abandonner.etymology: Inherited from Old French abandoner ('to surrender, leave at large, give up'), derived from the prepositional phrase mettre a bandon ('to place under someone's jurisdiction' or 'to leave unrestrained'). Old French bandon ('authority, proclamation, free disposal') comes from Frankish *bann ('public command, proclamation, jurisdiction'), with an ending reshaped under the influence of Latin donum ('gift').

history.meaning: at one's disposal; to hand over or leave unrestricted
to forsake, leave behind, give up

abandonner.notes: Despite ending in -donner, it is etymologically unrelated to donner ('to give'); in film production, abandonner un projet means to shelve or scrap a project.

rootFamily.gloss: public ban; banns of marriage (same Frankish root)

abat-jour.etymology: Compound formed in seventeenth-century French from abattre ('to beat or cast down', 3rd-person stem abat-) and jour ('daylight'). Before naming a lampshade, an abat-jour was a slanted cellar skylight angled to throw daylight downward into a basement.

history.meaning: reflector or shade casting lamp light downward

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: abat-jour (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: abat-jour

abat-jour.notes: Because **jour** sits inside the verb-object phrase *abattre le jour*, traditional grammar treats **des abat-jour** as invariable in the plural.

cognates.meaning: to knock down, slaughter (cognate base verb)
to knock down, fell (cognate base verb)

abattoir.etymology: Coined in French around 1806—following Napoleon's decree establishing municipal slaughterhouses on the outskirts of Paris—from abattre ('to fell, strike down, slaughter livestock') and the locative/instrumental suffix -oir (from Latin -orium). The verb abattre descends via Old French abatre from Vulgar Latin *abbattuere, formed from ad- ('to, down') + Classical Latin battere/battuere ('to beat, strike').

history.meaning: to beat down, strike to the ground

morphemes.meaning: place or instrument for an action

abattoir.notes: Borrowed directly into English as a genteel euphemism, whereas in French abattoir is the plain, everyday word for a slaughterhouse; aller à l'abattoir means 'to walk into certain defeat/doom'.

rootFamily.gloss: to fell, shoot down, slaughter; to demoralize

abcès.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Medical Latin abscessus ('a going away, departure; medically, a drawing off of humors into a localized suppuration', used by Celsus to calque Ancient Greek apostēma). Latin abscessus is the action noun of abscedere ('to go away, withdraw'), compounded from abs- ('away from') and cedere ('to go, yield').

history.meaning: medical abscess; figuratively, festering crisis or grievance

morphemes.meaning: to go, withdraw (from Latin cedere / cess-)

abcès.notes: Masculine noun with a silent final -s in both singular and plural; indispensable in the workplace/agency idiom crever l'abcès ('to lance the boil', i.e., confront a festering conflict head-on).

rootFamily.gloss: to accede, gain access (same Latin root cedere)

abeille.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Old Occitan abelha ('bee'), itself inherited from Classical Latin apicula ('little bee', diminutive of apis), replacing northern Old French ef / é after sound wear reduced apis to a single vowel.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: abeille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: abeille

abeille.notes: Because Latin **apis** eroded in northern French to a tiny monosyllable (**ef**, plural **és**), speakers adopted southern **abeille** so the word for 'bee' stayed clear and unmistakable.

cognates.meaning: plank, ship's side (Germanic cognate of bord)

abord.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Middle French from aborder ('to come alongside a ship, reach shore, approach someone'), itself built from a- (Latin ad- 'to, toward') + bord ('ship's side, edge, rim'). Old French bort was borrowed from Frankish *bord ('plank, side of a vessel'), gradually shifting from maritime docking to social approach and temporal priority.

history.meaning: plank, wooden side of a ship
to bring a vessel alongside, land on shore
act of approaching; initial impression or outset

abord.notes: The final -d is always silent; encountered constantly in d'abord ('first of all') and au premier abord ('at first glance / on first meeting').

rootFamily.gloss: to approach someone, broach a topic
edge, rim; board of a ship

abri.etymology: Abri derives as a back-formation from Old French abrier ('to cover, shelter from the cold', from Late Latin apricare 'to warm in the sun').
abri.notes: **À l'abri de la pluie** = sheltered from the rain.

cognates.meaning: state of being away or lacking

absence.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (12th–13th century) from Classical Latin absentia ('state of being away, non-appearance'), an abstract noun derived from absens, absentis, the present participle of abesse ('to be away from, be missing'), compounded from ab- ('away from') and esse ('to be').

history.meaning: state of being away or non-attendant
non-attendance, lack, brief lapse of attention

absence.notes: Pronounced with a voiceless /p/ by regressive assimilation (/ap.sɑ̃s/); avoir des absences means to space out momentarily or suffer brief memory lapses.

rootFamily.gloss: to leave the room, step out briefly

absent.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th century) from Classical Latin absens, accusative absentem ('being away, not present'), functioning as the present participle of abesse ('to be away, be distant from'), formed from ab- ('away') + esse ('to be', using a participial stem *sent- parallel to praesens).

history.meaning: being away from a place, non-attendant
absent, away; mentally vacant or distracted

absent.notes: Remember the French proverb Les absents ont toujours tort ('The absent are always in the wrong' — if you miss the meeting at ASK, you get blamed or sidelined!).

rootFamily.gloss: to step away, excuse oneself temporarily

absolu.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Latin absolutus ('freed from restraint, complete, unconditional'), past participle of absolvere ('to loosen from, set free, complete'), from ab- ('away from') + solvere ('to loosen, untie').

history.meaning: to untie, set free -> unrestricted, complete

absolument.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French from the adjective absolu ('unrestricted, complete, unconditional', borrowed from Classical Latin absolutus, past participle of absolvere 'to loosen from, set free, bring to completion', from ab- 'from' + solvere 'to loosen, untie') plus the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin mente, ablative of mens 'mind').

history.meaning: loosened, acquitted, brought to completion, unconditional

morphemes.meaning: adverbial suffix of manner (from Latin mente)

absolument.notes: A staple of Parisian talent-agent banter: standalone Absolument ! means 'Spot on / Definitely!', while Absolument pas ! means 'Out of the question!'.

rootFamily.gloss: to absolve, acquit (same Latin verb absolvere)

abstrait.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th century, initially in scholastic philosophy) from Late Latin abstractus ('drawn away, separated from matter or particulars'), the past participle of Classical Latin abstrahere ('to drag away, detach, divert'), compounded from abs- ('away from') and trahere ('to draw, pull').

history.meaning: to drag away; pulled away, detached

abstrait.notes: False-friend trap for academics: an academic 'abstract' (paper summary) is un résumé in French, whereas l'abstrait means 'the abstract realm'.

rootFamily.gloss: abstraction; faire abstraction de = to disregard

absurde.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (16th century) from Classical Latin absurdus ('out of tune, discordant, harsh-sounding; hence incongruous, irrational, pointless'), formed from intensive or separative ab- ('off, away') + surdus ('deaf, mute, dull-sounding'), showing a shift from acoustic dissonance to logical contradiction.

history.meaning: out of tune, dissonant; incongruous, silly

absurde.notes: Shares its Latin root surdus with French sourd ('deaf'); as a masculine noun, l'absurde is central to French culture via Camus and le théâtre de l'absurde.

rootFamily.gloss: deaf, muffled (inherited doublet of Latin surdus)

abîmer.etymology: Derived from Old French abisme ('abyss, bottomless depth', modern abîme, from Late Latin abyssimus, superlative alteration of Greek abyssos 'bottomless'); originally meant 'to cast into an abyss, swallow up', then weakened in modern French to 'to spoil, damage'.

history.meaning: to plunge into an abyss -> to ruin, damage

cognates.meaning: to buy up, hoard, corner the market

accaparer.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century (first attested in southern/Lyonnais merchant usage) from Italian accaparrare ('to secure goods with a deposit, buy up commodities to corner the market'), formed from a- + caparra ('earnest money, down payment'). Italian caparra arose from arra ('pledge, deposit', Latin arrha) crossed with capo ('head') or capere ('to seize, take').

history.meaning: earnest money; to lock in goods with a deposit, hoard
to hoard scarce commodities (especially grain) to drive up prices
to monopolize, hog someone's time or the spotlight

accaparer.notes: During the French Revolution, un accapareur ('grain hoarder') was a capital offense; today in social or set settings, accaparer quelqu'un/l'attention means to hog someone's time or steal the spotlight.

rootFamily.gloss: non-refundable deposit, earnest money (related Latin arrha)

cognates.meaning: way of pronouncing; stress or diacritic mark

accent.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Classical Latin accentus ('song added to speech, vocal pitch, intonation, stress'), coined by Roman grammarians as a morphological calque of Ancient Greek prosōidia (pros- 'to' + ōidē 'song') from Latin ad- ('to') + cantus ('singing, melody', derived from canere 'to sing').

history.meaning: musical pitch or modulation accompanying spoken syllables
vocal intonation, stress, orthographic diacritic mark
regional/foreign pronunciation, tone of voice, diacritic, emphasis

accent.notes: Covers regional pronunciation (accent du Midi), written diacritics (accent aigu, grave, circonflexe), and emphasis in mettre l'accent sur ('to emphasize/highlight').

rootFamily.gloss: song, singing (inherited doublet of Latin cantus)

accepter.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin acceptare ('to take or receive willingly'), frequentative of accipere ('to take to oneself, receive'), from ad- ('to') + capere ('to take').

cognates.meaning: accessory (cognate of the base noun accessoire)

accessoiriste.etymology: Coined in 19th-century French theatrical vocabulary from accessoire ('secondary item; theater/film stage prop') + the agentive occupational suffix -iste. French accessoire was borrowed in Middle French from Medieval Latin accessorius ('additional, subordinate'), derived from Classical Latin accedere ('to come to, be added to', from ad- + cedere 'to go').

history.meaning: subordinate element; stage object handled by actors (19th c.)

accessoiriste.notes: Essential film-set false friend: on a French movie set, un accessoire is a 'prop' (not just a fashion accessory), so l'accessoiriste (masc. or fem.) is the 'prop master'.

rootFamily.gloss: to access, reach (same Latin verb accedere)

accident.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin accidentem, present participle of accidere ('to fall upon, happen, come to pass'), from ad- ('to, upon') + cadere ('to fall').

history.meaning: to fall upon, happen -> chance event

accidentellement.etymology: Formed in Middle French (late fourteenth century) from the feminine accidentelle of accidentel ('happening by chance, accidental', from Medieval Latin accidentālis, built on Classical Latin accidēns, accidentem 'chance occurrence', present participle of accidere 'to fall upon, happen', ad- + cadere 'to fall') plus manner suffix -ment (< Latin ablative mente).
accidentellement.notes: Slightly more formal than conversational sans faire exprès ('without meaning to') or par erreur ('by mistake').

accompagner.etymology: Inherited from Old French acompaignier ('to take as a companion, go along with'), formed on compain / compagnon from Late Latin companionem (cum 'with' + panis 'bread' — literally 'one with whom you share bread').

history.meaning: to go with; to accompany musically

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: accompagner (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: accompagner

accompagner.notes: In both table fellowship and chamber music, **accompagner** preserves the warm image of sharing bread (**pain**) at the same table.

cognates.meaning: to achieve, fulfill (borrowed from Old French)
to fulfill, carry out (cognate of complere)

accomplir.etymology: Inherited from Old French acomplir ('to fill up, bring to completion, carry out'), formed either from Vulgar Latin *accomplere or within Gallo-Romance from a- (Latin ad-) + Old French complir ('to fill up, fulfill'), which continues Classical Latin complere ('to fill completely, complete', from com- 'altogether' + plere 'to fill').

history.meaning: to fill up to the brim, complete
to complete, fulfill a vow or duty

accomplir.notes: Regular second-conjugation (-ir / -issant) verb; reflexively, s'accomplir means 'to find personal/artistic fulfillment', and accompli means 'accomplished/consummate' (une actrice accomplie).

rootFamily.gloss: to fill up (close French relative from Latin plere)

accord.etymology: Accord is a noun formed from accorder, to bring into agreement. The Académie records the twelfth-century spelling acort.

history.meaning: to bring hearts into harmony (< cor, cordis)
agreement, pact; musical chord; grammatical agreement

accord.notes: Final -d is silent in pronunciation (/akɔʁ/), added in early modern spelling by analogy with Latin cor, cordis.

accorder.etymology: Inherited from Old French acorder ('to reconcile, bring into agreement'), from Vulgar Latin *accordare ('to be of one heart or mind'), formed from ad- ('to') + cor, cordis ('heart'); musical senses ('to tune strings') arose through blending with corde ('string').

cognates.meaning: to place, arrange (cognate of couchier < collocare)
to lay down, put to bed (cognate of collocare)

accoucher.etymology: Inherited from Old French acouchier ('to take to one's bed, lie down because of illness or childbirth'), formed from a- (Latin ad-) + couchier ('to lay down, lie in bed'). Old French couchier descends regularly from Classical Latin collocare ('to place together, lay on a couch or bed'), from com- ('together') + locare ('to place', from locus 'place').

history.meaning: to set in place, lay down on a bed
to take to one's bed, especially for childbed confinement
to give birth; figuratively, to laboriously bring forth an idea/script

morphemes.meaning: to lie down, bed (from Old French couchier < Latin collocare)

accoucher.notes: Notice prepositions: accoucher d'un bébé ('to give birth to a baby'); colloquially in meetings, Accouche ! means 'Spit it out!', and accoucher d'un scénario dans la douleur means to agonize over finishing a script.

rootFamily.gloss: to put to bed; se coucher = to go to bed

cognates.meaning: crook, shepherd's hook (Germanic cognate of croc)

accroc.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Early Modern French (16th–17th century) from accrocher ('to catch on a hook, snag, tear fabric on a sharp projection'), itself derived from a- (Latin ad-) + croc ('hook, fang'). Old French croc was borrowed from Old Norse krókr or Frankish *krōk ('hook, bend'), yielding first 'L-shaped rip in cloth' and then 'unexpected obstacle or snag'.

history.meaning: to fasten onto or catch on a hook
tear in fabric caught on a hook; figurative hitch, snag, or blunder

accroc.notes: Pronunciation trap: the final -c in accroc is completely silent (/a.kʁo/), unlike croc where it can be silent in croc-en-jambe or pronounced by some speakers; le tournage s'est déroulé sans accroc means 'shooting went off without a hitch'.

rootFamily.gloss: to hang up, hook; to captivate an audience
small hook; crochet; musical eighth note

accrocher.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in twelfth-century Old French (acrochier, 'to seize with a hook, hang on a hook') from prefix a- (< Latin ad- 'to, onto') + croc ('hook', borrowed from Old Norse krókr / Frankish *krōk 'hook, crook') + verbal ending -er.

history.meaning: to hook, catch on a hook

cognates.meaning: hooked staff, bend (from Old Norse krókr)
borrowed from Old French encrochier ('seize with a hook')

rootFamily.gloss: to unhook; to pick up the phone
to hang back up; to hang up the phone

accrocher.notes: Forms a vivid trio with décrocher ('unhook / pick up the phone') and raccrocher ('hang back up / end a phone call').

accueil.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (acueil, 12th c.) from accueillir ('to gather to oneself, welcome, receive').

cognates.meaning: cull (borrowed from Old French coillir, cognate base)

accueillant.etymology: Adjectival use of the present participle of accueillir ('to welcome, receive a guest'), inherited via Old French acoillir ('to gather together, associate, receive') from Vulgar Latin *accolligere, compounded from ad- ('to, toward') + Classical Latin colligere ('to gather together, collect', from com- 'together' + legere 'to gather, pick').

history.meaning: to gather to oneself, receive into a group
to gather, receive; hospitable, gracious toward guests
welcoming, warm, inviting (of people or spaces)

morphemes.meaning: to gather, pick (from Old French cueillir < Latin colligere)

accueillant.notes: Mind the tricky orthographic inversion -uei- (not *-eui-): the u is written right after c solely to keep c hard (/k/) before the front vowel e (/a.kœ.jɑ̃/).

rootFamily.gloss: to welcome, host, receive (a guest or film review)

accueillir.etymology: Inherited from Old French acueillir ('to gather together, associate, receive'), from Vulgar Latin *accolligere, formed from ad- ('to') + Classical Latin colligere ('to gather together').

accuser.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin accusare ('to call to account, blame, indict'), formed from ad- ('to') + causa ('cause, lawsuit').

history.meaning: to call to account, bring a charge against

accès.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin accessus ('an approaching, admittance; onset of a fever'), action noun from accedere ('to go toward, approach'), from ad- ('to') + cedere ('to go, yield').

history.meaning: means of approach, access; sudden fit

cognates.meaning: to assent to, attain an office or throne

accéder.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th–15th century) from Classical Latin accedere ('to approach, draw near, enter upon, be added, assent to'), compounded from assimilated ad- ('to, toward') and cedere ('to go, move, yield'). In the 20th century, alongside formal 'assent to / attain', it expanded to general physical and digital 'access'.

history.meaning: to draw near, enter upon, assent to
to adhere to a treaty, attain a rank or dignity
to reach, gain entry or digital access to; accede to a request

morphemes.meaning: to go, move, yield (from Latin cedere)

accéder.notes: Grammar alert: unlike English transitive 'to access a file/set', French accéder ALWAYS requires the preposition à — accéder au plateau ('to access the film set'), accéder à une demande ('to grant a request').

rootFamily.gloss: access, entry; sudden outburst or fit (accès de colère)
accession to power or property ownership

cognates.meaning: device or pedal that increases speed

accélérateur.etymology: Derived in French from accélérer ('to quicken, speed up') + the agentive/instrumental suffix -ateur (from Latin -ator, -atorem), originally as a 16th-century anatomical/scientific adjective-noun ('muscle or agent that hastens movement') and later reinforced by English accelerator in late 19th-century automotive engineering. Accélérer comes from Classical Latin accelerare, from ad- + celer ('swift').

history.meaning: anatomical muscle or physical agent that speeds up motion
automotive gas pedal/throttle; particle or business accelerator

accélérateur.notes: Used literally for a car's gas pedal and figuratively in agency/business talk: appuyer sur l'accélérateur ('to step on the gas / fast-track a project').

rootFamily.gloss: swiftness, promptness (formal noun from Latin celeritas)

cognates.meaning: bloodthirsty, fierce, relentless (cognate formation from carne)
carnal, carnage (from the same Latin root caro, carnis)

acharner.etymology: Inherited from Old French acharner ('to feed raw flesh to hunting hounds or falcons to whet their bloodlust for the quarry'), a denominal hunting verb formed from a- (Latin ad- 'to') + charn (Old French oblique form of char, modern chair 'flesh, meat', from Classical Latin caro, carnis) + -er. From hounds tearing at prey, it generalized to relentless human persistence or persecution.

history.meaning: to bait hounds or hawks with flesh to excite them for the hunt
to hound fiercely; reflexively, to persist or pick on relentlessly

morphemes.meaning: flesh, meat (Old French charn < Latin carnis)

acharner.notes: Almost always used pronominally today: s'acharner sur un texte ('to slave obsessively over a script'), s'acharner sur quelqu'un ('to hound/pick on someone'), or le sort s'acharne ('bad luck keeps striking').

rootFamily.gloss: relentless persistence, doggedness; acharnement thérapeutique = futile life support
flesh (inherited French noun from Latin caro, carnis)

acheter.etymology: Inherited from Old French achater ('to acquire, buy'), from Vulgar Latin *accaptare ('to acquire, obtain'), prefixed form of *captare / Classical Latin acceptare (from ad- + capere 'to take').

acheteur.etymology: Inherited from Old French achateor ('purchaser, buyer'), agent noun formed from achater / acheter ('to buy') + suffix -eur (from Latin -atorem).

acier.etymology: Inherited via Old French acier from Late Latin aciarium ('hardened edge-iron, steel'), derived from Classical Latin acies ('sharp cutting edge, blade point'), because steel was first forged specifically to give iron tools and weapons a durable edge.

history.meaning: hardened iron for cutting edges, steel

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: acier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: acier

acier.notes: From the same Indo-European sharpness root come French **aigu** ('sharp, high-pitched') and **aigre** ('sour').

acousticien.etymology: Formed in Modern French from acoustique ('acoustics') + agent/specialist suffix -ien.

acoustique.etymology: Learned borrowing (c. 1700, Sauveur) from Ancient Greek akoustikos ('relating to hearing'), derived from akouein ('to hear').

acquiescer.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin acquiescere ('to come to rest, find peace in, assent quietly to'), from ad- ('to') + quiescere ('to rest, keep quiet', from quies 'rest').

history.meaning: to rest in, assent quietly to

cognates.meaning: deed; division of a play; legal statute
deed, legal document, act of a play
deed, ceremony, act of a play

acte.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th century) from two converging Classical Latin derivatives of agere ('to drive, set in motion, do, perform'): masculine actus ('movement, dramatic performance, division of a play') and neuter actum, plural acta ('thing done, public transaction, official record'). Both derive from the past participial stem act-.

history.meaning: performance, division of a play / deed, official legal record
legal deed or certificate; philosophical reality; moral deed
deed, act of a play, official certificate (acte de naissance)

acte.notes: Rich in agency and legal idioms: prendre acte de ('to take formal note of'), passer à l'acte ('to act on an impulse/plan'), and faire acte de présence ('to put in a token appearance at an event').

rootFamily.gloss: to act, take action (inherited/adapted from Latin agere)

acteur.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French (originally in legal and general senses 'litigant, author, agent', then re-anchored to theater in the 16th–17th century) from Classical Latin actor, accusative actorem ('driver, doer, legal pleader, stage performer'), the agent noun formed on the supine stem act- of agere ('to drive, do, act on stage').

history.meaning: instigator, plaintiff in law; stage player
film or theater actor; key participant (acteur économique)

morphemes.meaning: do, perform (Latin stem act- of agere)

acteur.notes: Insider cinema nuance heard throughout Dix pour cent: French performers often distinguish un acteur (associated with cinema and screen persona) from un comédien (associated with theater craft and playing varied roles, not 'stand-up comic'!).

actif.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (12th–13th century, first contrasting la vie active 'worldly life of deeds' with la vie contemplative in Christian thought) from Classical Latin activus ('practical, pertaining to action rather than contemplation'), built on act-, the past participial stem of agere ('to drive, do, conduct').

history.meaning: practical, characterized by action; active voice in grammar
devoted to practical deeds (vie active vs. contemplative)
energetic, employed (population active); noun: credit/assets or credits

morphemes.meaning: do, act (Latin stem act- of agere)
tending to, characterized by (from Latin -ivus; fem. -ive)

actif.notes: Feminine is active; as a masculine noun (un actif), it means financial 'assets' AND appears in the career idiom avoir dix films à son actif ('to have ten films to one's credit / under one's belt').

rootFamily.gloss: to activate, speed up; s'activer = to bustle about

action.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (12th century, initially in legal usage) from Classical Latin actio, accusative actionem ('a setting in motion, performance, public proceeding, lawsuit, oratorical or dramatic delivery'), action noun of agere ('to drive, do'). In the 17th century it acquired the financial sense 'share of stock' as a semantic calque of Dutch actie (originally 'legal claim to dividends' in the Dutch East India Company).

history.meaning: legal claim; physical or moral deed; dramatic plot
deed, plot, director's 'Action!', corporate share of stock

morphemes.meaning: do, drive, perform (Latin stem act- of agere)
process or result of an action (from Latin -ionem)

action.notes: Central to BOTH worlds of Dix pour cent: on set, the director calls Action ! ('Action!'), while in the ASK agency boardroom, des actions are 'shares/equity stakes' in the company!

rootFamily.gloss: to operate a lever/mechanism; to sue

actionnaire.etymology: Coined in French at the beginning of the 18th century (popularized during John Law's joint-stock speculation boom around 1718–1720) from action in its financial sense ('equity share in a company', calqued on Dutch actie from Latin actio) + the agentive/possessive suffix -naire (from Latin -arius, modeled on pensionnaire and millionnaire).

history.meaning: transferable legal claim to company profits, stock share
holder of shares in a trading or colonial company

morphemes.meaning: person holding or associated with (from Latin -arius)

actionnaire.notes: False-friend alert: un actionnaire is a 'shareholder / equity partner' (like Andréa, Mathias, Gabriel, and Arlette fighting over ASK's shares), NOT an 'action hero' or 'man of action' (homme d'action).

cognates.meaning: female dramatic performer (influenced by French actrice)

actrice.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Late Latin actrix, accusative actricem ('female doer, female administrator or legal claimant'), the regular feminine agent noun corresponding to Classical Latin actor (from agere 'to drive, do, perform on stage'), and extended in 17th-century French from general 'female agent' to theatrical and later cinematic 'actress'.

history.meaning: woman who drives an action; female stage performer (17th c.)
female film or stage actor; key female player (actrice majeure)

morphemes.meaning: do, perform (Latin stem act- of agere)

actrice.notes: Unlike English, where 'actor' is increasingly used gender-neutrally for women, French consistently uses the grammatically feminine actrice (or comédienne) when referring to a female performer.

cognates.meaning: real, existing in fact (semantic false friend!)

actuel.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Late Latin actualis ('active, practical', used in medieval scholastic Latin to mean 'existing in act/reality as opposed to mere potentiality'), derived from Classical Latin actus ('act, accomplishment', from agere). Because what exists in act exists 'right now', French shifted the meaning in the 17th–18th century from 'real/effective' to 'present-day, current'.

history.meaning: active, practical; existing in reality rather than potential (medieval)
real, effective (e.g., péché actuel vs. péché originel)

actuel.notes: Classic false friend (#1 learner pitfall): actuel means 'current, present-day' (son agent actuel = 'her current agent'); to say 'actual/real', use réel, vrai, or véritable!

rootFamily.gloss: topicality; les actualités = current events / the news

actuellement.etymology: Formed in Middle French from the feminine form actuelle of actuel ('existing in reality; later, present, current', from Late Latin actualis) + the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin mente, ablative singular of mens 'mind'). Parallel to actuel, its meaning evolved from scholastic 'in reality, effectively' to temporal 'at the present moment, nowadays'.

history.meaning: in an active or real manner (scholastic components)

actuellement.notes: Notorious false friend: actuellement NEVER means 'actually / in fact' (use en fait, en réalité, or d'ailleurs for that) — it strictly means 'currently, at the moment' (elle tourne actuellement à Rome).

rootFamily.gloss: current events, news (les actus in slang)
to update, bring up to date

acupuncteur.etymology: Formed in 20th-century French from acupuncture by substituting the Latinate agent suffix -teur (masc.) / -trice (fem.) for -ture. Neo-Latin acupunctura was coined in 1683 by Dutch physician Willem ten Rhijne after observing traditional medicine in Japan, compounding Classical Latin acus ('needle', ablative acu 'with a needle') + punctura ('pricking, puncture', from pungere 'to prick').

morphemes.meaning: with a needle (Latin ablative acu of acus)
prick, pierce (Latin stem punct- of pungere)

acupuncteur.notes: Spelling & pronunciation variants exist in French: both acupuncteur (/a.ky.pɔ̃k.tœʁ/) and modernized acuponcteur are accepted, and the feminine form is acupunctrice (or acuponctrice).

rootFamily.gloss: puncture, medical tap (same Latin root punctura)
sharp, acute (from the same root family as Latin acus 'needle')

cognates.meaning: addition; café/bar bill (in parts of Latin America)

addition.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (13th century, first as an arithmetic term) from Classical Latin additio, accusative additionem ('an adding to, annexing'), action noun of addere ('to put to, join, annex, increase'), compounded from ad- ('to') + -dere (from PIE *dʰeh₁- 'to put, place', merged in Latin with dare 'to give'). In mid-19th-century Parisian cafés, la carte à payer became l'addition ('the summed-up tab').

history.meaning: arithmetic operation of summing numbers; marginal supplement
arithmetic sum; itemized restaurant/café bill; figurative 'heavy price'

addition.notes: Essential bistro phrase: L'addition, s'il vous plaît ! ('Check, please!'); figuratively, payer l'addition or une addition salée ('a salty/steep bill') means paying dearly for a mistake, whereas a general invoice is une facture and a banknote is un billet.

rootFamily.gloss: to add up numbers; s'additionner = to compound/accumulate

adieu.etymology: Univerbation in Old French (attested from the 12th century as a Deu / a Dieu) of the prepositional phrase à Dieu ('to God'), elliptical for formulas of parting benediction such as je vous commande à Dieu ('I commend you to God's keeping'). Preposition à comes from Latin ad ('to') and Dieu from Classical Latin Deus, accusative Deum ('God').

history.meaning: (I commend you) to God! — everyday parting greeting
solemn or permanent farewell; regional southern 'hello/goodbye'

adieu.notes: Register alert: in standard Parisian French, adieu implies a dramatic or permanent farewell ('goodbye forever', vs. everyday au revoir) — or dramatic hyperbole like Adieu les vacances ! ('Kiss the vacation goodbye!'), though in southern France/Switzerland it can still be a friendly 'hello!'.

rootFamily.gloss: God; plural dieux (adieu takes plural adieux: faire ses adieux)

rootFamily.word: bondieusard / débonnaire (related religious compounds; déifier = to deify)

administration.etymology: Learned borrowing into Old French (13th century) from Classical Latin administrātiōnem (accusative of administrātiō, 'aid, direction, management'), an action noun derived from administrāre ('to attend upon, manage, direct'), itself composed of ad- ('to, toward') and ministrāre ('to serve, attend'), from minister ('attendant, servant', built on minus 'less' with the comparative contrast suffix *-teros).

history.meaning: stewardship, management of property or public affairs
public bureaucracy, management, or government offices

administration.notes: Feminine noun (l'administration). In France, 'l'Administration' (often capitalized or definite singular) refers collectively to civil service bureaucracy and public offices rather than a specific presidential term as in American English.

admirable.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century (attested in Nicole Oresme) from Classical Latin admirābilis ('worthy of wonder, astonishing, admirable'), derived from admirārī ('to wonder at, regard with awe'), composed of intensive ad- ('at, toward') and mīrārī ('to marvel, be astonished'), from the adjective mīrus ('wonderful, strange').

history.meaning: astonishing, worthy of wonder or awe

admirable.notes: Invariant for masculine and feminine singular (un acteur admirable, une scène admirable). Unlike English 'admirable', where the stress shifts to the first syllable, French keeps even phrasing with final stress and pronounces the cluster -dm- clearly.

admirateur.etymology: Learned borrowing in the late 15th century from Classical Latin admirātōrem (accusative of admirātor, 'one who wonders at or reveres'), an agent noun formed on the past participial stem admirāt- of the deponent verb admirārī ('to marvel at, gaze at in wonder'), from ad- ('toward') and mīrārī ('to wonder').

history.meaning: one who marvels at or reveres
one who contemplates with wonder or devotion

morphemes.meaning: agent noun (one who performs the action)

admirateur.notes: Masculine form admirateur pairs with feminine admiratrice. In cinema and celebrity contexts (such as Dix pour cent), it bridges devoted artistic appreciation ('un grand admirateur de votre travail') and romantic pursuit ('un admirateur secret').

admiration.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin admirātiōnem (accusative of admirātiō, 'wonder, surprise, astonishment, high regard'), an action noun built on the supine stem admirāt- of admirārī ('to marvel at'), from ad- ('at, toward') + mīrārī ('to wonder'), gradually shifting from stunned surprise to enthusiastic esteem.

history.meaning: feeling of marvel before something extraordinary

admiration.notes: Feminine noun (une grande admiration). Used idiomatically in 'être en admiration devant quelqu'un' ('to be in awe of someone'), a staple phrase when talent agents flatter actors and directors.

admirer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin admirari ('to wonder at, regard with awe or esteem'), from ad- ('at, toward') + mirari ('to wonder, marvel', from mirus 'wonderful').

history.meaning: to marvel at, regard with wonder
to contemplate with wonder and esteem

adoption.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical Latin adoptiōnem (accusative of adoptiō, 'taking as one's child, legal adoption'), a syncopated derivative of adoptāre ('to choose for oneself, select, adopt into a family'), formed from ad- ('to, for oneself') and optāre ('to choose, wish for').

history.meaning: legal act of choosing and taking someone into one's family
spiritual or legal affiliation as child and heir
legal child adoption; formal approval of a law or project

adoption.notes: Feminine noun. Alongside legal child placement, 'd'adoption' is a very frequent post-nominal idiom meaning 'by choice / adopted' (e.g., 'Paris est sa ville d'adoption', 'son pays d'adoption').

adorable.etymology: Borrowed from Classical/Late Latin adōrābilis ('worthy of worship or veneration'), derived from adōrāre ('to speak to formally, entreat, revere, worship'), from ad- ('to') + ōrāre ('to speak, pray, plead', from ōs, ōris 'mouth'). Originally strictly religious in French before secularizing in the 17th-century salon register to mean 'utterly charming'.

history.meaning: worthy of divine worship or reverence
worthy of religious veneration (of God or relics)

adorable.notes: In everyday Parisian and industry speech ('Tu es adorable !'), calling an adult 'adorable' means 'You're a sweetheart / So kind of you!', whereas English 'adorable' often sounds infantilizing or purely cute.

adorer.etymology: Inherited and re-Latinized from Old French aorer ('to pray to, worship'), from Classical Latin adorare ('to speak to formally, entreat, worship'), from ad- ('to') + orare ('to speak, pray', from os, oris 'mouth').

history.meaning: to worship; by extension, to love dearly

adoucir.etymology: Formed in Old French (radoucir / adoucir, 12th c.) from prefix a- (from Latin ad-) + doux, douce ('sweet, soft, gentle', from Latin dulcis) + verbal suffix -ir.

adresse.etymology: Deverbal noun from Old French adrecier (modern adresser, 'to set straight, direct toward a goal'), from Vulgar Latin *addirectiare ('to make straight', from ad- + directus 'straight').

history.meaning: to direct straight -> skill, direction, destination

adresser.etymology: Inherited from Old French adrecier ('to straighten, set right, direct toward a goal'), formed from Vulgar Latin *addīrectiāre, a derivative of ad- ('to, toward') and *dīrectiāre ('to make straight'), itself built on Classical Latin dīrēctus ('straight, direct'), past participle of dīrigere ('to set straight, guide').

history.meaning: to make straight, guide directly toward
to straighten up, set on the right path, direct
to send, direct speech or mail to; (refl.) to speak to

adresser.notes: Watch the spelling difference from English: French 'adresser' (and 'adresse') has only ONE 'd' (unlike English 'address'). Reflexive 's'adresser à quelqu'un' is the standard way to say 'to speak to / inquire with someone'.

rootFamily.gloss: to set upright, train, draw up

adultère.etymology: Learned re-borrowing in the 14th century (replacing inherited Old French avoutire / avoutre) from Classical Latin adulterium ('marital infidelity, contamination') and adulter ('adulterer, unfaithful spouse'), derived from adulterāre ('to corrupt, falsify, commit adultery'), probably formed from ad- ('toward') + alter ('the other [person]'), i.e., approaching another outside marriage.

history.meaning: adultery, extramarital affair; adulterer or adulterous

morphemes.meaning: other, another (from Latin alter, reshaped as -ulter-)

adultère.notes: Unusually versatile in French: 'adultère' serves unchanged as the abstract masculine noun ('commettre un adultère'), a person noun ('un/une adultère'), and an adjective ('une liaison adultère'). Note: etymologically unrelated to 'adulte' (from adolescere)!

rootFamily.gloss: born of or relating to adultery

affaire.etymology: Univerbation in Old French (12th century, afaire) of the prepositional infinitive phrase à faire ('[something] to do, business to be done'), from Latin ad ('to, for') + facere ('to do, make'). Originally masculine in Old French (as an substantivized infinitive phrase) before becoming feminine in Modern French through frequent vowel-initial determiner ambiguity (l'affaire, une bonne affaire).

history.meaning: what has to be done, occupation, rank, difficulty
matter, business deal, scandal; (pl.) personal belongings or commerce

morphemes.meaning: to, for (from Old French preposition à)

affaire.notes: Feminine noun (une affaire) and a classic partial false friend: 'une affaire' means a business deal, bargain, legal case, or scandal — NOT a romantic affair (which is 'une liaison' or 'une aventure'). In the plural, 'mes affaires' means 'my stuff/belongings' and 'les affaires' means 'business'.

rootFamily.gloss: busy, bustling (lit. having much to do)

affamé.etymology: Past participle of affamer ('to starve, make hungry'), formed in Old French (afamer) from a- (Latin ad-) + faim ('hunger', from Latin famem).

affecter.etymology: Learned borrowing in the 14th–15th century blending two related Classical Latin verbs: (1) affectāre ('to strive after, aim at, feign', frequentative of afficere), yielding the senses 'to assign/allocate' and 'to feign'; and (2) afficere (supine affectum, 'to act upon, move emotionally, afflict', from ad- + facere 'to do to'), yielding the emotional sense 'to touch, distress'.

history.meaning: to act upon emotionally; to strive after or pretend
to aspire to, feign; to earmark for a use
to move or distress emotionally; to feign; to post/assign someone

affecter.notes: Carries three distinct uses learners should distinguish: emotional impact ('Cette rupture l'a beaucoup affecté'), pretense ('affecter l'indifférence'), and administrative assignment ('être affecté à un poste').

affection.etymology: Borrowed in the late 12th century from Classical Latin affectiōnem (accusative of affectiō, 'disposition, state of mind or body produced by an external influence, goodwill, love'), a noun of state built on afficere (past participle affectus, 'acted upon, moved'), from ad- ('toward, upon') + facere ('to make, do').

history.meaning: mental or bodily state, disposition, favorable feeling
inner inclination of the soul, devotion, zeal
tender fondness, warmth; (med.) organic disease or ailment

affection.notes: Feminine noun. Commonly paired with 'avoir de l'affection pour quelqu'un' or 'prendre quelqu'un en affection' ('to take a shine/fondness to someone'). In formal medical French, 'une affection' also means an ailment or disorder.

affectueux.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Late Latin affectuōsus ('full of inclination, loving, warm-hearted'), derived from Classical Latin affectus (fourth-declension noun, 'emotional state, passion, tender attachment'), from the past participial stem of afficere ('to move, touch', from ad- + facere).
affectueux.notes: Masculine 'affectueux' becomes 'affectueuse' in the feminine. Its adverb 'affectueusement' ('fondly, warmly') is a classic warm sign-off in personal letters and emails among close colleagues and friends.

affiche.etymology: Deverbal feminine noun formed in Old and Middle French from afficher ('to fasten, pin, post publicly'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *affīcticāre ('to fasten to, pin onto'), a frequentative derivative of Classical Latin affīgere (past participle affīxus, 'to fasten or attach to', from ad- + fīgere 'to fix, drive in'). Originally denoted a clasp or pin before meaning a posted public bill.

history.meaning: brooch, pin, clasp; thing fastened up
public placard, film/theater poster, star billing

affiche.notes: Essential Dix pour cent cinema idiom: 'être à l'affiche' means 'to be currently playing/starring', 'partager l'affiche' means 'to co-star', and 'tenir le haut de l'affiche' means 'to have top billing'. Feminine noun (une affiche).

rootFamily.gloss: index card, plug, form; to drive in

afficher.etymology: Derived in Middle French from affiche ('pin, clasp; posted notice'), itself a deverbal noun from Old French afichier ('to fasten, pin up'), from Vulgar Latin *affigicare, frequentative of Classical Latin affigere ('to fasten to').

history.meaning: to fasten or pin firmly to
to pin up -> to post a public notice, display

cognates.meaning: gone mad, infatuated (related formation from folle)

affolé.etymology: Past participial adjective of affoler ('to drive mad, throw into panic'), formed in Old French (afoler, 'to drive crazy, bewilder'; note a separate homonym meant 'to injure/trample' from fouler) from prefix a- (Latin ad-) + fol ('mad, foolish', modern fou/folle, from Late Latin follis 'windbag, bellows', hence 'empty-headed') + verbal suffix -er.

history.meaning: to make foolish, drive out of one's wits
bewildered, infatuated, or thrown into erratic motion (as a compass needle)

affolé.notes: Takes feminine -e (affolée). Very common in both participial form and the reflexive verb 's'affoler' ('Ne t'affole pas !' = 'Don't freak out / Don't panic!'). Originally applied in physics to a compass needle spinning wildly ('une boussole affolée').

rootFamily.gloss: to panic, send into a frenzy
panic, frantic frenzy (e.g., of heart or markets)

affreux.etymology: Inherited from Old French afreus / affreux ('frightful, inspiring terror', 12th century), derived with suffix -eux from the Old French noun afre / affre ('terror, dread, horror', surviving in Modern French plural les affres, as in les affres de l'angoisse). The noun affre is most likely borrowed from Frankish *aifrs ('bitter, harsh, terrifying'; cf. Old High German eivar, Old English āfor).
affreux.notes: Masculine 'affreux' (invariant in plural) becomes 'affreuse' in the feminine. In conversational French, its terrifying medieval force has softened into expressive hyperbole ('J'ai une migraine affreuse', 'Cette robe est affreuse !').

cognates.meaning: to set teeth on edge, provoke

agacer.etymology: Evolved from Old French aacier ('to set teeth on edge with sour fruit', 13th century), probably from Vulgar Latin *acaciāre, a derivative of Classical Latin aciēs ('sharp edge, point') and acidus ('sour, tart'). In Middle French, the spelling and sense shifted to agacer ('to tease, provoke, irritate') through folk-etymological crossing with agace ('magpie', a chattering, teasing bird, from Frankish *agatja).

history.meaning: to sharpen, set teeth on edge with acidity
to numb or irritate the teeth (as unripe fruit does)
to tease, needle, annoy, get on someone's nerves

agacer.notes: Requires a cedilla before 'a' or 'o' to keep the soft /s/ sound (nous agaçons, il agaçait). Milder and sleeker in register than 'énerver' or 'faire chier': 'Ça m'agace' means 'That rubs me the wrong way / gets on my nerves'.

agaçant.etymology: Lexicalized present participial adjective of agacer ('to irritate, needle, set on edge'), attested in the emotional sense from the 17th–18th centuries. Built on the stem agaç- (from Old French aacier 'to set teeth on edge', likely from Vulgar Latin *acaciāre 'to make sharp/acidic', reshaped by Middle French agace 'magpie') plus the participial suffix -ant (Latin -antem).

history.meaning: setting the teeth on edge (of sour foods)

agaçant.notes: The cedilla (ç) is mandatory before -ant to preserve the /s/ pronunciation ([agasɑ̃]); feminine is 'agaçante'. Ubiquitous in Parisian banter for exasperating people or habits ('Qu'il est agaçant !').

agence.etymology: A seventeenth-century French derivative of agent. The word developed the modern senses of an intermediary business, an official organisation, and the offices where such work takes place.
agence.notes:
- Common collocations: **agence de voyages**, **agence immobilière**, **agence de presse**.
- The word is feminine: **une agence**.

agenda.etymology: Learned borrowing (late 16th century) from Classical Latin agenda ('things to be done'), neuter nominative/accusative plural of agendus, future passive participle (gerundive) of agere ('to drive, set in motion, do, conduct'). In French it concretized early into a notebook or pocket planner listing daily appointments rather than an ideological program.

history.meaning: things that must be done or transacted
memorandum book for recording tasks to do
appointment calendar, personal diary, daily schedule

morphemes.meaning: Latin neuter plural gerundive ('things to be -ed')

agenda.notes: Classic false friend! In French (especially in talent agencies!), 'un agenda' (masculine, pronounced [aʒɛ̃da] with nasal -en-) means a calendar/planner/schedule ('vérifier mon agenda'). For a meeting's 'agenda', use 'l'ordre du jour'; for a 'hidden agenda', use 'arrière-pensée'.

agent.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (via Scholastic Latin or Italian agente) from Classical Latin agentem, present participle of agere ('to drive, do, act, conduct').

history.meaning: to act, do -> one who acts

agente.etymology: Feminine inflection of agent, which entered French in the 15th–16th century both directly from Medieval/Classical Latin agentem (accusative of agēns, present participle of agere 'to act, do, manage') and in the commercial/diplomatic sense ('representative managing someone else's affairs') via Italian agente. The inflected feminine agente gained wide currency in modern Francophone usage alongside epicene une agent.

history.meaning: representative acting on behalf of a prince or merchant (via Italian)
female talent agent, representative, or public officer

agente.notes: Central word of Dix pour cent: Andréa Martel is variously referred to as 'une agente (artistique)' (standard in Quebec, Switzerland, and increasingly France, pronouncing the final /t/) or epicene 'une agent'. 'Agent' also means police officer ('agent de police').

aggraver.etymology: Learned renovation (14th–15th century, refashioning inherited Old French agrever 'to weigh down, oppress') from Classical Latin aggravāre ('to make heavier, add to a burden, make worse'), formed from intensive/assimilated ad- ('to, upon') and gravāre ('to burden, weigh down'), from gravis ('heavy, serious, grievous').

history.meaning: to make heavier, add weight to, make more oppressive
to overburden physically or increase the severity of a fault
to make a situation, illness, or legal offense worse

aggraver.notes: Partial false friend with informal English: French 'aggraver' ONLY means 'to make worse' (e.g., 'aggraver son cas' = 'to dig oneself into a deeper hole'), NEVER 'to annoy/irritate a person' (for which French uses 'agacer' or 'énerver').

agir.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin agere ('to drive, set in motion, do, act'), adapted into the French -ir conjugation.

agitation.etymology: Learned borrowing (15th century) from Classical Latin agitātiōnem (accusative of agitātiō, 'frequent movement, tossing about, mental restlessness or activity'), derived from agitāre ('to drive to and fro, shake repeatedly, stir up'), the frequentative-intensive derivative of agere ('to drive, set in motion').

history.meaning: violent physical tossing (as of waves) or inner turmoil
bustle, nervous restlessness, or political unrest

agitation.notes: Feminine noun. Captures both bustling physical commotion on a film set or agency floor ('toute cette agitation') and inner nervous restlessness ('être dans une grande agitation').

rootFamily.gloss: to shake, wave, stir up; (refl.) to fidget/bustle

agneau.etymology: Inherited through Old French agnel (plural agniaus -> agneaux) from Classical/Late Latin agnellum (accusative of agnellus, 'little lamb'), an affectionate diminutive of Classical Latin agnus ('lamb', from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷnós; cf. English yean). As often in Vulgar Latin livestock terms, the expressive diminutive completely displaced the base noun agnus in Gallo-Romance.

history.meaning: young sheep; symbol of gentleness and Christian sacrifice
lamb (both the young animal and culinary lamb meat)

agneau.notes: Masculine noun (un agneau, plural des agneaux), pronounced [aɲo] with palatal 'gn'. Unlike English (which splits Germanic 'lamb/sheep' from French-derived 'mutton'), French uses 'agneau' seamlessly for both the live lamb and prime restaurant meat ('un gigot d'agneau'). Figuratively, 'doux comme un agneau' ('gentle as a lamb').

agonie.etymology: Learned borrowing (14th century, Oresme; widely diffused via ecclesiastical narratives of Christ's anguish at Gethsemane) from Ecclesiastical Latin agōnia ('extreme anguish, death struggle'), borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀγωνία (agōnía, 'contest for victory, athletic struggle, acute mental anguish'), derived from ἀγών (agṓn, 'assembly, stadium contest, struggle'), from ἄγειν (ágein, 'to lead, drive').

history.meaning: athletic contest, struggle for victory, acute anxiety
supreme spiritual anguish (especially of Christ); final struggle with death
final death throes just before dying; slow decline or dramatic death scene

agonie.notes: Crucial false friend! In French, 'être à l'agonie' does NOT mean 'to be in intense physical pain' (which is 'souffrir le martyre' or 'avoir atrocement mal'); it means 'to be on one's deathbed / in one's final death throes' (or figuratively on the verge of collapse). Feminine noun.

rootFamily.gloss: to lie dying, be in one's last throes

agressif.etymology: Formed in the late 18th to early 19th century on the learned Latin participial stem aggress- of Classical Latin aggredī (past participle aggressus, 'to approach, step up to, assail, attack', from ad- 'toward' + gradī 'to step, walk', from gradus 'step'), combined with the adjectival suffix -if (Latin -īvus).

history.meaning: to walk toward, approach, launch an attack against
hostile, combative; harsh or grating on the senses (of colors, light, tone)

agressif.notes: Spelled with a SINGLE 'g' in French (agressif, f. agressive), unlike English 'aggressive'. Also watch the business/agency register nuance: calling a pitch or negotiator 'agressif' in French is usually negative ('hostile/pushy') rather than a compliment meaning 'bold/ambitious' ('dynamique', 'offensif').

agréable.etymology: Derived in Old French (12th c.) from agréer ('to receive favorably, please', from à gré 'to one's liking', from Latin gratum 'pleasing') + suffix -able.

ah.etymology: This interjection continues an expressive cry rather than an ordinary noun. The Académie records eleventh-century A or Ha and notes the same exclamation in Latin.

history.meaning: exclamation of surprise, pain, or realization

ah.notes: Extremely frequent in conversational French feedback: Ah bon? ('Oh really?') signals mild surprise or attentive listening.

aha.etymology: Expressive interjection attested since Old French (a ha), combining the exclamations ah and ha to voice sudden discovery, surprise, or triumph.

aide.etymology: The noun was formed from the older French verb behind aider. Ninth-century aiudha meant the act of helping; the shorter form aïe is recorded in the twelfth century.

history.stage: Early Old French (9th c., Strasbourg Oaths)

aide.notes: Aiudha in the 842 Oaths of Strasbourg is one of the earliest recorded words in the history of French; feminine une aide means 'help', while un/une aide means 'an assistant'.

aider.etymology: Aider comes from Latin adjutare, a repeated-action form related to adjuvare, to help. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century.
aider.notes: Takes a direct object for the person helped and à before an infinitive: aider quelqu'un à faire quelque chose.

aigu.etymology: Inherited via Old French agu (later aigu with graphic/palatalized glide development) from Classical Latin acūtum (accusative of acūtus, 'sharpened, pointed, piercing, high-pitched in tone'), past participial adjective of acuere ('to sharpen, whet'), built on the PIE root *h₂eḱ- ('sharp, pointed'; cf. acus 'needle'). Substantivized in music and acoustics for a high-pitched note or treble register.

history.meaning: sharpened to a point; piercing to the ear, high-pitched
sharp-pointed (of weapons); shrill or piercing (of voice)
sharp, acute; (noun, m.) high note, upper vocal register, or audio treble

aigu.notes: As a masculine noun ('un aigu', 'les aigus'), it means a high note in singing ('chanter dans les aigus') or treble in sound mixing (paired with 'les graves' for bass/low notes). As an adjective, its feminine has a diaeresis: 'aiguë' (reformed 1990 spelling: 'aigüe'), pronounced [egy], ensuring the 'u' is not silent!

aiguille.etymology: Inherited via Old French aguille from Late Latin acucula ('small needle, pin'), diminutive of Classical Latin acus ('needle'), from the root of acutus ('sharp, pointed').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: aiguille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: aiguille

aiguille.notes: Notice the pronunciation **/eɡɥij/** (where *-gu-* before *-i-* sounds like */ɡɥi/*, unlike **guide** */ɡid/*), and how French uses **les aiguilles** for the hands of a clock.

ailleurs.etymology: Inherited from Old French aillors / ailleurs ('in another place', 11th century), continuing Vulgar Latin *aliōrsum (recorded in Late/Carolingian Latin as aliorsum), an adverbial contraction of Classical Latin aliō vorsum / aliō versum ('turned toward another direction, elsewhere'), from alius ('other, another') + vorsus/versus ('turned toward', from vertere 'to turn'), with final adverbial -s.

history.meaning: turned in another direction, toward another place
in or to another place, elsewhere
elsewhere, somewhere else; (in d'ailleurs) besides, moreover

morphemes.meaning: other, another place (from Latin alius, palatalized to aill-)

ailleurs.notes: Pronounced [ajœʁ]. Beyond literal 'elsewhere' ('chercher ailleurs', 'avoir la tête ailleurs' = 'to have one's mind elsewhere'), its prepositional phrase 'd'ailleurs' ('by the way, besides, for that matter') is one of the highest-frequency discourse connectors in spoken French.

rootFamily.gloss: alien, outsider; alibi (learned Latin relatives from alius)

aimable.etymology: Inherited/adapted in Old French from Classical Latin amabilis ('worthy of love, lovely, pleasant'), from amare ('to love'), reshaping the stem after French aimer.

history.meaning: to love -> worthy of love, pleasant

aimant.etymology: Remarkable case of folk-etymological convergence! Inherited via Old French adement / aiemant ('diamond, lodestone') from Classical Latin adamanta (accusative of adamās, 'hardest steel, diamond, lodestone'), from Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas, 'unconquerable, untamed', from privative ἀ- + δαμάω 'to tame'). In Gallo-Romance, loss of intervocalic -d- yielded aïmant -> aimant, which merged homophonously with aimant ('loving', present participle of aimer) because lodestones 'love' and attract iron.

history.meaning: unconquerable metal, diamond, and magnetic lodestone
diamond or magnetic stone (reinterpreted via aimer 'to love')
magnet (physical object or figurative person/place of attraction)

morphemes.meaning: magnet (historically Greek a-damant- 'untamed', reshaped after aim- 'love')

aimant.notes: Masculine noun (un aimant). It is a doublet of 'diamant' ('diamond')! Even though it did not originally come from 'aimer' ('to love'), French speakers have associated magnets with loving attraction since the Middle Ages ('attirer comme un aimant').

rootFamily.gloss: diamond (etymological doublet via Medieval Latin diamas)

aimer.etymology: Inherited through Old French amer (stressed stem aim- / eim- in singular forms like aime, unstressed stem am- in plural/infinitive amer, later analogically leveled to aimer in Middle French) from Classical Latin amāre ('to love, be fond of, like'), ultimately linked to a nursery/affective Indo-European root *am- ('mother, nurse, affection'; cf. Latin amīcus 'friend').

history.meaning: to love passionately or affectionately, be fond of
to love (romantically, filially, or spiritually), hold dear
to love (used unmodified with people) or to like/enjoy (with things or adverbs)

aimer.notes: Famous French nuance paradox! With a person, bare 'Je t'aime' is strong ('I love you'), whereas adding 'bien' softens it ('Je t'aime bien' = 'I like you / I'm fond of you' — the dreaded friend-zone phrase!). Notice how Old French unstressed 'am-' survives in 'amant', 'amour', and 'ami'.

ainsi.etymology: Inherited from Old French ensi / ainsinc ('thus, in this way'), probably from Vulgar Latin *in sic ('in thus, so'), reinforced by ainz ('before') or ac ('and') + sic ('thus').

air.etymology: From Old French air ('atmosphere, breeze; manner, look'), continuing Classical Latin aer, aerem ('air, lower atmosphere'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek aer ('mist, lower air').

aise.etymology: Inherited from Old French aise ('elbow room, opportunity, physical comfort, pleasure', 12th century; cf. Old Occitan aize), continuing Vulgar Latin *adjacia, neuter plural of *adjacium ('surrounding space, neighborhood, convenience'), formed from Classical Latin adjacēns, present participle of adjacēre ('to lie near, border on', from ad- 'at, near' + jacēre 'to lie'). Semantic shift ran from 'adjacent room to move' to 'unconstrained comfort'.

history.meaning: lying nearby; surrounding space, elbow room
free space, opportunity, material comfort, delight

morphemes.meaning: comfort, ease (historically from Latin ad- + jacēre 'lie near')

aise.notes: Feminine noun (une aise), vital in high-frequency idioms: 'être à l'aise' ('to feel comfortable / confident', or financially 'well-off'), 'mettre quelqu'un à l'aise' ('to put someone at ease'), 'mal à l'aise' ('uncomfortable / awkward'), and 'à votre aise' ('as you wish / take your time').

ajouter.etymology: Inherited from Old French ajoster ('to place side by side, join together'), from Vulgar Latin *adjuxtare, formed from ad- ('to') + juxta ('beside, close to').

history.meaning: to put side by side -> to add

alcool.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century via Medieval/Scientific Latin alcohol (popularized by Paracelsus for 'ultra-fine powder' and then 'quintessence obtained by distillation, rectified spirit of wine'), ultimately from Andalusi Arabic al-kuḥúl / Classical Arabic الكحل (al-kuḥl, 'antimony eyeliner powder, kohl', composed of the definite article al- + kuḥl). Alchemists extended the term from sublimated mineral powders to distilled volatile essences, before Lavoisier fixed the spelling alcool for spirits in 1787.

history.meaning: finely powdered antimony sulfide used as eye cosmetic (kohl)
impalpable sublimated powder; distilled quintessence of wine (Paracelsus)
ethyl alcohol, distilled spirits, alcoholic beverages

morphemes.meaning: historic Arabic definite article ('the', fused in borrowing)
distilled spirit (from Arabic kuḥl 'fine kohl powder')

alcool.notes: Masculine noun, pronounced [alkɔl] — do NOT pronounce the double 'oo' as /u/! Only a handful of French words have double 'oo' (alcool, zoo, scoop), and here both 'o's merge into a single open [ɔ] sound. 'Alcool fort' refers to hard liquor/spirits.

allemand.etymology: Inherited from Old French aleman, borrowed from Late Latin Alamannus, itself rendered from Proto-West Germanic *Alamaniz ('all men'), the confederation of Germanic tribes settled along the upper Rhine whom Gallo-Romans met first and generalized to all Germans (with an excrescent final -d added by suffix analogy with -and).

history.meaning: confederation of 'all men' (upper-Rhine Germanic tribal league)
member of the Alamanni tribe; a German

allemand.notes: Capitalized as a noun referring to a person (un Allemand, une Allemande), but always lowercase as an adjective or language name (le cinéma allemand, parler allemand); note also the idiom une querelle d'Allemand ('a fight picked over nothing').

aller.etymology: The Académie traces aller to Latin ambulare, to walk or move about. The proposed route through a shortened military command is uncertain. Other Latin verbs survive within its conjugation: ire in the future and conditional, and vadere in several present forms and the singular imperative.
aller.notes: Aller forms the near future: je vais manger. Allez ! and Allons ! can also encourage someone, roughly come on.

aller-retour.etymology: Modern French compound noun juxtaposing aller ('to go; outward journey') and retour ('return, trip back', from retourner).

history.meaning: outward and return journey; round-trip ticket

allergique.etymology: Derived in early 20th-century French from allergie plus the relational suffix -ique (modeled on German allergisch), after Austrian pediatrician Clemens von Pirquet coined German Allergie in 1906 from Ancient Greek állos ('other, altered') and érgon ('work, reactivity') to denote altered immune reactivity.

history.meaning: altered biological reactivity / reactive to an allergen

allergique.notes: Very common in conversational and agency banter in the figurative construction être allergique à quelque chose/quelqu'un ('to be unable to stand something or someone', e.g., allergique à la paperasse).

allez.etymology: Pragmaticalized discourse interjection from the second-person plural imperative of aller ('to go'), inherited via Old French aler from Vulgar Latin *allāre, most plausibly a rapid-speech phonetic reduction of Classical Latin ambulāre ('to walk, march') in military and colloquial commands.
allez.notes: One of spoken French's quintessential discourse markers—used regardless of whether addressing tu or vous—to encourage ('Allez, courage !'), concede ('Allez, d'accord'), wrap up a phone call ('Allez, salut'), or cheer a team.

cognates.meaning: to bind, fasten; set (teeth) on edge

allier.etymology: Inherited from Old French alier ('to bind, unite by treaty or marriage'), from Classical Latin alligāre ('to bind to, tie up, fetter'), composed of assimilating prefix ad- ('to') and ligāre ('to bind, tie'), shifting from physical tying to political union and harmonious blending of qualities.

history.meaning: to tie to, bind fast, fetter
to bind together, unite in alliance
to ally politically; to combine qualities harmoniously

allier.notes: In polished pitch and crítica prose, allier X et Y or allier X à Y ('to combine talent with charm') is high-register praise; pronominal s'allier avec/à means 'to team up or form an alliance with'.

allié.etymology: Allié began as the past participle of allier, to join or ally. The Académie records fourteenth-century alliet; the participle also became a noun for an ally.

history.meaning: to bind to, unite (< ad- + ligāre)

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French alier, alié

allié.notes: From the same Latin binding root ligāre come lier ('to tie') and une alliance ('an alliance' and 'a wedding band').

allumer.etymology: Inherited from Old French alumer ('to set alight, illuminate'), from Vulgar Latin *alluminare, altered from Classical Latin illuminare / adluminare (from ad- + lumen, luminis 'light').

history.meaning: to light, kindle; later to switch on

cognates.meaning: allure (actually a false-cognate lookalike from Old French alurer 'to lure', not aleüre!)

allure.etymology: Inherited from Old French aleüre ('way of walking, gait, pace'), derived from aler ('to go', from Vulgar Latin *allāre < Latin ambulāre) plus the deverbal suffix -ure (< Latin -ūra); originally describing a person's or horse's stride, it broadened to speed and stylish bearing or poise.

history.meaning: gait of a horse; pace of movement

allure.notes: Partial false friend with English allure: French allure is not 'temptation/seductiveness' (which came from Old French alurer, 'to lure a falcon', from leurre), though avoir de l'allure means 'to look classy/stylish'; also common in à toute allure ('at top speed').

allô.etymology: Allô is a nineteenth-century borrowing of American English hallo or hello. The early French spelling hallo preserves the link with that greeting.

rootFamily.gloss: are you still on the line? / paying attention?

allô.notes: Used specifically when answering or checking a phone connection (never as a face-to-face street greeting, unlike English 'hello').

alors.etymology: Alors joins à and the older adverb lors. It is recorded from the twelfth century, although the Académie notes that it remained uncommon until the fifteenth.

morphemes.meaning: then (< Old French l'ore < Latin illā hōrā)

history.meaning: then -> at that time, so, then

cognates.meaning: then, at that time, so (< ad illam hōram)

alors.notes: The final -s in lors / alors is the ‘adverbial s’ commonly added to Old French adverbs (compare toujours, volontiers); Italian allora reflects the exact same 'at that hour' formation.

alzheimer.etymology: Elliptical eponym from la maladie d'Alzheimer, calquing German Alzheimer-Krankheit, coined in 1910 by psychiatrist Emil Kraepelin in honor of his colleague Alois Alzheimer (1864–1915), who first described the neuropathology in 1906; the surname derives from a Rhineland-Palatinate habitational name (Alzheim, 'old/Alzey homestead').

history.meaning: presenile dementia described by Alois Alzheimer

alzheimer.notes: Used both formally in la maladie d'Alzheimer (capitalized) and colloquially as a masculine noun un alzheimer; in casual banter, actors forgetting lines sometimes quip j'ai un début d'alzheimer, though register sensitivity applies.

amande.etymology: Inherited via Old French almande / amande from Vulgar Latin amandula, an everyday alteration of Classical Latin amygdala, borrowed from Ancient Greek amygdálē ('almond').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: amande (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: amande

amande.notes: Learned anatomical French re-borrowed the Greek-Latin form directly as **amygdale** ('tonsil, amygdala', named for its almond shape).

amant.etymology: Inherited from Old French amant ('one who loves, courtly suitor'), from Classical Latin amantem, accusative of amāns ('loving; lover'), the substantivized present participle of amāre ('to love'); narrowed in post-classical French from any devoted suitor to an extramarital romantic partner.

history.meaning: male lover (especially in an affair); pl. les amants 'romantic lovers'

amant.notes: Crucial social nuance: singular mon amant almost always implies an extramarital or secret affair (whereas 'boyfriend' is mon copain / mon compagnon), though plural les amants remains poetic and literary ('the lovers').

ambassadeur.etymology: Borrowed in 14th-century Middle French from Old Italian ambasciatore (reinforced by Old Occitan ambaisador), derived from Medieval Latin ambactia ('official mission, service'), itself from Gaulish ambactos ('retainer, envoy, one sent around', recorded by Julius Caesar), from Proto-Celtic *ambi-ag-to- ('driven/sent around').

history.meaning: diplomatic envoy of a state or prince

ambassadeur.notes: In the cinema and luxury world of Paris agencies, un ambassadeur / une ambassadrice (note irregular feminine -drice, not *-deuse) frequently denotes a celebrity 'brand ambassador' for a fashion or cosmetics house (ambassadrice d'une grande maison).

ambiance.etymology: Coined in late 19th-century French literary circles (attested in Villiers de l'Isle-Adam and popularized by Edmond de Goncourt in 1891) from the adjective ambiant ('surrounding') plus suffix -ance, originally describing an enveloping artistic or spiritual aura before becoming the everyday word for mood or party vibe.

history.meaning: enveloping artistic milieu; mood, lively atmosphere

ambiance.notes: Watch key set phrases: mettre de l'ambiance ('to liven up the party'), casser l'ambiance ('to kill the mood'), and ironic bonne ambiance ! ('tense/awkward vibe in here!').

ambiant.etymology: Learned 16th-century borrowing (first used by surgeon Ambroise Paré in l'air ambiant) from Classical Latin ambientem, accusative present participle of ambīre ('to go around, encircle, encompass'), composed of prefix amb- ('around, on both sides') and īre ('to go').

history.meaning: physically surrounding or enveloping (especially of air)

ambiant.notes: Used both physically in à température ambiante ('at room temperature') and socially after abstract nouns to mean 'prevailing / all around us' (le pessimisme ambiant, la morosité ambiante).

rootFamily.gloss: ambition (from the same Latin verb ambīre!)

ambitieux.etymology: Learned borrowing (attested from the 13th–15th centuries) from Classical Latin ambitiōsus ('going around canvassing for votes; eager for public favor or honor'), derived from ambitiō ('a going around by Roman candidates soliciting votes'), itself an action noun from ambīre ('to go around', amb- + īre).

history.meaning: walking around to canvass voters for office
vote-courting, eager for public honor or display
driven by desire for success; bold in scope (of a project)

morphemes.meaning: go (Latin it-, supine stem of īre)

ambitieux.notes: Applied to a film or script (un projet ambitieux), it is warm praise; applied to a person (c'est un ambitieux), French usage can carry a sharper undertone of careerism ('social climber') than English 'ambitious'.

rootFamily.gloss: to aspire to, have ambitions for

cognates.meaning: amends (borrowed from Old French plural amendes)

amende.etymology: Inherited from Old French amende ('reparation, compensation for a fault, pecuniary penalty'), deverbal noun from amender ('to correct, set right'), semi-learned from Classical Latin ēmendāre ('to free from faults, correct', from ex- 'out' + menda 'fault, blemish'), with popular prefix substitution of a- for ē-.

history.meaning: to remove blemishes or errors, correct
to correct a fault, make reparation

amende.notes: Watch spelling and pronunciation against its near-homophone amande ('almond'—both pronounced /amɑ̃d/): payer une amende is 'to pay a fine/ticket', and faire amende honorable means 'to apologize publicly / eat humble pie'.

rootFamily.gloss: to amend (a bill); to reform oneself (s'amender)

amener.etymology: Formed in Old French (amener, 11th c.) from prefix a- (Latin ad- 'to, toward') + mener ('to lead, guide', from Late Latin minare 'to drive animals with shouts').

history.meaning: to lead or bring toward a place

ami.etymology: Ami continues Latin amicus, used both as an adjective and a noun. The eleventh-century French form amic still shows the older final consonant.
ami.notes: Be careful: un ami / une amie with a possessive (mon ami) can imply 'boyfriend / girlfriend', so French speakers often say un ami à moi or un copain for 'a friend of mine'.

amical.etymology: Learned borrowing (attested in Old/Middle French from the 13th–14th centuries) from Late Latin amīcālis ('of a friend, friendly'), preserving the intervocalic -c- lost in inherited ami, from Classical Latin amīcus ('friend'), itself built on the root of amāre ('to love').

history.meaning: friendly, warm, non-romantic or non-competitive (match amical)

amical.notes: Note the irregular masculine plural amicaux (des conseils amicaux); unlike English amicable (used mainly for divorces or settlements, which in French is à l'amiable!), French amical simply means 'friendly, warm'.

cognates.meaning: in a friendly way (from sibling stem amichevole)

amicalement.etymology: Formed in 14th-century Middle French from the feminine singular form amicale ('friendly', < Late Latin amīcālis) plus the productive Romance adverbial suffix -ment, grammaticalized from Classical Latin mente ('with a [friendly] mind', ablative of mēns).

history.meaning: in the manner of a friend, warmly

amicalement.notes: A go-to email and note sign-off among industry colleagues and acquaintances—warmer than Cordialement ('Regards') without being overly intimate ('Warmly / Best').

amitié.etymology: Inherited via Old French amistiet, amistié (with subsequent loss of preconsonantal -s-) from Vulgar Latin *amīcitātem (probably reshaped after *amīcitās or influenced by inimīcitās), replacing Classical Latin amīcitia ('friendship'), derived from amīcus ('friend') and amāre ('to love').

history.meaning: friendship, bond between friends or allies

amitié.notes: In the plural, Amitiés at the end of a message means 'Fond regards / Warm wishes', and Fais-lui mes amitiés means 'Give him/her my best'; note also une participation amicale / par amitié when a star appears in a film cameo for a director friend.

cognates.meaning: amortize (borrowed from Old French amortiss-, stem of amortir)

amortir.etymology: Inherited from Old French amortir ('to deaden, extinguish, alienate property in mortmain'), from Vulgar Latin *admortīre ('to make dead, deaden'), formed from prefix ad- ('to') and Classical Latin mors, mortis ('death'); semantically extended both to deadening physical shocks and to paying off or recouping financial costs.

history.meaning: to deaden (a blow or flame); transfer land into mortmain
to cushion a shock; to recoup or amortize an investment

morphemes.meaning: to, into a state of (Latin ad-)

amortir.notes: Equally common in physical contexts (amortir le choc, 'to cushion the blow'—literally or emotionally) and producer/agency finance (amortir le budget d'un film, 'to recoup/break even on a film's budget').

amour.etymology: Inherited via Old French amur, amor from Classical Latin amōrem, accusative of amor ('love, affection, desire'), related to amāre ('to love'); its modern -our vowel rather than regular Northern French *-eur (like douleur < dolōrem) reflects the prestige influence of Old Occitan troubadour lyric amor.
amour.notes: Famously one of three French nouns (with délice and orgue) that are masculine in the singular (un grand amour) but traditionally feminine in elevated/poetic plural (des amours tumultueuses); in everyday office praise, Tu es un amour ! means 'You're a sweetheart / lifesaver!'.

amour-propre.etymology: Compound noun forged in 16th–17th-century French moralist philosophy (famous in Pascal, La Rochefoucauld, and later Rousseau, who contrasted it with healthy amour de soi) as a calque of Scholastic Latin amor proprius ('self-love'), combining amour ('love') and propre ('one's own', < Latin proprius).

history.meaning: self-love (theological contrast to love of God)
self-centered vanity and attachment to one's own ego

amour-propre.notes: Indispensable for managing actors' egos in Dix pour cent: blesser / piquer l'amour-propre de quelqu'un means 'to wound/prick someone's pride', and une question d'amour-propre is 'a matter of personal pride'. Plural: des amours-propres.

amoureux.etymology: Inherited from Old French amorous, amoreus ('loving, enamored'), from Vulgar Latin *amōrōsus ('full of love'), derived from Classical Latin amor ('love') plus the productive adjectival suffix -ōsus ('abounding in, full of'); substantivized in French to denote a romantic partner or sweetheart.

history.meaning: full of love, inclined to love
in love (adj.); sweetheart, boyfriend (noun; fem. amoureuse)

amoureux.notes: Unlike amant (which implies an illicit affair), mon amoureux / mon amoureuse sounds affectionate, tender, or playfully Innocent ('my sweetheart / boyfriend / girlfriend'); tomber amoureux de = 'to fall in love with'.

ampoule.etymology: Inherited from Old French ampole ('small flask or phial, especially for holy oil; blister'), from Classical Latin ampulla ('small globular two-handled flask, phial'); extended in the late 19th century to the glass incandescent light bulb and sealed medical vial.

history.meaning: phial, water blister; electric light bulb

amusant.etymology: Lexicalized in 17th-century Classical French from the present participle of amuser ('to divert, entertain'), just as the verb softened from its older medieval sense 'to make stare idly, stall, deceive' (built on Old French muser 'to stare with snout in the air') into 'to pass the time pleasantly'.

morphemes.meaning: loiter, gawk (< Old French muser, from muse 'muzzle')
