amusant.notes: Slightly more polished and understated than drôle or marrant: c'est amusant can mean genuinely 'fun/entertaining' or dryly 'curious/funny how...' when an agent spots an ironic coincidence.

cognates.meaning: snout, muzzle (cognate of the underlying noun root)

amuser.etymology: Inherited from Old French amuser ('to make someone stare stupidly, trick, waste someone's time'), formed with causative prefix a- (< Latin ad-) and Old French muser ('to loiter, gawk with one's snout in the air'), itself from muse ('animal snout, muzzle', < Gallo-Romance/Medieval Latin musus); softened in the 17th century to 'divert, entertain'.

history.meaning: to make someone gawk, deceive, stall for time
to entertain, amuse; (s'amuser) to have fun

amuser.notes: Not related to the Greek Muses! Note the vital difference between transitive amuser la galerie ('to play to the crowd / clown around') and pronominal s'amuser ('to have fun, enjoy oneself'), plus ne t'amuse pas à faire ça ! ('don't you dare try doing that!').

rootFamily.gloss: to dawdle, waste time on trifles (preserves the older sense!)

améliorer.etymology: Re-formed with learned vocalism in 16th-century French (replacing native Old French ameillorer, amieudrer) from prefix a- (< Latin ad-) and Late/ Juridical Latin meliōrāre ('to make better, increase the value of an estate'), derived from Classical Latin melior ('better', suppletive comparative of bonus 'good').

history.meaning: better / to make better, improve property value
to make better, raise in quality
to improve, enhance; (s'améliorer) to get better

morphemes.meaning: toward, into a state of (< Latin ad-)

améliorer.notes: Unlike English ameliorate (stiff and formal), French améliorer is the everyday, standard verb for 'to improve' (améliorer un scénario); intransitive 'to improve / get better' MUST be reflexive: son jeu s'est amélioré (never *son jeu a amélioré).

rootFamily.gloss: better; best (inherited twin of the learned -mélior- stem!)

américain.etymology: Formed in 16th-century French (attested 1555–1575) from Amérique plus the ethnonymic suffix -ain (< Latin -ānus); Neo-Latin America was coined in Saint-Dié-des-Vosges in 1507 by cartographers Martin Waldseemüller and Matthias Ringmann from Americus, Latinized given name of Florentine navigator Amerigo Vespucci (ultimately Germanic Amalric, 'work/vigor-ruler').

history.meaning: Amerigo (Vespucci) → the newly charted Western landmass
indigenous inhabitant of the Americas; pertaining to the New World
of the Americas or specifically the United States; film day-for-night technique (nuit américaine)

américain.notes: Rich in French film-set idioms (made famous by Truffaut): une nuit américaine is 'day-for-night' shooting (filming night scenes in daylight with a filter), and un plan américain is a 'medium-long / cowboy shot' framed from mid-thigh up. Capitalized only as a person noun (un Américain).

an.etymology: An descends from Latin annus, year. The Académie dates the French noun to the eleventh century.

rootFamily.gloss: year (considered in its duration: bonne année!)

an.notes: An counts calendar units and ages (j'ai vingt ans, tous les ans), whereas derived année highlights duration or experience (toute l'année, bonne année!).

analyse.etymology: Learned 16th-century borrowing via Medieval and Renaissance Latin analysis from Ancient Greek análysis (ἀνάλυσις, 'an unloosing, dissolving, resolution of a whole into its constituent parts'), action noun from analýein ('to unloose, undo'), composed of aná- ('up, throughout, back') and lýein ('to loosen, untie').

history.meaning: unloosing; resolving a complex problem into simpler elements
logical or mathematical resolution into parts

analyse.notes: In Parisian artistic circles, être en analyse or faire une analyse very frequently serves as shorthand for 'undergoing psychoanalysis / seeing a therapist', alongside medical des analyses de sang ('blood tests') and en dernière analyse ('ultimately').

ancien.etymology: Inherited from Old French ancien ('old, belonging to earlier times'), from Vulgar Latin *antianus ('from before, former'), derived from Classical Latin ante ('before') + suffix -anus.

cognates.meaning: angel (borrowed from Old French angele, reinforced by Latin)

ange.etymology: Inherited with semi-learned church influence via Old French angele, angle, ange from Late/Ecclesiastical Latin angelus ('heavenly messenger'), borrowed from Ancient Greek ángelos (ἄγγελος, 'messenger, envoy'), which Septuagint translators used to render Biblical Hebrew mal'āḵ ('messenger [of God]').

history.meaning: angel, celestial spirit serving as God's messenger
angel; person of angelic sweetness or patience

ange.notes: Packed with vivid idioms: un ange passe ('there's an awkward silence in the room'—literally 'an angel is passing by'), être aux anges ('to be over the moon / on cloud nine'), and rire aux anges ('to smile blissfully to oneself'). Always masculine (un ange), even for a woman!

anglais.etymology: Inherited from Old French angleis ('English'), from Medieval Latin Anglicus / Vulgar Latin *Anglensis, derived from Angli ('the Angles', a Germanic people from Angeln who settled in Britain) + ethnic suffix -ensis (Old French -eis > -ais).

cognates.meaning: angle (borrowed from Old French) and ankle (distant Germanic cognate)

angle.etymology: Inherited via Old French angle ('corner, nook, geometric angle') from Classical Latin angulus ('corner, angle, retired nook'), originally a diminutive formation from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eng- / *ang- ('bend, corner, joint', cognate with Greek ankýlos 'bent' and Germanic *ankulaz 'ankle').

history.meaning: corner, bend, geometric angle, secluded nook
street corner, camera/geometric angle, editorial viewpoint

angle.notes: Essential in both cinema and city directions: à l'angle de la rue means 'on the street corner', un angle de prise de vue (or grand angle, 'wide-angle lens') is a 'camera angle', and arrondir les angles ('to round off the corners') means 'to smooth things over / ease tensions' in a negotiation!

cognates.meaning: fear, angst (from the same PIE root *h₂emǵʰ-)

angoisse.etymology: Inherited from Old French angoisse ('physical choking, chest constriction, acute torment'), from Classical Latin angustia (chiefly plural angustiae, 'narrowness, tight pass, straits, distress'), derived from augustus ('narrow, constricted'), from angere ('to squeeze, choke, throttle', PIE *h₂emǵʰ-).

history.meaning: spatial narrowness, tight defile; difficulty, distress
sensation of choking or chest tightness; agony
existential dread, acute anxiety; colloquially 'what a nightmare!'

angoisse.notes: Ranges from clinical/existential dread (une crise d'angoisse = 'a panic attack') to dramatic everyday hyperbole in Parisian speech: Quelle angoisse ! or C'est l'angoisse totale ! ('What a nightmare! / How stressful!').

rootFamily.gloss: to make anxious; (s'angoisser) to stress out

angoissé.etymology: Participial adjective from the past participle of angoisser ('to grip with anguish or anxiety'), inherited via Old French angoissier ('to choke, oppress, torment') from Christian Late Latin angustiāre ('to compress, hem in, afflict'), derived from angustia ('narrowness, distress').

history.meaning: to hem in tightly, afflict with distress
anxious, dread-ridden; (noun, un angoissé) a chronic worrier

angoissé.notes: Don't mix up angoissé ('feeling anxious', e.g., les acteurs sont toujours angoissés avant la première) with angoissant ('causing anxiety, nerve-wracking', e.g., un silence angoissant); also used as a noun: C'est un grand angoissé ('He's a total worrywart').

animal.etymology: Learned borrowing (attested 12th century, gradually overtaking native bête in scientific and general prose by the 16th century) from Classical Latin animal ('living, breathing creature'), substantivized neuter of animālis ('endowed with breath or life'), from anima ('breath, air, vital spirit, soul', PIE *h₂enh₁- 'to breathe').

history.meaning: breath, vital spirit → any living, breathing being
living creature (in scholastic and encyclopedic texts)

animal.notes: Irregular plural les animaux (/animo/); as an adjective in casting talk, un magnétisme animal ('animal magnetism') is high praise, while un animal politique ('a political animal') describes a master strategist. Note that 'pet' is un animal de compagnie.

rootFamily.gloss: soul (the inherited evolution of the very same Latin anima!)

animalier.etymology: Coined in early 19th-century French fine-arts criticism (attested around 1831 for sculptors like Antoine-Louis Barye as peintre/sculpteur animalier) from animal ('animal') plus the relational and occupational suffix -ier (< Latin -ārius), later extended to wildlife cinema, photography, and set animal wranglers.

history.meaning: relating to animals as subjects of film, care, or trade (dresseur animalier, documentaire animalier)

animalier.notes: Contrast the two adjectives from animal: animal means 'belonging to animal nature or biology' (le règne animal, l'instinct animal), whereas animalier means 'dealing with animals professionally or artistically'—crucial on film sets for un dresseur animalier ('animal wrangler/trainer') or un documentaire animalier ('wildlife documentary').

animation.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin animātiōnem (nominative animātiō), 'the act of imparting life or breath', a noun of action derived from animāre ('to quicken, endow with breath or soul'), itself from anima ('breath, vital spirit, soul'), from PIE *h₂enh₁- ('to breathe'). In French, it shifted from philosophical 'giving life' (14th–16th c.) to 'liveliness' (17th c.) and later to cinematic frame-by-frame motion under the influence of English animation in the 20th century.

history.meaning: act of imparting life or vital breath
bestowal of life; liveliness; cinematic animation

animation.notes: Feminine noun (une animation). In cinema (*cinéma d'animation*), it refers to animated filmmaking, while in everyday French it also means 'liveliness, bustle' or a hosted event/activity.

animé.etymology: Past participle adjective of animer ('to give life to, enliven'), borrowed in Old/Middle French from Classical Latin animātus ('endowed with breath or life, disposed'), perfect passive participle of animāre ('to fill with breath, quicken'), from anima ('breath, soul'). Alongside its adjectival sense of 'bustling, spirited', it joined dessin animé ('animated drawing, cartoon') in early 20th-century cinema.

history.meaning: endowed with breath or life; spirited

animé.notes: In film contexts, *un dessin animé* is any animated cartoon or feature, whereas standalone noun *un animé* specifically denotes Japanese animation (anime).

rootFamily.gloss: to bring to life, host, lead

anis.etymology: Inherited/borrowed via Old French anis (12th–13th c.) from Classical Latin anīsum (also anēsum), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄνῑσον (ánīson), Ionic/Attic variant of ἄνηθον (ánēthon, 'dill, anise'), likely a loanword from an Eastern Mediterranean or Egyptian substrate. In French café culture, the word came by metonymy to designate anise-flavored aperitifs such as pastis.

history.meaning: anise plant and its aromatic seed

anis.notes: Masculine noun (*un anis*). The final *-s* is silent in standard French (/a.ni/), though some southern speakers pronounce it (/a.nis/); ordering *un petit anis* at a café means a glass of pastis or anisette.

anniversaire.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical and Medieval Latin anniversarius ('returning every year'), compound of annus ('year') + versus ('turned', past participle of vertere).

history.meaning: day that comes round each year

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: anniversaire (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: anniversaire

anniversaire.notes: In everyday French, **un anniversaire** means both 'birthday' (**Joyeux anniversaire!**) and 'anniversary' (**anniversaire de mariage**).

annoncer.etymology: Inherited from Old French anoncier ('to make known, proclaim'), from Classical Latin annuntiare ('to bring news, announce'), from ad- ('to') + nuntiare ('to report, declare', from nuntius 'messenger').

annuel.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (anuel) from Late Latin annualis ('yearly'), variant of Classical Latin annalis, derived from annus ('year').

annuler.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Late Latin annullare ('to bring to nothing, abolish'), formed from ad- ('to') + nullum ('nothing', from ne- + ullus 'not any').

année.etymology: Inherited from Old French anee ('the full span or yield of a year'), from Vulgar Latin *annata, feminine participial noun formed on Classical Latin annus ('year') with suffix -ata.

history.meaning: the duration or produce of a year

anonyme.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century via Late Latin anōnymus from Ancient Greek ἀνώνυμος (anṓnymos, 'nameless, without a name'), formed from the privative prefix ἀν- (an-, 'without, un-') and ὄνυμα (ónyma), Aeolic/Doric dialectal form of ὄνομα (ónoma, 'name'), from PIE *h₁nómn̥ ('name'). Initially applied to unattributed texts and authors before broadening to unknown persons or featureless places.

history.meaning: nameless, uncelebrated, bearing no author's name

anonyme.notes: Invariable across masculine and feminine (*un appel anonyme*, *une lettre anonyme*). In corporate law, *société anonyme* (SA) means 'public limited company' (so named because shareholders are not named in the company title).

anse.etymology: Inherited from Latin ansa ('handle of a jug or cup, loop, grip'), which survived directly into Old French anse for the curved ear-like handle of a vessel or basket.

history.meaning: loop handle of a vessel, grip
curved handle of a pot, cup, or basket

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: anse (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: anse

anse.notes: French divides English 'handle' by shape: **une anse** is a curved loop (teacup, basket), **une poignée** is a grip/door handle, and **un manche** is a straight shaft (pan, broom, knife).

antispasme.etymology: Modern French medical and colloquial compound formed from the learned Greek-derived prefix anti- (from Ancient Greek ἀντί, antí, 'against, opposed to') and spasme ('involuntary muscular contraction'), borrowed via Latin spasmus from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós, 'convulsion, cramp, drawing'), derived from σπάω (spáō, 'to draw, pull, wrench'). Used in spoken French as a clipped nominal equivalent of un médicament antispasmodique.
antispasme.notes: Colloquial shorthand in spoken French for *un antispasmodique* (such as Spasfon, a ubiquitous French over-the-counter pill for stomach cramps). Formal medical writing strongly prefers *antispasmodique*.

antiterrorisme.etymology: Twentieth-century French compound combining the Greek-derived prefix anti- (ἀντί, 'against') with terrorisme, itself coined during the French Revolution (1794, after the Reign of Terror, la Terreur) from Latin terror ('great fear, dread', from terrēre, 'to frighten, make tremble', PIE *tres- 'to tremble') plus the suffix -isme. Designates state police, intelligence, and judicial policies aimed at preventing terrorism.

history.meaning: system of political rule by intimidation (the Jacobin Terror)

antiterrorisme.notes: Masculine noun (*l'antiterrorisme*). Notice that *terrorisme* itself originated in French during Thermidor 1794 to denounce Robespierre's *Terreur*; the related adjective is *antiterroriste* (e.g., *la brigade antiterroriste*).

appareil.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (apareil, 12th c., 'preparation, outfit, equipment') from apareillier ('to prepare, fit out'), from Vulgar Latin *appariculare ('to match together, make ready', from ad- + pariculus, diminutive of par 'equal').

apparemment.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French from the adjective apparent ('visible, manifest, seeming', borrowed from Latin appārentem, present participle of appārēre, 'to appear, come into sight', from ad- + pārēre) and the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin ablative mente, 'with a ... mind'). The spelling assimilation of -ent + -ment to -emment reflects regular Middle French phonetic lowering and nasalization before final -ment, leaving modern pronunciation /a.pa.ʁa.mɑ̃/.
apparemment.notes: Pronunciation trap: despite the *-emm-* spelling, the middle vowel is pronounced like an *a* (/a.pa.ʁa.mɑ̃/), just like *évidemment* (/e.vi.da.mɑ̃/) and *prudemment*. Also note double *p*, single *r*, double *m*.

appartement.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-16th century from Italian appartamento ('a separated suite of rooms within a palace or house'), derived from appartare ('to set apart, separate'), itself formed from a parte ('aside, apart'), from Latin ad partem ('to the side', from pars, partis, 'part, share'). French appartement was later borrowed into English as apartment in the 17th century.

history.meaning: private suite of rooms set apart in a residence
suite of rooms; self-contained flat or apartment

appartement.notes: Spelling watch: French *appartement* has double *p* (unlike English *apartment*). In casual spoken French (especially in Paris and on *Dix pour cent*), it is constantly clipped to *un appart'* (/a.paʁt/).

appartenir.etymology: Inherited from Old French apartenir ('to belong to, concern'), from Late Latin appertinere, intensive form of Classical Latin pertinere ('to reach to, belong to, concern'), from ad- + per- + tenere ('to hold').

history.meaning: to belong to, be the property or part of

appel.etymology: Appel is a noun formed from appeler, to call. It is recorded from the eleventh century; its modern telephone sense extends the older idea of a call.

history.meaning: call, roll call, appeal; phone call

appel.notes: Covers un appel téléphonique ('a phone call'), faire l'appel ('take attendance'), and faire appel ('lodge a legal appeal').

appeler.etymology: Appeler comes from Latin appellare, whose senses included approaching someone and addressing them. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century.

history.meaning: to accost, address, name, appeal to
to call, telephone; (s'appeler) to be named

appeler.notes: Doubles l to mark open /ɛ/ whenever the ending has a silent schwa: j'appelle, tu appelles, ils appellent vs. nous appelons.

applaudir.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin applaudere ('to strike upon, clap the hands in approval'), from ad- ('to, at') + plaudere ('to clap, strike, beat').

appliquer.etymology: Borrowed/semi-learned adaptation in Old French (apliier, then re-Latinized appliquer in the 14th c.) from Classical Latin applicāre ('to attach, join to, bring into contact, direct one's mind toward'), composed of ad- ('to, against') and plicāre ('to fold, bend, twine'), from PIE *plek- ('to plait, fold'). From physically laying one surface onto another, it developed abstract legal and practical senses of enforcing a rule or devoting effort.

history.meaning: to fold against, attach to, direct toward
to place upon, attach, bring to bear
to apply, put into practice, enforce

appliquer.notes: False-friend alert: *appliquer* does NOT mean 'to apply for a job' — use *postuler* or *candidater* for job applications! Reflexive *s'appliquer* means 'to apply oneself diligently' (or 'to apply/be relevant to').

apporter.etymology: Inherited from Old French aporter ('to carry to a place, bring'), from Classical Latin apportare ('to carry or bring to'), formed from ad- ('to') + portare ('to carry').

apprendre.etymology: Inherited from Old French aprendre ('to learn; to teach'), from Classical Latin apprehendere ('to seize hold of, grasp with the mind'), from ad- ('to') + prehendere ('to seize, catch').

history.meaning: to take hold of, grasp mentally

apprenti.etymology: Inherited from Old French aprentiz ('learner bound to a craft master'), formed with suffix -iz (< Latin -icius) on the stem of aprendre ('to learn'), from Latin apprehendere ('to take hold of, grasp with the mind').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: apprenti (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: apprenti

apprenti.notes: Old plural **apprentis** dropped the internal *-t-* before *-s*, and singular **apprenti** was later reshaped from the spoken plural.

approcher.etymology: Inherited from Old French aprochier ('to come near, bring near'), from Late Latin appropiare ('to draw near'), derived from ad- ('to') + prope ('near').

approuver.etymology: Inherited from Old French aprover ('to prove, test, judge good'), from Classical Latin approbare ('to assent to as good, approve, prove'), from ad- ('to') + probare ('to test, find good', from probus 'good, upright').

apprécier.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Late Latin appretiāre ('to set a price on, value, appraise'), formed from ad- ('to') and pretium ('price, worth, reward'), from PIE *per- / *pret- ('traffic, exchange, value'). Originally commercial and judicial ('to assess the monetary worth of'), it broadened in Classical and Modern French to 'esteem highly' and 'enjoy, like'.

history.meaning: to set a price upon, appraise commercially
to estimate the value or worth of
to assess; to value highly, enjoy, like

apprécier.notes: In French, *apprécier quelqu'un / quelque chose* is the natural, polite way to say you 'like' or 'fondly value' a colleague, friend, or work of art without the romantic intensity that *aimer* alone carries with people.

appuyer.etymology: Inherited from Old French apuier ('to support, prop up, lean upon'), from Vulgar Latin *appodiare ('to prop up on a support'), formed from ad- ('to, on') + podium ('raised base, support, hillock').

appétit.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (apetit, 12th c.) from Classical Latin appetītus ('eager desire, longing, natural craving, appetite for food'), action noun from appetere ('to strive after, reach toward, long for'), composed of ad- ('toward') and petere ('to seek, aim at, rush toward'), from PIE *peth₂- ('to rush, fly'). Narrowed in everyday usage from philosophical desire in general to physical hunger and gusto for food.

history.meaning: striving after, eager longing, natural craving

appétit.notes: Masculine noun (*un bon appétit*, liaison /bɔ.na.pe.ti/). Famous in the proverb coined by Rabelais (and earlier medieval table lore): *L'appétit vient en mangeant* ('Appetite comes with eating' — ambition grows once you start).

après.etymology: Inherited from Old French aprés ('after, behind, next'), from Late/Vulgar Latin ad pressum ('close behind, pressing hard upon'), from ad ('at, to') + pressum, neuter past participle of premere ('to press').

après-midi.etymology: Compound formed in Middle/Classical French from après ('after') + midi ('noon, midday', from Old French miedi < Latin medius dies 'middle of the day').

history.meaning: the part of the day after noon, afternoon

aquarelle.etymology: Borrowed in the late 18th century from Italian acquerello / acquarella ('thin water-based pigment wash'), derived from acqua ('water') < Classical Latin aqua.

cognates.meaning: from French aquarelle and Latin aqua
native inherited doublet of Latin aqua

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: aquarelle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: aquarelle

aquarelle.notes: **Aquarelle** (borrowed via Italian) and **eau** (inherited directly) both go back to the exact same four-letter Latin noun **aqua**.

arbre.etymology: Inherited from Old French arbre ('tree'), from Classical Latin arborem (nominative arbor, 'tree'), with dissimilation of the first r-r to r-b-r in Gallo-Romance.

arc.etymology: Inherited from Old French arc ('bow for shooting arrows; curved vault'), from Classical Latin arcus, arcum ('bow, arch, rainbow').

arche.etymology: Inherited from Old French arche ('chest, coffer; Noah's Ark; bridge arch'), from Classical Latin arca ('chest, strongbox; Noah's ark in Ecclesiastical Latin'), while the architectural sense ('vaulted bridge span') reflects merging with Vulgar Latin *arca from arcus ('arch').

architecte.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (via Italian architetto and Latin architectus) from Ancient Greek architekton ('master builder, chief artificer'), from archi- ('chief') + tekton ('carpenter, builder').

architecture.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin architectura ('the art of building'), derived from architectus ('master builder, architect').

ardeur.etymology: Inherited from Old French ardor / ardeur (12th c.), from Classical Latin ardōrem (nominative ardor), 'flame, fire, fierce heat, passionate eagerness', derived from ardēre ('to burn, blaze, be on fire'), from PIE *h₂eh₃s-d- ('to be dry, burn'). Both literal scorching heat (l'ardeur du soleil) and metaphorical emotional passion or work ethic survive side by side in French.

history.meaning: fervor, passion, spirited energy; intense heat

ardeur.notes: Feminine noun (*une grande ardeur*), like nearly all abstract French nouns in *-eur* (except *le bonheur*, *le malheur*, *l'honneur*, *le labeur*). Common agency/workplace idiom: *calmer les ardeurs de quelqu'un* ('to cool someone's enthusiasm / rein someone in').

argent.etymology: Inherited from Old French argent ('silver; silver coin, money'), from Classical Latin argentum ('silver; silver money'), from PIE *h2erg-nt-om ('the white or shining metal').

argile.etymology: From Latin argilla ('white potter's clay'), borrowed from Ancient Greek árgillos, built on argós ('shining, white') after the pale colour of fine kaolin and potter's earth.

rootFamily.gloss: silver; money (from the same Indo-European 'white/shining' root)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: argile (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: argile

aristocrate.etymology: Coined in French during the lead-up to and outbreak of the French Revolution (attested 1778–1789) as a back-formation from aristocratie, borrowed in the 14th century (by Nicole Oresme) via Medieval Latin from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατία (aristokratía, 'rule of the best-born or noblest'), from ἄριστος (áristos, 'best, noblest') and κράτος (krátos, 'strength, power, rule'). French aristocrate quickly spread into English and across European languages.

history.meaning: government by the best citizens or nobility
political regime ruled by nobles; the noble class
partisan of the Old Regime; member of the nobility

aristocrate.notes: Both masculine and feminine (*un/une aristocrate*). Colloquially shortened in French to *un/une aristo* (often slightly ironic or teasing). Famous Revolutionary song line: *Les aristocrates à la lanterne !*

arme.etymology: Inherited via Old French arme (10th–11th c., Chanson de Roland) from Classical Latin arma ('defensive and offensive gear, implements of war, shields and weapons'), originally a neuter plural collective noun that was reanalyzed in Vulgar Latin as a feminine singular first-declension noun (*arma, -ae). Ultimately related to Latin armus ('shoulder, upper arm') and ars ('fitting, skill') from PIE *h₂er- ('to fit, join together').

history.meaning: implements of war, armor, battle gear

arme.notes: Feminine noun (*une arme*). Do not confuse *une arme* ('a weapon') with *un bras* ('an anatomical arm')! Useful idioms: *rendre les armes* ('to surrender/give up') and *passer l'arme à gauche* (colloquial for 'to kick the bucket / die').

armoire.etymology: Inherited from Old French armaire / armoire ('wall niche or chest for tools, books, or weapons'), altered from Classical Latin armarium ('closet, chest, originally a place for storing arms or tools'), from arma ('tools, gear, weapons').

history.meaning: gear, weapons -> storage chest or cupboard

armure.etymology: Inherited from Old French armeüre (12th c.), regularly contracted in Middle French to armure, from Classical Latin armātūra ('equipment, armor, armed troops'), derived from armātus, past participle of armāre ('to equip with weapons, fit out'), from arma ('weapons, defensive gear'). Notice how the inherited popular form armure coexists as an etymological doublet with the later learned Renaissance borrowing armature ('structural framework').

history.meaning: military equipment, defensive gear; armed soldiers
defensive body armor worn in combat
suit of armor; protective shell or emotional defense

armure.notes: Feminine noun (*une armure*). Very frequent in psychological/dramatic French via the idiom *un défaut dans la cuirasse / fendre l'armure* ('to let one's guard down, show vulnerability beneath a tough exterior').

arrangement.etymology: Formed within French (attested early 16th c., popularized in the 17th–18th c.) from the verb arranger ('to set in rows, put in order, settle') and the action/result suffix -ment. Through the Frankish root *hring ('ring, circle, assembly rank'), the word moved from spatial ordering to musical adaptation and to diplomatic or business compromises ('a mutually convenient deal').

history.meaning: to draw up in ranks or rows, put in order
orderly disposition of parts; settlement of affairs
layout; musical adaptation; negotiated compromise or deal

arrangement.notes: In agent/business negotiations, *trouver un arrangement* means 'to work out a deal / reach an amicable settlement' (as in the proverb *Un mauvais arrangement vaut mieux qu'un bon procès*). Note the slight pejorative shade in *des petits arrangements avec la vérité* ('fudging the truth').

cognates.meaning: to make do, sort out (from French)

arranger.etymology: Inherited from Old French arrengier / arengier (12th c., 'to line up troops in battle order'), composed of a- (from Latin ad-, 'to') and rengier / ranger ('to place in a row'), derived from Old French renc (modern rang, 'row, rank, circle of people'), borrowed from Frankish *hring ('ring, circle of warriors or judges'), cognate with English ring and German Ring. Semantic shift went from military formation to tidying, repairing, and suiting someone's convenience.

history.meaning: to draw up soldiers in battle ranks
to put in order, fix, suit; (reflexive) to work out

arranger.notes: Essential conversational idioms in *Dix pour cent*: *Ça m'arrange !* ('That suits me / works out great for me!'), *Ça va s'arranger* ('Things will work themselves out'), and *Il ne s'arrange pas !* ('He's getting worse / not aging or behaving any better!'). Spelling note: *nous arrangeons* keeps the *e* before *-ons*.

arriver.etymology: Arriver comes from Vulgar Latin *arripare (ad + ripa 'riverbank, shore'): originally a maritime and river word meaning 'to reach the bank, come ashore', before generalising to 'to arrive, happen'!
arriver.notes: Takes **être** in the passé composé (*elle est arrivée*). **J'arrive!** = Coming! / On my way!

arrivée.etymology: Noun formed in Old/Middle French from the feminine past participle of arriver ('to reach the shore, arrive').

history.meaning: act of reaching one's destination, arrival

arrière.etymology: Inherited from Old French ariere (11th c.), from Vulgar Latin *ad retrō ('to the back, backward'), a reinforced prepositional compound combining Classical Latin ad ('to, toward') and retrō ('behind, backward', formed from re- + comparative suffix -trō). English borrowed both arrears ('unpaid debts left behind') and aphetic rear directly from Anglo-Norman/Old French ariere.
arrière.notes: Functions as adverb (*faire marche arrière*, 'to backpedal / reverse'), masculine noun (*à l'arrière du taxi*, 'in the back of the cab'), invariable adjective (*les sièges arrière*), and productive prefix (*arrière-pensée*, 'ulterior motive'; *arrière-plan*, 'background' in film).

rootFamily.gloss: behind, in back of (from de + retro)

arrogant.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French (13th–14th c.) from Classical Latin arrogantem (nominative arrogāns), 'assuming, overbearing, haughty', present participle of arrogāre ('to claim for oneself, appropriate unduly'), composed of ad- ('to, for oneself') and rogāre ('to ask, propose a law, demand'), from PIE *h₃reǵ- ('to straighten, direct'). An arrogant person literally 'claims or demands privileges for themselves without right'.

history.meaning: claiming unduly for oneself, presumptuous, haughty

arrogant.notes: Regular gender agreement: *arrogant* (/a.ʁɔ.ɡɑ̃/, silent *-t*) vs. feminine *arrogante* (/a.ʁɔ.ɡɑ̃t/, pronounced *-t*). Its underlying verb survives in elevated French *s'arroger un droit* ('to arrogate/usurp a right for oneself').

arrondissement.etymology: Formed in Classical French (16th–17th c.) from the verb arrondir ('to make round, round off, enlarge an estate') plus the nominal suffix -issement. Arrondir combines a- (from Latin ad-) and rond ('round'), inherited via Old French reont from Latin rotundum ('wheel-shaped, circular', from rota, 'wheel'). During the French Revolution (1795), arrondissement was adopted as a territorial administrative subdivision ('a rounded-off district').

history.meaning: to make round; to consolidate a property or territory
act of rounding; municipal or departmental administrative district (1795)

arrondissement.notes: Cultural essential for Paris (and Lyon/Marseille): Paris is divided into 20 numbered *arrondissements* spiraling outward clockwise like a snail shell (*l'escargot*) from the Louvre (1er) to Ménilmontant (20e); Parisians simply say *J'habite dans le dixième*.

rootFamily.gloss: to round off; to supplement (e.g. arrondir ses fins de mois)

arroser.etymology: Inherited from Old French aroser (12th c., 'to moisten with dew, sprinkle with water'), from Vulgar Latin *adrōsāre, a parasynthetic verb built on ad- ('to, upon') and Classical Latin rōs, rōris ('dew, moisture'), cognate with Sanskrit rasá ('moisture, sap') from PIE *h₁reh₁s- ('to flow, moisten'). From 'bedewing crops', it generalized to watering plants, basting roasts, and colloquially to celebrating with drinks or bribing.

history.meaning: to water plants; to baste; to toast with drinks or bribe

arroser.notes: Very lively agency/social slang! Beyond watering plants (*arroser les plantes*), *Ça s'arrose !* means 'That calls for a celebratory drink / champagne!', while *arroser quelqu'un* in crime or politics means 'to grease someone's palm / pay a bribe'. Also note the proverb *l'arroseur arrosé* ('the trickster tricked', title of the Lumière brothers' 1895 comedy film).

arrêt.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (arest, 12th c., 'halt, stay; court decree') from arester / arrêter ('to stop, stay').

history.meaning: act of stopping, halt; judicial ruling
stop, halt, bus stop; court judgment

arrêter.etymology: Inherited from Old French arester ('to bring to a halt, stop, stay'), from Vulgar Latin *arrestare, formed from ad- ('to') + restare ('to stand back, remain, stop', from re- + stare 'to stand').

history.meaning: to cause to stand still, stop

art.etymology: Inherited from Old French art (10th–12th c., 'craft, method, learned skill'), from Classical Latin artem (nominative ars), 'practical skill, trade, craftsmanship, method, work of art', derived from PIE *h₂értis ('a fitting together'), from the root *h₂er- ('to fit, join harmoniously'). Throughout the Middle Ages art meant technical mastery or liberal scholarship (les arts libéraux) before specializing in the 17th–18th centuries as aesthetic fine art (les beaux-arts).

history.meaning: creative aesthetic expression, fine art; technical mastery

art.notes: Masculine noun (*un art*, final *-t* is always silent: /aʁ/, never linked in liaison in the singular). In French culture, cinema is universally called *le septième art* ('the seventh art', a phrase coined by critic Ricciotto Canudo in 1911–1923).

article.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin articulus ('little joint, knuckle; clause of a text, grammatical particle'), diminutive of artus ('joint, limb').

history.meaning: joint -> small joint, distinct clause or item
numbered clause, newspaper piece, item of trade, grammatical article

articuler.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th–15th c.) from Classical Latin articulāre ('to divide into joints, utter distinctly syllable by syllable'), derived from articulus ('small joint, knuckle, clause, grammatical article'), diminutive of artus ('joint, limb'), itself from PIE *h₂er- ('to fit, join together' — the same ultimate root as art and arme). Originally anatomical and legal ('dividing into numbered clauses'), then phonetic ('enunciating distinctly').

history.meaning: to divide into joints; to pronounce distinctly
to set forth clause by clause; to join anatomically
to enunciate clearly; to structure or connect (s'articuler)

articuler.notes: In acting and voice coaching, *Articule !* means 'Enunciate / don't mumble!' Reflexive *s'articuler autour de...* is a favorite formal French expression meaning 'to be structured or organized around...'.

rootFamily.gloss: article (newspaper, shop item, grammar, law clause)

artisan.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (1546) from Northern Italian artigiano ('skilled craftsperson'), derived from Vulgar Latin *artitianus, itself built on Classical Latin ars, artis ('art, skill, craft'). During the Renaissance, Italian workshops exported both their decorative arts and their vocabulary across France. From French, the word was subsequently borrowed into English as artisan.
artisan.notes: In France, **un artisan boulanger** or **pâtissier** is a protected title indicating that bread and pastries are mixed and baked on the premises rather than industrially.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: artisan

artiste.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the late 14th century from Medieval Latin artista ('master of the liberal arts, university scholar, alchemist'), or reinforced by Italian artista ('practitioner of a fine art', used by Dante), built on Latin ars, artis ('skill, art') plus the Greek-origin agent suffix -ista (-iste). Only in the 17th–18th centuries did artiste separate cleanly from artisan to denote a creative painter, musician, or stage/screen performer.

history.meaning: student or master of the university liberal arts; alchemist
scholar of the arts; skilled practitioner or chemist
fine artist; stage or screen actor, singer, performer

artiste.notes: Core *Dix pour cent* vocabulary! Both masculine and feminine (*un/une artiste*). Unlike English *artist* (which defaults to visual arts unless specified), French *artiste* regularly means a stage/film actor or musical performer — hence *un agent artistique / agent d'artistes* ('talent agent') and *l'entrée des artistes* ('stage door').

artistique.etymology: Derived within French in the mid-18th century (attested c. 1752 in Enlightenment aesthetic criticism, Diderot era) from artiste ('fine artist, performer') and the relational adjectival suffix -ique (from Latin -icus / Greek -ικός). Replaced older adjectival uses of artiste to express 'pertaining to the arts, aesthetics, or performing artists' and was subsequently borrowed into English as artistic.

history.meaning: practitioner of the fine or performing arts
relating to the fine arts or aesthetic taste
artistic; relating to talent management or creative direction

artistique.notes: Signature *Dix pour cent* term: ASK (*Agence Samuel Kerr*) is *une agence artistique* ('a talent agency', NOT an 'art gallery'), *un agent artistique* is a 'talent agent', and *le directeur artistique (DA)* is the 'creative/artistic director'. Same form for masculine and feminine.

ascenseur.etymology: Coined in Paris in 1867 by French engineer Félix Léon Edoux for the hydraulic passenger lifts displayed at the Exposition Universelle, built as a learned agent/instrument formation from Latin ascēnsor ('one who climbs or mounts', from ascendere, 'to climb up', ad- + scandere, 'to climb, mount') on the pattern of French instrument nouns in -eur. The neologism immediately entered Italian (ascensore) and Spanish (ascensor).

history.meaning: to climb up; climber or rider mounting upward
hydraulic mechanical lift for raising passengers (coined 1867)
passenger elevator; vehicle of upward mobility

morphemes.meaning: climb up, mount (Latin ascend-, supine ascens-)

ascenseur.notes: Masculine noun (*un ascenseur*). Packed with idiomatic French expressions: *renvoyer l'ascenseur* ('to return a favor', especially in career networking), *l'ascenseur social* ('upward social mobility'), and Miles Davis's iconic 1958 French noir score *Ascenseur pour l'échafaud*.

aseptisé.etymology: Past participle adjective of aseptiser ('to sterilize, render free of germs', late 19th c.), derived from aseptique ('free from putrefaction or infection'), itself a 19th-century medical formation from Greek privative ἀ- (a-, 'without, non-') and σηπτικός (sēptikós, 'putrefying, causing rot'), from σήπω (sḗpō, 'to make rotten, decay'). In late 20th-century cultural criticism, aseptisé developed a vivid figurative sense: 'over-sanitized, bland, stripped of raw character'.

history.meaning: to sterilize surgical instruments or wounds against microbes
medically sterilized; (fig.) sanitized, clinical, soullessly polished

aseptisé.notes: High-frequency film/media critique word! When French directors or agents call a script, pop song, or Hollywood remake *trop aseptisé*, they mean it has been 'sanitized, watered down, made bland and risk-free'. Pronounced /a.sɛp.ti.ze/ (the *s* after *a-* stays voiceless /s/, never /z/).

assassiner.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-16th century from Italian assassinare ('to commit premeditated murder'), derived from assassino ('hired killer'), borrowed during the Crusades via Medieval Latin assassinus from Arabic حَشَّاشِين (ḥaššāšīn, 'hashish-users'), an epithet applied by rivals to the Nizari Ismaili sect of Syria and Persia famed for targeted political killings of Crusader and Muslim leaders. Generalized in French to any premeditated murder, as well as figurative character assassination.

history.meaning: hashish-consumers (polemical epithet for Nizari Ismaili operatives)
to murder treacherously or for hire
to commit premeditated murder; (fig.) to savage or bore to death

assassiner.notes: Broader than English *assassinate*! In French law and everyday speech, *assassiner* means ANY premeditated murder (*un assassinat*), whether the victim is a politician or an ordinary private citizen (whereas unpremeditated murder is *un meurtre*). Figuratively, critics *assassinent un film* ('savagely pan a movie').

rootFamily.gloss: murderer, assassin; murderous (adj., e.g. une critique assassine)

assemblée.etymology: Inherited from Old French asemblee (12th c., 'gathering, encounter, tournament or battle clash'), substantivized feminine past participle of asembler (modern assembler, 'to bring together'), from Vulgar Latin *assimulāre ('to gather into one group'), formed from ad- ('to, together') and simul ('at the same time, together'), from PIE *sem- ('one, together'). Italian assemblea, Spanish asamblea, and English assembly are all loans from French.

history.meaning: to bring together at the same place or time
gathering of people; feudal council or tournament clash
deliberative council, parliament; gathered audience or company

assemblée.notes: Feminine noun (*une assemblée*). Capitalized *l'Assemblée (nationale)* refers to the lower house of the French Parliament; in corporate life *l'assemblée générale (AG)* is the shareholders' meeting, and in social or theater contexts *toute l'assemblée* means 'the whole room / gathered crowd'.

rootFamily.gloss: together; outfit or set (from Latin in + simul)

cognates.meaning: to assess (from Latin assidere, 'to sit beside a judge')

asseoir.etymology: Inherited from Old French aseoir (11th c., 'to place, seat, establish, besiege'), from Vulgar Latin *assēdere (reshaping Classical Latin assidēre, 'to sit beside', by restoring the vowel of simple sedēre, 'to sit'), from ad- ('to, at') and sedēre ('to sit'), from PIE *sed- ('to sit'). The silent medial e in modern spelling asseoir reflects Middle French etymological/hiatus spelling before -oir (officially simplified to assoir in the 1990 rectifications, though asseoir remains dominant).

history.meaning: to sit beside; to seat or settle down
to seat, set in place; (reflexive) to sit down
to seat, establish firmly; (s'asseoir) to sit down

asseoir.notes: Famous for having TWO standard conjugations in modern French! Elevated/classic *je m'assieds, asseyez-vous* (/a.sɛ.je.vu/) coexists with everyday *je m'assois, assoyez-vous* (/a.swa.je.vu/); the *e* in *asseoir* is completely silent (/a.swaʁ/). Distinguish dynamic *s'asseoir* ('to sit down') from stative *être assis(e)* ('to be sitting'). Transitive *asseoir sa réputation / son autorité* means 'to firmly establish one's reputation or authority'.

assez.etymology: Inherited from Old French asez ('very much, sufficiently'), from Vulgar Latin *ad satis ('to sufficiency'), a univerbation of Classical Latin ad ('to, toward') and satis ('enough, sufficient'). As Classical satis weakened phonetically in Gaul, speakers reinforced it with the directional preposition ad, mirroring parallel Romance formations.

history.meaning: to sufficiency, up to what is enough

assez.notes: Before an adjective or adverb, 'assez' often means 'quite' or 'fairly' ('assez bon' = pretty good) rather than 'enough', whereas 'assez de' + noun expresses sufficient quantity.

assiette.etymology: Inherited from Old French assiete ('act of seating guests at table; the dish set at each diner's place'), feminine participial noun from asseoir ('to seat, set down') < Vulgar Latin assedere.

history.meaning: to sit beside, set in place
seating arrangement; course set before a guest

cognates.meaning: from Anglo-Norman asetz / assiette in legal accounting

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: assiette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: assiette

assiette.notes: The older sense 'way of sitting steady' survives in the idiom **ne pas être dans son assiette** ('to feel out of sorts').

assis.etymology: Inherited from Old French asis ('seated, situated'), past participle of asseoir ('to seat, set'), from Vulgar Latin *assedere (for Classical assidere 'to sit beside'), with participle modeled on Vulgar Latin *assissum.

assistant.etymology: Assistant is the present participle of assister used as a noun. The Académie dates this development to the fourteenth century.

rootFamily.gloss: to assist (dir. obj.); to attend (assister à)

assistant.notes: Remember the preposition split on parent verb assister: assister quelqu'un means 'to help someone', whereas assister à une réunion means 'to attend a meeting'.

assistante.etymology: Feminine inflection of assistant, borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin assistentem, the present participle of assistere ('to stand beside, attend, aid in court'), formed from ad- ('near, by') and sistere ('to take a stand, cause to stand'), a reduplicated stem of PIE *stā- ('to stand').

history.meaning: to stand beside, stand by to help or defend
female assistant (executive, production, or director's assistant)

assistante.notes: In French film and talent agencies (like ASK in Dix pour cent), an 'assistante' is a pivotal gatekeeper; watch out for the false friend 'assister à', which means 'to attend' (an event), whereas 'assister quelqu'un' means 'to assist someone'.

association.etymology: Entered Middle French via Medieval Latin associationem ('a joining together, fellowship'), noun of action derived from Classical Latin associare ('to unite, join as an ally or companion'), built on ad- ('to') and socius ('companion, partner, ally'). Under French law (notably the Loi 1901), it became the standard term for a non-profit organization as well as a business partnership.

history.meaning: act of uniting or joining in fellowship
union of persons for a common interest

association.notes: In everyday France, 'une association' (often shortened colloquially to 'une asso', pronounced [aso]) usually refers to a non-profit or charity (Loi 1901), though in agency business it also means 'partnership'.

associer.etymology: Borrowed in late Old French from Classical Latin associare ('to join to, unite with'), derived from ad- ('to, toward') assimilated before s- and sociare ('to join together, share'), itself from socius ('comrade, partner, ally', ultimately linked to the root of sequi 'to follow').

history.meaning: to join together, unite as companions or allies
to admit someone as a companion or co-holder
to associate, bring in as a partner, link

associer.notes: Used reflexively, 's'associer (avec quelqu'un)' means 'to go into business together' or 'team up as partners' — a recurring power move among senior talent agents.

associé.etymology: Participial noun and adjective from associer ('to join as a companion or partner'), borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin associare ('to unite, join together'), from ad- ('to') + socius ('companion, ally, partner').

history.meaning: to join as an ally or partner

associée.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of associer ('to unite, take on as a partner'), ultimately from Classical Latin associata ('joined together, allied'), built on ad- ('to') and socius ('partner, ally'). In commercial French, it came to designate a co-owner or equity partner in a firm or agency.

history.meaning: woman joined in a venture or fellowship
female business partner or equity co-owner

associée.notes: False-friend nuance: in corporate or agency French (such as Andréa Martel's title at ASK), 'une associée' is not a junior 'associate' in the American sense, but a senior equity 'partner' who owns shares in the company.

assorti.etymology: Past participle of assortir ('to match, group by kind, stock with matching goods'), formed in Old/Middle French from a- (Latin ad-) + sorte ('kind, sort, category').

history.meaning: matched by kind or color, well-paired

assumer.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French from Classical Latin assumere ('to take to oneself, adopt, claim, usurp'), composed of ad- ('to, toward', assimilated to as-) and sumere ('to take, pick up', itself from sub- 'up from under' + emere 'to take, buy').

history.meaning: to take up, adopt, receive to oneself
to shoulder responsibility; to own one's choices unapologetically

assumer.notes: Major false friend! French 'assumer' almost NEVER means 'to suppose/presume' (use 'supposer' or 'présumer' for that); it means 'to take full responsibility for' or colloquially 'j'assume !' ('I own it / I'm unapologetic about it!').

assurance.etymology: Inherited from Old French asseurance ('pledge, guarantee, security, confidence'), derived from the verb asseurer ('to make safe, reassure') plus the abstract nominal suffix -ance. Asseurer goes back to Vulgar Latin *assecurare, built on Classical Latin securus ('free from care or danger', from se- 'without' + cura 'care, worry'). In the 16th–17th centuries, maritime trade extended its sense to financial insurance contracts.
assurance.notes: Covers both English 'insurance' ('les assurances du tournage' = film shoot insurance, a huge issue for older or risky stars) and 'self-assurance' ('avoir de l'assurance' = to have poise).

assurance-vie.etymology: Modern French nominal compound formed by direct apposition of assurance ('insurance', from Old French asseurance < Vulgar Latin *assecurare, 'to make safe') and vie ('life', from Old French vie < Classical Latin vita, 'life'). It elliptically condenses the older prepositional phrase assurance sur la vie ('insurance upon one's life'), attested from the 18th–19th centuries with the rise of actuarial finance.

history.meaning: contract guaranteeing payment contingent on human life
life insurance policy and tax-advantaged savings vehicle

assurance-vie.notes: In France, an 'assurance-vie' functions not only as death-benefit life insurance (often contrasted with 'assurance décès') but also as the country's most popular long-term investment and estate-planning account; plural is 'des assurances-vie'.

assurer.etymology: Inherited from Old French asseurer ('to make safe, protect, pledge'), from Vulgar Latin *assecurare ('to render secure'), a parasynthetic verb formed from Latin ad- ('to') + securus ('free from care, safe', itself from se- 'apart, without' + cura 'care, anxiety') + -are. Syncope of the intervocalic velar produced Old French seür ('sure') and asseürer, which contracted to assurer.

history.meaning: to make safe from danger or worry
to secure, assure, insure; (colloquial) to perform brilliantly

assurer.notes: Beyond 'to insure' and 'to guarantee', colloquial French uses intransitive 'assurer' as high praise: 'Tu assures !' or 'Elle a grave assuré sur le plateau !' means 'You rock!' / 'She totally nailed it on set!'

atelier.etymology: Inherited from Old French astelier ('pile of wood chips; carpenter's yard or workshop'), derived from astele ('splinter, wood shaving, lath'), from Late Latin astella, diminutive of Classical Latin astula / assula ('splinter, chip of wood').

history.meaning: carpenter's woodyard -> craftsman's or artist's workshop

atmosphère.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-17th century from Neo-Latin atmosphaera, coined by astronomers (notably John Wilkins in 1638) from Ancient Greek ἀτμός (atmós, 'vapor, steam') and σφαῖρα (sphaîra, 'ball, globe, sphere') to describe the gaseous envelope around celestial bodies. From the late 18th century onward, French extended the term metaphorically to the social or emotional ambiance of a place.

history.meaning: sphere of vapor surrounding a planet or moon
gaseous envelope around the Earth (scientific usage)
planetary atmosphere; mood, ambiance, or tension in a room

atmosphère.notes: Iconic French cinema reference: Arletty's legendary line in Marcel Carné's 1938 classic Hôtel du Nord — 'Atmosphère ! Atmosphère ! Est-ce que j'ai une gueule d'atmosphère ?' — is quoted constantly by French actors and cinephiles.

cognates.meaning: at all, wholly (structural parallel: a tutto)

atout.etymology: Formed by univerbation of the Old and Middle French prepositional phrase à tout ('with everything, accompanied by; playing for all stakes'), from Latin ad ('to, at') + totum (accusative of totus, 'whole, all'). In 15th-century card games, 'jouer à tout' meant playing the dominant suit that beats all others, turning 'un atout' into a noun meaning 'trump card' before generalizing to 'major asset or advantage'.

history.meaning: with, entirely, for the whole stake
trump suit or trump card in card games
trump card; key asset, strength, selling point

atout.notes: Pronounce the first 't' but keep the final '-t' silent ([atu]); idioms like 'avoir tous les atouts en main' ('to hold all the cards / have every advantage') are staples of casting and contract negotiations.

attacher.etymology: Inherited from Old French atachier ('to fasten, nail, tie'), altered by prefix substitution (a- for es-) from Old French estachier ('to fasten to a stake'), from Frankish *stakka ('stake, post, peg').

history.meaning: stake, peg -> to fasten to a peg, attach

attaque.etymology: Deverbal noun created in Early Modern French (late 16th century) from attaquer ('to join battle, assail'), reinforced by Italian attacco ('engagement, assault'). Ultimately traces to a Germanic root *stakka ('stake, post') via Gallo-Romance/Old Italian verbal formations meaning 'to fasten onto, grapple with an enemy'.

history.meaning: attack, offensive; sudden medical fit; opening strike of a musical note

attaque.notes: The energetic idiom 'être d'attaque' ('Je suis d'attaque !') means 'to be raring to go, rested, and ready for action' — frequently heard early in the morning on a film set or at the agency.

rootFamily.gloss: to attack; to sue; to start briskly

cognates.meaning: to attack; doublets with to attach

attaquer.etymology: Borrowed in the late 16th century from Italian attaccare ('to fasten, join battle, assail', in phrases like attaccare battaglia 'to engage battle'), itself a cognate of Old French atachier ('to fasten to a stake', whence French attacher and English attach), ultimately built on ad- + a Germanic noun *stakka ('stake, post'). Thus 'attaquer' and 'attacher' are etymological doublets.

history.meaning: to fasten together, engage in combat
to assail militarily, initiate hostilities against
to attack; to sue in court; to tackle (work or a meal) briskly

attaquer.notes: In agency and entertainment law, 'attaquer quelqu'un (en justice)' means 'to sue someone' (e.g., for breach of contract); colloquially, 'On attaque ?' means 'Shall we dig in / get started?'.

atteindre.etymology: Inherited from Old French ateindre ('to touch upon, overtake, reach'), from Vulgar Latin *attingere for Classical Latin attingere ('to touch, reach, arrive at'), from ad- ('to') + tangere ('to touch').

history.meaning: to reach, attain, hit a mark

attendre.etymology: Attendre comes from Latin attendere, to direct one’s attention towards something. The eleventh-century French spelling was atendre; waiting and expecting developed around that idea of attention.

history.meaning: to stretch one's mind toward, pay heed

attendre.notes: Classic false friend with English: attendre means 'to wait for' (j'attends le bus, with no preposition!), whereas 'to attend' an event is assister à.

attente.etymology: Inherited from Old French atente ('expectation, hope, waiting'), formed on the Vulgar Latin participial/deverbal pattern *attenta from Classical Latin attendere ('to stretch toward, direct the mind or ear toward', from ad- 'toward' + tendere 'to stretch'). As French attendre shifted semantically from 'paying attention' to 'waiting for', attente followed suit from 'mental focus' to 'waiting and expectation'.

history.meaning: stretching the mind toward, directing attention
wait, waiting period; expectation (especially plural: les attentes)

morphemes.meaning: to stretch, wait (Latin tendere / French attendre)

attente.notes: Remember the core false-friend family: 'attendre' means 'to wait for' (not 'attend'), so 'salle d'attente' is a 'waiting room', 'être en attente' is 'to be on hold', and 'répondre aux attentes' is 'to meet expectations'.

attentif.etymology: Recorded from Old/Middle French attentif ('paying close heed'), derived on the learned stem of Latin attendere (past participle attentus, 'stretched toward, alert, heedful', via scholastic Latin attentivus), composed of ad- ('toward') + tendere ('to stretch [one's mind or ear]'). Unlike popular attendre ('to wait'), learned attentif preserved the Classical Latin sense of focused mental alertness.

history.meaning: having the mind stretched toward, alert, heedful

attentif.notes: Feminine is 'attentive'; note the contrast between 'attentif' ('focused, observant, paying close attention') and 'attentionné' ('thoughtful, considerate, caring toward someone').

attention.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin attentionem (nominative attentio, 'mental application, attentiveness'), noun of action from attendere ('to stretch the mind toward, heed'), from ad- + tendere ('to stretch').

history.meaning: to direct the mind toward -> attentiveness

cognates.meaning: marked for attention (bureaucratic false friend to French sense)

attentionné.etymology: Coined inside Early Modern French (attested early 18th century) from the noun attention ('thoughtful care, regard for others', from Classical Latin attentionem < attendere 'to direct one's mind toward') plus the adjectival suffix -é ('endowed with, characterized by', with consonant gemination -nn-). It specialized specifically around warm, solicitous gestures ('avoir des attentions pour quelqu'un').

history.meaning: mental focus; delicate gesture of kindness toward someone

attentionné.notes: Crucial learner distinction: 'un agent très attentionné' means a 'very thoughtful, caring agent' (who remembers flowers or a client's anxieties), NOT someone merely paying attention in a meeting (which is 'attentif').

attentivement.etymology: Formed in Middle French from the feminine form attentive (of attentif, 'alert, heedful', from Latin attentus < attendere 'to stretch the mind toward') and the adverbial suffix -ment, which descends from the Classical Latin ablative singular mente ('with a [certain] mind', from mens, mentis, feminine noun). Because Latin mens was feminine, French adverbs regularly attach -ment to the feminine adjectival stem.
attentivement.notes: Standard collocation in agency life: 'lire attentivement un scénario / les petits caractères d'un contrat' ('to read a script / the fine print of a contract closely').

atterrir.etymology: Parasynthetic verb created in Early Modern French (17th century) from à (assimilated to at-, from Latin ad 'to, toward') + terre ('earth, dry land', from Classical Latin terra) + second-group infinitive suffix -ir. Originally a nautical term meaning 'to sight or reach land after a sea voyage', it was adopted at the dawn of aviation (circa 1908–1910) for landing an airplane, inspiring parallel planetary coinages like alunir ('to land on the Moon').

history.meaning: to touch down on the ground (aircraft or jumper); figuratively, to come back to reality

morphemes.meaning: second-group verbal infinitive ending (-iss- in plural)

atterrir.notes: Spelling trap: double 't' AND double 'r' ('at-terr-ir', because of 'terre'). Colloquially, 'Faut atterrir !' means 'Come back down to earth / get real!' (e.g., when a diva makes impossible demands), and 'atterrir quelque part' means 'to wind up somewhere unexpectedly'.

attirant.etymology: Adjectival use of the present participle of attirer ('to draw toward oneself, entice'), attested with its figurative aesthetic and romantic sense from the 16th–17th centuries. Built on a- (assimilated to at-, from Latin ad- 'toward') + tirer ('to pull, draw', from Old French tirier) + participial suffix -ant (from Latin -antem).

history.meaning: drawing or pulling physically toward oneself
attractive, appealing, alluring (of a person, offer, or role)

attirant.notes: While English speakers often reach for 'attractif', French distinguishes the two: 'attirant' describes personal, physical, or emotional appeal (a person or intriguing film role), whereas 'attractif' mostly describes economic or financial appeal ('un salaire attractif', 'des prix attractifs').

attirer.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French from prefix a- (spelled at- by learned Latinizing orthography after ad-, 'toward') and tirer ('to pull, draw, tug'). While the compound morphology is completely transparent, the ultimate origin of Old French tirier ('to pull, suffer') is debated among Romance philologists — most plausibly derived via semantic shortening from Vulgar Latin *martyriare ('to torture on the rack, stretch, yank') or influenced by Germanic *tiran ('to tear, pull').

history.meaning: to pull or drag physically toward oneself
to attract, draw (audiences, attention, or trouble), entice

attirer.notes: Very common in entertainment and PR collocations: 'attirer l'attention' ('to draw attention'), 'attirer le public en salle' ('to draw audiences to theaters'), and reflexively 's'attirer des ennuis' ('to bring trouble on oneself').

attraper.etymology: Formed in Old French (atraper, 12th c., 'to catch in a trap, ensnare') from a- (Latin ad-) + trape ('snare, trap', modern trappe), borrowed from Frankish *trappa ('trap, snare').

history.meaning: trap -> to catch in a trap
to catch, grab, get hold of

atténuer.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (15th–16th century, initially medical and rhetorical) from Classical Latin attenuare ('to make thin, wear down, weaken, lessen'), formed from ad- ('to', assimilated to at-) and tenuare ('to make thin or slender'), from tenuis ('thin, fine, slight', from PIE *ten- 'to stretch thin').

history.meaning: to make thin, slender, or weak; to pare down style
to thin out bodily humors; to lessen severity
to diminish, soften, alleviate (pain, scandal, lighting, or blame)

atténuer.notes: Much more everyday in French than 'attenuate' is in English: used for softening wrinkles or harsh lighting on camera ('atténuer les cernes'), easing a media scandal ('atténuer le choc'), and in law 'circonstances atténuantes' ('mitigating circumstances').

au.etymology: Au is the contraction of the preposition à and the masculine article le. It is a grammatical combination, not the unrelated chemical symbol Au. The Académie describes its use under à.

history.meaning: to the, at the, in the (before consonant-initial m. sg. nouns)

au.notes: Mandatory contraction before masculine singular nouns starting with a consonant sound (au cinéma), whereas vowel-initial nouns take à l' (à l'hôpital).

cognates.meaning: actually, by the way (parallel factum phrase)
au fait (borrowed from the older French sense 'well-informed')

au fait.etymology: Idiomatic prepositional phrase composed of au (regular Old French contraction of à + le, 'to the') and fait ('deed, fact, point at issue', from Old French fait < Classical Latin factum, neuter substantivized past participle of facere 'to do, make'). Originally used in expressions like 'venir au fait' ('to come to the point') and 'être au fait de' ('to be apprised of the facts'), it grammaticalized in spoken French into a discourse marker introducing a sudden recollection ('speaking of facts / by the way').

history.form: venir au fait / estre au fait
history.meaning: to get to the heart of the matter; to be fully informed
by the way, incidentally (discourse marker); informed (être au fait)

au fait.notes: Pronunciation key! In 'Au fait, tu as vu Mathias ?' ('By the way, have you seen Mathias?'), the final '-t' of 'fait' IS pronounced ([ofɛt]), unlike in 'en fait' (also [ɑ̃fɛt]) vs. 'tout à fait' ([tutafɛ], silent '-t'). Also a false friend to English 'au fait', which retained only the formal French sense 'être au fait de' ('well-informed about').

au point.etymology: Idiomatic prepositional phrase formed from au (contraction of à + le, 'at the') and point ('exact mark, degree, prick', from Old French point < Classical Latin punctum, 'prick, dot, exact spot on a scale', substantivized neuter past participle of pungere 'to prick, pierce'). From medieval and early modern craft, cookery, and optics ('adjusted to the exact focal mark'), 'être au point' evolved to mean 'finely tuned, perfected, ready'.

history.meaning: at the exact proper degree or mark
perfected, finely tuned, mastered, ready for deployment

morphemes.meaning: at the, to the (contraction of à + le)

au point.notes: Essential agency & cinema collocations: 'Le scénario n'est pas encore au point' ('The script isn't quite ready/worked out yet'), 'mettre au point un plan' ('to devise/fine-tune a plan'), and in photography 'faire la mise au point' ('to focus the lens' / figuratively 'to set the record straight'). Don't confuse with steak 'à point' (medium-rare/medium).

au revoir.etymology: Elliptical farewell formula combining au (contraction of à + le, 'until the') with the substantivized infinitive revoir ('the act of seeing again'), formed from iterative prefix re- ('again') + voir ('to see', from Old French veeir < Classical Latin videre 'to see'). Attested from the 17th century (alongside 'jusqu'au revoir'), it gradually displaced 'adieu' ('to God') in everyday secular leave-taking whenever speakers expected to meet again.
au revoir.notes: In natural spoken Parisian French, the middle 'e' drops and 'au revoir' is routinely pronounced in two quick syllables ([oʁvwaʁ] or even [ɔʁvwaʁ]); unlike dramatic 'adieu' (final farewell), 'au revoir' works across every polite and casual register.

rootFamily.gloss: to see again; to revise/review (a contract)
reunion, meeting again (plural: les retrouvailles / au revoir)

au-delà.etymology: Compound adverb and preposition formed from au ('at the', contraction of à + le) + delà ('on the other side, beyond', from Old French de la < Latin de illac 'from that side').

au-dessus.etymology: Compound adverb formed from au ('at the', à + le) + dessus ('on top, above', from Old French desus < de + sus < Latin sursum 'upward').

aube.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin alba ('dawn'), substantivized feminine of Classical Latin albus ('dull white'), elliptical for alba lux ('the white light on the horizon before sunrise').

history.meaning: first white light of morning, daybreak

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: aube (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: aube

aube.notes: Latin *al-* vocalized regularly to *au-* before consonants in Old French (*alba* -> **aube**, *alterum* -> **autre**, *calidum* -> **chaud**).

aucun.etymology: Inherited from Old French alcun ('some, someone, any'), from Vulgar Latin *aliqui-unus, altered from Classical Latin aliquis ('someone, anyone') + unus ('one'); through frequent use with negation ne, its sense shifted from positive ('some, any') to negative ('no, none').

history.meaning: any, some -> (with ne) no, not any, none

audacieux.etymology: Derived in Middle French (15th century) from audace ('boldness, daring', borrowed from Classical Latin audacia) with the suffix -ieux (from Latin -iosus, 'full of'). Classical Latin audacia stems from audax ('bold, daring'), built on the semi-deponent verb audere ('to dare, venture'), itself contracted from avidere (related to avidus 'eager, yearning').

history.meaning: bold, daring, artistically or strategically innovative

audacieux.notes: Positive nuance alert: whereas English 'audacious' often sounds insolent or brazen, French 'audacieux' (feminine 'audacieuse') is usually high praise in cinema and art — 'un choix de mise en scène très audacieux' ('a bold, daring directorial choice').

rootFamily.gloss: avid, eager (distant Latin cognate via avidus)

cognates.meaning: audit (source of the modern French borrowing)

audit.etymology: Borrowed in the second half of the 20th century from English audit ('official examination of accounts'), which itself comes from Medieval and Classical Latin auditus ('a hearing, listening', noun of action from audire 'to hear, listen'). In medieval England and France, financial accounts were read aloud and verified orally before auditors ('hearers'), so audit re-entered modern French corporate terminology as a "boomerang" Latinism via Anglo-American accounting.

history.meaning: official hearing and verification of financial accounts

audit.notes: Pronounce the final '-t' clearly ([odit])! Note that while 'un audit' is used for an internal or consulting inspection of a company's finances, an official government tax audit in France (like the painful one hitting ASK in Season 2) is specifically called 'un contrôle fiscal'.

rootFamily.gloss: audition; judicial hearing; sense of hearing

audition.etymology: Learned borrowing (attested in Old/Middle French in legal and medical contexts) from Classical Latin auditionem ('act of hearing, listening to a lecture or witness'), derived from audire ('to hear'). Originally designating the physiological sense of hearing and the formal questioning of witnesses, it developed its theatrical and musical sense ('trial performance before a director') in late 19th-century French, later reinforced by cinema and English usage.

history.meaning: act of hearing, listening; lecture, rumor
judicial hearing of witnesses; physiological sense of hearing
hearing (sense or legal); theatrical/musical audition (alongside casting/essais)

audition.notes: Cinema insider tip: while 'passer une audition' is completely standard (especially for theater, voice, or music), French film agents and casting directors very often say 'passer un casting' or 'faire des essais (caméra)' specifically for an on-camera screen test! Also means medical 'hearing' ('perte d'audition') and a police/parliamentary 'hearing'.

rootFamily.gloss: to audition; to question formally (a witness)

auditionner.etymology: Formed in early 20th-century French by adding the productive first-group verbal suffix -er (with orthographic gemination of -n-) to audition ('trial performance; formal hearing', from Classical Latin auditionem < audire 'to hear'). Its dual modern usage covers both show-business casting trials and formal police or judicial questioning.

history.meaning: hearing; musical or theatrical trial performance
to audition (an actor/musician or for a role); to question a witness officially

auditionner.notes: Works both transitively ('Le réalisateur auditionne vingt comédiens' = 'The director is auditioning twenty actors') and intransitively ('Elle auditionne pour le premier rôle' = 'She's auditioning for the lead role'). In crime dramas, 'être auditionné par la police' means 'to be questioned/interviewed by the police'.

augmentation.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th century) from Late Latin augmentationem ('an increasing, enlargement'), noun of action from augmentare ('to increase, enrich'), itself built on Classical Latin augmentum ('growth, increase') from augere ('to make grow, enlarge, exalt', from PIE *h₂ewg- 'to increase, grow strong', cognate with English wax 'to grow').

history.meaning: growth in size, quantity, or value
increase, rise; salary raise (une augmentation de salaire)

augmentation.notes: Workplace essential: while English 'augmentation' sounds stiff and technical, French 'une augmentation' is the everyday word for a pay raise — 'demander une augmentation à son patron' ('to ask one's boss for a raise').

rootFamily.gloss: author (from Latin auctor < augere, 'one who originates/promotes')

augmenter.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Late Latin augmentare ('to increase, enlarge, multiply'), a denominative verb formed from Classical Latin augmentum ('increase, growth'), derived from augere ('to cause to grow, increase, strengthen', from PIE *h₂ewg- 'to grow, increase'). Unlike Italian and Spanish (which assimilated -gm- to -m-), French retained and pronounces the learned cluster -gm- ([ɔɡmɑ̃te] or [oɡmɑ̃te]).

history.meaning: to make greater in quantity, rank, or size
to increase, go up; to give someone a pay raise

augmenter.notes: Used transitively with a person as direct object, 'augmenter quelqu'un' specifically means 'to give someone a raise' ('Andréa refuse d'augmenter son assistante' = 'Andréa refuses to give her assistant a raise') — not to make them physically bigger!

augustin.etymology: Learned French adaptation of Classical Latin Augustinus ('belonging to Augustus'), a Roman cognomen formed with the relational suffix -inus on Augustus ('venerable, consecrated, majestic'), itself linked to augere ('to increase, exalt') and augur ('religious diviner'). The given name spread widely across Western Christendom through the prestige of Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430).
augustin.notes: In Dix pour cent, Augustin Trapenard appears as himself; historically, English 'Austin' is the contracted Anglo-Norman reflex of this exact name.

aujourd'hui.etymology: Univerbation of the Old/Middle French phrase au jour d'hui ('on the day of today'), where hui ('today', Old French ui) comes directly from Classical Latin hodie ('today' < hoc die 'on this day'); because hui was reduced to a single vowel, speakers reinforced it with au jour de ('on the day of').

history.meaning: literally 'on the day of today' -> today

auparavant.etymology: Formed in Middle French by the orthographic agglutination of the prepositional phrase au par avant ('in the time before'): au (contraction of Old French a le, 'at the') + par ('through, by', from Latin per) + avant ('before', from Late Latin abante, itself a compound of ab 'from' + ante 'before').
auparavant.notes: Unlike avant, auparavant is strictly an adverb and never takes a noun object directly (say 'avant le tournage', or 'auparavant' alone).

auprès.etymology: Agglutinated in Old and Middle French from au (contraction of a le, 'at the') and près ('near, close'), which descends from Late Latin pressum ('crowded closely, near'), adverbial accusative of Classical Latin pressus, the past participle of premere ('to press, squeeze closely together').
auprès.notes: In agency and diplomatic French, 'intervenir auprès de quelqu'un' is the standard idiom for lobbying, interceding, or making representations to someone.

aussi.etymology: Aussi developed from an older combination of al, meaning something else, and si, meaning thus. The Académie records twelfth-century alsi in a comparison expression; the modern adverb also acquired the sense too.

morphemes.meaning: other thing (< Old French al < Latin aliud)

aussi.notes: Position changes meaning: Elle vient aussi ('She's coming too'), aussi grand que ('as tall as'), and literary clause-initial Aussi est-il parti ('Therefore he left').

autant.etymology: Inherited from Old French altant, autant ('just as much'), compounded from al ('other, another such', neuter of Old French el from Vulgar Latin *allum for Classical Latin aliud, reinforced by analogy with autel 'likewise') + tant ('so much', from Classical Latin tantum). Vocalization of preconsonantal l to u produced autant.

history.meaning: so much, to such a degree
as much; might as well (with infinitive)

autant.notes: Followed directly by an infinitive ('autant te le dire tout de suite'), autant idiomatically means 'might as well'; also note the debated spelling of 'au temps pour moi' vs. 'autant pour moi' ('my bad').

auteur.etymology: Inherited from Old French autor, reshaped in Middle French as auteur after Classical Latin auctor ('originator, promoter, builder, literary creator'), an agent noun built on the supine stem auct- of augere ('to increase, originate, bring into being'). English 'author' acquired its 'th' from Renaissance scribal confusion of Latin auctor with Greek authentes.
auteur.notes: In French film culture ('cinéma d'auteur'), un auteur denotes a director whose personal artistic vision stamps a film as strongly as a novelist's prose; feminine forms are 'auteure' or 'autrice' (the latter directly reviving Latin auctrix).

auteur-réalisateur.etymology: Twentieth-century French cinema compound joining auteur (from Latin auctor, 'originator, writer') and réalisateur ('film director', literally 'one who brings into reality'), derived from réaliser ('to make real, direct a film'), itself built on réel (from Late Latin realis 'relating to things', from Classical Latin res 'thing, matter'). Popularized by the Nouvelle Vague and Cahiers du cinéma.

history.meaning: person who brings a project or film into reality
filmmaker who both writes the screenplay and directs

auteur-réalisateur.notes: Watch the false friend: un réalisateur is a film/TV director (never a 'producer', which is producteur, whereas metteur en scène is primarily used for theater). Feminine: auteure-réalisatrice or autrice-réalisatrice.

authentique.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (autentique, later restored with 'th') from Late Latin authenticus ('original, genuine, carrying legal authority'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek authentikos (αὐθεντικός, 'warranted, original, principal'), from authentes (αὐθέντης, 'one who accomplishes with one's own hand', from autos 'self' + -hentes 'doer, accomplisher').
authentique.notes: In French law as well as everyday speech, un acte authentique still carries its medieval technical sense of an official instrument certified by a notary, alongside the everyday sense 'genuine/sincere'.

autographe.etymology: Learned borrowing via Late Latin autographus ('written with one's own hand') from Ancient Greek autographos (αὐτόγραφος, 'written in one's own hand'), compounded from autos (αὐτός, 'self') and graphein (γράφειν, 'to scratch, draw, write').
