Originally an adjective describing an author's original manuscript before shifting in the 19th century to a celebrity's signature.
autographe.notes: Masculine noun ('signer un autographe'); contrast with une dédicace, which is a personalized inscription written for a fan or reader on a book or photo.

automne.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin autumnus ('autumn, harvest season'), a word of ancient Italic or Etruscan origin already opaque to Roman grammarians. The Latin -mn- spelling was restored in Middle French even though only /n/ is pronounced.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: automne (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: automne

automne.notes: The **-m-** is silent in **automne** (/otɔn/), resurging aloud in the adjective **automnal** (/otɔmnal/).

autorisation.etymology: Derived in Middle French from autoriser ('to vest with authority, empower, permit', borrowed from Medieval Latin auctorizare, built on Classical Latin auctor 'guarantor, originator') + the learned action-noun suffix -ation (from Latin -ationem).
autorisation.notes: Spelling trap for English speakers: French never uses 'th' in autorisation, autoriser, or autorité (unlike authentique). On film sets, une autorisation de tournage is the mandatory location shooting permit.

autour.etymology: Univerbation of the Old French phrase au tour ('in the turn or circuit of'), from au (à + le) + tour ('turn, circuit, circumference', deverbal from tourner).

history.meaning: in the circle of -> around, about

autre.etymology: Autre descends from Latin alter, the other of two. Tenth-century French distinguished masculine altre and feminine altra.
autre.notes: Plural 'other books' is d'autres livres (de + autres, not *des autres livres when indefinite).

autrefois.etymology: Univerbation of Old French autre feiz / autre fois ('another time'), from autre ('other', Latin alter) + fois ('time, occasion', from Latin vicem 'turn, change').

history.meaning: at another time -> in former times, formerly

autrement.etymology: Formed in Old French (altrement, autrement) from autre ('other', inherited from Classical Latin alterum, accusative of alter 'the other of two') + the Romance adverbial suffix -ment (from Classical Latin ablative mente, 'with a [specified] mind or disposition', grammaticalized into a manner suffix).
autrement.notes: Watch the common idiom 'autrement dit' ('in other words') and the intensifying colloquial use before an adjective: 'c'est autrement plus compliqué' ('it's far/way more complicated').

aux.etymology: Aux combines the preposition à with the plural article les. Like singular au, it belongs to the history of French preposition–article contractions rather than being an independent borrowed noun.

history.meaning: to the, at the, in the (plural)

aux.notes: Used before all plural nouns of either gender—linking with a /z/ liaison before vowel sounds (aux États-Unis /o.z‿e.ta.zy.ni/).

avaler.etymology: Avaler is derived from aval, downwards or downstream. Its eleventh-century intransitive sense was to descend; the swallowing sense developed as making something go down the throat.

history.meaning: to go down, lower -> make go down the throat

cognates.meaning: related Alpine Romance derivative of aval

rootFamily.gloss: downstream (en aval, opposite of en amont)
to swallow back; refurbish a building facade

avaler.notes: Delightful spatial pair with monter ('to go up a mountain'): Old French avaler originally meant 'to go down into the valley' before specializing into swallowing food down one's throat!

avance.etymology: Avance is a noun built from avancer ('to move forward', from Vulgar Latin *abantiare, built on ab + ante 'from before').
avance.notes: **Être en avance** = to be early (ahead of schedule); **à l'avance** = beforehand.

avancer.etymology: Inherited from Old French avancier ('to move forward, promote'), from Vulgar Latin *abantiare, derived from Late Latin abante ('in front, before', source of avant).

avant.etymology: Inherited from Old French avant ('in front, forward, before'), from Late Latin abante ('in front of, before'), a compound preposition formed from ab ('from, off') + ante ('before, in front').

avantage.etymology: Derived in Old French from avant ('ahead, in front', from Late Latin abante < ab + ante) + the collective/state nominal suffix -age (from Late Latin -aticum), originally denoting the spatial or tactical superiority of being positioned ahead of a rival. English 'advantage' borrowed the Old French word and later inserted an unetymological 'd' by false association with Latin ad-.
avantage.notes: No 'd' in French avantage (unlike English 'advantage')! In contract negotiations, 'avantages en nature' means fringe benefits or perks in kind (car, housing, wardrobe).

rootFamily.gloss: to favor, flatter, give an edge to

avantageux.etymology: Derived in Old and Middle French (avantageus, avantageux) from the noun avantage ('superiority, benefit', itself from avant 'ahead' + -age) + the adjectival suffix -eux (inherited from Classical Latin -osus, 'abounding in, characterized by').
avantageux.notes: Besides 'beneficial' (un contrat avantageux), describing a person's demeanor or outfit as avantageux ('se montrer sous un jour avantageux') means 'flattering'—or slightly 'self-important/vain'. Feminine: avantageuse.

rootFamily.gloss: to give an advantage to; to flatter

avc.etymology: Twentieth-century French medical initialism (AVC) for accident vasculaire cérébral ('cerebrovascular accident'): accident (from Latin accidentem, 'befalling event', from ad- + cadere 'to fall'), vasculaire (from Modern Latin vascularis, built on Classical Latin vasculum 'small vessel', diminutive of vas), and cérébral (from Latin cerebralis, from cerebrum 'brain').

history.meaning: acute disruption of blood flow to the brain

avc.notes: Always pronounced letter by letter (/a.ve.se/) and grammatically masculine ('faire un AVC' = 'to have a stroke'); for a transient mini-stroke/TIA specifically, doctors also say un AIT (accident ischémique transitoire), though laypeople often call it un petit AVC.

avec.etymology: Avec continues a reconstructed Popular Latin combination *apu(d)-hoc, approximately with this, strengthening apud, near or with. The early French forms avuec, avoc and avoec are recorded in the eleventh century.
avec.notes: While Italian (con) and Spanish/Portuguese (con / com) kept Classical Latin cum, Northern Gallo-Romance replaced cum with *apud hoc > avec; the final /k/ is always pronounced.

avenir.etymology: Formed by the univerbation and nominalization of the Old and Middle French infinitive phrase (le temps) a venir ('the time to come'), composed of the preposition à (from Latin ad, 'to, toward') and venir ('to come', from Classical Latin venire). Originally written as two words before coalescing into masculine l'avenir.
avenir.notes: French distinguishes l'avenir (human, personal, or career prospects: 'un acteur plein d'avenir', 'à l'avenir' = 'in the future / from now on') from le futur (grammatical tense or abstract/distant future).

aventure.etymology: Inherited from Old French aventure ('chance, fate, unforeseen occurrence, chivalric quest'), from Vulgar Latin *adventura ('things about to happen'), feminine singular reinterpretation of Classical Latin adventura, the neuter plural of the future active participle of advenire ('to arrive, happen', from ad- 'to' + venire 'to come').

history.meaning: things about to arrive or happen

aventure.notes: Context matters: alongside 'adventure' ('un film d'aventures'), 'avoir une aventure avec quelqu'un' is the standard polite idiom for having a brief romantic fling or affair.

avenue.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of Old/Middle French avenir ('to arrive, come up to', from Latin advenire 'to come to'); originally meant 'arrival, way of approach to a country house lined with trees', whence 'wide tree-lined thoroughfare'.

history.meaning: arrival, approach road to an estate

averse.etymology: Formed in early modern French by fusing the adverbial phrase à verse ('pouring down in buckets', as in il pleut à verse), built on verser ('to pour, tip over') from Latin versare.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: averse (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: averse

averse.notes: Compare **renverser** ('to spill or knock over') and **verser** ('to pour tea or soup'), both from the same root.

avertissement.etymology: Derived in Middle French from the extended stem avertiss- of avertir ('to turn someone's attention to, notify, warn', from Vulgar Latin *advertire, a fourth-conjugation reshaping of Classical Latin advertere 'to turn toward, direct one's mind to', from ad- + vertere 'to turn') + the action-noun suffix -ment (from Latin -mentum).

history.meaning: to turn the mind or attention toward
to notify, inform, put on guard

avertissement.notes: Classic false friend! Un avertissement NEVER means a commercial 'advertisement' (which is une publicité / une pub); it means a 'warning' (or a brief prefatory note in a book).

aveugle.etymology: Inherited from Old French avogle, aveugle ('sightless, blind'), descending from Late Latin aboculis ('deprived of eyes, eyeless'), a prepositional compound formed from Classical Latin ab ('away from, without') + oculis (ablative plural of oculus, 'eye'), likely calqued in Christian/medical Late Latin on Ancient Greek apommatos ('eyeless').
aveugle.notes: Key idioms: 'faire confiance aveuglément' ('to trust blindly') and 'à l'aveugle' ('blindly / sight unseen', as in casting or wine tasting). In polite modern usage for people, 'malvoyant' or 'non-voyant' is often preferred.

avion.etymology: Coined in 1875 by the French engineer and aviation pioneer Clément Ader for his bat-winged, steam-powered flying machine (Avion), learnedly constructed from Classical Latin avis ('bird') + the suffix -ion / -on (modeled on aviation, itself coined in 1863 by Gabriel La Landelle from avis + -ation). Generalized to all heavier-than-air aircraft during World War I.

history.meaning: Clément Ader's experimental winged flying apparatus

avion.notes: Notice the preposition contrast: 'prendre l'avion' ('to take a plane'), 'voyager en avion' ('to travel by plane'), and 'descendre de l'avion' ('to get off the plane').

avis.etymology: Univerbation of the Old French phrase ce m'est a vis ('it seems to me', literally 'that is to me by way of view'), from à ('to, in') + vis ('sight, view, opinion', from Classical Latin visum, neuter past participle of videre 'to see').

history.form: visum -> a vis (in ce m'est a vis)

avocat.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing in Old French from Classical Latin advocatus ('one summoned to give legal counsel or witness, pleader'), nominalized past participle of advocare ('to call to one's aid', from ad- 'to' + vocare 'to call', derived from vox, vocis 'voice'). Replaced earlier inherited Old French avoé in courtroom usage.

history.meaning: legal counselor summoned to assist a party in court
pleader in ecclesiastical or royal courts; intercessor

avocat.notes: Delightful homonymy: un avocat means both 'a lawyer' (from Latin advocatus) and 'an avocado' (reshaped by folk etymology from Spanish aguacate, ultimately Nahuatl ahuacatl)! Lawyers are addressed formally as 'Maître'.

avoir.etymology: Avoir descends from Latin habere. The Académie dates the French verb to the ninth century. Its central meaning concerns possession, and it also serves as an auxiliary in compound tenses.
avoir.notes:
- *Avoir* is used for age and many states: *avoir chaud, froid, faim, soif, peur, raison, tort*.
- *Il y a* means 'there is/are' and also 'ago': *il y a deux ans*.
- Along with *être*, it is one of the two auxiliary verbs of French.

cognates.meaning: to avow, declare openly (from Old French)

avouer.etymology: Inherited from Old French avoer ('to recognize someone as feudal overlord or protector, acknowledge an act as one's own, confess'), from Classical Latin advocare ('to call upon as patron, witness, or defender', from ad- + vocare 'to call'), later phonetically and semantically blended in Gallo-Romance with vouer ('to vow', from Vulgar Latin *votare).

history.meaning: to summon as legal patron or protector
to acknowledge a feudal lord; to own up to an act

morphemes.meaning: call upon / vow (Latin voc- blended with vot-)

avouer.notes: In conversational French (especially in Dix pour cent!), 'J'avoue !' or 'J'avoue que...' is constantly used casually to mean 'I have to admit!' or 'Fair enough / totally!', without any heavy criminal guilt.

avril.etymology: Inherited from Old French avril, regularly evolved (with lenition of intervocalic -p- to -v-) from Classical Latin Aprilis (sc. mensis, 'month of April'). Deeper within Italic, Aprilis was connected by Roman grammarians (Varro, Ovid) to aperire ('to open', as spring buds open), though modern philologists strongly favor an Etruscan mediation (*Apru) from Greek Aphrodite, goddess of April.

history.meaning: month of April (second month of the archaic Roman calendar)

avril.notes: Like all French month names, avril is lowercase and masculine ('en avril, ne te découvre pas d'un fil'). Also remember 'un poisson d'avril' ('April Fools' prank', literally 'an April fish').

axe.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin axis, axem ('axle, pivot, axis of the earth or sky'), from PIE *h2eks- ('axle').

history.meaning: geometric or mechanical axis, main line

aéroport.etymology: Early 20th-century compound (attested c. 1920s, reinforced by English airport and earlier French aérodrome), formed from the neoclassical combining element aéro- (from Ancient Greek aer, ἀήρ 'air, lower atmosphere', via Latin aer) + port ('harbor, haven', inherited from Classical Latin portus 'harbor, port, gateway').
aéroport.notes: Pronounce both 'a' and 'é' distinctly (/a.e.ʁo.pɔʁ/, four syllables—never 'éro-port'!). Adjective: aéroportuaire ('les taxes aéroportuaires').

aîné.etymology: Inherited from Old French ainsné ('firstborn, elder'), compound of ainz ('before, earlier', from Vulgar Latin *antius, comparative of ante 'before') + né ('born', from Latin natus).

aïe.etymology: Natural expressive exclamation of sudden sharp pain (attested since Old French aï / aïe), parallel to similar cries across Romance and European languages.

baby-sitter.etymology: Borrowed in the late 1940s directly from American English babysitter (first attested in 1937), a compound of baby ('infant', Middle English babi, of nursery/imitative origin) + sitter, agent noun from sit ('to stay in place and tend', from Old English sittan, ultimately Proto-Indo-European *sed- 'to sit').

history.meaning: person hired temporarily to look after children

baby-sitter.notes: Epicene in French ('un baby-sitter' or 'une baby-sitter') and traditionally hyphenated; for a regular daytime childminder or nanny, French uses une nounou or une assistante maternelle.

rootFamily.gloss: baby, infant (earlier English loan from 19th c.)

badigeonner.etymology: Derived in the 18th century from French badigeon ('whitewash, lime-wash coating used on stone walls'), a workshop word of uncertain provincial origin first recorded in 17th-century architectural treatises. Originally meaning to coat walls with limewash using a wide flat brush, the verb entered French culinary usage for brushing egg wash, melted butter, or warm honey glaze over pastries.

history.meaning: to coat with a wide brush; to glaze pastry

badigeonner.notes: In French baking recipes, **badigeonner au pinceau** is the standard instruction for brushing glaze or egg yolk across a cake or tart.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: badigeonner

bagage.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from bague (in its older plural sense bagues 'bundles, packs, personal belongings', from Old Norse baggi 'pack, bundle' or a Gallo-Romance root) + collective suffix -age; Originally denoted an army's supply train before meaning a traveler's luggage.

bagarre.etymology: Attested in 16th-century French in the sense of 'noisy tumult, crowd, mêlée', likely borrowed from Occitan/Provençal bagarra ('scuffle, brawl, clash'), whose deeper pre-Romance or expressive root remains debated (variously linked to Occitan baga 'bundle, baggage train'—where camp scuffles broke out—or to an expressive stem *bag- + pre-Latin suffix -arra).
bagarre.notes: Informal/everyday register for a scuffle, fistfight, or heated tussle ('chercher la bagarre' = 'to spoil for a fight'); the reflexive verb se bagarrer means 'to brawl / fight'.

bague.etymology: In the sense 'finger ring', borrowed in the 15th century from Old Occitan baga ('berry; metal ring or link'), from Classical Latin baca / bacca ('berry, pearl, link of a chain').

bail.etymology: Deverbal noun from Old French baillier ('to hand over, entrust, administer'), inherited from Classical Latin bajulare ('to carry a burden, take charge of'), from bajulus ('porter, carrier').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French bail / baillif

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: bail (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: bail

bail.notes: Plural **baux** preserves the historical vocalization of *-l* before *-s* (**un bail**, **des baux**), and colloquially **ça fait un bail!** means 'it has been ages!'.

bain.etymology: Inherited from Old French bain ('bath, bathing place'), from Vulgar Latin *banneum, phonetic reduction of Classical Latin balneum / balineum ('bath'), borrowed from Ancient Greek balaneion ('bath, bathhouse').

baiser.etymology: Nominalized infinitive of Old French baisier ('to kiss'), regularly inherited from Classical Latin basiare ('to kiss'), denominal verb built on basium ('a kiss'—originally an affectionate/colloquial word of Cisalpine Celtic origin popularized in Roman poetry by Catullus, which displaced Classical Latin osculum across Romance).

history.meaning: a kiss (noun); (verb shifted in modern slang)

baiser.notes: CRITICAL REGISTER TRAP: As a masculine noun ('un baiser', 'donner un baiser'), baiser is completely polite and romantic ('a kiss'). Used as a transitive verb without a body part ('baiser quelqu'un'), it is vulgar slang ('to have sex with' or 'to screw over')! Always use 'embrasser' for the verb 'to kiss'.

rootFamily.gloss: to kiss repeatedly; old-fashioned cheek kiss

baisse.etymology: Post-verbal feminine noun formed in Early Modern French from baisser ('to lower, bring down, decline'), inherited through Old French baissier from Vulgar Latin *bassiare ('to make low'), a derivative of Late Latin bassus ('short in stature, thickset, low', originally an Oscan-Sabellic Italic adjective seen in the Roman cognomen Bassus).

history.meaning: low, short in stature / to make lower
downward movement, drop in price, ratings, or morale

baisse.notes: Essential for TV/agency ratings and box-office talk: 'les audiences sont en baisse' ('ratings are down'), paired with its antonym 'en hausse' ('on the rise / up').

rootFamily.gloss: to lower; to go down, drop

baisser.etymology: Inherited from Old French baissier ('to lower, bring down'), from Vulgar Latin *bassiare ('to make low'), derived from Late Latin bassus ('low, short in stature').

balader.etymology: Derived in 19th-century colloquial/argotic French from the noun balade ('stroll', earlier 'itinerant singer's performance'), itself a semantic offshoot of Old and Middle French balade ('dancing song, lyric poem'), borrowed from Old Occitan balada ('dance, dancing song'), from balar ('to dance', from Late Latin ballare, from Ancient Greek ballizein 'to dance, jump about'). Street performers wandering from town to town sang balades, shifting the word from 'wandering song' to 'strolling'.

history.meaning: lyric ballad; mendicant singer's wandering performance
to take around; to stroll leisurely

balader.notes: Spelling distinction: 'une balade / se balader' ('a stroll / to stroll') takes ONE 'l', whereas poetic/musical 'une ballade' takes TWO! Also watch transitive slang 'balader quelqu'un' = 'to string someone along / give them the runaround'.

balancer.etymology: Formed in Old French from balance ('pair of scales'), which descends from Vulgar Latin *bilancia ('two-pan scale'), compound of bis ('twice') and lanx, lancis ('scale pan, platter'). Because the two pans of a balance rock up and down before coming to rest, balancer developed the sense of swaying, rocking, or swinging back and forth. Its reflexive form se balancer describes a tree swaying in the breeze or a child swinging.
balancer.notes: From **balancer** comes **une balançoire** ('a playground swing') and **un fauteuil à bascule / balancelle** ('porch swing').

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: balancer

balayer.etymology: Derived in Old French (baleiier, 12th c., 'to sweep with a broom') from balai ('broom, originally a bundle of broom twigs'), of Gaulish origin (*balatno- / *banatlo- 'broom plant, Genista', akin to Breton balan).

balcon.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian balcone ('projecting gallery or window platform'), itself derived from Lombardic *balko ('wooden beam, timber platform').

cognates.meaning: balcony via Italian; balk ('beam') from Old English balca

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: balcon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: balcon

balcon.notes: Renaissance Italian architecture brought **le balcon** into French cities, where wrought-iron railings later became a hallmark of classic facades.

balle.etymology: Inherited from Old French bale ('small spherical ball; rolled bundle'), borrowed from Frankish *balla ('ball, rounded mass', from Proto-Germanic *ballōn, ultimately Proto-Indo-European *bhel- 'to swell, inflate'). In the 16th century, reinforced by Italian palla/balla, it acquired the firearms sense 'musket ball, bullet' because early lead projectiles were spherical.

history.meaning: handball, small play ball; rolled bale of goods
small sports ball (tennis, golf); firearm bullet

balle.notes: Three indispensable senses: 1) small sports ball (tennis/ping-pong, vs. un ballon for a large inflated soccer/basketball); 2) firearm 'bullet' ('gilet pare-balles'); 3) colloquial slang for 'francs/euros' ('ça coûte cent balles' = 'it costs a hundred bucks').

rootFamily.gloss: bullet (in English) / small crumpled paper or meat ball
to pack up, wrap; to excite ('s'emballer')

banal.etymology: Derived in 13th-century Old French from ban ('feudal lord's proclamation, jurisdiction, compulsory public decree', borrowed from Frankish *ban 'command under penalty', from Proto-Germanic *bannaz) + the relational suffix -al. Originally a feudal legal adjective (four banal, moulin banal) designating communal manor facilities open to and obligatory for all serfs, it shifted by the late 18th century to 'shared by everybody, commonplace, unoriginal'.

history.meaning: public proclamation or command under penalty
subject to feudal lord's communal jurisdiction (mill, oven)

banal.notes: Famous plural quirk: in the everyday sense 'commonplace/trite', the masculine plural is 'banals' ('des scénarios banals')—one of the rare -al adjectives that does NOT become -aux (banaux is reserved for historical feudal 'fours banaux'!).

rootFamily.gloss: suburb (originally 'ban + lieue', league under a town's ban!)

banane.etymology: Borrowed into early 17th-century French (attested 1602 in travel accounts of Guinea) via Portuguese banana, which 16th-century Portuguese navigators adopted on the West African coast from a local Niger-Congo language, most likely Wolof banaana (or a neighboring Mande/Susu variety), denoting the cultivated fruit.

history.meaning: tropical banana fruit traded along the Guinea coast
banana fruit (earlier also the tree, before bananier)

banane.notes: Upbeat colloquial idiom: 'avoir la banane' means 'to have a huge grin from ear to ear / be beaming' (shaped like a banana!); 'un sac banane' (or just 'une banane') is a fanny pack / belt bag.

banc.etymology: Inherited from Old French banc ('long wooden seat; market counter'), borrowed early from Frankish *bank ('bench, shelf').

cognates.meaning: bench is the native Germanic cousin; bank came via Italian banca
italianate relatives from the same Germanic root

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: banc (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: banc

banc.notes: The final *-c* in **un banc** **/bɑ̃/** is completely silent (just like **blanc** **/blɑ̃/** and **franc** **/fʁɑ̃/**).

bande.etymology: Represents two converged Germanic borrowings in Old French: (1) 'strip, band, ribbon', from Frankish *binda ('band, fillet', akin to English bind); and (2) 'troop, company of people', via Old Occitan banda from Gothic bandwa ('standard, banner around which a troop rallies').

history.meaning: strip of cloth; troop under a banner
strip, tape, border; band or group of people

banlieue.etymology: Compounded in 12th-century Old French (modeled on Medieval Latin banleuca) from ban ('feudal proclamation or jurisdiction', from Frankish *ban) and lieue ('league', from Late Latin leuca of Gaulish origin). It originally designated the belt of land roughly one league wide surrounding a walled town over which municipal or feudal jurisdiction applied, before shifting in modern urbanism to suburbs and working-class housing estates.

history.meaning: territory of one league around a town subject to its jurisdiction
district around a city under municipal authority

banlieue.notes: Feminine noun (la banlieue); in modern French media and cinema, la banlieue often carries strong socio-economic connotations of peripheral housing estates (cités), unlike the affluent American image of 'suburbia'.

rootFamily.gloss: suburbanite; resident of the outer suburbs
to banish, exile (from the same Frankish root *ban)

banque.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century (first via Lyon merchant fairs) from Italian banca ('money-changer's wooden table or counter'), itself borrowed from Lombardic *banka ('bench'). It forms an etymological doublet with native French banc ('bench'), which entered Old French directly via Frankish *bank.
banque.notes: In film production (as in Dix pour cent), faire sauter la banque means 'to break the bank', while banque de données means 'database'.

rootFamily.gloss: bankruptcy (literally 'broken bench', from Italian banca rotta)

banquier.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Italian banchiere ('money-changer, financier'), derived from banca ('money-changer's table') with the agentive suffix -iere, and immediately aligned in Middle French with banque and the native occupational suffix -ier (< Latin -ārius).

history.meaning: financier, dealer in bills of exchange

banquier.notes: Feminine form is banquière; in French cinema jargon, les banquiers often refers wryly to risk-averse financiers backing a film purely for box-office return.

cognates.meaning: counter for serving drinks; rod, barrier

bar.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-19th century from English bar ('counter in a tavern or drinking house'), a classic Franco-English boomerang loan (aller-retour): English had earlier borrowed bar from Old French barre ('wooden rail or barrier', from Vulgar Latin *barra), referring to the barrier separating the tavern server and liquor casks from patrons.
bar.notes: Masculine noun (un bar); watch out for the homonym le bar meaning 'European seabass' (borrowed from Dutch baars, unrelated).

barbare.etymology: Learned 14th-century borrowing (first popularized by Nicole Oresme translating Aristotle) from Classical Latin barbarus ('foreign, non-Roman, uncivilized'), from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros, 'non-Greek-speaking, foreign'). The Greek word arose by reduplicative onomatopoeia (*bar-bar) mimicking unintelligible foreign speech, before acquiring moral connotations of cruelty and savagery.

history.meaning: foreigner outside classical civilization; cruel person

barbare.notes: Functions as both noun and epicene adjective (un peuple barbare, un barbare); figuratively, un nom barbare means an unpronounceable or overly technical term, not a cruel one.

rootFamily.gloss: lexical or grammatical error (originally foreign speech habit)
brave, spirited (doublet via Arabic Barbar 'Berber' or Greek barbaros)

barbecue.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-20th century from American English barbecue, itself adapted in the late 17th century from American Spanish barbacoa ('raised wooden framework used by Indigenous Caribbean peoples for sleeping or curing meat over smoke'), from Taíno barabicu. The popular French folk etymology linking it to 'de la barbe à la queue' ('from beard to tail', roasting a whole goat) is an entertaining 18th/20th-century myth.

history.meaning: sacred fire pit or wooden framework of sticks
wooden lattice for smoking meat or raised sleeping platform
gridiron for roasting meat; outdoor social cookout

barbecue.notes: Masculine noun (un barbecue), often shortened colloquially to barbuc or barbeuc; never believe the folk tale that French trappers coined it from barbe à queue!

rootFamily.gloss: historical French loan directly from Spanish barbacoa (buccaneer grill)

baromètre.etymology: Borrowed in 1666 from English barometer, coined shortly before (c. 1665) by physicist Robert Boyle from Ancient Greek βάρος (báros, 'weight, heaviness, pressure') and μέτρον (métron, 'measure, instrument for measuring'). By the late 18th century in French, it acquired its figurative sense of a sensitive gauge of public mood, politics, or box-office trends.
baromètre.notes: Masculine noun (un baromètre), like all French instrument compounds ending in -mètre; widely used in media and talent agencies for audience-rating or popularity trackers.

rootFamily.gloss: barometric, relating to pressure or opinion polls
isobar (weather contour line of equal pressure)

barre.etymology: Inherited from Old French barre ('bar, barrier, rod'), from Vulgar Latin *barra ('crossbar, barrier'), probably of pre-Roman or Gaulish origin.

barreau.etymology: Formed in Old French (barel / barreau, 12th c.) as the diminutive of barre ('bar, rod') with suffix -el (> -eau); refers both to a window/cage bar and to the railing separating lawyers in court, hence the legal 'bar'.

history.meaning: small bar or railing; the legal bar

barrer.etymology: Formed in 12th-century Old French from barre ('rod, crossbeam, barrier', from Vulgar Latin *barra of pre-Roman or Gaulish origin) plus the verbal ending -er. From physically bolting a door or blocking a road (barrer la route), it developed the scribal sense 'to strike out a line of text' (14th c.) and, in late-19th-century slang, the reflexive se barrer ('to bolt, take off, get out of here').

history.meaning: to fasten or block with a wooden bar
to strike out text; (reflexive slang) to clear out, leave

barrer.notes: Watch the huge register split: barrer un mot ('to cross out a word') and barrer la route ('to block the way') are standard, whereas je me barre ('I'm outta here') is informal conversational slang heard constantly in Dix pour cent.

rootFamily.gloss: bar, rod, helm of a boat

bas.etymology: Inherited from Old French bas ('low, not high'), from Late Latin bassus ('thickset, short, low in stature'), a word of Italic or Oscan origin originally used as a cognomen.

history.meaning: short, low, close to the ground

cognates.meaning: rocking lever, weighing scale (borrowed from French)
platform scale; to tilt (borrowed from French)

basculer.etymology: Derived in the late 16th century from bascule ('seesaw, counterpoised lever, drawbridge beam'), itself an alteration—reshaped under the semantic influence of bas ('low, downward')—of Middle French bacule ('seesaw, counterweight; paddle for spanking'). Middle French bacule was compounded from battre ('to beat, strike') and cul ('buttocks, rear end'), referring to the rear end of a beam striking the ground.

history.meaning: seesaw beam or counterpoise lever striking the ground
to tip over, swing abruptly into a new state

basculer.notes: A favorite dramatic verb in French screenwriting: faire basculer un récit or ma vie a basculé captures a sudden, irreversible tipping point in plot or fortune.

rootFamily.gloss: seesaw, rocking lever, toggle switch; turning point
tipping over, dramatic shift or upheaval
to beat, strike (initial element of bacule)

base.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin basis ('pedestal, architectural footing, foundation'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis, 'a stepping, footstep, pedestal, base'), an action/result noun formed from the root of βαίνω (baínō, 'I walk, step', from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- 'to go, come').

history.meaning: step, foot, pedestal on which something stands
pedestal of a column or statue; foundation
architectural plinth; fundamental principle or starting point

base.notes: Feminine noun (la base); don't confuse it with the adjective basse (feminine of bas, 'low', pronounced /bas/ vs. base /baz/). Colloquial à la base means 'originally' or 'fundamentally'.

rootFamily.gloss: basic, fundamental (modern borrowing/influence from English basic)

bassin.etymology: Inherited from Old French bacin ('wide bowl, water basin'), from Late/Medieval Latin baccinum ('water vessel'), widely traced to a Gaulish root *bacca ('trough, bowl').

history.meaning: fountain basin, garden pool, river basin

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: bassin (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: bassin

bassin.notes: In public French parks and squares, **le bassin** is the ornamental stone pool where fountains play and children sail toy boats.

bataille.etymology: Inherited via Old French bataille from Late and Vulgar Latin battualia / *battalia ('fencing and combat exercises of soldiers and gladiators'), originally a neuter plural collective noun reanalyzed in Gallo-Romance as a feminine singular, derived from Classical Latin battere / battuere ('to beat, strike, fence', likely an ancient Gaulish loan into Latin).

history.meaning: military and gladiatorial combat exercises; armed clash

bataille.notes: Remember the idiom cheval de bataille ('pet project, core issue, warhorse'), ubiquitous in agency negotiations and French political or workplace drama.

rootFamily.gloss: to fight, struggle hard, wage a campaign

cognates.meaning: steamboat, ferryboat (borrowed from Old French batel)

bateau.etymology: Inherited from Old French batel (plural bateaus, whence modern bateau via vocalization of -l before plural -s), formed with the diminutive suffix -el (< Latin -ellum) on Old French bat ('small boat'), which was borrowed from Old English bāt (or reinforced along the Norman coast by Old Norse bátr), from Proto-Germanic *baitaz ('dugout or split-plank vessel').

history.meaning: small boat, river barge, ship's tender

morphemes.meaning: boat (Old French bat < Old English bāt)

bateau.notes: Used invariantly as an invariable colloquial adjective, une question bateau or une excuse bateau means 'hackneyed, cliché, run-of-the-mill'; monter un bateau à quelqu'un means 'to string someone along with a tall tale'.

rootFamily.gloss: boatload; crowd of people arriving together

battant.etymology: Substantivized present participle of battre ('to beat, strike, fight', via Old French batre from Vulgar Latin *battere < Classical Latin battuere). Used since Old and Middle French for mechanical parts that strike or swing (a bell clapper, a swinging door leaf), its human sense 'scrappy fighter, energetic go-getter' emerged in 20th-century French, reinforced by se battre ('to fight hard') and English boxing/business usage of fighter.

history.meaning: beating; bell clapper, swinging wing of a double door

battant.notes: Feminine form is une battante ('a real fighter / go-getter'); also survives in the lively adverbial phrase tambour battant ('at a brisk clip, without wasting a second').

rootFamily.gloss: to beat, strike; (se battre) to fight

battre.etymology: Inherited from Old French batre ('to strike, beat'), from Vulgar Latin *battere, reduced from Classical Latin batuere / battuere ('to beat, strike, fence'), possibly an ancient Gaulish borrowing in Latin.

cognates.meaning: diagonal shoulder belt for a sword or bugle (via Old French)

baudrier.etymology: Inherited from Old French baudrei / baudrier ('ornate leather sword belt worn across the hip or shoulder'), reshaped with the suffix -ier. Its pre-Old French source is likely either Frankish/Old High German *balderich ('girdle, belt') or a Medieval Latin derivative *balteārius of Classical Latin balteus ('sword belt, girdle'), quite possibly reflecting a Germanic-Romance crossing of both forms.

history.meaning: knight's leather belt or shoulder strap supporting a sword
shoulder strap; mountaineering or stunt safety harness

baudrier.notes: In modern French (including film-set stunt work and climbing), un baudrier refers specifically to a safety or climbing harness, whereas English cognate baldric remains strictly historical/medieval.

rootFamily.gloss: historical maker of leather belts; currier of hides
thickened sole or harness leather (archaic technical derivative)

cognates.meaning: drool, dribble, foam (cognate with base bave)

bavard.etymology: Formed in 15th-century Middle French from the verb baver ('to drool, foam at the mouth', figuratively 'to prattle or spew idle talk', derived from bave 'saliva, drool' < expressive Late Latin *baba mimicking infant babbling and dribbling) plus the mildly pejorative agentive/adjectival suffix -ard (of Frankish origin, *-hard).

history.meaning: to drool; figuratively to prattle or mock
talkative, indiscreet, given to idle chatter

bavard.notes: In agency or legal contexts, être bavard can mean not merely 'chatty' but 'indiscreet / unable to keep a secret'; in film critique, un film trop bavard criticizes a dialogue-heavy script that tells instead of showing.

rootFamily.gloss: police or journalistic blunder, smear, smudge of ink/drool

cognates.meaning: chatter, prattle (19th-c. literary loan from French)

bavardage.etymology: Derived in Early Modern French (attested from the 16th–18th centuries) from bavarder ('to talk at length, chatter, gossip', itself formed on Middle French bavard 'talkative') with the productive action-noun suffix -age (< Latin -āticum). It preserves the playful underlying metaphor of speech flowing unchecked like saliva (bave).

history.meaning: to chat idly, talk excessively or indiscreetly
idle talk, small talk, indiscreet gossip

morphemes.meaning: nominal suffix denoting action or collective output

bavardage.notes: Masculine noun (un bavardage, souvent au pluriel les bavardages); French schoolteachers famously admonish pupils with Arrêtez les bavardages ! ('Stop chatting!').

bazar.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–17th centuries (through Portuguese, Italian, and diplomatic accounts of the Ottoman and Safavid empires) from Persian bāzār (بازار, 'covered public marketplace'), from Middle Persian wāzār ('market'). In 19th-century Paris, bazar came to designate inexpensive variety department stores (like the Bazar de l'Hôtel de Ville), whence colloquial French 'pile of personal stuff' and 'chaotic mess, shambles'.

history.meaning: clutter, jumble of belongings, chaotic situation

bazar.notes: Everyday polite substitute for stronger swear-word equivalents like bordel: Quel bazar ! ('What a mess / shambles!') and Range ton bazar ! ('Clean up your stuff!').

rootFamily.gloss: to sell off cheaply or get rid of clutter (colloquial)

beau.etymology: Beau continues Latin bellus, pretty or graceful. The eleventh-century French form bel survives as a modern alternative before certain vowel sounds.

cognates.meaning: borrowed from French beauté and beau

beau.notes: Preserves older Old French bel directly before masculine singular vowel or mute-h nouns: un bel arbre, un bel hôtel.

cognates.meaning: father-in-law (calqued via Anglo-Norman law vs. polite address)
handsome/fair + father (parallel Romance roots bello + padre)

beau-père.etymology: Compounded in 15th-century Middle French from beau ('fair, noble, dear', from Latin bellus, used in medieval courtly speech as an affectionate honorific in direct address to kin: beau père, belle mère) and père ('father', from Latin patrem). Once lexicalized, it displaced both Old French suire ('father-in-law' < Latin socerum) and parastre ('stepfather' < Latin patrastrum, which had grown pejorative).

history.meaning: respectful affectionate address ('dear/noble father') to a father or priest

morphemes.meaning: fair, honorific kinship modifier indicating affinity/remarriage

beau-père.notes: Covers BOTH 'father-in-law' and 'stepfather' (plural des beaux-pères); context usually clarifies, though speakers occasionally specify le mari de ma mère for stepfather when ambiguity arises.

beaucoup.etymology: Beaucoup joins beau, formerly able to mean large, and coup, a portion cut from a whole. The Académie records thirteenth-century biau cop with the sense of a large and fine thing.

history.meaning: 'a fine/big strike or cut', a great deal

cognates.meaning: literal cognate phrase ('nice shot/stroke', without the quantifier shift)

beaucoup.notes: Replaced older Old French moult (< Latin multum); remember beaucoup takes plain de (beaucoup d'amis, never *beaucoup des) and is never preceded by *très.

beauf.etymology: Created in 20th-century colloquial French by apocope (clipping) of beau-frère ('brother-in-law'), and immortalized in November 1973 by satirical cartoonist Cabu in Charlie Hebdo through his recurring character Le Beauf. The archetype satirized the smug, reactionary, chauvinistic brother-in-law pontificating over Sunday family lunch, turning a kinship clipping into a sociological label for narrow-minded vulgarity.

history.meaning: familiar clipping for brother-in-law; uncultured, reactionary petit-bourgeois stereotype

beauf.notes: Pronounced /bof/ (not like bof! 'meh'); culturally distinct from rural American 'redneck', un beauf targets loud, conformist, slightly vulgar or sexist bad taste (un humour de beauf) across any social class.

rootFamily.gloss: boorishness, smug vulgarity associated with the beauf stereotype
to turn vulgar, narrow-minded, or philistine

cognates.meaning: aesthetic attractiveness, beauty (borrowed from Old French)

beauté.etymology: Inherited via Old French beltet, biauté from Vulgar Latin *bellitātem (accusative of *bellitās, 'prettiness, attractiveness'), an abstract noun in -tās derived from Classical Latin bellus ('pretty, handsome, charming, neat'). Classical Latin bellus itself arose in Old Latin as an affectionate diminutive (*duenelos) of bonus ('good'), gradually replacing classical pulcher in spoken Romance.

history.meaning: pretty, charming → state of prettiness or elegance
beauty, aesthetic harmony, beautiful person or thing

morphemes.meaning: beautiful, handsome (from Old French bel / beau)

beauté.notes: Ending a career or scene en beauté means 'on a high note / in grand style'; grain de beauté is the idiomatic French term for a beauty mark or mole.

rootFamily.gloss: spell of fine weather; sudden improvement in prospects

bec.etymology: Inherited from Old French bec ('bird's bill, beak, spout'), from Classical Latin beccus ('beak'), explicitly recorded by Suetonius as a Gaulish word (*bekkos).

berceau.etymology: Inherited from Old French berçuel, bercel ('infant's cradle; arched trellis'), from Vulgar Latin *bertiolum, diminutive of Gallo-Roman *bertium ('wicker cradle, carrying basket'), which outlived Old French bers ('cradle'). The base *bertium is a substrate borrowing from Gaulish (related to Celtic roots for woven wickerwork or carrying, cf. Old Irish bert 'bundle, burden').

history.meaning: cradle, crib; birthplace or origin; barrel vault

berceau.notes: Just like English 'cradle', berceau is used figuratively for origins (le berceau du cinéma, 'the birthplace of cinema') and dès le berceau ('from infancy').

rootFamily.gloss: to rock gently in a cradle; soothe

bercer.etymology: Inherited from Old French bercier ('to rock a child in a cradle'), from Gallo-Roman / Vulgar Latin *bertiāre, a denominative verb formed directly on *bertium ('wicker cradle', of Gaulish origin, whence Old French bers and its diminutive berceau). From lulling infants to sleep, bercer developed the figurative sense of soothing or deluding someone with comforting illusions.

history.meaning: to rock a baby to sleep
to rock gently, lull; soothe with illusions

morphemes.meaning: first-conjugation infinitive ending (with cedilla ç before a/o)

bercer.notes: Spelling alert: requires a cedilla before -a- or -o- (nous berçons) to keep the /s/ sound; idiomatic se bercer d'illusions means 'to kid oneself / indulge in wishful thinking'.

besoin.etymology: The Académie traces besoin probably to reconstructed Old Low Franconian *bisun(n)i, care or need. Thirteenth-century French had besoing. The proposed Germanic source is probable rather than certain.
besoin.notes: Avoir besoin de ('to have need of') is French's primary way to express 'to need' (j'ai besoin d'aide).

beurre.etymology: Beurre comes from Latin butyrum, borrowed from Ancient Greek boútyron ('cow-cheese', from boûs 'cow' + tyrós 'cheese'), evolving through Old French burre into modern beurre.
beurre.notes: **Beurre doux** = unsalted butter; **beurre demi-sel / salé** = lightly salted / salted butter.

bibliothèque.etymology: Learned borrowing via Latin bibliotheca from Ancient Greek bibliothḗkē ('book repository, bookcase, library'), compounded from biblíon ('book, papyrus roll') and thḗkē ('case, chest, storage place', from tithénai 'to put').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: bibliothèque (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: bibliothèque

bibliothèque.notes: In French, **une bibliothèque** means both a public/private library AND a piece of furniture (a bookcase)—whereas **une librairie** is a bookshop.

cognates.meaning: large metal can, drum (borrowed from French)

bidon.etymology: As an adjective meaning 'fake, phony, trumped-up', attested in early-20th-century Parisian and WWI soldiers' argot via appositional use of the noun bidon ('metal canteen, jerrycan, hollow drum'; e.g., un coup bidon). The noun bidon first appeared in 16th-century Norman maritime usage for a wooden liquid cask, likely borrowed from Old Norse biða ('wooden tub, vessel'), with the slang shift driven by the image of an empty, hollow tin container (reinforced in Italian argot fare un bidone 'to swindle').

history.meaning: sailor's wooden jug; later soldier's metal canteen or fuel can

bidon.notes: As an adjective, bidon is completely INVARIABLE in both gender and number: une excuse bidon, des contrats bidon ('phony excuses, bogus contracts')—never *bidonne!

rootFamily.gloss: shantytown, slum (originally huts built from flattened oil drums)
to fake, rig, or doctor figures/news (colloquial)

bien.etymology: Bien descends from the Latin adverb bene, well. The Académie records it in French from the tenth century; the noun meaning a good or a possession developed from the adverb.
bien.notes: Bien modifies verbs and adjectives ('well, really'), whereas bon modifies nouns ('good')—though c'est bien! evaluates an idea or situation and c'est bon! praises taste or physical comfort.

cognates.meaning: secure, sure (borrowed via Old French seür)

bien sûr.etymology: Lexicalized affirmative adverbial phrase combining bien ('well, thoroughly, indeed', from Classical Latin bene) and sûr ('certain, confident', contracted via Old French seür from Classical Latin sēcūrus 'untroubled, free from anxiety', compounded from privative sē- 'without' + cūra 'care, worry'). The circumflex in sûr marks the historical loss of the Old French hiatus vowel in seür.

history.meaning: well + free from worry or danger
thoroughly confident, completely safe or certain

bien sûr.notes: Keep the circumflex on sûr ('sure') to distinguish it from the preposition sur ('on'); when followed by a clause, French adds que: Bien sûr que oui ! or Bien sûr qu'il viendra ('Of course he'll come').

rootFamily.gloss: safe, free from danger (learned doublet of sûr from Latin sēcūrus)

bientôt.etymology: Bientôt joins bien and tôt. Fourteenth-century bien tost meant in a short time, before the expression settled into its modern meaning soon.

history.meaning: in a short time, right quickly

bientôt.notes: À bientôt! ('See you soon!') is one of the warmest everyday farewells in French.

cognates.meaning: goodwill, kindness (from the same Latin source)

bienveillance.etymology: Evolved from Old French bienvoillance (alongside learned benevolence), remodeled on native bien ('well') and vouloir/veillant ('wishing') from Classical Latin benevolentia ('goodwill, friendly disposition, favor'), abstract noun from benevolēns ('wishing well', compounded from bene 'well' + volēns, present participle of velle 'to wish, will').

morphemes.meaning: wishing, willing (archaic participle stem of vouloir)

bienveillance.notes: A major 21st-century buzzword in French corporate, artistic, and parenting culture (management bienveillant), prized for warm supportiveness—though in cutthroat talent agencies like ASK it is sometimes invoked ironically.

rootFamily.gloss: unpaid volunteer (learned cognate from Latin benevolus)

cognates.meaning: welcome (parallel Germanic calque/cognate formation well + come)

bienvenu.etymology: Univerbated from the 12th-century Old French greeting phrase bien venu ('well arrived'), composed of bien ('well, happily', from Latin bene) and venu ('come, arrived', past participle of venir < Classical Latin venīre). Originally used predicatively to bless a traveler's safe arrival (soiez li bien venus), it fused into an inflecting adjective and noun.

history.meaning: happily or safely arrived (greeting to a guest)

bienvenu.notes: Distinguish spelling carefully: the adjective agrees in gender and number (il est le bienvenu, une pause bienvenue), whereas the greeting interjection 'Welcome!' and the noun 'a welcome' are always spelled feminine singular: Bienvenue ! / souhaiter la bienvenue.

bienvenue.etymology: Noun and adjective formed in Old French from bien ('well', from Latin bene) + venue, feminine past participle of venir ('to come', from Latin venire) — literally 'a good or happy arrival'.

bijou.etymology: Borrowed in 15th-century Middle French (initially in Brittany and western France) from Breton bizou ('finger ring'), derived from Breton biz ('finger', cognate with Welsh bys) with the suffix -ou. Initially restricted in French to an ornamental ring, it broadened in the 17th century to any finely crafted piece of jewelry or precious miniature object.

history.meaning: jewel, piece of fine jewelry; figurative gem

bijou.notes: Famous plural exception: takes -x in the plural (des bijoux), part of the classic French schoolroom mnemonic list bijou, caillou, chou, genou, hibou, joujou, pou. In film praise, un petit bijou means 'an absolute little gem'.

rootFamily.gloss: jewelry shop; the jewelry trade or collection

cognates.meaning: balance (from the same Late Latin bilanx via Old French)

bilan.etymology: Borrowed in the late 16th century (originally spelled bilans in merchant accounting) from Italian bilancio ('commercial balance sheet, equilibrium'), deverbal noun from bilanciare ('to weigh on scales, balance accounts'), derived from Italian bilancia ('two-pan scale') < Late Latin bilanx ('having two scale pans', from bi- 'two' + lanx 'plate, pan of a scale'). It is thus an Italianate commercial cousin of native French balance.

history.meaning: having two scale pans; two-pan weighing scale
weighing, equilibrium of debits and credits in bookkeeping
financial balance sheet; overall review, toll, or health checkup

bilan.notes: Extremely versatile in French: un bilan comptable is a financial balance sheet, un bilan de santé is a medical checkup, le bilan d'un accident is the casualty toll, and faire le bilan means 'to take stock / review how things went'.

rootFamily.gloss: weighing scale; balance (native French cognate from Late Latin bilancia)
relating to a company's balance sheet (e.g., hors-bilan)

billet.etymology: Formed in Middle French as a diminutive of bille ('short written note', an alteration of bulle 'sealed papal or official document', from Latin bulla 'leaden seal'); originally a short written note or pass, whence 'ticket' and 'banknote'.

history.meaning: short letter, written pass, ticket, banknote

biologique.etymology: Formed in the early 19th century from biologie ('science of living organisms', coined independently in 1802 by French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck and German physician Gottfried Reinhold Treviranus from Ancient Greek βίος bíos 'life' + -logie < λόγος lógos 'discourse, study') plus the learned adjectival suffix -ique (< Greek -ικός). In mid-20th-century French agronomy, agriculture biologique took on the specific sense of chemical-free 'organic' farming.

history.meaning: science of living organisms → relating to life processes
biological; organically grown without synthetic chemicals

biologique.notes: Classic false-friend trap in supermarkets and cafés: English 'organic food/wine' is nourriture/vin biologique (almost always clipped to bio, invariable: des légumes bio), whereas French organique is strictly scientific/chemical!

biopic.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century (becoming mainstream in French film journalism in the 1990s–2000s) from American English trade-press slang biopic (coined in Variety in the late 1940s), a syllabic blend (clipping compound) of biographical (from Ancient Greek βίος bíos 'life' + γράφω gráphō 'to write') and picture ('motion picture', from Latin pictūra 'painting').

history.meaning: dramatized feature film portraying a real person's life
biographical film or prestige star vehicle

biopic.notes: Masculine noun in French (un biopic), pronounced /bjo.pik/ (unlike English /ˈbaɪ.oʊ.pɪk/); a staple genre in Dix pour cent whenever Parisian stars vie for prestige historical roles, despite the Académie française recommending film biographique.

bip.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-20th century from English beep, an echoic word imitating a short, high-pitched electronic signal; its popularity in French surged in October 1957 through press coverage of Sputnik 1's recurring bip-bip radio transmission, later extending to answering machines, pagers, and censor tones.

history.meaning: short high-pitched horn or electronic sound
short electronic signal or censor tone

bip.notes: Masculine noun (un bip); plural is bips, and laisser un message après le bip sonore is the classic French voicemail prompt heard constantly by busy talent agents.

cognates.meaning: to emit a beep or page someone

biper.etymology: Coined in late-20th-century French as a first-conjugation verbal derivative of the noun bip ('electronic tone', from English beep) plus the infinitive suffix -er, initially meaning to contact someone via a pager (bipeur) and later to buzz someone's phone or scan a barcode.

history.meaning: to emit a beep; to page or buzz someone

biper.notes: In office and agency speech, biper quelqu'un casually means to ping, buzz, or call someone briefly on their mobile or intercom.

biscuit.etymology: Compound inherited from Old French bescuit ('twice-baked bread'), modeled on Latin panis bis coctus: bis ('twice') + cuit (past participle of cuire 'to bake'). Originally it named dry, durable ship's bread baked a second time to drive out moisture.

history.meaning: crisp sweet cookie; light sponge cake

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: biscuit (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: biscuit

biscuit.notes: Ceramicists also call unglazed once-fired pottery **le biscuit** by analogy with dry baked biscuit.

bisou.etymology: Formed in colloquial French from bise ('cheek kiss', an expressive labial formation closely tied to Old French baisier from Classical Latin bāsium 'affectionate kiss') combined with the endearing diminutive suffix -ou of Occitan and regional origin.
bisou.notes: Safe, affectionate, and non-sexual (faire un bisou / gros bisous), avoiding the dangerous trap of unplated baiser, which as a verb in modern spoken French means to have sex.

bisou-bisou.etymology: Colloquial reduplication of bisou ('informal kiss', itself derived from bise 'cheek kiss' + affectionate suffix -ou), iconically echoing the two-cheek kissing custom and used in spoken French—especially in entertainment and media circles—as a breezy phone sign-off.
bisou-bisou.notes: Classic showbiz and Parisian agency phone closer—warm on the surface, though often used briskly to end a call before the other person can object.

bizarre.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian bizzarro ('irascible, touchy, capricious, strange', derived from bizza 'fit of anger'), originally meaning 'hot-tempered, valiant' in French before settling into 'odd, strange, eccentric' in the 17th century.

history.meaning: flash of anger -> fiery, capricious, strange

bizarrement.etymology: Formed in French from the adjective bizarre (borrowed in the 16th century from Italian bizzarro 'irascible, fiery, capricious', which shifted in French to 'peculiar, odd') plus the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin mente, ablative singular of mēns 'mind').

history.meaning: in a strange or unexpected manner

bizarrement.notes: Used at the start of a sentence (Bizarrement, il a refusé le rôle), it works as a sentence adverb meaning 'Oddly enough' or 'Curiously'.

bière.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Middle Dutch bier (from West Germanic *beuzą 'barley brew'), gradually displacing Old French cervoise (from Gallo-Latin cervisia) as hopped beer from Flanders and Holland overtook unhopped grain ales in France.

history.meaning: fermented barley drink, brewer's yeast brew

bière.notes: Feminine noun (une bière); do not confuse with its literary homonym la bière ('coffin, funeral bier', from Frankish *bāra), which explains the classic French pun mise en bière ('bottling beer' vs. 'placing in a coffin').

cognates.meaning: belly; bellows (from the same Germanic root)

blague.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from Dutch balg ('inflatable skin, belly, pouch', from Proto-Germanic *balgiz) with metathesis of l; originally denoting a small pouch for pipe tobacco (blague à tabac), by c. 1800 it developed the slang sense 'bag of wind, boastful lie', softening into 'joke, prank'.

history.meaning: tobacco pouch; figuratively empty boasting or tall tale

blague.notes: Sans blague ! means 'No kidding! / Seriously!', while blague à part means 'joking aside'; the tobacco sense still survives in une blague à tabac.

blaireau.etymology: Inherited from Old French blarel / blaireau (14th century), most likely formed as a diminutive on Gaulish *blāros ('gray, white-marked, having a facial blaze'), naming the European badger after the striking white stripes running down its dark snout, and later transferred to a badger-hair shaving brush.

history.meaning: gray, white-spotted, marked with a blaze
badger; shaving brush; (slang) clueless loser or jerk

blaireau.notes: In modern conversational French (including Dix pour cent), quel blaireau ! rarely refers to woodland wildlife—it is a sharp colloquial insult meaning 'what a dork / uncultured idiot / loser'.

blanc.etymology: Blanc entered Gallo-Romance from Frankish *blank ('shining, gleaming white', cognate with English 'blank'), displacing Classical Latin albus in everyday speech.
blanc.notes: Feminine **blanche** preserves the palatalised final consonant: *une nappe blanche*.

blesser.etymology: Inherited from Old French blecier ('to bruise, crush, injure by a blow'), from Gallo-Romance *blettiāre ('to bruise or soften by crushing, like overripe fruit'), borrowed from Frankish *bletjan ('to make livid, bruise'), eventually displacing Old French navrer as the standard verb for physical and emotional wounding.

history.meaning: to bruise or injure with a blow
to wound, injure, or offend emotionally

blesser.notes: Classic false friend for English speakers: blesser NEVER means 'to bless' (which is bénir)—it strictly means 'to injure, wound, or hurt someone's feelings'.

blessure.etymology: Derived in 12th-century Old French (bleceüre) from the verb blecier ('to bruise, injure', from Gallo-Romance *blettiāre < Frankish *bletjan) plus the action/result nominal suffix -ure (from Latin -ūra), denoting both a physical bodily wound and a psychological slight to pride.

morphemes.meaning: noun suffix denoting result of an action

blessure.notes: Used constantly for fragile actor egos in uneven billing disputes: une blessure d'amour-propre / une blessure narcissique ('a wound to one's pride / ego').

blessé.etymology: Past participle adjective and substantivized noun of blesser (Old French blecié, from blecier 'to bruise, wound', itself via Gallo-Romance *blettiāre from Frankish *bletjan 'to bruise, make livid'), formed with the regular first-group participial ending -é (from Latin -ātus).
blessé.notes: Functions both as an adjective (elle est très blessée par sa remarque) and as a noun (les blessés 'the injured / casualties').

bleu.etymology: Inherited from Old French bloe / bleu ('blue, pale, livid'), borrowed from Frankish *blao ('blue, gleaming', from Proto-Germanic *blewaz, cognate with English blue and German blau), which displaced Latin caeruleus in Western Romance.

bleui.etymology: Past participle of bleuir ('to turn blue, make blue'), formed in Old/Middle French from the adjective bleu ('blue') + verbal suffix -ir.

cognates.meaning: blue (Germanic cognate of the root bleu)

bleuté.etymology: Formed in 18th-century French from bleu ('blue', inherited from Old French blo / bleu, borrowed from Frankish *blāo 'blue, livid, shimmering') with an epenthetic consonant -t- and the adjectival suffix -é ('tinged with'), expressing a subtle bluish cast of light or shadow.

history.meaning: tinted with a soft bluish hue

morphemes.meaning: having a tint or quality of

bleuté.notes: More poetic and aesthetically pleasing than bleuâtre ('bluish', which often suggests sickly or bruised skin); bleuté is favored in cinematography and lighting (une lumière bleutée).

bloc.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century (originally losc / bloc) from Middle Dutch blok ('felled tree trunk, heavy mass of wood or stone'), from Proto-Germanic *bluka-.

history.meaning: heavy log, solid mass of wood or stone
solid lump or block; unified group, notepad

blocage.etymology: Derived in early-20th-century French from bloquer ('to immobilize, obstruct', formed from Middle French bloc, borrowed from Middle Dutch blok 'felled tree trunk, solid mass of wood') plus the productive nominal suffix -age (from Latin -āticum), denoting mechanical jamming, political deadlock, or psychological inhibition.

history.meaning: felled tree trunk, heavy billet of wood
to hem in, besiege, or immobilize

blocage.notes: Covers both contract negotiations (un blocage dans les négociations 'a deadlock') and creative/acting freeze-ups (avoir un blocage psychologique 'to have a mental block').

blond.etymology: Inherited from Old French blont, feminine blonde (attested c. 1100 in the Chanson de Roland), from Medieval Latin blundus ('yellow-haired, fair'); philologists consider blundus most likely borrowed from Frankish *blund (possibly related to Germanic words for 'mixed, pale, or dazzling') though a pre-Romance substrate origin is also debated.

history.meaning: blond, fair-haired; pale (of beer or tobacco)

blond.notes: Beyond hair color, blond describes pale lager beer (une bière blonde) and mild Virginia-style tobacco (tabac blond); final -d is silent in the masculine (blond [blɔ̃]) and pronounced in the feminine (blonde [blɔ̃d]).

bloquer.etymology: Derived in the 15th century from bloc ('block, solid mass') or Middle Dutch blokken; originally a military verb meaning 'to hem in, blockade a fortress', later 'to jam, immobilize, block'.

history.meaning: to hem in, blockade -> to jam, immobilize, block

cognates.meaning: to deceive by feigned confidence in poker

bluffer.etymology: Adapted in late-19th-century French by adding the verbal ending -er to the noun bluff, borrowed from American English poker terminology bluff ('feigning a strong hand to intimidate opponents'), which itself likely came from Dutch bluffen ('to boast, swell up') and verbluffen ('to baffle, hoodwink').

history.meaning: to boast; to baffle or disconcert
to feign strength in poker to deceive opponents
to bluff; (modern colloquial) to astound or impress deeply

bluffer.notes: Crucial modern idiomatic shift: alongside 'to bluff' in negotiations, bluffer quelqu'un very frequently means 'to blow someone away / deeply impress them' (Son audition m'a bluffé !).

boire.etymology: Inherited from Old French boivre ('to drink'), from Classical Latin bibere ('to drink'), from PIE *pi-ph3-e- ('to drink').

bois.etymology: Bois descends from Medieval Latin boscus ('woodland, timber'), probably of Germanic origin (akin to English 'bush'). It means both a small forest ('woods') and the material 'wood'.
bois.notes: **En bois** = made of wood (e.g. *un train en bois*, *un escalier en bois*).

bol.etymology: In the sense 'hemispherical drinking or soup bowl', borrowed in the 17th–18th century from English bowl (Originally in punch bowl), from Old English bolla ('round vessel, bowl').

bombe.etymology: Borrowed in the late 16th century from Italian bomba ('explosive shell'), from Classical Latin bombus ('deep hollow booming or buzzing sound'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek βόμβος (bómbos, echoic of a low rumbling or humming noise); in 20th-century colloquial French it gained figurative senses of 'sensational hit' and 'stunningly attractive person'.

history.meaning: deep booming, humming, or rumbling sound

bombe.notes: Watch the polarity opposite to English: whereas a movie 'bomb' in English is a box-office flop, in French ce film, c'est de la bombe ! means 'this movie is dynamite / a total smash!', and une bombe means a knockout beauty (or a spray can, une bombe aérosol).

bon.etymology: Bon descends from Latin bonus, good. The Académie records tenth-century French buon; forms such as feminine bonne belong to this same adjective.

cognates.meaning: Latin borrowing and Old French bonté

bon.notes: Nasal /bɔ̃/ in masculine bon denasalizes to oral /bɔn/ in feminine bonne and in prenominal liaison (un bon ami /œ̃.bɔ.n‿a.mi/).

bonbon.etymology: Coined in early-17th-century French nursery speech (attested 1604) through expressive reduplication of the adjective bon ('good, tasty', inherited from Classical Latin bonus, Old Latin duenos), literally 'good-good', used by children and caregivers for sugared treats.

morphemes.meaning: nursery repetition denoting a tasty treat

bonbon.notes: Also used idiomatically in coûter bonbon ('to cost a fortune / cost a pretty penny'), and rose bonbon ('candy pink / bubblegum pink').

cognates.meaning: omen, augury (cognate of the second element -heur)

bonheur.etymology: Fused from the Old French phrase bon eür ('good fortune, favorable destiny'), combining bon ('good', from Latin bonus) and Old French eür ('luck, fate, omen', from Vulgar Latin *agurium < Classical Latin augurium 'divination by bird-flight, omen'); the unetymological silent h was added in Middle French by false analogy with heure ('hour' < hōra).

history.meaning: good luck (as in au petit bonheur), then deep happiness and joy

morphemes.meaning: luck, fate, omen (from Old French eür < Latin augurium)

bonheur.notes: Its original meaning of 'luck/chance' still lives in expressions like par bonheur ('luckily'), porter bonheur ('to bring good luck'), and au petit bonheur la chance ('haphazardly, trusting to luck'), alongside its antonym malheur ('misfortune').

rootFamily.gloss: happy, fortunate (derived from Old French eür + -eux)

bonjour.etymology: Bonjour joins bon and jour. The Académie records thirteenth-century bon jor with the sense of a good day or happy time. The wish developed into the familiar daytime greeting.
bonjour.notes: Use bonjour to greet someone during the day. Saying it when taking leave is regional; au revoir is the general farewell. Bonsoir is the usual evening greeting.

bonsaï.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from Japanese 盆栽 (bonsai, literally 'tray planting'), a Sino-Japanese compound of 盆 (bon 'shallow tray, basin', from Middle Chinese bwon) and 栽 (sai 'planting, cultivation', from Middle Chinese tsoj), itself adapted from Chinese 盆栽 (pénzāi); French orthography adds a diaeresis (ï) to preserve the diphthong [aj] rather than reading -ai as [ɛ].

history.meaning: potted miniature plant grown in a shallow tray
art of dwarfing trees in shallow containers

bonsaï.notes: Masculine noun (un bonsaï, plural des bonsaïs); the tréma on ï signals that a and i are pronounced separately as [bɔ̃saj] rather than merging into [ɛ].

rootFamily.gloss: potted samurai/Japanese loanword pattern with ï (cf. haïku, samouraï)

sources.title: CNRTL — Définition et étymologie de bonsaï

bonsoir.etymology: Univerbation of the greeting phrase bon soir ('good evening'), from bon ('good', Latin bonus) + soir ('evening', from Latin serum, neuter of serus 'late').

bonté.etymology: Inherited from Old French bontet / bonté ('goodness, moral worth, kindness'), from Classical Latin bonitatem (nominative bonitas, 'goodness, kindness'), derived from bonus ('good').

bord.etymology: Inherited from Old French bort ('ship's side, edge, rim'), borrowed from Frankish *bord ('plank, side of a ship, edge', cognate with English board).

history.meaning: side of a ship; edge, shore, rim

border.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from bord ('edge, side of a ship') + verbal ending -er; means 'to edge, hem, line along the border' or 'to tuck in bedsheets'.

history.meaning: to line the edge of; to tuck in

bordure.etymology: Formed in Middle French from border ('to edge, border') or bord ('edge') + suffix -ure.

borne.etymology: Inherited from Old French bodne / bozne / bone, altered with rhotacism to borne by the 12th–13th century, from Early Medieval Latin bodina / butina ('boundary stone'), of Gaulish (Celtic) origin *botina ('border marker, boundary mound'), surviving across modern tech and figurative senses of 'terminal' and 'limit'.

history.meaning: boundary stone or earthen border marker
milestone, limit, interactive kiosk, or charging terminal

borne.notes: Rich in everyday idioms: dépasser les bornes means 'to cross the line / go way too far', borné means 'narrow-minded / stubborn', and une borne interactive is a ticket or check-in kiosk.

rootFamily.gloss: to mark off, restrict; (se borner à) to limit oneself to
surveying and setting of boundary markers

cognates.meaning: bump, dent, embossing (cognate of base noun bosse)
raised knob or stud; to emboss (from Old French boce)

bosser.etymology: Attested in 19th-century popular and military slang as a verbal derivative of bosse ('hump, rounded swelling', from Old French boce, of uncertain Frankish or Gallo-Romance origin) plus -er, originally evoking laborers hunching their backs into a hump under heavy toil before becoming the ubiquitous everyday verb for working.

history.meaning: swelling, hump on the back, raised knob
hump, bump; knack or aptitude (avoir la bosse de)
to toil with bent back; (colloquial) to work, study hard

bosser.notes: Not related to English 'boss' ('employer', which comes from Dutch baas)! Bosser is the universal informal synonym of travailler heard in every Parisian office: Je bosse tout le week-end.

botox.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from the American English pharmaceutical trademark Botox, coined as a blend of bo(tulinum) and tox(in): New Latin botulinum derives from Classical Latin botulus ('sausage', because botulism poisoning was first studied in 18th-century Germany from tainted blood sausages), while toxin stems from Ancient Greek τοξικόν (toxikón 'arrow poison', from τόξον 'bow').

history.meaning: purified botulinum toxin type A trademarked for medical/cosmetic use

morphemes.meaning: clipped from toxin (ultimately Greek toxikón 'arrow poison')

botox.notes: In French film-industry banter (a staple plot point for aging stars in Dix pour cent), it immediately spawned the colloquial verb se faire botoxer and the adjective botoxé(e).

rootFamily.gloss: to inject with Botox; (se faire botoxer) to get Botox done
botulism (foodborne illness from the same root)

botte.etymology: Inherited from 12th-century Old French bote (originally a heavy ankle- or calf-high shoe worn by monks and riders in bad weather), attested in Medieval Latin as botta; its ultimate origin remains uncertain, variously traced by philologists to a Germanic root (compare Old Norse bóti 'patch, shoe-Gusset' or Frankish *bōta) or a pre-Latin substrate word.

history.meaning: sturdy monastic or riding footwear covering the foot and lower leg

botte.notes: French has three distinct homonyms spelled botte: 1) 'boot' (les bottes); 2) 'bundle/bunch' of radishes or hay (une botte de radis, from Low Franconian *bōt); and 3) 'fencing thrust' (une botte secrète 'a secret trump card', from Italian botta 'blow')—plus the slang verb ça me botte ! ('that really appeals to me / suits me!').

rootFamily.gloss: bootmaker; (figuratively) directory (le Bottin, by surname coincidence)
to outfit with boots; (slang) to suit or appeal to someone

bouche.etymology: Inherited from Old French boche ('mouth'), from Classical Latin bucca ('puffed-out cheek; in informal and Vulgar Latin, mouth'), which completely replaced Classical Latin os, oris in Romance.

bouche-à-bouche.etymology: Modern 20th-century French compound noun formed from bouche ('mouth') + preposition à ('to') + bouche ('mouth'), paralleling English mouth-to-mouth resuscitation; bouche itself descends from Old French boche, from Classical Latin bucca ('puffed-out cheek'), which in Vulgar Latin colloquially displaced Classical ōs ('mouth') across the Romance languages.
bouche-à-bouche.notes: Do not confuse le bouche-à-bouche ('mouth-to-mouth resuscitation', masculine, invariable in the plural) with le bouche-à-oreille ('word of mouth', crucial for indie film box office!).

sources.title: CNRTL — Définition et étymologie de bouche-à-bouche

boucher.etymology: Inherited from Old French bouchier ('to stop up an opening with a bundle of straw or twigs'), derived from Old French bousche ('handful of straw, bundle of brushwood', related to Gallo-Romance *boscus 'wood, thicket' > bois) rather than directly from bouche ('mouth'), though speakers early on reanalyzed it by folk etymology as closing an opening or 'mouth'.

history.meaning: bundle of twigs, wisp of straw used as a plug
to plug up with a bundle of straw or foliage
to cork, clog, obstruct, or block up

boucher.notes: Remarkable double trap: the verb boucher ('to clog/plug', from Old French bousche 'straw bundle') is etymologically unrelated both to bouche ('mouth' < bucca) AND to its exact homograph noun un boucher ('a butcher' < bouc 'he-goat')! Also note ça en bouche un coin ('that leaves one speechless').

rootFamily.gloss: to uncork, unclog, clear; to lead onto

cognates.meaning: butcher's trade; slaughter (borrowed from Old French)

boucherie.etymology: Inherited from 12th-century Old French boucherie ('slaughterhouse, meat market, carnage'), formed from Old French bouchier ('butcher', originally a slaughterer and seller of goat meat, derived from bouc 'billy goat', from Gaulish *bukkos or Frankish *bukk) plus the trade/place suffix -erie.

history.meaning: slaughterer of goats and livestock, butcher
butcher's shop; figuratively bloody slaughter or massacre

morphemes.meaning: shop, trade, or collective action suffix

boucherie.notes: In contemporary slang, c'est une tuerie / c'est une boucherie can paradoxically mean either 'it was a bloodbath/total disaster' (e.g. a butchered edit) OR, among younger speakers, 'it's killer / insanely good' depending on tone.

bouchée.etymology: Inherited from Old French bochiee ('a mouthful'), formed from bouche ('mouth') + suffix -ée denoting the quantity contained in something.

bouder.etymology: Attested since the 14th century ('to pout, sulk'), formed on an expressive root *bud- / *bod- évoquant puffed-out lips or a swollen belly (compare Old French boudine 'navel, paunch' and Provençal boudar 'to swell, pout').

bouger.etymology: Inherited from Old French bulgier / bougier ('to stir, bubble up, move'), from Vulgar Latin *bullicare ('to bubble, seethe, stir'), frequentative of Classical Latin bullire ('to boil, bubble').

cognates.meaning: wax candle; spark plug (borrowed from French)

bougie.etymology: Attested around 1300 in Old/Middle French as chandelle de Bougie and soon shortened to bougie, an eponymous borrowing from Bougie, the French name of the Algerian port city of Béjaïa (Arabic بجاية Bijāya in Kabylia), which supplied medieval France with fine North African beeswax superior to domestic tallow candles.

history.meaning: port city of Béjaïa in Algeria, major exporter of beeswax
fine candle made of imported North African beeswax
wax candle; automotive spark plug; unit of luminous intensity

bougie.notes: Bougie is the everyday word for any wax or birthday candle (souffler ses bougies) AND for a car's spark plug (bougie d'allumage), whereas chandelle mostly survives in idioms like dîner aux chandelles ('candlelit dinner') and tenir la chandelle ('to play third wheel').

rootFamily.gloss: small candleholder with a handle, chamberstick
restless fidgeting (unrelated homophonous root bouger, good contrast); wax-taper maker (cired bougier)

bouillir.etymology: Inherited from Old French bolir / bouillir ('to boil, bubble'), from Classical Latin bullire ('to bubble, boil'), derived from bulla ('water bubble').

cognates.meaning: to boil; boiler (borrowed from Old French bolir)
kettle, water heater (parallel formation from bollire)

bouilloire.etymology: Derived in Early Modern French (late 17th–18th century) from the stem of bouillir ('to boil', inherited from Old French bolir, from Classical Latin bullīre 'to bubble, seethe', itself from bulla 'water bubble') plus the feminine instrumental suffix -oire (from Latin -ōria), designating a spouted vessel for boiling water.

history.meaning: metal or electric kettle for boiling water

bouilloire.notes: Pronounced [bujwaʁ] (the -ill- represents the palatal glide [j], never an [l] sound); closely paired in everyday French home life with une bouillotte ('a hot-water bottle').

rootFamily.gloss: hot-water bottle for warming a bed

bouillon.etymology: Inherited from Old French boillon ('bubbling spring, boiling surge, broth'), derived from bouillir ('to boil') < Classical Latin bullire ('to bubble up'), itself from bulla ('water bubble').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from French bouillon and Old French boillir

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: bouillon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: bouillon

bouillon.notes: In 19th-century Paris, affordable neighborhood restaurants serving hot beef **bouillon** to workers gave rise to the classic Parisian **Bouillon** dining halls.

boulanger.etymology: Continued from Old Northern French / Picard boulenc (12th century) and boulengier, most plausibly traced by Bloch-Wartburg and the TLFi to Middle Dutch bolle ('round loaf of bread', related to boule). In medieval towns a boulanger baked round loaves, gradually displacing the older French word talmelier.
