sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: boulanger (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: boulanger

boulangerie.etymology: Derived in Middle French from boulanger ('baker'), earlier Picard and Old French boulenc / boulengier ('maker of round loaves'), borrowed from Middle Dutch or Old Picard bolle ('round ball-shaped loaf').

history.meaning: round loaf -> baker of round loaves

cognates.meaning: round loaf of country bread; ball

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: boulangerie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: boulangerie

boulangerie.notes: Medieval French originally called a baker **talmelier** (from sifting flour); **boulanger** won out because customers prized plump round loaves.

cognates.meaning: game of bowls (borrowed from Old French bole)

boule.etymology: Inherited from Old French bole ('round wooden or metal ball', 12th–13th century), from Classical Latin bulla ('air bubble on water, rounded boss or stud, spherical locket worn by freeborn Roman children'), whose regular phonetic outcome boule is an inherited doublet of the learned borrowing bulle ('bubble; papal bull').

history.meaning: water bubble, round metal stud, spherical amulet
spherical ball, especially for lawn games
solid ball or sphere; scoop of ice cream; (slang) head or nerves

boule.notes: Packed with vivid colloquialisms: perdre la boule ('to lose one's mind'), avoir les boules ('to be super pissed off / gutted'), avoir la boule au ventre ('to have a knot of anxiety in one's stomach' before going onstage), and une boule de glace ('a scoop of ice cream').

rootFamily.gloss: small ball, meatball, crumpled paper ball; blunder
to shatter, turn upside down ('overturn like a ball')

bouleau.etymology: Diminutive in -eau formed in Middle French on Old French boule / беоul ('birch tree'), which was inherited from Gaulish *betullos / *betua ('birch') via Late Latin betulla. The Celtic inhabitants of Gaul prized the white-barked birch for its flexible wood and waterproof tar, and their Celtic tree name survived directly into Gallo-Romance when Latin replaced Gaulish.
bouleau.notes: Like **chêne** ('oak') and **sapin** ('fir'), **bouleau** is one of the famous everyday French tree names inherited from ancient Celtic (Gaulish) rather than Latin.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: bouleau

bouleverser.etymology: Formed in 16th-century Middle French as a vivid compound of boule ('ball, sphere', from Latin bulla) and verser ('to overturn, tip over, spill', from Latin versāre, frequentative of vertere 'to turn'), originally meaning 'to send rolling head over heels, turn completely upside down' before extending to profound emotional upheaval.

history.meaning: round ball/stud + to turn over repeatedly
to overturn, throw into physical disorder like a rolling ball
to disrupt radically; to overwhelm, shatter, or move deeply

morphemes.meaning: to overturn, tip over (from Latin versāre)

bouleverser.notes: Essential cinema and critique vocabulary: un film bouleversant does not mean a 'disruptive' film in a bad way, but a 'deeply moving, emotionally shattering' masterpiece, and bouleverser le planning means to turn the shooting schedule upside down.

bouleversé.etymology: Past participle of Middle French bouleverser (16th century), a vivid compound of boule ('ball, sphere', from Classical Latin bulla 'bubble, round stud') and verser ('to overturn, pour, tip over', from Latin versāre, frequentative of vertere 'to turn'). Literally meaning 'to send rolling head over heels like a ball', it shifted from physical overthrow and turmoil to profound emotional shock or distress.

history.meaning: bubble, round object + to turn over repeatedly
to overturn completely, throw into disorder

bouleversé.notes: Stronger and more dignified than 'triste' or 'choqué'; in cinema and agency talk, 'Je suis bouleversé(e)' can mean being genuinely devastated or deeply moved to tears by an actor's performance.

cognates.meaning: bowl / bull (papal seal, via French/Latin bulla)

boulot.etymology: Formed in French from boule ('ball, round mass', inherited from Classical Latin bulla 'bubble, knob') with the diminutive suffix -ot. Originally an adjective and noun meaning 'short and plump' (a chubby person or small round loaf), it entered 19th-century Parisian artisans' and typographers' argot (cf. ça boulotte 'things are rolling along nicely') in the sense of 'steady work, everyday job'.

history.meaning: roundish object; plump person; small round loaf

boulot.notes: Ubiquitous informal synonym for 'travail' across France (famous from the Parisian routine 'métro, boulot, dodo'); completely natural in everyday office and agency conversation, though avoided in formal contracts.

rootFamily.gloss: to eat heartily; to jog along (colloquial)

bouquet.etymology: Borrowed into standard French from Norman-Picard dialectal bouquet (corresponding to Central Old French boschet), a diminutive in -et of bosc / bois ('wood, thicket'), itself borrowed from Frankish *busk ('bush, woodland'). Originally denoting a 'little wood, clump of trees' in the 14th century, it narrowed in Middle French to a decorative 'cluster of cut flowers' and figuratively a 'crowning culmination'.

history.meaning: bunch of flowers; aromatic profile of wine; grand finale

bouquet.notes: Beyond flowers and wine aroma, watch for the classic ironic idiom 'C'est le bouquet !' ('That tops it all!' / 'That's the last straw!'), drawn from 'le bouquet final' of a fireworks display.

cognates.meaning: jest, mockery (Scots/Middle English loan from Old French)

bourde.etymology: Inherited from Old French bourde ('lie, tall tale, jest, deception', 12th–13th century), whose ultimate origin is debated: most philologists connect it either to Late Latin burda ('reed, club, pack-saddle') via Old French bourder ('to joust with blunt lances, mock, fib') or to an expressive Gallo-Romance root *burd- denoting muddle and trickery. By the 17th century, the sense softened from an intentional falsehood to a clumsy blunder or gaffe.

history.meaning: clumsy mistake, verbal or social blunder

bourde.notes: Often paired with the verb 'faire' ('J'ai fait une grosse bourde' — 'I made a huge blunder'); very common in workplace comedies when someone accidentally leaks a secret to a client or journalist.

rootFamily.gloss: to fib, jest (archaic); to stall or balk

boussole.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Italian bussola ('mariner's compass housed in a small boxwood case'), from Late Latin buxida ('little box made of boxwood'), altered from Greek pyxís (from pýxos 'box tree').

history.meaning: small box holding a magnetized needle

cognates.meaning: native inherited doublet from the same Late Latin buxida!
likewise ultimately from Late Latin buxus/buxis ('boxwood')

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: boussole (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: boussole

boussole.notes: Astonishingly, **une boussole** ('compass') and **une boîte** ('box') are etymological twins — a compass was named after the little boxwood case protecting its needle!

bout.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (bot / bout, 'blow, thrust; extremity, end') from bouter ('to strike, push, thrust'), itself borrowed from Frankish *botan ('to strike, push, thrust', cognate with English butt).

history.meaning: to thrust -> end point, tip, small piece

bouteille.etymology: Inherited from Old French boteille ('bottle, flask'), from Late Latin butticula ('small cask or flask'), diminutive of buttis ('cask, wine-skin, barrel').

boutique.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Old Occitan botica ('shop, storehouse'), from Late Latin apotheca ('storehouse, wine-cellar, magazine'), itself from Ancient Greek apotheke ('repository, storehouse', from apotithenai 'to put away, store', the same Greek word that gave apothicaire and dépôt).

bouton.etymology: Inherited from Old French boton ('plant bud, shoot; round boss or garment fastener', 12th century), derived from the verb boter / bouter ('to push, thrust out, sprout'), which was borrowed from Frankish *bōtan ('to strike, push, thrust', from Proto-Germanic *bautaną). Because a flower bud visibly pushes outward from the stem, the noun came to denote any small round protuberance, including clothing buttons, pimples, and electrical switches.

history.meaning: plant bud; small round clasp or boss
garment button; flower bud; pimple; control switch

morphemes.meaning: to push, thrust out, sprout (from bouter)
nominal suffix denoting a small object or result

bouton.notes: Covers three distinct English words depending on context: a shirt 'button', an elevator/device 'button' or 'switch', a rose 'bud' ('bouton de rose'), and a skin 'pimple' ('avoir des boutons').

boutonner.etymology: Formed in Old French (12th century) from bouton ('bud of a plant; round button on a garment'), itself derived from Old French bouter ('to push out, sprout, thrust'), borrowed from Frankish *bōtan ('to strike, push, sprout'). Before buttons fastened clothing, bouton meant a flower bud pushing outward in spring, so boutonner meant both 'to bud' (of trees) and 'to fasten buttons'.

history.meaning: bud, button -> to bud; to button up

boutonner.notes: Adding the prefix **dé-** gives the opposite action: **déboutonner sa veste** ('to unbutton one's jacket').

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: boutonner

boîte.etymology: Inherited from Old French boiste ('small box, pyx'), from Vulgar Latin *buxida, borrowed from Late Greek pyxida (accusative of pyxis 'boxwood receptacle, small box'), derived from pyxos ('box tree, boxwood').

boîtier.etymology: Derived within French from boîte ('box') with the suffix -ier. Boîte itself goes back through Old French boiste to Late Latin buxida, from Greek pyxís ('small boxwood container', from pýxos 'box tree').

history.meaning: protective casing, watch case, junction box

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: boîtier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: boîtier

branche.etymology: Inherited from Old French branche ('tree bough, branch'), from Late Latin branca ('paw, claw of an animal'), which developed the metaphorical sense 'forking bough of a tree' in Gallo-Romance.

history.meaning: animal paw or claw -> branching limb

brancher.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from branche ('branch'); originally meant 'to perch on a branch' (or hang a thief from a tree), then in modern technical usage 'to connect a branch pipe or electrical lead, plug in'.

history.meaning: to perch on a branch -> to tap a line, plug in, connect

braquage.etymology: Formed in 20th-century French from braquer ('to aim a weapon, steer sharply, rob at gunpoint') + action suffix -age. Middle French braquer (15th–16th century) originally meant 'to pivot the shafts or carriage of a cannon or wagon to aim it', derived from Old French brac / braquet ('beam, arm'), ultimately going back to Classical Latin bracchium ('arm'). In mid-20th-century underworld argot, 'aiming a gun at someone' specialized into 'armed hold-up'.

history.meaning: to pivot a gun carriage or wagon pole; to aim a firearm
sharp steering turn; armed robbery, heist

morphemes.meaning: to aim a weapon, hold up (braquer)
noun suffix denoting an action or its result

braquage.notes: Standard term in crime dramas ('film de braquage' = 'heist movie') and Figuratively used in negotiations when an agent or producer feels fleeced ('C'est du braquage !' — 'That's daylight robbery!').

rootFamily.gloss: to aim, steer, rob at gunpoint; to antagonize (se braquer)

bras.etymology: Inherited from Old French braz ('arm'), from Classical Latin bracchium ('forearm, arm'), borrowed from Ancient Greek brachion ('upper arm, arm').

brave.etymology: Borrowed in the early 16th century (during the Italian Wars) from Italian bravo ('bold, untamed, fine') and Spanish bravo ('fierce, wild'), both generally traced to Vulgar Latin *brabus, a dissimilated variant of Classical Latin barbarus ('foreign, untamed, fierce', from Ancient Greek bárbaros). In French, the adjective developed a famous positional split between 'courageous' and 'good-hearted, decent, obliging'.
brave.notes: Classic word-order trap: after the noun, 'un homme brave' means 'a courageous man', whereas before the noun, 'un brave homme' means 'a decent, nice fellow' (sometimes with a slightly patronizing edge).

bravo.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from Italian bravo! ('well done!, bold!, admirable!'), exclamation of the adjective bravo ('bold, wild, untamed'), probably from Vulgar Latin *bravus (an alteration of barbarus 'untamed, wild' or pravus 'crooked, fierce').

bref.etymology: Inherited via Old French brief ('short in space or time', 11th century; feminine brieve, modernized to brève) from Classical Latin brevis ('short, small, concise'), itself from Proto-Indo-European *mréǵʰus ('short', cognate with Ancient Greek brakhýs). In Middle and Modern French, the masculine monophthongized from brief to bref, and its absolute discourse use ('Bref, ...') became one of the most frequent conversational summarizers in the language.

history.meaning: short in length or duration, concise
short, brief; in short, anyway (discourse marker)

bref.notes: As an interjection/discourse marker, 'Bref...' ('Anyway...', 'Long story short...') is indispensable in spoken French for cutting off a rambling anecdote and jumping to the point.

rootFamily.gloss: short news item; musical breve; feminine of bref

bricolage.etymology: Formed in Modern French from bricoler ('to do odd jobs, tinker; originally to rebound or zigzag', from Old/Middle French bricole 'catapult, rebound of a ball in court tennis', from Italian briccola) + suffix -age.

cognates.meaning: concise set of instructions; legal summary
letter (old loan from Late Latin breve)

brief.etymology: A classic 20th-century 'aller-retour' (boomerang) borrowing from English brief ('concise instructions, project summary', clipping of briefing or nominal brief), which English had earlier borrowed from Anglo-Norman and Old French brief ('official letter, writ, summary note'), itself from Late Latin breve ('short document, inventory'), neuter substantive of Classical Latin brevis ('short'). Popularized in French via advertising, communications, and film/talent agencies.

history.meaning: project instructions, preparatory briefing (reborrowed from English)

brief.notes: Pronounced /bʁif/ (masculine: 'un brief'). Staples of Parisian agency, PR, and casting life ('faire un brief avant le rendez-vous'), though the Académie française recommends 'breffage' or 'consignes'.

rootFamily.gloss: to brief, give instructions prior to a meeting

briefer.etymology: Coined in late 20th-century French professional and media jargon by adapting the English verb to brief ('to instruct or prepare someone concisely before an operation, meeting, or audition') into the productive French first conjugation with -er. Ultimately a boomerang borrowing: English brief stems from Anglo-Norman brief ('writ, summary letter'), from Late Latin breve, neuter of Classical Latin brevis ('short').

history.meaning: to summarize facts for counsel; to instruct before a mission
to prep or instruct a client, actor, or team member

briefer.notes: Pronounced /bʁi.fe/, conjugated regularly like 'parler' ('Je l'ai briefé avant son casting' — 'I prepped him before his audition'); ubiquitous in 'Dix pour cent' whenever agents coach actors before meeting a director.

rootFamily.gloss: to debrief, review after an event

brigade.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Italian brigata ('company, troop, band of soldiers or companions'), a participial noun from brigare ('to contend, strive, brawl'), derived from briga ('strife, quarrel, trouble'), which goes back to a pre-Roman Celtic/Gaulish root *brīga ('strength, might, valor', cf. Old Irish bríg). Beyond military and police units, Auguste Escoffier famously extended it in the late 19th century to the structured kitchen staff ('brigade de cuisine').

history.meaning: military/police unit; organized restaurant kitchen team

brigade.notes: In French cultural life, 'la brigade' immediately evokes three worlds: specialized police squads ('brigade criminelle'), a corporal's gendarmerie unit, or a restaurant's high-pressure 'brigade de cuisine'.

rootFamily.gloss: corporal/sergeant; stage manager's stick knocking three times in theater!
bandit, highwayman (originally a foot soldier in a brigata)
to campaign or scheme ambitiously for a post or award

brillant.etymology: Present participle of briller ('to shine, sparkle') used as an adjective and noun (for a cut diamond) since the 17th century.

briller.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian brillare ('to sparkle, glitter'), likely derived from Vulgar Latin *beryllare ('to gleam like a beryl crystal'), from Latin beryllus < Greek beryllos ('beryl, sea-green gemstone').

history.meaning: beryl gem -> to sparkle like a gem

brin.etymology: Attested since the 16th century ('slender shoot of a plant, blade of grass, strand of thread, tiny bit'), of uncertain origin—probably a figurative use of Old French brin ('noise, clamor, dash') or from a pre-Latin/Celtic root *brinos ('rod, shoot').

history.meaning: slender plant shoot, blade, strand, tiny bit

brioche.etymology: Brioche appears in fifteenth-century Norman French, built on the dialect verb brier (Old French broier, 'to knead or pound dough with a wooden roller').
brioche.notes: **Une brioche à la cannelle** = a cinnamon roll/bun.

brique.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century via Picard/Flemish from Middle Dutch brike ('broken piece, flat cake, fired clay brick', related to breken 'to break').

cognates.meaning: borrowed in the 15th c. via French/Flemish
unrelated in form, whereas English break shares the Germanic root

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: brique (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: brique

brique.notes: In French culinary slang, rectangular milk or juice cartons are also called **des briques** (**une brique de lait**).

brise.etymology: Attested from the 16th century as a nautical term ('steady northeast wind, light breeze'), cognate with Spanish brisa and English breeze; of uncertain ultimate origin (possibly related to Old French bise 'cold north wind').

cognates.meaning: bruise (partly blended with Old French brisier)

briser.etymology: Inherited from Old French brisier ('to break into pieces, smash, shatter', 11th century), continuing Gallo-Romance / Vulgar Latin *brīsiāre, borrowed from Gaulish *briss- ('to break, crush'; cf. attested Gaulish gloss bris- and Old Irish brissid 'breaks'), from Proto-Celtic *brissīti. Used both concretely for shattering rigid objects and figuratively for breaking hearts, careers, taboos, or silence.

history.meaning: to break, smash, crush into fragments
to break, shatter; to ruin emotionally or professionally

briser.notes: More dramatic and literary than everyday 'casser': you 'casses un verre' by accident, whereas you 'brises le silence', 'brises le cœur de quelqu'un', or 'brises une carrière' ('ruin a career').

bristol.etymology: Shortened from papier bristol (early 19th century), named after the English port city of Bristol, whose paper mills became famous around 1800 for smooth, heavy pasted card stock (Bristol board).

history.meaning: fine calling card, index card, or recipe card

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: bristol (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)

bristol.notes: In France today, **une fiche bristol** (or simply **un bristol**) is every student's, librarian's, and baker's favorite sturdy index card.

bromazépam.etymology: Coined in 20th-century international pharmaceutical nomenclature (patented by Roche in 1963) as a systematic chemical blend: brom- refers to bromine (French brome, coined in 1826 by chemist Antoine-Jérôme Balard from Ancient Greek brômos 'stench'), -az- indicates a nitrogen atom replacing carbon in a ring (from French azote 'nitrogen', Greek a- 'without' + zōḗ 'life'), and -épam is the standardized suffix for benzodiazepine anxiolytics modeled on diazépam.

history.meaning: stench (source of French brome) + lifeless (source of Lavoisier's azote)
history.stage: Ancient Greek roots in 18th–19th c. French chemistry

morphemes.meaning: nitrogen atom in heterocyclic ring (from azote)

bromazépam.notes: Best known in France under the iconic brand name 'Lexomil', culturally referenced in French films and series (including high-strung agents and actors) the way Americans reference Xanax or Valium.

bronze.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian bronzo ('copper-tin alloy, bell metal'), itself of debated origin—either from Medieval Latin aes Brundisinum ('copper of Brindisi, famous for bronze mirrors') or from Persian birinj ('copper, brass').

brouiller.etymology: Inherited from Old French broillier ('to dirty, mix up, confuse'), derived from broil / brouet ('broth, muddy mixture'), from a Gallo-Romance verb tied to Frankish *brod ('broth, brew', cognate with English broth).

history.meaning: broth, mixture -> to stir up, muddle, blur
to scramble, blur, jam, set at odds

cognates.meaning: broth (cognate with the underlying Germanic root *brod)

brouillon.etymology: Derived in the 16th century from the verb brouiller ('to mix up, muddle, blot with ink') with the suffix -on. Brouiller comes from Old French broillier ('to soil, stir into a mess'), derived from broil / brouet ('thick broth, muddy liquid'), itself borrowed from Frankish *brod ('broth, soup', from Proto-Germanic *bruþą). Originally a merchant's daybook or blotted worksheet, it came to mean any rough draft of a text or script.

history.meaning: to dirty, mix into a muddle, blot ink
daybook; rough draft of a writing; unmethodical, scatterbrained (adj.)

morphemes.meaning: to mix up, muddle, scribble over (brouiller)
nominal/adjectival suffix denoting a rough state or agent

brouillon.notes: Used both as a masculine noun ('un brouillon de scénario' — 'a rough script draft') and as an invariable-plural-hesitant colloquial adjective ('Il est un peu brouillon' — 'He's a bit disorganized/sloppy').

rootFamily.gloss: to muddle, scramble, cause a falling-out (se brouiller)

bruit.etymology: Substantivized past participle of Old French bruire ('to roar, rumble, rustle'), from Vulgar Latin *brugere, a blend of Classical Latin rugire ('to roar') and fremere / bracare.

history.meaning: to roar, rumble -> noise, sound, rumor

brume.etymology: Borrowed (partly via Old Occitan/Provençal nautical usage bruma) from Classical Latin brūma ('winter solstice; midwinter cold and winter mists'), which arose by regular syncope and assimilation from Archaic Latin *brevima (diēs), an ancient superlative of brevis ('short') literally meaning 'the shortest day of the year'. From 'wintry weather', the sense specialized into 'light mist or atmospheric haze'.

history.meaning: shortest day (winter solstice); midwinter cold and fog
light mist, atmospheric haze; mental haziness

brume.notes: Lighter, more poetic, and less opaque than 'brouillard' ('thick fog'); also spawned the Revolutionary calendar's autumn month 'Brumaire' ('month of mists') and cosmetic 'brumisateur' ('facial mist spray').

rootFamily.gloss: Month of Mists in the French Republican Calendar

brun.etymology: Inherited from Old French brun ('dark brown, dusky, gleaming'), borrowed from Frankish *brun ('brown, shining', from Proto-Germanic *brunaz, cognate with English brown).

cognates.meaning: brute; brut (dry champagne, borrowed from French)

brut.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th–15th century) from Classical Latin brūtus ('heavy, unwieldy, dull, irrational, insensible'), an Oscan-Umbrian loanword in Latin from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrūtós ('heavy', related to Latin gravis). Under the influence of Italian mercantile usage (brutto 'unrefined, including tare weight'), French developed the senses 'raw, unpolished, uncut' (gems, timber, raw talent) and 'gross' (before deductions).

history.meaning: unreasoning, rough; uncut or unrefined (of stones/goods)

brut.notes: Pronounce the final 't' (/bʁyt/)! Essential in contract negotiations ('salaire brut' = gross pay vs. 'salaire net' = take-home pay), champagne orders, and praising an actor's 'talent brut' ('raw talent') or 'brut de décoffrage' ('rough around the edges, unfiltered').

rootFamily.gloss: to deaden, stupefy, overwhelm with mindless toil

brutal.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Late Latin brūtālis ('belonging to beasts, irrational, coarse', attested in Macrobius), derived from Classical Latin brūtus ('heavy, dull, unreasoning; brute animal') + relational suffix -ālis. Initially contrasting animal instinct with human reason, it evolved in Modern French to mean 'violent, harsh' as well as 'sudden, abrupt, unvarnished' (e.g., un changement brutal).

history.meaning: bestial, savage, lacking refinement or gentleness

brutal.notes: Partial false friend: in French, 'brutal' very often means merely 'sudden, abrupt, or blunt' without physical cruelty—'un arrêt brutal' is a 'sudden stop' and 'une baisse brutale' is a 'sharp drop'.

bruyant.etymology: Adjective formed from the old present participle of bruire ('to roar, make noise', source of bruit).

brûlant.etymology: Present-participle adjective of brûler ('to burn'), attested since the 12th century as Old French bruslant. The verb brusler likely arose from a blend of Vulgar Latin *ustulare ('to scorch, singe', from Classical urere 'to burn') with an initial b- influenced by Germanic *brennan ('to burn') or broïr ('to char'). The circumflex in brûlant marks the historical loss of the s before l.
brûlant.notes: Between **froid** ('cold') and **brûlant** ('piping/scorching hot'), French uses **tiède** for 'lukewarm, pleasantly warm to the touch'.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: brûlant

brûler.etymology: Inherited via Old French brusler ('to burn, consume by fire', 11th century, gradually supplanting Old French ardre < Latin ārdēre) from Vulgar Latin *brūstulāre, a Gallo-Romance alteration of Late Latin ustulāre ('to scorch, singe', diminutive of Classical Latin ūrere, past participle ustus 'to burn'), crossed at the initial with Germanic/Frankish *brōjan ('to scald, burn') or *brunst ('burning'). The circumflex on û preserves the Old French s before l.

history.meaning: to singe, scorch + to scald, burn > to burn intensely
to burn, set on fire, be consumed by heat
to burn; to run a red light; to perform passionately on stage

brûler.notes: Essential theater and cinema idiom: 'brûler les planches' (literally 'to burn the floorboards') means to give an electrifying, passionate stage performance; meanwhile 'se brûler les ailes' means to get burned by overambition.

cognates.meaning: bulge (from the same Gaulish-Latin root bulga)
pouch, pocket, ditch in Dante's Malebolge (via Old French)

budget.etymology: A famous 18th-century 'aller-retour' (boomerang) loanword: borrowed in 1764 from English budget ('the Chancellor of the Exchequer's annual financial statement', named after the leather dispatch pouch in which he carried his papers), which English had borrowed from Old and Middle French bougette ('small leather wallet or travel bag'), diminutive of Old French bouge ('leather sack'), from Classical Latin bulga ('leather knapsack'), itself of Gaulish origin (*bulgā 'bag, belly').

history.meaning: small leather pouch, purse, or saddlebag
financial plan, allocated funds (reborrowed via English)

budget.notes: Pronounced the French way /byd.ʒɛ/ (silent final 't'); in French film production, 'un film à gros/petit budget' is a big-/low-budget film, and the adjective is 'budgétaire' (retaining the historical 't').

rootFamily.gloss: leather bag, closet, hovel (native survival of Latin bulga)

cognates.meaning: bush (from the same West Germanic root *busk)

buisson.etymology: Inherited from Old French buisson ('bush, thorny thicket, copse', 11th–12th century), continuing Gallo-Romance *būscōnem / *boscōnem, derived with the suffix -on from Late Latin *boscus ('wood, thicket'), itself borrowed from Frankish *busk ('bush, shrubbery, woodland', from Proto-Germanic *buskaz). Related to French bois and bouquet within the same Germanic-Romance word family.

history.meaning: bush, woodland > dense shrub or thicket

buisson.notes: Remember the classic French idiom 'faire l'école buissonnière' ('to play truant / skip school', literally 'to attend school in the bushes' rather than in the classroom).

rootFamily.gloss: relating to bushes; playing truant (école buissonnière)

bulle.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Latin bulla ('water bubble; round boss or amulet; leaden seal attached to papal documents').

history.meaning: papal bull; air or soap bubble, comic speech balloon

bureau.etymology: Inherited from Old French burel ('coarse woolen cloth'), derived from bure ('dark homespun wool cloth', from Late Latin burra 'shaggy wool'); shifted seamlessly from the coarse baize cloth covering a counting table -> the writing desk itself -> the office room -> the agency or staff working there.

history.meaning: coarse woolen cloth covering a counting-table
cloth-covered writing desk -> office room -> department

bus.etymology: Clipped in the 20th century from autobus ('motor bus'), itself modeled on omnibus (1828, from Latin omnibus 'for everyone', dative plural of omnis 'all').

cognates.meaning: buzzard (borrowed from Old French busard, from the same root)

buse.etymology: Inherited from Old French buise / buson ('buzzard, hawk of low hunting value', 12th century), from Vulgar Latin *būtiō / *būtēa, feminine collateral form of Classical Latin būteō ('buzzard, kind of hawk or falcon'), of onomatopoeic origin imitating the bird's plaintive mewing cry (compare Latin būbō 'eagle-owl'). Because medieval falconers considered the buzzard untrainable compared to noble falcons, 'buse' became a vivid metaphor for a dunce by the 16th century.

history.meaning: common buzzard; figuratively, a fool or hopeless incompetent

buse.notes: Frequently heard in exasperated spoken French as a mild insult for incompetence: 'Quelle buse !' ('What a dope!') or 'On ne saurait faire d'une buse un épervier' ('You can't make a silk purse out of a sow's ear'). Note: a homonym 'buse' ('pipe, nozzle') has a separate Dutch/Germanic origin.

rootFamily.gloss: harrier (bird of prey, from Old French busard)

business.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-19th century (attested in French around the 1840s–1870s) from English business ('commercial enterprise, trade, affairs'), itself from Middle English bisinesse, formed from bisi ('busy, diligent, anxious', Old English bisig) + abstract noun suffix -nesse. In French, it settled into both mainstream corporate/entertainment vocabulary (show-business) and colloquial talk for profitable or slightly opportunistic wheeling and dealing.

history.meaning: commerce, showbiz, lucrative or shady dealings (loanword)

business.notes: Masculine ('le business', pronounced /biz.nɛs/); in French cinema and talent representation, 'C'est le business' carries a pragmatic, unsentimental ring ('It's just business'), alongside 'le show-business' (often shortened to 'le showbiz').

cognates.meaning: archery target, mound behind a target; thick end (from Old French)

but.etymology: Attested in Old French since the 13th century as but ('archery target, mark aimed at; end, goal'), derived from Old French buter / bouter ('to strike, thrust, abut') crossed with Frankish *būt or Old Norse bútr ('stump, block of wood set up as a target'). From the physical wooden block at the end of a shooting range, the word naturally generalized to any abstract 'aim, purpose, objective' as well as a 'goal' in team sports.
but.notes: Pronunciation fluctuates in modern France: traditionally silent 't' before a consonant or in 'de but en blanc' (/by/), but increasingly pronounced /byt/ at the end of a phrase ('Quel est le but ?' and always in soccer 'But !'). Not related to English 'but'!

rootFamily.gloss: to stumble against, balk; to kill (slang)
mound, small hillock (originally the earth mound behind a target)

cognates.meaning: humming sound; excited media chatter or word of mouth

buzz.etymology: Borrowed around the turn of the 21st century from American English marketing and entertainment slang buzz ('excited word-of-mouth chatter, viral media attention'), a figurative extension of buzz ('the humming sound of bees or a murmuring crowd'), from Middle English bussen, of direct onomatopoeic origin. Rapidly integrated into French media and PR idiom in expressions such as faire le buzz.

history.meaning: to hum like an insect; low murmur of many voices
viral media hype, public sensation (faire le buzz)

buzz.notes: Masculine ('le buzz', pronounced /bœz/ in French!); watch out for the contrast between 'faire le buzz' (go viral / generate media hype) and 'un bad buzz' (a PR disaster or viral backlash—a classic French pseudo-anglicism collocation).

rootFamily.gloss: to go viral, generate media hype (colloquial verb)
intercom/game-show button (borrowed earlier from the same English root)

buée.etymology: Derived from Old French buer ('to wash linen in steaming hot lye-ash water'), borrowed from Frankish *bukon ('to steep laundry in beech-ash lye'); the noun shifted from 'washhouse steam' to 'mist/condensation on cold glass'.

history.meaning: to soak linen in hot lye
vapor condensation on windows or glasses

cognates.meaning: to steep linen in hot lye

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: buée (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: buée

buée.notes: Unlike **vapeur** (steam rising in the air), **la buée** specifically names the fine mist that fogs a windowpane or a pair of spectacles.

cognates.meaning: to baste (tack fabric loosely with long stitches, via Old French)
inner bark fiber used for binding and weaving

bâtir.etymology: Inherited from Old French bastir ('to build, erect; to weave or stitch together; to devise', 12th century), borrowed from Frankish *bastjan ('to bind or plait with bast fibers, construct wattle-and-daub walls'), derived from Proto-Germanic *bastaz ('bast, fibrous inner bark of lime trees'). The word uniquely preserves both ancient technical crafts in Modern French: constructing buildings/empires and 'basting' fabric with temporary stitches, with â marking the lost Old French s.

history.meaning: to plait with bark fiber, construct wattlework
to erect a structure; to stitch loosely; to contrive
to build, construct; to found or establish (a career, project); to baste cloth

bâtir.notes: More elevated and architectural or figurative than everyday 'construire': you 'bâtis un empire', 'bâtis une carrière', or describe someone vigorous as 'bâti comme une armoire à glace' ('built like a brick wall'). Regular 2nd-group (-ir/-issant) verb.

rootFamily.gloss: large rural house or country estate; fortified medieval new town (bastide)

cognates.meaning: baster (in sewing, from Old French bastir)

bâtisseur.etymology: Derived in Old and Middle French (bastisseor, 13th–14th century) from the extended stem bâtiss- of bâtir ('to build, construct', from Frankish *bastjan 'to weave wattlework with bast fibers') + the agentive suffix -eur (from Latin -ātōrem). Over the centuries, while maçon and constructeur took over routine construction, bâtisseur acquired a noble, visionary register denoting great architects, kings, and empire- or studio-builders.

history.meaning: one who erects buildings or fortifications
builder, founder of institutions, empires, or grand projects

morphemes.meaning: to build, construct (extended stem of bâtir)

bâtisseur.notes: Feminine is 'bâtisseuse'. Carries prestige and visionary scale ('les grands bâtisseurs de cathédrales', 'un bâtisseur d'empire')—for a regular building contractor, French uses 'entrepreneur' or 'constructeur'.

cognates.meaning: infant, young child (source of the 19th-c. French loan)

bébé.etymology: Adapted in the mid-19th century (popularized in France around 1840–1855) from English baby ('infant'), itself a Middle English diminutive (babi) of babe, originating in universal infantile labial babbling (ba-ba). In French, its rapid adoption and spelling bébé were reinforced both by native nursery reduplication and by the famous 18th-century nickname 'Bébé' borne by Nicolas Ferry, the beloved court dwarf of King Stanislas Leszczyński at Lunéville, which already meant 'little doll' in regional French.

history.meaning: doll, plaything; newborn or toddler; cherished project

bébé.notes: Always grammatically masculine ('un bébé', even for a baby girl: 'C'est un beau bébé !'). In agency and film-production talk, 'C'est mon bébé' ('This project/film is my baby') is used exactly as in English.

rootFamily.gloss: babysitter / babysitting (later reborrowings from the same English word)
foosball, table football (French pseudo-anglicism using English baby)

bénéfice.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old French (benefice, 12th–13th century, alongside the inherited phonetic doublet bienfait) from Classical Latin beneficium ('kindness, favor, service; legal privilege'), derived from beneficus ('generous, obliging'), a compound of bene ('well') and the stem of facere ('to do, make'). Initially denoting an ecclesiastical living or legal privilege (e.g., bénéfice du doute), it developed the commercial accounting sense of 'net financial profit' in the 17th–18th centuries.

history.meaning: kind deed, favor, legal privilege or grant
ecclesiastical endowment; legal privilege or advantage
financial profit, net gain; advantage (bénéfice du doute)

bénéfice.notes: Watch out for the false-friend nuance in business: 'les bénéfices' in corporate French means 'profits / net earnings' (often shortened in speech to 'faire du bénef'), whereas employee 'benefits/perks' are 'les avantages sociaux'.

rootFamily.gloss: good deed, benefit (popular inherited doublet of bénéfice)

cognates.meaning: beast (borrowed from Old French beste before s-loss)

bête.etymology: Inherited from Old French beste ('living creature, non-human animal; unreasoning person', 11th century), from Vulgar Latin bēsta, simplified from Classical Latin bēstia ('wild beast, animal lacking human reason'). As Old French preconsonantal s fell silent before t, beste became bête (marked with a circumflex, while learned derivatives like bestial kept the s). Used in apposition ('un homme bête', literally 'a beast-man'), the noun yielded the everyday French adjective for 'silly, foolish, stupid'.

history.meaning: animal, beast; figuratively, a dull-witted person

bête.notes: Softer and far more versatile than English 'stupid': 'C'est bête !' means 'What a shame / How silly!', 'Pas si bête !' means 'Clever idea!', and 'une bête de scène' is a powerhouse stage performer ('a stage animal').

rootFamily.gloss: silliness, blunder, nonsense; Cambrai mint candy
tiny creature, bug, critter (retaining the historical 's'!)
bestial, brutish (learned doublet from Latin bestiālis)

bêtement.etymology: Formed in Middle French (bestement, 15th century) by attaching the Romance adverbial suffix -ment to the adjective bête ('foolish, silly', from Old French beste < Vulgar Latin bēsta < Classical Latin bēstia 'beast'). As across Romance adverbs, -ment continues the Classical Latin ablative singular mente ('with a [foolish] mind, in a [foolish] frame of mind', from feminine mēns, mentis 'mind, intellect').

history.meaning: beast + with a ... mind (Latin ablative of manner)

morphemes.meaning: adverbial manner suffix ('-ly', from Latin mente)

bêtement.notes: Often means 'pointlessly / in a silly avoidable way' ('se blesser bêtement' = 'to injure oneself in a dumb accident') or, after 'tout', simply 'plain and simple' ('C'est tout bêtement un problème d'agenda' — 'It's quite simply a scheduling issue').

bêtise.etymology: Derived in Middle French from bête ('beast; foolish person', from Old French beste, inherited from Vulgar Latin *besta, altering Classical Latin bestia 'wild animal') + the abstract noun suffix -ise (from Latin -itia). Originally denoting beastly ignorance or stupidity, it softened in everyday speech to mean a silly mistake, nonsense, or childish mischief.
bêtise.notes: Extremely common in spoken French across registers: 'dire des bêtises' means talking nonsense, while 'faire une bêtise' ranges from a child's prank to a serious blunder.

c'est-à-dire.etymology: Lexicalized French explanatory locution formed from ce ('this/that', from Old French ço, Latin ecce hoc) + est ('is', Latin est) + à ('to', Latin ad) + dire ('to say', Old French dire, Latin dicere). Attested since Old French (c'est a dire) to gloss, clarify, or reformulate a preceding statement, mirroring Medieval Latin id est.
c'est-à-dire.notes: Used standalone with rising intonation ('C'est-à-dire ?'), it is the go-to polite prompt asking an interlocutor—like an evasive agent or producer—to clarify what they actually mean; abbreviated 'c.-à-d.' in writing.

cabinet.etymology: Formed in the 16th century (or reinforced by Italian gabinetto) as a diminutive of cabine ('small room, cabin'), denoting a small private room, study, closet, or professional office.

history.meaning: small private room, study, professional office, storage chest

cacher.etymology: Inherited from Old French cachier ('to press together, crush, tread down; later to conceal'), from Vulgar Latin *coacticare ('to press tightly together, stow away'), frequentative of Classical Latin coactare (from cogere 'to drive together, compress').

history.meaning: to press tightly together, pack away
to press down -> to tuck out of sight, hide

cachet.etymology: Derived in the 16th century from cacher in its etymological sense 'to press, compress, stamp' (from Vulgar Latin *coacticare 'to press together', frequentative of Classical Latin coactare, from cogere) + diminutive suffix -et. It first denoted a personal signet or wax seal on royal letters (lettre de cachet), then a stamped voucher redeemable for pay, and in the 19th–20th centuries an actor's or musician's per-performance fee.

history.meaning: signet ring, wax seal; mark of distinction
stamped fee voucher; artist's performance fee

cachet.notes: In French cinema and agency jargon (like ASK in Dix pour cent), 'le cachet' specifically means an actor's negotiated fee for a film or gig (compare 'intermittent du spectacle' pay rules), whereas 'avoir du cachet' means having distinctive charm—matching English 'cachet'.

rootFamily.gloss: to stamp, postmark, seal with wax

cachette.etymology: Formed in Middle French from cacher ('to hide, conceal', earlier Old French cachier 'to press, compact, stow away out of sight', from Vulgar Latin *coacticare 'to press together') + feminine diminutive suffix -ette. The semantic shift from 'pressing tightly' to 'stowing away' produced 'hiding', making cachette literally a 'little hiding spot'.

history.meaning: to press down; to stow away, conceal

cachette.notes: Watch the extremely frequent adverbial idiom 'en cachette' ('secretly, behind someone's back, on the sly'), e.g. reading a rival client's script 'en cachette'.

cadavre.etymology: Learned Middle French borrowing (14th–16th c.) from Classical Latin cadaver ('dead body, corpse'), a neuter noun derived from cadere ('to fall, fall dead in battle', from PIE *ḱad- 'to fall') with the rare suffix -aver. Literally 'that which has fallen', it replaced or supplemented older Old French charoigne and cors.

history.meaning: to fall, sink, die in battle

cadavre.notes: Masculine noun ('un cadavre'). Idiomatically, 'avoir des cadavres dans le placard' equals 'to have skeletons in the closet', and in colloquial French 'un cadavre' also jokingly means an empty bottle left after a party.

cadavérique.etymology: Formed in Early Modern French (late 17th c.) on the Latinate stem cadaver- (from Classical Latin cadaver 'corpse', from cadere 'to fall') + the learned relational suffix -ique (from Latin -icus, Greek -ikos), displacing or complementing cadavéreux (from Latin cadaverosus) especially in anatomical and clinical terminology before gaining figurative use for ghastly pallor.

history.meaning: pertaining to a corpse; ghastly pale

morphemes.meaning: relating to, having the nature of (-ic)

cadavérique.notes: Used medically in 'rigidité cadavérique' (rigor mortis) and figuratively in 'un teint cadavérique' (a deathly pale complexion—say, an actor exhausted after a night shoot).

cadeau.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Occitan capdel ('capital letter heading a chapter', from Latin capitellum 'little head'); calligraphers' ornate flourished capitals became 'festive flourishes / treats offered to please someone', and by the 18th century 'a gift'.

cognates.meaning: native northern French doublet from capitellum

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cadeau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cadeau

cadeau.notes: Originally a calligrapher's decorative flourish added 'purely for pleasure rather than utility', **un cadeau** came to replace **un présent** in everyday French.

cognates.meaning: core group of trained personnel (from French)

cadre.etymology: Borrowed in the early 16th century from Italian quadro ('square; picture frame; painting'), itself inherited from Classical Latin quadrum ('a square, four-sided figure', related to quattuor 'four'). From a physical picture frame it broadened to 'setting, environment', 'camera framing' in cinema, and (via military officer rosters) 'corporate executive/manager'.

history.meaning: square; decorative border or picture frame

cadre.notes: Polysemous powerhouse: 'dans le cadre de' ('within the framework/context of'), 'un cadre agréable' ('a pleasant setting'), 'un cadre supérieur' ('a senior executive'), and on a film set 'hors cadre' ('off-camera / out of frame').

rootFamily.gloss: camera framing, composition of a shot

café.etymology: Café ultimately comes from Arabic qahwa through Turkish qahve. The Académie considers Italian caveé or caffè the probable intermediary into French. It records the seventeenth-century French spellings cauueh and cafeh.
café.notes:
- *Un café* in France is normally a small, strong espresso. For a milky coffee, ask for *un café crème* or *un café au lait*.
- The same word names both the drink and the place.

cahier.etymology: Cahier comes from Old French quayer, cayer, from Vulgar Latin *quaternium (Latin quaternio, 'gathering of four folded sheets', from quattuor 'four'). English 'quire' (of paper) comes from the exact same Old French word!
cahier.notes: Used for school exercise books and large bound ledgers.

caisse.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Old Occitan caissa ('wooden chest, box'), inherited from Classical Latin capsa ('cylindrical box for book rolls, chest, coffer', from capere 'to hold, contain', doublets with native French châsse).

history.meaning: packing crate, cash box, checkout counter, car body

caler.etymology: Combines two sources: (1) 'to wedge, prop up with a chock', derived from cale ('wooden wedge', from Middle High German kil / dialectal German Keil 'wedge'); and (2) 'to lower a sail; to stall or give up', borrowed via Occitan calar from Late Latin chalare < Ancient Greek chalan ('to slacken, let down').

history.meaning: to lower a sail; to wedge firmly in place
to wedge steady; (of an engine) to stall

cognates.meaning: to shout, summon (source of English call)

call-back.etymology: Twentieth-century borrowing from American English theatrical and film-casting jargon callback (compound of call, from Old English ceallian / Old Norse kalla 'to summon loudly', + adverbial particle back, from Old English bæc). Adopted directly into Parisian casting and talent-agency French to denote a second-round audition when a director narrows down shortlisted actors.

history.meaning: second or subsequent audition for a role

call-back.notes: Masculine noun ('un call-back', plural 'des call-backs'); quintessential Parisian casting-agency anglicism alongside 'casting', 'self-tape', and 'showrunner'.

rootFamily.gloss: to phone back; to recall (native French equivalent)

calligraphie.etymology: Learned borrowing in the 16th–17th century from Ancient Greek kalligraphia ('beautiful handwriting'), a compound of kallos ('beauty', from kalos 'beautiful') and graphein ('to write, draw, engrave'). Humanist printers and writing masters revived the Greek compound to celebrate the art of shaping letters harmoniously with a reed or quill pen.

history.meaning: the art of fine handwriting, calligraphy

calligraphie.notes: Shares its first Greek element **kalli-** ('beautiful') with **kaléidoscope**.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: calligraphie

calme.etymology: Calme entered Middle French via Italian calma ('stillness free of wind at sea'), ultimately from Late Latin cauma and Ancient Greek kaûma ('midday heat', when flocks and winds rest).
calme.notes: Both adjective (*une cour calme*) and masculine noun (*le calme*).

cognates.meaning: in a calm manner (root borrowed via French)

calmement.etymology: Formed in French from the epicene adjective calme ('windless, tranquil', borrowed in the 15th century from Old Italian calmo / calma 'stillness at midday, lull at sea', from Late Latin cauma 'burning heat of the midday sun when everything rests', itself from Ancient Greek kaûma 'heat', from kaíein 'to burn') + the adverbial suffix -ment (from the Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind').

history.meaning: burning midday heat (when work and wind cease)
midday rest; windless lull at sea, calm

morphemes.meaning: adverbial manner suffix (-ly, from Latin mente)

calmement.notes: Because 'calme' already ends in a mute '-e', '-ment' attaches directly without change; its unexpected Greek root originally referred to the siesta stillness of blazing noon!

calmer.etymology: Derived in the 15th century from calme ('calm, windless stillness at sea'), borrowed via Italian calmo / calma from Late Latin cauma ('burning heat of the midday sun when the wind drops and all rests'), from Ancient Greek kauma ('burning heat', from kaiein 'to burn').

history.meaning: midday heat when winds die down -> stillness, calm
to make calm, soothe, quiet down

cognates.meaning: site of the Crucifixion; severe ordeal

calvaire.etymology: Learned borrowing (12th–13th c. as proper noun, 16th–17th c. figuratively) from Ecclesiastical Latin Calvaria ('Place of the Skull', translating Aramaic Golgotha via Greek Kraníou Tópos in the Vulgate Gospels), derived from Classical Latin calvaria ('skull, cranium'), from calvus ('bald'). From the Passion of Christ on Mount Calvary, it came to denote a wayside crucifix and, figuratively, any agonizing, drawn-out ordeal.

history.meaning: dome of the skull, cranium (from calvus 'bald')
wayside cross; prolonged torment or ordeal

calvaire.notes: Masculine noun ('un vrai calvaire!'); completely everyday in secular modern French to describe a nightmare shoot, a bureaucratic ordeal, or a disastrous promotional tour—without sounding overly religious.

rootFamily.gloss: baldness (from the same Latin root calvus)

camarade.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-16th century from Spanish camarada (or Italian camerata), originally a feminine collective noun meaning 'a chamberful of soldiers sharing quarters and meals', derived from cámara ('room, chamber', from Late Latin camara / Classical Latin camera 'vaulted room', from Ancient Greek kamára 'vault'). It soon individualized to mean a single bunkmate, classmate, or peer.

history.meaning: group of soldiers sharing a barracks room; bunkmate

camarade.notes: Epicene noun ('un/une camarade'): neutral and warm in 'camarade de classe' (classmate) or theatrical 'mes petits camarades' (fellow cast members), though standalone 'camarade!' also carries trade-union or left-wing political resonance.

rootFamily.gloss: bedroom, room (inherited doublet of Latin camera)

camion.etymology: Attested in the 14th century in northern French (Norman-Picard camion, originally 'very small pin' and later 'low heavy dray or cart'), of uncertain origin.

history.meaning: low heavy dray or wagon -> motor truck, lorry

camionnette.etymology: Formed in late nineteenth-century French as the diminutive (-ette) of camion ('heavy dray cart, truck'), originally a Norman-Picard dialect word (camion, 14th c.) for a low transport dray.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: camionnette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: camionnette

camomille.etymology: Borrowed via Medieval Latin camomilla from Ancient Greek khamaímēlon, literally 'ground-apple' (khamaí 'on the earth, low-growing' + mêlon 'apple'), because fresh chamomile blossoms give off a crisp scent of ripe apples.

cognates.meaning: chamomile (literally 'little apple', a calque of the Greek!)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: camomille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: camomille

camomille.notes: Spanish **manzanilla** ('little apple') translates the Greek metaphor directly into Romance.

cognates.meaning: organized military or media drive; sparkling wine region

campagne.etymology: Inherited in Old French (champaigne 'open plain') and reinforced in the 16th century by Italian campagna ('open country; seasonal military expedition in the field'), both from Late Latin campania ('level country, open plain', originally referring to the fertile plain around Naples), substantivized feminine of campanius, from Classical Latin campus ('open field, plain'). Armies took the field in spring, giving rise to the sense 'military, political, or promotional campaign'.
campagne.notes: Notice the double meaning: 'à la campagne' means 'in the countryside', whereas 'en campagne' or 'une campagne de promo' means campaigning (for an election, César award, or film release)—and capitalized 'la Champagne' is its native Old French phonetic twin!

rootFamily.gloss: field (native French evolution of Latin campus)

cognates.meaning: to pitch camp; to place boldly in a scene
to set up a camp (borrowed via French)

camper.etymology: Derived in the 16th century from camp ('military encampment', borrowed via Italian campo or Picard camp from Classical Latin campus 'open field, military drill ground') + first-group verbal suffix -er. From pitching an army's tents firmly on a position, it developed two rich idioms: standing firm ('camper sur ses positions') and, in theater/cinema, vividly embodying a character ('camper un personnage').

history.meaning: to pitch camp; stand firm; portray a role vividly

camper.notes: Essential in two *Dix pour cent* contexts: in tough contract negotiations 'camper sur ses positions' means refusing to budge an inch, and in film reviews 'camper un rôle' means bringing a character vividly to life on screen.

rootFamily.gloss: to pack up camp, clear out quickly

caméra.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century from English camera, itself a shortening of New Latin camera obscura ('dark chamber', optical device used by Renaissance painters and early photographers), from Classical Latin camera ('vaulted room, chamber'), borrowed from Ancient Greek kamára ('anything with an arched cover, vaulted room'). It is thus an etymological doublet of French chambre.

history.meaning: darkened optical chamber projecting an image

caméra.notes: Crucial false friend with English! In French, 'une caméra' shoots moving video or film (cinema, TV, webcam, surveillance), whereas a still photographic camera is 'un appareil photo'.

rootFamily.gloss: bedroom, chamber (inherited doublet from Latin camera)

canadien.etymology: Formed in 16th–17th century French from Canada—recorded by navigator Jacques Cartier in 1535 from Laurentian (St. Lawrence Iroquoian) kanata ('village, settlement', originally referring to Stadacona near present-day Quebec City)—plus the relational/demonym suffix -ien (from Latin -ianus). Historically in New France, 'Canadien' specifically designated French-speaking settlers of the St. Lawrence valley.

history.meaning: territory along the St. Lawrence River
pertaining to Canada or its inhabitants

canadien.notes: French capitalization rule: lowercase as an adjective ('le cinéma canadien', 'une coproduction franco-canadienne'), capitalized only as a noun for a person ('un Canadien, une Canadienne'). Feminine is 'canadienne'.

rootFamily.gloss: fleece-lined sheepskin/canvas winter jacket; small tent

cognates.meaning: overhanging fabric hood; bite-sized savory appetizer (from French)
upholstered settee; savory bread hors d'oeuvre

canapé.etymology: Evolved in Early Modern French (attested 17th c. as 'curtained couch') from Medieval Latin canapeum, an alteration of Classical Latin conopeum ('bed fitted with a mosquito net'), borrowed from Ancient Greek kōnōpeîon ('Egyptian couch with mosquito curtains'), derived from kṓnōps ('mosquito, gnat'). From a curtained day-bed, it shifted to an upholstered sofa, and metaphorically to a slice of bread 'cushioned' with savory toppings.

history.meaning: couch enclosed with a mosquito net (from kṓnōps 'mosquito')
upholstered sofa/couch; topped bread hors d'oeuvre

canapé.notes: Partial false friend: while 'petits canapés' can mean cocktail appetizers, in everyday French 'le canapé' (often shortened colloquially to 'le canap') almost always means the living-room sofa or couch—and in showbiz, 'la promotion canapé' means the 'casting couch'.

rootFamily.gloss: forest treetop canopy (re-borrowed via English canopy, same root!)

canard.etymology: Formed in Old and Middle French from cane ('female duck', originally 'quacking bird' from an onomatopoeic stem *kan- imitating the bird's nasal call, displacing Old French ane from Latin anas) + the masculine pejorative/augmentative suffix -ard (of Frankish origin, *-hard). From the bird's noisy quack, it gained secondary senses including a sour musical note, a hoax story ('vendre un canard à moitié'), and a slang word for a newspaper.

history.meaning: duck; false note; hoax/tabloid newspaper; sugar cube dipped in coffee/brandy

canard.notes: Rich slang in media circles: 'un canard' is colloquial for a newspaper (famously the investigative weekly *Le Canard enchaîné*), 'un vilain petit canard' is an ugly duckling, and 'il fait un froid de canard' means it's freezing cold (duck-hunting weather).

rootFamily.gloss: female duck (and source of 'marcher en canard')
to snipe at from cover; to hit sour notes

cancer.etymology: Learned 15th–16th century medical re-borrowing from Classical Latin cancer ('crab; creeping malignant tumor'), cognate with and modeled semantically on Ancient Greek karkínos ('crab; malignant ulcer', because physicians like Hippocrates and Galen likened the swollen veins radiating from a tumor to a crab's legs, from PIE *karkr-o-). It is a learned doublet of inherited French chancre.

history.meaning: crab; spreading tumor with crab-like veins

cancer.notes: Pronounced /kɑ̃.sɛʁ/ with an audible final '-r'. Its native Old French phonological twin is 'chancre' ('ulcer, tree canker'), illustrating how French often pairs an inherited popular word with a later learned Latin medical borrowing.

rootFamily.gloss: ulcer, canker (inherited popular doublet of Latin cancer)

candidat.etymology: Learned borrowing (14th–16th c., initially in Roman history contexts) from Classical Latin candidatus ('one clothed in glittering white; seeker of public office'), passive participle formation from candidus ('dazzling white, pure', from candere 'to shine brightly, glow white'). In republican Rome, citizens campaigning for magistracies wore a specially chalk-whitened toga (toga candida) in the Forum to signify civic purity and stand out in crowds.

history.meaning: man wearing a whitened toga while seeking public office
male applicant, exam taker, or award/election nominee

candidat.notes: Silent final '-t' (/kɑ̃.di.da/). Covers a broader range than English 'candidate': job applicants, game-show contestants, exam sitters ('candidat au bac'), and actors shortlisted for a role or César award.

rootFamily.gloss: ingenuous, naive (from the same Latin candidus 'pure white')

candidate.etymology: Regular French feminine inflection of candidat (attested progressively from the 18th–19th centuries as women entered examinations, stage competitions, and public life), ultimately from Classical Latin candidata, feminine of candidatus ('robed in a whitened toga as a seeker of office', from candidus 'gleaming white', candere 'to shine'). Adding final '-e' causes the final dental consonant /t/ to be pronounced.

history.meaning: seeker of an office, prize, or post

candidate.notes: Pronunciation contrast is key for listening comprehension: masculine 'candidat' ends in an open vowel /kɑ̃.di.da/, whereas feminine 'candidate' clearly pronounces the final /t/ (/kɑ̃.di.dat/).

canne.etymology: Inherited via Old French cane from Classical Latin canna ('reed, cane, hollow stem'), which was borrowed from Ancient Greek kanna and ultimately traces back to Semitic (compare Akkadian qanû and Hebrew qāneh 'reed'). Because sturdy, lightweight Mediterranean reeds were cut to make measuring rods and walking sticks, canne came to denote both the plant (canne à sucre) and a gentleman's walking stick.
canne.notes: The diminutive of **canne** gave **cannelle** ('cinnamon', literally 'little hollow reed', from the rolled shape of cinnamon bark) and **canon** ('tube, cannon').

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: canne

cannelle.etymology: Cannelle comes from Old French canele ('little reed or tube', diminutive of canne from Latin canna 'reed'), named after the rolled quill shape of dried cinnamon bark.
cannelle.notes: Italian *cannella* and Spanish *canela* share the exact same image of a rolled reed.

cognates.meaning: having the ability or capacity (borrowed from French)
spacious; able, competent (from Late Latin capax)

capable.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Late Latin capabilis ('able to hold, receptive; intelligible'), derived from Classical Latin capere ('to take, seize, hold, contain', from PIE *kap- 'to grasp'). Originally meaning 'spacious enough to contain' or legally 'fit to inherit', it evolved by the 17th century to mean 'having the skill, power, or nerve to do something'.

history.meaning: able to hold or grasp; receptive
able, competent; daring enough (capable de tout)

capable.notes: Takes the preposition 'de' ('être capable de faire quelque chose'). Colloquially shortened to 'cap' in dares ('Cap ou pas cap ?' — 'Dare or no dare?'), and 'il est capable du pire' warns someone stops at nothing!

rootFamily.gloss: to capture, pick up (a signal or attention; same Latin capere)

capitaine.etymology: Inherited from Old/Middle French capitaine, from Late Latin capitaneus ('prominent in size, chief, leader'), formed on Classical Latin caput, capitis ('head').

history.meaning: leader of a company or vessel

cognates.meaning: both borrowed from Old French forms of capitaneus
native doublet directly from Latin caput

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: capitaine (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: capitaine

capitaine.notes: **Chef** and **capitaine** both grow from Latin **caput** ('head'), one through popular Gallo-Romance sound change and the other through medieval administrative Latin.

cognates.meaning: chief, vital; accumulated wealth; seat of government
essential, chief; wealth or capital city

capital.etymology: Learned Old French borrowing (12th c. in 'peine capitale' and 'péché capital') from Classical Latin capitalis ('of the head; affecting life; chief, foremost'), derived from caput, stem capit- ('head', from PIE *káput 'head'). Because the head is the seat of life and leadership, 'capital' came to mean both 'punishable by loss of one's head' and 'of paramount, vital importance'.

history.meaning: relating to the head or life; foremost, chief

capital.notes: Watch plural and gender distinctions: masculine plural is 'capitaux' ('des enjeux capitaux' = crucial stakes; 'des capitaux' = financial funds), feminine noun 'une capitale' means a capital city or uppercase letter, and its native French twin from 'caput' is 'chef'!

rootFamily.gloss: leader, head; chef (inherited popular doublet from Latin caput)
to summarize main headings; to capitulate (from capitulum 'little head')

cognates.meaning: understood, got it (past participle of capire)
fitted, held (cognate participle of caber, from Latin capere)

capito.etymology: Informal colloquial borrowing from Italian capito ('understood!'), elliptical use of '(hai) capito?' ('have you understood?'), the masculine singular past participle of capire ('to understand, grasp mentally'), inherited from Classical Latin capere (1st sg. capio 'to seize, grasp, take in', shifted to the fourth conjugation in Vulgar Latin *capire). Grasp by hand became grasp by mind.
capito.notes: Playful, punchy colloquialism in spoken French (much like in English): tossed at the end of a firm instruction ('Pas un mot à la presse, capito ?') for brisk, mock-bossy emphasis.

rootFamily.gloss: to pick up, get/understand (colloquial: 'T'as capté ?', same Latin root capere)
capable (from Late Latin capabilis, same root capere)

cognates.meaning: shiver of fear; sudden whim, artistic fantasy
sudden unaccountable change of mood or behavior (via French)

caprice.etymology: Borrowed in the late 16th century from Italian capriccio, originally 'a sudden shiver of horror making one's hair stand on end', compound of capo ('head', from Latin caput) + riccio ('hedgehog; frizzy/curled', from Latin ericius 'hedgehog', literally 'hedgehog-head'). By folk association with capra ('goat', notorious for erratic leaps), it shifted in Italian and French to mean a sudden artistic fancy or erratic whim.

history.meaning: shiver making hair bristle like a hedgehog; sudden fancy
sudden artistic impulse; unpredictable whim or tantrum

caprice.notes: A signature *Dix pour cent* word: 'les caprices de star' refers to the diva demands and sudden whims of pampered movie stars that talent agents constantly have to soothe.

rootFamily.gloss: temperamental, fickle, prone to whims (or changeable weather)
to develop a sudden infatuation for (s'encapricer)

capricieux.etymology: Borrowed in the late 16th century from Italian capriccioso ('whimsical, subject to sudden starts'), derived from capriccio ('sudden shudder or whim', from capo 'head' + riccio 'hedgehog, curled/standing on end' — originally 'a head with hair standing on end').

capsule.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin capsula ('small box or coffer'), diminutive of capsa ('cylindrical box for papyrus rolls'), related to capere ('to hold, contain').

history.meaning: small sealed container, seed pod, time capsule

cognates.meaning: crate / reliquary box (doublets from Latin capsa)
borrowed via French from Latin capsula

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: capsule (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: capsule

capsule.notes: In everyday French, **une capsule** can mean a bottle cap, a coffee pod, a space capsule, or **une capsule temporelle** ('time capsule').

car.etymology: Inherited from Old French quar / car ('for, because, therefore'), phonetic reduction of Classical Latin quare ('by what means, wherefore, why, therefore', literally qua re 'by which thing').

history.meaning: by which thing, wherefore, for which reason

cognates.meaning: distinctive nature; written symbol; fictional personage

caractère.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (caractere 'magical sign, distinctive mark') via Classical Latin character ('branding iron; distinctive mark; literary style') from Ancient Greek kharaktḗr ('engraving tool; stamped impression on a coin; distinctive mark of a person's nature'), agent/result noun from kharássein ('to sharpen, scratch, engrave'). From an indelible stamp on metal, it came to denote a person's temperament.

history.meaning: engraving tool; stamped mark on a coin; distinctive nature
branded mark, symbol; distinctive style or disposition

caractère.notes: Major false friend in cinema & TV! 'Un caractère' means temperament or personality ('avoir bon/mauvais caractère', 'avoir du caractère'), NEVER a fictional role in a movie or script—a movie/story character is 'un personnage'!

carafe.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century from Italian caraffa ('glass water decanter'), from Arabic gharrafa ('drinking vessel, ladle, water-scoop'), derived from gharafa ('to draw or scoop up water').

history.meaning: vessel for scooping water -> glass decanter
flared glass water or wine pitcher

cardiaque.etymology: Learned borrowing (14th–16th c.) via Classical Latin cardiacus from Ancient Greek kardiakós ('pertaining to the heart or upper stomach orifice'), derived from kardía ('heart', from PIE *ḱḗr, gen. *ḱr̥d-ós 'heart', the same Indo-European root that yielded Latin cor -> French cœur and Proto-Germanic *hertō -> English heart).

history.meaning: heart / pertaining to the heart or stomach
relating to the heart or gastric ailment
pertaining to the heart; person with a heart condition

cardiaque.notes: Epicene adjective and noun ('une crise cardiaque' = a heart attack; 'un arrêt cardiaque' = cardiac arrest). In casual exaggeration, 'Tu vas me rendre cardiaque !' means 'You're going to give me a heart attack!'

rootFamily.gloss: heart (inherited Latin cousin from the same PIE root *ḱḗr)

cognates.meaning: slaughter, heap of flesh; fresh meat tax
slaughter, butchery; meat supply aboard ship

carnage.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-16th century from Italian carnaggio (or Norman/Old Provençal carnatge 'meat ration; slaughter'), derived from Medieval Latin carnaticum ('tribute paid in livestock/meat; flesh'), built on Classical Latin caro, stem carn- ('flesh, meat', from PIE *(s)ker- 'to cut', originally 'a cut piece of meat') + collective suffix -aticum (French -age). From butchered meat, it came to mean battlefield slaughter and, colloquially, a total wreck or disaster.

history.meaning: meat ration; mass butchery, heap of corpses
bloodbath, slaughter; (figurative) total shambles or disaster

carnage.notes: Masculine noun ('un carnage'). Very common figuratively and humorously in everyday French: 'C'était un vrai carnage !' can describe a chaotic film pitch, a trashed hotel suite, or a brutal box-office flop.

rootFamily.gloss: flesh (native French evolution of Latin carnem)
massacre, bloodbath (native French parallel formation on charn-)

carnet.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Old Occitan carnet / quernet ('small group of four folded sheets of paper, booklet'), diminutive of quern ('quire of four sheets', French cahier), from Vulgar Latin *quaternum (from quattuor 'four').

history.meaning: gathering of four folded sheets -> small notebook
pocket notebook, booklet of tickets or checks

carotte.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Latin carota ('carrot'), itself from Ancient Greek karōtón, replacing the older medieval French name pastenade.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: carotte (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: carotte

carotte.notes: Notice the spelling contrast between French **carotte** (one *r*, two *t*'s) and English **carrot** (two *r*'s, one *t*).

carreau.etymology: Inherited from Old French quarrel ('four-sided block, square tile, crossbow bolt'), from Vulgar Latin quadrellum, diminutive of quadrum ('square', related to quattuor 'four'). From 'little square', it came to name both floor tiles and rectangular windowpanes.

history.meaning: tile; windowpane; check pattern; diamonds (in cards)

cognates.meaning: (archaic) square-headed crossbow bolt, from Old French quarrel

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: carreau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: carreau

carreau.notes: In everyday French, **faire les carreaux** means 'to wash the windows'.

carrière.etymology: In the career sense, carrière was borrowed from Old Provençal carriera, street, ultimately from a Latin expression for a road for carts. Its sixteenth-century French sense concerned a space for running horses. The quarry noun has a separate origin.

rootFamily.gloss: chariot, float (native Northern French outcome of carrus)

carrière.notes: Homonym note: une carrière ('stone quarry', from Late Latin *quadrāria 'place where stones are squared') has a completely separate etymology from une carrière ('career').

carrousel.etymology: Borrowed in the early 17th century from Italian carosello (Neapolitan garosello), originally a courtly equestrian pageant in which horsemen threw perfumed clay balls at one another (famously staged by Louis XIV in 1662 at the Place du Carrousel by the Louvre), probably related to carro ('chariot, cart', from Latin carrus, of Gaulish origin) or caracollo. Training devices with wooden horses on a rotating arm for tilting practice evolved into the fairground merry-go-round.

history.meaning: festive mock cavalry tournament with clay balls and tilting
royal equestrian spectacle (1662); rotating wooden-horse trainer
merry-go-round; airport baggage carousel; rotating media gallery

carrousel.notes: In France, 'le Carrousel du Louvre' still preserves the memory of Louis XIV's 1662 royal horse tournament! For a children's merry-go-round in a park, French uses both 'un carrousel' and 'un manège' (another equestrian training term!).

rootFamily.gloss: chariot, float, tank (from the same Gaulish-Latin carrus family)

carré.etymology: Inherited from Old French quarré ('four-cornered, square'), from Classical Latin quadratus ('squared, four-sided'), past participle of quadrare ('to make square'), from quattuor ('four').

carte.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century (replacing native Old French charte in everyday senses) from Classical Latin charta ('sheet of papyrus, paper, document'), from Ancient Greek chartes ('leaf of papyrus').

history.meaning: sheet of papyrus or stiff paper

cartographe.etymology: Modern scholarly compound formed from carte ('map', from Latin charta 'sheet of papyrus') + -graphe (from Ancient Greek gráphein 'to draw, write, chart').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cartographe (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)

cartographe.notes: Note that French **une carte** covers 'map', 'postcard' (**carte postale**), 'menu/wine list', and 'playing card' all in a single word.

cartographie.etymology: Learned compound coined in the early 19th century from carte ('map', from Latin charta) + -graphie (from Ancient Greek graphein 'to write, draw').

history.meaning: the art and science of drawing maps

carton.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian cartone ('heavy pasteboard, full-scale preparatory drawing for a fresco'), augmentative of carta ('paper', from Latin charta) with suffix -one.

history.meaning: thick paper, pasteboard; artist's full-scale sketch

cognates.meaning: pasteboard; large preliminary drawing (source of French carton)
cardboard box; preliminary sketch / comic strip (both from carton/cartone)

cartonner.etymology: Derived from carton ('cardboard; pasteboard target at a fairground shooting gallery', borrowed in the 16th century from Italian cartone, augmentative in -one of carta 'paper, card', from Latin charta, Ancient Greek khártēs 'sheet of papyrus') + verbal suffix -er. From 'hitting the bull's-eye of the cardboard shooting target' (faire un carton) and 'crashing hard', it became lively 20th-century slang for smashing box-office or audience records.

history.meaning: heavy pasteboard, cardboard; full-scale artist's sketch
to bind in boards; to crash; (colloquial) to score a smash hit

cartonner.notes: Indispensable showbiz verb in *Dix pour cent*: 'Le film cartonne au box-office !' or 'Ça va cartonner !' means it's an absolute smash hit (likewise the noun phrase 'faire un carton'). Watch context though: on the road, 'cartonner sa voiture' means crashing your car!

rootFamily.gloss: cardboard, box; bull's-eye / smash hit ('faire un carton')
card, map, menu (from the same Latin charta)

cas.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin casus ('a falling, chance occurrence, event, grammatical case'), action noun from cadere ('to fall').

history.meaning: to fall -> a fall, chance event, circumstance

cognates.meaning: stepped waterfall; series of stages (borrowed from French)

cascade.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-17th century (initially for ornamental Italianate garden waterworks at royal châteaux) from Italian cascata ('a fall, waterfall'), substantivized feminine past participle of cascare ('to fall, tumble down'), from Vulgar Latin *casicare ('to fall repeatedly, totter'), frequentative built on Classical Latin casus ('a fall'), from cadere ('to fall'). In the late 19th and 20th centuries, acrobatics and cinema extended 'tumbling fall' to 'performed stunt'.

history.meaning: waterfall; rapid chain ('en cascade'); film/circus stunt

cascade.notes: Essential cinema vocabulary: alongside 'waterfall' and 'en cascade' ('one after another in a chain reaction'), 'une cascade' is a movie stunt ('régler ses propres cascades' = to do one's own stunts), and a stunt performer is 'un cascadeur / une cascadeuse'.

rootFamily.gloss: to tumble down; lead a wild life; perform stunts
case, event, fall (learned cousin from Latin casus, cadere)

casque.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Spanish casco ('potsherd, skull, helmet'), derived from cascar ('to crack, break open'), from Vulgar Latin *quassicāre, a frequentative of Classical Latin quassāre ('to shake violently, shatter'). In the 20th century, its sense of protective headgear extended to radio headsets and audio headphones (casque audio).

history.meaning: protective helmet; audio headset or headphones

casque.notes: On film sets (as in Dix pour cent), le casque (or casque retour) commonly refers to the director's or sound engineer's monitoring headphones rather than a safety helmet.

rootFamily.gloss: to break, shatter (distant Latin quassāre doublet)

cognates.meaning: to annul, reject legally (via Old French)

casse.etymology: Deverbal feminine noun formed in Middle French from casser ('to break, shatter'), inherited via Old French quasser from Classical Latin quassāre ('to shake repeatedly, batter, shatter'), frequentative of quatere ('to shake, strike'). From physical breakage it developed industrial senses of scrap metal and idiomatic expressions like mettre à la casse ('to scrap').
casse.notes: Watch the gender split: la casse (feminine) means breakage or the scrap heap (partir à la casse, limiter la casse 'to do damage control'), whereas un casse (masculine, from colloquial casser 'to burgle') means a heist or break-in.

casser.etymology: Inherited from Old French quasser ('to shatter, break into pieces'), from Classical Latin quassare ('to shake violently, batter, shatter'), frequentative of quatere ('to shake').

cognates.meaning: to throw; to assign roles to actors

caster.etymology: Late 20th-century French cinema and talent-agency verb formed from the English theatrical root cast ('to assign dramatic parts', originally 'to throw, mold', borrowed into Middle English from Old Norse kasta 'to throw') integrated with the productive French first-group infinitive suffix -er.

history.meaning: to throw; to distribute roles in a play
to audition or select an actor for a role
