clientèle.notes: Notice the grave accent in French (clientèle, pronounced /klijɑ̃tɛl/) that English dropped when borrowing the word. Talent agents fiercely guard their portefeuille de clients / clientèle when rival agencies poach stars.

cognates.meaning: to lean, slope, be disposed toward

clignotant.etymology: Substantivized 20th-century present participle (short for feu clignotant, 'blinking light') of clignoter ('to blink repeatedly, flicker'), a frequentative derived with -oter from cligner ('to wink, half-close the eyes'). Old French clignier descends from Vulgar Latin *cliniare, built on Classical Latin clinare ('to bend, incline, lower'), applied specifically to lowering the eyelids.

history.meaning: to incline, bend down / to lower the eyelids
to wink, squint (12th c.) / to blink repeatedly, twinkle (16th c.)
blinking; automotive turn-signal indicator light (mid-20th c.)

clignotant.notes: Literally 'blinker' (mettre son clignotant = 'to put on one's turn signal'). Figuratively in news and business French, tous les clignotants sont au rouge means 'all warning lights/indicators are flashing red'.

rootFamily.gloss: to blink repeatedly, flash on and off

clignoter.etymology: Frequentative verb formed in Middle French from cligner ('to blink, wink, half-close the eyes') with the iterative suffix -oter ('to do repeatedly in small bursts'). Cligner descends from Spoken Latin *cliniare, related to clinare ('to incline, lower').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: clignoter (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: clignoter

clinique.etymology: Borrowed via Late Latin clinicus ('bedridden patient; bedside physician') from Ancient Greek klinikos ('pertaining to a bed'), derived from kline ('bed, couch'), from klino ('to lean, recline', PIE *klei-). Used first as an adjective in French (médecine clinique, 'instruction at the patient's bedside'), la clinique became a standalone feminine noun for a medical teaching ward and then a private hospital.

history.meaning: bedside medical teaching (17th–18th c.); private hospital facility (19th–20th c.)

clinique.notes: Partial false friend: whereas an English 'clinic' usually suggests a small outpatient walk-in center, une clinique in France is typically a full-scale private inpatient hospital (where stars discreetly check in for surgery, childbirth, or rest cures, contrasted with un hôpital public).

rootFamily.gloss: to lean, bow (same PIE *klei- root via Latin)

cloche.etymology: Cloche comes from Medieval Latin clocca ('bell'), a word spread across Europe by early Irish missionary monks (Old Irish cloc 'bell', ultimately imitative of ringing). English 'clock' comes from the exact same root!
cloche.notes: Diminutive **la clochette** = small handbell or gate bell.

clocher.etymology: Inherited from Old French clochier ('bell tower, steeple'), derived from cloche ('bell', from Late Latin clocca, brought across Europe by Early Medieval Irish missionaries, cf. Old Irish clocc 'bell') + place suffix -ier.

clochette.etymology: Diminutive in -ette of cloche ('bell'), from Merovingian/Medieval Latin clocca ('handbell'), spread across Western Europe by early Irish missionary monks (compare Old Irish cloc 'bell').

cognates.meaning: originally a bell-striking timepiece, from the same clocca word

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: clochette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: clochette

clochette.notes: Because early mechanical tower clocks had no dials and announced hours purely by ringing a bell, Medieval Latin **clocca** gave French **cloche** ('bell') and English **clock**.

cloison.etymology: Inherited from Old French cloison ('enclosure, fence, partition wall'), from Vulgar Latin *clausionem, derived from claudere (past participle clausus, 'to close, shut off').

clope.etymology: First attested in late 19th-century Parisian argot (c. 1891, originally masculine un clope meaning 'discarded cigarette butt, cigar end' gathered by street pickers) before shifting in the 20th century to a mostly feminine colloquial noun (une clope) for a whole cigarette. Its ultimate origin is uncertain: philologists propose either an expressive onomatopoeia for puffing/popping lips or a playful argotic apheresis of cyclope ('Cyclops', likening a glowing cigarette tip in the dark to a single burning eye).

history.meaning: discarded cigarette or cigar butt (Parisian argot)

clope.notes: Ubiquitous on French film sets and café terraces: Tu as une clope ? / On va fumer une clope ? ('Got a smoke? / Wanna go grab a smoke?'). Today une clope (feminine) strongly predominates over older un clope.

rootFamily.gloss: butt-picker (19th-c. Parisian slang ramasseur de clopes)

cognates.meaning: comic circus entertainer; originally rustic boor

clown.etymology: Borrowed in the early 19th century (1808/1823) from English clown ('comic stage and circus performer', earlier 16th-century 'rustic peasant, clumsy boor'). The English word is of Scandinavian or Low German origin (compare Icelandic klunni 'clumsy oaf', Low German klönne), belonging to a Germanic word family denoting a heavy clod, lump, or log.

history.meaning: country bumpkin, rustic boor; comic stage fool
acrobatic English pantomime and circus jester
circus clown; figuratively buffoon or joker

clown.notes: Pronounced /klun/ (like 'kloon', never rhyming with English 'town'!). Faire le clown means 'to fool around / play the fool', and French cinema distinguishes le clown blanc (witty, authoritative straight man) from l'auguste (bumbling slapstick comic).

cognates.meaning: association, sports team, nightclub; heavy stick

club.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century from English club ('social or political association of gentlemen', notably thriving during the French Revolution as le Club des Jacobins, and re-borrowed in the 19th–20th centuries for sports clubs, resorts, and nightclubs). English club comes via Middle English clubbe from Old Norse klubba ('thick cudgel, clump'), which evolved in 17th-century England via 'clubbing together' into a lump sum or shared-expense gathering.

history.meaning: association of persons meeting periodically (from 'clubbing' expenses)
political society (18th c.); exclusive circle, sports club, nightclub (19th–20th c.)

club.notes: Pronounced /klœb/ (with the open French eu vowel of peur, not /klʌb/). At Cannes or in Paris nightlife, un club private venue contrasts with une boîte (de nuit), while un club sandwich is a brasserie staple.

rootFamily.gloss: member of a select club or nightclubber

clé.etymology: Clé (also spelled clef) comes from Latin clavis ('key, bolt'), related to claudere ('to close'). Final v dropped in spoken French while spelling preserved -f in clef until modern clé became standard.
clé.notes: **Fermer à clé** = to lock; **sous clé** = under lock and key.

clôture.etymology: Inherited via Old French closture from Late Latin claustura ('barrier, enclosure, fastening'), formed on claudere, clausum ('to shut, close').

cognates.meaning: from sister formations on Latin claudere

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: clôture (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: clôture

clôture.notes: Once again, the circumflex in **clôture** preserves the memory of the vanished *-s-* in Old French **closture**.

cocasse.etymology: First recorded in the mid-18th century (originally spelt coquasse in informal Parisian and Norman usage, meaning 'foolish, laughable, mocking'), likely formed from coq ('rooster', of expressive/onomatopoeic origin, long associated in French idiom with strutting vanity and folly) + the expressive/pejorative adjectival suffix -asse. Over the 19th century its sting softened from 'ridiculous' to 'quirkily comical, delightfully odd'.

history.meaning: oddly funny, quirky, droll (of a situation or detail)

cocasse.notes: A favorite slightly literary/witty adjective in French comedy writing: une situation cocasse isn't slapstick hilarious—it's 'wryly absurd, deliciously awkward, quirky' (classic farce-of-manners territory).

cognates.meaning: small triangular bone at the base of the spinal column

coccyx.etymology: Learned Renaissance anatomical borrowing (used in French by Ambroise Paré in the 16th century) via Medical Latin coccyx from Ancient Greek kokkyx ('cuckoo bird; human tailbone'). The Hellenistic anatomist Herophilus of Chalcedon named the fused terminal vertebrae after the cuckoo because their curved, pointed silhouette resembles a cuckoo's beak.

history.meaning: cuckoo bird; by anatomical metaphor, curved tailbone
terminal bone of the vertebral column

coccyx.notes: Unlike English, French has no everyday native compound like 'tailbone'—everyone, from doctors to someone slipping on a stunt set (se fêler le coccyx), uses le coccyx (/kɔksis/).

cognates.meaning: mixed alcoholic drink; appetizer or reception

cocktail.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-19th century (attested in French around 1859–1860) from American English cocktail (first defined in print in New York in 1806 as 'a stimulating liquor, composed of spirits of any kind, sugar, water, and bitters'), literally compounding cock ('rooster') + tail. In 18th-century England, cock-tailed described a non-thoroughbred horse whose docked tail stood up like a rooster's—hence 'mixed breed/adulterated' or 'perked-up stimulant'.

history.meaning: horse with docked upright tail; non-thoroughbred (mixed blood)
mixed drink; by ellipsis (20th c.), cocktail reception party

cocktail.notes: Crucial agency/premiere usage: in French, un cocktail alone very frequently means 'a cocktail party / standing reception with drinks and canapés' (le cocktail après l'avant-première), not just the drink in a glass!

rootFamily.gloss: shaker for mixing cocktails (anglicism alongside shaker)

cognates.meaning: fruit of the coconut palm (historically spelt cocoanut)

coco.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (via travel accounts of the Indies) from Portuguese and Spanish coco ('grimacing face, bogeyman, goblin; coconut'). Vasco da Gama's Portuguese sailors returning from India (1498–1499) nicknamed the hard shell coco because the three dark germination pores at its base resemble the two eyes and mouth of a grinning goblin face.

history.meaning: bogeyman, grinning skull-like mask used to frighten children
coconut (named for its three face-like indentations)
coconut palm fruit and its white flesh/milk

coco.notes: Watch out for lively French homonyms! Un coco / une noix de coco is 'coconut' (lait de coco), whereas mon coco is a teasing/affectionate 'my lad / kiddo' (from coq), un drôle de coco is 'a sketchy character', and la coco is slang for cocaine!

cognates.meaning: system of laws; cipher, PIN, programming instructions
code of laws, cipher, zip/PIN code

code.etymology: Inherited and semi-learned adaptation in Old French (code, 13th century, originally denoting the Codex Justinianus of Roman imperial law) from Classical Latin codex, earlier caudex ('tree trunk, wooden block; set of wax-coated wooden tablets bound together as a book; ledger or book of statutes'). From Napoleonic law books (Code civil), it extended in the 19th–20th centuries to telegraph ciphers, road rules, and electronic access PINs.

history.meaning: tree trunk; bound wooden writing tablets; compilation of laws
body of laws, social conventions, secret cipher, keypad entry PIN

code.notes: Quintessential Parisian survival word: C'est quoi le code ? at an apartment building means the street-door keypad code (digicode); passer le code means taking the written driver's license exam (Code de la route); and connaître les codes du milieu means knowing industry etiquette.

rootFamily.gloss: to encode; to set an access code

coffre.etymology: Inherited from Old French cofre ('strongbox, chest'), from Classical Latin cophinus ('wicker basket'), borrowed from Ancient Greek kophinos ('large basket'), with consonantal change -phn- > -fr- (doublet of couffin).

cogner.etymology: Inherited from Old French coignier ('to drive in a wedge, stamp coins with a die, strike hard'), from Classical Latin cuneare ('to wedge, force with a wedge'), derived from cuneus ('wedge', source of French coin).

history.meaning: to drive a wedge -> to knock, bang, bump against

coiffer.etymology: Inherited from Old French coifier ('to cover the head with a linen cap or mail hood under a helmet'), derived from coife (modern coiffe, 'headdress, cap'), from Late Latin cofia / cuphia ('cap, helmet liner', attested 6th century in Venantius Fortunatus), generally traced to a West Germanic borrowing (compare Old High German kuppha 'head covering'). Meaning evolved from putting on headgear to arranging and styling the hair itself.

history.meaning: close-fitting cap or padded helmet liner
to cover the head with a coif or mail hood
to dress or style hair; to top/crown; idiomatically to edge out at the finish line

coiffer.notes: On a film shoot, the HMC department stands for Habillage, Maquillage, Coiffure ('wardrobe, makeup, hair'); se coiffer means 'to do/comb one's hair', while coiffer quelqu'un au poteau ('to nose someone out at the finish post') means beating a rival actor to a role at the very last second!

rootFamily.gloss: traditional headdress or cap; outer nose cone of a rocket

coiffeur.etymology: Derived from the verb coiffer ('to dress hair, cover the head') with the agentive suffix -eur. Coiffer comes from Old French coife ('linen cap worn under a mail hood, headdress'), from Late Latin cofia ('cap, helmet liner'), likely borrowed from West Germanic *kupphjō ('headgear'), itself connected to Late Latin cuppa ('cup, vessel').

history.meaning: skullcap; to cover with a headdress or hood

morphemes.meaning: to style hair, cover with a cap

coiffeur.notes: On film sets (as in Dix pour cent), the chef coiffeur heads the hair department; the feminine form is coiffeuse (which also denotes a dressing table).

rootFamily.gloss: to style or do someone's hair

coiffure.etymology: Formed in Middle French from coiffer ('to cover the head, dress hair') plus the resultative suffix -ure. Ultimately from Old French coife ('headdress, cap worn beneath a helmet') and Late Latin cofia ('cap'), reflecting the shift from ornamental head-coverings to sculpted hair arrangements at the French court.

morphemes.meaning: to dress hair, cover the head
action or result of an action

coiffure.notes: Refers both to an individual's hairstyle (une belle coiffure) and to the hairdressing trade (un salon de coiffure); paired on film shoots as HMC (habillage, maquillage, coiffure).

coin.etymology: Inherited from Old French coin ('iron wedge; minting die; angle, corner'), from Classical Latin cuneus ('wedge; wedge-shaped block or corner').

coincer.etymology: Derived in the 17th century from coin ('wedge, corner'); originally a carpenter's and printer's term meaning 'to secure tightly with wedges', then 'to jam, trap in a corner'.

history.meaning: to wedge tight -> to jam, get stuck, corner

colis.etymology: Borrowed in the early eighteenth century by Lyon and Marseille merchants from the Italian plural colli ('bales or bundles of goods', singular collo 'bundle carried on the neck or shoulder', inherited from Classical Latin collum 'neck'). Because shipping bills listed multiple colli, French reanalysed the plural with a silent final -s as a singular noun un colis.

history.meaning: neck; merchant bale carried on the neck/shoulder
shipping bale -> postal or courier parcel

colis.notes: Pronounced [kɔli] with a silent final -s, and spelled identically in singular and plural (un colis, deux colis).

collaborateur.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin collaborātor ('fellow worker'), agent noun from collaborāre ('to work together'), composed of the assimilating prefix com- ('with, together') and laborāre ('to toil, work', from labor). Popularized in 19th-century administrative and artistic French for co-workers and co-authors.
collaborateur.notes: Watch the register: in modern French workplaces (like the ASK agency), mes collaborateurs politely means 'my staff/associates', whereas the WWII sense 'wartime collaborator' is usually shortened to collabo.

collant.etymology: Present participle of coller ('to glue, stick, cling closely'); used as an adjective ('sticky, skin-tight') and since the 20th century as a noun for tights or pantyhose.

colle.etymology: Inherited from Old French cole ('paste, glue'), from Late Latin colla, borrowed from Ancient Greek kolla ('glue, paste made from hides or fish').

collectif.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French from Classical Latin collectīvus ('gathered together, condensed'), derived from collectus, the past participle of colligere ('to gather together, assemble'), formed from com- ('together') and legere ('to gather, pick, read').

history.meaning: to gather together / gathered into one body
pertaining to a group as a whole, shared

collectif.notes: Used both as an adjective (féminin: collective) and as a masculine noun (un collectif d'acteurs, 'an actors' collective/ensemble').

coller.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French from colle ('glue, paste') + verbal suffix -er.

history.meaning: to glue, paste, stick or press closely against

colline.etymology: Borrowed in the sixteenth century from Italian collina ('gentle hill'), derived from Classical Latin collis ('hill', adjective collinus 'of a hill').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: colline (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: colline

colline.notes: Lyon is traditionally described through its two famous **collines**: Fourvière (*la colline qui prie*) and la Croix-Rousse (*la colline qui travaille*).

collègue.etymology: Learned 16th-century borrowing from Classical Latin collēga ('partner in office, fellow magistrate'), formed from com- ('with, together') and the stem of legāre ('to depute, commission, appoint by law', related to lēx, 'law') — literally 'one chosen alongside another for a duty'.

history.meaning: partner in public office or priesthood

collègue.notes: Epicene noun (un collègue / une collègue); in theater and cinema, actors traditionally call fellow performers camarade or partenaire rather than collègue, while doctors and lawyers use confrère/consœur.

colonne.etymology: Inherited from Old French colombe / colone ('pillar, column'), from Classical Latin columna ('pillar, post, column', related to columen 'summit, gable, prop').

history.meaning: architectural pillar, vertical column of text or troops

colossal.etymology: Coined in 16th-century French (attested in Rabelais) from colosse ('giant statue') plus the adjectival suffix -al. Colosse was borrowed via Classical Latin colossus from Ancient Greek κολοσσός (kolossós, 'large statue'), famously applied to the gigantic bronze statue of Helios at Rhodes.

history.meaning: statue, especially the giant statue at Rhodes

morphemes.meaning: pertaining to, having the scale of

colossal.notes: Irregular masculine plural colossaux (un budget colossal / des budgets colossaux), feminine colossale(s); a favorite showbiz intensifier for box-office figures or flops.

colère.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin cholera ('biliousness, choler, one of the four bodily humors in ancient medicine'), from Ancient Greek kholera / khole ('bile, gall, anger').

history.meaning: bilious humor believed to cause hot temper

combat.etymology: Post-verbal noun derived in Middle French from combattre ('to fight'), replacing earlier Old French combatement. Ultimately from Late Latin combattuere ('to fight with, beat together'), formed from intensive/associative com- and Classical Latin battuere ('to beat, strike, fence').

history.meaning: to strike or fence against one another

combat.notes: Final -t is silent; used figuratively in le parcours du combattant ('an obstacle course / bureaucratic nightmare', e.g., financing an independent French film).

combattre.etymology: Inherited through Old French combatre from Vulgar Latin *combattere, an alteration of Late Latin combattuere ('to beat or strike against another'), composed of com- ('with, together') and Classical Latin battuere ('to beat, strike, practice fencing', possibly a Gaulish loan into Latin).

history.meaning: to beat, fence / to fight together

combattre.notes: Conjugates exactly like battre (je combats, il combat, nous combattons, j'ai combattu) and takes a direct object without a preposition (combattre une injustice).

combien.etymology: Univerbation in Old French (com bien, 12th c.) of com ('how, as', from Vulgar Latin *quomo < Classical Latin quomodo 'in what manner') + bien ('well, much', from Latin bene).

coming.etymology: Late 20th-century borrowing from English coming (exclusively in the compound coming-out / coming out), verbal noun from Middle English comen and Old English cuman ('to come'), from Proto-Germanic *kwemaną (PIE *gʷem-, also the source of French venir via Latin). Adopted from American LGBT usage, originally modeled on a debutante's formal 'coming out' into society.

history.meaning: formal debut in society; public self-disclosure of sexual orientation
public disclosure of one's sexual orientation or identity

coming.notes: Never used alone in French outside the fixed masculine expression faire son coming-out ('to come out of the closet', and by extension to publicly admit a secret preference).

comique.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French from Classical Latin cōmicus ('pertaining to comedy'), from Ancient Greek κωμικός (kōmikós, 'of or for comedy'), derived from κῶμος (kômos, 'festal procession, revel, merrymaking'), from which theatrical comedy evolved in ancient Greece.

history.meaning: relating to revelry or theatrical comedy

comique.notes: Works as an adjective ('funny/comedic'), a person noun (un/une comique, 'a stand-up comic or comedic actor', distinct from un comédien, which means any dramatic actor!), and an abstract noun (le comique de situation, 'sitcom/situational humor').

comité.etymology: Borrowed in 1650 from Early Modern English committee (originally denoting a parliamentary body to whom a matter was entrusted), which English had formed from Anglo-Norman commettre / Latin committere ('to entrust, commit', from com- + mittere 'to send') — making comité a classic Franco-British 'boomerang' loanword.

history.meaning: to bring together, entrust a charge
person or parliamentary group entrusted with a matter
deliberative board, panel, or small group

comité.notes: Masculine noun (un comité de lecture, 'a script-reading panel' at CNC or a production house); also common in the idiom en petit comité ('in a small, intimate group').

commande.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (comande, 'entrusted deposit; order, command') from comander / commander.

commandement.etymology: Derived in Old French (comandement, 11th c.) from comander / commander ('to order, command') + nominal suffix -ment.

commander.etymology: Inherited from Old French comander ('to entrust to someone's care; to order, rule'), from Late Latin *commandare, altered from Classical Latin commendare ('to commit to one's charge, entrust') under the influence of mandare ('to order').

history.meaning: to entrust -> to give orders, command
to command, control; to order goods

comme.etymology: Comme developed from Latin quomodo, in what way, through later quomo. Early French had cum and com; com remained in use into the sixteenth century.
comme.notes: French split Latin quōmodo into comme ('like, as, since' and exclamatory Comme c'est beau!) and suffixed comment? ('how?').

commencer.etymology: Inherited from Old French comencier ('to begin'), from Vulgar Latin *cominitiare ('to initiate, enter upon'), formed from com- ('with, intensive') + initiare ('to begin, initiate', from initium 'beginning').

comment.etymology: Inherited from Old French coment ('in what way, how'), formed from com ('how, as', from Vulgar Latin *quomo < Classical Latin quomodo) + the adverbial suffix -ment.

commentaire.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French from Classical Latin commentārium (plural commentāria, 'notebook, memoir, explanatory notes', as in Caesar's Commentarii), derived from commentārī ('to think over thoroughly, study, compose'), frequentative of comminīscī ('to devise by thought', from com- + PIE *men- 'to think').
commentaire.notes: Covers both English 'comment' (un commentaire sur les réseaux sociaux, sans commentaire! 'no comment!') and 'commentary' (le commentaire audio d'un film).

commerce.etymology: Learned borrowing (14th century) from Classical Latin commercium ('trade, traffic, mercantile exchange, fellowship'), formed from com- ('with, together') and merx, mercis ('merchandise, wares, goods', related to mercārī 'to trade' and the god Mercurius).

history.meaning: trading of goods, commercial or social intercourse

commerce.notes: Besides macro-level 'trade/business' (une école de commerce, 'business school'), un commerce in everyday French means a neighborhood shop or storefront (les petits commerces).

commercial.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from English commercial (itself formed on Latin commercium 'trade, commerce', from com- + merx, mercis 'merchandise'), or formed directly on French commerce + -ial.

commettre.etymology: From Old French cometre ('to entrust, join, perpetrate'), reshaped after Classical Latin committere ('to bring together, unite, entrust, perpetrate an offense'), composed of com- ('together') and mittere ('to send, let go').

history.meaning: to entrust a duty; to perpetrate a fault
to commit (an error, crime, or indiscretion); to appoint

commettre.notes: False-friend alert: commettre means to commit a mistake, crime, or gaffe (commettre une erreur/impair), NOT 'to commit oneself' to a project or partner (which is s'engager or s'investir).

commission.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical and Medieval Latin commissiō, commissiōnem ('a bringing together; in Medieval Latin, delegation of authority or entrusted charge'), derived from commissus, past participle of committere ('to entrust, commit', from com- + mittere 'to send').

history.meaning: mandate entrusted to an agent; committee; brokerage percentage

commission.notes: Key Dix pour cent polysemy: une commission is a funding/review panel (la commission d'avance sur recettes), an agent's percentage fee (the famous 10%!), and in plural faire des commissions ('to run errands').

commun.etymology: Inherited through Old French comun from Classical Latin commūnis ('shared by all or many, public, general'), from Old Latin comoine(m), formed from com- ('together') and *moinis ('bound by shared duty or exchange', compare Latin mūnus 'public office, service, gift', from PIE *mey- 'to exchange').

history.meaning: shared in public duty, general, joint
belonging to several or all, ordinary

commun.notes: Key phrases: d'un commun accord ('by mutual agreement'), hors du commun ('extraordinary'), les transports en commun ('public transit'); as a feminine noun, une commune is a French municipality.

communication.etymology: Learned 14th-century borrowing from Classical Latin commūnicātiō, commūnicātiōnem ('an imparting, sharing, making common'), action noun from commūnicāre ('to share, impart, partake'), itself derived from commūnis ('common, shared').

history.meaning: sharing of news or ideas; passage, connection
interpersonal exchange; public relations and media messaging

communication.notes: In French media and talent agencies, la communication (informally shortened to la com' — c'est juste un coup de com'!) specifically means PR, spin, and publicity strategy.

compagne.etymology: Inherited from Old French compaigne ('female companion'), feminine counterpart of the old nominative compain (whose oblique case gave compagnon), from Late/Vulgar Latin *compāniō, *compāniōnem ('messmate, one who shares bread'), a calque on Germanic *gahlaibō (Gothic gahlaiba, from ga- 'with' + hlaifs 'loaf'), formed from Latin com- ('with') and pānis ('bread').

history.meaning: one who eats bread with another, fellow soldier or traveler

compagne.notes: Notice the asymmetry in modern romantic usage: ma compagne is the standard, respectful term for an unmarried female life partner, and its masculine counterpart is mon compagnon (not *compain, which died out).

compagnie.etymology: Inherited from Old French compaignie ('fellowship, retinue, band of soldiers'), derived from compain / compaigne ('bread-sharer, companion', from Late Latin *compāniō, from com- 'with' + pānis 'bread') with the collective/abstract suffix -ie.

history.meaning: presence of others; theater troupe; airline or insurance firm

compagnie.notes: Partial false friend in business: a general commercial 'company' is usually une entreprise, une boîte (informal), or une société, while compagnie is reserved for theater/dance troupes (une compagnie théâtrale), airlines, and insurance firms.

comparer.etymology: Borrowed/reshaped in Old French from Classical Latin comparāre ('to couple together, match, set side by side as equals'), formed from com- ('together') and pār ('equal, peer', also the source of French pair). Note that a homonymous Latin comparāre (from parāre 'to prepare, procure') yielded Spanish comprar ('to buy').

history.meaning: to pair up, match, examine side by side
to liken, evaluate similarities and differences

comparer.notes: Remember the French proverb comparaison n'est pas raison ('a comparison/analogy is not proof'); takes à or avec (comparer un scénario à/avec un autre).

complet.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin completus ('filled up, full, complete'), past participle of complere ('to fill up to the brim, fulfill'), from com- + plere ('to fill').

complexe.etymology: Learned borrowing (17th century) from Classical Latin complexus ('surrounding, encompassing, interwoven'), past participle of the deponent verb complectī ('to twine around, embrace, bind together'), from com- ('together') and plectere ('to plait, weave, braid', from PIE *plek- 'to plait, fold').

history.meaning: to embrace, weave together / interwoven, composite
composed of interconnected elements; psychological inhibition (20th c.)

complexe.notes: As a masculine noun, un complexe means either a building facility (un complexe cinématographique, 'multiplex') or a psychological hang-up/insecurity (avoir des complexes, être décomplexé 'uninhibited').

compliment.etymology: Borrowed in the early seventeenth century from Italian complimento ('courteous observance, compliment'), adapted from Spanish cumplimiento ('fulfilment of what courtesy requires', from cumplir 'to fulfil, complete'), ultimately from Classical Latin complēre ('to fill up, complete', com- + plēre). Originally denoted fulfilling every polite duty owed to someone before specialising to praise.

morphemes.meaning: fulfil, complete (via Italian/Spanish from Latin complēre)

history.meaning: fulfilment of polite duty -> act of courtesy

compliment.notes: Just like English compliment vs. complement, French distinguishes compliment (praise, via Italian/Spanish) from its Latinate doublet complément (something that completes a whole).

complimenter.etymology: Formed in the 17th century from compliment ('courteous expression of praise or respect', borrowed via Italian complimento and Spanish cumplimiento from Latin complere 'to fulfill what courtesy requires') + verbal suffix -er.

compliquer.etymology: Learned 14th-century borrowing from Classical Latin complicāre ('to fold together, roll up; in Late/Moral Latin, to entangle, confuse'), composed of com- ('together') and plicāre ('to fold', inherited natively into French as plier).

history.meaning: to fold or roll up together; to entangle
to combine intricately, make difficult to untangle

compliquer.notes: In Parisian conversation (and every episode of Dix pour cent), c'est compliqué is a polite, understated euphemism for 'it's a disaster / virtually impossible'; se compliquer la vie means 'to make things harder for oneself'.

rootFamily.gloss: to fold, bend (native doublet of plicāre)

compliqué.etymology: Past participle of compliquer ('to fold together, entangle, make complex'), borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin complicare ('to fold or roll up together'), from com- ('together') + plicare ('to fold').

cognates.meaning: secret plan, storyline (likely shortened or influenced by Old French complot)

complot.etymology: Inherited from Old French complot (12th c., originally 'dense crowd, compact press of struggling people'; 15th c., 'secret scheme'), whose pre-Old French origin is debated: most philologists derive it as a back-formation from *comploter ('to roll into a tight ball', from com- + pelote 'ball', Latin pīla), or from Latin *complicātum ('entangled together', from complicāre) crossed with pelote.

history.meaning: compact crowd, dense throng of combatants

complot.notes: Final -t is silent ([kɔ̃plo]); tramper dans un complot / ourdir un complot means 'to hatch a plot', and une théorie du complot is 'a conspiracy theory' (with complotiste for 'conspiracy theorist').

complètement.etymology: Formed in Middle French from the feminine adjective complète ('complete, full') + adverbial suffix -ment.

comportement.etymology: Formed in Middle French (16th century) from the verb (se) comporter ('to bear oneself, conduct oneself') plus the action/manner suffix -ment. Ultimately from Classical Latin comportāre ('to carry together, bring together', from com- + portāre 'to carry'), via the reflexive shift 'to carry oneself' -> 'to behave'.

history.meaning: to carry or gather together into one place
manner of bearing oneself, demeanor, conduct

morphemes.meaning: nominal suffix of action or manner

comportement.notes: The standard neutral French noun for 'behavior' (troubles du comportement, 'behavioral disorders'), whereas English 'comportment' is formal and archaic.

comporter.etymology: Inherited/adapted via Old French comporter ('to endure, bear, carry') from Classical Latin comportāre ('to carry together, collect, transport'), composed of com- ('together') and portāre ('to carry'). In Middle French, the reflexive se comporter developed the figurative sense 'to carry oneself, behave'.

history.meaning: to carry or bring together, collect
to comprise or entail (transitive); to behave (reflexive)

comporter.notes: Watch the transitive vs. pronominal split: se comporter means 'to behave' (il s'est mal comporté sur le tournage), whereas transitive comporter means 'to include, contain, or entail' (le contrat comporte trois clauses).

rootFamily.gloss: to carry away; (s'~) to lose one's temper

composer.etymology: Formed in Old French (composer, 12th c.) from com- ('together') + poser ('to place, set down', which came from Late Latin pausare 'to pause, rest' but took over the meanings of Classical Latin ponere, positum 'to put, place' and componere 'to put together').

compositrice.etymology: Feminine counterpart of compositeur ('one who puts together; musical composer'), borrowed from Latin compositor (from componere, compositum 'to put together, compose').

compost.etymology: Another Franco-English boomerang word: re-borrowed in the 18th century in its modern agricultural sense from English compost ('manure mixture'), which Middle English had borrowed from Old French compost ('mixture, pickled preserve, soil amendment'), itself from Classical Latin compositum ('something put together'), neuter past participle of compōnere (com- 'together' + pōnere 'to put, place'). Doublet of compote.

history.meaning: decomposed organic matter used as garden fertilizer

compost.notes: Both final consonants -st are pronounced ([kɔ̃pɔst]), preserving its re-borrowing from English — unlike its native French twin compote, where Old French preconsonantal s disappeared!

rootFamily.gloss: to compost; to punch/validate a train ticket

compote.etymology: Inherited from Old French composte ('condiment or mixture of stewed fruits and vegetables'), substantivized feminine of Latin composita ('put together, prepared'), past participle of compōnere ('to put together, assemble', from com- + pōnere 'to place'), with regular French loss of preconsonantal s (composte > compote). Etymological doublet of compost.

history.meaning: seasoned dish or preserve of stewed fruits/meats
sweet purée of stewed fruit (especially apples)

compote.notes: Beyond fruit purée (compote de pommes), en compote is vivid everyday slang for 'bruised, battered, aching all over' (avoir les jambes en compote, un œil en compote).

rootFamily.gloss: to stew gently over low heat

comprendre.etymology: Inherited from Old French comprendre ('to embrace, include, grasp with the mind'), from Classical Latin comprehendere ('to take hold of together, encompass, perceive'), from com- ('together') + prehendere ('to seize, grasp').

comptabilité.etymology: Derived in the 18th century from comptable ('accountable; accountant') plus the abstract noun suffix -ité. Comptable comes from compter ('to count, reckon'), Old French conter (later respelled with silent etymological p), inherited from Classical Latin computāre ('to sum up, reckon'), from com- ('together') and putāre ('to prune, clear up, calculate, think').

history.meaning: to sum up, calculate, reckon together

comptabilité.notes: The p is completely silent ([kɔ̃tabilite]); in office slang (like ASK's finance floor), la comptabilité is routinely clipped to la compta (passer à la compta).

compte.etymology: Inherited from Old French conte ('calculation, tally, narrative'), from Classical Latin computus ('a calculation, reckoning'), derived from computare ('to count, sum up', from com- + putare 'to reckon'); respelled compte with etymological p in Middle French to distinguish financial reckoning from conte ('story').

compter.etymology: Compter comes from Latin computare, to calculate. French originally wrote conter; an etymological spelling with p became associated with counting, while conter retained the storytelling sense.

history.meaning: to sum up, reckon (< com- + putāre)
to count; to recount (later split in spelling)
to count; intend; rely on (compter sur)

cognates.meaning: Old French borrowing and learned Latin doublet

compter.notes: The p in compter (/kɔ̃te/) is purely etymological and completely silent—reintroduced by Renaissance scribes to distinguish numerical counting (compter) from storytelling (conter).

comptoir.etymology: From Old French comptoir / conteoir ('counting room, counting table'), formed on compter ('to count, reckon', from Latin computare) + the place/instrument suffix -oir (Latin -atorium). Originally the merchant's table where coins were tallied.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: comptoir (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: comptoir

compétent.etymology: Learned borrowing (13th–14th century, originally in legal French) from Late/Legal Latin competēns, competentem ('coinciding, fitting, legally qualified'), present participle of Classical Latin competere ('to come together, coincide, be suitable or equal to a task'), formed from com- ('together') and petere ('to seek, aim for, go toward').

history.meaning: to meet together, be suitable / fitting, legally qualified
having legal jurisdiction; possessing required skill and capability

compétent.notes: Retains both its everyday meaning ('skilled, capable') and its original legal sense ('having jurisdiction': le tribunal compétent, 'the court of competent jurisdiction').

compétition.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin competītiō, competītiōnem ('rivalry for the same office or prize; judicial claim'), derived from Classical Latin competere ('to strive after something together with another', from com- 'together' + petere 'to seek, aim at'); its modern sporting and festival sense was reinforced in the 19th century by English competition.

history.meaning: joint striving after the same object, rivalry
rivalry for a post or title; organized sporting or artistic contest

compétition.notes: In French cinema, être en compétition officielle refers to vying for the Palme d'Or at Cannes! Note the false friend: commercial market 'competition' is usually la concurrence, while compétition is for contests, sports, and awards.

comtesse.etymology: Inherited from Old French contesse, from Medieval Latin comitissa ('wife or female equivalent of a count'), formed from Classical Latin comes, comitis ('companion, imperial attendant', later 'count', literally 'one who goes with', from com- + ire 'to go') and the feminine title suffix -issa (borrowed from Ancient Greek -issa).

history.meaning: wife of a count, female ruler of a county

comtesse.notes: Notice the silent 'm' (pronounced /kɔ̃.tɛs/): Middle French restored the etymological 'm' from Latin comes/comitis, whereas English 'countess' kept the Old French 'n' spelling.

comédie.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin comoedia, itself adapted from Ancient Greek kōmōidia (κωμῳδία, 'amusing spectacle, comic drama'), a compound of kōmos ('revel, merrymaking, festive procession') and ōidē ('song, ode'). Beyond humorous plays, French extended the word to Dramatic Arts as a whole and figuratively to 'putting on an act'.

history.meaning: dramatic play (light or serious), theatrical art

comédie.notes: In agency and showbiz French, 'jouer la comédie' means both 'to act professionally' and idiomatically 'to pretend / put on a sham' ('Arrête ton cinéma, arrête ta comédie !').

comédien.etymology: Derived in 16th-century French from comédie ('theatrical art, play') plus the agentive suffix -ien. Because classical French theater termed all stage acting 'la comédie' (as in La Comédie-Française), comédien generalized to mean any dramatic actor of stage or screen rather than strictly a comic performer.
comédien.notes: Crucial false friend in *Dix pour cent*: un comédien / une comédienne is a dramatic 'actor/actress' (especially valued for stage craft), whereas a stand-up 'comedian' is un(e) humoriste!

concentrer.etymology: Formed in early 17th-century French from prefix con- ('together') + centre ('center', from Latin centrum, itself from Ancient Greek kentron 'sharp point, stationary pin of a compass') + verbal suffix -er, possibly modeled on Italian concentrare. Originally a scientific term meaning 'to gather toward a single center', later applied to mental focus.

history.meaning: stationary compass point, center of a circle
to draw together to a common center; to condense

concentrer.notes: For mental focus without a direct object, French requires the reflexive form: 'se concentrer (sur son texte)' ('to focus on one's lines'), never bare *concentrer alone.

concept.etymology: Learned borrowing in the 15th century from Late Latin conceptus ('mental grasping, thought, plan'), action noun built on the past participial stem of Classical Latin concipere ('to take together, take in, conceive', from con- 'together' + capere 'to seize, take'). Revived in 20th-century media and creative industries via English 'concept' for a pitchable show or artistic idea.

history.meaning: to take in, gather, conceive in the womb or mind

concept.notes: In modern Paris agency/media slang, both final 'c' and 'pt' are pronounced (/kɔ̃.sɛpt/), unlike older French words where final '-pt' is silent (as in sept or prompt).

concernant.etymology: Grammaticalized in Middle French as an invariable preposition from the present participle of concerner ('to relate to, affect'), directly mirroring Medieval Latin legal and chancery usage concernentem ('having regard to, touching upon'). Ultimately from Latin con- ('together') + cernere ('to sift, distinguish').

history.meaning: relating to, affecting, having regard to
touching upon, regarding (in legal and administrative prose)

concernant.notes: Very frequent in contract and agent negotiations ('concernant votre cachet', 'en ce qui me concerne'); as a preposition it is strictly invariable and never agrees in gender or number.

concerner.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Medieval Latin concernere ('to relate to, regard, affect'), a semantic specialization of Late Latin concernere ('to mix or sift together, perceive jointly'), formed from con- ('together') + Classical Latin cernere ('to sift, separate, distinguish, decide').

history.meaning: to sift, separate, discern visually or mentally
to mingle together; in Medieval Latin, to relate to or affect
to touch upon, relate to, involve

concerner.notes: Watch the partial false friend: French 'concerner' means 'to be about / affect / be someone's business' ('Ça ne te concerne pas'), NOT 'to worry someone' (which is inquiéter or préoccuper).

concert.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian concerto ('agreement, harmony of voices or instruments'), deverbal noun from concertare ('to contend, strive together; to bring into harmony, arrange together'), from Latin concertare.

concession.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin concessio, concessionis ('a granting, yielding, permission, legal allowance'), noun of action derived from concedere ('to give way, yield, grant'), composed of con- ('completely, together') + cedere ('to go, withdraw, yield', participial stem concess-).

history.meaning: to withdraw, yield, grant a right
grant of privilege; act of yielding a point

concession.notes: Common in contract talks ('faire des concessions' = to compromise) and film praise ('un film sans concession' = an uncompromising, bold film); also means a car dealership or cemetery plot lease.

conclure.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Classical Latin concludere ('to shut up closely, enclose; to bring an argument to a close, infer'), from com- ('together, completely') + claudere ('to shut, close').

history.meaning: to shut up, bring to a close
to bring to an end, settle a deal, infer

conclusion.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin conclusio, conclusionis ('a shutting in, siege; end of a speech; logical consequence'), action noun from concludere ('to shut up closely, enclose, bring to an end'), formed from con- ('together, completely') + claudere ('to shut, close', compounding stem -cludere).

history.meaning: to shut in, enclose, bring to a close
final settlement, logical outcome, closing of an argument

conclusion.notes: Used both for logical wrap-ups ('En conclusion...') and finalizing deals ('la conclusion d'un contrat'); in legal French, plural 'les conclusions' means a lawyer's formal written pleadings.

rootFamily.gloss: to conclude, finalize a deal (or romantic conquest in slang)

concret.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French from Classical Latin concretus ('grown together, condensed, curds-like, hardened, solid'), past participle of concrescere ('to grow together, thicken, solidify'), from con- ('together') + crescere ('to grow, arise'). Scholastic philosophy contrasted concretus ('embodied in reality') with abstractus.

history.meaning: to grow together, curdle, condense into solid matter

concret.notes: Agents constantly ask 'Tu as du concret ?' ('Do you have a firm/tangible offer?'). Beware the building-material trap: English noun 'concrete' (cement mix) is 'le béton' in French, never *le concret!

concurrence.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Medieval Latin concurrentia ('meeting at the same point, coincidence, rivalry for the same prize or beneficio'), derived from the present participle of Classical Latin concurrere ('to run together, assemble, clash in combat, coincide'), from con- ('together') + currere ('to run').

history.meaning: to run together, collide, vie with one another
simultaneous occurrence; rivalry for an office or market

concurrence.notes: Major false friend: French 'la concurrence' means commercial/professional 'competition' or 'rival agencies' (e.g., StarMédia vs. ASK), NOT 'agreement' as in English 'concurrence'! (Sports competition is 'la compétition'.)

concurrent.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin concurrens, concurrentis, present participle of concurrere ('to run together, meet, clash, compete'), formed from con- ('together') + currere ('to run'). From 'running toward the same goal simultaneously', French developed the primary sense of 'competing, rival'.

history.meaning: striving for the same post or advantage, rival

concurrent.notes: False friend alert: 'une agence concurrente' means 'a competing / rival agency' (and noun 'un concurrent' = a competitor), whereas English 'concurrent' ('simultaneous') is usually 'simultané' in French.

rootFamily.gloss: to compete for a prize or exam

condition.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin condicionem (nominative condicio, 'agreement, stipulation, terms, social rank or state'), from condicere ('to talk over together, agree upon'), from com- + dicere ('to say, appoint').

history.meaning: to agree upon -> stipulation, state, rank

conditionnel.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Late and Juridical Latin conditionalis (variant of Classical condicionalis, 'subject to stipulations or conditions'), derived from condicio, condicionis ('agreement, stipulation, terms', from condicere 'to speak together, agree upon', from con- + dicere 'to say, declare').

history.meaning: dependent on legal terms or stipulations
subject to a condition; grammatical conditional mood

conditionnel.notes: In French media & agency talk, 'parler au conditionnel' means using the conditional tense for unverified rumors; in criminal law, 'la liberté conditionnelle' (often shortened to 'la conditionnelle') means 'parole'.

conduire.etymology: Inherited via Old French conduire ('to guide, escort, direct') from Vulgar Latin *conducere (with stress shift from Classical Latin conducere, 'to lead together, assemble, escort, hire'), composed of con- ('together') + ducere ('to lead, guide'). Extended from guiding horses and carriages to driving motor vehicles.

history.meaning: to lead together, assemble, escort, contract for
to escort, guide, direct along a path

conduire.notes: Irregular conjugation modeled on -uire verbs (je conduis, nous conduisons, j'ai conduit); reflexive 'se conduire' means 'to behave / conduct oneself', and 'le fil conducteur' is a script's 'common thread / storyline'.

rootFamily.gloss: driver; line producer (directeur de production / conducteur)
to renew/extend (a contract); to escort back

confiance.etymology: Confiance was borrowed from Latin confidentia, trust, related to confidere. The Académie records thirteenth-century confience.
confiance.notes: Faire confiance à quelqu'un means 'to trust someone', whereas une confidence in French is a private secret shared in confidence!

confidentiel.etymology: Derived in 18th-century French from confidence ('secret entrusted in private', influenced by Italian confidenza, from Classical Latin confidentia 'firm trust, self-assurance', from confidere 'to trust fully') + relational suffix -iel. Originally restricted to diplomacy and private letters before spreading to cinema distribution.

history.meaning: private disclosure of a secret under trust
communicated in secret, restricted to trusted parties

confidentiel.notes: Cinema nuance! Beyond 'top-secret' (as for a leaked script), 'un film confidentiel' in French film criticism means an 'arthouse / niche / limited-release film known only to a small audience'.

rootFamily.gloss: intimate secret shared in trust (false friend: not self-confidence!)

confier.etymology: Inherited via Old and Middle French confier from Vulgar Latin *confidare (first-conjugation regularization of Classical Latin semi-deponent confidere, 'to trust completely, rely firmly upon'), formed from intensive con- + fidere ('to trust', from the same Indo-European root as fides 'faith, loyalty').

history.meaning: to have full trust in, rely firmly upon
to trust, place in someone's keeping
to entrust to someone's care or secrecy

confier.notes: Transitive 'confier un rôle / un secret à quelqu'un' means 'to entrust a role/secret to someone'; reflexive 'se confier à quelqu'un' means 'to open up / confide in someone'.

confirmer.etymology: Re-Latinized in Middle French after Classical Latin confirmare ('to make firm, strengthen, establish, corroborate, ratify'), replacing inherited Old French confermer. Composed of intensive con- ('thoroughly, together') + firmare ('to make firm, steady', from firmus 'strong, steadfast, enduring').

history.meaning: to make firm, strengthen, ratify, corroborate

confirmer.notes: Everyday agency staple: 'Je te confirme les dates de tournage' ('I confirm the shoot dates for you'); idiomatically, 'L'exception confirme la règle' ('The exception proves the rule').

rootFamily.gloss: seasoned, established (of an actor or professional)

confirmé.etymology: Adjectival use of the past participle of confirmer, reflecting Classical Latin confirmatus ('made firm, strengthened, proven, established'). From 'whose worth has been proven by experience', modern French developed the common professional sense 'seasoned, accomplished, well-established in one's craft'.

history.meaning: verified, officially ratified; later proven and seasoned in a profession

confirmé.notes: Casting & résumé essential: 'un comédien confirmé / un réalisateur confirmé' does NOT mean 'booked/confirmed for the shoot' unless context says so — it means an 'experienced, established actor/director' (as opposed to 'débutant' or 'émergent').

confiture.etymology: Derived in Old French (confiture, 13th c., 'prepared medicinal preserve, candied fruit') from confire ('to prepare, preserve fruit in sugar or honey', from Latin conficere, confectum 'to prepare thoroughly').

history.meaning: to prepare, preserve in sugar -> fruit jam or preserve

conflit.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin conflictus ('a striking together, collision, shock of battle'), fourth-declension action noun from confligere ('to strike together, clash, contend'), composed of con- ('together') + fligere ('to strike, dash down'). Early spellings alternated between conflict and conflit, with silent final -t prevailing.

history.meaning: to strike together, collide, engage in combat
clash, dispute, collision of jurisdictions or interests

conflit.notes: Pronounced /kɔ̃.fli/ with a silent final 't'; essential in agency ethics ('un conflit d'intérêts') and screenwriting ('créer du conflit dramatique'). Note the derived adjective restores the Latin 'c': conflictuel.

rootFamily.gloss: to distress, afflict (shares Latin root fligere)

confondre.etymology: Inherited via Old French confondre ('to overthrow, ruin, mingle, put to shame') from Classical Latin confundere ('to pour together, mingle, blend, throw into disorder, perplex'), formed from con- ('together') + fundere ('to pour, melt'). Literally 'to pour two liquids together so they can no longer be told apart'.

history.meaning: to pour together, mix, throw into disorder

confondre.notes: Watch the distinction: 'confondre A et/avec B' means 'to mistake A for B / mix them up', while reflexive 'se confondre en excuses' means 'to apologize profusely' (and 'être confus' often means 'embarrassed/apologetic'!).

rootFamily.gloss: to melt, cast metal (from Latin fundere)

confort.etymology: A classic Franco-British semantic boomerang: Old French confort meant 'moral strengthening, solace, aid', back-formed from conforter (from Late Latin confortare 'to strengthen greatly', from con- + fortis 'strong'). Borrowed into English as comfort, it shifted to 'material ease and physical well-being', in which modern sense French re-borrowed confort in the early 19th century.

history.meaning: domestic ease, physical and material well-being (re-borrowed via English)

confort.notes: False friend nuance: modern French 'le confort' refers to physical/material ease ('la zone de confort', 'un hôtel tout confort'), whereas emotional 'comfort/solace' is 'le réconfort'!

rootFamily.gloss: to reinforce, bolster (an opinion or position)

confortable.etymology: Originally formed in Old/Anglo-Norman French as confortable ('consoling, strengthening, encouraging') from conforter (Late Latin confortare 'to strengthen') + -able. Adopted into English as comfortable, where it developed the modern sense 'affording physical ease and coziness', and re-imported into French in the 18th century with that English meaning.

history.meaning: affording physical ease and domestic convenience
physically cozy, financially cushioned (re-borrowed semantic shift)

confortable.notes: Idiom warning! Say 'Ce fauteuil est confortable' or 'un cachet confortable' (a handsome fee), NEVER *'Je suis confortable avec cette idée' (an Anglicism — say 'Je suis à l'aise avec cette idée').

confortablement.etymology: Formed regularly in French from the adjective confortable ('affording ease and material well-being', reshaped semantically via English comfortable from Old French conforter, Late Latin confortare 'to strengthen') + the Romance manner-adverb suffix -ment (from Classical Latin ablative mente, 'with a ... mind/manner').

history.meaning: in a consoling or helpful manner
in physical ease or financial security

confortablement.notes: Common in set phrases like 'être confortablement installé' ('to be comfortably seated/settled in') or 'vivre confortablement' ('to make a comfortable living').

confusion.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin confusionem (nominative confusio, 'a pouring or mingling together, disorder, blushing shame'), from confundere ('to pour together, mix up, throw into disorder').

history.meaning: to pour together -> mingling, disorder, embarrassment

cognates.meaning: leave of absence, farewell, military discharge

congé.etymology: Inherited via Old French congié ('permission to leave, farewell, authorization') from Classical Latin commeatus ('passage to and fro, military furlough, leave of absence, convoy'), derived from commeare ('to go back and forth', from com- + meare 'to go, pass'). Regular Gallo-Romance sound change palatalized Vulgar Latin *commiatu into *comjatu > congié > congé.

history.meaning: passage, military furlough, leave of absence

congé.notes: Used in workplace French for time off ('prendre un jour de congé', 'congé maternité', plural 'les congés payés' = paid vacation), whereas 'donner congé à quelqu'un' formally means to dismiss an employee or give notice to a tenant!

connaissance.etymology: Inherited via Old French conoissance (Middle French connoissance, modernized to -aiss- in the 1835 Académie spelling reform to reflect pronunciation /ɛ/) from conoissant, present participle of conoistre (modern connaître, from Classical Latin cognoscere 'to come to know, become acquainted with', from co- + gnoscere 'to know') + suffix -ance.

history.meaning: to become acquainted with, investigate, recognize

morphemes.meaning: state, faculty, or person associated with

connaissance.notes: Rich polysemy in Paris networking: 'une connaissance' = an acquaintance/contact; plural 'des connaissances' = scholarly/professional knowledge; 'perdre connaissance' = to faint / lose consciousness!

connaître.etymology: Inherited from Old French conoistre ('to know, recognize, be acquainted with'), from Classical Latin cognoscere ('to become acquainted with, learn, know'), formed from co- ('with') + gnoscere / noscere ('to come to know').

connexion.etymology: Learned borrowing in the 14th century from Classical Latin connexio, connexionis (variant of conexio, 'a binding together, joining, logical sequence'), action noun built on the participial stem of connectere / conectere ('to bind or fasten together'), from con- ('together') + nectere ('to tie, bind, weave').

history.meaning: a binding together, close union, logical link
affinity, close link between ideas or mechanisms

connexion.notes: Spelling trap for English speakers! The French noun is ALWAYS spelled with an 'x' ('une connexion internet', 'être en connexion avec son partenaire'), even though the verb is spelled with 'ct': connecter.

rootFamily.gloss: to connect; (se connecter) to log in
related, connected (e.g., droits connexes = neighboring rights in film/music)

connu.etymology: Inherited via Old French conëu from Vulgar Latin *cognutus, an analogical -utus past participle replacing Classical Latin cognitus, from cognoscere ('to get to know, become acquainted with, recognize', from co- + gnoscere 'to come to know'). Used adjectivally since Old French for 'widely recognized, famous'.

history.meaning: to come to know, recognize, ascertain

connu.notes: In everyday French, 'Il est très connu' is the most natural way to say 'He is very famous / a household name' (more idiomatic in speech than 'fameux', which usually means 'tasty/great' or 'that notorious...').

conseil.etymology: Inherited via Old French conseil from Classical Latin consilium ('deliberation, consultation, plan, wisdom, advice, advisory body'), closely linked to consulere ('to deliberate, take counsel, consult', from the Indo-European root *sel- 'to take, gather together'). Palatalized Latin -li- regularly yielded French -il (/j/).

history.meaning: deliberation, plan of action, advice, council of elders
deliberation, opinion, counsel, assembly of advisors

conseil.notes: Grammar gem: unlike uncountable English 'advice', French 'un conseil' is countable — 'un bon conseil' ('a good piece of advice') and 'des conseils' ('some advice'). Also means 'board/council' ('le conseil d'administration').

conseiller.etymology: Inherited via Old French conseillier ('to deliberate with, guide, aid with advice') from Vulgar Latin *consiliare, active regularization of Classical Latin deponent consiliari ('to take counsel, deliberate, advise'), derived from consilium ('deliberation, advice, council'). Note that the homophonous noun un conseiller comes separately from Latin consiliarius.

history.meaning: to deliberate, take counsel, give advice
to guide, advise, assist in deliberation

conseiller.notes: Valency pattern to master: 'conseiller quelque chose À quelqu'un' or 'conseiller À quelqu'un DE faire quelque chose' ('Je te conseille de lire ce scénario' — indirect object 'lui/leur', unlike English direct object!).

conseillère.etymology: Feminine agent noun corresponding to masculine conseiller (Old French conseillier, inherited from Classical Latin consiliarius 'counselor, advisor, assessor', from consilium 'deliberation, advice'), formed with the feminine agent suffix -ère (from Latin -aria). Long attested and fully standardized in modern administrative, artistic, and corporate titles.

history.meaning: advisor, counselor, member of a council
one who gives counsel, royal or personal advisor
female professional advisor, consultant, or council member

conseillère.notes: Notice the pronunciation shift between genders: masculine 'un conseiller' ends in /e/ (silent 'r'), whereas feminine 'une conseillère' opens the vowel and pronounces the 'r': /kɔ̃.sɛ.jɛʁ/ (e.g., 'conseillère artistique').

consentement.etymology: Formed in Old French (12th century) from the verb consentir ('to agree, yield') plus the action-noun suffix -ement. Consentir descends from Classical Latin consentire ('to feel together, be of one mind, accord'), uniting the comitative prefix con- ('together, with') and sentire ('to feel, perceive').

history.meaning: formal agreement, legal or personal consent

consentement.notes: Masculine noun (le consentement); central in both contract law (vice du consentement) and contemporary discussions of personal boundaries and intimacy coordination on film sets.

cognates.meaning: music or drama academy; originally charitable orphanage
school of music or dramatic arts; greenhouse

conservatoire.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from Italian conservatorio, originally denoting 16th-century Neapolitan and Venetian charitable institutions that sheltered ('preserved') orphans while training them intensely in music, from Medieval Latin conservatorium ('place for preserving'), derived from Classical Latin conservare ('to keep safe, preserve'). Institutionalized in France in 1795 for music and dramatic declamation.

history.meaning: orphanage providing musical training; music academy
public academy of music, dance, or dramatic art

morphemes.meaning: place or institution dedicated to an activity

conservatoire.notes: In French theater and cinema (as in Dix pour cent), le Conservatoire with a capital C refers specifically to the prestigious CNSAD (Conservatoire national supérieur d'art dramatique) in Paris—not a glass greenhouse (une véranda or une serre).

consigne.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 16th century from consigner ('to seal, deposit in custody, give formal orders to a sentry', from Latin consignare 'to seal, register, attest'); denotes both strict standing orders and a baggage checkroom or bottle deposit.

history.meaning: to register under seal -> sentry's orders, instructions; left-luggage office

constamment.etymology: Attested in Middle French (14th century, replacing earlier constantment), formed from the adjective constant—borrowed from Classical Latin constantem ('standing firm, steadfast'), present participle of constare ('to stand together, remain firm')—combined with the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin mente, ablative of mens 'mind, manner'), with regular phonetic assimilation of -nt-ment to -mment.
constamment.notes: Pronounced /kɔ̃.sta.mɑ̃/: as with all French adverbs ending in -amment (from -ant adjectives), the double m lowers and denasalizes the preceding vowel to an open 'a' sound.

cognates.meaning: sudden dismay or amazement (shared Latin root)

consterné.etymology: Past-participle adjective of consterner, borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin consternare ('to throw into confusion, dismay, terrify'), an intensive-causative formation closely allied to consternere ('to strew over, throw flat to the ground'), from con- ('completely') + sternere ('to spread out, strike down, prostrate').

history.meaning: to strike down in terror, throw into panic or confusion
to overwhelm with sudden shock or grief
dismayed, appalled, stunned by bad news or folly

consterné.notes: Slightly elevated yet punchy in everyday Parisian speech (je suis consterné !), often expressing exasperated disbelief at someone's incompetence rather than sheer terror.

cognates.meaning: to build; to interpret grammatically (shared Latin verb)

construire.etymology: Attested from Old and Middle French as a semi-learned adaptation of Classical Latin construere ('to heap together, pile up, build, arrange syntactically'), reshaped by analogy with instruire and détruire. Latin construere joins con- ('together') and struere ('to pile up, arrange in layers, erect'), from PIE *strew- ('to spread, pile').

history.meaning: to heap together, build, arrange words syntactically
to erect a building; to arrange grammatical elements
to build physically or develop (a career, character, story)

construire.notes: Conjugates irregularly like conduire and détruire (nous construisons, construit); in acting and screenwriting parlance, construire un personnage means fleshing out a character's arc.

cognates.meaning: office or premises of a consul

consulat.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French (13th–14th century) from Classical Latin consulatus ('the magistracy, rank, or term of office of a Roman consul'), formed from consul ('chief magistrate of the Roman Republic', tied to consulere 'to deliberate together') + the office-denoting suffix -atus. In medieval Mediterranean trade, the term shifted to commercial and diplomatic missions abroad.

history.meaning: office and term of a Roman supreme magistrate
municipal magistracy in southern towns; trade representation abroad
diplomatic consulate; also the 1799–1804 French regime (le Consulat)

consulat.notes: Essential on international film shoots for work visas (passer au consulat); capitalized as le Consulat, it denotes Napoleon Bonaparte's 1799–1804 government prior to the First Empire.

cognates.meaning: to seek advice or information from

consulter.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (15th century) from Classical Latin consultare ('to deliberate earnestly, reflect upon, ask the advice of'), the frequentative-intensive derivative of consulere ('to take counsel, deliberate in assembly'), formed from con- ('together') + an archaic verbal root related to gathering or sitting in council.

history.meaning: to deliberate together; to ask counsel repeatedly
to take counsel, examine documents or advisors
to seek professional advice, check a source, or see patients

consulter.notes: Works both transitively (consulter son avocat / un médecin — 'to see a lawyer/doctor') and intransitively when a physician holds office hours (le médecin consulte le mardi).

contact.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (initially in medical and physical contexts for direct touch between bodies) from Classical Latin contactus ('a touching, physical contact, contagion'), fourth-declension action noun built on contactus, the past participle of contingere ('to touch closely, reach'), from con- ('together') + tangere ('to touch').

history.meaning: direct physical touching of two bodies
physical touch, communication link, or professional insider connection

morphemes.meaning: to touch (from tangere, past-participle stem tact-)

contact.notes: Both final consonants -ct are pronounced (/kɔ̃.takt/); in talent-agency parlance, avoir un bon carnet de contacts or garder le contact is the lifeblood of dealmaking.

cognates.meaning: to reach out to, communicate with

contacter.etymology: Coined in mid-20th-century French from the noun contact + the productive verbal suffix -er, strongly reinforced by semantic and syntactic calquing on American and British English to contact. Ultimately rooted in Classical Latin contactus ('a touching'), from contingere (con- + tangere 'to touch').

history.meaning: to reach out to someone by phone, mail, or message

contacter.notes: Long frowned upon by the Académie française (which recommends prendre contact avec or joindre), contacter is nevertheless ubiquitous across professional, media, and agency French.

cognates.meaning: to make impure or infectious by contact

contaminer.etymology: Borrowed (attested isolatedly in Old French as 'to defile morally', re-borrowed steadily in the 15th–16th centuries) from Classical Latin contaminare ('to bring into contact, mingle, spoil, defile'), denominal verb from contamen ('contact, pollution'), built from con- ('together') + *tag-men, from the root of tangere ('to touch').

history.meaning: to blend together, defile by contact, corrupt
to defile morally or transmit pestilence
to infect biologically, pollute chemically, or spread an emotion

contaminer.notes: In French medical usage, contaminer someone means transmitting a virus or infection to them (where English often prefers 'to infect'), alongside figurative uses like contaminer tout le plateau avec son stress.

content.etymology: Content comes from Latin contentus, satisfied, the past participle of continere, to contain or hold within. The French adjective is recorded from the thirteenth century.
content.notes: Stronger and warmer in everyday French than English 'content': Je suis très content de te voir means 'I'm really happy/glad to see you'.

continu.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical Latin continuus ('joining together, uninterrupted, successive'), derived from continere ('to hold together', from com- + tenere).

continuer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin continuare ('to join together in an unbroken series, carry on without interruption'), derived from continuus ('uninterrupted').

history.meaning: unbroken -> to carry on without break

cognates.meaning: to draw together, enter into an agreement, catch an illness

contracter.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (15th century) from Classical/Medieval Latin contractare or formed directly on Latin contractus, past participle of contrahere ('to draw together, tighten, shrink, conclude a bargain'), combining con- ('together') and trahere ('to pull, draw, drag'). Replaced archaic Old French contraire in both legal and physical senses.

history.meaning: to draw together, tighten, conclude a deal
to enter into a formal agreement or debt
to tighten (muscles), incur (a debt/illness), or conclude an obligation

morphemes.meaning: to draw, pull (from trahere, stem tract-)

contracter.notes: Watch the false friend: contracter does NOT mean 'to hire an actor' (use engager or mettre sous contrat); reflexively, se contracter means 'to tense up'—the exact opposite of se décontracter ('to relax').

contraction.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century (first in medical treatises for muscular and nerve tightening) from Classical Latin contractio (accusative contractionem, 'a drawing together, shortening, abridgment, muscular spasm'), action noun derived from contrahere ('to draw together, tighten'), from con- ('together') + trahere ('to pull, draw').

history.meaning: a drawing together, shortening, muscular tightening
spasmodic drawing together of sinews or muscles
muscular tightening, uterine labor spasm, or grammatical vowel/word fusion

contraction.notes: In everyday spoken French, avoir des contractions without further qualification almost always refers to uterine labor pains before childbirth.

contradiction.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (12th–13th century, earlier contradicion) from Classical and Late Latin contradictio (accusative contradictionem, 'a speaking against, reply, objection, logical opposition'), derived from contradicere ('to speak against, oppose verbally'), combining contra- ('against') and dicere ('to say, speak').

history.meaning: inconsistency between statements or acts; verbal refutation

morphemes.meaning: to say, speak (from dicere, stem dict-)

contradiction.notes: Note the idiomatic expression avoir l'esprit de contradiction ('to be argumentative / contrary for the sake of it') and porter la contradiction ('to challenge someone's argument').

contrainte.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle (13th century, Old French constreinte, contrainte) of contraindre ('to compel, force, restrict'), inherited from Classical Latin constringere ('to bind together tightly, fetter, curb, compel'), formed from con- ('together') + stringere ('to draw tight, bind, press').

history.meaning: to tie tightly together, fetter, restrain
obligation, practical restriction, or creative rule

morphemes.meaning: to bind, draw tight (from stringere > traind-)

contrainte.notes: Common in production scheduling (contraintes budgétaires, contraintes de tournage) as well as French literary culture (Oulipo's famous écriture sous contrainte—writing under formal rules).

cognates.meaning: opposite in nature or direction (via Anglo-Norman)

contraire.etymology: Adapted in Old French (12th century, cuntraire, contraire, both adjective and noun) from Classical Latin contrarius ('lying over against, opposite, opposed, unfavorable'), derived via the suffix -arius from the preposition and adverb contra ('against, facing'), originally an ancient comparative formation on com- ('with').

history.meaning: the exact opposite (noun); opposing or harmful (adjective)

contraire.notes: As a noun it is always masculine (le contraire); discourse markers au contraire ('on the contrary') and bien au contraire are staples of animated French conversation and negotiation.

cognates.meaning: conflict, visual opposition of tones or figures

contraste.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century as a fine-arts term (denoting the dynamic opposition of poses, colors, or light and shadow) from Italian contrasto ('contention, visual opposition'), deverbal noun from contrastare ('to stand against, resist'), from Vulgar Latin *contrastare (Classical contra 'against' + stare 'to stand'). Replaced an older medieval borrowing meaning 'strife'.

history.meaning: dispute; artistic juxtaposition of opposing forms or light
striking difference between juxtaposed elements; cinematographic tonal range

contraste.notes: Masculine noun (un contraste saisissant); vital in cinematography for lighting ratios as well as casting complementary screen partners (jouer sur le contraste).

rootFamily.gloss: to contrast sharply; increase image contrast

contrat.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century (originally contract) from Classical Latin contractus ('a drawing together; a business agreement or bargain'), action noun from contrahere ('to draw together, conclude a bargain').

contre.etymology: Inherited from Old French contre ('against, facing'), from Classical Latin contra ('against, opposite to, facing'), originally an instrumental/ablative feminine form built on com- ('with, together') with contrastive suffix *-trād.

history.meaning: against, close up against, in exchange for

cognates.meaning: to oppose, parry, strike back (via Anglo-Norman contre)

contrer.etymology: Formed within Early Modern French (17th–19th century, popularized through fencing, boxing, and card games such as bridge where contrer means 'to double an opponent's bid') directly from the preposition and noun contre ('against, parrying blow'), inherited from Classical Latin contra ('against, opposite'), + first-conjugation verbal suffix -er.

history.meaning: to double a bid at cards; to parry, block, or thwart an opponent or rival offer

contrer.notes: Brisk, strategic verb used constantly in sports, politics, and talent agencies (contrer une offre concurrente — 'to fend off/counter a rival agency's offer').

contrôle.etymology: Contracted from Old and Middle French contrerolle ('duplicate parchment roll kept to verify an original tax or accounting register'), compound of contre ('against, alongside') + rôle ('scroll, roll' < Latin rotulus).

history.meaning: verification, inspection; later also 'mastery' via English

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: contrôle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: contrôle

contrôle.notes: This origin explains a classic French-English false friend: **un contrôle** in French usually means a 'check, inspection, or ticket check' (**liste de contrôle** = checklist), not domination.

cognates.meaning: to direct, command, or verify (borrowed from Anglo-Norman)

contrôler.etymology: Attested in Middle French as contreroller (14th–15th century, 'to verify accounts against a duplicate register'), denominal verb from contrerolle ('duplicate scroll kept to audit an official ledger'), from contre- ('against') + rôle (Old French rolle 'parchment scroll', from Latin rotulus 'little wheel, roll'). The modern sense 'to dominate, steer, master' was re-borrowed in the 19th–20th centuries from English to control, itself an earlier loan from French.

history.meaning: duplicate audit scroll; to verify records against a counter-register
to inspect officially, stamp, or audit (circumflex marking lost s/r cluster contraction)
both to inspect/check (tickets, IDs) and to command/manage (via English influence)

morphemes.meaning: scroll, register (from Old French rolle < Latin rotulus)

contrôler.notes: Crucial partial false friend: in daily life, contrôler very often means simply 'to check or inspect' (contrôler les billets on a train, un contrôle fiscal 'tax audit'), alongside 'to manage/keep under control' (contrôler son image).

convaincant.etymology: Lexicalized verbal adjective attested in the 17th century from the verb convaincre ('to prove conclusively, persuade') + the participial suffix -ant.
