Convaincre derives from Classical Latin convincere ('to overcome decisively, prove beyond doubt'), combining intensive con- with vincere ('to conquer, vanquish').

history.meaning: to establish guilt; later to win over by argument
persuasive, credible, compelling (especially of an argument or performance)

morphemes.meaning: to conquer, win over (from Latin vincere)

convaincant.notes: Classic French spelling trap: the adjective is spelled convaincant (une actrice très convaincante), whereas the invariable present participle verb form keeps 'qu': convainquant le réalisateur ('convincing the director').

cognates.meaning: to persuade; also legal 'convict' (from the Latin past participle)

convaincre.etymology: Semi-learned Old and Middle French adaptation (12th–14th century, remodeled on vaincre) of Classical Latin convincere ('to overcome completely, refute, prove guilty of a crime or error'), composed of intensive con- ('thoroughly') + vincere ('to conquer, defeat'). Its original judicial sense ('to convict') gradually yielded in the 16th–17th centuries to rational or emotional persuasion.

history.meaning: to conquer decisively, prove undeniably guilty or mistaken
to prove a charge against someone in court
to persuade someone of a truth or win them over

convaincre.notes: Irregular conjugation identical to vaincre: the third-person singular drops the -t after -c (il convainc), while plural and imperfect stems spell the /k/ sound with -qu- (nous convainquons).

cognates.meaning: agreeable, fitting (archaic borrowing from Old French)

convenable.etymology: Formed in Old French (12th century, originally covenable, later reshaped to convenable with Latinate n) from convenir (Old French covenir, 'to suit, harmonize, be fitting', from Classical Latin convenire 'to come together, fit') + the adjectival suffix -able (from Latin -abilis).

history.meaning: to come together, fit, be appropriate
socially decent, respectable, or reasonably satisfactory (e.g. of pay or conduct)

morphemes.meaning: capable of or worthy of being; fitting

convenable.notes: Depending on context, convenable means either 'socially proper/decent' (un comportement peu convenable) or 'fair/adequate' in negotiations (un cachet tout à fait convenable — 'a very decent fee').

cognates.meaning: to come together for a meeting (borrowed from the same Latin verb)

convenir.etymology: Inherited via Old French covenir (10th–11th century, restored to convenir under Latin orthographic influence) from Classical Latin convenire ('to come together, assemble; to harmonize, agree; to be fitting or suitable'), uniting con- ('together') and venire ('to come').

history.meaning: to assemble together; to harmonize, fit, be appropriate
to meet, reach an accord, be fitting
to suit someone (convenir à); to agree on a date or terms (convenir de)

convenir.notes: Watch auxiliary and preposition pairs: 'to suit' takes à and traditionally avoir (ça m'a convenu — 'that suited me'), whereas 'to agree upon' takes de and formally être (nous sommes convenus d'un rendez-vous), though avoir is now widespread in speech.

convenu.etymology: Lexicalized past participle of convenir ('to agree together, settle upon'), descending from Classical Latin conventus, past participle of convenire ('to come together, agree upon terms', from con- 'together' + venire 'to come'). From its neutral legal/social sense 'mutually agreed upon', it developed in 18th–19th-century aesthetic criticism the pejorative nuance 'conventional, formulaic, clichéd'.

history.meaning: settled by mutual agreement or custom
agreed upon (comme convenu); also predictable, hackneyed, or formulaic (of art/dialogue)

convenu.notes: Dual life in agency French: neutral and practical in comme convenu ('as agreed'), but a sharp script-reading critique in un scénario un peu convenu ('a rather predictable/formulaic script').

conversation.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin conversationem (nominative conversatio, 'frequent abode in a place, intercourse, way of life, company'), from conversari ('to live with, keep company with'); narrowed in the 16th–17th century to 'familiar talk, conversation'.

history.meaning: social company -> exchange of spoken words

cognates.meaning: firm belief; also a criminal guilty verdict

conviction.etymology: Borrowed in Early Modern French (16th–17th century, initially for conclusive judicial proof before shifting to deep inner certainty) from Late Latin convictio (accusative convictionem, 'demonstration, proof, refutation'), derived from convictus, past participle of Classical Latin convincere ('to overcome decisively, prove beyond doubt', from con- + vincere 'to conquer').

history.meaning: decisive evidence establishing guilt (pièce à conviction)
deep-seated belief or persuasive sincerity (jouer avec conviction)

morphemes.meaning: conquered, proven (from Latin vincere, stem vict-)

conviction.notes: False friend in criminal law: 'a criminal conviction' in French is une condamnation, NOT une conviction—though the older judicial sense survives frozen in pièce à conviction ('court exhibit / piece of evidence') and intime conviction ('juror's inner certainty').

cognates.meaning: moderately cold; calm, relaxed, fashionable (source word)
moderately cold; also borrowed from English as 'hip/relaxed'

cool.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-20th century from American English cool—first entering French in the late 1940s and 1950s via jazz criticism (le cool jazz, denoting understated, unhurried musical poise) and spreading into general colloquial French from the 1970s onward. English cool descends from Old English col ('moderately cold, calm, unexcited'), from Proto-Germanic *koluz, ultimately from PIE *gel- ('cold, to freeze', distant Indo-European cognate of French gel).

history.meaning: composed, hip, stylishly understated (African American & jazz slang)
laid-back, easygoing, nice, stress-free (vas-y cool, c'est cool)

cool.notes: Historically invariable in gender, cool now occasionally takes plural -s in casual writing (des gens cools); in French it leans much more toward 'laid-back, easygoing, chill' (reste cool, un réalisateur très cool) than 'edgy/hip'.

cognates.meaning: working together toward a shared end

coopération.etymology: Borrowed in Late Middle French (15th–16th century, initially in Christian theological writing for human alignment with divine grace, then secularized in political economy during the 18th–19th centuries) from Late Latin cooperatio (accusative cooperationem, 'a working together'), action noun from cooperari ('to work jointly'), from co- ('together') + operari ('to work', from opus, operis 'work').

history.meaning: joint action, working together (especially with divine grace)
concurrence of forces or divine/human agency
collaborative effort, mutual assistance, or international development aid

coopération.notes: Pronounced in five distinct syllables with a hiatus between the two o's (/kɔ.ɔ.pe.ʁa.sjɔ̃/), never merged into an English-style 'oo' vowel.

cognates.meaning: fellow traveler, friend (via Old French accusative compagnon)

copain.etymology: Descends from Old French compaing, the inherited nominative singular case of compagnon (from the oblique case companionem). Both trace to Late/Vulgar Latin *companio ('messmate, bread-sharer'), compounded from com- ('with, together') + panis ('bread') as an early Romance calque on Germanic *gahlaibo (Gothic gahlaiba, Frankish *gahlaibo, from *ga- 'with' + *hlaib- 'loaf of bread'). Denasalized colloquial copain spread nationwide from regional and student slang in the 18th–19th centuries.

history.meaning: one who shares bread, military messmate
history.stage: Late / Vulgar Latin (6th c. Salic Law)

history.meaning: pal, buddy; with possessive (mon copain), romantic boyfriend

copain.notes: Article vs. possessive matters enormously: un copain à moi means 'a (male) friend/buddy of mine', whereas mon copain without further context usually means 'my boyfriend' (and le copainisme means 'cronyism').

copeau.etymology: Inherited from Old French copel / coupeau ('wood chip, splinter shaved off with a blade'), derived from coper / couper ('to cut, strike off', from coup 'blow').

history.meaning: chip or shaving cut from wood
wood shaving, curl of planed wood or metal

cognates.meaning: duplicate, manuscript text; also 'copious' (from the same Latin noun)

copie.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical and Medieval Latin copia. In Classical Latin copia meant 'abundance, plenty, ample supply' (a contraction of *co-opia, from co- 'together, intensive' + ops, opis 'wealth, resources'); in Medieval Latin scribal usage, dare copiam ('to grant ample access or permission to transcribe') shifted copia itself to mean 'a written transcript or duplicate'.

history.meaning: abundance, plenty, ample means or supply
permission to transcribe; written reproduction of a manuscript
duplicate, student exam paper, or physical/digital film print

copie.notes: Rich French cinema and school polysemy: in filmmaking, une copie is a release print and la copie zéro is the first married answer print; in school and business, revoir sa copie means 'to go back to the drawing board / revise one's plan'.

copine.etymology: Feminine counterpart of copain, remodeled in Early Modern and Modern French (17th–19th century) with the productive feminine suffix -ine on the denasalized stem of copain, succeeding Old French compaigne ('female companion', from Late Latin *compania, feminine of *companio 'bread-sharer', from com- 'with' + panis 'bread').

history.meaning: female messmate or companion sharing bread
female friend, pal; with possessive (ma copine), girlfriend

copine.notes: Just like copain, une copine means 'a female friend' (used by speakers of any gender, e.g., voir des copines), whereas ma copine typically means 'my girlfriend' unless context clearly indicates platonic female friends.

rootFamily.gloss: to pal around; engage in cronyism

cognates.meaning: joint production between studios or countries

coproduction.etymology: Twentieth-century cinema and broadcasting compound (attested in the late 1940s alongside postwar Franco-Italian bilateral film treaties) uniting the prefix co- ('jointly, together', from Latin com-) and production, borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin productio ('a lengthening, bringing forth'), from producere (pro- 'forth' + ducere 'to lead').

history.meaning: act of bringing forth; economic or theatrical creation and financing
joint financing and making of a film, series, or stage work by multiple entities or nations

morphemes.meaning: to lead, bring forth (from Latin ducere, stem duct-)

coproduction.notes: Written solid without a hyphen in standard French (une coproduction franco-belge), and central to European film financing in Dix pour cent where television networks, regional funds, and foreign studios pool budgets.

rootFamily.gloss: to co-produce a film or show

coquin.etymology: Attested in Old French (~1170) in the pejorative sense of 'beggar, vagabond, rogue'; its ultimate origin is disputed, most plausibly derived either from coq ('rooster', suggesting a strutting or scrapping scavenger) or from Medieval Latin coquinus ('kitchen boy, scullion', from Classical Latin coquus 'cook'), before softening in the 17th–18th centuries into an affectionate term for someone playfully mischievous or saucy.

history.meaning: rascal, knave; sly or flirtatious person

coquin.notes: Tone depends heavily on context: gentle and teasing with children ('petit coquin' = 'little rascal'), but suggestive or risqué among adults ('un sourire coquin', 'lingerie coquine').

corail.etymology: Inherited via Old French coral / corail from Classical Latin corallium, borrowed from Ancient Greek korállion ('red Mediterranean coral').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: corail (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: corail

corail.notes: When used as a noun for reef coral, the plural is **des coraux**, whereas as a color modifier (**des lentilles corail**, 'red lentils') **corail** stays invariable.

corde.etymology: Inherited from Latin chorda ('catgut string of a lyre or harp, cord'), borrowed from Ancient Greek khordḗ ('gut string of a musical instrument'). The musical sense is actually the oldest meaning of the word, older than 'rope'!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: corde (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: corde

corde.notes: From Latin *accordare* (originally debated between *cor* 'heart' and *chorda* 'tuning strings together') comes **accorder un piano**.

cordial.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Medieval Latin cordialis ('of or pertaining to the heart, heartfelt'), derived from Classical Latin cor, cordis ('heart'); originally used in medieval medicine for tonics stimulating the heart before shifting to sincere or polite warmth in social relations.

history.meaning: heart; seat of feeling and mind
pertaining to the heart; invigorating the heart

cordial.notes: In French diplomacy and workplace culture, 'une entente cordiale' or 'des rapports cordiaux' signals polished, respectful warmth rather than deep intimacy.

cordialement.etymology: Formed in Middle French from the feminine adjective cordiale ('heartfelt, warm', from Medieval Latin cordialis, from Latin cor, cordis 'heart') plus the Romance adverbial suffix -ment (from Classical Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind/spirit').

history.meaning: sincerely, from the bottom of one's heart

cordialement.notes: The single most ubiquitous French professional email sign-off (equivalent to 'Best regards' or 'Kind regards'); adding 'Bien cordialement' softens its slightly brisk administrative feel.

cognates.meaning: cordon, ornamental braid or police barrier

cordon.etymology: Derived in Old French from corde ('rope, string, cord', inherited from Latin chorda, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek khordē 'gut, string of a musical instrument') plus the nominal/diminutive suffix -on, denoting a twisted strand, ribbon, or anatomical tether such as the umbilical cord.

history.meaning: animal gut, string of a lyre

cordon.notes: Appears in key everyday idioms: 'couper le cordon (ombilical)' ('to become independent of one's parents') and 'cordon-bleu' ('master cook', originally the blue ribbon of the Order of the Holy Spirit).

rootFamily.gloss: to string (a racket) or twist into rope

corporel.etymology: Adapted in Old French (corporel, alongside earlier corporal) from Classical and Late Latin corporalis ('bodily, physical, of the flesh'), an adjectival derivative of corpus, corporis ('body'), substituting the productive French suffix -el for Latin -alis.
corporel.notes: Common in acting and legal French alike: 'expression corporelle' ('physical movement/body language in drama training') and 'dommages corporels' ('bodily injury').

corps.etymology: Inherited via Old French cors ('living or dead body, person, trunk') from Classical Latin corpus ('body, flesh, mass, organized whole'); Renaissance humanists reintroduced the etymological Latin 'p' into the spelling while keeping the final '-ps' completely silent in pronunciation.
corps.notes: Both the 'p' and 's' are silent (/kɔʁ/), making singular and plural identical in speech ('un corps' / 'des corps'); in 'corps à corps' ('hand-to-hand'), a formal liaison /kɔʁ.za.kɔʁ/ is sometimes heard, though /kɔʁ.a.kɔʁ/ predominates.

corral.etymology: Borrowed from Spanish corral ('enclosed yard, livestock pen')—first noted by French travelers to Spain and later reinforced via American English Western vocabulary—which likely descends from Vulgar Latin *currale ('enclosure for carts and carriages'), derived from Classical Latin currus ('wheeled vehicle, chariot').

history.meaning: courtyard, livestock pen; open-air theater yard

corral.notes: Masculine ('un corral', plural 'des corrals'); used in French film sets and Western genres for horse pens, and historically for Golden Age Spanish courtyard theaters ('corrales de comedias').

rootFamily.gloss: curriculum, career path (shared Latin currus root)

corriger.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin corrigere ('to make straight, set right, reform, amend'), formed from the assimilating intensive prefix com- ('together, thoroughly') and regere ('to guide straight, direct, rule').

history.meaning: to straighten crooked things; to amend, chastise
to rectify faults, discipline, revise a text

corriger.notes: Spelling-change verb: insert an 'e' after 'g' before 'a' or 'o' ('nous corrigeons', 'il corrigeait') to preserve the soft /ʒ/ sound; 'se corriger' means to mend one's ways.

corset.etymology: Formed in Old French (13th century) as a diminutive of cors ('body', modern French corps, from Classical Latin corpus) plus the diminutive suffix -et; originally designating a laced outer tunic or bodice worn by both sexes before specializing into a whalebone-stiffened undergarment and, in modern medicine, a rigid spinal brace.

history.meaning: stiffened waist-shaping undergarment; orthopedic torso brace

corset.notes: Covers both period costume dramas ('film en costume / corset') and everyday medical usage ('porter un corset orthopédique' = 'to wear a back brace'); the verb 'corseter' figuratively means to straitjacket or overly restrict.

rootFamily.gloss: to constrict, fit with a corset; make tighter/spicier

cortisone.etymology: Borrowed around 1949 from English cortisone, coined by American biochemist Edward Calvin Kendall as a contracted name for 17-hydroxy-11-dehydrocorticosterone, combining Classical Latin cortex, corticis ('bark, outer rind', referring to the adrenal cortex) with the chemical suffix -one denoting a ketone steroid.

history.meaning: tree bark, outer shell or rind
adrenal-cortex steroid hormone used against inflammation

cortisone.notes: Feminine noun ('de la cortisone'); on film sets and stage tours, emergency 'piqûres de cortisone' (cortisone shots) are classic backstage remedies when an actor loses their voice before shooting.

costume.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century from Italian costume ('custom, historical usage, characteristic dress'), which developed from Vulgar Latin *consuetumen (replacing Classical Latin consuetudo, consuetudinis 'custom, habit', from consuescere 'to grow accustomed'); it is a learned Italianate doublet of inherited French coutume.

history.meaning: manner of living, historical dress appropriate to a period

costume.notes: Crucial partial false friend: in everyday life 'un costume' (colloquially 'un costard') means a business suit ('costume-cravate'), whereas 'fancy dress / Halloween costume' is usually 'un déguisement'—though in cinema/theater, 'les costumes' does mean stage or film wardrobe!

rootFamily.gloss: costume designer / wardrobe master in film & theater
dressed in a suit or period costume

coton.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century (via Italian cotone during Mediterranean trade) from Arabic quṭn / quṭun ('cotton').

cognates.meaning: borrowed directly from Andalusi Arabic al-quṭún (keeping article al-)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: coton (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: coton

coton.notes: Compare French **coton** (via Italian, without the Arabic article) and Spanish **algodón** (which kept Arabic **al-** 'the').

couche.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (couche, 12th c., 'bed, resting place') from couchier / coucher ('to lay down, lie down', from Classical Latin collocare 'to place together, lay in bed'); extended to a stratum or layer laid flat, a coat of paint, and a baby's diaper.

history.meaning: to lay down -> bed, layer, coat, diaper

coucher.etymology: Inherited via Old French culchier, later couchier ('to lay down flat, place in bed'), from Classical Latin collocare ('to put in place, arrange, lay down'), composed of com- ('together') and locare ('to place, set', from locus 'place'); it is the inherited vernacular doublet of learned colloquer.

history.meaning: to place together, station, lay down in bed or marriage
to lay horizontally, put to bed; (reflexive) lie down

coucher.notes: Watch the reflexive distinction carefully: 'se coucher' means 'to go to bed / lie down', transitive 'coucher les enfants' means 'to put the kids to bed', whereas non-reflexive 'coucher avec quelqu'un' strictly means 'to sleep with (have sex with) someone'.

coucou.etymology: Onomatopoeic word attested since Old French (cucu / coucou), directly imitating the two-note spring call of the European cuckoo (Cuculus canorus), and used playfully as a peek-a-boo greeting ('peekaboo!, hi there!').

coude.etymology: Inherited via Old French coute, later voiced to coude, from Classical Latin cubitus (or neuter cubitum, 'elbow; cubit measure'), itself derived from the verbal root of cubare ('to lie down, recline'), because diners in antiquity leaned on their elbow while reclining on couches.

history.meaning: elbow; sharp bend in a road or pipe

coude.notes: Rich in colorful idioms: 'se serrer les coudes' ('to stick together / support each other'), 'jouer des coudes' ('to elbow one's way up ambitiously'), and 'lever le coude' ('to drink alcohol heartily').

couic.etymology: Attested from the 19th century as a pure expressive onomatopoeia imitating a short, high-pitched squeak, snap, or choked cry—especially that of a small animal or bird having its neck wrung—hence its colloquial extension to an abrupt termination, cut-off, or sudden demise.

history.meaning: strangled squeak; sound of a neck snapping or sudden stop

couic.notes: Often paired with a throat-slitting gesture in 'et couic !' ('and curtains! / snip, it's over!') or 'faire couic' ('to croak / be abruptly killed off, e.g., a character cut from a script').

couler.etymology: Inherited from Old French coler ('to strain through a sieve, trickle, flow'), from Classical Latin colare ('to strain, filter a liquid'), derived from colum ('strainer, colander').

history.meaning: to trickle, flow, run; to cast metal; to sink

couleur.etymology: Inherited from Old French color / couleur ('color, hue, complexion'), from Classical Latin colorem (nominative color, 'hue, tint, complexion').

couloir.etymology: Formed from couler ('to flow, glide through', from Latin colare 'to strain, filter, flow') + -oir. Originally a strainer or narrow channel for liquids, by the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries un couloir came to mean a narrow indoor passageway through which people move from room to room.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: couloir (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: couloir

coup.etymology: Inherited from Old French colp ('blow, strike'), from Vulgar Latin *colpus, synced from Late Latin colaphus ('a blow with the fist, buffet, cuff'), borrowed from Ancient Greek kolaphos ('buffet, slap').

history.meaning: blow, stroke, sudden action, drink, shot

coupable.etymology: Inherited with semi-learned suffix retention via Old French culpable, evolving phonetically (through vocalization of 'l' before 'p' to 'u') into coupable, from Classical Latin culpabilis ('worthy of blame, reprehensible'), derived from culpa ('fault, offense, guilt').

history.meaning: fault, error, moral or legal blame
guilty of an offense, worthy of blame

coupable.notes: Functions as both adjective ('plaider coupable' = 'to plead guilty', 'plaisir coupable' = 'guilty pleasure') and noun ('le/la coupable' = 'the culprit'); learned relatives keep the Latin 'culp-' stem ('culpabiliser').

coupe.etymology: Convergence of two distinct etymological lines in French: (1) 'goblet, champagne glass, trophy', inherited via Old French cope from Late Latin cuppa ('drinking vessel', geminated variant of Classical Latin cupa 'tub, cask'); and (2) 'cut, haircut, garment cut, film edit', a postverbal noun formed in Old French from couper ('to cut, strike', derived from coup < Late Latin colaphus < Ancient Greek kolaphos 'blow').

history.meaning: drinking cup (cuppa); blow with the fist (colaphus)
stemmed drinking goblet; act of cutting wood or cloth

coupe.notes: At industry wrap parties, 'une coupe' (short for 'une coupe de champagne') means any glass of champagne—even when served in 'une flûte'—while in editing rooms and salons 'la coupe' means 'the cut'.

rootFamily.gloss: small saucer or dish (diminutive of cup sense)
blow, strike, shot (root of cut sense)

coupe-papier.etymology: Compound noun formed in the 19th century from the verb stem coupe- (from couper 'to cut') + papier ('paper') — literally 'paper-cutter'.

history.meaning: blade for slitting uncut book pages or envelopes, letter opener

couper.etymology: Couper is derived from coup, a blow. Its early literal sense was dividing something with a blow; the verb is recorded from the eleventh century.

history.meaning: blow -> to sever with a blow, cut

cognates.meaning: borrowed from French coup and couper ('cut-off slip')

couper.notes: Also used for turning off phones, engines, or microphones (couper le son, couper son téléphone) and interrupting someone (couper la parole).

couple.etymology: Inherited from Old French cople ('leash tying two hounds together; pair, married or loving twosome'), from Classical Latin copula ('band, tie, bond, link', from co- + apere 'to fasten').

history.meaning: pair of animals or things (fem.); pair of partners (masc.)

coupure.etymology: Derived in the 14th century from couper ('to cut, sever', itself a denominal verb from Old French colp / coup 'blow', via Late Latin colaphus from Ancient Greek kolaphos 'punch, slap') plus the resultative nominal suffix -ure (< Latin -ura); its meaning expanded from a skin gash to a press clipping, an editing cut or power outage, and a paper banknote denomination (originally detached from a counterfoil).

history.meaning: skin cut; press clipping; break/interruption; paper banknote

morphemes.meaning: result or act of an action (-ura)

coupure.notes: Remarkably polysemous in media and daily life: 'grosses/petites coupures' ('large/small bills of cash'), 'coupures de presse' ('press clippings'), 'coupure pub' ('commercial break'), and 'coupure au montage' ('editing cut').

cour.etymology: Cour descends from Popular Latin *curtis (from Classical Latin cohors, cohortis, 'enclosed yard, farmyard, retinue'). It denoted both an enclosed courtyard and a ruler's court; the dropped final t was never restored in spelling (unlike court 'short' from curtus).
cour.notes: **Donner sur la cour** = to overlook the courtyard (prized in French apartments and hotels for quiet).

courage.etymology: Inherited from Old French corage ('heart as the seat of feelings, inner spirit, valor'), from Vulgar Latin *coraticum, derived from Classical Latin cor, cordis ('heart') + suffix -aticum (> -age).

history.meaning: that which belongs to the heart, inner spirit

courageux.etymology: Formed in Old French (corageus, 12th century) from corage / courage ('heart as seat of inner feelings, spirit, valor', derived from Old French cor 'heart' < Classical Latin cor + collective/abstract suffix -age < Latin -aticum) plus the adjectival suffix -eux (< Classical Latin -osus 'full of').

history.meaning: inner disposition of the heart, spirit, resolve
spirited, bold, full of heart and determination

courageux.notes: Feminine is 'courageuse'; in everyday French, 'être courageux' often praises industriousness and grit (e.g., tackling a grueling workday or shoot) just as much as heroic bravery.

courant.etymology: Inherited via Old French corant, the present participle of courre / courir ('to run, flow rapidly'), descending from Classical Latin currere ('to run, hasten, flow'); used both as an adjective ('running, ordinary, fluent') and as a masculine noun for a flowing stream of water, air, electricity, or artistic thought.
courant.notes: Essential office/agency expressions: 'être au courant' ('to know / be in the loop'), 'tenir quelqu'un au courant' ('to keep someone posted'), and 'le courant passe bien entre eux' ('they click / have great chemistry').

courir.etymology: Inherited from Old French corre / courir ('to run'), from Classical Latin currere ('to run, hasten'), shifted from the Latin 3rd conjugation to the French -ir class.

courriel.etymology: Lexical blend (portmanteau) coined in Quebec in 1990 by terminologists at the Office québécois de la langue française—and officially endorsed by France's Commission générale de terminologie in 2003—fusing courrier ('mail', originally 'mounted messenger', from Italian corriere < Latin currere 'to run') and électronique ('electronic').
courriel.notes: Universally used in Quebec and standard in formal French administration/contracts, whereas in Parisian talent agencies ('Dix pour cent' style) speakers overwhelmingly say 'un mail' (/mɛl/) in casual conversation.

rootFamily.gloss: junk mail, spam (Quebec blend with pourriel)

courrier.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Old Occitan corrier or Italian corriere ('mounted messenger who rides posthaste'), derived from Latin currere ('to run'); transferred from the messenger to the mail he carries.

cours.etymology: Cours descends from Latin cursus, the action of running. Its extended senses include a course or sequence of study. This is distinct from the later specialised noun for a broad avenue.
cours.notes: Pronounced /kuʁ/ (with silent final -s in both singular and plural: un cours, des cours), distinguishing it in speech from la cour (/kuʁ/, 'courtyard/court') only by article gender and from la course (/kuʁs/, 'race/shopping').

course.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Italian corsa ('act of running, race, raid at sea'), feminine participial noun from correre (< Latin currere, cursum 'to run'), replacing or supplementing older French cours.

cognates.meaning: courser (swift horse, borrowed from Old French)

coursier.etymology: Derived in Old French (corsier, 12th century) from cors / cours ('run, race, swift journey', from Classical Latin cursus, action noun of currere 'to run') plus the suffix -ier (< Latin -arius), reinforced by Italian corsiere; historically denoting a fast battle charger or messenger ship before shifting in modern urban French to an express dispatch rider.

history.meaning: act of running, swift course, journey
poetic steed; urban scooter/bike courier delivering urgent packages

coursier.notes: A staple figure of Parisian film agencies: before encrypted PDFs, 'le coursier' on a scooter raced printed screenplays ('scénarios') and contracts across Paris—while in elevated poetry 'un coursier' still means a noble steed!

court.etymology: Inherited from Old French cort ('short, brief'), from Classical Latin curtus ('clipped, docked, mutilated, short', from PIE *(s)ker- 'to cut').

court-métrage.etymology: Twentieth-century cinematographic compound formed from court ('short', inherited from Classical Latin curtus 'cut short, truncated') and métrage ('measurement in meters, length of a film reel', derived from mètre < Ancient Greek metron 'measure' + -age), originally classifying 35mm films whose physical celluloid reel measured under roughly 1,600 meters.

history.meaning: film of short reel length (legally under 60 minutes in France)

morphemes.meaning: meter, unit of film length (< Greek metron)

court-métrage.notes: Spelled with or without a hyphen ('un court-métrage' or 'un court métrage', plural 'des courts-métrages') and often clipped in the film industry simply to 'un court', contrasted with 'un long-métrage' ('feature film') and 'un moyen-métrage'.

courtisane.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian cortigiana (feminine of cortigiano 'courtier', derived from corte 'princely court', from Classical Latin cohors, cohortis 'enclosed yard, retinue, imperial guard'); originally meaning a noblewoman attending court, it acquired in Renaissance Rome and Venice the euphemistic sense of a cultivated mistress of powerful men.

history.meaning: lady of a princely court; cultivated high-society mistress
refined woman kept by wealthy or aristocratic patrons

courtisane.notes: Asymmetrical gender pair: masculine 'un courtisan' still means 'a royal courtier' or 'sycophant/flatterer', whereas feminine 'une courtisane' almost exclusively means 'a courtesan' (historical/literary high-status mistress).

rootFamily.gloss: to court, woo, curry favor with

cousin.etymology: Inherited from Old French cosin ('cousin, kinsman'), from Vulgar Latin *cosinus, contracted in rapid kinship address from Classical Latin consobrinus ('mother's sister's child, first cousin', from com- + sobrinus < soror 'sister').

coussin.etymology: Inherited from Old French coissin / coussin, from Vulgar Latin *coxinum ('seat pad for the hips'), derived from Classical Latin coxa ('hip', which itself evolved into French cuisse 'thigh').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: coussin (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: coussin

coussin.notes: Contrast **un coussin** (seat or sofa cushion) with **un oreiller** (bed pillow, from *oreille* 'ear').

cousu.etymology: Inherited from Old French cosu ('sewn, stitched'), past participle of coudre ('to sew'), from Vulgar Latin *cosere < Classical Latin consuere ('to sew together', from com- + suere 'to sew').

couvent.etymology: Inherited via Old French covent ('gathering, assembly, monastic community') from Ecclesiastical Latin conventus ('religious congregation, monastery'), specialized from Classical Latin conventus ('assembly, meeting'), an action noun of convenire ('to come together', from com- + venire 'to come'); loss of preconsonantal 'n' yielded couvent alongside learned conventuel.

history.meaning: coming together, assembly, judicial or civic gathering
monastery or nunnery; conventual boarding school

couvent.notes: Pronounced /ku.vɑ̃/; historically applied to male friaries too ('un couvent de dominicains'), though in everyday usage 'entrer au couvent' strongly evokes becoming a nun or retreating into strict seclusion.

couver.etymology: Inherited via Old French cover ('to sit on eggs to warm and hatch them') from Classical Latin cubare ('to lie down, recline; of birds, to sit on eggs, brood'); from literal avian incubation it developed rich figurative senses of smoldering unseen (fire, illness, plot) and hovering overprotectively over a child or protégé.

history.meaning: to lie down; (of hens/birds) to sit on eggs
to incubate eggs; to harbor secretly
to brood eggs; brew an illness ('couver une grippe'); coddle ('couver du regard')

couver.notes: Three idiomatic uses worth mastering: 'couver quelqu'un' ('to coddle/fuss over someone'), 'couver quelqu'un des yeux' ('to gaze dotingly or amorously at someone'), and 'couver quelque chose' ('to be coming down with an illness').

rootFamily.gloss: brood of chicks, litter; clutch of eggs
hospital incubator (for premature babies) or egg hatchery

couvercle.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin cooperculum ('cover, lid'), an instrument noun built on cooperire ('to cover completely'—the same verb that gave French couvrir and English cover).

history.meaning: lid of a vessel or chest

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: couvercle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: couvercle

couverture.etymology: Inherited from Old French coverture ('covering, roof, bed-cover, dissimulation'), from Late/Vulgar Latin *cooperitura, formed on Classical Latin cooperire, coopertum ('to cover completely', source of couvrir).

history.meaning: roofing, bed blanket, book cover, insurance or media coverage

cognates.meaning: to cover (borrowed from Old French covrir)

couvrir.etymology: Inherited via Old French covrir ('to place something over, clothe, shield, hide') from Late and Classical Latin cooperire ('to cover completely, overwhelm, bury'), compounded from intensive co- (com-) and operire ('to cover, shut, conceal', the antonym of aperire 'to open', whence French ouvrir).

history.meaning: to cover all over, envelop, conceal
to cover, roof, clothe, protect in battle

morphemes.meaning: to cover/shut (parallel in conjugation to ouvrir)

couvrir.notes: Conjugates in the present tense like a regular '-er' verb ('je couvre, tu couvres') with irregular past participle 'couvert'; 'couvrir quelqu'un' means to cover for someone (provide an alibi or shield them from blame).

coéquipier.etymology: Formed in 20th-century French from prefix co- ('with, fellow') + équipier ('team member', from équipe 'team, crew').

coûter.etymology: Inherited from Old French coster ('to cost, require an outlay of money or effort'), from Classical Latin constare ('to stand together, stand firm; in commerce, to stand at a price, cost'), from com- + stare ('to stand').

history.meaning: to stand at a price, cost

craie.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin creta ('chalk, fine white clay, fuller's earth'). Regular loss of intervocalic -t- and diphthongisation of long ē turned creta into Old French creie, then craie.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: craie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: craie

craie.notes: English **crayon** was borrowed from French *crayon*, originally 'a small stick of **craie** (chalk)'.

cognates.meaning: to tremble, quake (from unblended Latin tremere)

craindre.etymology: Inherited via Old French creindre (earlier criembre 'to fear, dread') from a Gallo-Romance Vulgar Latin blend *cremere, formed when Classical Latin tremere ('to tremble, quake with fear') crossed with Gaulish *krit- ('to shake, shudder', cognate with Old Irish crith 'trembling' and Welsh crynu 'to tremble'), followed by epenthetic '-d-' between 'n' and 'r'.

history.meaning: to fear, stand in awe or dread of

craindre.notes: Irregular '-aindre' verb ('je crains, nous craignons, j'ai craint'); in formal French 'je crains que + subjunctive' means 'I'm afraid that...', whereas in casual slang 'ça craint !' means 'that sucks! / that's sketchy!'.

rootFamily.gloss: to tremble (related Latin tremere root via trembler)

crainte.etymology: Formed in Old French (creinte, 12th century) as the substantivized feminine past participle of creindre / craindre ('to fear, dread', from Gallo-Romance *cremere < Latin tremere × Gaulish *krit-), analogically remodeled after noun-participle pairs like plainte ('complaint') and feinte ('feint'), gradually displacing older Old French cremor.

history.meaning: feeling of dread, reverent awe, apprehension

crainte.notes: More elevated and cerebral than 'la peur' (visceral fear): 'de crainte que (+ subjunctive)' or 'de crainte de (+ infinitive)' translates neatly as 'for fear that / lest'.

cognates.meaning: crenel, battlement notch (from Old French crenel)

cran.etymology: Inherited from Old French cren (later lowered before nasal to cran, 'cut, indentation, notch'), descending from Vulgar Latin *crenna ('notch, incision, cleft'), widely regarded as a pre-Latin Gaulish substrate word (compare Classical manuscript reading crena in Pliny); its mechanical sense of a ratchet or gun-lock notch gave rise to idioms of tension and grit.

history.meaning: notch cut into wood, metal, or a crossbow catch

cran.notes: Packed with everyday idioms: 'être à cran' ('to be on edge / wound tight like a cocked trigger'), 'avoir du cran' ('to have guts/nerve'), and 'monter d'un cran' ('to go up a notch').

rootFamily.gloss: battlement notch; time slot or parallel-parking space

craquement.etymology: Derived in the 16th century from craquer ('to make a sharp dry snapping, creaking, or crunching noise', an expressive onomatopoeic verb reinforced by Germanic cognates like Middle Dutch craken and Old High German chrahhōn) plus the deverbal action-noun suffix -ment (< Classical Latin -mentum).

history.meaning: to emit a sharp snapping or creaking sound
dry snapping, creaking of wood/joints, or crunching sound

craquement.notes: Covers crisp acoustic sounds ('craquement de branches', 'craquement d'allumette', 'craquement d'articulations'), while its base verb 'craquer' in modern spoken French means 'to snap under pressure', 'to splurge', or 'craquer pour quelqu'un' ('to fall hard for someone').

rootFamily.gloss: to crack, creak; snap emotionally or fall for someone
to crackle, sputter (radio, fire, dry twigs)

cognates.meaning: to split or make a sharp noise

craquer.etymology: Formed in Middle French from the onomatopoeic root crac imitating a sudden snapping or splitting sound, reinforced by Middle Dutch kraken ('to crack, creak'). From physical snapping, 20th-century colloquial French developed the psychological senses 'to break down under stress' and 'to fall head over heels for someone'.

history.meaning: to make a cracking noise, split open
to crack; to snap emotionally or cave in

craquer.notes: Extremely versatile in spoken French and agency banter: 'je craque' means 'I'm losing my mind under pressure', while 'craquer pour quelqu'un' means to have a crush on someone.

rootFamily.gloss: nervous breakdown; sudden splurge or slip-up

cravate.etymology: Adopted in the mid-17th century as a phonetic adaptation of Croate ('Croatian'), naming the knotted linen neck-scarves worn by Croatian light horsemen serving in King Louis XIII and Louis XIV's Royal-Cravates regiment.

history.meaning: scarf knotted around the collar; necktie

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cravate (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cravate

cravate.notes: Croatia celebrates International Cravat Day every October in honor of how **la cravate** traveled from Croatian riders through Paris to wardrobes worldwide.

crayon.etymology: Crayon was formed in French from craie ('chalk', from Latin creta) + -on, originally meaning a piece of drawing chalk before naming the graphite pencil.
crayon.notes: False friend: **un crayon** is an ordinary pencil (*écrire au crayon* = 'write in pencil').

creuser.etymology: Derived in Old French from the adjective crues (modern creux, 'hollow, deep'), itself traced to a Vulgar Latin *crosus of probable Gaulish origin. Originally meaning 'to hollow out', it broadened to excavating earth and figuratively 'digging deeper' into an idea, script, or investigation.
creuser.notes: In creative meetings (like script development in Dix pour cent), 'il faut creuser cette idée' means 'we need to flesh out / dig deeper into this idea', while 'ça creuse' means 'that works up an appetite'.

creux.etymology: Inherited from Old French crues ('hollow, empty inside, deep'), from Vulgar Latin *crosus ('hollowed out'), a pre-Romance (likely Gaulish or Celtic) word also found in Old Occitan cros ('hollow, hole').

crever.etymology: Inherited through Old French crever from Classical Latin crepāre ('to rattle, crack, burst open with a sharp noise'). By Old French the verb already coupled physical bursting (such as puncturing an eye or a tire later on) with violent or wretched death, which yielded its blunt modern colloquial sense 'to die, kick the bucket'.

history.meaning: to rattle, crack, burst noisy open
to burst apart, break open; to perish

crever.notes: Register warning: using 'crever' for human death is blunt/vulgar ('kick the bucket'), though completely everyday in hyperbolic expressions like 'crever de faim' (to be starving) or 'crever l'écran' (to have magnetic screen presence!).

crevé.etymology: Adjectival past participle of crever, descending from Latin crepātus ('cracked, burst'). From describing a blown-out object or a foundered horse worked to the point of bursting, colloquial 19th- and 20th-century French generalized it to mean 'wiped out, dead tired'.
crevé.notes: Informal but ubiquitous in everyday speech ('je suis complètement crevé' = 'I'm totally wiped out'); more colloquial than 'épuisé' or 'fatigué', without the harshness of 'crever' meaning 'to die'.

rootFamily.gloss: to burst; to wear out; to die (colloquial)

crier.etymology: Inherited from Old French crier ('to proclaim publicly, shout, cry out'), from Vulgar Latin *critare, reduced from Classical Latin quiritare ('to raise a public outcry, appeal for help to the Quirites or Roman citizens').

history.meaning: to call on fellow citizens for help, cry aloud

crise.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century as a medical term ('decisive turning point of an illness') via Medieval Latin crisis from Ancient Greek krisis ('separation, decision, turning point of a disease'), from krinein ('to separate, decide, judge').

history.meaning: decisive judgment or turning point of a disease
medical turning point -> acute attack, social or economic crisis

critique.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Latin criticus, from Ancient Greek kritikós ('able to discern or judge'), derived from krīnein ('to separate, sift, decide'). The feminine noun (une critique) arose via ellipsis of art critique (ars critica) to denote both the discipline of criticism and an individual review.
critique.notes: Watch the gender change in cinema and publishing: 'la critique' (feminine) is a review or the press corps collectively ('la critique a adoré le film'), whereas 'un/une critique' is an individual reviewer.

cognates.meaning: to evaluate or find fault with

critiquer.etymology: Formed in Early Modern French (attested around the late 16th to 17th century) as a denominal verb from critique ('criticism, discerning judgment', ultimately from Ancient Greek kritikós / krīnein) plus the productive first-conjugation verbal suffix -er.

history.meaning: to examine critically; to find fault with

critiquer.notes: Unlike academic English 'to critique' (which can be neutral), 'critiquer' in everyday French almost always implies finding fault or speaking negatively unless clearly framed in an artistic context.

crochet.etymology: Diminutive formed in Old French from croc ('hook, curved fang') + -et, with croc borrowed from Frankish *krōk or Old Norse krókr ('hook').

cognates.meaning: hooked needlework (from French); curved staff (from Norse)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: crochet (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: crochet

crochet.notes: English borrowed **crochet** directly from French because the yarn is worked with a small hooked needle.

croire.etymology: Inherited from Old French creire ('to trust, have faith in, believe'), from Classical Latin credere ('to entrust, trust, believe', from archaic PIE compound *kred-dhe- 'to place one's heart or sacred trust').

croiser.etymology: Derived in Old French (croisier, 12th c., originally 'to take the Crusader's cross, mark with a cross, lay crosswise') from croiz / croix ('cross', from Classical Latin crucem).

history.meaning: cross -> to lay crosswise, take the cross
to cross, fold across, pass by each other, interbreed

cognates.meaning: waxing moon shape (borrowed from Old French)

croissant.etymology: Substantivized present participle of Old French croistre (modern croître, 'to grow, wax'), from Classical Latin crēscentem (accusative of crēscēns, 'growing, waxing [of the moon]', from crēscere). Applied first to the crescent moon, it was adopted in 19th-century Paris to name the Austrian Kipferl pastry popularized by August Zang's Boulangerie Viennoise, later remade with laminated puff-yeast dough.
croissant.notes: Beyond the bakery, 'croissant' is still an active adjective meaning 'growing, increasing' (e.g., 'un succès croissant' = 'growing success', 'par ordre croissant' = 'in ascending order').

croquis.etymology: Derived in the mid-18th century from the verb croquer ('to crunch', and figuratively among 17th-century painters 'to dash off or capture a subject briskly in a few strokes'), with suffix -is.

morphemes.meaning: result of an action (compare gâchis, fouillis)

cognates.meaning: borrowed in fashion and art drawing from French

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: croquis (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: croquis

croquis.notes: What a vivid studio metaphor: **un croquis** is a drawing 'bitten off' briskly from real life before the moment passes!

croustillant.etymology: Present participle of croustiller ('to crunch small crusts between the teeth'), formed in the 16th–17th century from croustille ('little crust'), diminutive of Old/Middle French crouste (modern croûte 'crust', from Latin crusta).

croyable.etymology: Evolved from Old French creable ('worthy of belief'), inherited or adapted from Classical Latin crēdibilis ('believable', from crēdere, 'to trust, believe'), and later reshaped to croyable on the stem croy- of croire. It forms an inherited-versus-learned doublet with crédible.
croyable.notes: In modern French, positive 'croyable' appears mostly in negative or interrogative contexts ('c'est à peine croyable' = 'it's barely believable') and in its ubiquitous derivative 'incroyable'; for positive plausibility (e.g., an actor's performance), French prefers 'crédible'.

croûte.etymology: Inherited from Old French croste ('hard outer layer of bread or a wound'), from Classical Latin crusta ('hard surface, rind, shell, bark, crust').

history.meaning: hard outer rind, shell, or crust

cru.etymology: Inherited through Old French cru from Classical Latin crūdus ('bloody, raw, unripe, undigested, harsh'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- ('raw flesh, clotted blood'). Regular loss of intervocalic -d- between Latin and Old French reduced crūdum to cru.
cru.notes: Watch out for homophones! Adjective 'cru' ('raw', 'blunt/explicit', e.g., 'une lumière crue' or 'des mots crus') is unrelated to past participle 'cru' (from croire, 'believed') and noun 'un cru' ('vintage vineyard growth', from croître).

rootFamily.gloss: raw, unvarnished harshness (of light or language)

cognates.meaning: willful infliction of suffering (from Old French)

cruauté.etymology: Inherited via Old French crualté (alongside learned crudélité, later lost) from Classical Latin crūdēlitātem (accusative of crūdēlitās, 'harshness, barbarity, cruelty'), abstract noun formed on crūdēlis ('unmerciful, fierce'), itself linked to crūdus ('raw, bloody'). Vocalization of preconsonantal -l- before -t- regularly turned crualté into cruauté.
cruauté.notes: Famous in French theater history through Antonin Artaud's 'Théâtre de la Cruauté' (Theater of Cruelty), where it denotes existential intensity and sensory rigor rather than mere physical sadism.

cruel.etymology: Inherited through Old French cruel from Classical Latin crūdēlis ('hard-hearted, unmerciful, fierce'), derived from the same root as crūdus ('bloody, raw') and crūor ('spilled blood'). Loss of intervocalic -d- yielded Old French cruel directly.
cruel.notes: Remember the feminine doubling of the final consonant: 'un monde cruel' vs. 'une décision cruelle'. Beyond malice, it often describes a painful dilemma ('un choix cruel').

cruellement.etymology: Formed in Old French by attaching the Romance adverbial suffix -ment (grammaticalized from the Classical Latin ablative mente, 'with a ... mind') to the feminine adjective cruelle ('cruel', < Latin crūdēlis). Alongside 'mercilessly', classical and modern French developed the intensive sense 'sorely, acutely' with verbs of lacking.
cruellement.notes: Very common as an idiomatic intensifier with 'manquer': 'nous manquons cruellement de temps / de budget' means 'we are sorely / desperately short of time / budget', with no literal malice implied.

cognates.meaning: infant bed, manger (from Old English cognate)

crèche.etymology: Inherited from Old French creche ('livestock manger, feeding trough'), borrowed from Old Low Franconian (Frankish) *krippja ('woven manger, crib'). Because the infant Jesus was laid in a manger, crèche came to designate the Christmas Nativity scene and, from 1844 in Paris (Firmin Marbeau's philanthropic infant nurseries), public daycare centers for babies and toddlers.
crèche.notes: In France, 'la crèche' is daycare specifically for children under age 3 (before 'l'école maternelle'). Bonus slang: the verb 'crécher' means 'to crash / live somewhere' ('tu crèches où ?' = 'where are you staying?').

crème.etymology: Inherited from Old French cresme ('rich fatty layer rising on milk'), from Late Latin chrisma ('consecrated anointing oil, chrism', borrowed from Ancient Greek khrisma 'unguent, anointing') blended in Gaul with Gaulish *crama ('cream of milk').

history.meaning: rich upper layer of milk, ointment

crève-cœur.etymology: Verb-object compound attested from Middle French, combining the third-person singular stem crève of crever ('to burst, split open', < Latin crepāre) with cœur ('heart', < Latin cor). Literally 'that which bursts the heart', it parallels Italian crepacuore and English heartbreak.

history.meaning: to break or burst the heart

crève-cœur.notes: Always masculine ('c'est un vrai crève-cœur de couper cette scène' = 'it's truly heartbreaking to cut this scene'). Since the 1990 spelling reform, plural 'des crève-cœurs' is accepted alongside traditional invariable 'des crève-cœur'.

rootFamily.word: écœurant / déchirant (cf. cœur family: cordial, courage)

créateur.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old French from Classical and Ecclesiastical Latin creātōrem (accusative of creātor, 'begetter, founder, divine Creator'), agent noun derived from creāre ('to bring forth, produce'). Secularized during the modern era, it became the standard prestigious French title for fashion designers, auteurs, and original showrunners.
créateur.notes: Feminine is 'créatrice'. In Paris fashion and television, 'un créateur / une créatrice (de mode, de série)' carries high artistic prestige where English uses 'designer' or 'showrunner'.

rootFamily.gloss: to create, originate (a role or work)

créatif.etymology: Formed on the Latin supine stem creāt- (from creāre, 'to produce, create') with the learned suffix -if (< Latin -īvus). Occasional in Early Modern philosophical prose ('having the power to create'), its modern everyday sense of 'imaginative, artistically inventive' expanded rapidly in the 20th century under the semantic influence of English creative in psychology, media, and advertising.

history.meaning: having the capacity to bring forth (Latin base)
endowed with generative power; artistically inventive

morphemes.meaning: adjectival suffix denoting tendency or capacity (fem. -ive)

créatif.notes: Also used as a noun in agency and advertising circles ('les créatifs', often shortened colloquially to 'les créas') for members of a creative team. Feminine: 'créative'.

crédible.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin crēdibilis ('worthy of belief, likely'), derived from crēdere ('to trust, entrust, believe'). Borrowed in Middle French alongside its inherited doublet croyable, crédible gained strong currency in the 20th century—partly reinforced by English credible—to express professional, political, or dramatic plausibility.
crédible.notes: Essential casting and acting vocabulary: 'elle n'est pas crédible dans ce rôle' ('she isn't convincing/believable in this role') always uses 'crédible', never 'croyable'.

crédit.etymology: Borrowed in the late 15th to 16th century from Italian credito ('commercial trust, sum loaned'), a Renaissance banking term continuing Classical Latin crēditum ('a loan, something entrusted'), the substantivized neuter past participle of crēdere ('to trust, entrust, believe').

history.meaning: reputation, influence; financial loan or credit

crédit.notes: Cinema false friend! Film 'credits' (opening/closing credits on screen) are NEVER 'les crédits' in standard French—they are 'le générique' ('le générique de début / de fin'). 'Un crédit' means a bank loan ('faire un crédit'), phone/account balance, or personal clout/credibility.

créer.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old French (originally spelled crier before being Latinized to créer to avoid homophony with crier 'to shout') from Classical Latin creāre ('to beget, bring forth, produce, elect to office'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *ḱer- ('to grow, make grow', shared with Latin crēscere).

history.meaning: to bring into being (originally divine creation)

créer.notes: Watch the double 'é' in present-tense forms and the feminine past participle ('elle a créé une agence' -> 'l'agence qu'elle a créée' has THREE e's in a row!). In French theater, 'créer un rôle' means to originate a role in its premiere production.

cognates.meaning: toothed rack, trammel hook (borrowed from French)

crémaillère.etymology: Derived via Old French cremailliere from cremascle ('notched iron trammel-hook'), continuing Late Latin cremasclum, an alteration of Ancient Greek kremastḗr ('suspender, something by which an object hangs', from kremánnȳmi, 'to hang'). In traditional homes, hanging the iron pot-hook in the chimney hearth marked the completion of moving in and cooking the first meal for helpers, giving rise to 'pendre la crémaillère' ('to throw a housewarming party').

history.meaning: chimney trammel hook; toothed rack gear

crémaillère.notes: Almost every learner encounters this word in the fixed idiom 'pendre la crémaillère' (verb) or 'une pendaison de crémaillère' (noun) = 'a housewarming party'—literally 'the hanging of the chimney pot-hook'.

cognates.meaning: rich fatty part of milk (from Old French)

crémière.etymology: Feminine agent noun formed from crème + -ière ('woman who makes or sells dairy products'). French crème (Old French cresme) arose from a phonetic and semantic blend of Gaulish crama ('cream of milk') with Ecclesiastical Late Latin chrisma ('anointing oil, unguent', from Ancient Greek khrîsma, 'unguent', from khrīō, 'to rub, anoint').

history.meaning: milk cream (Gaulish) blended with unguent (Late Latin)
dairywoman, keeper of a dairy shop

crémière.notes: Immortalized in the everyday French idiom for 'wanting to have your cake and eat it too': 'vouloir le beurre et l'argent du beurre'—often capped off jokingly with 'et le sourire (or le cul) de la crémière!' ('to want the butter, the money for the butter, and the dairymaid's smile!').

rootFamily.gloss: cream; the best ('la crème de la crème')

cuillère.etymology: Inherited from Old French cuillier ('spoon'), from Classical Latin cochlearium ('spoon with a pointed end for eating snails and eggs; measure of a spoonful'), derived from cochlea ('snail, spiral shell', from Greek kokhlias).

cuir.etymology: Inherited from Old French cuer / cuir ('skin, hide, tanned leather'), from Classical Latin corium ('thick hide of an animal, leather, rind').

cuire.etymology: Inherited from Old French cuire ('to cook, bake, burn, smart'), from Vulgar Latin *cocere, reduced from Classical Latin coquere ('to cook, bake, ripen, digest', from PIE *pekw-).

cuisine.etymology: Inherited from Old French cuisine ('kitchen, art of cooking, cooked food'), from Late Latin cocinae / coquina ('kitchen, art of cooking'), derived from coquus ('cook') and coquere ('to cook').

history.meaning: kitchen; style or art of cooking

cuisson.etymology: Inherited from Old French cuisson, from Vulgar Latin *coctionem (Classical Latin coctio, coctionis 'cooking, baking'), action noun of coquere ('to cook, bake').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cuisson (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cuisson

cuisson.notes: Whether asking how you'd like a steak cooked (**Quelle cuisson?**) or timing a brioche in the oven (**le temps de cuisson**), **la cuisson** is essential French kitchen vocabulary.

cognates.meaning: to prepare food by heat (from Latin coquus)

cuite.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of cuire ('to cook, bake, fire in a kiln, burn'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *cocere (Classical Latin coquere, past participle coctus -> feminine cocta > cuite). Originally referring to a batch of bricks or bread baked at one time, 19th-century slang extended 'être cuit' / 'prendre une cuite' to getting thoroughly 'cooked' or 'baked' with alcohol.

history.meaning: a baking, firing batch (of bricks, porcelain, sugar)

cuite.notes: Used in the classic colloquial phrase 'prendre une cuite' or 'se prendre une cuite' ('to get hammered / go on a drunken bender'). Related slang: 'c'est cuit' means 'it's over / we're toast / the deal is dead'.

cuivre.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cuprum (shortened from aes Cyprium, 'metal of Cyprus', because the island of Cyprus had the Roman world's chief copper mines). Cuprum yielded Old French cuevre / cuivre—just as it gave English copper.

cognates.meaning: copper (early Germanic borrowing from Latin cuprum)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: cuivre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: cuivre

cognates.meaning: buttocks, bottom; base of a bottle

culot.etymology: Formed in Middle/Early Modern French from cul ('bottom, rear, base of a vessel', inherited from Classical Latin cūlus, 'buttocks, fundament') plus the diminutive suffix -ot. First denoting the heavy metallic residue at the bottom of a crucible, the brass base of a lamp or cartridge, and a seasoned pipe bowl, 19th-century Parisian slang shifted 'avoir du culot' to having 'nerve, brass, cheeky audacity' (having a solid weighted base that won't tip over, reinforced by the earthy boldness of cul).

history.meaning: heavy bottom of a crucible, lamp base, youngest child/animal of a litter

culot.notes: Despite coming from 'cul' (which is vulgar on its own), 'avoir du culot' / 'quel culot !' ('to have nerve / what nerve!') is completely acceptable, lively colloquial French—neither coarse nor taboo! Final 't' is silent (/ky.lo/), though heard in the adjective 'culotté'.

rootFamily.gloss: to fall backward; to move back (reculer)

cognates.meaning: system of religious veneration; devoted pop-culture following
worship; iconic pop-culture work (film di culto)

culte.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle/Early Modern French as a noun from Classical Latin cultus ('care, cultivation, adornment, veneration, worship'), derived from colere ('to till, tend, inhabit, honor'). In the late 20th century, modeled on English cult film / cult classic, French began using culte appositively directly after a noun (un film culte, une réplique culte) as a quasi-adjective meaning 'iconic, revered by fans'.

history.meaning: tending, cultivation, worship of the gods
iconic, having a devoted fan following

culte.notes: False friend alert for the noun! A dangerous fringe 'cult' in English is 'une secte' in French, NOT 'un culte' (which simply means mainstream religious worship, as in 'un lieu de culte' = 'a place of worship'). As an adjective ('une série culte', 'des films cultes'), it means 'iconic / classic'.

cultiver.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Medieval Latin cultivare ('to till the soil'), derived from Late Latin cultivus ('tilled, arable'), from Classical Latin cultus, past participle of colere ('to till, tend, inhabit, worship').

history.meaning: to cultivate soil, grow crops; to foster the mind

cognates.meaning: arts, customs, and intellectual achievement (from French/Latin)

culture.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French from Classical Latin cultūra ('tilling of land, husbandry, care'), derived from the past participial stem cult- of colere ('to till, tend, inhabit'). Already used figuratively by Cicero in cultūra animī ('cultivation of the mind'), French expanded it during the Enlightenment from agriculture and personal education ('culture générale') to the collective arts, letters, and cinema.

history.meaning: tilling of soil; cultivation of the mind (Cicero)
tillage of land; intellectual and moral training

culture.notes: In France (and throughout Dix pour cent!), 'la Culture' (often capitalized in 'le ministère de la Culture') directly encompasses cinema, theater, literature, and state arts funding, whereas 'la culture générale' means broad well-rounded knowledge.

cumulé.etymology: Adjectival past participle of cumuler ('to heap together, hold multiple offices or incomes concurrently'), a learned Middle French borrowing from Classical Latin cumulāre ('to heap up, pile up, crown'), derived from cumulus ('a heap, pile, surplus').
cumulé.notes: Standard box-office and business term in French media: 'entrées cumulées' means 'cumulative ticket admissions / total box-office attendance to date'. Related noun 'le cumul (des mandats / d'emplois)' refers to holding multiple posts or jobs at once.

rootFamily.gloss: to combine, hold simultaneously, rack up

curieux.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (curios, 12th c., 'careful, eager to learn, inquisitive') from Classical Latin curiosus ('full of care, diligent, inquisitive, meddlesome'), derived from cura ('care, attention').

cv.etymology: Twentieth-century initialism (pronounced /se.ve/) of the Neo-Latin phrase curriculum vitae ('course of one's life'), composed of Classical Latin curriculum ('a running, racecourse, chariot, career', diminutive derived from currere, 'to run') and vītae (genitive singular of vīta, 'life').

history.meaning: biographical summary of qualifications and career

cv.notes: Look out for the classic Franco-English swap! Although English borrowed French 'résumé' for a job CV, in French 'un résumé' ONLY means a plot summary or abstract—a job or acting résumé is strictly 'un CV' (/œ̃ se.ve/, masculine, invariable in the plural: 'des CV').

rootFamily.gloss: to run (inherited verb from Latin currere)

cognates.meaning: thick rope or insulated wire; to wire (from Norman French)

câbler.etymology: Denominal verb formed from câble + -er (first in 19th-century maritime and telegraphy usage, then 20th-century television and electronics). French câble entered Old French via Norman-Picard/Provençal from Late Latin capulum ('lasso, halter, thick mooring rope'), derived from Classical Latin capere ('to seize, hold fast'). The circumflex â marks the historical loss of preconsonantal s in alternative Middle French spellings (chasble/cable) and preserves a back vowel quality.

history.meaning: to twist into a cable; to telegraph; to wire up for electricity or TV

câbler.notes: On film sets, 'câbler' refers to rigging power/video cables, and in media 'une chaîne câblée' is a cable TV channel. Figuratively, 'être câblé comme ça' means 'to be wired that way', and 'péter un câble' is a must-know idiom meaning 'to blow a fuse / freak out'!

cèdre.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (cedre, 12th c.) from Classical Latin cedrus ('cedar tree, cedar oil'), from Ancient Greek kedros ('cedar, juniper').

cognates.meaning: to yield territory or rights (borrowed from French)

céder.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (16th century) from Classical Latin cēdere ('to go, move away, withdraw, give ground, yield to authority or legally transfer'), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱeyd- ('to go, give way'). It supplies the base for a large Latinate prefix family in French and English (concéder, précéder, succéder).

history.meaning: to go away, withdraw, yield ground, grant rights
to hand over rights; to give in, yield to pressure

céder.notes: Crucial in both contract negotiations ('céder les droits d'adaptation' = 'to assign/sell the adaptation rights') and emotional standoffs ('céder au chantage / à la panique' = 'to give in to blackmail / panic'). Watch the accent flip: 'je cède' (grave) vs. 'nous cédons' (acute).

cognates.meaning: bachelorhood, single state (for men; nubilato for women)

célibat.etymology: Learned borrowing in the early 16th century from Classical Latin caelibātus ('the unmarried state, single life'), derived from caelebs ('unmarried, single, living alone'). While ecclesiastical usage applied it to priestly vows against marriage, everyday French preserved the broad secular Latin meaning of simply being unmarried or single.

history.meaning: unmarried status (secular or clerical), single life

morphemes.meaning: state or status noun (< Latin -ātus, silent -t)

célibat.notes: Major false friend! In French, 'le célibat' and 'être célibataire' simply mean 'single life' and 'being single / unmarried'—they do NOT mean sexual abstinence (which is 'la chasteté' or 'l'abstinence') unless explicitly 'le célibat des prêtres'! Silent final '-t' (/se.li.ba/).

cognates.meaning: abstaining from marriage or sexual relations

célibataire.etymology: Derived in 18th-century French from célibat ('unmarried state'), itself a learned borrowing from Classical Latin caelibātus ('celibacy, single life'), formed from caelebs ('unmarried, single'), of uncertain Indo-European etymology, combined with the agentive-relational suffix -aire (< Latin -ārius).
célibataire.notes: A classic false friend for English speakers: in everyday French, célibataire simply means 'single' (unmarried or unattached), not sexually abstinent ('chaste' or 'abstinent' expresses religious celibacy).

célèbre.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (15th century) from Classical Latin celeber (accusative celebrem), originally meaning 'frequented, populous, crowded' (of places or festivals) before shifting metaphorically in Classical Latin to 'honored, much talked of, renowned'.
célèbre.notes: Unlike 'connu' (merely well-known), célèbre implies genuine prestige or wide public acclaim, and is epicene in form (un acteur célèbre / une actrice célèbre).

cognates.meaning: to honor or mark an occasion

célébrer.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (12th century, originally used of officiating at Mass or a solemn rite) from Classical Latin celebrāre ('to frequent in great numbers, crowd, solemnize, honor, praise'), a denominative verb from celeber ('frequented, renowned').

history.meaning: to frequent in crowds, solemnize a rite, praise
to perform a religious ceremony or festival solemnly

célébrer.notes: More formal than 'fêter': on fête un anniversaire with friends, whereas on célèbre un mariage, une victoire, or un talent au festival de Cannes.

célébrité.etymology: Learned borrowing into Old/Middle French from Classical Latin celebritās (accusative celebritātem), originally 'a multitude, large gathering, concourse', then 'solemnity' and 'fame, renown', before acquiring the concrete count-noun sense 'famous public figure' in the 19th century.

history.meaning: solemnity of a ceremony; wide renown

célébrité.notes: In French showbiz (as at ASK in Dix pour cent), 'la célébrité' as an uncountable noun means 'fame', while 'une célébrité' (often alongside 'une star' or 'un people') refers to a famous person.

céramique.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries from Ancient Greek keramikḗ (tékhnē) ('the potter's art'), from kéramos ('potter's clay, earthenware jar'), which also named the Kerameikós potters' quarter of ancient Athens.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: céramique (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: céramique

céramique.notes: Covers earthenware (**la faïence**), stoneware (**le grès**), and porcelain (**la porcelaine**).

cérébralement.etymology: Formed in Modern French from the feminine adjective cérébrale (from learned Latin cerebrālis, derived from cerebrum 'brain', from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂-s-ro- 'head, horn') plus the adverbial suffix -ment (< Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind').

history.meaning: pertaining to the brain; intellectual rather than emotional

cérébralement.notes: In French film criticism and acting talk, 'cérébral' / 'cérébralement' describes an actor or auteur who approaches a role through intellect and analysis rather than instinct ('viscéralement').

cérémonie.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Ecclesiastical and Classical Latin caerimōnia ('sacredness, awe, religious rite'), a word of obscure origin that Roman grammarians connected by folk etymology with Caere, an ancient Etruscan city allied with Rome whose priests sheltered Roman sacred objects.
cérémonie.notes: In French cinema, 'la cérémonie' par excellence refers to 'la cérémonie des César' or the opening/closing ceremonies at Cannes; 'maître / maîtresse de cérémonie' is the awards host.

césar.etymology: Antonomasia (eponym) coined in 1976 for France's national film award after the French sculptor César Baldaccini (1921–1998), who designed the compressed-bronze trophy and whose given name continues Latin Caesar, the cognomen of Julius Caesar that became the imperial title of Rome.

history.meaning: Roman patrician cognomen; later imperial title
French masculine given name and imperial title
annual French national cinema trophy (created by Georges Cravenne and sculptor César in 1976)

césar.notes: France's equivalent of the Oscar; when capitalized as the proper institution ('les César'), it stays invariable, whereas as a common noun for the statuette itself ('remporter deux césars') it can take lowercase and plural -s.

rootFamily.gloss: recipient of a César film award

côte.etymology: Inherited from Old French coste ('rib, side of the body, hillside, seacoast'), from Classical Latin costa ('rib, side, wall').

history.meaning: anatomical rib; steep slope, hill; seacoast

côté.etymology: Inherited from Old French costé ('flank, side'), from Vulgar Latin *costatum ('the ribbed part of the body, flank'), neuter noun formed on Classical Latin costa ('rib').

cœur.etymology: Inherited from Old French cuer ('heart, courage, inner mind'), from Classical Latin cor ('heart, soul, mind', from PIE *kerd- 'heart').

history.meaning: heart, seat of feeling and courage

d'abord.etymology: Adverbial phrase formed in the 16th century from de ('of, from') + abord ('approach, landing against a shore or ship', deverbal from aborder, built on bord 'side of a ship, shore') — originally 'at the very first contact or approach', hence 'at first, first of all'.

history.meaning: at first approach -> at first, first of all

d'accord.etymology: This expression combines the elided preposition de with accord, agreement. Accord itself is a noun formed from accorder. In the fixed expression, the combination expresses being in agreement.

history.meaning: to be in agreement -> agreed, okay

d'accord.notes: Informal spoken French often shortens d'accord to d'acc! (/dak/).

d'ailleurs.etymology: Lexicalized adverbial phrase combining the preposition de ('from') with ailleurs ('elsewhere'), which evolved from Old French aillors via Vulgar Latin *aliōrsum ('toward another place'), remodeled from Classical Latin aliōvorsum / aliōrsum (aliō 'to another place' + vorsum 'turned toward', with adverbial -s).

history.meaning: in another direction, toward another place
from elsewhere; moreover, besides, by the way

d'ailleurs.notes: One of spoken French's most versatile discourse markers: literally 'from elsewhere' ('venir d'ailleurs'), in conversation it introduces a supporting point ('besides, moreover') or a casual tangential thought ('by the way').

dalle.etymology: Originally a Norman maritime and building word dale ('deck scupper trough; grooved flagstone channeled for rainwater; flat paving slab'), borrowed from Old Norse dœla ('small wooden gutter or trough aboard ship', related to dalr 'valley, hollow').

cognates.meaning: from related Old Norse dalr / Old English dæl ('valley')

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: dalle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: dalle

dalle.notes: From Viking ship gutters in Normandy to cathedral and courtyard flagstones across France, **une dalle** traveled a remarkable journey.

dame.etymology: Inherited via Old French dame from Classical Latin domina ('mistress of a household, lady'), feminine counterpart of dominus ('master, lord', from domus 'house').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: dame (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: dame

dame.notes: **Madame** is simply the fused possessive phrase *ma dame* ('my lady').

danger.etymology: Inherited from Old French dangier ('arbitrary power of a feudal lord, dominion, mastery, resistance'), from Vulgar Latin *dominiarium, derived from dominium ('lordship, ownership', from dominus 'lord'); shifted from 'being at someone's mercy or power' (estre en son dangier) to 'peril, risk, danger'.

history.meaning: feudal mastery -> exposure to harm, peril, danger

dangereusement.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French from the feminine adjective dangereuse (originally 'haughty, capricious, difficult', later 'perilous') plus the adverbial suffix -ment (< Latin ablative mente); ultimately rooted in Old French dangier ('lordly power, mastery, peril') from Vulgar Latin *dominiārium (< dominium 'lordship').

history.meaning: lordly authority, power of a master
arrogantly, reluctantly; later in a perilous manner

dangereusement.notes: Remember the famous literary title Les Liaisons dangereuses: everything in the 'danger' family originally referred to being at someone else's feudal mercy before shifting to physical or moral peril.

dangereux.etymology: Derived in Old French (dangereus, 12th century) from dangier ('power, control, resistance, peril') + -eus (< Latin -ōsus). Dangier reflects Gallo-Romance *dominiārium (derived from Latin dominium 'lordship, ownership', from dominus 'master'), shifting semantically from 'subject to a lord's arbitrary power' to 'difficult, risky, perilous'.

history.meaning: imperious, hard to please, reluctant; exposed to harm

dangereux.notes: Takes the preposition 'pour' before a person/noun ('dangereux pour sa carrière') and 'de' before an infinitive when impersonal ('il est dangereux de refuser ce rôle').

dans.etymology: Dans comes from later Latin deintus, inside, composed from an intensive de- and intus, within. The Académie dates its French history to the twelfth century.

history.meaning: in, inside, into; in (time from now)

dans.notes: In time expressions, dans dix minutes means 'ten minutes from now', whereas en dix minutes means 'taking ten minutes to complete'.

dansant.etymology: Present participle of danser ('to dance', from Old French dancier) used as an adjective meaning 'lively for dancing' or 'where dancing takes place' (as in une soirée dansante).

danse.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (12th century, danse / dance) from danser ('to dance'), which entered Old French from Old Low Franconian (Frankish), most likely *dansōn ('to draw, stretch out, move in a line Dance'), related to Old High German dansōn ('to pull, draw along'), whence French exported the word across Europe.

history.meaning: to draw out, stretch, lead a line dance

danse.notes: Watch the idiom 'entrer dans la danse' (to join the fray / enter the action) and 'mener la danse' (to call the shots / lead the pack) — frequent in agency negotiations!

cognates.meaning: to dance (borrowed back from Old French)

danser.etymology: Inherited through Old French dancier / danser (12th century), almost certainly borrowed from Frankish *dansōn ('to stretch, pull, move back and forth in a chain dance', cognate with Old High German dansōn, from Proto-Germanic *þansōną), displacing Classical Latin saltāre in northern Gallo-Romance.

history.meaning: to stretch out, pull along in a line
to perform rhythmic steps to music

danser.notes: Idiomatic gem in stressful workplace banter: 'ne plus savoir sur quel pied danser' means 'not to know which way to turn / not to know where one stands anymore'.

date.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Medieval Latin data ('indication of place and time on a document'), taken from the opening formula of Roman and medieval letters data (est epistola) Romae... ('[this letter was] given at Rome on...'), feminine past participle of dare ('to give, hand over to a courier').

history.meaning: calendar date of a document or event
