de.etymology: De continues the Latin preposition de. Its older senses included separation and origin; later everyday Latin also expanded its use in partitive and possessive relationships. French inherited those connecting uses.

history.meaning: of, from (taking over Latin genitive & ablative roles)

rootFamily.gloss: contraction de + les; plural indefinite article

de.notes: After a negated verb, indefinite un/une/du/de la/des usually reduces to plain de: J'ai du temps -> Je n'ai pas de temps.

deal.etymology: Twentieth-century borrowing from English deal ('business transaction, bargain', and separately 'illicit drug trade'), from Middle English deel and Old English dǣl ('part, share, portion distributed'), from Proto-Germanic *dailiz ('part, division').

history.meaning: distribution of cards; business bargain or transaction

deal.notes: Ubiquitous anglicism (masculine: 'un bon deal', 'conclure un deal') in Parisian talent agencies, startups, and media, though it also means drug trafficking depending on context ('le deal de drogue').

rootFamily.gloss: to negotiate a deal; to sell drugs (slang/colloquial)

dealer.etymology: Borrowed in the second half of the 20th century from American and British English (drug) dealer, an agent noun from the verb deal (Old English dǣlan 'to divide, distribute shares', from Proto-Germanic *dailijaną), semantically narrowed in French almost exclusively to narcotics.

history.meaning: merchant, trader; distributor of illicit drugs

morphemes.meaning: borrowed English agentive suffix (often adapted as -eur / feminine -euse)

dealer.notes: Crucial semantic narrowing: whereas English 'dealer' can be an art dealer ('marchand d'art') or car dealer ('concessionnaire'), French 'un dealer' (feminine 'une dealeuse') almost always means a drug dealer!

rootFamily.gloss: to traffic drugs; to negotiate informally

debout.etymology: Univerbation in Old/Middle French of the phrase de bout ('on end, upright'), from de ('of, on') + bout ('extremity, end', from Old French bouter 'to thrust, set').

history.meaning: standing on end -> upright, on one's feet, awake

dedans.etymology: Formed in Old French (dedenz, 11th c.) by reinforcing denz / dans ('inside, within', from Vulgar Latin *de intus 'from within') with a second initial preposition de.

degré.etymology: Inherited from Old French degré ('step of a staircase, rung, rank, gradation'), from Vulgar Latin *degradus, formed from de- + Classical Latin gradus ('step, pace, stair, rank').

history.meaning: stair step -> rank, level, unit of angle or temperature

dehors.etymology: Formed in Old French (defors / dehors, 11th c.) from de ('from, of') + hors (older fors, 'outside', from Classical Latin foris 'out of doors', related to forum and fores 'double doors').

demain.etymology: Demain developed from the later Latin expression de mane. That expression could refer to the morning and also to the morning of the following day; the latter reading became tomorrow.

history.meaning: early in the morning -> next morning

demain.notes: Demain names tomorrow relative to today, whereas le lendemain names 'the next day' relative to a past or future narrative point.

demande.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (12th century) from demander ('to ask, request'), inherited from Classical Latin dēmandāre ('to entrust, commit to someone's charge', from dē- + mandāre 'to put into one's hand, entrust, order'), which shifted in Late Latin to 'to ask for, request'.

history.meaning: to entrust, commit to someone's care

demande.notes: Major false friend: 'une demande' is a polite 'request' or 'application' ('une demande en mariage' = marriage proposal), whereas an English 'demand' is 'une exigence'!

demander.etymology: Demander comes from Latin demandare ('to entrust', and in Late Latin 'to request, ask for'). Unlike English 'demand', French demander is the polite everyday verb 'to ask'.

history.meaning: to entrust; Late Latin: to request

demander.notes: False friend: **demander** simply means 'to ask' (not 'demand', which is *exiger*).

demi.etymology: Inherited from Old French demi ('half'), from Vulgar Latin *dimedius, reshaped from Classical Latin dimidius ('halved, half'), compound of dis- ('apart') + medius ('middle').

demi-centimètre.etymology: Modern French compound noun formed from demi ('half') + centimètre ('centimeter').

cognates.meaning: a day's travel or work (archaic loanword)

demi-journée.etymology: Compound formed in French from demi ('half', via Old French demi from Vulgar Latin *dīmedius, Classical Latin dīmidius, from dis- 'apart' + medius 'middle') and journée ('day's duration or work', via Old French jornee from Vulgar Latin *diurnāta, derived from Classical Latin diurnus 'of a day', from diēs 'day').

history.meaning: half + span/work of a single day

demi-journée.notes: Orthographic rule: 'demi-' is invariable and hyphenated before a noun ('une demi-journée de tournage', plural 'des demi-journées'), whereas after the noun it agrees in gender only ('une journée et demie').

demi-sel.etymology: Modern French culinary compound formed from demi ('half') + sel ('salt', from Latin sal), designating butter or fresh cheese lightly salted (typically 0.5% to 3% salt).

demi-tour.etymology: Compound noun formed from demi ('half') + tour ('turn, revolution') — literally 'a half-turn (180 degrees)', hence 'an about-face or turning back'.

demi-verre.etymology: Compound noun formed from demi ('half') + verre ('drinking glass', from Latin vitrum 'glass').

cognates.meaning: tooth (native Germanic cognate via Grimm's Law)

dent.etymology: Inherited through Old French dent from Classical Latin dentem (nominative dēns 'tooth'), originally an active present participle of Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed- ('to eat'), *h₁d-ént-s literally meaning 'the biter / eater'. Feminine in Modern French despite being masculine in Latin and early Old French.

history.meaning: tooth (shifting from masculine to feminine in late medieval usage)

dent.notes: Watch the gender ('une dent', feminine!) and rich idioms: 'avoir une dent contre quelqu'un' (to hold a grudge against someone) and 'avoir les dents longues' (to be ruthlessly ambitious).

dentelle.etymology: Formed in the 16th century as a diminutive of dent ('tooth', from Classical Latin dentem); originally referred to the tiny tooth-like picots or scalloped points along the edge of openwork trimmings, before naming lacework as a whole.

depuis.etymology: Formed in Old French (depuis, 12th c.) from de ('from') + puis ('afterward, since', from Vulgar Latin *postius, comparative of Classical Latin post 'after, behind').

dernier.etymology: Dernier is a fifteenth-century contraction of derrenier, itself related to an older form ultimately derived from Latin deretro, behind. Its history connects being last with being at the back.

morphemes.meaning: behind, rear (< Old French derren- < dē retrō)

dernier.notes: Placement changes meaning: la semaine dernière ('last/previous week', after the noun) vs. la dernière semaine des vacances ('the final week of the holidays', before the noun).

derrière.etymology: Inherited from Old French deriere ('behind, at the back'), from Late/Vulgar Latin de retro ('from behind, at the rear'), compound of de ('from, at') + retro ('backward, behind').

history.meaning: behind, in back of; rear end

descendre.etymology: Inherited from Old French descendre ('to come or go down, dismount'), from Classical Latin descendere ('to climb down, go down, sink'), compound of de- ('down from') + scandere ('to climb').

history.meaning: to go down, come down, get off; to carry down

desserrer.etymology: Formed in Old French (desserrer, 12th c.) from reversative prefix des- / dé- (Latin dis-) + serrer ('to press tight, lock, clench', from Late Latin serare 'to bolt, bar').

dessin.etymology: Deverbal noun from dessiner ('to draw, sketch, design'); originally spelled dessein in both senses ('mental plan/purpose' and 'graphic drawing') until the 17th–18th century split the spellings into dessein ('intention') and dessin ('drawing').

history.meaning: purpose, design -> graphic drawing, sketch, pattern

dessiner.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian disegnare ('to draw, outline, plan'), from Classical Latin designare ('to mark out, trace, point out'), from de- + signare ('to mark with a sign', from signum).

history.meaning: to mark out in lines, trace, draw

dessous.etymology: Formed in Old French (desoz, 11th c.) from de ('from, at') + souz / sous ('under, below', from Classical Latin subtus 'beneath, underneath').

dessus.etymology: Formed in Old French (desus, 11th c.) from de ('from, at') + sus ('up, above', from Vulgar Latin *susum < Classical Latin sursum 'upward, on high').

cognates.meaning: predetermined course of events (via French destinée)

destin.etymology: Deverbal noun attested from Old and Middle French, derived from destiner ('to fix, ordain, intend') or influenced by Italian destino, ultimately from Classical Latin dēstināre ('to make fast, fix firmly, resolve, appoint'), from dē- + *stanāre (a causative formation built on the root of stāre 'to stand').

history.meaning: to fasten down, fix, determine, intend
fixed decree of fate, overarching course of existence

destin.notes: 'Le destin' usually evokes fate as an impersonal cosmic force (or a grand artistic trajectory, 'un destin hors du commun'), whereas 'la destinée' highlights the lived path or individual lot.

cognates.meaning: to ordain or intend for a purpose

destiner.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in Old French (12th century) from Classical Latin dēstināre ('to fasten, secure, fix upon, resolve, assign'), composed of the prefix dē- and a derivative *stanāre related to stāre ('to stand firm', Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-), evolving from 'fixing physically in place' to 'fixing by intention or fate'.

history.meaning: to make fast, fix firmly; determine, appoint
to fix in advance, ordain by fate, intend for

morphemes.meaning: to make stand firm, fix (< *stanāre / stāre)

destiner.notes: In everyday French, 'être destiné à' often simply means 'to be intended/designed for' ('un scénario destiné au grand public') rather than grand mythological fate.

deux.etymology: Deux continues Latin duos, an object-case form of duo, two. The Académie records earlier French dos, dous and deus before the spelling deux.

cognates.meaning: Indo-European cognate, Latin loan, and Old French borrowing

deux.notes: Silent -x becomes a voiced /z/ in liaison before a vowel: deux amis /dø.z‿a.mi/, deux heures /dø.z‿œʁ/.

deuxième.etymology: Deuxième was formed from deux ('two', from Latin duos) + the ordinal suffix -ième, providing a regular ordinal alongside older second.
deuxième.notes: Used interchangeably with *second(e)*, and preferred whenever a third (*troisième*) exists.

devant.etymology: Formed in Old French (devant, 11th c.) from de ('from, at') + avant ('in front, before', from Late Latin abante < ab + ante).

devenir.etymology: Inherited from Old French devenir ('to come to be, become'), from Classical Latin devenire ('to come down from, arrive at, reach a state'), from de- + venire ('to come').

deviner.etymology: Inherited from Old French deviner ('to practice divination, foretell, guess'), from Classical Latin divinare ('to foresee, prophesy, guess'), derived from divinus ('inspired by a god, prophetic', from divus / deus 'god').

history.meaning: prophetic -> to foretell by inspiration, guess
to foretell -> to guess, figure out

devoir.etymology: Devoir comes from Latin debere, to owe or be indebted. Its French use to express obligation is recorded from the ninth century. The noun meaning duty developed from the verb.

morphemes.meaning: owe, be bound to (< Latin dēb-)

history.stage: Old French (9th c., dover; 11th c., deveir)

history.meaning: must, have to, owe; duty, school homework (n.)

cognates.meaning: from Middle French se mettre en devoir and Anglo-Norman

devoir.notes: Masculine past participle dû carries a circumflex solely to distinguish it from the partitive/contracted article du (feminine due and plural dus drop the circumflex).

cognates.meaning: precious crystalline carbon; unyielding substance (doublet: adamant)

diamant.etymology: Inherited via Old French diamant (12th century) from Medieval/Vulgar Latin diamās (accusative diamantem), an alteration (likely influenced by diaphanus 'transparent' or di-) of Classical Latin adamās (accusative adamantem 'hardest steel, diamond'), borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas, 'untamable, unconquerable'), from privative ἀ- ('not') + δαμάω (damáō 'to tame').
diamant.notes: A fascinating etymological doublet of 'aimant' (magnet, also from Latin adamantem via Old French aimant) and English 'adamant'; idiomatically, 'un diamant brut' means 'a diamond in the rough' (e.g., raw acting talent).

diction.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (15th century, originally 'word, phrasing, style') from Classical Latin dictiō (accusative dictiōnem, 'a saying, utterance, mode of expression, delivery'), an action noun formed from dictus, past participle of dīcere ('to say, speak', from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- 'to point out, show').

history.meaning: word choice, literary phrasing; later vocal articulation (18th c.)

morphemes.meaning: say, speak (< Latin dict-, from dīcere)

diction.notes: Subtle nuance vs. English: while English 'diction' in literature often means 'word choice', French 'diction' today refers almost exclusively to vocal articulation and stage/screen delivery ('travailler sa diction au Conservatoire').

dieu.etymology: Inherited from Old French dieu ('God, a god'), from Classical Latin deus ('god, deity'), from PIE *deiwos ('celestial one, god', built on *dyew- 'bright sky, day').

cognates.meaning: injury to reputation by false statements

diffamation.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (13th century, diffamacion) from Classical/Late Latin diffāmātiō (accusative diffāmātiōnem), action noun of diffāmāre ('to spread abroad, divulge, noise abroad an ill report'), composed of dis- ('abroad, in all directions', assimilated to dif-) + fāma ('rumor, reputation', akin to fārī 'to speak').

history.meaning: to spread rumors abroad, divulge to someone's discredit
public disgrace, sullying of someone's good name

diffamation.notes: Watch the spelling difference from English ('diffamation' with -ff- and -i-, vs. 'defamation'), a constant legal flashpoint with French celebrity tabloids ('porter plainte pour diffamation').

cognates.meaning: hard to accomplish or deal with (back-formed from difficulty)

difficile.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (14th century) from Classical Latin difficilis ('hard to do, troublesome; hard to please, morose'), formed by vowel weakening in pre-Classical Latin from dis- ('away, not') + facilis ('easy, doable'), itself derived from facere ('to make, do').

history.meaning: hard to perform; obstinate, hard to please

morphemes.meaning: do, make (< Latin fac-, weakened to -fic- in compounds)

difficile.notes: Applied to a person ('un comédien difficile', 'ne fais pas le difficile !'), it means 'fussy, picky, or hard to work with' — preserving a sense already present in Classical Latin!

différemment.etymology: Formed in Middle French (15th century) from the adjective différent (< Latin differēns, present participle of differre 'to carry apart, differ') + the adverbial suffix -ment; because adjectives in -ent come from Latin one-termination -ēns stems, -ent + -ment assimilates regularly to -emment, pronounced /-amɑ̃/.
différemment.notes: Pronunciation trap for learners: the '-emment' ending is pronounced [a.mɑ̃] ('diffé-ra-ment'), not [ɛ.mɑ̃], and it is spelled with an acute accent on the first 'é' plus double 'm'.

différence.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (12th century, difference) from Classical Latin differentia ('diversity, distinction, difference'), abstract noun formed on differēns (stem different-), present participle of differre ('to carry in different directions, scatter, put off, be distinct'), from dis- ('apart') + ferre ('to carry').

history.meaning: carrying apart; diversity, distinction between species

morphemes.meaning: apart, in separate directions (< Latin dis-)

différence.notes: Useful prepositional contrast: 'à la différence de' means 'unlike / in contrast to' ('À la différence de son agent, elle adore le théâtre subventionné').

différent.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (14th century) from Classical Latin differēns (accusative differentem), present participle of differre ('to carry apart, disperse; to differ'), composed of dis- ('apart') + ferre ('to bear, carry', from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-).
différent.notes: Position changes meaning AND grammar: after a noun, 'des rôles différents' means 'different (distinct) roles', whereas before a plural noun with zero article, 'différents rôles' means 'various / several roles'. Also don't confuse with the noun 'un différend' (a dispute)!

cognates.meaning: to consider worthy (in 'deign', via Old French deignier)

digne.etymology: Entered Old French (11th century) as a semi-learned borrowing from Classical Latin dignus ('worthy, deserving, fitting, proper'), from Proto-Italic *deknos, derived with suffix *-nos from Proto-Indo-European *deḱ- ('to take, accept, conform, be fitting'; cognate with Latin decet 'it is fitting' and decus 'ornament, honor').

history.meaning: deserving of honor or respect; fitting

digne.notes: Has two key constructions: absolute 'rester digne' ('to remain dignified / keep one's composure') and relational 'digne de' ('worthy of', e.g. 'digne de confiance' = trustworthy, 'digne d'un César').

dignement.etymology: Formed in Old French (12th century) from the epicene adjective digne ('worthy, fitting, noble', from Latin dignus) and the adverbial suffix -ment (< Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind/disposition').

history.meaning: with a worthy or fitting disposition

dignement.notes: Often used slightly playfully in everyday French with 'fêter' or 'arroser': 'Il faut fêter ça dignement !' means 'We have to celebrate this properly / in style!'.

dignité.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French dinité / dignité) from Classical Latin dignitatem (nominative dignitas, 'worthiness, merit, honorable rank'), derived from dignus ('worthy, deserving').

cognates.meaning: embankment against flooding; excavated ditch (doublet: ditch)

digue.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th century, originally feminine digue / dique along the North Sea coast) from Middle Dutch dijc ('embankment, dam, ditch'), from Proto-West Germanic *dīk ('trench, earthwork embankment', since digging a drainage trench simultaneously raises an earthen seawall).

history.meaning: excavated channel and earthen seawall embankment
coastal embankment or breakwater holding back water

digue.notes: Used figuratively for emotional or institutional restraint giving way under pressure: 'les digues ont cédé' or 'faire sauter les digues' ('the floodgates broke / all restraint gave way').

rootFamily.gloss: to embank, contain, stem (a crisis or flood)

cognates.meaning: to break down food or assimilate mentally

digérer.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (14th–15th century) from Classical Latin dīgerere ('to carry apart, separate, distribute, arrange in order; dissolve or assimilate food in the body'), composed of dis- ('apart', becoming dī- before g-) + gerere ('to bear, carry, manage').

history.meaning: to carry apart, distribute, arrange; dissolve food in the stomach
to assimilate food physiologically; to ponder and absorb mentally

morphemes.meaning: apart, in separate directions (< Latin dis- / dī-)

digérer.notes: Very common figuratively in French for stomaching a setback or snub ('Il n'a toujours pas digéré son éviction du casting' = 'He still hasn't gotten over / stomached being cut from the cast'); note the stem alternation 'je digère / nous digérons'.

rootFamily.gloss: hard to digest; tediously dense (un scénario indigeste)

dimanche.etymology: Inherited from Old French diemenche ('Sunday'), from Ecclesiastical/Late Latin dies dominica (revised to *dia dominica, 'the Lord's day', translating Greek kyriake hemera), replacing pagan dies Solis ('day of the Sun').

dindon.etymology: Formed in Middle French from dinde ('turkey hen') plus the diminutive and masculine suffix -on (originally designating a young turkey poult before shifting to 'male turkey' and 'turkey' generally). Dinde itself arose by ellipsis and reanalysis of coq d'Inde or poule d'Inde ('rooster/hen of India'), reflecting 16th-century Europeans' misidentification of the newly discovered Americas (the West Indies), whence the domesticated bird was imported via Spain, as 'India'.
dindon.notes: Featured in the classic idiom être le dindon de la farce ('to be the dupe/fall guy'), often used in agency negotiations when someone gets outmaneuvered.

rootFamily.gloss: to dupe, make a fool of (archaic/literary)

dingue.etymology: Attested in late 19th- and early 20th-century Parisian slang, probably derived as a deverbal adjective from dinguer ('to stagger, fall, flail, be sent flying', as in envoyer dinguer), itself built on an expressive onomatopoeic stem ding- evoking erratic swinging or ringing. Semantic development toward 'mad, crazy' was likely reinforced by colonial military slang dingue / dengue ('dengue fever'), an illness notorious for causing high-fever delirium.

history.meaning: to stagger, fall over, be thrown aside

dingue.notes: Inversible for gender (un truc dingue, une histoire dingue) and ubiquitous in informal showbiz speech: c'est dingue ! ('that's insane!') or être dingue de quelqu'un ('to be crazy about someone').

rootFamily.gloss: to send flying; (envoyer dinguer) to brush off

diplomatique.etymology: Adapted from Neo-Latin diplomaticus ('pertaining to official charters and archival documents'), popularized by Jean Mabillon's treatise De re diplomatica (1681) on authenticating medieval charters, from Latin diploma ('folded state document'). In late 18th-century French (corps diplomatique), since treaties and state credentials were 'diplomas', the adjective shifted to foreign statecraft and thence to 'tactful, skilled in delicate negotiation'.

history.meaning: relating to ancient charters and official state documents
pertaining to ambassadors and international relations
diplomatic; tactful and discreet in handling people

diplomatique.notes: Watch the distinction: une réponse diplomatique means a tactful or strategically non-committal reply, whereas un diplomate is a diplomat (person).

diplôme.etymology: Learned borrowing in the 16th–17th centuries from Classical Latin diploma ('state letter of recommendation, official privilege granted by magistrates'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek díplōma ('paper folded in two, double tablet'), derived from diplóō ('to fold double'), from diploûs ('double, twofold'). From designating royal charters and medical licenses under the Ancien Régime, it generalized after the Revolution to academic degrees and professional certificates.

history.meaning: object folded in two; double-leaved passport or license
official state letter conferring privileges or safe-conduct
royal charter; academic degree or professional certificate

diplôme.notes: Masculine noun (un diplôme) despite ending in -e; in France it covers university degrees (equivalent to English 'degree') as well as vocational certificates.

diplômé.etymology: Past-participial adjective and noun formed in 19th-century French from the verb diplômer ('to confer an academic degree or official certificate upon'), itself derived from diplôme ('charter, degree'), ultimately via Latin diploma from Ancient Greek díplōma ('folded document'). It denotes someone officially certified by an institution.

history.meaning: to grant an official diploma or license to
certified, holding an academic or professional degree

diplômé.notes: Used both as an adjective (diplômé d'une grande école) and as a noun (un jeune diplômé, 'a recent college graduate').

dire.etymology: Dire continues Latin dicere, meaning to say or express something in words. The Académie dates the French verb to the tenth century. Declaring, naming and recounting are extensions of that central meaning.
dire.notes:
- Irregular: the *vous* form is *dites*, not *disez* (also *vous redites*, but *vous contredisez*).
- *Dire* is used with indirect speech: *dire que* + clause.

direct.etymology: Learned borrowing (14th century) from Classical Latin directus ('laid straight, aligned, level, straightforward'), past participle of dirigere ('to set in a straight line, guide, steer'), compounded from dis- / de- (intensive/directional) and regere ('to rule, guide straight'). Notice its inherited Old French doublet droit ('straight, right, law'), which underwent regular Vulgar Latin syncope (*directus > *drectus > dreit > droit).

history.meaning: set in a straight line, level, straightforward
unmediated, moving in a straight line

direct.notes: Essential media expression: en direct means 'live' (on air/television), and in colloquial French direct is also used as an invariable adverb meaning 'right away, straight up' (il a dit oui direct).

directement.etymology: Formed in Middle French (14th century) from directe, the feminine form of the learned adjective direct (from Latin directus, 'straight, unmediated'), combined with the adverbial suffix -ment (inherited from the Classical Latin ablative singular mente, 'with a ... mind/manner').

history.meaning: in a straight line, without intermediary

morphemes.meaning: adverbial suffix of manner (from Latin mente)

directement.notes: The internal mute e in -te- is generally pronounced in careful speech ([di.ʁɛk.tə.mɑ̃]) to break up the four-consonant cluster -ctm-.

directeur.etymology: Learned borrowing in the late 15th century from Late Latin director (accusative directorem, 'guide, leader, spiritual or administrative overseer'), agent noun formed on the supine stem direct- of Classical Latin dirigere ('to align, steer, guide'), from dis- and regere ('to rule, keep straight').

history.meaning: spiritual advisor; person who guides an enterprise
executive manager, school head, department head

directeur.notes: Crucial cinema false friend! A film 'director' in French is un réalisateur (or metteur en scène in theater), NOT un directeur—though cinema crews do have un directeur de casting ('casting director') and un directeur de la photographie ('cinematographer').

direction.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Late/Classical Latin directionem (nominative directio, 'a making straight, aiming in a straight line'), action noun from dirigere ('to set straight, guide, direct').

history.meaning: setting in a straight line, guidance
line of movement, direction; management, steering

directrice.etymology: Learned borrowing (16th century) from Late Latin directrix (accusative directricem, 'female guide, female ruler'), feminine agent noun corresponding to director, built on the participial stem direct- of Classical Latin dirigere ('to guide straight, govern'), from dis- and regere ('to rule, steer').

history.meaning: woman who guides or heads a religious or educational house
female executive, manager, school principal; guiding (adj., e.g. idée directrice)

directrice.notes: Unlike newer feminized titles, directrice is fully established in all registers; as an adjective (une ligne directrice, 'a guideline'), it translates 'guiding'.

diriger.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin dirigere ('to set in a straight line, align, guide, steer'), compound of dis- / de- + regere ('to keep straight, rule, guide').

discours.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical/Late Latin discursus ('a running to and fro; in Late Latin, conversation, treatise, reasoning'), from discurrere ('to run about, treat of a subject').

history.meaning: running about -> orderly exposition in speech

discret.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–13th century from Medieval/Ecclesiastical Latin discretus ('discerning, prudent, wise; separate, distinct'), originally the past participle of Classical Latin discernere ('to separate, distinguish, perceive clearly').

discrimination.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin discriminatio (accusative discriminationem, 'separation, distinction, rhetorical contrasting'), derived from Classical Latin discriminare ('to divide, part, distinguish'), from discrimen ('dividing line, interval, distinction'), built on discernere ('to separate, sift apart', from dis- 'apart' + cernere 'to sift, perceive'). While first used in French for neutral cognitive 'distinction', its modern sociopolitical sense of 'unfair prejudicial treatment' spread in the 20th century under the semantic influence of American English discrimination.

history.meaning: act of separating, contrasting, or distinguishing
faculty of distinguishing between things or concepts
unfair or prejudicial treatment of a person or group

discrimination.notes: Note that French discrimination almost exclusively carries the negative sense of 'prejudicial treatment'; for positive aesthetic 'discernment' or 'good taste', French uses discernement.

discrètement.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French (13th–14th centuries, originally 'wisely, with discernment') from discrète, feminine of discret, plus the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin mente). Discret was borrowed from Medieval and Ecclesiastical Latin discretus ('discerning, prudent, reserved'), specialized from the Classical Latin past participle of discernere ('to separate, distinguish', from dis- 'apart' + cernere 'to sift').
discrètement.notes: Notice the grave accent in discrètement (matching the feminine adjective discrète), whereas English splits the Latin root into two spellings ('discreet' vs. 'discrete') that French keeps under discret.

discréditer.etymology: Attested in 16th-century French (modeled on or reinforced by Italian discreditare, 'to ruin someone's commercial or moral credit'), formed with the privative/reversative prefix dis- and crédit ('trust, reputation, financial standing', borrowed via Italian credito from Latin creditum, 'loan, thing entrusted', neuter past participle of credere, 'to believe, trust').

history.meaning: to destroy someone's commercial trust or standing
to discredit, undermine the reputation or credibility of

discréditer.notes: Frequently used reflexively in PR and agency crises: se discréditer ('to ruin one's own credibility'). Conjugates with alternating accents like céder (il discrédite, nous discréditons).

rootFamily.gloss: to credit; to lend credence to

discrétion.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Late/Ecclesiastical Latin discretionem (nominative discretio, 'separation, power of distinguishing, discernment, prudence'), derived from discernere, discretum.

history.meaning: good judgment, reserve, tact; free judgment (à discrétion)

discuter.etymology: Learned borrowing (Old/Middle French, 13th–14th centuries) from Latin discutere ('to strike asunder, shatter, disperse, scatter', and in Late and Judicial Latin 'to examine, investigate, debate a point'), compounded from dis- ('apart, in pieces') and quatere ('to shake, strike'). In French it moved from medical 'dispersing a humor' and legal 'liquidating a debtor's assets' to examining arguments and finally everyday conversation.

history.meaning: to strike apart, disperse; (Late Latin) to examine judicially
to dissipate (medicine); to examine critically or debate
to talk over, chat, negotiate, or debate

discuter.notes: Grammar trap for English speakers: you cannot say *discuter un problème for 'discuss a problem' in everyday sense—use discuter de quelque chose ('talk about / discuss something') or discuter avec quelqu'un ('chat with someone'); transitive discuter un contrat / un prix specifically means 'to contest or haggle over'.

disparaître.etymology: Formed in the 15th century (replacing Old French despareir) from prefix dis- ('away, reversal') + paraître ('to appear, come into view', from Vulgar Latin *parescere, inchoative of Classical Latin parere 'to appear').

history.meaning: to pass out of sight, vanish, disappear

disponible.etymology: Learned legal borrowing (late 14th–15th centuries) from Medieval Latin disponibilis ('that of which one may freely dispose'), derived from Classical Latin disponere ('to distribute, set in order, arrange'), compounded from dis- ('apart, in distinct places') and ponere ('to put, place'). Originally restricted to property law (biens disponibles, 'unencumbered assets'), it broadened in the 18th–19th centuries to goods in stock and people free of commitments.

history.meaning: legally free to be disposed of or bequeathed
available, free, open (of schedules, actors, or goods)

morphemes.meaning: adjectival suffix of capability ('able to be')

disponible.notes: In talent agencies and workplaces, it is endlessly shortened to the invariable clipped form dispo: Tu es dispo mardi pour le tournage ? ('Are you free Tuesday for the shoot?').

rootFamily.gloss: to arrange; (disposer de) to have at one's disposal

disposition.etymology: Learned borrowing (12th–13th centuries) from Classical Latin dispositio (accusative dispositionem, 'regular arrangement, ordering, management, rhetorical structure'), action noun formed on the participial stem disposit- of disponere ('to set in different places, distribute, arrange'), from dis- ('apart') and ponere ('to place').

history.meaning: arrangement, state of mind or bodily condition
layout, legal provision, inclination; (à la disposition de) disposal/service

morphemes.meaning: placed, arranged (from ponere, past participle positus)

disposition.notes: Polite professional staple: Je reste à votre entière disposition translates 'Please do not hesitate to reach out / I remain at your disposal', while une disposition légale means a 'clause or legal provision' in a contract.

rootFamily.gloss: to arrange; to have at one's disposal

dispute.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Middle French (originally 'formal scholastic debate', then 'heated argument, quarrel') from disputer ('to debate, argue').

disputer.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin disputare ('to weigh or examine from all sides, discuss, debate'), compound of dis- ('apart, in different directions') + putare ('to reckon, consider, clear up').

history.meaning: to debate -> to contend for, quarrel, scold

disque.etymology: Learned borrowing in the 17th century from Classical Latin discus ('quoit, flat circular plate'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek dískos ('throwing quoit, round platter'), derived from the verb dikeîn ('to throw, cast'). Initially referring to the Greek athletic discus and astronomical discs, it was adopted in the late 19th and 20th centuries for flat phonograph records, musical albums, and computer hard drives. Its inherited Old French doublet is dais ('table, canopy platform').

history.meaning: quoit, flat circular plate or sundial face
athletic discus; musical record/album; hard drive (disque dur)

disque.notes: Rich in idiomatic speech: changer de disque ('change the record / stop harping on the same topic') and un disque d'or ('a gold record').

distance.etymology: Borrowed in 13th-century Old French from Classical Latin distantia ('standing apart, remoteness, interval, difference, diversity'), abstract noun formed on distans (stem distant-), present participle of distare ('to stand apart, be separate or distant'), compounded from dis- ('apart') and stare ('to stand').

history.meaning: discord, difference; spatial or temporal interval

distance.notes: Key expressions: à distance ('remotely', e.g. travailler à distance) and prendre ses distances avec quelqu'un ('to distance oneself from someone').

rootFamily.gloss: to outstrip, leave behind; to distance

distingué.etymology: Past-participle adjective of distinguer ('to distinguish, set apart'), borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin distinguere ('to separate by pricking, mark off, differentiate'), from dis- ('apart') + -stinguere ('to prick, mark', related to stimulus and English sting). By the 17th-century classical age, distingué came to describe a person whose bearing, manners, or talent stands out with quiet elegance.
distingué.notes: In formal French letters, **mes salutations distinguées** is the classic polite closing formula.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: distingué

cognates.meaning: built on the same Latin verb distinguere

distribuer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin distribuere ('to divide and deal out among several, apportion'), compound of dis- ('apart') + tribuere ('to assign, allot, grant').

distributeur.etymology: Learned borrowing (Middle French, 14th–16th centuries) from Late and Ecclesiastical Latin distributor (accusative distributorem, 'one who divides, apportions, or dispenses'), agent noun built on the supine stem distribut- of Classical Latin distribuere ('to divide, deal out, apportion'), from dis- ('apart, individually') and tribuere ('to allot, assign, grant').

history.meaning: one who apportions or dispenses shares
person who deals out alms, goods, or roles
commercial/film distributor; ATM or vending machine

distributeur.notes: Dual meaning to know! In the film industry (Dix pour cent), le distributeur is the film distribution company that releases a movie to theaters; on the street, un distributeur (de billets) is an ATM or vending machine.

rootFamily.gloss: to distribute, hand out; to cast (roles in a film)
distribution; cast of actors in a film or play

divin.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin divinus ('of a god, godlike, prophetic, supremely admirable'), derived from divus ('god, deity', akin to deus).

diviser.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century (replacing native Old French deviser in mathematical and physical senses) from Classical Latin dividere, divisum ('to force apart, separate into parts, distribute').

divorce.etymology: Learned borrowing in 14th-century Middle French (notably by Nicole Oresme) from Classical Latin divortium ('parting of ways, fork in a road or river, separation, legal dissolution of marriage'), derived from divertere / archaic divortere ('to turn aside, go in different directions, leave one's spouse'), compounded from dis- ('apart, in opposite directions') and vertere ('to turn').

history.meaning: fork in a road; separation, dissolution of marriage
marital separation; breach or discord between parties
legal dissolution of marriage; figurative split or rift

divorce.notes: Masculine noun (un divorce); frequently used figuratively in politics and business for an irreconcilable split (le divorce est consommé entre l'acteur et son agent).

rootFamily.gloss: various, diverse (from the same Latin root divertere)

divorcer.etymology: Derived in Middle French (late 14th–15th centuries, reinforced by Late Latin divortiare) from the noun divorce ('dissolution of marriage', from Classical Latin divortium, 'parting of ways', from dis- + vertere 'to turn') plus the productive first-conjugation verbal suffix -er. It gained widespread legal currency when civil divorce was instituted during the French Revolution in 1792.

history.meaning: to dissolve a marriage; to separate

divorcer.notes: Watch both syntax and spelling: French uses an intransitive construction—divorcer de quelqu'un or divorcer d'avec quelqu'un (NOT *se divorcer or direct transitive *divorcer son mari)—and inserts a cedilla before a/o (nous divorçons).

dix.etymology: Dix descends from Latin decem, ten. Eleventh-century French spellings included dis and diz.
dix.notes: Has three pronunciations depending on context: /dis/ standalone (j'en ai dix), /di/ before a consonant (dix livres), and /diz/ in liaison before a vowel (dix ans /di.z‿ɑ̃/).

dix-huit.etymology: Inherited from Old French dis et oit / dis-uit ('eighteen'), additive compound of dix ('ten', from Latin decem) + huit ('eight', from Latin octo), replacing Classical Latin subtractive duodeviginti ('two from twenty').

dix-huitième.etymology: Formed in French by attaching the ordinal suffix -ième (from Old French -isme / -iesme, generalized from Vulgar Latin *-esimus) to the additive compound cardinal numeral dix-huit ('eighteen'). Dix-huit continues Old French dis et uit, reflecting Late/Vulgar Latin decem (et) octo ('ten and eight'), which replaced the Classical Latin subtractive formation duodeviginti ('two from twenty').
dix-huitième.notes: Pronunciation rule: the x in dix-huitième voices to [z] ([di.zɥi.tjɛm]) by internal liaison despite the silent Latinate h of huit, and in Paris le dix-huitième refers to the 18th arrondissement (Montmartre).

dix-neuf.etymology: Inherited from Old French dis et nuef / dis-nuef ('nineteen'), additive compound of dix ('ten', from Latin decem) + neuf ('nine', from Latin novem), replacing Classical Latin subtractive undeviginti ('one from twenty').

dix-sept.etymology: Inherited through Old French dis et set (later juxtaposed without conjunction as dis-set, respelled etymologically dix-sept) from Late/Vulgar Latin decem (et) septem ('ten [and] seven'), an analytic ten-first compound that supplanted Classical Latin septemdecim ('seven-ten') across the Western Romance languages. Combining Classical Latin decem ('ten') and septem ('seven').
dix-sept.notes: Pronounced [dis.sɛt] (or assimilated to [di.sɛt] in rapid speech): here x is voiceless [s] before the voiceless s- of sept, and the p in sept is completely silent while the final t is always pronounced.

dizaine.etymology: Inherited from Old French disaine ('group of ten'), formed from dis / dix ('ten', from Latin decem) + collective numerical suffix -aine (from Latin -ena).

do.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th–18th century from Italian do, introduced by music theorists (traditionally linked to Giovanni Battista Doni or the syllable of Dominus 'Lord') as a more open, singable vowel to replace Guido d'Arezzo's original first solfège syllable ut.

history.meaning: first note of the diatonic scale (C)

docteur.etymology: Learned borrowing in late 12th-century Old French from Classical Latin doctor (accusative doctorem, 'teacher, instructor, trainer'), agent noun built on the supine stem doct- of docere ('to teach, show, cause to know'), originally a causative formation from Proto-Indo-European *deḱ- ('to take, accept, perceive'). In medieval universities and Church usage it meant an authorized master teacher (docteur de l'Église, docteur en droit) before extending in the 16th–19th centuries to medical physicians.

history.meaning: learned theologian, university master empowered to teach
holder of a doctorate (PhD); medical doctor (physician)

docteur.notes: Register nuance: Docteur is the standard polite form of address (Bonjour, Docteur) and denotes a PhD holder (docteur ès lettres), whereas in third-person formal prose the profession 'physician' is un médecin (aller chez le médecin is preferred in careful style over colloquial aller chez le docteur).

document.etymology: Learned borrowing in 12th-century Old French from Classical Latin documentum ('lesson, example, warning, specimen, proof'), formed from the verb docere ('to teach, demonstrate, instruct') plus the resultative/instrumental noun suffix -mentum. For five centuries in French it meant 'teaching, moral lesson, instruction' before specializing in the 17th–18th centuries into 'written evidence, official record, archival paper'.

history.meaning: written record, official paper, digital file

morphemes.meaning: to teach, show, prove (from Latin docere)

document.notes: Often clipped in casual office and agency speech to un doc (Je t'envoie les docs par mail).

rootFamily.gloss: to document; (se documenter) to do background research

documentaire.etymology: Formed in late 19th-century French (1870s) from document ('official record, factual evidence', from Latin documentum) plus the relational suffix -aire (modeled initially on English documentary in the legal/archival sense 'based on documents'). Crucially for film history, French cinema critics coined le documentaire as a noun in the 1900s–1920s for non-fiction travelogues and factual films—a sense that Scottish filmmaker John Grierson then calqued back into English as documentary in 1926.

history.meaning: based on or serving as archival/written proof
non-fiction factual film or broadcast program

documentaire.notes: Masculine as a noun (un documentaire, informally un docu in television and film production); hybrid docudramas are called des docu-fictions.

doigt.etymology: Inherited from Old French doi ('finger'), from Classical Latin digitus ('finger, toe; inch-like measure'), respelled doigt in Middle French with silent etymological g and t after Latin digitus.

dollar.etymology: Borrowed in the late 18th century (especially around American independence) from English dollar, which had adapted Low German and Dutch daler, a clipped form of Early New High German Joachimstaler ('silver coin minted at Sankt Joachimsthal', modern Jáchymov in Bohemia, from 1519 onward). The German compound combines the saint's name Joachim with Tal (older spelling Thal, 'valley') + relational suffix -er ('of the valley'). French also borrowed the German coin name directly as thaler / taler.

history.meaning: large silver coin from Joachim's Valley in Bohemia
Spanish-American peso/piece of eight; US currency unit (1785)
dollar (currency of the US, Canada, Australia, etc.)

dollar.notes: Pronounced [dɔ.laʁ] with a silent plural -s, and masculine in gender (un million de dollars—remember the preposition de after million/milliard before a currency noun!).

rootFamily.gloss: historical German silver coin (doublet of dollar)
conversion of an economy to US dollars

domaine.etymology: Evolved from Old French demaine / demeine ('feudal lord's personal landholding, hereditary property'), altered in Middle French to domaine through re-Latinizing influence of Latin dominus ('lord, master') and domus ('house'). It continues Classical Latin dominium ('ownership, property right, lordship, feast'), derived from dominus ('master of a household'), itself built on domus ('house, home'). From landed estates (such as wine estates), it extended figuratively in the 17th–18th centuries to fields of knowledge and expertise.

history.meaning: lord's hereditary estate or crown land
country/wine estate; sphere of activity, field of expertise, web domain

domaine.notes: Versatile across registers: dans mon domaine ('in my field of expertise'), tomber dans le domaine public ('to enter the public domain', crucial for literary/film adaptations), and un domaine viticole ('a wine estate').

domestique.etymology: Learned borrowing in 14th-century Middle French from Classical Latin domesticus ('belonging to the house or household, family, private, native'), derived from domus ('house, home, household', from Proto-Indo-European *dóm- / *dem- 'house, household'). Originally an adjective meaning 'living under the same roof, tame (of animals)', it was substantivized in the 16th century to designate members of a nobleman's household retinue and later paid household servants.

history.meaning: belonging to the house or family; private
belonging to the household; tamed (of animals)
household servant; domestic (relating to the home)

domestique.notes: Double watch-out: as a noun (un/une domestique) for 'servant', it now sounds dated or period-drama (replaced in modern speech by employé(e) de maison); as an adjective, 'domestic flight' is traditionally un vol intérieur in proper French rather than the anglicism *vol domestique.

dominer.etymology: Learned borrowing (attested in the 12th century, popularized in the 14th) from Classical Latin dominari ('to be lord and master, rule over, hold sway'), a deponent verb derived from dominus ('master of a household, lord, owner'), itself formed with the leadership suffix -nus on domus ('house, household'). Beyond ruling or overpowering, it developed physical senses ('to tower over a landscape') and psychological senses ('to keep emotions under control').

history.meaning: to be lord and master, exercise sovereignty
to exercise authority or rule over
to dominate, overpower, tower over; (se dominer) to control oneself

dominer.notes: Reflexive se dominer is high-grade idiomatic French for 'to keep one's composure / master one's temper' under pressure.

cognates.meaning: damage; what a pity (che danno, regional/older)

dommage.etymology: Inherited from Old French damage / domage ('harm, injury, financial loss'), where the initial vowel a labialized to o before the nasal m (probably aided by folk-etymological association with dom / dominus, 'lord'). Old French damage derives regularly from Vulgar Latin *damnaticum ('harm, penalty'), built with the collective/abstract suffix -aticum (> French -age) on Classical Latin damnum ('loss, harm, legal fine'). English damage was borrowed directly from the older unrounded Anglo-Norman/Old French form damage.

history.meaning: material or moral harm, detriment, misfortune

dommage.notes: Everyday conversational essential: C'est dommage ! or Quel dommage ! means 'What a shame / Too bad!', whereas the plural dommages retains the legal/material sense in dommages et intérêts ('monetary damages' in a lawsuit).

rootFamily.gloss: to compensate, indemnify for a loss

don.etymology: Inherited from Old French don, from Classical Latin dōnum ("gift, present, votive offering"), itself from Proto-Indo-European *déh₃nom ("gift"), a nominal derivative of the root *deh₃- ("to give"). Beyond a material offering or legal grant, Christian Latin and Old French extended the word to spiritual grace and thence to an innate artistic or intellectual aptitude.

history.meaning: donation; innate talent or natural gift

don.notes: In casting and agency talk, avoir un don ("to have a natural gift") contrasts raw, effortless charisma with learned conservatory technique; also used for charitable giving (faire un don).

donateur.etymology: Learned borrowing (attested in legal French by the 14th century) from Classical Latin dōnātor (accusative dōnātōrem, "giver, bestower"), agent noun formed from dōnāre ("to present, bestow"), itself from dōnum ("gift"). It forms an etymological doublet with the inherited vernacular noun donneur, preserving a more formal, juridical, and philanthropic register.

history.meaning: person making a formal legal donation

donateur.notes: Distinguish register carefully: un donateur gives money, art, or patronage (gala fundraisers, foundations), whereas un donneur gives biological tissue (donneur de sang, donneur d'organes). Feminine: donatrice.

donc.etymology: Inherited from Old French donc / donques ('then, at that time; therefore'), from Vulgar Latin *dunc / *dumque, formed on Classical Latin dum ('while, then') blended with tunc ('then, at that time').

cognates.meaning: to give; deal (in card games: dare le carte)

donne.etymology: Deverbal feminine noun formed in Early Modern French from donner ("to give; to deal cards"), inherited via Old French doner from Vulgar Latin dōnāre ("to give", displacing Classical dare), from Classical Latin dōnum ("gift"). Originating at the gaming table for the distribution of cards, it broadened metaphorically in the 20th century to the prevailing balance of power or set of circumstances.

history.meaning: to bestow a gift; (Vulgar Latin) to give
act of dealing cards; cards dealt in a round
card deal; strategic situation or state of play

donne.notes: Essential in the high-frequency idiom changer la donne ("to change the game / alter the whole situation") and nouvelle donne ("new deal / new reality")—a staple of crisis negotiations at ASK.

donner.etymology: Inherited from Old French doner ('to give'), from Classical Latin donare ('to present as a gift, bestow'), derived from donum ('gift'), which displaced irregular Classical Latin dare across Gaul.

history.meaning: to present with a gift -> to give

donneur.etymology: Inherited from Old French doneor ("giver"), derived regularly from doner (Modern French donner, "to give") + the agentive suffix -eor (Modern French -eur), reflecting Vulgar Latin dōnātōrem. English donor was borrowed directly from the Anglo-Norman form donour, while French later re-borrowed Classical Latin dōnātōrem as the learned doublet donateur.
donneur.notes: Beyond medical contexts (donneur d'organes) and business (donneur d'ordre, "client/commissioning party"), watch out for the sharp idiom donneur de leçons ("preachy, sanctimonious person"). Feminine: donneuse.

dormeuse.etymology: Feminine form of dormeur ("sleeper"), attested since Old French (dormeor, feminine dormeuse), built on the stem of dormir ("to sleep") + the agentive suffix -euse (from Latin -ōsam / -ātōrem). Dormir continues Classical Latin dormīre ("to sleep"), from Proto-Indo-European *drem- ("to sleep"). In the 18th and 19th centuries dormeuse also acquired specialized senses for a daybed, a sleeping carriage, and sleeper earrings worn overnight.

history.meaning: sleeping woman, sleepyhead; chaise longue; sleeper earring

dormeuse.notes: Affectionate or teasing when used for a person (Quelle dormeuse !, "What a sleepyhead!"), while in costume and jewelry departments des dormeuses specifically refers to clasp-back earrings safe to sleep in.

rootFamily.gloss: to lull to sleep; to fool someone

dormir.etymology: Dormir continues Latin dormire, to sleep. The Académie records the French verb from the twelfth century.

cognates.meaning: from Old French dormant and Latin dormītōrium

dormir.notes: Drops stem-final -m- in singular present forms: je dors, tu dors, il dort, before restoring it in nous dormons, ils dorment.

doré.etymology: Past participle of dorer ('to gild, coat with gold, brown to a golden hue'), inherited from Old French dorer, from Late Latin deaurare ('to gild over'), compound of de- + aurare (from aurum 'gold').

dos.etymology: Inherited from Old French dos ('back'), from Vulgar Latin *dossum, assimilation of Classical Latin dorsum ('back of a person or animal, ridge').

history.meaning: anatomical back, reverse or spine of an object

dossier.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from dos ('back') + suffix -ier; originally meant 'chair-back or headboard against which one leans one's back', and in the 18th century acquired the sense 'bundle of legal or administrative papers labeled on the back or spine (au dos)'.

history.meaning: chair-back -> bundle of papers labeled on the spine, file, case

double.etymology: Inherited from Old French doble ('twofold, double'), from Classical Latin duplus ('twofold, twice as much'), formed from duo ('two') + *-plos ('-fold').

doublure.etymology: Derived in Old French (doublëure, 13th century) from doubler ("to double, fold in two, line a garment") + the resultative suffix -ure (from Latin -ūram). Doubler stems from Late Latin duplāre ("to double"), from Classical Latin duplus ("twofold, twice as much"). Originally denoting a protective inner lining sewn inside clothing or armor, the word shifted in late 18th-century theater to an understudy and in 20th-century cinema to a stand-in, body double, or stunt double.

history.meaning: inner fabric lining of a garment or shield
garment lining; theatrical understudy; film stand-in or body double

morphemes.meaning: noun suffix denoting result, lining, or function

doublure.notes: Core film-set vocabulary in Dix pour cent: film crews distinguish doublure lumière (lighting stand-in), doublure corps (body double), and doublure cascade (stunt double), whereas voice dubbing is doublage (performed by a comédien de doublage).

rootFamily.gloss: to double; to dub a film; to overtake

doucement.etymology: Formed in Old French (doucement, 12th c.) from the feminine adjective douce ('sweet, soft, gentle', from Latin dulcis) + adverbial suffix -ment.

douche.etymology: Borrowed in the late 16th century from Italian doccia ('water pipe, gutter, jet of water poured over the body at thermal baths'), deverbal from docciare ('to pour in a stream'), from Vulgar Latin *ductia ('water conduit'), from Classical Latin ducere, ductum ('to lead, conduct').

douleur.etymology: Inherited from Old French dolor / douleur ('physical pain, grief, sorrow'), from Classical Latin dolorem (nominative dolor, 'ache, bodily pain, anguish'), derived from dolere ('to feel pain, grieve').

douloureux.etymology: Inherited from Old French doloros, dolereus ("full of grief or physical pain"), from Late Latin dolōrōsus ("painful, sorrowful"), formed with the adjective suffix -ōsus from Classical Latin dolor ("bodily pain, mental anguish, grief"), itself derived from dolēre ("to feel pain, suffer, grieve"). Retains both physical ("aching, tender") and emotional ("heartbreaking, distressing") senses in Modern French.

history.meaning: afflicted with grief or bodily torment

morphemes.meaning: adjectival suffix ("full of, characterized by"; fem. -euse)

douloureux.notes: Covers both physical soreness (une épaule douloureuse) and emotional trauma (un souvenir douloureux). Note the colloquial noun la douloureuse ("the restaurant bill"—literally "the painful one").

rootFamily.gloss: to cause pain or grief (archaic/literary: se douloir)

doute.etymology: Post-verbal noun derived in Old French (dote, doute, 12th century, meaning both "fear, dread" and "uncertainty") from doter (Modern French douter, "to fear, hesitate, doubt"), ultimately from Classical Latin dubitāre ("to waver between two opinions"). Originally feminine in Old and Middle French (like Spanish la duda), its gender shifted to masculine by the 16th–17th centuries. English doubt was borrowed from Old French, with Renaissance scribes reinserting a silent etymological b after Latin dubitāre.
doute.notes: Masculine noun (un doute, sans aucun doute). Watch the contrast between sans doute ("probably, no doubt" in a weakened hedging sense) and sans aucun doute ("without a shadow of a doubt, definitely").

rootFamily.gloss: formidable, fearsome (retaining the Old French "fear" sense)

cognates.meaning: to feel uncertain (via Old French); indubitable (via Latin)

douter.etymology: Inherited from Old French doter, douter ("to fear, dread; to hesitate, doubt"), from Classical Latin dubitāre ("to waver in opinion, hesitate, be uncertain"), a frequentative verb derived from dubius ("moving in two directions, wavering"), built on the root of duo ("two"). The medieval semantic branch "to fear" survives today in redouter ("to dread").

history.meaning: to oscillate between two options, hesitate, question
to fear, hold in awe; to be uncertain
to doubt (douter de); to suspect or surmise (se douter de)

douter.notes: Crucial learner trap: douter que / douter de means "to doubt", whereas reflexive se douter de / se douter que means the exact opposite—"to suspect, guess, have a hunch" (Je m'en doutais !, "I suspected as much!").

doux.etymology: Inherited from Old French douz (feminine douce, 'sweet to the taste, gentle, soft, mild'), from Vulgar Latin *dulcius, remodeled from Classical Latin dulcis ('sweet, pleasant, gentle').

douzaine.etymology: Formed in twelfth-century Old French (dozaine) from douze ('twelve', Latin duodecim) plus the collective numeral suffix -aine (from Latin -ena). English dozen was borrowed directly from Old French dozaine.

cognates.meaning: group of twelve (from Old French dozaine)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: douzaine (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: douzaine

douze.etymology: Inherited from Old French doze ('twelve'), from Vulgar Latin *dodece, contracted from Classical Latin duodecim ('twelve', compound of duo 'two' + decem 'ten').

cognates.meaning: to provide with a talent or income (via Old French douer)

doué.etymology: Participial adjective from the past participle of douer ("to endow"), inherited from Old French doer ("to provide a marriage dowry; to bestow qualities upon"), from Classical Latin dōtāre ("to endow, portion"), derived from dōs, dōtis ("marriage portion, dowry; natural gift or quality"), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *deh₃- ("to give"). Already in Classical Latin, dōtēs ingenī meant "gifts of the mind".

history.meaning: provided with a dowry; richly endowed
endowed with property, grace, or faculties

doué.notes: Constructed with pour for skills (très doué pour l'improvisation) and de in formal prose for possessing an attribute (doué de raison, "endowed with reason"). Also gives surdoué ("intellectually gifted / prodigy").

cognates.meaning: head of a faculty or cathedral (via Anglo-Norman deien)

doyen.etymology: Inherited from Old French deien, doien ("ecclesiastical dean, leader of ten"), from Late Latin decānus ("commander of ten soldiers; monk supervising ten others; chief astrologer of a ten-degree zodiacal division"), derived from Classical Latin decem ("ten"). From medieval monastic and cathedral administration, it passed into universities ("dean of a faculty") and general usage for the oldest or longest-serving member of any body.

history.meaning: leader of ten soldiers or ten monks
cathedral dean, head of a guild or faculty
university dean; most senior or oldest member of a group

doyen.notes: Feminine is doyenne (borrowed into English as doyenne for a respected senior woman in a field, such as la doyenne de la Comédie-Française). Pronunciation note: oi + y sounds like "dwa-yen" [dwajɛ̃].

cognates.meaning: to pull along; to dredge a riverbed

draguer.etymology: Derived in the late 17th century from drague ("dredge, dragnet"), borrowed from English drag or Middle Dutch dragge ("grapnel, sweep-net"), from Proto-Germanic *draganą ("to draw, pull"). Originally a maritime and river-engineering verb meaning "to dredge silt or sweep for mines and fish", it entered mid-20th-century Parisian slang for strolling up and down boulevards or cafés "trawling" for romantic encounters, before becoming the standard informal verb for flirting or hitting on someone.

history.meaning: sweep-net or dredging scoop pulled across the seabed
to dredge a harbor or sweep a channel with a dragnet
to dredge; (colloquial) to cruise, flirt with, hit on

draguer.notes: Informal but ubiquitous in everyday French: draguer quelqu'un ("to hit on someone"), la drague ("flirting/picking up"), and un dragueur ("a flirt / pickup artist"). Completely unrelated to drogue ("drug")!

rootFamily.gloss: flirt, pickup artist; minesweeper (dragueur de mines)

cognates.meaning: relating to drama; striking or grave

dramatique.etymology: Learned borrowing (attested in Middle French by the 15th–16th centuries as dramatic, dramatique) from Late Latin dramaticus ("theatrical, pertaining to stage plays"), itself from Ancient Greek δραματικός (dramatikós, "fit for or relating to drama"), derived from δρᾶμα, δράματος (drâma, drámatos, "deed, action, stage performance"), from δράω (dráō, "to do, act"). Alongside its neutral theatrical meaning (art dramatique), it developed a stronger everyday sense of "tragic, catastrophic" than English dramatic.

history.meaning: relating to theatrical action or stage plays
belonging to stage drama (as opposed to narrative epic)

dramatique.notes: Subtle false-friend nuance: in theatre and TV, art dramatique ("acting") and une dramatique ("a TV drama") are neutral, but in news or conversation une situation dramatique means "a tragic, dire, catastrophic situation", not merely "exciting" or "impressive" (for which French prefers spectaculaire).

rootFamily.gloss: to blow out of proportion, make a tragedy of

drame.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin drāma ("play, theatrical piece"), from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma, "deed, action; stage play, especially tragedy"), formed with the result suffix -μα (-ma) from δράω (dráō, "to do, accomplish, perform"). Popularized in 18th-century French theatrical theory by Diderot and Beaumarchais (le drame bourgeois) for serious plays bridging classical tragedy and comedy, before extending in the 19th century to real-life tragedies and emotional crises.

history.meaning: deed, action; theatrical performance on stage
theatrical play in verse or prose
serious theatrical/film genre; real-life tragedy or crisis

drame.notes: Masculine noun despite ending in -e (un drame, like poème, thème, système—a hallmark of Greek neuter nouns in -ma). En faire tout un drame means "to make a huge fuss/tragedy out of it".

drap.etymology: Inherited from Old French drap ('woven woolen cloth, piece of fabric, bedsheet'), from Late Latin drappus ('piece of cloth', attested in the 6th-c. Capitularies and Oribasius), probably of Gaulish origin (*drappo-).

cognates.meaning: medicinal substance or narcotic (borrowed from Middle French drogue)
dry (probable source of droge vate, "dry barrels")

drogue.etymology: Attested in 14th-century Middle French (drogue) for dried apothecary herbs, spices, and dyestuffs; most plausibly borrowed from Middle Dutch droge vate ("dry barrels, dry goods"), in which droge ("dry", from Proto-Germanic *drūgiz, cognate with English dry and drought) was reanalyzed by French merchants as a noun designating the dried medicinal substances packed inside. French drogue subsequently diffused across Europe, yielding English drug, Italian droga, and Spanish droga.

history.meaning: dried medicinal ingredient, spice, chemical dyestuff

drogue.notes: Important register false friend: in contemporary French, la drogue almost exclusively means illegal narcotics or an addiction—NEVER over-the-counter or prescription medicine, which is toujours un médicament! (Hardware/cleaning-supply stores, however, keep the old chemical sense in une droguerie.)

rootFamily.gloss: to drug, dope; (se droguer) to take narcotics

droit.etymology: Inherited from Old French dreit / droit ('straight, upright, right-hand; law, rightful claim'), from Vulgar Latin *derectus, syncopated from Classical Latin directus ('laid straight, direct, upright, just'), past participle of dirigere ('to set straight').

history.meaning: straight, right (not left); law, legal right

cognates.meaning: right hand, right side (from Latin dīrēcta)
straight, unmediated (learned borrowing from Latin dīrēctus)

droite.etymology: Substantivized feminine of droit ("straight, upright, right"), inherited from Old French dreit, droit, from Vulgar Latin *drīctus, a syncopated form of Classical Latin dīrēctus ("laid straight, aligned, direct"), past participle of dīrigere ("to set straight, guide", from dis- + regere, "to rule, straighten"). As a noun, la droite arose by ellipsis of la main droite ("the straight/capable hand"), replacing Classical Latin dextra across much of Western Romance.

history.meaning: straight; right hand or right-hand side
right-hand side; straight line (geometry); political right wing

droite.notes: The political sense of la droite ("the right wing") vs. la gauche ("the left wing") was born directly in France during the 1789 National Constituent Assembly, where royalist supporters of the king's veto sat to the president's right. On stage, côté cour ("courtyard side") traditionally corresponds to stage left (audience's right).

rootFamily.gloss: straight; right; law or legal entitlement (un droit)

drôle.etymology: Appeared in the 15th–16th century as a noun meaning 'merry fellow, rascal, wag', probably borrowed from Middle Dutch drol ('little fat fellow, goblin, jester, bowling pin'); used as an adjective ('amusing, comical, odd') from the late 16th century.

du.etymology: Du is the contraction of de and the masculine singular article le. The ninth-century form del shows an earlier stage of the combination. Modern uses depend on whether the phrase expresses a relationship or an unspecified quantity.

history.meaning: of the, from the; some/any (masculine partitive)

du.notes: Serves two vital jobs: preposition + article contraction (la porte du bureau 'the office door') and masculine partitive article for uncountable nouns (boire du café 'drink [some] coffee').

cognates.meaning: wife of a duke or female sovereign of a duchy (via Old French)

duchesse.etymology: Inherited from Old French duchesse (12th century), formed from duc ("duke", from Classical Latin dux, ducis, "military commander, leader, guide", root of dūcere, "to lead") + the feminine aristocratic suffix -esse (from Late Latin -issa, borrowed from Ancient Greek -ισσα, -issa). Passed directly into Middle English as duchesse (Modern English duchess) and inspired Italian duchessa.

history.meaning: leader, military commander (+ feminine title suffix)
wife of a duke or female ruler of a duchy
duchess; (colloquial) haughty woman; lustrous satin fabric (satin duchesse)

duchesse.notes: Notice the palatalization of c [k] in duc to ch [ʃ] in duchesse and duché ("duchy"). In ironic conversational French, jouer les duchesses means "to put on airs / act high and mighty", and pommes duchesse are piped, golden-baked mashed potato swirls.

duo.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian duo ('musical piece for two voices or instruments'), from Classical Latin duo ('two').

history.meaning: two -> musical piece for two performers
musical duet; pair of people working together

dur.etymology: Inherited from Old French dur ('hard, firm, harsh, difficult'), from Classical Latin durus ('hard to the touch, tough, stern, arduous', from PIE *deru- 'firm, solid like oak').

cognates.meaning: to last, bear hardship (via Old French endurer); duration

durer.etymology: Inherited from Old French durer ("to hold out, resist, continue in time"), from Classical Latin dūrāre ("to make hard, harden; intransitively, to hold out, endure, last"), derived from the adjective dūrus ("hard, firm, solid, hardy"), from Proto-Indo-European *dewh₂-ró-s ("long-lasting, firm"). The semantic shift from physical hardness ("solid like oak or stone") to temporal persistence ("continuing without wearing out") had already occurred in Classical Latin.

history.meaning: to harden; to hold out, endure, continue in existence
to hold fast, last in time, extend in space
to last, continue over a span of time

durer.notes: In idioms, faire durer le plaisir means "to draw out the pleasure / milk the moment", and ça ne peut plus durer means "this cannot go on any longer". Note how English duration and durable come from this exact family.

cognates.meaning: unlawful coercion (via Anglo-Norman duresce, from the same Latin root)

dureté.etymology: Inherited from Old French durté, dureté ("physical hardness; harshness of character, pitilessness"), from Classical Latin dūritātem (accusative of dūritās, "hardness, firmness, austerity, rigor"), derived from dūrus ("hard, stern, unyielding"). Reshaped in Middle French with a medial -e- by analogy with the feminine adjective dure.

history.meaning: physical hardness; sternness, harshness of manner
solidity of stone or metal; severity, callousness
hardness (of materials, water); harshness, severity, toughness

dureté.notes: Used for physical materials (la dureté du diamant), water mineral content (la dureté de l'eau), and human ruthlessness—e.g. la dureté du métier ("the brutal toughness of the acting profession"). Older idiom dur d'oreille parallels dureté d'oreille ("hardness of hearing").

rootFamily.gloss: to harden; to make tougher against hardship

cognates.meaning: characterized by force, change, or energy (via French)

dynamique.etymology: Introduced into French in 1692 by philosopher-mathematician Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (writing in French) as a feminine noun la dynamique ("the science of forces in motion", contrasting with statique), borrowed from Ancient Greek δυναμικός (dynamikós, "powerful, efficacious"), from δύναμις (dýnamis, "power, strength, faculty"), from δύναμαι (dýnamai, "to be able"). Extended as an adjective in the 18th–19th centuries from physics and aesthetics to personal vigour, enterprise, and momentum, whence English dynamic.

history.meaning: branch of mechanics studying forces that produce motion (Leibniz, 1692)
energetic, enterprising, active; group momentum (une dynamique)

dynamique.notes: Works both as an adjective (un jeune agent très dynamique) and as a feminine noun (créer une bonne dynamique d'équipe, "to build strong team momentum"). Shares its Greek root with Alfred Nobel's 1867 coinage dynamite.

rootFamily.gloss: high explosive; powerhouse (coined from Greek dýnamis)

dynamisme.etymology: Coined in early 19th-century French philosophical prose from the Greek stem δυναμ- (dynam-, from δύναμις, dýnamis, "force, power, potentiality") + the doctrinal suffix -isme (from Latin -ismus, Greek -ισμός). Initially denoting Leibnizian philosophical systems that explain matter through active forces rather than inert mass, it shifted by the early 20th century into everyday praise for energetic drive, initiative, and vitality.

history.meaning: philosophical doctrine viewing force as the essence of matter

morphemes.meaning: noun suffix denoting a doctrine, quality, or tendency

dynamisme.notes: Masculine noun (le dynamisme), prized in corporate, artistic, and CV language (faire preuve de dynamisme, "to show drive/initiative"). Pronounced [-ism] with both the s and m clearly articulated.

dès.etymology: Inherited from Old French des ('starting from, right from'), from Vulgar Latin *de ex, compound of Classical Latin de ('down from, from') + ex ('out of, directly from').

history.meaning: right out from, from the very moment or point of
from, right from, as early as

dé.etymology: In the sense of 'gaming die' and 'small cube' (un dé de carotte), inherited via Old French dé from Classical Latin datum ('that which is given or cast', neuter past participle of dare 'to give, throw'), used in Roman gaming slang for throwing dice.

history.meaning: something given or thrown (a cast of the dice)
die; small culinary cube (couper en dés)

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French dé / dés

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: dé (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: dé

dé.notes: Homonym note: **un dé à coudre** ('thimble') has a completely different origin—from Latin *digitale* ('finger cap', from *digitus* 'finger')!

cognates.meaning: soft magnesium silicate mineral; talcum powder

dé-talquer.etymology: Transparent modern privative formation (spelled détalquer or hyphenated dé-talquer for morphological clarity in spoken/scripted dialogue) combining the reversative prefix dé- (from Old French des-, Latin dis-, expressing removal) with talquer ("to dust or coat with talcum powder"). The base noun talc entered 16th-century French via Medieval Latin talcum and Spanish talco from Arabic طَلْق (ṭalq, "mica, talc, asbestos"), itself borrowed from Persian تَلْک (talk).

history.meaning: to dust skin, gloves, or surfaces with talcum powder
to brush or wipe off excess talcum or setting powder

dé-talquer.notes: Illustrates how productively French wardrobe and HMC (habillage, maquillage, coiffure) film crews coin ad-hoc dé- + verb formations on set (like démaquiller, décoiffer, défroisser) when too much mattifying powder shows under studio lights.

cognates.meaning: to leave a ship or aircraft (adapted from French débarquer)

débarquer.etymology: Formed in 16th-century Middle French (desbarquer, modeled alongside Italian sbarcare and Spanish desembarcar) as the antonym of embarquer, combining the reversative prefix dé- (Old French des-, from Latin dis-) + barque ("small sea vessel, barge", from Late Latin barca) + -er. From stepping ashore off a boat or landing troops (le Débarquement of June 1944), colloquial French vividly extended the verb to arriving unannounced, piling into an office, or being cluelessly new to a situation.

history.meaning: to go ashore from a ship, unload cargo or troops
to disembark; (colloquial) to turn up unexpectedly; to be out of the loop

débarquer.notes: High-frequency conversational gem in Dix pour cent: Il débarque dans mon bureau sans prévenir ! ("He barges/shows up in my office unannounced!"), Tu débarques ou quoi ? ("Did you just land from Mars / Are you totally out of the loop?"), and se faire débarquer ("to get ousted/fired from a project").

rootFamily.gloss: to board a ship; to drag someone into an affair

débarrasser.etymology: Formed in the 16th century from reversative prefix dé- (Latin dis-) + embarrasser ('to obstruct, encumber with barriers') or directly on barras ('barrier, obstacle', from barre 'bar').

history.meaning: to clear away obstacles, free from encumbrance, clear the table

cognates.meaning: accounting entry for a sum owed (borrowed from French débit / Latin dēbitum)

débit.etymology: Attested in the 16th century with two intertwined commercial senses: first, a learned adaptation of Classical Latin dēbitum ("sum owed, debt", neuter past participle of dēbēre, "to owe", whence inherited dette); second, a deverbal noun from débiter ("to sell goods piecemeal at retail; to saw timber into measured pieces; to rattle off speech"). From "steady dispensing of goods or words" (débit de boissons, débit vocal), 19th-century engineers extended débit to fluid flow rate and 20th-century telecommunications to data bandwidth.

history.meaning: something owed, pecuniary debt or obligation
accounting debit; retail sale of wares; delivery rate of speech
bank debit; vocal delivery speed; water flow rate; internet bandwidth (haut débit)

débit.notes: Remarkably polysemous: in tech, le haut débit means "high-speed broadband"; in acting/voice coaching, avoir un débit trop rapide means "to deliver one's lines too fast"; in law, un débit de boissons is a licensed bar/pub; and in banking, carte de débit is a debit card.

rootFamily.gloss: to retail; to charge an account; to rattle off lines
debt (inherited vernacular doublet of Latin dēbita)

débloquer.etymology: Formed in the 16th–17th century from reversative prefix dé- + bloquer ('to blockade, jam, lock'); originally 'to raise a military siege', later 'to unjam a mechanism, unfreeze funds, unlock'.

history.meaning: to raise a blockade -> to unjam, unfreeze, unlock

cognates.meaning: edge, ship's side (from Old English bord, Germanic cognate of French bord)

débordant.etymology: Participial adjective formed from the present participle of déborder ("to spill over the edge, overflow"), attested since Middle French (desbordant). Déborder combines the prefix dé- (Old French des-, Latin dis-, indicating movement beyond a boundary) with bord ("ship's side, river bank, edge"), borrowed into Gallo-Romance from Frankish *bord ("plank, side of a ship", from Proto-Germanic *burdą). Metaphorically transferred from flooding rivers to exuberant energy, imagination, or affection.

history.meaning: wooden plank, side of a vessel
spilling over its banks (of a river or vessel)

débordant.notes: Almost always positive and vibrant when followed by de: une énergie débordante ("boundless energy"), une imagination débordante ("a fertile, overflowing imagination")—contrasting sharply with its stressed cousin débordé ("swamped with work")!

rootFamily.gloss: to overflow, spill over; to go too far

cognates.meaning: margin, boundary (via Old French bordure, from the same Frankish root *bord)
to overflow, jut beyond the edge

débordé.etymology: Participial adjective from the past participle of déborder ("to overflow a bank; in military tactics, to outflank an army's wing"), formed from dé- (Old French des-, Latin dis-) + bord ("edge, flank, ship's side", from Frankish *bord). Combining the imagery of riverbanks submerged by floodwaters and a defensive line overrun on its flanks, être débordé settled into everyday modern usage for being swamped by obligations and short of time.
