history.meaning: to overflow riverbanks; to extend past a line of battle
overwhelmed, swamped with work or demands

débordé.notes: Perhaps the single most-uttered adjective in a Parisian talent agency: Je suis complètement débordé(e) en ce moment ! ("I'm completely swamped right now!"). Pair it with débordant to remember active "-ing" ("brimming") vs. passive "-ed" ("swamped").

cognates.meaning: liquid soup; muddle ("too many cooks spoil the broth", cognate with Frankish *broþ)
to untangle, get out of a jam (parallel formation on broglio)

débrouiller.etymology: Formed in 16th-century Middle French (desbrouiller) with the reversative prefix dé- (Old French des-, Latin dis-) + brouiller ("to mix up, muddle, cloud, tangle"), from Old French broillier ("to soil, stir into a murky soup"), derived from Gallo-Romance *brodiculāre, based on Frankish *broþ ("broth, gravy", cognate with English broth and Old High German brod). Literally "to clear up a murky mess or untangle knotted threads", its reflexive form se débrouiller became a prized 19th-century cultural watchword ("to manage, improvise, fend for oneself").

history.meaning: broth → to stir into a cloudy mixture, soil, confuse
to untangle threads, clear up confusion or disorder
to untangle; (reflexive) to manage, get by resourcefully

débrouiller.notes: Cultural touchstone: le Système D (D for débrouille / débrouillard) celebrates French street-smart resourcefulness—improvising a fix under pressure when official channels fail. Imperative Débrouille-toi ! means "Figure it out yourself!".

rootFamily.gloss: to muddle, scramble (radio); to fall out with someone (se brouiller)

cognates.meaning: lying in wait in the woods (via Old French embuschier, same Germanic *busk- root)
to flush game from cover; to ferret out

débusquer.etymology: Entered 16th-century French hunting and military vocabulary (desbusquer, reinforced by Italian sbuscare) from the prefix dé- (Old French des-, Latin dis-, "out of") + Old French busc ("wood, thicket, copse", standard Modern French bois), from Late Latin boscus ("woodland"), borrowed from Frankish *busk ("bush, thicket", cognate with English bush). Literally "to drive deer or boar out of the underbrush into the open", it generalized to unearthing hidden talent, secrets, or fugitives.

history.meaning: to drive hunted game or ambushed soldiers out of the woods
to flush out game; to track down, ferret out, uncover

morphemes.meaning: woods, thicket (Old French busc / Late Latin boscus)

débusquer.notes: Notice the exact hunting symmetry with embusquer / embuscade ("to hide in the woods / ambush"): embusquer puts someone into hiding in the bush, while débusquer flushes them out! Agents use it for scouting elusive new actors (débusquer la perle rare).

rootFamily.gloss: small wood, grove (via Italian boschetto / Provençal bosquet)
wood, forest (native French reflex of boscus)

début.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 16th century from débuter ('to play the first stroke toward the mark in bowls or billiards; to make one's first appearance'), itself formed from dé- + but ('target, goal, mark').

history.meaning: first throw toward the mark -> beginning, first appearance

cognates.meaning: deliberate trickery or fraud (borrowed from Middle French before French shifted meaning!)

déception.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (decepcion, 12th century, "fraud, trickery, illusion") from Late Latin dēceptiōnem (accusative of dēceptiō, "deceit, ensnaring"), noun of action from Classical Latin dēcipere ("to catch in a snare, beguile, cheat, disappoint expectations"), formed from dē- ("away, astray") + capere ("to seize, catch"). While English preserved the medieval sense of intentional fraud, 18th- and 19th-century French shifted décevoir and déception almost wholly to the passive feeling of dashed hopes ("disappointment").
déception.notes: One of the most notorious French–English false friends! Une grande déception ALWAYS means "a huge disappointment / letdown" (e.g., box-office flop or missed role), NEVER "fraud" or "deceit" (which is une tromperie, une supercherie, or une duperie).

rootFamily.gloss: to disappoint, let down (false friend: NOT "to deceive")

cognates.meaning: release, unloading, firing (borrowed from Old French descharge)

décharge.etymology: Deverbal feminine noun formed in Old French (descharge, 13th century) from deschargier (Modern French décharger, "to unload a beast or wagon, relieve of a burden"), composed of des- (Latin dis-) + chargier ("to load"), from Late Latin carricāre ("to load onto a cart"), itself from Classical Latin carrus ("four-wheeled Celtic wagon", borrowed from Gaulish *karros, from PIE *ḱers-, "to run"). From physically unloading a cart, it branched into legal liability waivers, exculpatory testimony, bursts of energy/adrenaline, and waste dumps.

history.meaning: to load goods onto a wheeled wagon
act of unloading cargo; relief from a tax or obligation
liability release/waiver; defense testimony (à décharge); adrenaline/electric surge; landfill

décharge.notes: In film production and legal contexts, signer une décharge means "to sign a liability waiver / release form" (e.g., before an actor performs a risky stunt), while témoigner à décharge means "to testify for the defense" (as opposed to à charge, "for the prosecution"). Also watch une décharge d'adrénaline ("an adrenaline rush") and une décharge publique ("a garbage dump").

rootFamily.gloss: to unload, relieve, discharge; (se décharger) to shift responsibility
load, burden, responsibility; prosecution evidence (à charge)

décharger.etymology: Inherited from Old French deschargier ('to unload a burden, relieve of a duty or accusation'), formed from prefix des- / dé- + chargier / charger ('to load', from Late Latin carricare).

history.meaning: to unload cargo, relieve of a burden, discharge

déchirer.etymology: Inherited from Old French deschirer ('to tear apart, rend, scratch'), formed from intensive prefix des- (Latin dis-) + Frankish *skerian / Old High German skerran ('to scrape, scratch, tear', cognate with English shear).

history.meaning: to claw, rend, tear to pieces

décibel.etymology: Borrowed in the 1920s from English decibel, coined by telephone engineers at Bell Laboratories from metric prefix deci- ('one-tenth', from Latin decimus) + bel (unit named in honor of Alexander Graham Bell, 1847–1922).

history.meaning: one-tenth of a bel (logarithmic unit of sound intensity)

décider.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th century) from Classical Latin dēcīdere ('to cut off', and figuratively 'to cut short a dispute, settle, determine'), composed of dē- ('off, away') and caedere ('to cut, strike'), from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂eyd-.

history.meaning: to cut off; to settle a matter, determine
to settle a legal dispute, resolve
to decide, make up one's mind

décider.notes: Watch prepositions: décider de + infinitive means 'to decide to do something', whereas se décider à + infinitive emphasizes finally making up one's mind after hesitation.

décision.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin decisionem (nominative decisio, 'a cutting off; a settlement, agreement'), derived from decidere ('to cut off; to settle a matter once and for all', from de- + caedere 'to cut').

déclaration.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (14th century) from Classical Latin dēclārātiōnem, accusative of dēclārātiō ('a making clear, disclosure, public announcement'), noun of action derived from dēclārāre ('to make clear, reveal'), ultimately based on clārus ('bright, clear, loud').
déclaration.notes: Covers both lofty romantic or press statements (une déclaration d'amour, une déclaration à la presse) and mundane administrative filings (déclaration d'impôts 'tax return').

déclarer.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (13th century, alongside inherited desclairier) from Classical Latin dēclārāre ('to make clear, make evident, announce aloud'), formed from intensive dē- ('thoroughly') and clārāre ('to brighten, clarify'), from clārus ('clear, bright, distinct').
déclarer.notes: In French labor and entertainment contexts, déclarer quelqu'un specifically means 'to register an employee officially for payroll and social contributions' (as opposed to working au noir).

décliner.etymology: Adapted in Old French decliner (11th–12th century) from Classical Latin dēclīnāre ('to bend aside, turn away from, inflect grammatically'), composed of dē- ('down, away') and clīnāre ('to lean, bend'), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- ('to lean').

history.meaning: to bend aside, turn away, inflect words
to sink, deviate, recount in detail
to turn down politely, wane, state (identity)

décliner.notes: In talent-agency parlance, décliner un rôle / une offre is the diplomatic verb for turning down a part; note also the idiomatic décliner son identité ('to state one's full name and details', from grammatical declension).

décompresser.etymology: Coined in 20th-century French from the reversative prefix dé- and compresser ('to compress, pressurize'), from Late Latin compressāre, frequentative of Classical Latin comprimere ('to press together', from com- + premere 'to press'); shifted from deep-sea diving and aviation medicine in the 1930s to everyday psychological relief ('to unwind') in the 1970s.

history.meaning: to squeeze or press tightly together
to relieve gas or cabin pressure

décompresser.notes: Used intransitively without an object (J'ai besoin de décompresser après le tournage — 'I need to unwind after the shoot'), whereas décomprimer stays strictly technical or medical.

décor.etymology: Back-formed in late 17th-century French from décorer ('to adorn, embellish'), itself borrowed from Classical Latin decorāre ('to adorn, honor'), derived from decus, decoris ('ornament, grace, dignity') alongside Latin decor ('seemliness, beauty'), from Proto-Indo-European *deḱ- ('to take, be fitting').

history.meaning: to ornament, confer an honor upon

décor.notes: Essential cinema vocabulary: un décor naturel means an on-location setting (as opposed to un décor en studio 'studio set'), and chef décorateur is the production designer; plural les décors often translates simply as 'the sets'.

décourager.etymology: Inherited from Old French descouragier (12th–13th century, 'to dishearten, deprive of spirit'), formed with privative des- (modern dé-) + courage ('heart, inner disposition, ardor', from Old French corage < Vulgar Latin *corāticum, derived from Classical Latin cor, cordis 'heart') + verbal suffix -er.

history.meaning: feelings of the heart, inner spirit
to turn away one's heart, dishearten

décourager.notes: Transitive décourager quelqu'un means 'to discourage someone', while pronominal se décourager corresponds to English intransitive 'to get discouraged / lose heart'.

découverte.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle (attested in the 15th–16th century, initially for military reconnaissance and maritime exploration) of découvrir ('to uncover, reveal, find'), from Old French descovrir < Late Latin discooperīre ('to uncover, lay bare').

history.meaning: to uncover, remove a covering from

découverte.notes: In cinema and talent agencies, une belle découverte refers to a breakout newcomer or hidden gem spotted by an agent or casting director.

découvrir.etymology: Inherited from Old French descovrir ('to remove a cover, expose, reveal a secret'), from Late Latin discooperīre ('to uncover, lay bare'), formed from reversative dis- and Classical Latin cooperīre ('to cover completely', from co- + operīre 'to cover, shut').

history.meaning: to uncover physically, disclose a secret

découvrir.notes: Conjugates like ouvrir despite ending in -ir (je découvre, j'ai découvert), and retains its literal physical sense ('to uncover a pot / take off a layer of clothing') alongside 'to discover'.

décrocher.etymology: Formed in Middle French descrochier (14th–15th century, 'to unhook, detach from a hook'), from reversative des- (modern dé-) + croc ('hook', borrowed into Old French from Old Frankish *krōk or Old Norse krókr 'hook') + verbal suffix -er; the telephone sense arose from lifting the earpiece off its switchhook, while 'landing' a prize comes from snatching the ring or trophy off a high hook (cf. décrocher la timbale).

history.meaning: to detach or pull down from a hook
to unhook; to pick up the phone; to land a role/award

décrocher.notes: A staple verb in Dix pour cent with two vital senses: answering a ringing phone (Décroche !) and landing a coveted part or César award (décrocher le premier rôle); its telephone opposite is raccrocher ('to hang up').

rootFamily.gloss: to hang up (phone or picture), hook onto

décès.etymology: Décès was borrowed from Latin decessus, departure or death. The Académie records the French word from the eleventh century.
décès.notes: Standard in official notices, news reports, and condolences (acte de décès 'death certificate'), sounding gentler and more formal than la mort.

décéder.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (15th century, initially in legal and administrative records, back-influenced by older noun décès) from Classical Latin dēcēdere ('to go away, withdraw, depart', used elliptically for dēcēdere dē vītā 'to depart from life'), composed of dē- ('away from') and cēdere ('to go, yield').

history.meaning: to go away, withdraw; (euphemistic) to depart from life

décéder.notes: Conjugated with être in compound tenses (il est décédé) and restricted to formal, medical, news, or polite euphemistic register (never used for animals or plants, which take mourir).

dédicace.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (15th–16th century, replacing Old French dedicasse / dedicacion for the consecration of a church) from Classical and Ecclesiastical Latin dēdicātiō ('consecration, formal dedication of a temple or literary work'), adapted with the semi-learned suffix -ace, from dēdicāre ('to proclaim, consecrate', from dē- + dicāre 'to proclaim, consecrate').

history.meaning: consecration of a shrine; literary dedication
church consecration feast; epistle dedicating a book
signed inscription, book-signing event, radio/TV shout-out

dédicace.notes: False friend alert: dédicace never means 'hard work / devotion' (which is dévouement or implication); in French media and publishing, une séance de dédicaces is a book- or poster-signing session, and faire une dédicace is to give someone a personal shout-out or signed note.

rootFamily.gloss: to sign/autograph with a personal note
to dedicate (a work or life to someone)

dédicacer.etymology: Coined in mid-19th-century French directly from the noun dédicace ('personal inscription or literary dedication', ultimately from Latin dēdicātiō < dēdicāre 'to consecrate') + first-group verbal suffix -er, filling a lexical gap alongside dédier ('to dedicate abstractly') for the physical act of writing and signing a personalized inscription.

history.meaning: to inscribe and autograph (a book, photo, album)

dédicacer.notes: Keep dédicacer distinct from dédier: an actor or author will dédicacer une photo / un livre (physically sign a note on a copy), whereas a director will dédier un film à quelqu'un (dedicate the work itself to someone's memory); remember the cedilla before a/o (nous dédicaçons).

déduire.etymology: Re-borrowed or refashioned in Middle French (14th–15th century) after Classical Latin dēdūcere ('to lead down, draw out, subtract from a sum, derive in argument'), from dē- ('down, from') and dūcere ('to lead'), supplanting Old French deduire which had shifted semantically to 'to pass time pleasantly, amuse oneself'.

history.meaning: to lead down, subtract, derive logically
to recount in order, subtract, infer

déduire.notes: Covers both English 'to deduce' (J'en déduis que... 'I gather/deduce from this that...') and 'to deduct' in accounting or agency commissions (déduire les frais 'to deduct expenses').

cognates.meaning: lack, fault (difetto is from dēfectus; diffalta from *dēfallita)

défaut.etymology: Inherited from Old French defaut (12th century, 'absence, lack, shortcoming, failure to appear in court'), masculine participial/verbal noun derived from defaillir ('to fail, run short, give way'), from Vulgar Latin *dēfallīre, regularized from dē- + Classical Latin fallere ('to deceive, slip, fail').

history.meaning: to fail, be lacking, give out
lack, absence, legal non-appearance, moral failing
character flaw, manufacturing defect, lack (à défaut de)

morphemes.meaning: to fail, be lacking (from faillir / fallere)

défaut.notes: Final -t is completely silent (/de.fo/); distinguish un défaut ('a character flaw or product defect') from une faute ('a mistake, moral transgression, or foul'), and note the high-utility phrase à défaut de ('failing that / for lack of').

rootFamily.gloss: to fail, almost do; go bankrupt

défendre.etymology: Inherited from Old French defendre (attested from the 10th–11th century, 'to ward off, protect, forbid'), from Classical Latin dēfendere ('to ward off, repel, protect'), composed of dē- ('away') and the bound root *-fendere ('to strike, push', seen also in offendere), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen- ('to strike').

history.meaning: to ward off, strike away, protect
to protect in battle, bar access to, forbid
to defend, stand up for, forbid (formal)

défendre.notes: In cinema/theater talk, défendre un rôle / un projet means 'to champion a project or deliver a committed performance that does justice to a difficult character'; remember it also means 'to forbid' on signs (Défense de fumer).

défier.etymology: Inherited from Old French desfier / defier (11th–12th century, originally a feudal term meaning 'to renounce one's oath of fealty to a lord and declare open hostility'), from Vulgar Latin *disfīdāre ('to renounce trust'), composed of privative dis- and Latin fīdus ('faithful') / fīdere ('to trust', from fidēs 'faith, trust').

history.meaning: to renounce feudal allegiance, challenge to combat
to challenge, defy; (se défier de) to distrust

défier.notes: Notice how the feudal origin bridges both meanings: active défier quelqu'un means 'to challenge or defy someone', while reflexive se défier de quelqu'un preserves the root sense of 'to distrust / be wary of someone' (close to se méfier de).

défigurer.etymology: Inherited from Old French desfigurer (12th century, 'to mar the form or features of, make unrecognizable'), formed from privative/pejorative des- (modern dé-) + figure ('form, shape, human face', borrowed from Classical Latin figūra 'shape, form', from fingere 'to mold, fashion') + -er, reinforced by Medieval Latin dēfigūrāre.

history.meaning: to spoil the form or countenance of, disguise
to disfigure (a face); to spoil or distort (a landscape, a work)

défigurer.notes: Remember that French figure means 'face' as well as 'figure/shape', so défigurer means specifically 'to mar someone's face' (and figuratively 'to butcher/distort an artwork, script, or historic neighborhood').

cognates.meaning: defile — narrow gorge or single-file march (from French)

défilé.etymology: Substantivized masculine past participle (late 17th century) of défiler ('to march past one behind another', originally 'to unthread'), formed from dé- + file ('single line, row', deverbal of filer 'to spin thread' < Classical Latin fīlum 'thread'); denoted first a narrow mountain pass forcing soldiers into single file, then the military review itself, and by the 20th century a couture runway show.

history.meaning: narrow mountain pass requiring single-file passage
military parade, protest march, fashion runway show

morphemes.meaning: line, thread (from file / fil < Latin fīlum)

défilé.notes: In Paris celebrity and agency life, un défilé (or un défilé de mode) is a runway fashion show (e.g., during Fashion Week), while le défilé du 14 Juillet is the Bastille Day military parade and un défilé incessant means an endless stream of visitors.

rootFamily.gloss: to march past, walk the runway, scroll by

définir.etymology: Adapted in Old French defenir (12th century, re-Latinized to définir in Middle French) from Classical Latin dēfīnīre ('to mark out boundaries, limit, determine, explain precisely'), composed of dē- ('completely, off') and fīnīre ('to bound, limit, end'), derived from fīnis ('boundary marker, border, end').

history.meaning: to set boundaries to, limit, explain precisely
to settle, bring to an end, formulate the meaning of
to define, establish parameters or terms

définir.notes: Conjugates as a regular second-group -ir verb with the -iss- stem extension in plural and imperfect forms (nous définissons, ils définissaient).

définitif.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th century, initially in canon and civil law for a final judgment, sentence définitive, as opposed to an interlocutory ruling) from Late Latin dēfīnītīvus ('explanatory, decisive, final'), derived from dēfīnītus, past participle of Classical Latin dēfīnīre ('to bound, determine').

history.meaning: settling a lawsuit once and for all

définitif.notes: In filmmaking, le montage définitif is the 'final cut'; also note the fixed discourse marker en définitive ('ultimately / when all is said and done').

définitivement.etymology: Formed in Middle French (15th century) from the feminine stem définitive (from Late Latin dēfīnītīvus 'final, decisive', from dēfīnīre 'to bound, determine') + the Romance adverbial suffix -ment (inherited from Classical Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind').

history.meaning: by final judicial decree, without appeal
once and for all, permanently, irrevocably

définitivement.notes: Classic false friend: traditionally définitivement means 'permanently / for good' (Il quitte définitivement l'agence = 'He is leaving the agency for good'), NOT 'certainly / definitely' (use absolument, sans aucun doute, or clairement, even though younger speakers increasingly copy the anglicism).

cognates.meaning: to knock the bottom out, break through
to knock the bottom out of, wreck

défoncer.etymology: Inherited from Old and Middle French desfonser / défoncer (13th–14th century, literally 'to stave in or knock the bottom out of a cask or barrel'), formed from privative des- (modern dé-) + Old French fons ('bottom', modern fond, from Classical Latin fundus 'bottom, foundation, estate') + verbal suffix -er.

history.meaning: bottom (of a vessel), base, piece of land
to knock the bottom out of a barrel; break open
to smash in, break down (a door); (slang) to thrash or get wasted

défoncer.notes: Appears across registers: standard in défoncer une porte ouverte ('to state the obvious', lit. 'break down an open door'), colloquial/vulgar in se défoncer ('to give 110% effort' OR 'to get high/wasted') and défoncé ('wasted / wrecked').

rootFamily.gloss: to break down, force open (a door)

cognates.meaning: to disengage / gage, wage (from Old French)

dégager.etymology: Formed in Old French desgagier (13th century, originally 'to redeem an object left in pawn, free from a pledge or obligation'), from reversative des- (modern dé-) + gage ('pledge, security', via Vulgar Latin *wadium from Old Frankish *wadi 'pledge', cognate with English wed and wage) + -er.

history.meaning: to redeem a pledged item, release from obligation
to clear (space), emit (charisma/odor), free up; (colloq.) to get lost!

dégager.notes: Extremely versatile in Dix pour cent: polite/neutral in dégager du temps ('free up time') or Elle dégage quelque chose d'incroyable ('She radiates incredible screen presence'), vs. brusque/rude in Dégage ! ('Beat it! / Get out!') or se faire dégager ('to get booted/fired').

cognates.meaning: degage — unconcerned, easygoing; ballet step (borrowed from French)

dégagé.etymology: Adjectival past participle (16th–17th century) of dégager ('to free from a pledge or obstacle, clear'), from Old French desgagier (reversative des- + gage 'pledge' < Frankish *wadi); evolved from 'redeemed from pawn' to 'unencumbered in movement or bearing' and 'clear, open, unobstructed' of spaces, skies, or facial features.

history.meaning: redeemed from pledge, released from debt
free and graceful in posture, unencumbered

dégagé.notes: Common in Paris real estate, set scouting, and hairstyling: une vue dégagée ('an unobstructed view'), un ciel dégagé ('clear sky'), and dégagé autour des oreilles ('trimmed clear around the ears').

dégonfler.etymology: Formed in Middle/Modern French from reversative prefix dé- (Latin dis-) + gonfler ('to swell, inflate', from Vulgar Latin *conflare 'to blow up').

history.meaning: to deflate, let the air out of, reduce swelling

cognates.meaning: to disgust (borrowed from Middle French desgouster)

dégoûter.etymology: Formed in Middle French desgouster (16th century, 'to spoil someone's appetite, make someone lose their taste for food', influenced by Italian disgustare), from privative des- (modern dé-) + goût ('taste, appetite', Old French goust < Classical Latin gustus 'tasting, flavor', from PIE *ǵews- 'to taste, choose') + -er.

history.meaning: to take away appetite, cause distaste for food
to disgust, sicken, put off; (colloq. être dégoûté) to be gutted

dégoûter.notes: Both spellings dégoûter (traditional) and dégouter (1990 spelling reform) exist; in everyday spoken French, Je suis dégoûté(e) ! very often means 'I'm so bummed / gutted!' (e.g., after losing a role) rather than literal nausea.

dégrisement.etymology: Derived in 19th-century French from dégriser ('to sober up, dispel intoxication or euphoria') + action-noun suffix -ment; dégriser is formed from reversative dé- + griser ('to make tipsy, exhilarate', 17th century), itself derived from colloquial gris ('tipsy, slightly drunk', literally 'grey', borrowed into Old French from Old Frankish *grīs 'grey').

history.meaning: to make slightly drunk, intoxicate, exhilarate

dégrisement.notes: Encountered both in French legal/police terminology (une cellule de dégrisement = 'drunk tank / sobering-up cell') and figuratively for coming back down to earth after the intoxicating rush (griserie) of fame or success.

rootFamily.gloss: to sober up, bring back to reality

cognates.meaning: to disguise (borrowed from Old French desguiser); wise ('manner')

déguiser.etymology: Inherited from Old French desguiser (12th century, 'to alter from one's customary manner or dress, conceal one's identity'), formed from privative/alterative des- (modern dé-) + guise ('manner, way, fashion', borrowed from Old Frankish *wīsa 'manner, custom', from PIE *weyd- 'to see, know', cognate with English wise in clockwise) + -er.

history.meaning: to dress in an unusual fashion, conceal identity
to disguise, conceal; (se déguiser) to dress up in costume

déguiser.notes: Whereas se déguiser is normal for costume parties or Halloween ('to dress up as...'), professional actors on set wear un costume (costumer / habiller) rather than un déguisement — calling a film costume un déguisement sounds dismissive or amateurish!

rootFamily.gloss: manner, way (à sa guise = as one pleases)

cognates.meaning: to degenerate, get out of hand

dégénérer.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (late 15th century) from Classical Latin dēgenerāre ('to fall away from one's ancestral stock or noble kind, grow worse'), derived from the adjective dēgener ('departing from its race, ignoble'), formed from dē- ('away from, down from') and genus, generis ('birth, lineage, kind'), from PIE *ǵenh₁- ('to beget').

history.meaning: to fall short of one's noble lineage, worsen
to lose the qualities of one's lineage or kind
to degenerate; (of a situation) to escalate, get out of hand

dégénérer.notes: In everyday French conversation and news, Ça a dégénéré ! is the idiomatic way to say 'Things escalated / got out of hand!' (e.g., an argument on set turning into a brawl), much milder and more situational than English 'degenerate'.

déjeuner.etymology: Déjeuner developed from a reconstructed Popular Latin verb *disjunare, shortened from *disjejunare, breaking a fast. Twelfth-century French used a reflexive form for taking the morning meal; in modern metropolitan French the usual meal is lunch.

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old French disner from the same *disjējūnāre!

déjeuner.notes: As meal hours shifted later in Paris, déjeuner moved to midday ('lunch', requiring petit-déjeuner for breakfast), whereas in Belgium, Switzerland, and Quebec déjeuner still means 'breakfast'!

déjà.etymology: Univerbation in Old/Middle French (des ja, 13th c.) of dès ('right from', < Vulgar Latin *de ex) + ja ('now, already', from Classical Latin jam 'now, already').

délicat.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th–15th century) from Classical Latin dēlicātus ('alluring, voluptuous, dainty, tender, fastidious'), etymologically tied to dēliciae ('delight, charm, luxury') and dēlicere ('to entice, lure away', from dē- + lacere 'to lure, ensnare'), with secondary semantic attraction to dēdicātus and līquēre.

history.meaning: refined, dainty, sensitive in constitution or taste

délicat.notes: In workplace and agency diplomacy, un sujet délicat / une situation délicate means 'a touchy, awkward, or tricky matter requiring tact', while C'est très délicat de votre part praises someone for being thoughtful and considerate.

délicatesse.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian delicatezza ('refinement, daintiness, tact'), derived from delicato, itself from Classical Latin delicatus ('alluring, dainty, luxurious, tender'), closely connected to deliciae ('delight, pleasure') and delicere ('to entice, lure away').
délicatesse.notes: In professional and agency contexts, 'indélicatesse' means a breach of trust or minor embezzlement, whereas 'avec délicatesse' highlights diplomatic tact when handling fragile egos.

délicieux.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Late Latin deliciosus ('delightful, luxurious, dainty'), derived from Classical Latin deliciae ('delights, pleasures, luxuries', related to delicere 'to allure, entice').

cognates.meaning: civil wrong or misdemeanor in Roman/civil law

délit.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing in the 14th century from Classical Latin delictum ('fault, offense, transgression'), substantivized neuter past participle of delinquere ('to fail, fall short of duty, offend'), formed from intensive/away prefix de- + linquere ('to leave behind, forsake'). Distinct from obsolete Old French delit ('delight', from delectare).

history.meaning: to fail in duty, fall short, transgress

délit.notes: In French criminal law, 'délit' sits between a minor 'contravention' and a major 'crime'; common idioms include 'flagrant délit' (caught red-handed) and 'délit de fuite' (hit-and-run).

démantèlement.etymology: Derived in the 16th century from démanteler ('to tear down defensive walls', literally 'to strip of a cloak') + action suffix -ment; built on privative dé- + Old French mantel ('cloak', metaphorically 'protective curtain wall of a fortress'), from Classical Latin mantellum ('cloak, covering').

history.meaning: to strip a fortress of its ramparts
dismantling of structures, networks, or corporate assets

démantèlement.notes: Notice the grave accent in 'démantèlement' reflecting the open vowel [ɛ] before a mute syllable; in business French (as in agency buyouts), it specifically denotes breaking up and selling off a company's divisions.

cognates.meaning: diplomatic step or initiative (borrowed from French)

démarche.etymology: Post-verbal feminine noun from démarcher ('to step, walk, pace'), composed of dé- + marcher ('to walk, tread'). Old French marchier ('to trample underfoot, stride') comes from Frankish *markōn ('to mark, press with the foot'). Semantic shift progressed from 'physical gait' (16th c.) to 'step taken toward an objective, procedure, or artistic approach' (17th c.).

history.meaning: to mark out, press with the foot
gait, bearing; purposeful step or approach

démarche.notes: In cinema and arts circles, 'une démarche artistique' means an artist's guiding vision or creative method, whereas plural 'des démarches (administratives)' means bureaucratic paperwork and errands.

démarrer.etymology: Formed in the 15th–16th century as a nautical verb ('to unmoor a ship, cast off') from reversative prefix dé- + amarrer ('to moor a vessel with cables', borrowed from Middle Dutch maren 'to tie, moor').

history.meaning: to untie mooring lines, cast off
to cast off -> to start moving, start up an engine

cognates.meaning: act of stepping down or relinquishing office (archaic/formal)

démissionner.etymology: Coined in the late 18th–early 19th century as a denominal verb from démission ('resignation, relinquishment of office') + -er. Démission was borrowed from Classical/Medieval Latin demissio ('a letting down, lowering, sinking'), noun of action from demittere ('to send down, let fall, lay down an office'), from de- ('down') + mittere ('to send, let go').

history.meaning: to send down, lower, relinquish post
to resign formally from a position

démissionner.notes: Unlike English 'dismiss', 'démissionner' is almost always intransitive ('to resign, quit'); colloquially, 'être démissionné' (used in the passive) is an ironic idiom meaning to be forced to resign.

cognates.meaning: to tear down, destroy (via Middle French demoliss-)

démolir.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin demoliri (regularized in Late Latin as active *demolire), meaning 'to pull down, throw down, destroy', formed from reversative de- + moliri ('to build up, construct with effort, heave'), itself derived from moles ('massive structure, pier, heavy mass').

history.meaning: shapeless mass, boulder, monumental dike or structure
to pull down a heavy structure, raze
to tear down buildings; figuratively to ruin or crush

démolir.notes: In showbiz and media French, 'démolir un film' means for critics to pan a movie ruthlessly, and 'être complètement démoli' means to be emotionally crushed or exhausted.

rootFamily.gloss: pier, breakwater; massive block (from Latin moles)

démon.etymology: Borrowed via Ecclesiastical Latin daemon ('evil spirit, pagan god') from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn, 'divine power, tutelary spirit, lesser deity, allotted fate'), originally derived from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂y- / Greek δαίομαι (daíomai, 'to divide, apportion destinies'). Christian Latin narrowed the morally neutral Greek spirit to a malevolent fiend.

history.meaning: divine power, guiding spirit, allotted destiny
fiend, devil; inner obsession or creative genius

démon.notes: Retains both Christian and Greek shades in French idioms: 'ses vieux démons' (one's recurring vices/obsessions) and 'le démon de midi' (midlife crisis / sudden romantic infatuation in middle age).

démonter.etymology: Formed in Old French (desmonter, 12th c., originally 'to unhorse a rider, throw from a mount') from prefix des- / dé- + monter ('to mount, go up, assemble'); extended in the 16th–17th century to taking apart an assembled mechanism.

history.meaning: to unhorse -> to take apart, disassemble; to disconcert

cognates.meaning: household management, three-way relationship (loan from French ménage)
house, mansion (cognate with base Latin mansio)

déménager.etymology: Formed in Middle French (desmenagier) from reversative/ablative dé- + ménage ('household, furniture, domestic goods') + -er. Old French mesnage ('dwelling, household') continues Vulgar Latin *mansionaticum ('that which belongs to a house'), derived from Classical Latin mansio, mansionem ('staying, dwelling place'), from manere ('to remain, abide').

history.meaning: to remove one's household furniture to another dwelling

déménager.notes: Distinguish 'déménager' (focusing on leaving the old place or moving house in general) from 'emménager' (moving into the new home); in slang, 'ça déménage !' means 'it really rocks / packs a punch!'

rootFamily.gloss: to move into a new home

déménageur.etymology: Formed in the 19th century from déménager ('to move one's household goods to a new residence', from dé- + ménage 'household') + agent suffix -eur.

dénouer.etymology: Inherited from Old French desnoer ('to untie a knot, unravel'), formed from prefix des- / dé- (Latin dis-) + noer / nouer ('to tie in a knot', from Classical Latin nodare < nodus 'knot').

history.meaning: to untie a knot; to unravel a plot or crisis

cognates.meaning: to strip of covering or vegetation

dénuder.etymology: Learned borrowing (15th century) from Classical Latin denudare ('to lay bare, uncover, strip, disclose'), composed of intensive/privative prefix de- + nudare ('to make naked, strip'), derived from nudus ('naked, bare, unadorned'), from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷós ('naked').

history.meaning: to lay completely bare, strip off covering
to bare, expose; (reflexive) to appear nude

morphemes.meaning: naked, bare (Latin nud-, cf. French nu)

dénuder.notes: In casting and film contract negotiations (a staple of *Dix pour cent*), reflexive 'se dénuder à l'écran' is the standard polite expression for doing a nude scene, whereas 'dénué de' (without 'd') means 'devoid of'.

rootFamily.gloss: low-cut or revealing; stripped of foliage

cognates.meaning: roadside repair or emergency assistance (borrowed from French)

dépannage.etymology: Formed in early 20th-century automotive and aviation French from dépanner ('to get a vehicle out of a breakdown, repair') + action suffix -age. Dépanner combines privative dé- + panne ('mechanical breakdown'), originally a 17th-century naval term ('mettre en panne', to heave to by backing sails so the ship stands motionless), probably linked to Old French pan / penne ('piece of sailcloth, yardarm tip', from Latin pannus / pinna).

history.meaning: (of a sailing ship) hove-to, immobilized with backed sails
emergency repair, towing, or quick favor in a pinch

dépannage.notes: Beyond roadside towing ('dépannage auto') or tech troubleshooting, 'en dépannage' and 'dépanner quelqu'un' are everyday spoken French for helping someone out in a jam (e.g., filling in last-minute on a shoot).

rootFamily.gloss: to fix, bail out, help out in a pinch
repair technician, tow-truck driver, convenience store (Québec)

départ.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (depart, 12th c., 'separation, division; act of leaving') from departir ('to divide, separate; to set out, leave', from Vulgar Latin *departire).

history.meaning: separation -> act of setting out, departure, start of a race

dépasser.etymology: Formed in Middle French from prefix dé- + passer ('to pass, step beyond', from Vulgar Latin *passare < passus 'step').

history.meaning: to go beyond, overtake, exceed, rise above

cognates.meaning: to rely on, be contingent upon

dépendre.etymology: Inherited/adapted in Old French (dependre) from Classical Latin dependere ('to hang down, hang from; figuratively to be derived from or dependent upon'), composed of de- ('down from') + pendere ('to hang, be suspended'). In French, the literal physical sense ('to unhook/take down what is hanging') split off from the figurative stative sense ('to rely on, be contingent on').

history.meaning: to hang down from, be governed by
to hang from; to be subject to or contingent upon

dépendre.notes: Always takes the preposition 'de' (never 'sur', a classic English interference error from 'depend on'): 'Ça dépend de toi' ('It depends on you').

dépenser.etymology: Rebuilt in Middle French from dépense ('expenditure, pantry', from Late Latin dispensa, feminine past participle of dispendere 'to weigh out money, disburse'), replacing older dépendre ('to spend').

déplacer.etymology: Formed in Middle French (desplacer, 15th c.) from prefix des- / dé- + place ('place, spot') + verbal ending -er.

history.meaning: to move from its place, shift; (reflexive) to travel

déplier.etymology: Inherited from Old French despleier ('to unfold, spread open', doublet of déployer), from Late/Vulgar Latin displicare ('to unfold, scatter'), from dis- + plicare ('to fold').

dépoli.etymology: Past participle of dépolir ('to remove the polish or gloss from a surface'), formed in the 17th century from privative prefix dé- + polir ('to polish', from Latin polire).

history.meaning: deprived of gloss; frosted or ground (of glass)

cognates.meaning: to lay down, depose, testify (from Latin deponere)
to remove from office, testify under oath (borrowed from French)

déposer.etymology: Formed in Old French (deposer) from dé- + poser ('to set down, place'), remodeling Classical Latin deponere ('to lay down, entrust, remove from office'). Remarkably, French poser phonetically descends from Late Latin pausare ('to pause, halt, rest', from Greek παῦσις paûsis), which completely usurped the semantic field of Classical Latin ponere ('to put, place') in Gallo-Romance.

history.meaning: to halt, rest (pausare) / to lay down, entrust (deponere)
to remove from office, lay down, entrust
to set down, drop someone off, file legally, or deposit

déposer.notes: Extremely versatile false-friend trap: while it includes legal 'testify/file' ('déposer plainte', 'déposer le bilan' = file for bankruptcy), in everyday life 'Je te dépose ?' simply means 'Can I give you a ride / drop you off?'

rootFamily.gloss: to place, put down, ask (a question)

cognates.meaning: to press down, lower spirits (via Latin past participle depressus)

déprimer.etymology: Learned borrowing (14th century) from Classical Latin deprimere ('to press down, weigh down, sink deep, humble'), composed of downward prefix de- + premere ('to press, squeeze, bear down upon', weakened to -primere in compounds by Latin vowel reduction). Psychological senses ('to lower someone's morale') arose in the 19th century alongside medical usage.

history.meaning: to press, squeeze, exert weight upon
to press down, sink low, humble
to lower physically; to sadden or feel downhearted

déprimer.notes: Can be used both transitively ('Ce scénario me déprime' = This script bums me out) and intransitively in casual speech ('Arrête de déprimer !' = Stop moping / feeling down!).

déprimé.etymology: Past participial adjective of déprimer ('to press down, dishearten'), borrowed from Classical Latin deprimere ('to press down, sink', from de- + premere 'to press'). Originally used in anatomy and botany for flattened surfaces (16th–18th c.), it acquired its psychological meaning ('dejected, low-spirited') in late 19th-century psychiatric and everyday French.

history.meaning: flattened, sunken, weakened (e.g., pulse or organ)

déprimé.notes: Careful with register and clinical nuance: 'être déprimé' usually describes feeling down or blue, whereas 'être dépressif' describes someone suffering from clinical depression or prone to depressive episodes.

cognates.meaning: to send off quickly (via Italian/Spanish from Gallo-Romance)

dépêcher.etymology: Inherited from Old French despeechier ('to free from a fetter or hindrance, disentangle, send off swiftly'), formed as the exact antonym of empeechier (modern empêcher, 'to hinder'). Built on privative des- (dé-) + Late Latin *pedicare / impedicare ('to shackle, snare the feet'), from Classical Latin pedica ('fetter, foot-snare'), derived from pes, pedis ('foot').

history.meaning: foot-snare, shackle / to entangle the feet
to unshackle, free from obstacles, expedite
to send urgently; (reflexive se dépêcher) to hurry up

morphemes.meaning: fetter, foot-snare (from Latin pedica, root ped- 'foot')

dépêcher.notes: Unrelated to 'pêcher' ('to fish', < piscari) or 'pécher' ('to sin', < peccare)! Reflexive 'se dépêcher' means 'to hurry', while transitive 'dépêcher un envoyé' means 'to dispatch an envoy'.

dérangement.etymology: Formed in the 16th–17th century from déranger ('to throw out of order, disturb') + nominal suffix -ment.

déranger.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French (desrengier, 13th c., 'to break military ranks, throw out of line') from prefix des- / dé- + rangier / ranger ('to set in a row or rank', from rang < Frankish *hring 'circle, ring of warriors').

history.meaning: to throw out of line -> to disarrange, disturb, bother

désastre.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-16th century from Italian disastro ('ill-starred misfortune, calamity'), a Renaissance astrological coinage combining pejorative prefix dis- ('badly, unfavorably') + astro ('star, planet, celestial influence'), from Classical Latin astrum, itself from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, 'star, constellation'). Literally 'an unfavorable alignment of the stars'.

history.meaning: misfortune caused by an unfavorable star

désastre.notes: Masculine noun ('un désastre'); in film production and box-office talk, 'un désastre industriel' refers to a big-budget flop that loses massive sums of money.

cognates.meaning: to abandon one's post or forsake (from French déserter)

déserter.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Late Latin desertare ('to forsake, abandon, leave uninhabited'), frequentative built on desertus, past participle of Classical Latin deserere ('to sever ties with, undo one's link to, abandon'), formed from reversative de- + serere ('to join together, bind in a row, entwine'). Literally 'to unbind oneself from the ranks'.

history.meaning: to unbind from a series, sever ties, forsake
to abandon a military post or leave a place empty

déserter.notes: Pronounced with [z] ('dé-zer-ter') because single 's' sits between vowels (contrast 'dessert' [de.sɛʁ], sweet course, from 'desservir' 'to clear the table'). Often used transitively: 'Le public a déserté les salles' (Audiences abandoned movie theaters).

cognates.meaning: runaway soldier or defector (borrowed from French)

déserteur.etymology: Adapted in the 15th century from Classical Latin desertor, desertorem ('one who forsakes, runaway soldier, defector'), agent noun built on the supine stem of deserere ('to sever ties, abandon one's post', from de- + serere 'to bind together in a line'), with Latin -orem reshaped into the productive French agent suffix -eur.

history.meaning: one who forsakes duty or military service
military deserter; figuratively someone who bails out on a commitment

déserteur.notes: Famous in French cultural memory through Boris Vian's iconic 1954 pacifist song *Le Déserteur*; figuratively used playfully or critically for an actor or colleague who walks off a project.

désespérément.etymology: Formed in Middle French from désespéré ('hopeless, driven to despair', past participle of désespérer) + adverbial suffix -ment (from Classical Latin ablative mente, 'with a ... mind'). Désespérer continues Old French desesperer, reshaping Classical Latin desperare ('to give up hope', from privative de- + sperare 'to hope', from spes 'hope') with the reinforced prefix des- + esperer.

history.meaning: to have no hope, give up hope
to lose all hope, fall into despair
without hope; intensely, at all costs

désespérément.notes: Like English 'desperately', it shifted in modern usage from tragic hopelessness to hyperbolic intensity ('chercher désespérément un rôle' = desperately hunting for a role, echoed in the French title *Recherche Susan désespérément*).

cognates.meaning: casual or state of partial undress (borrowed from French déshabillé)
able, skillful (from Old French abile, root of habiller)

déshabiller.etymology: Formed in Middle French (deshabillier) from reversative dés- + habiller ('to dress', originally in Old French 'to prepare, fit out, trim logs into timber'). Remarkably, habiller derives from Old French abile ('fit, suitable, nimble', modern habile), borrowed from Classical Latin habilis ('easily handled, suitable, fit'), from habere ('to hold, have'). Clothing was conceived as 'fitting someone out for action'.

history.meaning: to prepare, equip, outfit, and later to clothe
to divest of equipment or strip off clothing

déshabiller.notes: Note the obligatory liaison [de.za.bi.je] because the 'h' in 'habiller' is mute (h muet), restored only graphically by Renaissance scribes imitating Latin 'habilis'. Idiom: 'déshabiller Pierre pour habiller Paul' (rob Peter to pay Paul).

rootFamily.gloss: to dress; costume designer on set (habilleur/habilleuse)
skillful, clever (doublet of the base adjective)

cognates.meaning: longing, wish (borrowed from Old French desir)

désir.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in Old French (desir, gradually replacing earlier desirrier < Vulgar Latin *desideriarium) from the verb desirer ('to long for, miss'), inherited from Classical Latin desiderare ('to long for what is absent, miss, wish for'), traditionally linked to de- + sidus, sideris ('star, constellation').

history.meaning: longing for something lost or absent, grief, wish
conscious wish, longing, or sensual passion

désir.notes: Stronger and more emotionally or sensually charged than 'envie' in everyday French; in cinema/celebrity culture, 'se faire désirer' means to play hard to get or make people wait eagerly for one's arrival.

cognates.meaning: to long for, wish (via Old French desirer)

désirer.etymology: Inherited from Old French desirer ('to long for, miss, wish for'), from Classical Latin desiderare ('to long for what is absent, regret, await'). Roman grammarians and modern philologists connect desiderare (alongside considerare 'to observe the stars closely') to de- + sidus, sideris ('star, constellation') — originally augural/military slang meaning 'to look in vain to the stars' or 'to miss soldiers absent under the night sky'.

history.meaning: to miss what is absent, long for, regret
to wish for formally, or to desire passionately

désirer.notes: Register split: with a person or art object it expresses deep passion, whereas with an infinitive or in hospitality ('Vous désirez ?') it is formal/polite service French. Idiom: 'laisser à désirer' ('to leave much to be desired').

rootFamily.gloss: stellar, staggering (learned relative from Latin sidus, sideris)

désolé.etymology: Désolé is the past participle of désoler, also used as an adjective. The Académie traces the verb to Latin desolare, to depopulate or devastate. The everyday apology uses a milder sense of distress or regret.
désolé.notes: Je suis désolé(e) (or simply Désolé!) is French's most natural everyday way to say 'I'm sorry'.

désordre.etymology: Formed in the 14th century from privative/negative prefix dés- + ordre ('regular arrangement, rank'), replacing earlier Old French desordene. Ordre descends via Old French ordene from Classical Latin ordo, ordinem ('row of threads in a loom, military line, regular series, social rank').

history.meaning: row of threads in a loom, rank, regular arrangement
breach of rule, confusion, military rout
physical mess, organizational chaos, or civil unrest

désordre.notes: Unlike English medical 'eating disorder' or 'anxiety disorder' (which French translates with 'trouble': 'trouble alimentaire', 'trouble anxieux'), French 'désordre' means a physical mess ('ma chambre est en désordre') or organizational turmoil.

cognates.meaning: by now, from now on (ora + mai, parallel compound)

désormais.etymology: Univerbation (fusion into a single word) of the Old French adverbial phrase des ore mais ('from this hour onward, henceforth'), composed of three elements: des ('from, since', modern dès < Vulgar Latin *de ex) + ore ('now, at this hour' < Classical Latin hora 'hour') + mais ('more, further' < Classical Latin magis 'more'). Literally 'from-now-more'.

history.meaning: from now on, henceforth, now (contrasting with the past)

morphemes.meaning: now, this hour (Old French ore < Latin hora)

désormais.notes: Slightly elevated compared to 'à partir de maintenant', yet ubiquitous in journalism, contract talks, and dramatic turning points ('Désormais, c'est moi qui décide'); shares Old French 'ore' ('now') with 'd'ores et déjà' and 'dorénavant' (d'ore en avant).

déstabiliser.etymology: Formed in mid-20th-century French from reversative prefix dé- + stabiliser ('to make stable'), itself a learned derivation from Classical Latin stabilis ('firm, steadfast, able to stand'), built on the root of stare ('to stand') + instrumental/adjectival suffix -bilis, plus verbalizing -iser (from Late Latin -izare / Greek -ίζειν).

history.meaning: to render physically or economically stable
to upset political/physical balance; personally to rattle or throw off guard

déstabiliser.notes: Major register difference from English: whereas English 'destabilize' sounds geopolitical, French 'déstabiliser quelqu'un' is everyday interpersonal vocabulary meaning 'to rattle, fluster, or throw someone off balance' (e.g., during an audition or negotiation).

cognates.meaning: affliction, hardship (historical source of 'stress' via Old French destrece)

déstresser.etymology: Late 20th-century French formation combining privative dé- + stresser ('to subject to stress'), built on the 20th-century borrowing stress from English. Crucially, this completes a philological round-trip ('aller-retour'): English stress arose by apheresis from Middle English destresse, borrowed from Old French destrece ('narrowness, oppression, anguish', modern détresse), from Vulgar Latin *districtia, built on Latin distringere ('to draw tight, hinder').

history.meaning: to relieve tension, unwind, calm someone down

déstresser.notes: Used transitively ('Ça me déstresse'), intransitively ('Il faut que tu déstresses avant le tournage' — relax before the shoot!), or reflexively ('se déstresser'); its inherited French cousin from the exact same Latin root is 'détresse' ('distress').

rootFamily.gloss: distress, anguish (native French doublet of stress)

détail.etymology: Post-verbal noun attested from the 12th century from Old French detaillier ('to cut into small pieces, slice up, sell in small quantities'), formed from intensive/divisive dé- + tailler ('to cut, carve, prune'). Tailler descends from Late Latin taliare ('to split, cut shoots'), derived from Classical Latin talea ('cutting, graft twig, wooden rod'). Evolved from 'retail cutting of cloth' to 'itemized particulars' (17th c.).

history.meaning: plant cutting, rod / to split, prune, cut
cutting into pieces; selling cloth or goods in small portions
retail trade; small particular or fine element of a whole

détail.notes: Preserves its original commercial meaning in 'vente au détail' ('retail', opposed to 'vente en gros' 'wholesale'), just as English 'retail' comes from Old French 'retaillier' ('to cut off a piece')! Plural is 'détails'.

rootFamily.gloss: to detail, itemize; to size someone up

cognates.meaning: easing of diplomatic hostility (borrowed from French noun détente)

détendre.etymology: Inherited from Old French destendre ('to unbend a bow, slacken a rope, take down a tent'), reflecting Late/Classical Latin detendere ('to unstretch, strike a tent') merged with *distendere (from reversative dis-/de- + Classical Latin tendere 'to stretch, pull taut', from Proto-Indo-European *ten- 'to stretch'). Metaphorical relaxation of mind and muscles developed from slackening bowstrings.

history.meaning: to stretch taut / to unstretch, take down tents
to unstring a bow, slacken a taut cord
to slacken tension; (reflexive se détendre) to relax, unwind

détendre.notes: For 'to relax' intransitively, French requires the reflexive 'se détendre' ('Détends-toi !' = Relax!); used transitively, 'détendre l'atmosphère' means 'to break the ice / ease the tension in the room'.

rootFamily.gloss: relaxation, trigger of a firearm, diplomatic thaw
to stretch, tighten; to hold out

détendu.etymology: Past participial adjective of détendre ('to unbend, slacken, relax'), continuing Old French destendu ('unstrung, slackened, loosened'), built on privative des- (dé-) + tendu, the Gallo-Romance weak past participle (*tendutus, replacing Classical Latin tentus / tensus) of Latin tendere ('to stretch, draw tight'). Literally 'no longer pulled taut'.

history.meaning: (of a bow or rope) unstrung, slackened
relaxed, calm, laid-back, free of tension

détendu.notes: Its exact antonym is 'tendu' ('tense, uptight, dicey'); in French workplace and film-set banter, 'ambiance détendue' describes an easygoing, low-pressure vibe. Feminine adds '-e' ('détendue', silent in pronunciation).

cognates.meaning: firmness of purpose, act of defining (borrowed via Old/Middle French)

détermination.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical and Scholastic Latin determinatio, determinationem ('boundary, conclusion, fixing of limits'), noun of action from determinare ('to enclose within boundaries, fix limits, settle'), composed of intensive/delimiting de- + terminare ('to mark off boundaries, end'), from terminus ('boundary stone, limit'). The modern sense 'unwavering willpower' crystallized in the 17th–18th centuries under philosophical and English influence.

history.meaning: boundary stone / to enclose within fixed limits
fixing of boundaries; scholastic conclusion of a debate
precise definition; resolute firmness of purpose

détermination.notes: Always feminine in French (like nearly all nouns ending in '-tion': 'une grande détermination'); covers both character grit ('faire preuve de détermination') and grammar/science ('la détermination du prix').

déterrer.etymology: Formed in Old French (desterrer, 12th c.) from prefix des- / dé- ('out of, away from') + terre ('earth, ground', from Latin terra) + -er.

history.meaning: to dig up out of the ground, unearth, unearth a secret

détester.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin detestari ('to curse while calling the gods to witness, execrate, abhor'), compound of de- ('away, down') + testari ('to call to witness, invoke', from testis 'witness').

history.meaning: to curse by calling the gods as witness, abhor
to execrate -> to hate intensely, detest

détritus.etymology: Learned 19th-century borrowing (initially in geology for rock debris worn away by erosion) from Classical Latin dētrītus ('a rubbing away, wearing down'), action noun and past participle of dēterere ('to rub off, wear out, grind down'), compounded from dē- ('down, away') and terere ('to rub, thresh'). In colloquial French it extended from physical refuse to an insult for a worthless person or piece of junk.

history.meaning: to rub away, wear down; the act or product of wearing down
geological rock fragments produced by disintegration; organic residue
trash, garbage, refuse; (figurative) piece of junk or scumbag

morphemes.meaning: to rub, grind, wear down (Latin terere, past participle trītus)

détritus.notes: Insoluble final -s is pronounced (/detʁitys/); invariable in the plural (des détritus), and used colloquially in fiery agency arguments as a harsh personal insult ('trash').

rootFamily.gloss: trite, worn out by overuse (via English/Latin trītus)

détruire.etymology: Inherited via Old French destruire from Vulgar Latin *dēstrūgere, a remodeling (influenced by trahere/tractus and the perfect stem strūxī) of Classical Latin dēstruere ('to pull down, unbuild, dismantle'), formed from reversative dē- ('down, un-') and struere ('to pile up, arrange, build'). English destroy was borrowed directly from the Old French stem.

history.meaning: to pull down, dismantle what has been built
to ravage, demolish, bring to ruin

détruire.notes: Conjugates irregularly like construire and conduire (je détruis, nous détruisons, past participle détruit); colloquially, ça m'a détruit can mean 'that wiped me out / crushed me'.

rootFamily.gloss: to build, construct (antonymic prefixation on struere)
to instruct, equip mentally (from Latin instruere)

cognates.meaning: laid waste; overwhelmed with grief or shock

dévasté.etymology: Past participial adjective of dévaster, a learned borrowing from Classical Latin dēvastāre ('to lay completely waste, depopulate'), formed from intensive dē- ('thoroughly') and vastāre ('to ravage, make empty'), itself from vastus ('empty, desolate, immense'). While traditionally restricted in French to physical ruin of land or buildings, its psychological use ('emotionally crushed') surged in modern media and cinema circles under the influence of English devastated.

history.meaning: to lay completely waste, ravage territory
to ravage, plunder, desolate a region or building
physically ruined; emotionally shattered or heart-stricken

dévasté.notes: Purists flag je suis dévasté(e) ('I'm devastated' emotionally) as a late-20th-century anglicism—traditional French prefers anéanti, effondré, or bouleversé—making it delightfully on-brand for dramatic actors and agents in Dix pour cent.

cognates.meaning: process of growing, elaborating, or unfolding (borrowed from French)

développement.etymology: Formed within French (attested 15th century as desvelopement) by suffixing the action-noun formant -ment to développer ('to unwrap, unfurl, expand'). The semantic trajectory moves from physically unrolling a wrapped bundle or scroll, to unfolding an idea in discourse, to biological, economic, and cinematic script development (le développement d'un projet).

history.meaning: act of unwrapping, unrolling, or unfurling
exposition of an idea; organic growth or expansion

morphemes.meaning: to wrap, roll up (Old French voloper)

développement.notes: In French film and TV production, être en développement refers specifically to the pre-greenlight phase where screenwriters and producers shape a concept, treatment, and financing.

rootFamily.gloss: to wrap up, enclose (the morphological antonym)
envelope, outer wrapping or budget allocation

cognates.meaning: to unfold, grow, elaborate (borrowed from French)

développer.etymology: Inherited from Old French desvoloper ('to unwrap, unfurl, free from coverings'), formed with reversative prefix des- (modern dé-) on the Old French verbstem voloper / vloper ('to wrap up', preserved in envelopper). That Gallo-Romance base is most plausibly traced to Late Latin faluppa ('chaff, bundle of straw, scrap', whence Italian viluppo 'tangle, bundle') via a verb *faluppāre ('to bundle in straw'), with labial assimilation.

history.meaning: wisp of straw, bundle; to wrap in a bundle
to unwrap, unroll, clear of coverings

développer.notes: Notice the spelling asymmetry with English: French writes a single l and double p (développer), just like envelopper ('to wrap'), its exact historical opposite.

rootFamily.gloss: paper envelope; total financial budget ('une enveloppe budgétaire')

cognates.meaning: to eat up hungrily or consume eagerly

dévorer.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (devorer, 12th century, originally church Latin for the devil or beasts swallowing prey) from Classical Latin dēvorāre ('to swallow down, gulp whole, engulf'), compounded from dē- ('down') and vorāre ('to swallow greedily', from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerh₃- 'to swallow', the same root seen in gorge and vorace).

history.meaning: to swallow down whole, gulp greedily, engulf
to eat up like a beast of prey, swallow alive
to devour ravenously; to read or gaze at avidly

dévorer.notes: Frequently used figuratively in arts and media: dévorer un scénario ('to tear through a script in one sitting') or dévorer quelqu'un des yeux ('to devour someone with one's eyes').

cognates.meaning: misled, tricked (via Old French decevoir, before semantic divergence)

déçu.etymology: Past participial adjective of décevoir, inherited via Old French deceü ('tricked, misled, frustrated in expectation') from Classical Latin dēceptus, past participle of dēcipere ('to catch in a snare, beguile, cheat'), from dē- ('away, astray') + capere ('to take, seize'). Between Classical and Modern French, the sense softened from deliberate fraud ('tricked') to dashed hopes ('let down, disappointed').

history.meaning: tricked, betrayed, frustrated in one's hopes

déçu.notes: Classic false friend: déçu means 'disappointed' (and décevoir means 'to disappoint', une déception 'a disappointment'), whereas English 'deceived' is trompé or dupé! Notice the cedilla (ç) keeping the soft /s/ sound before u.

rootFamily.gloss: to receive (parallel formation from Latin recipere)

dîner.etymology: Inherited from Old French disner ('to take the first main meal of the day, break one's fast'), from Vulgar Latin *disjejunare ('to break one's fast', the tonic-accented doublet of déjeuner), formed from dis- + jejunare ('to fast', from jejunus 'fasting').

history.meaning: midday meal -> evening meal, dinner; to dine

cognates.meaning: trunk, traveling case (native descendant of Old French male, source of English mail)

e-mail.etymology: Borrowed in the 1980s–1990s from American English e-mail, clipping of electronic mail. Remarkably, mail is an etymological boomerang (aller-retour): Middle English male ('traveling bag, mail pouch') was borrowed from Anglo-Norman/Old French male ('leather bag, trunk', modern French malle), itself from Frankish *malha ('wallet, sack'), while electronic stems ultimately from Ancient Greek ēlektron ('amber').

history.meaning: leather pouch, traveling bag (carried by royal couriers)
messages transmitted digitally over computer networks

morphemes.meaning: post, message system (English mail < Old French male 'bag')

e-mail.notes: Masculine (un e-mail); in everyday Parisian office speech, clipped simply to un mail (/mɛl/), whereas official language commissions promote courriel (blend of courrier électronique, dominant in Quebec and formal writing).

rootFamily.gloss: colloquial clipping for an email message in France
traveling trunk (native French twin of English mail)
official French blend (courrier + électronique) for email

sources.title: CNRTL – Étymologie de malle (origin of mail)

eau.etymology: Eau descends intact through speech from Latin aqua ('water')! Intervocalic -qu- softened and dropped, leaving Old French ewe, eaue, modern eau — five Latin letters transformed into three vowels pronounced simply /o/.
eau.notes: **Eau chaude / froide** = hot / cold water; **eau gazeuse** = sparkling water.

cognates.meaning: to wipe out, make inconspicuous (borrowed from French)

effacer.etymology: Formed in Old French (esfacier, 12th century) from the privative/ablative prefix es- (from Latin ex- 'out, away', assimilated to ef- before f) and face ('face, visible surface', from Vulgar Latin *facia, Classical Latin faciēs 'form, visage') plus -er. Literally 'to remove the face from' or 'wipe from the surface', whence 'to rub out writing, erase, obliterate'.

history.meaning: to wipe away from the surface, destroy the likeness of
to rub out writing or marks, obliterate
to erase, delete, cause to fade; (reflexive) to step aside or keep a low profile

morphemes.meaning: out, off, away (Latin ex- assimilated before f)
first-conjugation infinitive ending (with c → ç before a/o)

effacer.notes: Reflexive s'effacer means either 'to fade away' (memories, stains) or socially 'to step aside / stay discreetly in the background' (s'effacer devant une star), giving the adjective effacé ('self-effacing, meek').

effet.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French (efet, effect, 13th century) from Classical Latin effectus ('accomplishment, execution, result'), fourth-declension verbal noun from efficere ('to work out, accomplish, bring about'), compounded from ex- ('out, thoroughly') and facere ('to make, do', weakened to -ficere in compounds).

history.meaning: result, impression, impact; (plural) personal belongings or special effects

morphemes.meaning: out, thoroughly (Latin ex- assimilated to ef-)

effet.notes: Watch the crucial discourse false friend: en effet confirms what was just said ('indeed, quite so'), whereas 'in effect / actually' introducing a correction or contrast is en fait or dans les faits! In cinema, effets spéciaux = 'special effects'.

rootFamily.gloss: to carry out, perform (from Medieval Latin effectuāre)

efficace.etymology: Learned 14th-century borrowing from Classical Latin efficāx, genitive efficācis ('powerful, effectual, productive'), an adjective formed with the inclination/capacity suffix -āx on the stem of efficere ('to bring to pass, accomplish', from ex- 'out' + facere 'to make, do'). Unlike English, which split effective and efficient, French efficace covers both meanings.

history.meaning: producing its intended theological or medicinal effect
effective (achieving results) and efficient (working briskly without waste)

efficace.notes: Covers both English 'effective' and 'efficient' when praising a capable assistant or agent; French effectif is a false friend meaning 'actual, in force' (or as a noun, 'staff headcount').

cognates.meaning: strenuous physical or mental exertion (borrowed from French)

effort.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (esforz, late 11th century: 'strength, military force, exertion') from esforcier ('to strengthen, exert oneself', modern s'efforcer), descending from Vulgar Latin *exfortiāre ('to put forth strength'), built from intensive ex- ('out') and Classical Latin fortis ('strong, brave') / Late Latin fortia ('strength').

history.meaning: to put forth strength, compel, exert
display of might, troop force, strenuous exertion
conscious physical, intellectual, or financial exertion

morphemes.meaning: out, forth (Old French es- < Latin ex-, respelled ef-)

effort.notes: Silent final -t (/efɔʁ/); in contract negotiations (a staple of Dix pour cent), faire un effort often specifically means 'to make a financial concession' on a fee or price.

cognates.meaning: brawl, commotion; to frighten (borrowed from Old French esfrei / esfreer)
peace (cognate with the Germanic root *friþu inside effrayer)

effrayant.etymology: Present participial adjective of effrayer ('to frighten'), from Old French esfreer ('to disturb, throw into turmoil, terrify'). Esfreer derives from Gallo-Romance / Vulgar Latin *exfridāre ('to break the peace of, cast out of peace'), a Gallo-Frankish hybrid combining Latin privative ex- ('out of') with Frankish *friþu ('peace, public order'). English affray and afraid ultimately descend from the Anglo-Norman variant of this same verb.

history.meaning: to put out of peace, disturb public quiet

morphemes.meaning: out of (Latin ex- assimilated to ef-)
peace, tranquility (from Frankish *friþu via Old French esfreer)

effrayant.notes: Pronounced /efʁɛjɑ̃/; alongside literal terror, conversational French uses c'est effrayant hyperbolically ('it's appalling / staggering') when reacting to someone's incompetence, cynicism, or box-office flop.

cognates.meaning: hey, eh (interjection of inquiry or call)

eh.etymology: Primary expressive exclamation attested since Old French (e, eh, 11th century) and directly continuing or paralleling Classical Latin ēh / ehem, a natural vocalic interjection used to call attention, express surprise, soften a rejoinder, or buy thinking time before a reply (especially in the ubiquitous compound discourse marker eh bien).

history.meaning: ha! hey! exclamation of surprise or attention
alas, hey, oh (vocative or emotive interjection)
hey, well (attention-getter or conversational opener, esp. eh bien / eh oui)

eh.notes: Spelling tip even native speakers mix up: eh (exclamation/discourse opener: eh bien !, often clipped in speech to ben ! or bah !) vs. hé (hailing someone from afar: hé là-bas !) vs. et ('and').

elle.etymology: Elle continues Latin illa, the feminine of the demonstrative ille, that one. The Académie records ninth-century ele as a subject form and thirteenth-century elle as an object form. Modern elle can therefore be understood against a history with different grammatical uses and spellings.

emballer.etymology: Formed in the 14th century from prefix en- / em- ('in, into') + balle ('bale, tightly tied bundle of merchandise', from Frankish *balla 'ball, rounded bundle'); originally 'to pack goods into a bale', and figuratively in modern French 'to carry away with enthusiasm'.

history.meaning: to pack into a bale, wrap up; to thrill, get carried away

cognates.meaning: to put or go on board a ship
to load onto a vessel, board
to board a ship; to begin an enterprise (borrowed from French)

embarquer.etymology: Attested in the 16th century, borrowed from or modeled on Provençal/Spanish embarcar and Italian imbarcare ('to put on board a boat'), formed from prefix em- (Latin in- 'into, onto') + barque ('small decked vessel', from Late Latin barca) + -er. In 19th–20th-century colloquial French it developed vivid figurative senses: 'to rope someone into an affair', 'to walk off with', and 'to haul off to the police station'.

history.meaning: small boat, ship's tender or barge
to load cargo or passengers onto a ship; to set sail
to board (a ship/plane); colloquially to drag someone in, swipe, or arrest

morphemes.meaning: in, into, aboard (Latin in- assimilated before labial b)

embarquer.notes: Beyond airport boarding (porte d'embarquement), listen in French TV dialogue for se faire embarquer par les flics ('to get hauled in / arrested by the cops') and embarquer quelqu'un dans une galère ('to rope someone into a mess').

rootFamily.gloss: boarding (passengers) or loading onto a vessel/flight
to disembark, land; colloquially 'to turn up unexpectedly / be clueless'

cognates.meaning: hindered; (in modern Spanish, specialized to) pregnant!

embarrassé.etymology: Past participial adjective of embarrasser, borrowed in the late 16th century from Spanish embarazar ('to hinder, obstruct, encumber'), itself likely from Portuguese embaraçar ('to entangle in a cord or noose'), built on em- ('in') + baraço ('halter, cord, twine', of uncertain pre-Roman Hispano-Celtic or Arabic origin, often cross-associated with barra 'bar'). The physical sense 'encumbered, blocked' evolved into 'quandaried, awkward, sheepish'.

history.meaning: to entangle with a cord, obstruct, impede movement
to encumber physically; to put in a quandary or bind
awkward, sheepish, ill at ease, or torn over a dilemma

embarrassé.notes: Subtle false friend: être embarrassé is milder and more practical than English 'embarrassed'—it often means 'put in a tight spot / conflicted / awkward' (compare l'embarras du choix 'spoiled for choice'). For acute social mortification, French prefers gêné or mort de honte.

rootFamily.gloss: to encumber, put in an awkward spot, bother
to clear away clutter, rid of (antonymic prefixation)

cognates.meaning: squared timber beam, ridge (cognate with Frankish *balko)
to corrupt or seduce away from duty (borrowed from French débaucher)

embauche.etymology: Deverbal feminine noun (18th century) from embaucher ('to hire a worker', 16th century). Embaucher originally belonged to carpentry guild jargon ('to trim rough timber, lay out beams, start framing work in the shop'), formed from em- ('in, onto') + Old/Middle French bauch / bauche ('wooden beam', from Frankish *balko 'beam, balk'). Putting a journeyman onto the timber frame came to mean 'engaging a worker', while its twin débaucher meant 'luring a worker away from the workshop' (and later 'corrupting morals').

history.meaning: to square timber; to set a craftsman to work in a workshop
the act of hiring, recruitment, or starting employment

morphemes.meaning: beam, workshop framing; hiring (from Old French bauch)

embauche.notes: Key workplace collocation: un entretien d'embauche ('a job interview'). Notice its astonishing etymological twin débaucher, which still means both 'to poach a rival agency's talent/employee' and 'to lead into debauchery'!

rootFamily.gloss: to poach an employee; to lay off; to lead into debauchery
rough sketch, first draft (parallel carpentry derivative esbaucher)

embaucher.etymology: Formed in the 16th century (originally in carpentry, 'to square a rough log into a beam', then 'to set a journeyman to work, hire') from em- ('in') + bauche / bauch ('squared timber beam; workshop', opposite of débaucher 'to entice away from the workshop').

history.meaning: to trim timber / bring into the workshop -> to hire, take on staff

embouteillage.etymology: Derived from embouteiller ('to pour wine into bottles', from en- + bouteille 'bottle' < Late Latin butticula 'small cask'); applied figuratively in Paris around the 1890s–1900s to vehicles wedged into a narrow street like liquid in a bottleneck.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: embouteillage (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)

embouteillage.notes: Colloquial French carries the wine-bottle pun one step further by calling a traffic jam **un bouchon** ('a cork')!

cognates.meaning: box, small container (both from Late Latin buxida < Greek puxis)
boxwood; compass housing (from the same Greco-Latin root)

emboîter.etymology: Formed in Old French (emboister, 13th century, originally anatomical/carpentry: 'to set a bone into its socket, fit tenon into mortise') from prefix em- (Latin in- 'in, into') + boîte (Old French boiste 'small box, bone socket', from Late Latin buxida, accusative buxidem, borrowed from Ancient Greek puxis 'boxwood container', from puxos 'box tree') + -er.

history.meaning: to enclose in a box; to set a bone into a joint socket
to fit neatly together, nest, interlock

morphemes.meaning: box, socket, casing (Old French boiste, modern boîte)

emboîter.notes: Master the high-frequency idiom emboîter le pas à quelqu'un ('to follow right on someone's heels', figuratively 'to follow someone's lead / follow suit' immediately). The circumflex î marks the vanished Old French s of boiste.

rootFamily.gloss: interlocking, nesting; car pile-up / rear-end collision
to unbox, dislocate a joint, pull out into a passing lane

cognates.meaning: to hug, clasp in one's arms; accept eagerly (borrowed from Old French)
to hug, clasp in the arms
to hug, hold in one's arms

embrasser.etymology: Inherited from Old French embracier (12th century, 'to clasp in one's arms, hug'), formed from prefix em- (Latin in- 'in') + bras ('arm', Old French braz, from Classical Latin bracchium 'forearm, arm', borrowed from Ancient Greek brakhiōn) + -er. In the 17th century, because French courtiers and bourgeois greeted one another by clasping arms while touching cheeks, embrasser shifted to replace baiser (which became taboo/sexualized) as the everyday verb for 'to kiss'.

history.meaning: to take or clasp in one's arms, hug
to kiss (on the lips or cheeks); in elevated prose, to encompass or espouse

embrasser.notes: Essential false friend: embrasser in everyday speech means 'to kiss' (or greet with cheek kisses—je t'embrasse is the standard affectionate sign-off on phone calls and emails among agents and actors!), NOT 'to hug' (serrer dans ses bras / faire un câlin). Never use the verb baiser to mean 'kiss' in modern French, as it is strictly vulgar slang for sex!

rootFamily.gloss: solemn hug or embrace (retains the older 'arms' sense)
bracelet, wristband (diminutive of Old French bracel 'little arm')

cognates.meaning: animal, brute (borrowed from Old French beste, same root as bête)

embêter.etymology: Coined in 18th-century French from em- ('into') + bête ('beast; foolish, silly', inherited via Old French beste from Vulgar Latin *bēsta, Classical Latin bēstia 'wild animal') + -er. Initially meaning 'to make stupid, reduce to brute dullness', it almost immediately took on the everyday colloquial sense 'to annoy, pester, bore', boosted by its phonetic service as a polite euphemistic stand-in (starting with emb-) for vulgar emmerder.

history.meaning: to dull the wits, stupefy; to weary or bother
to annoy, pester, hassle; (reflexive) to be bored or go to needless trouble

morphemes.meaning: beast; silly, foolish (Old French beste > bête)

embêter.notes: Sits right in the conversational sweet spot: milder and far politer than emmerder or faire chier, yet more natural in spoken dialogue than formal importuner or contrarier. C'est embêtant means 'that's annoying / inconvenient'.

rootFamily.gloss: stupidity, foolish blunder, piece of nonsense

emmener.etymology: Formed in Old French (enmener, 11th–12th c.) from adverbial pronoun en ('away from here', from Latin inde 'thence') + mener ('to lead, guide', from Late Latin minare).
