history.meaning: to lead or take someone away with oneself

cognates.meaning: domestic establishment; trio (borrowed from French ménage)
large dwelling house (borrowed from Old French mansion < Latin mansiō)

emménager.etymology: Formed in early Modern French (attested 17th–18th century, first 'to set furniture in order inside a house', then intransitively 'to move into a new home') from prefix em- ('into', pronounced with a nasal vowel /ɑ̃/ before m!) + ménage ('household, domestic affairs', Old French mesnage, from Vulgar Latin *mansionāticum 'that which pertains to a dwelling', built on Classical Latin mansiō 'staying, abode', from manēre 'to remain, dwell') + -er.

history.meaning: to arrange household furniture inside a new residence
to move in (take up residence in a new home or office)

emménager.notes: Pronunciation & vocabulary trap: initial em- is nasalized (/ɑ̃menaʒe/, NOT /ɛm-/!), which keeps emménager ('to move in') audible next to aménager (/amenaʒe/, 'to fit out/renovate a space') and pairs cleanly with its opposite déménager ('to move out / relocate').

rootFamily.gloss: to move out, change residence or offices
to lay out, fit out, convert a space

cognates.meaning: supreme realm or vast business conglomerate (borrowed from Old French)

empire.etymology: Semi-learned adaptation in Old French (emperie, empire, 11th–12th century) of Classical Latin imperium ('military command, supreme authority, sovereign dominion'), derived from imperāre ('to command, order, requisition'), itself from in- ('upon, over') + parāre ('to prepare, arrange, furnish'). Alongside territorial sovereignty, French retains the Classical abstract sense of 'sway, ascendancy' (sous l'empire de la colère) and modern corporate 'business empire'.

history.meaning: sovereign rule, realm governed by an emperor
political empire; vast corporate conglomerate; psychological sway or grip

morphemes.meaning: upon, over (Latin in- > im- > French em-)

empire.notes: Watch two look-alikes: the noun un empire ('an empire' or 'sway', e.g., un empire médiatique, sous l'empire de l'alcool) vs. the unrelated verb empirer ('to get worse', built on pire 'worse' < Latin peior), whose third-person singular il empire is spelled identically!

emploi.etymology: Deverbal masculine noun attested in Middle French (15th century: 'use to which money or resources are put') from employer ('to apply, devote, engage'). Employer descends via Old French empleier ('to fold into, entangle, devote oneself to, spend') from Classical Latin implicāre ('to enfold, entwine, involve, engage'), compounded from in- ('in') + plicāre ('to fold'), making employer an inherited doublet of learned impliquer.

history.meaning: to fold into, entangle, engage, involve
to apply, devote, put to use
use, utilization; paid job; theatrical type-role

morphemes.meaning: fold, engage, apply (Old French pleier < Latin plicāre)

emploi.notes: Rich cinema and theater polysemy! Alongside un emploi ('a job'), mode d'emploi ('instructions for use'), and emploi du temps ('schedule'), in French acting jargon un emploi means an actor's signature casting type or stock range (e.g., jeune premier, ingénue), whence contre-emploi ('casting against type').

rootFamily.gloss: casting against type (acting idiom built on emploi)

cognates.meaning: person working for wages or salary (borrowed directly from French employé)

employé.etymology: Substantivized in the 17th century from the past participle of employer ('to use, engage in service'), originally designating an official appointed to a financial or administrative post. Employer continues Old French empleier from Classical Latin implicāre ('to enfold, involve, engage', from in- 'in' + plicāre 'to fold'). English borrowed French employé in the early 19th century, adapting the -é/-ée suffix into employee.

history.meaning: enfolded, entangled, engaged in an affair
put to use, assigned to a post or duty

morphemes.meaning: to fold in, engage, put to work (from Latin plicāre)

employé.notes: Inflects for gender in spelling (un employé / une employée, pronounced identically /ɑ̃plwaje/). In French labor law and corporate culture, employé specifically contrasts with cadre ('executive / salaried manager') as non-executive office or service staff.

cognates.meaning: to carry, bear (cognate with base verb porter)
easy to carry; transporter (from French porter < Latin portāre)

emporter.etymology: Agglutinated in Old French (originally two words, en porter, 10th–11th century) from the directional adverb en ('away from there, hence', from Classical Latin inde 'from that place, thence', nasalized and spelled em- before labial p) + porter ('to carry', from Classical Latin portāre 'to carry, convey'). Crucially, its em- means 'away' (Latin inde), NOT 'in' (Latin in-)!

history.meaning: to carry away from a place, bear off
to take along, sweep away, prevail; (reflexive) to lose one's temper

morphemes.meaning: away, from there (Old French adverb en < Latin inde, spelled em- before p)

emporter.notes: Distinguish emporter ('to carry away' portable objects; à emporter = 'takeout / to go') from emmener ('to take along' people or animals on foot/by vehicle). Also note three vivid idioms: l'emporter ('to win out / prevail'), s'emporter ('to fly off the handle'), and emporté ('hot-tempered').

rootFamily.gloss: to bring an object to a place (ad- + portāre, directional opposite)
outburst of temper, transport of passion

emprunter.etymology: Inherited from Old French emprunter ('to obtain as a loan, borrow'), from Vulgar Latin *improntare / *impromutuare, altered from Classical Latin in + promutuari ('to advance as a loan', from mutuum 'loan').

history.meaning: to borrow (money, an object, a word, or a route)

cognates.meaning: to accuse formally; originally 'to hinder, fetter' (borrowed from Old French empeechier!)
to pledge, pawn, commit (from related Vulgar Latin formation, alongside impedir)
to entangle, hinder, obstruct (from the same Late Latin verb)

empêcher.etymology: Inherited via Old French empeechier / empeschier ('to shackle, entangle, obstruct, hinder', 12th century) from Late Latin impedicāre ('to catch in a snare, fetter the feet'), formed from in- ('in') + pedica ('foot-snare, shackle, fetter', derivative of pēs, genitive pedis 'foot') + -āre. Remarkably, Anglo-Norman carried Old French empeechier into English as impeach (originally 'to impede', then 'to challenge/accuse').

history.meaning: foot-snare, fetter; to entangle or shackle the feet
to prevent, stop, keep from doing; (reflexive) to refrain from

morphemes.meaning: foot-snare, fetter (Late Latin -pedic- from pēs, pedis 'foot', with circumflex ê from Middle French s)

empêcher.notes: Grammar & dialogue gem: empêcher quelqu'un de faire quelque chose ('to stop someone from doing something'); je ne peux pas m'en empêcher ('I can't help myself'); and colloquial sentence-initial n'empêche (que)... ('still / all the same / be that as it may...'). Unrelated to pêcher ('to fish') or pécher ('to sin')!

rootFamily.gloss: hindrance, last-minute obstacle or tie-up ('j'ai eu un empêchement')
to free from a trap, extricate; colloquially 'to hurry up' (se dépêcher)
trap, snare (native descendant of Latin pedica 'foot-snare'!)

en.etymology: As a preposition, en descends from Latin in. It survives in many old fixed expressions, even where dans now serves other location senses. The pronoun en has a different Latin source, inde, from there.

history.meaning: two distinct Latin words converging in French
in, by, while (prep.); of it, some, from there (pron.)

cognates.meaning: Italian keeps Latin in and inde distinct!

en.notes: Seeing Italian in vs. ne illuminates French's two homonymous words spelled en: preposition en (< Latin in: en France, en train) and pronoun en (< Latin inde: j'en veux 'I want some [of it]', j'en viens 'I come from there').

cognates.meaning: live on the air (exact broadcast parallel: in diretta)
live on air (exact broadcast parallel: en directo)

en direct.etymology: 20th-century radio and television broadcast locution (attested from the 1930s–1950s as émissions en direct, elliptical for en transmission directe 'in direct, unrecorded transmission'), combining the preposition en (from Classical Latin in) with learned adjective/noun direct, borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin dīrēctus ('laid straight, aligned, unmediated'), past participle of dīrigere (dis- + regere 'to guide, rule straight').

history.meaning: to set in a straight line; straight, level, without detour
broadcast live (simultaneously with the event, without pre-recording)

en direct.notes: Essential media/broadcast pair in Dix pour cent: passer en direct ('to go on the air live', e.g., on France Inter radio or the César Awards) vs. en différé ('pre-recorded / tape-delayed'); un direct is also a masculine noun meaning 'a live broadcast'. Pronounce both final consonants of direct (/ɑ̃ diʁɛkt/).

rootFamily.gloss: to direct, manage, steer (from Latin dīrigere)

sources.title: CNRTL – Étymologie de direct (locution en direct)

cognates.meaning: indeed, as a matter of fact (from in + fatto)

en fait.etymology: Adverbial and discourse-marking phrase formed from preposition en (< Classical Latin in) + masculine noun fait ('deed, reality, fact', inherited via Old French fait from Classical Latin factum 'something done, deed, real event', substantivized neuter past participle of facere 'to do, make'). Originating in medieval legal French in opposition to en droit ('in law' vs. 'in concrete fact', mirroring Latin dē factō vs. dē iūre), it grammaticalized into Modern French's primary conversational corrective ('actually').

history.meaning: in an accomplished deed or actual event
in point of material reality as opposed to legal theory
actually, in reality, as a matter of fact (conversational pivot)

morphemes.meaning: deed, fact, reality (Old French fait < Latin factum)

en fait.notes: Pronunciation rule: in modern French, the final -t of en fait IS pronounced (/ɑ̃ fɛt/)! Never confuse en fait ('actually / as a matter of fact', correcting or clarifying) with en effet ('indeed', agreeing) or au fait (/o fɛt/, 'by the way').

rootFamily.gloss: fact, deed; past participle of faire
to do, make (from Classical Latin facere)
by the way, speaking of which (companion phrase with pronounced -t)

sources.title: CNRTL – Étymologie de fait (locution en fait)

cognates.meaning: kind, category; 'sort of' (borrowed from Old/Middle French sorte)
lot, fate; kind, manner (in qualche sorta)
luck, fate; manner, kind (de alguna suerte)

en quelque sorte.etymology: Idiomatic adverbial phrase attested since Middle and Classical French, composed of en ('in', < Latin in) + indefinite determiner quelque ('some', fused in Old French quel que from Latin quālis 'of what kind' + quam / quid) + sorte ('manner, category, kind'). Sorte derives via Gallo-Romance/Old Occitan or Italian sorta from Classical Latin sors, genitive sortis ('divination lot, allotted share, rank, condition', whence 'category, way').

history.meaning: wooden lot drawn in divination; allotted share, rank, or condition
in a way, so to speak, after a fashion, sort of

morphemes.meaning: some, a certain (Old French quel + que)
kind, manner, way (from Latin sors, sortis)

en quelque sorte.notes: More polished and articulate than English filler 'kinda/sorta': French speakers use en quelque sorte in interviews, pitches, and diplomatic excuses to soften a bold metaphor or delicate comparison ('so to speak / in a sense').

rootFamily.gloss: kind, sort, manner (feminine noun); compare masculine le sort ('fate')
fate, lot, spell (masculine twin from Latin sors)
so that, in such a way that (conjunctive locution)

sources.title: CNRTL – Étymologie de sorte (en quelque sorte)

encadrer.etymology: Formed in the 17th century from prefix en- ('in') + cadre ('square border, picture frame; staff of officers', borrowed from Italian quadro < Latin quadrum 'square') + -er.

history.meaning: to put in a frame, surround; to supervise or train a team

cognates.meaning: pregnant (direct sister descendant of Late Latin incincta)

enceinte.etymology: Inherited via Old French enceinte (12th century) from Late Latin incincta ('pregnant'), famously glossed by Isidore of Seville (Etymologiae 10.151) as 'ungirdled, wearing no belt' (privative in- 'not, un-' + cincta, feminine past participle of cingere 'to gird, encircle with a belt', because expectant women loosened their girdles). Modern philologists note that Late Latin incincta likely remodeled the rarer Classical Latin adjective inciēns, incientis ('pregnant, near delivery') by folk etymology on cincta.

history.meaning: near delivery, pregnant; reinterpreted as 'ungirdled, beltless'

morphemes.meaning: un-, without (Latin privative in- > Old French en-)
girdled, belted (from Latin cincta, past participle of cingere)

enceinte.notes: Fascinating homonym split! As an adjective (femme enceinte), en- comes from Latin privative in- ('ungirdled' = pregnant, used for humans—animals are pleine); as a feminine noun (une enceinte), en- comes from Latin locative in- ('girdled in'), meaning 'fortified enclosure, compound' or 'stereo loudspeaker'!

rootFamily.gloss: to gird, encircle (from Classical Latin cingere)
enclosure wall, arena; audio speaker cabinet (homonymous noun)

enchanté.etymology: Past participle of enchanter ('to cast a magic spell by singing, bewitch, delight'), inherited from Old French enchanter < Classical Latin incantare ('to chant a magic formula over'), from in- + cantare ('to sing'); used elliptically for je suis enchanté (de faire votre connaissance) as a polite greeting upon meeting someone.

history.meaning: to chant a spell over, bewitch

cognates.meaning: to bind in chains (borrowed via Old French)

enchaîner.etymology: Inherited from Old French enchaener (12th century), either continuing Late Latin incatenare ('to put in chains') or formed directly in Gallo-Romance from en- + chaîne, itself from Classical Latin catena ('chain, fetter'). From physical fettering, the verb broadened in Middle and Modern French to linking ideas, scenes, or shoots in unbroken succession.
enchaîner.notes: In film and agency slang, enchaîner les tournages means shooting projects back-to-back without a break, while On enchaîne! on set cues the crew to move straight to the next take or scene.

rootFamily.gloss: sequence, series of events or shots

cognates.meaning: to surround or shut in (via Old French)

enclos.etymology: Substantivized masculine past participle of Old French enclore ('to shut in, fence around'), from Vulgar Latin *inclaudere, a recomposition of Classical Latin includere (in- + claudere 'to shut, close') that restored the unweakened root vowel of claudere. By the 12th century, the participle enclos designated a walled or hedged parcel of land.

history.meaning: walled or fenced plot of ground

enclos.notes: Masculine noun taking a silent final -s in both singular and plural (un enclos, des enclos); closely related to clos, the prestigious term for a walled French vineyard.

encore.etymology: Encore is traced to a reconstructed Popular Latin expression *hinc ha hora or *hinc ad horam, approximately from here until this hour. The French word is recorded from the eleventh century.

history.meaning: from here until this hour, still now

encore.notes: Covers both 'still' (il dort encore) and 'again / more' (encore un café); paradoxically, when French concertgoers shout for an 'encore', they usually shout Une autre! or Bis! rather than Encore!

cognates.meaning: to give support or confidence (borrowed from French)

encourager.etymology: Formed in Old French as encoragier (late 12th century) from the prefix en- + corage ('heart, spirit, inner disposition'), itself derived from Classical Latin cor ('heart') via Vulgar Latin *coraticum. Originally meaning 'to put heart or mettle into someone', it yielded English encourage through Anglo-Norman.

history.meaning: inner seat of feelings, spirit, heart
to inspire with boldness or resolve

morphemes.meaning: first-conjugation infinitive ending (retaining e before a/o)

encourager.notes: Spelling alert: like manger, it retains an orthographic e after g before a or o to preserve the soft [ʒ] sound (nous encourageons, encourageant), and takes the preposition à before an infinitive (encourager quelqu'un à faire).

encre.etymology: Inherited from Old French enque / encre, from Late Latin encaustum ('purple ink used by Roman emperors'), borrowed from Ancient Greek énkauston ('burned in, heat-prepared pigment', from enkaíein 'to burn in') with proparoxytonic stress shift.

cognates.meaning: ink was borrowed from Old French enque

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: encre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: encre

encre.notes: English **ink** comes straight from the older Old French form **enque**, before French inserted an *-r-* to give **encre**.

cognates.meaning: to fall asleep, lull to sleep
to put to sleep, fall asleep

endormir.etymology: Inherited from Old French endormir (11th century), formed with the prefix en- on dormir ('to sleep'), or continuing Late Latin indormire ('to fall asleep upon, slumber over'), from Classical Latin in- + dormire ('to sleep', ultimately from PIE *drem-). In French it developed a causative transitive use ('to put to sleep') alongside reflexive s'endormir ('to fall asleep').

history.meaning: to fall asleep in or over something
to put to sleep; (reflexive) to fall asleep

endormir.notes: Used transitively, endormir means 'to put to sleep', 'to anesthetize', or figuratively 'to hoodwink/lull someone's suspicions' (endormir la méfiance de quelqu'un); for 'to fall asleep' oneself, the reflexive s'endormir is required.

endroit.etymology: Univerbation in Old French (en droit, 'right opposite, in the exact line of') of en ('in', < Latin in) + droit ('straight line, right side', < Latin directum); came to mean both 'a specific place or spot' and 'the right or finished side of a fabric'.

history.meaning: in the right line -> particular place, spot; right side of cloth

enfance.etymology: Inherited through twelfth-century Old French enfance from Classical Latin īnfantia ('inability to speak; early infancy'), abstract noun built on īnfāns, īnfantem ('unable to speak, very young child'), from negative in- ('not') + fāns, present participle of fārī ('to speak', from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- 'to speak').
enfance.notes: Broader than English infancy: French enfance spans all of childhood up to adolescence (souvenirs d'enfance, ami d'enfance).

enfant.etymology: Inherited from Old French enfant ('young child; noble youth or page'), from Classical Latin infantem (nominative infans, 'speechless, newborn babe not yet able to speak'), compound of negative prefix in- ('not') + fans, present participle of fari ('to speak').

enfer.etymology: Inherited from Old French enfern, enfer (10th century), from Late/Ecclesiastical Latin infernum ('hell, the netherworld'), originally the neuter singular or masculine plural (inferni) of Classical Latin infernus ('lower, subterranean'), derived from infra ('below', from PIE *ndher- 'under'). Christian Latin specialized the spatial adjective for the abode of the damned.
enfer.notes: Pronounced [ɑ̃.fɛʁ] with an audible final -r (unlike -er infinitives). Note its slang antiphrasis: d'enfer means 'fantastic, incredible' (un casting d'enfer), whereas un enfer means 'a living nightmare'.

rootFamily.gloss: restricted library reserve for banned books (figurative extension of enfer)

enfermer.etymology: Formed in Old French (enfermer, 11th c.) from prefix en- ('in, inside') + fermer ('to close, lock, make fast', from Classical Latin firmare 'to make firm, secure').

history.meaning: to shut or lock inside, enclose

cognates.meaning: to line up, head straight along
gunfire directed along the length of a line (military loan from French)

enfiler.etymology: Created in Old French as enfiler (12th century) from en- + fil ('thread'), inherited from Classical Latin filum ('thread, filament, string'). Originally denoting the literal act of threading a needle or stringing pearls on a cord, by Middle French it extended figuratively to slipping limbs smoothly through sleeves, trousers, or coats, and tossing back drinks in succession.

history.meaning: to thread a needle; to string beads onto a thread
to slip into a garment quickly; to do in rapid succession

enfiler.notes: More dynamic and casual than mettre: in costume fittings or backstage rushes, enfiler une veste/robe means throwing or slipping a garment on in one swift motion (and idiomatic enfiler des perles means wasting time on trivialities).

rootFamily.gloss: row, alignment; suite of aligned rooms
to unthread, unravel; to parade down a runway

enfin.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French of the Old French prepositional phrase en fin ('in the end, at last'), from en ('in', < Latin in) + fin ('end', < Latin finem).

history.meaning: in the end, at last, finally

cognates.meaning: to pledge, hire, or involve (borrowed from French)
to hire, recruit, join battle (from Old French)
pledge or payment for labour (via Anglo-Norman)

engager.etymology: Formed in Old French as engagier (12th century) from en- + gage ('pledge, security, pawn'), borrowed from Frankish *wadi ('pledge', from Proto-Germanic *wadją, cognate with Gothic wadi and Latin vas). Originally a legal-economic verb meaning 'to pawn property or bind oneself by a pledge', by the 16th–17th centuries it extended to binding soldiers, servants, or actors under contract.

history.meaning: to put up as security, bind by pledge
to enlist, hire under contract, initiate

engager.notes: Essential false friend in romance contexts: être fiancé(e) (not engagé!) means 'to be engaged to be married'. In agency life, engager un comédien means to hire/cast an actor, and s'engager means to commit oneself contractually or morally.

rootFamily.gloss: pledge, token, guarantee (pl. gages = domestic wages)
commitment, contract, signing of an artist
to redeem a pledge; to release from an obligation; to clear space

cognates.meaning: politically or socially committed (loanword from French)
politically or artistically committed (calqued on French)

engagé.etymology: Past participial adjective of engager (from Old French engagier, built on Frankish *wadi 'pledge'). While it originally meant 'pawned' or 'bound by promise', in 20th-century French intellectual life—decisively popularized by Jean-Paul Sartre around 1945 (littérature engagée)—it acquired the cultural sense of an artist, writer, or citizen actively committed to political and social causes.

history.meaning: put in pawn, bound by a pledge
enlisted, under contract, involved in action

engagé.notes: In French cinema and press, un film engagé or un acteur engagé praises socially conscious, activist art—never 'engaged to be married' (fiancé) nor merely 'busy' (occupé / pris).

rootFamily.gloss: withdrawal from a commitment; political detachment

cognates.meaning: motor or machine (borrowed from Old French engin)

engin.etymology: Inherited from Old French engin (11th century, 'inborn wit, cleverness, ruse, war machine'), directly from Classical Latin ingenium ('innate disposition, natural talent, cleverness'), formed from in- + gignere ('to beget, produce', PIE *ǵenh₁-). Already in Late Latin (Tertullian, military writers), ingenium shifted metonymically from the inventor's cleverness to a mechanical contrivance or siege engine.

history.meaning: clever device, mechanical contrivance, war machine
wit, trickery; siege machine or tool

engin.notes: False friend nuance: whereas English engine usually means a motor (French moteur), French engin refers either technically to heavy equipment/craft (engin de chantier, engin spatial) or colloquially and humorously to any bizarre contraption or gadget ('What is that thing?!').

cognates.meaning: to make drunk (learned borrowing from Latin)

enivrer.etymology: Inherited from Old French enivrer (12th century), from Late Latin inebriare ('to make drunk, saturate'), formed from in- + Classical Latin ebrius ('drunk, intoxicated'). Through regular Gallo-Romance lenition and palatalization, Latin ebrius became ivre, giving enivrer both its literal sense of alcoholic intoxication and its poetic sense of heady elation.

history.meaning: to make drunk; to overwhelm the senses

enivrer.notes: Pronunciation trap! Despite the single n, enivrer retains a nasal vowel as if prefix + root were separate: [ɑ̃.ni.vʁe] (like s'enamourer), never *[ɛ.ni.vʁe]. In modern speech it is chiefly literary or figurative (enivré par le succès = intoxicated by fame).

rootFamily.gloss: drunk; intoxicated with joy or pride

enlever.etymology: Formed in Old French (enlever, 12th c.) from prefix en- (combining Latin in- and inde 'away') + lever ('to raise, lift', from Classical Latin levare); evolved from 'to lift up' to 'to carry off, abduct, remove, take off'.

history.meaning: to lift up -> to carry away, remove, take off

enlèvement.etymology: Derived in Middle French (14th–15th century) with the nominal suffix -ment from enlever ('to lift up, carry away, remove'), itself formed in Old French from en- (representing Latin inde 'thence, away' fused with in-) + lever ('to raise', from Classical Latin levare 'to lighten, lift', from levis 'light in weight'). From 'lifting away', it specialized legally into 'abduction, forcible carrying off'.

history.meaning: to lift up, carry off, snatch away
removal of goods; forcible abduction of a person

enlèvement.notes: Standard French legal and thriller term for 'kidnapping/abduction' (though English loan kidnapping also exists in media), while in logistics enlèvement simply means 'collection/pickup' of parcels or towed cars!

rootFamily.gloss: to remove, take off, or kidnap
uprising; lifting or heave of emotion

cognates.meaning: hostile adversary (borrowed via Old French enemi)

ennemi.etymology: Inherited from Old French enemi (9th century, Sequence of Saint Eulalia: inimi), from Classical Latin inimicus ('unfriendly, personal foe'), formed by vowel weakening from privative in- ('not') + amicus ('friend', allied to amare 'to love'). In Late Latin, inimicus displaced Classical hostis ('public wartime enemy', which shifted to 'army') as the general Romance word for 'enemy'.

morphemes.meaning: friend (from Latin -micus < amicus, opaque in modern French)

ennemi.notes: Unlike enivrer, the initial e- before double nn in ennemi is oral, NOT nasal: pronounce [ɛn.mi] or [ɛ.nə.mi], never *[ɑ̃n.mi]. Functions both as a noun (un ennemi, une ennemie) and an adjective (les lignes ennemies).

rootFamily.gloss: friend (sharing the underlying Latin amicus root)
enmity, hostility (learned formation from Latin inimicitia)

cognates.meaning: to irritate (borrowed earlier from Old French enoiier)

ennui.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French as enui, enoi (12th century) from enoiier ('to vex, torment, weary'), descending from Late Latin inodiare ('to make hateful or loathsome'), itself verbalized from the Classical Latin colloquial idiom mihi in odio est ('it is hateful/odious to me', from odium 'hatred'). Remarkably strong in Old French ('deep grief, torment'), it softened by the 17th–18th centuries to 'wearisome boredom' and 'minor trouble'.

history.meaning: (to be) an object of hatred or revulsion
world-weariness, boredom; pl. troubles or hassles

ennui.notes: Pronunciation & polysemy alert: ennui HAS a nasal initial vowel [ɑ̃.nɥi]! In the singular, l'ennui means 'boredom' (or 'the snag is...': l'ennui, c'est que...), whereas plural des ennuis always means 'troubles, headaches, legal/financial problems' (avoir des ennuis avec le fisc).

rootFamily.gloss: odious, hateful (learned cognate from Latin odiosus)

cognates.meaning: to irritate, bother (borrowed from Anglo-Norman/Old French)

ennuyer.etymology: Inherited from Old French enoiier, enuier (12th century, 'to grieve, torment, weary'), from Late Latin inodiare ('to inspire disgust or loathing, make hateful'), built on Classical Latin in odio ('held in hatred', from odium 'hatred, aversion'). Borrowed into Middle English as anoyen (modern annoy), the French verb retained both the active sense 'to bother/inconvenience' and the experiential sense 'to bore'.

history.meaning: to hold in loathing, render hateful
to bore; to bother, trouble, or inconvenience

morphemes.meaning: first-conjugation infinitive ending (y alternates with i before mute e)

ennuyer.notes: Pronounced with initial nasal [ɑ̃.nɥi.je], and y shifts to i before silent endings (ça m'ennuie). Watch context: s'ennuyer means 'to be bored', whereas Ça m'ennuie de vous déranger politely means 'I hate to bother you / It troubles me to disturb you'.

ennuyeux.etymology: Derived in Old French (enoios, 12th c., 'troublesome, vexing, wearisome') from ennui ('grief, vexation, boredom', from Old French enoi / enui, back-formed from enoiier < Late Latin inodiare 'to make hateful', from the phrase mihi in odio est 'it is hateful to me').

cognates.meaning: to enter officially in a list (via Medieval Latin/French)

enregistrer.etymology: Formed in Middle French (late 14th century, enregistrer) from en- + registre ('ledger, official roll'), borrowed from Medieval Latin registrum, an alteration of Late Latin regesta ('things recorded, list', neuter plural past participle of Classical Latin regerere 'to carry back, transcribe into a book', from re- + gerere 'to carry, conduct'). With late-19th-century phonography and cinema, it expanded from chancery ledgers to audio-visual recording and airport check-in.

history.meaning: matters transcribed back into a record book
to enter officially into a public ledger or roll
to record sound/film; to check in luggage; to register data

enregistrer.notes: Covers a huge range in studio and travel life: enregistrer une voix off ('to record a voice-over'), enregistrer un fichier ('to save a computer file'), and enregistrer ses bagages ('to check in luggage').

rootFamily.gloss: ledger, official log; vocal or tonal register

enrouler.etymology: Formed in Middle French from prefix en- ('in, around') + rouler ('to roll', from Old French roler < Vulgar Latin *rotulare, from rotula 'little wheel').

history.meaning: to roll up, wind or coil around

enseigne.etymology: Inherited from Old French enseigne ('mark, token, military banner, battle cry'), from Vulgar Latin *insignia (treated as a feminine singular noun from Classical Latin neuter plural insignia 'badges of office, standards, distinguishing marks', from signum 'mark, sign').

history.meaning: banner, standard -> shop sign, commercial brand

ensemble.etymology: Inherited from Old French ensemble ('together, at the same time'), from Vulgar Latin *insimul, reinforced from Classical Latin simul ('at the same time, together', cognate with English same and assemble); used as a noun ('harmonious whole, outfit, group') since the 16th century.

history.meaning: at the very same time, together
together (adv.); unified whole, matching outfit, musical group (noun)

ensuite.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French of the Old French phrase en suite ('in continuation, following right after'), from en ('in') + suite ('following, train, continuation', participial noun from suivre 'to follow').

history.meaning: in the train of -> next, afterward, then

entendre.etymology: Inherited from Old French entendre ('to direct one's attention or mind toward, understand, hear'), from Classical Latin intendere ('to stretch out, direct one's mind or ears toward, intend'), from in- + tendere ('to stretch'); displaced Old French oïr (< Latin audire) as the everyday verb for 'to hear'.

history.meaning: to stretch toward, direct attention to
to pay heed, understand -> to hear

enterrer.etymology: Formed in Old French (enterrer, 11th c.) from prefix en- ('in, into') + terre ('earth, ground', from Latin terra) + verbal suffix -er.

history.meaning: to put into the earth, bury, inter

cognates.meaning: person filled with eager passion; fanatical devotee (originally)

enthousiaste.etymology: Learned borrowing (early 17th century) from Ancient Greek enthousiastēs ('person inspired or possessed by a god'), agent noun of enthousiazein ('to be divinely inspired'), from entheos ('having a god within', from en 'in' + theos 'god'). Initially used in French for prophetic rapture or religious fanaticism, during the Enlightenment and Romantic era it secularized into passionate artistic zeal and everyday eagerness.

history.meaning: one possessed or inspired by a deity
visionary seized by divine or poetic transport; religious zealot
eager, ardent admirer (noun and invariable-gender adjective)

enthousiaste.notes: Ends in -e, so masculine and feminine forms are identical (un agent enthousiaste, une actrice enthousiaste), whereas the related verbal adjective enthousiasmant means 'exciting/inspiring'.

rootFamily.gloss: to thrill, excite, fill with enthusiasm

entier.etymology: Inherited from Old French entier ('unbroken, whole, intact, upright'), from Classical Latin integrum (nominative integer, 'untouched, whole, complete', from in- 'not' + root of tangere 'to touch', learned doublet of intègre).

entièrement.etymology: Formed in Old French as entierement (12th century) from entier ('whole, intact, unbroken'), in its feminine agreement form entière, plus the adverbial suffix -ment (from the Classical Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind'). Entier itself evolved by regular Gallo-Romance sound change from Classical Latin integrum (accusative of integer 'untouched, whole, unblemished', from in- 'not' + tangere 'to touch').

morphemes.meaning: adverbial suffix of manner or degree (< Latin mente)

entièrement.notes: Notice the doublets from Latin integer: popular phonetic evolution produced entier ('whole'), while a later learned borrowing produced intègre ('morally upright, incorruptible'). Idiom: Je suis entièrement d'accord ('I completely agree').

entourer.etymology: Formed in the 15th–16th century from entour ('surroundings, circuit', from en + tour 'turn, circuit') + verbal suffix -er.

history.meaning: to form a circle around, surround, encircle

cognates.meaning: to pull behind; to teach or drill (from Old French traïner)

entraîner.etymology: Formed in Old French as entraïner (12th century, 'to drag away, pull along with oneself') from en- + traîner ('to drag, trail'), descending from Vulgar Latin *traginare, an iterative derivative of *tragere for Classical Latin trahere ('to draw, drag, pull'). While French retained 'to sweep along / cause' (entraîner des retards), its modern athletic sense 'to coach, practise' was reinforced in the 19th century by semantic calquing on English to train (itself an earlier loan from French traîner!).

history.meaning: to drag away, sweep along in one's wake
to entail/cause; (19th c., influenced by English) to coach or practise

entraîner.notes: Watch its two major meanings: non-reflexive entraîner often means 'to lead to, cause' (entraîner un scandale) or 'to coach an athlete', whereas reflexive s'entraîner means 'to work out, practise, rehearse'. (Since the 1990 spelling reform, entrainer without circumflex is also accepted, though entraîner remains dominant.)

rootFamily.gloss: to drag, lag behind, hang around

entre.etymology: Inherited from Old French entre ('between, among'), from Classical Latin inter ('between, among, during').

cognates.meaning: bold undertaking or business firm (borrowed from French)

entreprise.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of Old French entreprendre (12th century, 'to undertake, seize upon, attack'), formed from entre- (Latin inter 'between, among') + prendre ('to take', from Classical Latin prehendere 'to grasp, seize'). Originally denoting any bold venture, chivalric feat, or contracted project, from the 17th–18th centuries onward it acquired its core economic meaning of a commercial firm or business organization.

history.meaning: to grasp, seize between or in hand
contracted project; commercial company or firm

morphemes.meaning: taken, seized (feminine past participle of prendre)

entreprise.notes: Standard French word for a 'company/business' of any size (PME = petites et moyennes entreprises), while English entrepreneur is a direct borrowing from its agent noun!

entrer.etymology: Inherited from Old French entrer ('to go inside, enter'), from Classical Latin intrare ('to go into, penetrate'), derived from intra ('inside, within').

history.meaning: to enter, come in, go in

entretien.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 15th century from entretenir ('to hold together, keep in good repair, support; to converse with', from entre- 'mutually' + tenir 'to hold').

history.meaning: upkeep, maintenance; formal conversation or interview

entrée.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle formed in Old French (entree, 12th c.) from entrer ('to enter').

history.meaning: act or place of entering, entrance, admission, starter dish

enveloppe.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old/Middle French from envelopper ('to wrap up, cover around').

history.meaning: outer wrapping or covering; folded paper letter envelope

envelopper.etymology: Inherited from Old French enveloper ('to wrap up, fold inside, entangle'), formed from prefix en- ('in') + root *vlopp- / *faluppa (found in Old French veloper / développe, from Late Latin faluppa 'chaff, bundle of straw or fibers, wrapping').

history.meaning: to wrap up in a bundle, enfold

cognates.meaning: turned upside down or opposite in order (from Latin inversus)

envers.etymology: Inherited from Old French envers (10th century), descending from Classical Latin inversus ('turned upside down, reversed, inside out'), past participle of invertere (in- + vertere 'to turn'), while the prepositional sense ('towards') arose from Late Latin in versus ('turned toward'). Substantivized as a masculine noun (l'envers), it came to denote the reverse face of fabric, a coin, or social appearances.

history.meaning: reverse side, lining, hidden underside (noun); toward (preposition)

envers.notes: Know the iconic backstage idiom l'envers du décor ('behind the scenes / the unvarnished reality behind the set'), as well as à l'envers ('inside out / upside down / backwards', opposite of à l'endroit). Also functions as a preposition meaning 'towards' feelings-wise (gentil envers quelqu'un).

rootFamily.gloss: reverse side of a coin or setback (revers de fortune)

envie.etymology: Inherited from Old French envie ('jealousy, begrudging; ardent desire, longing'), from Vulgar Latin *invidia for Classical Latin invidia ('envy, jealousy, ill will'), derived from invidere ('to look askance at, cast an evil eye upon', from in- + videre 'to look').

history.meaning: envy; strong wish, craving (avoir envie de)

cognates.meaning: surroundings (borrowed from Old French plural environs)
natural world or surroundings (via Old French environement)

environ.etymology: Univerbation in Old French (11th–12th century, environ 'around, in a circle') of en + viron ('circle, circuit, surrounding area'), derived from virer ('to turn, veer'), itself from Vulgar Latin *virare (likely altered from Classical Latin gyrare 'to turn in a circle' or Celtiberian/Latin viria 'armlet, ring'). From spatial 'round about', it shifted naturally to numerical approximation ('roughly, about').

history.meaning: in a circle around, round about (spatial adverb/preposition)

morphemes.meaning: circle, turn (Old French viron, related to virer)

environ.notes: Watch the singular vs. plural distinction: invariable adverb environ means 'roughly, about' (environ dix pour cent), whereas masculine plural noun les environs means 'the surrounding area / outskirts' (dans les environs de Paris).

rootFamily.gloss: to turn, veer; to fire/sack someone (colloquial); bank transfer (virement)

cognates.meaning: to contemplate or foresee as a possibility (borrowed from French)
a person's face or countenance (via Old French)

envisager.etymology: Coined in Early Modern French (late 16th century; popularized in the 17th century) from en- + visage ('face, countenance'), itself derived in Old French from vis ('face', from Classical Latin visus 'sight, appearance, look', past participial noun of videre 'to see') + collective/augmentative suffix -age. Originally literal ('to look someone squarely in the face'), by the mid-17th century (Pascal, Molière) it shifted to mentally confronting or contemplating a plan or possibility.

history.meaning: act of seeing, gaze, outward appearance
to look directly at a person's face
to contemplate, consider, view as a future possibility

morphemes.meaning: face, countenance (from Old French vis < Latin visus)
first-conjugation infinitive ending (keeps e before a/o)

envisager.notes: High-frequency negotiation verb in agency meetings: envisager de faire quelque chose ('to consider doing something') or envisager un rôle ('to consider taking a role'). Takes de before an infinitive and retains e before a/o (nous envisageons).

rootFamily.gloss: to stare intently at; to disfigure

envoyer.etymology: Envoyer continues later Latin inviare, to travel along or reach a place, which also developed the sense send. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century.

history.meaning: to travel along a road; set someone on their way

cognates.meaning: from French envoyé and Middle French envois

envoyer.notes: Future and conditional swap the regular stem for irregular enverr- (j'enverrai, j'enverrais), modelled on voir -> je verrai.

erreur.etymology: Erreur comes from Latin error, errorem ('wandering astray, mistake', from errare 'to wander, err'). Like most Latin abstract nouns in -or, it became feminine in French.
erreur.notes: **Par erreur** = by mistake; **mon erreur** uses *mon* before a vowel despite feminine gender.

cognates.meaning: scaling walls with ladders; (back-formed verb) to escalate

escalade.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (late 15th century, during the Italian Wars) from Northern Italian scalada (standard Italian scalata), participial noun of scalare ('to scale with a ladder'), from Classical Latin scala ('ladder, flight of steps', from *scand-sla, related to scandere 'to climb'). Initially a military siege term for storming ramparts with ladders, in the 19th–20th centuries it became both the sport of rock climbing and figurative 'escalation' of conflict.

history.meaning: storming a fortified wall with ladders
siege scaling; rock climbing; mutual escalation of tension

morphemes.meaning: ladder, step (from Italian scala < Latin scala; prosthetic e-)

escalade.notes: Covers both athletics (faire de l'escalade = to go rock climbing / bouldering) and media/agency drama (l'escalade de la violence / des exigences = escalating conflict or demands). Notice native French cousin échelle ('ladder') from the same Latin scala!

rootFamily.gloss: to climb, scale (a wall, cliff, or fence)
staircase (also borrowed via Provençal/Italian from Latin scalarium)
ladder; scale of measurement (inherited native doublet from Latin scala)

escalier.etymology: Borrowed in the sixteenth century from Old Provençal escalier (from Late Latin scalarium, built on scala 'ladder, flight of steps'). Earlier French used degré or montée; notice the prosthetic e- before sc- (compare scala -> échelle).
escalier.notes: **Monter / descendre l'escalier** = to go upstairs / downstairs.

cognates.meaning: enslaved person (borrowed via Old French esclave)
slave (also source of Venetian greeting ciao < schiavo!)

esclave.etymology: Attested in Old French from the 13th century as esclave, borrowed via Medieval Latin sclavus / sclava (often transmitted through Italian/Mediterranean trade ports), originally the ethnonym Sclavus ('Slav', from Byzantine Greek Sklabēnos, rendering Proto-Slavic *slověninъ). Because vast numbers of pagan Slavic captives were sold into servitude across early medieval Europe and the Mediterranean, the ethnonym displaced Classical Latin servus ('slave', which shifted to feudal serf) as the general word for an enslaved person.

history.meaning: enslaved person; one enthralled by passion or work

esclave.notes: Epicene noun (ending in -e, identical form for masculine and feminine: un esclave, une esclave). Note that 'to enslave' in French is réduire en esclavage or asservir (never *esclaver).

rootFamily.gloss: pro-slavery advocate or slave trader; taskmaster (figurative)

espace.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French espace) from Classical Latin spatium ('room, expanse, distance, interval of time, racecourse').

history.meaning: open room, distance, interval of space or time
space, expanse, interval; printer's typographical space

espagnol.etymology: Attested in Old French from the 12th century (espaignol), borrowed via Old Occitan espanhol (which itself passed the word into Spanish as español!), descending from Vulgar Latin *Hispaniolus, a diminutive ethnic formation built on Classical Latin Hispania ('Iberian Peninsula, Spain'). Prosthetic e- developed regularly before initial sp-, and palatalized -ni- yielded the palatal nasal written gn [ɲ].

history.meaning: Spanish; person from the Christian kingdoms of Spain

espagnol.notes: Orthography rule: in French, adjectives of nationality and language names are NEVER capitalized (parler espagnol, un réalisateur espagnol), whereas the noun referring to a person IS capitalized (un Espagnol, une Espagnole). Idiom: une auberge espagnole means a potluck or eclectic melting pot (immortalized by Cédric Klapisch's film!).

rootFamily.gloss: Hispanic, Spanish-speaking world (learned stem from Latin Hispanicus)
spaniel dog breed (Old French chien espagneul 'Spanish dog')

espoir.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (espoir, 12th c.) from the stem of espérer ('to hope', Old French 1st-person singular espoir < Latin spero).

history.meaning: expectation of a desired good, hope

espresso.etymology: 20th-century borrowing from Italian caffè espresso ('pressed-out coffee' and 'coffee made expressly to order on the spot'), past participle of Italian esprimere ('to press out, express'), from Classical Latin expressus, past participle of exprimere (ex- 'out' + premere 'to press'). In Italian café culture following late-19th- and early-20th-century steam/piston machines in Turin and Milan, espresso combined both literal mechanical pressure and rapid, made-to-order preparation.

history.meaning: squeezed out, pressed forth, distinctly portrayed
coffee brewed under pressure expressly to order

espresso.notes: In Parisian cafés and agency breakrooms, you will see both spellings un espresso and francicized un expresso, though the absolute everyday way to order one at the counter is simply Un café, s'il vous plaît! or Un petit noir!

rootFamily.gloss: francicized variant of espresso; also fast train / rapid delivery
to express (from Latin exprimere 'to press out')
explicit, formal (adj., e.g. défense expresse, fem. expresse — inherited/learned from Latin expressus)

cognates.meaning: vital animating principle, soul, mood (via Anglo-Norman)

esprit.etymology: Semi-learned Old French borrowing (10th–11th century, esperit, later syncopated to esprit) from Classical and Ecclesiastical Latin spiritus ('breath, breeze, breath of life, soul, courage'), action noun of spirare ('to breathe, blow'). Under Christian theology (translating Greek pneuma) and later Cartesian philosophy and salon culture, French esprit broadened extraordinarily to encompass 'soul', 'human mind/intellect', and 'sparkling wit'.

history.meaning: breath, blowing of wind, breath of life, inspiration
divine spirit (Saint Esperit), soul, vital breath
mind, intellect, mood, ghosts, and sparkling verbal wit

esprit.notes: Translates English 'mind' just as often as 'spirit'! Avoir de l'esprit means 'to be witty', garder à l'esprit means 'to keep in mind', and un bel esprit is an intellectual wit. Note pronunciation: final -t is ALWAYS silent [ɛs.pʁi].

rootFamily.gloss: spiritual; witty, clever (un mot spirituel = a witty remark!)
to breathe (sharing the Latin spirare root)

espèce.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–13th century from Classical Latin species ('outward appearance, form, sort, kind; in Late Latin, spices, coins, goods', from specere 'to look at, behold', doublet of épice).

history.meaning: kind, sort, biological species; (plural espèces) cash

espérer.etymology: Inherited from Old French esperer ('to hope, wait for'), from Classical Latin sperare ('to hope, look forward to', from spes 'hope'), later reshaped in spelling and stem vowels after the Latin model.

essai.etymology: Inherited from Old French essai ('test of metal or wine, trial, attempt'), from Late Latin exagium ('a weighing, balance, standard weight'), derived from exigere ('to drive out, weigh accurately, examine', from ex- + agere); immortalized in the literary sense by Montaigne's Essais (1580).

history.meaning: trial, test, attempt; literary essay (Montaigne, 1580); rugby try

cognates.meaning: literary composition or attempt (borrowed from French essai)
testing, rehearsal, sample (from Late Latin exagium)

essayage.etymology: Derived in Modern French (late 18th / 19th century) from essayer ('to try, test, try on') + action suffix -age. Essayer itself comes from Old French essai ('trial, test, weighing of metal'), inherited from Late Latin exagium ('act of weighing, balance, standard weight'), derived from Classical Latin exigere ('to drive out, examine, weigh accurately', from ex- + agere 'to drive, do'). From testing metals and armor, essayer specialized in tailoring and couture into trying on garments.

history.meaning: to put to the test, try out, try on clothing
trying on garments or costumes; technical trial run

essayage.notes: Staple word on film sets and in shops: les essayages costumes ('costume fittings' for actors before shooting) and la cabine d'essayage ('fitting/changing room' in a clothing store), distinct from les essais ('screen tests / auditions').

rootFamily.gloss: to try, attempt; to try on (clothes)
trial, attempt, literary essay; screen test (essais caméra)

essayer.etymology: Inherited from Old French essaier ('to test the quality of, put to the proof, attempt'), from Vulgar Latin *exagiare ('to weigh, test'), derived from Late Latin exagium ('a weighing').

history.meaning: to try, test, try on clothes

essentiel.etymology: Borrowed as a Scholastic philosophical term in Old/Middle French (13th–14th century, essenciel, remodeled as essentiel) from Late and Medieval Latin essentialis ('pertaining to the fundamental being of a thing'), derived from Classical/Late Latin essentia ('being, essence', coined by Cicero/Seneca on the model of Greek ousia from esse 'to be'), and later substantivized as masculine noun l'essentiel ('the core, what matters most').

history.meaning: intrinsic being, substance -> pertaining to essence
constituting the intrinsic nature of a being (Scholastic philosophy)
indispensable (adj.); the main point, bare necessities (noun)

essentiel.notes: As a masculine noun with the definite article, l'essentiel means 'the main thing / bottom line' (L'essentiel, c'est qu'elle signe le contrat; aller à l'essentiel = 'to get straight to the point'), immortalized by Saint-Exupéry's L'essentiel est invisible pour les yeux.

rootFamily.gloss: essentially, mainly, for the most part
fifth and purest essence, epitome (quinta essentia)

essuyer.etymology: Inherited from Old French essuier ('to dry off, wipe dry'), from Classical Latin exsucare ('to press or drain the juice/moisture out of'), compound of ex- ('out') + sucus ('juice, moisture').

history.meaning: to drain of moisture, dry off
to wipe dry, wipe; figuratively, to endure (a storm or refusal)

est.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century (via Anglo-Norman est) from Old English east ('the east, direction of sunrise', from Proto-Germanic *austra-, cognate with Latin aurora 'dawn' from PIE *h2ews- 'to shine, dawn').

cognates.meaning: is (3sg. of essere < Latin est) + this (< ecce hoc)

est-ce.etymology: Syntactic inversion of est ('is', inherited from Classical Latin est, 3rd-person singular present indicative of esse 'to be', from PIE *h₁ésti) + demonstrative pronoun ce ('this/it', from Old French ço, ce, descending from Vulgar Latin *ecce hoc 'behold this!'). Originally a literal cleft question in Old and Middle French (est-ce que...? = 'is it the case that...?'), by the 16th century it grammaticalized into an invariable yes/no interrogative marker allowing speakers to keep standard subject-verb word order.

history.meaning: is it this (that...)? — literal cleft question

est-ce.notes: Pronounced as a single syllable [ɛs] (the t is completely silent before ce!). Followed by que (est-ce que, [ɛs.kə]), it neatly turns any statement into a neutral-register question without awkward verb inversion (Qu'est-ce que c'est ? = literally 'What is-it that this is?').

rootFamily.gloss: it is / this is (declarative counterpart of est-ce)
would it only be / even just (subjunctive counterpart of est-ce)

cognates.meaning: it is that / the thing is that

est-ce que.etymology: Grammaticalized interrogative particle formed in Old and Middle French from the inverted cleft construction est-ce que ('is it [the case] that...'), combining estre ('to be', from Latin esse), the demonstrative pronoun ce (from Vulgar Latin *ecce hoc), and the complementizer que (from Latin quid/quod). By the 16th century it had fused into an invariable yes/no question marker allowing speakers to preserve subject-verb word order.

history.meaning: interrogative marker introducing a polar question

est-ce que.notes: Pronounced /ɛs kə/ (or /ɛs k/ before a vowel, as in est-ce qu'il vient ?); neutral in register between formal subject-verb inversion and casual rising intonation.

rootFamily.gloss: what (object question phrase, lit. 'what is it that')

esthéticienne.etymology: Feminine agent noun derived in the mid-20th century from esthétique ('aesthetics, beauty care') with the professional suffix -ienne. Esthétique was borrowed in the 18th century from New Latin aesthetica (coined by German philosopher Alexander Gottlieb Baumgarten in 1735), itself from Ancient Greek aisthētikós ('perceptive, sensitive, relating to sensory perception'), from aisthánomai ('I perceive, feel').

history.meaning: of or for perception by the senses
philosophical science of sensory cognition and beauty

esthéticienne.notes: In everyday French, une esthéticienne always means a licensed cosmetologist/beautician (waxing, facials, makeup on film sets), never an academic philosopher of art (who is un esthéticien / une philosophe de l'art).

et.etymology: Et continues the Latin conjunction et, and. French had the ninth-century form e before the spelling was remodelled in the twelfth century; the written final t is not pronounced in the conjunction.
et.notes: Crucial French liaison rule: liaison is strictly forbidden after the conjunction et—the -t in et (/e/) is NEVER pronounced, even before a vowel (et elle /e.ɛl/).

euh.etymology: Natural vocalic hesitation filler in spoken French, representing the mid central rounded vowel /ø/ or /ə/ uttered while pausing for thought.

euphorisant.etymology: Present participial adjective from euphoriser ('to induce euphoria, exhilarate'), formed in 20th-century medical and psychological French from euphorie + -iser. Euphorie derives via Medical Latin euphoria from Ancient Greek euphoría ('power of enduring easily, vigour, well-being'), from eúphoros ('bearing well'), combining εὖ (eû, 'well') and φέρω (phérō, 'to bear, carry').

history.meaning: ability to bear easily, healthy bodily condition
sense of physical well-being; intense elation

euphorisant.notes: Used both as a pharmacological noun (un euphorisant, 'a mood-elevating substance/upper') and figuratively as an adjective for an intoxicating success, cocktail, or piece of good news.

rootFamily.gloss: euphoric, elated (of a person or mood)

euro.etymology: Coined and officially adopted by the European Council in Madrid (December 1995) as a clipping of Europe / européen for the single European currency introduced in 1999/2002.

history.meaning: unit of currency of the eurozone

européen.etymology: Derived from Europe with the relational suffix -éen (modeled on Latin -aeus, Greek -aîos), replacing earlier Middle French europois and européen variants in the 16th–17th centuries. The continent name comes via Latin Eurōpa from Ancient Greek Eurṓpē, in mythology the Phoenician princess abducted by Zeus; its ultimate etymology is debated between Greek eurýs ('wide') + ṓps ('face, eye') and Akkadian erēbu ('to set, go down [of the sun], west').
européen.notes: Capitalized as a noun referring to a person (un Européen, une Européenne), but always lowercase as an adjective (le cinéma européen, l'Union européenne); watch the feminine doubling -éenne.

eux.etymology: Inherited from Old French els, eus, evolved regularly from Classical Latin illōs, the masculine accusative plural of the distal demonstrative ille ('that one, he'). Vocalization of preconsonantal /l/ to /w/ before final -s produced the diphthong spelling -eu- (with orthographic -x originally a scribal abbreviation for -us), giving modern eux /ø/ as the disjunctive (stressed) pronoun alongside unstressed subject ils (from Vulgar Latin *illī).
eux.notes: Used after prepositions (pour eux, chez eux), in cleft focus (c'est eux or formal ce sont eux), and with -mêmes (eux-mêmes, 'themselves'); silent final -x links as /z/ only in fixed expressions like eux aussi.

rootFamily.gloss: they / them (feminine plural subject & stressed pronoun)

ex.etymology: Colloquial nominalization via clipping of compounds formed with the prefix ex- (such as ex-mari, ex-femme, ex-compagnon), strongly reinforced in the mid-20th century by colloquial English ex ('former spouse or romantic partner'). The prefix ex- itself is a learned borrowing from Latin ex ('out of, from'), used since Late Latin (e.g., ex-consul) to designate someone who formerly held an office or status.

history.meaning: out of, from; formerly holding the office of (in Late Latin compounds)

ex.notes: Invariable in both gender and number (mon ex, ton ex, mes ex); because ex begins with a vowel, feminine possessive ma regularly shifts to mon (mon ex, even when referring to a woman!).

exact.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Classical Latin exactus ('weighed out, precise, accurate, finished'), past participle of exigere ('to drive out, measure, weigh accurately, demand').

exactement.etymology: Formed in the 16th century from the feminine adjective exacte ('accurate, exact') + adverbial suffix -ment.

exagérer.etymology: Learned 16th-century borrowing from Classical Latin exaggerāre ('to heap up, pile up; to amplify, magnify in speech'), formed from intensive ex- ('out, thoroughly') + aggerāre ('to heap up'), itself a denominative verb from agger ('earthwork, mound, rampart, heap'), built on ad- ('to, toward') + gerere ('to carry, bring'). The metaphor shifted from piling up earth to piling on rhetorical hyperbole.

history.meaning: mound, heap → to pile up earth
to heap up high; to magnify or amplify in words
to overstate, go beyond reasonable bounds

morphemes.meaning: to heap, carry toward (from ad + gerere)

exagérer.notes: Used intransitively in everyday spoken French to mean 'to push it / go too far' (Tu exagères ! = 'You're pushing it!' or 'Come on, that's unfair!'), a staple complaint in Parisian workplaces; note stem alternation j'exagère / nous exagérons.

examen.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin exāmen ('swarm of bees; tongue or pointer of a balance scale; weighing, scrutiny, consideration'), contracted from *ex-ags-men, built on ex- ('out') + agere ('to drive, set in motion, weigh') + instrumental noun suffix -men. From the oscillating needle of a scale used to test weight accurately came the senses of careful scrutiny, medical checkup, and academic test.

history.meaning: pointer of a balance; act of weighing, testing, or examining
academic test, medical checkup, thorough inspection

examen.notes: Pronounced /ɛɡ.za.mɛ̃/ (ending in the nasal vowel /ɛ̃/, never /-mɛn/ like amen!). False-friend alert on the verb: passer un examen means 'to take/sit an exam', whereas 'to pass an exam' is réussir un examen!

examinateur.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Late Latin exāminātor ('one who weighs, judges, or investigates'), agent noun from Classical Latin exāmināre ('to weigh accurately, test, scrutinize'), itself derived from exāmen ('tongue of a balance scale', from ex- + agere). In modern France, it commonly denotes an official academic jury member or state driving-test inspector.

history.meaning: to weigh with a balance, test, ponder
official who conducts an examination or inspection

examinateur.notes: Feminine form is examinatrice; in France's famously strict driver's license test (le permis de conduire), l'examinateur or l'inspecteur sits beside the candidate evaluating every maneuver.

excellent.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin excellentem (nominative excellens, 'rising above others, lofty, superior'), present participle of excellere ('to rise high, surpass, excel', from ex- + *cellere 'to rise, project', related to celsus 'high').

exception.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century (originally in legal prose) from Classical Latin exceptiō, accusative exceptiōnem ('an excepting, restriction, reservation, or legal plea in defense'), action noun from excipere ('to take out, withdraw, exempt from a general rule'), formed from ex- ('out') + capere ('to take, seize'). In French cultural policy, l'exception culturelle designates cinema and arts protected from pure free-market rules.

history.meaning: exclusion from a general rule; extraordinary case

exception.notes: Key expressions in the film and talent world include l'exception culturelle française (state support/quotas protecting French cinema) and d'exception ('world-class, extraordinary', e.g. un acteur d'exception).

exceptionnel.etymology: Formed in the late 18th century within French from exception + adjectival suffix -el (from Latin -ālis), initially meaning 'constituting a legal or procedural exception' (especially during the French Revolution for tribunaux or lois d'exception) before broadening in the 19th century to the laudatory sense 'extraordinary, far above the norm'. English exceptional was likely borrowed from or modeled on French exceptionnel.

history.meaning: case departing from a general rule
pertaining to an exception; remarkably superior

morphemes.meaning: relational adjective suffix ('of the nature of')

exceptionnel.notes: Note the double n in French (-nnel, feminine exceptionnelle) versus single n in English exceptional; agents constantly pitch scripts and performances as absolument exceptionnel.

excitant.etymology: Present participial adjective of exciter, borrowed in the 12th–14th centuries from Classical Latin excitāre ('to call out, rouse, wake up, stir up, kindle'), frequentative of exciēre ('to summon forth, rouse'), from ex- ('out, forth') + ciēre ('to set in motion, stir, summon', from PIE *ḱey- 'to set in motion'). In the 20th century, under partial semantic influence from English exciting, it gained the everyday sense 'thrilling, stimulating' alongside physiological arousal.

history.meaning: to summon forth → to rouse, awaken, kindle, stir up
to rouse, provoke; stimulating substance (18th c.)

morphemes.meaning: to rouse, set in motion (citāre / ciēre)

excitant.notes: Crucial false-friend trap with the related participle excité: un projet très excitant safely means 'a very exciting project', whereas saying je suis excité(e) about a person often implies sexual arousal or manic hyper-agitation—use j'ai hâte or je suis enthousiaste for 'I'm excited'!

rootFamily.gloss: to arouse, stir up, get worked up

excitation.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Late Latin excitātiō, accusative excitātiōnem ('a rousing, incitement, awakening'), action noun derived from Classical Latin excitāre ('to rouse forth, stir up, kindle'), frequentative of exciēre (ex- 'forth' + ciēre 'to put in motion'). Originally referring to moral or physiological stimulation, it expanded to nervous agitation, sexual arousal, and feverish anticipation.

history.meaning: to rouse, wake up, stir into action
physiological stimulation, nervous agitation, feverish thrill

excitation.notes: Stronger and more physical/nervous in tone than English 'excitement'—depending on context, l'excitation can mean frantic bustle (l'excitation d'une première), jittery agitation, or sexual arousal; for purely joyful enthusiasm, enthousiasme or effervescence is often preferred.

exclure.etymology: Semi-learned remodelling (14th century, replacing Old French esclore 'to hatch, shut out') from Classical Latin exclūdere ('to shut out, shut off, keep out, prevent'), composed of ex- ('out') + claudere ('to close, shut', which becomes -clūdere in prefixed compounds). Its conjugation in -ure aligns by analogy with conclure and inclure.

history.meaning: to shut out, cut off, hinder
to shut out, bar from a group or right
to expel, bar, rule out as impossible

exclure.notes: Watch the past participle: exclu / exclue (with NO final -s in the masculine singular, unlike inclus / incluse!). C'est exclu ! ('Out of the question! / No way!') is a classic crisp refusal in French negotiations.

rootFamily.gloss: to include (antonym from the same root)

exclusif.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th centuries from Medieval scholastic and legal Latin exclūsīvus ('serving to exclude or bar'), formed on exclūsum, the supine stem of Classical Latin exclūdere ('to shut out', from ex- 'out' + claudere 'to shut'), plus the adjectival suffix -īvus. From legal privileges that shut out all others, it developed the commercial and media sense of sole representation or rights.

history.meaning: having the power or effect of excluding others
shutting others out; sole, unshared (contract, interview)

exclusif.notes: Feminine form is exclusive (/ɛk.skly.ziv/); in talent agencies and entertainment journalism, un contrat exclusif binds an actor to a single agent or brand, while describing a partner as très exclusif means possessive.

exclusivité.etymology: Coined in French in the late 18th century (first attested around the 1790s) from the feminine stem exclusiv- of exclusif + abstract noun suffix -ité (from Latin -itātem). Built ultimately on Latin exclūsus, past participle of exclūdere ('to shut out', ex- + claudere). In 20th-century publishing, journalism, and cinema, it came to mean both contractual sole representation and a media scoop.

history.meaning: state of being exclusive; sole rights; media scoop

exclusivité.notes: Essential agency and press vocabulary: avoir l'exclusivité means holding sole representation or broadcast rights, and en exclusivité on a magazine cover or trailer means 'an exclusive / world premiere'.

excuse.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Middle French (15th c.) from excuser ('to clear of blame, excuse', borrowed from Classical Latin excusare < ex- 'out of' + causa 'legal charge, accusation').

history.meaning: to free from a charge -> plea or apology offered to clear oneself

excuser.etymology: Excuser was borrowed from Latin excusare, to remove from blame, justify or excuse. The Académie records it from the twelfth century.

history.meaning: to clear from blame, plead in excuse

excuser.notes: Excusez-moi ('Excuse me') gets someone's attention politely on the street or apologizes for bumping past.

excès.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin excessus ('a departure, going out, digression, overstepping of bounds'), action noun from excēdere ('to go out, step beyond, surpass'), formed from ex- ('out, beyond') + cēdere ('to go, yield, step'). From stepping physically outside a boundary, the noun specialized into moral, emotional, or legal overstepping of a limit.

history.meaning: to go out, step beyond a boundary
departure; projection; stepping beyond proper bounds
immoderation, overindulgence, exceeding of a legal limit

morphemes.meaning: to go, step (Latin cēdere, supine cessum)

excès.notes: Invariable in spelling between singular and plural (un excès, des excès, pronounced /ɛk.sɛ/). Note the everyday compound excès de vitesse ('speeding / speeding ticket') and excès de zèle ('being overzealous').

exemplaire.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical Latin exemplar ('model, pattern, transcript, copy') and Late Latin exemplarium ('copy of a book'), derived from exemplum ('sample, model, example').

history.meaning: model to imitate; transcribed copy of a text
serving as a model (adj.); single printed copy of a book or issue (noun)

exemple.etymology: Refashioned in Middle French after Classical Latin exemplum ('sample, specimen, pattern, warning, precedent'), replacing inherited Old French essample (whence English sample). Latin exemplum derives from *ex-em-lom, built on eximere ('to take out, single out from a group'), from ex- ('out') + emere ('to take', later 'to buy') + instrumental suffix -lum: literally 'one item taken out of a batch to show what the rest is like'.

history.meaning: to take out → a sample singled out, pattern, model

exemple.notes: Masculine (un bon exemple), pronounced /ɛɡ.zɑ̃pl/ (with voiced /ɡz/). Besides par exemple ('for example'), older oridiomatic colloquial French uses Ça, par exemple ! as an exclamation of surprise ('Well I never! / Fancy that!').

rootFamily.gloss: exemplary (adj.); copy/issue of a book or script (noun)

exigeant.etymology: Present participial adjective of exiger, attested as an adjective in the 17th century. Notice the orthographic silent e inserted after g (-geant) so that g keeps its soft postalveolar fricative value /ʒ/ before a. Ultimately from Classical Latin exigere (present participle exigēns, exigentem), 'to drive out, weigh out, demand payment, enforce strict standards', from ex- ('out') + agere ('to drive, act').

history.meaning: requiring much care, hard to please, exacting

exigeant.notes: Spelling trap! The e in exigeant (feminine exigeante) is kept purely to keep the g soft (/ɛɡ.zi.ʒɑ̃/), whereas the noun exigence ('demand, high standard') drops the a and becomes -ence with no extra e! In French cinema, un réalisateur exigeant is a polite euphemism for a perfectionist auteur.

rootFamily.gloss: collectible, due and payable (of a debt/fee)

exiger.etymology: Learned 14th–15th century borrowing (initially fiscal and legal: 'to levy or exact a tax or due') from Classical Latin exigere ('to drive out, thrust forth; to demand payment, collect; to measure, weigh'), compounded from ex- ('out') + agere ('to drive, set in motion, do', weakened to -igere in unstressed medial position). English exact comes from its Latin past participle exactus.

history.meaning: to drive out; to demand or enforce payment; to measure
to levy or collect by legal authority (taxes, dues)
to insist upon authoritatively, require as indispensable

exiger.notes: Much stronger and more authoritative than demander ('to ask for'): when exiger que introduces a clause, the verb that follows MUST take the subjunctive (Elle exige que sa loge soit prête, 'She demands that her dressing room be ready'). Also inserts e before a/o: nous exigeons.

rootFamily.gloss: exact, accurate (from Latin past participle exactus)

exister.etymology: Learned borrowing (16th–17th centuries, popularized by philosophical Latin such as Descartes's writings, following 14th-century existence) from Classical Latin exsistere / existere ('to step forth, stand out, emerge, come into being, be manifest'), composed of ex- ('out, forth') + sistere ('to cause to stand, take a stand'), the reduplicated stem of stāre ('to stand', PIE *steh₂-). Literally 'to stand forth into reality'.

history.meaning: to step out, emerge, appear, be
to have real being (philosophical & theological prose)
to exist, live, count or be recognized socially

exister.notes: Pronounced /ɛɡ.zis.te/ (voiced /ɡz/). Idiomatically used in French showbiz and relationships to mean 'to matter, be noticed, have a real presence' (exister à l'écran = 'to have real screen presence'; je n'existe plus pour lui = 'I'm invisible to him').

exotique.etymology: First introduced into French in 1548 by François Rabelais (marchandises exotiques) as a humanistic borrowing from Classical Latin exōticus ('foreign, imported from abroad'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek exōtikós ('foreign, alien, from the outside'), derived from éxō ('outside, out of doors'), an adverb built on the preposition ex / ek ('out of'). In 19th-century Romanticism it shifted from 'non-native' to 'alluringly distant or tropical'.

history.meaning: outside → belonging to the outside, foreign, alien
foreign, imported (especially of luxury goods or customs)
foreign to Europe; strikingly or alluringly unfamiliar

exotique.notes: Applies equally to both genders (masculine & feminine exotique). In contemporary casting or social commentary, calling a French actor of non-European heritage exotique can carry a patronizing or tokenizing undertone, though it remains neutral for travel, plants, and cuisine (fruits exotiques).

expert.etymology: Refashioned in the 14th century (replacing Old French espert) after Classical Latin expertus ('tried, proved, tested, experienced'), the past participle of the deponent verb experīrī ('to try thoroughly, put to the test, learn by experience'), composed of ex- ('out, thoroughly') + the root *per- ('to try, risk, test', also seen in Latin perīculum 'trial, danger' and Greek peîra 'attempt'). Substantivized in French first for court-appointed appraisers.

history.meaning: to put to the test → tested, experienced, skilled through trial

expert.notes: Pronounced /ɛk.spɛʁ/ (unvoiced /ks/ before /p/, silent final -t in the masculine, sounded in the feminine experte /ɛk.spɛʁt/). Common compound: expert-comptable ('chartered accountant / CPA', vital to every talent agency!).

rootFamily.gloss: experience, experiment (from the same verb experīrī)

explication.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin explicātiō, accusative explicātiōnem ('an unfolding, uncoiling; exposition, interpretation, explanation'), action noun from explicāre ('to unfold, unroll [a scroll], disentangle, set forth clearly'), formed from ex- ('out') + plicāre ('to fold, plait'). Unrolling a folded papyrus scroll or untangling a knot provided the enduring metaphor for making a complex meaning clear.

history.meaning: to unfold, unroll → unfolding, clear exposition of meaning
textual interpretation, clarification of something obscure
explanation; frank confrontation to clear the air

explication.notes: Everyday French word for 'explanation' (whereas English explication is academic, as in the classic French school exercise explication de texte). Note the idiom avoir une explication avec quelqu'un: 'to have it out / have a frank heart-to-heart confrontation with someone'.

rootFamily.gloss: to explain; (s'expliquer) to make oneself clear / argue it out

explicite.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–17th centuries from Classical and Medieval Latin explicitus, originally an alternative past participle of explicāre ('to unfold, disentangle, set forth fully', from ex- 'out' + plicāre 'to fold'). In medieval manuscripts, explicitus liber (abbreviated explicit, 'the book is unrolled [to the end]') marked the end of a scroll; in scholastic logic explicitus contrasted with implicitus ('folded in') to mean 'openly and fully stated'.

history.meaning: to unfold, unroll a scroll, set out plainly
unfolded, expressly stated rather than implied
clearly and unmistakably expressed; graphic (of cinema/content)

explicite.notes: Primarily means 'unambiguous, crystal clear' (une clause explicite dans le contrat), though under recent English influence it also describes graphic film scenes (scènes explicites); its exact etymological twin-opposite is implicite ('folded in / implied').

rootFamily.gloss: to make explicit, spell out clearly

expliquer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin explicare ('to unfold, unroll a scroll; to set forth clearly, expound'), compound of ex- ('out') + plicare ('to fold', learned doublet of éployer).

history.meaning: to unfold, unroll -> to make clear, expound

cognates.meaning: exploit (bold feat, borrowed from Old/Middle French)

exploit.etymology: Inherited from Old French esploit ('revenue, advantage, vigorous execution, achievement', later re-spelled exploit with etymological x), from Vulgar Latin *explicitum, neuter substantive of Classical Latin explicitus ('unfolded, settled, brought to completion'), past participle of explicāre ('to unfold, bring to an issue, accomplish', from ex- + plicāre). From 'matter successfully brought to completion', chivalric literature narrowed it to 'heroic deed or feat'.

history.meaning: execution, profit, vigorous action, chivalric deed
remarkable feat or achievement; bailiff's writ (legal)

exploit.notes: Pronounced /ɛk.splwa/ (silent -t). Unlike English where 'to exploit' is mostly negative, the noun un exploit in French is overwhelmingly positive ('a remarkable feat, triumph', e.g., réaliser un exploit), whereas negative 'exploitation' uses exploiter / exploitation. (In French law, un exploit d'huissier also survives in the archaic sense of a bailiff's formal summons!)

rootFamily.gloss: to operate/run (a cinema, farm); to exploit, make the most of
operation/screening (cinéma d'exploitation = movie theater distribution); exploitation
cinema theater operator/exhibitor; farm operator; exploiter

exploser.etymology: Back-formed or derived in late 18th-century French from explosion (replacing earlier Latinate exploder), ultimately from Classical Latin explōdere (supine explōsum), which originally belonged to Roman theater! Compounded from ex- ('out, off') + plaudere ('to clap the hands, stamp'), Latin explōdere meant 'to drive a bad actor off the stage by loud clapping, hissing, and stamping', before shifting in Early Modern science to 'drive out violently with a loud bang'.

history.meaning: to clap or hoot an actor off the stage; drive out with noise
to burst violently, detonate, erupt in emotion or fame

exploser.notes: Delightful theater trivia: exploser shares its root plaudere with applaudir ('to applaud')—originally it meant clapping an actor *off* the stage! In modern showbiz French, exploser means both 'to lose one's temper' (exploser de colère / de rire) and 'to skyrocket / break out as a star' (sa carrière a explosé).

explosif.etymology: Formed in the 18th century (alongside or slightly influenced by scientific English explosive) on the Latin supine stem explōs- of explōdere ('to drive off stage by clapping, expel with a loud noise', from ex- + plaudere 'to clap') + the adjectival suffix -if (from Latin -īvus). Nominalized in the 19th century (un explosif) with the invention of nitroglycerin and dynamite, and widely used figuratively for volatile situations or dynamic energy.

history.meaning: to drive out by clapping or noisy outburst
tending to burst violently or detonate
explosive substance; volatile, bursting with energy, bombshell

morphemes.meaning: noisy clap or burst (Latin plaudere, stem -plōs-)

explosif.notes: Feminine form is explosive (/ɛk.splo.ziv/). Figuratively describes anything from a high-voltage performance (un duo explosif) to a tabloid scandal or tense meeting ready to blow up (une ambiance explosive, des révélations explosives).
