fraction.notes: Most frequent in everyday speech in une fraction de seconde ("a split second"); political "splinter group" can be either une fraction or its doublet une faction (though faction comes from facere, not frangere!).

rootFamily.gloss: to divide up into smaller parts or installments

fracture.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old/Middle French from Classical Latin frāctūra ("a breach, cleft, broken fragment, bone fracture"), formed from frāctus ("broken"), past participle of frangere ("to break, shatter") + resultative suffix -ūra.

history.meaning: rupture, surgical bone break, forced breach
bone fracture; deep societal or数字 divide

morphemes.meaning: noun suffix of result or state

fracture.notes: Widely used metaphorically in French public discourse: la fracture sociale ("the social divide") and la fracture numérique ("the digital divide").

rootFamily.gloss: to break open (a lock/door) or fracture (a bone)

cognates.meaning: easily broken; (frail via Old French doublet)

fragile.etymology: Learned 14th-century borrowing from Classical Latin fragilis ("easily broken, brittle, perishable"), formed from the unnasalized root frag- of frangere ("to break") + suffix -ilis ("capable of or prone to being"). It is an etymological doublet of inherited frêle ("frail, slender"), which underwent regular Old French sound change (fraile > frêle).

history.meaning: delicate, breakable, emotionally or financially vulnerable

fragile.notes: Applies equally to glass, health, ego, or a shaky film deal (un équilibre fragile); compare its inherited doublet frêle, which specifically evokes slender physical frailty.

fragiliser.etymology: 20th-century French derivative built on fragile ("delicate, easily broken", from Latin fragilis) + the productive causative suffix -iser (from Late Latin -izāre, Ancient Greek -ίζειν), meaning "to render fragile, undermine the stability or confidence of".

history.meaning: to make fragile, weaken structurally or psychologically

fragiliser.notes: Very common in psychology, media, and business French where English would say "to undermine", "to shake", or "to leave vulnerable" (cette rumeur l'a beaucoup fragilisé).

rootFamily.gloss: process of weakening or making precarious

frais.etymology: As an adjective ('cool, fresh, newly made', fem. fraîche), inherited from Old French freis / fresche, borrowed from Frankish *frisk ('fresh, untainted, cool', cognate with English fresh); as a plural noun (des frais 'expenses, costs'), from Medieval Latin fredum ('peace-fine paid to a magistrate', from Frankish *frithu 'peace').

fraise.etymology: Inherited from Old French frese / fraise ('wild strawberry'), from Vulgar Latin *fraga (originally the neuter plural of Classical Latin fragum 'strawberry', reinterpreted as a feminine singular noun, with intervocalic -g- > -y- / -z-).

history.meaning: strawberry; ruffled collar (16th c.); rotary milling cutter

franc.etymology: Inherited from Old French franc ('free by birth, noble, sincere, candid'), from Late Latin Francus ('a Frank; under Frankish rule in Gaul, a free man exempt from tributary servitude', from Proto-Germanic *Frankon); the coin name franc comes from the 1360 gold coin inscribed Francorum Rex ('King of the Franks').

history.meaning: a Frank -> free man, noble, candid
free, candid, outspoken (adj.); French currency unit (noun)

franchement.etymology: Formed in Old French (franchement, 12th c., originally 'freely, nobly', then 'openly, candidly') from the feminine adjective franche ('free, frank, sincere') + adverbial suffix -ment.

franchir.etymology: Derived in Old French (franchir, 12th c.) from franc ('free, unhindered'); originally meant 'to set free, exempt', then evolved in the 16th century to 'to clear an obstacle freely at a single bound, cross over a threshold or boundary'.

history.meaning: to set free -> to leap clear over an obstacle, cross a boundary

cognates.meaning: voting right; commercial or film license (borrowed from Old French)

franchise.etymology: Formed in Old French from franc / feminine franche ("free, not servile, noble, sincere", from Frankish *frank "a Frank, free man", since only Franks held full freeman status in early Merovingian Gaul) + abstract suffix -ise (from Latin -itia). Evolved from "legal freedom or immunity" to moral "candor, outspokenness", and was later re-borrowed semantically from English for commercial and cinematic "franchises".

history.meaning: member of the Frankish people; free man
status of a freeman, chartered privilege, nobility of character
candor, frankness; insurance deductible; film/brand franchise

morphemes.meaning: abstract noun suffix of quality or status

franchise.notes: Polysemous powerhouse: en toute franchise means "in all candor / quite frankly", une franchise d'assurance means an "insurance deductible", and une franchise de cinéma is a movie series!

rootFamily.gloss: to free, emancipate; to stamp mail (affranchir une lettre)

français.etymology: Inherited through Old French franceis, later françois (spelled with -ois until the Académie française officially adopted -ais in 1835 after the diphthong leveled to [ɛ] in Parisian speech), from Early Medieval Latin franciscus ("Frankish, relating to the Franks"), formed from Frankish *Frank ("a Frank") + Germanic-Latin ethnic suffix -iscus.

history.meaning: French, of the Kingdom of France or Île-de-France

français.notes: Remember capitalization rules: lowercase for the adjective and language (parler français, le cinéma français), capitalized ONLY for a person/citizen (un Français, une Française); en bon français idiomatically means "in plain, blunt terms".

rootFamily.gloss: to make French or adapt a foreign word into French

cognates.meaning: chilled/iced (borrowed from past participle of frapper)

frappant.etymology: Lexicalized present participle of frapper ("to strike, hit, knock"), attested figuratively for "vividly impressing the mind or eye" since the 17th century. Old French fraper itself is likely of Germanic or expressive onomatopoeic origin (compare Middle Dutch flappen "to strike with a flat blow", with rhotacism of fl- > fr- evoking a sharp slap or impact).

history.meaning: to hit, strike a physical blow
hitting; (figuratively, 17th c.) vividly arresting to the mind

frappant.notes: Pairs naturally with nouns of impression or likeness: une ressemblance frappante ("a striking resemblance"), un contraste frappant ("a stark/striking contrast").

rootFamily.gloss: to hit, knock, strike; to amaze
keystroke, minting of coins, or military strike

frapper.etymology: Inherited from Old French fraper ('to strike, hit, beat'), formed on an expressive or Germanic root *frapp- / *hrapp- imitating a sharp blow or lash.

history.meaning: to strike, hit, knock at a door; to chill with ice; to impress deeply

fredonner.etymology: Derived in sixteenth-century French from fredon ('musical trill, vocal ornament, refrain'), an expressive onomatopoeic formation imitating rapid hummed notes.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fredonner (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fredonner

cognates.meaning: to hold back, abstain (via Old French refrener)

frein.etymology: Inherited through Old French frein ("horse's bit, bridle, restraint") from Classical Latin frēnum ("bridle, bit, curb, check"), probably from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer- ("to hold firmly, support"). Extended in the 19th century from horse-drawn carriage drag-shoes to railway and automobile brakes.

history.meaning: bridle bit, check on passions or actions
mechanical vehicle brake; obstacle or check

frein.notes: Equestrian origins live on in vivid idioms: ronger son frein ("to champ at the bit / chafe impatiently while waiting") and mettre un frein à ("to put the brakes on / curb").

rootFamily.gloss: to brake, slow down, hold back
to restrain, hold back an impulse (refréner)

friable.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (by Bernard Palissy) from Classical Latin friabilis ('easily crumbled or broken into small pieces'), derived from friare ('to rub, crumble, break into small pieces').

history.meaning: crumbly, friable (of rock, soil, or pastry)

fric.etymology: Attested in mid-19th-century French argot with disputed origin. The leading philological hypothesis derives it by apocope from fricot ("hearty stew, feast; illicit profit", from fricasser), following the pervasive French slang pattern equating food with money (like blé "wheat", oseille "sorrel", galette "flatbread"); an alternative links it to thieves' cant ferrique ("small coin, metal scrap", from Latin ferrum "iron").

history.meaning: stew, rich fare, windfall (or small metal coin)

fric.notes: Uncountable masculine slang noun (du fric = "cash / dough / bucks"), completely mainstream in spoken French alongside pognon, blé, and thune; un film à fric is a big-budget commercial cash-grab.

rootFamily.gloss: stew, feast; shady profit (probable source word)

frigo.etymology: Colloquial 20th-century clipping (with popular -o suffix) of frigorifique ('refrigerating apparatus, cold storage', coined in the 19th century from Latin frigorificus < frigus, frigoris 'cold' + -ficare 'to make').

cognates.meaning: sudden thrill or shiver of excitement (borrowed from French)
coldness, chill (via shared Latin frīgus influence)

frisson.etymology: Inherited through Old French friçon, frisson ("trembling fit, feverish chill") from Gallo-Romance *frīctiōnem, representing Classical Latin frīctiōnem ("a rubbing", from fricāre) semantically and phonetically crossed in Vulgar Latin with frīgus / frīgere ("cold, to be stiff with cold"), evoking goosebumps and involuntary shivering from chill, fear, or intense emotion.

history.meaning: rubbing / tingling sensation blended with chill
shivering fit from cold, fever, or dread
shiver, goosebumps, aesthetic or emotional thrill

frisson.notes: Masculine noun; avoir des frissons or ça me donne des frissons means "it gives me chills / goosebumps" (from a great performance or suspense), and le grand frisson means an ultimate thrill.

rootFamily.gloss: to shiver, shudder, quiver with emotion or cold
chilly, sensitive to cold; overly cautious or risk-averse (frileux)

cognates.meaning: batter-fried cake or morsel (via Old French friture)

friture.etymology: Inherited from Old French friture, from Late Latin frīctūra ('a frying, fried dish'), formed with the action/result suffix -tūra on frīctus, the past participle of Classical Latin frīgere ('to roast, parch, fry in oil'), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵ- ('to roast, bake'). In the 20th century, the sizzling sound of hot frying oil inspired the figurative telecommunications sense 'crackling static on a line'.

history.meaning: act of frying; small fried dish
frying fat; dish of fried food (especially small fish)

friture.notes: Beyond the kitchen ('fried food' or 'frying oil'), il y a de la friture sur la ligne is a classic French idiom meaning 'there is static/interference on the phone line' — or figuratively, tension in a relationship.

froid.etymology: Froid descends from Popular Latin *frigidus / *frigdu ('cold', Classical Latin frigidus). Loss of the unstressed vowel and palatalisation of -gd- produced Old French freit, froit, modern froid.
froid.notes: **Avoir froid** = to feel cold (of a person); **refroidir** = to cool down.

fromage.etymology: Fromage comes from Late Latin *(caseus) formaticus — 'cheese shaped in a mould' (from forma 'mould, form'). Through metathesis of r, Old French formage became modern fromage, while Italian formaggio kept the original order.
fromage.notes: Same Latin phrase gave Italian *formaggio* and Catalan *formatge*.

froncer.etymology: Inherited from Old French froncier ('to wrinkle, pleat, pucker'), from Frankish *hrunkjan ('to wrinkle, crease', related to Old High German runza 'wrinkle', with initial Germanic hr- rendered as fr- in Gallo-Romance).

history.meaning: to pleat fabric; to knit the brow (froncer les sourcils)

front.etymology: Inherited from Old French front ('forehead, brow; front line of an army'), from Classical Latin frontem (nominative frons, 'forehead, brow, forepart').

cognates.meaning: borderland, outer edge of settlement (from Old French)

frontière.etymology: Inherited from Old French frontiere, originally the feminine form of the adjective frontier ('facing, confronting, situated on the front line', as in terre frontiere 'bordering land'), derived from front ('forehead, military front') + -iere (< Latin -āria), ultimately from Classical Latin frōns, frontis ('forehead, brow, forepart'). Initially military ('front line facing an enemy'), it generalized by Middle French to any political or figurative boundary.

history.meaning: military front line; fortified borderland facing an enemy

frontière.notes: Unlike English 'frontier' (which often evokes unexplored wilderness), French frontière is the everyday, neutral word for any national 'border' (passer la frontière, Médecins Sans Frontières).

frote.etymology: Colloquial phonetic spelling reflecting a rapid, syncopated pronunciation of contemporary French slang frérot ('little brother, close buddy, bro'). In urban French youth speech, the historically silent final -t of frérot is commonly pronounced ([fʁeʁot]), and fast allegro elision of the unstressed first syllable yields [fʁot] (spelled frote in informal transcripts). Frérot itself combines frère ('brother', from Classical Latin frāter) with the affectionate diminutive suffix -ot.
frote.notes: Purely spoken, informal street/youth register; avoid confusing this slang vocative with la frotte ('polishing/rubbing') or present-tense forms of frotter ('to rub').

frotter.etymology: Inherited from Old French froter ('to rub, chafe, scrub'), probably from Vulgar Latin *frictare, frequentative built on Classical Latin fricare, frictum ('to rub').

fruit.etymology: Inherited from Old French fruit ('produce of the earth or trees, fruit, profit'), from Classical Latin fructus ('enjoyment, proceeds, produce, fruit of a tree or crops', from frui 'to enjoy, have the use of').

history.meaning: edible plant fruit; outcome or reward of labor

frère.etymology: Frère descends from Latin frater, fratrem ('brother'), with regular lenition of intervocalic -tr- to -r- through Old French frere.
frère.notes: **Grand frère / petit frère** = older / younger brother.

cognates.meaning: to visit often, hang out with

fréquenter.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin frequentāre ('to visit regularly, crowd, populate, celebrate often'), a denominative verb formed from frequēns, frequentis ('crowded, crammed, repeated, constant'), a word of uncertain deeper Indo-European origin possibly connected with farcīre ('to stuff, cram'). Semantic range in French covers attending places, keeping company with people, and dating.

history.meaning: crowded, thronging, repeated at short intervals
to crowd into, visit repeatedly, celebrate
to visit regularly; to keep company with

fréquenter.notes: With a person as direct object (fréquenter quelqu'un), it means 'to hang out with, associate with' (and in slightly dated or regional usage, 'to date/court'); mal fréquenté describes a sketchy or seedy venue.

fuir.etymology: Inherited from Old French fuïr ('to flee, run away from danger'), from Vulgar Latin *fugire, remodeled from Classical Latin fugere ('to flee, take flight', from PIE *bhewg-).

history.meaning: to flee, shun; (of a pipe or roof) to leak

fuite.etymology: Inherited from Old French fuite ('act of fleeing, flight'), from Vulgar Latin *fugita, feminine participial noun formed on *fugire (Classical Latin fugere 'to flee').

history.meaning: flight, escape; leak of water, gas, or secret information

cognates.meaning: short-lived, fleeting (from the same Latin root fugere)

fuiter.etymology: Modern 20th-century French denominal verb formed from fuite ('flight, escape; fluid leak; unauthorized disclosure of information') + verbal suffix -er, semantically reinforced by English to leak in journalism, politics, and entertainment media. Fuite itself descends from Old French fuite, from Vulgar Latin *fugita (substantivized feminine past participle replacing Classical fuga), from Classical Latin fugere ('to flee').

history.meaning: to flee > act of fleeing, escape
flight, escape; later fluid leak and information leak
to leak out (of confidential news, scripts, or data)

fuiter.notes: A staple of press and agency jargon (le scénario a fuité, 'the script leaked'): traditionally intransitive ('to be leaked'), though transitive faire fuiter or fuiter un document ('to leak something') is increasingly common.

cognates.meaning: to emit vapor or rage (via Old French fumer)

fumer.etymology: Inherited from Old French fumer ('to emit smoke or steam, burn incense; to be enraged'), from Classical Latin fūmāre ('to smoke, steam, reek'), a denominal verb derived from fūmus ('smoke, steam, vapor'), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós ('smoke, swirling vapor'). Following the introduction of New World tobacco in the late 16th century, it acquired the transitive and absolute sense 'to smoke tobacco'.

history.meaning: smoke, steam > to emit smoke or vapor
to give off smoke; figuratively to fume with anger
to smoke (tobacco); to cure food in smoke; to fume

fumer.notes: In colloquial French, fumer also retains its medieval figurative heat: ça me fait fumer ('that makes me fume with anger'), and transitively in slang fumer quelqu'un means 'to crush, wipe out, or Chew out someone'.

fumée.etymology: Inherited from Old French fumee ('smoke, vapor, steam, breath'), formed as the substantivized feminine past participle of fumer ('to emit smoke', corresponding to Gallo-Romance *fūmāta), replacing Old French fun (< Classical Latin fūmus, which became homophonous with awkward monosyllables). Ultimately from Classical Latin fūmus ('smoke, steam'), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós.

history.meaning: to emit smoke (that which has been smoked/emitted)
plume of smoke, steam, exhaled vapor

fumée.notes: Feminine noun (la fumée): note key idioms partir en fumée ('to go up in smoke') and il n'y a pas de fumée sans feu ('there's no smoke without fire').

cognates.meaning: burial ceremony (via Old French funerailles / Medieval Latin)

funérailles.etymology: Borrowed in the late 14th century (Middle French funerailles) from Late Latin fūnerālia ('funeral rites, obsequies'), the substantivized neuter plural of Classical/Late Latin fūnerālis ('pertaining to a funeral'), derived from Classical Latin fūnus, fūneris ('funeral procession, burial rites, corpse, violent death'). As routinely happened with Latin neuter plurals in -ia, French reanalyzed the ending as a feminine plural (-ailles).

morphemes.meaning: plural suffix for solemn ceremonies (cf. fiançailles, épousailles)

funérailles.notes: Always feminine plural (les funérailles) and relatively formal or solemn in register (e.g., state or celebrity funerals); in everyday speech, French speakers more commonly say l'enterrement or les obsèques.

furieux.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin furiōsus ('full of madness, raging, frenzied, inspired'), derived with the adjectival suffix -ōsus ('full of') from furia ('violent passion, madness, rage; avenging deity'), itself linked to furere ('to rage, rave, be out of one's mind'). In French it weakened from literal clinical insanity ('raving mad', still preserved in fou furieux) to intense anger or extreme intensity.

history.meaning: seized by madness or battle frenzy; violently angry

furieux.notes: Watch the colloquial idiom un fou furieux ('a raving lunatic; a total fanatic'), and pre-nominal intensifier usage like une furieuse envie de... ('a fierce/overwhelming urge to...'). In informal speech, furieux is often clipped to furax!

rootFamily.gloss: fury, rage; unleashing (faire fureur 'to be all the rage')

fusain.etymology: Inherited via Old French fusain ('spindle tree') from Vulgar Latin *fusago, *fusaginem, derived from Classical Latin fusus ('spinning spindle'), because its dense fine wood was prized first for carving spindles and later for charring into artists' charcoal sticks.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fusain (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fusain

fusain.notes: Even when modern charcoal sticks are made from willow twigs, French artists still call every charcoal drawing **un dessin au fusain**.

fusible.etymology: Originally a fourteenth-century learned adjective from Medieval Latin fusibilis ('capable of melting', from fundere, fusum 'to melt, pour'). In late nineteenth-century electricity, un coupe-circuit fusible was shortened to un fusible: the calibrated wire designed to melt first and protect the circuit.

history.meaning: safety fuse in an electrical circuit

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: fusible (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: fusible

cognates.meaning: time yet to come; upcoming (via Old French futur)

futur.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin futūrus ('about to be, yet to come'), the suppletive future active participle of esse ('to be'), formed with the future participial suffix -tūrus on the stem fu- (seen in perfect fuī 'I was'), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- ('to become, grow, come into being'). Used in French as a grammatical term, an adjective ('upcoming, prospective'), and a noun ('the future').

history.meaning: about to be, destined to exist
future (grammatical tense and theological/philosophical time to come)

futur.notes: Nuance vs. avenir: as a noun, l'avenir refers personally and concretely to what lies ahead in someone's life or career (un acteur d'avenir), whereas le futur is more abstract, philosophical, technological, or grammatical — though as an adjective (mon futur mari, son futur film), futur has no rival.

rootFamily.gloss: was (3rd sg. past historic of être, from the same Latin fu- stem)

fâché.etymology: Past participle of fâcher ('to anger, displease, vex'), inherited from Old/Middle French faschier ('to weary, disgust, annoy'), from Vulgar Latin *fasticare, contracted from Classical Latin fastidiare ('to feel loathing or distaste', from fastidium 'aversion, weariness').

history.meaning: angry, cross, sorry, on bad terms

félicitation.etymology: Formed in the 15th–17th centuries from féliciter ('to congratulate', originally 'to make happy or blessed') + action-noun suffix -ation, or modeled on Late Latin fēlīcitātiō. Féliciter was borrowed from Late Latin fēlīcitāre ('to make happy'), derived from Classical Latin fēlīx, fēlīcis ('fruitful, fertile, auspicious, fortunate, happy'), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *dʰeh₁(y)- ('to suckle, nourish, produce').

history.meaning: fruitful, fortunate > to make happy or blessed
to render happy; later (17th c.) to congratulate on good fortune
act or words of congratulating, official praise

félicitation.notes: Almost always used in the plural as an exclamation — Félicitations ! ('Congratulations!') or Toutes mes félicitations ! — while the singular appears in formal phrases like une lettre de félicitation or recevoir les félicitations du jury (highest honors).

rootFamily.gloss: to congratulate; se féliciter de 'to be pleased about'

félicitations.etymology: Plural of félicitation ('act of wishing someone joy or congratulating them'), derived in the 17th century from féliciter ('to congratulate').

history.meaning: expressions of joy for another's success, congratulations

féliciter.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical/Late Latin felicitare ('to make happy'), derived from felix, felicis ('happy, fortunate'); shifted in 17th-century French from 'to make happy' to 'to congratulate someone on their good fortune'.

cognates.meaning: cat-like; member of the cat family

félin.etymology: Learned borrowing (attested in Middle French and re-established in the 18th–19th centuries via natural history) from Late Latin fēlīnus ('of or belonging to a cat'), formed with the relational suffix -īnus from Classical Latin fēlēs (also fēlis, 'wildcat, small carnivorous mammal such as a marten or polecat, and later domestic cat'). Extended figuratively to graceful, supple, or stealthy human movement.

history.meaning: wildcat, marten, small predator; domestic cat
belonging to or characteristic of a cat
feline, cat-like, lithe (adj.); big cat or felid (noun)

félin.notes: Used both as a zoological noun (les grands félins, 'big cats' like lions and panthers) and as a flattering descriptive adjective for actors or dancers possessing lithe, magnetic grace (une démarche féline).

rootFamily.gloss: member of the biological cat family Felidae

cognates.meaning: female, womanly; grammatical gender (via Old French)

féminin.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century (Old French femenin) from Classical Latin fēminīnus ('female, womanly; belonging to the feminine grammatical gender'), derived with the relational suffix -īnus from fēmina ('woman, female'), literally 'she who suckles', an archaic middle-passive participial formation in *-m̥h₁no- from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- ('to suckle, nurse').

history.meaning: woman, female > womanly, female, of feminine gender
belonging to women; feminine grammatical gender

féminin.notes: Crucial translation trap: French féminin covers BOTH English 'feminine' (stylistic/gendered qualities) AND 'female' / 'women's' whenever femelle would sound purely zoological (hence un rôle féminin 'a female role', l'équipe féminine 'the women's team', la gent féminine 'womankind').

rootFamily.gloss: woman, wife (inherited directly from Latin fēmina)

cognates.meaning: quality of being feminine (via Old/Middle French)

féminité.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French (feminité) from Late Latin fēminitās, fēminitātis ('womanhood, female nature'), formed from Classical Latin fēmina ('woman, female', from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- 'to suckle') + the abstract quality suffix -itās, -itātis (> French -ité). Re-popularized in 19th- and 20th-century literary and cultural discourse.

history.meaning: womanly nature, condition of being a woman

morphemes.meaning: abstract noun suffix denoting quality or state

féminité.notes: Notice that French drops a syllable compared with English 'fem-i-nin-i-ty': it is fé-mi-ni-té (built directly on Latin fēmina + -ité rather than on féminin + -ité).

cognates.meaning: banquet, religious celebration (borrowed from Old French feste)

fête.etymology: Inherited from Old French feste ('religious feast day, festival, rejoicing'), with regular loss of preconsonantal -s- recorded by the circumflex accent (ê). Derived from Vulgar Latin festa (a feminine singular noun reanalyzed from Classical Latin festa, the neuter plural of festum 'holiday, feast'), from the adjective festus ('festive, solemn, joyful'), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁s- ('sacred, divine', cognate with Latin fēriae and fānum).

history.meaning: sacred, joyful > religious holidays, festal observances
church feast day, saint's day, courtly celebration
party, public holiday, saint's name day, celebration

fête.notes: Covers everything from a house party (faire la fête 'to party') and national holidays (la Fête nationale) to one's saint's name day (Bonne fête ! — Note: in Metropolitan France, Bonne fête is for name days or Mother's/Father's Day, whereas Bon anniversaire is for birthdays, though Quebec uses Bonne fête for birthdays!).

cognates.meaning: to honor lavishly with celebrations (borrowed from Modern French)

fêter.etymology: Inherited from Old French fester ('to observe a holy day, abstain from work, celebrate joyously'), a denominal verb formed from feste (> fête 'feast, festival, party') + -er, ultimately from Vulgar Latin festa / Classical Latin festus ('solemn, festal, joyful'). Preconsonantal -s- disappeared in pronunciation by Middle French, yielding the modern spelling fêter while learned derivatives like festif kept -s-.

history.meaning: to observe a religious feast day; to welcome with festivities
to celebrate (an occasion, achievement, or birthday); to toast

fêter.notes: Ça se fête ! ('That calls for a celebration / a drink!') is one of the most frequent celebratory idioms at French offices, film wraps, and agency signings; note the vowel alternation [ɛ] in je fête vs. [e] or [ɛ] in fêter.

cognates.meaning: social blunder (borrowed from 19th–20th c. French); also fishing gaff (earlier borrowing)
hook, staple; jinx/bad luck; (pl. gafas) eyeglasses hooked over ears

gaffe.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French as a nautical and river-craft term meaning 'iron-tipped boathook, gaff' from Old Occitan gafa ('hook'), verbal noun of gafar ('to seize, hook, snatch'), likely of pre-Roman or Germanic origin (often compared with Gothic *giban or Proto-Germanic *gabalō 'fork'). In 19th-century popular and military slang, gaffe developed two rich figurative branches: 'lookout, sentry duty' (whence faire gaffe 'to watch out') and 'clumsy jab, social blunder, faux pas'.

history.meaning: long pole with an iron hook used by boatmen and fishermen
clumsy social blunder (faire une gaffe); watchfulness (faire gaffe)

gaffe.notes: Master the crucial article contrast: faire UNE gaffe means 'to make a blunder / put one's foot in one's mouth', whereas faire gaffe (no article: Fais gaffe !) means 'to be careful / watch out!'.

rootFamily.gloss: to blunder, put one's foot in it
blunder-prone person (famously comic hero Gaston Lagaffe)

cognates.meaning: to acquire, profit (borrowed via Middle French gagner)
to earn, win (borrowed via Old French/Germanic)

gagnant.etymology: Adjectival and substantivized present participle of gagner ('to win, earn') + -ant. Gagner descends from Old French gaaignier ('to till the soil, harvest crops, forage, capture booty, make a profit'), borrowed from Frankish *waidanjan ('to graze, pasture, hunt or forage for food'), derived from *waidu ('pasture, meadow, food'). The semantic shift moved from agricultural harvesting and military plunder to financial earning and competitive victory.

history.meaning: to pasture, forage, hunt for food
to cultivate land, reap a harvest, win booty > cultivator, earner

gagnant.notes: Used both as a noun (le grand gagnant, la gagnante) and in the business/negotiation calque donnant-donnant or gagnant-gagnant ('win-win', e.g. un accord gagnant-gagnant).

gagner.etymology: Inherited from Old French gaaignier ('to till the soil, forage, capture booty, earn by labor'), borrowed from Frankish *waidanjan ('to pasture, forage, hunt for food', from *waida 'pasture, hunting').

history.meaning: to harvest, earn -> to win, gain, reach

cognates.meaning: scabbard, sheath, pod (vanilla is its diminutive vainilla!)
anatomical canal (learned Latin borrowing of the exact etymon of gaine)

gaine.etymology: Inherited from Old French gaïne ('sword scabbard, knife sheath, case'), descending from Classical Latin vāgīna ('scabbard, sheath, ear-husk of grain'). Initial Latin v- shifted irregularly to Gallo-Romance gw- > g- (compare gué < vadum and gâter < vastāre) through phonetic crossing with a synonymous Frankish word beginning in *w-. From 'close-fitting sheath' it extended in modern French to 'protective cable conduit' and 'shaping girdle / shapewear'.

history.meaning: sword scabbard, sheath, protective husk of grain
scabbard for a blade; fitted leather case
sheath; electrical conduit; body-shaping girdle or corset

gaine.notes: A classic costume-department word on film sets ('shapewear, girdle'), while its derivative gainage is the standard modern French fitness term for 'core-strengthening planks'! Also look out for dégainer ('to unsheathe/draw a weapon').

rootFamily.gloss: to draw from a sheath (dégainer une arme / son téléphone)
to sheathe; to sculpt/firm the figure; core plank (gainage)
vanilla (via Spanish vainilla 'little sheath/pod', diminutive of Latin vāgīna)

cognates.meaning: chivalrous, brave, courtly toward women (borrowed from Middle French)
handsome, courtly; leading man in theater (galán, from French)

galant.etymology: Lexicalized present participle of Old French galer ('to make merry, rejoice, live sumptuously, amuse oneself') + -ant, derived from Old French gale ('pleasure, festivity, lively entertainment'), generally traced to Frankish *wala ('well, wealth, good fortune', cognate with Old High German wola and English well / weal). Evolved from 'lively, dashing reveler' in Middle French to 'courtly, chivalrous gentleman' and 'amorous, romantic'.

history.meaning: merrymaking, pleasure > to rejoice, live dashingly
lively, stylish, spirited; chivalrous man of court
attentive/chivalrous toward women; romantic or amorous (aventure galante)

galant.notes: Position changes meaning subtly: un homme galant is 'courteous/chivalrous' (holding doors, polite manners), un galant homme (before the noun, literary) means 'an honorable gentleman', and after nouns like aventure galante or rendez-vous galant it means 'romantic/amorous'.

rootFamily.gloss: gala celebration (borrowed back via Italian/Spanish from Old French gale)

cognates.meaning: playful leap or caper (borrowed in 16th c. from French gambade)

gambader.etymology: Derived in Middle French (16th century) from gambade ('playful leap, caper, bound') + -er. Gambade was borrowed from Occitan or Northern Italian gambada ('kick, bound of the legs'), derived from Late Latin gamba ('fetlock or hock of a quadruped, leg'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek kampē ('bend, joint, flexure'). Because central French palatalized Latin ga- to ja- (yielding jambe 'leg'), initial g- in gambader betrays its southern Romance borrowing path.

history.meaning: bend, joint > animal hock, leg (in veterinary Late Latin)
leap, kick of the legs, caper (in dance or horsemanship)
to frolic, skip, scamper about joyously

gambader.notes: Evokes carefree, bouncy physical energy — kids, puppies, or joyous characters scampering across a field or park — and shares its hidden 'leg' root with jambe, jambon ('ham'), and gambettes ('legs', affectionate slang).

rootFamily.gloss: leg (the native central French reflex of Late Latin gamba)
legs, pins (colloquial affectionate diminutive from northern dialect gambe)

cognates.meaning: play, sport, competitive contest (source of the French borrowing)

game.etymology: Contemporary masculine borrowing from English game, inherited from Middle English game, gamen and Old English gamen ('joy, mirth, sport, pastime'), from Proto-Germanic *gamaną ('shared joy, amusement, fellowship', formed with collective prefix *ga- + *mann- 'person'). In French, it entered first through tennis scoring, then through commercial pseudo-anglicisms like laser game ('laser tag') and escape game ('escape room'), as well as hip-hop/media slang le game ('the competitive scene').

history.meaning: arcade/activity venue (laser game, escape game); competitive industry arena (le game)

game.notes: Classic French pseudo-anglicism alert: French people say un laser game for 'laser tag' and un escape game for 'an escape room' (plus être dans le game 'to be a major player in the industry'), whereas everyday 'game' remains un jeu or une partie.

cognates.meaning: playfully mischievous, boyish, waif-like (borrowed from French gamin/gamine)

gamin.etymology: Entered general Parisian French in the early 19th century (immortalized by Victor Hugo's street urchin Gavroche in Les Misérables, 1862) from eastern and central French regional dialects (Burgundy, Lorraine, Franche-Comté), where gamin was attested in the 18th century for a young boy assistant in glassworks and masonry workshops. Its ultimate etymology remains debated: leading hypotheses derive it from German gemein ('common, ordinary rank-and-file helper') or from regional gamber ('to scamper, run errands').

history.meaning: young apprentice helper in eastern French glassworks and trades

gamin.notes: Informal, warm everyday synonym for enfant ('kid', feminine gamine) alongside gosse and môme; calling an adult un vrai gamin can either tease them affectionately ('a big kid at heart') or criticize childishness ('so immature').

gamme.etymology: Inherited from Old French game / gamme ('musical scale'), from Medieval Latin gamma, the Greek letter G (Γ) placed by Guido d'Arezzo at the bottom of the medieval musical scale to denote the lowest bass note (gamma ut, which also gave English gamut).

history.meaning: lowest note of Guido's hexachord -> entire musical scale
musical scale; full range or product line

gant.etymology: Inherited from Old French guant / gant, borrowed from Frankish *want ('glove, hand-wrapping', related to Germanic *windan 'to wind, wrap around').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French gantelet ('little/armored glove')

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: gant (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: gant

gant.notes: Initial Frankish *w-* regularly became *gu-* -> *g-* in French (just as *wardon* gave **garder** and *werra* gave **guerre**).

cognates.meaning: assurance, pledge (guarantee via French; doublet warrant via Old Northern French warant)

garantie.etymology: Inherited from Old French garantie ('protection, legal surety, defense'), formed with the abstract suffix -ie on garant ('protector, legal voucher, guarantor'; Old Northern French warant, source of English warrant). Garant was borrowed from Frankish *warjand / *warōnd ('defender, warrantor'), a substantivized present participle of *warjan ('to defend, fend off') crossed with *warōn ('to watch over, vouch for'), from Proto-Germanic *warjaną / *warōną.

history.meaning: defender, protector, one who vouches for another
feudal protector, legal surety > protection, pledge of truthfulness

garantie.notes: Covers both English 'guarantee' (je te donne ma garantie) and commercial 'warranty' (sous garantie 'under warranty'), as well as film-financing minimum garanties (MG, 'minimum guarantee' advances from distributors).

rootFamily.gloss: guarantor, voucher (se porter garant 'to vouch for')

cognates.meaning: watch, protector (guard via French; native Germanic cognate ward)

garde.etymology: Inherited from Old French garde (Northern dialect warde), a post-verbal noun formed from garder ('to watch over, protect, keep safe'), borrowed from Frankish *wardōn ('to keep watch, stand guard, attend to'), from Proto-Germanic *wardōną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wer- ('to perceive, watch out for', cognate with Latin verērī and English aware / ward). Frankish initial *w- regularly developed into gw- > g- in central Gallo-Romance.

history.meaning: to keep watch, guard / act of watching, sentry duty

garde.notes: Gender changes meaning! Feminine LA garde means 'custody, watch, on-call duty, or collective guard force' (la garde des enfants 'child custody', garde alternée 'joint custody', être de garde 'to be on call', prendre garde 'to watch out'); masculine UN garde is an individual guardsman or ranger (un garde du corps 'bodyguard').

rootFamily.gloss: to look at (originally 'to look back/watch closely')

garder.etymology: Inherited from Old French garder ('to watch over, protect, keep'), borrowed from Frankish *wardon ('to stand guard, watch over, protect', from Proto-Germanic *wardona, cognate with English ward and guard).

history.meaning: to guard, look after, keep, retain

cognates.meaning: protector (guardian via Old French; doublet warden via Anglo-Norman wardein)

gardien.etymology: Inherited from Old French gardien (altered by suffix substitution with -ien from earlier Old French gardenc, Anglo-Norman wardein), borrowed from Frankish *warding ('watchman, keeper, protector'), a derivative formed with the Germanic patronymic/agentive suffix *-ing on the stem of *wardōn ('to watch, guard'). English borrowed this word twice: from Anglo-Norman wardein as warden, and from central Old French gardien as guardian.

history.meaning: building concierge/caretaker, goalkeeper, guardian (e.g. ange gardien)

gardien.notes: False friend in family law: a child's legal 'guardian' in French is un tuteur / une tutrice (NOT un gardien!). In everyday Parisian life, le gardien or la gardienne refers to an apartment building's resident superintendent/caretaker, a museum guard, or a soccer goalkeeper (gardien de but), while adjectival gardien appears in ange gardien ('guardian angel').

rootFamily.gloss: caretaker's role or residential security monitoring

gare.etymology: Gare originally meant a sheltered river dock where boats pulled aside (from garer 'to moor, shelter', of Frankish origin *waron 'to watch out, protect'). In the railway age, river-dock terminology transferred directly to train stations!
gare.notes: For bus or tram stops, French says **un arrêt**; for metro, **une station**; for trains, **la gare**.

garer.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century (originally in river navigation, 'to berth a boat in a sheltered cove or dock out of the main current') from Old Occitan garar ('to watch out, shelter, protect'), itself from Frankish/Gothic *waron ('to heed, protect', cognate with gare 'river basin -> railway station').

history.meaning: to shelter, put in a safe berth
to dock a boat, shunt a train -> to park a car

cognates.meaning: boy, apprentice, waiter (borrowed from Old French garçon)
young man, waiter (borrowed from Old French)
unfortunate outcast (native Germanic cognate of Frankish *wrakjō!)

gars.etymology: Inherited from Old French gars, a remarkable fossil of the medieval Old French two-case declension system: gars (*warkjōs) was the nominative singular (cas sujet), whereas garçon (*warkjōnem) was the oblique singular (cas régime) of the exact same noun! Both derive from Gallo-Romance *warkjō, borrowed from Frankish *wrakjō ('exile, roaming warrior, young retainer or servant', cognate with Old High German reckeo 'warrior, hero' and Old English wrecca 'exile, wretch').

history.meaning: page, servant lad, boy (at times pejorative 'knave')
guy, lad, fellow, buddy (warm colloquial masculine noun)

gars.notes: Pronunciation trap: both the -r- and -s are traditionally silent in standard colloquial French — un gars is pronounced [ɡɑ] or [ɡa] ('ga')! Very common in friendly address: mon gars ('my boy / buddy'), un bon gars ('a good guy'), les gars ('guys / fellas').

rootFamily.gloss: boy, young man; waiter (the historical oblique-case twin of gars!)
tomboy (garçon manqué) or 1920s flapper girl; bachelor flat

garçon.etymology: Inherited from Old French garçon (originally the oblique case of gars, meaning 'serving-boy, camp-follower, valet, young lad'), from Frankish *wrakjo ('retainer, mercenary, exile, young warrior', cognate with English wretch).

gauche.etymology: Gauche emerged in Middle French, probably from gauchir ('to veer aside, bend', from Frankish *wenkjan 'to waveringly turn aside', cognate with English 'wink' and 'flinch'), replacing older senestre ('left').

gazeux.etymology: Formed in the late 18th century (Lavoisier, 1787) from gaz ('gas', coined by the Flemish chemist J. B. van Helmont in the 17th c. after Greek khaos 'chaos, air') + adjectival suffix -eux.

history.meaning: gaseous; carbonated, sparkling (of water or drinks)

cognates.meaning: traditional Japanese female entertainer (borrowed from Japanese)

geisha.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th century (first attested in French travelogues and Japonisme literature in the 1880s–1890s, partly via English) from Japanese geisha (芸者, literally 'person of the arts, performing artist'), a Sino-Japanese compound combining gei (芸, traditional 藝, from Middle Chinese ngjejH, 'art, artistic skill, performance') + sha (者, from Middle Chinese tsjaeX, 'person who practices an activity'). Originally applied in 18th-century Edo Japan to male as well as female entertainers before specializing to classically trained female hostesses.

history.meaning: professional artist-entertainer skilled in music, dance, and conversation
traditional Japanese hostess and classical performing artist

geisha.notes: Pronounced [ɡɛjʃa] or [ɡejʃa] in French; cultural note — in Japan a geisha (or Kyoto geiko) is a rigorously trained classical musician, dancer, and conversationalist, despite long-standing Western orientalist misconceptions conflating the profession with courtesans (oiran).

rootFamily.gloss: traditional Japanese martial or performing arts (shares Sino-Japanese root gei- in geijutsu 'art' — within French loanwords, compare fellow Edo cultural loanwords like kimono and kabuki; strictly morphologically standalone in French aside from plural geishas)
geisha-like or relating to geisha aesthetics (occasional literary derivative)

cognates.meaning: to freeze (with regular loss of initial Latin g-/h- in pronunciation)
to set into a gel; also cold/congealed (via Latin gelāre / gelū, cognate with cold!)

geler.etymology: Inherited from Old French geler ('to turn to ice, freeze, be stiff with cold'), from Classical Latin gelāre ('to freeze, congeal, stiffen with frost'), a denominal verb derived from gelū (also gelum, 'icy cold, frost, ice'), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵel- ('cold, to freeze', the same root that gave Proto-Germanic *kaldaz > English cold and Latin glaciēs > French glace).

history.meaning: frost, ice > to cause to freeze or turn into ice
to freeze over (impersonal il gèle); to stiffen with cold
to freeze (water, food, or figuratively prices, hiring, and bank accounts)

geler.notes: Stem-changing spelling verb: e becomes è before silent endings (il gèle 'it is freezing', ça me gèle 'I'm freezing'). Very common in impersonal weather expressions (il gèle à pierre fendre 'it's freezing hard enough to split stone') and colloquial se les geler ('to freeze one's butt off').

rootFamily.gloss: frost, freeze; hair/shower gel; asset freeze (le gel des avoirs)

cognates.meaning: ice cream (literally 'frozen', substantivized past participle of gelare)

gelé.etymology: Adjectival past participle of geler ('to freeze'), inherited from Old French gelé, continuing Classical Latin gelātus ('frozen, congealed, frosted'), past participle of gelāre ('to freeze'), from gelū ('frost, ice', from Proto-Indo-European *ǵel- 'cold'). Exact Romance cognate of Italian gelato and Spanish helado, though French specialized glace for 'ice cream' and kept gelé as an adjective.

history.meaning: covered in frost, turned to ice, numb with cold
frozen solid; freezing cold (person); blocked/frozen (funds or negotiations)

gelé.notes: Just like English 'I'm freezing!', French speakers say Je suis complètement gelé(e) ('I'm freezing cold!'). For commercial frozen foods at the supermarket, however, French prefers surgelé ('deep-frozen') or congelé rather than gelé.

cognates.meaning: congealed fruit preserve (borrowed from Old French)

gelée.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of geler ('to freeze'), inherited via Old French gelee from Latin gelata, feminine past participle of gelare ('to freeze, congeal'), itself derived from gelu ('frost, icy cold'). From the literal meteorological sense of 'morning frost', Old French developed the culinary sense of a meat broth or fruit juice clarified and set by cooling, whence English 'jelly'.

history.meaning: frost, extreme cold / to freeze solid
frost; congealed meat stock or fruit juice

gelée.notes: Covers both weather ('les premières gelées', first frosts) and food/cosmetics ('gelée de groseilles', 'gelée royale'), whereas ice cream is 'glace'.

genre.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French gendre / genre) from Classical Latin genus, generis ('birth, descent, race, stock, kind, sort, grammatical gender', from PIE *gene- 'to give birth, beget').

history.meaning: kind, sort, artistic genre, grammatical gender, manner

gens.etymology: Inherited from Old French gent (plural genz / gens, 'race, nation, people, folk'), from Classical Latin gentem (nominative gens, 'clan, Roman patrician family, tribe, people', from PIE *gene- 'to beget').

cognates.meaning: well-born, mild (borrowed from Old French); non-Jewish (learned doublet)

gentil.etymology: Inherited from Old French gentil ('noble, high-born, valiant, courteous'), from Classical Latin gentilis ('belonging to the same clan or gens; of noble lineage'), derived from gens, gentis ('clan, Roman patrician family, birth'). In medieval chivalric culture, noble birth was equated with refined conduct, gradually broadening in Middle and Modern French from 'aristocratic' to 'pleasant, kind, and considerate'.

history.meaning: belonging to the same clan (gens); of good family

gentil.notes: Silent final '-l' in the masculine singular [ʒɑ̃ti], pronounced as a palatal glide in the feminine 'gentille' [ʒɑ̃tij]; in workplace banter (as at ASK), calling someone 'bien gentil' can carry patronizing irony ('sweet, but naive').

cognates.meaning: chivalrous, well-bred man (source of the French borrowing)

gentleman.etymology: Re-borrowing (aller-retour) from English gentleman, first attested in French contexts describing England in the 16th–17th centuries and naturalized in the 18th–19th centuries. English gentleman was itself formed in Middle English as a partial calque of Anglo-Norman gentilz hom (Modern French gentilhomme), combining Old French gentil ('noble-born') with native English man.

history.meaning: man of gentle birth or honorable conduct
man of impeccable manners, fair play, and elegance

gentleman.notes: Unlike archival 'gentilhomme' (aristocrat), 'gentleman' emphasizes gallant fair play and understated elegance (e.g., 'un accord de gentleman', 'gentleman-cambrioleur'); standard plural is 'gentlemen' or regularized 'gentlemans'.

germer.etymology: Inherited from Old French germer ('to sprout, put forth shoots'), from Classical Latin germinare ('to bud, sprout, spring forth'), denominal verb from germen, germinis ('sprout, bud, offshoot, embryo'), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁-men- ('offspring, seed', from *ǵenh₁- 'to beget, produce'). Used figuratively since medieval French for ideas or projects taking root in the mind.

history.meaning: to sprout; to take shape figuratively
to germinate; (of an idea) to dawn or develop

germer.notes: Very frequent figuratively in creative and film-pitch contexts: 'une idée qui germe' (an idea taking shape) or 'faire germer un projet'.

cognates.meaning: bodily movement; playful remark (from Old French geste 'exploit')

geste.etymology: Masculine noun borrowed in the 15th century from Classical Latin gestus ('bodily carriage, posture, theatrical movement of the hands'), action noun from gerere, gestum ('to bear, carry, comport oneself, perform'). Distinct from, though etymologically kindred to, Old French feminine la geste ('chronicle of heroic deeds', as in chanson de geste), which came from Latin neuter plural gesta ('things accomplished').

history.meaning: bearing, posture, expressive motion of an orator or actor
physical gesture; symbolic act or concession

geste.notes: Masculine ('un beau geste', 'faire un geste commercial' = offer a discount/concession in negotiations); feminine 'la geste' survives only in literary expressions for epic cycles.

rootFamily.gloss: management (from the same Latin root gerere)

gestion.etymology: Learned borrowing (late 15th century, initially in legal Latin sense negotiorum gestio 'handling of affairs') from Classical Latin gestio, gestionis ('carrying out, performance, management, administration'), action noun built on the supine stem gest- of gerere ('to carry on, conduct, administer').

history.meaning: conducting, carrying out, administration of affairs
legal administration of another's property or estate

morphemes.meaning: noun suffix of action or process

gestion.notes: False friend alert: 'gestion' means 'management' or 'administration' (e.g., 'gestion de carrière', 'gestion de crise'), never 'digestion' or 'suggestion'.

gifle.etymology: Inherited from Old French gifle / giffle ('cheek, jowl'), which survived in regional dialects before entering general colloquial Parisian French in the early 19th century via metonymy from 'cheek' to 'a blow struck across the cheek' (parallel to joue -> jouée or gueule -> gueulée). The ultimate origin of Old French gifle is likely an expressive Gallo-Romance or Germanic formation *gif- evoking puffed-out cheeks.

history.meaning: cheek, fleshy side of the face
slap across the cheek (regional, then general French)
slap across the face; stinging humiliation or setback

gifle.notes: Standard word for an open-handed slap in the face (colloquial synonym: 'une baffe' or 'une claque'); figuratively used for a box-office or electoral humiliation ('prendre une gifle').

gifler.etymology: Denominal verb derived in French from gifle ('slap on the cheek', earlier Old French 'cheek') + first-conjugation suffix -er. Attested in regional usage in the late 18th century and popularized in standard French literature and theater over the 19th century alongside the noun gifle.

history.meaning: cheek (Old French); slap on the cheek (Modern dialectal)
history.stage: Old to Early Modern French base

history.meaning: to strike across the cheek with the open hand

gifler.notes: Classic French boulevard and cinema trope ('scène de ménage'); takes a direct person object ('gifler quelqu'un', to slap someone), unlike English 'slap at'.

gilet.etymology: Appeared in the 17th–18th century for a sleeveless waistcoat; traditionally traced either to Gille (the stock comic buffoon of French fairground theater who wore a sleeveless jerkin) or via Spanish jileco / Algerian Arabic jalika from Turkish yelek ('sleeveless vest').

glace.etymology: Inherited from Old French glace ('ice'), from Vulgar Latin *glacia, feminine singular reshaped from Classical Latin glacies ('ice'); extended in the 16th–17th century to polished plate-glass mirrors and to frozen desserts (ice cream).

history.meaning: ice; plate-glass mirror or car window; ice cream

glacé.etymology: Past participle of glacer ('to freeze, turn to ice, chill, coat with a glossy sugar icing'), derived in Old French from glace ('ice').

history.meaning: frozen, icy cold; glazed, glossy, iced

glaçage.etymology: Formed in the 18th–19th century from glacer ('to glaze, coat pastry with shiny sugar icing') + nominal suffix -age.

history.meaning: glossy finishing glaze; sugar icing or frosting on a cake

cognates.meaning: to move smoothly (from the same Germanic root *glidan)

glissant.etymology: Adjectival present participle of glisser ('to slip, slide'), formed in Old and Middle French as an expressive remodeling (influenced by glace 'ice' and glacer) of Old French glier ('to slip, glide'), itself borrowed from Frankish *glidan ('to glide, slide'), from Proto-Germanic *glīdaną.
glissant.notes: Used both on road signs ('chaussée glissante') and in delicate agency or PR situations: 'un terrain glissant' ('a slippery slope / touchy subject').

rootFamily.gloss: to slip, slide; to slip something in

glisser.etymology: Inherited from Old French glier / glicier ('to slip, slide, glide'), borrowed from Frankish *glidan ('to glide, slip smoothly', cognate with English glide) crossed with Old French glacier ('to slip on ice', from glace).

history.meaning: to slide, slip, glide, slip something in discreetly

gond.etymology: Inherited via Old French gont from Late Latin gumphus / gomphus ('iron hinge pin, peg, joint'), borrowed from Ancient Greek gómphos ('wooden peg, iron bolt, molar tooth').

history.meaning: vertical iron pintle supporting a door or shutter

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: gond (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: gond

gond.notes: Because a shutter lifted off its *gonds* swings out of control, **sortir de ses gonds** means 'to lose one's temper'—literally 'to come off one's hinges'!

cognates.meaning: to swell, inflate (intermediary or cognate Romance form)
to fuse together (learned borrowing from Latin conflare)

gonflable.etymology: Derived in 19th-century French from gonfler ('to swell, puff up, inflate') + adjectival suffix -able ('capable of being'). The verb gonfler continues Classical Latin conflare ('to blow together, blow up a fire or bladder, inflate'), from com- ('together') + flare ('to blow'), showing Western Romance voicing of initial c- to g- after nasal prefixes or via Southern Gallo-Romance/Italian influence.

history.meaning: to blow up, kindle, swell with wind
capable of being inflated with air or gas

gonflable.notes: Literal in 'matelas gonflable' or 'canot gonflable', while the base verb has rich slang uses: 'être gonflé' ('to have some nerve!') and 'ça me gonfle' ('that really annoys me').

rootFamily.gloss: to deflate; (reflexive) to lose one's nerve

gonflé.etymology: Past participle of gonfler ('to blow up, swell, inflate'), inherited via Old French / Occitan gonflar from Classical Latin conflare ('to blow together, blow up a fire or bladder'), from com- + flare ('to blow').

cognates.meaning: narrow ravine; to stuff oneself (borrowed from Old French)

gorge.etymology: Inherited from Old French gorge ('throat, gullet, neck, bosom'), from Late Latin gurga ('whirlpool; throat'), a first-declension feminine remodeling of Classical Latin gurges, gurgitis ('whirlpool, eddy, abyss', and figuratively 'insatiable gullet'), ultimately an expressive reduplicated Indo-European root *gʷerh₃- ('to swallow, devour').
gorge.notes: Anchors many vivid idioms: 'avoir la gorge serrée' (to have a lump in one's throat), 'rire à gorge déployée' (to laugh heartily), and 'avoir le couteau sous la gorge' (to be under extreme pressure).

rootFamily.gloss: to slit the throat; to fleece financially

gorgée.etymology: Formed in Old French (gorgiee, 12th c.) from gorge ('throat, gullet', from Late Latin gurga < Classical Latin gurges 'whirlpool, abyss, throat') + suffix -ée denoting the amount swallowed at one time.

history.meaning: a mouthful or swallow of liquid, sip, gulp

gosse.etymology: Attested in Parisian argot at the end of the 18th century ('young lad, apprentice, street urchin'), of uncertain origin. Leading philological hypotheses connect it either to regional French gosse ('small dog, pup', used affectionately or disparagingly for a child, compare loupiot or chiard) or to a truncation of Old/Middle French gosselin ('gosling, silly youngster').

history.meaning: kid, child (epicene); handsome guy in 'beau gosse'

gosse.notes: Major regional false friend! In France, 'un/une gosse' means 'a kid' and 'un beau gosse' (abbreviated BG) means 'a hunk / handsome guy', whereas in Quebec French 'les gosses' is vulgar slang for testicles.

gourmandise.etymology: Formed in Middle French (attested 14th–15th centuries) from the adjective/noun gourmand ('fond of good food, greedy') + abstract feminine suffix -ise (from Late Latin -itia). Originally denoting the capital sin of gluttony (replacing Old French gloutonie), it softened from the 17th–18th centuries onward to mean appreciative fondness for fine food, and concretely a sweet treat or delicacy. (The base gourmand itself is of debated medieval origin, possibly altered from Old French gromme 'wine-merchant's lad, taster'.)

history.meaning: immoderate greed for food, sin of gluttony
fondness for delicacies; sweet treat or pastry (especially plural)

morphemes.meaning: abstract quality or concrete treat noun suffix

gourmandise.notes: In modern French, calling someone 'gourmand(e)' or praising their 'gourmandise' is warm and positive ('food-loving, having a sweet tooth'), unlike harsh 'gloutonnerie' (gluttony); 'un café gourmand' is an espresso served with mini-desserts.

rootFamily.gloss: fond of good food and sweets; greedy
connoisseur of fine food and wine (originally wine-broker's assistant)

goutte.etymology: Inherited from Old French gote ('drop of liquid; trace amount, nothing at all in ne... goutte; gout'), from Classical Latin gutta ('falling drop of liquid').

goût.etymology: Inherited through Old French goust ('sense of taste, flavour, appetite') from Classical Latin gustus ('tasting, sip, flavour'), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵews- ('to taste, try, choose', cognate with English choose). Preconsonantal s fell silent in late Old French, leaving the circumflex accent in modern goût.
goût.notes: The circumflex on û commemorates the vanished s of Old French goust — which still surfaces in learned relatives like déguster ('to savour') and gustatif ('gustatory').

goûter.etymology: Inherited from Old French goster ('to taste, sample food or drink'), from Classical Latin gustare ('to taste, take a little of, enjoy'), derived from gustus ('taste, sipping'); as a noun (le goûter), denotes the light afternoon snack.

goûteur.etymology: Formed in Middle/Modern French from goûter ('to taste, test food or wine') + agent suffix -eur.

cognates.meaning: cereal seed (borrowed from Old French grain)

graine.etymology: Inherited from Old French graine ('seed, berry, scarlet dye grain'), from Vulgar Latin *grana, a collective feminine singular reanalyzed from the Classical Latin neuter plural grana of granum ('seed, kernel, small particle'), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm ('worn-down particle, ripened grain', cognate with English corn).

history.meaning: plant seed; budding talent ('graine de star')

graine.notes: Distinguish feminine 'une graine' (a plant seed to sow; figuratively 'une graine de star' = a star in the making, 'mauvaise graine' = bad seed) from masculine 'un grain' (a grain of sand, wheat, coffee, or folly: 'un grain de folie').

gramme.etymology: Borrowed in 1793–1795 by the founders of the French metric system from Late Latin gramma / Ancient Greek gramma ('written character; small weight equal to one twenty-fourth of an ounce, scruple'), from graphein ('to write').

history.meaning: base metric unit of mass (weight of one cubic centimeter of water)

grand.etymology: Grand comes from Latin grandis ('full-grown, tall, great'), which completely displaced Classical Latin magnus in spoken Gallo-Romance.
grand.notes: Before a vowel or mute h, liaison sounds final d as /t/ (*un grand hôtel* /ɛ̃ ɡʁɑ̃t‿otɛl/).

cognates.meaning: much, any great deal (in 'non è granché')

grand-chose.etymology: Fossilized nominal phrase inherited from Old French grant chose ('great thing, much'), preserving the etymological Old French feminine singular grant without final -e. Because Classical Latin grandis was a third-declension two-termination adjective with identical masculine and feminine forms, Old French said grant chose, grant mere, grant rue; when analogical feminine grande generalized in Middle French, fixed expressions kept grant-, today spelled with a hyphen (replacing a mistaken 16th-century apostrophe grand'chose). Chose descends from Latin causa ('cause, legal matter, thing').

history.meaning: great matter, much (used especially in negative/interrogative clauses)

grand-chose.notes: Invariably singular and used almost exclusively in negative or conditional contexts ('ce n'est pas grand-chose', 'il ne reste plus grand-chose') with neuter/masculine agreement ('pas grand-chose de nouveau').

rootFamily.gloss: grandmother (built with the same fossilized feminine grand-)

grand-mère.etymology: Compound kinship noun formed in Old/Middle French from grand ('great, elder', retaining its archaic invariable feminine form grand without -e from Latin grandis) + mère ('mother', from Latin matrem).

grand-père.etymology: Compound kinship noun formed in Middle French (replacing older aïeul) from grand ('great, elder', from Latin grandis) + père ('father', from Latin patrem).

cognates.meaning: imposing, magnificent (source of the French word)
imposing or extravagantly ambitious (borrowed via French)

grandiose.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (originally in travelers' accounts of Italian architecture, painting, and opera) from Italian grandioso ('imposing, majestic, noble in scale'), derived from grande ('great, large', from Latin grandis) + augmenting adjectival suffix -oso (from Latin -osus).

history.meaning: imposing, noble in artistic style and scale

morphemes.meaning: full of, characterized by (from Italian -oso / Latin -osus)

grandiose.notes: Subtle false friend: English 'grandiose' is often pejorative ('pretentious, overblown'), whereas French 'grandiose' is genuinely admiring ('un spectacle grandiose', 'un décor grandiose' = breathtaking, magnificent).

grandir.etymology: Inherited from Old French grandir ('to grow tall, increase, make great'), from Vulgar Latin *grandire (for Classical Latin grandescere), derived from grandis ('large, tall, full-grown').

history.meaning: to grow up, grow taller, increase

cognates.meaning: country estate or outlying monastic farm (from Anglo-Norman)

grange.etymology: Inherited from Old French grange ('barn for storing sheaves of grain; outlying monastic farmstead'), from Gallo-Roman / Medieval Latin *granica (attested as granica in medieval charters), substantivized feminine of *granicus ('pertaining to grain'), derived from Classical Latin granum ('grain, cereal seed') with regular palatalization of *-ica to -ge.

history.meaning: farm barn for hay, straw, and unthreshed grain

grange.notes: Denotes specifically a high-roofed stone or timber barn for storing hay/crops (often renovated into country homes or indie film locations), whereas animal stalls are 'une étable' (cattle) or 'une écurie' (horses).

rootFamily.gloss: to gather crops into the barn; figuratively to rack up profits/awards

gratter.etymology: Inherited from Old French grater ('to scratch, scrape, claw'), borrowed from Frankish *kratton ('to scratch, scrape', from Proto-Germanic *krattōną, cognate with German kratzen and English scratch).

gratuit.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Classical Latin gratuitus ('done without pay or profit, spontaneous, free of charge'), derived from gratia ('favor, kindness, thanks') and gratis ('for nothing').

history.meaning: done out of favor without payment, free
free of charge; unprovoked or unfounded (of an act or claim)

gratuitement.etymology: Formed in the 15th–16th century from the feminine adjective gratuite ('free of charge, unprovoked') + adverbial suffix -ment.

history.meaning: free of charge, for nothing; without justification

grave.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century (replacing native Old French grief in most senses) from Classical Latin gravis ('heavy, weighty, serious, deep in pitch, pregnant', from PIE *gwerh2- 'heavy').

history.meaning: serious, solemn, severe; low-pitched (in music); grave accent (`)

graver.etymology: Inherited from Old French graver ('to make a part in the hair; to incise, carve into wood, stone, or metal'), borrowed from Frankish *graban ('to dig,hollow out, carve', from Proto-Germanic *grabana, cognate with English grave and engrave).

history.meaning: to engrave, carve, etch; to burn a disc or memory

grenier.etymology: Grenier descends from Latin granarium ('granary, grain loft above a house', from granum 'grain'). Because grain was stored dry under the rafters, le grenier became the everyday word for an attic.
grenier.notes: Compare English 'granary' and 'garner' (borrowed from Old French).

grille.etymology: Inherited from Old French greïlle / grille ('iron gridiron for broiling; grating of iron bars'), from Late Latin craticula ('small hurdle, fine gridiron'), diminutive of Classical Latin cratis ('wickerwork hurdle, lattice, harrow').

history.meaning: iron grating, wrought-iron gate; crossword or schedule grid

cognates.meaning: to broil on a grate; to question intensely (from French)

griller.etymology: Denominal verb derived in Old French (graïllier, later griller) from gril / graïl ('gridiron, cooking grate') + -er. Old French graïl descends from Late Latin craticula ('small wicker hurdle; iron gridiron'), diminutive of Classical Latin cratis ('wickerwork, latticework, hurdle'), with voicing of initial cr- to gr- (compare gras from crassus). From scorching meat on a grate arose rich figurative senses of burning out a bulb, running a red light, and ruining someone's cover or industry reputation.

history.meaning: small latticework hurdle; iron cooking grate
to broil over hot coals, scorch, torture on a gridiron
to grill; to blow (a fuse); to expose or blacklist someone

griller.notes: Essential showbiz and everyday idiom: 'être grillé dans le métier' means to be blacklisted / washed up in the industry; 'griller un feu rouge' = run a red light; 'se faire griller' = get busted/caught red-handed.

rootFamily.gloss: iron gate, railing; TV schedule ('grille des programmes')

grillé.etymology: Past-participle adjective of griller ('to toast, roast, grill'), formed in Old French from gril / grille ('iron gridiron, grate'). The noun descends from Late Latin craticula ('small hurdle or gridiron'), diminutive of Classical Latin cratis ('wickerwork, lattice, hurdle'). Anything toasted over heat—from morning bread (pain grillé) to roasted almonds (amandes grillées)—is described in French as grillé.

history.meaning: gridiron -> to roast on a grid

grillé.notes: Notice how English splits the meanings that French unites in **grillé**: **du pain grillé** is 'toast', **des amandes grillées** are 'toasted/roasted almonds', and **du poisson grillé** is 'grilled fish'.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: grillé

grimper.etymology: Appeared in the 15th century ('to climb up by clutching with hands and feet'), altered with nasalization from Old French griper ('to seize, clutch with claws'), borrowed from Frankish *gripan ('to grip, clutch', cognate with English grip and gripe).

history.meaning: to clutch with hands or claws -> to climb, clamber up

grincement.etymology: Formed in the 16th century from grincer ('to gnash the teeth, creak, grate', from Old French grincier < Frankish *grinitjan 'to snarl, bare or gnash the teeth') + nominal suffix -ment.

history.meaning: gnashing of teeth; harsh grating or squeaking sound

cognates.meaning: flu (borrowed from French in the 18th century)
to seize tightly (from the same Germanic root *gripan); archival 'la grippe' for flu

grippe.etymology: Deverbal noun from Middle French gripper ('to seize, clutch, snatch with claws'), itself borrowed from Frankish or Middle Dutch *gripan / gripen ('to grasp, seize'). Originally meaning 'a sudden seizure, whim, or clawing grasp' (preserved in prendre quelqu'un en grippe, 'to take a sudden dislike to someone'), it became the medical and popular name for epidemic influenza around the 1743 outbreak because the illness 'seizes' sufferers abruptly with chills and aches (reinforcement by Russian khrip 'hoarseness' has also been suggested for later 1782 waves, though the French term predates them).
grippe.notes: Beyond 'avoir la grippe' (to have the flu), note the very common interpersonal idiom 'prendre quelqu'un en grippe' ('to take a strong, persistent dislike to someone').

rootFamily.gloss: to jam, seize up mechanically (originally 'to clutch')
suffering from the flu; jammed (of an engine)

gris.etymology: Inherited from Old French gris ('gray; gray squirrel fur'), borrowed from Frankish *gris ('gray', from Proto-Germanic *grisaz, cognate with Old Saxon gris and German greis 'hoary, gray-haired').

gros.etymology: Inherited from Old French gros ('thick, bulky, coarse, large'), from Late Latin grossus ('thick, coarse, big', attested from the 4th c.), which replaced Classical Latin crassus for physical bulk.

grossesse.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French from grosse ('pregnant', specialized feminine use of gros 'thick, big, swollen', as in femme grosse 'woman big with child') + abstract state suffix -esse (from Late Latin -itia). While Old French grossece could mean both physical bulk and pregnancy, Modern French split the senses cleanly between grosseur ('swelling, size') and grossesse ('pregnancy'). Gros itself derives from Late Latin grossus ('thick, bulky, coarse').

history.meaning: thickness, volume; state of a woman big with child

morphemes.meaning: big, swollen with child (fem. of gros)
abstract noun suffix of state or condition

grossesse.notes: Standard, neutral medical and everyday noun for pregnancy ('congé de maternité', 'test de grossesse'), whereas the adjective for 'pregnant' today is 'enceinte' (archaic 'être grosse' now sounds blunt or rustic).

cognates.meaning: to swell, grow bigger or thicker
large-scale, coarse, total (borrowed from Old French gros)

grossir.etymology: Inherited from Old French grossir ('to become or make thick, swell, increase'), formed from the adjective gros ('thick, large, stout', from Late Latin grossus 'thick, bulky') + second-conjugation inchoative/factitive suffix -ir (inflected with -iss- from Latin inchoative -iscere).

history.meaning: to swell, grow thick or large
to gain weight; to magnify (optically) or exaggerate

grossir.notes: Used intransitively for putting on weight ('j'ai grossi') and transitively for magnifying or making someone look heavier ('ce costume me grossit', 'verre grossissant' = magnifying glass, 'grossir le trait' = caricature/exaggerate).

cognates.meaning: cave, cavern (source of the French word)

grotte.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian grotta ('natural or ornamental cave, subterranean chamber'), inherited via Vulgar Latin *crupta from Classical Latin crypta ('vaulted underground passage, tunnel'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κρύπτη (kryptē, 'concealed vault'), from κρύπτειν (kryptein, 'to hide, conceal'). Popular Romance doublet of the learned ecclesiastical borrowing crypte.

history.meaning: hidden underground vault or covered gallery
natural cave (e.g. Lascaux) or ornamental garden grotto

grotte.notes: Standard French word for any natural rock cave ('la grotte de Lascaux'), whereas 'une cave' is a false friend meaning 'wine cellar / basement'! Notice also 'grotesque', originally naming whimsical Roman frescoes unearthed in buried 'grottos'.

cognates.meaning: knot, cluster, group (source of the French word)
assemblage of people or things (borrowed from French)

groupe.etymology: Borrowed in the late 17th century (1668, first in painting and sculpture theory for a harmonious cluster of figures in a single composition) from Italian gruppo ('knot, tangle, cluster of sculpted figures'), itself from Lombardic (Germanic) *kruppa ('round mass, lump, knot'), from Proto-Germanic *kruppaz ('lump, rounded body'), making it an etymological doublet of native French croupe ('rump, rounded ridge').

history.meaning: rounded mass, knot; cluster of sculpted or painted figures
artistic cluster of figures (17th c.); general assemblage of people or things (18th c.)

groupe.notes: Masculine ('un groupe'); besides a band ('un groupe de rock') or cast ensemble, 'un grand groupe' in French media business refers to a major corporate conglomerate.

grâce.etymology: Inherited/adapted in Old French (grace, 12th c.) from Classical Latin gratia ('favor, esteem, charm, goodwill, thanks; in Christian Latin, divine grace'), derived from gratus ('pleasing, welcome, thankful').

grès.etymology: From twelfth-century Old French gres ('gritstone, sandstone, cobblestone'), borrowed from Old Low Franconian *greot ('coarse sand, gravel'—cognate with Old English greot, modern English grit). Later applied to dense, high-fired stoneware pottery whose vitrified body is as hard as sandstone.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: grès (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: grès

cognates.meaning: armed conflict (borrowed from Old Northern French werre)

guerre.etymology: Inherited from Old French guerre (Old Northern French werre), borrowed via Early Medieval Latin *werra from Frankish *werra ('confusion, tumult, sedition, strife'), from Proto-Germanic *werzō ('confusion, quarrel'; compare Old High German werra 'strife' and German verwirren 'to confuse'). In Western Romance, Germanic *werra completely replaced Classical Latin bellum ('organized war'), partly because bellum collided phonetically with Late Latin bellus ('handsome, fine').

history.meaning: confusion, discord, armed brawl or strife

guerre.notes: Initial 'gu-' represents the standard Central French adaptation [g] of Germanic [w] (whereas Norman kept 'w-', giving English 'war'); source of English loans 'nom de guerre' and 'à la guerre comme à la guerre' ('making do in tough circumstances').

rootFamily.gloss: to wage minor skirmishes, bicker constantly

cognates.meaning: to stay in readiness (from Old Northern French waitier); native cognate 'watch'

guet.etymology: Postverbal noun derived in Old French (guait, guet) from guaitier (Modern French guetter, 'to watch intently, keep lookout'), borrowed from Frankish *wahton ('to keep watch, stand guard'), denominal verb from *wahta ('night watch, guard duty'), from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō ('vigil, watch'), ultimately from PIE *weǵ- ('to be vigorous, awake', whence Latin vigil).

history.meaning: night guard, vigil / to stand watch
lookout, watch (especially in 'faire le guet' and 'avoir l'œil au guet')

guet.notes: Silent final '-t' [gɛ]; thrives in idioms like 'faire le guet' (to keep a lookout, e.g., outside a celebrity's hotel), 'être aux aguets' (to be on high alert), and 'un guet-apens' (an ambush/setup).

rootFamily.gloss: to watch intently for, lie in wait for

guide.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Old Occitan guida or Italian guida ('person who shows the way'), deverbal noun from guidar / guidare ('to guide, direct'), itself from Gothic/Frankish *witan ('to watch over, show the way, direct').

history.meaning: to show the way -> leader, guide
person who leads the way; guidebook, mechanical guide-rail

cognates.meaning: to defend against, ward off (from the same Germanic verb)

guérir.etymology: Inherited from Old French garir / guerir ('to protect, defend, shelter, save from danger', and consequently 'to restore to health'), borrowed from Frankish *warjan ('to defend, ward off, protect'), from Proto-Germanic *warjaną ('to ward off, defend'). Over Middle French, the military/protective senses yielded to garantir and protéger, specializing guérir in medical and emotional recovery.

history.meaning: to protect, save; to cure of illness

guérir.notes: Works both transitively ('ce traitement l'a guéri' = cured him) and intransitively ('la blessure guérit vite' / 'guérir d'un chagrin d'amour' = to heal/recover).

guêpe.etymology: Guêpe developed from reconstructed Gallo-Romance *wespa, a blend of Latin vespa and Frankish *waspa, both meaning wasp. The Académie records twelfth-century wespe.
guêpe.notes: Initial gu- (/ɡ/) betrays Frankish *w- crossing with Latin vespa (just like guerre < *werra and garder < *wardōn); taille de guêpe means a 'wasp waist'.

gymnastique.etymology: Learned Renaissance borrowing (attested 16th century first as an adjective, then substantivized from l'art gymnastique) via Classical Latin gymnasticus from Ancient Greek γυμναστικός (gymnastikos, 'fond of or skilled in bodily exercise'), from γυμνάζειν (gymnazein, 'to train naked, exercise strenuously'), itself derived from γυμνός (gymnos, 'naked, unclad'), because Greek athletes trained unclothed in the palaestra.

history.meaning: pertaining to athletic training performed unclothed
ancient art of bodily exercise and health training
gymnastics, calisthenics; complex mental or logistical juggling

gymnastique.notes: Often clipped to 'la gym' for everyday workouts or PE class; figuratively 'toute une gymnastique' describes intricate scheduling or diplomatic contortions (like juggling two film shoots at once!).

rootFamily.gloss: indoor sports hall / gymnasium (whereas German Gymnasium = 'lycée')

cognates.meaning: to cleanse with water (from the same Germanic root *waskaną)
