Unlike English impressive (formed directly on the Latin stem impress- + -ive), French builds the adjective on the denominal verb stem impressionn-.

history.meaning: to stir emotionally, strike the mind

morphemes.meaning: nominal stem (-ion-) extended for verb derivation

impressionnant.notes: Avoid the classic Anglophone trap *impressif (which does not exist in standard French — always use impressionnant for 'impressive', and sensible/influençable for 'impressionable'!).

impressionner.etymology: Coined in French in the late 18th century (attested around the Revolutionary era) as a denominal first-conjugation verb from impression ('imprint, strong mental effect', < Classical Latin impressiō, from imprimere 'to press into'), differentiating emotional/psychological impact (impressionner) from physical printing on paper (imprimer). In the 19th century it also acquired the photographic/cinematographic sense 'to expose light-sensitive film'.

history.meaning: imprint, strong effect on the senses or mind
to move deeply, dazzle, intimidate; to expose film stock

impressionner.notes: Can mean both positively 'to dazzle/impress' and 'to intimidate/faze': ne te laisse pas impressionner ! ('don't let yourself be intimidated / starstruck!'), a constant pep talk before auditions.

imprimer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin imprimere ('to press into, stamp, imprint on wax or the mind'), compound of in- ('into, upon') + premere ('to press'); applied from c. 1470 to Gutenberg's movable-type printing press.

history.meaning: to press into, stamp a mark upon
to imprint, stamp -> to print books or documents

improbable.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Classical Latin improbābilis ('not deserving approval, objectionable; hard to prove'), composed of privative in- ('not', > im-) + probābilis ('worthy of approval, credible, likely'), from probāre ('to test, approve, prove', itself from probus 'good, upright'). As probable shifted toward statistical/epistemic likelihood in early modern science, improbable came to mean 'unlikely, far-fetched'.
improbable.notes: Huge colloquial vogue in contemporary Parisian French: une histoire improbable or un casting improbable means 'wildly bizarre / surreal / outlandish', not merely statistically unlikely!

improvisation.etymology: Derived in the late 18th century from French improviser + -ation (modeled on Italian improvvisazione), initially describing the Italian art of composing verse or music on the spot. Improviser was borrowed in the 17th century from Italian improvvisare, from improvviso ('unforeseen, extemporaneous'), continuing Classical Latin imprōvīsus ('unforeseen'), from privative in- ('not') + prōvīsus, past participle of prōvidēre ('to foresee').

history.meaning: to compose verse or music extemporaneously

improvisation.notes: In French drama schools and comedy troupes, routinely clipped to l'impro (faire de l'impro, un match d'impro), feminine noun.

improviser.etymology: Improviser is a seventeenth-century borrowing from Italian improvvisare, with the same sense of producing something without prior preparation.

history.meaning: to compose verse or music extempore

improviser.notes: Entered French through Italian poetic and musical performance culture, alongside à l'improviste ('out of the blue').

improvisé.etymology: Past participle adjective of improviser ('to compose on the spot, put together without preparation'), borrowed in the mid-17th century from Italian improvvisare ('to sing or compose extempore'), built on improvviso ('unexpected, offhand') < Classical Latin imprōvīsus ('unforeseen', especially in the ablative phrase dē imprōvīsō 'unexpectedly'), from in- ('not') + prō- ('beforehand') + vīsus ('seen').

history.meaning: to compose poetry or music extempore
performed off the cuff; impromptu, hastily arranged

improvisé.notes: Used neutrally or fondly for spontaneous gatherings (une fête improvisée = 'an impromptu party') as well as ad-libbed lines on set (une réplique improvisée), though un travail improvisé criticizes amateurishness.

imprésario.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-18th century (first attested via descriptions of Italian opera houses by Charles de Brosses and Rousseau) from Italian impresario ('theatrical contractor, opera manager'), formed from impresa ('undertaking, enterprise, theatrical venture') + agentive suffix -ario (< Latin -ārius). Italian impresa is the substantivized feminine past participle of imprendere (< Vulgar Latin *imprehendere, 'to undertake, seize upon'), making imprésario an exact etymological cousin of French entrepreneur!

history.meaning: contractor managing an opera house or theatrical season
tour promoter; (dated/wry) celebrity talent manager or agent

imprésario.notes: Directly evokes Dix pour cent's world: in modern French cinema, professionals call themselves agent (artistique), treating imprésario (spelled with é, plural imprésarios) as charmingly old-school music-hall/tour jargon.

imprévu.etymology: Formed within Classical French (17th century) as an adjective and quickly substantivized as a masculine noun (un imprévu), combining privative in- (assimilated to im-) with prévu, past participle of prévoir ('to foresee, plan for'). Prévoir was remodeled from Latin praevidēre ('to see beforehand', from prae- 'before' + vidēre 'to see') after native French voir. It forms a native French counterpart to the Italian-mediated borrowing improvisé.

history.meaning: unforeseen (adj.); unexpected hitch or last-minute snag (noun)

imprévu.notes: An everyday lifesaver for excusing delays or schedule changes: J'ai eu un imprévu ('Something came up last minute!') or sauf imprévu ('barring anything unforeseen').

impulsif.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century (originally a medical and mechanical term meaning 'driving onward, propelling', as in vertu impulsive) from Medieval Latin impulsīvus, built on Classical Latin impulsus, past participle of impellere ('to push against, drive forward, incite, urge on'), from directional in- ('against, onward', > im-) + pellere ('to push, drive, strike', from PIE *pelh₂-). Its psychological sense ('acting rashly on sudden urge') crystallized in the 19th century.

history.meaning: to strike against, drive onward, incite
exerting a propelling physical or humoral force
prone to acting rashly on sudden emotion or whim

impulsif.notes: Feminine form changes -f to -ve: un acteur impulsif / une actrice impulsive; can also be used as a noun (c'est un grand impulsif).

rootFamily.gloss: to propel; to expel (same pellere/puls- root)

impôt.etymology: Inherited from Old French impost, from Medieval/Classical Latin impositum ('assessment or charge laid upon', substantivized neuter past participle of imponere 'to place upon').

history.meaning: to lay upon -> charge laid upon

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Middle French impost / imposer

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: impôt (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: impôt

impôt.notes: As always in French spelling, the circumflex on **impôt** marks the historical *-s-* of Old French **impost**.

inacceptable.etymology: Borrowed or modeled in the 16th century on Late Latin inacceptābilis ('unwelcome, not worthy of acceptance'), or formed directly in French from privative in- ('not') + acceptable ('worthy of being received'). Acceptable derives from Late Latin acceptābilis, from Classical Latin acceptāre ('to take willingly, receive regularly'), frequentative of accipere ('to take to oneself, receive', from ad- 'to' + capere 'to take').

history.meaning: that cannot or ought not be accepted (of conditions or offers)
intolerable, out of the question (of behavior or contract terms)

morphemes.meaning: to take, receive (Latin cept-, from capere)

inacceptable.notes: Pronounced [inaksɛptabl] with an oral [in] (never nasal [ɛ̃], because in- precedes a vowel!), a signature sharp word in contract standoffs: C'est totalement inacceptable !

inachevé.etymology: Formed in the 18th century from negative prefix in- ('not') + achevé ('finished, completed', past participle of achever 'to bring to a head or end', from à + chef 'head, end').

inattendu.etymology: Formed within French in the late 15th–16th century from the privative prefix in- ('not') + attendu ('awaited, expected'), past participle of attendre ('to wait for, expect'). Attendre evolved from Classical Latin attendere ('to stretch toward, direct one's mind or attention to'), composed of ad- ('to, toward', > at-) + tendere ('to stretch, aim', from PIE *ten- 'to stretch'). French shifted attendere from 'paying attention' to 'waiting/expecting'.

history.meaning: to stretch toward, direct attention to
to wait for, look forward to, expect

inattendu.notes: Pronounced [inatɑ̃dy] (oral [in-] before a vowel); whereas imprévu stresses something unscheduled or disruptive, un succès inattendu or un rebondissement inattendu ('plot twist') often carries welcome surprise.

rootFamily.gloss: to wait for; (s'attendre à) to expect

incarner.etymology: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnāre ('to make flesh'), formed from in- ('into') + carō, carnis ('flesh'); originally theological for Christ's incarnation before extending in the 17th–19th centuries to theater and cinema for embodying a role.

history.meaning: to take bodily form; later, to embody an artistic role

incarner.notes: In cinema and agency parlance (as in Dix pour cent), incarner un personnage is higher-register than jouer un rôle, implying an actor fully inhabits the character rather than merely performing lines.

incertain.etymology: Formed in Old French from negative prefix in- ('not') + certain ('sure, settled'), which derives via Vulgar Latin *certānus from Classical Latin certus ('resolved, determined', originally past participle of cernere 'to sift, decide').
incertain.notes: Placed after a noun (un avenir incertain), it means objectively unpredictable; occasionally before abstract nouns or in literary usage, it stresses vague or wavering quality.

incognito.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century from Italian incognito ('unknown, unrecognized', especially in viaggiare incognito 'to travel anonymously'), continuing Classical Latin incognitus ('unexamined, unknown'), from in- ('not') + cognitus, past participle of cognōscere ('to come to know, recognize').

history.meaning: anonymously, without revealing one's celebrity or rank

morphemes.meaning: Italian masculine singular ending retained in adverbial borrowing

incognito.notes: In French, incognito functions primarily as an invariable adverb (voyager incognito) or masculine noun (garder l'incognito 'to keep a low profile'—essential celebrity vocabulary).

incompréhensible.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Late Latin incomprehensibilis ('that cannot be seized, boundless, unfathomable'), formed from in- ('not') + comprehensibilis ('graspable'), from Classical Latin comprehendere ('to seize together, encompass, grasp with the mind').

history.meaning: to grasp together, seize, take in mentally
unable to be grasped or encompassed; boundless

incompréhensible.notes: Applies both to utterances that cannot be decoded ('unintelligible') and to erratic behavior—like a diva's sudden refusal to shoot—that defies rational explanation.

inconnu.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French (inconu, 14th c.) from negative prefix in- ('not') + connu ('known', past participle of connaître).

history.meaning: unknown, unfamiliar; an unknown person or stranger

cognates.meaning: not conscious (note sense divergence from reckless)

inconscient.etymology: Substantivized in 19th-century philosophy and psychology (reinforced as a calque of German das Unbewusste in Hartmann and Freud) from the adjective inconscient, formed from in- ('not') + conscient, itself from Latin cōnsciēns, present participle of cōnscīre ('to be privy to, be conscious of').

history.meaning: to know jointly, be conscious of (especially guilt)
lacking awareness of one's state or actions

inconscient.notes: Watch the dual usage: as a masculine noun, l'inconscient means the psychological unconscious/subconscious; as an adjective describing a person (il est inconscient !), it usually means 'reckless, irresponsible', not 'knocked out' (évanoui / sans connaissance).

incorporer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Late Latin incorporare ('to embody, unite into one body'), composed of in- ('into') and corporare (from corpus, corporis 'body'). Originally a legal, philosophical, and alchemical term for blending substances into a single body, it became a cornerstone of French culinary terminology for gently folding flour, ground almonds, or beaten egg whites into a batter.

history.meaning: body -> to unite into one body
to incorporate; to fold into a batter

incorporer.notes: In French pastry recipes, **incorporer délicatement** translates the English baking term 'to fold in gently' with a spatula.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: incorporer

cognates.meaning: from the same Late Latin incorporare

incorrigible.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Late Latin incorrigibilis ('incapable of being set straight or amended'), composed of negative in- ('not') + corrigibilis, from Classical Latin corrigere ('to make straight, set right, reform'), itself from com- (intensive) + regere ('to guide, rule').

history.meaning: incapable of amendment or moral reform
impervious to correction; playfully hopeless in habit

incorrigible.notes: Often used with affectionate exasperation in conversational French (Tu es incorrigible !) when someone repeats a charmingly predictable flaw.

incroyable.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French (increable -> incroyable) from negative prefix in- ('not') + croyable ('believable', from croire 'to believe'), replacing Classical Latin incredibilis.

indice.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin indicium ('disclosing sign, token, proof'), related to index ('forefinger, pointer') and indicare ('to point out, make known').

history.meaning: to point out -> revealing sign, clue

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: indice (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: indice

indice.notes: False-friend alert: English *index* (at the back of a book) is **un index** in French too, whereas **un indice** primarily means a 'clue' or 'revealing sign'!

indiquer.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Classical Latin indicare ('to point out, make known, declare'), derived from index, indicis ('pointer, forefinger, informer, sign', from in- + dicare / dicere 'to point out, say').

indiscret.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Late Latin indiscrētus ('unseparated, undistinguished; hence lacking discernment or reserve'), formed from negative in- ('not') + discrētus, past participle of Classical Latin discernere ('to separate, distinguish, judge').

history.meaning: lacking tact; prying into private matters

indiscret.notes: Beyond blabbing secrets, French indiscret very frequently means 'nosy' or 'prying': une question indiscrète is an overly personal question, and Sans être indiscret... means 'If you don't mind my asking...'.

indisponible.etymology: Formed in late 18th-century French (originally legal for property that could not be freely disposed of) from negative prefix in- ('not') + disponible ('at one's disposal, available'), from Medieval Latin disponibilis, derived from Classical Latin dispōnere ('to set in order, arrange, distribute').

history.meaning: to place here and there, arrange, assign
capable of being arranged or freely assigned
legally inalienable; later, busy or out of stock

indisponible.notes: In talent-agency scheduling, être indisponible politely covers everything from conflicting film-shoot dates (dates de tournage) to medical leave, without the bodily illness implied by indisposé ('unwell').

rootFamily.gloss: to arrange, have at one's disposal

industrie.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin industria ('diligence, purposeful activity, assiduity'), derived from industruus, built on archaic Old Latin indu- ('within, inside') + struere ('to pile up, build, contrive'); shifted in the 18th century from personal ingenuity to large-scale organized production.

history.meaning: skill, ingenuity, dexterity in a craft
organized economic production or sector (e.g., cinema)

industrie.notes: While English speakers casually call show business 'the industry', French prefers le métier or le milieu among insiders, reserving l'industrie du cinéma for economic or institutional discussions.

cognates.meaning: for an unlimited or unspecified period

indéfiniment.etymology: Formed in 17th-century French from the adjective indéfini (borrowed from Late Latin indēfīnītus 'unbounded, vague', from in- 'not' + dēfīnītus 'bounded', from fīnis 'boundary') + the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind').

history.meaning: without fixed end or limit, endlessly

indéfiniment.notes: Because indéfini ends in a vowel, -ment attaches directly to the masculine-looking form rather than adding an extra -e- (unlike lentement), yielding /ɛ̃.de.fi.ni.mɑ̃/.

indélébile.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Classical Latin indelebilis ('imperishable, that cannot be erased or blotted out'), compound of in- ('not') + delebilis (from delere 'to wipe out, erase, destroy').

indépendant.etymology: Formed in the 16th century from negative prefix in- ('not') + dépendant ('hanging upon, subordinate'), the present participle of dépendre, borrowed from Classical Latin dēpendēre ('to hang down from, be governed by', from dē- 'down from' + pendēre 'to hang').

history.meaning: to hang down from; figuratively, to rely upon

indépendant.notes: Crucial in French labor and film: un indépendant is a freelancer/self-employed worker, while le cinéma indépendant (or un film indé) designates arthouse or non-major-backed productions.

indésirable.etymology: Coined around 1900 (partly influenced by English undesirable in diplomatic and administrative contexts) from negative prefix in- ('not') + désirable ('worth desiring'), from désirer, which descends from Classical Latin dēsīderāre ('to long for, miss', originally an augural term related to sīdus, sīderis 'star, constellation').

history.meaning: to await from the stars; to long for or miss
unwelcome, persona non grata; harmful side effect

morphemes.meaning: long for, wish (from désirer < Latin dēsīderāre)

indésirable.notes: Used both socially as a noun/adjective (être indésirable sur le plateau 'to be persona non grata on set') and in tech/medicine: courrier indésirable ('spam') and effets indésirables ('side effects').

cognates.meaning: localized tissue necrosis from blocked blood supply

infarctus.etymology: Learned 19th-century medical borrowing from Modern Scientific Latin infarctus ('stuffing, obstruction of a blood vessel'), derived from Classical Latin īnfarctus (variant of īnfartus), past participle of īnfarcīre ('to stuff into, cram'), from in- ('into') + farcīre ('to stuff, cram'—the same root that gave French farcir 'to stuff culinary dishes').

history.meaning: myocardial infarction; everyday French for heart attack

morphemes.meaning: Latin fourth-declension noun ending retained in medical borrowing

infarctus.notes: Unlike English, where 'infarction' sounds strictly clinical, faire un infarctus is standard everyday French for having a heart attack (even hyperbolically: Tu vas me faire faire un infarctus !), and final -s is always pronounced (/ɛ̃.faʁk.tys/).

rootFamily.gloss: to stuff (cooking); to put up with (slang: se farcir)
stuffing; prank or farce (originally 'interlude stuffed into liturgy')

infidélité.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th century) from Classical Latin īnfidēlitās ('unfaithfulness, untrustworthiness, perfidy'), abstract noun from īnfidēlis ('unfaithful, disloyal'), composed of negative in- ('not') + fidēlis ('trustworthy, faithful'), from fidēs ('trust, faith, loyalty').

history.meaning: lack of religious faith; breach of feudal or personal loyalty
romantic unfaithfulness; playful betrayal of a brand or agent

infidélité.notes: Beyond romantic cheating, faire une infidélité à quelqu'un is often used lightly in professional or consumer contexts—for instance, an actor signing a one-off deal with a rival agency or switching cafés.

infiniment.etymology: Formed in Middle French from the adjective infini (borrowed from Classical Latin īnfīnītus 'unbounded, endless, countless', from in- 'not' + fīnītus, past participle of fīnīre 'to bound, limit', from fīnis 'border, end') + the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin ablative mente).

history.meaning: without spatial or numerical limit (chiefly of God)
limitlessly; in polite formulas, exceedingly or very much

infiniment.notes: Merci infiniment ('Thank you so very much') is a staple of polished, gracious French—warm yet refined in high-stakes professional emails and backstage thank-yous.

infirmier.etymology: Evolved from Old and Middle French enfermier, reshaped on Latin spelling from Medieval Latin īnfirmārius ('monastic officer in charge of the infirmary or sickbay'), derived from Classical Latin īnfirmus ('weak, frail, unwell', from in- 'not' + firmus 'strong, steadfast') + agent suffix -ārius.

history.meaning: monk responsible for tending sick brethren
attendant of the sick; modern registered male nurse

infirmier.notes: Unlike English 'nurse' (from Old French norrice 'wet nurse', Latin nūtrīcia), French infirmier literally means 'tender of the infirm', while nourrice / nounou means 'nanny' or 'childminder'.

infirmière.etymology: Feminine counterpart of infirmier, continuing Medieval Latin īnfirmāria ('nun charged with caring for sick sisters in a convent') via Old French enfermiere, re-Latinized with in- after Classical Latin īnfirmus ('frail, sick', from in- 'not' + firmus 'strong') + feminine occupational suffix -ière (Latin -āria).

history.meaning: religious sister tending a convent sickbay

infirmière.notes: Pronounce the final -r clearly with the open vowel /ɛ̃.fiʁ.mjɛʁ/ (contrasting with masculine infirmier /ɛ̃.fiʁ.mje/, where the final -r is silent).

cognates.meaning: to have an effect on character or behavior

influencer.etymology: Coined in late 18th-century French (popularized around the French Revolution) as a denominal verb from influence, itself borrowed in the 13th century from Medieval Latin īnfluentia ('astrological fluid or power flowing from the stars onto human destiny'), from Classical Latin īnfluere ('to flow into', from in- + fluere 'to flow').

history.meaning: to sway or shape someone's decisions or views

morphemes.meaning: abstract noun formant retained in verbal stem

influencer.notes: Spelling watch: before -a or -o, the c takes a cedilla to keep its /s/ sound (nous influençons, il influençait), and modern French uses influenceur / influenceuse for social-media influencers.

info.etymology: Twentieth-century French colloquial apocope (clipping) of information, which entered Old French as informacion from Classical Latin īnfōrmātiō, īnfōrmātiōnis ('outline, mental conception, instruction'), derived from īnfōrmāre ('to give shape to, sketch, educate').

history.meaning: piece of news, tip-off; in plural les infos, the news broadcast

morphemes.meaning: clipped stem of form- (Latin fōrma 'shape, mold')

info.notes: Unlike uncountable English 'info/information', French info is countable and feminine: une info means 'a piece of news / a tip' (J'ai une info exclusive !), and les infos means 'the TV/radio news'.

rootFamily.gloss: computer science, IT (blend of information + automatique)

cognates.meaning: to give facts or knowledge to

informer.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (originally also spelled enformer) from Classical Latin īnfōrmāre ('to give form to, fashion, sketch out; figuratively, to form an idea of or instruct someone's mind'), from in- ('into') + fōrmāre ('to shape', from fōrma 'form, mold').

history.meaning: to shape, mold; to instruct or educate the mind
to give shape to; to instruct or apprise of facts
to notify, apprise; pronominally s'informer, to inquire

informer.notes: Notice the syntax: informer quelqu'un de quelque chose ('to inform someone of something'), whereas reflexive s'informer (sur quelque chose) means 'to find out / look into / keep up with the news'.

cognates.meaning: to steep in liquid; to instill

infuser.etymology: Built in Middle French (15th century) on Latin īnfūsus, the past participle of Classical Latin īnfundere ('to pour into, drench, administer a liquid; figuratively, to impart'), composed of in- ('into') + fundere ('to pour, melt, cast metal').

history.meaning: to pour in or upon, moisten, impart
to steep medicinal plants; to instill divine knowledge
to steep tea or herbs in hot water; figuratively, to sink in

morphemes.meaning: poured (Latin fūsus, past participle of fundere)

infuser.notes: Everyday kitchen phrase: laisser infuser cinq minutes ('let steep for five minutes'); also echoed in the ironic idiom avoir la science infuse ('to act like a know-it-all', literally 'to possess divinely instilled knowledge without studying').

cognates.meaning: drink prepared by steeping; introduction of a new element

infusion.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Classical and Late Latin īnfūsiō, īnfūsiōnis ('a pouring in, watering, drenching'), action noun from īnfundere ('to pour in', from in- 'into' + fundere 'to pour'); specialized in apothecary practice for herbal extracts steeped in boiling water.

history.meaning: act of pouring into or wetting
pouring in of grace; apothecary steeping of herbs

infusion.notes: On French café and restaurant menus, une infusion (or une tisane) specifically means a caffeine-free herbal tea (like verveine or camomille), whereas un thé means true Camellia sinensis tea—and medical 'IV infusion' is une perfusion, not infusion!

ingénieur.etymology: Continues Old French engigneor ('designer and builder of siege engines'), reshaped in the 16th century with initial in- under the influence of Italian ingegnere and Classical Latin ingenium ('innate disposition, cleverness, contrivance', from in- 'in' + gignere 'to beget, bring forth').

history.meaning: inborn nature, talent, cleverness; Late Latin war machine
builder of military siege engines; clever contriver

ingénieur.notes: On French film sets, un ingénieur du son (colloquially l'ingé son) is the production sound mixer; more broadly in France, ingénieur is a prestigious protected academic title from a grande école, with feminine forms une ingénieur or une ingénieure.

ingérence.etymology: Derived in early 19th-century political and legal French from the pronominal verb s'ingérer ('to meddle, thrust oneself into an affair without authority'), borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin īngerere ('to carry into, pour in, force oneself upon'), from in- ('into') + gerere ('to carry, conduct, manage').

history.meaning: to carry into; reflexively, to thrust oneself into, intrude
to meddle uninvited in an estate or another's business

ingérence.notes: High-register word beloved in French politics (le droit d'ingérence 'right of humanitarian intervention') and film-production clashes when producers or agents meddle in a director's creative cut.

initiale.etymology: Substantivized feminine form (supplying lettre, 'initial letter') of the adjective initial, borrowed in the 14th–16th century from Late Latin initialis ('of the beginning'), from Classical Latin initium ('entrance, beginning', from inire 'to go into, enter upon').

history.meaning: first letter of a word or name

cognates.meaning: not based on fairness or right

injuste.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin iniūstus ('unrighteous, wrongful, inequitable, harsh'), composed of negative prefix in- ('not') + iūstus ('righteous, lawful, equitable'), itself derived from iūs, iūris ('right, law, justice').

history.meaning: contrary to law or equity, wrongful, harsh
unrighteous, contrary to divine or human justice

injuste.notes: Because French lacks a separate Germanic word like 'unfair', C'est injuste ! covers everything from grave systemic inequity to everyday complaints ('That's so unfair!').

injustice.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century (notably via Nicole Oresme's translations of Aristotle) from Classical Latin iniūstitia ('unjustness, unfairness, wrongful treatment'), abstract noun built on iniūstus ('unjust', from in- 'not' + iūstus 'lawful, fair', from iūs 'law, right').

history.meaning: wrongful conduct, violation of law or equity
moral or legal iniquity (contrasted with Aristotelian justice)
unfairness; countable, an unfair act or slight

injustice.notes: Used both uncountably (lutter contre l'injustice) and countably (subir une injustice 'to suffer an unfair slight', such as being cut from a film's final edit).

rootFamily.gloss: fairness, accuracy of tone (la justesse de son jeu 'the spot-on truth of her acting')

cognates.meaning: unforgettable (related Vulgar Latin *oblītāre root in uita)

inoubliable.etymology: Formed in 19th-century French from negative prefix in- ('not') + oubliable ('forgettable'), from oublier ('to forget'), which evolved via Old French oblier from Vulgar Latin *oblītāre, a regular first-conjugation verb built on oblītus, past participle of Classical Latin oblīvīscī ('to lose remembrance of, forget').

history.meaning: to let slip from memory, neglect

inoubliable.notes: Note the oral pronunciation: unlike initial in- before consonants (/ɛ̃/), in- before a vowel denasalizes to /in/, so inoubliable is pronounced /i.nu.bli.jabl/.

inquiet.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin inquiētus ('restless, unquiet, agitated, sleepless'), formed from negative prefix in- ('not') + quiētus ('at rest, calm, peaceful'), past-participial adjective of quiēscere ('to rest, keep quiet', from PIE *kʷyeh₁- 'to rest').

history.meaning: worried, anxious about a person or outcome

inquiet.notes: Feminine spelling takes a grave accent rather than doubling the t: inquiète (/ɛ̃.kjɛt/), matching the adjective's masculine pronunciation /ɛ̃.kjɛ/; contrast the learned Latinate borrowing inquiet with inherited French coi ('speechless, still', as in rester coi), which comes from the very same Latin quiētus!

rootFamily.gloss: to worry; reflexively s'inquiéter, to worry (Ne t'inquiète pas !)
serene peace of mind (learned doublet); cf. inherited coi 'silent/still'

inquiéter.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Late Latin inquietare ('to disturb the rest of, agitate, trouble'), derived from Classical Latin inquietus ('restless, unquiet', from in- 'not' + quietus 'at rest, calm').

cognates.meaning: to write or carve words upon a surface

inscrire.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin īnscrībere ('to write in or upon, engrave, title a book, enter a name in a public list'), composed of in- ('in, upon') + scrībere ('to scratch, draw lines, write'); reshaped on the inherited conjugation pattern of écrire.

history.meaning: to carve or write upon; to enter in an official register
to engrave on stone; to record formally in a roll
to enter a name, enroll, sign up (for a course, casting, or festival)

inscrire.notes: False-friend nuance: while English 'inscribe' sounds solemn or epigraphic, French inscrire (and reflexive s'inscrire à) is the everyday verb for signing up, enrolling at school/gym, or submitting a film to Cannes.

rootFamily.gloss: registered, enrolled; listed heritage site (monument inscrit)

insecte.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin īnsectum (used in plural animalia īnsecta by Pliny the Elder, literally 'notched or segmented creatures'), a morphological calque of Aristotelean Ancient Greek ἔντομον (éntomon, 'cut into pieces', whence 'entomology'), from the neuter past participle of Latin īnsecāre ('to cut into, notch', from in- + secāre 'to cut').

history.meaning: to cut into, notch; creature with a segmented body (calquing Greek éntomon)
small segmented creeping or flying creature
six-legged arthropod; colloquially any small bug

morphemes.meaning: cut, notched (Latin sectum, past participle of secāre)

insecte.notes: Etymological gem: Latin in-sectum ('cut into') mirrors Greek en-tomon piece-for-piece because insects look nearly 'cut into sections' between head, thorax, and abdomen—sharing the secāre ('cut') root of section and sécateur ('pruning shears').

rootFamily.gloss: section, division (shared Latin secāre / sect- root)

insignifiant.etymology: Formed in French from the privative prefix in- ('not') and signifiant, present participle of signifier ('to mean, to signify'), from Latin significāre ('to show by signs, indicate'), itself from signum ('mark, sign') + facere ('to make').

cognates.meaning: too small or unimportant to be worth consideration

history.meaning: devoid of clear meaning; of little importance

insignifiant.notes: In modern spoken French, used both of trivial sums or details (un détail insignifiant) and dismissively of an unremarkable person.

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

insistance.etymology: Derived from insister ('to persist, press upon') with the action-noun suffix -ance, modeled on Latin īnsistentia ('persistence, steadfastness'), from īnsistere ('to stand upon, press on').

cognates.meaning: the fact or quality of insisting on something

history.meaning: act of dwelling firmly on a request or gaze

insistance.notes: Common in the phrase avec insistance ('pointedly, persistently', e.g., regarder quelqu'un avec insistance).

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

insister.etymology: Borrowed from Latin īnsistere ('to stand upon, set foot on, press upon, persevere'), formed from in- ('on, upon') + sistere ('to cause to stand, place firmly'), a reduplicated formation from the Proto-Indo-European root *steh₂- ('to stand').

cognates.meaning: to demand something forcefully, not accepting refusal

history.meaning: to stand upon, press on, persevere
to dwell on a point in argument; to urge

insister.notes: Takes the preposition sur before a noun (insister sur un détail) and pour before an infinitive or que-clause.

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

inspecteur.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–17th century from Classical Latin inspectorem (nominative inspector, 'one who looks into, examiner, overseer'), agent noun from inspicere, inspectum ('to look into, examine closely', from in- + specere 'to look').

history.meaning: official examiner, school or police inspector

inspection.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin inspectio, inspectionis ('a looking into, examination, review'), action noun from inspicere (past participle inspectus, 'to look into, examine closely'), composed of in- ('into, upon') and specere ('to look at, observe'). It shares the Indo-European visual root *spek- with spectacle, respect, and perspective.
inspection.notes: The verb corresponding to **une inspection** is **inspecter**, and the official who carries it out is **un inspecteur / une inspectrice**.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: inspection

inspectrice.etymology: Feminine counterpart of inspecteur ('inspector, overseer'), formed with the Latinate feminine agent suffix -trice.

inspiration.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–13th century from Late Latin inspirationem (nominative inspiratio, 'a breathing into; divine or creative breathing into the soul'), from Classical Latin inspirare ('to blow or breathe into, kindle', from in- + spirare 'to breathe').

history.meaning: inhalation of air; creative or divine impulse
drawing in of breath; sudden creative idea or inspiration

inspirer.etymology: Borrowed from Latin īnspīrāre ('to blow into, breathe upon, instill into the mind'), composed of in- ('into') + spīrāre ('to breathe, blow').

cognates.meaning: to fill someone with the urge or ability to do or feel something; to breathe in
to inhale; to arouse creative thought

history.meaning: to blow into, breathe upon, inspire
to infuse divine breath or creative thought into the soul

inspirer.notes: Retains both the physiological sense ('inhale', opposite of expirer) and the figurative creative sense, plus pronominal s'inspirer de ('to draw inspiration from').

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

installer.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Medieval Ecclesiastical Latin installare ('to place a canon or dignitary solemnly in his choir stall'), formed from in- ('in') + stallum ('choir stall', from Frankish *stal 'standing place, stall'); later broadened to settling people or fitting equipment into place.

history.meaning: to seat in a choir stall, induct into office
to induct -> to set up in a place, install equipment

instant.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–16th century from Classical Latin instantem (nominative instans, 'standing near, pressing closely, present, immediate'), present participle of instare ('to stand upon, press closely, be at hand', from in- + stare 'to stand').

instinct.etymology: Borrowed from Latin īnstīnctus ('instigation, impulse, inward prompting'), noun use of the past participle of īnstinguere ('to incite, impel, goad on'), from in- ('toward, on') + *stinguere ('to prick, goad'), from PIE *(s)teyg- ('to prick, be sharp').

cognates.meaning: an innate, typically fixed pattern of behavior; natural intuition

instinct.notes: The final -ct is silent in standard French pronunciation (/ɛ̃.stɛ̃/).

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

institutionnel.etymology: Formed in French from institution ('established body or practice', from Latin īnstitūtiō, from īnstituere 'to set up, establish') + the relational adjective suffix -el (Latin -ālis).

morphemes.meaning: to set up, place (from Latin statuere)
noun suffix of action or result

cognates.meaning: of, in, or like an institution or official organization
relating to public or corporate institutions

history.meaning: pertaining to political or corporate institutions

institutionnel.notes: In media and agency contexts (as in Dix pour cent), un film institutionnel means a corporate promotional video.

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

institutrice.etymology: Feminine form of instituteur ('founder, instructor, primary school teacher'), borrowed from Latin īnstitūtor / īnstitūtrīx ('one who establishes or trains'), from īnstituere ('to set up, instruct, educate').

morphemes.meaning: to set up, instruct (from Latin statuere)

institutrice.notes: Although officially replaced in administrative terminology by professeure des écoles in 1990, institutrice (and colloquial instit') remains universal in everyday French.

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

insulter.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Latin īnsultāre ('to leap upon, bound at, scoff at, abuse insolently'), frequentative of īnsilīre ('to leap into or upon'), from in- ('upon') + salīre ('to leap, jump').

morphemes.meaning: to leap repeatedly (from Latin salīre 'to jump')

cognates.meaning: to speak to or treat with disrespect or scornful abuse

history.meaning: to leap upon, scoff at, revile
to attack suddenly; to abuse verbally

insulter.notes: In elevated literary French, insulter à quelque chose ('to be an affront to', e.g., insulter au malheur) preserves the older indirect construction.

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

insupportable.etymology: Formed from the privative prefix in- ('not') and supportable ('bearable, endurable'), or borrowed from Late Latin īnsupportābilis ('unbearable'), from supportāre ('to carry from beneath, endure').

cognates.meaning: unable to be endured or justified

insupportable.notes: False friend note: French supporter commonly means 'to tolerate, put up with', so insupportable is the standard everyday word for 'unbearable, obnoxious'.

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

intact.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin intactus ('untouched, unharmed, undefiled, whole'), compound of negative prefix in- ('not') + tactus, past participle of tangere ('to touch').

intellectuel.etymology: Borrowed from Late and Medieval Latin intellēctuālis ('pertaining to the understanding or mind'), derived from intellēctus ('perception, discernment, intellect'), from intelligere ('to understand, choose between'), from inter- ('between') + legere ('to gather, choose, read').

cognates.meaning: relating to the intellect; a person of high mental pursuits
relating to the mind; scholar or thinker

history.meaning: pertaining to the mind; (from 1898) public thinker

intellectuel.notes: Often shortened colloquially to intello in modern French.

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

intelligent.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Latin intelligēns (stem intelligent-), present participle of intelligere ('to understand, perceive, discern'), composed of inter- ('between') + legere ('to pick out, choose, read').

cognates.meaning: having or showing intelligence, quick of mind

intelligent.notes: Frequently used antiphrastically in spoken French (C'est malin ! / C'est intelligent, ça ! — 'Real smart!').

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

intense.etymology: Borrowed from Latin intēnsus ('stretched tight, strained, vigorous'), past participle of intendere ('to stretch out, strain, direct one's attention'), from in- ('toward, upon') + tendere ('to stretch').

cognates.meaning: of extreme force, degree, or strength

intense.notes: Pairs with adverbs like très or extrêmement to describe emotions, gazes, traffic, or work rhythms.

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

intensité.etymology: Formed in French from intense ('stretched tight, acute') + the abstract noun suffix -ité (after Latin -itās), replacing earlier medieval intension.

morphemes.meaning: abstract noun suffix of quality or degree

cognates.meaning: the measurable amount of a property, or quality of being intense

history.meaning: degree of physical or emotional force

intensité.notes: Used both technically (electrical current, sound volume) and figuratively (l'intensité dramatique d'une scène).

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

intention.etymology: Borrowed in twelfth-century Old French (entencion, reshaped to intention) from Classical Latin intentiō, intentiōnem ('stretching, mental effort, attention, purpose'), action noun of intendere ('to stretch out toward, aim one's mind at', from in- + tendere 'to stretch', Proto-Indo-European *ten-).

morphemes.meaning: stretch, aim (supine stem of Latin tendere)

history.meaning: to stretch toward -> mental direction, purpose

intention.notes: Built on the image of drawing a bowstring toward a target (intendere arcum); anchors avoir l'intention de ('to intend to').

intentionné.etymology: Participial adjective formed in French from intention ('purpose, aim', from Latin intentiō 'a stretching out, effort, attention, purpose') + -é.

history.meaning: disposed toward a certain motive (bien/mal intentionné)

intentionné.notes: Rarely stands alone without bien or mal; contrast with intentionnel ('deliberate, intentional').

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

interdiction.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical Latin interdictionem (nominative interdictio, 'prohibition, legal restraining order'), derived from interdicere ('to interpose by speech, forbid by decree', from inter- + dicere 'to say, pronounce').

interdire.etymology: Inherited and partly reshaped from Classical Latin interdīcere ('to interpose by speech, forbid by decree, prohibit'), composed of inter- ('between') + dīcere ('to say, pronounce authoritatively').

history.meaning: to place under ecclesiastical ban; to forbid

interdire.notes: Conjugates like dire except in the 2nd person plural present indicative and imperative: vous interdisez (unlike vous dites).

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

interdit.etymology: From the past participle of interdire ('to forbid'), reflecting Latin interdictus ('prohibited by decree; placed under legal ban'), past participle of interdīcere.
interdit.notes: Note the dual meaning: 'forbidden' (sens interdit, c'est interdit) and 'taken aback, speechless' (Il est resté tout interdit).

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

interférence.etymology: Borrowed in the early 19th century from English interference (coined in optics by Thomas Young in 1801), itself derived from Old French s'entreferir ('to strike each other'), from entre- (Latin inter- 'between, mutually') + ferir (Latin ferīre 'to strike').

cognates.meaning: the combination of wave crests/troughs; unwanted meddling or radio noise

rootFamily.gloss: to strike (archaic, in sans coup férir)

history.meaning: mutual interaction of light waves; meddling

interférence.notes: Old French ferir survives in modern French only in the fossilized idiom sans coup férir ('without striking a blow, effortlessly').

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

international.etymology: Borrowed from English international, coined in 1780 by the philosopher and jurist Jeremy Bentham (in An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation) from Latin inter- ('between, among') + national (from nātiō 'birth, nation').

cognates.meaning: existing, occurring, or carried on between two or more nations

international.notes: Frequently used in the phrase à l'international ('internationally, in foreign markets').

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

internet.etymology: Borrowed from American English Internet (shortened from internetwork / internetworking in 1974 DARPA TCP specifications by Vint Cerf, Yogen Dalal, and Carl Sunshine), from inter- ('between, interconnected') + net (clipped from network).

cognates.meaning: the global system of interconnected computer networks

internet.notes: Often used without a definite article after sur (chercher sur Internet / sur internet), though l'internet is also standard.

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

interphone.etymology: Compound formed from the prefix inter- ('between, mutual') and the Greek-derived combining form -phone (from Ancient Greek φωνή phōnē 'voice, sound'), modeled on téléphone and mid-20th-century English trade name Interphone.

cognates.meaning: internal telephone or intercom system (esp. in aviation)

history.meaning: two-way building entry buzzer or intercom

interphone.notes: In apartment buildings in France, l'interphone is the audio entry buzzer, while the keypad code panel beside it is le digicode.

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

interrompre.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin interrumpere ('to break apart between, break off, cut short'), compound of inter- ('between') + rumpere ('to break', source of French rompre).

history.meaning: to break off in the middle

interrupteur.etymology: Adapted in nineteenth-century physics and electrical engineering from Latin interruptor ('one who breaks off', from interrumpere 'to break between, interrupt'): a switch opens or closes a gap in the electrical current.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: interrupteur (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: interrupteur

interruption.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Latin interruptiō (stem interruptiōn-, 'a breaking off, gap'), derived from interrumpere ('to break apart, break off, sever'), from inter- ('between') + rumpere ('to break, burst').

morphemes.meaning: noun suffix of action or state

cognates.meaning: the action of interrupting or state of being interrupted

interruption.notes: Very common in sans interruption ('non-stop, continuously').

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

intervenir.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Latin intervenīre ('to come between, interrupt, step in, mediate'), formed from inter- ('between') + venīre ('to come').

cognates.meaning: to come between so as to prevent or alter a result
to step in, take part, audit
to step in, speak up, attend

history.meaning: to enter a legal dispute; to step in or take the floor

intervenir.notes: Like venir, it is conjugated with the auxiliary être in compound tenses (Je suis intervenu).

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

interview.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th century from English interview ('a journalistic meeting to question a public figure'), which was itself borrowed in the 16th century from Middle French entrevue ('a face-to-face meeting'), verbal noun of s'entrevoir ('to see one another briefly'), from entre- + voir (Latin vidēre).

morphemes.meaning: sight, seeing (from Old French veue, from voir)

cognates.meaning: a formal consultation or journalistic questioning

history.meaning: journalistic questioning of a public figure

interview.notes: In France, une interview (feminine) is used for press/media interviews, whereas a job interview is un entretien d'embauche (and Quebec French prefers entrevue for both).

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

intime.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Latin intimus ('inmost, deepest, most secret, most close in friendship'), superlative formed on the preposition/adverb intus / in ('inside, within') with the archaic superlative suffix -timus (compare ultimus, optimus).

history.meaning: closely bound in friendship; private, innermost

intime.notes: In French legal language, l'intime conviction du juge/jury is the fundamental standard of inner moral certainty required to convict.

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

intimider.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin intimidāre ('to frighten, strike fear into'), formed from in- ('into') + timidus ('fearful, timid'), from timēre ('to fear, be afraid').

cognates.meaning: to make shy or fearful, daunt

history.meaning: to cow an adversary; to make shy or self-conscious

intimider.notes: In everyday French, Tu m'intimides often means simply 'You make me feel shy/self-conscious' rather than 'You are threatening me'.

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

intimité.etymology: Formed in French from intime ('inmost, close, private', from Latin intimus) + the abstract noun suffix -ité.

morphemes.meaning: abstract noun suffix of state or quality

intimité.notes: Crucial translation note: French has no single direct cognate for English 'privacy'; l'intimité (or la vie privée) is the natural equivalent.

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

intéressant.etymology: Present participial adjective of intéresser ('to concern, hold the attention of'), from Latin interesse ('to be between, make a difference, concern').

cognates.meaning: arousing curiosity or interest; holding the attention

history.meaning: to be between, make a difference, concern

intéressant.notes: In commercial contexts, un tarif intéressant or une offre intéressante specifically means 'a good deal / competitive price'.

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

intéresser.etymology: Derived in the 16th century from the noun intérêt (earlier interest, from Latin interest 'it makes a difference, it concerns', 3rd person singular present of interesse, from inter- 'between' + esse 'to be'), replacing an older sense 'to damage, prejudice'.

cognates.meaning: to excite the curiosity or attention of

history.meaning: to be between, be of importance
to give a financial stake in; to engage the attention of

intéresser.notes: Pronominal s'intéresser à quelque chose means 'to take an interest in something'.

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

intéressé.etymology: Past participial adjective and noun from intéresser ('to give a stake in; to hold the attention of'), ultimately from Latin interesse ('to be between, be of importance').

cognates.meaning: showing curiosity; having a personal stake

history.meaning: having a financial stake in an affair

intéressé.notes: Watch placement and syntax: être intéressé par quelque chose = 'to be interested in something'; être intéressé (with no complement, describing character) = 'to be self-serving / mercenary' (opposite of désintéressé).

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

intérieur.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Classical Latin interiorem (nominative interior, 'inner, Situated further inside'), comparative built on intra / inter ('within').

history.meaning: inner, internal (adj.); the inside, domestic life or home (noun)

intérim.etymology: Borrowed from Latin interim ('in the meantime, meanwhile'), an adverb formed from inter- ('between') + the archaic locative/accusative demonstrative suffix -im (compare olim, statim).
intérim.notes: Pronounced /ɛ̃.te.ʁim/ (with final -m sounded); gives rise to intérimaire ('temp worker; acting/interim').

sources.title: TLFi — Trésor de la langue française informatisé

intérêt.etymology: Borrowed and adapted from Medieval Latin interesse ('compensation for loss, legal stake'), a substantivized use of the Classical Latin infinitive interesse ('to be between, differ, be of importance'), from inter- ('between') + esse ('to be'). In Middle French, interest acquired a final -t by analogy with past participles before shifting to intérêt as preconsonantal s dropped under a circumflex.

history.meaning: to be between, make a difference, matter
legal compensation for damages or loss

intérêt.notes: In agency and business French, 'avoir intérêt à faire quelque chose' is an idiomatic warning or strong recommendation ('you had better do something'), while the plural 'intérêts' often refers specifically to financial interest or stakes.

inutile.etymology: Learned borrowing via Old French inutile from Classical Latin inūtilis ('useless, unprofitable, unserviceable, harmful'), formed with the privative prefix in- ('not') attached to ūtilis ('useful, serviceable'), itself derived from the deponent verb ūtī ('to use, make use of').
inutile.notes: Frequently used in brisk spoken French in the elliptical construction 'Inutile de + infinitive' ('No point in...', 'Needless to...'), e.g., 'Inutile d'insister' ('There's no point pushing it').

inventer.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Late and Medieval Latin inventāre, a frequentative verb built on inventum, the supine stem of Classical Latin invenīre ('to come upon, discover, find out, contrive'), composed of in- ('in, upon') + venīre ('to come'). Semantic focus shifted from accidental discovery ('coming upon') to deliberate creation or fabrication.

history.meaning: to discover, create, fabricate a story

inventer.notes: In everyday conversation and showbiz banter, 'inventer' very often means 'to make up out of thin air'—as in 'Je n'invente rien !' ('I'm not making this up!') or 'Il n'a pas inventé l'eau chaude' ('He's not the sharpest tool in the shed').

inverse.etymology: Borrowed as a learned term from Classical Latin inversus ('turned upside down, transposed, reversed'), the past participle of invertere ('to turn upside down, turn about, pervert'), composed of in- ('in, onto') + vertere ('to turn'). First used as an adjective in logic and mathematics before nominalizing as 'l'inverse' ('the opposite').

history.meaning: inverted in order or direction; the opposite

inverse.notes: As a masculine noun ('l'inverse'), it pairs constantly with 'au contraire' and the set phrase 'à l'inverse (de)' ('conversely / unlike').

inverser.etymology: Formed within Modern French (19th century) as a regular first-conjugation verb directly from the adjective and noun inverse ('opposite, inverted'), itself borrowed from Classical Latin inversus, past participle of invertere ('to turn upside down, reverse', from in- + vertere 'to turn'), largely displacing older invertir in everyday senses.

history.meaning: inverted, opposite in direction or order
to reverse the order, direction, or roles of

inverser.notes: Common in idiomatic agency negotiations such as 'inverser les rôles' ('to turn the tables / swap roles') and 'inverser la tendance' ('to reverse the trend').

investir.etymology: Initially borrowed from Medieval Latin investīre ('to clothe in robes of office, endow with feudal possession, surround'), from Classical Latin investīre ('to clothe, cover,deck'), from in- ('in') + vestīre ('to dress', from vestis 'garment'). In the 20th century, its modern financial and psychological sense ('to commit capital or personal energy') was reinforced by semantic borrowing from Italian investire and English invest.

history.meaning: to clothe with insignia of office, grant feudal tenure
to endow with authority; besiege; commit capital or effort

investir.notes: Conjugates as a regular second-group (-ir / -issant) verb; reflexively, 's'investir dans un rôle / un projet' means 'to throw oneself wholeheartedly into a role or project'.

investissement.etymology: Derived in Middle French from investir ('to surround, besiege, endow') + nominal suffix -ment (< Latin -mentum), originally designating a military encirclement or feudal investiture. In the early 20th century, under the influence of English investment (and psychoanalysis via German Besetzung for emotional cathexis), it gained its primary modern senses of financial capital outlay and personal dedication.

history.meaning: feudal conferral; military encirclement of a fortress
allocation of financial capital; deep personal or emotional commitment

investissement.notes: Unlike English 'investment', French 'investissement personnel' very naturally means 'personal dedication / emotional commitment' to a film shoot or artistic work without sounding overly corporate.

invisible.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (12th century, originally used in theological contexts of God and spiritual beings) from Classical and Christian Latin invīsibilis ('unseen, incapable of being seen'), formed from negative in- ('not') + vīsibilis ('visible'), itself from vīsus, past participle stem of vidēre ('to see').
invisible.notes: Colloquially, 'devenir invisible' or 'jouer l'homme invisible' refers to someone dodging calls or vanishing when agents or producers are trying to track them down.

invitation.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin invītātiōnem (nominative invītātiō, 'an invitation, incitement, challenge, entertainment'), noun of action from invītāre ('to invite, treat, summon, challenge'), a verb of uncertain Indo-European root (possibly related to *weie- 'to pursue, wish for').

history.meaning: summons to a feast, inducement, challenge
act of inviting a guest or formal card/request to attend

morphemes.meaning: action or concrete result noun suffix

invitation.notes: In Parisian cinema and VIP culture, 'une invitation' (often shortened in speech to 'une invit'', pronounced with a final /t/) specifically means a complimentary pass or guest-list spot for a premiere or gala.

inviter.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–16th century from Classical Latin invitare ('to ask as a guest, entertain, summon, allure').

history.meaning: to ask as a guest, treat, induce
to invite, treat to a meal or outing

invité.etymology: Substantivized past participle of inviter ('to invite'), designating a guest who has been invited to a home, meal, or event.

inédit.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th–18th century from Classical Latin ineditus ('not yet published or made known'), compound of negative prefix in- ('not') + editus, past participle of edere ('to give out, publish').

cognates.meaning: trap (from Old French trappe, same Germanic root)

irrattrapable.etymology: Formed within Modern French from the assimilated negative prefix ir- (< Latin in- 'not' before r-) + rattrapable ('recoverable, capable of being caught again'), from rattraper ('to catch up with again, recoup, make up for'), itself composed of re- + attraper ('to catch in a trap', from à + trappe, borrowed from Frankish *trappa 'trap, snare').

history.meaning: to catch again, overtake, make good a mistake
impossible to catch up with or salvage

irrattrapable.notes: Pronounced with a geminated (lengthened) /ʀ/ sound in careful speech ([iʀ.ʀa.tʀa.pabl]); used both for lost time on a film schedule and for a PR blunder beyond repair.

rootFamily.gloss: to catch up with, salvage, make up for
catch-up session, make-up exam, remedial fix

irremplaçable.etymology: Formed in 18th–19th-century French from the assimilated negative prefix ir- (< Latin in- 'not') + remplaçable ('replaceable'), derived from remplacer ('to put back in the place of, succeed'), composed of re- + en- + place ('place, open square', via Vulgar Latin *plattea from Classical Latin platēa 'courtyard, broad street', from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα 'broad way') + -able.

history.meaning: to take the place of, substitute for

irremplaçable.notes: Note the mandatory cedilla (ç) before -able to preserve the soft /s/ sound of 'remplacer', and remember the wry French maxim 'Personne n'est irremplaçable' ('No one is irreplaceable').

irresponsable.etymology: Created at the end of the 18th century from the assimilated privative prefix ir- (< Latin in- 'not') + responsable ('answerable, accountable'), itself derived in Medieval/Middle French legal usage from Latin respōnsus, past participle of respondēre ('to answer, promise in return, be answerable', from re- 'back' + spondēre 'to pledge solemnly').

history.meaning: to pledge in return, answer a legal claim

irresponsable.notes: Used both as an adjective ('un comportement irresponsable') and as a cutting noun ('C'est un irresponsable !' — 'He's completely reckless!'), as well as in law for diminished capacity ('pénalement irresponsable').

isolant.etymology: Present participle of isoler ('to isolate, insulate', borrowed in the 17th c. from Italian isolato 'made like an island, detached', from isola < Latin insula 'island'); used in physics and building since the 19th century for an electrical, thermal, or acoustic insulator.

history.meaning: cutting off like an island -> insulating material or adjective

isolement.etymology: Derived in 18th-century French from isoler ('to set apart like an island, separate') + action suffix -ment. The verb isoler was borrowed from Italian isolato ('detached, standing free like an island', past participle of isolare), from isola ('island'), inherited from Latin īnsula ('island; detached city block').

history.meaning: standing detached like an island; to separate
state of social, physical, or political solitude

morphemes.meaning: island, set apart (from Italian isola < Latin īnsula)

isolement.notes: Watch the false-friend split with French 'isolation': 'isolement' refers to human solitude, quarantine, or social seclusion, whereas French 'isolation' almost always means thermal or acoustic insulation in buildings!

itinéraire.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin itinerarium ('road map, travel account'), derived from Classical Latin iter, itineris ('walk, road, journey', related to ire 'to go').

cognates.meaning: from the same Late Latin stem

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: itinéraire (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: itinéraire

itinéraire.notes: On French road signs, **Itinéraire bis** marks a scenic or secondary detour route avoiding holiday traffic!

ivoire.etymology: Inherited through Old French ivurie / ivoire from Latin eboreus ('made of ivory', from ebur 'ivory'—itself borrowed via Egyptian ābu 'elephant, ivory').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: ivoire (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: ivoire

ivre.etymology: Inherited through Old French ivre from Vulgar Latin *ebrius, reflecting Classical Latin ēbrius ('drunk, sated with wine, intoxicated'), an ancient adjective whose antonym sōbrius ('sober') shares the same obscure second element (traditionally connected to a root for drinking or wine-vessels). Regular Gallo-Romance palatalization and lenition reduced ēbrius to ivre.
ivre.notes: Slightly elevated or literary when meaning literally 'drunk' (colloquial speech favors 'bourré' or 'saoul'), except in strong idioms like 'ivre mort' ('blind drunk') and figurative expressions like 'ivre de joie / de colère' ('beside oneself with joy / rage').

cognates.meaning: already (cognate with first element ja < iam)

jadis.etymology: Univerbation of the Old French adverbial phrase ja a dis ('there are already days, days ago'), composed of three inherited Latin words: Old French ja ('already, formerly' < Classical Latin iam 'already, now'), a ('there is/are', 3rd singular of avoir < Latin habet), and dis ('days', oblique plural of di < Classical Latin diēs 'day').

history.meaning: days ago, a while back, formerly
in bygone times, once upon a time

morphemes.meaning: days (Old French dis < Latin diēs, fused with a < habet)

jadis.notes: The final -s IS pronounced (/ʒa.dis/); literary or playfully nostalgic in register ('comme jadis', 'les stars de jadis'), contrasting with neutral everyday 'autrefois' or 'avant'.

jalousie.etymology: Formed in 12th-century Old French from jalous (modern jaloux, 'ardent, possessive, jealous') + suffix -ie (or reinforced by Old Occitan gelosia in courtly love lyric). Ultimately traces back through Late Latin zēlōsus ('full of zeal') to Late Latin zēlus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, 'ardor, emulation, fierce rivalry').

history.meaning: passionate possessiveness in love, envy, suspicion

morphemes.meaning: abstract quality or state noun suffix

jalousie.notes: Besides romantic jealousy and fierce professional rivalry among actors, 'une jalousie' also denotes a louvered shutter through which one can peek out unseen—borrowed into English as 'jalousie window'.

cognates.meaning: jealous (from Old French) and zealous (learned doublet)

jaloux.etymology: Inherited (likely mediated or shaped by Old Occitan troubadour lyric gelos) from Late Latin zēlōsus ('full of zeal, passionately ardent'), derived from zēlus ('zeal, emulation, jealousy'), a borrowing from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, 'eager rivalry, fervor'), where Vulgar Latin initial z- palatalized to /dʒ/ > /ʒ/ in Gallo-Romance.

history.meaning: full of religious or passionate zeal
ardent, fearful of losing a beloved, envious

jaloux.notes: Feminine is 'jalouse' (/ʒa.luz/); note the idiom 'faire des jaloux' ('to make people green with envy') and the literary construction 'être jaloux de son indépendance' ('to guard one's independence fiercely').

jamais.etymology: Jamais combines Old French ja ('already, ever', from Latin iam) + mais ('more', from Latin magis): literally 'ever more'. Paired with ne, it came to mean 'never'.
jamais.notes: Without *ne* in questions (*Si jamais...*), it can still mean 'ever'.

jambe.etymology: Inherited from Old French jambe ('leg'), from Late Latin gamba ('hock or fetlock joint of a horse; leg'), borrowed from Ancient Greek kampe ('a bending, curve, joint of a limb'), which displaced Classical Latin crus in Western and Central Romance.

jardin.etymology: Jardin comes from Gallo-Roman *hortus gardinus ('enclosed garden'), built on Frankish *gardo ('enclosure, yard', cognate with English 'yard' and 'garden'). Old French jardin passed straight into English 'garden' via Norman.

cognates.meaning: garden (via Anglo-Norman) and yard (native Germanic cognate)

jardiner.etymology: Formed in Middle French from jardin ('garden') + verbal ending -er. The noun jardin descends through Old French jardin / jart from Gallo-Romance *hortus gardīnus ('enclosed kitchen garden'), derived from Frankish *gardo (oblique stem *gardin-, 'enclosure, fenced yard'), from Proto-Germanic *gardô ('enclosure').

history.meaning: to cultivate or tend a garden

jardiner.notes: While 'jardiner' means tending plants, theatre and cinema insiders should also recall 'côté jardin' ('stage right' from the audience's perspective, literally 'côté du jardin des Tuileries' in historic Paris theatres, opposite 'côté cour').

rootFamily.gloss: garden; stage left (actor's view) / audience's left

jaune.etymology: Inherited from Old French jalne / jaune ('yellow'), from Classical Latin galbinus ('greenish-yellow, pale yellow'), derived from galbus ('yellow').

jazz.etymology: Borrowed in 1917–1918 (initially often as jazz-band) from American English jazz, popularized in France when African American military bands such as James Reese Europe's regiment performed during World War I. The American English musical term grew out of early 20th-century West Coast and New Orleans slang jazz / jasm ('pep, vigor, spirited energy'), whose ultimate origin remains debated.

history.meaning: syncopated African American musical genre and ensemble

jazz.notes: Masculine noun ('le jazz') pronounced /dʒaz/ in French; Paris quickly became a second homeland for jazz in the interwar years and New Wave film scores (e.g., Miles Davis's soundtrack for Louis Malle's 'Ascenseur pour l'échafaud').

rootFamily.gloss: to play in a jazz style (colloquial/rare)

je.etymology: Je descends from Late Latin eo, itself continuing Classical Latin ego, I. The Académie dates the French pronoun to the eleventh century. Its earlier Latin forms help explain a history that is not obvious from the very short modern word.

jeter.etymology: Inherited from Old French geter / jeter ('to throw, hurl, cast out'), from Vulgar Latin *jectare, altered from Classical Latin jactare ('to throw, toss repeatedly'), frequentative of jacere ('to throw'), which displaced jacere across Romance.

jeu.etymology: Inherited from Old French gieu / jeu ('play, sport, game, jest'), from Classical Latin jocus ('joke, jest, pastime, verbal play'), which in Popular Latin replaced ludus for every kind of game and play.

history.meaning: play, game, deck or set, acting, mechanical clearance

jeudi.etymology: Jeudi developed from Latin Jovis dies, day of Jupiter. The Académie records the twelfth-century form juesdi.

rootFamily.gloss: fellow compounds preserving Old French di 'day'

jeudi.notes: Without an article, jeudi means 'on Thursday' (one specific occasion); with the definite article, le jeudi means 'on Thursdays / every Thursday'.

jeune.etymology: Inherited from Old French jovene / jeune ('young'), from Classical Latin juvenis ('young, youthful; a young person', from PIE *h2yuh1en- 'young', cognate with English young).

history.meaning: young, in the prime of youth

jeunesse.etymology: Inherited through Old French jovenece / jonesce from Vulgar Latin *iuvenitia ('state of being young, youth'), formed as an abstract noun from Classical Latin iuvenis ('young, young person', cognate with English young via Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁en-) + abstract suffix -itia (replacing Classical Latin iuventūs and iuventa).

morphemes.meaning: abstract state or collective noun suffix (< -itia)

jeunesse.notes: Used both uncountably ('sa jeunesse', 'la jeunesse dorée') and appositively without a preposition in publishing/cinema ('un film jeunesse', 'littérature jeunesse' — 'children's / YA film or books').

rootFamily.gloss: to make or look younger, rejuvenate

cognates.meaning: joy (from Old French) and gaudy (from Latin gaudium)

joie.etymology: Inherited through Old French joie from Late/Vulgar Latin gaudia (feminine singular), a reanalysis of the Classical Latin neuter plural gaudia ('delights, pleasures, expressions of gladness'), plural of gaudium ('inward joy, delight'), derived from gaudēre ('to rejoice'). Initial g- before au regularly palatalized to j- in northern Gallo-Romance.
joie.notes: Often used ironically in the plural in workplace complaints—'les joies du métier !' ('the joys of the job!')—as well as in the internationally famous expression 'la joie de vivre'.

cognates.meaning: to join (from Old French joindre) and yoke (PIE cognate)

joindre.etymology: Inherited via Old French joindre from Classical Latin iungere ('to yoke together, harness, unite, attach'), formed with a nasal infix from Proto-Indo-European *yewg- ('to yoke, join'; cf. Latin iugum 'yoke', Sanskrit yuj-). Phonologically, syncope of *iung're triggered an epenthetic -d- between palatalized n and r, yielding joindre.

history.meaning: to attach, enclose, reach someone by phone

joindre.notes: Irregular verb on the -oindre/-eindre pattern (je joins, nous joignons, j'ai joint); essential in agency phone tag ('Impossible de le joindre !' — 'I can't get hold of him!') and email attachments ('pièce jointe', abbreviated PJ).

joint.etymology: Inherited from Old French joint ('junction, seam, articulation'), substantivized past participle of joindre ('to join'), from Classical Latin junctus (past participle of jungere 'to yoke together, join').

history.meaning: point where two parts meet, mortar seam, watertight gasket or seal

joli.etymology: Inherited from Old French jolif (nominative jolis, originally 'festive, merry, gay, amorous', later 'pretty, pleasing'), probably derived from Old Norse jol ('Yule, midwinter pagan feast', English Yule) + Romance suffix -if.

joue.etymology: Inherited via Old French joe / joue from Gallo-Romance and Western Romance *gauta ('cheek'), a pre-Latin word generally traced to Gaulish (probably connected to Gaulish *gaba 'crop, throat, jowl'), which displaced Classical Latin gena ('cheek') and bucca ('puffed cheek' > French bouche 'mouth'). Initial g- before au regularly palatalized to j- in French.
joue.notes: Do not confuse the feminine noun 'la joue' ('cheek') with forms of the verb 'jouer' ('il joue' — 'he plays/acts'); common idioms include 'tendre l'autre joue' ('to turn the other cheek') and 'coucher en joue' ('to aim a rifle at').

rootFamily.gloss: slap on the cheek (archaic/literary) or jawpiece

jouer.etymology: Inherited from Old French joer ('to play, sport, make merry'), from Vulgar Latin *jocare, active reshaping of Classical Latin deponent jocari ('to jest, joke'), derived from jocus ('jest, game').

history.meaning: to jest -> to play a game or instrument
to play, act a role, gamble

joueur.etymology: Inherited through Old French jooür / joueor, reflecting Late/Vulgar Latin iocātōrem (nominative iocātor, 'jester, joker, player'), agent noun from Classical Latin iocārī ('to jest, joke'), which replaced Classical lūdere ('to play') across Romance, derived from iocus ('jest, joke, pastime').
joueur.notes: Feminine is 'joueuse'; used as an adjective ('Tu es joueur !' / 'Elle est très joueuse'), it describes someone playful who loves taking cheeky risks, bluffing, or raising the stakes in a negotiation.

rootFamily.gloss: to play, gamble, act a role
game, acting style (le jeu d'acteur), stake

jour.etymology: Inherited from Old French jorn ('day, daylight'), from Late/Vulgar Latin diurnum (sc. tempus, 'daytime'), neuter of Classical Latin diurnus ('of the day, daily', derived from dies 'day').

jour-là.etymology: Hyphenated noun-plus-enclitic unit inside ce jour-là ('that day'), combining jour ('day, daylight', inherited via Old French jorn from Late Latin diurnum, neuter of Classical Latin diurnus 'of the day', from diēs) with the distal adverbial particle -là ('there, then', inherited from Latin illāc 'that way, over there').

morphemes.meaning: there, that one (distal pointer < Latin illāc)

cognates.meaning: that day (parallel formation from diurnum + illāc)

jour-là.notes: Always preceded by ce (ce jour-là) and joined by a hyphen, contrasting a specific past or future day with ce jour-ci / aujourd'hui.

journal.etymology: Inherited from Old French jornal ('daily; day's work or land plowed in a day; book of daily accounts'), from Classical Latin diurnalis ('daily'), derived from diurnus ('of the day'); came to mean a daily chronicle and then a printed newspaper (17th c.).

journaliste.etymology: Coined at the end of the 17th century (initially for editors and reviewers of scholarly periodicals) from journal ('daily chronicle, newspaper') + agentive suffix -iste (< Latin -ista < Greek -ιστής). The noun journal was substantivized in Old French from the adjective journal ('daily'), inherited from Late Latin diurnālis ('daily'), from Classical Latin diēs ('day').

history.meaning: daily account book, chronicle, periodical newspaper
contributor to a periodical; news reporter

journaliste.notes: Epicene noun—identical in masculine and feminine singular ('un journaliste' / 'une journaliste')—and remember that French 'journal' means 'newspaper' or 'TV news bulletin' ('le journal de 20 heures'), not merely an academic journal or diary.

journée.etymology: Journée is derived from jour, day. The twelfth-century form journee already belongs to this French word family.

history.meaning: day -> a day's span, day's travel or work
day (in its duration or lived experience)

cognates.meaning: working day, stage of a journey
borrowed from Old French journee ('a day's travel')!

journée.notes: English 'journey' originally meant literally 'one day's travel' (from Old French journee); in modern French Bonne journée! wishes someone a pleasant whole day ahead.

cognates.meaning: jewel (diminutive of gioia, from Old French)

joyau.etymology: Evolved from Old French joiel / joel ('precious gift, trinket, ornament', plural joiaus > joyaux, whence refashioned singular joyau). It goes back to Gallo-Romance *iocāle ('plaything, delightful object', neuter of Latin iocālis from iocus 'game, jest'), phonetically and semantically reshaped early on by association with joie ('joy, delight' < Latin gaudia).

history.meaning: cut precious stone, crown jewel, masterpiece

joyau.notes: Plural takes -x ('des joyaux'); higher in register than everyday 'bijou' ('piece of jewelry'), 'joyau' denotes either crown jewels / museum-grade gems or figuratively a crowning treasure ('le joyau du cinéma français').

judo.etymology: Borrowed at the start of the 20th century from Japanese 柔道 (jūdō, literally 'the gentle or yielding way'), coined in 1882 in Tokyo by educator Kanō Jigorō as a modern pedagogical and competitive refinement of jūjutsu, from Sino-Japanese jū (柔 'gentle, supple, pliant' < Middle Chinese *nyuw) + dō (道 'way, path, spiritual discipline' < Middle Chinese *dawX).

history.meaning: gentle way; modern martial art and philosophy
Japanese grappling martial art and Olympic sport

judo.notes: Pronounced /ʒy.do/ in French (unlike /dʒaz/ for 'jazz', initial j- here uses standard French /ʒ/); judo is exceptionally popular in France, and a practitioner is called 'un/une judoka'.

rootFamily.gloss: judo practitioner (epicene in French, or fem. judokate)
jujitsu, traditional Japanese grappling art (柔術)

juge.etymology: Inherited via Old French juge from Classical Latin iūdicem (nominative iūdex, 'judge, magistrate, arbiter'), an ancient root compound formed from iūs ('law, legal right, sacred formula') + the zero/full grade of dīcere ('to speak, point out, pronounce'), literally 'one who declares the law'.

history.meaning: one who pronounces the law; magistrate, umpire

juge.notes: Epicene in contemporary French ('un juge' / 'une juge', or formally 'Madame la juge'), and central to the classic idiom 'être juge et partie' ('to have a conflict of interest', literally 'to be both judge and litigant').

rootFamily.gloss: judicial, pertaining to courts (learned cousin from iūdiciārius)
