jugement.etymology: Formed in earliest Old French (11th century) from jugier (modern juger, 'to judge, render a verdict', < Latin iūdicāre) + the action/result noun suffix -ment (< Latin -mentum), supplanting Classical Latin iūdicium in inherited French vocabulary.

history.meaning: court ruling; critical opinion, discernment, appraisal

morphemes.meaning: action, verdict, or faculty noun suffix

jugement.notes: Used both for an official court decision ('rendre un jugement') and for interpersonal evaluation ('porter un jugement de valeur' — 'to make a value judgment', 'erreur de jugement' — 'lapse in judgment').

cognates.meaning: to judge (from Old French jugier) and adjudicate (learned doublet)

juger.etymology: Inherited through Old French jugier from Classical Latin iūdicāre ('to examine judicially, pass sentence, decide, deem'), denominative verb built on iūdex, iūdicis ('judge', from iūs 'law, right' + dīcere 'to declare'). Syncope of unstressed i in *iūdicāre led via palatalization to jugier and modern juger.

history.meaning: to pass legal sentence, decide, deem
to try in court, sentence, form an opinion

juger.notes: Spelling-change verb: insert a silent 'e' after 'g' before 'a' or 'o' ('nous jugeons', 'il jugeait') to keep the soft /ʒ/ sound; idiomatic 'juger bon de faire...' means 'to see fit to do...'.

juin.etymology: Inherited through Old French juin from Classical Latin Iūnius (short for mēnsis Iūnius, 'month of Juno'), traditionally derived from the Roman goddess Iūnō, protectress of marriage and women, or linked to the Roman gens Iūnia. Regular Gallo-Romance palatalization and nasalization reduced Iūnium to juin.

history.meaning: month sacred to Juno, fourth month of the early Roman calendar
sixth month of the Julian year

juin.notes: Like all French month names, juin is masculine and never capitalized in running prose; notice the nasal vowel [ʒɥɛ̃] with the semivowel [ɥ], distinct from jeune or jeun.

rootFamily.gloss: of Jupiter / jovial; mythologically paired with Juno

jumeau.etymology: Inherited from Old French jumel (feminine jumele, 'twin'), altered with labial rounding of the initial vowel from Classical Latin gemellus ('twin-born, paired'), diminutive of geminus ('twin').

junior.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin iūnior ('younger'), the contracted comparative of iuvenis ('young, youthful'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yéwHō. Re-energized in 19th- and 20th-century French via British and American English in sports, corporate, and agency hierarchies.

history.meaning: younger member of a monastery or family

junior.notes: In Parisian talent agencies and corporate offices (as in Dix pour cent, e.g., agent junior), junior stays invariable in gender (une agente junior) though it takes -s in the plural according to most modern usage.

rootFamily.gloss: young person; young (inherited doublet of iuvenis)

jupe.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century via Southern Italian or Sicilian jupa from Arabic jubba (جُبَّة, 'long woollen outer garment with wide sleeves'). In Old and Middle French jupe designated a man's quilted tunic or doublet worn under armor before shifting in the 17th century to a woman's waist-down skirt.

history.meaning: long outer garment or robe with wide sleeves
long tunic or quilted doublet worn by men or women
woman's skirt hanging from the waist

jupe.notes: Colloquial expressions include être pendu aux jupes de sa mère ('to be tied to one's mother's apron strings') and courir le jupon ('to womanize').

cognates.meaning: member of a sworn body (via Anglo-Norman)

jurer.etymology: Inherited through Old French jurer from Classical Latin iūrāre ('to swear an oath, take an oath, conspire'), a denominal verb formed from iūs, iūris ('law, right, sacred formula'). Like English 'to swear', it developed both the solemn legal-religious sense and the sense of uttering profanities.

history.meaning: to utter a sacred formula, take a solemn oath
to pledge by oath; to blaspheme

jurer.notes: Beyond 'to swear an oath' (je te jure!) and 'to curse', jurer avec means 'to clash aesthetically' (of colors or styles: cette veste jure avec le décor).

juridique.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin juridicus ('relating to the administration of justice, judicial'), compound of jus, juris ('law, right') + dicere ('to say, pronounce').

history.meaning: relating to the law, legal, juridical

jus.etymology: Inherited from Old French jus ('broth, gravy, sap or liquid squeezed from meat, herbs, or fruit'), from Classical Latin jus ('broth, soup, gravy, sauce', from PIE *yewHs- 'broth', homonymous in Latin with jus 'law').

history.meaning: broth, soup, vegetable or meat juice
gravy, squeezed fruit or vegetable juice; (colloquial) electric current

jusqu'à.etymology: Compound preposition combining jusque—inherited via Old French jusque / dusque from Late Latin dē ūsque ('all the way from/to', reinforcing Classical Latin ūsque 'continuously, all the way')—with the preposition à (< Latin ad, 'to, toward'). Initial d- palatalized or assimilated to j- in Old French (influenced by joste or inde ūsque).

history.meaning: all the way → continuously up to
up to (space), until (time), even to the point of

morphemes.meaning: all the way, continuously (from dē ūsque)

jusqu'à.notes: Before a vowel, jusque obligatorily elides its final -e (jusqu'à demain, jusqu'ici); when followed by a clause rather than a noun, use jusqu'à ce que + subjunctive.

jusque.etymology: Jusque descends from Latin inde usque ('from there all the way to'), blending de + usque ('all the way, continuously') into Old French jusque, jusques.
jusque.notes: Usually elides before *à* or *au*: **jusqu'à demain**, **jusqu'au deuxième étage**.

cognates.meaning: there, in that place (cognate of là)

jusque-là.etymology: Compound adverb formed within French from jusque ('all the way to', from Late Latin dē ūsque) and the locative adverb là ('there', inherited from Classical Latin illāc 'that way, over there'). Used first spatially ('as far as that spot') and rapidly extended to temporal boundaries ('up to that moment').

history.meaning: all the way + by that way / over there
as far as that place; up to that time

jusque-là.notes: Retains its hyphen (unlike jusqu'ici, which elides without a hyphen). Very frequent in conversational pivots: Jusque-là, tout va bien ('So far, so good'—immortalized by the film La Haine).

juste.etymology: Juste was borrowed from Latin justus, just or right. The adjective is recorded from the twelfth century; adverbial uses such as just or only developed alongside it.

history.meaning: fair, accurate, tight-fitting (adj.); just, only, barely (adv.)

rootFamily.gloss: precisely, as a matter of fact

juste.notes: Notice c'est un peu juste ('it's a bit tight'—of clothes, budget, or catchable train time), alongside chanter juste ('to sing in tune').

justement.etymology: Formed in Old French (justement, 12th c.) from the adjective juste ('just, righteous, exact', from Classical Latin justus < jus 'right, law') + adverbial suffix -ment.

history.meaning: justly, rightfully -> preciesly, as it happens

justice.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing in early Old French (justise, justice) from Classical Latin iūstitia ('righteousness, equity, administration of law'), derived from iūstus ('just, lawful, upright'), itself built on iūs ('law, right'). Anglo-Norman exported the French word directly into Middle English.

history.meaning: moral equity; feudal jurisdiction and court authority

justice.notes: In French, la justice often denotes the entire judicial system or courts (traduire en justice = 'to prosecute / take to court'), whereas de justesse means 'barely, by a hair's breadth'.

rootFamily.gloss: subject to the jurisdiction of the courts, litigant

cognates.meaning: cosmic retribution; personal luck or vibe

karma.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century (via English and Orientalist scholarship) from Sanskrit karman (कर्मन्, nominative karma, 'act, deed, ritual performance, moral consequence of actions'), from the verbal root kṛ- ('to do, make'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷer- ('to do, build'). Secularized in late 20th-century colloquial French to mean personal luck or fate.

history.meaning: deed, ritual act; causal moral consequence across rebirths
Buddhist and Hindu doctrine of moral causation
cosmic payback, personal luck or aura in everyday speech

karma.notes: Masculine noun (un bon / mauvais karma); in Parisian showbiz banter, avoir un mauvais karma playfully means being jinxed or paying the price for past arrogance.

kiffer.etymology: Formed in late 20th-century French slang by adding the verbal suffix -er to kif ('hashish; keen pleasure'), borrowed in the mid-19th century via Algerian and Moroccan Arabic kīf (from Classical Arabic kayf, كَيْف, 'state, condition, well-being, pleasurable mood'). Broadened in youth and urban French to mean 'to really enjoy, love, or have a crush on'.

history.meaning: how, state of mind → well-being, marijuana mixture
cannabis mixture; carefree bliss or favorite thing
to thoroughly enjoy, dig, or fancy someone

kiffer.notes: Informal/colloquial register (familier) ubiquitous across generations today (Je kiffe ce scénario !); the noun c'est mon kif means 'that's my thing / guilty pleasure'.

kilo.etymology: Conversational clipping (attested since the early 19th century) of kilogramme ('one thousand grams'), formed in 1795 from the metric prefix kilo- (an adaptation of Ancient Greek khilioi 'thousand').

kilomètre.etymology: Coined in France in 1795 during the Revolutionary establishment of the metric system from kilo- (adapted from Ancient Greek khílioi, χίλιοι, 'thousand') and mètre (from Greek métron, μέτρον, 'measure'). Exported from French into nearly every modern language worldwide.

history.meaning: metric unit of length equal to 1,000 meters

morphemes.meaning: measure, unit of length (from Greek métron)

kilomètre.notes: Often clipped in speech to bornes (faire cent bornes); figuratively, un texte au kilomètre means bloated copy written in bulk without care.

rootFamily.gloss: mileage, total distance in kilometers; figuratively overly long

cognates.meaning: study of body movement (shares Greek kínēsis)

kiné.etymology: Everyday apocope (clipping) of kinésithérapeute ('physical therapist') or kinésithérapie ('physical therapy'), scientific compounds coined in French from Ancient Greek kínēsis (κίνησις, 'movement, motion', from kineîn 'to move'—the same root as cinéma!) and therapeía (θεραπεία, 'medical care, healing').

history.meaning: therapeutic rehabilitation through movement; practitioner thereof

morphemes.meaning: clipped from kinési- (Greek kínēsis, movement) + thérapeute

kiné.notes: Un(e) kiné is the universal everyday French word for a physical therapist (aller chez le kiné); remarkably, kiné and cinéma share the exact same Greek root kineîn ('to move').

rootFamily.gloss: kinetic, relating to motion (doublet via c-)

la mort.etymology: Combines the feminine definite article la (< Classical Latin illa, 'that') with mort, inherited through Old French mort from Classical Latin mors, mortis ('death'), an abstract -ti- stem from Proto-Indo-European *mŕ̥tis ('dying, death'), built on the verbal root *mer- ('to die, disappear').

history.meaning: death (often personified as feminine in Romance)

morphemes.meaning: feminine singular definite article (< Latin illa)

la mort.notes: Feminine in French (just like in Latin mors), explaining why Death is personified as a woman (la Grande Faucheuse) in French cinema and theater. Idiomatically, à mort in slang means 'totally, intensely' (je kiffe à mort).

rootFamily.gloss: mortal; deadly; in slang, 'hilarious' or 'dead boring'

cognates.meaning: lake (borrowed from Old French), loch (Celtic cognate)

lac.etymology: Inherited via Old French lac from Classical Latin lacus ('lake, basin, tank, vat'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lókus ('pond, pool, body of standing water'), cognate with Old Irish loch and Old English lagu.
lac.notes: Pronounced [lak] with an audible final [k]. Famous idiom: Il n'y a pas le feu au lac ! ('There's no rush / no need to panic!', gently teasing calm Swiss pacing around Lake Geneva).

rootFamily.gloss: gap, hiatus, deficiency (learned borrowing from lacūna)

cognates.meaning: cord, ornamental openwork fabric (from Old French laz)

lacet.etymology: Diminutive formed in Old French (lacet, 'small cord or snare') from las / laz (Modern French lacs, 'snare, love-knot'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *lacium for Classical Latin laqueus ('noose, snare, trap'). Specialized for cords threaded through eyelets on bodices and shoes.

history.meaning: cord, noose → thin cord for lacing garments or trapping game
shoelace; hairpin bend on a mountain road

morphemes.meaning: cord, loop (Old French laz / lacs < laqueus)

lacet.notes: False friend alert: French lacet means 'shoelace' (or 'switchback road': route en lacets), whereas English 'lace' (delicate fabric) is dentelle in French!

rootFamily.gloss: to lace up (shoes or a corset)
to embrace, clasp in one's arms; to intertwine

laine.etymology: Inherited from Old French laine ('sheep's wool'), from Classical Latin lana ('wool, fleece, down', from PIE *h2wlh1neh2 'wool', cognate with English wool).

laisser.etymology: Inherited from Old French laissier ('to let go, leave behind, permit'), from Classical Latin laxare ('to loosen, slacken, release, unbind', from laxus 'loose, slack'), which took over the semantic field of Classical sinere and relinquere.

lait.etymology: Lait comes from Popular Latin *lacte (Classical Latin lac, lactis, 'milk'). The Latin -ct- cluster regularly palatalised to -it in French (compare noctem -> nuit, factum -> fait).
lait.notes: Gives **le laitier** ('milkman, dairy') and **café au lait**.

laitier.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from lait ('milk', from Vulgar Latin *lactem < Classical Latin lac, lactis) + suffix -ier.

history.meaning: dairy farmer or milkman (noun); relating to milk or dairy (adj.)

laiton.etymology: From Old French laton / laiton ('brass, copper-zinc alloy'), attested across medieval Western Romance and Mediterranean trade (compare Arabic lāṭūn 'copper/brass'), reshaped in French under the influence of lait ('milk') because of the pale sheen of freshly polished brass.

cognates.meaning: medieval sheet brass (from Old French laton)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: laiton (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: laiton

lame.etymology: Inherited from Old French lame ('thin metal plate, tombstone slab, sword blade'), from Classical Latin lamina (syncopated to lamna in spoken Latin, 'thin plate of metal, wood, or stone, blade').

history.meaning: thin sheet or plate of metal, blade
thin strip or slat, knife or razor blade, microscope slide, ocean wave

lampadaire.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin lampadārium ('chandelier, lampstand') and Late Latin lampadārius ('torchbearer slave'), derived from Classical Latin lampas, lampadis ('torch, luster'), itself from Ancient Greek lampás (λαμπάς, 'torch, beacon'), from lámpein ('to shine'). Adopted for urban streetlamps and tall floor lamps.

history.meaning: torch-bearing attendant; branched lamp-holder in churches
ornamental lamp-post, streetlamp, or tall standard floor lamp

lampadaire.notes: Covers both an outdoor municipal streetlight (réverbère / lampadaire) and an indoor freestanding floor lamp (lampadaire halogène).

lampe.etymology: Lampe comes via Late Latin lampada from Ancient Greek lampás, lampádos ('torch, oil lamp', from lámpein 'to shine').
lampe.notes: **Lampe de chevet** = bedside lamp; **lampe de poche** = pocket flashlight.

cognates.meaning: to hurl, set in motion (from Anglo-Norman lancer)

lancer.etymology: Inherited through Old French lancier ('to hurl a spear, fling, lunge') from Late Latin lanceāre ('to wield or throw a lance'), a denominal verb from Classical Latin lancea ('light spear, javelin'), itself likely of Celtiberian or Gaulish origin. Broadened to throwing any projectile and metaphorically launching projects or careers.

history.meaning: light javelin → to brandish or hurl a spear
to hurl weapons, charge on horseback, fling
to throw; to launch a product, film, or career; to quip

lancer.notes: Essential agency/cinema verb: lancer un acteur ('to launch an actor's career'), lancer le tournage ('to kick off filming'), and se lancer ('to take the plunge'). Spelling takes ç before a/o (nous lançons).

rootFamily.gloss: launch (of a film, campaign, or rocket)
momentum, impetus, run-up (être sur sa lancée)

cognates.meaning: system of human speech (from Old French langage)

langage.etymology: Derived in Old French (langage, 12th c.) from langue ('tongue, language', < Classical Latin lingua) + the collective/functional suffix -age (< Late Latin -āticum). Old French exported langage both to Middle English ('language') and to neighboring Romance languages (Italian linguaggio, Spanish lenguaje).

history.meaning: anatomical tongue; speech, idiom of a people
faculty of speech, discourse, manner of speaking

langage.notes: Crucial Saussurean and everyday distinction: une langue (feminine) is a specific national tongue (le français, l'anglais), whereas le langage (masculine) is the human faculty of communication, register (langage familier), body language (langage corporel), or programming language.

lanterne.etymology: Lanterne comes from Latin lanterna ('lantern, torch'), itself an early borrowing (via Etruscan) from Ancient Greek lamptḗr ('torch, lamp', from lámpein 'to shine').
lanterne.notes: Shares its ultimate Greek root 'to shine' with **la lampe**.

cognates.meaning: young rabbit, leveret (likely same Pre-Roman Iberian base)

lapin.etymology: Attested in late Middle French (lapin, 15th c.), gradually displacing Old French conil / connin (< Latin cunīculus, 'rabbit', which fell taboo due to homophony with con). Its ultimate origin is debated: most philologists link it via southwestern Gallo-Romance or Iberian *lapparo ('burrow-dweller / young rabbit', from a pre-Roman substrate *lappa 'flat stone, hollow') or an expressive alteration influenced by laper ('to lap').

history.meaning: rocky hollow or young rabbit sheltering under stones
wild or domesticated rabbit (eclipsing taboo connin)

lapin.notes: Two classic French idioms: poser un lapin à quelqu'un ('to stand someone up on a date or meeting') and chaud lapin ('randy fellow'). Furthermore, the word lapin is famously taboo backstage on French theater sets and ships (called l'animal aux longues oreilles instead)!

rootFamily.gloss: rabbit hutch; cramped apartment building (cage à lapins)

large.etymology: Inherited from Old French large ('generous, bountiful; broad, wide'), from Classical Latin largus ('abundant, copious, liberal in giving'), which in Gallo-Romance displaced latus as the ordinary adjective for physical width.

history.meaning: generous -> wide, broad; the open sea (le large)

cognates.meaning: for the most part (root borrowed from Old French large)

largement.etymology: Formed in Old French (largement, 'generously, abundantly, broadly') from the adjective large (< Classical Latin largus, 'abundant, bountiful, wide') + the adverbial suffix -ment (< Latin ablative mente, 'with a [wide/bountiful] mind'). Retains the Latin core of 'abundance' alongside spatial width.

history.meaning: munificently, generously; across a wide expanse
widely; amply, with plenty to spare, more than enough

largement.notes: In everyday spoken French, largement most often means 'easily, with plenty to spare' rather than merely 'mostly': On a largement le temps ('We have more than enough time') or Ça suffit largement ! ('That's plenty!').

rootFamily.gloss: wide, broad; generous (not a synonym of 'big' = grand!)
to widen, broaden; to release from custody

largeur.etymology: Formed in the 15th century from large ('wide, broad') + abstract suffix -eur (replacing Old French largece / laize in the dimensional sense).

larguer.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century as a nautical term ('to slacken or let go a sail or mooring rope') from Provençal or Spanish/Portuguese largar ('to loosen, let go, set sail'), descending from Vulgar Latin *largāre, built on Classical Latin largus ('ample, loose, generous'). Extended in modern colloquial French to dropping cargo and 'dumping' a romantic partner or inconvenient client.

history.meaning: to slacken ropes, unfurl sails, head out to open sea
to cast off moorings; to airdrop; colloquially to dump someone

morphemes.meaning: loose, open sea (from largus via Romance largar)

larguer.notes: Nautical imagery persists in larguer les amarres ('to cast off moorings / break free'), while colloquially Il m'a larguée means 'He dumped me' and être complètement largué means 'to be totally out of one's depth / lost'.

larme.etymology: Inherited via Old French lairme / larme from Classical Latin lacrima (archaic Old Latin dacrima), descending from the same Indo-European root as English tear.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: larme (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: larme

larme.notes: Colloquially in French cafés and kitchens, **une larme de lait / de miel** also means 'just a tiny drop' in a cup.

laser.etymology: Borrowed around 1960 directly from American English laser, an acronym coined in 1957–1959 by physicist Gordon Gould for 'Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation', following the model of maser (1954). Assimilated into French as a masculine noun and invariable appositive modifier.

history.form: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation → laser
history.meaning: optical maser producing a coherent monochromatic light beam
laser device or beam in physics, surgery, and entertainment

laser.notes: Pronounced [lazɛʁ] with a voiced [z]. When used as an adjective in French (des imprimantes laser, la chirurgie laser), laser remains invariable in both gender and number.

cognates.meaning: laser tag (genuine English idiom corresponding to French pseudo-anglicism)

laser game.etymology: Late 20th-century French commercial pseudo-anglicism (generalized from franchise brand names in the 1990s) combining laser ('Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation') and English game (from Old English gamen, 'joy, amusement, sport', < Proto-Germanic *gamaną). English speakers normally say 'laser tag' rather than 'laser game'.

history.meaning: indoor recreational laser-tag arena or match

laser game.notes: Classic French faux anglicisme (like un footing for 'a jog' or un parking for 'a parking lot'): un laser game refers both to the venue and the activity that Anglophones call 'laser tag'.

rootFamily.gloss: video gamer (related English borrowing in French)

latte.etymology: Inherited from Old French late ('thin wooden strip or lath supporting roof tiles'), borrowed from Frankish *latta ('lath, thin split board', cognate with English lath and German Latte).

history.meaning: wooden roof lath, bed slat, ruler

laver.etymology: Inherited from Old French laver ('to wash, cleanse with water'), from Classical Latin lavare ('to wash, bathe', from PIE *lewh3- 'to wash', cognate with English lather and lye).

le.etymology: The article le and feminine la continue object-case forms of Latin demonstratives ille and illa. The direct-object pronouns le and la share that historical source, although articles and pronouns do different jobs today.

history.form: le (f. la, pl. les; elided l')

rootFamily.gloss: mandatory contractions with de and à

le.notes: Elides to l' before any vowel or mute h (l'ami, l'hôtel), and doubles as the direct-object pronoun 'him/it' before verbs (je le vois).

cognates.meaning: lush greenness (borrowed via Old French verdure)

le vert.etymology: Nominalized masculine phrase combining the definite article le (< Latin illum) with vert, inherited through Old French vert from Vulgar Latin *virdis (syncopated from Classical Latin viridis, 'green, fresh, vigorous, blooming'), derived from virēre ('to be green, flourish, be full of sap').

history.meaning: green in hue; fresh, unseasoned, youthful
the color green; nature, countryside; ecological politics

morphemes.meaning: masculine singular definite article (< Latin illum)

le vert.notes: Just as lapin is taboo in French theaters, le vert (green costumes) is traditionally considered bad luck onstage because Molière supposedly collapsed in green—while donner le feu vert means 'to green-light a project' and se mettre au vert means 'to retreat to the countryside to recharge'.

rootFamily.gloss: to turn green; to grow green again (reverdir)

lecture.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Medieval Latin lectura ('act of reading, public reading or commentary on a text'), derived from Classical Latin legere, lectum ('to gather, read').

history.meaning: act of reading or lecturing on a text

lendemain.etymology: Classic case of French article agglutination: Old French formed endemain ('the following day') from en (< Latin in) + demain ('tomorrow', < Late Latin dē māne, 'early in the morning'). Because l'endemain was constantly heard with the elided article l', Middle French speakers reinterpreted the l- as part of the noun itself, producing le lendemain ('the-the-next-day').

history.meaning: at daybreak, early in the morning; tomorrow
the day following a given day
the next day; aftermath or future consequences (les lendemains)

morphemes.meaning: tomorrow (< dē māne, in the morning)

lendemain.notes: Learner trap: demain = 'tomorrow' (measured from today, 'now'), whereas le lendemain = 'the next day' (measured from a past or future reference point: Le lendemain de la première, la presse était dithyrambique). Un lendemain de veille means 'a hangover'.

rootFamily.gloss: two days later, the day after the next day

lent.etymology: Inherited/borrowed from Classical Latin lentus ('pliable, flexible, sticky, tenacious; hence sluggish, slow-moving, calm').

lentement.etymology: Formed in Old French (lentement, 12th c.) from the feminine adjective lente ('slow') + adverbial suffix -ment.

lentille.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin lenticula ('lentil'), diminutive of Classical Latin lens, lentis ('lentil'). In the seventeenth century, physicists named curved optical glass 'lentilles' (and English 'lenses' directly from Latin lens) because a biconvex glass disc is shaped just like a lentil seed.

cognates.meaning: from Old French lentille / directly from Latin lens

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: lentille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: lentille

lentille.notes: In French, eyeglass lenses in frames are usually called **les verres de lunettes**, while contact lenses and camera lenses are **des lentilles**.

lequel.etymology: Univerbation in Old French (li quels / lequel) of the definite article le ('the', < Latin illum) + interrogative/relative adjective quel ('which, what kind of', < Classical Latin qualis).

cognates.meaning: to pay the costs of (borrowed from French défrayer)

les frais.etymology: Plural noun phrase combining les (< Latin illōs) with frais, plural of archaic singular frai ('damage, fine, outlay'), inherited via Old French frait / frais from Medieval Latin fractum ('breach of peace, damage fine, expense incurred'), neuter past participle of Classical Latin frangere ('to break'). Completely unrelated etymologically to its homograph frais ('fresh, cool', < Frankish *frisk)!

history.meaning: to break, shatter → broken thing; feudal fine for breach or damage
expenses, costs, outlays (used almost exclusively in the plural)

morphemes.meaning: costs, outlays (< Old French frait < fractum, + plural -s)

les frais.notes: Rich in agency and business idioms: note de frais ('expense report'), aux frais de la princesse ('on the company's / taxpayer's dime'), faire les frais de quelque chose ('to bear the brunt of / pay the price for'), and en être pour ses frais ('to have wasted one's effort').

rootFamily.gloss: to cover someone's expenses; défrayer la chronique ('to make scandalous headlines')
fragile, breakable (learned cognate from Latin frangere)
fracture, break (learned doublet of Old French frait)

cognates.meaning: process of washing out soluble matter (learned Latinate cognate)

lessivé.etymology: Past participial adjective of lessiver ('to scrub or boil with lye, launder'), derived from lessive ('lye-water, laundry'), inherited via Old French lessive from Late Latin lixīva (elliptical for aqua lixīva, 'alkaline ash-water'), from Classical Latin lixīvus ('made into lye'), built on lix ('ashes, lye'). Because harsh wood-ash lye left linen wrung-out and bleached, lessivé developed the vivid colloquial sense 'utterly drained, wiped out'.

history.meaning: alkaline water steeped in wood ashes for washing cloth
lye wash, laundry → to launder or scour thoroughly
bleached/washed; figuratively exhausted, completely wiped out

lessivé.notes: Colloquial favorite after a grueling film shoot or crisis day: Je suis complètement lessivé(e) ('I'm totally wiped out / wrung dry'—exact semantic parallel to English 'washed out').

rootFamily.gloss: to wash down walls; to exhaust someone or purge a team
thorough scrubbing; wholesale purge or firing spree in an office

lettre.etymology: Lettre comes from Latin littera ('written character', and in the plural litterae 'epistle, written message'), evolving through Old French letre into both French lettre and English 'letter'.

leur.etymology: Inherited from Old French lor / leur ('of them, to them; their'), from Classical Latin illorum ('of those ones, of them', genitive plural of ille 'that one, he'), used both as an indirect object pronoun ('to them') and as a possessive determiner ('their').

lever.etymology: Inherited from Old French lever ('to raise, lift, rise'), from Classical Latin levare ('to make light, lighten, lift up, raise'), derived from levis ('light in weight').

history.meaning: to raise, lift; (reflexive) to get up, rise

cognates.meaning: rigid bar pivoting on a fulcrum (borrowed from Old French levier)

levier.etymology: Derived in Old French (levier, 12th c., 'crowbar, pry-bar') from lever ('to raise, lift', < Classical Latin levāre, 'to lighten, lift up', from levis, 'light in weight') + the instrumental suffix -ier (< Latin -ārium). Extended from physical mechanics and gearshifts to financial and strategic 'leverage' in negotiations.

history.meaning: to make light, raise, lift up
wooden or iron bar used to pry and lift heavy loads
mechanical lever, gearstick; strategic or financial leverage

levier.notes: In contract negotiations and business French, effet de levier means 'leverage' and avoir un levier (or un moyen de pression) means having bargaining power.

rootFamily.gloss: to lift, raise; se lever ('to get up')
lifting; removal of an obstacle or ban (levée)
to raise higher, elevate; to bring up (a child)

cognates.meaning: instruction, unit of study (borrowed from Old French leçon)

leçon.etymology: Inherited via Old French leçon from Classical Latin lēctiō, lēctiōnis ('a reading aloud, perusal of a text'), action noun of legere ('to gather, choose, read'). In medieval monastic and university practice, teaching consisted of reading and glossing authoritative texts aloud, turning 'a reading' into 'a lesson'—leaving lecture as its later learned doublet for silent 'reading'.

history.meaning: act of reading aloud from a scroll or codex
liturgical scripture reading; master's oral commentary to students
instructional session, moral takeaway, or textual variant in philology

leçon.notes: Pair of doublets to master: leçon (inherited) = 'lesson' (donner une leçon à quelqu'un = 'to teach someone a lesson / lecture them'), whereas lecture (learned) = 'reading' (not 'a lecture', which is un cours or une conférence!).

rootFamily.gloss: reading (learned doublet of leçon from Medieval Latin lectūra)

liberté.etymology: Borrowed and adapted in Old French (liberté, 12th–14th c., replacing earlier inherited leauté/franchise in legal senses) from Classical Latin lībertās, lībertātis ('civil status of a free person as opposed to a slave, political independence, candor'), derived from līber ('free, unrestricted'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰeros ('belonging to the people, free').

history.meaning: legal status of a freeborn citizen; political self-rule
exemption from servitude, civic privilege, moral autonomy
fundamental freedom, artistic autonomy, or release from custody

liberté.notes: First word of the French Republican motto (Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité); in cinema and contracts, liberté artistique ('creative freedom') and prendre des libertés avec le scénario ('to take liberties with the script') are staple expressions.

rootFamily.gloss: to free, release, clear up (one's schedule)

libraire.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical Latin librarius ('copyist of manuscripts, bookseller'), derived from liber ('inner bark of a tree used for writing; book').

cognates.meaning: shifted in English to 'public/lending collection', whereas French librairie kept 'bookshop'

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: libraire (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: libraire

libraire.notes: Classic false friend: **un / une libraire** sells books in **une librairie** ('bookshop'), while a librarian in **une bibliothèque** is **un / une bibliothécaire**.

librairie.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from libraire ('copyist or seller of books', from Classical Latin librarius < liber 'book'); meant 'library, collection of books' in Old and Classical French (whence English library) before specializing in Modern French to 'bookshop, bookstore'.

history.meaning: collection of books, library -> bookshop, book trade

libre.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century (replacing native Old French franc in general usage) from Classical Latin liber, libera, liberum ('free, unrestricted, not enslaved', originally 'belonging to the free people', from PIE *h1lewdh- 'people, growth').

librement.etymology: Formed in Middle French (14th c.) from the adjective libre ('free, unconstrained', semi-learned reflex of Classical Latin līber) + the adverbial suffix -ment (< Latin ablative mente, 'with a [free] mind'). Signifies acting without external coercion, censorship, or rigid literalness.

history.meaning: freely, openly, candidly; loosely (in artistic adaptations)

librement.notes: Appears constantly in French film credits in the formula librement inspiré de... ('loosely based on / freely adapted from...'), signaling creative departure from source material or real-life figures.

libérer.etymology: Learned 15th-century borrowing from Classical Latin līberāre ('to set free, release from bondage or obligation'), formed on the adjective līber ('free, unrestricted'), from Proto-Italic *louðeros and PIE *h₁lewdʰeros ('belonging to the people, free'). It forms an etymological doublet with the inherited verb livrer ('to hand over, deliver'), which underwent regular Gallo-Romance phonetic erosion.

history.meaning: to set free, emancipate, release from debt or duty
to discharge from an obligation, set free
to free, release, clear up (time or space)

libérer.notes: In agency and film-shoot scheduling (as in Dix pour cent), 'se libérer' means to clear one's calendar or get out of a prior commitment ('Tu peux te libérer mardi ?').

lier.etymology: Inherited via Old French liier, lier ('to tie, fasten, bind by oath') from Classical Latin ligāre ('to bind, tie up, bandage, unite'), with regular loss of intervocalic -g- between vowels in Gallo-Romance. Ultimately from PIE *leyg- ('to bind, tie'). Contrast learned Latinate borrowings that preserve the velar consonant, such as ligature and obligation.

history.meaning: to tie physically; to bind by feudal or legal obligation
to bind, connect, link; to thicken a sauce

lier.notes: In talent-agency legalese, 'être lié par contrat' means to be contractually bound, while 'lier d'amitié' means to strike up a close friendship.

lierre.etymology: Formed in Middle French by agglutinating the elided definite article l' onto Old French ierre ('ivy'): l'ierre ('the ivy') was reanalyzed by speakers as a single noun le lierre! Old French ierre itself came regularly from Classical Latin hedera ('ivy').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: lierre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: lierre

lierre.notes: The same article fusion created French **le lendemain** ('the next day', from *l'endemain*) and **la luette** ('uvula', from *l'uette*).

lieu.etymology: Inherited from Old French leu / lieu ('place, spot'), from Classical Latin locus ('place, spot, locality, position, rank').

lifting.etymology: Mid-20th-century French pseudo-anglicism (attested around 1951), formed by elliptical clipping of English face-lifting ('cosmetic surgical tightening of facial skin'), itself from the verb lift (from Old Norse lypta, 'to raise into the air', related to lopt, 'air, sky') plus the gerundial suffix -ing.

history.meaning: cosmetic surgery to tighten facial tissues
surgical facelift; figurative revamp or renovation

morphemes.meaning: English action-noun suffix used in French borrowings

lifting.notes: Classic false anglicism: English speakers say 'facelift', never bare 'a lifting'. Masculine in French ('un lifting'), and also used figuratively for renovating a brand or building ('faire un lifting').

rootFamily.gloss: to give a facelift or revamp (colloquial)

ligne.etymology: Inherited from Old French ligne ('flax thread, plumb line, stroke, row'), from Classical Latin linea ('linen thread, string, plumb-line, geometric line'), feminine of lineus ('made of flax or linen', from linum 'flax').

history.meaning: linen thread, plumb line, drawn stroke
line, row, fishing line, transport route, silhouette

limite.etymology: Borrowed in 14th-century Middle French from Classical Latin līmes, accusative līmitem ('cross-path between fields, boundary marker, fortified frontier of the Empire'), related to līmus ('transverse, oblique') and līmen ('threshold'). Semantic scope broadened from physical land borders to abstract thresholds of time, patience, or legality.

history.meaning: balk or path marking a boundary between estates; frontier
limit, boundary, outer edge; (colloquial adj./adv.) borderline

limite.notes: Feminine noun ('la limite', unlike masculine Italian 'il limite' and Spanish 'el límite'). In casual spoken French, 'limite' is ubiquitous as an invariable adjective or adverb meaning 'borderline, dicey, almost' ('C'est un peu limite !').

limousine.etymology: Substantivized feminine of the regional adjective limousin ('of Limoges or the Limousin province'), which derives from Late Latin Lemovīcīnus, from Classical Latin Lemovīcēs, the Gaulish tribe (*Lemo-wīkes, 'elm-warriors') who inhabited the region. First designating a heavy hooded wool or goat-hair cloak worn by Limousin shepherds, the word was transferred around 1902 to an early closed-cabin automobile body whose projecting roof sheltered the driver like that cloak, and thence to a luxury chauffeur-driven car.

history.meaning: Gaulish tribe of central-western Gaul (around Limoges)
heavy hooded shepherd's cloak from the Limousin region
enclosed carriage-style automobile; luxury chauffeured car

limousine.notes: Besides VIP festival cars at Cannes, 'la limousine' (or 'vache limousine') also denotes the prized reddish-brown beef cattle breed native to the Limousin region.

rootFamily.gloss: rough masonry; (figurative, from 1914) to dismiss a general to Limoges

lin.etymology: Inherited via Old French lin from Classical Latin linum ('flax plant, linen thread, linen cloth'), cognate with Ancient Greek línon.

cognates.meaning: lingerie comes from French linge (< lineus 'made of linen')

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: lin (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: lin

lin.notes: Normandy and northern France remain among the world's premier growers of flax (**le lin**), woven into tablecloths, bookbinding thread, and summer clothes.

lindy.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from American English Lindy (short for Lindy Hop), the exuberant African American swing dance developed in Harlem ballrooms (notably the Savoy Ballroom) in 1927–1928. Popularized by dancer George 'Shorty' Snowden, the name played on newspaper headlines celebrating aviator Charles Lindbergh ('Lucky Lindy') and his historic nonstop solo transatlantic 'hop' from New York to Paris in May 1927.

history.meaning: syncopated Harlem swing partner dance named after Lindbergh's flight

lindy.notes: Masculine in French ('danser le lindy' or 'le lindy hop'); its origin carries a transatlantic Franco-American link, since Lindbergh's famous 1927 'hop' landed at Le Bourget outside Paris.

linge.etymology: Inherited from Old French linge ('made of linen; linen cloth or garment'), from Classical Latin lineus ('of flax, linen', derived from linum 'flax').

history.meaning: linen cloth -> household linen, underwear, laundry

lion.etymology: Inherited through Old French lion (attested c. 1100 in the Chanson de Roland) from Classical Latin leō, accusative leōnem ('lion'), with raising of unstressed Latin e in hiatus to i before o. Latin borrowed the word from Ancient Greek λέων (léōn), itself likely an ancient loanword from an Afroasiatic or Near Eastern substrate language (compare Semitic *labiʾ-).

history.meaning: lion; emblem of courage or fierceness

lion.notes: In cinema parlance, 'le Lion d'or' is the top prize at the Venice Film Festival; idiomatically, 'avoir bouffé du lion' means to be unusually fired up and full of energy.

rootFamily.gloss: lion-like; leonine (e.g., contrat léonin, an unfair one-sided contract)

lipofilling.etymology: Late-20th-century medical and aesthetic-surgery hybrid compound adopted in international surgical jargon, combining the neoclassical Greek prefixoid lipo- (from Ancient Greek λίπος, lípos, 'animal fat, lard, grease') with the English verbal noun filling ('act of restoring volume', from Old English fyllan, 'to make full'). It denotes harvesting a patient's own adipose tissue and reinjecting it to plump hollow facial contours.

history.meaning: fat (Greek) + act of filling in volume (English)
autologous fat transfer used in reconstructive and cosmetic surgery

lipofilling.notes: Masculine ('un lipofilling'); in French aesthetic medicine, doctors also use the transparent native term 'lipomodelage' or 'transfert graisseux', though 'lipofilling' dominates glossy celebrity talk.

liquide.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical Latin liquidus ('flowing, fluid, clear, limpid'), derived from liquere ('to be fluid or clear').

history.meaning: fluid, liquid (adj. & noun); ready cash (argent liquide)

lire.etymology: Inherited from Old French lire ('to read'), from Classical Latin legere ('to gather, pick out, trace letters with the eye, read aloud', from PIE *leg- 'to collect, speak').

history.meaning: to gather, pick out -> to read

lisse.etymology: Inherited from Old French lisse ('smooth, polished, sleek'), from Vulgar Latin *liscia / verb *lisciare ('to smooth'), borrowed from Frankish *lisi ('smooth, softly gliding', related to Old High German lisi 'gentle, quiet').

liste.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (in the sense 'written roll or catalogue of names or items') from Italian lista ('narrow strip of cloth or paper; roll of names'), itself sharing the same Germanic origin (*lista 'border, strip') as native Old French liste ('border, edge, tournament lists').

history.meaning: strip of paper bearing a series of names

lit.etymology: Lit descends regularly from Latin lectus ('couch, bed'): -ct- developed to -it and short e merged into i, producing Old French and modern French lit (with silent final t).
lit.notes: Gives **la literie** ('bedding'); **faire le lit** = to make the bed.

lividité.etymology: Learned derivative attested in Middle French (14th–15th c.), formed on the adjective livide or borrowed from Medieval Latin līviditās (accusative līviditātem), from Classical Latin līvidus ('dull leaden-blue, black-and-blue from bruising; figuratively spiteful or envious'), itself from the stative verb līvēre ('to be bluish or lead-colored'). In Modern French the color sense shifted from dark bruise-blue toward a ghastly, bloodless pallor.

history.meaning: lead-colored or bruised discoloration of skin (medical)
ghastly ash-white paleness; postmortem skin discoloration

lividité.notes: Subtle false friend with English: whereas English 'livid' usually means 'furiously angry' (flushed red or dark), French 'livide' and 'lividité' evoke turning deathly pale or chalk-white from shock, fear, or illness.

cognates.meaning: setting free, release (learned doublet via Latin)

livraison.etymology: Inherited via Old French livraison, livreson ('action of handing over; allotted ration or payment') from Late and Medieval Latin līberātiōnem (Classical līberātiō, 'setting free, discharge from an obligation'). Following the Gallo-Romance semantic shift of līberāre > livrer from 'releasing goods from one's control' to 'handing over, supplying', livraison came to mean 'delivery', making it an inherited doublet of learned libération.

history.meaning: handing over of goods; feudal allowance or ration
commercial delivery, shipment; serialized issue of a publication

livraison.notes: Notice the classic French doublet pair: inherited '-aison' in 'livraison' (delivery of a package or final cut of a film) versus learned '-ation' in 'libération' (setting someone free).

rootFamily.gloss: to deliver, hand over; to confide

livre.etymology: Represents two distinct Latin words that converged in spelling: (1) masculine le livre ('book'), from Classical Latin liber, librum ('inner bark of a tree used for writing, scroll, book'); and (2) feminine la livre ('pound weight; former currency unit'), from Classical Latin libra ('balance, pair of scales, Roman pound of twelve ounces').

local.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century as an adjective from Late Latin localis ('belonging to a place'), derived from Classical Latin locus ('place'); used as a masculine noun (un local, pl. des locaux) since the 18th century for a room or business premises.

locataire.etymology: Borrowed in 16th-century Middle French legal usage from Medieval Latin locātārius ('person who takes property on lease'), derived from Classical Latin locātus, past participle of locāre ('to place, put; to let out for hire or rent'), itself a denominative verb from locus ('place, spot').

history.meaning: to place, station; to lease or rent out for money
tenant, renter of an apartment or building

locataire.notes: Epicene noun ('un locataire' / 'une locataire'), and remember its parent false friend: 'location' in French means 'rental/lease' (e.g., 'appartement en location'), NEVER 'geographical location' ('emplacement' or 'lieu'—or on film sets, 'décor naturel' / 'repérage').

locomotive.etymology: Borrowed in the 1830s from English locomotive (short for locomotive engine, coined in the early 19th c.), built on New Latin locomotivus from Classical Latin loco (ablative of locus 'from a place') + Medieval Latin motivus ('causing motion', from movere 'to move').

cognates.meaning: attic; open-plan apartment in a converted industrial building

loft.etymology: Borrowed in the 1970s from American English loft ('spacious open-plan dwelling converted from a former factory, artist's studio, or warehouse floor', originally 'upper story, attic'), from Late Old English loft ('upper chamber, sky, air'), itself borrowed from Old Norse lopt ('air, sky, upper room'), from Proto-Germanic *luftuz ('air, roof, canopy').

history.meaning: air, sky; upper room or balcony under the roof
attic, warehouse floor; converted open-plan urban apartment
upscale open-plan apartment in a converted workshop or factory

loft.notes: In Paris real estate (and successful actors' homes in Dix pour cent), 'un loft' specifically implies high ceilings, industrial windows, and converted workshop ('atelier') chic in districts like the Marais or Bastille, rather than a dusty attic ('grenier').

rootFamily.gloss: contestant in the 2001 French reality show Loft Story

cognates.meaning: small house, cabin; Masonic or porter's lodge (from Old French)
entrance hall, foyer (from Medieval Latin lobia, same Germanic root)
open gallery, opera box (borrowed from Old French)

loge.etymology: Inherited via Old French loge (12th c., 'leafy arbor, rustic shelter, merchant's or mason's booth, gallery') from Frankish *laubja ('shelter of foliage, bower, covered gallery'), from Proto-Germanic *laubijǭ, a derivative of *laubą ('leaf, foliage'). In theatrical life, the word specialized in two directions: elevated private spectator boxes in an opera house or theater, and backstage dressing rooms for actors.

history.meaning: leafy bower, thatched shelter, covered porch
arbor, tournament viewing gallery, artisan's workshop hut
actor's dressing room; opera/theater box; concierge's office; Masonic lodge

loge.notes: Essential showbiz vocabulary: on a film set or in a theater, 'la loge' (or 'loge maquillage') is an actor's private dressing room—when a star locks themselves 'dans sa loge', the agent is usually summoned to coax them out!

rootFamily.gloss: home, dwelling (poetic or real-estate: 'le corps de logis')

cognates.meaning: temporary accommodation (parallel formation on Old French loger)

logement.etymology: Formed in Old French (12th–13th c., originally denoting the pitching of camp or military quartering) from the verb loger ('to build shelters, quarter troops, accommodate', itself from loge < Frankish *laubja, 'leafy shelter') plus the action/result nominal suffix -ment (from Latin -mentum). By Middle French it generalized to civilian housing and living quarters.

history.meaning: to encamp, quarter soldiers, provide shelter
act of quartering troops; temporary lodging or inn room

morphemes.meaning: nominal suffix forming nouns of action or concrete result

logement.notes: More administrative and practical than 'maison' or 'appartement': used in phrases like 'chercher un logement', 'logement de fonction' (employer-provided apartment), or 'la crise du logement'.

rootFamily.gloss: dressing room, concierge's booth, theater box

loger.etymology: Derived in Old French (logier, 12th c., 'to camp in huts or arbors, quarter troops, lodge') from loge ('arbor, leafy shelter, hut', borrowed from Frankish *laubja 'shelter of boughs or foliage', from *laub 'leaf', cognate with English lodge and lobby).

history.meaning: to shelter in a hut or quarters
to lodge, house, reside, fit into

cognates.meaning: logic (shared Greco-Latin root of first element)

logiciel.etymology: Deliberate French neologism coined in 1967 by computer science pioneer Philippe Dreyfus to render English software without borrowing the anglicism. It blends logique ('logic', via Latin logica from Ancient Greek λογική, logikḗ, 'art of reasoning', from λόγος, lógos) with the relational suffix -iel, directly mirroring the ending and semantic contrast of matériel ('hardware, physical equipment').
logiciel.notes: One of the most successful official French tech coinages in history, universally used instead of 'software' and spawning an entire family ('progiciel', 'ludiciel', 'didacticiel', 'malveillant / maliciel').

loi.etymology: Inherited through Old French lei -> loi (tenth–twelfth century) from Classical Latin lēx, lēgem ('statute, binding rule, law'), with regular Gallo-Romance loss of intervocalic -g- and diphthongisation of tonic closed ē (lēgem -> *leie -> lei -> loi [lwa]), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- ('to gather, lay down').
loi.notes: Compare popular inherited loi / loyal (where Latin -g- disappeared completely) with learned legal vocabulary légal and législateur, re-borrowed directly from Latin lēgālis.

loin.etymology: Inherited from Old French loing / loin ('far, far off'), from Classical Latin longe ('far off, at a distance, at length'), adverb formed from longus ('long').

history.meaning: far off, at a great distance

lointain.etymology: Inherited via Old French lointain ('distant in space or time', famed in troubadour Jaufré Rudel's 'amor de lonh' / 'amour lointain') from Vulgar Latin *longitānus ('situated far off'), formed from the Classical Latin adverb longē ('far away, at a distance', from longus, 'long') plus the relational suffix -tānus. Palatalization and vocalization of the medial velar cluster yielded the nasal diphthong oin-.

history.meaning: distant, remote (adj.); distant background of a view or painting (noun)

lointain.notes: While 'loin' is strictly an adverb ('habiter loin'), 'lointain / lointaine' is the corresponding adjective ('un souvenir lointain', 'un cousin lointain').

long.etymology: Inherited from Old French lonc (feminine longue, 'long'), from Classical Latin longus ('long in space or time', from PIE *dlonghos, cognate with English long).

longtemps.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French of the Old French phrase long temps ('a long time'), from long ('long', < Latin longum) + temps ('time', < Latin tempus).

history.meaning: for a long time, a long while

cognates.meaning: at length, for a long time

longuement.etymology: Inherited from Old French longuement (attested from the 10th–11th c.), formed regularly from longue, the feminine form of long (from Classical Latin longa, feminine of longus, 'long'), combined with the Romance adverbial suffix -ment, which grammaticalized from the Classical Latin ablative noun mente ('with a [long] mind, in a [prolonged] manner').

history.meaning: with a steadfast/enduring mind or manner (ablative phrase)
at length, thoroughly, for a long while

longuement.notes: Nuance vs. 'longtemps': 'longtemps' simply measures clock or calendar duration ('attendre longtemps'), whereas 'longuement' highlights thoroughness, deliberation, or lingering intensity ('en parler longuement', 'réfléchir longuement').

rootFamily.gloss: length; slow/drawn-out passage in a film or script ('des longueurs')

cognates.meaning: to peer, look out (dialectal/archaic lugen, shared West Germanic root)

look.etymology: Borrowed in the late 1970s and popularized in 1980s fashion and media French from English look ('visual style, curated outfit and personal image', as in Christian Dior's 1947 'New Look'), from Middle English loken, Old English lōcian ('to gaze, behold, appear'), from Proto-West Germanic *lōkōn ('to look'). French rapidly created native derivatives around it such as relooker.

history.meaning: to gaze, look, direct one's sight
characteristic fashion silhouette or personal appearance
curated style, outfit, overall visual image

look.notes: Masculine ('un nouveau look'); exclusively a noun in French meaning 'style/outfit/image' (never a glance or the verb 'to look'), and productively adapted into French verbs like 'relooker' (to restyle / give a makeover).

rootFamily.gloss: to give a style makeover, redesign
styled in a striking or trendy way (colloquial)

loquet.etymology: Diminutive formed in twelfth-century Old French from loc ('lock, bolt'), an early borrowing from Old English loc or Frankish/Old Norse lok ('fastener, bar, lock'). English latch and lock belong to the very same Germanic family.

cognates.meaning: lock; small hinged case (locket borrowed back from French loquet)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: loquet (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: loquet

cognates.meaning: person who fails or loses; social underdog

loser.etymology: Borrowed in late-20th-century colloquial French from American English loser ('habitual failure, hapless person, social underdog'), an agent noun formed from the verb lose (from Old English losian, 'to perish, go astray, be lost', derived from los, 'destruction, loss', from PIE *lews-, 'to loosen, separate') plus the agentive suffix -er.

history.meaning: to perish, be destroyed, slip away
one who loses a contest; chronic failure or misfit (slang from 1950s)

loser.notes: Frequently misspelled 'looser' online even in France, and it spawned the uniquely French colloquial noun 'la lose' ('avoir la lose' = to have a streak of pathetic bad luck, as poor Hervé or Mathias might lament!).

rootFamily.gloss: chronic bad luck, pathetic failure ('avoir la lose')

louche.etymology: Inherited via Old French louce / louche ('large long-handled spoon, ladle') from Frankish *lōtja ('ladle, scoop'), from Proto-Germanic *lōtjō, related to Old High German lōz and Old English lōd ('ladle'). Brought into Gallo-Romance through domestic Germanic kitchenware, une louche displaced Latin cochlear/trulla for the deep soup ladle used at the stove and table.
louche.notes: Do not confuse the feminine noun **une louche** ('a soup ladle', from Frankish) with the homophonous adjective **louche** ('squinting, shady, suspicious', from Latin *luscus*!).

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: louche

louer.etymology: Convergence of two distinct Latin verbs that became homophones in Old French: (1) 'to rent, hire, let out', from Classical Latin locare ('to place, let out for hire', from locus 'place'); and (2) 'to praise, commend', from Classical Latin laudare ('to praise', from laus, laudis).

history.form: locare ('to let for hire') / laudare ('to praise')
history.meaning: to place or rent out; to praise

loup.etymology: Inherited via Old French leu (northern regular phonetic outcome, still preserved in the frozen idiom 'à la queue leu leu', 'in single file like wolves') and dialectal/analogical loup from Classical Latin lupus, accusative lupum ('wolf'). Middle French scribes restored the final -p on the Latin model, though it remains silent in pronunciation. Latin lupus (with -p- rather than native Roman *lucus) is itself likely a Sabine/Oscan Italic loanword from PIE *wĺ̥kʷos ('wolf').

history.meaning: wolf; sea bass; theatrical mistake or technical glitch on set/stage

loup.notes: Pronounced /lu/ (the '-p' is completely silent!). In French theater and film jargon, 'un loup' means a glaring mistake, continuity error, or technical botch—whence the everyday verb 'louper' (to miss a train, botch an audition).

rootFamily.gloss: to miss, botch, mess up (from theatrical 'loup')

lourd.etymology: Inherited from Old French lort / lourd (originally 'dull-witted, stunned, clumsy', then from the 13th–14th c. 'physically heavy', displacing Old French pesant in everyday speech), from Classical Latin luridus ('pale yellow, wan, ghastly, livid') or Vulgar Latin *lurdus ('bleary, stunned, heavy').

loyauté.etymology: Inherited via Old French leauté, loiauté ('feudal fidelity, uprightness, adherence to law and honor') from Classical Latin lēgālitās, accusative lēgālitātem ('conformity to law'), derived from lēgālis ('relating to the law'), from lēx, lēgis ('statute, binding law'). Regular Gallo-Romance loss of intervocalic -g- and vocalization of -l- before -t- produced loyauté, an inherited doublet of learned légalité.
loyauté.notes: At ASK in Dix pour cent, 'la loyauté' between an agent and a longtime actor—or between agents poaching clients—is the central moral currency; in contract law, 'obligation de loyauté' means the duty of good faith.

rootFamily.gloss: law (shared inherited root from Latin lēx)

loyer.etymology: Inherited from Old French loier ('recompense, wage, hire, rent'), from Classical Latin locarium ('money paid for a lodging or stall, rent'), derived from locare ('to let out for hire', from locus 'place').

history.meaning: payment for a leased place, rent
wage -> rent paid for housing or premises

lui.etymology: Lui continues Latin illi, a dative form of the demonstrative ille or illa. The Académie records ninth-century li. Modern lui can be an indirect-object form or a stressed pronoun.

history.meaning: to him, to her (indirect clitic); him (stressed pronoun)

lui.notes: Crucial French grammar point: before a verb, lui means BOTH 'to him' AND 'to her' (je lui parle = 'I speak to him / to her'), whereas after a preposition (avec lui vs. avec elle) lui is strictly masculine!

lui-même.etymology: Compound emphatic pronoun formed by joining the masculine singular disjunctive (tonic) pronoun lui—from Vulgar Latin *illūi, remodeled dative of Classical Latin ille ('that one, he') on the analogy of interrogative cui—with the intensive particle même, from Old French meïsme, medisme, which descends from Vulgar Latin *metipsimus, an emphatic superlative compounding Classical Latin enclitic -met ('-self') + ipse ('himself, very').

history.meaning: to/for that very one himself (emphatic Vulgar Latin syntagm)
he himself, in his very own person

lui-même.notes: Always hyphenated in French ('lui-même', 'elle-même', 'eux-mêmes'); indispensable in celebrity cameos where stars play 'son propre rôle' or appear 'en personne, lui-même'.

cognates.meaning: emitting light, clear (via Middle French / Latin)

lumineux.etymology: Borrowed in 14th-century Middle French from Classical Latin lūminōsus ('full of light, bright, well-lit, conspicuous'), derived from lūmen, genitive lūminis ('light, lamp, daylight, radiance'), from prehistoric Latin *louksmen, built on the PIE root *lewk- ('to shine, be bright', whence also lūx and lūna), adapted with the native French adjectival ending -eux (< -ōsus).

history.meaning: bright, sunlit (of a room); radiant (of a performer); brilliant (of an idea)

lumineux.notes: High praise in French cinema and real estate alike: 'un appartement très lumineux' means flooded with natural light, while calling an actress 'lumineuse à l'écran' praises effortless screen charisma, and 'une idée lumineuse' means a stroke of genius.

lumière.etymology: Inherited from Old French lumiere ('light, lamp, torch, eyesight'), from Late/Vulgar Latin luminaria (originally plural of Classical Latin luminare 'lamp, torch, celestial body, window opening'), derived from lumen, luminis ('light').

lundi.etymology: Inherited from Old French lunsdi ('Monday'), from Vulgar Latin *lunis dies, transposition of Classical Latin Lunae dies ('day of the Moon', a calque of Ancient Greek hemera Selenes).

cognates.meaning: relating to the moon (learned Latin borrowing)

lune.etymology: Inherited unchanged in spelling from Old French lune (11th c.), from Classical Latin lūna ('the moon; month'), attested in Old Latin (Praenestine mirror inscription) as losna, descending from Proto-Italic *louksnā and PIE *lówksneh₂ ('the shining or luminous one'), a feminine derivative of the root *lewk- ('bright, to shine').

history.meaning: the moon; moonlight; lunar goddess Luna
moon; alchemical silver; whimsical mood (from Middle French)
moon, natural satellite; mood or daydreaming in idioms

lune.notes: Packed with everyday idioms for volatile temperaments: 'être dans la lune' (to be daydreaming/spaced out), 'être bien/mal luné' (to be in a good/foul mood), and 'promettre la lune' (to promise the impossible).

rootFamily.gloss: Monday ('day of the Moon', Latin Lūnae diēs)

lunettes.etymology: Lunette is the diminutive of lune ('moon', from Latin luna): a 'little moon' first meant a small round mirror or round glass lens in the Middle Ages, and in the plural **lunettes** came to mean a pair of eyeglasses.
lunettes.notes: Always plural for spectacles: **mes lunettes**, **une paire de lunettes**.

lutherie.etymology: Formed from luthier ('maker and repairer of stringed instruments'), derived from luth ('lute') < Old French leüt, borrowed via Old Occitan/Spanish from Arabic al-ʿūd ('the wood; the oud/lute').

cognates.meaning: all trace back to Arabic al-ʿūd

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: lutherie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: lutherie

lutherie.notes: Even after violins eclipsed lutes in the 17th century, French kept **luthier** and **lutherie** for all bowed and plucked wooden instruments.

lutte.etymology: Inherited via Old French luite, lute ('hand-to-hand wrestling bout, combat, strenuous effort') from Late Latin lucta ('wrestling match, struggle'), a post-Classical back-formation alongside Classical Latin luctātiō from the deponent verb luctārī ('to wrestle, lock arms, strain, contend'), ultimately from PIE *lewg- ('to bend, twist, lock limbs'). Palatalization of Latin -ct- yielded Old French -it-, later reduced to -t- (spelled -tt-) after u.

history.meaning: wrestling match; armed or moral struggle
struggle, social or political fight; sport of wrestling

lutte.notes: Retains its ancient Roman sense as the Olympic sport of 'wrestling' ('la lutte gréco-romaine'), alongside political and personal struggle ('la lutte des classes', 'une lutte acharnée').

rootFamily.gloss: reluctant (learned English/Latin cognate via re- + luctārī)

luxueux.etymology: Derived in 18th-century French (with isolated 16th-century precursors) from luxe ('luxury, sumptuousness, refinement'—borrowed in the 17th c. from Classical Latin luxus, 'excess, extravagant living, splendor, dislocation') plus the adjectival suffix -eux (from Latin -ōsus). French needed luxueux because the older Latinate adjective luxurieux (from luxuria) had narrowed exclusively to the theological sin of 'lustful, lecherous'.
luxueux.notes: Crucial false friend trap: always translate English 'luxurious' as 'luxueux / luxueuse'—NEVER 'luxurieux' (which means 'lustful/lecherous') nor 'luxuriant' (which means 'lush, overgrown' of vegetation or hair!).

rootFamily.gloss: lust, lechery (false friend with English luxury!)

cognates.meaning: lecture hall or classical institution (via Latin/Greek)

lycée.etymology: Borrowed in 16th-century Humanist French via Classical Latin Lycēum from Ancient Greek Λύκειον (Lúkeion), originally a wooded sanctuary and gymnasium just outside Athens sacred to Ἀπόλλων Λύκειος (Apollo Lyceus, variously interpreted as 'wolf-slayer' or 'god of light/Lycia'), where Aristotle founded his Peripatetic school in 335 BCE. In 1802, Napoleon Bonaparte revived the classical name to establish France's state secondary schools preparing students for the baccalauréat.

history.meaning: Athenian gymnasium of Apollo where Aristotle taught philosophy
Aristotle's school; salon or academy of arts and sciences (18th c.)
history.stage: Middle to Early Modern French (16th–18th c.)

history.meaning: upper secondary school (ages ~15–18, Seconde to Terminale)

lycée.notes: Masculine despite the final '-ée' ('un lycée', like 'un musée'). In France's school system, 'le collège' is middle school (ages 11–15), whereas 'le lycée' is senior high school (ages 15–18, ending with 'le bac')—a double false friend for English speakers!

cognates.meaning: lily flower (borrowed directly from Latin līlia)

lys.etymology: Inherited via Old French lis (12th c.; later often spelled lys with an etymologizing Greek y) from Classical Latin līlia, plural of līlium ('white lily'), treated collectively with final -s retained from the Old French nominative singular / oblique plural inflection. Latin līlium (with dissimilation of r to l) was borrowed from Ancient Greek λείριον (leírion, 'Madonna lily'), itself from an Eastern Mediterranean or Egyptian/Coptic substrate word (compare Coptic hreri, Demotic ḥrrt, 'flower').

history.meaning: lily flower; stylized royal emblem of the Capetian monarchy

lys.notes: Pronunciation quirk: the final '-s' IS pronounced /lis/ in standalone 'un lys' ('un bouquet de lys'), EXCEPT in the historic heraldic compound 'fleur de lys / fleur-de-lis', where it is traditionally silent (/flœʁ də li/). Both spellings 'lys' and 'lis' are valid.

rootFamily.gloss: resembling a lily in whiteness; pertaining to the lilies of France

là.etymology: Là comes from Latin illac or illa, by that way or there. It is recorded in French from the eleventh century.

rootFamily.gloss: there is, here you go (< vois là)

là.notes: Carries a grave accent solely to distinguish it visually from the article/pronoun la; in spoken French je suis là usually means 'I'm here / present', leaving là-bas for distant 'over there'.

cognates.meaning: down there, over there (parallel compound là + basso / giù)

là-bas.etymology: Compound spatial adverb attested from Middle French (15th–16th c.), uniting the distal deictic adverb là ('there', via Old French la from Classical Latin illāc, 'by that way, on that side') with bas ('low, down below', from Late Latin bassus, 'thickset, short, low in stature'). Originally literal ('down there below'), its vertical sense bleached so that in Modern French it serves as the standard everyday adverb for 'over there' on any horizontal plane.

history.meaning: that way / there + low, short (Latin ancestors)
down there, in a lower place
over there, yonder; back in that country or city just mentioned

là-bas.notes: Because bare 'là' in spoken French often weakens to 'here / right now' ('Je suis là' = I'm here!), speakers rely on 'là-bas' whenever they truly mean 'over there' at a distance—or anaphorically for a city/set being discussed ('Il tourne à Rome, il adore vivre là-bas').

rootFamily.gloss: there; here (in spoken French); particle of emphasis

là-dedans.etymology: Compound adverb formed from deictic adverb là ('there', from Latin illac) + dedans ('inside, within').

cognates.meaning: on top of that, thereupon (parallel compound là + sopra)

là-dessus.etymology: Compound pronominal and discourse adverb attested from Old/Middle French, combining the deictic adverb là ('there, on that point', from Classical Latin illāc) with the adverbial preposition dessus ('on top, above', Old French desus, fused from Late/Vulgar Latin dē sūsum, where sūsum reflects Classical Latin sūrsum < *sub-vorsum, 'turned from below upward'). It evolved from physical placement ('on top of that object') to temporal sequence ('thereupon') and conversational topic reference ('about that').

history.meaning: on top of it; thereupon, with that; on that topic/subject

là-dessus.notes: Super idiomatic in rapid French dialogue as a pronoun replacement for 'sur + non-human noun': 'On est d'accord là-dessus' ('We agree on that'), 'Je travaille là-dessus' ('I'm working on it'), or as a brisk exit cue: 'Bon, là-dessus, j'y vais !' ('Well, on that note, I'm off!').

rootFamily.gloss: on top, above; upper hand ('prendre le dessus')
underneath that; in that secret matter ('là-dessous')

là-haut.etymology: Compound adverb formed from là ('there', from Latin illac) + haut ('high, up above').

lâche.etymology: Deverbal adjective and noun formed in Old French (lasche, 12th c., 'slack, loose; faint-hearted, cowardly') from laschier / lâcher ('to slacken, let go', from Vulgar Latin *lascare < Classical Latin laxare).

history.meaning: slack, loose, not taut -> cowardly, craven; coward

lâchement.etymology: Formed in Old French as laschement from the adjective lâche ('slack, loose', figuratively 'faint-hearted, cowardly') and the adverbial suffix -ment (from the Latin ablative mente, 'with a [specified] mind'). Lâche itself derives via Vulgar Latin *lascus from Classical Latin laxus ('wide, loose, slack'), undergoing metathesis of -ks- to -sk- before palatalizing in Gallo-Romance; the moral shift from physical slackness of bowstrings or muscles to moral cowardice was already established in medieval chivalric literature.
lâchement.notes: Carries strong moral condemnation in French ('in a cowardly or underhanded way'), often used in agency drama when someone backs out of a contract or betrays a client behind their back.

lâcher.etymology: Inherited from Old French laschier ('to slacken, loosen, release'), from Vulgar Latin *lascare, metathesized from Classical Latin laxare ('to loosen, slacken, unbind', from laxus 'loose', doublet of laisser).

history.meaning: to loosen, let go, release, drop

cognates.meaning: labial (learned borrowing); native lip is cognate via PIE *leb-

lèvre.etymology: Inherited through Old French levre from Classical Latin labra, originally the neuter plural of labrum ('lip, rim, edge'), reanalyzed in Vulgar Latin as a feminine singular first-declension noun (*labra, -ae) because of its collective dual nature. Latin labrum stems from Proto-Indo-European *leb- ('to hang loosely, lip'), making it an ancient cognate of Germanic *lepjô (English lip).

history.meaning: lip, rim, margin of a vessel

lèvre.notes: Feminine noun (une lèvre) despite deriving from a Latin neuter; appears in key expressions like du bout des lèvres ('reluctantly, half-heartedly') and être pendu aux lèvres de quelqu'un ('to hang on someone's every word').

légal.etymology: A 14th-century learned borrowing from Classical Latin lēgālis ('pertaining to the law'), derived from lēx, lēgis ('statute, enacted law') plus the relational suffix -ālis. It forms an etymological doublet with the inherited Old French adjective loial (modern loyal), which underwent regular Gallo-Romance intervocalic lenition of -g- to yod and diphthongization, whereas légal preserved the Latin consonantism for strictly juridical and statutory contexts.

history.meaning: pertaining to or conformable to law

légal.notes: Watch the plural masculine légaux; also note that 'legal advice' or 'legal department' in French business and entertainment contracts is conseil juridique / service juridique, whereas légal strictly means 'permitted or mandated by statute'.

légendaire.etymology: Derived in the early 16th century from légende ('saint's life, legend') with the learned suffix -aire (Latin -ārius), modeled on Medieval Latin legendārius (originally a noun meaning 'book of saints' lives to be read aloud'). Légende itself comes from Medieval Latin legenda, reanalyzed feminine singular from the neuter plural gerundive of Classical Latin legere ('to gather, read'), literally 'things to be read' during monastic matins.

history.meaning: collection of saints' lives; compiler of legends

légendaire.notes: In cinema and talent-agency parlance, légendaire describes both iconic screen stars and notoriously difficult traits (e.g., sa ponctualité légendaire, often used ironically).

légende.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Medieval Ecclesiastical Latin legenda ('things to be read, specifically the book of saints' lives appointed to be read aloud at matins and in monastery refectories'), neuter plural (reanalyzed as feminine singular) of the gerundive of Classical Latin legere ('to read').

history.meaning: saint's life -> traditional wonder-tale, legend; coin inscription, map or picture caption

léger.etymology: Inherited from Old French legier ('light in weight, nimble, swift, fickle'), from Vulgar Latin *leviarius, formed on Classical Latin levis ('light in weight, swift, slight').

légume.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin legumen ('pulse, bean or pea plant whose seeds grow in pods and are gathered by hand'), connected with legere ('to gather, pick'); broadened in 17th-century French to any edible kitchen vegetable.

légèrement.etymology: Formed in Old French (12th century, legierement) by adding the adverbial suffix -ment to légère, the feminine form of léger ('light in weight, gentle, slight'). The adjective descends from Vulgar Latin *leviarius, an extension of Classical Latin levis ('light in weight, swift, slight'). Thus légèrement expresses doing something with a light touch or to a slight degree.
légèrement.notes: Shows the regular French adverb rule: take the feminine adjective (**légère**) and add **-ment** -> **légèrement**.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: légèrement

cognates.meaning: coconut biscuit (via earlier French) and pasta (via Italian)

macaron.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-16th century (attested in Rabelais, 1552) from Italian maccarone / maccherone (especially Venetian macaron), originally denoting a small pasta dumpling or almond-paste confection. The Italian word probably derives from Late Greek makarōnía ('funeral meal made with barley or pasta'), from makários ('blessed'), or alternatively from southern Italian maccare ('to crush, bruise, knead vigorously'), referring to pounding almonds or dough.

history.meaning: kneaded pasta dumpling or almond sweetmeat

macaron.notes: Do not confuse French macaron (the delicate Parisian almond-meringue sandwich pastry ubiquitous in luxury catering and gift boxes) with macaronis (tubular pasta) or English macaroon (usually a coconut cluster); macaron also denotes a round lapel badge or steering-wheel emblem.

rootFamily.gloss: tubular pasta (later re-borrowing from Italian plural)

machin.etymology: Attested in colloquial French since the early 19th century (1808) as a masculine back-formation or playful alteration of machine ('device, contraption', borrowed from Latin māchina and Doric Greek mākhanā, 'contrivance'). Shifting the gender from feminine la machine to masculine le machin turned a concrete technical noun into a generalized placeholder ('gizmo, thingamajig, what's-his-name') for any object or person whose exact name escapes the speaker.
machin.notes: Informal spoken French indispensable in fast-paced dialogue (often reduplicated as machin-chouette or paired with truc); when referring to a person (Monsieur Machin), it sounds dismissive, so avoid it in polite professional settings.

rootFamily.gloss: stagehand, grip (in theater and film sets)

machine.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–16th century from Classical Latin machina ('contrivance, mechanical device, siege engine, stage crane, stratagem'), borrowed from Doric Greek makhana (Attic mekhane, 'device, means, contrivance').

madame.etymology: Madame combines ma, my, and dame, lady. The Académie records this form of address from the twelfth century.
madame.notes: Notice that plural mesdames (like messieurs and mesdemoiselles) still inflects the internal possessive ma -> mes!

mademoiselle.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French of the possessive phrase ma demoiselle ('my young noblewoman'). Demoiselle (Old French damoisele) descends from Vulgar Latin *domnicella, an affectionate diminutive of Latina domina ('mistress of a household, lady', feminine of dominus, 'master, lord'). Originally reserved in medieval and Ancien Régime society for unmarried noblewomen and even married women of the bourgeoisie, it gradually generalized into the standard polite title for unmarried women.

history.meaning: little mistress, young lady of rank
polite title of address for an unmarried woman

mademoiselle.notes: Removed from French administrative forms in 2012 in favor of Madame, yet famously retained as a prestigious honorific for legendary French stage and screen actresses (e.g., 'Mademoiselle Deneuve' or 'Mademoiselle Adjani') regardless of age or marital status.

mafia.etymology: Borrowed in the 1860s–1870s from Sicilian and Italian mafia (popularized by the 1863 Palermo play I mafiusi di la Vicaria), where mafiusu originally meant 'bold, swaggering, proud, fearless' (and of objects, 'fine, exquisite') before acquiring the sense of a clandestine criminal brotherhood. Sicilian mafia is most plausibly traced to Arabic mahyah ('boasting, bragging') or ma'āfir (name of an Arab tribe that ruled Palermo), introduced during the Emirate of Sicily.
mafia.notes: Beyond organized crime, colloquial French frequently uses une mafia figuratively and ironical-pejoratively for any insular, nepotistic professional clique or gatekeeping network in cinema, publishing, or politics.
