magasin.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century (via Old Occitan or Italian magazzino, originally 'maritime storehouse, warehouse for goods and munitions') from Arabic makhazin, plural of makhzan ('storehouse, depot, treasury'), derived from khazana ('to store up, guard').

history.meaning: warehouse, ammunition magazine -> retail shop, department store

magazine.etymology: An 18th-century re-borrowing (attested 1741, initially for British journals like The Gentleman's Magazine) from English magazine ('periodical miscellany, storehouse of information'), which English had earlier borrowed from Middle French magasin ('warehouse, storehouse'). Magasin entered French via Old Provençal or Italian magazzino from Arabic makhāzin, plural of makhzan ('storehouse, depot, treasury'), derived from the verbal root khazana ('to store up, guard').
magazine.notes: Classic spelling/pronunciation trap: le magazine (/ma.ga.zin/, ending in -ine) is a glossy print periodical or TV feature show, whereas its French doublet le magasin (/ma.ga.zɛ̃/, ending in -in) means a retail shop or store!

magicien.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French (14th century) from magique ('magical, art of magic') or directly on the stem of Latin magicus with the agentive suffix -ien (from Latin -iānus). The ultimate source is Classical Latin magus and Ancient Greek mágos ('member of the learned Persian priestly caste, sorcerer'), borrowed from Old Persian maguš (from Proto-Indo-European *magh-, 'to be able, have power').

history.meaning: member of the Median/Persian priestly caste

magicien.notes: Feminine is magicienne; in French entertainment circles, calling an agent, editor, or lighting director un magicien is high praise for pulling off seemingly impossible scheduling or creative miracles.

magie.etymology: Borrowed in the late 14th to 15th century from Classical Latin magīa ('sorcery, occult art'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek mageía ('the theology and ritual of the Persian Magi; enchantment, wizardry'). Greek mageía derives from mágos, rendering Old Persian maguš ('priest'), from the Indo-European root *magh- ('to be able, have power', also underlying English might and may).

history.meaning: ritual of the Magi; sorcery, enchantment

magie.notes: Frequently heard in la magie du cinéma ('movie magic'); remember that magie is strictly the noun ('magic'), whereas the adjective ('magic/magical') is always magique.

magique.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin magicus ('relating to magic or sorcery'), from Ancient Greek magikos ('of the Magi, magical'), derived from magos < Old Persian magush ('Zoroastrian priest, magus').

magnifique.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin magnificus ('doing great deeds, noble, sumptuous, splendid'), compound of magnus ('great') + -ficus (from facere 'to make, do').

history.meaning: performing on a grand scale, splendid

magnétique.etymology: Entered French in the early 17th century via Scientific Neo-Latin magnēticus, formed from Classical Latin magnēs, magnētis ('lodestone, magnet') and Ancient Greek Magnē̂tis líthos ('Magnesian stone'). The lodestone was named after Magnēsía, a mineral-rich region in Thessaly or Lydia in Asia Minor; following 18th-century Mesmerism ('animal magnetism'), the adjective acquired its vivid figurative sense of irresistible personal charisma.

history.meaning: pertaining to the lodestone or attraction

magnétique.notes: Note the everyday distinction: French uses aimant (not *magnet, except for fridge magnets) for a physical magnet, while magnétique serves as the standard adjective for both physics (bande magnétique, 'magnetic tape') and screen charisma (un regard magnétique).

mai.etymology: Inherited from Old French mai ('the month of May; green bough or maypole planted on May Day'), from Classical Latin Maius (sc. mensis, 'month of Maia, the Italic goddess of spring growth and increase', related to magnus / major).

history.meaning: month of the goddess Maia, May

cognates.meaning: mesh, tights, swimsuit (cognate with base maille)
mail (as in chain mail, from Old French maille)

maillot.etymology: Derived in Old French as a diminutive in -ot of maille ('mesh of a net, link of chain mail, knitted stitch'), originally denoting an infant's swaddling cloth wrapped tightly around the body (from emmailloter, 'to swaddle'). Maille descends from Classical Latin macula ('spot, blemish; mesh or hole in a woven net'). In the 19th century, maillot shifted to theatrical and acrobatic body-hugging knitwear (tights, leotards), and subsequently to sports jerseys and swimsuits.

history.meaning: spot, stain; mesh of a net
net mesh, ring of armor, knitted stitch
swaddling cloth; later close-fitting knitted garment

maillot.notes: Context determines the garment: un maillot de bain (often shortened to maillot at the pool or beach) is a swimsuit, whereas in sports un maillot is a team jersey (like the famous maillot jaune of the Tour de France).

rootFamily.gloss: mesh, knit stitch; link of chain mail
to swaddle a baby; to wrap up tightly

main.etymology: Inherited from Old French main ('hand'), from Classical Latin manus, manum ('hand; power, control; handwriting; band of men').

history.meaning: hand, handwriting, quire of paper, turn in cards

maintenant.etymology: Formed in Old French (maintenant, 12th c., originally 'immediately, without letting go, while still holding in the hand') from the present participle of maintenir ('to hold in the hand, keep up', from main 'hand' + tenir 'to hold').

history.meaning: while holding in the hand -> right away, immediately

maintenir.etymology: Inherited from Old French maintenir ('to protect, support, keep'), descending from Vulgar Latin *manūtenēre, a syntactic univerbation of Classical Latin manū tenēre ('to hold in the hand'), combining manū (ablative singular of manus, 'hand') and tenēre ('to hold, keep, grasp', from PIE *ten-, 'to stretch'). From physically holding fast by hand, the verb developed legal and administrative senses of upholding a right, keeping something in place, or confirming a scheduled event.
maintenir.notes: Conjugates exactly like tenir and venir (je maintiens, nous maintenons, il maintiendra, maintenu); in scheduling and production talk, Le tournage est maintenu means 'The shoot is still on (not canceled)'.

maire.etymology: Inherited from Old French maire ('head magistrate, chief official'), which reflects the nominative singular case of Classical Latin maior ('greater, superior, elder', irregular comparative of magnus, 'great', from PIE *meg-, 'great'). Under the Merovingians, maior domūs ('mayor of the palace') designated the chief steward of the royal household, while in medieval chartered communes maire became the title of the chief municipal magistrate; meanwhile, the Latin accusative maiōrem yielded the doublet majeur.

history.meaning: chief steward of an estate; head of a municipality

maire.notes: A rare survivor of the Old French nominative case (contrast majeur from the oblique case); pronounced /mɛʁ/ identically to mère ('mother') and mer ('sea'), and a female mayor is Madame la maire (or colloquially mairesse in Canada/some regions).

mairie.etymology: Derived in Old French (mairie, 13th c., 'office or jurisdiction of a mayor') from maire ('mayor, head official of a municipality', from Classical Latin major 'greater, elder, chief') + suffix -ie.

history.meaning: office of mayor -> town hall, municipal administration

mais.etymology: Mais developed from Latin magis, more or rather. The French word is recorded from the tenth century; its history helps explain the move from preference or contrast to but.

history.meaning: more, henceforth (n'en pouvoir mais) -> rather, but

mais.notes: The older sense 'more' of Latin magis still echoes inside jamais ('nevermore'), désormais, and the idiom je n'en peux mais; as an exclamation, Mais oui! means 'Why yes, of course!'.

maison.etymology: Inherited from Old French maison ('dwelling, house'), from Classical Latin mansionem (nominative mansio, 'a staying, remaining, night quarters, inn'), derived from manere, mansum ('to remain, dwell, stay the night'), which displaced domus in Gallo-Romance.

majeur.etymology: Borrowed/adapted from Classical Latin majorem (nominative major, 'greater, larger, elder', comparative of magnus 'great', learned doublet of maire); as a noun (le majeur), denotes the middle (longest) finger.

history.meaning: greater, larger, of full legal age
greater, major, of legal age (adj.); middle finger (noun)

majoritaire.etymology: Coined in 19th-century French political and corporate vocabulary (first attested around 1842–1877) from majorité ('majority, greater number', borrowed via Medieval Latin maioritās from Classical Latin maior, 'greater') plus the relational suffix -aire (from Latin -ārius). It spread from parliamentary voting systems (scrutin majoritaire) to corporate governance to designate whoever holds a controlling stake of shares.

history.meaning: greater number of votes; legal adulthood

majoritaire.notes: Essential corporate vocabulary in agency boardroom storylines (e.g., ASK in Dix pour cent): un actionnaire majoritaire is a 'majority/controlling shareholder', contrasted with minoritaire.

rootFamily.gloss: to increase, mark up (a price or fine)

mal.etymology: Inherited from Old French mal ('evil, harm, pain, illness; badly'), from Classical Latin malum ('evil, misfortune, harm', neuter of adjective malus 'bad, evil') and adverb male ('badly, ill').

malade.etymology: Inherited via Old French malade from Late/Vulgar Latin male habitus ('in a bad condition, indisposed, poorly kept'), an idiomatic phrase attested since Plautus and Celsus, formed from male ('badly, ill', adverb of malus) and habitus (past participle of habēre, 'to have, hold, keep oneself'). Syncope of the unstressed vowel in *malabitu triggered cluster assimilation and voicing (*malabdu > malade) in Gallo-Romance.

history.meaning: badly kept, in poor physical condition, indisposed

malade.notes: Functions as both adjective ('sick') and noun (un/une malade, 'a patient'); in colloquial spoken French, c'est un grand malade or un truc de malade means 'he's completely crazy' or 'something totally insane/wild'.

maladie.etymology: Formed in Old French (attested c. 1150) by adding the abstract quality/state suffix -ie (from Latin -ia) to the adjective malade ('ill, unwell', from Late Latin male habitus, 'in poor condition'). While English borrowed Old French maladie as malady with a literary or poetic register, French maladie became the everyday, unmarked word for any medical illness, disease, or disorder.
maladie.notes: Unlike the elevated English cognate malady, French maladie is completely neutral and everyday (e.g., assurance maladie for 'health insurance', arrêt maladie for 'sick leave').

cognates.meaning: mischance (parallel formation using mis- + Old French cheance)

malchance.etymology: A 19th-century compound (earlier Old/Middle French used mescheance, whence English mischance) combining the pejorative prefix mal- (from Latin male / malus, 'bad, ill') with chance ('luck, fortune'). Chance itself evolved from Old French cheance ('the way dice fall, befalling'), from Vulgar Latin *cadentia ('a falling'), neuter plural present participle of Classical Latin cadere ('to fall').

history.meaning: fall of the dice, fortune, luck
bad luck, streak of ill fortune

malchance.notes: Whereas chance used alone in French usually means 'good luck' (avoir de la chance = 'to be lucky'), malchance unambiguously means 'bad luck' (alongside colloquial la poisse or pas de bol).

malentendu.etymology: Substantivized in the mid-17th century from the Middle French adjectival phrase mal entendu ('poorly understood, misheard, ill-conceived'), uniting the adverb mal (from Latin male, 'badly, wrongly') with entendu, past participle of entendre ('to understand, hear'). Entendre comes from Classical Latin intendere ('to stretch toward, direct one's attention or mind toward', from in- + tendere), which in Gallo-Romance meant 'to understand' before also taking over 'to hear'.

history.meaning: to stretch out, direct one's attention toward

malentendu.notes: Preserves the older Classical French sense of entendre ('to understand', still alive in bien entendu, 'of course'); classic comedy-of-errors fuel in French farce (dissiper un malentendu = 'to clear up a misunderstanding', closely related to un quiproquo).

cognates.meaning: maugre (archaic: 'in spite of', borrowed from Old French)

malgré.etymology: Univerbation of the Old French noun phrase mal gré (also maugré), literally 'ill will, displeasure', combining mal ('bad, ill', from Latin malus) and gré ('will, liking, pleasure, gratitude', from Classical Latin grātum, neuter substantive of grātus, 'pleasing, welcome, thankful'). Used in absolute constructions like mal gré mien ('to my displeasure, against my wishes'), it grammaticalized into the general concessive preposition 'despite, in spite of'.

history.meaning: that which is pleasing or agreeable; favor
ill will, displeasure; against the wishes of

malgré.notes: Followed directly by a noun or pronoun (malgré la pluie, malgré lui — never *malgré de!); also avoid the debated construction *malgré que in formal French, preferring bien que + subjunctive instead.

rootFamily.gloss: liking, free will (de plein gré = willingly)

cognates.meaning: bad omen (parallel reflex of malum augurium)

malheur.etymology: Formed in Old French as mal eür ('ill fate, bad omen, misfortune'), uniting mal ('bad, evil', from Latin malus) with Old French eür ('omen, destiny, luck'). Eür descends via Vulgar Latin *agurium from Classical Latin augurium ('divination by observing birds, omen, portent', related to augur). Later folk etymology falsely associated eür with heure ('hour', from Latin hōra), introducing the unetymological silent h in malheur and bonheur.

morphemes.meaning: omen, fate, fortune (spelled with unetymological h-)

malheur.notes: Etymological surprise: the -heur in malheur and bonheur has nothing to do with heure ('hour')—it comes from Latin augurium ('omen')! Used dramatically as an exclamation (Malheur !, 'Woe / Disaster!') or in par malheur ('unfortunately').

malheureusement.etymology: Formed in the 15th–16th century from the feminine adjective malheureuse ('unfortunate, unhappy', from malheur 'bad luck, misfortune' < Old French mal + eür < Latin malum augurium 'ill omen') + adverbial suffix -ment.

malhonnête.etymology: Derived in Middle French (14th century, malhonneste) from the negative/pejorative prefix mal- ('badly, un-', from Latin male) and honnête ('honorable, upright, decent'). Honnête comes via Old French honeste from Classical Latin honestus ('regarded with honor, respectable, virtuous'), itself derived from honōs / honor ('honor, esteem, public dignity'). Its meaning narrowed from socially unseemly or impolite (17th-century honnête homme ideal) to modern financial or moral dishonesty.
malhonnête.notes: Pronounced /ma.lɔ.nɛt/ with seamless resyllabification across the mute h; in modern French it primarily means 'crooked, deceitful, unethical' (e.g., une clause malhonnête), though older speakers occasionally retain its Classical sense of 'rude, ill-mannered'.

malin.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century (feminine maligne) from Classical Latin malignus ('of an evil or grudging nature, spiteful, stingy', from malus 'bad' + -gnus < gignere 'born'); in popular French, le Malin ('the Evil One, the Devil, renowned for his cunning') softened the word's everyday sense to 'clever, shrewd, mischievous'.

history.meaning: malignant (in medicine); shrewd, clever, sly (in everyday speech)

cognates.meaning: sane (borrowed from Latin sānus, cognate with base sain)

malsain.etymology: Attested in Old French (12th–13th centuries, malsain) as a compound of the pejorative prefix mal- ('badly, ill', from Latin male) and sain ('healthy, sound, whole'), inherited from Classical Latin sānus ('healthy in body, sound in mind'). Originally applied to a sickly body or pestilential climate/air, it extended by the 18th and 19th centuries to morally corrupting, toxic, or twisted psychological atmospheres and relationships.

history.meaning: healthy, whole, sound in body or mind

malsain.notes: Frequently used psychologically in modern French where English says 'toxic', 'creepy', or 'twisted' (une ambiance malsaine, une curiosité malsaine, une relation malsaine), not just for diet or air quality.

maman.etymology: Affectionate nursery word formed by reduplication of the syllable ma- (attested in French since the 13th c., parallel to Latin mamma and Greek mamme), with nasalization of the final vowel in French.

mamie.etymology: An affectionate French family term that arose through two converging paths: on one hand, a nursery diminutive in -ie of maman ('mom', reduplicated infantile syllable *mam-, paralleled in Latin mamma, 'mother, breast'); on the other, univerbation of the tender address m'amie ('my [female] friend, sweetheart', Old French elision of ma amie before a vowel, from Latin amīca). By the 20th century, mamie settled specifically as the standard endearing term for 'grandma'.
mamie.notes: Paired with papy / papi ('grandpa'); warm and affectionate within the family, though calling an unfamiliar older woman une mamie can sound slightly patronizing depending on tone.

manche.etymology: Feminine la manche ('sleeve') is inherited from Classical Latin manica ('long tunic sleeve reaching over the hand, handcuff'), derived from manus ('hand').

history.meaning: shirt or coat sleeve; narrow sea channel (la Manche)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: manche (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: manche

manche.notes: Masculine **le manche** ('broom or pan handle') comes from a closely related Latin derivative *manicus* ('part held in the hand').

manger.etymology: Inherited from Old French mangier ('to eat'), from Late/Vulgar Latin manducare ('to chew, chomp, eat ravenously', derived from Manducus, a comic mask with chomping jaws, from Classical Latin mandere 'to chew'), which displaced Classical edere in Gallo-Romance and Italian.

manifestation.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–14th centuries from Late/Ecclesiastical Latin manifestātiō, manifestātiōnis ('revelation, making plain'), action noun from Classical Latin manifestāre ('to show clearly, expose'), from manifestus ('palpable, caught in the act, evident'—compound of manus, 'hand', and *festus, akin to infestus / 'struck by the hand'). In mid-19th-century France, the sense of 'public display of opinion' specialized into an organized street protest or march.

history.meaning: caught red-handed, palpable, plain to see
outward expression; organized public protest march

manifestation.notes: Classic false friend: while manifestation can mean an 'outward sign' or a 'cultural/sporting event' (manifestation culturelle), in everyday Parisian news and conversation une manifestation (colloquially une manif) means a 'street protest / demonstration'—cause of endless Parisian traffic jams!

rootFamily.gloss: to demonstrate, protest; to show, express

cognates.meaning: sleeve; gang of rogues (cognate via Latin manica)

manigance.etymology: Attested in French since the mid-16th century ('covert trickery, underhanded maneuver'), almost certainly borrowed from Occitan/Provençal manigança ('secret handling, shady contrivance'). Occitan manigança derives ultimately from a Vulgar Latin derivative of Classical Latin manus ('hand')—via manica ('long sleeve; gauntlet', whence tricks hidden up one's sleeve) or a frequentative verb *manicāre ('to handle, work covertly with the hands').

history.meaning: hand / long tunic sleeve covering the hand

manigance.notes: Usually plural (des manigances); lighter and pettier than un complot ('conspiracy'), it perfectly captures the backstage scheming, poaching of clients, and rival agent tricks in Dix pour cent.

manigancer.etymology: First attested in the early 17th century (1611 in Cotgrave), either formed within French as a denominal verb in -er from manigance ('underhanded scheme, covert maneuver') or borrowed alongside it from Occitan manigançar ('to handle secretly, contrive, plot'). Through Occitan, the root traces back to Latin manus ('hand') via manica / *manicāre, preserving the metaphor of deftly working strings or hiding sleight-of-hand up one's sleeve.

history.meaning: to handle, contrive, engineer in secret
to concoct, plot, engineer behind the scenes

manigancer.notes: Watch the orthographic cedilla before a or o to keep the soft /s/ sound (nous manigançons, il manigançait); a classic dialogue line when catching a colleague red-handed is Qu'est-ce que tu manigances encore ? ('What are you cooking up / scheming again?').

manipulateur.etymology: Derived in late 18th-century French (1780s) from manipuler ('to handle apparatus; to influence cunningly') with the learned agentive/adjectival suffix -ateur (from Latin -ātor). Originally denoting a chemist, pharmacist, or telegraph/film technician who physically operates delicate instruments by hand (from Medieval Latin manipulāre, ultimately Classical Latin manipulus, 'handful'), it developed its dominant modern psychological sense of an emotionally or politically calculating schemer.

history.meaning: handful, bundle of hay; infantry company
person who artfully controls others, schemer

manipulateur.notes: Feminine is manipulatrice (not *-ateuse!); used both as a noun (un manipulateur) and an adjective (un agent très manipulateur), though in hospitals manipulateur radio retains the neutral technical sense of 'radiology technician'.

rootFamily.gloss: liturgical vestment worn on the arm; handful (doublet)

manipuler.etymology: Entered standard French in the late 18th century (1760s–1770s) among chemists and apothecaries from Medieval/Scientific Latin manipulāre ('to lead by the hand; to prepare substances in measured handfuls'), derived from Classical Latin manipulus ('handful, bundle', from manus, 'hand', + the root of plēre, 'to fill'). During the French Revolution and early 19th century, the concrete laboratory sense ('to work materials with skilled hands') broadened figuratively to rigging votes, doctoring accounts, or covertly steering people's behavior.

history.meaning: to lead by the hand; to compound by handfuls
to handle instruments/substances; to control people covertly

manipuler.notes: Unlike English manipulate (which almost always sounds sinister unless very technical), French manipuler is still completely normal on warning labels for physical handling: Manipuler avec précaution ('Handle with care')!

cognates.meaning: way of doing something; social deportment

manière.etymology: Inherited from Old French maniere ("way of acting, sort, kind"), substantivized feminine of the adjective manier ("done by hand, skillful, habitual"), from Vulgar Latin *manarius, derived from Classical Latin manus ("hand"), tracing semantic shift from manual handling to general style or mode of action.

history.meaning: manual skill, way of acting, custom

manière.notes: Feminine noun (une manière); in the plural (faire des manières), it means to put on airs or fuss—common when describing diva actors on set.

cognates.meaning: jointed artist's figure; display dummy; model

mannequin.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Middle Dutch manneken ("little man, figurine"), a diminutive formed from man ("man") plus the diminutive suffix -ken. First used in French for an artist's jointed wooden figure and dressmaker's dummy before extending in the 19th century to live fashion models.

history.meaning: jointed figurine used by painters and sculptors

mannequin.notes: Always grammatically masculine (un mannequin), even when referring to a female fashion model—a classic gender trap in agency and casting talk.

manquant.etymology: Present participle of manquer ('to be lacking, be missing'), used as an adjective and noun since the 16th–17th century.

manque.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from manquer ("to be lacking, fail, miss"), itself borrowed in the 16th century from Italian mancare ("to be insufficient, dwindle"), derived from Classical Latin mancus ("maimed, crippled in the hand, defective").
manque.notes: Masculine noun (un manque de temps, être en manque de); do not confuse with the feminine noun la manque ("absence/failure" in military slang).

manquer.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian mancare ('to be lacking, fail, fall short'), derived from Classical Latin mancus ('maimed in the hand, crippled, defective, incomplete', source of Old French manc / manchot).

history.meaning: to be defective, fall short, be lacking
to miss, lack, run short of, fail

manteau.etymology: Manteau comes from Latin mantellum ('cloak, cloth covering') via Old French mantel; vocalisation of final -el before plural -s produced manteau (compare English 'mantle' and 'mantelpiece').

manuel.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–15th century from Classical Latin manualis ('belonging to or held in the hand') and Late Latin manuale ('small book that can be held in the hand', translating Greek enkheiridion), from manus ('hand').

history.meaning: done by hand, manual (adj.); textbook, handbook (noun)

maquillage.etymology: Derived in the 19th century from maquiller ("to paint the face, disguise") with the action/result suffix -age; first popularized in theatrical slang for greasepaint and stage cosmetics before entering everyday cosmetics and film production vocabulary, alongside figurative senses of falsification.

history.meaning: to work, cheat, disguise one's face for the stage

morphemes.meaning: action or material result of a verb

maquillage.notes: On French film sets, passer au maquillage ("heading to hair & makeup") is daily call-sheet routine; figuratively, maquillage de comptes means cooking the books.

maquiller.etymology: Originated in thieves' argot ("to do, fabricate, cheat at cards, disguise"), likely via Picard makier ("to make, work") from Middle Dutch maken ("to make"). Adopted by 19th-century theater actors for applying stage paint to transform one's face, remarkably paralleling English "to make up".

history.meaning: to fake, disguise; to apply stage cosmetics

maquiller.notes: Reflexive se maquiller means to put on one's own makeup, whereas transitive maquiller quelqu'un is what a set makeup artist does—or, in crime dramas, maquiller un crime ("to stage/cover up a crime").

marche.etymology: Combines two sources: (1) deverbal noun from marcher ('to walk, tread'), giving 'act of walking, military march, stair step (tread), operation of a machine'; and (2) Old French marche ('borderland, frontier'), from Frankish *marka ('boundary, borderland', cognate with English mark and march).

history.meaning: act of walking, pace, stair step, working order

marcher.etymology: Inherited from Old French marchier ('to trample underfoot, tread down, stamp'), borrowed from Frankish *markon ('to mark, impress with the foot, tread heavily', from *marka 'mark, footprint'); broadened in the 15th–16th century to 'to walk, go on foot' (replacing Old French aler a pié).

history.meaning: to leave a footprint, tread heavily
to trample -> to walk, march; (of a device) to work, function

marché.etymology: Inherited from Old French marchié ('marketplace, trade, commercial bargain'), from Classical Latin mercatus ('trade, traffic, marketplace, public fair'), derived from mercari ('to trade', from merx, mercis 'merchandise, wares').

history.meaning: open market, economic market, deal or bargain (bon marché)

mardi.etymology: Mardi continues Latin Martis dies, day of Mars. The twelfth-century French form marsdi preserves the older name more visibly.

cognates.meaning: Germanic calque ('Tiw's day', equating Tiw with Mars)

mardi.notes: English borrowed Mardi Gras verbatim for the festive Tuesday before Ash Wednesday when households used up rich fats and eggs.

marge.etymology: Adapted in Old and Middle French from Classical Latin margo, marginem ('edge, border, riverbank').

history.meaning: blank border of a page; leeway

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old/Middle French or directly from Latin marginem

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: marge (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: marge

marge.notes: French school notebooks famously feature a red vertical line marking **la marge** on the left side of every squared page.

mari.etymology: Inherited via Old French mari ("husband") from Classical Latin maritus ("married man, husband; conjugal"), originally an adjective meaning "provided with a spouse, paired", ultimately connected to an Indo-European root denoting a young man or bride/groom.
mari.notes: Silent final consonant historically lost in both spelling and speech (unlike Latin maritus); pairs in formal register with époux, while conjoint/compagnon covers unmarried partners too.

mariage.etymology: Inherited from Old French mariage (12th century, "wedlock, matrimony, dowry"), formed within Gallo-Romance from marier ("to wed") plus the collective/action suffix -age (from Latin -aticum); subsequently borrowed into Middle English as marriage.
mariage.notes: Covers both English "marriage" (the ongoing union) and "wedding" (the ceremony: aller à un mariage = "to go to a wedding"); spelled with a single r in French vs. double rr in English.

cognates.meaning: to wed, harmonize (e.g. wine and food)

marier.etymology: Inherited from Old French marier ("to join in wedlock, give in marriage"), from Classical Latin maritare ("to wed, unite, impregnate, tie vines to trees"), denominative verb built on maritus ("husband, married").

history.meaning: to wed, give in marriage; pair vines with trees
to give in marriage, unite spouses

marier.notes: Watch argument structure: marier quelqu'un means to officiate someone's wedding or marry off a child; "to marry someone" is se marier avec quelqu'un (or épouser quelqu'un, never *marier quelqu'un for your own spouse!).

marin.etymology: Inherited/adapted in the 12th century from Classical Latin marinus ('of the sea'), derived from mare ('sea'); used both as an adjective ('marine, seagoing') and as a noun ('sailor, seaman').

history.meaning: of or belonging to the sea

marié.etymology: Past participle of marier used adjectivally and nominally since Old French, continuing Latin maritatus ("joined in marriage, wedded"), past participle of maritare ("to wed").
marié.notes: As a noun, le marié is the groom, la mariée is the bride, and les jeunes mariés means "the newlyweds".

marmite.etymology: From Middle French marmite ('deep lidded cooking pot'), substantivized feminine of Old French adjective marmite ('demure, secretive, hiding one's face'), humorously applied to a covered pot that conceals what simmers inside.

cognates.meaning: named after the French earthenware cooking pot pictured on its label

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: marmite (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: marmite

marmite.notes: In French home cooking, **faire bouillir la marmite** ('keep the soup pot boiling') idiomatically means 'to keep the household fed and running'.

marque.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 14th–15th century from marquer ('to mark, stamp'), borrowed via Old Occitan marcar / marca from Germanic *markon / *marka ('boundary sign, distinguishing stamp or brand').

history.meaning: distinguishing sign, brand, trademark, token, score

cognates.meaning: to place a visible sign on (Germanic cognate)

marquer.etymology: Attested from the 15th–16th centuries (replacing earlier Old French merker / merchier), influenced by Italian marcare or Old Occitan marcar, ultimately from Germanic *markon ("to set a boundary sign, stamp, brand"), derived from Proto-Germanic *marko ("boundary, sign").

history.meaning: to mark a boundary, blaze, stamp
to stamp, indicate, leave an impression, score

marquer.notes: In cinema and agency parlance, marquer les esprits means to make a lasting impression, and un rôle marquant is a career-defining role; on set, marquer au sol refers to actor floor marks.

marquise.etymology: Feminine form of marquis ("nobleman ruling a borderland"), formed in Middle French from Old French marchis ("defender of a frontier march"), ultimately from Frankish *marka ("borderland, frontier") via Medieval Latin marchensis; later reshaped under Italian marchese / marchesa influence.

history.meaning: wife of a marquis; marchioness in her own right

marquise.notes: Beyond period-drama nobility, une marquise in Paris architecture is the ornate glass-and-iron canopy over hotel, theater, and agency entrances—and in pastry, a rich chocolate mousse dessert.

marre.etymology: Colloquial argot attested from the late 19th century in en avoir marre ("to have enough of, be sick of"). Its exact origin is disputed: philologists propose either Old/Middle French marri ("afflicted, aggrieved", from Frankish *marrjan "to hinder, vex"), argot marre ("share, portion" — i.e., "to have had one's fill"), or Spanish marra ("lack, want").

history.meaning: to be fed up, have had one's fill

marre.notes: Informal spoken staple (j'en ai marre !, marre de tout ça !); never used with très—intensify with en avoir vraiment marre or the stronger colloquialism en avoir ras-le-bol.

rootFamily.gloss: funny, amusing (originally: bored/fed up in slang se marrer)

marron.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Franco-Provençal or Northern Italian marrone ('large cultivated sweet chestnut'), from a pre-Latin Alpine word *marra; used as an invariable color adjective ('chestnut-brown, brown') since the 18th century.

mars.etymology: Inherited from Old French marz / mars, from Classical Latin Martius (short for mensis Martius, "month of Mars"), derived from Mars (stem Mart-), the Roman god of war and agricultural renewal whose festival inaugurated the original Roman year.

history.meaning: month dedicated to the god Mars

mars.notes: Unlike English "March", French month names are never capitalized (en mars, le 15 mars), and the final -s IS pronounced /maʁs/—just like the planet Mars and Paris's Champ-de-Mars.

marteau.etymology: Inherited from Old French martel, from Late Latin martellus ('hammer'), diminutive of Imperial Latin martulus (an alteration of Classical Latin marculus 'small smith's hammer').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: marteau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: marteau

marteau.notes: Around 1709 Bartolomeo Cristofori invented the *gravicembalo col piano e forte* by replacing harpsichord plucks with tiny leather-and-felt **marteaux**.

cognates.meaning: face covering (borrowed from Middle French masque)

masque.etymology: Borrowed in the early 16th century from Italian maschera ("mask"), which blends Pre-Romance/Lombardic *maska ("mesh, specter, witch, blackened face") and Arabic maskhara ("buffoonery, object of ridicule", from sakhira "to mock"). Entered English directly from French.

history.meaning: carnival or theatrical face covering; masked figure

masque.notes: Masculine noun (un masque)—a frequent error for English speakers because words in -que often look feminine; in acting, le jeu masqué ("masked acting") is classic conservatory training, and lever le masque means to drop all pretense.

cognates.meaning: to conceal or cover with a mask

masquer.etymology: Formed in the 16th century as a denominative verb from masque ("mask") or adapted directly from Italian mascherare ("to disguise with a mask"), rapidly extending from literal carnival disguise to obscuring views, emotions, or inconvenient truths.

history.meaning: to put on a mask, disguise
to cover with a mask; block from view, conceal

masquer.notes: On a film set, masquer un partenaire ("to block/upstage a fellow actor from the camera") is a cardinal framing sin; on phones, un numéro masqué means a blocked/withheld caller ID.

massage.etymology: Coined in early 19th-century French from masser ("to knead the body") plus -age. The verb masser (first recorded by French travelers in India and Egypt in the late 18th century) likely derives from Arabic massa ("to touch, feel, palpate"), possibly reinforced by Portuguese amassar ("to knead dough", from Latin massa).

history.meaning: to touch, feel with the hands
to rub and knead muscles after a bath

massage.notes: A genuine French export to world languages (including English, German, and Italian); masculine noun (un massage), with practitioners called un masseur / une masseuse (or medically un kiné).

massif.etymology: Derived in the 14th century from masse ('lump, mass, solid block', from Classical Latin massa < Ancient Greek maza 'barley cake, lump of dough') + adjectival suffix -if; used as a noun in geography and gardening for a mountain massif or flowerbed.

history.meaning: solid, heavy, bulky (adj.); mountain group, thick clump of shrubs (noun)

match.etymology: Borrowed in the early 19th century from English match ("contest between equals, sporting game"), itself from Middle English macche ("companion, mate, equal adversary") and Old English gemæcca ("mate, spouse, counterpart").

history.meaning: mate, companion, one of a pair

match.notes: Masculine noun (un match); plural is usually des matchs (1990 spelling reform and standard usage, though des matches also occurs). Note that English "match" meaning fire-stick is une allumette, never un match!

rootFamily.gloss: to match, pair up (recent informal/dating/tech verb)

maternité.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French from Medieval/Ecclesiastical Latin maternitas ("quality or state of being a mother"), derived from Classical Latin maternus ("maternal, of a mother"), itself from mater ("mother", from PIE *méh₂tēr). Extended in the 19th century to specialized maternity hospitals (such as Port-Royal in Paris).

history.meaning: motherhood; maternity hospital or ward; Virgin-and-Child artwork

maternité.notes: Used standalone with an article, la maternité / une maternité commonly means "the maternity hospital / maternity ward" (aller à la maternité), alongside abstract motherhood and congé maternité ("maternity leave").

matin.etymology: Inherited from Old French matin ('morning'), from Classical Latin matutinum (sc. tempus, 'early morning hours'), neuter of matutinus ('of the early morning', derived from Matuta, the Roman goddess of dawn, akin to maturus 'timely, early').

matinal.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French from matin ("morning", from Latin matutinum, neuter of matutinus "of the morning", linked to Mater Matuta, Roman goddess of dawn) plus the relational suffix -al, modeled on Late Latin matutinalis.

history.meaning: of the early morning / morning time
belonging to the morning; rising early

matinal.notes: Applied to a person, Vous êtes bien matinal ! means "You're up bright and early!"; in French media/PR (crucial for talent agents booking press tours), la matinale (feminine noun) is the flagship morning radio or TV talk show.

matinée.etymology: Formed in Old French (matinee, 12th c.) from matin ('morning') + suffix -ée denoting the full duration or activities of that part of the day.

history.meaning: the course or duration of the morning; afternoon theatrical performance

cognates.meaning: physical substance; topic (borrowed from Anglo-Norman matere)

matière.etymology: Semi-learned adaptation in Old French (matere, matiere) of Classical Latin materia ("building timber, woody substance of a tree, raw stuff, subject of discourse"), derived from mater ("mother, trunk of a tree producing shoots").

history.meaning: timber, trunk-wood; raw substance; theme or topic

matière.notes: Rich polysemy: physical fabric/substance, school subject, legal domain (en matière de contrats), and in film editing/writing, il y a de la matière means "there's great raw footage / rich story material to work with".

mature.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin maturus ("ripe, timely, fully grown, occurring at the proper hour"), doubly inherited in French alongside its popular phonetic descendant mûr ("ripe, mature", via Old French meür). Its psychological sense ("emotionally grown-up") was strongly reinforced in the 20th century by English mature.
mature.notes: Learned doublet of mûr: fruit is mûr (never *mature), careful reflection is mûre réflexion, whereas mature specifically describes emotional/personal maturity (très mature pour son âge) or a mature market/audience.

cognates.meaning: physical substance; equipment (also borrowed as matériel)

matériel.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old/Middle French from Late Latin materialis ("composed of matter, physical"), derived from Classical Latin materia ("timber, substance"). Substantivized in the 18th–19th centuries as le matériel ("physical equipment, gear, apparatus") in contrast to le personnel ("staff").
matériel.notes: Classic false friend as a noun: le matériel is an uncountable collective noun meaning "equipment / hardware / camera & sound gear" (not sewing cloth, which is tissu, nor raw building material, which is matériau).

mauvais.etymology: Inherited from Old French malvais ('bad, wicked, worthless, cowardly'), from Vulgar Latin *malifatius ('ill-fated, born under a bad sign'), compound of Classical Latin malus ('bad') + fatum ('fate, destiny', parallel to Old Occitan malvatz).

maximum.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (first in mathematics and physics, then in everyday prose) directly from Classical Latin maximum, neuter singular of maximus ('greatest, largest, highest'), the irregular superlative of magnus ('great, large'). Along with its opposite minimum, it kept its Latin -um ending while becoming a fully naturalized French masculine noun.
maximum.notes: Although borrowed from Latin **-um**, in French **maximum** is pronounced **/maksimɔm/** (with an open **/ɔ/** before the final **/m/**, just like **album** and **aquarium**).

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: maximum

cognates.meaning: from the same Latin neuter superlative
one in authority or skilled (via Old French maistre)

maître.etymology: Inherited via Old French maistre from Classical Latin magister ("chief, director, teacher, helmsman"), formed with the contrastive/comparative suffix *-teros from the root of magis ("more") and magnus ("great")—literally "the greater one" (opposed to minister, "the lesser one, attendant"). The circumflex marks the lost Old French s.

history.meaning: master, expert, primary teacher, attorney title

maître.notes: Capitalized Maître (abbr. Me) is the mandatory honorific when addressing lawyers (avocats) and notaries—indispensable whenever agency contracts turn litigious! Un coup de maître is a masterstroke.

cognates.meaning: female teacher, mistress of a craft
woman in authority; lover (borrowed from Old French maistresse)

maîtresse.etymology: Inherited from Old French maistresse, formed from maistre ("master") plus the feminine agentive/status suffix -esse (from Late Latin -issa, of Greek origin). Evolved across domains to denote a woman in command, a female schoolteacher, a pet's female owner, and an extramarital lover (via courtly love's "mistress of one's heart").

history.meaning: woman with authority, governess, lady beloved by a suitor
female teacher; woman of the house; pet owner; romantic mistress

maîtresse.notes: Context completely governs register: completely innocent for a primary-school teacher (la maîtresse d'école), a dog's owner (sa maîtresse, as with Jean Gabin in Dix pour cent!), or a pillar idea (idée maîtresse), yet means extramarital lover in avoir une maîtresse.

me.etymology: Inherited from Old French me ('me, to me'), unstressed clitic development of Classical Latin me (accusative and ablative of ego 'I').

history.meaning: me, to me, myself (1st-person singular object pronoun)

mec.etymology: Attested in Parisian criminal argot from the early 19th century first as "master, boss, God" (le mec des mecs) and "pimp", before bleaching in the 20th century into everyday "guy, fellow, boyfriend". Etymology debated: either a clipping mac / mec of maquereau ("pimp"), or from earlier dialectal/argot mèque ("lord, ruler", tenuously linked to Latin magnus).
mec.notes: Ubiquitous informal word for "guy/dude" (un mec sympa) or "boyfriend/partner" (mon mec, son mec); its Verlan (backslang) mirror keum is also heard in casual speech.

meilleur.etymology: Inherited from Old French meillor ('better, best'), from Classical Latin meliorem (nominative melior, 'better'), synthetic comparative of bonus ('good').

cognates.meaning: threat, danger (borrowed from Old French menace)

menace.etymology: Inherited via Old French menace / manace from Classical Latin minaciae ("threats, overhanging perils", plural of Late/Vulgar Latin minacia), derived from minax ("jutting out, overhanging, threatening"), from minae ("projecting battlements of a wall; threats").

history.meaning: projecting wall parapets; threats / overhanging, threatening
declaration of hostile intent, impending danger

menace.notes: Less melodramatic than English "menace": une menace is the normal, everyday French word for any "threat" (mettre ses menaces à exécution = "to carry out one's threats").

cognates.meaning: to threaten, endanger (from Old French menacier)

menacer.etymology: Inherited from Old French menacier ("to threaten, warn of harm"), from Vulgar Latin *minaciare, a denominative verb formed on minacia ("threat"), ultimately rooted in Classical Latin minari ("to jut out, overhang, threaten").

history.meaning: to intimidate with threats; portend danger
to threaten; be on the verge of collapsing or failing

menacer.notes: Spelling rule: c takes a cedilla before a and o to stay soft /s/ (il menaçait, menaçant); governs de + infinitive (menacer de claquer la porte = "to threaten to walk out").

menacé.etymology: Past participle of menacer ("to threaten", from Old French menacier < Vulgar Latin *minaciare) used adjectivally; broadened in modern administrative, ecological, and labor usage to mean "at risk of closure, dismissal, or extinction".

history.meaning: under threat; at risk (of job loss, cancellation, or extinction)

menacé.notes: Covers both personal danger (se sentir menacé = "to feel threatened/insecure", e.g. by a rival agent) and institutional/ecological peril (espèce menacée = "endangered species", tournage menacé = "shoot in jeopardy").

cognates.meaning: relying on alms; beggar (from Latin mendicans)

mendiant.etymology: Inherited from Old French mendiant (12th–13th century, notably applied to the mendicant friar orders), present participle of mendier ("to beg for alms"), from Classical Latin mendicare ("to ask for alms, beg"), itself built on mendicus ("needy, indigent; originally having a physical defect/blemish", from mendum "bodily defect, fault").

history.meaning: physical defect -> disabled, reduced to penury, beggar
mendicant friar; person begging for alms

mendiant.notes: Feminine is mendiante; culturally, les mendiants (or quatre mendiants) are also classic French Christmas chocolate disks topped with dried fruits and nuts whose colors evoked the robes of the four medieval mendicant orders.

mener.etymology: Inherited from Old French mener ('to lead, guide, drive'), from Late/Vulgar Latin minare ('to drive cattle onward with shouts and threats'), active reshaping of Classical Latin minari ('to threaten, jut out', from minae 'threats').

history.meaning: to drive animals with cries -> to lead, conduct
to lead, guide, direct, carry on

mensonge.etymology: Inherited via Old French mençonge / mensonge (originally feminine) from Late/Vulgar Latin *mentionia ("falsehood, fabrication"), formed from Classical Latin mentiri ("to lie, fabricate, feign"), itself derived from mens, mentis ("mind, intention, invention"—i.e., devising something purely in one's head).

history.meaning: to invent in the mind, speak falsely, deceive

morphemes.meaning: abstract nominal suffix (from *-ionia, reshaped after songe)

mensonge.notes: Masculine noun (un mensonge, un pieux mensonge = "a white lie") despite ending in -e and having been feminine in Old French (it shifted to masculine by analogy with le songe, "dream").

menteur.etymology: Inherited from Old French menteor (originally the oblique case alongside nominative mentere), from Late Latin mentitorem (nominative mentitor, 'liar, deceiver'), an agent noun derived from Classical Latin mentiri ('to speak falsely, fabricate'), itself built on mens, mentis ('mind, invention').

history.meaning: to fabricate in the mind, speak falsely

menteur.notes: Inflects irregularly in the feminine as menteuse (not -eure); in talent-agency banter, 'beau menteur' describes a charming smooth-talker rather than a malicious deceiver.

menthe.etymology: Inherited via Old French mente from Classical Latin mentha ('mint'), borrowed from Ancient Greek mínthē (in myth, the nymph Minthe transformed into the fragrant herb).

cognates.meaning: early West Germanic borrowing from Latin mentha

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: menthe (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: menthe

menthe.notes: Hot green **thé à la menthe** steeped with fresh spearmint leaves is a beloved café staple across France.

mentir.etymology: Inherited via Old French mentir from Vulgar Latin *mentire, an active re-formation of Classical Latin deponent mentiri ('to lie, cheat, feign, invent'), derived from mens, mentis ('mind, intellect'), reflecting a semantic shift from 'forming a mental construct' to 'inventing a falsehood'.

history.meaning: to devise in the mind, feign, lie

mentir.notes: Conjugates like sentir, dropping the stem-final -t in singular present forms (je mens, tu mens, il ment) while keeping it in the plural (nous mentons).

menton.etymology: Inherited via Old French menton from Vulgar Latin *mentonem, enlarged from Classical Latin mentum ('chin', from an Indo-European root *men- 'to jut out', also seen in promontoire and éminent).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: menton (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: menton

menton.notes: Watch out for the look-alike verb **mentir** ('to tell a lie', from Latin *mentiri* 'to fabricate in the mind' < *mens*) — completely unrelated to **le menton**!

menu.etymology: Inherited from Old French menu ('small, fine, finely chopped, detailed'), from Classical Latin minutus ('made small, minute, petty', past participle of minuere 'to lessen, chop small'); as a noun (18th c.), originally the detailed list (le menu détail) of dishes to be served at a banquet, hence 'restaurant menu'.

history.meaning: slender, fine, minor (adj.); detailed bill of fare, menu (noun)

menuisier.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from menuise ('small work, fine craftsmanship', from menuiser 'to make small, carve fine details', from Vulgar Latin *minutiare < minutus 'small'); designated a craftsman working in small, finely fitted woodwork (joinery and cabinetry) as opposed to a heavy structural charpentier.

history.meaning: craftsman of fine fitted woodwork, joiner, carpenter

mer.etymology: Inherited from Old French mer ('the sea'), from Classical Latin mare ('sea', from PIE *mori 'body of salt water, marsh', cognate with English mere and German Meer).

merci.etymology: Merci comes from Latin merces, which meant pay or a price and later favour or grace. The Académie records ninth-century mercit with the sense of grace or mercy. Modern merci is the everyday expression of thanks; the older sense survives in sans merci.

history.meaning: pay, price; later favour or grace

merci.notes:
- Answer to *merci* is usually *de rien* or *je vous en prie*.
- *Non, merci* declines an offer; *Oui, merci* accepts it.

mercredi.etymology: Inherited from Old French mercresdi ('Wednesday'), from Vulgar Latin *Mercurii dies, transposition of Classical Latin dies Mercurii ('day of the god Mercury', translating Greek hemera Hermou).

merde.etymology: Inherited directly via Old French merde from Classical Latin merda ('dung, ordure, excrement'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *smerd- ('foul-smelling, filth'). Beyond its literal and expletive uses, French theatrical tradition adopted 'Merde !' in the 19th century as a superstitious wish for success, recalling the horse droppings left outside packed playhouses.

history.meaning: expletive of frustration; theatrical 'break a leg!'

merde.notes: In French cinema and theater (ubiquitous in Dix pour cent), wishing an actor 'Merde !' before an audition or premiere means 'Break a leg!' — never reply 'merci' (said to jinx it).

cognates.meaning: wonder, astonishing thing (borrowed from Old French)

merveille.etymology: Inherited from Old French merveille, from Vulgar Latin mirabilia ('wonderful things'), originally the neuter plural of Classical Latin mirabilis ('astonishing, extraordinary') reanalyzed in Gallo-Romance as a feminine singular collective noun, from mirari ('to wonder at, gaze in admiration').

history.meaning: wonderful things, objects of admiration (neuter plural)

merveille.notes: Always feminine (une merveille); the adverbial phrase 'à merveille' ('wonderfully, to perfection') is a staple compliment for an actor's screen test or performance.

merveilleux.etymology: Formed in Old French (merveillos, 11th–12th c.) from merveille ('wonder, marvel', from Vulgar Latin *mirabilia, neuter plural of Classical Latin mirabilis 'wonderful', from mirari 'to wonder at') + suffix -eux.

message.etymology: Inherited from Old French message ('errand, official communication; originally also the messenger himself'), from Medieval/Vulgar Latin *missaticum, derived from mittere, missum ('to send') + suffix -aticum.

history.meaning: that which is sent, mission, message
messenger -> spoken or written communication, message

messagerie.etymology: Formed in Middle French from messager ('messenger, courier') plus the collective/institutional suffix -ie, itself built on Old French message from Vulgar Latin *missaticum ('that which is sent, dispatch'), derived from missus, past participle of Classical Latin mittere ('to send'). It evolved from stagecoach and parcel-delivery services to modern voicemail and digital messaging.

history.meaning: official dispatch, mission entrusted to an envoy
office of a messenger; coach and parcel transport service
electronic mail system, voicemail inbox, instant messaging

messagerie.notes: On French mobile phones, 'tomber sur la messagerie' is the standard idiom for a call going straight to voicemail — a constant plot beat for frantic talent agents.

mesure.etymology: Inherited from Old French mesure ('measurement, standard vessel, moderation, musical time'), from Classical Latin mensura ('a measuring, standard of measure, proportion'), derived from metiri, mensus ('to measure').

history.meaning: act or unit of measuring, proportion
measure, dimension, moderation, musical bar, step/action

mesurer.etymology: Inherited from Old French mesurer ('to ascertain the dimensions of, apportion, moderate'), from Late Latin mensurare ('to measure'), derived from Classical Latin mensura ('measure').

cognates.meaning: meddler, one who puts in (from meter)

metteur.etymology: Derived in Old and Middle French as an agent noun from mettre ('to put, place, set') plus -eur. Mettre continues Classical Latin mittere ('to send, release, throw'), which underwent a sweeping Gallo-Romance semantic shift to 'put, place' (displacing Classical ponere). In the 19th century, 'metteur en scène' crystallized for the person who stages a theatrical production.

history.meaning: to put, place, set in position
placer, setter; stage or film director

metteur.notes: Rarely stands alone outside compounds; in French cinema, 'réalisateur' is standard for a film director, while 'metteur en scène' means theater director or honors a film director's artistic auteurship.

rootFamily.gloss: to hand over, postpone, put back

mettre.etymology: Inherited from Old French metre ('to put, place, set'), from Classical Latin mittere ('to send, let go, throw'); in Late and Popular Latin, mittere shifted from 'to send' to 'to put, place' (while Classical ponere narrowed to 'to lay eggs', French pondre).

history.meaning: to send, let go -> to put, place, set
to put, place, put on clothing, spend time

meuble.etymology: Shortened from biens meubles ('movable goods'), inherited from Spoken Latin *movibilis (Classical Latin mobilis, 'movable', from movere 'to move'). In medieval law property was either immeuble ('immovable': land and buildings) or meuble ('movable': chests, tables, beds).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: meuble (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: meuble

micro.etymology: Twentieth-century French apocope (clipping) of microphone, itself adapted from English microphone (popularized in its modern acoustic-electrical sense by David Edward Hughes in 1878), a learned neoclassical compound of Ancient Greek mikros ('small, faint') and phone ('voice, sound'), originally denoting an instrument that amplifies faint sounds.
micro.notes: Watch the homonym: 'un micro' most commonly means 'a microphone' on set or radio (e.g., 'micro-cravate' = lapel mic), whereas 'un micro-ondes' (often shortened to 'le micro-ondes', never just 'micro') is a microwave oven.

midi.etymology: Midi combines the older French elements mi, middle, and di, day. They descend from Latin medius and dies. The combination originally identifies the middle of the day.

history.meaning: middle of the day, noon; south

midi.notes: French never says *douze heures for 12:00—always il est midi ('it's noon') and il est minuit ('it's midnight').

miel.etymology: Miel comes directly from Latin mel ('honey'), with regular diphthongisation of stressed short e into ie (as in caelum -> ciel).

mien.etymology: Inherited from Old French mien ('mine, my own'), stressed tonic development of Classical Latin meum (accusative of meus 'my, mine', with the vowel modeling of tien / sien after tuum / suum).

history.meaning: mine (possessive pronoun); my own kin (les miens)

miette.etymology: Double diminutive formed in Old French from mie ('soft inner crumb of bread, tiny bit') + -ette, inherited from Classical Latin mica ('crumb, grain of salt, tiny morsel').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: miette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: miette

miette.notes: Modern French still distinguishes **la croûte** ('crust'), **la mie** ('soft inside of the loaf'), and **les miettes** ('loose crumbs').

mieux.etymology: Inherited from Old French mielz / mieus ('better, best'), from Classical Latin melius ('better'), neuter singular of melior used adverbially.

cognates.meaning: obsequious follower, servile subordinate (borrowed from Middle French)

mignon.etymology: Attested in 15th-century Middle French as both noun ('royal favorite, darling') and adjective ('graceful, dainty, cute'), built on an expressive Gallo-Romance stem mign- (likely influenced by Celtic *min- 'gentle, small, soft' or pet-names for cats such as minet) denoting smallness, delicacy, and affectionate charm.
mignon.notes: Classic false friend with English 'minion' (which borrowed the 16th-century French court-favorite sense 'les mignons d'Henri III'): French 'mignon' (fem. mignonne) simply means 'cute, sweet, or handsome', though 'péché mignon' means an indulgent 'guilty pleasure'.

rootFamily.gloss: miniature bottle or petit four pastry

mijoter.etymology: Attested from Middle/Classical French in regional northern usage (originally 'to coddle, store fruit gently in straw or crumbs to ripen', then 'to cook very slowly over low heat'), expressive derivative built on Old French mie / Picard mijot.

history.meaning: to simmer slowly over gentle heat

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mijoter (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mijoter

mijoter.notes: Figuratively, **Qu'est-ce que vous mijotez?** means 'What scheme or surprise are you cooking up?'.

milieu.etymology: Univerbation in Old French (mi leu / milieu, 12th c.) of mi ('middle, half', from Classical Latin medius 'middle') + lieu ('place', from Classical Latin locus) — literally 'the middle place'.

history.meaning: middle place, center; social or natural environment

militant.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical and Ecclesiastical Latin militantem, present participle of militare ('to serve as a soldier, campaign'), from miles, militis ('soldier'). First used in theology for the earthly 'Église militante' ('Church Militant' striving against evil), it secularized in late 19th-century labor and political movements to denote a committed grassroots campaigner.

history.meaning: serving as a soldier, waging war
grassroots activist, union or party campaigner

militant.notes: Crucial nuance false friend: in French, 'un militant / une militante' neutrally means 'an activist, grassroots organizer, or campaigner' (e.g., 'un film militant' = a socially engaged film), without the violent or extremist overtones of English 'militant'.

rootFamily.gloss: to campaign actively for a cause

mille.etymology: The number mille was borrowed from Latin mille, thousand. Its French history is recorded from the eleventh century; the number does not take an ordinary plural s.

cognates.meaning: from Roman mīlle passūs ('1,000 paces') and mīlle

mille.notes: Unlike vingt and cent, numerical mille is completely invariable—it NEVER takes plural -s (deux mille ans, dix mille euros)!

cognates.meaning: Roman milestone; unit of a thousand paces (via Latin)

millier.etymology: Inherited via Old French milier from Late Latin miliarium ('group of a thousand; milestone marking a thousand paces'), substantive neuter of Classical Latin miliarius ('containing a thousand'), derived from mille ('one thousand'). Unlike the invariable numeral mille, millier functions as an approximate collective noun.

history.meaning: milestone (1,000 paces); vessel or unit of a thousand
approximate count or group of a thousand

millier.notes: Whereas the cardinal number 'mille' never takes a plural -s ('trois mille euros'), the collective noun 'millier' behaves like 'dozen' and takes plural -s plus 'de' ('des milliers de spectateurs' = thousands of viewers).

millimètre.etymology: Coined in 1793–1795 as part of the French metric system from combining form milli- ('one-thousandth', from Classical Latin mille 'thousand') + mètre ('meter').

million.etymology: Borrowed in 14th-century Middle French from Early Italian milione (literally 'a great thousand'), formed in medieval Italian merchant accounting from mille ('thousand', from Classical Latin mille) plus the augmentative suffix -one, and famously popularized across Europe as the nickname of Marco Polo's travelogue Il Milione.
million.notes: Grammatically a noun rather than a pure determiner, so it takes a plural -s and requires 'de' before a direct noun ('deux millions d'entrées' = two million box-office admissions).

cognates.meaning: to chop finely; to soften speech ('minced oath', from Old French mincier)

mince.etymology: Attested in the 19th century as a polite minced-oath interjection ('darn!, shoot!') substituting euphemistically for merde ! by sharing its initial m-. The word itself is the adjective mince ('thin, slender'), back-formed in Old French from mincier ('to chop into tiny pieces'), from Vulgar Latin *minutiare, derived from Classical Latin minutus ('small, minute').

history.meaning: to chop finely, reduce to small bits

mince.notes: Remarkable double coincidence: French 'mince !' is literally a 'minced oath' for 'merde !', and English 'to mince one's words' actually comes from the exact same Old French verb 'mincier' ('to chop small').

rootFamily.gloss: to make or become thinner, slim down

cognates.meaning: air, bearing, facial expression (borrowed from French)

mine.etymology: Attested in 15th-century Middle French ('faire mine de', facial look or bearing), most plausibly borrowed from Breton min ('beak, snout, muzzle, mouth'; compare Welsh min 'lip, edge'), shifting metonymically from the mouth/muzzle to a person's facial expression, complexion, and outward demeanor. It is an accidental homonym of mine ('mineral pit; pencil lead').
mine.notes: Essential everyday idioms: 'avoir bonne mine' means looking healthy and radiant, 'avoir petite mine' means looking exhausted or pale, and 'mine de rien' means 'casually, unassumingly, without looking like it'.

rootFamily.gloss: to pull coy or affected faces, simper

cognates.meaning: under-age person; lesser (via Old French and Latin)

mineur.etymology: Inherited and reinforced via Old French menor, mineur from Classical Latin minorem (accusative of minor, 'smaller, lesser, younger'), the irregular comparative of parvus ('small'). Already in Roman law (minor viginti quinque annis), minor designated a person below full legal age, yielding the modern French noun and adjective for an under-age person.

history.meaning: lesser in rank or age; person under guardianship

mineur.notes: Homonym alert: 'un mineur' is both 'an under-age minor' (fem. une mineure, from Latin minorem; crucial in child-actor labor rules on French film sets) and 'a coal/ore miner' (from mine + -eur).

rootFamily.gloss: state of being under legal age; minority group

miniature.etymology: Borrowed in the late 16th century from Italian miniatura ('manuscript illumination, tiny painted portrait'), derived from Medieval Latin miniare ('to rubricate or paint with red pigment'), from Classical Latin minium ('cinnabar, red lead'). Etymologically unrelated to Latin minimus ('smallest'), it acquired the sense 'tiny scale model' through folk-etymological attraction to minimum and minute, since monastic illuminations were delicately small.

history.meaning: monastic manuscript illumination; small portrait locket
small-scale painting or tiny replica ('en miniature')

morphemes.meaning: paint with red lead, illuminate (from Latin minium)
result or art of an action (from Italian -atura)

miniature.notes: One of philology's great surprises: 'miniature' originally meant 'painted in red lead (minium)', not 'small' — indeed, modern 'mini-' (minijupe, minibus) was ultimately extracted from 'miniature'! In digital media, 'une miniature' also means a video 'thumbnail'.

minimum.etymology: Learned 17th-century borrowing (initially in mathematical and philosophical treatises by Leibniz and French geometers before entering everyday speech) from Classical Latin minimum, neuter singular of minimus ('smallest, least'), the suppletive superlative paired with parvus ('small') and comparative minor ('smaller'), from Proto-Indo-European *mey- ('small, lessen').

history.meaning: the smallest amount, very least (neuter superlative)
lowest mathematical value; lowest acceptable threshold

minimum.notes: Always masculine ('le minimum syndical' = 'the bare minimum required'); in the plural, both 'des minimums' (everyday standard) and Latinate 'des minima' (formal, e.g., 'les minima sociaux' = minimum welfare benefits) are accepted.

rootFamily.gloss: very slight, tiny (learned doublet from fem./masc. minimus)

ministre.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin ministrum (nominative minister, 'attendant, servant, subordinate helper'), formed from the stem of minus ('less') with the contrastive comparative suffix -ter. It was coined in direct structural opposition to magister ('master, chief', from magis 'more'), before rising from 'royal servant' to 'cabinet minister of state'.

history.meaning: servant of God or of a sovereign; agent
high government official heading a portfolio; Protestant pastor

ministre.notes: Since 1998 and affirmed by the Académie française in 2019, feminine titles use the feminine article 'Madame la ministre' or 'une ministre' (e.g., 'la ministre de la Culture', a frequent guest or foil in French film-world comedies).

ministère.etymology: Learned borrowing via Middle French from Classical Latin ministerium ('office of an attendant, service, employment, administration'), derived from minister ('servant, subordinate attendant') plus the abstract office suffix -ium. Note that popular inherited evolution of the exact same Latin word ministerium yielded French métier ('trade, craft, profession') — making ministère and métier true etymological doublets!

history.meaning: service of an attendant, duty, administration
ecclesiastical or official service; intermediary agency
government department or cabinet office; public prosecutor ('ministère public')

ministère.notes: Fascinating doublet: learned 'ministère' ('government ministry') and everyday 'métier' ('profession, the acting craft') both descend from Latin 'ministerium' — one borrowed intact by scholars, the other worn down by centuries of spoken Old French (*menestier > mestier > métier).

minuit.etymology: Compound inherited from Old French mienuit ('the middle of the night'), combining feminine mie (< Latin media 'middle') and nuit (< Latin noctem 'night'), exactly parallel to midi (< medius dies 'midday').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: minuit (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: minuit

minuit.notes: Originally feminine because *nuit* is feminine, **minuit** shifted to masculine on the model of **midi**.

minuscule.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–18th century from Classical Latin minusculus ('rather small, tiny', originally in paleography littera minuscula 'small cursive or lowercase script' as opposed to majuscula), double diminutive formed on minor, minus ('less, smaller').

minute.etymology: The time word minute comes from medieval Latin minuta, a noun use of the feminine of minutus, small. The Académie records it from the thirteenth century. The separate document-draft sense has its own specialised history.

history.meaning: first small division (1/60th of an hour or degree)

rootFamily.gloss: small, slender; restaurant menu (inherited doublet of minūtus!)

minute.notes: Note that une minute is feminine in French (attends une minute!), whereas Italian il minuto and Spanish el minuto are masculine; 'second' (pars minūta secunda, the 'second' small division) gave une seconde!

minuteur.etymology: Formed in 20th-century French from minuter ('to time to the minute, regulate duration', from minute 'sixtieth of an hour') + instrument suffix -eur.

miracle.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 11th–12th century from Classical Latin miraculum ('object of wonder, marvel; in Christian Latin, supernatural work of God'), derived from mirari ('to wonder at, marvel', from mirus 'wonderful').

miroir.etymology: Miroir comes from Old French mireor, built on mirer ('to look at, gaze at', from Latin mirari 'to wonder at, admire'). English 'mirror' was borrowed directly from Old French.
miroir.notes: **Regarder dans le miroir** = to look in the mirror.

mise.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of mettre ('to put, place, set, stake'), inherited from Old French mise, continuing Gallo-Romance *missa from Classical Latin missa (feminine of missus, past participle of mittere 'to send, release'). Because mettre became French's core verb of placement, mise developed an exceptionally wide range of nominal senses: 'placing, staging, outfit,赌 stake, and software update'.

history.meaning: sent, released (feminine past participle of mittere)
act of placing, outlay of money, arbitration
placing, wager, styling; head of compounds like mise à jour and mise en scène

morphemes.meaning: put, place (suppletive participial stem of mettre)

mise.notes: Powerhouse noun in French idioms: 'mise à jour' (update), 'mise en scène' (staging/direction), 'mise en pli' (hair set), 'mise au point' (clarification/focusing), and 'être de mise' (to be called for / appropriate).

cognates.meaning: miser (FALSE FRIEND — unrelated! English miser is from Latin miser 'wretched')

miser.etymology: Denominal verb coined in late 18th-century French from the gambling sense of mise ('stake, money placed on a gaming table') plus the first-conjugation verbal suffix -er, literally 'to place one's stake'. From casinos and horse-racing it rapidly generalized into business and everyday figurative speech ('miser sur quelqu'un' = to bet on / invest hopes in someone).

history.meaning: wager, stake placed in a game
to place a bet; figuratively to bank on or invest in

miser.notes: Total false friend with English 'miser' (a stingy hoarder, which translates as 'un avare' or 'un radin'): 'miser sur un jeune acteur' means 'to bet on / back a young actor's potential'.

rootFamily.gloss: to bet again, raise the stakes

mission.etymology: Learned borrowing in the 16th century from Classical Latin missionem (nominative missio, 'a sending away, dispatching, release from duty'), action noun formed on missus, past participle of mittere ('to send'). Initially adopted in Jesuit and theological usage for sending clergy abroad, it broadened in the 17th–20th centuries to diplomatic envoys, military tasks, and professional consulting assignments.
mission.notes: In everyday French workplace vocabulary, 'une mission' simply means a temporary project, freelance gig, or business trip ('être en mission' = on a work assignment), not necessarily something heroic.

mode.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French from Classical Latin modum (nominative modus, 'measure, standard, rhythm, musical scale, grammatical mood, manner'), from Proto-Indo-European *med- ('to measure, take appropriate measures'). Middle French split the single Latin word into two nouns differentiated by gender: masculine le mode ('method, musical/grammatical mode, device setting') and feminine la mode ('prevailing manner, fashion').

history.meaning: measure, musical rhythm, grammatical mood, manner
logical/grammatical mood; customary way of living or dressing
operating mode, setting, method (masc.) vs. fashion, trend (fem.)

mode.notes: Textbook gender pair to memorize: masculine 'le mode' means mode, method, or device setting ('mode avion' = airplane mode, 'mode d'emploi' = user manual), whereas feminine 'la mode' means fashion or trend ('être à la mode').

moderne.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Late Latin modernus ('of the present time, recent, contemporary', coined in the late 5th c. from Classical Latin adverb modo 'just now, recently', on the model of hodiernus from hodie).

cognates.meaning: unassuming, moderate in size or ego

modeste.etymology: Learned borrowing in 14th-century Middle French from Classical Latin modestus ('keeping due measure, restrained, temperate, unassuming'), built on an archaic neuter s-stem *modes- related to modus ('measure, limit, proper bound'; compare moderari 'to keep within bounds'). Its core etymological image is staying gracefully within one's measure.

history.meaning: keeping due measure, temperate, orderly, discreet

modeste.notes: Position changes nuance slightly, and watch English 'modest' in the dress sense: French 'modeste' means humble, unassuming, or small in scale ('une somme modeste', 'fausse modestie'), while 'modest clothing' is usually 'une tenue pudique' or 'sobre'.

modification.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French from Classical Latin modificationem (nominative modificatio, 'a measuring off, metrical regulation'), action noun from modificare ('to set bounds to, regulate'), a compound of modus ('measure, manner') and -ficare ('to make', from facere). In French, its meaning shifted from 'imposing a limit' to 'altering the form or terms of something without replacing its essence'.

history.meaning: act of measuring off, metrical arrangement
restriction, moderation of a clause or penalty
partial change, revision, amendment (e.g., to a script or contract)

modification.notes: In French film and agency offices, 'les modifs' (colloquial feminine clipping of 'modifications') is constantly used for last-minute script rewrites or contract tweaks.

modifier.etymology: Learned borrowing in 14th-century Middle French from Classical Latin modificare / deponent modificari ('to measure off, set bounds to, regulate, moderate'), compounded from modus ('measure, manner') and -ficare (unstressed combining form of facere, 'to make, do'). From 'moderating or qualifying a legal clause', it broadened to 'making partial adjustments or edits'.

history.meaning: to measure properly, keep within limits, regulate
to alter, edit, adjust without total replacement

modifier.notes: Standard button label across all French software and phones for English 'Edit' ('Modifier le profil', 'Modifier le scénario').

cognates.meaning: scale replica, exemplar, fashion model (borrowed via French)

modèle.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-16th century from Renaissance Italian modello ('architectural scale model, sculptor's mold, artist's figure'), from Vulgar Latin *modellus, a suffix-substituted variant of Classical Latin modulus ('small measure, architectural standard of proportion'), diminutive of modus ('measure'). Note that Latin modulus also entered Old French directly via popular inheritance as moule ('casting mold').

history.meaning: sculptor's or architect's scale pattern; artist's subject

modèle.notes: Subtle fashion/cinema false friend: an artist's figure model or role model is 'un modèle', whereas a runway or fashion model is ordinarily called 'un mannequin' (always grammatically masculine even for women: 'elle est mannequin').

rootFamily.gloss: casting mold (inherited doublet from Latin modulus)

moi.etymology: Moi continues Latin me, me. The Académie records ninth-century French mi. It is the stressed object form rather than the subject form je.
moi.notes: Used after prepositions (pour moi, chez moi), for emphasis (Moi, je pense que...), and enclitically after affirmative imperatives (donne-moi!).

moi-même.etymology: Compound intensive/reflexive pronoun formed from stressed pronoun moi ('me, I', from Latin me) + même ('self, same').

cognates.meaning: lesser, slightest (from nominative minor, exact structural cognate)

moindre.etymology: Inherited directly via Old French meindre, moindre from Classical Latin nominative singular minor ('smaller, lesser'), as opposed to mineur which continues the accusative minorem. In Gallo-Romance, syncope of the unstressed vowel brought n and r into contact (*minre), triggering regular epenthesis of a transitional -d- (*mindre > meindre > moindre), just as in cinerem > cendre and ponere > pondre.

history.meaning: smaller in size, rank, or importance
lesser; slightest, least (with definite article le moindre)

moindre.notes: One of only three inherited synthetic comparatives in everyday French (with meilleur and pire); with a definite article and negation ('sans le moindre doute', 'pas la moindre idée'), it translates idiomatically as 'not the slightest'.

moineau.etymology: Diminutive in -eau (Old French moignel) of moine ('monk' < Late Latin monachus), affectionately naming the house sparrow after the brown-and-grey hood of its plumage, which reminded medieval observers of a friar's cowl.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: moineau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: moineau

moineau.notes: Older French called a sparrow **un passereau** (from Latin *passer*), which survives in **les passereaux** ('songbirds'), while cheeky little **moineau** ('little monk') won everyday speech!

moins.etymology: Inherited from Old French meins / moins ('less, fewer'), from Classical Latin minus ('less'), neuter comparative of parvus ('small', from root *mei- 'small, diminish').
