mois.etymology: Inherited from Old French meis / mois ('month'), from Vulgar Latin *mense, Classical Latin mensem (nominative mensis, 'month', from PIE *meh1ns- 'moon, month', cognate with English month and moon).

cognates.meaning: flabby, limp, spoiled (from related Vulgar Latin *muccidus)

moisi.etymology: Past-participial adjective of moisir ('to grow moldy, mildew'), inherited via Old French moisir from Vulgar Latin *mucire, a fourth-conjugation reshaping of Classical Latin mucere ('to be moldy, musty, or flat, especially of wine'), derived from the same root as mucus ('slime, moldy film, nasal mucus').

history.meaning: to be moldy, musty, or spoiled (of wine or bread)
moldy, mildewed; figuratively stale or pathetic

moisi.notes: Beyond moldy bread or damp walls ('ça sent le moisi' = 'it smells musty'), colloquial modern French loves 'moisi' as vivid slang for 'lame, corny, or terrible' ('une blague moisie' = a terrible joke, 'un scénario moisi' = a trashy script).

moitié.etymology: Inherited from Old French meitié ('half'), from Classical Latin medietatem (nominative medietas, 'the middle, place in the middle, half', coined by Cicero from medius 'middle').

cognates.meaning: Cuban rum, mint, and lime cocktail; little citrus sauce
sauce, gravy, bundle of herbs (probable source of Spanish mojo)

mojito.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from Cuban Spanish mojito (originating in early 20th-century Havana), diminutive of Spanish mojo ('citrus-and-garlic seasoning sauce' brought from the Canary Islands to Cuba, itself likely from Portuguese molho 'sauce, herb bundle', ultimately tied to Latin molliare 'to wet, soften'). Popular Havana bar lore also connects it to Afro-Cuban mojo ('magic charm') or mojadito ('slightly wet').

history.meaning: Canarian and Cuban citrus seasoning sauce
Havana cocktail of white rum, lime, sugar, mint, and soda water

mojito.notes: Pronounced in French either with an approximated Spanish velar fricative [mɔxito], an English-style [mɔdʒito], or a naturalized [mɔʒito] — France is one of the world's top consumers of the drink at Parisian café terraces and wrap parties.

rootFamily.gloss: to wet, dampen, soak (distant Romance cousin via Vulgar Latin *molliare)
soft (inherited Romance relative from Latin mollis)

moment.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin momentum ('movement, impulse, small weight that turns the scale, brief particle of time'), contracted from *movimentum, derived from movere ('to move').

history.meaning: decisive weight on a scale -> brief span of time
moment, instant, short while; mechanical torque

mon.etymology: Mon and its feminine counterpart ma descend from Latin meus, mea and meum. The Académie records tenth-century mo. Modern forms agree with the possessed noun rather than naming the owner’s gender.
mon.notes: Before any feminine singular noun starting with a vowel or mute h, French uses mon (with /n/ liaison) instead of ma for smooth euphony: mon amie, mon idée, mon histoire!

cognates.meaning: earthly, secular; dull and ordinary (FALSE FRIEND in modern tone!)

mondain.etymology: Inherited and semi-learnedly adapted in Old French (mondain, 'belonging to this earthly world, secular' as opposed to monastic life) from Late and Ecclesiastical Latin mundanus ('earthly, secular'; in Classical Latin, 'cosmopolitan, citizen of the world'), derived from mundus ('world, universe'). Through 17th- to 19th-century Parisian aristocratic salon culture (Proust's 'le grand monde'), 'worldly' specialized into 'glamorous, high-society, socialite'.

history.meaning: citizen of the universe (Classical); earthly, secular (Ecclesiastical)
secular, attached to earthly pleasures rather than the cloister
high-society, glamorous, pertaining to fashionable elite circles

mondain.notes: Spectacular false friend with English 'mundane' ('boring, humdrum', which is 'banal' in French): French 'mondain' means the exact opposite — glamorous, jet-setting, high-society ('un dîner mondain' = a swanky society dinner, 'les chroniques mondaines' = society gossip columns).

rootFamily.gloss: world; people; high society ('le beau monde')

monde.etymology: Monde, world, descends from Latin mundus with the same meaning. It is recorded from the twelfth century. The rare adjective monde, clean, is a different dictionary entry.

history.meaning: ordered universe, cosmos, world (calquing Greek kósmos)

monde.notes: In everyday French du monde means 'people / a crowd' (il y a beaucoup de monde ici), and tout le monde means 'everyone'.

mondial.etymology: Coined in late nineteenth-century French (attested around 1875–1885) from monde ('world') plus the learned relational suffix -ial (from Latin -ialis). French monde descends from Classical Latin mundus, originally an adjective meaning 'clean, neat, orderly' that came to mean 'ordered universe, world' as a semantic calque of Ancient Greek kósmos.

history.meaning: relating to the entire world, global

mondial.notes: In film and agency contexts, une sortie mondiale means a global theatrical release, whereas globalization is la mondialisation (contrast with globalisation, which feels anglicized).

moniteur.etymology: Learned sixteenth-century borrowing from Classical Latin monitor ('one who reminds, warner, adviser, theatrical prompter'), agent noun formed from monēre ('to remind, warn, instruct', from PIE causative *mon-éye- 'to make think') and the agentive suffix -tor. Its modern technical senses ('video playback screen, medical display') entered twentieth-century French as a semantic calque of English monitor.

history.meaning: instructor; electronic display screen or tracking device

moniteur.notes: On a French film set, directors check playback on le moniteur (or simply le combo, 'video assist'), whereas outside tech contexts un moniteur usually means a driving, ski, or camp instructor.

monnaie.etymology: Inherited from Old French moneie ('coined money, mint'), from Classical Latin moneta ('mint, coined money', from the title of the goddess Juno Moneta on the Capitoline Hill in Rome, near whose temple the Roman mint was established).

cognates.meaning: marriage or partnership with one person at a time

monogamie.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French via Ecclesiastical Latin monogamia from Ancient Greek monogamía (μονογαμία, originally 'the state of marrying only once in a lifetime', opposed to remarriage after widowhood), compounded from mónos (μόνος, 'single, alone') and gámos (γάμος, 'marriage, wedlock') with the abstract noun suffix -ía. Modern French broadened the sense to exclusivity to a single partner at one time.

history.meaning: marrying only once in one's life
system or practice of having a single spouse or partner

monogamie.notes: In modern relationship banter (such as in Dix pour cent), monogamie routinely refers to romantic fidelity in unmarried couples as well as legal marriage; the adjective is monogame.

cognates.meaning: extended speech by one actor or speaker
dramatic speech by a single character

monologue.etymology: Coined in French around the turn of the sixteenth century as a theatrical term, built on Ancient Greek monólogos (μονόλογος, 'speaking alone') from mónos (μόνος, 'alone, solitary') and lógos (λόγος, 'speech, discourse, word'), modeled directly in contrast to dialogue. English monologue was subsequently borrowed from French in the seventeenth century.

history.meaning: theatrical scene in which a character speaks alone on stage

monologue.notes: Essential audition vocabulary (préparer un monologue); figuratively, faire un monologue chides someone who dominates a conversation without letting anyone else speak.

rootFamily.gloss: conversation between two or more people; script lines

monsieur.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French of the Old French honorific form of address mon sieur ('my lord'), where sieur is a reduced proclitic form of seigneur ('lord, master'), from Classical Latin seniorem (comparative of senex 'old, elder').

monstre.etymology: Inherited through Old French mostre and reshaped as semi-learned monstre from Classical Latin mōnstrum ('divine omen, portent, unnatural prodigy', later 'misshapen or terrifying creature'). Latin mōnstrum derives via *-dhrom from monēre ('to warn, advise'), because an aberration in nature was interpreted by Roman augurs as a warning from the gods.
monstre.notes: In French cinema and theater, un monstre sacré ('sacred monster', coined by Jean Cocteau) is high praise for a larger-than-life legendary star; colloquially, monstre also works as an invariable intensifier (un succès monstre, 'a smash hit').

rootFamily.gloss: to show, point out (from sibling root monstrare)

monstrueux.etymology: Borrowed in fourteenth-century Middle French (monstrueus) from Imperial and Late Latin mōnstruōsus (a variant of Classical mōnstrōsus, 'strange, unnatural, portentous'), formed from mōnstrum ('divine portent, monster') plus the suffix -ōsus ('abounding in, having the nature of').
monstrueux.notes: Feminine is monstrueuse; in everyday Parisian speech, monstrueux frequently loses its horror sense to mean 'enormous, insane' (un embouteillage monstrueux, un talent monstrueux).

cognates.meaning: composite sequence of shots (borrowed from French)

montage.etymology: Formed in Middle and Early Modern French from monter ('to go up, mount, assemble piece by piece', from Vulgar Latin *montāre, denominal of Latin mōns, montis 'mountain') and the action/result suffix -age (from Latin -āticum). Originally denoting physical hoisting or mechanical assembly, it was adopted around 1912–1920 by French and Soviet filmmakers for the cutting and sequencing of film strips.

history.meaning: to ascend a mountain, climb up
act of carrying up; assembling mechanical parts into a whole
film editing; financial or theatrical structuring

morphemes.meaning: action or result of an action

montage.notes: False-friend trap in cinema: English 'montage' means a compressed musical sequence of quick shots, whereas French le montage simply means 'film editing' as a whole (la salle de montage = editing room; un montage financier = financial package for a film).

rootFamily.gloss: to climb; to edit (a film); to produce (a play)

montagne.etymology: Inherited from Old French montaigne ('mountain'), from Vulgar Latin *montanea ('mountainous region, mountain'), feminine noun from Late Latin montaneus ('of a mountain'), derived from Classical Latin mons, montis ('mountain').

cognates.meaning: upright post; total sum, prize pool

montant.etymology: Substantivated masculine present participle of Old French monter ('to rise, climb, add up to', from Vulgar Latin *montāre, denominal of Classical Latin mōns, montis 'mountain'). From the sense 'rising to a given level' (compare Old French amonter, source of English amount), Middle French developed the accounting noun le montant for the total sum a calculation reaches.

history.meaning: vertical post; total sum of an account or fee

montant.notes: Crucial talent-agency noun: le montant du cachet means the exact amount of an actor's fee; in architecture or sports, les montants refers to upright doorposts or goalposts.

rootFamily.gloss: to go up, rise, amount to

monter.etymology: Monter comes from later Latin montare, to go up, derived from mons or montis, mountain. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century; riding and mounting are related extensions.

history.meaning: to go up, climb; carry up; assemble/edit

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old and Modern French

rootFamily.gloss: to go back up; wind up (a watch)

monter.notes: Switches auxiliary by transitivity: intransitive je suis monté ('I went upstairs', with être) vs. transitive j'ai monté les valises ('I carried the suitcases upstairs', with avoir)!

montre.etymology: Montre is a noun built from montrer ('to show, display', from Latin monstrare). It first named a shop display case and the visible dial that 'showed' the hours, before naming a pocket watch or wristwatch.

montrer.etymology: Inherited from Old French mostrer ('to show, point out'), from Classical Latin monstrare ('to point out, show, indicate, teach'), derived from monstrum ('divine omen, sign', from monere 'to warn, remind').

montée.etymology: Substantivated feminine past participle of Old French monter ('to ascend, climb', from Vulgar Latin *montāre, derived from Classical Latin mōns, montis 'mountain, hill') with the participial ending -ée (from Latin -āta, expressing a completed action or stretch). Attested since the twelfth century for both an upward path and the act of ascending.
montée.notes: In French cinema culture, la montée des marches refers specifically to the glamorous red-carpet walk up the Palais des Festivals steps at the Cannes Film Festival.

cognates.meaning: to ridicule, imitate derisively (borrowed from Old French)
to wipe a nose; to jeer at

moquer.etymology: Attested in Old French as moquier ('to deride, scoff at, deceive'), likely from a Popular Romance expressive root *mukk- / *mokk- imitating a jeering grimace of the lips, or through a figurative extension of Late Latin muccāre ('to blow or wipe the nose', from muccus 'snot', as 'wiping someone's nose' meant 'duping or sneering at a fool'). English mock was borrowed from Old French moquer in the fifteenth century.

history.meaning: to make fun of; to disregard completely

moquer.notes: Almost always pronominal in modern French: se moquer de quelqu'un ('to make fun of someone'), or idiomatically je m'en moque ('I couldn't care less', polite equivalent of je m'en fous).

cognates.meaning: spirits, confidence (borrowed from French moral, respelled)

moral.etymology: Eighteenth-century masculine substantivation (le moral, 'mental disposition, spirits, psychological resolve', contrasted with le physique) of the adjective moral, borrowed in the fourteenth century from Classical Latin mōrālis ('pertaining to manners, character, or conduct'). Cicero coined mōrālis from mōs, mōris ('custom, habit, character') to render Ancient Greek ēthikós.

history.meaning: pertaining to character, manners, or ethics
relating to conduct, customs, or non-material mind

moral.notes: Watch gender and spelling: masculine le moral (no -e!) corresponds to English 'morale' (avoir le moral à zéro = 'to feel really down'), whereas feminine la morale means 'ethics, morality' or 'the moral of a story'.

rootFamily.gloss: ethics, morality; moral of a story

cognates.meaning: small bite-sized piece of food (borrowed from Old French morcel)
bit of a horse's bridle; vise, clamp

morceau.etymology: Inherited from Old French morcel ('mouthful, bitten-off piece, small fragment'), formed with the diminutive suffix -el (modern -eau, from Latin -ellum) on Old French mors ('a bite'), itself from Classical Latin morsum, neuter past-participle noun of mordēre ('to bite'). Over time the literal biting sense faded to mean any detached piece, chunk, or musical composition.

history.meaning: piece, chunk, musical track or excerpt

morceau.notes: Beyond 'a piece' (un morceau de pain), un morceau is the everyday word for a song/track on an album, and un gros morceau figuratively means a daunting task or heavyweight opponent.

rootFamily.gloss: to fragment, parcel up into small pieces

mordre.etymology: Inherited through Old French mordre from Vulgar Latin *mordĕre, a regular third-conjugation shift of Classical Latin second-conjugation mordēre ('to bite, sink teeth into, sting, grip', ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂merd- 'to bite, crush', cognate with English smart 'to sting with pain').

history.meaning: to bite, seize with the teeth; cut into

mordre.notes: Rich in idioms: mordre à l'hameçon ('to take the bait' in a negotiation), s'en mordre les doigts ('to bitterly regret something'), and être mordu de cinéma ('to be crazy about cinema').

morgue.etymology: Attested in fifteenth-century Middle French first with the sense 'solemn, haughty facial expression, arrogant air', tied to the verb morguer ('to look sourly at, scrutinize closely') and Occitan morga ('face, snout', of uncertain pre-Romance or expressive origin). In seventeenth-century Paris, la morgue named the entry room of the Grand Châtelet prison where turnkeys scrutinized incoming prisoners' faces for identification, then the room where unidentified corpses from the Seine were displayed to the public, yielding modern 'mortuary'.

history.meaning: prison vestibule where detainees' faces were inspected
public mortuary for identifying dead bodies; also haughtiness

morgue.notes: Notice that morgue has NO etymological link to mort ('death')! In literary French, avoir de la morgue still preserves its original 15th-century meaning: 'to have an arrogant, supercilious demeanor'.

mort.etymology: Inherited via Old French mort from Vulgar Latin *mortus, a phonetically shortened and regularized form of Classical Latin mortuus ('dead, deceased, lifeless'), the irregular past-participial adjective of morī ('to die', from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥-tós 'dead', root *mer- 'to die, pass away').
mort.notes: Serves as the irregular past participle of mourir (conjugated with être: elle est morte) and an everyday hyperbole: je suis mort(e) ('I'm exhausted'), mort de rire (MDR, French texting equivalent of LOL), and c'est mort ('no way / the deal is dead').

cognates.meaning: subject to death; lethal (borrowed from Old French)

mortel.etymology: Inherited and partly learned via Old French mortel (eleventh century) from Classical Latin mortālis ('subject to death, human, transient; causing death, fatal'), derived from mors, mortis ('death', from PIE *mér-ti-s) plus the relational suffix -ālis. Colloquial French extended 'fatal' in two opposite hyperbolic directions: 'deadly boring' and, in youth slang, 'killer, amazing'.
mortel.notes: Tone and generation decide the meaning of c'est mortel!: older or exasperated speakers mean 'it's deadly dull' (un ennui mortel), while younger speakers mean 'it's killer / awesome!'.

mortier.etymology: Inherited via Old French mortier from Classical Latin mortarium ('stone or wooden trough in which lime and sand — or kitchen herbs — are pounded together; the mortar mixed in it').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French mortier and Latin mortarium

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mortier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mortier

mortier.notes: Just as in English, **un mortier** means both the mason's lime-and-sand mix between flagstones and the kitchen mortar used with a pestle (**un pilon**).

mot.etymology: Inherited from Old French mot ('utterance, speech, remark, word'), from Late/Vulgar Latin muttum ('grunt, murmur, uttered sound', as in non muttum facere 'not to utter a sound', from the expressive root of muttire 'to mutter, mumble'), which replaced Classical Latin verbum across Gallo-Romance.

moteur.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin motorem (nominative motor, 'one who moves, mover'), agent noun from movere, motum ('to move'); applied in the 19th century to mechanical engines.

history.meaning: prime mover, driving force (adj. & noun); mechanical engine, motor

motivé.etymology: Past-participial adjective of motiver (attested in early eighteenth-century French first as 'to state the grounds or reasons for a legal decision'), formed from motif ('motive, driving impulse') plus -er. French motif comes from Medieval Latin mōtīvus ('moving, impelling'), itself derived from Classical Latin mōtus, past participle of movēre ('to move, set in motion'). Its psychological sense 'keen, enthusiastic, driven' expanded in the twentieth century alongside English motivated.

history.meaning: backed by stated legal or logical grounds

motivé.notes: In French work culture, every job application includes une lettre de motivation ('cover letter'), while in legal French un jugement motivé still means 'a ruling accompanied by formal written reasons'.

rootFamily.gloss: motive; decorative pattern; ground for absence

moto.etymology: Early twentieth-century apocopated clipping (attested around 1903) of motocyclette ('motorcycle'), coined in France in 1897 by the Werner brothers from moto- (combining form of moteur 'engine', from Classical Latin mōtor 'mover', agent noun of movēre 'to move') and cyclette, diminutive of cycle (from Ancient Greek kýklos 'wheel, circle').

history.stage: Classical Latin and Ancient Greek roots

moto.notes: Despite ending in -o, une moto is feminine because it retains the grammatical gender of une motocyclette! In jammed Parisian traffic, celebrities and executives famously rely on un moto-taxi to make flights and shoots on time.

motus.etymology: Playful 17th-century mock-Latin interjection built on French mot ('word' < Late Latin muttum 'muttered sound') + humorous Latinate ending -us, popularized in classical comedy for '(not a) word! hush!'.

history.meaning: not a word! mum's the word!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: motus (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: motus

motus.notes: Because of its mock-Latin disguise, the final *-s* of **motus** **/mɔtys/** is always pronounced aloud, especially in the beloved idiom **Motus et bouche cousue!** ('Mum's the word and lips sealed!').

mou.etymology: Inherited from Old French mol (feminine mole / molle, 'soft, yielding, weak'), from Classical Latin mollis ('pliable, supple, soft, gentle, weak', from PIE *mel- 'soft, crush').

cognates.meaning: nasal mucus (from the same Latin root muccus)
nasal mucus; candle snuffer (mocador in Catalan = handkerchief)

mouchoir.etymology: Attested in fifteenth-century Middle French (mouchoir), derived from moucher ('to wipe or blow the nose', Old French mouchier, inherited from Popular Latin muccāre, denominal of Classical/Late Latin muccus 'nasal mucus, snot') and the instrumental noun suffix -oir (from Latin -ōrium, 'place or tool for doing an action').

history.meaning: to blow someone's nose; trim a candlewick
cloth (and later paper tissue) for wiping the nose

morphemes.meaning: to blow or wipe the nose

mouchoir.notes: Un mouchoir en papier (or kleenex) is a disposable tissue; idiomatically, dans un mouchoir de poche ('inside a pocket handkerchief') means 'neck and neck / within a tiny margin', and sortir les mouchoirs describes a tearjerker film.

rootFamily.gloss: to blow one's nose (se moucher); put someone in their place

mouette.etymology: Formed in Middle French (fourteenth century) with the diminutive suffix -ette on Old French moue (Norman/Picard variant of maue, 'gull'), borrowed along the Channel coast from Old English mǣw or Old Low Franconian *māu ('seagull'), from Proto-Germanic *maiwiz, an imitative formation echoing the bird's high-pitched wailing cry.
mouette.notes: French ornithology distinguishes une mouette (smaller black-headed gull) from un goéland (large herring gull), though casual beachgoers call most gulls mouettes; in theater, La Mouette is Anton Chekhov's classic play The Seagull.

rootFamily.gloss: gull (archaic/regional base form preserved in place names)

mouillé.etymology: Past participle of mouiller ('to wet, soak, drench'), inherited from Old French moillier < Vulgar Latin *molliare ('to soften by soaking in water'), derived from Classical Latin mollis ('soft, supple').

history.meaning: to soften by steeping in water -> to wet

moule.etymology: Inherited via Old French modle / molle ('mold, hollow form for casting or baking') from Classical Latin modulus ('small measure, rhythmic pattern, architectural module'), diminutive of modus ('measure, manner'). Through regular Old French sound change, the internal cluster -dl- vocalized and simplified, turning modulus into moule. In the kitchen, un moule (masculine) is any baking tin or cake pan.
moule.notes: Famous French gender pair: **le moule** (masculine, from Latin *modulus*) means 'the cake pan / mold', whereas **la moule** (feminine, from Latin *musculus*) means 'the mussel' (shellfish)!

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: moule

mourir.etymology: Inherited through Old French morir from Vulgar Latin *morīre, a fourth-conjugation active remodeling of Classical Latin deponent morī ('to die, pass away, wither', attested already in Plautus as morīrī), ultimately descending from the Proto-Indo-European root *mer- ('to die, disappear'). Vowel alternation under stress produced present-stem forms like meurt (< *mŏrit) beside unstressed mourons.

history.stage: Old French (9th–10th c., Sequence of Saint Eulalia)

history.meaning: to die; to fade away; (hyperbolic) to long or suffer intensely

mourir.notes: Conjugated with être in compound tenses (il est mort) and stem-changing in stressed persons (je meurs, ils meurent, future je mourrai with double r!); onstage, mourir d'envie ('to be dying to') and mourir de trac ('to die of stage fright') are constant idioms.

cognates.meaning: hair on the upper lip (borrowed from French)

moustache.etymology: Borrowed in the late fifteenth century from Italian mostaccio (plural mostacchi, 'upper lip, mustache'), itself taken from Byzantine Greek moustákion (μουστάκιον), diminutive of Ancient Doric Greek mýstax (μύσταξ, 'upper lip, facial hair on the upper lip', connected to mástax 'jaws, mouth'). English mustache/moustache was subsequently borrowed from French in the late sixteenth century.

history.meaning: upper lip; hair on the upper lip

moustache.notes: Singular une moustache usually refers to a person's whole mustache, whereas plural les moustaches is standard for an animal's whiskers (les moustaches d'un chat).

cognates.meaning: act of moving; campaign or artistic trend (via Old French)

mouvement.etymology: Inherited from twelfth-century Old French movement ('motion, impulse, stir'), formed from movoir (modern mouvoir, 'to move', from Classical Latin movēre) plus the action-noun suffix -ment (from Latin -mentum; compare Medieval Latin movimentum). Semantic extensions later encompassed clockwork mechanisms, symphonic sections, and social or cinematic movements (such as la Nouvelle Vague).

history.meaning: to move, set in motion, stir
motion, camera movement, artistic trend, strike action

mouvement.notes: On a film set, un mouvement d'appareil means a camera movement (pan, dolly, tracking shot), whereas in French news un mouvement social is the standard euphemism for a labor strike or protest.

cognates.meaning: method, resources (borrowed from Old French meien)
middle, medium, means (cognate via Latin medius/medianus)

moyen.etymology: Substantivated from the Old French adjective meien, moien ('situated in the middle, intermediate'), inherited regularly from Classical and Late Latin mediānus ('in the middle'), derived from medius ('middle', from PIE *médʰyos). From denoting an 'intermediary link or middle course between person and goal', Middle French developed the noun sense 'instrument, method, or financial resource'.

history.meaning: way, method; (plural) financial or production resources; average

moyen.notes: Singular un moyen means 'a way' (il n'y a pas moyen = 'no way!'), plural les moyens means 'financial resources / production budget' (avoir les moyens = 'to be able to afford it'), and as an adjective moyen means 'average, so-so'.

rootFamily.gloss: in exchange for, for the price of

muet.etymology: Old French diminutive built on mu ('mute, silent', from Latin mutus) + -et. As one-syllable mu risked homophony in speech, the fuller form muet replaced it completely by Middle French.

cognates.meaning: silent (from Latin mutus / Old French muet)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: muet (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: muet

cognates.meaning: individual quick-bread cupcake or flat griddle cake
small cake (Low German Muffe, likely source of English)

muffin.etymology: Borrowed into French from English muffin (first noted in nineteenth-century travel and culinary writing for the British tea cake, then re-borrowed widely in the late twentieth century for the American domed sweet pastry). English muffin (attested 1703) is itself of uncertain origin, usually connected either to Low German Muffen (plural of Muffe, 'small cake') or to Old French moufflet ('soft, fluffy', said of bread).

history.meaning: light round yeast cake toasted for tea; later sweet domed quick bread

muffin.notes: Pronounced in French either close to [mœfin] or [mafin] rather than with the English [ʌ]; always masculine (un muffin aux myrtilles = 'a blueberry muffin'), a staple of Parisian café and film-set craft tables.

rootFamily.gloss: soft, padded mitten or bread roll (possible Old French distant relative)

sources.title: CNRTL — Définition et origine de muffin

mug.etymology: Borrowed in the second half of the 20th century from English mug ('large cylindrical drinking cup with a handle, used without a saucer'), itself of Scandinavian origin (compare Swedish mugg, Norwegian mugge 'pitcher, mug').

history.meaning: large ceramic coffee or tea mug

municipal.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin municipalis ('belonging to a self-governing town or municipium'), derived from municipium ('free town whose citizens shared Roman civic duties', from munia 'public duties' + capere 'to take').

history.meaning: relating to a commune or town council, municipal

mur.etymology: Inherited from Old French mur ('stone or brick wall'), from Classical Latin murus ('city wall, defensive rampart, masonry wall').

murmurer.etymology: Inherited and reinforced in the 12th century from Classical Latin murmurare ('to murmur, mutter, rustle, hum'), derived from the reduplicated onomatopoeic noun murmur ('low continuous sound of water, wind, bees, or soft voices'). The repeated syllable mur-mur- directly imitates the soft, vibrating resonance of hushed speech or a babbling fountain.

history.meaning: low humming sound -> to murmur, whisper

murmurer.notes: Alongside **chuchoter** (which imitates the *shh-shh* of a whisper), **murmurer** emphasizes a soft, low, melodious tone of voice.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: murmurer

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French murmurer / Latin murmur

muscle.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin musculus ('a muscle of the body; literally, a little mouse', diminutive of mus 'mouse', calquing Ancient Greek mys 'mouse; muscle', because the rippling of a flexed biceps under the skin resembled a mouse darting beneath a cloth).

cognates.meaning: relating to music; stage or film musical

musical.etymology: Borrowed in fourteenth-century Middle French from Medieval Latin mūsicālis ('pertaining to music'), derived from Classical Latin mūsica ('the art of music and lyric poetry'), itself from Ancient Greek mousikḗ (tékhnē) (μουσική τέχνη, 'art of the Muses'), feminine adjective of Moûsa (Μοῦσα, 'Muse, goddess of song and inspiration').

history.meaning: art of the Muses; poetry and music

musical.notes: Watch the false friend in cinema and theater: English 'a musical' is normally une comédie musicale in French (not *un musical*, though hip industry insiders occasionally use the anglicism); note masculine plural musicaux.

musicien.etymology: Formed in the 14th century from musique ('music', from Latin musica and Ancient Greek mousikē [tekhnē], 'the art of the Muses') + the agent suffix -ien (from Latin -ianus). Originally denoting a scholar of musical harmony as well as an instrumentalist or singer, musicien became the universal French noun for anyone who performs or composes music.
musicien.notes: Nouns and adjectives in **-ien** double the **n** in the feminine, changing the nasal vowel **/ɛ̃/** to oral **/ɛn/**: **un musicien** /myzisjɛ̃/ -> **une musicienne** /myzisjɛn/.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: musicien

musique.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French musique) from Classical Latin musica, from Ancient Greek mousike (sc. tekhne, 'the art of the Muses, encompassing poetry, song, and instrumental harmony'), derived from Mousa ('Muse').

mutuel.etymology: Borrowed and adapted in fourteenth-century Middle French from Classical Latin mūtuus ('borrowed, lent; done in exchange, reciprocal'), replacing the Latin -uus ending with the productive French relational suffix -el (< Latin -ālis). Latin mūtuus derives from the same Indo-European root *mey- ('to change, exchange') as mūtāre ('to change, swap').

history.meaning: lent, borrowed; reciprocal, done in return
reciprocal, exchanged equally between two or more parties

mutuel.notes: In contract and divorce scenes, d'un commun accord or par consentement mutuel ('by mutual consent') is the standard legal phrasing; feminine is mutuelle.

mutuelle.etymology: Nineteenth-century elliptical feminine noun shortened from société de secours mutuels or compagnie d'assurance mutuelle ('mutual-aid or mutual-insurance society'), using the feminine form of mutuel ('reciprocal', from Classical Latin mūtuus 'shared in exchange' + -el). With the rise of the post-1945 French welfare state, une mutuelle became the everyday term for non-profit supplementary health insurance.

history.meaning: mutual insurance organization; top-up health insurance plan

mutuelle.notes: Essential French life-admin vocabulary: France's public Sécurité sociale ('la Sécu') reimburses most medical costs, and employers must also provide une mutuelle ('top-up health insurance') to cover the remainder, dental, and glasses.

mystère.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Latin mysterium, from Ancient Greek mystḗrion ('secret rite, hidden truth'), derived from mýstēs ('initiate') and mýein ('to close the eyes or lips').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mystère (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mystère

mystère.notes: Note the medieval homograph: Old French *mestier* ('craft, guild', modern **métier**, from Latin *ministerium*) was sometimes spelled *mystère* when craft guilds staged medieval 'mystery plays'!

mystérieux.etymology: Derived in the 15th–16th century from mystère ('religious mystery, hidden secret', from Latin mysterium < Ancient Greek mysterion 'secret rite of initiation', from myein 'to close the eyes or lips') + adjectival suffix -ieux.

mère.etymology: Inherited from Old French mere ('mother'), from Classical Latin matrem (nominative mater, 'mother', from PIE *meh2ter- 'mother', cognate with English mother).

mètre.etymology: Coined in 1791–1793 by the French Academy of Sciences (following Borda's proposal) as the fundamental unit of length of the decimal metric system, from Ancient Greek metron ('measure, rule, standard of length', which had already entered Old French for poetic meter).

history.meaning: poetic meter -> base unit of length in the metric system

cognates.meaning: bad luck, mishap (borrowed from Old French mescheance, same verb!)
to fall amiss (parallel formation from minus + cadere)

méchant.etymology: Lexicalized present participle of Old French mescheoir ('to turn out badly, fall amiss, suffer misfortune'), formed from the pejorative prefix mes- (modern mé-, blending Frankish *missi- 'wrongly, awry' with Latin minus 'less') and cheoir ('to fall, happen by lot', from Vulgar Latin *cadēre < Classical Latin cadere 'to fall'). Originally meaning 'unlucky, wretched, pitiful' (twelfth century), it shifted via 'of poor quality, worthless' to 'malicious, nasty, unkind' by Middle French.

morphemes.meaning: to fall, befall (Old French cheoir < Latin cadere)

méchant.notes: In movies and storytelling, le méchant / la méchante is the standard noun for 'the villain / bad guy'; colloquially, pas méchant means 'harmless / no big deal' (ce n'est pas bien méchant).

rootFamily.gloss: due date, deadline (from sister compound échoir < cadere)

cognates.meaning: dissatisfied person, rebel (borrowed from French malcontent, parallel prefix)

mécontent.etymology: Formed in late fourteenth-century Middle French (mescontent) by attaching the negative and pejorative prefix mé- (Old French mes-, from Frankish *missi- 'amiss' reinforced by Latin minus) to content ('satisfied, pleased', borrowed from Classical Latin contentus 'satisfied, self-restrained', originally past participle of continēre 'to hold together, contain').

history.meaning: contained; satisfied with what one has

mécontent.notes: Slightly more formal than pas content (used constantly in speech: il n'est pas content!); often appears in journalism and workplace diplomacy as les mécontents ('disgruntled clients/staff') or exprimer son mécontentement.

mécène.etymology: Eponymous borrowing in 16th-century French from Classical Latin Maecēnās, the family name of Gaius Cilnius Maecenas (70–8 BCE), a wealthy Roman statesman of Etruscan lineage and trusted advisor to Emperor Augustus who generously financed poets such as Virgil, Horace, and Propertius.

history.meaning: Gaius Cilnius Maecenas; proverbially, a generous patron of literature
wealthy protector of writers, artists, and scholars

mécène.notes: Masculine noun (un mécène), used equally for male and female patrons in traditional style (une femme mécène or une mécène in modern usage); in French cinema and arts funding, mécénat carries tax-deductible prestige distinct from commercial parrainage ('sponsorship').

médaille.etymology: Borrowed in the late 15th century from Italian medaglia ('small coin, commemorative medallion'), itself from Vulgar Latin *medālia, originally a neuter plural of Late Latin medālis or mediālis denoting a small coin worth half a denarius (from Classical Latin medius 'middle, half',compare Old French maille 'half-obol coin').

history.meaning: fractional coins worth half a denarius

médaille.notes: Key idiom: le revers de la médaille ('the flip side of the coin / the downside of success'), constantly heard in talent agencies when sudden stardom brings unwanted tabloid scrutiny.

médecin.etymology: Developed in Old and Middle French (medecin, displacing earlier Old French miege < medicus) by back-formation from médecine ('art of healing') or from Late Latin medicīnus ('pertaining to healing'), derived from Classical Latin medicus ('physician, healer'), from medeor ('to heal, cure'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *med- ('to measure, take appropriate remedial measures').
médecin.notes: Watch the spelling and pronunciation: médecin has e-acute then mute e ([medsɛ̃]), unlike English medicine. False friend alert: un médecin is the person ('doctor'), whereas 'medicine' (the field or substance) is la médecine or un médicament.

média.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-20th century from American English (mass) media, itself the Classical Latin neuter plural of medium ('middle, center, public arena, intermediary'), substantivized from the adjective medius ('in the middle'). French reanalyzed the Latinate plural media as a masculine singular count noun (un média, des médias).

history.meaning: medium or outlet of mass communication

média.notes: Unlike English, French treats média as a regular countable masculine noun with a written plural -s: un média ('a media outlet'), les médias ('the media'). Académie française orthography includes the acute accent.

rootFamily.gloss: relating to the media; high-profile in the press

médical.etymology: Learned borrowing (attested isolately in the 16th century and established in the 18th century) from Late Latin medicālis ('pertaining to a physician or to healing'), formed from Classical Latin medicus ('physician, healer', from medeor 'to heal') plus the relational adjectival suffix -ālis.

history.meaning: relating to a physician or medical treatment

médical.notes: Takes a regular masculine plural in -aux: un certificat médical, des examens médicaux (unlike fatal or naval). In film production, la visite médicale is mandatory before insuring lead actors on a shoot.

médicament.etymology: Learned borrowing in the 14th century from Classical Latin medicāmentum ('remedy, curative potion, salve, drug, dye'), formed from the verb medicāre / medicārī ('to heal, cure, treat with remedies', from medicus 'healer') and the instrumental noun suffix -mentum.

history.meaning: curative drug, salve, potion, or poison

médicament.notes: Essential distinction: always use un médicament for pills or medication you take (prendre des médicaments), never la médecine (which means the medical profession/science) and never la drogue (which means illicit narcotics).

méditation.etymology: Learned borrowing in the 12th century (Old French meditacion, initially in monastic spiritual usage) from Classical and Ecclesiastical Latin meditātiō, meditātiōnem ('mental preparation, study, reflection, devotional contemplation'), action noun derived from the deponent verb meditor ('to ponder, reflect upon, practice').
méditation.notes: Covers both secular/spiritual mindfulness (la méditation de pleine conscience) and classic philosophical reflection (Descartes's Méditations métaphysiques).

méditer.etymology: Learned borrowing in the 14th century from Classical Latin meditor, meditārī ('to think over, reflect upon, plan, rehearse'), an iterative-frequentative formation from Proto-Indo-European *med- ('to measure, weigh mentally, give counsel'), thus sharing its ultimate Indo-European root with médecin and modérer.

history.meaning: to contemplate deeply, ponder, or plot

méditer.notes: Notice its Valency shift: méditer (intransitive) means 'to practice meditation', méditer sur un sujet means 'to reflect on a topic', and transitive méditer un projet / une vengeance means 'to plot or quietly plan something'.

méfiant.etymology: Present participial adjective of se méfier ('to be wary, distrust'), continuing Old French mesfier, formed with the pejorative/reversal prefix mes- (modern mé-, from Vulgar Latin *minus 'less, wrongly') attached to Old French fier ('to trust, entrust'), from Vulgar Latin *fīdāre, derived from Classical Latin fīdus ('faithful, trustworthy').
méfiant.notes: Subtle nuance: méfiant describes cautious wariness ('guarded, on alert', se méfier de quelqu'un), whereas soupçonneux implies actively suspecting wrongdoing and défiant is stiffer/literary ('deeply distrustful', not 'defiant'!).

mélancolique.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old French (melancolique, 13th century) from Late Latin melancholicus ('atrabilious, suffering from excess black bile'), from Ancient Greek melankholikos (μελαγχολικός), derived from melankholia (μελαγχολία 'black bile'), a humoral-medicine compound of melas, melanos ('black, dark') and khole ('bile, gall').

history.meaning: having excess black bile in humoral medicine; irascible or despondent

mélancolique.notes: French drops the Greek 'h' in spelling (mélancolique, not *mélancolhique*), though choléra keeps it—both share Greek khole ('bile'). In French cinema reviews, mélancolique is often praise for poetic wistfulness rather than clinical depression.

mélanger.etymology: Formed in Middle French (16th century) as a denominal verb from mélange ('mixture', earlier meslange), which itself was derived in Old French from the verb mesler ('to mix', modern mêler, from Vulgar Latin *misculāre, frequentative of Classical Latin miscēre 'to mix') with the collective/action suffix -ange.
mélanger.notes: Spelling trap: remember the retained 'e' before -ons/-ais to keep the soft 'g' sound (nous mélangeons). Idiom: tout mélanger ('to get everything mixed up') and ne pas mélanger le travail et les sentiments (a classic ASK agency rule constantly broken).

mélodie.etymology: Learned borrowing via Late Latin melodia from Ancient Greek melōidía ('singing, choral song, tune'), compounded from mélos ('limb; musical phrase') and ōidḗ ('song', source of ode).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: mélodie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: mélodie

mémoire.etymology: Borrowed early into Old French (memorie, memoire, 11th–12th century) from Classical Latin memoria ('faculty of remembering, remembrance, historical record'), an abstract noun derived from the adjective memor ('mindful, remembering'), from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European root *(s)mer- ('to remember, care for').

history.meaning: faculty of recall, remembrance, monument or record
memory (fem.); written report, thesis, or memoirs (masc.)

mémoire.notes: Classic gender pair: la mémoire (feminine) is the mental faculty of memory (avoir bonne mémoire, trou de mémoire 'blanking on one's lines'), whereas un mémoire (masculine) is a master's thesis or legal brief, and ses Mémoires (masc. pl.) are published memoirs!

cognates.meaning: household management (borrowed or cognate via Old French)

ménage.etymology: Inherited from Old French mesnage, maisnage ('household, domestic establishment, family members living under one roof'), from Vulgar Latin *mānsiōnāticum ('everything pertaining to a dwelling or household'), formed from Classical Latin mānsiō, mānsiōnem ('staying, dwelling, abode', from manēre 'to remain, dwell', source of French maison) plus the suffix -āticum.

history.meaning: appurtenances and management of a dwelling

ménage.notes: Faire le ménage means literally 'to clean the house', and figuratively in office/agency politics 'to clean house / fire deadwood'. Compare faire bon ménage ('to get along well together') and ménage à trois.

rootFamily.gloss: to handle carefully, spare; to arrange
to move into a new home

mériter.etymology: Derived in Old French (meriter, 12th–13th c.) from mérite ('worth, reward, desert', from Classical Latin meritum 'that which is earned, service, reward', neuter past participle of merere / mereri 'to earn, deserve').

history.meaning: to earn, be worthy of, deserve

mérité.etymology: Past participial adjective of mériter ('to deserve, earn'), attested in Old French (meriter, 12th century) as a denominal verb from merite ('worth, reward, desert'), borrowed from Classical Latin meritum ('that which is earned, pay, service, value'), substantivized neuter past participle of mereō / mereor ('to earn, deserve, serve as a soldier for pay').

history.meaning: earned pay, reward, just desert, service rendered
to earn, be worthy of reward or punishment

mérité.notes: C'est amplement mérité ! ('It's richly deserved!') is the quintessential congratulatory line at the César awards or after a grueling film shoot; contrast with immérité ('undeserved').

métal.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French metal) from Classical Latin metallum ('mine, quarry; mineral, metal'), from Ancient Greek metallon ('mine, quarry; ore, metal').

métallique.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin metallicus ('of a mine or metal'), from Ancient Greek metallikos ('relating to mines or metals'), derived from metallon ('mine, metal').

history.meaning: made of or resembling metal, metallic

métaphore.etymology: Learned rhetorical borrowing in Middle French (metafore, métaphore, 15th–16th century; isolated Old French metaphe) from Classical Latin metaphora, borrowed from Ancient Greek metaphora (μεταφορά 'transference, carrying across, shift of a word to a new sense'), derived from metaphero (μεταφέρω: meta- 'across, over' + phero 'to carry, bear').

history.meaning: transport, transference, rhetorical transfer of meaning
rhetorical figure of speech transferring a term's sense

métaphore.notes: Fun cultural connection: in modern Athens, a moving van still says μεταφορές (metaphores, literally 'transports')! Idiom: filer la métaphore ('to sustain/extend a metaphor'). Feminine noun: une métaphore.

méthode.etymology: Learned Renaissance borrowing (16th century) from Late Latin methodus ('systematic mode of teaching or inquiry, medical regimen'), from Ancient Greek methodos (μέθοδος 'pursuit of knowledge, systematic investigation, way of inquiry'), compounded from meta (μετά 'after, in pursuit of') and hodos (ὁδός 'way, road, path').

history.meaning: pursuit, mode of inquiry, systematic path
systematic procedure in medicine or rhetoric
systematic method, technique, or instructional manual

méthode.notes: Gender trap for Romance speakers: la méthode is feminine in French (following Greek feminine ἡ μέθοδος and Latin feminine methodus), unlike Italian il metodo and Spanish el método! In acting, la Méthode refers to Lee Strasberg's Method acting (l'Actors Studio).

métier.etymology: Inherited from Old French mestier ('service, function, need, craft, guild'), from Vulgar Latin *misterium, contracted from Classical Latin ministerium ('office, service, attendance, occupation', derived from minister 'attendant, servant', learned doublet of ministère).

métro.etymology: Apocopic clipping coined in Paris around 1900 from (Chemin de fer) métropolitain ('metropolitan railway'), itself modeled on London's Metropolitan Railway (opened 1863). Métropolitain derives from Late Latin mētropolītānus, from Ancient Greek metropolites (μητροπολίτης 'inhabitant of a mother-city'), compounded from meter ('mother') and polis ('city').
métro.notes: Paris's iconic cultural shorthand for the daily grind is métro, boulot, dodo ('commute, work, sleep', coined in a 1951 poem by Pierre Béarn). Notice how Hector Guimard's Art Nouveau station arches still read MÉTROPOLITAIN in full.

météo.etymology: 20th-century colloquial clipping of météorologie ('meteorology, weather forecasting', from Ancient Greek meteorologia 'study of phenomena high in the air', from meteoros 'raised on high, atmospheric').

history.meaning: study of atmospheric phenomena -> weather forecast or service

mêler.etymology: Inherited from Old French mesler, medler ('to mix, blend, mingle; to embroil in conflict'), from Vulgar Latin *misculāre, an expressive frequentative-diminutive built on Classical Latin miscēre ('to mix, mingle, stir up'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meyk- ('to mix'). The circumflex accent on ê marks the loss of Old French preconsonantal s.

history.meaning: to mix, blend; to clash or meddle
to mix, entangle; (reflexive) to get involved or meddle

mêler.notes: English borrowed this verb twice: Anglo-Norman medler gave English meddle, while the feminine participial noun gave English melee (une mêlée). Crucial conversational idiom: Mêle-toi de tes affaires ! ('Mind your own business!').

même.etymology: Inherited from Old French medisme / meïsme / mesme ('same, self, even'), from Vulgar Latin *metipsimus, a superlative reinforcement of the emphatic pronoun phrase *-met ipse (as in egomet ipse 'I my very own self', combining intensive particle -met + ipse 'himself, very').

môme.etymology: Attested in early 19th-century Parisian argot (originally thieves' cant for a youngster or juvenile prisoner), most likely derived from dialectal and Old French momer ('to wear a mask, pull faces, mumble') and mome ('mummer, grimace'), built on an expressive onomatopoeic labial root *momm- imitating a child's or masked mummer's babbling.

history.meaning: to masquerade, pull faces; mummer's disguise
youngster, street urchin (Parisian argot); kid, young woman

môme.notes: Informal, affectionate Parisian slang for 'kid' (un môme / les mômes); in older Belleville slang une môme also meant a petite young woman or girlfriend, immortalized by Édith Piaf's stage name La Môme Piaf (and the Oscar-winning biopic La Môme, titled La Vie en Rose in English).

mûr.etymology: Inherited from Old French meür ('ripe, full-grown, timely, wise'), from Classical Latin mātūrus ('ripe, occurring at the proper time, early, fully developed'). Regular Gallo-Romance lenition deleted intervocalic -t- (mātūrum > *maduro > meür), and Middle French contraction of the hiatus eü to [y] is commemorated by the circumflex in mûr.

history.meaning: ripe (of fruit); of mature age or judgment

mûr.notes: The circumflex distinguishes mûr ('ripe, mature' < mātūrus) in writing from its exact homophone mur ('wall' < mūrus), though the feminine mûre traditionally dropped or kept it before the 1990 reform (and une mûre also means 'blackberry'). Idiom: après mûre réflexion ('after careful consideration').

n'importe quoi.etymology: Lexicalized in early Modern French (17th century) from the negated impersonal clause (il) n'importe ('it does not matter, it is of no consequence') followed by the stressed interrogative/indefinite pronoun quoi ('what'): ne (< Latin nōn) + importe (from importer 'to matter', borrowed in the 16th century from Italian importare < Latin importāre 'to bring in, entail') + quoi (< Latin quid).

history.meaning: to carry in, bring about / what
no matter what, anything whatsoever (indefinite pronoun)
anything at all; utter nonsense, rubbish, reckless behavior

morphemes.meaning: matters, is of consequence (3sg of importer)

n'importe quoi.notes: One of the most frequent spoken French expressions! As an object, dire/faire n'importe quoi means 'to talk nonsense / act recklessly'; as a standalone exclamation, C'est n'importe quoi ! means 'That's ridiculous / total nonsense!'.

cognates.meaning: to navigate (learned borrowing from the same Latin verb)

nager.etymology: Inherited from Old French nagier ('to row, sail, travel by boat'), from Classical Latin nāvigāre ('to sail, go by sea', from nāvis 'ship' + agere 'to drive'). In Middle French, nager shifted from 'to sail/row' to 'to swim' in order to replace Old French noer ('to swim' < Latin natāre), which had collided homophonically with noier/noyer ('to drown' < Latin necāre)—a classic case of therapeutic lexical replacement!

history.meaning: to sail, steer a vessel, travel by sea
to row, propel a boat, travel by water

nager.notes: Colloquial agency/office idiom: je nage complètement ('I'm completely lost / out of my depth') or nager en plein délire ('to be in total madness/surreality'). Keep the 'e' in nous nageons! Its learned doublet from the exact same Latin verb is naviguer ('to sail').

naissance.etymology: Formed in 12th-century Old French from the present participle stem naiss- of naistre (modern naître 'to be born', from Vulgar Latin *nāscere, regularized from Classical Latin deponent nāscī, Old Latin gnāscī 'to be born, spring forth', from PIE *genh₁- 'to beget, give birth') plus the abstract nominal suffix -ance (< Latin -antia).

history.meaning: to be born, arise, spring forth

naissance.notes: Used both literally (date et lieu de naissance, acte de naissance 'birth certificate') and figuratively in arts/cinema: donner naissance à un chef-d'œuvre ('to give birth to a masterpiece').

nappe.etymology: Nappe comes from Latin mappa ('napkin, signal cloth'), with dissimilation of initial m- to n- before -pp- in Popular Latin *nappa. English 'napkin' and 'apron' (originally 'a napron') both come from this French word!
nappe.notes: False friend: **la nappe** is a tablecloth; a napkin is **une serviette**.

national.etymology: Derived in 16th-century Middle French from nation ('people united by origin or territory', from Classical Latin nātiō, nātiōnem 'birth, breed, stock, tribe, people', formed from nātus, past participle of nāscī 'to be born') plus the learned relational suffix -al (< Latin -ālis); propelled into modern political vocabulary across Europe by the French Revolution of 1789.

history.meaning: pertaining to a people or kingdom
pertaining to the sovereign nation or state

national.notes: Pronunciation note: the 't' in nation and national is pronounced [s] ([nasjɔnal]), never [t] despite initial nat-. Plural is nationaux; une route nationale (often shortened to une nationale) is a major state highway.

nature.etymology: Borrowed early into Old French (nature, early 12th century) as a semi-learned term from Classical Latin nātūra ('birth, innate character, natural disposition, constitution of the universe'), formed from nātus (past participle of nāscī 'to be born') and the abstract suffix -ūra.

history.meaning: birth, inborn quality, course of things, universe
cosmic creative order, innate temperament, essence
natural world, human disposition, kind or unflavored state

nature.notes: Used invariable as a postposed adjective meaning 'plain, unflavored, or unfiltered': un yaourt nature ('plain yogurt'), un café nature, or être très nature ('to be completely unpretentious / spontaneous'—rare praise for a movie star!). Also payer en nature ('to pay in kind').

naturel.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French naturel) from Classical Latin naturalis ('by birth, according to nature, innate'), derived from natura ('birth, inborn character, nature', from nasci, natus 'to be born').

naturellement.etymology: Formed in Old French (naturelment, 12th c.) from the adjective naturel ('natural') + adverbial suffix -ment.

naufrage.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (15th century) from Classical Latin naufragium ('shipwreck, loss at sea; figuratively, ruin or catastrophe'), abstract noun derived from naufragus ('shipwrecked'), a transparent Latin compound of nāvis ('ship', reduced to nau- in composition) and the root of frangere ('to break, shatter').

history.meaning: shattering of a ship, shipwreck; ruin
wrecking of a vessel at sea; utter disaster

naufrage.notes: Widely used metaphorically in French criticism and conversation: un naufrage artistique ('an artistic trainwreck'), faire naufrage ('to founder/fail disastrously'), and Chateaubriand's famous phrase about old age: la vieillesse est un naufrage.

rootFamily.gloss: wrecker who lures ships onto rocks (figuratively, destroyer)

cognates.meaning: navew (via French naveau, from Latin nāpus)

navet.etymology: Formed in Old and Middle French (13th–14th century) with the diminutive suffix -et on the stem nav- of Old French nef / naveau ('turnip'), inherited from Classical Latin nāpus ('turnip', with regular intervocalic lenition -p- > -v-). Its sense 'artistic flop, dud' arose in late 18th- and 19th-century Parisian art-academy slang, mocking stiff, pale, lifeless nude paintings as looking like peeled white turnips before spreading to theater and cinema.

history.meaning: turnip; (slang) lifeless painting, then terrible play or movie flop

navet.notes: Signature Dix pour cent cinema slang! Whereas English calls a terrible movie a 'turkey' or 'lemon', French calls it un navet ('a turnip'—or affectionately un nanar when it's 'so bad it's hilarious'). Also note avoir du sang de navet ('to be spineless/anemic').

rootFamily.gloss: rape, colza (oilseed turnip relative, Brassica napus)

naviguer.etymology: Learned Renaissance borrowing (late 15th–16th century) from Classical Latin nāvigāre ('to sail, steer a ship, travel by sea'), compounded from nāvis ('ship') and -igāre (the combining form of agere 'to drive, guide, set in motion'). Re-borrowed into French as a learned maritime doublet after inherited nāvigāre > nager had shifted its meaning from 'to sail' to 'to swim'.

history.meaning: to sail, steer a ship, voyage by water
to sail, pilot a vessel or aircraft
to sail; to navigate tricky situations; to browse the web

naviguer.notes: Keep the 'u' throughout conjugation to preserve the hard [g] sound (je navigue, nous naviguons), though the related noun and adjective drop it before 'a': la navigation, navigable! Idiom: naviguer à vue ('to play it by ear / fly blind without a long-term plan').

cognates.meaning: navy (via Old French navie, from shared Latin nāvis)

navire.etymology: Developed from Old French navilie, navire (initially feminine collective meaning 'fleet, shipping', becoming masculine 'large seagoing vessel' by the 14th–15th century, probably via Old Occitan navili with rhotacism or suffix substitution), from Vulgar Latin *nāvilium, an alteration of Classical Latin nāvigium ('vessel, ship; sailing'), derived from nāvis ('ship', PIE *néh₂us 'boat').

history.meaning: fleet of ships (fem.), then single large seagoing vessel (masc.)
large seagoing ship (merchant, cruise, or naval vessel)

navire.notes: Register & gender note: despite ending in -ire, un navire is masculine! It specifically denotes a large seagoing ship (un navire de croisière, un navire-amiral 'flagship'), whereas un bateau is the everyday word for boats of any size. Idiom: quitter le navire ('to abandon a sinking ship/project').

rootFamily.gloss: nave of a church (literally 'ship' < Latin nāvis)
shuttle (boat-shaped loom shuttle or transit shuttle)

navré.etymology: Past participial adjective of navrer, inherited from Old French navrer ('to wound gravely, pierce, slash in battle', attested in the Song of Roland, 11th century, via metathesis of *narver), borrowed from Frankish *narwōn ('to constrict, scar, inflict a wound'), from Proto-Germanic *narwōną ('to tighten, leave a narrow scar'). Its sense softened from mortal physical wounds to deep heartbreak and finally to polite social apology.

history.meaning: to wound severely with a weapon in combat

navré.notes: Polite, slightly upscale alternative to désolé: Je suis navré(e) ('I'm terribly sorry'—a staple of smooth Parisian agents delivering bad news to clients!). Meanwhile, the present participial adjective navrant means 'pitiful, pathetic, dismal' (un spectacle navrant).

rootFamily.gloss: to distress deeply, break someone's heart

naître.etymology: Inherited via Old French naistre from Vulgar Latin *nascere, an active-voice reshaping of Classical Latin deponent nasci (Old Latin gnasci, 'to be born, arise, spring forth'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- ('to beget, give birth'). Syncope of *nasc're triggered an epenthetic -t- before -r-, later signaled by the circumflex after loss of preconsonantal s.

history.meaning: to be born, be begotten, spring forth
to be born, come into existence

naître.notes: Takes être in compound tenses (je suis né) and keeps its circumflex before -t- (il naît, naître) under traditional spelling, though post-1990 orthography allows naitre/nait; its irregular past participle né comes directly from Latin natus.

naïf.etymology: Inherited via Old French naif ('native, natural, genuine, unspoiled') from Classical Latin nativum (accusative of nativus, 'inborn, natural, produced by nature, native'), derived from natus, past participle of nasci ('to be born'). Originally praising unaffected naturalness, the adjective shifted in Early Modern French toward 'artless, unsophisticated, gullible', forming an inherited doublet of learned natif.
naïf.notes: The tréma (ï) keeps a-i in hiatus (/na.if/ masculine, /na.iv/ feminine naïve) rather than merging into /ɛ/; English borrowed naive directly from the French feminine form.

ne.etymology: The negative ne continues Latin non. Its French history is recorded from the tenth century. The chemical abbreviation Ne belongs to an unrelated Greek-derived name.

history.meaning: not (paired with pas, jamais, rien, plus...)

ne.notes: Standard written French frames the verb with ne ... pas (Je ne sais pas), whereas informal spoken French very frequently drops ne (Je sais pas / J'sais pas).

nerf.etymology: Inherited via Old French nerf ('sinew, tendon, bowstring, vigor') from Classical Latin nervum (accusative of nervus, 'sinew, tendon, cord, string of a musical instrument; vigor'), cognate with Ancient Greek neuron from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₁wr̥ ('sinew, tendon'). Anatomical science gradually narrowed the singular to neural fibers while the plural retained emotional and temperamental senses.
nerf.notes: Pronunciation shifts with number: singular nerf sounds the final -f (/nɛʁf/), whereas plural nerfs drops it (/nɛʁ/), as in avoir les nerfs à vif ('to have frayed nerves') or taper sur les nerfs ('to get on someone's nerves').

nerveux.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin nervosus ('sinewy, muscular, vigorous', from nervus 'sinew, tendon, bowstring, nerve'); shifted in modern medicine and everyday usage from 'muscular, sinewy' to 'relating to the nerves, high-strung, excitable'.

history.meaning: sinewy, wiry -> relating to the nervous system, tense, irritable

net.etymology: Inherited from Old French net ('clean, pure, spotless, clear'), from Classical Latin nitidus ('shining, bright, sleek, neat', from nitere 'to shine', cognate with English neat); reinforced in commercial senses ('net weight or price, free of deductions') by Italian netto.

nettoyer.etymology: Inherited via Old French netoiier ('to cleanse, purify, clear away') from Vulgar Latin *nitidiare ('to make clean or shining'), a verbal derivative of Classical Latin nitidus ('shining, bright, sleek, neat'), itself from nitere ('to shine, glitter'). Within French, it remains transparently linked to its base adjective net ('clean, clear-cut').
nettoyer.notes: Conjugates with a y → i stem alternation before silent e (je nettoie, nous nettoyons); figuratively, nettoyer un texte or faire du nettoyage in a script or agency roster means cutting clutter ruthlessly.

neuf.etymology: Convergence of two distinct Latin words that became homophones in Old French: (1) the number neuf ('nine'), from Old French nuef < Classical Latin novem ('nine', from PIE *h1newn); and (2) the adjective neuf (feminine neuve, 'brand-new, newly made'), from Old French nuef < Classical Latin novus ('new', from PIE *newos).

neurodégénératif.etymology: Modern 20th-century medical compound formed from the neoclassical combining element neuro- (from Ancient Greek neuron, 'sinew, nerve') and dégénératif ('causing progressive deterioration'), itself derived from dégénérer, a learned borrowing from Classical Latin degenerare ('to fall away from one's ancestral kind or quality', from de- + genus, generis 'birth, race, kind').

history.meaning: sinew, nerve (Greek) + to fall away from one's stock (Latin)
characterized by progressive tissue or functional decline
involving progressive loss of structure or function of neurons

neurodégénératif.notes: Written as a single unhyphenated word in French (feminine neurodégénérative, e.g., une maladie neurodégénérative) and confined to formal clinical or journalistic registers.

neutre.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old and Middle French from Classical Latin neutrum (neuter form of neuter, 'neither of the two'), a pronominal compound of ne ('not') and uter ('which of two'). First adopted as a grammatical term for the neuter gender, it broadened during the Renaissance to political non-alignment, emotional detachment, and subdued tones.

history.meaning: neither of the two; grammatical neuter
belonging to the neuter gender; taking neither side

neutre.notes: Invariable across masculine and feminine in the singular (un ton neutre, une couleur neutre); in diplomacy and institutions, neutralité is paired with both neutre and the narrower adjective neutral.

neuvième.etymology: Formed in Old French (nuevieme, 12th c.) from neuf ('nine', using the voiced stem neuv- of neuve) + ordinal suffix -ième.

nez.etymology: Inherited from Old French nes ('nose'), from Classical Latin nasus / nasum ('nose', from PIE *nas- 'nose', cognate with English nose).

history.meaning: nose; sense of smell or flair

ni.etymology: Inherited from Old French ne / ni ('neither, nor'), from Vulgar Latin *nec, reduced from Classical Latin nec / neque ('and not, nor').

niche.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 13th–14th century from nichier / nicher ('to build a nest, nestle'), from Vulgar Latin *nidicare ('to make a nest'), derived from Classical Latin nidus ('nest', source of French nid); extended to an arched wall recess and a doghouse.

history.meaning: recess in a wall; doghouse, kennel

niveau.etymology: Inherited via Old French livel and dissimilated nivel ('plumb-line, carpenter's level') from Vulgar Latin *libellum, masculine reshaping of Classical Latin libella ('small balance, carpenter's water-level or plumb-level'), diminutive of libra ('pair of scales, pound'). Dissimilation of the two l-sounds (l...l > n...l) produced French niveau, whereas English level reflects earlier Old French livel.
niveau.notes: Takes an -x plural (des niveaux); in colloquial spoken French (and agency banter), niveau + bare noun acts like a shorthand preposition meaning 'when it comes to' (e.g., niveau budget, niveau casting), though purists prefer au niveau du budget.

nièce.etymology: Inherited via Old French niece from Vulgar Latin *neptia ('niece'), an enlarged feminine reshaping in *-ia of Classical Latin neptis ('granddaughter', and in Late Latin 'brother's or sister's daughter'), feminine counterpart of nepos ('grandson; nephew') from Proto-Indo-European *népōts. Palatalization of *-tia yielded Old French -ce, later borrowed directly into Middle English as niece.
nièce.notes: Its masculine counterpart is the phonetically distant neveu (< Latin nepotem); note the grave accent in nièce (/njɛs/), which distinguishes it visually from the Riviera city Nice (/nis/).

noble.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing in Old French from Classical Latin nobilem (accusative of nobilis, 'well-known, renowned, celebrated; of high birth'), originally Old Latin gnobilis ('knowable, noteworthy'), derived from noscere / gnoscere ('to come to know', from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- 'to know'). Used both as an adjective and substantively as a noun denoting a member of the aristocracy.
noble.notes: Functions identically as a masculine/feminine noun (un noble, une noble) and adjective; the idiom lettres de noblesse ('credentials, artistic respectability') is ubiquitous in French film criticism when a genre earns prestige.

nocturne.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French from Classical Latin nocturnus ('of or belonging to the night, nightly'), formed from nox, noctis ('night', from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts) with the temporal suffix -urnus (modeled alongside diurnus, 'of the day'). Because inherited nuit lacked an everyday relational adjective, learned nocturne filled that lexical slot.

history.meaning: belonging to the night, occurring by night
nightly, nocturnal; night office in liturgy

nocturne.notes: Serves as the standard relational adjective for nuit (e.g., tournage nocturne, 'night shoot', tapage nocturne, 'nighttime noise disturbance'); as a feminine noun (une nocturne), it denotes a museum or store staying open late at night, while un nocturne is a musical nocturne.

noir.etymology: Inherited from Old French neir / noir ('black, dark'), from Classical Latin nigrum (nominative niger, 'shining black, dark, sable'), which displaced ater across Romance.

noix.etymology: Inherited via Old French nois ('walnut, hard-shelled nut') from Classical Latin nucem (accusative of nux, nucis, 'walnut, nut, nut-tree'), an ancient Mediterranean or Italic root of uncertain deeper Indo-European origin. Regular Gallo-Romance palatalization of final -cem produced -is/-ix, while the unshifted stem survives in derived forms like noyer ('walnut tree') and cerneau.
noix.notes: By itself, une noix means specifically 'walnut' (not any generic nut — use fruits à coque for mixed tree nuts), though compounds name others (noix de coco, noix de cajou); colloquial à la noix means 'rubbish, bogus' (un scénario à la noix).

nom.etymology: Inherited from Old French nom / non ('name, reputation, noun'), from Classical Latin nomen ('name, title, clan name, grammatical noun', from PIE *h1nomn- 'name', cognate with English name).

nombreux.etymology: Adapted in Middle French from Classical Latin numerosus ('rhythmical, harmonious; manifold, populous, numerous'), reshaped morphologically on French nombre ('number', inherited from Latin numerum with syncope and epenthetic -b-) plus the productive adjectival suffix -eux (< Latin -osus). Initially used of prose cadence as well as quantity, the quantitative sense prevailed.

history.meaning: harmonious in rhythm; large in number

nombreux.notes: In the singular, nombreux takes a collective noun (un public nombreux, une équipe nombreuse); in the plural before a noun, de replaces des (de nombreux acteurs, never *des nombreux acteurs).

nomination.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French from Classical Latin nominationem (accusative of nominatio, 'a naming; proposal or appointment to public office'), noun of action from nominare ('to call by name, appoint'), derived from nomen ('name', PIE *h₃néh₃mn̥). Its traditional French meaning 'official appointment to a post' was expanded in the 20th century under English awards-ceremony influence to mean 'award shortlisting'.

history.meaning: naming; naming as candidate or appointee to office
official appointment to an office or benefice

nomination.notes: In cinema parlance (Césars, Oscars), une nomination aux César is universally said, even though the Académie française officially objects that French nomination means 'definitive appointment to a job' and recommends sélection instead.

nommer.etymology: Inherited from Old French nomer ('to call by name, give a name to, appoint'), from Classical Latin nominare ('to name, call by name, nominate for office'), derived from nomen, nominis ('name').

history.meaning: to name, call, appoint to a post

nommé.etymology: Substantivized past participle of nommer ('to name, appoint, shortlist'), inherited via Old French nomer from Classical Latin nominare ('to call by name, designate for office, make famous'), denominal verb of nomen ('name'). In contemporary French film and literary awards, un nommé / une nommée was promoted as the idiomatic French noun for an award nominee.

history.meaning: called by name, designated for office

nommé.notes: Crucial cinema-world shibboleth: the Académie des César officially calls contenders les nommés (from nommer) and frowns upon the anglicism les nominés, a correction talent agents and journalists make constantly.

rootFamily.gloss: to name, appoint, shortlist for a prize

non.etymology: Non continues Latin non. The Académie analyses the older Latin expression as *ne oinum, not a single one; the asterisk marks a reconstructed earlier form.

history.meaning: not a single one -> not, no

non.notes: Answers an affirmative question negatively (Tu viens? — Non), while contradicting a negative question with 'yes, I AM!' requires si! instead of oui.

non-stop.etymology: Twentieth-century borrowing from English non-stop (attested in French rail and aviation contexts by the 1920s–1930s), compounded in English from the Latinate negative prefix non- ('not') and stop (from Old English *stoppian, 'to plug, halt'). Generalized rapidly in spoken French to describe continuous workdays, broadcasts, and shoots without breaks.

history.meaning: making no intermediate halts (of trains or flights)

non-stop.notes: Completely invariable in both gender and number as an adjective (des réunions non-stop) and equally common as an adverb (bosser non-stop, 'to work around the clock'); formal prose prefers sans interruption or en continu.

rootFamily.gloss: to stop, halt (earlier borrowing from English)

nord.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century (via Anglo-Norman nort / nord) from Old English north ('the north', from Proto-Germanic *nurtha-).

nord-ouest.etymology: Compound compass noun formed in Old/Middle French from nord ('north') + ouest ('west', borrowed from Old English west).

normal.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th–18th century from Classical Latin normalis ('made according to the carpenter's square, right-angled; conforming to a rule'), derived from norma ('carpenter's T-square, rule, pattern, standard').

history.meaning: conforming to the standard or rule, regular, normal

norme.etymology: Learned borrowing (sporadic in Middle French, established in the 19th century) from Classical Latin norma ('carpenter's square or T-square for right angles; figuratively rule, pattern, precept'), itself likely borrowed into Latin via Etruscan from Ancient Greek gnomon ('carpenter's square, sundial pin, criterion'). From a physical squaring tool it evolved into social, legal, and technical standards.
norme.notes: Note the invariable prepositional phrase hors norme or hors normes ('extraordinary, unconventional', e.g., un acteur hors norme), whereas être aux normes (always plural) means 'to be up to safety/regulatory code'.

nostalgie.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from New Latin nostalgia, a medical neologism coined in 1688 by Swiss physician Johannes Hofer in his Basel dissertation to translate German Heimweh ('homesickness'), combining Ancient Greek nostos ('homecoming, return journey', as in Odyssey narratives) and algos ('pain, grief, ache'). Originally diagnosing acute, potentially fatal homesickness among Swiss mercenaries abroad, it softened in the 19th century into wistful longing for the past.

history.meaning: acute homesickness; wistful yearning for a bygone era

nostalgie.notes: Still occasionally retains an echo of spatial longing in phrases like la nostalgie du pays ('homesickness') or la nostalgie de la boue ('yearning for degradation'), alongside temporal wistfulness.

notaire.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old French from Classical Latin notarius ('shorthand writer, stenographer, secretary', and in Late and Medieval Latin 'official drafter and custodian of legal deeds'), derived from nota ('written mark, cipher, shorthand symbol') plus the agentive suffix -arius. Under civil law, the office evolved from court scribe into a state-appointed public officer authenticating property and inheritance deeds.

history.meaning: drafter and authenticator of legal instruments
public official authenticating deeds and wills

notaire.notes: Major cultural false friend: unlike an Anglo-American notary public who merely witnesses signatures, a French notaire is a highly trained civil-law jurist holding a state monopoly over real-estate sales, marriage contracts, and estate settlements.

rootFamily.gloss: note, written mark, grade (< Latin nota)

note.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin nota ('mark, sign, written character, musical symbol, marginal remark, brand'), related to noscere, notum ('to know').

history.meaning: musical note, brief written jotting, footnote, school grade, bill/check

noter.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin notare ('to mark, designate with a sign, write down, observe'), derived from nota ('mark, sign, note').

history.meaning: to write down, take note of, grade

notre.etymology: Notre comes from Latin noster, our. Ninth-century French had nostro. Modern plural nos belongs to this same possessive series.

history.stage: Early Old French (9th c., Strasbourg Oaths)

notre.notes: Notice the vowel & spelling contrast: unstressed determiner notre (/nɔtʁ/, no circumflex: notre maison) vs. stressed pronoun le nôtre (/noːtʁ/, with circumflex: c'est le nôtre).

cognates.meaning: nurse (from Old French norrice, base of nounou)
wet nurse, nanny (< Late Latin nutricia)

nounou.etymology: Late 19th-century French nursery formation created by hypocoristic apocope and syllable reduplication (nou- + nou) of nourrice ('wet nurse, nanny'), itself inherited via Old French norrice from Late Latin nutricia ('wet nurse, governess', feminine substantive of Classical Latin nutricius 'suckling, nursing', from nutrix). Comparable to child-speech formations like dodo (from dormir) and tata (from tante).

morphemes.meaning: reduplicated initial syllable of nourrice ('nurse, nanny')

nounou.notes: Informal but completely standard in everyday family life (plural des nounous), whereas administrative paperwork uses assistante maternelle or garde d'enfants; figuratively on film sets, playing someone's nounou means babysitting a high-maintenance star.

nourrir.etymology: Inherited via Old French norrir / nurrir ('to suckle, rear, educate, feed') from Classical Latin nutrire ('to suckle, breastfeed, nourish, bring up, foster'), closely bound to nutrix ('wet nurse') from a Proto-Indo-European root *(s)neh₂u- ('to flow, let flow milk').
