Assimilation into the inchoative second-conjugation (-ir / -iss-) paradigm produced plural stems like nourrissons, whence English nourish.

history.meaning: to breastfeed, bring up a child, sustain with food

nourrir.notes: Regular -ir verb with -iss- extension (nous nourrissons); beyond literal feeding, se nourrir de ('to draw inspiration from', e.g., un acteur qui se nourrit de son vécu) is a staple of artistic interviews, and nourri means 'hearty, sustained' (des applaudissements nourris).

nous.etymology: Nous descends from Latin nos, meaning we or us. The Académie dates the French pronoun to the ninth century. Modern nous still has both subject and object uses, so its history fits a wider range than the single English gloss we.

nous-mêmes.etymology: Emphatic compound pronoun joining nous ('we, us', inherited via Old French nos from Classical Latin nos) and plural mêmes ('selves'), inherited via Old French meïsmes / medismes from Vulgar Latin *metipsimos, an intensive superlative coalescing the Classical Latin enclitic -met ('-self', as in egomet, nosmet) with ipsissimus (superlative of ipse, 'himself, very self').
nous-mêmes.notes: Always hyphenated and takes plural -s whenever nous refers to two or more people, though polite/royal nous referring to a single person writes nous-même in the singular; remember that ordinary reflexive verbs use plain nous (nous nous voyons), reserving nous-mêmes for contrast or prepositions (par nous-mêmes).

nouveau.etymology: Nouveau descends from Latin novellus, young or recent, itself related to novus, new. Twelfth-century French had novel; the alternative nouvel preserves that older shape.

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old and Modern French

rootFamily.gloss: feminine form; piece of news; novella

nouveau.notes: French keeps both neuf (< novus, 'brand-new from the factory', un téléphone neuf) and nouveau (< novellus, 'another/different, new to me', mon nouvel appartement; note nouvel before vowel/mute h!).

nouveau-né.etymology: Compound noun and adjective formed in Middle and Early Modern French from adverbial nouveau ('newly, freshly', inherited via Old French novel from Late Latin novellum, diminutive of Classical Latin novus 'new') and né ('born', inherited via Old French né from Classical Latin natum, past participle of nasci). Because nouveau modifies né adverbially ('newly born'), it stayed invariable for centuries before noun agreement emerged.
nouveau-né.notes: Watch the famous grammar trap: as a noun, plural is des nouveau-nés (nouveau stays invariable because it means 'newly'!) and feminine noun is une nouveau-née; as an adjective, both parts remain invariable for masculine/feminine in traditional grammar or only né agrees (une fille nouveau-née, des enfants nouveau-nés), never *nouveaux-nés!

cognates.meaning: novelty, news, new release (< Latin novitatem)
novelty, news, new release (< Latin novitatem)

nouveauté.etymology: Inherited via Old French nuveltet / novelté ('newness, innovation, fresh tidings') from Late Latin novellitatem (accusative of novellitas, 'newness'), derived from novellus ('young, fresh, new', diminutive of Classical Latin novus), which replaced shorter Classical novitas in Gallo-Romance. Vocalization of preconsonantal -l- before -t- turned novelté into nouveauté, while Anglo-Norman preserved novelty for English.

history.meaning: novelty, new fashion, newly released work or product

morphemes.meaning: abstract quality or item noun suffix (-itatem > -té)

nouveauté.notes: Unlike English novelty (which often implies a cheap gimmick or trinket), French les nouveautés in publishing, cinema, and streaming neutrally means 'new releases' or 'what's new in the catalog'.

nouvelle.etymology: The noun nouvelle, news, comes from Latin novella, a noun use of the neuter plural of novellus, new or recent. Its plural use for news should be distinguished from the adjective nouvelle and from the later literary sense short story.

morphemes.meaning: feminine/collective ending (< Latin n. pl. novella)

history.meaning: new things, tidings (neuter plural of novellus)
piece of news (pl. news); short story / novella

cognates.meaning: literary genre names from this same Romance word

nouvelle.notes: Literary false friend: in French une nouvelle is a short story or novella, whereas a full-length 'novel' is un roman!

novateur.etymology: Learned borrowing in Early Modern French from Late Latin novatorem (accusative of novator, 'renewer, introducer of changes'), agent noun of Classical Latin novare ('to make new, renew, alter, invent'), derived from novus ('new', PIE *néwos). Initially viewed with suspicion in religious and political writing ('subversive reformer'), it gained strongly positive prestige in modern arts and technology ('pioneering, groundbreaking').

history.meaning: reformer introducing religious or political changes

novateur.notes: Takes the feminine novatrice (un réalisateur novateur, une mise en scène novatrice); stylishly preferred over innovant in cultural criticism when praising daring artistic vision.

noyer.etymology: Inherited from Spoken Latin *nucarius ('walnut tree'), derived from Classical Latin nux, nucis ('nut, walnut'—which itself gave French noix). Like chêne or merisier, the tree name also names its timber.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: noyer (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: noyer

noyer.notes: An accidental homograph of the verb **noyer** ('to drown', from Latin *necare*), which has a completely separate origin.

nu.etymology: Inherited from Old French nu (feminine nue, 'naked, bare'), from Classical Latin nudus ('naked, bare, uncovered, stripped', from PIE *nogw-do-, cognate with English naked).

nuage.etymology: Formed in Middle French from Old French nue ('cloud', inherited from Vulgar Latin *nuba, a first-declension feminine reshaping of Classical Latin nubes, nubis 'cloud, mist,暗 overcast') plus the collective suffix -age (< Latin -aticum). Originally denoting a mass or bank of clouds collectively, nuage gradually displaced monosyllabic nue as the everyday singular word for 'cloud'.
nuage.notes: Masculine (un nuage), even though its poetic ancestor la nue is feminine (preserved in idioms like tomber des nues, 'to be flabbergasted', and porter aux nues, 'to praise to the skies'); un nuage de lait means 'a splash of milk'.

rootFamily.gloss: nuance, subtle shade (originally 'shifting cloud-tint' from nuer)

nudité.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French from Classical Latin nuditatem (accusative of nuditas, 'nakedness, bareness; plainness of rhetorical style, destitution'), derived from nudus ('naked, bare, uncovered', from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷós, cognate with English naked). It superseded the inherited Old French formation nueté while preserving the Latin -d- lost in French nu ('naked').
nudité.notes: Standard term in film contracts (clause de nudité, scène de nudité, doublure nudité for a body double); note how French pairs the inherited short adjective nu with the learned Latinate noun nudité.

rootFamily.gloss: naked, bare; a nude artwork (< Latin nudum)
to strip bare, expose, lay bare

nuit.etymology: Nuit continues Latin nox, with the stem noct-. The Académie records tenth-century noit before the modern spelling.
nuit.notes: Compare how Latin -ct- (noctem, lactem, factum) evolves across Romance: French nuit, lait, fait; Portuguese noite, leite, feito; Spanish noche, leche, hecho; Italian notte, latte, fatto.

nul.etymology: Inherited and reinforced via Old French nul ('no, not any, nobody') from Classical Latin nullum (accusative of nullus, 'not any, none, nobody, of no account'), contracted from negative ne and ullus ('any', diminutive *oinolos of unus 'one', literally 'not even a little one'). From legal 'void, invalid' and mathematical 'zero' (match nul), modern colloquial French developed the vivid evaluative sense 'rubbish, hopeless, incompetent'.

history.meaning: no, not any, no one (negative determiner/pronoun)

nul.notes: Spans two opposite registers: high-register literary pronoun/determiner with ne (Nul n'est censé ignorer la loi; sans nul doute) and everyday colloquial adjective with être (C'est nul ! 'It sucks!', Je suis nul en maths 'I'm hopeless at math', feminine nulle).

numéro.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–17th century (originally in merchant bookkeeping as an abbreviation N° written on bales of goods) from Italian numero ('assigned number in a series'), from Classical Latin numerus ('number', native doublet of nombre).

history.meaning: serial or identifying number, issue of a periodical, variety act

numéroter.etymology: Derived in the 17th–18th century from numéro ('serial number') + verbal suffix -ter (with linking -t- on the model of abricoter / chapeauter).

history.meaning: to assign sequential numbers to, number pages or items

nécessaire.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old French (necessaire) from Classical Latin necessarius ('unavoidable, indispensable, urgent; closely bound by kinship or patronage'), derived from indeclinable necesse ('unavoidable, inevitable'), probably formed from ne- ('not') + cedere ('to yield, withdraw' — literally 'from which there is no backing away'). Used both as an adjective and, since Early Modern French, as a noun for a travel kit.

history.meaning: unavoidable, indispensable; closely bound friend or kinsman

nécessaire.notes: Watch the spelling contrast with English: French has one c and double s (nécessaire, acute accent on é); the idiom faire le nécessaire ('to take care of whatever is needed / handle it') is constant office and agency shorthand.

négliger.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French from Classical Latin neglegere / negligere ('to disregard, slight, be indifferent to, overlook'), compounded from Archaic/Classical nec ('not') and legere ('to pick up, gather, choose, read'). Literally 'not to pick up or single out for care', it was coined in Latin as the exact structural antonym of diligere ('to single out, prize, be diligent toward').

history.meaning: not to pick up; to disregard, slight, pay no heed to
to leave uncared for, fail to attend to

négliger.notes: Takes an orthographic e after g before a or o to keep /ʒ/ soft (nous négligeons) and alternates é → è before silent syllables (il néglige /nɛ.ɡliʒ/ vs. je néglige — note that é stays written é before -ge in néglige, unlike céder → cède, wait: il néglige keeps é!); non négligeable ('substantial, nothing to sneeze at') is a classic French litotes, and un air négligé means 'studiedly casual or disheveled'.

rootFamily.gloss: negligible, minor (or substantial in non négligeable)

négociateur.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French from Classical Latin negotiatorem (accusative of negotiator, 'wholesale merchant, banker, business agent'), agent noun of negotiari ('to carry on business, trade'), itself from negotium ('business, occupation, affair'), a transparent compound of nec ('not') + otium ('leisure, ease'). From wholesale commerce, its sense specialized in diplomacy, contracts, and crisis mediation.

history.meaning: lack of leisure; occupation, business affair
merchant; diplomatic envoy or contract bargainer

négociateur.notes: Feminine is négociatrice (spelled with c in French: négocier, négociateur, unlike English negotiate with t); a talent agent's core identity in Dix pour cent is être un fin négociateur ('a shrewd dealmaker'), distinct from un négociant ('a wine or wholesale merchant').

négociation.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin negōtiātiōnem, noun of action from negōtiārī ('to carry on business, trade'), itself derived from negōtium ('business, occupation'), literally 'lack of leisure', formed from nec ('not') + ōtium ('leisure, ease'). In French it shifted from wholesale commercial trading (14th c.) to diplomatic and contractual bargaining by the 17th century.

history.meaning: commercial trade; diplomatic or contractual bargaining

négociation.notes: Feminine noun (une négociation); central to talent-agency life in Dix pour cent, especially in 'être en pleine négociation' (to be deep in contract talks) over an actor's cachet.

négocier.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin negōtiārī ('to do business, act as banker or merchant'), deponent verb built on negōtium ('occupation, business, affair'), a compound of nec ('not') and ōtium ('leisure'). Originally restricted to mercantile trade in Middle French before broadening to brokering agreements and terms.

history.meaning: to conduct commerce; to discuss terms of an agreement

négocier.notes: Used both transitively ('négocier un contrat', 'négocier un virage') and with 'avec'; remember stem spelling keeps 'c' throughout, while nouns like 'négoce' drop the '-i-'.

nôtre.etymology: Inherited from Old French nostre ('our, ours'), from Vulgar Latin *nostrum for Classical Latin noster, nostrum ('our, ours', derived from nos 'we, us'); retains the circumflex accent (le nôtre) as a stressed tonic possessive pronoun.

objet.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Medieval Scholastic Latin objectum ('something placed before the eyes or mind'), substantivized neuter past participle of Classical Latin objicere ('to throw or set before, present to sight', from ob- 'in front of, against' + jacere 'to throw').

history.meaning: that which is placed before the senses or mind
tangible thing, object; aim, subject matter

obligation.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin obligātiōnem ('a binding, pledging, legal bond'), action noun from obligāre ('to bind up, bandage, put under moral or legal bond'), composed of ob- ('toward, against, around') and ligāre ('to tie, bind'). Its earliest French sense was strictly juridical—a formal deed binding a debtor—before generalizing to moral and social duty.

history.meaning: written legal bond or debt commitment
moral, social, or contractual duty; financial bond

obligation.notes: Feminine noun; besides 'duty' (des obligations professionnelles / promotionnelles for film stars), in finance 'une obligation' means a corporate or government bond (not a stock, 'une action').

obliger.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old French from Classical Latin obligāre ('to bind around, tie up; figuratively, to bind by oath, law, or favor'), formed from ob- ('around, over') + ligāre ('to bind', source of inherited French lier). French retained both senses of the Latin metaphor: compelling someone by constraint and winning gratitude through a favor.

history.meaning: to bind up; to place under legal or moral obligation
to bind by oath or contract; to compel

obliger.notes: Watch preposition choice: in the active voice, 'obliger quelqu'un à faire quelque chose' takes 'à', whereas passive 'être obligé de faire' overwhelmingly takes 'de' in modern spoken French; spelling adds 'e' before 'a/o' (nous obligeons).

obligé.etymology: Adjectival use of the past participle of obliger, attested from Old French obligié and reflecting Classical Latin obligātus ('bound up, tied; bound in duty or gratitude'), perfect passive participle of obligāre (ob- + ligāre). Alongside its sense of 'compelled' or 'grateful', it developed the rhetorical sense of 'inevitable, standard' (as in un passage obligé).

history.meaning: bound, tied up; mortgaged, under obligation
bound by promise or feudal duty
compelled, indebted; inevitable (of a step or scene)

obligé.notes: Very common in screenwriting and agency talk in 'un passage obligé' (an essential scene/stop you cannot skip) and colloquially as a clipped interjection: 'Obligé !' ('Definitely! / Have to!').

observation.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin observātiōnem ('watching, attentiveness, adherence to custom or rule'), action noun from observāre ('to watch over, heed, keep'), composed of ob- ('toward, over') + servāre ('to keep safe, watch, guard'). In Middle French it first meant compliance with religious or legal rules before shifting toward empirical watching and critical remarks.

history.meaning: compliance with a rule or monastic order
act of watching closely; critical remark or medical monitoring

observation.notes: Note the pronunciation assimilation: the 'b' before voiceless 's' is pronounced [p] ([ɔpsɛʁvasjɔ̃]); 'faire une observation à quelqu'un' often means to mildly reprimand or point out a fault, whereas religious 'observance' uses the doublet 'observance'.

observer.etymology: Inherited and reinforced by learned borrowing from Classical Latin observāre ('to watch, attend to, guard, comply with'), formed from ob- ('in front of, over') and servāre ('to watch over, keep safe', from PIE *ser- 'to protect', unrelated to servus 'slave'). In French, it bridges visual scrutiny, silent pause (observer une minute de silence), and adherence to rules.

history.meaning: to guard, keep safe, watch over
to watch closely, heed, respect a law
to follow a rule; to examine attentively

observer.notes: Pronounced [ɔpsɛʁve] with regressive devoicing of 'b' before 's'; actors preparing for a role often 'observent' professionals in the field to build character authenticity.

obtenir.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin obtinēre ('to hold fast, occupy, maintain, prevail, acquire'), composed of ob- ('against, toward') + tenēre ('to hold'). Remodeled in French conjugation on the inherited verb tenir (j'obtiens, nous obtenons, obtenu), shifting semantically from 'holding onto possession' to 'securing something sought after'.

history.meaning: to hold fast, keep possession of, prevail
to succeed in securing a grant, right, or request

obtenir.notes: Conjugates exactly like 'tenir' and 'venir' (j'obtiens, ils obtiennent, j'obtiendrai), with 'b' devoiced to [p] ([ɔptəniʁ]); the go-to verb for landing a coveted lead ('obtenir le premier rôle').

occasion.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–13th century from Classical Latin occasionem (nominative occasio, 'favorable moment, opportunity'), derived from occidere, occasum ('to fall down, happen, set', from ob- + cadere 'to fall').

history.meaning: favorable opportunity, occasion; bargain, secondhand item (d'occasion)

occuper.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin occupāre ('to seize first, take possession of, forestall, employ'), formed from intensive ob- ('over, against') + a verbal stem built on capere ('to take, seize'). From physical or military seizure of space, French developed the reflexive construction s'occuper de ('to busy oneself with, look after').

history.meaning: to seize beforehand, take possession of, fill up time
to take possession of a place; to keep someone busy

morphemes.meaning: over, completely (intensive ob- assimilated to oc-)

occuper.notes: Crucial reflexive idiom in Dix pour cent: 'Je m'en occupe !' ('I'm on it! / Leave it to me!') and 's'occuper d'un client' (to represent/look after a talent).

occupé.etymology: Past participle of occuper ('to take possession of, fill up space or time, keep busy'), borrowed in Old/Middle French from Classical Latin occupare ('to seize beforehand, take possession of, employ'), from ob- + capere ('to take, seize').

history.meaning: to seize hold of, fill, employ

octave.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Medieval Latin octava (sc. dies 'the eighth day after a church feast', or pars / consonance 'interval of eight diatonic degrees'), feminine of Classical Latin octavus ('eighth', from octo 'eight').

history.meaning: eight-day liturgical period; eight-note musical interval
musical interval of eight degrees, octave

océan.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century (Old French occean) from Latin Ōceanus, itself from Ancient Greek Ὠκεανός (Ōkeanós), the Titan and great outer river believed by the ancients to encircle the flat habitable earth disk, probably of Pre-Greek Mediterranean substrate origin. In the Age of Discovery it shifted from the single mythic world-stream to the major basins of the globe.

history.meaning: great outer river encircling the earth; Titan deity
the outer sea surrounding the known world

océan.notes: Masculine noun (un océan, l'océan Atlantique); used hyperbolically in conversational French ('un océan de larmes', 'boire la tasse dans un océan de galères').

odeur.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French odor / odeur) from Classical Latin odorem (nominative odor, 'smell, scent, fragrance, stench', from PIE *h3ed- 'to smell', cognate with Greek ozein and Latin olere).

odieux.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin odiōsus ('hateful, offensive, tiresome, annoying'), derived from odium ('hatred, aversion, disgust'), linked to the defective verb ōdī ('I hate'). While English 'odious' feels bookish or elevated, French odieux remains vigorous and natural in everyday speech for insufferably rude behavior.

history.meaning: arousing hatred or moral disgust; insufferably obnoxious

odieux.notes: Much more common in spoken French than English 'odious': saying a diva actor 'a été odieux sur le plateau' simply means they behaved obnoxiously or horribly on set (feminine: odieuse).

rootFamily.gloss: in an odious or obnoxious manner

offensive.etymology: Substantivized feminine of the adjective offensif (18th century, originally elliptical for guerre offensive or marche offensive), derived from Medieval Latin offēnsīvus, from Classical Latin offēnsum, supine of offendere ('to strike against, dash upon, attack'), from ob- ('against') + *fendere ('to strike, thrust', also in dēfendere).

history.meaning: to strike against, bump into, attack
serving to attack rather than defend
coordinated military attack; strategic campaign or initiative

offensive.notes: False friend alert as an adjective/noun: in French, 'une offensive' is an attack or PR push ('passer à l'offensive', 'une offensive de charme'), NEVER 'insulting/offensive' in the social sense (which is 'offensant' or 'blessant').

officiel.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–18th century from Late Latin officialis ('relating to a public office or duty; magistrate's attendant'), derived from Classical Latin officium ('service, duty, public office', contracted from *opificium < opus 'work' + facere 'to do').

history.meaning: pertaining to an office or magistrate

officiellement.etymology: Formed in the late 18th century from the feminine adjective officielle ('official') + adverbial suffix -ment.

officier.etymology: Attested from Old French oficier ('holder of an office or household charge'), derived from Medieval Latin officiārius ('official, magistrate'), built on Classical Latin officium ('service, duty, ceremonial function, magistracy'), a contraction of *opificium from opus ('work') + facere ('to do, perform'). It later specialized in military command, civil registry, and orders of merit.

history.meaning: person holding an ecclesiastical or royal charge
holder of a public duty; military commander or civil registrar

officier.notes: Covers military officers, civil registrars ('officier d'état civil' conducting French town-hall weddings), and cultural honors ('Officier des Arts et des Lettres', prized by French actors); as a verb, 'officier' also means to officiate or practice.

rootFamily.gloss: office, duty, tourist bureau, worship service

offre.etymology: Deverbal feminine noun formed in the 12th century (Old French ofre) from offrir ('to offer, present'), which descends via Vulgar Latin *offerīre from Classical Latin offerre ('to bring before, present, bestow'), composed of ob- ('toward, before') + ferre ('to carry, bring'). Originally a religious or feudal presentation, it expanded to commercial bids and employment proposals.

history.meaning: act of offering; gift, bid, or proposal

morphemes.meaning: to bring, carry (from Latin ferre via offrir)

offre.notes: Feminine noun ('une offre ferme', 'la loi de l'offre et de la demande'); note that its parent verb 'offrir' conjugates like a first-group '-er' verb in the present singular ('j'offre', 'il offre').

rootFamily.gloss: to offer, give as a gift

offrir.etymology: Inherited from Old French ofrir ('to present as a gift or religious offering'), from Vulgar Latin *offerire, remodeled from Classical Latin offerre ('to bring before, present, offer'), compound of ob- ('toward, before') + ferre ('to carry, bring').

history.meaning: to offer, give as a gift

oh.etymology: Oh is an expressive interjection recorded in French from the sixteenth century. The Académie considers borrowing from the same Latin exclamation probable, rather than presenting that route as certain.

history.meaning: oh! (interjection of surprise, admiration, or protest)

rootFamily.gloss: expressive exclamation of surprise, awe, or dismay

oh.notes: Oh là là! expresses everything from sympathy or exasperation ('oh dear!') to genuine amazement—not the suggestive cliché it acquired in English.

oignon.etymology: Inherited from Old French oignon, from Classical Latin unionem (accusative of unio, 'oneness, single large pearl; country Latin word for a single-bulb onion', contrasted with multi-clove garlic).

cognates.meaning: onion was borrowed from Old French oignon; union is its learned Latin doublet!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: oignon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: oignon

oignon.notes: Old French wrote *oign-* to represent palatal /ɲ/ after *o*; the 1990 spelling reform also permits **ognon** to match modern pronunciation /ɔɲɔ̃/.

oiseau.etymology: Inherited from Old French oisel ('bird'), from Late/Vulgar Latin aucellus ('little bird, bird'), diminutive formed on *auca (from Classical Latin avica, derived from avis 'bird'), which completely replaced Classical avis in Gallo-Romance and Italian (uccello).

ok.etymology: Borrowed from American English OK (attested steadily in French from the early 20th century and popularized after World War I and II), proven by philologist Allen Walker Read to originate in an 1839 Boston Morning Post humorous abbreviation fad: O.K. for 'oll korrect' (facetious respelling of 'all correct'), reinforced in 1840 by Martin Van Buren's campaign nickname 'Old Kinderhook'.
ok.notes: Pronounced [ɔke] in French (not with the English diphthong [oʊˈkeɪ]), NEVER spelled out with French letter names *[okɑ]; invariable as a predicate adjective ('Ils sont ok pour tourner demain').

okay.etymology: Phoneticized spelling borrowing from American English okay (attested in English as okeh/okay by the late 19th–early 20th century as a spelled-out rendering of initialism O.K., originally 1839 Boston newspaper slang for 'oll korrect' = 'all correct'). Adopted into French script dialogue and informal writing to represent the disyllabic pronunciation [ɔke].

history.meaning: all right, agreed (colloquial French discourse marker)

okay.notes: Frequent in screenplays, subtitles, and text messages alongside 'ok'; in brisk office exchanges at ASK in Dix pour cent, 'Okay, on fait comme ça' signals snappy, modern agreement compared with the slightly more traditional 'D'accord'.

olive.etymology: Inherited from Old French olive ('olive fruit, olive tree'), from Classical Latin oliva ('olive, olive tree'), borrowed from archaic Ancient Greek *elaiwa (Attic elaia, 'olive').

olympique.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin Olympicus, from Ancient Greek Ὀλυμπικός (Olympikós, 'relating to Mount Olympus or to Olympia in Elis'), built on Ὄλυμπος (Ólympos), home of the twelve Olympian gods, and the Panhellenic sanctuary of Olympia where quadrennial games honoring Zeus were held from 776 BCE; revived internationally by Baron Pierre de Coubertin in French in 1894.

history.meaning: of Mount Olympus or the sanctuary and games of Olympia
pertaining to Olympia or the Olympic festival
pertaining to the Olympic Games; serenely majestic

olympique.notes: Know two classic idioms: 'avoir la forme olympique' (to be in peak form) and 'un calme olympien' (note 'olympien' = godlike/Olympian for serenity, though 'un calme olympique' occurs colloquially by blend).

rootFamily.gloss: Mount Olympus; legendary Paris concert hall L'Olympia

ombre.etymology: Inherited directly from Classical Latin umbra ('shadow, shade'), with regular Romance lowering of short Latin u to /o/ nasalised before m + consonant.

cognates.meaning: little shade (via Italian ombrello from Latin umbra)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: ombre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: ombre

on.etymology: On descends from Latin homo, meaning a human being. The Académie records om in the ninth century and hom or hum in the eleventh. A noun referring to a person became a subject pronoun; its older noun-like construction also explains l’on.
on.notes: The possessive can depend on the meaning: general on can go with son/sa/ses; when on means nous, notre/nos is common.

oncle.etymology: Inherited from Old French oncle ('uncle'), from Classical Latin avunculus ('mother's brother, maternal uncle', literally 'little grandfather', affectionate diminutive of avus 'grandfather'), which displaced paternal patruus across Romance.

onze.etymology: Inherited from Old French onze ('eleven'), from Vulgar Latin *undece, contracted from Classical Latin undecim ('eleven', compound of unus 'one' + decem 'ten').

opportunité.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin opportūnitātem ('fitness, suitability, favorable time, advantage'), abstract noun from opportūnus ('favorable, seasonable'), originally a maritime metaphor from ob- ('toward') + portus ('harbor, port'), describing seasonal winds blowing a ship safely toward port. Its modern sense of 'career or business opening' was reinforced by English opportunity in the 20th century.
opportunité.notes: Purists including the Académie française traditionally restrict 'opportunité' to 'timeliness/advisability' ('juger de l'opportunité d'une mesure') and recommend 'occasion' for 'a good opportunity', though 'une belle opportunité' is ubiquitous in business and cinema agencies.

optimisme.etymology: Coined in French in 1737 in the Jesuit Mémoires de Trévoux (and immortalized satirically by Voltaire's Candide, ou l'Optimisme in 1759) from Classical Latin optimum ('the best thing'), neuter superlative of bonus ('good'), + philosophical suffix -isme, to name Leibniz's theodicy that God created 'the best of all possible worlds' before broadening to a hopeful temperament.

history.meaning: Leibnizian doctrine of the best of all possible worlds

optimisme.notes: Originally a French philosophical coinage exported across Europe! Masculine noun ('garder son optimisme', 'un optimisme béat' = naive, overly rosy optimism).

optimiste.etymology: Formed in mid-18th-century French (first attested around 1752–1759 in Enlightenment debates over Leibniz) from optimisme by substituting the suffix -iste, built on Classical Latin optimus ('best', superlative of bonus). Initially denoting a partisan of Leibniz's metaphysical system, it shifted by the early 19th century to anyone inclined to expect favorable outcomes.

history.meaning: hopeful, inclined to see the bright side

optimiste.notes: Functions identically as both adjective ('un agent très optimiste') and noun ('un/une optimiste'), invariant for gender in the singular thanks to final '-e'.

option.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century as a legal and ecclesiastical term from Classical Latin optiōnem ('free choice, liberty to choose'), derived from optāre ('to choose, wish for, select', related to ops and PIE *h₃ep- 'to choose, prefer'). In the 20th century, contract law and cinema/publishing reinforced the sense of a time-limited right of first refusal.

history.meaning: legal right to choose; elective subject or contractual hold

option.notes: Essential film-industry idiom: 'poser / mettre une option sur un livre ou sur les dates d'un acteur' means optioning adaptation rights or placing a temporary hold on an actor's shooting schedule.

opéra.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-17th century (under Cardinal Mazarin's introduction of Italian lyric theater to Paris) from Italian opera ('work, composition', clipped from opera in musica, 'work in music'), from Classical Latin opera (feminine singular collective formed from the neuter plural of opus, operis, 'work, artistic labor', which separately yielded inherited French œuvre).

history.meaning: dramatic work set entirely to music
sung dramatic work; opera house or company

opéra.notes: Masculine in French ('un opéra magnifique', 'aller à l'Opéra Garnier') despite ending in '-a' and descending from feminine Italian 'opera'! Also names the rich layered Parisian coffee-chocolate cake ('un gâteau opéra') and the central Paris metro hub/district.

opération.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old French (12th–13th c.) from Classical Latin operātiōnem ('work, labor, performance, activity'), action noun from operārī ('to work, labor, be effective'), derived from opus, operis ('work'). Across Middle and Modern French it specialized into surgical intervention, arithmetic calculation, military deployment, and publicity or financial campaigns.

history.meaning: working, activity, performance; almsgiving in Christian Latin
action, workings of nature or medicine
surgical procedure, calculation, financial or PR campaign

morphemes.meaning: work, activity (Latin oper-, stem of opus)

opération.notes: In media and talent-agency French, 'une opération séduction' or 'une opération de com'' refers to a coordinated PR/charm campaign to repair a star's public image.

opérationnel.etymology: Twentieth-century formation (spreading during and after World War II under the influence of English operational, notably in recherche opérationnelle) built on French opération + relational suffix -nel (modeled on pairs like fonction / fonctionnel), ultimately from Classical Latin operātiōnem ('work, performance') and opus ('work').

history.meaning: coordinated action, military or technical procedure
fit for deployment, up and running; ready to work

opérationnel.notes: Applied colloquially to people as well as systems: 'Je ne suis pas encore opérationnel avant mon café' or 'Il faut être opérationnel dès 7h sur le tournage' ('ready to roll / sharp and functioning'). Feminine: opérationnelle.

opérer.etymology: Learned borrowing (attested from the 15th–16th century, replacing inherited ouvrer in technical senses) from Classical Latin operārī ('to work, labor, take effect, perform rites'), built on the stem oper- of opus ('work, deed'). It serves as a learned doublet of ouvrer ('to work, craft'), preserving the Latin 'p' that lenited to 'v' in popular Gallo-Romance.

history.meaning: to labor, be busy with, have an effect
to produce an effect, carry out, perform surgery

opérer.notes: Stem-changing accent (`é` -> `è` before silent syllable: 'le charme opère', 'j'opère'); note how 'le charme opère' means 'the magic/charm is working', whereas operating a machine is 'faire fonctionner' (not *opérer une machine).

rootFamily.gloss: to craft, work (inherited doublet of opérer)

or.etymology: Represents two converged Latin words: (1) noun or ('gold'), from Old French or < Classical Latin aurum ('gold'); and (2) conjunction/adverb or ('now, well now, whereas'), from Old French or / ore ('at this hour, now'), from Classical Latin hac hora ('at this hour').

orage.etymology: Inherited from Old French orage (originally 'strong wind, gust of air'), from Vulgar Latin *auraticum, built on Classical Latin aura ('breeze, breath of air', borrowed from Greek aúra).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: orage (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: orage

orage.notes: Unrelated to *or* ('gold')—its initial *or-* reflects Latin *au-* (*aura* -> *or-*), just as *aurum* gave *or*.

orange.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century (via Old Occitan auranja / Italian arancia, with blending of initial o- after French or 'gold' and the town name Orange) from Arabic naranj, from Persian narang, ultimately from Sanskrit naranga ('orange tree').

oranger.etymology: Formed in Middle French (15th century) from orange + fruit-tree suffix -er (from Latin -ārius, compare pomme -> pommier). French orange itself came via Old Italian melarancia and Arabic nāranj from Persian nārang and Sanskrit nāraṅga ('orange tree', likely of Dravidian origin); initial 'n-' was lost by rebracketing (une narange -> une arange), and the vowel shifted to o- by folk-etymological blend with or ('gold') or Provençal town Orange.

history.meaning: orange tree; source of orange-blossom water

oranger.notes: Masculine noun ('un oranger'); prized in French pastry and calming herbal remedies via 'l'eau de fleur d'oranger' (orange-blossom water), and architecturally famous from royal 'orangeries' (like the Musée de l'Orangerie in the Tuileries).

rootFamily.gloss: conservatory for citrus trees; Orangerie museum

ordinaire.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin ōrdinārius ('in regular order, customary, usual'), derived from ōrdō, ōrdinis ('row, rank, regular arrangement, originally a line of threads on a loom'). From ecclesiastical and legal regularity (juge ordinaire), it broadened to everyday custom, average quality, and the adverbial phrase d'ordinaire ('usually').

history.meaning: row of threads, rank, regular order
arranged in regular order, customary, regular
conforming to normal rule; everyday, average; daily meal ration

ordinaire.notes: Notice position-sensitive nuance: after a noun ('un homme ordinaire') it means 'everyday/average' (or slightly pejorative 'common/banal'), while 'd'ordinaire' is an elegant synonym for 'd'habitude' ('usually').

rootFamily.gloss: to order, arrange; to ordain or prescribe

ordinateur.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin ordinatorem (nominative ordinator, 'one who puts in order, regulator', from ordinare); proposed in April 1955 by the Latinist Jacques Perret at the request of IBM France to translate English electronic computer ('a machine that puts information into systematic order').

history.meaning: one who arranges or puts in order

ordre.etymology: Inherited/adapted in Old French (ordene -> ordre) from Classical Latin ordinem (nominative ordo, 'straight row, line of threads in a loom, rank, regularity, command').

history.meaning: order, tidiness, command, religious or chivalric order

cognates.meaning: filth, horrider dirt (archaic Cognate root orrido)

ordure.etymology: Derived in the 12th century within Old French from the adjective ort, orde ('filthy, foul, repulsive') + abstract/collective suffix -ure. Old French ort comes from Classical Latin horridus ('bristling, rough, shaggy, dreadful, uncouth'), from horrēre ('to bristle, shudder'). Semantically it moved from rough/foul filth to household refuse (les ordures ménagères) and, in singular invective, a despicable person ('scumbag').

history.meaning: filth, refuse; morally vile person (in modern insult)

morphemes.meaning: filthy, foul (Old French ort/orde, from Latin horridus)

ordure.notes: Plural 'les ordures (ménagères)' is neutral everyday French for 'household trash/garbage', whereas singular 'Quelle ordure !' / 'C'est une ordure !' is a strong insult meaning 'What a scumbag / piece of trash!' (feminine even when aimed at a man).

rootFamily.gloss: horrid, dreadful (learned doublet of Old French ort)
horror, dread (from the same Latin horrēre root)

oreille.etymology: Inherited from Classical/Colloquial Latin auricula ('earlobe, little ear'), diminutive of Classical Latin auris ('ear'). Across all Romance languages, spoken Latin preferred the expressive diminutive auricula over short auris.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: oreille (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: oreille

oreille.notes: Adding *-er* to *oreille* produced **un oreiller**—literally 'the thing for your ear', i.e. a pillow!

oreiller.etymology: Inherited from Old French oreillier ('bed pillow'), derived from oreille ('ear', from Classical Latin auricula, diminutive of auris 'ear') + suffix -ier — literally 'that on which one rests one's ear'.

history.meaning: cushion for resting the ear/head, pillow

cognates.meaning: little ear; atrium of the heart; dog-ear

oreillette.etymology: Diminutive formed in Old French (13th century, originally 'little ear' or ear-guard on a helmet) from oreille ('ear') + diminutive suffix -ette. French oreille itself descends from Classical Latin auricula ('earlobe, little ear', already a diminutive of auris 'ear' that displaced the simplex across Vulgar Latin), making oreillette historically a double diminutive. In late-20th-century broadcasting it took on the sense of a discreet in-ear monitor.

history.meaning: helmet ear-piece; heart atrium; broadcast in-ear receiver

oreillette.notes: Ubiquitous on TV sets, Cannes red carpets, and award ceremonies in Dix pour cent ('parler dans l'oreillette' = prompting a host or actor via a hidden earpiece); also means an atrium of the heart and a crisp Provençal Mardi Gras pastry!

organisateur.etymology: Coined in French at the end of the 18th century during the French Revolution (famously applied to Lazare Carnot as 'l'organisateur de la victoire') from organiser ('to endow with organs; to structure systematically') + agent suffix -ateur. Ultimately from Medieval Latin organizāre and Classical Latin organum, from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon, 'tool, instrument, bodily organ'), akin to ἔργον (érgon, 'work').

history.meaning: implement, tool, musical instrument, bodily organ
to form living organs; later, to arrange into an ordered whole
one who structures an institution, campaign, or event

organisateur.notes: Feminine form is 'organisatrice' ('les organisateurs du Festival de Cannes'); also used as an adjective ('le comité organisateur', 'avoir un talent organisateur').

organiser.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin organizare ('to play the organ; to furnish with organs'), derived from Classical Latin organum ('musical instrument, implement, bodily organ'), itself from Ancient Greek órganon ('tool, instrument, sense organ', from the PIE root *werǵ- 'to work'). In Middle French it first meant 'to endow a body with living organs', shifting in the 18th century to 'structuring an institution, event, or plan systematically'.

history.meaning: to play the organ; to furnish with organs
to endow with organs; later, to arrange systematically

organiser.notes: In production and agency talk, 'organiser un casting / une tournée' covers both high-level planning and practical logistics; reflexive 's'organiser' means 'to get oneself sorted out'.

orientation.etymology: Formed in the 18th–19th century from orienter ('to position facing the east or a compass point', from orient 'the east, point of sunrise' < Latin orientem, present participle of oriri 'to rise') + suffix -ation.

history.meaning: alignment with the points of the compass; direction, career guidance

original.etymology: Learned borrowing (14th century) from Late Latin originalis ('primitive, existing from the beginning, innate'), derived from Classical Latin origo, originis ('beginning, source, birth, lineage'), from the verb oriri ('to rise, come forth, be born'). Originally purely chronological ('first, uncopied'), it developed aesthetic and psychological senses ('creative, unconventional, eccentric') in late 17th-century artistic criticism.

history.meaning: pertaining to the origin; later, novel or eccentric

original.notes: Watch word position and tone: 'un scénario original' means an unadapted screenplay, whereas calling a person 'un original' (or saying 'C'est... original !' with a pause) politely implies 'weird' or 'eccentric'.

origine.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Classical Latin originem (nominative origo, 'birth, source, lineage, beginning'), derived from oriri ('to rise, spring forth, be born').

history.form: oriri ('to rise, spring up') -> origo, originem

orphelin.etymology: Inherited from Old French orfenin ('parentless child'), extended with the diminutive/relational suffix -in from Late and Ecclesiastical Latin orphanus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek orphanós ('bereaved, fatherless, destitute'), cognate with Latin orbus ('bereft'). The shift from Old French orfenin to Middle French orphelin arose through liquid dissimilation of the two nasals (n...n > l...n), combined with learned restoration of the ph spelling.
orphelin.notes: Used both as a noun ('un orphelin / une orpheline') and figuratively with 'de' ('orphelin de son mentor' = bereft of one's mentor).

orteil.etymology: Inherited from Old French arteil ('toe'), from Classical Latin articulus ('little joint, knuckle, digit'), whose initial vowel shifted from a- to o- in Gallo-Romance through the influence of Gaulish ordiga ('big toe').

cognates.meaning: learned doublet of orteil from Latin articulus

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: orteil (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: orteil

orteil.notes: Few pairs look more surprising than **un orteil** ('a toe') and **un article** ('a newspaper article'), yet both trace back to Latin *articulus*!

orthophoniste.etymology: Twentieth-century medical-professional derivative formed from French orthophonie ('study and correction of speech and voice disorders', coined in 1828 by physician Marc Colombat de l'Isère) plus the agentive suffix -iste. Orthophonie combines Ancient Greek orthós ('straight, upright, correct') and phōnḗ ('voice, vocal sound'), literally 'straightening or correcting the voice'.

history.meaning: medical correction of stammering and speech defects
specialist in speech and language therapy

orthophoniste.notes: Epicene in form ('un / une orthophoniste'); actors in French cinema also consult an orthophoniste or coach vocal to correct diction, lisp, or vocal strain.

os.etymology: Inherited via Old French os from Vulgar Latin ossum, reshaped from Classical Latin os, ossis ('bone'), which descends from Proto-Indo-European *h₂óst ('bone', cognate with Ancient Greek ostéon and Sanskrit ásthi). Because Old French plural os lost its final sibilant before pauses while singular os preserved /s/, Modern French retains a striking pronunciation alternation between singular and plural.
os.notes: Crucial pronunciation asymmetry: singular 'un os' is pronounced /ɔs/ (with audible -s), whereas plural 'des os' is pronounced /de.zo/ (silent -s, closed /o/)! Idiom: 'tomber sur un os' = 'to hit a snag / run into an unexpected obstacle'.

oser.etymology: Inherited from Old French oser ('to dare, have the boldness to'), from Vulgar Latin *ausare ('to dare'), frequentative formed on the past participle ausus of Classical Latin audere ('to dare, venture', from avidus 'eager').

ou.etymology: Inherited from Old French o / ou ('or'), from Classical Latin aut ('or, either... or').

ouais.etymology: Colloquial expressive alteration of oui ('yes'), attested since the late 16th and 17th centuries (spelled ouay, ouais in Molière as an exclamation of surprise, skepticism, or reluctant assent). Oui itself evolved from Old French oïl ('yes', contrasting with southern Occitan òc), contracted from Vulgar Latin hoc ille ('that [did] he', a reply echoing the subject pronoun).
ouais.notes: Ubiquitous in spoken French (/wɛ/); depending on intonation, 'ouais' ranges from brisk agreement ('yeah') to skeptical 'ouais, bof...' ('yeah, right / meh'). Avoid in formal correspondence.

rootFamily.gloss: to say yes to everything, rubber-stamp (informal/rare)

oublier.etymology: Inherited from Old French oblier ('to forget'), from Vulgar Latin *oblitare, frequentative built on Classical Latin oblivisci, oblitus ('to lose remembrance of, forget').

ouf.etymology: Onomatopoeic interjection (attested since the 17th century) imitating a deep exhalation of breath upon being relieved from a burden, fear, or exhaustion.

ouh.etymology: Expressive vocalic interjection attested since Old/Middle French (ou / hou), imitating a hooting cry to express playful fright, teasing, booing, or chill.

history.meaning: expressive hoot of teasing, surprise, or shivering ('ooh!')

oui.etymology: Oui developed from Old French oïl, an affirmative response. The Académie dates the modern form to the fourteenth century.

cognates.meaning: yes (< Latin hoc alone, giving Languedoc its name!)

oui.notes: Dante famously classified Western Romance by its word for 'yes': langue d'oïl (Old French oïl > oui), langue d'oc (Occitan òc), and lingua del sì (Italian sì < Latin sīc). Note also that oui behaves like a consonant-initial word (le oui, que oui, no elision!).

oups.etymology: Modern expressive interjection (reinforced in the 20th century by English oops / whoops, alongside older French houp / hop) uttered upon making a slight slip, stumble, or mistake.

history.meaning: exclamation over a minor blunder or slip ('oops!')

ours.etymology: Inherited through Old French ors from Classical Latin ursus ('bear'), descending from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ŕ̥tḱos ('bear', cognate with Ancient Greek árktos, source of 'arctic', and Sanskrit ṛkṣa). Figuratively applied in French since the 17th century to an unsociable, gruff person ('un ours mal léché', from the medieval belief that bear cubs were born shapeless and licked into form by their mothers).
ours.notes: Pronounced /uʁs/ with an audible final /s/ in both singular and plural. In cinema, 'l'Ours d'or' (Golden Bear) is the top prize at the Berlin International Film Festival (Berlinale), while calling a director 'un vrai ours' means they are gruff and anti-social.

out.etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English out ('outside, out of bounds, openly revealed'), from Old English ūt, from Proto-Germanic *ūt ('out'). First borrowed into French at the turn of the 20th century in tennis and boxing ('out of play / knocked out'), then re-borrowed in late 20th-century media and queer terminology via the phrase coming-out (clipped from English coming out of the closet).

history.meaning: out of bounds; openly declaring LGBTQ+ identity
out of play; public disclosure of identity or secret

out.notes: Encountered chiefly in 'faire son coming-out' (to come out publicly, also used playfully for admitting a secret passion), 'être out' (to be out of fashion / eliminated), and the verb 'outer quelqu'un' (to out someone against their will).

rootFamily.gloss: public disclosure of one's sexual orientation or secret

outil.etymology: Inherited from Old French ostil / outil ('implement, working tool'), from Vulgar Latin *usitilium, altered (under the influence of uti, usus 'to use') from Classical Latin utensilia ('things for use, tools, utensils', neuter plural of utensilis).

ouvert.etymology: Ouvert is the past participle and adjective of ouvrir ('to open'), descending from Vulgar Latin *opertus (for Classical Latin apertus 'open, uncovered').
ouvert.notes: Feminine **ouverte** sounds the final t (/uvɛʁt/). English 'overt' was borrowed from Old French.

ouverture.etymology: Inherited from Old French overture ('opening, aperture, beginning'), from Vulgar Latin *apertura / *operitura, altered from Classical Latin apertura ('an opening', from aperire 'to open') under the influence of ovrir / ouvrir.

ouvrir.etymology: Ouvrir descends from Vulgar Latin *operire (a blend of Classical Latin aperire 'to open' with cooperire 'to cover', which gave couvrir). Intervocalic -p- voiced and softened to -v-.
ouvrir.notes: Conjugates like a -er verb in the singular present (*j'ouvre, tu ouvres, il ouvre*) despite its -ir infinitive; past participle **ouvert**.

où.etymology: Où descends from Latin ubi, where. The Académie records the French question word from the tenth century.

cognates.meaning: where (literary ove < ubi; everyday dove < dē ubi)

où.notes: The only word in the entire French language containing the letter ù—written with a grave accent solely to distinguish où ('where') from ou ('or' < Latin aut).

pacte.etymology: Learned 14th-century borrowing (replacing inherited Old French pate) from Classical Latin pactum ('agreement, covenant, treaty'), the nominalized neuter past participle of pacisci ('to strike a bargain, agree upon'), built on the same PIE root *peh₂ǵ- ('to fasten, fix firmly') as pangere ('to drive in, fix') and pax ('peace, settlement').
pacte.notes: Stronger and more solemn or conspiratorial than 'accord' or 'contrat' — e.g. 'signer un pacte avec le diable' or 'un pacte de non-agression' between rival talent agents.

rootFamily.gloss: to make a pact (often pejorative: collude with)

page.etymology: Represents two distinct words: (1) feminine la page ('side of a leaf of paper in a book'), borrowed in the 12th–15th century from Classical Latin pagina ('column of writing, leaf of papyrus; originally a trellis of vines', from pangere 'to fasten'); and (2) masculine le page ('young nobleman attending a knight or prince'), borrowed via Italian paggio from Medieval Greek paidion ('little boy', diminutive of pais 'child').

history.meaning: page of a book (f.); young court page (m.)

cognates.meaning: sequin (also borrowed as paillette); straw flake

paillette.etymology: Formed in late Old / Middle French (14th century) as the diminutive of paille ('straw, chaff; tiny flake of metal') + suffix -ette, where paille descends from Classical Latin palea ('chaff, husks of grain'). Originally denoting tiny flat spangles of gold, silver, or copper found in river sand or sewn onto courtly attire, it came to symbolize showbiz glamour as 'les paillettes'.

history.meaning: straw; tiny flake of metal or gold
tiny metal spangle sewn onto clothing; sequin, glitter

paillette.notes: In plural, 'les strass et les paillettes' ('rhinestones and sequins') is the quintessential French idiom for the glitz, glamour, and superficiality of red-carpet celebrity life.

rootFamily.gloss: to fleck or spangle with glitter/gold

pain.etymology: Pain descends from Latin panis ('bread, loaf'). From Old French onward it has stood at the centre of daily meals and expressions such as gagner son pain ('to earn one's living') and copain (literally 'one who shares bread').

paire.etymology: Inherited from Old French paire ('matched set of two'), from Classical Latin paria ('equals, pairs'), neuter plural (reanalyzed as feminine singular) of the adjective par ('equal, matching').

paisible.etymology: Formed in Old French (paisible, 12th c.) from pais / paix ('peace', from Latin pacem) + adjectival suffix -ible.

history.meaning: inclined to peace, tranquil, peaceful, quiet

paisiblement.etymology: Formed in Old French (paisiblement, 12th century) from the adjective paisible ('tranquil, peace-loving', derived from Old French pais 'peace' < Classical Latin pacem, accusative of pax) + the adverbial suffix -ment (from the Classical Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind').
paisiblement.notes: Notice the /z/ sound spelled with 's' between vowels (/pɛ.zi.blə.mɑ̃/), preserving the Old French stem 'pais-' related to 'paix' and 'apaiser'.

paix.etymology: Inherited from Old French pais ('peace, reconciliation, silence'), from Classical Latin pacem (nominative pax, 'peace, treaty, calm', related to pacisci 'to make a pact' and pangere 'to fix, fasten').

palier.etymology: Attested since the 14th–15th century ('level landing between flights of stairs'), probably derived from paille ('straw', from Latin palea, originally denoting a straw mat placed on a stair landing or the level floor of a granary); extended in modern French to a level plateau or stage.

history.meaning: stair landing; level stage or threshold, shaft bearing

palme.etymology: From Old French palme ('palm branch, token of triumph'), semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin palma ('palm of the hand', transferred to the 'palm tree / palm frond' because its spreading leaves resemble an outstretched hand, and hence 'emblem of victory' awarded to triumphant athletes and gladiators in antiquity). Note that the inherited doublet for 'palm of the hand' became French paume.

history.meaning: palm of the hand; palm frond; prize of victory
palm branch (martyrdom or triumph); supreme honor

palme.notes: Essential Cannes Film Festival term: 'la Palme d'or' (created in 1955, inspired by the palm on the coat of arms of Cannes) is the festival's highest award; figuratively, 'remporter la palme' means 'to take the cake / win first prize'. (Plural 'des palmes' also means 'swim fins'!)

panade.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Provençal/Occitan panada ('bread soup made by boiling stale bread in water with a little butter or oil'), derived from Occitan pan ('bread') < Classical Latin panis ('bread'). Because soggy bread soup was humble peasant or invalid fare and had a sticky, mushy consistency, 'être dans la panade' evolved in 19th-century slang to mean 'to be destitute' and then 'to be stuck in a mess or jam'.

history.meaning: bread soup; (figuratively, 19th c.) poverty, sticky mess

panade.notes: Almost always heard in the lively informal idiom 'être dans la panade' ('to be in a real jam / up the creek'), a polite alternative to 'être dans la merde' or 'être dans le pétrin'.

pancarte.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Medieval Latin pancarta / pancharta ('official charter confirming all of a holder's possessions, posted tariff sheet'), a compound of Greek pan- ('all') and Latin charta ('sheet of papyrus or paper', from Greek khartēs). From a large public sheet posted at city gates listing tolls and laws, pancarte broadened to mean any placard or hand-held sign.

history.meaning: comprehensive public charter or posted sheet

pancarte.notes: Notice the family resemblance with **une carte** ('card, map'), which comes from the same Greco-Latin **charta**.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: pancarte

panier.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin panarium ('breadbasket'), derived from panis ('bread', French pain) + -arium. Long after baskets came to carry everything at market, the word still preserves 'bread' at its core.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: panier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: panier

panique.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (originally in the adjective phrase terreur panique, Rabelais) via Latin panicus from Ancient Greek panikos ('of the god Pan'), because the ancients attributed sudden, groundless collective terror in lonely woods or armies to the woodland god Pan.

history.meaning: sudden terror inspired by the god Pan

paniquer.etymology: Formed in the 20th century from panique ('sudden fear, panic') + verbal suffix -er (reinforced by English to panic).

history.meaning: to be seized by panic, cause to panic

panne.etymology: Originated as a nautical term (mettre en panne, 17th c., 'to heave to, bring a sailing ship to a standstill by backing the sails'), from Old French panne / pene ('sail yard or upper corner of a sail; plush fabric or fur lining', from Latin penna 'feather, wing'); transferred around 1900 to the sudden breakdown or stalling of a motor vehicle.

history.meaning: to stop a ship by backing its sails
mechanical breakdown, power outage, fuel shortage

panneau.etymology: Inherited from Old French panel ('piece of cloth placed under a saddle, section of a net or wall'), from Vulgar Latin *pannellus, diminutive of Classical Latin pannus ('piece of cloth, garment, rag', source of French pan).

history.meaning: small piece of fabric, saddle pad
wooden wainscot panel, signboard, road sign, trap/snare

pantalon.etymology: Eponymous noun derived in the 17th century from Pantalon, the French adaptation of Pantalone, the stingy old Venetian merchant stock character in Italian commedia dell'arte (whose name traditionally reflects San Pantaleone, a popular patron saint in Venice, from Greek Panteléēmōn 'all-compassionate'). Because Pantalone wore long tight-fitting ankle-length hose instead of aristocratic knee-breeches (culottes), the garment took his name and became standard wear during the French Revolution ('les sans-culottes').

history.meaning: Venetian commedia dell'arte character wearing long hose
stage costume; later (late 18th c.), full-length trousers

pantalon.notes: Always singular in French for a single pair of trousers ('un pantalon', never *des pantalons unless referring to multiple pairs), just like 'un jean' or 'un short'.

papa.etymology: Formed by labial reduplication (pa-pa) universal in infant speech, reinforced in learned and courtly French (where royal children addressed the king as papa in the 16th–17th centuries, whence it spread into bourgeois usage and then English) by Classical Latin pappa ('daddy; pap food') and Ancient Greek páppas ('father, daddy' in child language).
papa.notes: Used both by children and adults in warm family contexts; also appears in classic cultural idioms like 'le cinéma de papa' (stuffy, old-fashioned cinema — famously attacked by the French New Wave) and 'un fils à papa' (spoiled rich kid / nepo baby).

rootFamily.gloss: sugar daddy / doting older dad (slang: 'papa gâteau')
pope (ultimately same Greek/Latin nursery-turned-ecclesiastical root pappas)

cognates.meaning: celebrity press photographer (singular paparazzo, plural paparazzi)

paparazzi.etymology: Borrowed in the 1960s from Italian paparazzi, plural of Paparazzo, the surname given by director Federico Fellini and screenwriter Ennio Flaiano to the relentless scooter-riding press photographer (played by Walter Santesso) in the 1960 film La Dolce Vita. Fellini and Flaiano drew the name from southern Italian dialect paparazzo ('large buzzing mosquito' or 'noisily chattering sparrow') or a Calabrian hotelier surname encountered in George Gissing's travelogue By the Ionian Sea.

history.meaning: intrusive tabloid photographer in Fellini's La Dolce Vita (1960)
press photographer pursuing celebrities (singular or plural)

paparazzi.notes: In everyday French, 'un paparazzi' (plural 'des paparazzis' or invariable 'des paparazzi') is completely standard in the singular, unlike Italian where 'paparazzo' is singular; also spawned the verb 'paparazzer' ('to snap tabloid photos of a celebrity').

paperasse.etymology: Formed in the 16th century from papier ('paper') + pejorative/augmentative suffix -asse (modeled on Italian scartafaccio / carta).

history.meaning: waste paper, tedious red-tape documents, paperwork

papier.etymology: Papier comes via Latin papyrus from Ancient Greek pápyros ('Nile papyrus sedge, writing sheet'), shifting in the late Middle Ages to rag-and-pulp paper.

paquet.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century (during the Anglo-Flemish wool trade) from Middle English paket / Middle Dutch pak ('small bundle or bale of wool or goods') + diminutive suffix -et.

par.etymology: Inherited from Old French par ('through, by, by means of'), from Classical Latin per ('through, across, during, by means of', partially blended in Gallo-Romance with pro).

par-dessus.etymology: Compound preposition and adverb formed in Old French from par ('through, over', < Latin per) + dessus ('on top, above', < de + sus < Latin sursum).

history.meaning: over, on top of, above and beyond

paragraphe.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–15th century via Medieval Latin paragraphus from Ancient Greek paragraphos (sc. gramme, 'short horizontal stroke drawn in the margin to mark a break in sense or change of speaker'), from para- ('beside') + graphein ('to write').

history.meaning: marginal stroke marking a new section of text
marginal symbol (§); distinct subdivision of a text, paragraph

paralyser.etymology: Coined in late 18th-century French (popularized during the French Revolution in both medical and figurative political-economic rhetoric, and subsequently borrowed into English) from paralysie ('paralysis, palsy') + verbal suffix -iser. Paralysie entered French via Late Latin paralysis from Ancient Greek parálysis ('loosening at the side, disabling of nerves'), from pará ('beside, amiss') + lýein ('to loosen, untie, dissolve').

history.meaning: loosening on one side, disabling palsy
medical loss of movement or sensation
to strike with paralysis; figuratively, to bring to a standstill

paralyser.notes: Very common figuratively in high-pressure environments: 'être paralysé par le trac' (paralyzed by stage fright) or 'une grève qui paralyse le tournage' (a strike bringing the shoot to a halt).

cognates.meaning: paranoia / paranoid mood (colloquial clipping: para / paranoico)

parano.etymology: Late 20th-century colloquial French apocope (clipping after the -o- linking vowel, a productive colloquial truncation pattern alongside mégalo, schizo, mytho, prolo) of paranoïaque ('paranoid; paranoid person') and paranoïa ('paranoia'), ultimately from Ancient Greek paránoia ('mental derangement, folly', from pará 'beside, awry' + noûs 'mind').

history.meaning: overly suspicious, anxious (adj./noun); bout of paranoia (fem. noun)

parano.notes: Extremely frequent in conversational French: 'Arrête d'être parano !' ('Stop being paranoid!') or 'faire une crise de parano'. As an adjective, it does not add feminine -e ('elle est complètement parano'), though plural 'paranos' is written.

paranoïa.etymology: Learned late 19th-century psychiatric borrowing (diffused internationally through German psychiatric nosology, notably Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum and Emil Kraepelin, from Neo-Latin paranoia) from Ancient Greek paránoia ('madness, distraction, derangement of mind'), composed of pará ('beside, astray, amiss') + noûs (contracted from nóos, 'mind, perception, intellect').

history.meaning: clinical paranoia; figuratively, acute suspicion or distrust

paranoïa.notes: Notice the tréma (diaeresis) on the 'ï' in 'paranoïa' (/pa.ʁa.nɔ.ja/), which keeps the 'o' and 'i' in separate syllables instead of merging into the French /wa/ sound!

rootFamily.gloss: metanoia, profound change of mind (same Greek root noûs)

paranoïaque.etymology: Coined in early 20th-century French psychiatric vocabulary from paranoïa ('delusion of persecution, paranoia', from Ancient Greek paránoia 'madness', from pará 'beside, awry' + noûs 'mind') + the Greek-derived medical adjectival/nominal suffix -aque (modeled on maniaque 'maniac' and hypocondriaque 'hypochondriac').

history.meaning: afflicted with or characteristic of paranoia

morphemes.meaning: pertaining to or afflicted by (medical suffix)

paranoïaque.notes: Whereas English distinguishes clinical 'paranoiac' from everyday 'paranoid', standard French uses 'paranoïaque' (epicene: 'un acteur / une actrice paranoïaque') for both, reserving 'paranoïde' strictly for clinical 'schizophrénie paranoïde'.

cognates.meaning: flourish of a signature (noun parafe / rúbrica)

parapher.etymology: Derived in Middle French (15th century) from the noun paraphe (also spelled parafe, earlier paragrafe / paraffe, 'distinctive flourish under a signature; abbreviated initials'), contracted from Medieval Latin paragraphus ('sign marking a section of text'), from Ancient Greek parágraphos ('short stroke drawn in the margin beside a text', from pará 'beside' + gráphein 'to write'). It is thus an etymological doublet of paragraphe!

history.meaning: marginal stroke written beside a text
section mark; distinctive signature flourish or initials
to endorse every page of a document with one's initials; to sign formally

parapher.notes: Key contract-law and talent-agency verb: in France, before signing the final page of a film contract, parties must 'parapher chaque page' (initial the bottom corner of every page); in journalism, 'parapher un contrat' also means 'to officially sign a deal'.

rootFamily.gloss: initials or flourish on a contract page
signature book / folder held by executives for signing mail and contracts

parasite.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century via Classical Latin parasitus from Ancient Greek parasitos ('one who eats at another's table, sponger, flatterer in Greek comedy; originally a temple assistant who shared the sacred grain'), from para- ('beside') + sitos ('wheat, grain, food').

history.meaning: social freeloader; biological parasite (18th c.); static interference

paraître.etymology: Inherited from Old French pareir / paroistre ('to come into view, show oneself, seem'), from Vulgar Latin *parescere, inchoative form of Classical Latin parere ('to appear, be visible').

parc.etymology: Inherited from Old French parc ('fenced livestock pen, enclosed royal hunting preserve'), from Early Medieval Latin parricus ('enclosure', attested in the Lex Ripuaria and Lex Baiuvariorum), of debated pre-Romance substrate or West Germanic (*parruk 'fencing, fold') origin. From fenced medieval deer preserves, the meaning broadened in the 17th–19th centuries to aristocratic palace grounds, urban public gardens, and even 'fleet/stock of equipment' ('parc automobile').

history.meaning: landscaped grounds, public park; fleet of vehicles/gear

parc.notes: Beyond green spaces ('le parc Monceau') and amusement parks ('parc d'attractions'), 'parc' in French business also means 'installed fleet or inventory' ('parc informatique', 'parc automobile') and 'playpen' for a baby!

rootFamily.gloss: to pen in, cram people or animals into a tight space
parquet flooring (originally a small enclosed court space, diminutive of parc)

parce.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French (primarily in the causal conjunction parce que 'because') of the Old French phrase par ce (que) ('by this [fact that]'), from par ('by, through', < Latin per) + demonstrative pronoun ce ('this', < Vulgar Latin *ecce hoc).

parce que.etymology: Compound causal conjunction crystallized across Old and Middle French from three elements: the preposition par ('by, through' < Classical Latin per), the neuter demonstrative pronoun ce ('this, that' < Old French ço < Vulgar Latin *ecce hoc 'behold this'), and the subordinating conjunction que ('that' < Latin quid/quod). Literally meaning 'by this [fact] that', it gradually displaced Old French car and por ce que in causal subordinate clauses.

history.form: par ço que > par ce que
history.meaning: by reason of the fact that, because

parce que.notes: Always written as two words ('parce que', eliding to 'parce qu'il / qu'elle' before a vowel), though in rapid casual speech it routinely compresses to /paskə/! Contrast with three-word 'par ce que' ('by what', e.g., 'touché par ce que tu as dit').

rootFamily.gloss: whereas, from the moment that ('dès lors que' / 'puisque')

pardon.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (pardon, 11th c.) from pardoner / pardonner ('to forgive, remit a debt or offense', from Late/Medieval Latin perdonare 'to give wholeheartedly, remit', from per- 'thoroughly' + donare 'to give').

history.meaning: forgiveness of an offense; polite apology ('excuse me, pardon')

cognates.meaning: to pardon (borrowed from Old French pardoner)

pardonner.etymology: Inherited from Old French pardoner ('to remit a debt or penalty, grant mercy, forgive'), from Early Medieval and Vulgar Latin perdonare ('to give wholeheartedly, remit unconditionally'), composed of the intensive prefix per- ('thoroughly, completely', becoming par- in French) + Classical Latin donare ('to give, bestow', from donum 'gift'). Notice the striking Germanic calque in English forgive (for- + give) and German vergeben!

history.meaning: to give wholeheartedly, remit a debt or offense

pardonner.notes: Watch the syntax carefully: you forgive SOMETHING TO SOMEONE — 'pardonner quelque chose à quelqu'un' ('Je lui pardonne son retard'), though 'pardonner quelqu'un' occurs informally; 'Ça ne pardonne pas' means 'There's no room for error / It's unforgiving'.

pareil.etymology: Inherited from Old French pareil ('equal in rank, matching, alike'), descending regularly from Vulgar Latin *pariculus ('matching, equal'), an expressive diminutive formation built on Classical Latin par, paris ('equal, like, matching; a pair'). The Vulgar Latin cluster -cl- regularly palatalized into the French palatal lateral spelled -il (/j/).
pareil.notes: Essential spoken responses: 'C'est pareil' ('It's the same thing'), 'Pareil pour moi !' ('Same for me!'), and before a noun 'un scandale pareil' ('such a scandal'). Feminine doubles the 'l': 'pareille'.

parent.etymology: Inherited from Old French parent ('father or mother; blood relative, kinsman'), from Classical Latin parens, parentem ('father or mother, progenitor; in plural, ancestors and kin'), originally the substantive aorist/present active participle of parere ('to bring forth, give birth to, produce', from PIE *perh₃- 'to produce, procure'). Unlike English, French preserved both the narrow Classical sense ('father/mother') and the broader Late Latin sense ('relative, kin').

history.meaning: to give birth to > father or mother; ancestor, kinsman

parent.notes: Classic partial false friend: in the plural 'mes parents' almost always means 'my parents (mom and dad)', whereas 'un parent éloigné' or 'des parents de province' means 'a distant relative / relatives'! Also note the idiom 'le parent pauvre' ('the neglected stepchild / underfunded branch').

rootFamily.gloss: related by blood or style ('apparenté à')

parental.etymology: Learned borrowing (sporadically attested in 16th-century humanist French, then strongly revived in the mid-20th century under the reinforcement of English sociological and legal usage parental) from Late and Classical Latin parentalis ('pertaining to parents or deceased ancestors', as in Parentalia, the Roman festival honoring dead kin), derived from parens, parentis ('parent').

history.meaning: pertaining to parents or ancestral rites
pertaining to parents and parental authority/care

parental.notes: Masculine plural is 'parentaux' ('les congés parentaux', 'les droits parentaux'), feminine plural 'parentales' ('l'autorité parentale', 'les obligations parentales'). Unlike 'parent', 'parental' strictly means 'of parents', never 'of extended relatives'.

parfait.etymology: Inherited/adapted in Old French (parfit / parfait, 11th–12th c.) from Classical Latin perfectus ('completed, fully accomplished, flawless'), past participle of perficere ('to carry through to the end, complete', from per- 'thoroughly' + facere 'to make, do').

cognates.meaning: perfectly (re-Latinized from Middle English parfitly < Old French)

parfaitement.etymology: Formed in Old French (parfitement, 12th century, later reshaped to parfaitement) from the feminine form parfaite of parfait ('completed, accomplished, faultless', from Classical Latin perfectus, past participle of perficere 'to carry through to the end, accomplish', from intensive per- 'thoroughly' + facere 'to make, do') + the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind').

history.meaning: to carry through to completion > finished, complete, flawless

morphemes.meaning: thoroughly, to the end (< Latin per-)

parfaitement.notes: Used standalone ('Parfaitement !') in lively French dialogue, it serves as an emphatic, sometimes indignant or triumphant 'Absolutely! / Quite so! / Spot on!'.

parfois.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French of the Old French phrase par feiz / par fois ('by times, at times'), from par ('by', < Latin per) + fois ('time, occasion', < Classical Latin vicem 'turn, succession').

parfum.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 16th century from parfumer ('to scent by burning aromatic smoke').

history.meaning: aromatic smoke -> pleasant scent, perfume, culinary flavor

parfumer.etymology: Borrowed in the early 16th century from Old Occitan perfumar or Italian perfumare ('to fill with aromatic smoke, fumigate with incense or herbs'), compound of per- ('through and through') + fumare ('to smoke', from Latin fumus 'smoke').

history.meaning: to scent thoroughly with fragrant smoke

parisien.etymology: Formed in Old and Middle French from Paris + the relational/demonymic suffix -ien (< Latin -ianus). The city name Paris evolved from Late Roman civitas Parisiorum ('city of the Parisii', replacing earlier Gallo-Roman Lutetia), named after the Celtic Gaulish tribe Parisii who inhabited the Seine islands and basin in antiquity (often linked to a Celtic root *kʷar-io- 'cauldron' or *par- 'commanders/spearmen', though the ultimate Gaulish etymon remains debated).

history.meaning: chief settlement of the Gaulish Parisii tribe on the Seine
of or belonging to the city of Paris

morphemes.meaning: Paris (city on the Seine < Gaulish Parisii)

parisien.notes: Capitalized as a noun referring to a resident ('un Parisien / une Parisienne'), lowercase as an adjective ('le milieu parisien' = the insular Parisian cultural/media elite — a recurring satire target in *Dix pour cent*, alongside 'le parisianisme').

rootFamily.gloss: Greater Paris metropolitan area ('la région parisienne')
Parisian woman; baguette-style loaf or font/newspaper title

cognates.meaning: parking lot (borrowed or calqued as parcheggio)
the act of parking vehicles (source of the French noun)

parking.etymology: Early 20th-century borrowing (attested c. 1920 with the rise of automobile traffic) from English parking, the gerund/verbal noun of to park ('to enclose in a park; later, to station vehicles in an enclosure'), which English had originally borrowed from Old French parc! This makes parking a classic Franco-English lexical boomerang ('aller-retour'), reanalyzed in French from an action noun into a concrete count noun ('a parking lot / garage').

history.meaning: enclosure (OF) > to station vehicles > act/area of parking (Eng.)
car park, parking lot or underground garage

morphemes.meaning: enclose, station a vehicle (< English park < Old French parc)
English -ing suffix, often reinterpreted as a place/activity noun in French

parking.notes: Classic pseudo-Anglicism trap: in France, 'un parking' means 'a parking lot / parking garage' (NOT the abstract act of parking, which is 'le stationnement'). In Quebec French, 'un stationnement' is strongly preferred over 'un parking'.

rootFamily.gloss: to park / pen in (Swiss/Belgian/regional 'parquer sa voiture'; France prefers 'se garer')

parler.etymology: Parler continues Christian Latin parabolare, to speak, related to parabola, speech. That word was borrowed from Greek parabolê, comparison or parable. The French verb is recorded from the tenth century.

cognates.meaning: all borrowed from Old French parler derivatives

parler.notes: Used with no preposition before language names in everyday speech (parler français, parler italien), and as a masculine noun le parler ('local speech variety').

parmi.etymology: Univerbated in Old French from the prepositional phrase par mi ('through the middle of'), combining par (< Classical Latin per, 'through, across') and mi (< Classical Latin medium, neuter substantive of medius, 'middle'). Originally governing singular nouns in the spatial sense 'right through the middle of', it shifted in Middle French to plural and collective complements meaning 'among, amid'.

history.meaning: through the middle of, right across

parmi.notes: Unlike entre ('between', often for two distinct entities or reciprocal relations), parmi requires a plural or collective noun (e.g., parmi les acteurs, parmi la foule) and cannot be followed by stressed disjunctive pronouns like *parmi eux without care—though parmi eux/elles is standard, *parmi nous autres is colloquial.

parole.etymology: Inherited from Old French parole ('spoken word, speech, pledged word'), from Late/Ecclesiastical Latin parabola ('comparison, proverb, parable in the Gospels; hence speech, word'), borrowed from Ancient Greek parabole ('juxtaposition, comparison, parable'), which displaced Classical verbum in Western and Central Romance.

history.meaning: spoken word, faculty of speech, word of honor, song lyric
