part.etymology: Inherited from Old French part ('portion, share, side, direction'), from Classical Latin partem (nominative pars, 'part, portion, share, side, party').

history.meaning: share, portion, side (quelque part, de la part de)

partager.etymology: Derived in the 15th–16th century from partage ('division into shares', formed in Old French from partir 'to divide into parts' + suffix -age).

history.meaning: to divide into shares, share with others

partant.etymology: Lexicalized in French from the present participle of partir ('to set out, depart'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *partīre (Classical Latin partīrī, 'to divide, share out', from pars, partis, 'part'). From the Old French reflexive soi partir ('to separate oneself, leave'), the participial adjective developed the 20th-century colloquial sense 'ready to set off', hence 'game, willing, on board' for a project.

history.meaning: to divide; to separate oneself, set out
departing; ready to join in, willing

partant.notes: Very common in everyday and agency French in the idiom être partant(e) pour ('to be up for / on board with', e.g., Je suis partante pour le tournage); in formal written French, invariable partant also survives as an adverb meaning 'consequently, therefore'.

partenaire.etymology: Borrowed in the late 18th century (first in card games, then dance, business, and theater) from English partner, with French phonetic and orthographic adaptation modeled on words in -aire. Remarkably, this is a re-borrowing (aller-retour): English partner altered Middle English parcener, itself borrowed from Anglo-Norman and Old French parçonier ('joint heir, sharer'), from parçon ('share, portion') < Latin partītiōnem.
partenaire.notes: Epicene noun (un/une partenaire): in French cinema and theater, partenaire (or partenaire de jeu) specifically denotes a co-star or scene partner (donner la réplique à son partenaire), as well as a romantic partner in modern usage.

participation.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old French (12th century, initially theological and legal) from Late Latin participātiōnem (nominative participātiō), noun of action from Classical Latin participāre ('to share in, partake of'), a compound of pars, partis ('part, share') and capere ('to take, seize') via particeps ('sharing, partaking'). In film and television billing, it specialized to denote a guest or special appearance.
participation.notes: In French screen credits and talent contracts, avec la participation (exceptionnelle) de signals a prestigious cameo or special guest appearance by an established star, a staple negotiation point in Dix pour cent.

participer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin participare ('to share in, partake of, participate'), derived from particeps ('taking a share, partner'), a compound of pars, partis ('part, share') and the root of capere ('to take'). Etymologically, to participate is literally 'to take one's part or share' in a collective endeavor.

history.meaning: taking a share -> to share in

participer.notes: Remember the construction: where English says 'participate **in** a festival', French always uses **à** (**participer à un festival, participer au concours**).

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: participer

particulier.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th century) from Late Latin particulāris ('concerning a small part, specific, individual'), derived from Classical Latin particula ('small part, particle, bit'), diminutive of pars, partis ('part, share'), with French adaptation of the learned suffix -āris to -ier. Alongside 'private, individual', it developed the nuanced evaluative sense 'peculiar, unusual, acquired-taste'.

history.meaning: specific to an individual, private, distinct

particulier.notes: Watch the polite understatement: calling a script, director, or performance très particulier in French often means 'weird, eccentric, hard to sell' rather than merely 'specific'; as a noun, un particulier means a private individual (as opposed to a company).

particulièrement.etymology: Formed in Middle French (late 14th century) from the feminine inflection particulière of the adjective particulier ('specific, individual, special', < Late Latin particulāris, from Classical Latin particula, diminutive of pars, 'part') plus the adverbial suffix -ment (< Classical Latin mente, ablative singular of mēns, 'mind, manner, intent'). It shifted from 'individually, in detail' to an intensifier meaning 'especially'.

history.meaning: in an individual or specific manner (analytic source components)

particulièrement.notes: Retains the feminine e + grave accent spelling (particulièrement) from particulière, though in brisk Parisian speech the internal schwa is frequently dropped ([paʁtikyljɛʁmɑ̃]).

cognates.meaning: social gathering; political or legal party

partie.etymology: Substantivized in Old French (12th century) from the feminine past participle partie of partir ('to divide, share out', < Vulgar Latin *partīre, Classical Latin partīrī, from pars, partis, 'part, portion'). Literally 'that which has been divided off', it came to denote a portion of a whole, a litigant side in law, a match or round of play, and a social outing.

history.meaning: share, portion, divided fraction; opposing side
part of a whole, game, legal party

partie.notes: False friend & gender trap: une partie (f.) means 'part of a whole', 'a game/match', or 'a contracting party' (faire partie de = 'to belong to / be part of'), whereas un parti (m.) means a 'political party', 'choice/course' (prendre parti), or 'marriage catch', and 'a party' (celebration) is une fête or une soirée!

partir.etymology: Inherited from Old French partir ('to divide into parts, separate; reflexively se partir de, to separate oneself from a place, set out, leave'), from Vulgar Latin *partire, active reshaping of Classical Latin partiri ('to divide, share', derived from pars, partis 'part').

history.meaning: to divide -> to separate oneself, set out, leave, depart

partition.etymology: From Latin partitio ('division into parts', from partiri 'to divide'). In seventeenth-century music (matching Italian partitura), une partition meant dividing an ensemble piece onto aligned staves on one page so every voice or hand could be read together—hence 'musical score / sheet music'.

history.meaning: musical score arranged in aligned staves

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: partition (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: partition

partout.etymology: Univerbation of the Old French phrase par tot / par tout ('throughout all, in every place'), from par ('through, throughout', < Latin per) + tout ('all, everything', < Vulgar Latin *tottum).

pas.etymology: The negative pas began as the noun for a step, from Latin passus. It first strengthened negatives with movement verbs by referring to even a tiny distance, then became a general spoken negative marker.

history.meaning: step, pace (from pandere 'to stretch the legs')
step -> minimal-distance emphatic negator ('not [a] step' with motion verbs)

pas.notes: Classic textbook example of Jespersen's Cycle: je ne marche pas originally meant literally 'I don't walk a single step', before pas generalized to negate every verb in French!

passage.etymology: Formed in Old French (passage, 11th–12th c.) from passer ('to pass, cross over') + nominal suffix -age.

history.meaning: act or place of passing, crossing, corridor, excerpt of a text

passager.etymology: Derived in Old French (passagier, 12th–14th centuries) from passage ('act or place of passing across', from passer, 'to step, pass', < Vulgar Latin *passāre, from Classical Latin passus, 'step, pace') plus the relational and agentive suffix -ier / -er (< Latin -ārius). As a noun it denoted a traveler paying passage; as an adjective (originally of migratory birds like faucon passager) it came to mean 'transient, fleeting, short-lived'.

history.meaning: traveler crossing a passage; migratory, transient

passager.notes: Functions as both noun (un passager, 'a passenger') and adjective (passager, f. passagère, 'fleeting, temporary', as in une crise passagère or un succès passager); note that English passenger gained an intrusive -n- (like messenger from messager).

passant.etymology: Present participle of passer ('to pass by, walk along'), used as a noun since Old/Middle French for a passerby on the street (or a belt loop through which a strap passes) and as an adjective ('busy with foot traffic', as in une rue passante).

history.meaning: passerby, belt loop (noun); busy with pedestrians (adj.)

passer.etymology: Passer comes from a reconstructed later Latin *passare, derived from passus, step. The Académie records the French verb from the eleventh century.

history.meaning: step -> to step across, pass by
to pass, go by; spend (time); take (an exam)

rootFamily.gloss: to happen, take place (qu'est-ce qui se passe?)

passer.notes: Famous exam false friend: passer un examen means 'to SIT / TAKE an exam' (not necessarily pass it!—'to pass an exam' is réussir un examen). Also switches auxiliary: je suis passé chez toi vs. j'ai passé une bonne soirée.

passerelle.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century (via Provençal passerello or directly from Italian passerella, 'narrow footbridge, gangplank'), ultimately derived from Vulgar Latin *passāre ('to step across, pass', from Classical Latin passus, 'step, pace', influenced in Italian by passera, 'sparrow', via the image of stepping stones across a stream). In French it broadened from maritime gangways and pedestrian bridges to institutional or career 'bridges'.

history.meaning: footbridge, overhead studio walkway, bridging pathway

passerelle.notes: Beyond a physical footbridge, boarding bridge, or film-studio lighting catwalk, faire passerelle / une passerelle is widely used figuratively in French media and education for a crossover pathway between fields (e.g., from theater or stand-up to cinema).

passion.etymology: Borrowed in early Old French (10th century, Passion de Clermont) from Christian Late Latin passiōnem (nominative passiō, 'suffering, martyrdom, disturbance of the soul', calquing Ancient Greek páthos), formed from passus, past participle of Classical Latin patī ('to suffer, endure, undergo'). From Christ's Passion and philosophical 'affection undergone passively by the soul', it shifted in courtly and Classical French to overpowering romantic desire or devotion.

history.meaning: physical suffering, martyrdom; emotion undergone by the soul
Christ's suffering; intense emotion, ardent love affair

passion.notes: In French relationship and cinema talk, une grande passion or vivre une passion often specifically means an all-consuming love affair, while passionner ('to fascinate') yields passionnant ('thrilling, engrossing'—much more common than *intéressant for high praise).

passionnément.etymology: Formed in Middle French (15th century) from passionné ('impassioned, filled with ardent emotion', past participle of passionner, itself from passion < Late Latin passiōnem, 'suffering, strong emotion', from Classical Latin patī, 'to suffer, undergo') plus the adverbial suffix -ment (< Latin mente). Notably, the acute accent on -é- reflects an older long vowel assimilation where the silent feminine -e of passionnée merged phonetically before -ment.

history.meaning: suffering, strong emotion of the soul

passionnément.notes: Culturally iconic as the third petal in the French daisy-plucking game effeuiller la marguerite: Il/Elle m'aime un peu, beaucoup, passionnément, à la folie, pas du tout—and notice the irregular spelling -ément (dropping the feminine -e of passionnée).

passé.etymology: Substantivized in Old French (12th century, le passé) from the masculine singular past participle passé of passer ('to step across, go by, elapse'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *passāre, a denominative verb built on Classical Latin passus ('step, pace', originally from pandere, 'to spread, stretch out the legs'). Literally 'that which has gone by', it came to denote bygone time and a person's prior life or record.
passé.notes: Beware the English loanword trap: in English, passé means 'outdated, unfashionable', whereas in French that sense requires démodé or ringard (or passé de mode); French le passé (m.) means 'the past' or someone's 'track record / backstory' (avoir un lourd passé).

pastille.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (originally via Spanish pastilla for a scented aromatic pellet, reinforcing an earlier medical borrowing) from Classical Latin pastillus ('little loaf, roll, aromatic lozenge'), diminutive of pānis ('bread, loaf') or closely linked to pasta ('dough, paste' < Ancient Greek pástē, 'barley porridge'). From perfumed and medicinal tablets, it generalized to throat lozenges, mints, and small round badges or video inserts.

history.meaning: small roll of bread, aromatic lozenge
small cake of dough, scented or medicinal tablet
lozenge, throat drop, mint; small round sticker or short TV clip

pastille.notes: In everyday French une pastille is a mint or throat lozenge (pastille Vichy, pastille pour la gorge), while in French television and digital media jargon une pastille (humour) also refers to a short, punchy 1–3 minute comedy sketch or video segment!

pastis.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century (commercialized in Marseille in the 1930s by Paul Ricard after the ban on absinthe) from Provençal (Occitan) pastis ('mash, mixture, pie, muddle'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *pasticium ('dough preparation, pie'), a derivative of Late Latin pasta ('dough, paste', from Ancient Greek pástē). The aperitif took its name from being a 'blend' or 'concoction' of star anise, licorice root, sugar, and Provençal herbs.

history.meaning: pie, mash, blended mixture; tricky mess

pastis.notes: Always pronounce the final -s ([pastis])! Because of its Provençal sense 'mixture, muddle', être dans un beau pastis also survives in colloquial southern-flavored French for 'to be in a fine mess / pickle'.

rootFamily.gloss: pâté, meat pie (native northern French doublet)

patate.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (originally batate, then patate) via Spanish patata, a Renaissance Spanish blend of Taíno (Arawakan) batata ('sweet potato', Ipomoea batatas) and Quechua papa ('Andean white potato', Solanum tuberosum). In standard metropolitan French, pomme de terre ('earth apple') became the formal term for the white potato while patate designated the sweet potato (patate douce) and colloquial 'spud'.

history.meaning: edible tuber, sweet potato and later white potato
sweet potato; (colloquial) white potato, head, punch

patate.notes: Register & idiom goldmine: pomme de terre is neutral, whereas patate is informal (though standard in Canadian French) and powers vivid expressions like avoir la patate ('to feel great / full of energy'), en avoir gros sur la patate ('to feel heavy-hearted / resentful'), and refiler la patate chaude ('to pass the buck').

paternité.etymology: Learned borrowing (attested in Old and Middle French from Christian Latin) from Late Latin paternitātem (nominative paternitās, 'fatherhood, fatherly care'), derived from Classical Latin paternus ('of a father, paternal'), itself from pater, patris ('father', from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr). Alongside biological and legal fatherhood, Classical and Modern French extended it to intellectual or artistic authorship of a work or idea.

history.meaning: of or belonging to a father, fatherly
biological/legal fatherhood; authorship of a creative work

paternité.notes: In both family subplots and French copyright law (droit moral), paternité carries dual weight: congé de paternité ('paternity leave') vs. revendiquer la paternité d'un scénario / d'un film ('to claim authorship/credit for a script or film').

pathétique.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (16th century, Rabelais) via Late Latin pathēticus from Ancient Greek pathētikós ('capable of feeling, sensitive, stirring deep emotion or pathos'), derived from páthos ('experience, suffering, deep emotion', from páskhein, 'to suffer, undergo'). For centuries in French aesthetics and rhetoric, pathétique meant 'deeply moving, tragic, poignant' (as in Beethoven's Sonate Pathétique) before acquiring its modern colloquial pejorative sense under late 20th-century English influence.

history.meaning: susceptible to emotion, stirring pity or strong feeling
deeply moving, poignant; (recent colloquial) pitiful, lame

pathétique.notes: Crucial register split: in literature, theater criticism, and classical music, le pathétique / une scène pathétique is high praise meaning 'poignant, deeply moving', whereas in contemporary dialogue (like Dix pour cent: T'es pathétique !) it mirrors the English pejorative 'pitiful, sad, lame'.

patiemment.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French (paciement -> patiemment) from the adjective patient ('patient, enduring') + adverbial suffix -ment (with assimilation of -nt-m- to -mm-).

patience.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French pacience) from Classical Latin patientia ('quality of bearing or suffering calmly, endurance, forbearance'), derived from pati, patiens ('to suffer, endure, bear').

cognates.meaning: enduring calmly (adj.); person under medical care (n.)

patient.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (12th century as adjective 'enduring hardship calmly', 14th century in Ambroise Paré's surgical tradition as noun 'one undergoing medical treatment') from Classical Latin patientem (nominative patiēns), present participle of the deponent verb patī ('to suffer, endure, bear, undergo'). Both the moral virtue ('forbearing') and the clinical noun ('sufferer under a physician's action') stem directly from 'one who undergoes'.

history.meaning: bearing, enduring, capable of suffering hardship
enduring trials without complaint; opposite of philosophical agent
person receiving medical care; patient, calm (adj.)

patient.notes: Notice the hidden etymological kinship with passion: both come from Latin patī ('to suffer/undergo', present stem pati-, past participial stem pass-); pronounce the second t as [s] ([pasjɑ̃], f. patiente [pasjɑ̃t]), never [t]!

patienter.etymology: Formed inside Middle French (late 16th century, Montaigne) as a first-conjugation deadjectival verb from patient ('enduring calmly, forbearing', < Classical Latin patientem, present participle of patī, 'to suffer, bear, endure') plus the verbal infinitive suffix -er. Originally meaning 'to exercise fortitude under pain', it specialized in modern polite usage into 'to wait a little while, hold the line'.

history.meaning: to bear suffering with patience, take heart
to wait calmly, hold on briefly

patienter.notes: Essential office, reception, and phone French (heard constantly from agency assistants in Dix pour cent): Veuillez patienter un instant ('Please hold / wait a moment') or faire patienter quelqu'un ('to keep someone waiting politely').

patrimoine.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin patrimonium ('inheritance passed down from a father', from pater, patris 'father'). Expanded in modern French from family estate to shared cultural and architectural heritage (le patrimoine historique).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: patrimoine (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: patrimoine

patron.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th–13th century from Classical Latin patronus ('protector of clients or freedmen, defender, advocate', derived from pater 'father'); evolved in Medieval and Modern French to mean 'patron saint', 'master of a ship or workshop, boss', and 'dressmaker's paper pattern (model)'.

history.meaning: patron saint; employer, boss, shop owner; paper sewing pattern

cognates.meaning: mistress, female owner or boss; patron saint

patronne.etymology: Feminine form of patron, borrowed in Old French (12th century, first as 'patron saint, protector, model', later 'shipmaster' via Occitan/Mediterranean usage, and in the 19th century 'employer, head of a firm or café') from Classical Latin patrōnus ('protector of clients, defender, advocate, former master of a freedman'), derived from pater, patris ('father'). Patronne reflects regular French feminine gemination (-on > -onne).

history.meaning: protector, defender, former master/mistress of freedpersons
female boss, company head, bistro owner

patronne.notes: Classic false friend with English patron: un patron / une patronne means 'boss, CEO, owner' (never 'customer', which is un client / une cliente!), while un patron (m. only) also means a sewing 'pattern' or template.

patte.etymology: Attested in Old French (12th century, pate, 'animal paw, foot'), widely traced by Romance philologists (Wartburg, FEW; CNRTL) to a pre-Latin or Gallo-Romance expressive onomatopoeic root *patt- imitating the flat slap or heavy tread of a foot striking the ground (compare *paut- in Occitan pauta and German Pfote). From animal paws and bird feet, it acquired rich metaphorical extensions for human hands, handwriting, signature style, and clothing flaps.

history.meaning: flat slap or tread of a foot (expressive root)
paw or foot of a quadruped or bird
animal paw; (colloquial) hand, distinctive artistic touch

patte.notes: Beyond animal paws (à quatre pattes, 'on all fours') and playfully gruff Bas les pattes ! ('Hands off!'), la patte d'un réalisateur is high-register cinema praise for a director's unmistakable stylistic signature, while graisser la patte means 'to grease someone's palm / bribe'.

rootFamily.gloss: to splash/paddle in mud or water

paume.etymology: Inherited from Old French paume, from Classical Latin palma ('palm of the hand; palm tree frond whose spread leaves resemble an open hand'), with regular vocalization of Latin -l- before -m-.

history.meaning: palm of the hand; palm branch

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French paume / Latin palma

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: paume (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: paume

paume.notes: Striking a ball with the bare **paume** gave medieval France **le jeu de paume** ('real/court tennis'), the direct ancestor of modern tennis.

pause.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th century, initially for a musical rest or rhetorical cadence, then a cessation of activity) from Classical Latin pausa ('halt, cessation, stop, end'), itself an early borrowing from Ancient Greek paûsis ('a stopping, ceasing, rest'), verbal noun from paúō ('I stop, bring to an end, check'). It generalized in modern French to any work or shooting break.

history.meaning: halt, pause in speech or action
musical/poetic rest; temporary break in work

pause.notes: Spelling/homophone alert: do not confuse une pause ([poz], 'a break', as in faire une pause, pause-café, pause déjeuner) with une pose ([poz], 'striking a pose' for photographers or 'installation' of equipment, from poser)!

rootFamily.gloss: to pause briefly, mark a pause
cessation of menstrual cycles (Greek compound cognate)
to place, rest (contaminated in Late Latin pausāre)

pauvre.etymology: Inherited from Old French povre ('poor, destitute, unfortunate'), from Vulgar Latin *pauperus, 1st/2nd-declension remodeling of Classical Latin pauper ('producing little, poor, of small means', compound of paucus 'few, little' + parere 'to produce, bring forth').

pavé.etymology: Substantivized past participle of paver ('to pave with stones or tiles'), inherited from Old French paver ('to beat down earth or lay stones flat'), from Vulgar Latin *pavare, altered from Classical Latin pavire ('to beat, ram, tread down earth or pavement').

history.meaning: to lay a beaten or stone floor
cobblestone, paved street; thick heavy book or steak

payer.etymology: Inherited from Old French paier ('to appease, satisfy a creditor, pay'), from Classical Latin pacare ('to make peaceful, pacify, appease', derived from pax, pacis 'peace'); in Vulgar Latin, 'to pacify an angry creditor' came to mean 'to pay what is owed'.

history.meaning: to pacify, appease -> to satisfy a creditor

pays.etymology: Inherited through Old French païs (two syllables: [pa.is], 10th–11th centuries) from Late Latin pāgēnsis (sc. ager or locus, 'rural district, territory of a canton'), relational adjective of Classical Latin pāgus ('country district, rural community, boundary marker fixed in the earth', related to pangere, 'to fasten, fix'). In Modern French the letter y represents two i-elements: pays splits phonetically as paï-is > [pe.i], preserving two syllables.

history.meaning: rural district, canton / pertaining to a rural district
country, sovereign nation; local home region

pays.notes: Pronunciation trap: pays is two syllables—[pe.i] (like pé-i), never *[pɛ]! That same split-y explains paysan ([pe.i.zɑ̃]) and paysage ([pe.i.zaʒ]); also note mal du pays ('homesickness') and être dépaysé ('to feel refreshed/out of one's usual element abroad').

rootFamily.gloss: to take someone out of their familiar surroundings

paysage.etymology: Coined in 16th-century French (1549, Robert Estienne, originally as an art-historical calque on Dutch landschap to describe Flemish paintings depicting an expanse of countryside) from pays ('country, rural region', < Late Latin pāgēnsis, from Classical Latin pāgus) plus the collective/spatial suffix -age (< Latin -āticum). From painted views, it broadened to natural scenery and metaphorical institutional 'landscapes'.

history.meaning: belonging to a rural district or canton
painting representing an expanse of countryside
natural view, scenery; overall panorama of a sector

paysage.notes: Pronounced in three syllables ([pe.i.zaʒ]); in French film and television industry talk, le PAF stands for le Paysage Audiovisuel Français ('the French broadcasting landscape'), and faire partie du paysage means 'to be a familiar fixture'.

paysan.etymology: Inherited through Old French païsant / païsan (12th century, 'inhabitant of the local region, countryman, tiller of the soil') from Gallo-Romance *pāgēnsānus, formed from Late Latin pāgēnsis ('of a rural canton', from Classical Latin pāgus, 'country district, village') plus the suffix -ānus. Anglo-Norman païsant was borrowed into Middle English as peasant, while Classical Latin pāgānus ('villager; non-Christian') separately yielded French païen ('pagan').

history.meaning: inhabitant of a rural district or canton
smallholder farmer, person of the countryside

paysan.notes: Pronounced [pe.i.zɑ̃] (feminine paysanne [pe.i.zan]); while agriculteur is the formal occupational term ('farmer'), paysan has been proudly reclaimed in France for artisanal, small-scale farming (agriculture paysanne, pain paysan), though used as an insult by snobs it means 'bumpkin'.

cognates.meaning: animal hide, fur; thin skin (via Anglo-Norman)

peau.etymology: Inherited through Old French pel, oblique plural pels > peaus > peau (with regular vocalization of preconsonantal -l to -u before plural -s, subsequently leveled across the paradigm) from Classical Latin pellem (nominative pellis, 'animal hide, pelt, human skin'), from Proto-Indo-European *pel- ('to cover, wrap; skin, hide', cognate with English fell and film). It largely displaced Latin cutis in French for human skin.

history.meaning: human or animal skin, fruit peel

peau.notes: Essential actor's idiom: entrer / se glisser dans la peau d'un personnage ('to get under the skin of / inhabit a character') and être bien dans sa peau ('to feel comfortable in one's own skin'), whereas avoir la peau de quelqu'un means 'to bring someone down / finish them off'.

rootFamily.gloss: to peel, shed skin; fur coat (pelisse)
furrier's pelt trade (preserving Old French stem pel-)

peindre.etymology: Inherited from Old French peindre ('to paint, depict in colors'), from Classical Latin pingere ('to embroider, tattoo, paint, adorn with color', from PIE *peyg- 'to mark, cut, paint').

peine.etymology: Inherited through early Old French peine (10th century, 'punishment, torment, grief, strenuous effort') from Classical Latin poena ('compensation, retribution, punishment, penalty; hardship'), itself an early borrowing from Ancient Greek poinḗ (Doric poinā, 'blood-money, fine, penalty, vengeance', from PIE *kʷoynéh₂). Semantic bleaching extended it from judicial penalty (peine de prison) and sorrow (faire de la peine) to 'effort, bother' and 'barely' (à peine).

history.meaning: legal sentence; emotional grief; effort or trouble

peine.notes: Polysemy powerhouse: Ce n'est pas la peine ('Don't bother / No need'), Ça vaut la peine ('It's worth the trouble'), faire de la peine à quelqu'un ('to hurt someone's feelings / make them sad'), à peine ('barely, hardly'), and peine de cœur ('heartache')—but physical 'pain' is douleur, not peine!

rootFamily.gloss: to grieve, hurt someone's feelings; to struggle laboriously
penal, criminal (learned doublet from Latin poenālis)

peinture.etymology: Inherited from Old French peinture ('art or work of painting, pigment'), from Vulgar Latin *pinctura, altered (after the nasalized verb stem ping-) from Classical Latin pictura ('painting, picture', from pingere, pictum 'to paint').

cognates.meaning: long-napped velvety fabric; luxurious (borrowed from French)
lint, fuzz, nap; stuffed toy (peluche from French)
plush fabric, stuffed toy (borrowed from French)

peluche.etymology: Attested in 16th-century French (pluche, peluche, first meaning 'tuft of hair, shaggy nap, lint', then 'shaggy velvet-like fabric'), either borrowed from Italian peluzzo / peluccia ('fine hair, fuzz, lint') or formed natively from Old French pelucher ('to pick off lint, fluff up'), ultimately from Vulgar Latin *pilūcāre ('to pluck hairs one by one'), a derivative of Classical Latin pilus ('hair'). In the 20th century, par métonymie from ours en peluche ('plush bear'), une peluche came to mean any cuddly stuffed animal.

history.meaning: hair / to pluck or pick hairs
tuft of fibers, shaggy velvet-like fabric
plush fabric; stuffed toy animal; sweater pilling

peluche.notes: Remarkable reverse loan: English plush (fabric and 'luxurious') was borrowed in the late 16th century from the syncopated French variant pluche! In modern French, une peluche (f.) means both a cuddly stuffed toy and a little lint ball/pill on a sweater (pelucher = 'to pill').

rootFamily.gloss: to shed lint, pill (of knitwear); to scrutinize (éplucher)
animal hair, coat (native evolution of Latin pilus)

pencher.etymology: Inherited from Old French penchier ('to tilt, incline, slope downward'), from Vulgar Latin *pendicare ('to hang down, incline'), frequentative of Classical Latin pendere ('to hang, be suspended').

history.meaning: to hang or slope toward one side

pendaison.etymology: Formed in Old French (pendison, pendaison, 12th–13th centuries, 'act of hanging') from the stem of pendre ('to hang, suspend', < Classical Latin pendere, 'to cause to hang, weigh', merged in Vulgar Latin with pendēre, 'to hang down') plus the action-noun suffix -aison (inherited regularly from Classical Latin -ātiōnem, the popular counterpart of learned -ation). By itself pendaison means execution or suicide by hanging, whereas in pendaison de crémaillère it preserves the literal medieval sense 'hanging up the hearth pot-hook'.

history.meaning: to suspend, weigh / to hang down
act of hanging or suspending (especially on gallows)

pendaison.notes: Handle with care! Alone, une pendaison means 'a hanging' (gallows/suicide); for a housewarming party you must include the pot-hook—une pendaison de crémaillère (or the verb phrase pendre la crémaillère), recalling the medieval tradition of hanging the notched iron cauldron hook over the fireplace before serving the first meal to helpers in a new home.

pendant.etymology: Originated in 13th–14th-century legal French as the present participle of pendre ('to hang, be suspended') in absolute constructions modeled on Scholastic Latin pendente lite / pendente processu ('while the lawsuit is hanging/pending, during the trial'), whence the general preposition pendant ('during').

history.meaning: while the case is pending -> during (prep.); matching counterpart or earring (noun)

penser.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in Early Old French (penser, 10th–11th c.) from Classical Latin pensare ('to weigh carefully, ponder, consider'), frequentative of pendere, pensum ('to weigh in the scales', native doublet of panser).

history.meaning: to weigh in the mind, ponder

cognates.meaning: garden flower Viola tricolor ('remembrance', from French)

pensée.etymology: Substantivized in Old French (pensee, 12th century) from the feminine past participle of penser ('to think, reflect, intend'), inherited as a semi-learned verb from Classical Latin pēnsāre ('to weigh carefully, ponder, counterbalance, estimate'), frequentative of pendere ('to weigh, suspend'). Note the doublets: popular phonetic evolution of pēnsāre gave French peser ('to weigh physically'), while semi-learned preservation of -n- gave penser ('to weigh in the mind, think') and pensée ('thought').

history.meaning: act of thinking, reflection, mind, intention

pensée.notes: Contrast une pensée (f., 'a specific thought, philosophical thought, remembrance, or pansy flower'—which gave English pansy via Shakespeare's Ophelia: 'There's pansies, that's for thoughts') with le penser (archaic) or la réflexion; and marvel at the doublet penser ('to weigh mentally') vs. peser ('to weigh on scales')!

rootFamily.gloss: to weigh (popular inherited doublet of penser)

pente.etymology: Deverbal/participial noun formed in Old/Middle French from pendre ('to hang down, slope', from Latin pendere), modeled on feminine past participles in -te (like vente, rente, tente).

percer.etymology: Inherited from Old French percier ('to bore or thrust through'), from Vulgar Latin *pertusiare, a verb formed on Classical Latin pertusus, the past participle of pertundere ('to thrust or bore through'), itself composed of intensive per- ('through') and tundere ('to beat, strike'). In modern French, alongside physical piercing, it developed the intransitive career sense 'to break through to public recognition'.

history.meaning: to beat or bore right through

percer.notes: In cinema and talent-agency French (Dix pour cent), percer used intransitively ('il va finir par percer') specifically means to get one's big break and achieve stardom.

percée.etymology: Formed in French by substantivizing the feminine past participle of percer ('to pierce, bore through', from Old French percier < Vulgar Latin *pertusiare < Classical Latin pertusus). Originally designating a clearing cut through a forest or wall (16th–17th c.), it acquired the military sense of breaking through enemy lines before broadening in the 20th century to an artistic, commercial, or political breakthrough.

history.meaning: forest clearing; military or career breakthrough

percée.notes: Faire une percée ('to make a breakthrough') is standard both in box-office reporting and politics; remember it is feminine (une percée) because it derives from a feminine past participle.

perdre.etymology: Perdre descends from Latin perdere, originally to give wastefully and later to destroy or ruin. The Académie records the French verb from the ninth century.

history.meaning: to give away to ruin, destroy, lose

perdre.notes: Perdre son temps means 'to waste one's time', while manquer or rater (un train) is usual in France for missing a train.

perfectionniste.etymology: Coined in 19th-century French (first in philosophical and theological contexts, reinforced by English perfectionist) from perfection + suffix -iste, with regular doubling of the -n-. Perfection itself was borrowed from Classical Latin perfectionem ('completion, accomplishment'), a noun of action from perficere ('to carry through to the end, finish thoroughly', from per- + facere 'to make, do').

history.meaning: to bring to completion; thorough accomplishment
believer in moral perfection; exacting person

perfectionniste.notes: Watch the French double n (perfectionniste vs. English single n); on film sets, calling an auteur director perfectionniste is often a diplomatic euphemism for tyrannical over endless retakes.

perle.etymology: Attested in Old French perle (12th–13th c.), probably via Gallo-Romance or Italian perla from a Vulgar Latin diminutive *pernula ('little pearl-shell, pearl'), derived from Classical Latin perna ('ham, leg of pork', applied by visual analogy to a triangular sea mussel that produces pearls), with dissimilation/assimilation of -rn-l- to -rl-. Figuratively applied since the Middle Ages to a person of rare worth.

history.meaning: ham; a species of sea mussel

perle.notes: Calling an assistant or talent agent une perle (or une perle rare) means they are an absolute gem, whereas enfiler des perles idioms can mean wasting time on trifles, and une perle in school/media slang can also mean a hilarious blunder or howler!

rootFamily.gloss: to bead up (of sweat or dew)

permettre.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin permittere ('to let pass through, let go, give leave, allow'), compound of per- ('through') + mittere ('to let go, send').

history.meaning: to let pass through, grant leave

permis.etymology: Substantivized masculine past participle of permettre ('to allow, authorize'), borrowed and adapted in Middle French from Classical Latin permissus, past participle of permittere ('to let pass through, give up, grant leave'), formed from per- ('through') + mittere ('to send, let go'). As an independent noun ('written authorization, license'), un permis became established in administrative French in the 18th–19th centuries.

history.meaning: to let pass through, surrender, allow
official permit; driver's license (permis de conduire)

permis.notes: Used alone (avoir/passer son permis), le permis almost always means a driver's license (permis de conduire); note the silent final -s in masculine singular permis, pronounced /pɛʁ.mi/, contrasting with feminine permise (/pɛʁ.miz/).

permission.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin permissionem (nominative permissio, 'a letting go, leave, authorization'), derived from permittere, permissum ('to allow, permit').

persil.etymology: Inherited via Old French perresil / persil from Late Latin petrosilinum, borrowed from Ancient Greek petrosélinon ('rock celery', compound of pétra 'rock' + sélinon 'celery, parsley').

cognates.meaning: blended from Old English petersilie and Old French perresil

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: persil (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: persil

persil.notes: Greek **sélinon** in the second half of **persil** is also the exact source of French **céleri** ('celery')!

persister.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th–15th c.) from Classical Latin persistere ('to continue steadfastly, stand firm, abide'), a compound of intensive per- ('through to the end, thoroughly') + sistere ('to cause to stand, take a stand, stand still'), itself a reduplicated present stem derived from the Indo-European root of stare ('to stand').

history.meaning: to persevere firmly in an action or state

persister.notes: The legal-turned-everyday idiom je persiste et signe ('I stand by every word I said') is a favorite emphatic retort in French arguments and agency negotiations; persister takes the preposition dans or à.

rootFamily.gloss: to insist; to resist (sister verbs on -sister)

personnage.etymology: Derived in Old French (personage, 12th–13th c., first denoting an ecclesiastical benefice or dignity, then an important person and by the 15th c. a theatrical role) from persone ('person', from Classical Latin persona 'actor's mask, dramatic role, character', likely borrowed via Etruscan φersu) + suffix -age (< Latin -aticum). Remarkably, the derivative circled back to the theatrical 'character' sense of Latin persona.

history.meaning: actor's mask, dramatic character, legal person
theatrical or fictional character; colorful figure

personnage.notes: Essential cinema false friend: un personnage (always masculine, even when referring to a female role!) is a fictional character in a script or film, whereas English 'character' in the moral sense is caractère, and a real-life human being is une personne.

personne.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French persone) from Classical Latin persona ('actor's theatrical mask, dramatic character or role, legal individual', probably via Etruscan phersu 'masked figure'); through frequent use in negative sentences (ne... personne), also became the negative pronoun 'no one, nobody'.

history.meaning: theatrical mask -> dramatic role, human individual
person, individual (fem. noun); anyone / no one (pronoun)

personnel.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (personel, 12th c.) from Late Latin personalis ('pertaining to an individual person', used in Roman law for personal actions and by grammarians for personal pronouns), derived from Classical Latin persona ('actor's mask, role, individual') + relational suffix -alis. In the 19th century, the masculine adjective was substantivized as le personnel ('workforce, staff') in contrast to le matériel.

history.meaning: individual, done in one's own person

personnel.notes: One French word covers two English ones: as an adjective (personnel / personnelle) it means 'personal', while as a masculine singular collective noun (le personnel) it means 'staff, crew, personnel'.

personnellement.etymology: Formed in Old French (personelment, 13th c., later remodeled as personnellement once feminine adjectives in -el generalized distinct feminine -elle by analogy) from the feminine stem of personnel (< Late Latin personalis, from Classical Latin persona 'mask, individual') + adverbial suffix -ment (< Classical Latin mente, ablative singular of mens 'mind, disposition, manner').

history.meaning: in a personal frame of mind or manner

personnellement.notes: In casual spoken French (and office banter at ASK), personnellement is very frequently clipped to perso at the start of a sentence ('Perso, j'adore le scénario').

perspective.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Medieval Latin (ars) perspectiva ('science of optics'), substantivized feminine of Late Latin perspectivus ('optical, looking closely'), built on Classical Latin perspectus, past participle of perspicere ('to look through, inspect thoroughly', from per- 'through' + specere 'to look at'). Reinforced in the 16th century by Renaissance Italian prospettiva in the artistic sense of linear depth, which soon yielded the figurative sense 'future prospect, outlook'.

history.meaning: to look right through, examine closely
pictorial depth; future outlook or prospect

perspective.notes: Semi-false friend alert: while la perspective means visual/mental 'perspective', in plural or phrases like perspectives d'embauche or en perspective ('un beau rôle en perspective'), it best translates to English 'prospects' or 'on the horizon'.

pesant.etymology: Inherited from Old French pesant ('heavy, weighty, burdensome', 11th–12th c.), lexicalized from the present participle of peser ('to weigh'), reflecting Vulgar Latin *pesantem for Classical Latin pensantem, present participle of pensare ('to weigh carefully, counterbalance, ponder'), frequentative of pendere ('to hang scales, weigh'). Both physical weight and psychological oppressiveness have coexisted since Old French.
pesant.notes: While lourd is the everyday word for physically heavy luggage, pesant excels for atmosphere and mood (un silence pesant, une ambiance pesante — 'a heavy, oppressive silence'); note also the idiom valoir son pesant d'or ('to be worth one's weight in gold', where pesant is an archaic noun).

cognates.meaning: poise (borrowed from Old French stem peis-/pois-)

peser.etymology: Inherited from Old French peser ('to weigh, have weight, cause grief or burden'), from Vulgar Latin *pesare (with regular early loss of nasal n before s), continuing Classical Latin pensare ('to weigh carefully, estimate, ponder'), intensive-frequentative of pendere ('to suspend from balance scales, weigh, pay out'). This explains the learned French doublet penser ('to think, weigh in mind') alongside inherited peser ('to weigh').

history.meaning: to weigh out on scales; to ponder mentally
to weigh; to burden or grieve someone

peser.notes: Remember that peser and penser ('to think') are etymological twins from Latin pensare! Conjugation undergoes a stem-vowel alternation: nous pesons (/pə.zɔ̃/) vs. je pèse / ça me pèse (/pɛz/, 'it weighs heavily on me').

rootFamily.gloss: to think (learned doublet from Latin pensare)

pessimiste.etymology: Coined in late 18th- / early 19th-century French alongside pessimisme (deliberately modeled as the antonym of optimisme / optimiste, which Jesuits had coined in 1737 to critique Leibniz's 'best of all possible worlds' and Voltaire popularized in Candide), built on Classical Latin pessimus ('worst', suppletive superlative of malus 'bad') + suffix -iste.

history.meaning: philosophical view that everything tends for the worst; gloomy person

pessimiste.notes: Unlike English, which distinguishes noun 'pessimist' from adjective 'pessimistic', French pessimiste is invariant for gender in singular (un agent pessimiste, une actrice pessimiste) and serves as both noun and adjective.

peste.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (15th c.) from Classical Latin pestis ('deadly epidemic disease, plague, destruction, bane'), a root of uncertain pre-Latin Italic origin. Already in Cicero and Plautus, pestis was hurled metaphorically at ruinous or intolerable people; French preserved both the medical sense ('bubonic plague') and the lively interpersonal sense ('scheming nuisance, mischievous brat').

history.meaning: epidemic plague; malicious or troublesome person

peste.notes: Context decides severity: la peste noire is the Black Death, fuir quelqu'un comme la peste is 'to avoid someone like the plague', while calling a child or diva actress une petite peste means 'a little brat / scheming vixen' (not an insect — agricultural 'pests' are nuisibles or ravageurs!).

rootFamily.gloss: to rail, fume, curse under one's breath
to stink up; to poison the atmosphere

petit.etymology: Petit is traced to a Gallo-Romance form *pit- expressing smallness. Medieval Latin pititus provides evidence for that family; the reconstructed base is marked with an asterisk.

cognates.meaning: early Anglo-Norman borrowing and modern French loan

petit.notes: One of French's core prenominal adjectives (un petit café), forming kinship compounds like petit-fils ('grandson') and petit ami ('boyfriend').

petit-bourgeois.etymology: Compound solidified in 19th-century French social and literary criticism (Balzac, Proudhon, Marx) from petit ('small, minor', Old French petit < Gallo-Romance *pittittus, an expressive root) + bourgeois ('town-dweller, middle-class citizen', Old French borjois < Late Latin burgensis 'inhabitant of a fortified settlement', from Late Latin burgus, reinforced by Frankish *burg 'fortified town'). It shifted from socio-economic description (shopkeepers, minor clerks) to cultural satire of narrow-minded respectability.

history.meaning: small + inhabitant of a fortified town
townsman of modest rank or means

petit-bourgeois.notes: In Parisian artistic circles, petit-bourgeois is a classic aesthetic insult for safe, conventional, status-anxious taste; note that both parts inflect in feminine (petite-bourgeoise, plural petits-bourgeois / petites-bourgeoises), and in liaison petit sounds its t (/pə.ti.buʁ.ʒwa/ — actually no liaison before consonant b! Feminine petite /pə.tit.buʁ.ʒwaz/ sounds the t).

petit-déjeuner.etymology: Modern French compound noun (19th c.) formed from petit ('small, light') + déjeuner ('breakfast, literally breaking the fast'); coined when urban déjeuner shifted from the morning meal to the midday lunch.

petit-fils.etymology: Compound kinship noun formed in the 16th–17th century (replacing Old French neveu in the sense 'grandson' after neveu narrowed to 'nephew') from petit ('little, younger') + fils ('son', from Latin filius).

peu.etymology: Peu continues Latin paucum, few or little. Early French spellings included pou, poi and po before peu became established.
peu.notes: Subtle contrast like English 'little' vs. 'a little': peu de temps means 'scarcely any time', whereas un peu de temps means 'a little bit of time'.

peur.etymology: Inherited from Old French paor / peeur ('fear, dread'), from Classical Latin pavorem (nominative pavor, 'trembling, quaking, panic, dread'), derived from pavere ('to be struck with terror, quake with fear').

peut-être.etymology: Peut-être joins peut, the he/she present form of pouvoir, and être, to be. Twelfth-century expressions included put cel estre and puet estre; the hyphenated form is recorded in the seventeenth century.
peut-être.notes: Built the exact same way as English 'maybe' ('may + be'); at the start of a clause, Peut-être que... avoids formal subject-verb inversion (Peut-être qu'il viendra vs. Peut-être viendra-t-il).

pharmacie.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–16th century via Late Latin pharmacia from Ancient Greek pharmakeia ('use or preparation of drugs, medicines, or potions'), derived from pharmakon ('medicinal herb, drug, remedy, poison').

history.meaning: science of preparing medicines; chemist's shop, pharmacy, medicine cabinet

pharmacien.etymology: Formed in Classical French from pharmacie ('apothecary art, pharmacy'), via Medieval Latin pharmacia from Ancient Greek pharmakeía ('preparation of remedies'), from phármakon ('medicinal herb, remedy').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: pharmacien (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: pharmacien

pharmacien.notes: In 1777, a royal declaration in France officially established the *Collège de pharmacie*, replacing the older guild title **apothicaire** with **pharmacien**.

photo.etymology: Conversational clipping (attested since the second half of the 19th century) of photographie ('photography; photograph', coined in the 1830s from Ancient Greek phos, photos 'light' + graphein 'to draw, write').

photocopier.etymology: Formed in 20th-century French from photocopie ('photographic reproduction of a document', attested late 19th/early 20th c.) or by prefixing neo-classical photo- (from Ancient Greek φῶς, φωτός [phôs, phōtós] 'light') to copier ('to copy, transcribe', borrowed in Old/Middle French from Medieval Latin copiare 'to transcribe in abundance', derived from Classical Latin copia 'plenty, abundance').

history.meaning: abundance -> to transcribe in multiple copies
light-based document copy -> to reproduce by photocopier

photocopier.notes: In agency office life, assistants spend hours photocopier des scénarios; like copier, verbs in -ier keep both i's in the imperfect and subjunctive (nous photocopiions), though rare outside playful grammar tests.

photocopieuse.etymology: Derived in mid-20th-century French from photocopier ('to photocopy', composed of Greek-derived photo- < φῶς, φωτός 'light' + copier < Medieval Latin copiare 'to transcribe abundantly') + the productive feminine instrumental suffix -euse (originally ellipsis of machine photocopieuse, where -euse continues Latin -osa / agentive -orem). French routinely forms household and office appliances in the feminine with -euse (perceuse, tondeuse, imprimante).
photocopieuse.notes: Everyday French overwhelmingly says la photocopieuse (feminine, like une perceuse 'drill' or une agrafeuse 'stapler'), though corporate IT catalogs occasionally use the masculine un photocopieur for heavy industrial units.

photographe.etymology: Coined in 1839 at the dawn of photography (simultaneously in French alongside photographie around Daguerre's and Arago's announcements, and in English photographer/photography popularized by Sir John Herschel and Hercules Florence's earlier French notes of 1833–1834), from neo-classical photo- (< Ancient Greek φῶς, φωτός [phôs, phōtós] 'light') + -graphe (< Ancient Greek -γράφος [-gráphos] 'one who draws or writes', from γράφειν [gráphein]).

history.meaning: of light + one who draws or records

photographe.notes: Photographe is epicene (same spelling and form for men and women: un photographe / une photographe); on a French film set, distinguish le photographe de plateau ('stills photographer') from le directeur de la photographie ('cinematographer / DP').

photogénique.etymology: Coined in 1839 by French physicist François Arago (parallaling William Henry Fox Talbot's English photogenic drawing in the same year) from photo- (< Ancient Greek φῶς, φωτός [phôs, phōtós] 'light') + -génique (< Ancient Greek -γενής [-genḗs] 'born of, producing', from γίγνομαι / γένος + French -ique). Originally a technical physics term meaning 'produced by or sensitive to light', it was repurposed by early French cinema theorists (like Louis Delluc around 1919–1920) to mean 'captivating on camera'.

history.meaning: image produced chemically by the action of light
naturally expressive and flattering on camera or film

photogénique.notes: French film criticism gave the world the modern meaning of photogénique and la photogénie ('screen magnetism'): casting directors contrast actors who are merely beaux in person with those who are truly photogéniques on lens.

phrase.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century via Late Latin phrasis from Ancient Greek phrasis ('way of speaking, diction, expression'), derived from phrazein ('to point out, declare, tell, express').

history.meaning: manner of speech, turn of phrase
turn of phrase -> grammatical sentence, musical phrase

physique.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century (Old French fisique, originally 'natural science and the art of medicine') via Classical Latin physica from Ancient Greek physike (sc. episteme, 'knowledge of nature'), derived from physis ('nature, natural growth', from phyein 'to bring forth, grow').

history.meaning: physical (adj.); physics (fem. noun); bodily build or appearance (masc. noun)

phénomène.etymology: Borrowed in 16th-century French via Late Latin phaenomenon from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, 'that which appears, observable event, celestial appearance'), neuter singular middle-passive present participle of φαίνω (phaínō, 'to bring to light, show'; middle φαίνομαι 'to shine forth, come into view'). By the late 18th and 19th centuries, it expanded from natural philosophy to a sensation, prodigy, or eccentric character.

history.meaning: that which appears; observable celestial sign
natural phenomenon; prodigy or eccentric character

phénomène.notes: Always masculine (un phénomène), even when describing a woman! Exclaiming 'Quel phénomène !' or 'C'est un sacré phénomène' in conversational French affectionately or wryly means 'What a character / piece of work!' rather than a scientific marvel.

rootFamily.gloss: phantom, fantasy (distant Greek phainō relatives via phantasma)

piano.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from Italian piano, both as a musical dynamic marking ('softly, quietly', from Latin planus 'flat, level, even, soft in sound') and as a clipping of pianoforte / forte-piano (invented by Bartolomeo Cristofori in Florence c. 1709 as gravicembalo col piano e forte 'harpsichord with soft and loud').

history.meaning: softly; keyboard instrument capable of playing both soft and loud

pic.etymology: Inherited from Old French pic ('iron pickaxe; sharp mountain peak; woodpecker'), from Vulgar Latin *piccus ('sharp point, woodpecker'), built on an expressive/pre-Latin root *pikk- ('to strike with a sharp point, peck').

history.meaning: pickaxe, sharp mountain peak, peak level, woodpecker

pied.etymology: Inherited from Old French piet / pié ('foot'), from Classical Latin pedem (nominative pes, 'foot; metrical foot; twelve-inch measure of length', from PIE *ped- 'foot', cognate with English foot).

history.meaning: anatomical foot, base or leg of furniture, plant stalk, foot measure

pierre.etymology: Pierre comes from Latin petra ('rock, stone', borrowed from Ancient Greek pétra). Diphthongisation of open e to ie and lenition of -tr- to -rr- yielded Old French piere, pierre.
pierre.notes: Also the source of the first name *Pierre* ('Peter'); **en pierre** = made of stone.

pile.etymology: Represents two Latin words that converged: (1) 'stack, heap, bridge pier, Voltaic battery (originally a stacked column of zinc and copper discs invented by Volta in 1800)', from Old French pile < Classical Latin pila ('stone pier, pillar'); and (2) 'reverse side of a coin; right on the dot (pile à l'heure)', from the medieval minting die pile ('under-iron').

history.meaning: masonry pier -> neat vertical stack, electric battery; coin face -> right on the dot

cognates.meaning: pill (via Middle Dutch/Middle French from Latin pilula)

pilule.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th–15th c., originally spelled pillule, simplified to pilule by the 18th c.) from Classical Latin pilula ('little ball, globule, medicinal pill'), regular diminutive of pila ('playing ball, sphere'). Because apothecaries gilded bitter medicinal pellets in gold leaf to mask their taste, French coined enduring idioms around swallowing unpleasant truths.
pilule.notes: With the definite article alone, prendre la pilule specifically means 'to take the contraceptive pill' (general tablets are comprimés or cachets); in agency diplomacy, faire passer / dorer la pilule means 'to sugarcoat bad news so the client swallows it'.

rootFamily.gloss: to form into pellets; to pill (of fabric)
pelota, ball of yarn (from same Latin pila 'ball' root)

cognates.meaning: pigment; pimento (learned & Spanish doublets from Latin pigmentum)

pimenté.etymology: Adjectival past participle of pimenter ('to season with chili or hot spice', 19th c.), derived from piment ('chili pepper, hot spice'). Piment was inherited from Old French piment ('spiced honeyed wine, aromatic balm'), from Late Latin pigmentum ('plant juice, spice, drug'), a semantic shift from Classical Latin pigmentum ('coloring matter, paint, pigment', built on pingere 'to paint, tint'). Figuratively extended to racy or thrilling stories and relationships.

history.meaning: paint, coloring dye; in Late Latin, aromatic spice or herb extract
spiced wine, aromatic seasoning; later New World chili pepper
seasoned with chili; figuratively spicy, racy, provocative

pimenté.notes: Delightful etymological surprise: pimenté ('spicy/racy') and pigment ('color pigment') come from the exact same Latin word! Used figuratively (un scénario un peu pimenté), it means 'spicy, risqué, full of zest'.

rootFamily.gloss: to spice up, add excitement to

pince.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old/Middle French from pincier / pincer ('to pinch, grip tightly', from Vulgar Latin *pinctiare / expressive root *pints-).

history.meaning: gripping tool, pliers, tongs, tweezers, crab claw, dress dart

pinceau.etymology: Inherited from Old French pincel, from Vulgar Latin *penicellus, a variant of Classical Latin penicillus ('painter's fine brush', originally 'little tuft of tail hair', double diminutive of penis 'tail').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French pincel (originally a fine camel-hair brush before graphite!)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: pinceau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: pinceau

pinceau.notes: Watch the false friend: English *pencil* came from Old French *pincel*, but in modern French **un pinceau** is a paintbrush and **un crayon** is a pencil (and **penicillin** was named in Latin for its brush-shaped mold!).

pincée.etymology: Formed in Middle French from pincer ('to pinch between thumb and forefinger') + suffix -ée denoting the quantity held.

history.meaning: amount taken between two fingers, pinch (of salt, spice)

pipi.etymology: Attested since the late 17th century in French nursery and familiar speech (faire pipi), formed by infantile syllabic reduplication (pi-pi) both from expressive onomatopoeia imitating the sound of a thin stream of liquid and by nursery shortening of pisser ('to urinate', Old French pissier, itself an onomatopoeic Gallo-Romance verb *pissiare).
pipi.notes: Unlike pisser (which sounds vulgar in French), faire pipi and une pause pipi ('bathroom break') are mild, playful, and universally used by adults in casual or family conversation; pipi de chat ('cat pee') is classic slang for weak, terrible wine or tepid coffee.

pire.etymology: Inherited from Old French pire ('worse, worst'), directly continuing the Classical Latin nominative singular pejor ('worse', synthetic comparative of malus 'bad'; the Latin accusative pejorem gave the archaic/literary French pis).

piscine.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (piscine, 12th–13th c., originally denoting Biblical bathing pools like Siloam and church ablution basins) from Classical Latin piscina ('fishpond', and already under the Roman Empire 'heated or cold artificial pool for swimming and bathing'), derived from piscis ('fish') + locative/pertaining suffix -ina. Revived in secular urban life in the 19th century for modern swimming pools.

history.meaning: fish -> fishpond; Roman bathing or swimming tank
Biblical healing pool; liturgical ablution basin

piscine.notes: Hidden inside piscine (/pi.sin/, silent sc = /s/) is Latin piscis — the ancestor of French poisson ('fish')! In Saint-Tropez or Cannes wine bars, commander une piscine means ordering champagne or rosé served over a giant goblet full of ice cubes.

piste.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (originally in horsemanship) from Italian pista ('beaten track left by hooves, trail'), feminine participial noun of Late Latin pistare ('to pound, tread down', frequentative of pinsere).

history.meaning: trail, clue track, ski run, bike lane

cognates.meaning: pounded basil sauce (from the same Late Latin pistare!)
ski run or fencing strip, borrowed from French

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: piste (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: piste

piste.notes: **Une piste** ('trodden trail') and Italian **pesto** ('pounded sauce') come from the very same verb meaning 'to pound or tread down'!

pistonner.etymology: Derived in late 19th-century French slang from piston in its figurative student and Grande École sense of 'pull, string-pulling, influential backing' (attested mid-19th c., from the mechanical metaphor of a pump piston pushing someone upward or forward). Mechanical piston itself was borrowed in the 16th–18th centuries from Italian pistone ('pestle, pump plunger'), an augmentative derived from Vulgar Latin pistare ('to pound, ram'), frequentative of Classical Latin pinsere ('to beat, crush').

history.meaning: to pound/ram -> large pestle, pump plunger
to pull strings for, get someone hired through connections

pistonner.notes: Indispensable French entertainment-industry verb: se faire pistonner or avoir du piston means getting a role, internship, or job through nepotism and insider connections rather than open audition; slightly pejorative compared to neutral recommander.

rootFamily.gloss: engine piston; insider clout/connections (avoir du piston)
person hired via connections, nepotism hire

cognates.meaning: pestle (via Old French pestel from Latin pistillum)

pistou.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th–20th century from Provençal (Occitan) pistou ('pounded garlic, basil, and olive-oil sauce', and in Nice/Provence also 'pestle'), derived from Provençal pistar ('to pound in a mortar'), from Late/Vulgar Latin pistare ('to pound, crush, bray'), frequentative of Classical Latin pinsere (past participle pistus, 'pounded, crushed'). It is the exact Provençal cousin of Ligurian/Italian pesto.

history.meaning: to beat, crush in a mortar -> to pound repeatedly
to pound -> pestle; pounded garlic-and-basil paste
Provençal basil, garlic, and olive-oil sauce (soupe au pistou)

pistou.notes: Culinary distinction prized in southern France: unlike Italian pesto, authentic Provençal pistou (famous in soupe au pistou) contains crushed basil, garlic, and olive oil — traditionally NO pine nuts! Also shares its 'pounding' root with pistonner.

rootFamily.gloss: engine piston (Italian cousin from same Vulgar Latin pistare)
to track, tread down (from Latin pistare 'to tread/pound')
beaten track, trail; film/audio track; dance floor

cognates.meaning: well (inherited cousin of English pit via Latin puteus)

pitbull.etymology: Borrowed in late 20th-century French (1980s–1990s) from American English pit bull (shortened from American Pit Bull Terrier), a compound of English pit ('sunken arena for dogfighting or rat-baiting', from Old English pytt, an early Germanic borrowing from Classical Latin puteus 'well, shaft, pit') + bull (short for bulldog, bred historically for bull-baiting, from Middle English bole / Old Norse boli 'bull'). Rapidly adopted in French metaphor for an attack-dog negotiator or agent.

history.meaning: pit bull dog; tenacious, aggressive enforcer or agent

pitbull.notes: Pronounced /pit.bul/ in French (with French /u/ as in poule, not English /ʊ/); in talent-agency and legal slang, calling an agent or lawyer un vrai pitbull praises (or fears) their refusal to ever let go of a contract clause.

rootFamily.gloss: bulldog (earlier 18th-c. French adaptation of English bulldog)
cockpit; orchestra pit/traders' pit cousins via English pit
well, shaft (native French descendant of Latin puteus, source of English pit!)

pitié.etymology: Inherited via Old French pitet, pitié ('compassion, mercy, tenderness', 10th–11th c.) through popular/semi-learned phonetic evolution from Classical Latin pietatem (accusative of pietas, 'dutifulness toward gods and family, loyalty, tender affection', and in Christian Late Latin 'mercy, compassion toward suffering'), derived from pius ('dutiful, devout'). Classical Latin pietas split in French into inherited pitié ('pity, mercy') and learned borrowing piété ('religious piety').

history.meaning: dutiful devotion; in Late Latin, Christian mercy and compassion
compassion, mercy, sorrow for another's suffering

pitié.notes: Pitié and piété ('piety') are textbook French doublets from Latin pietatem! Watch the sharp contrast between avoir pitié de quelqu'un ('to feel compassion/mercy for someone') and faire pitié ('to look pathetic/pitiful'); standing alone, 'Pitié !' means 'Have mercy! / Spare me!'.

rootFamily.gloss: piety, religious devotion (learned doublet from Latin pietatem)

pitoyable.etymology: Formed in Old French (piteable, pitoyable, 12th–13th c., built on pitié / Old French verb piteer, pitoyer 'to feel pity, show mercy', ultimately from Latin pietas 'dutifulness, compassion') + suffix -able (< Latin -abilis). Remarkably, throughout Old and Classical French pitoyable first meant 'compassionate, merciful' (preserved in its antonym impitoyable 'merciless'), before shifting to passive 'inspiring pity' and finally pejorative 'wretched, pathetic'.

history.meaning: full of mercy, compassionate toward the poor

morphemes.meaning: pity, mercy (alternating stem pitoy- of pitié)

pitoyable.notes: Fascinating semantic flip: pitoyable today almost always expresses scorn ('pathetic, dismal', e.g., une excuse pitoyable), yet its negative impitoyable ('ruthless, merciless', e.g., un milieu impitoyable) froze the medieval meaning 'merciful'!

rootFamily.gloss: to move to pity; s'apitoyer 'to wallow in self-pity'

pièce.etymology: Pièce is traced to reconstructed Gaulish *pettia, a small piece. Its French history is recorded from the eleventh century. The theatre sense is one of several later uses of this general noun.

history.meaning: room (in a flat); coin; play (pièce de théâtre); piece/part

pièce.notes: Real-estate essential: un trois-pièces in France counts ALL main living rooms + bedrooms (excluding kitchen and bath), so a trois-pièces usually has one living room and two bedrooms!

piège.etymology: Inherited from Old French piege ('snare that catches an animal by the foot'), from Late Latin pedica ('foot-snare, fetter, shackle'), derived from Classical Latin pes, pedis ('foot').

cognates.meaning: pawn; peon (via Anglo-Norman/Spanish from sister Vulgar Latin *pedonem)

piéton.etymology: Inherited and remodeled from Old and Middle French pieton ('foot soldier, infantryman', attested 14th c., replacing earlier peon / pion), descending from Vulgar Latin *peditonem (accusative of *pedito), an augmented reshaping of Classical Latin pedes, peditis ('one who goes on foot, foot soldier'), derived from pes, pedis ('foot'). By the 17th–18th centuries its military sense yielded wholly to civilian 'person walking on foot'.

history.meaning: civilian pedestrian, walker in street traffic

piéton.notes: Used both as a noun (un piéton / une piétonne) and as an adjective (une rue piétonne 'a pedestrianized street', un passage piéton 'crosswalk'); also cognate with un pion ('chess pawn / school hall monitor'), which came from the parallel Vulgar Latin *pedonem!

rootFamily.gloss: to trample underfoot; to stall/make no progress
pawn, game piece (doublet via Old French peon < *pedonem)

placard.etymology: Derived in the 15th century from plaquer ('to lay flat, plaster, post a bill on a wall', from Middle Dutch placken 'to patch, plaster, stick on'); evolved from 'posted wall bill' -> 'wooden door frame or paneling applied to a wall' -> 'built-in wall cupboard or closet'.

history.meaning: posted broadside, wall paneling -> built-in wall cupboard, closet

place.etymology: Place came through Latin platea from Greek plateia hodos, a broad street. The French noun is recorded from the eleventh century; its modern senses include a location, space or seat.
place.notes: Covers a city square (la place de la Concorde), available room (il n'y a plus de place), and a cinema/train seat or ticket (deux places, s'il vous plaît); a general 'place/location' is un endroit or un lieu.

cognates.meaning: action of placing; job or product placement

placement.etymology: Formed in Middle French from the verb placer ('to put in a place') plus the action-noun suffix -ment, ultimately tracing through Old French place ('open space, town square') to Vulgar Latin *plattea and Classical Latin platea ('broad street, courtyard'), borrowed from Ancient Greek plateia (hodos) ('broad way'). In modern finance and media, it expanded from physical positioning to capital investment and cinema 'placement de produit'.

history.meaning: to set in a place, assign a spot
act of placing; financial investment or positioning

morphemes.meaning: action or result of an action

placement.notes: Masculine noun; in film and talent-agency contexts (like Dix pour cent), 'placement de produit' ('product placement') and 'placement d'acteurs' are staple industry terms, alongside financial 'placement' ('investment').

cognates.meaning: to put in a particular position

placer.etymology: Derived in late Old and Middle French (placier, placer) as a denominal verb from place ('open space, spot, rank'), itself via Vulgar Latin *plattea from Latin platea ('broad street, courtyard') and Ancient Greek plateia ('broad [way]', feminine of platys 'flat, wide'). Its sense broadened from stationing someone in a public square to putting objects, seating guests,investing money, or pitching clients into roles.

history.meaning: to put in a designated spot, station

placer.notes: Spelling note: takes a cedilla before 'a' or 'o' to keep the soft /s/ sound (nous plaçons, il plaçait). Idiomatically, 'placer un mot' means 'to get a word in edgewise', and an agent tries to 'placer un comédien sur un film'.

plafond.etymology: Originally spelled plat-fonds or plat fond in sixteenth-century architecture—literally 'flat bottom / flat underside' (plat 'flat' + fond 'bottom, background'), describing a flat boarded or plastered ceiling underside as opposed to an open arched vault. Fused into plafond in the seventeenth century.

history.meaning: flat underside of an upper floor

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: plafond (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: plafond

plage.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian piaggia ('gently sloping shore, coast'), itself continuing Late Latin plagia ('coast, flat stretch of land'), derived from Classical Latin plaga ('region, tract, expanse') or influenced by Ancient Greek plagios ('sloping, oblique'). Originally a nautical term in French for a flat, harborless stretch of coastline before becoming the everyday word for a sandy beach and later a time slot on radio or TV schedules.

history.meaning: flat coastal stretch, tract of land

plage.notes: Feminine noun (la plage). Beyond the seaside (crucial for the Cannes Film Festival!), media professionals constantly use 'plage horaire' to mean a 'time slot' or broadcast window.

cognates.meaning: to argue a case in court; make an emotional appeal

plaider.etymology: Inherited from Old French plaidier ('to go to court, hold a legal assembly, argue a suit'), derived from plait ('lawsuit, judicial assembly, agreement'), which comes from Classical Latin placitum ('opinion, decree, that which pleases', neuter past participle of placere 'to please'). In medieval Frankish and Carolingian law, placitum denoted the sovereign's judicial session, shifting the verb from 'attending court' to 'defending a cause'.

morphemes.meaning: plea, legal suit (from Old French plait/plaid)

plaider.notes: Used both transitively ('plaider coupable' = to plead guilty; 'plaider la cause de quelqu'un' = to champion someone's case) and intransitively for courtroom advocacy.

plaie.etymology: Inherited from Old French plaie ('wound, blow, affliction'), directly continuing Classical Latin plaga ('blow, stroke, wound', and in Christian Latin 'divine scourge, pestilence'), itself an early borrowing from Doric Greek plaga (Attic plege, 'blow, strike'). While its literal medical sense ('open wound') endures, colloquial French extended the Biblical 'plaies d'Égypte' ('plagues of Egypt') to describe an unbearable person or nuisance.

history.meaning: blow, stroke, surgical or battle wound; divine scourge

plaie.notes: Feminine noun (une plaie). In everyday spoken French, calling someone or something 'une vraie plaie' means 'a total pain in the neck / a nightmare', whereas 'remuer le couteau dans la plaie' means 'to rub salt in the wound'.

rootFamily.gloss: wound-healing (compound medical root, cf. vulnéraire); idiom: 'plaies et bosses' (bumps and bruises)

plainte.etymology: Inherited from Old French plainte ('lamentation, cry of grief, legal grievance'), substantivized feminine past participle (*plancta) of Vulgar Latin *plangere, from Classical Latin plangere ('to strike, beat one's breast in mourning, lament aloud'). The semantic shift from ritual mourning cries to formal legal accusation occurred already in medieval feudal courts, where an injured partyvoiced their grievance before a lord.

history.meaning: to beat the breast in grief, lament aloud
lament, cry of sorrow; legal accusation

plainte.notes: Feminine noun. Note the key legal collocation 'porter plainte (contre quelqu'un)' ('to press charges / file a formal police complaint'), without an article before 'plainte'.

rootFamily.gloss: to pity; (reflexive se plaindre) to complain

plaire.etymology: Plaire is a remodelling of the older French verb plaisir, itself descended from Latin placere, to be pleasing. The Académie dates plaire to the twelfth century.

history.meaning: to please (older infinitive became the noun le plaisir!)

rootFamily.word: s'il vous plaît / s'il te plaît

plaire.notes: Ça me plaît ('That appeals to me / I like it') reverses the English subject and object, just like Italian mi piace and Spanish me gusta.

plaisanter.etymology: Derived in Middle French (16th century) from the adjective plaisant, which originally meant 'pleasing, agreeable' (present participle of plaire 'to please', from Latin placere) before specializing in Classical French to mean 'amusing, witty, comical'. Adding the verbalizer -er yielded plaisanter ('to make witty remarks, jest, not be serious').
plaisanter.notes: Very frequent in spoken dialogue: 'Tu plaisantes ?' ('Are you kidding?') and 'Sans plaisanter' ('Seriously / All joking aside'). Beware the modern adjective 'plaisant', which today mostly means 'pleasant' rather than 'funny' (except in fixed phrases like 'un mauvais plaisant', a prankster).

plaisir.etymology: Inherited from Old French plaisir, originally the infinitive of the verb meaning 'to please, be agreeable' (modern plaire), from Classical Latin placere ('to please, seem good to'), substantivized as a masculine noun ('delight, enjoyment, favor').

plan.etymology: Plan blends two related Latin origins: planus ('flat, level surface', giving a flat architectural drawing or town map) and plantare ('to lay out on the ground'), expanding from a floor plan to any project or scheme.
plan.notes: **Un plan de la ville** = a city map; **un bon plan** = a good idea/deal.

planche.etymology: Inherited from Old French planche ('flat wooden board, footbridge'), from Late Latin planca ('flat board, slab', recorded by Palladius and Festus), related to Classical Latin plancus ('flat-footed') from PIE *plak- ('flat').

history.meaning: wooden plank, shelving board, engraved plate, garden bed

plancher.etymology: Derived in Old French (planchier, 12th c.) from planche ('wooden board, plank') + suffix -ier.

history.meaning: timber floor of a room, floorboards, ceiling structure; minimum floor level

cognates.meaning: act or process of making plans

planning.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century from English planning (gerund-noun of to plan, itself borrowed earlier from French plan 'ground-plan, flat projection'). In French management, office, and film-production usage, the anglicism underwent semantic narrowing: whereas English 'planning' denotes the abstract process of devising plans (French planification), French 'un planning' denotes a concrete visual schedule, timetable, or call sheet.

history.meaning: process of organizing activities in advance

planning.notes: Classic pseudo-anglicism / semantic shift (masculine: 'le planning'): in French, 'le planning de tournage' means 'the shooting schedule', NOT the abstract act of planning (which is 'la planification'). Essential agency vocabulary in Dix pour cent!

plante.etymology: Represents two senses from the same Latin word: (1) 'sole of the foot' (la plante des pieds), inherited from Old French plante < Classical Latin planta ('sole of the foot, used to tamp down earth around a new shoot'); and (2) 'living vegetable organism, plant', borrowed in the 13th–16th century from Classical Latin planta ('sprout, slip, cutting, young plant').

history.meaning: sole of the foot; plant slip or shoot
sole of the foot; botanical plant

cognates.meaning: to set in the ground to grow; fix firmly
to plant; to abandon abruptly (piantare in asso)
to plant; to stand someone up (dejar plantado)

planter.etymology: Inherited from Old French planter ('to set shoots in soil, drive in firmly'), from Classical Latin plantare ('to set in the earth, fix in place, propagate from shoots'), derived from planta ('sprout, slip, cutting', also 'sole of the foot' used to tamp down soil). From the image of leaving someone rooted like a post on the spot, Romance languages developed the vivid colloquial sense 'to ditch, stand up, or walk out on' (parallel to Italian piantare and Spanish dejar plantado).

history.meaning: to set shoots in the earth, fix firmly in place
to plant, drive in, station upright
