programme.etymology: Borrowed in the late 17th century via Late Latin programma ('public proclamation, edict') from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma, 'public written notice, agenda'), derived from προγράφω (prográphō, 'to write beforehand or post in public'), a compound of πρό (pró, 'before, in front') and γράφω (gráphō, 'to write'). Extended from university notices to theater playbills (18th–19th c.), broadcast schedules, politics, and computing (20th c.).

history.meaning: public written notice, posted order of business
playbill, schedule, broadcast lineup, software program

morphemes.meaning: before, publicly in front (from Greek pró-)

programme.notes: Masculine noun ('un programme') despite ending in '-amme' (a Greek neuter '-ma' loanword, like 'un drame', 'un problème', 'un télégramme'); idiom 'quel est le programme ?' means 'what's the plan / schedule?'.

progression.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th–15th c.) from Classical Latin progressio, progressionis ('a going forward, advance, gradual growth, rhetorical or mathematical progression'), action noun derived from the past participial stem progress- of progredi ('to step forward, advance'), from pro- ('forward') + gradi ('to step, walk', related to gradus 'step, degree').

history.meaning: gradual development, dramatic build-up, statistical rise

morphemes.meaning: step, walk (from Latin gradi, supine gressum)

progression.notes: Used both for narrative pacing ('la progression dramatique du scénario') and box-office or ratings growth ('une progression de 15 % des entrées').

progressivement.etymology: Formed in 18th-century French from progressive (feminine of progressif 'advancing step by step', built on Classical Latin progressus, past participle of progredi 'to step forward', from pro- 'forward' + gradi 'to walk, step') plus the adverbial suffix -ment (< Latin mente 'in a ... manner').

history.meaning: by successive degrees, gradually, little by little

morphemes.meaning: step, walk (from Latin gradi, supine gressum)

progressivement.notes: Subtle false friend: in everyday French, 'progressivement' almost always means 'gradually / step by step' (synonym of 'peu à peu'), NOT politically 'in a progressive/left-leaning way' (French distinguishes 'progressif' = gradual vs. 'progressiste' = politically progressive).

progrès.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Classical Latin progressus ('a going forward, advance, growth, improvement'), action noun from progredi ('to step forward, advance', from pro- 'forward' + gradi 'to step, walk').

projection.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (originally in alchemy, then geometry and cartography) from Classical Latin proiectio, proiectionis ('a throwing forward, stretching out'), derived from proicere ('to throw forth, cast out', from pro- 'forward' + iacere 'to throw'). Applied in the 17th–19th centuries to optical magic lanterns, it became the standard French term for a 'film screening' with the birth of cinema in 1895.

history.meaning: act of throwing forward or extending outward
alchemical transmutation; geometric/optical casting of lines or rays

morphemes.meaning: throw, cast (from Latin iacere, supine iectum)

projection.notes: In the French film industry, a 'screening' is 'une projection' (colloquially clipped on *Dix pour cent* to 'une projo', e.g., 'une projection de presse' = 'press screening', 'salle de projection' = 'screening room').

rootFamily.gloss: to project, screen a film, plan

projet.etymology: Evolved from Late Old/Middle French pourjet (14th–15th c., originally architectural: 'jutting balcony or overhang', then 'preliminary draft, plan thrown out on paper'), deverbal noun from pourjeter ('to throw forward, sketch out'), later Latinized in spelling to projet after Classical Latin proiectum / proiectus ('something thrown forward, jutting out'), from proicere (pro- 'forward' + iacere 'to throw').

history.meaning: thrown forth, jutting out; architectural prominence
architectural overhang; preliminary sketch or intended plan
planned undertaking, film/artistic project, draft bill

morphemes.meaning: throw, cast (from Latin iacere, supine iectum)

projet.notes: Silent final '-t' (/pʁɔ.ʒɛ/); in agency parlance 'avoir un beau projet' means having an exciting script/film package in development, while in politics 'un projet de loi' is a government-sponsored bill.

prolonger.etymology: Inherited/adapted in the 12th–13th century (Old French prolongier) from Late Latin prolongare ('to lengthen, extend in space or time'), compound of pro- ('forward') + longus ('long').

history.meaning: to extend in time or length, prolong

promenade.etymology: Formed in the 16th century with suffix -ade from promener ('to take for a walk, walk back and forth'), earlier Old French pormener (por- 'forth' + mener 'to lead' < Late Latin minare 'to drive/lead onward').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: promenade (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: promenade

promenade.notes: **Une promenade** names both the act of strolling (**faire une promenade**) and the scenic tree-lined avenue itself.

promener.etymology: Inherited from Old French por mener and promener, formed from Late Latin promināre ('to drive animals forward'), a prefixation of pro- ('forth, forward') + mināre ('to drive cattle with shouts'), itself from Classical Latin minārī ('to threaten, jut out'). Semantic shift moved from driving livestock ahead to taking someone out for a walk.

history.meaning: to threaten; to drive cattle with cries
to lead forth, take out walking

promener.notes: Transitive promener means to walk someone or a pet (promener le chien), whereas reflexive se promener means to go for a stroll oneself; colloquially envoyer promener quelqu'un means to tell someone to get lost.

promesse.etymology: Inherited from Old French promesse ('pledge, vow'), from Late/Vulgar Latin promissa ('a promise'), feminine singular reshaped from Classical Latin neuter plural promissa ('things promised'), past participle of promittere ('to send forth, foretell, promise').

prometteur.etymology: Derived within French from promettre ('to promise') + agentive/adjectival suffix -eur (from Latin -ātōrem / -ōrem). Originally denoting a person who makes excessive promises (12th–16th c.), it acquired its modern positive adjectival sense ('giving hope of future success, auspicious') in the 19th century, influenced by English promising.

history.meaning: to send forth; to foretell, promise

prometteur.notes: Feminine form is prometteuse; in talent-agency parlance (as in Dix pour cent), un jeune talent prometteur is the standard phrase for a breakout newcomer.

promettre.etymology: Inherited from Old French prometre ('to pledge one's word, promise'), from Classical Latin promittere ('to let go forward, send forth; to give assurance, promise'), compound of pro- ('forth') + mittere ('to send').

history.meaning: to put forth -> to pledge, promise

promis.etymology: Past participle of promettre used adjectivally and interjectionally, inherited from Old French promis, from Classical Latin prōmissus, perfect passive participle of prōmittere ('to let go forward, send forth; to pledge, vow'), composed of prō- ('forward') + mittere ('to send, release').
promis.notes: Used standalone in spoken French as a reassuring interjection—'Promis !' or 'Promis, juré !' ('Cross my heart! / I swear!'). Feminine singular adds silent -e (promise), which triggers pronunciation of the /z/.

promotion.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th c.) from Late Latin prōmōtiōnem (nominative prōmōtiō, 'advancement in rank or preferment'), a noun of action from prōmovēre ('to move forward, advance'). The media, cinema, and commercial sense ('publicity tour, press campaign') developed in the 20th century under American English influence.

history.meaning: advancement to higher office or rank
elevation to a dignity or post
career advancement; graduating cohort; publicity campaign

promotion.notes: In French film industry slang, promotion is routinely clipped to la promo (faire la promo d'un film = to do the press tour); note also the institutional French sense 'graduating class/year group' (camarade de promotion).

cognates.meaning: to advance in rank; to publicize

promouvoir.etymology: Borrowed and adapted in the 14th century from Classical Latin prōmovēre ('to move forward, push onward, advance, bring to light'), remodeled on native mouvoir ('to move'). Composed of prō- ('forward') + movēre ('to move, set in motion'), from PIE *mewH- ('to push away, move').

history.meaning: to move forward, push onward, advance
to elevate to an office or dignity

promouvoir.notes: Highly defective/irregular verb conjugated like mouvoir, though mostly encountered in the infinitive promouvoir and past participle promu (without circumflex in the feminine/plural: promue, promus, unlike dû).

prononcer.etymology: Inherited/semi-learned adaptation in Old French (prononcier, late 12th c.) from Classical Latin prōnūntiāre ('to proclaim publicly, announce, recite, articulate'), formed from prō- ('forth, in public') + nūntiāre ('to announce, report'), itself from nūntius ('messenger, herald').
prononcer.notes: Spelling requires a cedilla before a or o (nous prononçons) to preserve the soft /s/; reflexively se prononcer sur quelque chose means 'to take an official stance / give a verdict on something'.

rootFamily.gloss: to denounce; to terminate a contract

prophétie.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th century (Old French profecie) from Ecclesiastical Latin prophetia, from Ancient Greek propheteia ('gift of interpreting the will of the gods, prediction'), derived from prophetes ('spokesperson for a god, prophet', from pro- + phanai 'to speak').

proportion.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin proportionem (nominative proportio, coined by Cicero to translate Greek analogia from the phrase pro portione 'in accordance with each part's share').

propos.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (propos, 12th c., 'resolution, aim, subject of discussion, spoken remarks') from proposer ('to set forth, intend, propose').

history.meaning: purpose, subject at hand (à propos), spoken remarks

proposer.etymology: Proposer was borrowed from Latin proponere, to place before someone or set forth. Its French shape was influenced by poser. The Académie records it from the twelfth century.

history.meaning: to set forth, suggest (blended with poser)

proposer.notes: Watch the romance false friend: French proposer simply means 'to suggest / offer' (je te propose un café)—NOT 'to propose marriage' (demander en mariage)!

proposition.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (12th c.) from Classical Latin prōpositiōnem (nominative prōpositiō, 'a setting forth, statement of a theme, premise in logic'), derived from prōpositus, past participle of prōpōnere ('to set before, display, propose'), from prō- ('before, forth') + pōnere ('to place, set').

history.meaning: setting forth; rhetorical theme or logical premise
statement put forward for discussion; offer

proposition.notes: False-register alert: unlike English proposition (which often implies an improper sexual advance), French proposition is the everyday neutral noun for any offer, casting pitch, or suggestion (faire une proposition = to make an offer).

propre.etymology: Inherited from Old French propre ('belonging exclusively to someone, one's own, fitting, neat'), from Classical Latin proprius ('one's own, special, particular, characteristic'); in 16th–17th-century French, 'well-groomed, fitting' developed into the modern everyday sense 'clean, not dirty' (displacing net).

history.meaning: one's own (before noun); clean, tidy, literal (after noun)

proprement.etymology: Formed in Old French (12th century) from the adjective propre + adverbial suffix -ment. In Classical Latin, proprius meant 'one's own, particular, proper' (hence the older sense proprement dit, 'properly speaking'); in 17th-century French, propre also developed the everyday meaning 'clean, neat, well-kept', giving proprement its modern sense of 'neatly, cleanly'.
proprement.notes: Just as **propre** means 'own' before a noun (**ma propre cour**) and 'clean' after a noun (**des chaussures propres**), **proprement** means 'neatly, cleanly' in everyday life.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: proprement

propriétaire.etymology: Propriétaire comes from Late Latin proprietarius ('owner of property', from proprietas 'ownership', built on proprius 'one's own').
propriétaire.notes: Same form for masculine and feminine (**le / la propriétaire**).

propriété.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old French (proprieté, 12th c.) from Classical Latin proprietātem (nominative proprietās, 'peculiar nature, special characteristic; legal ownership' in Imperial jurists), derived from proprius ('one's own, personal, special, lasting'), probably contracted from *prō prīvō ('in an individual/private manner').

history.meaning: peculiar quality; legal right of ownership

propriété.notes: Notice the doublet with propreté ('cleanliness'), which evolved from propre after its semantic shift to 'clean, neat'; propriété means 'ownership, real estate, or inherent attribute' (e.g., propriété intellectuelle).

propulser.etymology: Formed in 19th-century French (first attested 1877) by back-formation from propulsion or directly as a learned borrowing from Classical Latin prōpulsāre ('to drive back, ward off, push onward'), frequentative of prōpellere ('to drive forth, hurl forward'), from prō- ('forward') + pellere ('to drive, strike').

history.meaning: to push forward repeatedly; to repel
to drive mechanically; to catapult to fame

propulser.notes: Very common figuratively in entertainment journalism: propulser quelqu'un au rang de star / sur le devant de la scène ('to catapult someone to stardom / into the spotlight').

protecteur.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th c.) from Late Latin prōtēctōrem (nominative prōtēctor, 'bodyguard, defender, imperial guard'), agent noun from Classical Latin prōtegere ('to cover in front, roof over, shield, defend'), composed of prō- ('in front') + tegere ('to cover, roof'), from PIE *(s)teg- ('to cover').

history.meaning: to cover in front, shield, defend

protecteur.notes: Irregular Latinate feminine: protectrice (e.g., une figure protectrice). Functions both as an adjective ('protective, patronizing') and as a noun ('protector, arts patron').

protection.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Late Latin protectionem (nominative protectio, 'a covering over, shelter, defense'), derived from Classical Latin protegere, protectum ('to cover in front, roof over, shield').

protocole.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (protokolle, c. 1330) from Medieval Latin protocollum ('authenticating flyleaf, notarial register of minutes'), from Late Greek prōtókollon ('first sheet glued onto a papyrus roll bearing date and authentication'), compound of prōtos ('first') + kólla ('glue'). Semantic evolution progressed from notarial formula book to diplomatic etiquette and procedural rules.

history.meaning: first sheet glued onto a papyrus scroll

protocole.notes: Masculine noun (le protocole); at Cannes or official French galas, le service du protocole strictly governs red-carpet order, seating, and VIP etiquette, while un protocole d'accord means a memorandum of understanding.

protéger.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century from Classical Latin protegere ('to cover in front, roof over, defend, shield'), compound of pro- ('in front of') + tegere ('to cover, roof').

history.meaning: to cover in front, shield from harm

prouver.etymology: Inherited from Old French prover (11th c., alternating between stem-stressed prueve and ending-stressed prouvons, later leveled to prouv-), from Classical Latin probāre ('to test the quality of, inspect, find good, approve, demonstrate'), derived from probus ('upright, sound, good'), from PIE *pro-bʰh₂u-o- ('growing straight/well').

history.meaning: to test, put to trial, establish as true

prouver.notes: Whereas Old French prover meant both 'to test' and 'to prove', Modern French split the duties: tester/essayer/éprouver handle 'testing/experiencing', while prouver means strictly 'to prove/demonstrate', though the older vowel alternation survives in preuve ('proof').

rootFamily.gloss: to feel, experience; to test severely

provenir.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (15th c.) from Classical Latin prōvenīre ('to come forth, appear, sprout, arise, turn out'), adapted to the conjugation of native venir. Composed of prō- ('forth, out') + venīre ('to come'), from PIE *gʷem- ('to step, come').

history.meaning: to come forth, sprout, originate, succeed
to issue forth, derive or originate from

provenir.notes: Conjugated exactly like venir and forms its compound tenses with être (ces fonds sont provenus de...), always followed by de to indicate source or origin.

provoquer.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (provoquier, 12th c.) from Classical Latin prōvocāre ('to call forth, summon out, challenge to combat, appeal to a higher tribunal'), composed of prō- ('forth, out') + vocāre ('to call'), from vōx ('voice'), ultimately from PIE *wekʷ- ('to speak').

history.meaning: to call forth, challenge, appeal legally

provoquer.notes: Besides 'to bait or antagonize a person', provoquer is standard neutral French for 'to cause or trigger' an event (provoquer un scandale / un fou rire), where English 'provoke' might sound overly intentional.

cognates.meaning: wise and judicious in practical affairs

prudent.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (late 13th c.) from Classical Latin prūdentem (nominative prūdēns, 'foreseeing, sagacious, skilled, practical'), a syncopated contraction of prōvidēns, present participle of prōvidēre ('to foresee, look ahead, provide for'), from prō- ('ahead, before') + vidēre ('to see').
prudent.notes: False-register nuance: while English prudent sounds formal or financial, French prudent is the everyday word for 'careful/safe' (Sois prudent sur la route ! = 'Drive safely / Be careful!').

près.etymology: Inherited from Old French pres ('near, close by'), from Classical Latin pressus ('pressed together, compact, close'), past participle of premere ('to press'), used adverbially in Late Latin (pressum 'closely').

précaution.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (late 14th–15th c.) from Late Latin praecautiōnem (nominative praecautiō, 'advance guard against danger, forewarning'), derived from Classical Latin praecavēre (past participle praecautus, 'to guard against beforehand, take care in advance'), composed of prae- ('before, in advance') + cavēre ('to beware, take heed').

history.meaning: to guard against beforehand, beware in advance
measure taken to prevent harm or indiscretion

précaution.notes: Often used in plural diplomatic/agency idioms like prendre des précautions oratoires ('to cushion bad news with diplomatic phrasing / disclaimers')—a staple skill for Parisian talent agents.

rootFamily.gloss: security deposit, guarantee, bail (from same Latin cavēre)

précieux.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 11th–12th century (Old French precios) from Classical Latin pretiosus ('of great value, costly, dear'), derived from pretium ('price, worth, value').

history.meaning: valuable, precious; affected in speech or manner

cognates.meaning: steep cliff face; brink of disaster

précipice.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (15th c.) from Classical Latin praecipitium ('a steep place, sheer drop; a falling headlong'), derived from praeceps (genitive praecipitis, 'headfirst, headlong, steep'), an exocentric compound of prae- ('before, forward') + caput ('head')—literally 'head-foremost'.
précipice.notes: Masculine noun (un précipice), despite ending in -ice; figuratively au bord du précipice ('on the brink of disaster/bankruptcy') is a frequent dramatic trope when ASK faces financial ruin.

cognates.meaning: to cause suddenly; to separate from solution

précipiter.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th c.) from Classical Latin praecipitāre ('to throw or cast down headlong, plunge, hasten'), denominative verb from praeceps, praecipitis ('headfirst, headlong'), composed of prae- ('forward, ahead') + caput ('head').

history.meaning: to hurl headfirst, cast down; to hurry on
to cast into an abyss; to accelerate rashly

précipiter.notes: Transitive précipiter means 'to hasten/trigger prematurely' (ne précipitons pas les choses = let's not rush things), whereas reflexive se précipiter means 'to dash, bolt, or scramble' somewhere.

précis.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–16th century from Classical Latin praecisus ('cut off short, abridged, brief, exact'), past participle of praecidere ('to cut off in front, cut short', from prae- 'before, in front' + caedere 'to cut').

history.meaning: strictly defined, exact, precise (adj.); concise summary textbook (noun)

précisément.etymology: Formed in Middle French (late 14th c.) from the feminine adjective précise ('exact, strictly defined', borrowed from Classical Latin praecīsus, 'cut off short, abridged', past participle of praecīdere, from prae- 'in front' + caedere 'to cut') + adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin ablative mente, 'with a ... mind').
précisément.notes: Note the acute accent added on the e of précise before -ment (précis -> précise -> précisément), matching a small closed class of French adverbs like profondément and énormément.

prédateur.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (16th c., initially in the sense 'pillager, plunderer') from Classical Latin praedātōrem (nominative praedātor, 'plunderer, pillager, hunter'), agent noun from praedārī ('to plunder, take booty, catch prey'), from praeda ('booty, spoil, game caught in the chase'), from archaic *prae-heda ('what is seized beforehand', root *gʰed- 'to seize'). The zoological and figurative 'predator' senses spread in the 20th century via English.

history.meaning: plunderer (16th c.); carnivorous hunter or exploitative abuser (20th c.)

prédateur.notes: Shares its Latin root praeda with the inherited French word proie ('prey'), showing the classic contrast between popular phonetic evolution (praeda -> proie) and learned borrowing (prédateur; feminine prédatrice).

rootFamily.gloss: prey, quarry (inherited doublet from Latin praeda)

préférer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin praeferre ('to carry in front, hold forth, place before in esteem, choose rather'), compound of prae- ('before, in front') + ferre ('to bear, carry').

history.meaning: to bear before -> to value more highly, prefer

préféré.etymology: Past participle of préférer ('to prefer'), used as an adjective and noun meaning 'favorite, best-liked'.

prémédité.etymology: Past participle adjective of préméditer, borrowed in Middle French (15th–16th c.) from Classical Latin praemeditātus, participle of the deponent verb praemeditārī ('to think over beforehand, rehearse mentally, deliberate in advance'), composed of prae- ('before, in advance') + meditārī ('to ponder, reflect upon, practice'), from PIE *med- ('to measure, consider').

history.meaning: to ponder or rehearse in advance

prémédité.notes: Originally a legal term distinguishing homicide avec préméditation ('first-degree/premeditated murder') from crimes of passion, it is widely used ironically in everyday speech for calculated social or PR maneuvers (un coup médiatique prémédité).

prénom.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (originally explaining the Roman praenomen) from Classical Latin praenomen ('first or personal name placed before the family clan name nomen'), compound of prae- ('before') + nomen ('name'); adopted during the French Revolution and modern civil registration to replace nom de baptême ('baptismal name').

history.meaning: fore-name placed before the family name

cognates.meaning: to worry, concern; formerly to occupy first
to absorb the mind; originally to seize beforehand

préoccuper.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th–16th c.) from Classical Latin praeoccupāre ('to seize beforehand, anticipate, take possession of first'), composed of prae- ('before') + occupāre ('to seize, take hold of', from ob- + capere 'to take'). Figuratively applied to seizing or biasing the mind in advance, whence Modern French 'to absorb anxiously, worry'.

history.meaning: to seize beforehand, take prior possession of
to bias the mind beforehand; to absorb with worry

préoccuper.notes: Nuance alert: English preoccupied usually just means 'distracted/lost in thought', whereas French préoccuper and être préoccupé carry a strong emotional charge of 'to worry / to be anxious' (Ça me préoccupe beaucoup = That really worries me); se préoccuper de means 'to care about / attend to'.

préparation.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin praeparationem (nominative praeparatio, 'a making ready beforehand'), derived from praeparare ('to prepare').

history.meaning: preparation, readiness, compounded medicine or culinary mixture

préparer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin praeparare ('to make ready beforehand, equip, fit out'), compound of prae- ('beforehand') + parare ('to make ready, procure').

cognates.meaning: state of being present; stage charisma

présence.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in Old French (presence, 12th c.) from Classical Latin praesentia ('a being at hand, presence in person; immediate efficacy'), abstract noun from praesēns, praesentis ('at hand, immediate, in person'), participle of praeesse ('to be before, be at hand, preside over'), from prae- ('before') + esse ('to be').

history.meaning: being at hand in person; immediate readiness

présence.notes: In French theater and cinema, avoir de la présence (or une présence à l'écran) is high praise for an actor's magnetic screen charisma; acte de présence (faire acte de présence) means making a brief obligatory appearance at an event.

présent.etymology: Inherited/adapted in Old French (present, late 11th c.) from Classical Latin praesentem (nominative praesēns, 'being before one, at hand, in person, immediate'), formed as the present participle of praeesse ('to be in front of, be at hand'), composed of prae- ('before, in front') + sēns (archaic participial stem of esse 'to be', from PIE *h₁sónts).
présent.notes: Watch the false-friend contrast with actuel ('current, present-day'): both à présent ('now') and actuellement ('currently') refer to the present time, whereas un présent ('a gift', derived via en présent = 'brought into someone's presence') is elevated/literary compared to everyday cadeau.

présentation.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (presentacion, 12th–13th c., originally ecclesiastical and legal) from Late Latin praesentātiōnem (nominative praesentātiō, 'a placing before, exhibition'), noun of action from Classical Latin praesentāre ('to place before the eyes, exhibit, show immediately'), from praesēns ('present, at hand').

history.meaning: social introduction; display, pitch, or screening

présentation.notes: Crucial social false friend: in plural, faire les présentations means 'to introduce people to each other' (NOT 'to give slideshows'), whereas English 'introduction' of a person is never *une introduction in French!

présenter.etymology: Inherited/adapted in Old French (presenter, late 11th c., 'to offer formally, bring into someone's presence') from Classical Latin praesentāre ('to place before, show, exhibit in person'), denominative verb from praesēns, praesentis ('at hand, before one's eyes').

history.meaning: to place before, show in person, exhibit
to bring before a lord; to proffer a gift

présenter.notes: Essential learner rule: to 'introduce' someone in French is ALWAYS présenter quelqu'un (Je te présente mon agent) and reflexively se présenter ('to introduce oneself / show up / run for office')—never *introduire, which sounds awkward or anatomically suggestive!

cognates.meaning: to presume; to boast, show off
to suppose on probability; to take liberties

présumer.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (presumer, 12th–13th c.) from Classical Latin praesūmere ('to take beforehand, anticipate, take for granted, dare'), composed of prae- ('beforehand, in advance') + sūmere ('to take, take up', itself contracted from sub- + emere 'to take, buy'). In Late Latin Jurists it acquired the evidentiary meaning 'to infer or suppose prior to proof'.

history.meaning: to take in advance, anticipate; to dare, suppose
to dare overconfidently; to suppose by conjecture

présumer.notes: Watch construction differences: transitive présumer que ('to assume/presume that', or juridical présumé innocent) vs. intransitive présumer de ses forces ('to overestimate one's own strength'). Also avoid using *assumer for 'to suppose'—French présumer/supposer translate English 'assume'!

cognates.meaning: claimant to a throne or title

prétendant.etymology: Substantivized present participle of prétendre ('to lay claim to, aspire to'), attested from the 16th century first for a dynastic claimant to a crown or office, and from the 17th century (classic Molière/salon usage) for a romantic suitor aspiring to a woman's hand in marriage. Ultimately from Latin praetendere ('to stretch forth, hold out before').

history.meaning: claimant to a title or throne (16th c.); romantic suitor (17th c.)

prétendant.notes: Covers three distinct English nouns depending on context: a romantic 'suitor/admirer', a royal 'pretender' (prétendant au trône), or a 'contender' for an award or film role (prétendant à la Palme d'or / au César).

rootFamily.gloss: to claim, assert; to aspire to

cognates.meaning: to feign, make believe; formerly to lay claim

prétendre.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (late 14th c.) from Classical Latin praetendere ('to stretch forth in front, hold before as a screen, allege as an excuse or claim'), remodeled on native tendre ('to stretch'). Composed of prae- ('in front, before') + tendere ('to stretch, aim'), from PIE *ten- ('to stretch').

history.meaning: to stretch out before; to put forward as a claim or screen
to lay claim to, aspire to; to assert as true

prétendre.notes: Classic false friend (#1 trap for anglophones): prétendre means 'to claim, maintain, or assert' (Il prétend être innocent = He claims to be innocent) or 'to aspire to' (prétendre à un rôle); to say 'to pretend / make believe', use faire semblant!

cognates.meaning: ostensible reason hiding the real motive

prétexte.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (16th c.) from Classical Latin praetextum / praetextus ('outward ornament, cloak, ostensible reason, excuse'), derived from praetexere (past participle praetextus, 'to weave in front, border a garment with a purple stripe, disguise, allege as a cover'), composed of prae- ('in front') + texere ('to weave'), from PIE *teks- ('to weave, fabricate'). Literally 'a woven front or decorative border masking what lies behind'.

history.meaning: to weave a border in front; to cloak or disguise
ornamental border (as on the toga praetexta); outward excuse
alleged reason concealing the true motive

prétexte.notes: Etymologically related to texte and textile ('something woven in front as a cover'), not to prétendre! Memorize the high-frequency prepositional phrases sous prétexte de + infinitive and sous prétexte que + indicative/subjunctive ('on the pretext that...').

rootFamily.gloss: to give as a pretext or excuse

prévenant.etymology: Present participial adjective of prévenir, borrowed from Classical Latin praevenīre ('to come before, anticipate'), from prae- ('before, in front') + venīre ('to come'). In 17th-century classical French, anticipating another person's wishes before they even needed to ask gave rise to the social sense 'considerate, obliging, attentive'.

history.meaning: anticipating, favorably disposing (first in theological grace, then manners)
thoughtful, considerate, attentive to others' needs

prévenant.notes: False-friend alert: unlike English 'preventive', prévenant describes a warm, attentive host or assistant who anticipates your needs; for 'preventive', French uses préventif.

prévenir.etymology: Learned 15th-century borrowing from Classical Latin praevenīre ('to come before, anticipate, forestall'), composed of prae- ('before') + venīre ('to come'), conjugated in French on the irregular pattern of venir. From 'acting ahead of an event' branched both 'to forestall' and the dominant modern conversational sense 'to notify or warn in advance'.

history.meaning: to anticipate, act ahead of, forestall
to warn, let someone know; formally, to prevent

prévenir.notes: Classic false friend: in everyday dialogue (e.g., 'Préviens-moi quand il arrive !'), prévenir means 'let me know' or 'warn me', not 'prevent' (which is empêcher, save in proverbs like 'mieux vaut prévenir que guérir').

prévoir.etymology: Formed in the 13th–15th century (remodeling Old French porveoir after Latin praevidere) from prefix pré- (Latin prae- 'beforehand') + voir ('to see', from Latin videre).

history.meaning: to see beforehand, foresee, plan for

prêt.etymology: Represents two related words: (1) adjective prêt ('ready, prepared'), inherited from Old French prest < Late Latin praestus ('at hand, ready, prompt', from Classical adverb praesto 'here, at hand'); and (2) masculine noun un prêt ('a loan'), deverbal from prêter ('to lend', from Classical Latin praestare 'to stand surety for, furnish, lend').

history.meaning: at hand, ready; to furnish or lend
ready (adj.); loan of money or goods (noun)

prêter.etymology: Inherited via Old French prester from Vulgar Latin *praestāre, continuing Classical Latin praestāre ('to stand before, excel, guarantee, furnish, supply'), formed from prae- ('before, in front') + stāre ('to stand'). In Late Latin legal and commercial usage, 'to furnish or supply' narrowed to 'to advance on loan'. Pre-consonantal s-loss is marked by the circumflex ê.

history.meaning: to stand before, guarantee, furnish, provide
to lend; to attribute or lend oneself to

prêter.notes: Notice the circumflex in prêter, preserving the memory of Old French prester (still audible in learned relatives like prestation 'performance/benefit'); also distinguish prêter ('to lend') from emprunter ('to borrow').

psychiatre.etymology: Nineteenth-century scientific formation modeled on German Psychiater (coined alongside Psychiatrie in 1808 by physician Johann Christian Reil), built from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, 'breath, soul, mind') + ἰατρός (iatrós, 'physician, healer', from ἰᾶσθαι 'to heal'). Entered French medical usage in the mid-19th century as a replacement for aliéniste.
psychiatre.notes: In casual Parisian speech (and constantly in Dix pour cent), both psychiatre and psychologue/psychanalyste are clipped to le/la psy; pronounce every consonant at the start (/psi.kjatʁ/).

pub.etymology: Twentieth-century colloquial apocope (clipping) of la publicité ('advertising, commercial'), retaining the feminine gender of the full noun. Ultimately traces back to Latin pūblicus ('of the people, public', earlier poplicus from populus 'people'). Popularized in postwar French radio, television, and film-agency jargon.
pub.notes: Gender distinguishes two homographs: une pub (feminine, clipped from publicité) is an ad or commercial ('tourner une pub' = to shoot a commercial), whereas un pub (masculine, borrowed from English) is an Irish or British tavern!

public.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical Latin publicus ('pertaining to the people or state, common, open to all', altered from Old Latin poplicus under the influence of pubes 'adult population', from populus 'people').

history.meaning: of the people or state, open to all

publicitaire.etymology: Formed in mid-19th-century French from publicité ('advertising') + relational/agentive suffix -aire (< Latin -ārius), built ultimately on Latin pūblicus ('of the people, public', from populus). First attested as an adjective ('pertaining to commercial advertising') around the 1860s and soon substantivized for an advertising agent or copywriter.
publicitaire.notes: False-friend nuance: un(e) publicitaire is an advertising executive or ad-maker (like Mad Men), whereas a film/celebrity 'publicist' in French is called un(e) attaché(e) de presse.

cognates.meaning: media attention, public notice (borrowed from French)

publicité.etymology: Derived in the late 17th century from public + abstract noun suffix -ité (< Latin -itātem), initially a legal term meaning 'the public nature of proceedings or notoriety'. With the rise of mass-circulation newspapers in the 1820s–1830s, its meaning shifted to paid commercial announcements and advertising.

history.meaning: belonging to the people or state, public
state of being public; public legal notoriety
commercial advertising; print or broadcast ad

publicité.notes: Semi-false friend: English 'publicity' means press coverage or media attention (French médiatisation or coup de pub), whereas French publicité primarily means paid 'advertising' or 'commercials'.

publier.etymology: Inherited/semi-learned via Old French publier (12th c.) from Classical Latin pūblicāre ('to confiscate for public use, throw open to the public, make universally known'), verbal derivative of pūblicus ('of the people'). Shifted from 'proclaiming aloud by herald' to 'issuing in print' with the advent of the printing press, and today also 'posting online'.

history.meaning: to make public property, make known to the public
to publish (books/articles); to post on social media

publier.notes: In publishing and media, publier means to release a work publicly, whereas éditer means to act as publisher (un éditeur = a publisher, not a copy-editor!).

puce.etymology: Inherited via Old French pulce, puce from Vulgar Latin *pūlicem, syncopated (*pūlcem) accusative of Classical Latin pūlex ('flea'). Its tiny, lively nature inspired the affectionate pet name ma puce ('my little darling') by the 18th century and, in the late 1970s, a figurative calque/coinage for a silicon microchip (puce électronique).

history.meaning: flea; affectionate pet name; electronic microchip / SIM card

puce.notes: Packed with idioms: 'ma puce' ('sweetie'), 'marché aux puces' ('flea market', from garment-lined stalls), 'mettre la puce à l'oreille' ('to tip someone off / arouse suspicion'), and 'carte à puce' ('chip card').

rootFamily.gloss: to rid an animal of fleas; to debug code

puis.etymology: Inherited from Old French puis ('afterward, next, then'), from Vulgar Latin *postius, comparative adverb built on Classical Latin post ('behind, after').

puissance.etymology: Formed in Old French (poissance, puissance, 12th c.) from the adjective poissant / puissant ('powerful') + abstract suffix -ance (< Latin -antia). Displaced direct outcomes of Classical Latin potentia in everyday French, while potentia was later re-borrowed as the learned doublet potence and potentialité.

history.meaning: sovereign authority, military or spiritual might
power, strength, great nation, mathematical exponent

puissance.notes: Nuance vs. pouvoir: pouvoir emphasizes institutional authority or ability to act ('le pouvoir politique'), whereas puissance emphasizes sheer force, clout, intensity, or geopolitical stature ('une grande puissance', 'montée en puissance').

cognates.meaning: powerful, mighty (literary, via Old French; doublet of potent)

puissant.etymology: Inherited via Old French poissant, puissant (11th c., Roland) from Vulgar Latin *possientem, an analogical remodeling of Classical Latin potentem (accusative of potēns 'able, mighty', old present participle of posse 'to be able') reshaped after Vulgar Latin *possiō (for possum). Note how its stem puiss- still matches the subjunctive que je puisse!

history.meaning: mighty, strong in arms or lordship

morphemes.meaning: to be able (subjunctive/participial stem of pouvoir)

puissant.notes: Grammar insight: puissant shares the exact stem of the present subjunctive of pouvoir (que je puisse, que tu puisses), both descended from Vulgar Latin *possiō / *possiat.

pull.etymology: 20th-century clipping of pull-over ('knitted sweater pulled on over the head'), borrowed in the 1920s from English pullover (from pull + over).

pupitre.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (pupiltre -> pupitre) from Classical Latin pulpitum ('wooden platform, reading stand, lectern'—the same Latin word that gave English pulpit).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: pupitre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: pupitre

pur.etymology: Inherited from Old French pur ('unmixed, clean, spotless, sheer'), from Classical Latin purus ('clean, free from dirt or admixture, chaste, plain', from PIE *pewH- 'to cleanse, purify').

purement.etymology: Attested from 12th-century Old French purement, regularly formed from the feminine adjective pure (< Classical Latin pūrus, pūra 'clean, unmixed, spotless') + the Romance adverbial suffix -ment (< Classical Latin ablative mente 'with a [pure] mind/disposition'). Evolved from 'cleanly, without admixture' to 'strictly, exclusively'.

history.meaning: with a pure or unmixed mind/intent
cleanly, chastely, without condition or mixture

purement.notes: Very frequent in legal and contract negotiations in the emphatic binomial 'purement et simplement' ('purely and simply / outright / unconditionally', e.g. 'annuler purement et simplement un contrat').

putréfaction.etymology: Fourteenth-century learned medical borrowing from Late Latin putrefactiōnem (nominative putrefactiō, 'rotting, decay'), noun of action from Classical Latin putrefacere ('to make rotten, cause to decay'), a compound of putēre ('to stink, be rotten', akin to putris 'rotten' and pūs) + facere ('to make, do').

history.meaning: making rotten; process of rotting or decaying
organic corruption of humors or flesh

putréfaction.notes: High-register medical/scientific noun often deployed in French satire or theatrical exaggeration to express visceral disgust at moral or artistic decay; its everyday inherited cousin from the same root family is pourrir ('to rot').

rootFamily.gloss: to rot (inherited verb via Latin putrēscere)

pygmalion.etymology: Lowercase antonomasia from Latin Pygmaliōn, from Ancient Greek Πυγμαλίων (Pugmalíōn, itself adapted from a Phoenician royal name *Pumayyaton). In Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book X), Pygmalion is the Cypriot sculptor who falls in love with his ivory statue, brought to life by Venus. Cemented as 'star-making mentor' via Rousseau (1762) and G. B. Shaw's play Pygmalion (1913).

history.meaning: legendary king/sculptor of Cyprus in Greco-Roman myth
artist enamored of his own creation (Ovidian literary allusion)
mentor or director who molds and launches a protégé's career

pygmalion.notes: A quintessential French cinema and pop-music trope (think Serge Gainsbourg, Roger Vadim, or veteran directors/agents in Dix pour cent): 'jouer les pygmalions' means to mold a raw newcomer into a star—often with controlling undertones.

rootFamily.gloss: relating to a Pygmalion-like mentor relationship

pyjama.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th century from British English pyjamas, itself adopted under colonial rule in India from Hindustani/Urdu pāyjāma (پاجامہ) and Persian pāyjāma (پايجامه, 'loose leg garment, trousers tied at the waist'), a compound of Persian pāy ('foot, leg', cognate with Latin pēs) + jāma ('garment, clothing').

history.meaning: loose sleeping suit adopted by Europeans in India

pyjama.notes: Number trap for English speakers: whereas English 'pyjamas/pajamas' is plural ('my pajamas are...'), French un pyjama is masculine singular ('mon pyjama est propre', 'être en pyjama').

rootFamily.gloss: casual loungewear/tracksuit ('pilou' or indoor pyjama idiom: 'pyjama pilou')

pâle.etymology: Inherited from Old French pale / pasle ('wan, pallid, light-colored'), from Classical Latin pallidus ('pale, wan, colorless', derived from pallere 'to be pale', with an unetymological s inserted in Middle French that left the circumflex accent).

pâleur.etymology: Inherited/semi-learned via Old French palor, paleur (12th c.) from Classical Latin pallōrem (accusative of pallor, 'wan color, paleness, ashiness of fear or illness'), derived from the stative verb pallēre ('to be pale'). The modern circumflex â in pâleur is purely analogical, copied in the 18th century from pâle (Old French pasle < pallidus).

history.meaning: loss of facial color from emotion, faintness, or sickness

pâleur.notes: Like toutes les qualités en -eur (la chaleur, la peur, la couleur, except le bonheur/malheur/labeur/honneur), la pâleur is feminine ('une pâleur mortelle').

rootFamily.gloss: to turn pale, blanch; to fade

pâlir.etymology: Formed in Old French (palir, 12th c.) from the adjective pale / pâle ('pale') + inchoative suffix -ir (continuing Latin pallescere).

history.meaning: to turn pale, grow dim or fade

pâte.etymology: Inherited from Old French paste ('dough, kneaded mixture'), from Late Latin pasta ('dough, medicinal lozenge, paste'), borrowed from Ancient Greek paste ('barley porridge or salted mess of flour and sauce', from passein 'to sprinkle with salt').

pâtisser.etymology: Inherited from Old French pasticier ('to knead dough, make pies and pastries'), from Vulgar Latin *pasticiare, derived from Late Latin pasta ('dough').

pâtisserie.etymology: Attested in Middle French as patisserie (15th c.), derived from pâtissier ('maker of meat pies and dough crusts') + -erie, itself from Old French pastiz ('savory pie or crusted dish', modern pâté) < Vulgar Latin *pastīcium, from Late Latin pasta ('dough, paste') < Ancient Greek παστά (pastá, 'barley porridge'). The circumflex marks lost s before t.

history.meaning: dough/paste > food baked in a dough crust
craft and guild trade of baking pies, tarts, and crusts
sweet pastry, cake-baking art, or pastry shop

pâtisserie.notes: Triple polysemy in one word: la pâtisserie means (1) the art of pastry-making, (2) the pastry shop itself, and (3) une pâtisserie, an individual fancy cake—all cousin to pâtes ('pasta') and pâté!

rootFamily.gloss: savory pie or meat terrine (originally 'baked in pastry')

pâté.etymology: Inherited from Old French pasté ('meat or fish baked inside a pastry crust'), participial noun from pasteler / pâte ('dough', < Late Latin *pastatum); later extended to the seasoned minced meat mixture itself even when cooked in a terrine without crust, as well as a child's sandcastle (pâté de sable) or inkblot.

history.meaning: savory dish baked in a pastry crust
meat pie, savory meat spread (pâté), block of houses, sandcastle, inkblot

père.etymology: Inherited via Old French pedre (9th–11th c., Saint Alexis) and pere from Classical Latin patrem (accusative of pater, 'father, head of household'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr. Shows hallmark Gallo-Romance lenition: Latin stressed open a > è, and intervocalic -tr- > -dr- > -r- (contrast learned derivatives in patr-).
père.notes: Notice the classic French split between eroded popular inheritance (père) and intact Latin learned borrowings for adjectives and abstractions: paternel ('paternal'), paternité ('paternity'), patrie ('homeland').

rootFamily.gloss: fatherhood, paternity; authorship of a work

pédale.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–17th century (originally for the foot-keys of a pipe organ) from Italian pedale ('organ foot-lever'), substantivized from Classical Latin pedalis ('of the foot, a foot long'), derived from pes, pedis ('foot'); extended in the 19th century to piano, sewing-machine, and bicycle pedals.

history.meaning: organ, piano, bicycle, or automobile foot pedal

pédaler.etymology: Derived from pédale + verbal suffix -er. French borrowed pédale in the early 17th century from Italian pedale ('organ foot-lever'), substantivized from Latin pedālis ('of or belonging to the foot'), from pēs, pedis ('foot', PIE *pōds). Initially meant 'to work organ foot-pedals' before booming in the 1860s–1890s with velocipedes and bicycles.

history.meaning: pertaining to the foot > pipe-organ foot lever
to play the foot-pedals of a musical instrument
to pedal a bicycle; figuratively, to flounder effortfully

pédaler.notes: Beloved workplace idiom: 'pédaler dans la semoule' or 'pédaler dans la choucroute' ('to pedal in semolina/sauerkraut') means to spin one's wheels, get bogged down, or lose the plot in a chaotic situation!

pénible.etymology: Pénible is derived from peine, trouble or effort. The Académie dates the adjective to the twelfth century. It is not explained by simply assigning a generic meaning to the ending -ible.

cognates.meaning: from Old French peine and Latin poenālis

pénible.notes: Usually describes exhausting, tedious, or irritating situations (un voyage pénible, qu'il est pénible!) rather than sharp bodily pain (douloureux).

cognates.meaning: peril, grave danger (via Old French peril)
danger (with metathesis of r/l from perīculum)

péril.etymology: Inherited via Old French peril (10th–11th c.) from Classical Latin perīculum (syncopated Vulgar Latin *perīclum, 'trial, attempt, test, risk, danger'), formed with the instrumental suffix -culum on the verbal root *per- seen in experīrī ('to try, test') and perītus ('experienced'). Regular Gallo-Romance palatalization turned -cl- into -l/-il.

history.meaning: mortal danger, hazard at sea or in battle

péril.notes: Pronunciation & idiom: final -l IS pronounced (/pe.ʁil/, unlike outil or fusil); used in elevated idioms like 'mettre en péril' ('to jeopardize'), 'à ses risques et périls' ('at one's own risk'), and 'il n'y a pas péril en la demeure' ('there's no urgent crisis').

rootFamily.gloss: to perish (historically distinct from perīre, often associated in usage); expert (from same *per- root via perītus)

pétillant.etymology: Substantivized present participle of pétiller ('to crackle like fire, sparkle, fizz'), attested from the 15th century and formed from péter ('to burst, crack, pop, break wind', inherited from Classical Latin pēdere, PIE *pezd-) + the diminutive-frequentative verbal suffix -iller ('to make little popping sounds repeatedly').

history.meaning: to break wind, make a sharp cracking noise
to crackle (of sparks in a fire), to bubble and sparkle

morphemes.meaning: to pop, crack, burst (stem of péter)

pétillant.notes: Delightful etymological surprise: glamorous French 'pétillant' (bubbly wine, sparkling eyes, or a vivacious actress—'elle est pétillante !') and 'pétard' ('firecracker') both come from péter ('to pop / fart')!

rootFamily.gloss: to sparkle, fizz, bubble with energy
to burst, pop, snap; (colloquial) to fart

pétrir.etymology: Inherited from Old French pestrir ('to knead dough'), from Late/Vulgar Latin *pisturire, built on Classical Latin pistura ('pounding grain, baking') and pistor ('baker', originally 'grain-pounder', from pinsere 'to crush, knead').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: pétrir (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: pétrir

pétrir.notes: The wooden kneading trough in a traditional French bakery is called **le pétrin** (whence the idiom *être dans le pétrin*, 'to be in a sticky jam').

pôle.etymology: Borrowed in late 14th-century Middle French (pole) from Classical Latin polus ('end of an axis, celestial pole, sky'), itself from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos, 'pivot, axis around which the heavens revolve'), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- ('to turn, revolve', cognate with wheel and cycle). Extended in late-20th-century French administration and business to 'center of activity, division, hub'.

history.meaning: pivot, axis of rotation, celestial pole
geographical or magnetic pole; point of attraction
pole; corporate division, institutional cluster, or hub

pôle.notes: Essential modern French corporate/agency buzzword: where English says 'department', 'division', or 'hub', French offices say le pôle ('le pôle fiction', 'le pôle talents', 'le pôle juridique', and formerly 'Pôle emploi' for the national job agency).

rootFamily.gloss: to polarize, focus all attention on

qu'est-ce.etymology: Qu'est-ce contracts que ('what', from Latin quid) + est ('is', from Latin est) + ce ('that/it', from Latin ecce hoc), forming the standard spoken French opening for 'what' questions (*qu'est-ce qui*, *qu'est-ce que*).
qu'est-ce.notes: Pronounced /kɛs/ as a single smooth syllable before *qui* or *que*.

qu'est-ce que.etymology: This question expression combines interrogative que, the verb est and the demonstrative ce, followed by que. The Académie treats the interrogative construction under que. Its pieces became a familiar way to introduce a question about an object.
qu'est-ce que.notes: Pronounced smoothly as two syllables (/kɛsk(ə)/), it lets French ask 'what...?' while keeping comfortable subject-verb word order (Qu'est-ce que tu fais? vs. formal Que fais-tu?).

cognates.meaning: what is it that... (parallel cleft construction)

qu'est-ce qui.etymology: Grammaticalized interrogative cleft periphrasis forged across Old and Middle French (12th–16th c.) to preserve subject-verb word order and disambiguate grammatical case: interrogative pronoun que ('what', < Latin quid) + est ('is', < est) + demonstrative ce ('this/it', Old French ço < Vulgar Latin *ecce hoc) + subject relative pronoun qui ('which/that', < Latin quī), literally 'what is this that [does X]?'.

history.meaning: emphatic cleft question: 'what is it that...'

qu'est-ce qui.notes: Crucial grammar contrast: use qu'est-ce qui when 'what' is the SUBJECT of the following verb ('Qu'est-ce qui se passe ?' = What is happening?), and qu'est-ce que when 'what' is the OBJECT ('Qu'est-ce que tu veux ?' = What do you want?). Pronounced briskly as /kɛs.ki/.

quai.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–13th century from Norman-Picard cai / quai ('earth embankment, stone wharf along a river or harbor', corresponding to Central Old French chai 'wine cellar'), from Gaulish *kagion ('hedge, wattled enclosure, retaining bank', cognate with Welsh cae 'enclosure, hedge').

history.meaning: stone embankment, harbor quay, railway station platform

qualification.etymology: Borrowed or derived in 15th–16th-century Middle French from Medieval Scholastic Latin quālificātiō ('attribution of a quality or legal characterization'), action noun from quālificāre ('to attribute a quality to'), built from Classical Latin quālis ('of what sort or kind') + -ficāre (combining form of facere 'to make'). Extended from legal/logical classification to professional credentials and sports rounds.

history.meaning: attribution of a defining property or quality
act of characterizing or naming the legal nature of an act
professional skill/credential; legal classification; sports qualifying

qualification.notes: In French labor and contract law (including film-crew conventions collectives), la qualification denotes an employee's official job grade/classification, while in criminal law la qualification des faits means the exact legal charge applied to an act.

rootFamily.gloss: to characterize, describe as; to qualify

qualité.etymology: Learned 12th-century Old French borrowing from Classical Latin quālitātem (nominative quālitās, 'property, nature, condition'), famously coined by Cicero (Academica 1.24–25) from quālis ('of what kind', PIE pronominal stem *kʷo-) + -tās to translate Plato's and Aristotle's Greek philosophical neologism ποιότης (poiótēs, 'what-sort-ness'). Developed secondary senses of 'noble rank', 'virtue', and 'official capacity'.

history.meaning: inherent property, moral attribute, noble station
excellence, personal virtue ('une grande qualité'), official capacity ('en qualité de')

qualité.notes: Usage tip: in plural portrait descriptions ('ses qualités et ses défauts'), une qualité specifically means a positive character trait or 'virtue' (its antonym is un défaut, 'flaw'), whereas 'en qualité d'agent' means 'in the capacity of agent'.

rootFamily.gloss: to describe as, characterize; to qualify
which, what kind of (inherited outcome of Latin quālis)

quand.etymology: Quand continues Latin quando, when. The Académie records the French word from the eleventh century.
quand.notes: In liaison before a vowel, final -d devoices to /t/: quand il arrive (/kɑ̃.t‿i.l‿a.ʁiv/); also remember French uses the future tense after temporal quand when referring to the future (quand tu viendras).

cognates.meaning: even so, all the same (parallel concessive idiom)
even when / all the same (quand + metipsimus cognates)

quand même.etymology: Concessive adverbial phrase crystallized in the 18th–19th centuries by ellipsis of classical conditional clauses introduced by quand même + conditional ('even if / even though [he should refuse]...' -> 'quand même !', 'even so, all the same!'). Combines quand (< Latin quandō 'when') + même (Old French meïsme < Vulgar Latin *metipsimus, emphatic superlative of *metipse 'his very self').

history.meaning: all the same, anyway, still; standalone exclamation ('honestly! / wow!')

quand même.notes: One of the most quintessentially French conversational discourse markers: besides 'anyway / all the same' ('Merci quand même !'), standalone 'Quand même !' expresses polite disbelief, reluctant concession, or relief ('Ah, quand même !' = 'Well, about time!'). Pronounced /kɑ̃.mɛm/ (silent d).

quarante.etymology: Inherited from Old French quarante ('forty'), from Vulgar Latin *quarranta, contracted from Classical Latin quadraginta ('forty', derived from quattuor 'four').

quarante-cinq.etymology: Additive decimal compound joining quarante ('forty', via Old French quarante from Vulgar Latin *quadrāginta, reduced from Classical Latin quadrāgintā 'four tens') and cinq ('five', via Old French cinc from Vulgar Latin *cīnque, dissimilated from Classical Latin quīnque, PIE *pénkʷe). Since the 1990 orthographic guidelines (and traditionally for compound tens), linked by a hyphen without et.
quarante-cinq.notes: Pronunciation & culture: final -q of cinq is pronounced here (/ka.ʁɑ̃t.sɛ̃k/); as a masculine noun, un quarante-cinq tours ('a 45-rpm vinyl single') remains a classic French music-industry term.

quarante-deux.etymology: Additive compound numeral uniting quarante ('forty', via Old French quarante from Vulgar Latin *quadrāginta < Classical Latin quadrāgintā, 'four tens', related to quattuor) and deux ('two', via Old French dous, deus from Classical Latin duōs, masculine accusative plural of duo, PIE *dwóh₁). Directly juxtaposed with a hyphen, unlike 41 (quarante et un).
quarante-deux.notes: Pattern reminder: French uses 'et' only before un/onze (quarante et un), jumping straight to a hyphen for 2–9 (quarante-deux, quarante-trois...); final -x is silent unless followed by a vowel liaison (/z/).

quarante-quatre.etymology: Compound cardinal numeral formed from quarante ('forty') + quatre ('four').

quart.etymology: Inherited from Old French quart ('fourth; a fourth part, quarter'), from Classical Latin quartus ('fourth', ordinal of quattuor 'four').

history.meaning: one-fourth, quarter (of an hour, pound, etc.); sailor's watch

quartier.etymology: Inherited from Old French quartier ('one-fourth part of something divided in four; one of the four administrative wards of a town; military camp quarters'), from Classical Latin quartarius ('fourth part of a measure, gill'), derived from quartus ('fourth').

history.meaning: quarter slice (of fruit or moon), city neighborhood/district, military quarters

quatorze.etymology: Quatorze descends from Latin quattuordecim, built from the words for four and ten. It is recorded in French from the twelfth century.
quatorze.notes: Le Quatorze Juillet (Bastille Day) and Louis Quatorze (Louis XIV, illustrating how French uses cardinal numbers from II upward for monarchs) make quatorze culturally iconic.

quatre.etymology: Inherited from Old French quatre ('four'), from Vulgar Latin *quattor for Classical Latin quattuor ('four', from PIE *kwetwores, cognate with English four).

cognates.meaning: eighty + ten (structural Celtic vigesimal parallel: dek warn-ugent / pevar-ugent)
ninety (decimal outcome of Latin nōnāgintā, cf. Belgian/Swiss nonante)

quatre-vingt-dix.etymology: Surviving fossil of the medieval Old French vigesimal (base-20) counting system—widely attributed to Gaulish/Celtic substratum or Norman reinforcement—combining quatre ('four' < Latin quattuor) × vingt ('twenty' < Latin vīgintī) + dix ('ten' < Latin decem), literally 'four-twenties-ten'. In Standard France French, it prevailed in the 17th century over Old French nonante (< Latin nōnāgintā).

history.meaning: four scores and ten (90, competing with nonante)

quatre-vingt-dix.notes: Spelling & regional rule: quatre-vingts ('80') takes an -s on vingt, but drops that -s as soon as another number follows: quatre-vingt-dix! Meanwhile, Belgium, Switzerland, and the DRC sensibly keep the inherited decimal nonante.

rootFamily.gloss: Royal 13th-century Paris hospital for 300 ('fifteen-twenties') blind veterans

quatre-vingts.etymology: Inherited from Old French quatre vinz ('four twenties, eighty'), a vestige of the vigesimal (base-20) counting system widespread in medieval French (which also produced l'hôpital des Quinze-Vingts '300' and formerly six-vingts '120'), often attributed to Gaulish/Celtic or Norman substrate influence.

quatrième.etymology: Formed in Old French (quatrieme, 12th–13th c., gradually replacing older ordinal quart) from quatre ('four') + ordinal suffix -ième.

que.etymology: Several older words converged in French que. Interrogative que continues Latin quid; relative que continues quem; the connecting conjunction developed from quia. These histories help explain why one spelling has different grammatical jobs.

history.meaning: phonological merger into one unstressed form

que.notes: Unlike English, French NEVER omits conjunction que ('that'): Je pense qu'il a raison ('I think [that] he's right').

quel.etymology: Quel descends from Latin qualis, of what kind or nature. The Académie records the French word from the tenth century.

history.meaning: of what kind, what sort of

quel.notes: All four forms (quel, quelle, quels, quelles) sound identical (/kɛl/) before a consonant, differing only in liaison before vowels (/kɛl.z‿/ in the plural) and in written agreement.

quelqu'un.etymology: Quelqu’un combines the indefinite quelque and un. The Académie records the compound from the thirteenth century. The apostrophe marks the joining of these two pieces.
quelqu'un.notes: Before an adjective, quelqu'un links with de + masculine singular: quelqu'un de gentil ('someone kind'), quelqu'un d'autre ('someone else').

quelque.etymology: Quelque was formed from quel and the conjunction que. The Académie records the combination from the eleventh century.

cognates.meaning: some, a few (followed by singular in Italian!)

quelque.notes: In everyday French, plural quelques + plural noun means 'a few' (quelques minutes, quelques amis); invariable adverbial quelque before a number means 'approximately' (quelque cent personnes).

quelque chose.etymology: Grammaticalized in Old and Middle French (13th–15th c.) from the indefinite determiner quelque ('some, whatever', formed in Old French from quel < Latin quālis 'of what kind' + que < quid/quam) + the feminine noun chose ('thing', inherited from Classical Latin causa 'cause, legal case, affair', which completely displaced Latin rēs for 'thing' across Romance).

history.meaning: whatever matter, some affair or thing (originally feminine)

quelque chose.notes: Two classic traps: (1) even though une chose is feminine, the pronoun quelque chose is MASCULINE and requires de before an adjective: 'quelque chose de beau / d'intéressant' (never *quelque chose belle!); (2) in fast speech it contracts to 'kekchose' (/kɛk.ʃoz/).

question.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin quaestionem (nominative quaestio, 'a seeking, inquiry, judicial investigation, subject of debate'), derived from quaerere, quaesitum ('to seek, ask, inquire').

questionnaire.etymology: Derived within French from question ('question, inquiry', inherited via Old French from Classical Latin quaestiōnem, accusative of quaestiō 'seeking, investigation', from quaerere 'to seek, ask') + the collective/instrumental noun suffix -aire (from Latin -ārium). Originally denoting a judicial torture official or a scholastic compendium of questions, it acquired its modern administrative sense of a printed survey list in the 19th century.

history.meaning: series of methodical questions, survey form

questionnaire.notes: Masculine noun (un questionnaire); English borrowed the word directly from French in the late 19th century, retaining the double n.

qui.etymology: Relative qui continues Latin qui, while interrogative qui continues Latin quis. The Académie records the relative in the ninth century and the question word in the tenth; their modern spellings coincide.
qui.notes: Key French rule: unlike que (qu'), relative and interrogative qui NEVER elides before a vowel (la femme qui arrive, NOT *qu'arrive)!

quiche.etymology: Borrowed in the early 19th century from Lorrain regional French quiche (attested at Nancy in 1605 as cuische), itself adapted from Rhine Franconian / Lorrain German Küchel or Küche, diminutive of German Kuchen ('cake, tart'), from Old High German kuocho, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *kōkō. In late-20th-century colloquial French, une quiche developed the slang figurative sense 'hopeless amateur, incompetent fool', alongside food metaphors like être une tarte.

history.meaning: savory open-faced custard tart of Lorraine

quiche.notes: In Dix pour cent / informal Parisian speech, être une quiche (en quelque chose) means 'to be hopeless/useless (at something)', much like calling someone a total dud.

quincaillerie.etymology: Formed in the 17th century (by assimilation of initial c- to qu- from earlier clincaillerie, 16th c.) from clincaille / quincaille ('small clinking articles of iron, copper, or tinware'), derived from Middle Dutch klinken ('to clink, ring, jingle', cognate with English clink).

history.meaning: jingle of small metal wares -> hardware, hardware store

quinoa.etymology: Borrowed through Spanish quinua / quinoa from Classical Quechua kinwa (also kinuwa), the indigenous Andean name for Chenopodium quinoa, a domesticated pseudocereal cultivated for millennia around Lake Titicaca and the Altiplano. First recorded in French travel and botanical accounts (as quinua in the 16th–18th centuries), it entered everyday metropolitan French in the late 20th century with health-food and trendy Parisian bistro culture.

history.meaning: Andean goosefoot plant and its edible grain

quinoa.notes: Masculine noun in French (du quinoa) and pronounced /ki.nɔ.a/ (kee-no-ah), unlike the English pronunciation /ˈkiːnwɑː/; in Parisian satire it often stereotypes trendy agency lunches.

quinzaine.etymology: Formed in Old French (quinzaine, 12th century) from quinze ('fifteen', inherited from Classical Latin quīndecim 'fifteen', from quīnque 'five' + decem 'ten') + the collective/approximative feminine suffix -aine (from Latin -ēna, feminine plural/collective of distributive numerals in -ēnī). Because inclusive counting in medieval French treated two weeks from Sunday to Sunday as fifteen days, une quinzaine became the standard idiom for a fortnight.

history.meaning: set of fifteen; period of fifteen days (inclusive two weeks)

quinzaine.notes: Just as huit jours means 'a week', une quinzaine (or quinze jours) means 'two weeks' due to traditional inclusive counting—and la Quinzaine des cinéastes is a famous Cannes sidebar!

quinze.etymology: Inherited from Old French quinze ('fifteen'), from Vulgar Latin *quindece, contracted from Classical Latin quindecim ('fifteen', compound of quinque 'five' + decem 'ten').

cognates.meaning: free from obligation; even (as in 'call it quits')

quitte.etymology: Inherited from Old French quite ('discharged of an obligation, exempt, free'), a medieval legal borrowing adapted from Medieval Latin quītum / quiētum, accusative of Classical Latin quiētus ('at rest, peaceful, free from trouble'; in medieval law 'cleared of a claim or debt'), past participle of quiēscere ('to rest, keep quiet'). From clearing a financial debt arose the reciprocal sense être quitte ('to be even, square').

history.meaning: legally discharged of debt or feudal obligation

quitte.notes: Besides nous sommes quittes ('we're even'), watch for the high-frequency idiom quitte à + infinitive ('even if it means having to...').

cognates.meaning: to stop, leave, resign (borrowed from Old French)
to calm; to grant a receipt for debt

quitter.etymology: Derived in Old French (quiter, 11th–12th centuries) from the legal adjective quite ('free, discharged of obligation', from Medieval Latin quītus, Classical Latin quiētus 'at rest'). Originally meaning 'to release someone from a feudal duty or debt' and then 'to cede, surrender, abandon a claim or place', by Middle and Classical French it generalized into the standard transitive verb for leaving a person, room, or job.

history.meaning: to pacify; in medieval law, to release from a claim
to exempt, discharge, yield up, abandon
to leave (a place or person), hang up, take off clothing

quitter.notes: Grammar trap: quitter is strictly transitive and requires a direct object (quitter Paris, quitter son mari); on the phone, Ne quittez pas ! means 'Hold the line!'.

quoi.etymology: Quoi is the stressed descendant of Latin quid ('what?'), where Latin short i opened to e and diphthongised in stressed position through ei and oi to /kwa/.
quoi.notes: Used after prepositions (*avec quoi?*, *de quoi?*) or at the end of spoken questions (*C'était quoi?*).

quotidien.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old French (cotidian, later refashioned with Latinizing qu- as quotidien) from Classical Latin cotīdiānus / quotīdiānus ('daily, recurring every day, ordinary'), derived from the adverb cotīdiē / quotīdiē ('every day'), itself a compound of quot ('how many, as many as') + diēs ('day'). Its semantic trajectory runs from ecclesiastical 'daily bread' (pain quotidien) to modern everyday life and daily newspapers.

history.meaning: belonging to every day, daily, ordinary
daily, everyday; (as noun) daily life or daily newspaper

morphemes.meaning: as many days as, every day (Latin quotīdiē)

quotidien.notes: Pronounced /kɔ.ti.djɛ̃/ (silent u after q); unlike formal English 'quotidian', français quotidien is completely natural everyday vocabulary, and le quotidien means both 'daily life' and 'daily newspaper'.

rabat.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old/Middle French from rabattre ('to beat or fold back down, turn down, deduct from a price'); denotes a folded-down collar, clerical bands, or the top flap of an envelope, pocket, or binder.

history.meaning: folding flap (of an envelope or pocket), turned-down collar

rabat-joie.etymology: Verb-object exocentric compound attested since the 16th–17th centuries, formed from rabattre ('to beat down, lower, dampen', from Old French rabatre = re- + abatre, from Late Latin abbattuere 'to beat down') + joie ('joy, merriment', inherited from Old French joie, from Late Latin gaudia, neuter plural of Classical Latin gaudium 'inward joy'). Literally 'one who beats down joy', mirroring English 'killjoy' or 'spoilsport'.

history.meaning: event or person that dampens celebration, spoilsport

rabat-joie.notes: Traditionally invariable in the plural (des rabat-joie, though des rabat-joies exists under the 1990 spelling reform) and used as both a noun and an adjective (Arrête d'être si rabat-joie !).

rootFamily.gloss: to fold down, pull down, dampen

raccourci.etymology: Substantivized past participle (16th–17th century) of raccourcir ('to shorten': re- + accourcir, built on court 'short' < Classical Latin curtus).

cognates.meaning: from Latin curtus and Middle French courtault

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: raccourci (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: raccourci

raccourci.notes: Today **un raccourci** means both a cobbled alley shortcut (**prendre un raccourci**) and a keyboard shortcut (**un raccourci clavier**).

raccrocher.etymology: Formed in Middle French from iterative prefix r- / re- ('again, back') + accrocher ('to hang on a hook', from croc 'hook'); acquired the modern sense 'to hang up the telephone receiver' from hanging the earpiece back on its switchhook.

history.meaning: to hang back on a hook -> to hang up the phone

rachat.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (rachat, 12th century) from rachater / racheter ('to buy back, redeem'), paralleling achat from acheter. Ultimately reflects re- ('back, again') + Vulgar Latin *accaptāre ('to acquire, purchase', formed from ad- + Classical Latin captāre 'to strive to seize', frequentative of capere 'to take'). From medieval feudal redemption of land or captives, it evolved into modern corporate 'buyout' and 'repurchase'.

history.meaning: to acquire back, recover by payment
ransom, feudal right of redemption, moral atonement

rachat.notes: Essential business vocabulary in Dix pour cent (le rachat d'ASK = the buyout/acquisition of the agency): it covers buying out a company's shares even when the buyer never owned them before.

rootFamily.gloss: to buy back, buy out, redeem

racheter.etymology: Inherited from Old French rachater, racheter ('to buy back, ransom, redeem a soul'), composed of the iterative/restorative prefix re- (elided to r-) + achater (Modern French acheter 'to buy'), which derives from Vulgar Latin *accaptāre ('to acquire, obtain', from ad- + Classical Latin captāre 'to try to catch, seize', frequentative of capere). Its senses span commercial buyouts, buying a replacement, and moral redemption (se racheter).

history.meaning: to strive to seize → to acquire, buy
to ransom a captive, redeem pledged property or sin
to buy back, buy out a business, make amends (se racheter)

racheter.notes: Watch two key idiomatic uses: racheter une boîte ('to buy out/acquire a company') and the reflexive se racheter ('to make it up to someone / redeem oneself' after a blunder).

cognates.meaning: radish (from Latin rādīcem via French/Italian); radical

racine.etymology: Inherited from Old French racine (12th century), descending from Late or Vulgar Latin rādīcīna ('root, small root'), an extended suffixed derivative in -īna of Classical Latin rādīx, rādīcem ('plant root, base, origin'), from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds ('root, branch', cognate with English wort and root). The suffixed form *rādīcīna replaced the simplex rādīcem in Gallo-Romance to preserve phonetic substance.

history.meaning: root of a plant, foot of a mountain, origin
botanical root; hair root; linguistic or cultural origin

racine.notes: In actor styling and salon talk, se refaire les racines means 'to touch up one's hair roots', while prendre racine idiomatically means 'to stand waiting forever'.

cognates.meaning: to scrape, grate; to clear one's throat

raclure.etymology: Derived in Middle French (rascleure, 14th century) from racler ('to scrape, grate off') + the resultative suffix -ure (from Latin -ūra). Old French rascler descends from Vulgar Latin *rāsiculāre ('to scrape repeatedly'), formed via *rāsicāre from Classical Latin rāsus, past participle of rādere ('to scrape, shave, scratch'). Literally 'filings or filth scraped off the bottom', it shifted figuratively (like raclure de bidet) to 'vile scumbag'.

history.meaning: scrapings, shavings removed by a scraper

morphemes.meaning: result or waste product of an action

raclure.notes: Harsh derogatory register: calling an unscrupulous rival agent une raclure (short for raclure de fond de tiroir or raclure de bidet) equates them with scraped-off grime—stronger than salaud in contempt.

rootFamily.gloss: to scrape, grate, clear one's throat
heavy thrashing/beating; Alpine melted-cheese dish scraped onto plates

raconter.etymology: Formed in Old French (raconter, 11th–12th c.) from prefix re- + aconter ('to count up, reckon, relate in detail', from à + conter < Classical Latin computare 'to reckon, recount').

history.meaning: to recount in detail, narrate, tell a story

radiateur.etymology: Formed in the mid-19th century by French physicists and engineers from the stem of radier ('to radiate heat or light', from Classical Latin radiare < radius 'ray, spoke') + instrument suffix -teur.

history.meaning: heat-radiating heating unit or engine cooling radiator

cognates.meaning: wireless transmission, broadcast receiver or station

radio.etymology: Twentieth-century clipping of radiotélégraphie, radiotéléphonie, or radiodiffusion ('wireless broadcasting'), built with the scientific combining form radio- ('electromagnetic radiation, ray'), taken from Classical Latin radius ('spoke of a wheel, beam of light, rod'). Note that French also clipped radiographie ('X-ray image') to une radio, making the same feminine short form serve both media broadcasting and medical imaging.

history.meaning: wheel spoke, measuring rod, beam of light
wireless voice transmission by electromagnetic waves
radio broadcasting, station, receiver; X-ray radiograph

radio.notes: Feminine noun (la radio) whether it means 'radio station/broadcast' (passer à la radio 'to be on the radio' during a press tour) or 'medical X-ray' (passer une radio); by contrast, un radio is a ship's radio operator.

cognates.meaning: inflexible, stiff (learned borrowing from the same Latin source)

raide.etymology: Inherited via Old French reide, roide ('stiff, inflexible, steep, fierce') directly from Classical Latin rigidus ('stiff, numb, unbending, stern'), derived from rigēre ('to be stiff or numb'). Regular Gallo-Romance lenition and syncope reduced Latin rigidum to *regdu > reide > roide, whose diphthong split in Early Modern French between conservative spelling roide and Parisian pronunciation /ɛ/, standardized as raide. Rigide was later re-borrowed as a learned doublet.

history.meaning: stiff, hard, inflexible, numb with cold
stiff, tense, steep; (colloquial) broke, dead drunk, or harsh

raide.notes: Doublet of learned rigide; in conversational French, raide appears everywhere: être raide dingue de quelqu'un ('madly in love'), être raide ('stone broke' or 'stiff/uptight' on camera), and C'est un peu raide ! ('That's a bit harsh!').

raison.etymology: Inherited from Old French raison ('reckoning, account, faculty of thought, argument, justice, speech'), from Classical Latin rationem (nominative ratio, 'reckoning, calculation, account, faculty of judgment, motive', derived from reri, ratus 'to reckon, think').

history.meaning: faculty of reason, good sense, motive, rightness (avoir raison)

cognates.meaning: sensible, fair, moderate (borrowed from Old French)

raisonnable.etymology: Inherited from Old French raisonable, resonable (12th century), adapted from Classical Latin ratiōnābilis ('endowed with reason, rational'), reshaped under the phonological influence of Old French raison ('reason, reckoning, speech', inherited from Latin ratiōnem, accusative of ratiō 'calculation, account, faculty of reason', from rērī 'to reckon, think') + suffix -able (Latin -ābilis). It shifted from 'possessing rational thought' to 'sensible, moderate, fair'.

history.meaning: rational, equitable, in accordance with justice
sensible, level-headed, moderate (in conduct or price)

raisonnable.notes: Spelling tip: raison takes one n, whereas raisonner and raisonnable double the n; telling a client Soyons raisonnables is classic polite French negotiation for 'Let's be realistic'.

rootFamily.gloss: to reason, think through; bring someone to their senses
