cognates.meaning: to slow down (borrowed via French ralentir)
to soften, yield, slacken (ultimately from Latin lentus via Old French)

ralentir.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Classical French (17th century, replacing earlier alentir) from the prefix re- + a- (from Latin ad-) + the adjective lent ('slow', inherited from Classical Latin lentus 'pliable, viscous, sluggish, slow') + second-conjugation verbal suffix -ir. Originally used of slackening physical speed or ardor, it later furnished cinema terminology such as au ralenti ('in slow motion').

history.meaning: to slow down (transitively or intransitively), decelerate

ralentir.notes: Regular -ir verb (nous ralentissons); on a film set, le ralenti means 'slow motion' (tourner au ralenti), while vivre au ralenti means functioning in low gear.

rootFamily.gloss: slow motion; idle speed of an engine

rallumer.etymology: Formed in Old French (ralumer, 12th c.) from iterative prefix r- / re- ('again') + allumer ('to light, kindle').

history.meaning: to relight, rekindle, switch back on

ramener.etymology: Formed in Old French (ramener, 11th–12th c.) from prefix r- / re- ('back, again') + amener ('to bring, lead toward').

history.meaning: to bring back, lead back, restore

cognates.meaning: bitter, long-standing resentment (borrowed via Old French)

rancœur.etymology: Inherited from Old French rancor, rancuer ('bitterness, festering grudge'), borrowed from Late and Christian Latin rancor, rancōrem ('rancid smell or taste; figuratively, deep-seated spite or resentment', used by St. Jerome and Church Fathers), from Classical Latin rancēre ('to be rancid, stink'). The Modern French spelling rancœur (with œu) reflects a folk-etymological crossing with cœur ('heart'), reinterpreting festering bitterness as 'sickness of the heart'.

history.meaning: rancidness, staleness; (Christian Latin) moral bitterness, grudge
lingering bitterness or resentment after a disappointment or slight

rancœur.notes: Feminine noun (la rancœur, spelled with the œ ligature because speakers historically associated it with le cœur 'heart', even though its true root is rance 'rancid'); slightly more elevated and poignant than rancune ('petty grudge').

cognates.meaning: haphazard, chance (borrowed from Old French randon 'impetuous rush')
to run, race (from the same Germanic root)

randonnée.etymology: Feminine participial noun from Middle French randonner ('to run swiftly, course around'), derived from Old French randon ('impetuous rush, headlong speed', preserved in English at random), itself from Old Frankish *rant ('a running, swift course'; compare Old High German rennen 'to make run', English run). Originally a hunting term for the circuit a stag runs when pursued by hounds, it softened in the 19th century into a long recreational excursion or hike.

history.meaning: impetuous rush → to gallop or circle wildly (of hunted game)
long excursion on foot, horseback, bicycle, or skis; hike

morphemes.meaning: action or circuit spanned (feminine participial noun ending)

randonnée.notes: Colloquially clipped to une rando ('a hike'); remarkably, cozy French hiking (faire de la randonnée) and English 'random' both spring from the same medieval Frankish word for a wild headlong sprint!

rang.etymology: Inherited from Old French renc ('circle of spectators or combatants, row, line of soldiers'), borrowed from Frankish *hring ('ring, circle, assembly of warriors or judges standing in a circle', cognate with English ring).

history.meaning: circle, ring of men gathered for battle or council
circle -> line, row, tier, social rank

ranger.etymology: Derived in Old French (rengier, 12th c., 'to draw up troops in battle lines, arrange in rows') from renc / rang ('row, line, rank').

history.meaning: to line up in rows -> to put in order, tidy away, park

rapide.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–17th century from Classical Latin rapidus ('tearing away, rushing, swift, impetuous', originally describing a torrent or fire), derived from rapere ('to seize, snatch, carry off').

history.meaning: fast, swift, rapid (adj.); river rapids, express train (noun)

cognates.meaning: rapidly (root borrowed from Latin rapidus via French)

rapidement.etymology: Regularly formed in Early Modern French from the adjective rapide ('swift, fast', a 15th–16th-century learned borrowing from Classical Latin rapidus 'seizing, rushing, impetuous, swift', originally 'carrying away', from rapere 'to snatch, seize') + the adverbial suffix -ment (inherited from the Classical Latin ablative singular mente 'with a ... mind'). Unlike English 'rapidly', which sounds somewhat formal, rapidement is everyday French for 'quickly, soon'.

history.meaning: rushing, swift, snatching away (of currents or winds)
quickly, swiftly; briefly, in short order

rapidement.notes: In workplace French, On se voit rapidement ('Let's meet up soon / briefly') can mean either 'very soon' or 'just for a quick moment' depending on context.

rootFamily.gloss: to delight, snatch away (same Latin root rapere)

rappeler.etymology: Rappeler is a French derivative of appeler. The Académie records it from the eleventh century. The additional beginning can contribute the sense of calling again or calling back.

history.meaning: to call back; remind; (se rappeler) remember

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Anglo-Norman rapeler ('revoke/call back a law')!

rootFamily.gloss: reminder, callback, vaccine booster, curtain call

rappeler.notes: Subtle grammar point: se rappeler takes a DIRECT object in standard grammar (je me rappelle cette histoire, je me le rappelle, lit. 'I recall it to myself'), unlike se souvenir de!

cognates.meaning: harmonious connection (borrowed from French); report (from Old French raporter)

rapport.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (raport, 13th century) from raporter (Modern French rapporter 'to bring back, yield, relate, connect'), itself from re- ('back') + aporter (apporter 'to bring', from Classical Latin apportāre 'to carry to', from ad- + portāre 'to carry'). From 'bringing back an account' came 'official report' and 'financial yield', while from 'bringing two things together mentally' arose 'connection, relationship, ratio', and plural 'sexual intercourse'.

history.meaning: to carry to → to carry back, recount, yield produce
witness account brought back, revenue yield
written/oral report; connection, relationship; ratio; yield

rapport.notes: False-friend alert: English 'rapport' always implies warm harmony, whereas French rapport neutrally means 'report', 'link' (Quel rapport ? = 'What's that got to do with anything?'), 'relationship', or in the plural (des rapports) 'sexual relations'.

rootFamily.gloss: to bring back, report, yield money
spokesperson/drafter of a committee; protractor; tattletale

rapporter.etymology: Formed in Old French (raporter, 11th–12th c.) from prefix r- / re- ('back, again') + apporter ('to bring, carry to').

history.meaning: to bring back, yield profit, report, tell on

cognates.meaning: reconciliation (borrowed from French rapprochement); approach (from approcher)

rapprocher.etymology: Formed in Old French (raprochier, 12th century) from the iterative/intensive prefix re- (elided to r-) + aprochier (Modern French approcher 'to come near, bring near'), which descends from Late Latin appropiāre ('to draw near'), derived from ad- + Classical Latin prope ('near', comparative propior). It combines physical 'bringing closer' (camera framing, seating) with figurative 'comparing' and interpersonal 'reconciling / growing closer' (se rapprocher).

history.meaning: to bring near again, draw closer
to move closer together, compare, reconcile (se rapprocher)

rapprocher.notes: In filmmaking, un plan rapproché is a 'medium close-up shot'; socially, se rapprocher de quelqu'un means 'to grow closer to someone' or 'to get in touch with someone professionally'.

rare.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (14th century, displacing Old French clersemé and escars) from Classical Latin rārus ('wide apart, loose-textured, thinly scattered, infrequent, extraordinary'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁r̥h₁-ró- ('separated, loose-knit'). Retaining both the concrete sense of 'sparse, thin' (cheveux rares) and the quantitative sense of 'uncommon, exceptional', it became the standard adjective for scarcity and distinction.

history.meaning: thinly spaced, loose in texture, infrequent, uncommon

rare.notes: False-friend trap at the restaurant: French rare NEVER refers to steak doneness—a 'rare' steak in French is saignant ('bleeding') or bleu ('very rare'), never *rare!

cognates.meaning: seldom, infrequently (formed on borrowed French rare)

rarement.etymology: Formed in Middle French (14th–15th centuries) from the feminine form of the adjective rare ('infrequent, scarce', borrowed from Classical Latin rāra, feminine of rārus 'thinly scattered, uncommon') + the Romance adverbial suffix -ment (from the Classical Latin ablative singular mente 'with a ... mind', matching Classical Latin rārō 'seldom'). It functions both as a frequency adverb ('seldom') and an intensifying degree adverb ('exceptionally').

history.meaning: rarely, seldom; (literary before an adjective) extraordinarily

rarement.notes: When placed at the very start of a formal or dramatic sentence, rarement triggers subject-verb inversion: Rarement un acteur aura été aussi capricieux ('Rarely will an actor have been so temperamental').

cognates.meaning: to demolish completely (borrowed from French); razor (from Old French rasor)
to shave closely, graze, level to the ground
to skim, level off; arrasar 'to demolish'

raser.etymology: Inherited from Old French raser ('to scrape, shave close, skim along'), descending from Vulgar Latin *rāsāre, a frequentative built on rāsus, the past participle of Classical Latin rādere ('to scrape, shave, scratch, graze'), replacing Old French rere (< rādere). Its semantic range unites shaving hair (se raser), demolishing buildings flush with the ground (raser un immeuble), skimming close to walls (raser les murs), and colloquially boring someone stiff.

history.meaning: to scrape, shave → to shave or scrape repeatedly/closely
to shave hair, graze closely, level fortifications
to shave; to demolish; to hug/skim; (colloquial) to bore to death

raser.notes: Watch two colorful agency idioms: raser les murs ('to slink along the walls' in embarrassment) and Tu me rases ! ('You're boring me to tears!', whence the adjective rasoir 'tedious').

rassembler.etymology: Formed in Old French (rasembler, 11th–12th c.) from prefix r- / re- ('together, again') + assembler ('to bring together', from Vulgar Latin *assimulare < ad + simul 'together').

history.meaning: to gather together, collect, reassemble, summon up

cognates.meaning: serving to restore confidence (modeled on/borrowed from French)
calm, secure (from Latin sēcūrus; compare asegurar)

rassurant.etymology: Participial adjective formed from the present participle of rassurer ('to restore confidence, calm fears'), attested in Old French as raseürer ('to guarantee anew, put at ease again'), from re- + aseürer (Modern French assurer 'to make secure, assure'). Assurer descends from Vulgar Latin *assēcūrāre ('to make safe'), built on ad- + Classical Latin sēcūrus ('free from care or danger', itself from sē- 'without' + cūra 'care, anxiety').

history.meaning: free from anxiety → to make safe or confident
to make secure again, dispel fear or doubt

rassurant.notes: Agents spend half their day trying to sound rassurant to panicked actors—often used ironically in French litotes: C'est pas très rassurant, tout ça ('That's not very comforting at all').

rassurer.etymology: Formed in Old French (rasseürer, 12th c.) from prefix r- / re- + assurer ('to make secure, give confidence', from Vulgar Latin *assecurare < securus 'free from care, safe').

history.meaning: to restore confidence to, calm someone's fears, reassure

rater.etymology: Attested from the 16th–17th century; originally meant 'to be eaten by rats' or (in hunting/firearms, prendre un rat) 'to misfire, fail to go off' (comparing a flintlock that clicks without firing to a trap that snaps without catching a rat), whence 'to miss a target, fail an exam, miss a train'.

history.meaning: to misfire (of a gun) -> to miss, fail, bungle

cognates.meaning: to catch in a snare (trap borrowed via Old English/Old French from Germanic *trappō)
to catch, ensnare (from the same Germanic root)
to catch, capture (borrowed from French attraper)

rattraper.etymology: Formed in Middle French (ratraper, 15th century) from the restorative/iterative prefix re- (elided to r-) + attraper ('to catch, snare'), which arose in Old French (atraper) from a- (Latin ad-) + trape ('animal snare, trap'), borrowed from Old Frankish *trappa ('snare, foot-trap'). From 'recapturing an escaped person or falling object', it broadened into 'catching up on lost time or work' and reflexively se rattraper ('to make up for a mistake').

history.meaning: animal trap → to catch in a trap, seize
to catch again, recapture someone fleeing
to catch before falling, catch up with, make up for lost time or a blunder

rattraper.notes: Super versatile: rattraper le temps perdu ('make up for lost time'), rattraper le coup ('salvage a botched situation'), se rattraper ('make amends'), and les rattrapages ('make-up exams').

cognates.meaning: rat; rato 'failed/dud' does not exist, compare rata 'rat'

raté.etymology: Nominalized and adjectival past participle of rater ('to misfire, miss a target, fail'), attested since the 17th century and derived from rat ('rat', a medieval Romance/Germanic word of expressive or uncertain ultimate origin). In 17th-century musketry slang, prendre un rat ('to catch a rat') meant for a flintlock firearm to click without igniting—comparing the balking mechanism to a rat darting into a hole or gnawing through a trap without springing it. By the 19th century, un raté denoted a 'washout, failed artist, loser'.

history.meaning: rat → for a firearm to misfire (17th-c. idiom)
to misfire, miss a shot, fail in an attempt
botched attempt, defective item; washout, failure, loser (person)

morphemes.meaning: miss, misfire, fail (from rater, originally derived from rat)

raté.notes: In artistic and cinema circles, un raté (feminine une ratée) cuts deep—it specifically evokes a bitter 'failed artist / washed-up has-been' whose career never took off, while rater son train simply means 'to miss one's train'.

rootFamily.gloss: to miss (a train/shot), fail, mess up
rat; (ballet slang) petit rat de l'Opéra 'young ballet student'

ravi.etymology: Past participle of ravir ('to snatch away by force, carry off to heaven in ecstasy, delight'), inherited from Old French ravir < Vulgar Latin *rapire for Classical Latin rapere ('to seize, carry off').

history.meaning: carried away with joy, delighted, thrilled

cognates.meaning: delightful, entrancing (borrowed directly from Old/Middle French)
to abduct, carry off (learned from Latin raptāre)

ravissant.etymology: Participial adjective formed in Old and Middle French from ravissant, present participle of ravir ('to snatch away by force; to transport with delight'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *rapīre, a fourth-conjugation remodeling of Classical Latin rapere ('to seize, snatch, carry off, plunder'). Via religious mysticism—being 'snatched up' into heavenly ecstasy (compare St. Paul's raptus)—violent abduction softened into aesthetic enchantment: 'delightful, utterly charming'.

history.meaning: to seize violently, snatch away, carry off
to carry off, transport into spiritual ecstasy → entrancing
delightful, lovely, charming (of people, outfits, or places)

morphemes.meaning: inchoative verbal stem extension (-iss- of second-conjugation verbs)

ravissant.notes: Much lighter in register than English 'ravishing': telling a colleague Vous êtes ravissante ce soir or C'est un appartement ravissant means 'lovely / charming' without melodrama, whereas un ravisseur still preserves the violent sense 'kidnapper'!

rootFamily.gloss: to delight (être ravi 'to be delighted'); to abduct

cognates.meaning: beam of light (borrowed from Old French rai); radiate (learned from Latin)
to draw lines on, scratch, grate

rayer.etymology: Inherited from Old French raier ('to shine forth in rays; to flow in streams; to mark with lines or furrows'), descending from Classical Latin radiāre ('to emit beams, shine, furnish with spokes'), derived from radius ('wheel spoke, rod, beam of light'). From tracing radial lines or ruling parchment with a stylus, rayer developed the graphic senses 'to stripe', 'to scratch a surface', and 'to strike out / cross off a name from a list'.

history.meaning: to furnish with spokes, emit beams of light
to beam, stream; to rule lines or score grooves
to stripe, scratch (glass/vinyl), strike or cross out from a list

morphemes.meaning: line, stripe, ray (raie / Old French rai < Latin radius)

rayer.notes: Notice the semantic network: une chemise rayée ('a striped shirt'), un disque rayé ('a scratched record'—used figuratively when someone repeats themselves!), and rayer un nom de la liste ('cross a name off the casting list').

cognates.meaning: radius (learned Latin); ray (via Old French rai); rayon fabric (coined from French rayon)

rayon.etymology: Derived in Old French (raion, 12th century) from rai ('beam of light, wheel spoke', inherited from Classical Latin radius, radium 'wheel spoke, measuring rod, beam') + the suffix -on (originally diminutive/individualizing, from Latin -ōnem), eventually replacing simplex rai. Its rich semantic evolution branched from 'sunbeam' and 'wheel spoke / geometric radius' to 'furrow / honeycomb cell', then 'bookshelf / store rack' (17th c.), and finally 'store aisle, department, or area of expertise'.

history.meaning: spoke of a wheel, rod, beam of light
beam of light; furrow; honeycomb frame
ray, radius, bicycle spoke, store shelf/department, field of expertise

morphemes.meaning: ray, spoke (Old French rai < Latin radius)

rayon.notes: Beyond un rayon de soleil ('ray of sunshine') and supermarket aisles (le rayon vins), learn the very idiomatic C'est pas mon rayon ! ('That's not my department / area of expertise!').

rootFamily.gloss: to shine, radiate (e.g., rayonner de bonheur)

cognates.meaning: spoke of a wheel; ray, beam

rayonnant.etymology: Present participial adjective of rayonner ('to shine forth, radiate'), derived from rayon ('ray, beam, spoke'), itself an Old French diminutive (rai + -on) of rai, inherited from Classical Latin radius ('staff, spoke of a wheel, beam of light'). The figurative shift from emitting physical light to glowing with joy, charisma, or success emerged in Classical French.

history.meaning: spoke of a wheel, rod, beam of light

rayonnant.notes: In cinema and talent-agency parlance, être rayonnant(e) à l'écran praises an actor's effortless screen magnetism; in architecture, gothique rayonnant names the 13th-century French style of radial rose windows.

rayure.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French from rayer ('to scratch with a line, stripe, strike out', from raie 'furrow, line, stripe' < Gallo-Romance *rica 'furrow') + nominal suffix -ure.

history.meaning: decorative stripe, scratch on glass or metal, rifling groove

rayé.etymology: Past-participle adjective of rayer ('to draw lines on, stripe, scratch'), derived in Old French from raie ('line, furrow, stripe'), which comes from Gallo-Roman *rica ('furrow') of Gaulish origin (*rikā, 'plough furrow'). From the parallel furrows cut by a plough across a field, raie and rayé came to describe any fabric, box, or awning patterned with parallel stripes.
rayé.notes: A single stripe on a shirt or box is **une rayure** (**à rayures** = 'with stripes'), derived from the same verb **rayer**.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: rayé

rebelle.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old French from Classical Latin rebellis ('waging war again, renewing hostilities, insurgent'), formed from the prefix re- ('again, back') and bellum ('war', Old Latin duellum). Originally applied to conquered peoples rising up anew against Rome, it broadened in French to anyone defying authority, convention, or even physical taming (as with unruly hair).
rebelle.notes: Epicene in form (un acteur rebelle / une actrice rebelle); beyond politics and image-making, it appears in everyday collocations like cheveux rebelles ('unruly hair').

rebondir.etymology: Formed in Old French from re- ('back, again') and bondir ('to leap, bound'), which originally meant 'to resound, ring out, echo' (especially of hunting horns) from Vulgar Latin *bombitire, an onomatopoeic derivative of Classical Latin bombus ('booming or buzzing sound', from Ancient Greek βόμβος). The sense shifted from a reverberating sound bouncing off walls to physical elastic recoil, and figuratively to recovering after a setback.

history.meaning: to echo back; to spring or leap back
to bounce back, recover; to follow up on a point

rebondir.notes: Regular second-conjugation (-ir / -issant) verb; in workplace and agency meetings, rebondir sur ce que tu dis means 'to piggyback/follow up on what you're saying', while rebondir professionally means recovering from a flop.

rootFamily.gloss: plot twist, dramatic turn of events

rebonjour.etymology: Colloquial modern French greeting formed from iterative prefix re- ('again') + bonjour ('hello, good day'), used when seeing the same person a second time in the same day.

rebord.etymology: Formed in the 15th century from prefix re- ('turned back, projecting') + bord ('edge, rim').

history.meaning: raised or folded rim, ledge, windowsill, lapel/brim

rebours.etymology: From Old French rebors ('bristling the wrong way, contrary'), inherited from Late Latin reburrus ('with hair standing up backward', from re- 'back' + burra 'shaggy wool, coarse nap'). Brushing cloth or fur à rebours meant stroking it against the grain—hence 'in reverse' and un compte à rebours ('countdown').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: rebours (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: rebours

recette.etymology: Inherited via Old French receite ('money or goods received; medical/culinary formula') from Medieval Latin recepta, substantivized feminine/neuter plural of Classical Latin receptus (from recipere 'to receive, take'), echoing the apothecary heading Recipe ('Take...').

history.meaning: to take, receive -> things received; formula

cognates.meaning: receipt came from Anglo-Norman receite (note old cookbooks called recipes 'receipts'!)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: recette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: recette

recette.notes: **Une recette** still keeps both historical meanings in French: **une recette de cuisine** ('a recipe') and **les recettes** ('box-office or shop takings').

recevoir.etymology: Inherited from Old French receivre / recevoir ('to take in, welcome, receive'), from Classical Latin recipere ('to take back, take to oneself, admit, receive'), compound of re- + capere ('to take').

rechange.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (rechange, 12th–13th c.) from rechangier ('to exchange again, replace'); preserved chiefly in the phrase de rechange ('spare, replacement', as in une roue de rechange 'spare tire', des vêtements de rechange).

history.meaning: replacement, spare part or change of clothes

recherche.etymology: Sixteenth-century deverbal noun from rechercher ('to seek out thoroughly, investigate'), replacing earlier recerche. Ultimately traces through Old French cerchier ('to go around, patrol, inspect') to Late Latin circare ('to wander around, traverse in a ring'), derived from Classical Latin circus ('circle, ring'). The spatial notion of circling an area thoroughly yielded the intellectual sense of systematic inquiry and artistic refinement.

history.meaning: search, quest, scholarly or artistic research

morphemes.meaning: search, seek (from chercher < Late Latin circare)

recherche.notes: Singular la recherche usually denotes academic/scientific research or an artistic quest (à la recherche d'un rôle), whereas plural les recherches often refers to concrete searches or police/casting inquiries.

cognates.meaning: to surround, fence in (from the older spatial sense of circare)

rechercher.etymology: Formed in Old French (recerchier, later assimilated to rechercher) from intensifying re- and cerchier ('to inspect, scrutinize, search'), inherited from Late Latin circare ('to go around, patrol'), itself derived from Classical Latin circus ('circle'). While simple chercher became the neutral verb 'to look for', rechercher retained the heightened sense of actively pursuing, prizing, or investigating carefully.

history.meaning: to walk around, patrol in circles
to inspect closely, rummage through, seek anew
to seek out deliberately, pursue, prize

rechercher.notes: More formal and purposeful than chercher: casting notices say on recherche un comédien ('seeking an actor'), and its past participle recherché means both 'wanted (by police)' and 'stylistically refined'.

recommander.etymology: Formed in Old French (recomander, 12th c.) from prefix re- + comander / commander ('to entrust to someone's care, commend'); in postal usage (recommander une lettre), means to register a letter for tracked, guaranteed delivery.

history.meaning: to entrust to someone's favor, speak in favor of, advise; to register mail

recommandé.etymology: Substantivized past participle of recommander (supplying envoi or pli recommandé, 'registered mail item'), attested since the 19th century.

recommencer.etymology: Formed in Old French (recomencier) from iterative re- ('again') and comencier ('to begin'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *cominitiare, a prefixed verbal formation from Classical Latin cum- (intensive) and initiare ('to initiate, consecrate, begin'), itself from initium ('entrance, beginning', from inire 'to go into').
recommencer.notes: Spelling watch: takes a cedilla before a or o to keep the soft /s/ sound (nous recommençons). On a film set, on recommence ! means 'let's do another take from the top!'.

cognates.meaning: reconnaissance (borrowed in the military sense from French)

reconnaissance.etymology: Derived in Old French (reconoissance) from the present participial stem of reconoistre (modern reconnaître, 'to recognize, acknowledge') + -ance. Reconnaître continues Classical Latin recognoscere ('to know again, recall to mind, inspect, authenticate'), composed of re- ('again'), co- ('with, together'), and gnoscere / noscere ('to come to know', from PIE *ǵneh₃-). The moral sense 'gratitude' arose from formally acknowledging a debt or favor received.

history.meaning: to recall to mind, examine, certify
act of recognizing, admission, feudal acknowledgement

reconnaissance.notes: Polysemous false-friend trap for English speakers: while English reconnaissance is strictly military/scouting (often repérages in filmmaking), French la reconnaissance everyday means 'gratitude' or 'peer acclaim/recognition' (la reconnaissance du métier).

rootFamily.gloss: to recognize, admit, be grateful for

reconnaître.etymology: Inherited from Old French reconoistre ('to identify again, acknowledge, explore'), from Classical Latin recognoscere ('to know again, recall to mind, examine, certify'), compound of re- ('again') + cognoscere ('to come to know').

reconquérir.etymology: Formed from re- ('again, back') and conquérir ('to conquer, win over'), which reshaped Old French conquerre along -ir conjugations. Conquerre descends from Vulgar Latin *conquaerere (rebuilt with the simplex vowel of quaerere), corresponding to Classical Latin conquirere ('to seek out earnestly, collect, procure'), from com- ('thoroughly') + quaerere ('to seek, ask'). Semantic shift moved from procuring by effort to winning by force or charm.

history.meaning: to win back by arms or effort
to reconquer, win back (territory, audience, or lover)

reconquérir.notes: Conjugates identically to acquérir (je reconquiers, ils reconquièrent, past participle reconquis); frequently used figuratively in showbiz and romance: reconquérir son public ('to win back one's audience').

cognates.meaning: to recruit (borrowed from French recrue / recruter)

recruter.etymology: Seventeenth-century verbal derivative built on dialectal/Eastern French recrute (standard French recrue, 'new growth, fresh levy of soldiers'), preserving the intervocalic -t- of Vulgar Latin *recruta, feminine past participle of recroître ('to grow again, spring up anew'), from re- + croître (< Classical Latin crescere, 'to grow, increase'). Originally agricultural ('second growth of grass or timber'), it shifted to replenishing depleted regiments and then to hiring talent.

history.meaning: to grow back, sprout anew (new growth)
second crop; fresh levy of troops to fill ranks
to enlist troops; to hire or sign new talent

morphemes.meaning: growth, fresh levy (from dialectal recrute / recrue < croître)

recruter.notes: Notice how recrue ('new recruit/hire', always feminine in grammar even for a man: une excellente recrue !) lacks the -t- that survives in recruter and recrutement.

recul.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French from reculer ('to draw back, move backward, retreat'), itself transparently derived from re- ('back') + cul ('buttocks, rear end, bottom', inherited from Classical Latin culus) + -er. Despite the anatomical bluntness of its root, both reculer and recul lost any vulgarity early on, developing physical senses ('recoil of a firearm, setback in space') and elevated intellectual senses ('critical distance, hindsight').

history.meaning: to move backward; act of retreating
backward distance, recoil; emotional perspective, hindsight

recul.notes: Completely neutral and polite in standard and formal registers despite containing cul: prendre du recul ('to step back and get perspective') and avec le recul ('in hindsight') are essential idiomatic expressions.

rootFamily.gloss: to step back, retreat, back down

reculer.etymology: Formed in Old French (reculer, 12th c., 'to move backward, draw back') from prefix re- ('back') + cul ('backside, rear end, bottom', from Classical Latin culus) + verbal ending -er.

history.meaning: to move tail-first, step backward, retreat, postpone

cognates.meaning: to come to pass, turn into (devenir)

redevenir.etymology: Formed in Old French from iterative re- ('again') + devenir ('to become'), inherited from Classical Latin devenire ('to come down from, arrive at, reach a state'), itself a compound of de- ('down from, off') and venire ('to come', from PIE *gʷem-). In Late Latin, arriving at a destination generalized into reaching a new state or condition ('becoming'), which re- reverses or restores to a prior state.

history.meaning: to come down to, arrive at, end up in
to turn into / to become once again
to revert to being, become again

morphemes.meaning: again, back to a former state

redevenir.notes: Like venir and devenir, it conjugates with the auxiliary être in compound tenses and agrees with the subject: elle est redevenue une star incontournable ('she became an unmissable star again').

redonner.etymology: Formed in Old French (redoner, 11th–12th c.) from prefix re- ('back, again') + donner ('to give').

history.meaning: to give back, restore, give again

redoutable.etymology: Derived in Old French (redotable) from redouter ('to dread, fear greatly') + -able ('worthy of being'). Redouter combines intensive re- with Old French douter ('to fear, be afraid of; to hesitate'), inherited from Classical Latin dubitare ('to waver between two opinions, hesitate', related to duo 'two'). In medieval French, douter meant 'to fear' before Latinizing influence narrowed simple douter to 'doubt', leaving the older 'dread' sense preserved inside redouter and redoutable.

history.meaning: to dread deeply / inspiring awe and fear

morphemes.meaning: dread, fear (archaic sense of douter < Latin dubitare)

redoutable.notes: Often a high compliment in negotiations or agency life: un négociateur redoutable means 'a formidable/razor-sharp negotiator'—nothing to do with 'doubtful' (which is douteux).

redresser.etymology: Formed in Old French (redrecier, 12th c.) from prefix re- ('back, again') + dresser ('to set upright, straighten', from Vulgar Latin *directiare < directus 'straight').

history.meaning: to set upright again, straighten out, right a wrong

refermer.etymology: Formed in Old French (refermer, 12th c.) from prefix re- ('again, back') + fermer ('to close, shut').

refiler.etymology: Formed from re- ('onward, back, over') and filer ('to spin thread; colloquially to pay out a line, slip, hand over'), itself derived from fil ('thread'), inherited from Classical Latin filum ('thread, string, filament'). Just as a card sharp or merchant smoothly pays out a thread or slips a counterfeit coin into someone's hand (filer quelque chose à quelqu'un), refiler specialized in nineteenth-century colloquial French for unloading or palming off something unwanted onto another person.

history.meaning: thread / to spin or draw out thread
to spin; to pay out cable; colloquially to slip or hand over
to pass along, palm off, saddle someone with

refiler.notes: Informal/colloquial register (familier): agents constantly complain about colleagues trying to refiler un mauvais scénario ('palm off a terrible script') or refiler le bébé ('dump a problem on someone')—or catching a cold (refiler son rhume).

rootFamily.gloss: to spin; to dash off; colloquially to hand over

reflet.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 17th century (originally in painting science, translating Italian riflesso) from refléter ('to throw back light or color', itself an alteration of réfléchir < Classical Latin reflectere 'to bend or turn back').

history.meaning: reflected gleam of light, glint, mirror image

refroidir.etymology: Formed in Old French (refroidir, 12th c.) from prefix re- + froidir / froid ('cold', from Vulgar Latin *frigidus for Classical frigidus).

history.meaning: to make or become cold again, cool down, chill

refuge.etymology: Borrowed and adapted in Old French from Classical Latin refugium ('a taking refuge, place of safety, recourse'), derived from the verb refugere ('to flee back, run away, escape'), composed of re- ('back, away') + fugere ('to flee', from PIE *bʰewg-). Alongside physical sanctuary, French developed psychological expressions such as trouver refuge dans le travail ('to seek solace/escape in one's work').

history.meaning: to flee back / place of escape, shelter
shelter, sanctuary, alpine hut, emotional haven

refuge.notes: Masculine noun (un refuge); also used in apposition as valeur refuge ('safe-haven asset/bet', e.g., casting a bankable star when financiers get nervous).

rootFamily.gloss: to take refuge, seek shelter (se réfugier)

cognates.meaning: refuse (verb and noun, borrowed from Old French)

refus.etymology: Twelfth-century deverbal noun from Old French refuser ('to reject, spurn, decline'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *refusare. This Vulgar Latin verb arose as a blend of Classical Latin recusare ('to make an objection against, decline', from re- + causa) with the past participial stem fus- of refundere ('to pour back, give back, repel', from re- + fundere 'to pour').

history.meaning: to decline, object × to pour back, repel
to reject, turn down / act of declining

refus.notes: Final -s is completely silent (/ʁə.fy/) and the noun is invariable in the plural (un refus, des refus); essuyer un refus is the idiomatic phrase for 'to meet with a rejection' after an audition or pitch.

rootFamily.gloss: to challenge/recuse a judge (learned doublet from recusare)

refuser.etymology: Inherited from Old French refuser ('to reject, decline'), from Vulgar Latin *refusare, frequentative built on the past participle refusus of Classical Latin refundere ('to pour back, give back, reject, spurn') blended with recusare ('to refuse, object to').

history.meaning: to pour or push back, reject

cognates.meaning: reward (Anglo-Norman doublet from Old Northern French rewarder)

regard.etymology: Deverbal noun from Old French regarder ('to look back at, observe attentively, watch over'), composed of re- ('back, attentively') and garder ('to watch, protect, keep'), itself borrowed from Frankish *wardōn ('to keep watch, guard', from Proto-Germanic *wardōną, related to English ward). From 'keeping watch over', French specialized regarder as the ordinary verb for 'looking at', giving regard its rich meaning of 'gaze, look, artistic point of view'.

history.meaning: to watch over, inspect, gaze upon / attentive look
gaze, look, expression of the eyes; perspective

regard.notes: False friend alert: un regard almost always means a physical 'look/gaze' or a director's 'artistic vision' (avoir un vrai regard de cinéaste), whereas English 'regards' (greetings) is amitiés or salutations, and 'respect/consideration' is égards.

rootFamily.gloss: to look at, watch; to concern

regarder.etymology: Regarder was formed in Old French from re- + garder ('to watch, guard', from Frankish *wardon 'to keep watch', cognate with English 'ward' and 'regard').
regarder.notes: No preposition for 'at': **regarder l'étiquette** = 'to look at the label'.

registre.etymology: Inherited from Old French registre, from Medieval Latin registrum, an alteration of Late Latin regesta ('matters recorded or entered in a book', neuter plural past participle of regerere 'to carry back, transcribe').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: registre (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: registre

registre.notes: From organ stops (**tirer les registres**), **le registre** also entered music and linguistics to mean vocal range or tone of speech (`tu` vs `vous`).

regret.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French from regreter ('to bewail the dead, lament someone's absence'). Most philologists trace regreter to the prefix re- combined with Frankish *grētan or Old Norse gráta ('to weep, bewail, groan', from Proto-Germanic *grētaną; cf. Old English grætan, Scots greet 'to cry'). From loud medieval lamentation for a lost hero, regret softened into inward sorrow, remorse, or wistful longing.

history.meaning: lamentation, grief over loss or death

regret.notes: Final -t is silent (/ʁə.ɡʁɛ/); à regret means 'reluctantly' (accepter un rôle à regret), while avoir des regrets expresses remorse over choices made or missed opportunities.

rootFamily.gloss: late, dearly departed (e.g. le regretté cinéaste)

cognates.meaning: to regret (borrowed from Middle French regreter)
to weep, cry (from Old Norse gráta)

regretter.etymology: Inherited from Old French regreter (attested already in the eleventh-century Life of Saint Alexis and Song of Roland as 'to mourn aloud, call back the dead with tears'), most plausibly formed from re- + Frankish *grētan (reinforced in Normandy by Old Norse gráta, 'to weep, lament'). Across Middle and Classical French, the verb shifted from ritualized mourning of the absent or deceased to feeling sorry for an action or missing a bygone state.

history.meaning: to weep, cry out in grief
to bewail the dead, mourn an absent person
to feel remorse for, be sorry; to miss sorely

regretter.notes: Preserves its medieval sense of 'missing' what is gone: je regrette le bon vieux temps ('I miss the good old days'); when followed by a clause, it triggers the subjunctive (je regrette qu'il parte) or de + past infinitive (je regrette d'avoir dit ça).

reine.etymology: Inherited through Old French reïne (disyllabic before contracting to reine) from Classical Latin regina ('queen'), an ancient feminine derivative of rex, regis ('king'), built on the Proto-Indo-European root *h₃rēǵ- ('to straighten, direct, rule'; remarkably parallel to Sanskrit rājñī and Old Irish rígain). Intervocalic Latin -g- lenited and disappeared regularly before a front vowel in Gallo-Romance.

history.meaning: queen; figuratively undisputed star or doyenne

reine.notes: Pronounced identically to renne ('reindeer') and the city Rennes (/ʁɛn/); figuratively common in showbiz as la reine du box-office or la reine de la soirée.

cognates.meaning: to reject (learned borrowing from Latin reiectus)

rejeter.etymology: Formed in Old French from re- ('back, away') and jeter ('to throw, cast'), inherited from Late/Vulgar Latin *iectare, an alteration of Classical Latin iactare ('to toss about, hurl repeatedly'), the frequentative of iacere ('to throw', from PIE *yeh₁-). While English borrowed learned reject directly from Latin reicere/reiectus, French evolved rejeter organically from the popular frequentative stem, encompassing both physical throwing back and abstract refusal.

history.meaning: to hurl back, drive back, cast off

rejeter.notes: Stem-changing orthography: doubles the t before a mute e to indicate open /ɛ/ (je rejette, ils rejettent, vs. nous rejetons). Idiom: rejeter la faute sur quelqu'un ('to pin/shift the blame onto someone').

rejoindre.etymology: Formed in Old French (rejoindre, 12th–13th c.) from prefix re- ('together again, back') + joindre ('to join', from Classical Latin jungere).

history.meaning: to join together again, reunite with, catch up with, meet

relais.etymology: Thirteenth-century deverbal noun from Old French relaissier ('to release, leave behind, allow to rest'), composed of re- + laissier ('to let go, leave', inherited from Classical Latin laxare 'to loosen, slacken'). Originally a medieval venery (hunting) term denoting fresh hounds posted along the chase route and unleashed to relieve exhausted dogs, it extended to staging posts with fresh horses (relais de poste), broadcast transmitters, and work shifts.

history.meaning: pack of fresh hunting hounds held in reserve along a chase
coaching inn with fresh horses; relay, go-between, work shift

morphemes.meaning: leave, let go (from laisser < Latin laxare)

relais.notes: Invariable in singular and plural (un relais, des relais); prendre le relais ('to take over from someone / step in') and relayer une info ('to pass along/amplify news in media') are ubiquitous in PR and agency life.

rootFamily.gloss: to relieve someone, pass on, broadcast

relation.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old French from Classical Latin relatio, relationem ('a carrying back, official report to the Senate, philosophical reference or connection'), formed on relatus, the suppletive past participle of referre ('to carry back, report, refer', from re- + ferre 'to bear, carry'). In French, the earlier sense 'narrative account' yielded center stage to 'interpersonal bond, romantic affair, or influential contact'.

morphemes.meaning: carried, borne (Latin suppletive stem lat- of ferre)

relation.notes: False friend nuance: English 'my relations' (= relatives/kin) is ma famille or mes proches, NEVER mes relations! In French, avoir des relations means 'to have influential connections/pull'—vital currency for a Parisian talent agent.

relever.etymology: Inherited from Old French relever ('to raise up again, relieve a feudal tenant or sentry'), from Classical Latin relevare ('to lift up again, lighten, alleviate'), compound of re- ('again, up') + levare ('to lift').

history.meaning: to raise up again, turn up, note down (a meter), spice up food, relieve on watch

cognates.meaning: relief (both comfort and raised sculpture, via French/Italian)

relief.etymology: Twelfth-century deverbal noun formed on the stressed stem (relief-) of Old French relever ('to raise up again', from Classical Latin relevare, 'to lift up, lighten', from re- + levare, itself from levis 'light in weight'). Originally denoting feudal dues paid to 'take up' an estate or leftover dishes lifted from a lord's table, it gained its visual and aesthetic sense ('raised sculpture, depth, vividness') in the Renaissance under the semantic influence of cognate Italian rilievo.

history.meaning: to lift up again, lighten, alleviate
lifting up; feudal succession fee; table remnants
sculptural projection, topography; vividness, depth of character

morphemes.meaning: raise, lift (tonic stem of lever < Latin levare)

relief.notes: Crucial false friend! French le relief NEVER means emotional comfort or alleviation (= le soulagement); instead it means 3D depth, terrain, or dramatic punch: un rôle sans relief is a flat, one-dimensional role, while mettre en relief means 'to highlight'.

rootFamily.gloss: to raise again, season, take up a challenge
takeover, next generation, changing of the guard

relire.etymology: Formed in Old French (relire, 12th c.) from iterative prefix re- ('again') + lire ('to read', from Latin legere).

cognates.meaning: release (borrowed from Old French variant relessier)

relâcher.etymology: Inherited through Old French relaschier ('to loosen, untie, set free') from Classical Latin relaxare ('to widen again, unbend, slacken, ease'), composed of re- + laxare ('to loosen', from laxus 'wide, loose, slack'). Preconsonantal -s- silenced in Middle French, leaving the circumflex accent over â as its historical trace (relascher > relâcher), while learned relaxer was later re-borrowed directly from Latin.

history.meaning: to stretch out, loosen, slacken, ease
to unbind, free a prisoner, slacken tension
to release, let go, slacken effort, relax (se relâcher)

morphemes.meaning: loose, slack (lâcher < Latin laxare; â marks lost s)

relâcher.notes: Notice the doublet pair: inherited relâcher ('to release a suspect, slacken pressure, let one's standards slip' with se relâcher) vs. modern learned se relaxer ('to unwind/chill'). In theater, faire relâche means 'to have a dark night (no performance)'.

rootFamily.gloss: to let go, drop, give up; cowardly (lâche)

cognates.meaning: relief of a guard, relay, replacement
to relieve a guard, take over (rilevare)

relève.etymology: Modern deverbal noun formed from relever in its military sense ('to relieve a sentry on watch, replace tired troops with fresh ones'), inherited from Classical Latin relevare ('to lift up again, lighten a burden', from re- + levare 'to raise, lighten', from levis 'light'). From the changing of the guard (la relève de la garde), the word generalized to the rising generation poised to succeed established veterans.

history.meaning: to raise up again, lighten, relieve
to replace a soldier on guard duty
changing of the guard, relief shift; rising new generation

relève.notes: In French cinema and sports, la relève est assurée ('the next generation of talent is in good hands') is the classic praise for promising young actors stepping into veterans' shoes.

rootFamily.gloss: to lift up again, relieve, meet a challenge

remarquable.etymology: Derived in sixteenth-century Middle French from remarquer ('to note attentively, single out, observe') + -able ('worthy of being'). Remarquer itself builds on marquer ('to put a distinguishing sign on'), from marque, of Frankish/Germanic origin (*marka 'boundary marker, sign'; cf. English mark). What is remarquable is literally 'worthy of being marked out from the crowd'.

history.meaning: to mark out, take special note of

remarquable.notes: Strongly positive in Modern French ('outstanding, admirable', e.g., une interprétation remarquable), whereas English 'remarkable' can sometimes simply mean 'unusual/surprising'.

remarquablement.etymology: Formed in Early Modern French by adding the adverbial suffix -ment to the adjective remarquable ('remarkable, noteworthy'), itself derived from remarquer ('to notice, mark again'), from re- + marquer (built on marque 'mark, boundary sign', of Germanic *marka origin). The adverb highlights a quality that immediately catches the eye and deserves special notice.
remarquablement.notes: Because **remarquable** already ends in **-e**, the adverb simply adds **-ment** without changing the vowel: **remarquablement**.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: remarquablement

remarque.etymology: Late sixteenth-century deverbal noun formed from remarquer ('to observe attentively, take note of'), itself from re- + marquer ('to mark'), derived from Frankish/Germanic *marka ('border sign, boundary mark, token'). Originally meaning an act of attentive mental observation or a marginal note in a text, remarque shifted in Classical French toward a spoken comment, critique, or pointed observation.

history.meaning: act of noting carefully, distinguishing sign
spoken or written comment, critical observation

remarque.notes: Watch register and tone: faire une remarque à quelqu'un often implies mild criticism or telling someone off ('to make a pointed comment / reprimand'), whereas imperative discourse marker remarque ! means 'mind you / come to think of it!'.

cognates.meaning: to remark (borrowed from French, though with a narrower sense)

remarquer.etymology: Formed in Middle French (attested ca. 1500 first literally as 'to mark again', then swiftly as 'to single out mentally, observe, notice') from re- + marquer ('to stamp, mark'), derived from marque, of Frankish/Germanic origin (*marka 'boundary sign, mark'). Semantic bleaching of the literal 're-stamping' yielded the primary cognitive verb for noticing something with the eyes or mind.

history.meaning: to stamp with a sign or boundary mark
to mark anew; to single out, note attentively
to notice, spot, call attention to (faire remarquer)

remarquer.notes: Classic semi-false friend: French remarquer primarily means 'to notice' silently (j'ai remarqué un détail = 'I noticed a detail'), NOT 'to say/remark aloud'—to mean 'remark/point out verbally', say faire remarquer.

rootFamily.gloss: to mark, score, leave an impression

remboursement.etymology: Formed in the 15th–16th century from rembourser ('to put money back into someone's purse, repay', from re- + embourser, built on bourse 'purse') + nominal suffix -ment.

cognates.meaning: to reimburse, put back in the purse

rembourser.etymology: Sixteenth-century financial formation from re- ('back') + embourser ('to put into a purse, pocket', from en- > em- before labial b + bourse 'purse' + -er), strongly reinforced by Renaissance Italian banking terminology rimborsare. Bourse descends via Late Latin bursa ('leather moneybag') from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa, 'dressed animal hide, wineskin'), the same root behind English bursar and French bourse ('stock exchange; scholarship').

history.meaning: animal hide, leather pouch > money purse
to pocket in a purse / to restore money to a purse

morphemes.meaning: in, into (assimilated from en- before b)

rembourser.notes: In French cinemas and theaters, unhappy spectators famously shout « Remboursez ! » ('Give us our money back!'); also note se faire rembourser ('to get refunded / reimbursed by insurance').

rootFamily.gloss: to shell out, spend money (literally 'take out of the purse')

remercier.etymology: Formed in the 14th century from prefix re- + mercier ('to thank', derived from Old French merci 'favor, grace, thanks' < Classical Latin mercedem 'reward, wages, favor').

history.meaning: to express gratitude to, thank; (euphemistically) to dismiss an employee

remettre.etymology: Inherited from Old French remetre ('to put back in place, hand over, postpone, forgive'), from Classical Latin remittere ('to send back, slacken, give up, forgive'), compound of re- ('back, again') + mittere ('to send; in Romance, to put').

history.meaning: to put back, hand over/deliver, put on again, postpone, recognize

remonter.etymology: Formed in Old French (remonter, 12th c.) from prefix re- ('up again, back') + monter ('to go up, mount, assemble').

history.meaning: to go back up, wind a clock, reassemble, trace back in time, cheer up

cognates.meaning: to replace (modeled on/borrowed from French remplacer)

remplacer.etymology: Formed in sixteenth-century French from re- ('again, in place of') + emplacer ('to set in a place, position', from en- > em- before labial p + place + -er). Place descends from Vulgar Latin *plattea, from Classical Latin platea ('courtyard, broad street'), borrowed from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa [hodós], 'broad [way]', feminine of platús 'flat, wide'). Unlike English replace, French kept the nasal prefix em- intact.

history.meaning: to substitute for, stand in for, succeed

morphemes.meaning: in, into (assimilated from en- before p; elided before e-)

remplacer.notes: Double trap for English speakers: spelling retains nasal -m- (remplacer, NOT *replacer, which means 'to put back where it was'!), and takes a cedilla before a/o (nous remplaçons, un remplaçant 'stand-in/understudy').

remplaçant.etymology: Substantivized present participle of Middle/Early Modern French remplacer ('to put back in place, succeed someone in an office or role'), formed from the prefix re- ('again, in return') and emplacer ('to set in a place'). Emplacer derives from en- + place, inherited from Vulgar Latin *plattea ('courtyard, open square'), an alteration of Classical Latin platea ('broad street, courtyard'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek plateia (hodos) ('broad [way]').

history.meaning: to assign a place; to take the place of another
one who stands in for another, substitute

remplaçant.notes: Feminine form is remplaçante. On French film sets, a lighting/camera stand-in or stunt double is usually called une doublure, whereas un remplaçant replaces someone who is absent (e.g., an assistant or cast member).

remplir.etymology: Formed in Old French (raemplir -> remplir, 11th–12th c.) from intensive/iterative prefix re- + emplir ('to fill', from Classical Latin implere 'to fill up').

history.meaning: to fill up completely, refill, fulfill a duty, fill out a form

remporter.etymology: Inherited from Old French remporter ('to carry back, take away again'), prefixed with re- onto emporter ('to carry off, take away'). Emporter compounds Old French en ('away from there', from Classical Latin inde 'thence') with porter ('to carry'), from Classical Latin portare ('to carry, convey, bear'). From the concrete sense of carrying trophies or spoils away from the field of contest, the verb developed the standard modern sense 'to win' (a prize, award, or victory).

history.meaning: to carry back, take away with oneself
to carry off (a prize), win; to take back away

remporter.notes: The go-to verb in awards season (remporter un César, remporter la Palme d'or, remporter un franc succès); unlike gagner, it always takes a direct object and cannot be used intransitively.

remuer.etymology: Formed in Old French (remuer, 12th c.) from prefix re- ('again, thoroughly') + muer ('to change, move, shift', from Classical Latin mutare 'to change, move').

history.meaning: to move about, stir, shake, fidget

rencontre.etymology: Deverbal noun from Old French rencontrer ('to meet face to face, come upon, clash with'), formed from re- + encontrer ('to meet, confront'). Encontrer derives from Late Latin incontrare ('to meet in front of'), verbalized from Classical Latin in + contra ('against, opposite, face to face'). Originally used both for armed clashes and chance meetings, the noun stabilized as feminine in Classical and Modern French.

history.meaning: to come face to face with, meet opposite
to clash with, chance upon; a meeting or skirmish
meeting, personal or professional encounter, sports match

morphemes.meaning: against, face to face (< Latin contra)

rencontre.notes: Always feminine (une belle rencontre). Whereas une réunion is a scheduled work meeting and un rendez-vous is an appointment, une rencontre highlights human connection, an artistic pairing, or a public Q&A.

rootFamily.gloss: in opposition to (in à l'encontre de)

rencontrer.etymology: Formed in Old French (rencontrer, 12th c.) from prefix r- / re- + encontrer ('to meet face to face, come upon', from Late Latin incontrare, derived from in + contra 'against, facing').

history.meaning: to come upon face to face, meet, encounter

rendez-vous.etymology: Rendez-vous began as an instruction: the polite or plural imperative of se rendre. The Académie records the expression used as a noun from the sixteenth century.

history.meaning: military order: 'present yourselves (at such a place)!'
appointed meeting place or time, appointment

rootFamily.gloss: to go to, proceed to (se rendre au travail)

rendez-vous.notes: In English 'rendezvous' sounds romantic or secretive, whereas in French un rendez-vous is the completely ordinary everyday word for a doctor's, dentist's, or business appointment (un rendez-vous chez le médecin; romantic = un rendez-vous amoureux/galant)!

rendre.etymology: Inherited from Old French rendre ('to give back, hand over, yield'), from Vulgar Latin *rendere, nasalized alteration (under the influence of prendre 'to take') of Classical Latin reddere ('to give back, return, restore', from red- 'back' + dare 'to give').

history.meaning: to give back, return, yield, make (+ adj.)

cognates.meaning: to formally give up or reject

renoncer.etymology: Adapted from Old French renoncier ('to retract, disclaim, abandon'), borrowed from Classical Latin renuntiare ('to bring back word, report officially, revoke a contract, break off relations'), composed of re- ('back, against') and nuntiare ('to announce, declare'), from nuntius ('messenger, message'). Legal and ecclesiastical Latin usage shifted the core sense from revoking a notice to formally relinquishing a right, claim, or attachment.

history.meaning: to report back, revoke a notice, disclaim
to repudiate, abjure, abandon a right
to give up, forgo, withdraw from

renoncer.notes: Takes the preposition à before nouns and infinitives (renoncer à un rôle, renoncer à tourner), and takes a cedilla before a or o (nous renonçons) to preserve the soft /s/ sound.

renseigner.etymology: From Middle French renseigner ('to indicate anew, point out by tokens or directions'), formed from re- + enseigner ('to show by a sign, instruct'). Old French enseignier comes from Vulgar Latin *insignare ('to mark out, point out'), an alteration of Classical Latin insignire ('to distinguish with a mark'), derived from insigne ('badge, mark, sign'), itself from in- + signum ('mark, token, sign').

history.meaning: to mark with a token, point out
to point out again, guide by indications
to provide information to; (reflexive) to make inquiries

renseigner.notes: Transitive renseigner quelqu'un means 'to inform someone', while reflexive se renseigner (sur) means 'to look into, check up on, gather intel'—essential agent jargon before negotiations.

rentrer.etymology: Formed in Old French (rentrer, 11th–12th c.) from prefix r- / re- ('back, again') + entrer ('to go in, enter').

history.meaning: to go or come back in, return home, resume school after vacation, bring inside

renverser.etymology: Formed in Old French (renverser, 12th c.) from prefix r- / re- + enverser ('to turn upside down, throw on one's back', derived from envers < Classical Latin inversus 'turned upside down').

history.meaning: to knock over, spill, overturn, reverse

renvoyer.etymology: Formed in Old French (renvoier, 12th c.) from prefix r- / re- ('back, again') + envoyer ('to send on one's way', from en + voie 'way' < Latin via).

history.meaning: to send back, return, dismiss/fire, refer, reflect

reparler.etymology: Inherited from Old French reparler ('to speak again, resume a discussion'), composed of iterative re- + parler ('to speak'). Parler descends from Christian Late Latin parabolare ('to speak, discourse, tell parables'), derived from Latin parabola ('comparison, proverb, speech'), borrowed from Ancient Greek parabole ('juxtaposition, comparison, allegory'), from para- ('beside') + ballein ('to throw').

history.meaning: to discuss again, revisit a topic

reparler.notes: Ubiquitous in agency brush-offs and deal-making: On s'en reparle ! ('Let's circle back on that / talk it over later!'), where en replaces de + topic.

repartir.etymology: Formed in Old French (repartir, 12th c.) from iterative prefix re- ('again, back') + partir ('to set out, leave').

history.meaning: to set off again, leave again, start up again

cognates.meaning: formal or literary word for a meal

repas.etymology: Inherited from Old French repas (earlier repast, 'nourishment, feeding, meal'), from Late Latin repastus ('a feeding'), derived from the past participle of repascere ('to feed again, nourish'), composed of re- + Classical Latin pascere (past participle pastus, 'to feed, lead to pasture, nourish'), from Proto-Indo-European *peh2- ('to protect, shepherd, feed'). Preconsonantal and final -t ceased to be pronounced in Middle French, leaving silent final -s.

history.meaning: to lead to pasture, feed; nourishment
food taken at one time, nourishment

repas.notes: Invariable in the plural (un repas, des repas) with a silent final -s; un repas d'affaires ('business meal') is where half of French cinema deals are sealed.

repasser.etymology: Formed in Old French (repasser, 12th c.) from prefix re- ('again, back') + passer ('to pass'); developed the specialized senses of passing a blade over a whetstone ('to sharpen'), passing a hot iron over linen ('to iron clothes'), and going over a lesson again.

history.meaning: to pass by again; to whet a blade; to iron clothes

repeindre.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French from iterative prefix re- ('again, anew') + peindre ('to paint').

history.meaning: to paint again, give a fresh coat of paint to

repenser.etymology: Inherited from Old French repenser ('to think over again, reflect anew'), formed from re- + penser ('to think, reflect'). Penser represents a semi-learned early Romance adaptation of Classical Latin pensare ('to weigh carefully, counterbalance, ponder, judge'), the frequentative of pendere ('to hang, cause to hang, weigh out'); its inherited popular doublet in French is peser ('to weigh').

history.meaning: to reflect again, call back to mind
to think back on (repenser à); to rethink or redesign (repenser + direct object)

repenser.notes: Watch the transitivity contrast: repenser à quelque chose means 'to think back on / remember something', whereas transitive repenser un scénario means 'to rethink / overhaul a script'.

replier.etymology: Formed in Old French (repleier / replier, 12th c.) from prefix re- ('back, again') + plier ('to fold, bend').

history.meaning: to fold back, fold up again, tuck in; (reflexive) to fall back, withdraw

cognates.meaning: to dive or thrust suddenly downward
to fall straight down like lead, plummet
to plumb, check verticality with a lead line

replonger.etymology: Inherited from Old French replongier ('to immerse again, dive back down'), formed from re- ('back, again') + plonger ('to dive, immerse'). Old French plongier derives regularly from Vulgar Latin *plumbicare ('to heave a sounding lead, sink like lead'), formed from Classical Latin plumbum ('lead metal'); palatalization of -mbic- before -a- yielded Old French -ng-.

history.meaning: lead metal; to sink like a lead weight
to immerse or dive back into water
to plunge back in, immerse again, relapse into a habit or mood

replonger.notes: Takes an orthographic e after g before a or o (nous replongeons). Used both positively (se replonger dans un rôle 'to immerse oneself back in a role') and for relapsing into addiction or depression.

rootFamily.gloss: high-angle camera shot; diving; dishwashing station

cognates.meaning: to give an account of, carry back news
to carry back, bring forward, report

reporter.etymology: Inherited from Old French reporter ('to carry back, bring word back, transfer'), continuing or re-forming Classical Latin reportare ('to carry back, bring back word'), from re- + portare ('to carry'). In financial accounting and administrative French, 'carrying forward' an entry to a later page or date produced the modern scheduling sense 'to postpone, defer' (reporter un rendez-vous).

history.meaning: to carry back, bring back word from afar
to carry back, recount, transfer forward
to postpone to a later date, carry forward, transfer (emotions) onto

reporter.notes: Classic false friend! The verb reporter (/ʁə.pɔʁ.te/) means 'to postpone' (reporter un tournage), NOT 'to report news' (which is rapporter or faire un reportage). Meanwhile, the noun un reporter (/ʁə.pɔʁ.tɛʁ/) was borrowed back from English for 'journalist'.

rootFamily.gloss: to bring back, report, yield profit

repos.etymology: Inherited from Old French repos ('cessation of labor or movement, peace'), a deverbal noun from reposer ('to rest, set back down'). Reposer derives from Late Latin repausare ('to cause to pause, take rest'), formed from re- + pausare ('to halt, cease'), from Classical Latin pausa ('a halt, cessation'), borrowed from Ancient Greek pausis ('stopping, ceasing'), from pauein ('to stop').

history.meaning: a halt, stop; to pause, rest from toil

repos.notes: Silent final -s (pronounced /ʁə.po/). Note the ironic French idiom de tout repos, almost always used in the negative: Ce tournage n'est pas de tout repos ('This shoot is anything but a walk in the park').

rootFamily.gloss: to rest, set down (se reposer 'to rest')

reposer.etymology: Inherited from Old French reposer ('to rest, take rest, set down again'), from Late Latin repausare ('to cause to rest, pause'), compound of re- + pausare ('to pause, cease', from pausa 'a halt, pause' < Greek pausis).

history.meaning: to rest, lie at rest; to put back down

reprendre.etymology: Formed in Old French (reprendre, 11th–12th c.) from prefix re- ('back, again') + prendre ('to take', from Latin prehendere).

history.meaning: to take back, resume, have a second helping, alter a garment, reprove

cognates.meaning: to express disapproval or disappointment to

reprocher.etymology: Inherited from Old French reprochier ('to bring back close before someone, cast in someone's teeth, blame'), from Vulgar Latin *repropiare ('to bring near again, confront with'). Formed symmetrically with approcher (< Late Latin appropiare) from re- + Classical Latin prope ('near, close at hand'); palatalization of the cluster -pi- in Gallo-Romance regularly produced -ch-.

history.meaning: near; to bring close up to someone again
to confront someone with a fault, cast blame
to reproach, blame, hold against someone

reprocher.notes: Syntax mirrors dire/donner: reprocher quelque chose à quelqu'un ('to blame someone for something') or reprocher à quelqu'un de faire quelque chose—the person blamed is always an indirect object (lui/leur).

représentante.etymology: Feminine form of représentant ('representative, agent, commercial traveler'), substantivized present participle of représenter ('to make present again, depict, act on behalf of', from Latin repraesentare).

history.meaning: female representative, delegate, or sales agent

cognates.meaning: depiction, acting on behalf of another

représentation.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (representacion) from Classical Latin repraesentatio (accusative repraesentationem, 'a vivid placing before the eyes, image, immediate cash payment'), noun of action from repraesentare ('to make present, exhibit immediately'), itself from re- + praesentare ('to place before, show'), derived from praesens ('present, at hand'). From the 16th–17th centuries it specialized in French theater for staging a play before an audience.

history.meaning: vivid exhibition before the eyes; cash payment
theatrical performance/screening; legal or artistic representation; mental image

représentation.notes: In performing arts, une représentation is a single show or run performance of a play/opera (la dernière représentation = closing night), whereas une performance usually means an athletic feat or avant-garde performance art.

cognates.meaning: to act or speak for, depict, symbolize

représenter.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (representer) from Classical Latin repraesentare ('to make present again, bring directly before the eyes, perform immediately'), formed from re- + praesentare ('to place before, exhibit'), from praesens (stem praesent-, 'being before one, at hand'), originally the participle of praeesse ('to be in front of, preside over', from prae- + esse 'to be').

history.meaning: to place before the eyes, make immediately present
to exhibit visually, depict, stand in the place of
to act as agent for, stand for, stage, mean to someone

représenter.notes: The core verb of ASK in Dix pour cent ('to represent talent': Je représente Isabelle Huppert). Reflexive se représenter something means 'to picture / imagine' how big or difficult it is.

cognates.meaning: to go regularly to a place; to fix; a haunt/lair
to return to one's homeland (learnèd doublet)
to return someone to their homeland

repérer.etymology: Coined in late 18th-century technical French ('to mark out alignments or reference points') from the noun repère ('benchmark, alignment mark, landmark'). Repère is an orthographic variant of repaire ('haunt, den, home base'), deverbal from Old French repairier ('to return home, frequent a place'), inherited from Late Latin repatriare ('to return to one's native land'), from re- + patria ('fatherland', from pater 'father').

history.meaning: to go back to one's native country
to return home, frequent; a home base or haunt
reference mark; to locate by landmarks, spot, scout

morphemes.meaning: landmark, reference point (< Old French repaire < Late Latin repatriare)

repérer.notes: Stem vowel alternates between é and è (je repère, nous repérons). In film production, faire des repérages means 'location scouting', while repérer un jeune talent means 'to spot/discover new talent'.

rootFamily.gloss: location scouting (for a film shoot); spotting
lair, hangout (historical spelling doublet of repère)

cognates.meaning: Mass for the dead (proposed source under Norman hypothesis)

requin.etymology: First attested in late 16th-century Norman maritime accounts as requien; ultimate origin disputed. Traditional folk and maritime etymology derives Norman requien from Latin Requiem ('rest [for the dead]', opening word of the Catholic Mass for the dead), because a swimmer bitten by the predator needed immediate last rites. Modern Romance philologists (Bloch-Wartburg, CNRTL) often favor a derivation from Middle French/dialectal rechigner, Old French reschignier ('to bare one's teeth menacingly, grimace', from Frankish *kinan 'to split, gape open'), alluding to the shark's exposed rows of teeth.

history.meaning: to bare the teeth, grimace (or 'rest' for the dead)
large predatory sea fish, shark (Norman sailor usage)
shark; ruthless cutthroat competitor in business

requin.notes: Just like English 'shark', un vrai requin in Dix pour cent describes a ruthless rival agent or producer (such as Mathias Barneville or StarMedia executives) ready to poach clients without mercy.

rootFamily.gloss: to balk, pull a grimace (probable etymological relative)
guitar shark / top session musician (slang: requin de studio)

cognates.meaning: esteem, due regard for someone's feelings or rights

respect.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French from Classical Latin respectus ('the act of looking back, regard, consideration, refuge'), action noun formed on the past-participial stem of respicere ('to look back at, gaze upon, have mindful regard for'), from re- ('back') + specere ('to look at, observe'), from Proto-Indo-European *spek- ('to observe').

history.meaning: to look back at; a looking back, mindful consideration
relation, regard, deference toward rank or merit
high regard, deference, compliance (with rules or deadlines)

morphemes.meaning: look at, regard (< Latin specere / spectus)

respect.notes: Both final consonants -ct are completely silent in Modern French (/ʁɛs.pɛ/), though /k/ resurfaces in derivatives like respecter (/ʁɛs.pɛk.te/) and respectueux.

rootFamily.gloss: to respect, abide by (a contract or schedule)

respecter.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin respectare ('to look back at repeatedly, regard with deference or consideration'), frequentative of respicere, respectum ('to look back at, have regard for', from re- + specere 'to look').

history.meaning: to look back upon, show regard for
to treat with deference, respect, abide by (a rule)

cognates.meaning: the physiological act or process of breathing

respiration.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French (respiracion) from Classical Latin respiratio (accusative respirationem, 'breathing out and in, exhalation, pause to catch one's breath'), action noun of respirare ('to breathe back out, recover breath, find relief'), composed of re- ('back, repeatedly') + spirare ('to breathe, blow'). Already in Cicero's rhetorical prose, respiratio also meant a 'breathing space' or rhythmic pause in delivery.

history.meaning: breathing, exhalation, pause to catch breath
act of drawing breath, vital breath
breathing; rhythmic pause or comic relief in a dramatic work

respiration.notes: Beyond everyday 'breathing' (as opposed to medical English 'respiration'), screenwriters and editors use une respiration for a 'breather'—a lighter scene that lets the audience exhale after high drama.

rootFamily.gloss: to breathe; to exude (respirer le bonheur)
to inspire, breathe in; to sigh (soupirer)

respirer.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–14th century from Classical Latin respirare ('to breathe out, fetch one's breath, breathe, recover breath'), compound of re- ('back and forth, again') + spirare ('to blow, breathe').

history.meaning: to breathe, take a breather, exude

resplendissant.etymology: Participial adjective from the present participle of resplendir ('to shine brightly, gleam'), inherited in Old French with a conjugation shift to -ir from Classical Latin resplendere ('to shine back, reflect light brightly, glitter'), composed of intensive/reflective re- + splendere ('to shine, gleam, be bright'), the same Latin root behind splendeur and splendide.

history.meaning: to shine back, glitter, reflect light brightly
radiant, glowing with beauty, health, or glamour

resplendissant.notes: Red-carpet praise par excellence: Vous êtes resplendissante ce soir ! ('You look radiant tonight!') or resplendissant de santé ('glowing with health').

cognates.meaning: duty, accountability, state of being responsible

responsabilité.etymology: Derived in late 18th-century French (attested c. 1783 in political theory alongside English responsibility) from Middle French responsable ('answerable in law, accountable') + abstract noun suffix -ité. Responsable was borrowed from Medieval Latin responsabilis ('answerable'), built on Classical Latin responsum / responsare, from respondere ('to promise in return, answer solemnly'), from re- ('in return') + spondere ('to pledge solemnly').

history.meaning: to pledge in return, answer; legally answerable
accountable, liable to answer for something
moral, managerial, or legal responsibility and liability

responsabilité.notes: Watch the spelling vowel a (responsabilité, responsable), contrasting with English responsibility/responsible! Un poste à responsabilités means 'a senior/executive position'.

rootFamily.gloss: responsible; person in charge / manager (un responsable)

responsable.etymology: Formed in the 13th–14th century in legal French from Medieval Latin responsabilis ('answerable in court'), derived from the supine stem respons- of Classical Latin respondere ('to answer, promise in return, be answerable for').

ressembler.etymology: Inherited from Old French resembler ('to be like, look like'), formed from prefix re- + sembler ('to seem, be alike', from Classical Latin similare 'to make like, resemble', from similis 'similar').

history.meaning: to bear a likeness to, resemble

cognates.meaning: bitter indignation at unfair treatment (also philosophical loan ressentiment)

ressentiment.etymology: Formed in 16th-century French from ressentir ('to feel deeply, feel the aftereffects of') + action/state suffix -ment. In 16th- and 17th-century Classical French, ressentiment meant any strong lingering feeling—whether physical pain, tender gratitude (un vif ressentiment de vos bontés), or anger at an insult—before specializing almost exclusively in the negative sense of harbored bitterness and grievance (the sense later adopted into philosophy by Nietzsche).

history.meaning: act of feeling deeply again; lingering physical or moral impression
harbored bitterness, grudge, sense of injury

morphemes.meaning: deeply, back again (doubled s to preserve /s/)
noun suffix denoting emotional state or result

ressentiment.notes: While English 'resentment' is everyday vocabulary, French ressentiment belongs to a slightly more psychological/elevated register; in casual speech people often say rancune ('grudge') or amertume ('bitterness').

rootFamily.gloss: overall emotional impression, gut feeling (noun: le ressenti)

cognates.meaning: to feel bitterness at (semantic narrowing from French)
to feel the effects of, be affected by
to begin to weaken, feel pain or resentment

ressentir.etymology: Inherited from Old French ressentir ('to feel strongly, experience inwardly, feel the effects of'), formed from intensive re- (spelled res- intervocalically so the sibilant remains voiceless /s/ rather than voicing to /z/) + sentir ('to feel, perceive, smell'), inherited from Classical Latin sentire ('to perceive by the senses, feel, discern, think').

history.meaning: to perceive by the senses, feel, be aware of
to experience deeply, feel the reverberation of
to feel or experience (an emotion or physical sensation); se ressentir de 'to suffer aftereffects of'

ressentir.notes: Crucial false friend: ressentir means 'to feel deeply' (ressentir de la joie, ressentir un malaise), NOT 'to resent'! To translate 'I resent him for that', French says Je lui en veux pour ça.

rootFamily.gloss: subjective feeling, lived impression (quel est ton ressenti ?)

resserrer.etymology: Formed in Old French (resserrer, 12th c.) from prefix re- ('again, more tightly') + serrer ('to press close, tighten, lock').

history.meaning: to tighten again, draw closer together, narrow

cognates.meaning: to obtain by lot, emerge, go out
to go out, emerge, stand out
rapid defensive sally; weekend trip (loan from French sortie)

ressortir.etymology: Inherited from Old French ressortir ('to spring back, rebound, go out again'), formed from re- (with orthographic doubling to res- to maintain voiceless /s/) + sortir ('to go out, emerge'). Old French sortir continues Gallo-Romance *sortire, generally traced to Classical Latin sortiri ('to cast lots, obtain by lot, allot', from sors, sortis 'lot, fate'), which developed senses of 'obtaining an outcome, escaping, emerging', likely reinforced by Old French saillir / sourdre.

history.meaning: to draw lots, obtain an outcome; (Gallo-Romance) to come forth, escape
to rebound, spring back, go out again
to go out again, resurface, stand out vividly, emerge from facts

morphemes.meaning: again, back out (doubled s to preserve /s/)

ressortir.notes: Conjugates like sortir (il ressort, nous ressortons) with auxiliary être when intransitive (un vieux dossier est ressorti 'an old scandal resurfaced'), or avoir when transitive ('to pull out again'). Faire ressortir means 'to highlight / make stand out'.

rootFamily.gloss: to go out, release (sortir un film)
exit, outing, theatrical film release (la sortie en salles)

cognates.meaning: dining establishment (borrowed from French); cf. restorative

restaurant.etymology: Substantivized present participle of restaurer ('to rebuild, renew, refresh with food'), borrowed from Classical Latin restaurare ('to rebuild, restore, renew'), from re- + *staurare (related to Latin instaurare 'to set up anew', from Proto-Indo-European *stau-ro- 'standing post, firm').
