From the 16th century un restaurant denoted a rich, restorative meat bouillon; in 1760s Paris, bouillon-sellers' shops (famously Boulanger's) gave the name by metonymy to public establishments serving individual dishes at private tables.

history.meaning: to rebuild, renew, restore to strength
restorative meat broth or cordial strengthening the sick or weary
public dining establishment serving meals from a menu

morphemes.meaning: set up firm, renew (< Latin restaurare)

restaurant.notes: Colloquially clipped to resto (/ʁɛs.to/) in everyday speech: On se fait un resto après la projo ? ('Shall we grab dinner out after the screening?').

rootFamily.gloss: to restore (a film print/building), to feed (se restaurer)
catering/food-service industry; art or film restoration

restaurer.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th–14th century from Classical Latin restaurare ('to rebuild, renew, repair, restore'), from re- ('again') + *-staurare (built on the PIE root *sta- 'to stand', as in instaurare); in 18th-century Paris, un bouillon qui restaure ('a restorative broth') gave rise to restaurant.

history.meaning: to repair a building or artwork; to refresh with food and drink

cognates.meaning: the remaining part or people (borrowed via Middle French)

reste.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Middle French from rester ('to remain behind, be left over'), adapted from Classical Latin restare ('to stand firm, stay behind, remain, survive'), composed of re- ('back, behind') + stare ('to stand'), from Proto-Indo-European *steh2- ('to stand'). Note that English has two homonyms 'rest': 'repose' is Germanic (Old English ræst), whereas 'the rest / remainder' was borrowed from French reste!

history.meaning: to stand back, stay behind, remain left over
that which remains unpaid or left over (originally often feminine)
remainder, balance (singular le reste); leftovers or mortal remains (plural les restes)

reste.notes: Masculine (le reste). Useful idioms: du reste ('besides / moreover'), ne pas demander son reste ('to beat a hasty retreat'), and avoir de beaux restes ('to still look impressive with age').

rester.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin restare ('to stand back, stay behind, remain, be left over'), compound of re- ('back, behind') + stare ('to stand').

history.meaning: to remain, stay, be left over

retard.etymology: Retard is a noun formed from retarder, to delay. The Académie dates the noun to the seventeenth century. The modern expression en retard means late.

rootFamily.gloss: to delay, postpone; run slow (of a watch)

retard.notes: To say 'I am late' for an appointment, French uses être en retard (never *être tard, which is impersonal: il est tard 'it's late at night'!).

retardement.etymology: Inherited from Old/Middle French retardement ('action of holding back, slowing down, postponement'), derived from retarder ('to slow down, delay') + action-noun suffix -ment. Retarder continues Classical Latin retardare ('to slow down, hinder, detain'), formed from re- ('back') + tardare ('to make slow, tarry'), from tardus ('slow, sluggish, late').

history.meaning: to slow down, impede, hold back
deliberate time-delay mechanism or delayed reaction (chiefly in à retardement)

retardement.notes: Everyday lateness is un retard (être en retard); retardement survives primarily in the vivid phrase à retardement ('time-delayed'), as in une bombe à retardement ('ticking time bomb') or réagir à retardement ('to have a delayed reaction').

rootFamily.gloss: to delay, run slow (of a watch)
late (in the day or behind schedule)

retenir.etymology: Inherited from Old French retenir ('to hold back, keep, detain, remember'), from Vulgar Latin *retenire for Classical Latin retinere ('to hold back, keep, preserve'), compound of re- ('back') + tenere ('to hold').

history.meaning: to hold back, detain, keep in memory, book/reserve, carry a digit

cognates.meaning: to withdraw from a post or active work (borrowed from French)
to pull back, withdraw, collect (via Gallo-Romance)

retirer.etymology: Inherited from Old French retirer ('to pull back, draw back, lead away'), formed from re- ('back, away') + tirer ('to pull, draw, tug'). While the prefixal derivation of retirer is completely transparent, Old French tirer (attested from the 11th century) has a debated root: either an apheretic shortening of Old French martirer ('to stretch on the torture rack, maltreat', from Latin martyr) or a borrowing from a Germanic verb akin to Gothic tairan / Old English teran ('to tear, pull apart').

history.meaning: to tug, draw back, pull away
to remove, pull off; (reflexive) to retreat into privacy or from battle
to take off (clothing), withdraw (money, a bid, a statement), pick up (tickets/packages)

retirer.notes: High-frequency polysemy: retirer son manteau ('take off one's coat'), retirer de l'argent ('withdraw cash'), retirer ses invitations ('pick up VIP invitations at will-call'), and se retirer d'un projet ('pull out of a project'). 'To retire from work' is usually prendre sa retraite!

rootFamily.gloss: to pull, shoot (also tirer un portrait / tirer profit)

cognates.meaning: to knock down, throw down, lie down

retomber.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French from re- ('again, back down') + tomber ('to fall, tumble'). Old French tomber ('to fall, do acrobatics, somersault') derives either from Frankish *tumon ('to turn, tumble, dance acrobatics', cognate with Old English tumbian > English tumble) or from an expressive Vulgar Latin *tumbare imitating the dull thud (*tumb-) of a body hitting the ground.

history.meaning: to somersault, fall with a thud
to tumble, fall back down again
to fall again, subside (of tension/hype), land back on one's feet

retomber.notes: Conjugates with être in compound tenses (le soufflé est retombé 'the hype fizzled out'). Agents live by retomber sur ses pieds ('to land back on one's feet') and les retombées médiatiques ('media fallout / press buzz').

rootFamily.gloss: nightfall (la tombée de la nuit); fall

cognates.meaning: to improve or repair slightly by adding small touches (loan from French)
to retouch, touch up, adjust slightly

retoucher.etymology: Formed in Middle French from re- ('again, anew') + toucher ('to touch, strike lightly'). Old French tochier descends from Vulgar Latin *toccare ('to knock, strike a bell, touch'), a pan-Romance expressive creation built on the onomatopoeic syllable *tok- imitating a light tap. In the 17th century retoucher became a fine-arts term for reworking a painting or copperplate engraving, later passing naturally into photography, makeup, and digital editing.

history.meaning: to knock, tap, strike a bell, touch
to touch again; to rework brushstrokes or engraved lines
to touch up (makeup/garments), airbrush or digitally alter (photos/footage)

retoucher.notes: Covers physical tailoring, set-side makeup touch-ups (une petite retouche maquillage avant de tourner !), and Photoshop airbrushing on magazine covers or movie posters (photo non retouchée).

rootFamily.gloss: to touch, move emotionally, collect (toucher un cachet 'collect a fee')

retour.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (retor / retour, 11th–12th c.) from retorner / retourner ('to turn back, return').

history.meaning: act of coming or going back, return, recurrence

retourner.etymology: Formed in Old French (retorner, 10th–11th c.) from prefix re- ('back, in the opposite direction') + torner / tourner ('to turn', from Classical Latin tornare 'to turn on a lathe').

history.meaning: to turn over, turn inside out, go back, return

retraite.etymology: Inherited from Old French retraite ('act of drawing back, military withdrawal, place of refuge'), substantivized feminine past participle of retraire ('to draw back, withdraw', from Classical Latin retrahere 'to draw back'); acquired the modern sense 'retirement from working life and old-age pension' in the 17th–19th centuries.

history.meaning: drawing back, military retreat, quiet refuge
military retreat, spiritual retreat; retirement and pension

retrouvailles.etymology: Formed in the 19th–20th century as a feminine plural noun from retrouver ('to find again, meet again after a separation') + festive/collective suffix -ailles (on the model of épousailles, fiançailles).

history.meaning: joyful reunion after a long separation

retrouver.etymology: Formed in Old French (retrover, 11th–12th c.) from prefix re- ('again') + trover / trouver ('to find').

history.meaning: to find again, recover, meet up with, recognize

cognates.meaning: to assign a higher value to; cf. valorize
to enhance or restore the value of

revaloriser.etymology: Early 20th-century French formation (originally macroeconomic, 'to restore the purchasing power or parity of a currency') combining re- ('again, upward') with valoriser ('to give value to, enhance'). Valoriser was built on Latin valor (accusative valorem, 'worth, strength, courage', whence French valeur), derived from Classical Latin valere ('to be strong, be healthy, be worth'), + causative suffix -iser (from Late Latin -izare, Greek -izein).

history.meaning: to be strong, be worth; strength, worth
to confer value upon, make profitable or respected
to revalue upward, raise (pay/fees), restore prestige or status to

revaloriser.notes: Prime contract-negotiation verb in French agencies and unions: revaloriser le cachet d'une actrice ('to bump up/increase an actress's fee') or revaloriser un métier ('to restore prestige and fair pay to a profession').

rootFamily.gloss: to showcase, make someone feel valued (valoriser un talent)
value, worth; mettre en valeur 'to highlight/flatter'

revanche.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from Middle French revancher ('to avenge, retaliate'), altered from Old French revenchier, composed of the intensive/iterative prefix re- and Old French venchier (modern venger), which descends from Classical Latin vindicare ('to lay legal claim to, avenge, punish').
revanche.notes: Unlike vengeance (serious moral or personal retribution), revanche often denotes playful payback, a sporting rematch, or the set phrase en revanche ('on the other hand').

revenir.etymology: Inherited from Old French revenir ('to come back'), from Classical Latin revenire ('to come back, return'), compound of re- ('back, again') + venire ('to come').

history.meaning: to come back, return, recover consciousness, cost, brown lightly in pan

cognates.meaning: income of an organization or state

revenu.etymology: Substantivized masculine past participle of revenir ('to come back, return'), originally denoting 'that which comes back' from an estate, investment, or harvest. Revenir continues Old French revenir, from Late Latin revenire, formed from Classical Latin re- ('back') and venire ('to come').
revenu.notes: Masculine (un revenu, des revenus); do not confuse with English 'revenue' (corporate/tax turnover, which in French business parlance is usually chiffre d'affaires or recettes fiscales).

revers.etymology: Borrowed and adapted in Old French from Late Latin reversus ('turned back, reversed'), past participle of Classical Latin revertere ('to turn back, fold back'), from re- ('back') + vertere ('to turn'). Because a coat or jacket lapel is formed by folding the front edge of the cloth back upon itself, tailors named it le revers; the same word also denotes the reverse side of a coin or a backhand stroke in tennis.

history.meaning: back side; folded lapel of a garment

revers.notes: Because the singular **revers** already ends in **-s** (silent **/ʁəvɛʁ/**), the singular and plural are spelled and pronounced identically.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: revers

cognates.meaning: to give new energy or strength to

revigorer.etymology: Formed within French (first attested in the 16th century as ravigorer, later reshaped as revigorer) from the prefix re- ('again, anew') + Old/Middle French vigorer ('to strengthen') or directly on Latin vigor ('liveliness, force, thriving strength'), from vigere ('to thrive, be lively').

history.meaning: to restore energy or vitality to

revigorer.notes: Shares colloquial space with its expressive cousin ravigoter ('to perk up', as in sauce ravigote); revigorer belongs to standard everyday and journalistic register.

revisser.etymology: Formed in Modern French from iterative prefix re- ('again, back') + visser ('to screw in, fasten with screws', from vis 'screw').

history.meaning: to screw back on or tighten a screw again

revoir.etymology: Revoir is derived from voir, to see, with the idea of seeing again. The Académie records tenth-century revedeir and twelfth-century reveoir.

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Middle French reveue (< revoir)

revoir.notes: Au revoir! is ellipsis for jusqu'au revoir ('until the seeing-again'), matching Italian arrivederci and German Auf Wiedersehen.

rez-de-chaussée.etymology: Compound noun formed in the 16th–17th century from archaic preposition rez ('flush with, at the exact level of', from Old French res < Classical Latin rasus 'scraped flat, level', past participle of radere) + de ('of') + chaussée ('paved street, roadway') — literally 'at street level'.

history.meaning: level with the street -> ground floor of a building

riche.etymology: Inherited from Old French riche ('powerful, mighty, noble; wealthy'), borrowed from Frankish *riki ('powerful, mighty, royal', from Proto-Germanic *rikijaz, cognate with English rich and German reich, itself an ancient Germanic borrowing from Celtic *rix 'king').

rideau.etymology: Formed in Old/Middle French (ridel / rideau, 13th–14th c., 'pleated cloth hanging around a bed or window') from rider ('to wrinkle, gather into pleats', from Frankish *hridan 'to twist, pleat, wrinkle').

history.meaning: pleated bed or window hanging -> curtain, stage curtain

ridicule.etymology: Learned 15th-century borrowing from Classical Latin ridiculus ('laughable, funny, absurd'), derived from ridere ('to laugh, smile'). In French, the sense shifted rapidly from 'eliciting good-natured laughter' to 'deserving mockery, absurdly humiliating'.
ridicule.notes: Functions as both an adjective (un cachet ridicule, 'a laughably tiny fee') and a masculine noun, famous in the proverb le ridicule ne tue pas ('embarrassment won't kill you').

ridiculiser.etymology: Coined in the late 16th to 17th century from the French adjective ridicule ('absurd, laughable', from Classical Latin ridiculus) plus the factitive verbal suffix -iser (from Late Latin -izare, Ancient Greek -izein), literally meaning 'to render ridiculous'.

history.meaning: to expose to mockery, make foolish

ridiculiser.notes: Very common reflexively (se ridiculiser, 'to make a fool of oneself') in showbiz and social settings when a pitch or audition goes badly wrong.

rien.etymology: Rien descends from Latin rem, the object-case form of res, thing. The French word is recorded from the tenth century; negative constructions gave this older thing-word its familiar modern meaning nothing.

cognates.meaning: nothing / anything (exact parallel shift of Latin rēs!)

rootFamily.gloss: a tiny trifle (preserving the positive noun 'a little thing'!)

rien.notes: Remarkable semantic flip: Latin rem meant 'a thing' (preserved in un rien l'amuse 'a tiny thing amuses him'), which frequent use in negative clauses (je ne vois rien) turned into 'nothing'!

rigoler.etymology: Inherited from Old French rigoler ('to mock, banter, make merry, dance'), whose ultimate origin remains uncertain. Philologists propose an expressive onomatopoeic root *rig- evoke lively movement or laughter, possibly related to Old Franconian or Low German forms, rather than Latin ridere.

history.meaning: to laugh, joke around, have fun

rigoler.notes: Informal everyday verb meaning both 'to laugh' and 'to kid/joke': Tu rigoles ! means 'You're kidding!' and Sans rigoler means 'No joke / seriously'.

rime.etymology: Inherited from Old French rime ('accentual verse, correspondence of terminal sounds in poetry'), derived via Medieval Latin rithmus from Ancient Greek rhythmos ('measured flow, cadence, proportion'); in medieval Latin poetry, rhythmus designated accentual rhymed verse as opposed to classical quantitative meter (metrum).

rire.etymology: Inherited from Old French rire ('to laugh'), from Vulgar Latin *ridere, 3rd-conjugation shift of Classical Latin ridere ('to laugh, smile').

risotto.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from Northern Italian (Milanese/Lombard-influenced Italian) risotto, formed from riso ('rice', from Latin oryza via Greek) + the masculine suffix -otto (expressing a substantial or characteristic dish made from the base ingredient).
risotto.notes: Pronounced /ʁi.zɔ.to/ in French (voiced /z/ between vowels, single consonant timing, final stress), and grammatically masculine (un risotto aux truffes).

risque.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian risco (modern rischio), a maritime insurance term from Medieval Latin risicum ('hazard at sea'). Its deeper origin is likely Byzantine Greek rhizikon ('cliff, reef; soldier's luck/fortune', from rhiza 'root, cliff base'), or possibly Arabic rizq ('allotted sustenance, fortune').

history.meaning: maritime hazard insured in shipping contracts
exposure to danger or potential loss

risque.notes: Originally feminine on arrival from Italian in the 1500s before stabilizing as masculine (un risque); English 'risk' was borrowed directly from this French word in the 17th century.

cognates.meaning: to expose to danger or loss

risquer.etymology: Attested in the late 16th century, derived from French risque ('hazard, peril') or adapted directly alongside Italian arriscare / rischiare ('to venture a ship or cargo, put in peril'), from Medieval Latin risicum.

history.meaning: to put cargo or oneself in hazard
to hazard, expose to danger; to be likely to

risquer.notes: Watch the construction risquer de + infinitive: Il risque de pleuvoir (or même Il risque de gagner !) often simply means 'It is likely to...' even for neutral or positive outcomes.

risqué.etymology: Adjectival past participle of French risquer ('to hazard, expose to danger'), formed on risque ('peril, commercial or personal hazard', from Italian risco / Medieval Latin risicum) with the regular first-conjugation participial suffix -é (from Latin -atus).

history.meaning: to expose to hazard or loss

risqué.notes: Classic false friend! In French, un projet risqué simply means 'a risky/dangerous project' (financially or artistically); for English 'risqué' (racily suggestive), French uses osé, grivois, or coquin.

rival.etymology: Learned late 15th-century borrowing from Classical Latin rivalis ('competitor in love; originally, one who shares the same irrigation brook with a neighbor'), derived from rivus ('stream, brook'). Neighbors sharing water rights frequently clashed, shifting the sense to competition.

history.meaning: neighbor sharing a brook; competitor in love
competitor for love, prestige, or success

rival.notes: Irregular masculine plural: un rival -> des rivaux (feminine une rivale -> des rivales); etymologically tied to streams, just like dériver ('to divert water; drift').

rivière.etymology: Inherited from Old French riviere ('riverbank, riverside hunting ground, river'), from Vulgar Latin *riparia (scilicet terra, 'land along a bank'), the substantivized feminine of Classical Latin riparius ('of a riverbank'), derived from ripa ('steep bank, shore').

history.meaning: steep bank of a stream, shore

morphemes.meaning: bank, shore (from Latin ripa / French rive)

rivière.notes: French distinguishes une rivière (an inland river flowing into another river, like the Marne) from un fleuve (a major river emptying into the sea, like the Seine); une rivière de diamants also means a single-strand diamond necklace on the red carpet!

riz.etymology: Inherited via Old French ris from Old Italian riso, from Vulgar Latin *orizum, Classical Latin oryza, borrowed from Ancient Greek oryza ('rice'), which traveled westward through Indo-Iranian trade routes from an ancient South Asian / Dravidian or Indo-Aryan source (cf. Tamil arici).

history.meaning: rice grain imported from the East

riz.notes: The final -z is completely silent (/ʁi/), so du riz sounds identical in isolation to du rire without its final /ʁ/; invariant in the plural.

robe.etymology: Inherited from Old French robe (originally 'booty, spoils stripped from a fallen enemy, pillaged garments', then 'suit of outer clothing, gown'), borrowed from Frankish *rauba ('spoils of war, plunder, captured clothing', from Proto-Germanic *raubo, cognate with English rob and reave).

history.meaning: garment, judicial/academic gown, woman's dress, animal's coat, color of wine

robinet.etymology: Appeared in the 15th century as a nickname from Robin (pet form of the given name Robert, also used in medieval folklore as the name of the sheep in the Roman de Renart) because water spigots on casks and fountains were commonly cast with a decorative ram's head whose knob was turned to let water or wine flow.

history.form: Robin (name given to the ram) -> robinet
history.meaning: ram's-head cask spigot -> water tap, faucet, valve

romantique.etymology: Borrowed in the late 17th century from English romantic ('resembling medieval chivalric tales'), which had itself been formed from early modern French romant (modern roman, 'vernacular tale, novel', originally Old French romanz 'in the Romance vernacular', from Vulgar Latin *romanice 'in the Roman manner').

history.meaning: speaking in the Roman vernacular (not Latin)
verse or prose narrative in French
evocative of chivalric tales; passionate idealist

romantique.notes: Used as a noun (un grand romantique, une romantique incurable) for a dreamy sentimentalist, or in cinema for une comédie romantique ('rom-com').

rompre.etymology: Inherited from Old French rompre ('to break, shatter, rout an army'), evolving regularly from Classical Latin rumpere ('to break, burst, tear asunder, annul a treaty'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *Hrewp- ('to break, tear, snatch').

history.meaning: to burst, break open, violate a pact
to shatter, smash through military ranks
to snap, sever a contract, break up romantically

rompre.notes: In contemporary spoken French, physical breaking uses casser, while rompre specializes in relationships and contracts: rompre avec quelqu'un ('to break up with someone'), rompre un contrat, or rompre le silence.

rond.etymology: Inherited from Old French reont / roont ('round, circular'), from Classical Latin rotundus ('wheel-shaped, circular, spherical, well-rounded'), derived from rota ('wheel').

ronronner.etymology: Nineteenth-century French verb built on the reduplicated onomatopoeia ronron ('a cat's purr'), imitating a steady low vibration.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: ronronner (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: ronronner

cognates.meaning: enclosed chamber in a building; open space

room.etymology: 20th-century hospitality borrowing from English room (chiefly in fixed luxury-hotel compounds like room service or show-room), which descends from Middle English roum and Old English rum ('open space, dimensional extent'), from Proto-Germanic *rumaz ('spacious, wide space').

history.meaning: interior chamber or hotel guest suite

room.notes: Never used alone in French to mean a bedroom or hotel room (use une chambre or une pièce); encountered almost exclusively in le room service at luxury hotels frequented by film stars, or un showroom in fashion.

rose.etymology: Inherited/adapted in Old French (rose, 11th–12th c.) from Classical Latin rosa ('rose flower and bush', an ancient Mediterranean word parallel to Greek rhodon); used as an adjective and noun for the color pink since the Middle Ages.

history.meaning: rose flower (fem. noun); pink color (adj. & masc. noun)

roue.etymology: Inherited from Old French roe ('wheel'), from Classical Latin rota ('wheel of a chariot or potter, disk', from PIE *roteh2 'wheel', built on *ret- 'to run, roll').

rouge.etymology: Inherited from Old French roge / rouge ('red'), from Classical Latin rubeus ('red, reddish', originally applied to cattle and hides, derived from ruber 'red' < PIE *h1rewdh- 'red'), which displaced ruber in Gallo-Romance.

rouleau.etymology: Inherited from Old French rolel / rouleau ('rolled-up scroll, cylinder'), diminutive of rôle (in its original sense 'parchment roll'), from Vulgar Latin *rotularius / Classical Latin rotulus ('little wheel, scroll'), diminutive of rota ('wheel').

history.meaning: scroll, cylindrical roller, rolling pin, paint roller, breaking wave

cognates.meaning: to move by turning over and over (borrowed from Old French)

rouler.etymology: Inherited from Old French roler / rouler ('to roll along, wrap in a scroll'), from Vulgar Latin *rotulare ('to turn like a little wheel'), derived from Classical Latin rotula ('small wheel'), diminutive of rota ('wheel'), from Proto-Indo-European *Hret- ('to run, roll').

history.meaning: to make revolve like a wheel
to roll, travel on wheels, drive

rouler.notes: Packed with idioms: Ça roule ? ('How's it going? / All good?'), rouler quelqu'un (dans la farine) ('to scam/rip someone off'), and on film sets Ça roule ! ('Rolling!').

rootFamily.gloss: scroll, roller; actor's role (doublet via Old French role)

cognates.meaning: gambling game with a spinning wheel (loanword)

roulette.etymology: Formed in Old French as rolete ('little wheel, caster'), diminutive of roe (modern roue, 'wheel') or directly derived from roler / rouler ('to roll', from Latin rotula) with the diminutive suffix -ette; applied to the spinning-wheel gambling game in the 18th century.

history.meaning: caster wheel; revolving gambling wheel game

roulette.notes: Gives the sunny expression aller comme sur des roulettes ('to go like clockwork / go smoothly, as if on little wheels'), as well as la roulette russe ('Russian roulette') and, terrifyingly, the dentist's drill!

roulé.etymology: Substantivized past participle of rouler ('to roll, roll up'), designating a rolled pastry (biscuit roulé, Swiss roll) or rolled roast.

cognates.meaning: way or course taken; utter defeat (rout)

route.etymology: Inherited from Old French rote ('cleared road, path through woods; troop detachment'), from Late/Vulgar Latin (via) rupta ('a way broken or hacked open through forest or rock'), feminine past participle of Classical Latin rumpere ('to break, force open').
route.notes: Une route typically connects towns or regions (unlike une rue, a street lined with buildings inside a city); en route ! ('let's hit the road!') was borrowed straight into English.

rootFamily.gloss: routine, habitual path (originally diminutive of route)
to break (inherited verbal base of rupta)

cognates.meaning: networking device that forwards data packets

routeur.etymology: Late 20th-century computing adaptation of English router ('device forwarding data packets along network paths'), re-gallicized with French agent/instrument suffix -eur. An etymological boomerang: English router derives from route, itself borrowed from Old French route (Latin via rupta).

history.meaning: device directing data packets across networks

routeur.notes: In everyday French home life, people often call their Wi-Fi router/modem unit une box (e.g., redémarrer la box), reserving routeur for technical or IT contexts.

rootFamily.gloss: to divert or reroute (a plane or shipment)

rouvrir.etymology: Formed in Old French (rovreir / rouvrir, 12th c.) from iterative prefix r- / re- ('again') + ouvrir ('to open').

cognates.meaning: pertaining to a monarch; real (doublet via Spanish/Latin)

royal.etymology: Inherited from Old French reial / roial ('kingly, sovereign'), regularly evolved (with Old French diphthongization ei > oi) from Classical Latin regalis ('worthy of or belonging to a king'), derived from rex, regis ('king'), from Proto-Indo-European *h3reǵ- ('to straighten, rule').

history.meaning: belonging to or worthy of a monarch

royal.notes: Colloquially means 'grand, ultra-generous, effortless'—and royalement ('royally') appears constantly in se ficher royalement de quelque chose ('to couldn't care less about something').

cognates.meaning: kingdom, sovereign domain (borrowed from Old French)

royaume.etymology: Inherited from Old French reiaume / roiaume ('kingdom, sovereign dominion'), descending from Vulgar Latin *regiminem (accusative of Classical Latin regimen 'rule, governance, guiding authority'), remodeled in Gallo-Romance under the phonological and semantic attraction of roi / roial (Latin regalis).

history.meaning: king's rule; territory governed by a king

morphemes.meaning: nominal suffix denoting collective domain (from -amen / regimen)

royaume.notes: English 'realm' was borrowed straight from the Old French spelling reaume; in modern French, le Royaume-Uni is 'the United Kingdom'.

ruban.etymology: Attested in thirteenth-century Old French as riban / ruban, likely borrowed from Middle Dutch ringhband ('neckband, collar ribbon'). Middle English riban—modern English ribbon—came straight from the Old Northern French form.

cognates.meaning: narrow woven strip (from Old French riban)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: ruban (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: ruban

rude.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin rudis ('unwrought, raw, uncultivated, rough'), originally applied to unworked stone, wood, or raw wool before extending to harsh weather, grueling labor, and unpolished manners.

history.meaning: rough to the touch, harsh, unrefined

rude.notes: Major false friend! French rude usually means 'tough, grueling, harsh' (une rude journée de tournage = 'a grueling day of filming'; la concurrence est rude = 'competition is fierce'), whereas English 'rude' (impolite) is impoli, malpoli, or grossier.

rootFamily.gloss: erudite, learned (literally 'brought out of rawness', ex + rudis)

rue.etymology: Rue comes from Late Latin ruga ('wrinkle, furrow', and by extension a 'wheel-rutted path' or 'lined street between houses'), developing into Old French rue ('town street').
rue.notes: Diminutive **une ruelle** = a narrow alley or side lane.

ruelle.etymology: Formed in Old French (ruele, 12th c.) as a diminutive of rue ('street', from Late Latin ruga 'wrinkle, furrow; wheel-rut, street lined with houses') + diminutive suffix -elle.

history.meaning: narrow lane or alley; space beside a four-poster bed

cognates.meaning: to destroy, reduce to poverty or collapse

ruiner.etymology: Formed in Middle French (14th century) from the noun ruine ('collapse, fallen building', borrowed from Classical Latin ruina 'headlong fall, tumbling down, disaster', from ruere 'to rush down, collapse, fall violently') + verbal suffix -er.

history.meaning: headlong collapse of a structure, catastrophe
to demolish, destroy, or drive into bankruptcy

ruiner.notes: Pronounced in two or three syllables (/ʁɥi.ne/); reflexively se ruiner is widely used hyperbolically when splurging ('to spend a fortune / break the bank').

ruiné.etymology: Adjectival past participle of French ruiner ('to demolish, impoverish'), derived from ruine (from Classical Latin ruina 'collapse, downfall', from ruere 'to tumble headlong') with the regular participial suffix -é (Latin -atus). By the 16th–17th centuries, the financial sense 'stripped of fortune' became standard.

history.meaning: to cause to collapse, lay waste
reduced to rubble; stripped of wealth and credit

ruiné.notes: Applied to people (Je suis ruiné !), it almost always means 'financially wiped out / broke', whereas applied to buildings or health (un château ruiné, une santé ruinée) it retains the destructive sense.

rumeur.etymology: Inherited/adapted via Old French rumor / rumeur ('clamor, uproar, public talk') from Classical Latin rumor, rumoris ('low dull noise, murmur of a crowd, hearsay, popular talk'), linked to an Indo-European acoustic root *h3rew- ('to bellow, murmur, roar').

history.meaning: noisy commotion, public outcry, unverified news
circulating gossip; ambient hum of a city

rumeur.notes: Feminine noun (une rumeur court, 'a rumor is going around'), like nearly all abstract French nouns ending in -eur (la peur, la chaleur, la valeur—with le bonheur and le malheur as famous masculine exceptions).

rupture.etymology: Learned 14th-century borrowing (first in surgical texts for hernias and fractures, then figurative) from Late Latin ruptura ('fracture, breaking of a limb or vein'), formed on rupt-, past participial stem of Classical Latin rumpere ('to break, burst, tear apart') + -ura.

history.meaning: physical breach; romantic breakup or contract termination

rupture.notes: Extremely versatile in everyday French: une rupture amoureuse ('a romantic breakup'), une rupture conventionnelle ('mutual employment termination'), and en rupture de stock ('out of stock').

russe.etymology: Attested in French since the 14th–16th centuries via Medieval Latin Russus, from Old East Slavic Rus' (Русь, the Kievan realm and its Varangian elite). The Slavic ethnonym was borrowed from Finnic Ruotsi ('Swedes; coastal oarsmen'), ultimately from Old Norse *roþs- ('men who row', from the root of 'row').

history.meaning: Russian (adjective and language); capitalized Russe for a person

russe.notes: In French orthography, adjectives and language names stay lowercase (le cinéma russe, parler russe), whereas nationality nouns take a capital letter (un Russe, une Russe); note also les montagnes russes ('roller coaster', literally 'Russian mountains'!).

rythme.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century via Classical Latin rhythmus from Ancient Greek rhythmos ('measured motion, regular recurrence, cadence, proportion', related to rhein 'to flow' — learned doublet of rime).

history.meaning: musical, poetic, or biological rhythm, pace

règle.etymology: Inherited/semi-learned adaptation in Old French (reule / riule -> règle) from Classical Latin regula ('straight wooden lath, ruler, measuring rod; moral or monastic standard, rule'), derived from regere ('to keep straight, guide, rule').

règlement.etymology: Formed in the 15th–16th century from régler ('to rule lines, regulate, settle an account') + nominal suffix -ment.

history.meaning: body of regulations, bylaws; settlement or payment of a bill or dispute

ré.etymology: Second syllable of the hexachord introduced by Guido d'Arezzo (c. 1025), taken from the initial syllable of the second half-line (Resonare fibris) of the Latin hymn to St. John the Baptist Ut queant laxis.

history.meaning: second solfège note of the scale (D)

cognates.meaning: action or response to a stimulus

réaction.etymology: Coined in Scholastic Medieval Latin reactio (and adopted into Middle/Early Modern French in scientific mechanics before entering psychology and politics during the French Revolution), from re- ('back, in opposition') + actio ('doing, driving force', from Classical Latin agere 'to drive, do, act').

history.meaning: to drive, perform -> a doing, physical motion
reciprocal physical counter-action of a body
physical, chemical, emotional, or political response

réaction.notes: Covers everything from emotional response (avoir une bonne réaction) to aviation: un avion à réaction is a 'jet plane' (literally 'reaction-propelled aircraft', hence un réacteur for a jet engine).

cognates.meaning: to respond to an event or stimulus

réagir.etymology: Formed in the 16th century (alongside Scholastic Latin reagere, originally in physics and alchemy) from the prefix ré- ('back, against, in response', variant of re- before a vowel) + French agir ('to act', borrowed from Classical Latin agere 'to drive, set in motion, perform').

history.meaning: to exert reciprocal force against an agent
to exert counterforce; respond to an event or provocation

morphemes.meaning: back, in response (prevocalic form of re-)

réagir.notes: Conjugates as a regular second-group -ir verb with the -iss- stem extension in plural/imperfect forms (nous réagissons, ils réagissent, je réagissais), just like agir and finir.

rootFamily.gloss: to act; s'agir de ('to be about')

cognates.meaning: one who makes real or achieves

réalisateur.etymology: Derived in early 19th-century French from the verb réaliser ('to make real, bring into existence') plus the agentive suffix -ateur (from Latin -ātōrem). Originally denoting someone who turns ideas into reality, it specialized in early 20th-century French cinema for the film director who brings a screenplay to life on screen.

history.meaning: one who brings into reality; (20th c.) film or television director

réalisateur.notes: False friend alert: French 'directeur' means manager or executive (like a casting or production manager), whereas a film director is always a 'réalisateur' (often shortened informally on set to 'le réal').

rootFamily.gloss: to direct (a film); to realize, achieve

réalisatrice.etymology: Formed as the feminine counterpart to réalisateur from the stem of réaliser ('to bring into reality, direct a film') with the learned feminine agentive suffix -atrice, borrowed from Latin -ātrīcem. Its cinematic sense ('female film director') established itself alongside réalisateur in 20th-century French film terminology.

history.meaning: belonging to the thing itself, real
woman who actualizes; female film or TV director

réalisatrice.notes: Unlike some professions where French historically hesitated over feminine forms (like 'auteure'/'autrice'), 'réalisatrice' is completely standard and universally used in the French film industry; colloquially shortened to 'la réal'.

rootFamily.gloss: to direct a film; to carry out

réaliser.etymology: Derived in the 15th–16th century (originally in law and philosophy, 'to make real or actual, convert property into cash') from Medieval Scholastic Latin realis ('actual, relating to things', from Classical Latin res 'thing'); acquired the additional sense 'to become fully aware of, realize' in the late 19th century under the influence of English to realize.

history.meaning: to make real, carry out, direct a film; to realize mentally

réaliste.etymology: Derived from Medieval Latin realis ('relating to actual things', from Classical Latin rēs 'thing') with the learned suffix -iste. First attested in French in philosophical usage (scholastic realism, later influenced by German Realist), it broadened in the mid-19th century around Courbet and Champfleury to aesthetic realism and practical clear-sightedness.
réaliste.notes: Functions as both an adjective ('un scénario réaliste' — a realistic script) and an invariable-stem epicene noun ('un/une réaliste' — a realist).

réalité.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Medieval Scholastic Latin realitatem (nominative realitas, coined by Duns Scotus for 'actual existence as a thing'), derived from Late Latin realis ('relating to actual things'), from Classical Latin res ('thing, fact').

rébellion.etymology: Borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin rebelliōnem (nominative rebelliō), originally meaning 'a renewal of war' by a conquered people, derived from rebellis ('waging war again, insurgent'), itself compounded from re- ('again, back') and bellum ('war'). In everyday French it softened from armed uprising to personal defiance against authority.

history.meaning: renewal of war, revolt of the vanquished

rébellion.notes: Note the acute accent in 'rébellion' versus the mute 'e' in the related noun/adjective 'rebelle' [ʁəbɛl] and verb 'se rebeller' — a frequent French spelling trap.

récemment.etymology: Formed in Middle French from the adjective récent ('fresh, new, recent') and the adverbial suffix -ment (from the Latin ablative mente 'with a mind'). Because adjectives in -ent derive from Latin third-declension stems in -ent-, the vowel assimilates before -ment, yielding spelled -emment pronounced [-amɑ̃].

history.meaning: newly, freshly, a short time ago

récemment.notes: Pronunciation key: '-emment' is always pronounced [amɑ̃] ('ré-sa-man'), never [ɛmɑ̃], matching adverbs like 'évidemment' and 'fréquemment'.

récent.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (14th century) from Classical Latin recentem (nominative recēns), meaning 'fresh, young, newly arrived, vigorous', built on the prefix re- and a participial root *ken- ('to arise, begin anew', cognate with Sanskrit kanīna 'young' and Old Church Slavonic na-čęti 'to begin').
récent.notes: Unlike shorter age adjectives such as 'nouveau' or 'jeune', 'récent' normally follows the noun ('un film récent', 'une version récente'), preceding only for rhetorical emphasis.

réception.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin receptionem (nominative receptio, 'a taking in, receiving, sheltering'), derived from recipere, receptum ('to receive').

history.meaning: receipt of goods/signals, formal social reception, hotel front desk

réceptionniste.etymology: Formed in the 20th century (modeled on English receptionist) from réception ('hotel or office reception desk') + specialist suffix -iste.

cognates.meaning: to claim back, demand the return of

réclamer.etymology: Re-Latinized in Middle French from Old French reclamer ('to call upon, invoke, summon back a hawk'), inherited from Classical Latin reclāmāre ('to cry out against, protest loudly'), from re- ('back, again, against') + clāmāre ('to shout, cry out'). Semantic shift moved from vocal outcry and hawking calls to insistent demand or legal claim.

history.meaning: to cry out against, shout in protest
to call back (a falcon), implore, invoke
to demand insistently, claim as one's due

réclamer.notes: In agency and contract negotiations, 'réclamer un cachet' means to demand a fee; its noun 'une réclamation' means a formal customer complaint, whereas old-fashioned 'la réclame' meant commercial advertising.

récompenser.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Late/Christian Latin recompensāre ('to weigh again in return, counterbalance, requite'), composed of re- ('in return, back') and Classical Latin compensāre ('to weigh one thing against another'), frequentative of compendere from pendere ('to hang, weigh out silver on scales').

history.meaning: to pay back in balance, requite good or ill
to make amends for; to reward merit

récompenser.notes: Very frequent in cinema awards contexts: 'un film récompensé à Cannes' means 'an award-winning film at Cannes', and 'une récompense' is both a general reward and an industry prize/award.

réconcilier.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Classical Latin reconciliāre ('to bring together again, regain, restore to favor or harmony'), formed from re- ('again, back') and conciliāre ('to assemble, unite, win over'), itself from concilium ('assembly, council', from com- 'together' + root *kal- 'to call, summon').

history.meaning: to reunite, restore harmony between parties
to restore to friendship or church communion

morphemes.meaning: to unite, bring into council (Latin conciliare)

réconcilier.notes: Used transitively to patch things up between two feuding stars ('réconcilier deux acteurs') or reflexively with 'avec' ('se réconcilier avec quelqu'un' — to make up with someone).

réconfort.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (originally reconfort) from reconforter ('to strengthen again, console, cheer'), built on re- ('again') + conforter, from Late Latin confortāre ('to strengthen greatly, invigorate'), derived from com- (intensive) + Classical Latin fortis ('strong, brave').

history.meaning: to strengthen greatly, give courage to

réconfort.notes: Crucial distinction for English speakers: 'le confort' means material/physical convenience (a plush hotel), whereas emotional comfort or solace in distress is 'le réconfort' (preserved in the proverb 'après l'effort, le réconfort').

cognates.meaning: to regain health or recover losses
to get back (via Old French recovrer, doublet)

récupérer.etymology: Learned Middle French borrowing (15th century) from Classical Latin recuperāre ('to get back, regain possession of, revive'), an etymological doublet of inherited Old French recovrer (Modern French recouvrer). In modern spoken French, récupérer vastly expanded into an everyday multipurpose verb for picking up, retrieving, or resting up.

history.meaning: to regain possession of, win back
to regain lost property or health
to get back, pick up (someone/something), catch up on rest

morphemes.meaning: to take, seize back (Latin -cuperare, linked to capere)

récupérer.notes: Workhorse verb of daily spoken French: 'récupérer un dossier' (grab/retrieve a file), 'récupérer un acteur à la gare' (pick up an actor at the station), or 'récupérer d'un tournage' (recover after a shoot). Note stem change: 'je récupère'.

cognates.meaning: to edit or censor text for publication

rédiger.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (late 15th century) from Classical Latin redigere ('to drive back, gather together, bring into a specified state or order'), compounded from red- (prevocalic variant of re-, 'back, again') and agere ('to drive, do, lead'). From 'putting scattered notes into order', it specialized into drafting formal texts.

history.meaning: to drive back, collect, reduce to order
to compile and arrange in written form
to draft, draw up, compose formally in writing

rédiger.notes: Major false friend with English 'redact': 'rédiger un contrat / un scénario' means to write up or draft a text from scratch, NEVER to black out classified lines (which is 'caviarder' or 'occulter').

réduction.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin reductionem (nominative reductio, 'a leading or bringing back, restoration'), derived from reducere, reductum ('to lead back, bring to a smaller state'); developed the senses of scaling down a drawing, boiling down a sauce, and granting a price discount.

history.meaning: decrease, price discount, scaled-down copy, thickened culinary sauce

cognates.meaning: to make smaller or less in amount

réduire.etymology: Inherited through Old French reduire (re-accented réduire by scholarly Latin influence) from Classical Latin redūcere ('to lead back, bring back, withdraw, restore, bring to a lesser state'), compounded from re- ('back') and dūcere ('to lead'). The modern sense of diminishing size or cost arose from 'bringing down to a smaller scale'.

history.meaning: to lead back, escort home, bring to a state
to bring back, subdue, turn into
to reduce, scale down, cut back

réduire.notes: Conjugated like 'conduire' and 'produire' ('nous réduisons', past participle 'réduit', NOT *réduis): in agency talk, 'réduire le budget' (cut the budget) or 'tarif réduit' (discounted ticket price).

réel.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French (originally reel, real) from Late and Medieval Latin realis ('pertaining to things themselves, actual'), derived from Classical Latin rēs ('thing, object, fact, property'). Originally a legal and scholastic philosophy term contrasting tangible things or rights with mere names (nominalis) or persons.

history.meaning: pertaining to property or actual existence

réel.notes: Irregular feminine doubling: 'réel' -> 'réelle'. Watch the false friend with adverb 'réellement' ('really, genuinely'), whereas English 'actually' (= in fact) translates to 'en réalité' or 'en fait', NOT 'actuellement' ('currently').

cognates.meaning: to test or attempt again (via Old French essai)
to taste or try again (from parallel exagium)

réessayer.etymology: Prefixed formation in French combining iterative ré- ('again') with essayer ('to try, test'), inherited from Old French essaier, from Late Latin exagiāre ('to weigh out, test the weight of'), derived from Late Latin exagium ('a weighing, balance, standard weight'), from Classical Latin exigere ('to drive out, measure, examine').

history.meaning: act of weighing, standard weight on scales
to put to the test, assay, attempt
to try again, make another attempt

morphemes.meaning: to try, test (from Old French essai < Late Latin exagium)

réessayer.notes: Like 'essayer' and 'payer', -ayer verbs allow two accepted present-tense spellings and pronunciations: 'je réessaie' [ʁe.e.sɛ] or 'je réessaye' [ʁe.e.sɛj]. Contrasted in colloquial speech with the syncopated variant 'ressayer'.

rootFamily.gloss: trial, attempt, screen test ('des essais caméra'), essay

cognates.meaning: to throw back light; to ponder deeply
to reflect light; to think over

réfléchir.etymology: Remodeled into the -ir conjugation in Middle French from Classical Latin reflectere ('to bend back, turn back, turn one's mind back'), composed of re- ('back') and flectere ('to bend, curve'). From the optical sense of bending light rays back (14th–16th c.), it developed the figurative Cartesian sense of turning thought inward to deliberate.

history.meaning: to bend or bounce back (light, sound)
to reflect (light); to think over, deliberate

réfléchir.notes: Takes the preposition 'à' ('réfléchir à une proposition' — to think over an offer), which becomes the pronoun 'y' ('J'y réfléchis' — I'll think about it / sleep on it, a classic agent stalling tactic!).

rootFamily.gloss: to bend, give way (unprefixed verb from flectere)

cognates.meaning: displaced person seeking safety (borrowed from French réfugié)

réfugier.etymology: Derived in Middle French (late 15th century, primarily pronominal se réfugier) from the noun refuge ('shelter, safe haven'), borrowed from Classical Latin refugium ('a place to flee back to, shelter, recourse'), from refugere ('to flee back, escape'), compounded of re- ('back, away') and fugere ('to flee').

history.meaning: place of safety to which one flees back
to flee for shelter; to retreat figuratively (into work, silence)

réfugier.notes: In modern French the verb is almost exclusively pronominal ('se réfugier dans sa loge' — to hide away in one's dressing room). Its past participle 'réfugié(e)' was borrowed into English after 1685 for Huguenot exiles, giving English 'refugee'.

rootFamily.gloss: to flee, run away (inherited from Latin fugere)

cognates.meaning: system of government (borrowed from French); dietary regimen

régime.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Classical Latin regimen ('guidance, steering, rule, government'), formed from regere ('to steer straight, rule, direct', from PIE *h₃reǵ- 'to straighten') + instrumental noun suffix -men. In medieval medical Latin (regimen sanitatis), it designated a prescribed rule of living and eating, yielding modern 'diet'.

history.meaning: prescribed medical rule of diet and lifestyle
political system; dietary regimen; social-security scheme

morphemes.meaning: result or means of action (from Latin -imen)

régime.notes: Triple meaning in French showbiz: 1) weight-loss diet ('être au régime'), 2) political regime, and 3) 'le régime des intermittents du spectacle' — France's famous unemployment benefit scheme for film and stage workers!

rootFamily.gloss: stage management, production office, control room
stage manager, location/production manager on set

région.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–13th century from Classical Latin regionem (nominative regio, 'direction, boundary line, district, province, quarter of the sky or earth'), derived from regere ('to direct in a straight line, rule').

history.meaning: geographical or administrative region, body area

régler.etymology: Inherited/adapted in Old/Middle French from Late Latin regulare ('to direct by a rule, regulate'), derived from Classical Latin regula ('straightedge ruler, rule'); combines the senses 'to draw straight lines with a ruler', 'to adjust a clock or machine', and 'to settle a bill or problem'.

history.meaning: to rule paper, adjust/set a mechanism, settle an account

régulier.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th–13th century (originally in Church usage for clergy bound by a monastic rule, règle, as opposed to secular clergy) from Classical Latin regularis ('relating to a bar or rule'), derived from regula ('straightedge, rule').

history.meaning: bound by a rule -> uniform, steady, punctual, regular

cognates.meaning: restoration of a building to good condition

rénovation.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old/Middle French from Classical and Christian Latin renovātiōnem (nominative renovātiō, 'renewal, spiritual rebirth, restoration'), action noun from renovāre ('to renew, restore, make new again'), composed of re- ('again') + novāre ('to make new'), from novus ('new').
rénovation.notes: Note the single 'n' in 'rénovation' and 'rénover' (learned Latin borrowings) versus the 'ou' in inherited French 'renouveler' ('to renew a contract') and 'nouveau' ('new').

rootFamily.gloss: new (inherited doublet root from Latin novus)

réouverture.etymology: Formed in the 18th–19th century from iterative prefix ré- ('again') + ouverture ('opening').

réparation.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Late Latin reparationem (nominative reparatio, 'restoration, renewal'), derived from Classical Latin reparare ('to restore, repair').

history.meaning: mending, repair; amends or compensation for damage

réparer.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–13th century from Classical Latin reparare ('to get again, recover, renew, restore, put back in good order'), compound of re- ('again') + parare ('to prepare, make ready').

history.meaning: to make ready again, restore, mend
to repair, mend, fix, make amends for

répartir.etymology: Formed in Old French as repartir ('to divide again, share out'), later differentiated by an acute accent (répartir) from intransitive repartir ('to leave again, reply'), built on re- (distributive/intensive) + partir in its original Old French transitive meaning 'to divide into shares', from Classical Latin partīrī ('to share, divide'), from pars, partis ('part').

history.meaning: to divide up into shares; also to set out again

répartir.notes: Crucial accent & conjugation pair: 'répartir' (with é) means 'to distribute/allocate' and conjugates regularly with -iss- ('nous répartissons les rôles'), whereas 'repartir' (no accent) means 'to leave again' ('nous repartons'). 'La répartition' also means a film's cast list!

rootFamily.gloss: distribution, allocation; cast list of roles in a play/film

cognates.meaning: bioengineered android (coined for 1982 film Blade Runner)

réplicant.etymology: Late 20th-century French science-fiction borrowing (1982) adapted from English replicant, coined by screenwriter David Peoples (suggested by his microbiologist daughter from biological replication) for Ridley Scott's film Blade Runner, ultimately built on Classical Latin replicāns (stem replicant-), present participle of replicāre ('to fold back, repeat, copy').
réplicant.notes: A quintessential pop-culture/cinema word in French (often cited when joking about emotionless executives or actors or discussing sci-fi roles), Gallicized with an acute accent and nasalized final [-ɑ̃] (feminine 'réplicante').

rootFamily.gloss: replica; actor's line in a script

réplique.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Middle French from répliquer ('to answer back, counter in legal debate') and reinforced in artistic senses by Italian replica, ultimately from Late/Juridical Latin replicāre ('to unfold again, repeat, make a formal legal rejoinder'), from Classical Latin re- ('back') + plicāre ('to fold'). In 17th–18th-century theater, the 'reply' cue generalized to any spoken line in a script.

history.meaning: to fold back, unroll a scroll again; (legal) make a counter-plea
formal legal rejoinder, sharp verbal retort
actor's line or cue in a script; retort; replica; aftershock

réplique.notes: Essential acting & *Dix pour cent* idiom: 'une réplique culte' is an iconic movie line, and 'donner la réplique à quelqu'un' means either to act opposite a co-star on screen or to read lines with an actor to help them rehearse!

répondre.etymology: Inherited from Old French respondre ('to answer, reply, correspond, stand surety for'), from Vulgar Latin *respondere, 3rd-conjugation shift of Classical Latin respondere ('to promise in return, answer, reply', from re- 'in return' + spondere 'to pledge solemnly').

history.meaning: to answer, reply, meet expectations, vouch for

réponse.etymology: Inherited from Old French response ('answer, reply'), from Vulgar Latin *responsa, feminine singular reshaped from Classical Latin neuter plural responsa ('answers, especially of jurists or oracles'), past participle of respondere ('to answer').

cognates.meaning: widespread estimation in which a person is held

réputation.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th century) from Classical Latin reputātiōnem (nominative reputātiō, 'a reckoning, calculation, thinking over'), derived from reputāre ('to count over, reckon, consider'), composed of re- ('over again') and putāre ('to prune vines; settle accounts; reckon, think'). Semantic shift moved from 'how one is reckoned' to public standing.

history.meaning: to trim/prune; clear accounts; reckon, judge
public opinion or standing of a person's worth

réputation.notes: In talent-agency French, 'avoir la réputation d'être ingérable' ('to have a reputation for being unmanageable') and 'être réputé pour...' ('to be renowned for...') are constant industry currency.

rootFamily.gloss: to attribute, impute (shared Latin putare root)

répéter.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–13th century from Classical Latin repetere ('to strike at again, return to, begin anew, say or do over again'), compound of re- ('again') + petere ('to seek, aim at').

history.meaning: to seek again, say or do over again
to repeat; to rehearse a play or concert

répétition.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Classical Latin repetītiōnem (nominative repetītiō, 'a demanding back, saying over again'), action noun from repetere ('to seek again, return to, repeat'), from re- ('again') + petere ('to aim at, seek, go toward'). In 17th-century French theater (Molière's era), repeating scenes before opening night yielded 'rehearsal'.

history.meaning: reclaiming; saying or doing over again
repetition; theatrical, musical, or film rehearsal

répétition.notes: Classic theater & cinema false friend: 'être en répétition' (colloquially 'en répète') means 'to be in rehearsal', and 'la répétition générale' (or simply 'la générale') is the final dress rehearsal!

rootFamily.gloss: to repeat; to rehearse a play, scene, or concert
dialogue coach / vocal or ballet rehearsal coach

cognates.meaning: netlike pattern or anatomical network (from same Latin root)
net, network, television channel (from Latin rete)
net, network, social media/signal (from Latin rete)

réseau.etymology: Evolved from Old French resel (plural reseaus > réseau), diminutive of rois/rei ('hunting or fishing net'), from Vulgar Latin *rēticellum, diminutive of Classical Latin rēte ('net, snare, mesh'). From physical hunting nets and anatomical webs of veins, it expanded in the 19th–21st centuries to rail networks, social connections, and mobile phone reception.

history.meaning: fishing or hunting net / small net
small net for catching birds or hairnet
interconnected network, professional contacts, mobile phone signal

morphemes.meaning: net, mesh (from Latin rete > Old French res-)

réseau.notes: Three vital everyday meanings in *Dix pour cent*: 1) 'Je n'ai pas de réseau' ('I have no cell service/bars!'), 2) 'les réseaux sociaux' ('social media', plural in `-x`), and 3) 'avoir du réseau' ('to have industry connections').

rootFamily.gloss: retina of the eye (Medieval Latin retina, from rete 'net')

réservation.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century (originally in canon law for the papal reservation of benefices) from Medieval Latin reservationem, derived from Classical Latin reservare ('to keep back, save up'); acquired the modern travel/hospitality sense ('advance booking of a seat, room, or table') in the 19th–20th century (reinforced by English reservation).

history.meaning: advance booking of a room, table, or ticket

réserve.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 14th–15th century from réserver ('to keep back for a later time, save', from Classical Latin reservare < re- 'back' + servare 'to keep, preserve').

history.meaning: stock kept back for future need, nature reserve, storeroom, cautious restraint

réserver.etymology: Réserver was borrowed from Latin reservare, to put aside or keep. The Académie records the French verb from the twelfth century.

rootFamily.gloss: to keep, preserve (same Latin servāre 'keep', distinct from servir 'serve'!)

réserver.notes: Built on Latin servāre ('to guard, keep safe', also in conserver, observer, préserver), NOT servīre ('to be a servant').

résolu.etymology: Originated as the past participle of résoudre, remodeled in Middle French after Classical Latin resolūtus ('untied, loosened, melted, dispelled'), past participle of resolvere ('to untie, unbind, dispel doubts'). Once mental hesitation is 'untied' or dispelled, a person becomes firm and unwavering—giving the adjectival sense 'resolute, determined'.

history.meaning: solved (of a problem); resolute, determined (of a person)

résolu.notes: Dual usage: after a noun like 'problème', it means 'solved' ('affaire résolue'); describing a person ('un agent résolu', 'être résolu à agir'), it means 'determined, resolute'. (Archaic chemical participle 'résous' only means 'dissolved'.)

résonner.etymology: Borrowed/adapted in the 12th–15th century (reshaping Old French resoner) from Classical Latin resonare ('to sound again, echo back, resound'), compound of re- ('back, again') + sonare ('to sound', from sonus 'sound').

cognates.meaning: to settle or find a solution to; decide firmly

résoudre.etymology: Inherited via Old French resoldre (re-accented résoudre) from Classical Latin resolvere ('to untie, unfasten, loosen, melt, unravel a difficulty'), formed from re- ('back, un-') and solvere ('to loosen, untie, release, pay', itself from se- 'apart' + luere 'to set free'). Notice the phonological epenthetic -d- between l (> u) and r in French (-lv'r- > -udr-).

history.meaning: to untie, unbind, unravel a knot or difficulty
to dissolve, untangle, settle a question
to solve (a crisis/problem); (se résoudre à) bring oneself to

résoudre.notes: Tricky irregular conjugation! The '-d-' disappears whenever '-lv-' resurfaces in plural stems: 'je résous, il résout', but 'nous résolvons, ils résolvent', past participle 'résolu'. Reflexive 'se résoudre à' means 'to resign/bring oneself to do something'.

rootFamily.gloss: to dissolve (parallel verb from Latin dissolvere)

cognates.meaning: result, outcome (direct source of French noun)

résultat.etymology: Borrowed in the early 17th century (or adapted on the model of Italian risultato and Scholastic Latin resultātum) alongside the verb résulter, from Medieval/Classical Latin resultāre ('to spring back, rebound, echo', and in Scholastic philosophy 'to follow as a logical consequence'), frequentative of resilīre from re- ('back') + saltāre / salīre ('to leap').

history.meaning: logical consequence; outcome that springs from an action
outcome, score, box-office or medical result

morphemes.meaning: to leap, spring (from Latin saltare / salire)
noun suffix from Latin/Italian past participle (-atum / -ato)

résultat.notes: In conversational French, 'Résultat :' (or 'Résultat des courses :') at the start of a sentence is a super-idiomatic way to say 'Bottom line:' or 'End result:'. In cinema, 'les résultats du premier jour' means opening-day box-office numbers.

rootFamily.gloss: to result, follow from ('il en résulte que...')
resultant force or overall outcome (feminine noun)
to jump, leap (cognate inherited from Latin saltare)

cognates.meaning: summary; (North America) curriculum vitae (borrowed from French)

résumé.etymology: Substantivized masculine past participle (16th–17th century) of the verb résumer ('to sum up, recapitulate concisely'), itself a learned Middle French borrowing from Classical Latin resūmere ('to take back, take up again, recover'), from re- ('back, again') + sūmere ('to take, pick up'). In Scholastic Latin, 'taking up main points again' shifted to 'summarizing'.

history.meaning: to take up again, recover, renew
concise summary, plot synopsis; ('en résumé') in short

résumé.notes: Top-tier false friend! In French, 'un résumé' NEVER means a job application résumé (that is 'un CV' [se.ve]) — it strictly means a summary or plot recap ('le résumé d'un scénario'). Likewise, French 'résumer' means 'to summarize', NEVER 'to resume/restart' ('reprendre').

rootFamily.gloss: to take on, own up to (shared Latin sumere root)
to presume, suppose (shared Latin sumere root)

rétablissement.etymology: Derived in Middle/Early Modern French from the verb rétablir ('to restore, set back on firm footing, heal', Old French restablir) + action suffix -issement, from re- ('back, again') + établir (Old French establir, with loss of preconsonantal s marked by é-), inherited from Classical Latin stabilīre ('to make firm, steady'), from stabilis ('standing firm', root of stāre 'to stand').

history.meaning: to make firm, steady, establish securely
to set back upright, restore to a former state
restoration (of order, truth, service); recovery of health

morphemes.meaning: to make stable, establish (Old French establir < Latin stabilire)
extended stem of -ir verbs + action noun suffix

rétablissement.notes: Standard polite formula when someone is sick or injured: 'Bon rétablissement !' or 'Prompt rétablissement !' ('Get well soon! / Wishing you a speedy recovery!'). Also used technically for restoring power or phone service ('rétablissement de la ligne').

rootFamily.gloss: to restore, re-establish; ('se rétablir') to recover one's health
stable, steady (learned doublet from Latin stabilis)

réunion.etymology: Réunion is derived from réunir. Its fifteenth-century senses included reconciliation or agreement before the broader idea of bringing together and the modern meeting sense.

cognates.meaning: borrowed from French (narrowed in English to nostalgic re-gatherings!)

réunion.notes: Workplace false friend: in French une réunion is any ordinary office or committee 'meeting' (je suis en réunion 'I'm in a meeting'), not just a family or class reunion!

réunir.etymology: Formed in the 15th–16th century from iterative prefix ré- ('again, together') + unir ('to unite, join as one', from Late Latin unire < Classical Latin unus 'one').

history.meaning: to join together again, gather, bring together, convene a meeting

réussir.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian riuscire ('to come out again, turn out, succeed'), formed from iterative ri- ('again') + uscire ('to go out'). Italian uscire descends from Classical Latin exīre ('to go out, result'), whose initial vowel shifted under the influence of ūstium/ōstium ('door'). French originally inherited exīre directly as Old French issir ('to go out', surviving in issue), before re-importing the Italianate semantic development from 'turn out well' to 'succeed'.

history.meaning: to go out, come forth, turn out
to come out again, turn out, succeed
to have an outcome; to achieve success

morphemes.meaning: to go out, turn out (from Italian uscire < Latin exīre)

réussir.notes: Watch the transitive vs. intransitive patterns: réussir à un examen ('to pass an exam') or réussir dans le cinéma, whereas direct transitive réussir un film/un casting means 'to pull off successfully'.

rootFamily.gloss: way out, outcome (native reflex of Latin exīre)
emerging, descended from (archaic past participle of issir)

réussite.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-16th century from Italian riuscita ('outcome, result, success'), the substantivized feminine past participle of riuscire ('to come out again, turn out, succeed'), ultimately from Latin re- + exīre ('to go out'). Like réussir, réussite initially denoted any outcome—good or bad—before narrowing in the 17th century to designate a favorable result, triumph, or (later) a game of solitaire.

morphemes.meaning: go out, turn out (from Italian usc- < Latin exīre)

réussite.notes: Always feminine (une belle réussite); in cinema and agency talk, une réussite critique et commerciale refers to a film that wins over both reviewers and the box office, and faire une réussite also means 'to play solitaire'.

réveil.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Old French (resveil, 12th–13th c., 'act of waking from sleep') from resveillier / réveiller ('to awaken', from re- + esveillier < Vulgar Latin *exvigilare 'to wake up'); also used by ellipsis for réveille-matin ('alarm clock').

réveiller.etymology: Réveiller is derived from éveiller, to wake. The Académie records the derivative from the twelfth century. The reflexive se réveiller describes waking up oneself.

history.meaning: to wake (someone) up; (se réveiller) wake up

cognates.meaning: military wake-up bugle call (from French réveillez!)

réveiller.notes: Un réveil is an alarm clock; remember reflexive je me réveille ('I wake up' on my own) vs. transitive le bruit me réveille ('the noise wakes me up').

cognates.meaning: vigilant, awake (from the same Latin root vigil)

réveillé.etymology: Past participial adjective of réveiller ('to wake up, rouse'), descending from Old French resveillier, formed from intensive/iterative re- + esveillier ('to awaken'). Old French esveillier derives from Vulgar Latin *exvigilāre ('to wake out of sleep'), itself compounded from Classical Latin ex- ('out of') + vigilāre ('to stay awake, keep watch'), from vigil ('awake, alert, brisk').Figurative use for mental sharpness ('sharp, alert') is well established since Classical French.

history.meaning: to wake up again, stir to alertness

réveillé.notes: Distinguish être réveillé ('to be awake'—resulting state, or figuratively 'bright, switched-on') from être éveillé ('to be awake; intellectually curious, perceptive', e.g., un enfant très éveillé).

rootFamily.gloss: to stay up late, keep watch

réverbère.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 15th–18th century from réverbérer ('to reflect back light or heat', from Late Latin reverberare 'to beat back, reflect'); in 1745–1766, oil streetlamps fitted with concave polished metal reflectors (lanternes à réverbère) were installed across Paris, making réverbère the standard French word for a streetlamp.

history.meaning: reflecting mirror on an oil lamp -> streetlamp, lamppost

réviser.etymology: Attested first as reviser (14th–16th c.) and reshaped with learned ré-, borrowed from Medieval Latin revīsāre ('to examine anew'), a frequentative built on Classical Latin revīsere ('to come back to see, revisit, inspect again'), from re- ('again') + vīsere ('to look at attentively, go to see'), itself the desiderative/intensive of vidēre ('to see'). It developed three modern domains: re-examining a text or contract, servicing machinery, and studying for an exam or audition.

history.meaning: to go back to see, revisit, inspect again

morphemes.meaning: look at, inspect (from Latin vīs-, vidēre)

réviser.notes: Like British English 'revise', French réviser commonly means 'to study/review material before a test or rehearsal' (réviser son texte = 'to go over one's lines'), alongside 'to amend' (réviser un contrat).

rootFamily.gloss: to aim at, inspect, stamp a visa

cognates.meaning: capable of being revoked or annulled

révocable.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century as a legal and administrative term from Late Latin revocābilis ('capable of being called back or recalled'), formed from Classical Latin revocāre ('to call back, withdraw, annul, rescind'), itself composed of re- ('back') + vocāre ('to call, summon', derived from vōx, vōcis, 'voice'). In French contract and corporate law, it specifically characterizes a mandate or appointment that can be terminated at will.

history.meaning: able to be recalled or undone

révocable.notes: In agency and company law (such as managing ASK in *Dix pour cent*), un mandat révocable ad nutum means an executive or agent mandate that can be terminated at any moment at a nod of the board.

cognates.meaning: causing intense disgust or moral outrage (calqued/borrowed from French)

révoltant.etymology: Present participial adjective (18th c.) of révolter in its psychological sense 'to stir to moral indignation, shock, sicken'. French révolter was borrowed in the 16th century from Italian rivoltare ('to turn upside down, overthrow, incite to rebellion'), from Vulgar Latin *revolvitāre, an iterative of Classical Latin revolvere ('to roll back, turn over', from re- + volvere, 'to roll'). The semantic shift mirrors 'stomach-turning' or 'stirring inner rebellion'.

history.meaning: to roll back, unroll, turn over
to turn over, invert, stir to rebel

morphemes.meaning: roll, turn (from Italian volt- < Latin volvere)

révoltant.notes: Subtle false friend of degree: while English 'revolting' primarily means physically nauseating ('gross'), French révoltant more often expresses moral outrage ('appalling, scandalous, infuriating'), e.g., C'est révoltant d'être traité ainsi !

cognates.meaning: orbital rotation; political or cultural upheaval

révolution.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Late Latin revolūtiō, revolūtiōnem ('a revolving, cyclical return, transmigration'), action noun derived from Classical Latin revolvere, revolūtum ('to roll back, unwind, come full circle'), from re- ('back') + volvere ('to roll, turn'). For centuries primarily astronomical (the full orbital return of planets), it acquired the sense of political upheaval via Italian rivoluzione and 17th-century English events before 1789 cemented its modern sense globally.

history.meaning: complete rotation; radical political or artistic upheaval

révolution.notes: Capitalized with the definite article, la Révolution refers specifically to the French Revolution of 1789; in everyday speech, faire sa révolution means to radically reinvent one's methods or career.

rootFamily.gloss: completed, bygone (past participle of archaic révolvir)

révélation.etymology: Borrowed in the late 12th century (first in Christian theology) from Ecclesiastical Latin revēlātiō, revēlātiōnem ('an uncovering, unveiling of divine truth'), action noun from Classical Latin revēlāre ('to draw back a veil, uncover, bare'), from reversive re- ('back, un-') + vēlāre ('to cover with a veil'), derived from vēlum ('veil, curtain, sail'). In 19th- and 20th-century theatre and cinema, it extended to a 'breakout newcomer' unveiled to the public.

history.meaning: divine manifestation; disclosure of a secret

morphemes.meaning: veil, cover (from Latin vēlum; native French voile)

révélation.notes: Essential French cinema vocabulary: at the César Awards, Meilleure Révélation (féminine/masculine) is the prize for 'Most Promising Newcomer / Breakout Star' (e.g., la révélation du Festival de Cannes).

rootFamily.gloss: to reveal, disclose; bring to light
to unveil (native French doublet built on voile < vēlum)

cognates.meaning: to disclose, make known (via Old French reveler)

révéler.etymology: Learned borrowing (13th–14th c. as reveler) from Classical Latin revēlāre ('to draw back the veil, lay bare, uncover the head or face'), formed from reversive prefix re- ('back') + vēlāre ('to veil, cover, wrap'), from vēlum ('cloth, curtain, veil'). In Ecclesiastical Latin it took on the figurative meaning 'to make known hidden truths', while French also preserved the inherited doublet voiler/dévoiler from the same Latin noun vēlum.

history.meaning: to draw back a veil, uncover, bare
to make known a secret or divine truth
to disclose, bring to prominence; (se révéler) prove to be

révéler.notes: Watch the stem-changing accent alternation in conjugation (il révèle, nous révélons, il révélera), and note two key uses: révéler un acteur ('to launch/discover an actor') and se révéler + adjective ('to turn out/prove to be').

réécrire.etymology: Formed in Modern French (18th–19th c.) with the full vowel-preserving iterative prefix ré- ('again, anew') + écrire ('to write'), purposefully distinguishing 'to redraft/rewrite a text' from older récrire (12th c., which had specialized in 'to write back, reply by letter', though today both forms can mean 'rewrite'). Écrire descends via Old French escrire (with prothetic e- before s + consonant) from Classical Latin scrībere ('to scratch, incise, write').

history.meaning: to write again, redraft a text or screenplay

morphemes.meaning: write (from Old French escrire < Latin scrībere)

réécrire.notes: Pronounced with two distinct close-mid front vowels [ʁe.e.kʁiʁ] (remember both acute accents in spelling!); in French film development, réécrire le scénario ('doing script rewrites') is a constant tug-of-war between directors, producers, and stars.

réécriture.etymology: Modern French compound (attested 20th c., popularized in literary theory and screenwriting) formed from iterative ré- ('again, anew') + écriture ('writing, script, style'). Écriture descends via Old French escriture from Classical Latin scrīptūra ('a writing, written composition', and in Ecclesiastical Latin 'Holy Scripture'), derived from scrīptus, the past participle of scrībere ('to write').

history.meaning: act of writing, written text, inscription

réécriture.notes: In French film production (as seen constantly in *Dix pour cent*), partir en réécriture means sending a screenplay back into a rewrite phase before financing or shooting can proceed.

rééducation.etymology: Formed in 19th-century French from restorative/iterative prefix ré- ('again, back to normal') + éducation ('training, upbringing'). Éducation was borrowed in the 14th–16th centuries from Classical Latin ēducātiō, ēducātiōnem ('a breeding, rearing, bringing up'), action noun of ēducāre ('to rear, nourish, train'), closely linked to ēdūcere ('to lead forth, draw out'). Around 1900 in French neurology and orthopedics, rééducation specialized to mean restoring lost motor or speech functions.

morphemes.meaning: rear, lead, train (from Latin ducāre / dūcere)

rééducation.notes: Major false friend! While English 're-education' sounds ominously political (ideological brainwashing), French faire de la rééducation almost always means 'doing physical therapy / medical rehab' after an injury, surgery, or childbirth.

rêve.etymology: Rêve is a noun formed from rêver. The Académie records the noun from the seventeenth century; this account does not claim a settled deeper origin for rêver.

history.meaning: to wander, rave, daydream -> dream during sleep
dream (displacing older songe in everyday speech)

cognates.meaning: from Old French resver and Middle French resverie!

rêve.notes: In medieval and 16th-century French, sleeping dreams were called un songe (< Latin somnium, like Italian sogno and Spanish sueño), while resver meant 'to wander/deliriously muse'—until rêve took over in the 1600s!

rêver.etymology: Inherited from Old French resver (12th c., originally 'to wander about deliriously, rave, talk wildly'), of debated origin (possibly from Vulgar Latin *re-ex-vadere 'to wander off track' or an expressive root); in the 16th–17th century it gradually took over the sense 'to dream while sleeping or daydreaming', displacing Old French songier (< somniare).

history.meaning: to wander about, rave in delirium

cognates.meaning: dramatic part (reborrowed from French); scroll/list (borrowed earlier from Old French)

rôle.etymology: From Old French rolle ('parchment scroll, legal docket, tax register'), a semi-learned reflex of Late/Medieval Latin rotulus ('little wheel; cylindrical scroll of parchment'), diminutive of Classical Latin rota ('wheel').
