In medieval mystery and passion plays, each actor's lines were copied onto an individual rolled-up parchment strip (un rolle) rather than a costly full manuscript, whence the metonymic shift (16th c.) to 'an actor's part' and 'social function', marked by a circumflex after -ll- simplified.

history.meaning: parchment scroll, court docket; strip with an actor's lines

rôle.notes: Pronounced with a closed [o] ([ʁol]) thanks to the historical circumflex; core *Dix pour cent* compounds include décrocher un rôle ('to land a part'), le rôle-titre ('title role'), and un contre-emploi ('role against type').

rootFamily.gloss: scroll, roll, roller (diminutive of Old French rolle)
to roll; to drive (from Old French roler < rotulāre)
to verify against a register (contre-rôle) -> to check, inspect

cognates.meaning: to cook by dry heat; roasted meat (borrowed from Old French rostir)
to roast, toast (from Old High German rōsten)

rôti.etymology: Substantivized masculine past participle (Middle French rosti, replacing earlier noun rost, modern rôt) of rôtir ('to roast'), from Old French rostir. Borrowed into Gallo-Romance from Frankish *hraustijan ('to cook on a gridiron or spit', akin to Old High German rōsten, from *hraust, 'gridiron, grate'). Loss of preconsonantal -s- before -t- lengthened the preceding vowel and yielded the modern circumflex in rôti.

history.meaning: to broil on a grate, roast over fire
joint of roasted meat (beef, pork, veal, poultry)

morphemes.meaning: roast over fire (from Old French rost- < Frankish *hraustijan)

rôti.notes: Besides Sunday dinner (un rôti de bœuf / de porc), colloquial French keeps the old proverb s'endormir sur le rôti ('to fall asleep while tending the spit', i.e., to slack off at the crucial moment).

rootFamily.gloss: to roast; (colloq.) to broil in the sun
roast meat (archaic/literary, preserved in rôt-de-bif -> rosbif)

rôtir.etymology: Inherited from Old French rostir ('to roast meat on a spit or gridiron over an open fire'), borrowed from Frankish *raustjan ('to roast on a gridiron', from *raust 'gridiron', cognate with Old High German rosten and English roast).

history.meaning: to broil on a grate, roast over fire

cognates.meaning: shepherd's or bishop's hooked staff (borrowed from Old French croc/croche)

s'accrocher.etymology: Pronominal form of accrocher ('to fasten with a hook, hang up'), formed in Middle French (14th–15th c., replacing earlier encrochier) from prefix a- (from Latin ad-, 'to, onto') + croc / croche ('hook') + verbal suffix -er. Old French croc ('hook, grapple') was borrowed from Old Norse krókr or Frankish *krōk ('hook, bend'). Reflexive s'accrocher evolved from 'getting caught on a hook' to 'clinging tightly, hanging in there stubbornly, or clashing'.

history.meaning: hook; to seize or hang with a hook
to cling onto, persevere tenaciously; to clash with someone

s'accrocher.notes: Imperative Accroche-toi ! / Accrochez-vous ! means both 'Hold on tight / brace yourself!' before shocking news and 'Hang in there, don't give up!'—whereas décrocher means both 'to pick up the phone' and 'to land (a role/contract)'.

rootFamily.gloss: hook; fang; (faire un croc-en-jambe) trip someone up
to unhook; pick up the phone; land a role

cognates.meaning: to act, agent (from Latin agere, agēns, āctus)
to act, operate (learned from Latin agere)

s'agir.etymology: Impersonal pronominal verb (occurring exclusively in third-person singular il s'agit de, 'it is a question/matter of'), attested in 15th-century French courtroom usage ('the issue under litigation is'). Built on agir ('to act, pursue a lawsuit'), a learned borrowing from Classical Latin agere ('to drive, set in motion, conduct, plead a case'), directly calquing the Classical Latin impersonal passive idiom agitur dē ('at stake is, the discussion concerns').

history.meaning: to drive, conduct, plead; 'at issue is...'
the legal matter being pleaded concerns...
to be a matter of, be about, involve

s'agir.notes: Strictly impersonal—only il is ever the grammatical subject (Il s'agit d'un film d'auteur; De quoi s'agit-il ?), never a personal subject (*ce film s'agit de... is a classic learner error; use ce film parle de... instead).

cognates.meaning: flat dish, plate; plateau (borrowed from Old/Modern French plat/plateau)

s'aplatir.etymology: Pronominal form of aplatir ('to make flat'), formed in Old French (aplatir, 13th c.) from prefix a- (Latin ad-) + adjective plat ('flat') + verbal suffix -ir. French plat descends from Vulgar Latin *plattus ('flat, spread out'), borrowed from Ancient Greek platús (πλατύς, 'broad, flat, wide', cognate with Latin lātus and English flat). Reflexive s'aplatir literally means 'to flatten oneself against the ground', whence colloquial 'to grovel, kowtow, cave in'.

history.meaning: to flatten oneself; (colloq.) to grovel, cave in spinelessly

morphemes.meaning: to, into state of (from Latin ad-)

s'aplatir.notes: Spelled with a single p (unlike appeler or applaudir—French academy spelling kept aplatir simple!), and vivid in office/agency slang: s'aplatir devant un producteur means 'to grovel/kowtow before a producer', closely echoing faire des courbettes or se mettre à plat ventre.

rootFamily.gloss: tray; film set / TV studio stage; highland

cognates.meaning: to appeal (borrowed from Old French apeler)
to call upon, appeal; roll call (appello)

s'appeler.etymology: Pronominal form of appeler ('to call, summon, name'), from Old French apeler ('to address, summon, accuse in court, call by name'), inherited from Classical Latin appellāre ('to accost, address, call upon, entreat, name'). Latin appellāre was formed from ad- ('toward') + *-pellāre, an intensive stem related to pellere ('to drive, push, strike'). Reflexive s'appeler ('to call oneself' -> 'to be named') became the standard French way to state a name.

history.meaning: to accost, address, call upon, name
to summon, appeal; to bear the name of
to be called, have as one's name

s'appeler.notes: Doubles the l wherever the ending is silent to reflect open [ɛ] (je m'appelle, ils s'appellent, il s'appellera) vs. single l with schwa [ə] (nous nous appelons, vous vous appelez).

rootFamily.gloss: call, phone call, appeal, casting call (appel à casting)

s'arrêter.etymology: Pronominal form of arrêter ('to stop, bring to a halt'), from Old French s'arester (< Vulgar Latin *arrestare, from ad- + restare 'to stand still, remain').

history.meaning: to come to a halt, stop oneself
to stop, pause, cease doing something

s'asseoir.etymology: Asseoir descends from Vulgar Latin *assedere (Classical Latin assidere, ad + sedere 'to sit beside'). Reflexive **s'asseoir** means 'to sit down'.

cognates.meaning: to attend, direct attention to (borrowed via Old French)
to pay attention to, look after, serve

s'attendre.etymology: Pronominal construction (s'attendre à, 'to expect, anticipate, count on') of attendre ('to wait for'), descending from Old French atendre ('to direct one's mind toward, strive for, wait'). Inherited from Classical Latin attendere (originally attendere animum, 'to stretch one's mind toward, pay heed to'), composed of ad- ('to, toward') + tendere ('to stretch, aim'). While simple attendre shifted to 'wait for', pronominal s'attendre preserved the mental orientation toward a future event ('expect').

history.meaning: to stretch toward, direct one's mind to, heed
to apply oneself to, rely on, await
to expect, anticipate, be prepared for

s'attendre.notes: Crucial contrast + false friend: attendre quelqu'un = 'to wait for someone' (NOT 'attend', which is assister à!), whereas s'attendre à quelque chose (or s'attendre à ce que + subjunctive) = 'to expect something' (Je m'y attendais = 'I saw that coming').

rootFamily.gloss: wait, expectation (contre toute attente = against all expectations)

cognates.meaning: to break through the bottom, burst through
to knock the bottom out of; (desfondarse) run out of steam
foundation, bottom, founder (from Latin fundus via French)

s'effondrer.etymology: Pronominal form of effondrer ('to cave in, break the bottom out of'), altered in the 14th century with an epenthetic -r- (through contamination by fondre, 'to melt, sink, swoop down') from Old French esfonder ('to knock the bottom out, sink, gut'). Old French esfonder continues a Vulgar Latin *exfundāre, formed from privative ex- ('out') + fundus ('bottom, floor, foundation'). S'effondrer captures both structural collapse and emotional breakdown.

history.meaning: to knock out the bottom or foundation
to stave in, gut, cause to cave in
to collapse structurally; to break down in tears or despair

morphemes.meaning: out, away (from Old French es- < Latin ex-)

s'effondrer.notes: Used equally for physical structures, box-office numbers (les entrées s'effondrent en deuxième semaine), and actors or agents breaking down emotionally (s'effondrer en larmes = 'to collapse in tears').

cognates.meaning: bale (of goods), ball (via Old French bale < Frankish *balla)
to pack up; (imballarsi) to stall or race (of an engine)

s'emballer.etymology: Pronominal form of emballer ('to pack into bales, wrap up'), attested since the 14th century from em- (en-, 'into') + balle ('bale of merchandise; ball', from Frankish *balla, 'rounded bundle, ball') + -er. In the 19th century, equestrian usage developed un cheval qui s'emballe ('a horse bolting uncontrollably with the bit between its teeth', perhaps influenced by balle 'bullet' or 'bundling off'), whence 'to race out of control' (of a heart or engine) and 'to get overly excited or carried away'.

history.meaning: to pack goods into a bale or bundle
to bolt (of a horse), race (engine/heart), get carried away

s'emballer.notes: In everyday dialogue, Ne t'emballe pas ! means 'Don't get ahead of yourself / Don't get carried away!', while transitive ça m'emballe (pas trop) means 'I'm (not really) thrilled/sold on that!'.

rootFamily.gloss: runaway escalation, racing (of heart or media frenzy)
to unpack; (colloq.) to spill secrets or lay out goods

cognates.meaning: to hug, clasp in the arms (borrowed from Old French embracier)

s'embrasser.etymology: Reciprocal pronominal form of embrasser, from Old French embracier ('to clasp in one's arms, hug'), formed from em- (en-, 'in') + bras (Old French braz, 'arm', from Classical Latin plural bracchia, 'both arms', borrowed from Greek brakhíōn) + -er. Because the older verb baiser ('to kiss', < Latin bāsiāre) became taboo as vulgar slang for sexual intercourse from the 17th–19th centuries, embrasser euphemistically took over the standard meaning 'to kiss' (on the lips or cheeks).

history.meaning: to encircle or clasp in one's arms, hug
to hug; to kiss one another (cheeks or lips)

s'embrasser.notes: Classic false friend! In Modern French, embrasser / s'embrasser almost always means 'to kiss' (including greeting kisses on the cheek, Je t'embrasse = 'Lots of love / kisses' at the end of a call or email), whereas 'to hug' is prendre dans ses bras or faire un câlin, and verbal baiser is strictly vulgar!

rootFamily.gloss: warm hug, ceremonial embrace (retains the older 'hug' sense)

s'endormir.etymology: Pronominal form of endormir ('to put to sleep'), formed in Old French (soi endormir, 11th–12th c.) from inchoative/intensive prefix en- (Latin in-) + dormir ('to sleep', from Classical Latin dormire).

cognates.meaning: to understand one another, agree, get along
to understand one another, come to terms
to intend (from Latin intendere via Old French)

s'entendre.etymology: Reciprocal and reflexive form of entendre ('to hear; earlier, to understand'), inherited via Old French entendre ('to direct one's attention, understand, mean') from Classical Latin intendere ('to stretch out, strain toward, direct one's mind or ears to'), from in- ('toward') + tendere ('to stretch'). While simple entendre largely shifted from 'understand' to 'hear' in the 16th–17th centuries, reciprocal s'entendre preserved the cognitive sense 'to understand one another', hence 'to get along harmoniously' or 'reach an agreement'.

history.meaning: to stretch toward, direct attention to
to understand, intend; to understand one another
to get along well; to reach a mutual agreement; to hear oneself

s'entendre.notes: Notice how the older sense 'understand' survives in idioms: bien entendu ('of course'), un sous-entendu ('innuendo'), un malentendu ('misunderstanding'), C'est entendu ! ('Agreed!'), and bien s'entendre avec quelqu'un ('to get along well with someone').

rootFamily.gloss: agreement, harmony, cordial understanding (e.g. Entente cordiale)

s'envoler.etymology: Pronominal verb formed in Old French (soi en voler -> s'envoler) from adverbial pronoun en ('away from here', from Latin inde 'thence') + voler ('to fly', from Classical Latin volare).

history.meaning: to fly away, take wing, take off (of an aircraft), vanish

cognates.meaning: to pardon, justify, excuse (via Old French)

s'excuser.etymology: Pronominal form of excuser ('to absolve from blame, pardon'), attested in Old French (12th c., escuser, reshaped with learned ex-) from Classical Latin excūsāre ('to release from a charge, plead in defense'), formed from ex- ('out of, free from') + causa ('judicial charge, accusation, lawsuit, cause', with regular Latin vowel weakening -au- > -ū- in compounds, as in accūsāre). Reflexive s'excuser literally meant 'to clear oneself of blame' before becoming the everyday verb 'to apologize'.

history.meaning: to release from a legal charge, justify, plead as an excuse

s'excuser.notes: Etiquette nuance: strict French purists warn against saying Je m'excuse ('I absolve myself'!), preferring Excusez-moi, Pardonnez-moi, or Je vous prie de m'excuser in polished settings—though Je m'excuse is heard constantly in real life (including at ASK!).

rootFamily.gloss: apology (pl. présenter ses excuses) or pretext/excuse (sg.)
to accuse, blame (parallel Latin compound ad- + causa)

cognates.meaning: to humiliate; humble (from the same Latin root humilis / humus)

s'humilier.etymology: Pronominal form of humilier ('to make low, humble, degrade'), borrowed in the 12th century from Late and Ecclesiastical Latin humiliāre ('to abase, make humble', widely used in the Vulgate Bible: qui se humiliat exaltabitur). Derived from Classical Latin humilis ('low-lying, close to the earth, lowly, modest'), itself built on humus ('earth, soil, ground'). Originally denoting virtuous Christian self-humbling, in secular Modern French it shifted strongly toward 'demeaning or debasing oneself'.

history.meaning: earth, soil > close to the ground, lowly
to humble oneself; to demean or humiliate oneself

morphemes.meaning: reflexive marker se (elided before mute h)
lowly, close to earth (from Latin humil- < humus)

s'humilier.notes: Starts with a mute h (h muet), requiring elision (s'humilier) and liaison (ils s'humilient [il.sy.mi.li]); unlike spiritual s'abaisser avec humilité, modern s'humilier implies painful loss of dignity.

rootFamily.gloss: humble, modest (inherited reflex of Latin humilem)

cognates.meaning: if you please (archaic/formal se ti piace)
if it pleases you (literary/older courtesy formula)
please (shortened from 'if you please', calqued on French!)

s'il te plaît.etymology: Lexicalized polite clause literally meaning 'if it pleases you' (addressed to a single person using informal tutoiement), continuing Old and Middle French se il te plaist (structurally mirroring Classical Latin sī tibī placet). Composed of conditional conjunction s' (si < Latin sī, 'if'), impersonal neuter subject il (< Vulgar Latin *illī / Classical ille), unstressed dative pronoun te (< Latin tē / tibī, 'to you'), and plaît (Old French plaist < Latin placet, 3rd sg. present of placēre, 'to be pleasing, seem good').

history.meaning: if it seems good / pleasing to you

morphemes.meaning: if (si elided before il; never elided before elle!)
pleases (3rd sg. of plaire < Latin placet)

s'il te plaît.notes: Often abbreviated STP in texts/emails and compressed in fast spoken French to [sitplɛ] or [stəplɛ]; under the 1990 French spelling rectifications, dropping the circumflex (s'il te plait) is also accepted, though plaît remains dominant.

rootFamily.gloss: to please, appeal to (from Old French plaisir/plaire < placēre)
pleasure, favor (originally the infinitive noun of plaire)

cognates.meaning: please (clipped from 'if it please you' / 'if you please', modeled on s'il vous plaît!)
please (als het u belieft, calqued on French s'il vous plaît)

s'il vous plaît.etymology: Lexicalized deferential formula ('if it pleases you'), descending from Old French se il vos plaist (matching Classical Latin sī vōbīs placet). Built from conditional s' (si < Latin sī, 'if'), impersonal subject il, polite or plural dative pronoun vous (< Latin vōs, replacing vōbīs), and plaît (< Old French plaist < Latin placet, from placēre, 'to please'). English 'please' itself arose in Early Modern English by shortening 'if you please', a direct calque of French s'il vous plaît.

history.meaning: if it pleases you (plural or courtly singular)

morphemes.meaning: to you (formal singular or plural dative)
pleases (3rd sg. of plaire < Latin placet)

s'il vous plaît.notes: Abbreviated SVP (also used noun-like or adverbially: un café avec un croissant, SVP !), and uttered with rising intonation (S'il vous plaît ?) either to get a waiter's/colleague's attention or in sharp disbelief ('Excuse me?! / Come again?!').

s'occuper.etymology: Pronominal form of occuper ('to take possession of, employ, busy'), from Classical Latin occupare; with de, means 'to take care of, attend to, look after'.

history.meaning: to keep oneself busy; to take care of, handle

sable.etymology: Inherited from Old French sable (alongside sablon, 'sand, gravel'), from Classical Latin sabulum ('coarse sand, gravel', which displaced arena in northern Gaul).

sac.etymology: Sac comes from Latin saccus ('bag, sack'), borrowed via Ancient Greek sákkos from Semitic *śaq ('coarse cloth, sack').
sac.notes: **Sac à main** = handbag; **sac à dos** = backpack.

cognates.meaning: religious offering; selfless renunciation (borrowed from Old French)

sacrifice.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century (in Old French biblical translations) from Classical Latin sacrificium ('a making sacred, priestly offering to a deity, immolation'), derived from adjective sacrificus ('performing sacred rites'). Sacrificus combines sacer, sacrum ('sacred, consecrated to the gods', from Proto-Italic *sakros) + -ficus, unstressed combining stem of facere ('to make, perform'). Secular figurative use ('giving up something prized for a higher cause') expanded from the 17th century onward.

history.meaning: rite of making sacred, offering to a god
ritual offering; costly renunciation or cut-price sale

sacrifice.notes: Always masculine (faire un lourd sacrifice); in commerce and production budgets, vendre à prix sacrifié means selling at a steep markdown ('slashed/giveaway prices').

rootFamily.gloss: sacred, holy; (before noun) damned/hell of a

cognates.meaning: to offer as a sacrifice; give up (via Old French)

sacrifier.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin sacrificāre ('to make a sacrifice, offer up to a deity'), compound verb formed from sacer ('sacred, consecrated') + -ficāre (combining verbal form of facere, 'to make, render', literally 'to render sacred'). From ancient and biblical ritual immolation, the verb broadened in Classical French to mean giving up personal interests, sacrificing a scene in the editing room, or complying with a tradition (sacrifier à la mode).

history.meaning: to perform a sacred rite, offer a victim to the gods
to sacrifice, give up; (se sacrifier) devote oneself selflessly

sacrifier.notes: Note the idiomatic prepositional construction sacrifier à la tradition / à la coutume, which does NOT mean giving up tradition, but rather 'paying tribute to / observing tradition'!

cognates.meaning: holy, consecrated (borrowed from Old French sacré, past participle of sacrer)

sacré.etymology: Originally the past participle of Old French sacrer ('to consecrate, anoint a sovereign'), borrowed/adapted from Classical Latin sacrātus ('consecrated, holy'), past participle of sacrāre ('to dedicate to a deity, declare inviolable'), from sacer, sacrum ('set apart from the profane—hence either holy or accursed, forfeited to the underworld gods', as in auri sacra fames, 'accursed hunger for gold'). Remarkably, Modern French preserves this ancient Latin ambivalence depending on word order!

history.meaning: set apart for the gods (holy or accursed) > consecrated

sacré.notes: Textbook adjective-position shift! After the noun, sacré means 'holy, sacred' (un lieu sacré, un monstre sacré du cinéma = 'a legendary icon of cinema'); before the noun, it means 'a hell of a / quite a / damned' (un sacré talent, un sacré numéro, Sacré Mathias !).

rootFamily.gloss: coronation/anointing; crowning triumph (le sacre aux César)
to consecrate; devote; crown an artist's career

sage.etymology: Inherited from Old French sage ('wise, learned, prudent'), from Vulgar Latin *sabius, contracted from Classical/Late Latin sapidus ('having taste or flavor; discerning, wise', derived from sapere 'to taste, have good discernment, be wise').

history.meaning: wise, sensible, well-behaved (of a child); wise person, sage (noun)

sage-femme.etymology: Compound attested in Old French from the 13th century, uniting sage ('wise, experienced, skilled', from Vulgar Latin *sabius, blending Classical Latin sapidus and nescius, from sapere 'to have discernment') and femme ('woman', from Classical Latin femina). Literally 'skilled woman', naming the experienced practitioner who assists at childbirth.
sage-femme.notes: Plural is sages-femmes; remarkably, French retains the title sage-femme even for male midwives (un homme sage-femme), alongside the rarer clinical term maïeuticien.

sagesse.etymology: Formed in 12th-century Old French from the adjective sage ('wise, discerning', via Vulgar Latin *sabius from Classical Latin sapidus 'tasty, discerning', derived from sapere 'to taste, understand') and the abstract quality suffix -esse (from Classical Latin -itia).
sagesse.notes: Ranges from philosophical 'wisdom' to everyday 'good behavior' in children (être d'une grande sagesse) and dentistry's dents de sagesse ('wisdom teeth').

saigner.etymology: Inherited from Old French saignier ('to lose blood, let blood medically'), from Classical Latin sanguinare ('to bleed, be bloodthirsty'), a denominative verb from sanguis, sanguinis ('blood'). From medieval bloodletting arose the figurative sense 'to drain someone's finances, extort'.
saigner.notes: In agency negotiations (as in Dix pour cent), saigner quelqu'un à blanc ('to bleed someone dry') vividly describes extracting ruinous fees or concessions, while saignant means 'rare' for steak.

cognates.meaning: to seek (Germanic cognate of the Frankish root)

saisir.etymology: Inherited from Old French saisir, seisir ('to put someone in feudal possession of, take possession of'), from Early Medieval Latin sacire ('to lay legal claim to, appropriate'), borrowed from Frankish *sakjan ('to claim in court, dispute', from Proto-Germanic *sokijana). Later generalized from feudal property law to physical grasping and mental comprehension.

history.meaning: to lay legal claim to, prosecute
to put in possession of, appropriate
to take possession of, grasp, understand

saisir.notes: Spans physical ('grab'), legal ('impound', saisir la justice 'refer to court'), digital ('input data'), and conversational ('get/catch a point': Tu saisis ?).

saison.etymology: Inherited from Old French saison, seison ('time of sowing, favorable moment, season of the year'), from Classical Latin sationem (accusative of satio, 'a sowing, planting'), derived from serere, satum ('to sow'). Its modern audiovisual meaning ('season of a TV series') is a 20th-century semantic calque of American English season.

history.meaning: act or time of sowing seeds
favorable agricultural period, time of year
calendar season; series run on television

saison.notes: Essential TV industry term (la saison deux, tourner une nouvelle saison); note the phonetic shift in its derivative saisonnier (/sɛ.zɔ.nje/, 'seasonal').

salade.etymology: Borrowed in 14th-century Middle French from Northern Italian salata (or Old Provençal salada, 'dish of herbs seasoned with salt and oil'), feminine substantive of the past participle of salare ('to salt'), ultimately from Classical Latin sal ('salt').

history.meaning: salad, cold mixed dish; (plural) tall tales

salade.notes: Colloquially, raconter des salades means 'to spin tall tales / talk nonsense'—a staple phrase when agents or actors make flimsy excuses.

rootFamily.gloss: to salt; salty, steep (of a bill)

salaire.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical Latin salarium ('allowance given to Roman soldiers to buy salt; stipend, pay'), originally neuter substantive of the adjective salarius ('pertaining to salt'), from sal ('salt').
salaire.notes: While office employees earn un salaire, film stars and stage performers in France are typically paid un cachet ('performance fee').

sale.etymology: Inherited via Old French sale ('murky, dull, soiled', 12th century) from Frankish *salu ('dull, dusky, dark-colored, dirty'), from Proto-Germanic *salwaz ('dusky, sallow'). Unrelated to Latin sal ('salt') or French salle ('room').
sale.notes: Word order flips the meaning: après-nom (une affaire sale, une chemise sale) means literally or morally 'dirty', whereas avant-nom (un sale coup, un sale quart d'heure) means 'nasty, awful, rotten'.

cognates.meaning: sallow (from the shared Germanic adjective root)

salir.etymology: Formed in 12th-century Old French as a deadjectival second-conjugation verb from sale ('murky, dirty', borrowed from Frankish *salu 'dusky, soiled') plus the verbal suffix -ir, meaning 'to make dirty' both physically and morally.

history.meaning: to dirty, stain; to sully a reputation

salir.notes: Conjugates regularly in -iss- (nous salissons); in media scandals, salir l'image / la mémoire de quelqu'un means 'to smear or tarnish someone's image'.

salle.etymology: Salle came through Latin sala from reconstructed Old Low Franconian *sal, a dwelling consisting of a single room. The French word is recorded from the eleventh century.
salle.notes: Designates functional or public rooms (salle de réunion, salle de classe, salle de cinéma, salle de bains), whereas a private bedroom is une chambre.

salon.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century from Italian salone ('great reception hall in a palace'), augmentative of sala ('hall, room', borrowed from Lombardic/Frankish *sala 'single-room dwelling, hall', source of French salle).

history.meaning: reception room, living room, literary gathering, trade exhibition, hair salon

saluer.etymology: Inherited from Old French saluer ('to wish health and safety to, greet, bow to'), from Classical Latin salutare ('to wish health to, greet, pay one's respects'), derived from salus, salutis ('health, safety, welfare, greeting').

history.meaning: to wish good health to, greet
to greet, say hello to, salute, hail

salut.etymology: Salut descends from Latin salus, physical well-being or health, related to salvus, safe or well. Wishing someone good health helped the word develop its greeting sense.
salut.notes: Just like Italian ciao, casual Salut! works both on arrival ('Hi!') and on departure ('Bye!') among friends, while formal contexts keep le salut ('salvation, safety').

salé.etymology: Inherited from Old French salé ('salted, salty'), past participle of saler ('to salt, cure with salt'), from Classical Latin salare / *salire, derived from sal ('salt').

history.meaning: salty, savory (as opposed to sweet); steep (of a bill)

samedi.etymology: Inherited from Old French samedy / sambedi ('Saturday'), from Vulgar Latin *sambati dies (attested across Gaul, northern Italy, and the Balkans, reflecting a nasalized vernacular Greek pronunciation *sambaton), from Ecclesiastical Latin sabbati dies ('day of the Sabbath'), from Ancient Greek sabbaton < Hebrew shabbat ('rest, Sabbath').

samu.etymology: Twentieth-century French acronym SAMU, standing for Service d'Aide Médicale Urgente ('Urgent Medical Aid Service'), pioneered in Toulouse by physician Louis Lareng in 1968 and codified nationwide in 1986; lexicalized as a common masculine noun pronounced as a single two-syllable word (/sa.my/).

history.meaning: hospital-based mobile emergency medical dispatch service

samu.notes: Always masculine (appeler le samu / le SAMU, emergency number 15 in France); unlike firefighter ambulances (les pompiers, 18), SAMU dispatches mobile intensive-care physicians.

rootFamily.gloss: social emergency outreach for the homeless

sanguin.etymology: Learned borrowing in 12th-century Old French from Classical Latin sanguineus ('of blood, bloody, blood-colored'), derived from sanguis, sanguinis ('blood'). Through medieval humoral medicine, where an excess of blood produced a fiery, passionate temperament, it acquired its psychological meaning.

history.meaning: of blood; having a predominant blood humor

sanguin.notes: Beware the false friend with English 'sanguine' ('cheerfully optimistic'): in French, une personne sanguine describes someone hot-blooded, quick-tempered, and explosive!

sans.etymology: Inherited from Old French senz / sans ('without'), from Vulgar Latin *senis / Classical Latin sine ('without', reinforced in Gallo-Romance with adverbial -s, possibly blended with absentia in legal formulas).

santé.etymology: Inherited from Old French santé, santeit ('physical soundness, well-being'), from Classical Latin sanitatem (accusative of sanitas, 'health of body or mind'), formed from sanus ('sound, healthy') with abstract suffix -itas.

history.meaning: soundness of body and mind, health

santé.notes: Used standalone when clinking glasses (Santé !, short for À ta/votre santé !) or even after someone sneezes in some regions alongside À tes souhaits !

sashimi.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from Japanese 刺身 (sashimi, 'thinly sliced raw fish or seafood'), a compound of 刺し (sashi, continuative stem of 刺す sasu 'to pierce, stick', originally referring to piercing the sliced flesh with the fish's tail fin to identify its species) and 身 (mi, 'body, flesh, meat').

history.meaning: pierced flesh; thinly sliced raw fish served with condiments
Japanese dish of raw fish slices

sashimi.notes: Masculine in French (un sashimi, des sashimis), pronounced /sa.ʃi.mi/; a staple of trendy Parisian power-lunches among talent agents and actors.

rootFamily.gloss: vinegared rice dish with fish (fellow Japanese culinary loan)
skewered grilled chicken (fellow Japanese culinary loan)

satisfait.etymology: Lexicalized adjective from the past participle of Middle French satisfaire (14th century), adapted from Classical Latin satisfactus, past participle of satisfacere ('to do enough for, content, discharge an obligation'), a compound of satis ('enough, sufficiently') and facere ('to do, make').

history.meaning: having been given sufficient amends or fulfillment

satisfait.notes: Takes the preposition de before nouns and infinitives (être satisfait d'un contrat / d'avoir signé), and occurs in the commercial guarantee satisfait ou remboursé ('money-back guarantee').

cognates.meaning: sausage (borrowed via Old Northern French saussiche)

saucisse.etymology: Inherited/adapted via Old French saucice (12th–13th century) from Late Latin salsicia ('seasoned salted meat stuffed in casing', feminine singular reanalyzed from neuter plural of salsicius 'prepared with salt'), derived from salsus ('salted'), past participle of sallere ('to salt'), from sal ('salt').

history.meaning: cased minced meat seasoned with salt and spices

saucisse.notes: Crucial culinary distinction: une saucisse is fresh or cooked (like chipolata, merguez, saucisse de Toulouse), whereas un saucisson is dry-cured and sliced cold as an apéritif snack.

rootFamily.gloss: to slice up time/budgets into tiny pieces

sauf.etymology: Inherited from Old French salf / sauf ('unharmed, safe; save, except'), from Classical Latin salvus ('whole, uninjured, safe and sound'); the prepositional sense ('except, save for') arose from Latin ablative absolute constructions like salvo jure / salvo honore ('with one's right/honor kept intact, saving...').

history.meaning: safe and sound; keeping intact, excepting
safe and sound (sain et sauf, adj.); except, save for (prep.)

sauter.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin saltare ('to dance, leap, jump about'), frequentative of salire ('to leap, spring, bound').

history.meaning: to leap -> to jump repeatedly, dance

sauvage.etymology: Inherited from Old French salvage, sauvage ('living in the woods, untamed, wild'), from Late/Vulgar Latin salvaticus, an alteration (by vowel assimilation or folk association with salvus) of Classical Latin silvaticus ('belonging to the forest, wild'), derived from silva ('forest, woodland'). Used both as an adjective and substantivized as a noun.

history.meaning: of the woods, growing or living wild in forests
wild, untamed; unsociable person or wild creature

sauvage.notes: Far milder in everyday French than English 'savage': faire le sauvage often just means being shy or unsociable at a party, while grève sauvage means 'wildcat strike' and affichage sauvage 'fly-posting'.

sauver.etymology: Sauver comes from Late Latin salvare ('to save, preserve', built on Classical Latin salvus 'safe, unharmed'). Vocalisation of l before v turned salvare into Old French salver, sauver.
sauver.notes: Related to **sauf** ('safe' in *sain et sauf*, and preposition 'except').

sauveur.etymology: Inherited from Old French salveor, sauveor ('deliverer, Redeemer'), from Late/Ecclesiastical Latin salvatorem (accusative of salvator, 'preserver, savior', coined by early Christian Latin translators to render Greek soter), agent noun from salvare ('to save'), from Classical Latin salvus ('safe, unharmed, whole').
sauveur.notes: Traditional religious feminine is salvatrice, though secular usage often employs sauveuse ('Mon sauveur / Ma sauveuse !' when a colleague rescues a doomed film deal).

saveur.etymology: Inherited from Old French savor, saveur ('taste, flavor, culinary sauce, zest'), from Classical Latin saporem (accusative of sapor, 'taste, flavor, refined discernment'), derived from the verb sapere ('to have a taste, be discerning, know')—making saveur an etymological cousin of savoir ('to know').
saveur.notes: Used both gastronomically and figuratively for wit or piquancy (une anecdote pleine de saveur); contrast fade or sans saveur ('bland, flavorless').

rootFamily.gloss: to know (from the same Latin verb sapere)

savoir.etymology: Savoir continues Latin sapere. That verb could refer both to taste or smell and to discernment or wisdom. The Académie dates French savoir to the ninth century: the history connects sensory judgement with knowing.
savoir.notes:
- *Savoir* is for facts and learned skills; *connaître* is for people, places and being familiar with something.
- *Je ne sais pas* is often shortened in speech to *chais pas*.

savon.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin saponem (nominative sapo, 'hair dye or tallow-and-ash mixture used by Gauls and Germans'), borrowed from Proto-Germanic *saipōn ('dripping resin, soap').

savonneux.etymology: Derived in the 14th century from savon ('soap', from Late Latin saponem) with the adjectival suffix -eux (from Latin -osus, 'full of, having the nature of').

savourer.etymology: Derived in the 12th century from Old French savour ('taste, flavor, relish', modern saveur, from Classical Latin saporem, from sapere 'to taste, have flavor').

scandale.etymology: Learned refashioning (replacing inherited Old French escandle, esclandre) from Ecclesiastical Latin scandalum ('stumbling block, temptation to sin, cause of moral offense'), borrowed from Ancient Greek σκάνδαλον (skandalon, 'spring-stick of a trap, snare, stumbling block'). Note that French esclandre ('public scene/outburst') is its popular doublet!

history.meaning: stumbling block, occasion of sin or public offense
public moral outrage, disgraceful affair, uproar

scandale.notes: Faire un scandale or crier au scandale means 'to make a scene / cry foul'; its inherited doublet un esclandre specifically means a noisy public row that PR agents scramble to hush up.

rootFamily.gloss: noisy public outburst (popular doublet of scandale)

scandaleux.etymology: Derived in 15th-century Middle French (modeled on Ecclesiastical Latin scandalosus 'causing offense') from scandale ('public offense, outrage', from Latin scandalum < Greek σκάνδαλον 'trap, stumbling block') plus the productive adjectival suffix -eux (from Latin -osus, 'full of').
scandaleux.notes: Feminine is scandaleuse; in everyday French C'est scandaleux ! ('That's outrageous!') reacts just as readily to an unfair fee or late train as to a tabloid affair.

sceau.etymology: Inherited via Old French seel ('signet ring, stamped wax emblem') from Classical Latin sigillum ('little figure, seal impression'), diminutive of signum ('mark, sign'); spelled sceau with etymological sc- from the Renaissance.

cognates.meaning: seal was borrowed from Old French seel!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: sceau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: sceau

sceau.notes: Famous French homophone quartet **/so/**: **un sceau** ('a wax seal'), **un seau** ('a bucket'), **un saut** ('a jump'), and **sot** ('foolish')!

sceller.etymology: Derived from Old French seel ('seal, signet', modern sceau, inherited from Classical Latin sigillum 'small figure, seal impression', diminutive of signum 'mark, sign').

history.meaning: to affix a seal, seal shut

sceptique.etymology: Learned borrowing in 16th-century Middle French (popularized by Montaigne's Essais) via Late Latin scepticus from Ancient Greek σκεπτικός (skeptikos, 'thoughtful, inquiring, examining carefully', applied to Pyrrho's philosophical school that suspended dogmatic judgment), derived from σκέπτομαι (skeptomai, 'to look closely, examine, reflect').

history.meaning: inquiring, reflective; follower of Pyrrhonian inquiry

sceptique.notes: Pronounced /sɛp.tik/ (the initial sc- is simply /s/, never /sk/!); do not confuse in writing or speech with septique (/sɛp.tik/, 'septic', as in fosse septique 'septic tank', a classic French joke).

cognates.meaning: science fiction (source of the French calque)

science-fiction.etymology: Mid-20th-century French lexical calque (attested around 1950) of American English science fiction (popularized by editor Hugo Gernsback in 1929), uniting two French nouns of Classical Latin origin: science (from scientia 'knowledge', from scire 'to know') and fiction (from fictio 'a fashioning, feigning', from fingere 'to shape, invent').

history.meaning: knowledge + act of shaping or inventing
speculative literary genre grounded in imagined science

science-fiction.notes: Feminine singular (la science-fiction, un film de science-fiction), very frequently abbreviated in cinema pitches as la SF (/ɛs.ɛf/); figuratively C'est de la science-fiction ! means 'That's pure fantasy / totally unrealistic!'

scooter.etymology: Borrowed in the early 1950s (in the motorized two-wheeler sense popularized across Europe by Italian Vespa and Lambretta models) from English scooter, originally 'child's foot-propelled kick scooter', an agent noun from to scoot ('to dart, glide swiftly'), itself likely of North Germanic/Scandinavian origin (compare Old Norse skjota 'to shoot, dart').

history.meaning: glider, child's foot-propelled kick scooter, then motor scooter

scooter.notes: Pronounced /sku.tœʁ/ (and informally clipped to un scoot); in French, un scooter is strictly motorized (the ubiquitous Parisian vehicle for weaving through traffic to castings), whereas a kick/electric stand-up scooter is une trottinette.

cognates.meaning: script, text of a play or film

script.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century in its theatrical, cinematic, and typographic senses from English script (both a learned borrowing from Classical Latin scriptum 'something written' and a clipping of manuscript / typescript), ultimately the neuter past participle of Latin scribere ('to write', alongside native French écrit).

history.meaning: handwriting style; working text of a play or film
shooting script, continuity text; unjoined handwriting

script.notes: Film-set trap: while un script (m.) means a script/shooting text (often secondary to scénario), un scripte / une scripte (formerly script-girl) is a person—the continuity supervisor on set!

rootFamily.gloss: continuity supervisor on a film set
written work; past participle of écrire (native doublet)

scrupule.etymology: Learned borrowing in 14th-century Middle French from Classical Latin scrupulus ('uneasiness, moral anxiety, lingering doubt', and literally 'a tiny sharp pebble'—such as one caught in a sandal that constantly pricks the foot—as well as a small apothecary weight), diminutive of scrupus ('jagged stone; anxiety').

history.meaning: tiny sharp pebble; nagging uneasiness or moral hesitation

scrupule.notes: Most often heard in sans scrupules ('unscrupulous, ruthless'—a classic descriptor for rival agents poaching clients) and avoir des scrupules à faire quelque chose ('to have qualms about doing something').

sculpter.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century (originally sculper, then reshaped after sculpteur / sculpture) from Classical Latin sculpere, past participle sculptus ('to carve,grave, chisel in stone, wood, or metal').

scène.etymology: Learned borrowing in 14th–15th-century Middle French from Classical Latin scaena, scena ('theatrical stage, backdrop wall'), from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skene, originally 'tent, covered booth' where Greek actors changed masks and costumes behind the orchestra, later 'stage building, stage, dramatic scene').

history.meaning: tent, actor's changing booth, stage backdrop
stage; dramatic or cinematic scene; public quarrel

scène.notes: Covers both English 'stage' (monter sur scène 'go on stage', mise en scène 'direction/staging') and 'scene' (tourner une scène 'shoot a scene', faire une scène de ménage 'have a domestic row').

scénario.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-18th century from Italian scenario ('sheet pinned backstage in commedia dell'arte outlining scene divisions and actors' entrances and exits'), derived from scena ('stage, scene', from Latin scaena < Greek σκηνή) with the suffix -ario (from Latin -arium). Extended at the birth of cinema (c. 1908) to mean a complete film screenplay.

history.meaning: backstage plot outline for improvised commedia dell'arte plays
theatrical or operatic plot outline, then film screenplay

scénario.notes: False-friend alert: while English 'scenario' usually means a hypothetical situation, French un scénario is first and foremost 'a screenplay/movie script' (lire un scénario); standard plural is des scénarios (rarely Italianate scénarii).

rootFamily.gloss: to adapt or structure into a screenplay

scénariste.etymology: Coined in early 20th-century French cinema (attested around 1918) from scénario ('screenplay', borrowed from Italian scenario, from Latin scaena < Greek σκηνή 'stage') by replacing the final -o with the professional agent suffix -iste (from Latin -ista < Greek -ιστής).

history.meaning: author of film, television, or comic-book scripts

scénariste.notes: Epicene noun (un scénariste / une scénariste); in French cinema and bande dessinée (comics), the scénariste enjoys strong auteur status alongside the réalisateur ('director') or dessinateur ('illustrator').

scénographie.etymology: Learned borrowing in 16th-century Renaissance architectural treatises (via Vitruvius) from Classical Latin scaenographia ('perspective drawing of buildings and stage fronts'), from Ancient Greek σκηνογραφία (skenographia, 'scene-painting, illusionistic backdrop painting'), compounding σκηνή (skene, 'tent, theatrical stage') and -γραφία (-graphia, 'drawing, writing', from γράφω grapho).

history.meaning: painting of theatrical stage backdrops in perspective
perspective representation; art of theatrical, exhibition, or film set design

scénographie.notes: Widely used in French not only for theater and opera stage design, but also for museum exhibitions, fashion runway shows, and film production design.

rootFamily.gloss: relating to stage or exhibition design

se.etymology: Se continues Latin se, oneself. It is recorded in French from the ninth century. Its modern reflexive uses belong to that pronoun history, not to the chemical abbreviation Se.
se.notes: Every French pronominal verb is listed in dictionaries with se (se lever, s'appeler, se réveiller), adapting to me, te, nous, vous across persons.

cognates.meaning: to fight (especially in a duel or for a cause)

se battre.etymology: Reciprocal/pronominal construction attested since Old French (soi batre 'to fight one another, struggle'), combining the reflexive pronoun se (from Classical Latin se) with battre ('to beat, strike'), inherited via Late/Vulgar Latin battere from Classical Latin batuere, battuere ('to beat, strike, fence as gladiators'), itself widely considered an early borrowing into Latin from Gaulish.

history.meaning: to strike, beat, practice fencing blows
to strike each other, engage in combat
to fight physically or struggle tenaciously for a goal

se battre.notes: Because it is pronominal, compound tenses always take être (elle s'est battue pour décrocher le rôle 'she fought hard to land the role'); contrast transitive battre ('to beat/defeat').

cognates.meaning: to bring toward a common center; to focus mental effort

se concentrer.etymology: Pronominal form of concentrer (attested c. 1600), created in French from prefix con- ('together, with') and centre ('center'), itself borrowed from Classical Latin centrum and ultimately Ancient Greek kentron ('sharp point, stationary leg of a pair of compasses'). Originally a geometric and physical term meaning 'to gather toward a single center', its reflexive psychological sense 'to focus one's mind or attention' emerged in the 18th century.

history.meaning: sharp point, goad, stationary center-point of a compass
center of a circle or sphere
to draw to a common center; (reflexive) to focus one's mind

se concentrer.notes: Takes the preposition sur when specifying the object of focus (se concentrer sur un rôle, 'to concentrate on a role'); indispensable on film sets when actors prepare before a take.

cognates.meaning: to untangle, manage, get out of trouble
to entangle in conflict or confusion (from the same French root brouiller)

se débrouiller.etymology: Pronominal use of débrouiller (16th century, 'to untangle, clear up confusion'), formed from privative prefix dé- (from Latin dis-) and brouiller ('to mix up, muddle', Old French broillier), which derives via Gallo-Romance from a root linked to Frankish *brod ('broth, thick liquid, sludge'). In the 19th century, the reflexive se débrouiller shifted colloquially from 'clearing up a muddle' to 'managing resourcefully on one's own'.

history.meaning: to dirty, mix up, muddle together
to untangle, sort out what is confused
to extricate oneself; to manage resourcefully, get by

se débrouiller.notes: Embodies a prized French cultural trait known as le système D (D for débrouille / débrouillardise): resourceful street-smart improvisation—essential for talent agents fixing last-minute crises.

rootFamily.gloss: to muddle, scramble, cause a falling-out

cognates.meaning: to challenge openly (originally 'to renounce trust', via Old French desfier)

se méfier.etymology: Pronominal verb attested in the 16th century (continuing Old French soi mesfier), composed of the pejorative prefix mé- (from Old French mes-, derived from Frankish *missa- 'wrongly, amiss' blended with Latin minus) and fier ('to entrust, trust'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *fidare, an alteration of Classical Latin fidere ('to trust, put confidence in', related to fides 'faith, trust').

history.meaning: to distrust, be on one's guard against

se méfier.notes: Always followed by de when naming what one distrusts (se méfier d'un producteur, 'to be wary of a producer'); standalone impérative Méfie-toi ! means 'Watch out! / Don't trust them!'.

rootFamily.gloss: to trust, rely on (se fier à)

cognates.meaning: to move past, elapse, take place (borrowed from Old French)

se passer.etymology: Pronominal development of passer, inherited from Old French passer and Vulgar Latin *passare ('to step, walk through, traverse'), a denominal verb formed from Classical Latin passus ('a step, pace', originally the past participle noun of pandere 'to stretch out, spread the legs in walking'). From spatial movement and temporal elapsing ('time passes'), the reflexive se passer acquired the eventive sense 'to unfold, happen, take place' in Middle French.

history.meaning: step, stride / to step across, traverse
to cross over, go beyond, elapse
to elapse; to take place, happen, go (well or badly)

se passer.notes: Watch the crucial construction contrast: Ça s'est bien passé ('It went well' — e.g. an audition) versus se passer de quelque chose ('to do without something').

rootFamily.gloss: crossing, corridor, brief scene or excerpt

se souvenir.etymology: Pronominal construction of souvenir ('to come to mind, remember'), inherited from Classical Latin subvenire ('to come up from under, come to aid, occur to the mind'), from sub- ('under, up from below') + venire ('to come').

history.meaning: it comes to mind -> to remember

cognates.meaning: trumpet, horn (from the same Germanic/expressive noun)
trumpet; to fabricate or 'trump up' (from Old French tromper)

se tromper.etymology: Pronominal form of tromper ('to deceive, cheat'), attested in Middle French (14th century). Originally meaning 'to blow the horn (trompe)', it was used in the idiom se jouer de quelqu'un à la trompe ('to mock or make fun of someone by blowing a horn at them'), from Old French trompe ('horn, trumpet', likely from Frankish *trumpa or an expressive onomatopoeic root). From 'mocking' it shifted to 'deceiving', and reflexively se tromper came to mean 'to deceive oneself, be mistaken'.

history.meaning: to sound a horn or trumpet
to be mistaken, make an error

se tromper.notes: Compare transitive vs. reflexive: tromper quelqu'un means 'to deceive someone' or 'to cheat on a romantic partner', whereas se tromper simply means 'to make a mistake' (se tromper de texte = 'to get one's lines/script wrong').

seau.etymology: Inherited via Old French seel from Vulgar Latin *sitellum, masculine diminutive of Classical Latin situla ('well bucket, pail').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: seau (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: seau

seau.notes: Famous French homophone trio all pronounced `/so/`: **un seau** ('a bucket'), **un sceau** ('a wax seal', < *sigillum*), and **un saut** ('a jump', < *saltum*).

sec.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin siccus ('dry, parched, without moisture; sober').

cognates.meaning: second in rank or order (borrowed from Old French)

second.etymology: Inherited from Old French segont, second (12th century), from Classical Latin secundus ('following, next in time or rank; favorable, with the current'), originally an old participial adjective built on the verb sequi ('to follow', from Proto-Indo-European *sekw- 'to follow'). Because what follows the first is number two, Latin secundus replaced older duo formations for the ordinal 'second'.

history.meaning: second in rank, order, or series

second.notes: Pronunciation exception: the letter 'c' in second (and its derivatives seconder, secondaire) is pronounced as a voiced [g] ([səgɔ̃]), and in cinema un second rôle is a 'supporting role' or 'character actor'.

rootFamily.gloss: unit of time (1/60th of a minute); second class/gear

cognates.meaning: secondary, of lesser rank or importance

secondaire.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (14th century) from Classical Latin secundarius ('of the second class, rank, or quality; inferior'), derived with the relational suffix -arius from secundus ('following, next, second'), itself from sequi ('to follow'). Originally applied in astronomy and scholastic philosophy to subordinate causes before broadening to general rank and importance.

history.meaning: belonging to the second class or inferior quality

morphemes.meaning: pertaining to, of the nature of

secondaire.notes: Pronounced with a hard [g] sound ([səgɔ̃dɛʁ]), just like second; in film casting, un personnage secondaire is a supporting/minor character, and un effet secondaire is a 'side effect'.

seconde.etymology: From Medieval Latin (pars) minuta secunda ('second small division [of an hour or degree]'), feminine of Classical Latin secundus ('following, second in rank or order', from sequi 'to follow').

history.meaning: second (of time or arc); second class/gear

cognates.meaning: assistance and relief in distress (via Old French)

secours.etymology: Inherited from Old French secors, socors (11th century), derived from Medieval Latin succursus ('help, aid, relief'), an action noun built on Classical Latin succurrere (past participle succursus, 'to run under, hasten to the aid of'), composed of prefix sub- ('under, up to') and currere ('to run', from Proto-Indo-European *kers- 'to run').

history.meaning: to run under, hasten to help someone in danger

morphemes.meaning: under, up to support (< Latin sub-)

secours.notes: Invariant final -s in both singular and plural (un secours, des secours); Au secours ! is the standard cry for 'Help!' in an emergency, while une issue de secours is an 'emergency exit'.

rootFamily.gloss: to rescue, come to the aid of

secret.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin secretus ('set apart, hidden, private') and its neuter noun secretum ('hidden thing, mystery, secluded place'), past participle of secernere ('to separate, set apart'), from se- ('apart') + cernere ('to sift, distinguish').

history.meaning: to separate -> set apart, hidden thing

cognates.meaning: secretly (built on the same Latin root secretus)

secrètement.etymology: Formed in Old and Middle French (12th–13th century, secretement) from secrète, the feminine form of the adjective secret (borrowed from Classical Latin secretus 'set apart, hidden, private', past participle of secernere 'to separate, sift apart', from se- 'apart' + cernere 'to sift, distinguish'), combined with the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind').

history.meaning: to set apart, separate / isolated, hidden, private
apart from others, in private, covertly
secretly, covertly (with grave accent marking open [ɛ])

secrètement.notes: Notice the accent shift from acute in le secret / secrète (Wait: secrète already has the grave accent!—unlike discret -> discrètement, secret has no accent in the masculine, then adds the grave accent in secrète and secrètement to mark the open [ɛ] before a mute syllable).

rootFamily.gloss: to secrete (physiological discharge, same Latin root)

cognates.meaning: secretary (borrowed via Middle French and Medieval Latin)

secrétaire.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (12th–13th century, secretaire) from Medieval Latin secretarius ('confidant, trusted advisor, privy clerk, notary'), a substantive use of Late Latin secretarius ('pertaining to secret or private counsels'), derived from Classical Latin secretum ('a secret, mystery, private place'), neuter noun from secretus ('set apart, confidential'). Originally denoted a trusted keeper of royal or ecclesiastical secrets before shifting to administrative assistant.

history.meaning: something set apart, mystery, confidential matter
confidant; administrative officer or office assistant; writing desk

morphemes.meaning: agent or person connected with (< Latin -arius)

secrétaire.notes: Epicene for people (un secrétaire / une secrétaire for an assistant or Secrétaire d'État), whereas strictly masculine un secrétaire also means a traditional writing bureau/desk! In modern French talent agencies like ASK, agents' assistants usually prefer assistant(e) over secrétaire.

section.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (14th century, originally in surgical anatomy and geometry for 'a cutting or intersection') from Classical Latin sectio (stem section-, 'a cutting, severing, division of confiscated property'), noun of action formed from secare (past participle sectus, 'to cut, cleave, divide', from Proto-Indo-European *sek- 'to cut'). Broadened in the 18th–19th centuries to administrative departments and festival categories.

history.meaning: to cut, slice / act of cutting, division
anatomical dissection; geometric point of intersection
subdivision of a text, organization, or festival program

section.notes: Always feminine (une section), like nearly all French nouns ending in -tion; in French cinema, major festivals like Cannes divide selections into sections such as Un Certain Regard (une section parallèle).

cognates.meaning: anatomical cavity or hollow (learned borrowing of the same Latin word)

sein.etymology: Inherited from Old French sein (11th century), from Classical Latin sinus ('curve, hollow, fold of a toga draped across the chest, bosom, gulf, bay'). Because Romans used the curved fold of their toga over the chest both as a pocket and as a place of embrace, Latin sinus meant both 'bosom/chest' and 'protective interior', yielding French sein for both anatomical 'breast' and the formal spatial idiom au sein de ('within, in the heart of').

history.meaning: curved fold of a garment over the chest, bosom, bay
female breast; (figurative) interior, midst (au sein de)

sein.notes: Exact homophone of sain ('healthy') and saint ('holy, saint')—all pronounced [sɛ̃]; note how elevated prose constantly uses au sein de l'agence ('within the agency') with zero anatomical connotation.

rootFamily.gloss: winding, sinuous (learned borrowing from Latin sinuosus)
to insinuate, slip subtly into the mind (< in- + sinuare)

seize.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin sedecim ('sixteen'), compound of sex ('six') + decem ('ten').

sel.etymology: Inherited directly from Classical Latin sal ('salt'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ls, one of the oldest and best-preserved culinary words across European languages.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: sel (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: sel

sel.notes: Latin *sal* also gave French **la salade** ('salted greens'), **la sauce** (*salsa* 'salted dressing'), and **le salaire** (*salarium*).

cognates.meaning: self-portrait photograph taken with a smartphone or webcam
self, same (cognate with the Germanic base self)

selfie.etymology: Borrowed in the early 2010s from English selfie, itself first attested in 2002 in Australian English internet forum slang and formed from English self (inherited from Old English self, from Proto-Germanic *selbaz 'oneself') plus the informal hypocoristic suffix -ie. Entered major French dictionaries (Petit Robert, Larousse) around 2015–2016 amid smartphone and red-carpet celebrity culture.
selfie.notes: Masculine in French (faire un selfie, 'to take a selfie'); Québec French actively promotes the clever portmanteau égoportrait, though un selfie overwhelmingly dominates in France.

rootFamily.gloss: self-service cafeteria or store (earlier French anglicism from self)

sources.title: Académie française – Dire, ne pas dire : selfie

selle.etymology: Inherited from Old French sele ('stool, seat, horse's saddle'), from Classical Latin sella ('seat, stool, chair, magistrate's curule chair'), derived from archaic *sedla (from the Proto-Indo-European root *sed- 'to sit' + instrumental suffix *-la; compare Classical Latin sedere 'to sit'). As mounted riding spread in Late Antiquity, sella specialized in Late Latin and Gallo-Romance to mean a horse's saddle.

history.meaning: stool, chair, seat (without back); Late Latin: riding saddle
saddle (for horse or bicycle); medical plural: bowel movements

selle.notes: Watch the equestrian idioms essential in agency talk: remettre quelqu'un en selle means 'to get someone back in the game / revive their career', and être bien en selle means 'to be firmly established'. Homophone of sel ('salt') and celle ('that one').

semaine.etymology: Semaine descends from Christian Latin septimana, related to an adjective meaning concerning the number seven. The French word is recorded from the eleventh century.

rootFamily.gloss: weekend (standard in Quebec; end of the workweek in France)

semaine.notes: Notice that the adjective for 'weekly' in French is learned Greek-derived hebdomadaire (from Greek hebdomás 'seven'), rather than a derivative of semaine!

cognates.meaning: outward appearance or show (via Old French semblance)

semblant.etymology: Substantive use in Old French (11th–12th century, semblant 'facial expression, outward look, appearance') of the present participle of sembler ('to seem, appear, resemble'), inherited from Late Latin similare (a variant of Classical Latin simulare 'to make like, imitate, feign'), derived from similis ('like, similar', from Proto-Indo-European *sem- 'one, together').

history.meaning: like, similar / to copy, imitate, feign
pretense, feigned show (faire semblant), faint trace (un semblant de)

semblant.notes: Crucial everyday idiom: faire semblant (de faire quelque chose) means 'to pretend (to do something)'—literally 'to make an appearance of'—ubiquitous in acting and diplomatic agency white lies!

sembler.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin similare ('to resemble, be like, imitate'), derived from similis ('like, similar').

sens.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin sensus ('faculty of perceiving, feeling, understanding, meaning, direction'), from sentire ('to feel, perceive'), Later reinforced in directional meanings by Frankish *sinn ('direction, way').

cognates.meaning: physical feeling; public excitement or stir

sensation.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (14th century) from Medieval Scholastic Latin sensatio (stem sensation-, 'understanding, sensory perception'), derived from Late Latin sensatus ('gifted with sense') and Classical Latin sensus ('faculty of perceiving, feeling, sense'), built on the past participial stem of sentire ('to perceive by the senses, feel'). The media sense 'public excitement, stir' (faire sensation) emerged in the 18th century.

history.meaning: sensory perception, cognition through the senses
physical or emotional impression; thrilling stir (18th c.)

sensation.notes: In showbusiness French, faire sensation (no article!) means 'to cause a sensation / be a smash hit' (e.g., Son film a fait sensation à Cannes), while sensations fortes means 'thrills'.

cognates.meaning: capacity for emotional/aesthetic responsiveness (cf. Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility)

sensibilité.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (14th century) from Late Latin sensibilitas (stem sensibilitat-, 'capacity for sensation or feeling'), an abstract quality noun derived from Classical Latin sensibilis ('perceptible by the senses; capable of feeling'), itself from sensus ('perception, feeling'), past participle noun of sentire ('to feel, perceive'). Developed strong aesthetic and emotional overtones during 18th-century Enlightenment literature.

history.meaning: perceptible, capable of feeling / faculty of sensation
physical capacity to feel sensory impressions
emotional responsiveness, artistic temperament, technical sensitivity

morphemes.meaning: capable of feeling, sensitive (< Latin sensibil-)

sensibilité.notes: Covers both English 'sensitivity' (emotional tenderness, allergies, photographic ISO film speed) and 'sensibility' (an actor's or director's artistic temperament: une grande sensibilité artistique).

rootFamily.gloss: to raise awareness, make sensitive to

cognates.meaning: practical, reasonable (semantic shift from earlier 'capable of feeling/perceptible')

sensible.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (13th century) from Classical Latin sensibilis, which originally had a passive meaning ('perceptible by the senses') before acquiring an active meaning in Late Latin ('endowed with feeling, responsive to impressions'), derived from sensus ('feeling, perception'), from sentire ('to feel'). French preserved both the passive ('noticeable, appreciable') and active ('emotionally sensitive, delicate') senses.

history.meaning: perceptible by the senses; (Late Latin) capable of feeling
capable of sensation; tangible to the senses
emotionally sensitive, touchy; noticeable (une baisse sensible)

sensible.notes: Classic top-tier false friend! French sensible means 'sensitive' (emotionally delicate, or a touchy topic: un sujet sensible), NEVER English 'sensible' ('level-headed, practical'), which is sensé or raisonnable!

rootFamily.gloss: level-headed, sensible, reasonable (do not confuse with sensible!)

sensuel.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (15th century) from Late Christian Latin sensualis ('endowed with feeling, pertaining to the bodily senses or carnal appetites'), coined by early Latin church writers (such as Tertullian and Jerome) from Classical Latin sensus (u-stem noun, 'sense, physical perception', from sentire 'to feel') in theological contrast to spiritualis ('spiritual'). Shed its strictly moralizing stigma in modern aesthetic usage.

history.meaning: physical perception / pertaining to bodily senses rather than spirit
governed by physical senses and earthly pleasures
voluptuous, physically alluring, gratifying to the senses

morphemes.meaning: physical sense, perception (< Latin u-stem sensu-)

sensuel.notes: Doubles the final consonant in the feminine: sensuel -> sensuelle (une voix sensuelle, 'a sultry/sensual voice'); unlike sexy, sensuel carries a refined, artistic, and tactile register prized in French cinema criticism.

rootFamily.gloss: philosophical doctrine that all knowledge comes from senses

cognates.meaning: opinion, emotional attitude, tenderness (borrowed from French)

sentiment.etymology: Attested in Old French as sentement (12th century, 'physical sensation, smell, awareness'), formed natively from sentir ('to feel, perceive, smell', inherited from Classical Latin sentire) plus the action/result suffix -ment (from Latin -mentum). In the 16th century, its spelling and pronunciation were reshaped to sentiment under the combined influence of Medieval Latin sentimentum and Italian sentimento, shifting primarily to emotional feeling and inner conviction.

history.meaning: to perceive through the senses, feel, think

sentiment.notes: Much broader and less mawkish than English 'sentiment': un sentiment is the standard everyday French word for 'a feeling' or 'an impression' (J'ai le sentiment qu'il ment), and in the plural avoir des sentiments pour quelqu'un means 'to have romantic feelings for someone'.

rootFamily.gloss: sentimental, romantic (e.g., la vie sentimentale = 'love life')

sentimental.etymology: Borrowed in 1769 from English sentimental (popularized by Laurence Sterne's A Sentimental Journey through France and Italy, 1768), formed on sentiment ('feeling', itself from French sentiment) + -al.

history.meaning: characterized by tender emotion or feeling

sentir.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin sentire ('to perceive by the senses, feel, hear, smell, think').

history.meaning: to perceive by the senses, feel

sept.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin septem ('seven'), from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥ ('seven'). The silent p was reintroduced in Middle French orthography by learned Latinizing spelling.

septième.etymology: Attested in Old French as setisme, later refashioned etymologically to septiesme and septième, replacing earlier Old French setme (which had descended directly from Classical Latin septimus 'seventh'). Formed from the cardinal numeral sept ('seven', from Classical Latin septem, Proto-Indo-European *septm) and the productive French ordinal suffix -ième (Old French -iesme, derived from Vulgar Latin *-esimus on the model of centesimus).

history.meaning: seventh; (substantive) seventh floor or seventh art

septième.notes: The 'p' is completely silent ([sɛtjɛm], never *[sɛptjɛm]!); culturally iconic in French: le septième art ('the seventh art') is the standard, beloved synonym for cinema (coined by critic Ricciotto Canudo in 1923), and être au septième ciel means 'to be on cloud nine'.

rootFamily.gloss: person in their seventies (learned from Latin septuagenarius)
September (originally the seventh month of the early Roman calendar)

cognates.meaning: serenely (from the same Latin adjective serenus)

sereinement.etymology: Formed in Middle French from sereine, the feminine singular of the adjective serein ('clear, calm, untroubled', borrowed/adapted from Classical Latin serenus 'clear, cloudless, bright, fair' of the sky and weather, and figuratively 'tranquil, cheerful'), combined with the adverbial suffix -ment (from Classical Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind').

history.meaning: clear, cloudless, fair (of sky/weather); calm, untroubled

sereinement.notes: Frequently used in professional French (aborder un tournage sereinement, 'to approach a shoot with peace of mind / without stress') where English might say 'calmly' or 'confidently' rather than the poetic 'serenely'.

rootFamily.gloss: serene, calm, relaxed about an outcome
evening outdoor music ('serenade', via Italian serenata from sereno/sera)

cognates.meaning: to shut, lock, clench, press tightly
closely compacted or crowded together (military/literary borrowing from French serré)

serrer.etymology: Inherited from Old French serrer ('to shut fast, bolt, lock up, press closely together'), from Vulgar Latin *serrare, a geminated alteration (likely influenced by ferrum 'iron' or serra 'saw') of Late Latin serare ('to fasten with a bolt, bar, shut'), derived from Classical Latin sera ('a movable wooden bar or bolt for fastening doors'). In French, as fermer took over the general meaning 'to close', serrer specialized in 'tightening, squeezing, clasping'.

history.meaning: door-bar, bolt / to bar, bolt, shut fast
to lock up, shut tight, crowd closely together

serrer.notes: Packed with high-frequency idioms: serrer la main ('to shake hands'), serrer quelqu'un dans ses bras ('to hug someone'), avoir le cœur serré ('to feel a pang of anguish'), un emploi du temps serré ('a tight schedule'), and un café serré ('a short, strong espresso').

rootFamily.gloss: lock (for a door, preserving the original Latin 'bolt' sense!)
to tighten further; to bring closer together

serrure.etymology: Derived in the 12th century from serrer ('to bar, lock up, fasten tightly', from Late Latin serare 'to bolt, bar', from sera 'door-bar') + instrumental noun suffix -ure.

serré.etymology: Past participle of serrer ('to press close, tighten, lock'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *serrare, alteration of Late Latin serare ('to bolt, fasten shut', from Classical Latin sera 'crossbar, bolt') blended with serrare ('to saw').

cognates.meaning: servant (borrowed from Old French masculine/epicene servant)

servante.etymology: Formed in Old French (12th–13th century) as the feminine substantive of servant, the present participle of servir ('to serve, wait upon'), inherited from Classical Latin servire ('to be a slave, serve, be in service to'), derived from servus ('slave, bondman'). While masculine servant became restricted to specialized liturgical or artillery roles (replaced generally by serviteur), feminine servante remained the standard historical term for a female domestic servant.

history.meaning: slave / to be in slavery, serve
woman in service, female attendant or maidservant
maidservant (historical/literary); rolling side-table; theatrical ghost light

servante.notes: Beloved backstage theater vocabulary: une servante is the 'ghost light'—the single standing lamp left lit center-stage overnight when a theater is empty, watching over the stage! For modern housecleaners, say femme de ménage or employée de maison, as servante sounds dated or period-drama.

cognates.meaning: person who serves food/drinks or tennis ball; computer server

serveur.etymology: Attested in Old French as serveor ('one who serves, attendant'), formed natively from servir ('to serve', from Classical Latin servire 'to be a slave, serve') and the agentive suffix -eur (from Latin -orem / -atorem). Largely eclipsed for centuries by serviteur and garçon (de café), serveur was revived in the 20th century as the respectful, gender-paired professional term (serveur / serveuse) for restaurant waitstaff, and later adopted for sports and computing via English server.

history.meaning: to be a slave, perform service
attendant, person who serves or waits at table
waiter / waitress; tennis server; network computer server (late 20th c.)

serveur.notes: Etiquette alert in Paris cafés: never snap your fingers or shout Garçon ! (now considered patronizing and rude); make eye contact and say S'il vous plaît / Excusez-moi, Monsieur / Madame when addressing un serveur or une serveuse.

rootFamily.gloss: briefcase; towel or napkin (things used for service)

service.etymology: Borrowed in the 11th century from Classical Latin servitium ('condition of a slave, servitude; body of servants'), derived from servus ('slave, servant'), broadened in medieval feudal and courtly usage to 'duty rendered, helpful act, table service'.

serviette.etymology: Serviette was formed in Middle French from servir ('to serve at table', from Latin servire) + diminutive -ette: originally the cloth used when serving at table, and later also a bath towel or briefcase.
serviette.notes: Context tells you whether **une serviette** is a napkin at breakfast or a towel in a hotel bathroom.

servir.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin servire ('to be a slave or servant, be subject to, serve, be useful to'), derived from servus ('slave, servant').

history.meaning: servant -> to serve, be of use

cognates.meaning: attendant, servant (archaic/Scottish legal borrowing from Middle French)

serviteur.etymology: Borrowed or adapted in Old French (12th century, servitor, serviteur) from Late and Christian Latin servitor (accusative servitorem, 'servant, attendant, follower of God'), an agent noun built on the supine stem of Classical Latin servire ('to be a slave, serve', from servus 'slave'). Replaced native Old French serveor as the elevated and general masculine noun for a household, royal, or public servant.

history.meaning: to serve / attendant, devoted follower (Late Christian Latin)
retainer, servant of a lord or of God
manservant; devoted civil/public servant (serviteur de l'État)

serviteur.notes: No modern feminine *serviteuse exists in standard usage (its functional feminine for domestic roles was historically servante); playfully used in conversation as votre serviteur ('yours truly / your humble servant') to refer to oneself with ironic modesty.

cognates.meaning: sitting, meeting, studio recording or training period

session.etymology: Learned borrowing in Middle French (14th century) from Classical Latin sessio (stem session-, 'a sitting, seat, tarrying; sitting in assembly'), derived from the past participial stem sess- of sedere ('to sit', from Proto-Indo-European *sed-). Originally restricted to sittings of church councils, courts, parliament, and university exams, its modern studio/training senses (une session d'enregistrement, une session de casting) expanded in the 20th century under English semantic influence.

history.meaning: to sit / act of sitting, sitting together in discussion
formal sitting of a council, tribunal, or parliamentary assembly
exam/parliamentary sitting; recording, training, or computer session

session.notes: Compare session vs. séance: a movie showing at the cinema, a photo shoot, or a therapy appointment is une séance (séance de cinéma, séance photo), whereas une session refers to a multi-day block/round (exam session, training workshop) or a studio music/dubbing session.

rootFamily.gloss: sitting, screening, single meeting (< Old French seoir < sedere)
assessor, assistant judge who 'sits beside' (< ad- + sedere)

seul.etymology: Seul continues Latin solus, alone or only. The Académie records the French adjective from the tenth century.

history.meaning: alone (diphthongization of tonic free ō > eu)

seul.notes: Position changes meaning: un seul billet (before the noun) means 'a single / only one ticket', whereas un homme seul (after the noun) means 'a man who is alone'.

seulement.etymology: Formed in the 12th century from the feminine adjective seule ('alone, single, only', from Classical Latin solus) + the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind').

cognates.meaning: discrimination or prejudice based on sex or gender

sexisme.etymology: Borrowed around 1970 from American English sexism (coined between 1965 and 1968 in the women's liberation movement on the structural model of racism), transparently adapted into French morphology from sexe ('biological sex', borrowed in Old French from Classical Latin sexus 'male or female division, sex', likely related to secare 'to divide') and the suffix -isme (from Latin -ismus, Ancient Greek -ismos), denoting an ideology, attitude, or systemic practice.

history.meaning: state of being male or female, gender division
systemic prejudice or discrimination based on sex (modeled on racism)

sexisme.notes: Frequently paired with sexiste (both adjective and epicene noun: un propos sexiste, 'a sexist remark'); a central theme in French cinema debates over ageism and double standards for actresses over forty.

sexy.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-20th century (first attested occasionally in the 1920s–1930s, popularized after World War II via Hollywood cinema and fashion magazines) from English sexy (attested c. 1925), formed from English sex—itself an earlier borrowing from Middle French sexe and Classical Latin sexus ('male or female division')—plus the English adjectival suffix -y ('characterized by'). Thus represents a lexical 'boomerang' returning a Latin-French root in English dress.

history.meaning: physically attractive, glamorous; (figurative) appealing, exciting (un projet sexy)

sexy.notes: Invariable for gender (un acteur sexy, une robe sexy) and traditionally invariable in the plural too (des tenues sexy), though des tenues sexys is permitted under the 1990 spelling rectifications; in agency pitch meetings, un projet très sexy figuratively means an 'appealing, marketable project'.

cognates.meaning: act of firing a weapon or filming/photographing (source of the French borrowing)

shooting.etymology: Late 20th-century French media and fashion borrowing (often analyzed as an elliptical pseudo-anglicism from photo shooting / shooting session) from English shooting, the verbal noun of to shoot (inherited from Old English sceotan 'to hurl a missile, dart forth', from Proto-Germanic *skeutana), which acquired the figurative photographic and cinematographic sense 'to capture with a camera' in the late 19th century. In French, un shooting specialized exclusively to mean a photographic shoot.

history.meaning: to shoot an arrow or missile, dart swiftly
to photograph or film with a camera / act of photographing or filming
professional fashion or publicity photo shoot

morphemes.meaning: capture with a camera (originally 'discharge a projectile')

shooting.notes: Dangerous reverse false friend for French speakers speaking English!
