In Paris talent agencies, J'ai un shooting demain simply means 'I have a photo shoot tomorrow' (official French: une séance photo; film shoots use un tournage), whereas saying 'a shooting' in English means a gun attack!

rootFamily.gloss: to photograph, kick a ball, or inject drugs (French verb built on English shoot)
shot glass; single photographic shot or adrenaline rush (anglicism)

sources.title: Académie française – Dire, ne pas dire : shooting (photo)

showbiz.etymology: Twentieth-century borrowing (attested in French around 1966) from American English showbiz, a colloquial clipping and respelling of show business ('the entertainment industry', coined in the mid-nineteenth century from show + business).
showbiz.notes: Masculine noun (le showbiz), often pronounced /ʃobiz/; ubiquitous in talent-agency banter alongside le métier ('the craft/industry') with a slightly flashier, more commercial ring.

rootFamily.gloss: live stage spectacle, television variety show

shui.etymology: Late twentieth-century borrowing via English feng shui from Mandarin Chinese shuǐ (水, 'water'), descending from Middle Chinese sywijX and Old Chinese *s.turʔ; in Chinese geomancy fēngshuǐ (風水, literally 'wind-water') designates the harmonious flow of vital energy across landscapes and interiors.

history.meaning: wind and water; geomantic siting of tombs and dwellings

shui.notes: In French, shui occurs exclusively inside the invariable loan phrase feng shui (used both as a masculine noun, le feng shui, and adjectivally, un bureau très feng shui) and is commonly pronounced /fɛŋ ʃɥi/ or /fɛŋ ʃwi/.

rootFamily.gloss: practitioner or consultant of feng shui (neologism)

si.etymology: The conditional si continues Latin si, if. The affirmative reply si has a different source, Latin sic, thus or yes. The musical note with the same spelling has a separate history.

history.meaning: two distinct Latin words converging in French
if (conj.); so (adv.: si beau); yes! (contradicting a negative)

cognates.meaning: Italian kept sī and sīc distinct in vowel quality!
Spanish distinguishes them by written accent

si.notes: Three everyday jobs in one tiny word: 1) S'il pleut ('If it rains'—eliding ONLY before il/ils!), 2) C'est si bon ('It's so good'), and 3) Tu ne viens pas? — Si! ('You're not coming? — Yes I am!').

sien.etymology: Inherited from Old French suen, later remodeled to sien by analogy with first-person mien (< Latin meum) and second-person tien (< Vulgar Latin *tuum), ultimately continuing Classical Latin suum, accusative singular of the reflexive possessive suus ('one's own, his, her, its'), from Proto-Indo-European *sewos.

history.meaning: his, her, or its own (stressed possessive)

sien.notes: Agrees in gender and number with the thing possessed, NOT the possessor (le sien, la sienne, les siens, les siennes); plural les siens alone means 'one's family/loved ones', and faire des siennes idiomatically means 'to be up to one's old tricks'.

sieste.etymology: Borrowed in the seventeenth century from Spanish siesta ('midday heat, afternoon nap'), inherited from Latin (hōra) sexta ('the sixth hour of the day'), which in Roman timekeeping—counting twelve daylight hours from sunrise—corresponded to high noon, the hottest moment of the day when work paused.

history.meaning: the sixth hour after dawn, midday

sieste.notes: Feminine noun (la sieste); the standard idiom is faire la sieste or faire une petite sieste ('to take a nap'), whereas un somme (faire un somme) is a slightly more literary or traditional synonym.

rootFamily.gloss: to take a nap (colloquial denominal verb)
midday office prayer (canonical sixth hour, doublet)

signal.etymology: Formed in Old French (or borrowed from Medieval Latin signale, neuter substantive of Late Latin signalis 'serving as a sign'), derived from Classical Latin signum ('mark, token, sign, watchword'). Originally denoting a military or maritime beacon, bell chime, or flag movement agreed upon in advance, signal entered English directly from French in the late 14th century.
signal.notes: Belongs to the same family as **un signe** ('sign, wave of the hand') and **signer** ('to sign'); its plural is **des signaux**.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: signal

signaler.etymology: Derived in the 16th–17th century from signal ('visual or acoustic sign', from Medieval Latin signale, neuter of signalis, from signum 'mark, sign') or borrowed via Italian segnalare ('to mark out, distinguish').

signature.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Medieval Latin signatura ('matrix of a seal, official mark, handwritten name'), derived from Late Latin signare ('to mark, stamp, sign', from Classical Latin signum).

history.meaning: to seal, sign -> seal mark, signature

signe.etymology: Borrowed or semi-learned inheritance from Classical Latin signum ('identifying mark, token, signal, military standard, constellation').

signer.etymology: Signer was remodelled after signe from older French seigner, which came from Latin signare, to mark or seal. The Académie distinguishes the thirteenth-century sense make a sign from the sixteenth-century signature sense.

history.meaning: to mark, stamp with a seal
to make the sign of the cross -> sign one's name (remodelled on signe)

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French seigner / signer

signer.notes: Older seigner still survives specifically as reflexive se signer ('to cross oneself'), alongside general signer un contrat ('to sign a contract').

signifier.etymology: Semi-learned twelfth-century borrowing (Old French senefier, later restored to signifier) from Classical Latin significāre ('to show by signs, point out, portend, mean'), a compound of signum ('identifying mark, token, sign') and -ficāre, theunstressed combining form of facere ('to make, produce').

history.meaning: to indicate by signs, portend, express
to mean; to notify formally (in law)

signifier.notes: Slightly higher register than vouloir dire ('to mean') in everyday speech, and in legal or executive contexts signifier quelque chose à quelqu'un means 'to serve formal notice of something' (e.g., signifier son congé, 'to give formal notice of dismissal').

silence.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin silentium ('state of being noiseless or still, silence'), derived from silens (present participle of silere 'to be noiseless, keep quiet').

silencieux.etymology: Learned borrowing (attested in Old/Middle French from the twelfth to fourteenth centuries) from Classical Latin silentiōsus ('perfectly still, hushed, silent'), derived via the suffix -ōsus ('full of') from silentium ('stillness, absence of noise'), itself built on silēns, present participle of silēre ('to be still or noiseless').
silencieux.notes: Feminine form is silencieuse; Watch out for cinema false friends: 'silent film' is cinéma muet ('mute cinema'), NOT *cinéma silencieux*, whereas un silencieux as a masculine noun means a gun suppressor or car muffler.

rootFamily.gloss: silence, hush (including film-set command 'Silence, on tourne !')

silhouette.etymology: Eponymous coinage from 1759 after Étienne de Silhouette (1709–1767), Louis XV's short-lived Controller-General of Finances whose unpopular austerity policies inspired the phrase à la Silhouette ('done on the cheap, stripped down'), soon applied to inexpensive cut-paper shadow portraits; his surname represents a Frenchified form of Basque Zilueta (from zilo/zulo 'hole, hollow' + locative-collective suffix -eta).

history.meaning: place of hollows (Basque surname adapted into French)
outline, bodily figure; non-speaking walk-on film extra

silhouette.notes: In French film and casting jargon (central to Dix pour cent), une silhouette is a specific union contract tier above simple figurant ('background extra'): an actor with a distinct visual interaction or brief camera focus (silhouette muette or silhouette parlante with up to five words).

rootFamily.gloss: to sketch in outline, cast in profile

simple.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin simplex, accusative simplicem ('single, uncompounded, plain, straightforward, guileless'), from Proto-Indo-European *sem- ('one') + *-plek- ('fold', cf. plicare 'to fold').

simplement.etymology: Formed in the 12th century from the adjective simple ('plain, straightforward', from Classical Latin simplex) + the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin ablative mente).

sincère.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin sincerus ('clean, pure, sound, unspoiled, genuine, candid'), traditionally connected since antiquity with sine ('without') + cera ('wax', i.e. marble or honey free of wax), though modern Indo-Europeanists prefer *sm̥-kēros ('of one growth, whole, unmixed').

sincèrement.etymology: Formed in Middle French from the feminine adjective sincère ('pure, genuine, frank', borrowed from Classical Latin sincērus, 'clean, sound, unmixed, unadulterated', likely from Proto-Indo-European *sm̥-kʷēros, 'of one growth') plus the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin ablative mente, 'with a ... mind').

morphemes.meaning: adverbial suffix of manner (< Latin mente)

sincèrement.notes: False friend in letter sign-offs: French speakers rarely close business emails with Sincèrement alone (an anglicism calqued on 'Sincerely'); standard French closings use Cordialement or Bien à vous, while sincèrement functions mainly as a sentence adverb ('frankly, honestly').

sincérité.etymology: Learned Middle French borrowing (late fifteenth century) from Classical Latin sincēritās (accusative sincēritātem, 'cleanliness, purity, soundness, moral integrity'), derived from sincērus ('unadulterated, whole, genuine', probably from PIE *sm̥-kʷēros 'of a single growth'; the popular story sine cēra 'without wax' in marble sculpture is a Renaissance folk etymology).
sincérité.notes: In French acting criticism, la sincérité praises naturalistic emotional truth on camera (playing 'juste' rather than overacting); remember the acute accent é here versus the grave accent è in sincère and sincèrement.

sinon.etymology: Formed in Old French (se non, si non) from the conditional conjunction si ('if', from Latin si) + the negation non ('not', from Latin non), modeling Classical Latin sinon / si non ('if not, otherwise').

site.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (fourteenth century) from Classical Latin situs ('local position, layout, terrain', originally a verbal noun from sinere, past participle situs, 'to set down, let lie'); in the 1990s it gained the digital sense 'website' by semantic calque on English (web)site (site web / site internet).

history.meaning: physical location, filming location, or website

site.notes: Masculine noun (un site); in media and production contexts un site can mean either a website (un site internet) or an on-location site/facility (sur site, 'on-site').

rootFamily.gloss: to locate, situate, place in context
state of affairs, position, dramatic setup

situation.etymology: Coined or borrowed in Middle French (late fourteenth century, situacion) from Medieval Latin situātiō (accusative situātiōnem, 'spatial placement, topographical arrangement'), derived from Late/Medieval Latin situāre ('to place, locate'), itself built on Classical Latin situs ('site, position').

morphemes.meaning: to place, locate (< situer / Latin situs)

situation.notes: Beyond 'circumstances', une belle situation traditionally means 'a secure, well-paid career/social standing', while comique de situation ('situational comedy') is a staple screenwriting term.

rootFamily.gloss: to place, locate; se situer 'to stand/be situated'

six.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin sex ('six'), from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs ('six').

siècle.etymology: Early semi-learned borrowing (tenth-century Old French secle, siecle) from Ecclesiastical and Classical Latin saeculum (syncopated saeclum, 'breed, generation, human lifetime, spirit of an age, and in Christian Latin the temporal world as opposed to eternity'), from Proto-Italic *sai-tlom; the modern strict sense 'hundred-year period' consolidated in the sixteenth century.

history.meaning: generation, lifetime, epoch; temporal world (Christian Latin)

siècle.notes: French always writes numbered centuries in Roman numerals with ordinal reading (le XXIe siècle = le vingt et unième siècle), and colloquially ça fait un siècle ! means 'it's been ages!'.

rootFamily.gloss: secularization (transfer from church to civil sphere)

siège.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 12th century from Old French asegier / segier ('to seat, settle, besiege'), from Popular Latin *sedicare, derived from Classical Latin sedere ('to sit', cf. sedes 'seat').

smoking.etymology: Pseudo-anglicism attested in French around 1888–1890 by ellipsis of British English smoking jacket (from smoking, verbal noun of to smoke, < Old English smocian), originally a velvet lounging jacket worn by gentlemen in smoking rooms to protect formal tailcoats from cigar ash and odor, which Continental tailors and fashion writers conflated with the black-tie dinner jacket.

history.meaning: informal velvet jacket worn while smoking cigars
tailless black evening jacket for gentlemen
tuxedo, black-tie evening suit (including iconic Yves Saint Laurent women's suit)

smoking.notes: Classic false friend: un smoking (masculine) NEVER means 'the act of smoking' (le tabagisme / fumer)—it strictly means a 'tuxedo / dinner jacket', indispensable on the Cannes red carpet (montée des marches en smoking).

sms.etymology: Borrowed in the 1990s from the English telecommunications initialism SMS (Short Message Service), co-developed by Franco-German GSM engineers in the mid-1980s to transmit 160-character alphanumeric messages over mobile signaling channels; lexicalized in French as an invariable masculine noun for an individual text message.

history.meaning: GSM mobile protocol for short text transmission

sms.notes: Pronounced letter by letter (/ɛs.ɛm.ɛs/) and masculine (un SMS, des SMS); in everyday Metropolitan French it competes on equal footing with un texto (while Quebec French prefers un texto or message texte).

rootFamily.gloss: to send a text message (colloquial verb, rare beside texter)

cognates.meaning: social climber or elitist who looks down on others

snob.etymology: Borrowed in the 1840s (popularized across Europe by William Makepeace Thackeray's 1848 Book of Snobs) from English snob, originally late eighteenth-century British dialect for a cobbler and Cambridge University slang for a townsman (as opposed to an aristocratic student), before shifting to 'pretentious social climber or elitist'; the viral claim that it abbreviates Latin sine nobilitate ('without nobility') is an unhistorical folk etymology.

history.meaning: shoemaker; non-university townsman; ostentatious social climber
person affecting elite tastes or looking down on popular culture

snob.notes: Functions as both a noun (un/une snob) and an adjective that takes plural -s (des gens très snobs) without changing for gender; immortalized in Boris Vian's satirical chanson 'J'suis snob'.

rootFamily.gloss: to snub, treat with haughty disdain

snober.etymology: Twentieth-century French denominal verb (attested around 1951) formed from snob plus the first-conjugation verbal ending -er ('to treat like a snob would'), strongly shaped in meaning by association with the phonetically similar English verb to snub ('to slight, rebuff coldly', itself of Old Norse origin via Middle English snubben).

history.meaning: to cold-shoulder, ignore out of elitism
to snub, boycott, pointedly ignore someone or an event

snober.notes: Transitive verb (snober quelqu'un, snober les César = 'to boycott/skip the César Awards', NOT *snober à quelqu'un*); pronounced /snɔbe/ with an open o.

sobre.etymology: Borrowed in twelfth-century Old French from Classical Latin sōbrius ('not drunk, temperate in drink, moderate, sensible'), formed from the Latin privative prefix sē- / sō- ('apart, without') and the root of ēbrius ('drunk, intoxicated'), thus etymologically 'free from intoxication'.

history.meaning: moderate in eating and drinking, continent
temperate; understated, pared-back, tasteful (in style or acting)

sobre.notes: Partial false friend: while sobre can mean 'temperate', French rarely uses it for 'not currently drunk tonight' (use à jeun instead!)—in fashion and acting (un jeu très sobre, une tenue sobre), it is high praise meaning 'understated, restrained, effortlessly tasteful'.

rootFamily.gloss: restraint, simplicity, moderation (and energy conservation: sobriété énergétique)

socio.etymology: Twentieth-century colloquial and university student apocope of sociologie ('sociology'), using the productive French clipping pattern that truncates words after -o- (like philo, éco, psycho); sociologie itself was coined in 1830 by French philosopher Auguste Comte as a Greco-Latin hybrid of Latin socius ('companion, fellow') and Greek -logia ('discourse, study').

history.meaning: scientific study of human society (coined by Auguste Comte, 1830)
sociology as an academic major or lens (student clipping)

morphemes.meaning: connecting vowel preserved as colloquial clipping suffix

socio.notes: Feminine in student slang because the full noun la sociologie is feminine (faire de la socio, être en fac de socio), whereas in Spanish/Italian un socio means 'a business partner/club member' (French un associé).

société.etymology: Learned twelfth-to-fourteenth-century borrowing from Classical Latin societās (accusative societātem, 'fellowship, union, political alliance, commercial partnership'), derived from socius ('companion, ally, sharer'), which reflects Proto-Indo-European *sokʷ-yo- ('follower, companion'), built on the verbal root *sekʷ- ('to follow').

history.meaning: human society; incorporated business company or production firm

morphemes.meaning: abstract state or collective body (< Latin -etātem)

société.notes: Crucial dual meaning in agency and film life: la société means 'society at large', while une société means 'a business company/firm' (e.g., une société de production = 'a production company', SA = société anonyme).

rootFamily.gloss: social, relating to society or labor welfare
business partner, shareholder (like the four senior agents at ASK!)
permanent shareholding troupe member (notably at the Comédie-Française)

soda.etymology: Borrowed in the early nineteenth century from English soda (short for soda-water, effervescent water prepared with sodium bicarbonate), which English took from Italian and Medieval Latin soda ('sodium carbonate, glasswort ash'), likely borrowed from Arabic suwwād, the name of a coastal saltwort plant burned to extract alkali.

history.meaning: saltwort plant → alkaline sodium carbonate ash

soda.notes: In Metropolitan France, un soda (masculine) specifically means a sugary fizzy soft drink (cola, orangeade), NOT plain sparkling mineral water (which is eau gazeuse or eau pétillante), whereas chemical 'baking soda' is bicarbonate de soude.

rootFamily.gloss: caustic soda / sodium carbonate (earlier French doublet via Medieval Latin)

soi.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin se (stressed accusative and ablative reflexive pronoun 'oneself, himself, herself, themselves'), from Proto-Indo-European *swé ('oneself').

soie.etymology: Inherited via Old French seie / soie from Classical Latin saeta ('coarse animal hair, bristle'), which in Late Latin phrases like seta serica ('Seric/Chinese strand') shifted to mean 'silk thread, silk fabric'.

cognates.meaning: borrowed via French from Arabic zaytūnī

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: soie (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: soie

soie.notes: Notice **le papier de soie**: in French, crisp ultra-thin wrapping tissue paper is poetically called 'silk paper'.

soif.etymology: Inherited via Old French soi, seif, soif from Classical Latin sitis (accusative sitim, 'thirst, aridity, eager desire'), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰgʷʰi-ti- ('wasting away, dryness'); regular Gallo-Romance loss of intervocalic -t- yielded Old French soi, to which an unetymological final -f was attached in the twelfth century (by analogy with words alternating -f/-s in inflection or dialectal labialization).

history.meaning: thirst; figurative hunger or ambition (soif de gloire)

soif.notes: Feminine noun (la soif) whose final -f is always pronounced (/swaf/); French expresses being thirsty with avoir soif ('to have thirst', NEVER *être soif*), and rester sur sa soif means 'to be left unsatisfied / wanting more'.

rootFamily.gloss: parched, thirsty; eager for (assoiffé de succès)

cognates.meaning: legal excuse for non-appearance in court (via Anglo-Norman)

soigner.etymology: Inherited from Old French soignier ('to concern oneself with, attend to, look after'), from Vulgar Latin / Gallo-Romance *soniāre, itself borrowed from Frankish *sunnijōn ('to care for, busy oneself with, offer a lawful justification'), related to Frankish *sunnja ('care, concern, legal impediment'; compare Gothic sunja, 'truth').

history.meaning: to attend to, justify, concern oneself with
to watch over, attend to, provide for
to treat medically, nurse; to polish or craft meticulously

soigner.notes: Dual everyday sense: medically 'to treat/care for a patient' (unlike guérir, which means 'to cure completely'), and stylistically 'to take great pains over'—soigner son image or soigner sa sortie ('to craft a polished exit') is classic celebrity-agent vocabulary.

soigneusement.etymology: Formed in Old French (twelfth century, soignosement) from the feminine adjective soigneuse ('attentive, diligent, painstaking', derived from soin 'care' + suffix -eux/-euse < Latin -ōsus/-ōsa) combined with the adverbial suffix -ment (< Latin ablative mente, 'with an attentive mind').
soigneusement.notes: Conveys thorough, deliberate neatness or precaution (choisir soigneusement ses rôles, éviter soigneusement un sujet = 'to studiously avoid a topic'), contrasting with prudemment ('cautiously, to avoid danger').

soigné.etymology: Past participle of soigner ('to take care of, attend to carefully'), derived from Old French soin ('care, attention, concern', from Frankish *sunnja 'legal excuse, care, solicitude').

history.meaning: care -> to tend carefully -> neat, well-groomed, carefully done

cognates.meaning: excuse for absence from court (via Old French essoine)

soin.etymology: Inherited from Old French soing, soin ('worry, diligent attention, upkeep, legal excuse'), from Gallo-Romance *sonium (or back-formed from *soniāre > soigner), borrowed from Frankish *sunnja / *sunni ('concern, care, lawful impediment'), from Proto-Germanic *sunjō ('truth, valid justification').

history.meaning: care, meticulous attention; plural soins: medical or spa treatments

soin.notes: Rich in idioms: prendre soin de ('to take care of'), être aux petits soins pour quelqu'un ('to pamper / wait hand and foot on someone'—every assistant's job with diva actors!), and plural les soins ('medical care' or 'skincare products').

rootFamily.gloss: to care for, treat, craft carefully
need, necessity (built on the same Frankish root: be- + soin)

soir.etymology: Soir descends from Latin serus, late or of the evening. The Académie records tenth-century ser before the twelfth-century form soir.

history.meaning: late; late hour of the day

soir.notes: Notice French says ce soir ('this evening') and hier soir ('last night' before bed), reserving cette nuit / la nuit dernière for the sleeping hours after midnight.

soirée.etymology: Soirée is derived from soir. It is recorded from the thirteenth century and can refer to the evening as a period spent doing something, or to an evening event.

history.meaning: evening (lived duration); evening party or performance

soirée.notes: Matches the jour / journée, matin / matinée, and an / année pairs: Bonne soirée! ('Have a lovely evening!') is the standard parting wish from late afternoon onward.

soit.etymology: Grammaticalization of Old French seit > soit, the third-person singular present subjunctive of estre / être ('may it be, let it be'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *siat, an analogical subjunctive remodeling Classical Latin sit (from esse, 'to be', < PIE *h₁es-); paired correlatively (soit... soit) it means 'be it X, be it Y', hence 'either... or'.

history.meaning: may it be (present subjunctive of esse)
be it; let it be so!
either... or (soit... soit); namely/that is; 'very well!' (/swat/)

soit.notes: Pronunciation trap: as 'either... or' or 'that is to say' (trois jours, soit 72 heures), the final -t is silent (/swa/ before consonants), whereas when used standalone as a resigned concession ('Fine! So be it!': Soit !), the -t is pronounced (/swat/).

rootFamily.gloss: to be (infinitive of the same paradigm)
so be it, amen (liturgical formula preserving verbal sense)

soixante.etymology: Inherited via Old French seissante, soissante from Vulgar Latin *sexanta (attested in late Roman inscriptions), a contracted popular form of Classical Latin sexāgintā ('sixty', literally 'six tens'), composed of sex ('six', < PIE *sweḱs) and the decimal suffix -āgintā ('tens', < PIE *dḱm̥t-).
soixante.notes: Spelling vs. sound alert: despite the letter x (introduced by medieval scribes under the influence of Latin sexāgintā), the x in soixante is ALWAYS pronounced as a voiceless double s (/swasɑ̃t/), never /ks/ or /gz/.

rootFamily.gloss: about sixty; sixty-year-old age bracket (la soixantaine)

cognates.meaning: sixty + ten (cognate components; Spanish uses setenta for 70)
sixty + ten (cognate components; Italian uses settanta for 70)

soixante-dix.etymology: Additive compound of soixante ('sixty', < Vulgar Latin *sexanta < sexāgintā) and dix ('ten', < Classical Latin decem); attested alongside decimal septante (< Latin septuāgintā) in medieval French as part of a partial vigesimal (base-20) counting system, and canonized by seventeenth-century Parisian grammarians and the Académie française.
soixante-dix.notes: Standard in France and Quebec, whereas speakers in Belgium, Switzerland, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo use the regular decimal form septante ('seventy'), which avoids adding teens onto sixty!

rootFamily.gloss: seventy (Belgian and Swiss French decimal equivalent)

soixante-neuf.etymology: Compound cardinal numeral joining soixante ('sixty', < Vulgar Latin *sexanta < Classical Latin sexāgintā) and neuf ('nine', via Old French nuef < Classical Latin novem, from PIE *h₁néwn̥); in late eighteenth-century post-Revolutionary French erotic pamphlets (attested c. 1790), the rotational symmetry of the Arabic digits 69 also generated an internationally borrowed slang noun.

history.meaning: sixty-nine (cardinal number; also department code for Rhône/Lyon)

soixante-neuf.notes: Joined with a hyphen (no et, which is reserved for 61 and 71: soixante et un, soixante et onze); in French geography le 69 (le soixante-neuf) immediately evokes Lyon and the Rhône department, while Serge Gainsbourg and Jane Birkin famously played on its double entendre in '69 année érotique'.

cognates.meaning: sixty + fifteen (cognate components; Spanish uses setenta y cinco)
sixty + fifteen (cognate components; Italian uses settantacinque)

soixante-quinze.etymology: Additive compound numeral combining soixante ('sixty', < Vulgar Latin *sexanta < sexāgintā) with quinze ('fifteen', via Old French quinze < Classical Latin quīndecim, itself a contraction of quīnque 'five' + decem 'ten'), continuing the Parisian French sixty-plus-teens counting series for 70 through 79.

history.meaning: seventy-five; administrative code for the city of Paris (le 75)

soixante-quinze.notes: Cultural shorthand across France: because French postal codes and license plates use department numbers, le 75 (le soixante-quinze) is everyday metonymy for intramural Paris itself (unlike Belgium and Switzerland, where 75 is septante-cinq).

rootFamily.gloss: fifteen (and quinze jours = 'two weeks / a fortnight')

sol.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th century from Classical Latin solum ('bottom, ground, floor, soil, foundation').

cognates.meaning: soldier (borrowed earlier from Old French soudeier / soudier)

soldat.etymology: Borrowed in the sixteenth century during the Italian Wars from Italian soldato ('mercenary, man-at-arms receiving military pay', substantivized past participle of soldare, 'to hire for pay'), derived from soldo ('coin, military wage'), which continues Late Latin solidus, the pure gold coin introduced by Emperor Constantine I (from Classical Latin solidus, 'firm, whole, solid'). Displaced native Old French soudoier and soudard.

history.meaning: coin, military wage → hired fighting man

morphemes.meaning: military pay, coin (< Italian soldo < Latin solidus)
substantivized past participle ('one provided with pay', < Italian -ato)

soldat.notes: Notice the silent final -t (/sɔlda/) and the surprising etymological link to money: solidus gave French both la solde ('military pay'), les soldes ('seasonal clearance sales'), un sou ('a penny'), and un soldat ('one who fights for pay')—often used figuratively in agency offices as un bon petit soldat ('a loyal, unquestioning team player').

rootFamily.gloss: military pay (feminine: la solde) vs. account balance / retail clearance sale (masculine: le solde)
rough, brutal mercenary (older French derivative from the same root)
solid, sturdy (learned doublet of Latin solidus)

soleil.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *soliculum (originally diminutive 'little sun', replacing short Classical Latin sol in Gallo-Romance), from Classical Latin sol ('sun') + diminutive suffix -iculus.

solidaire.etymology: Coined in 16th-century French jurisprudence from solide ('whole, firm') plus the relational suffix -aire, translating the Roman legal formula in solidum ('for the whole sum'), from Classical Latin solidus ('dense, undivided, entire'). Originally meaning 'jointly and severally liable for a debt', it broadened in the late 18th and 19th centuries to mutual moral and social support.

history.meaning: whole, undivided; for the entire sum in Roman law
jointly and severally liable in a legal obligation
united by shared responsibility, mutually supportive

solidaire.notes: In contract law (like agency representation agreements), être solidaire still retains its strict legal sense of 'jointly liable', alongside its everyday moral sense 'supportive' (être solidaire de quelqu'un).

solidarité.etymology: Formed in late 17th-century French from solidaire ('jointly liable') with the abstract noun suffix -ité (< Latin -itātem), ultimately rooted in Classical Latin solidus ('whole, firm') via the legal phrase obligātiō in solidum. Popularized in the 1830s–1840s by social philosopher Pierre Leroux to name organic social interdependence, whence English borrowed solidarity.

history.meaning: for the whole amount (of shared legal liability)
joint legal and financial liability among co-debtors
mutual fellowship, collective support within a community

solidarité.notes: French exported solidarité directly into English, German (Solidarität), and Polish (Solidarność); in workplace French, grève de solidarité means a sympathy strike.

solide.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin solidus ('dense, compact, whole, firm, substantial'), related to salvus ('whole, safe') and solus ('whole').

solitaire.etymology: Learned borrowing in Old French (12th c.) from Classical Latin sōlitārius ('alone, isolated, living by oneself'), derived from sōlus ('alone, single, sole'). As a noun, un solitaire came to denote first a hermit, later a single-set diamond (18th c.) and a solo peg-jumping board game.
solitaire.notes: Watch the game false friend: the card game English speakers call 'solitaire' is usually called la patience or la réussite in French, while le solitaire traditionally refers to peg solitaire (or a single-diamond ring).

solitude.etymology: Borrowed in 14th-century Middle French from Classical Latin sōlitūdō (accusative sōlitūdinem, 'loneliness, desert place, state of being forsaken'), formed from sōlus ('alone') plus the abstract state suffix -tūdō. It replaced earlier Old French seulleté.

history.meaning: state of being alone, uninhabited wilderness, isolation
secluded place; condition of living or feeling alone

solitude.notes: Unlike English, which distinguishes 'solitude' (peaceful seclusion) from 'loneliness' (painful isolation), French la solitude covers both senses; context or adjectives (pesante vs. choisie) clarify the tone.

cognates.meaning: to ask for, seek to obtain

solliciter.etymology: Learned 14th-century borrowing from Classical Latin sollicitāre ('to stir up, agitate, disturb, urge insistently'), from sollicitus ('wholly moved, restless, anxious'), an Old Latin compound of sollus ('whole, entire', an Oscan-related word) and citus ('aroused, set in motion', past participle of ciēre). It is the learned doublet of inherited soucier.

history.meaning: to agitate, trouble, urge or entice
to entreat earnestly, petition, call upon

solliciter.notes: In talent-agency and professional French, être très sollicité means 'to be in high demand / flooded with offers'—completely neutral or flattering, without the shady legal connotations English 'solicit' can carry.

cognates.meaning: answer to a problem; liquid mixture

solution.etymology: Borrowed in 12th-century Old French from Classical Latin solūtiō (accusative solūtiōnem, 'an unbinding, loosening, payment of a debt, explanation'), action noun from solvere (past participle solūtus, 'to untie, release, dissolve, pay'), itself from se- ('apart') + luere ('to loose, release').

history.meaning: to untie, loosen, release, pay off
loosening, payment, explanation of a difficulty
resolution of a problem; dissolution of a substance

solution.notes: In formal French, the set phrase solution de continuité is a classic false friend: because solution preserves its Latin sense of 'unbinding/break', une solution de continuité means a 'break or gap in continuity', not continuity itself!

cognates.meaning: capable of being solved (false friend in sense); cf. solvent

solvable.etymology: Formed in 15th-century Middle French from old verb solver ('to pay, settle a debt', borrowed from Classical Latin solvere 'to loosen, release from obligation, pay') plus the potential suffix -able. In French it specialized strictly in the financial sense of Latin solvere ('to discharge a debt').

history.meaning: to untie, release, discharge a financial obligation
to pay off, settle a sum owed
having the financial means to pay one's debts

solvable.notes: Major false friend: French solvable ONLY means financially 'solvent / creditworthy' (essential when renting a Paris apartment or financing a film); 'solvable' (of a puzzle or problem) is résoluble or soluble.

sombre.etymology: Post-verbal adjective formed in the 14th century from Old French sombrer ('to shade, be in shadow'), from Vulgar Latin *subumbrare ('to put under shade'), from Classical Latin sub- ('under') + umbra ('shadow, shade').

history.meaning: under shadow -> to cast into shade

somme.etymology: Inherited through Old French some ('total, chief point, amount') from Classical Latin summa ('highest part, main essence, total amount', short for summa pars or summa linea), feminine of summus ('highest, topmost', < *sup-mos, superlative of sub). Because Roman accountants added columns upward and wrote the total on the top line, summa came to mean the grand total.

history.meaning: topmost line; total figure written at the top of an account
total quantity, amount of money, compendium
sum, amount of money; synthesis (en somme)

somme.notes: Distinguish three French homographs: feminine la somme ('sum, amount', < Latin summa), masculine un somme ('a nap', faire un petit somme, < Latin somnus), and feminine bête de somme ('pack animal', < Late Latin sagma 'pack-saddle').

sommeil.etymology: Inherited through Old French someil ('sleep, drowsiness') from Vulgar Latin *somniculus, a diminutive of Classical Latin somnus ('sleep', < Proto-Indo-European *swep-no-, from *swep- 'to sleep'). As often in Gallo-Romance (compare soleil < *sōliculus, oreille < auricula), the expressive diminutive replaced the short Classical base word in everyday usage.

history.meaning: state of sleep, need to sleep

sommeil.notes: To say 'I am sleepy', French uses avoir without an article: j'ai sommeil (literally 'I have sleep'), never *je suis sommeil.

son.etymology: The possessive son, with feminine sa, continues Latin suus, sua and suum. The Académie dates it to the ninth century. It is historically separate from the nouns son meaning sound or bran.
son.notes: Essential trap for English speakers: son/sa agrees with the grammatical gender of the POSSESSED NOUN, never the owner—so 'her book' is son livre and 'his car' is sa voiture (and before a vowel, sa shifts to son: son amie)!

sondage.etymology: Formed in early 19th-century French from sonder ('to fathom, probe with a lead line') plus the action suffix -age; sonder itself derives from sonde ('sounding line'), likely borrowed by Norman sailors from Old English sundlīne or Old Norse sund ('sea channel, strait, swimming'). First used for hydrographic depth-taking and geological core-drilling, sondage acquired its modern sense of 'public opinion poll / ratings survey' in the late 1930s.

history.meaning: nautical lead line; to measure water depth
maritime depth-sounding, surgical probing, or borehole drilling
statistical opinion poll, audience or market survey

sondage.notes: Essential media and politics term: un sondage d'opinion is an opinion poll, and un sondage d'audience gauges viewership or box-office appeal before or after a release.

cognates.meaning: to measure depth; to test cautiously ('sound out')

sonder.etymology: Attested from the 12th–14th centuries as a denominal verb from sonde ('plumber's lead line used to measure water depth'), which entered northern Gallo-Romance maritime vocabulary likely from Old English sund ('sea, strait, swimming', as in sundgyrd 'sounding rod' and sundlīne 'sounding line') or Old Norse sund. By the 16th century (Montaigne), sonder figuratively meant probing someone's hidden intentions.

history.meaning: sea strait, water; nautical sounding line
to fathom seabed depth with a weighted line
to probe medically; to sound out intentions or poll opinions

sonder.notes: In negotiations and talent management, sonder le terrain ('to test the waters / put out feelers') and sonder quelqu'un ('to sound someone out discreetly') are indispensable idioms.

sonner.etymology: Sonner comes from Latin sonare ('to sound, ring, resound', from sonus 'sound'). It covers both ringing a bell and a clock striking the hour.
sonner.notes: Gives **la sonnette** ('bell, buzzer') and **la sonnerie** ('ringtone, chime').

sonnerie.etymology: Derived in the 14th century from sonner ('to ring, sound', from Classical Latin sonare, from sonus 'sound') + the collective/action noun suffix -erie.

sonnette.etymology: Derived in the 13th–14th century as a diminutive in -ette of Old French sonne ('little bell'), post-verbal noun from sonner ('to ring, sound', from Classical Latin sonare).

sophistiqué.etymology: Past participle adjective of Middle French sophistiquer ('to falsify with deceptive subtlety, adulterate'), from Medieval Latin sophisticāre, derived from Latin sophisticus and Ancient Greek sophistikos ('of a sophist, captious, cleverly deceptive'), from sophistēs ('master of craft, rhetorician') < sophos ('wise, skilled'). Originally pejorative ('adulterated, over-artificial'), it gained its positive modern senses ('worldly, refined, technically advanced') in the 20th century as a semantic loan from English sophisticated.

history.meaning: characteristic of a sophist, clever, captiously argued
to quibble, falsify, or adulterate a product (such as wine)
refined, elegant, technically intricate (under English influence)

sophistiqué.notes: Even today, sophistiqué applied to a person or style in French can occasionally retain a slight hint of 'overdone / artificial / contrived', unlike the almost purely complimentary English 'sophisticated'.

sorte.etymology: Attested from the 13th–14th centuries (reinforced by Old Occitan sorta and Northern Italian sorta), reflecting Vulgar Latin *sorta, a feminine first-declension reshaping of Classical Latin sors (accusative sortem, 'lot drawn in divination, share, rank, category'). Meanwhile, Classical Latin sortem regularly yielded masculine French le sort ('fate, spell').

history.meaning: lot, share assigned by chance, rank, class
kind, species, way (de la sorte, en quelque sorte)

sorte.notes: Mind the gender split between doublets: feminine la sorte means 'kind, sort, manner' (faire en sorte que 'to make sure that', en quelque sorte 'in a way'), whereas masculine le sort means 'fate, lot, or magical spell'.

rootFamily.gloss: to match harmoniously; to stock with varieties

cognates.meaning: operational flight or sudden sally by troops (borrowed from French)

sortie.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle (attested 13th–15th c.) of sortir ('to go out, emerge'). The verb sortir most likely reflects Gallo-Romance *surctīre ('to rise up, spring forth', formed on *surctus, variant past participle of Classical Latin surgere 'to rise'), blended in form and conjugation with Latin sortīrī ('to draw lots, obtain as one's share, issue in').

history.meaning: to rise up, spring forth / to draw lots, come out with
act or place of exiting; outing; public release of a book or film

sortie.notes: In French cinema and publishing (central to Dix pour cent), la sortie means a film's theatrical 'release' (la sortie en salles, sortie nationale), while faire une sortie can also mean making an outspoken public remark or outburst.

rootFamily.gloss: to go out, exit; to release (transitive)
to stand out, emerge again; fall under jurisdiction

sortir.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin sortiri ('to draw lots, obtain by lot, divide'), which in Late and Gallo-Romance usage shifted via 'to obtain one's share and depart' (or blended with *surctus from surgere 'to rise') to 'to go out, come out, exit'.

history.meaning: to go out, exit, take out

souci.etymology: Souci derives from Old French soucier ('to trouble, worry', from Latin sollicitare 'to disturb, make anxious').
souci.notes: **Pas de souci!** = No worries! / No problem!

cognates.meaning: to ask for, entreat (via learned doublet solliciter)

soucier.etymology: Inherited through Old French solcier, soucier ('to trouble, disturb, feel anxiety') by regular phonetic erosion from Classical Latin sollicitāre ('to agitate, disturb, make anxious, stir wholly'), from sollicitus ('anxious, restless'). Through syncope of unstressed vowels and palatalization (sollicitāre > *solcitare > solcier > soucier), it became the popular inherited doublet of learned solliciter.

history.meaning: to disturb, make restless, trouble with anxiety
to trouble, grieve; (reflexive) to worry about
to care about, be concerned with, worry

soucier.notes: Almost always reflexive in modern French: se soucier de quelque chose ('to care/worry about something'), famously negated in se soucier de quelque chose comme de l'an quarante ('not to care in the slightest').

soucoupe.etymology: Formed from sous ('under') + coupe ('cup, goblet', or modelled on Italian sottocoppa). Originally a small footed salver held underneath a goblet when serving wine at table; with the arrival of tea, coffee, and chocolate in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, it became the modern saucer.

history.meaning: tray held beneath a drinking goblet
porcelain or earthenware saucer under a teacup

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: soucoupe (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: soucoupe

cognates.meaning: occurring unexpectedly and quickly (borrowed from Anglo-Norman)

soudain.etymology: Inherited through Old French sodain, soudain from Vulgar Latin *subitānus, a suffixal simplification of Classical Latin subitāneus ('sudden, unexpected'), itself derived from subitus ('having come up stealthily, unexpected'), past participle of subīre ('to go under, approach secretly'), from sub- ('under') + īre ('to go').

morphemes.meaning: sudden, coming up unexpectedly (< Latin subit-)

soudain.notes: Besides being an adjective (un départ soudain) and a literary invariable adverb (Soudain, la porte s'ouvrit), it appears in the everyday conversational phrase tout à coup / tout d'un coup, and in learned doublet subit (mort subite 'sudden death').

cognates.meaning: quickly and unexpectedly (hybrid cognate from Anglo-Norman sodain + -ly)

soudainement.etymology: Formed in 12th-century Old French (sodainement) from soudaine, feminine of soudain ('sudden', < Vulgar Latin *subitānus < Classical Latin subitāneus), plus the Romance adverbial suffix -ment, which evolved from the Classical Latin ablative noun mente ('with a [sudden] mind/manner', feminine, hence requiring the feminine adjective stem).
soudainement.notes: In casual spoken French, tout d'un coup or d'un seul coup is much more frequent than the five-syllable adverb soudainement (pronounced [su.dɛn.mɑ̃], dropping the internal schwa).

cognates.meaning: joined with melted metal filler (via Old French solder)

soudé.etymology: Past participle adjective of souder ('to weld, solder, fuse'), inherited through Old French solder ('to fasten firmly, join metal, close a wound') from Classical Latin solidāre ('to make firm, make dense, consolidate'), denominal verb of solidus ('whole, firm, dense'). Vocalization of syllable-final l before d regularly turned solder into souder, and its participle developed the warm figurative sense 'welded together, tight-knit'.

history.meaning: to make firm, fasten solidly together
to join metals by fusion; to unite or heal a fracture

soudé.notes: A classic positive team/family descriptor in French (une équipe très soudée 'a tight-knit team', as the agents at ASK strive to be); contrast with soudoyer ('to bribe'), which comes via solde ('soldier's pay'), though ultimately from the same Latin solidus (a gold coin)!

rootFamily.gloss: to weld, solder; to unite closely
solid, firm (learned doublet of the base)

souffle.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 12th century from souffler ('to blow, breathe'), inherited from Classical Latin sufflare ('to blow up from below, inflate, puff'), from sub- ('under, up') + flare ('to blow').

souffler.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin sufflare ('to blow up from below, inflate, puff out'), compound of sub- ('under, up from beneath') + flare ('to blow').

cognates.meaning: to experience pain; (archaic) to allow, tolerate (borrowed from Anglo-Norman)

souffrir.etymology: Inherited through Old French sofrir ('to endure, bear patiently, tolerate, undergo pain') from Vulgar Latin *sufferīre, a fourth-conjugation regularization of Classical Latin irregular sufferre ('to hold up from beneath, bear, endure, undergo'), composed of sub- ('under') + ferre ('to carry, bear', < PIE *bher-).

history.meaning: to bear from underneath, endure, submit to
to endure hardship, tolerate, permit, feel pain
to feel physical or emotional pain; (literary) to tolerate

morphemes.meaning: infinitive ending (conjugated like ouvrir in present)

souffrir.notes: Although ending in -ir, souffrir conjugates like an -er verb in the present tense (je souffre, tu souffres) with irregular past participle souffert; in elevated style, je ne peux pas le souffrir still keeps the older sense 'I cannot stand/tolerate him'.

rootFamily.gloss: suffering, pain, distress; (en souffrance) pending delivery

souhaiter.etymology: Formed in the 12th century (Old French soushaidier) from sous- ('under', from Latin sub-) + Old French haitier ('to cheer, wish well, gladden'), derived from Frankish *hait ('promise, vow, command, wish').

history.meaning: to cheer, wish -> to desire, wish for

soulagement.etymology: Derived in the 14th century from soulager ('to lighten a burden, relieve, comfort') + -ment; soulager comes from Old French soulas ('relief, solace', from Classical Latin solacium) blended with léger ('light in weight', from Vulgar Latin *leviarius).

history.meaning: relief, easing of pain or worry

cognates.meaning: to lift up, relieve, comfort (from Classical sublevāre)
to lift up; to stir into revolt (from Classical sublevāre)
consolation, relief (from Latin sōlācium, which influenced Old French)

soulager.etymology: Inherited through Old French solagier, soulagier ('to lighten a burden, comfort, relieve') from Late/Vulgar Latin *subleviāre ('to lighten from underneath'), altered from Classical Latin sublevāre ('to lift up from beneath, support, lighten, alleviate') under the influence of levis ('light in weight'; compare *alleviāre > alléger, where -viāre regularly palatalized to -gier/-ger), with possible semantic reinforcement from Old French solacier ('to console' < sōlācium).

history.meaning: to lift from beneath, lighten a load, alleviate
to lighten someone's burden, comfort, ease pain
to relieve physical pain or emotional anxiety

soulager.notes: Ouf, ça me soulage ! ('Phew, that's a load off my mind!') is the quintessential conversational expression of relief; note also ironic slang soulager quelqu'un de son portefeuille ('to relieve someone of their wallet').

rootFamily.gloss: relief, comfort, easing of pain or worry

soulever.etymology: Soulever comes from Old French souzlever (sous 'under' + lever 'to raise', from Latin sublevare): literally 'to lift from underneath'.

soupe.etymology: Soupe comes from Late Latin suppa (of Germanic origin, related to English 'sop' and 'sup'), originally meaning the slice of bread placed in a bowl over which hot broth was poured, and later the soup itself.
soupe.notes: **Un bol de soupe chaude** = a bowl of hot soup.

souple.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin supplex, accusative supplicem ('bending the knees, humble, submissive, entreating'), from sub- ('under, down') + plac- / *plek- ('to fold, bend'); in French the physical sense 'bending easily, pliant, flexible' prevailed.

soupçonner.etymology: Derived in 12th–13th century Old French (sospeçoner, soupeçonner) from soupçon ('suspicion, inkling', Old French sospeçon), which evolved from Late Latin suspectiōnem (accusative of suspectiō), a crossing of Classical Latin suspīciō ('mistrust, distrust') with suspectus, past participle of suspicere ('to look up at from beneath, look askance at, mistrust'), from sub- ('from under') + specere ('to look').

history.meaning: to look askance at, mistrust; suspicion
mistrust, apprehension > to mistrust, hold under suspicion
to suspect someone of wrongdoing; to surmise, have an inkling of

morphemes.meaning: suspicion, slight trace (< Late Latin suspectiōnem)

soupçonner.notes: Pronunciation and spelling trap: the p in soupçon and soupçonner is pronounced ([sup.sɔ.ne], restored on the Latin model suspect-), and the cedilla ç keeps the [s] sound before o; meanwhile un soupçon de... means 'a hint/dash of' (borrowed into culinary English).

rootFamily.gloss: suspicion; tiny hint or dash of something

cognates.meaning: origin, spring, informant (borrowed from Old French)
risen, sprung forth (past participle of sorgere)

source.etymology: Inherited from 12th-century Old French sorse, sourse ('spring of water, welling up'), the substantivized feminine past participle of sourdre ('to gush forth, spring up from the ground'), from Vulgar Latin *surcta (altering Classical Latin surrēcta), feminine past participle of surgere ('to rise up, well up'), a contraction of sub- ('from below') + regere ('to direct straight').

history.meaning: to rise up from below, spring forth
natural spring of water gushing from the earth
water spring; origin; confidential media or industry informant

source.notes: In French, eau de source literally means 'natural spring water', while in journalism and entertainment gossip (de source sûre 'from a reliable source'), une source means an insider or informant.

rootFamily.gloss: to well up, spring forth (literary base verb)
resource, means (parallel derivative of re- + sourdre)

sourcil.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin supercilium ('eyebrow; ridge, pride'), compound of super- ('above, over') + cilium ('eyelid', whence French cil 'eyelash').

cognates.meaning: irrational root; voiceless consonant (learned borrowing from Latin surdus)

sourd.etymology: Inherited through Old French sort, sourt (feminine sorde) from Classical Latin surdus ('deaf, unhearing; silent, indistinct, muffled in sound, dull in color'), probably from a Proto-Indo-European root *swer- / *surd- originally meaning 'dark, dull, indistinct'. Already in Classical Latin, surdus combined both 'unable to hear' and 'making a dull, muted sound'.

history.meaning: deaf, hard of hearing; muffled (bruit sourd), unspoken (colère sourde)

sourd.notes: Final d is silent in masculine sourd [suʁ] (except in liaison or feminine sourde [suʁd]); idiomatic staples include faire la sourde oreille ('to turn a deaf ear') and un dialogue de sourds ('a conversation where nobody listens').

rootFamily.gloss: to deafen; to muffle or soundproof
mute, damper; en sourdine ('quietly, on the sly')

souriant.etymology: Present participle used as an adjective of sourire ('to smile'), inherited from Classical Latin subridere ('to smile slightly'), from sub- ('under, slightly') + ridere ('to laugh').

sourire.etymology: Substantivized infinitive of sourire ('to smile'), inherited from Classical Latin subridere (Vulgar Latin *subridere), compound of sub- ('under, slightly, quietly') + ridere ('to laugh').

souris.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *soricem (reshaped from Classical Latin sorex, accusative soricem 'shrew-mouse', from Greek hyrax), which displaced Classical Latin mus ('mouse') in Gallo-Romance.

sous.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin subtus ('below, underneath'), adverbial derivative of sub ('under').

cognates.meaning: to value or rate too low (structural model; estimate < Latin aestimāre)

sous-estimer.etymology: Formed in early 20th-century French from prefix sous- ('under, below standard', < Old French soz < Classical Latin subtus 'underneath', adverb from sub) + estimer ('to appraise, value, judge', borrowed in the 13th–14th c. from Classical Latin aestimāre 'to determine the monetary value of, appraise'), modeled on or reinforced by English underestimate.

history.meaning: underneath + to appraise the value or price of
to appraise below real monetary worth; to underrate abilities or risks

sous-estimer.notes: Pronounced with obligatory internal liaison [su.zɛs.ti.me]; its antonym surestimer ('to overestimate') is written as one word without a hyphen, whereas sous-estimer always keeps the hyphen so s between vowels isn't misread cleanly or merged.

rootFamily.gloss: to value, estimate, hold in esteem

cognates.meaning: to place, allocate (learned cognate of louer < Latin locāre)

sous-louer.etymology: French compound attested since the 17th century (1611), combining sous- ('under, sub-', < Old French soz < Classical Latin subtus 'underneath') with louer ('to rent, let out, lease'), which evolved regularly through Old French loer from Classical Latin locāre ('to place, put out on contract, rent out'), denominal verb of locus ('place').

history.meaning: to place, let out property or labor for hire
to rent out OR rent from someone
to sublet (as a tenant to a subtenant) or rent via sublease

sous-louer.notes: Like louer itself, sous-louer works in BOTH directions in French: it can mean 'to sublet out' your apartment to someone else OR 'to sublease from' the primary tenant; note also the homonym louer 'to praise' (< Latin laudāre).

cognates.meaning: outer or ritual robe (from Old French vestement)

sous-vêtement.etymology: 19th-century French compound (attested 1840s) formed from sous- ('under, worn beneath', < Old French soz < Classical Latin subtus) + vêtement ('garment'), inherited through Old French vestement from Classical/Late Latin vestīmentum ('article of clothing, garment'), derived from vestīre ('to clothe, dress') < vestis ('garment, attire', < PIE *wes- 'to clothe'). The circumflex in vêtement marks the historical loss of s before t.

history.meaning: garment worn directly next to the skin beneath outer clothes

sous-vêtement.notes: Unlike uncountable English 'underwear', sous-vêtement is countable in French (plural des sous-vêtements, taking -s on vêtement while sous- stays invariable).

cognates.meaning: to keep going, endure, bear up (borrowed from Old French sostenir)

soutenir.etymology: Inherited through Old French sostenir ('to hold up, endure, aid, defend') from Vulgar Latin *sustenīre, a remodeling (aligned on Simple *tenīre for tenēre) of Classical Latin sustinēre ('to hold up from below, prop up, check, endure, maintain'), composed of subs- / sus- (variant of sub- 'from under, upward') + tenēre ('to hold', < PIE *ten- 'to stretch, hold').

history.meaning: to hold upright from beneath, prop up, endure
to bear weight, withstand an attack, give aid to
to prop up physically; to back, champion, or defend (a thesis or person)

soutenir.notes: Covers English 'support' in moral, financial, and intellectual contexts (soutenir un projet, soutenir un acteur, soutenir une thèse 'to defend a PhD dissertation'), whereas French supporter usually means 'to put up with / endure' (je ne le supporte plus !).

cognates.meaning: sustenance, upkeep (related Old French derivative sostenement)

soutien.etymology: Deverbal masculine noun formed in 12th–13th century Old French (sostien) directly from the present-tense stem (il sostient > soutient) of soutenir ('to hold up, prop, back', < Vulgar Latin *sustenīre < Classical Latin sustinēre, from sus- 'up from below' + tenēre 'to hold'), paralleling maintien from maintenir.

history.meaning: physical prop, pillar, or act of aiding in battle
structural prop; moral, political, or financial backing

soutien.notes: Because le support in modern French mostly means a 'physical stand' or 'storage/media format' (un support numérique), always use le soutien for human, artistic, or financial backing (merci pour votre soutien); also forms soutien-gorge ('bra').

souvenir.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin subvenire ('to come up from beneath, come to mind, occur to someone'), from sub- ('under, up') + venire ('to come'); used both as a verb ('to remember') and as a substantivized infinitive ('memory, keepsake').

history.meaning: to come up, come to mind

souvent.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin subinde ('immediately after, repeatedly, from time to time'), compound of sub ('under, close upon') + inde ('thence, after that').

cognates.meaning: striking sight, public display; (pl.) eyeglasses (via Old French)

spectacle.etymology: Learned borrowing in late 12th–13th century Old French from Classical Latin spectāculum ('public sight, stage play, arena show, spectator seating'), formed with the instrumental/locative suffix -culum from spectāre ('to watch, gaze at, attend a show'), frequentative of specere ('to look at, behold', < PIE *spek- 'to observe').

history.meaning: to watch intently > public show, theatrical or amphitheater performance
impressive sight; staged dramatic or musical performance
live stage show; show business as a whole (le monde du spectacle)

morphemes.meaning: means, place, or object of action (< Latin -culum)

spectacle.notes: False friend in register: while English 'spectacle' sounds grand or scandalous ('making a spectacle of oneself' = se donner en spectacle), French un spectacle is the everyday neutral word for ANY live show (play, stand-up comedy, concert, dance), and les intermittents du spectacle are France's freelance performing-arts and cinema workers!

spectaculaire.etymology: Derived in late 19th- and early 20th-century French on the learned Latin stem spectācul- (from Classical Latin spectāculum 'public show, sight', < spectāre 'to watch') plus the adjectival suffix -aire (< Latin -āris), strongly reinforced in the early 1900s by English spectacular (itself attested from the late 17th century). Initially meaning 'theatrical, relating to stage shows', it quickly generalized to 'strikingly impressive, dramatic'.

history.meaning: pertaining to grand stage productions; visually striking, dramatic

spectaculaire.notes: Used both positively (un succès spectaculaire 'a smash success') and dramatically (un accident spectaculaire 'a dramatic-looking crash'—often implying it looked worse than its casualties).

spectateur.etymology: Learned 16th-century borrowing from Classical Latin spectātor (accusative spectātōrem, 'watcher, observer, theatergoer'), an agent noun derived from spectāre ('to watch, gaze at, observe'), the frequentative of specere ('to look at, behold'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *spek- ('to observe').

history.meaning: to watch intently, observe, attend a show
watcher, observer, member of a theater audience

spectateur.notes: Feminine is 'spectatrice'; in television and cinema industry talk, 'téléspectateur' specifies a TV viewer while 'spectateur' refers to cinema or live theater audiences.

spectral.etymology: Derived in early 19th-century French from spectre ('ghostly apparition, phantom' and later 'optical spectrum') plus the relational adjectival suffix -al; spectre itself is a 16th-century learned borrowing from Classical Latin spectrum ('image, apparition, vision'), from specere ('to look at, behold').

history.meaning: ghostly, phantom-like; pertaining to an optical spectrum

spectral.notes: Masculine plural is 'spectraux' (though rare in everyday speech); used both literally in physics ('analyse spectrale') and figuratively for a pale, gaunt, or eerie appearance.

spirituel.etymology: Borrowed in 12th-century Old French (esperituel, later refashioned to spirituel) from Late and Ecclesiastical Latin spīrituālis ('belonging to breath or the spirit'), derived from Classical Latin spīritus ('breath, inspiration, spirit, soul'), from spīrāre ('to breathe'). In French salon culture, paralleling the polysemy of esprit ('spirit' and 'wit'), it developed the secondary secular meaning 'witty, clever, sparkling with humor'.

history.meaning: of or belonging to breathing or the spiritual realm
relating to the soul; later also witty, full of clever esprit

spirituel.notes: Watch the classic French double sense: describing a person or remark as 'très spirituel' in secular conversation usually means 'very witty/clever' (having 'de l'esprit'), not 'deeply religious'.

splendide.etymology: Learned borrowing in 15th-century Middle French from Classical Latin splendidus ('bright, shining, glittering, sumptuous, magnificent'), an adjective formed from the verb splendēre ('to shine, gleam, be radiant').
splendide.notes: Invariable across masculine and feminine singular ('un décor splendide', 'une actrice splendide'); favored as an enthusiastic, slightly theatrical exclamation in showbiz settings.

cognates.meaning: sport, recreation (calqued/adapted from Old Provençal/French deport)

sport.etymology: Borrowed in 19th-century French from English sport ('pastime, outdoor recreation, athletic competition'), which is an aphetic shortening of Middle English and Anglo-Norman disport ('diversion, amusement'), itself from Old French desport / deport ('pleasure, recreation, diversion'), a deverbal noun from soi desporter ('to divert oneself, carry oneself away from work'), from des- ('away') + porter ('to carry', from Latin portāre). It is thus a classic Franco-English round-trip loanword (aller-retour).
sport.notes: Used colloquially as an invariable predicative adjective ('c'est sport !' or 'ça va être sport') meaning 'that's going to be tricky, hectic, or a real challenge', besides 'fair-play/sporting'.

rootFamily.gloss: to carry away, deport (shared etymological base)

spécial.etymology: Borrowed in 12th-century Old French as especial (later re-Latinized to spécial without the prosthetic e-) from Classical Latin speciālis ('individual, particular, belonging to a specific kind'), derived from speciēs ('appearance, form, sort, kind, species'), itself from specere ('to look at, behold').

history.meaning: individual, particular, belonging to a specific sort
particular, distinct from the general, unusual

spécial.notes: Placed after a person ('il est un peu spécial'), it is a polite conversational euphemism for 'eccentric, weird, or difficult to deal with'; masculine plural is 'spéciaux'.

cognates.meaning: to specialize, focus on a specific field

spécialiser.etymology: Formed in 19th-century French from the adjective spécial ('particular, specific', from Classical Latin speciālis) combined with the factitive verbal suffix -iser (from Late Latin -izāre, Ancient Greek -ίζειν).

history.meaning: particular, individual, specific to a kind
to restrict or dedicate to a specific branch of activity or study

spécialiser.notes: Most frequently used pronominally with the preposition 'dans' or 'en' ('se spécialiser dans le cinéma d'auteur') meaning 'to specialize in'.

spécialité.etymology: Borrowed in Old French as especialité and later refashioned to spécialité after Late Latin speciālitās (accusative speciālitātem, 'peculiarity, particular property or feature'), an abstract noun derived from Classical Latin speciālis ('individual, particular'), from speciēs ('appearance, kind, sort').

history.meaning: area of professional expertise, signature skill, or regional culinary dish

morphemes.meaning: abstract feminine noun suffix of quality or domain (-ity)

spécialité.notes: Covers professional fields (medical or agency 'spécialité'), culinary signature dishes ('la spécialité de la maison'), and personal quirks ('les retards, c'est sa spécialité').

square.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from English square ('open landscaped urban square'), itself from Anglo-Norman esquire / Old French esqarre ('square', from Vulgar Latin *exquadrare, from Latin quadrus 'square').

history.meaning: small fenced public garden in a city

stable.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–14th century from Classical Latin stabilis ('standing firm, steadfast, enduring, unwavering'), derived from stare ('to stand') + instrument/ability suffix -bilis.

cognates.meaning: stage, phase, platform (borrowed from Old French estage)
internship (modern borrowing from French); hostage/sojourn (archaic staggio)

stage.etymology: Re-borrowed in the 17th century from Medieval Latin stagium ('customary period of residence required of a new canon in a cathedral chapter before receiving full benefits'), which was itself a medieval Latinization of Old French estage ('dwelling, residence, standing, story of a building', whence modern French étage), from Vulgar Latin *staticum ('standing place, abode'), derived from Classical Latin stāre ('to stand'). In the 19th and 20th centuries, the ecclesiastical sense of probationary residence broadened to mandatory professional training for lawyers, doctors, and finally any corporate internship or training course.

history.meaning: dwelling, story of a building; required canonical residence period
probationary training period, internship, or intensive training course

stage.notes: Major false friend with English: French 'un stage' is NEVER a theater stage ('la scène' or 'les planches') or a developmental phase ('une étape'); it means an internship or a short training camp ('un stage de théâtre'), and it is pronounced /staʒ/.

rootFamily.gloss: floor, story of a building (native doublet from Old French estage)
to stagnate, stand still (shared Latin stāre root)

stagiaire.etymology: Formed in early 19th-century French from stage ('required period of probationary residence or professional training', originally in canon law and later in the legal and medical professions) plus the agentive and relational suffix -iaire (modeled on Latin -ārius with palatalized stem vowel).

history.meaning: required probationary residence of a canon; professional training period
canon or lawyer completing a probationary period; later any intern or trainee

morphemes.meaning: agent/relational suffix indicating a person performing a role

stagiaire.notes: Epicene noun ('un stagiaire' / 'une stagiaire') and also used as an adjective ('avocat stagiaire'); in French office culture, 'le/la stagiaire' is stereotypically tasked with making coffee and photocopying.

rootFamily.gloss: floor, level of a building (doublet of stage)

stand.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from English stand ('raised platform or spectator grandstand at a racecourse; exhibition booth, shooting stall'), from the verb stand (Old English standan, from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-).

history.meaning: exhibition booth, market stall, shooting range, pit stop

cognates.meaning: stand-up comedy performed solo before a live audience

stand-up.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from American and British English stand-up (ellipsis of stand-up comedy), referring to comedic monologues delivered standing alone on stage directly addressing the audience; compounded from English stand (from Old English standan, Proto-Germanic *standaną, ultimately from PIE *steh₂- 'to stand') and the particle up (from Old English ūp).

history.meaning: to stand upright on one's feet
solo live comedy performed standing before an audience
genre of solo live comedy monologue or a show in that style

morphemes.meaning: to remain upright on one's feet

stand-up.notes: Masculine noun ('faire du stand-up', 'un spectacle de stand-up'); the performer is called 'un stand-uppeur' / 'une stand-uppeuse' or more traditionally 'un humoriste'.

rootFamily.gloss: exhibition booth or stall (earlier borrowing from English stand)
social status, prestige, upscale quality (from English standing)

cognates.meaning: star (distant Indo-European cognate via Latin stēlla)

star.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-19th century from English star in its theatrical figurative sense ('celebrated leading actor or singer'), which derives from Middle English sterre, Old English steorra ('luminous celestial body'), from Proto-Germanic *sternǭ, and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr ('star', the same root that yielded Latin stēlla and native French étoile).

history.meaning: celestial star in the night sky
celestial body; figuratively a famous lead performer (from early 19th c.)
celebrity, cinema or music idol, headlining performer

star.notes: Always grammatically feminine in French ('une grande star', 'c'est une star internationale'), even when referring to a male actor or musician, following the gender of its native synonym 'une vedette' or 'une étoile'.

rootFamily.gloss: young aspiring female actress or minor celebrity
to turn someone into a celebrity or star

cognates.meaning: statute, written law; status (from Latin status)

statut.etymology: Learned borrowing in 13th-century Old French from Late and Medieval Latin statūtum ('law, decree, regulation, established order'), the substantivized neuter past participle of Classical Latin statuere ('to set up, establish, ordain'), which is derived from status ('posture, standing, condition'), an action noun from stāre ('to stand', from PIE *steh₂-). In the 20th century, under the influence of English status and sociological terminology, statut also absorbed the sense of 'social, professional, or legal standing/status'.

history.meaning: to set up, station, establish, decree
that which is established; statute, rule, decree
codified rule or bylaws; legal or social status and standing

statut.notes: The final '-t' is silent (/staty/); note that French 'statut' covers both English 'status' (professional/marital/social status, e.g., 'le statut d'intermittent du spectacle') and 'statutes/bylaws' (especially in the plural, 'les statuts d'une société').

rootFamily.gloss: to rule formally, hand down a legal decision
state, condition (native reflex of Latin status)

cognates.meaning: thick slice of meat or fish for grilling or frying
roast, cut of meat for roasting

steak.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century (alongside the earlier phonetic adaptation bifteck from beefsteak) from English steak ('thick slice of meat cut for grilling or frying'), which comes from Middle English steke, borrowed from Old Norse steik ('roast meat, slice of meat roasted on a spit'), related to the Old Norse verb steikja ('to roast on a spit').

history.meaning: meat roasted on a spit or fire
thick slice of beef or other meat for broiling or frying
slice of grilled meat or minced beef patty (steak haché)

steak.notes: Pronounced /stɛk/; in French bistro culture, 'un steak-frites' is an iconic quick lunch, and 'un steak haché' refers to a ground beef burger patty served with or without a bun.

rootFamily.gloss: beefsteak (older phonetic borrowing of English beefsteak)
restaurant specializing in grilled beef cuts

stop.etymology: Borrowed in the late 18th–19th century (first in nautical, telegram, and traffic usage) from English stop ('halt! stop!'), from Old English *stoppian, ultimately from Late Latin stuppare ('to plug with tow').

history.meaning: to halt; halt command or traffic sign

cognates.meaning: to plug with tow; to stop a ball in sports
burlap, coarse flax tow (from Latin stuppa)

stopper.etymology: Formed in the 19th century from the borrowed English verb to stop plus the French first-group infinitive suffix -er. English stop descends from Old English *stoppian (attested in forstoppian 'to plug up, stifle'), an early West Germanic borrowing from Late Latin stuppāre ('to plug or caulk with tow or oakum'), derived from Classical Latin stuppa ('coarse part of flax, tow, hards', from Ancient Greek στύππη). Thus stopper is an etymological doublet of native French étouper ('to caulk with tow') and closely related to étouffer ('to suffocate').

history.meaning: to plug up or caulk a hole with coarse flax fibers (stuppa)
to plug, block, obstruct, bring to a halt
to halt abruptly, stop a vehicle or process; also to mend fabric invisibly

stopper.notes: Used both transitively ('stopper un projet', 'stopper l'hémorragie') and intransitively; more punchy and abrupt in register than 'arrêter'.

rootFamily.gloss: to plug or caulk with tow (native doublet from Latin stuppāre)

stratège.etymology: Learned borrowing (first in the 16th century as an ancient history term for an Athenian general, then generalized in the 19th century) via Classical Latin stratēgus from Ancient Greek στρατηγός (stratēgós, 'army leader, general, chief magistrate'), a compound of στρατός (stratós, 'army, encamped host') and ἄγω (ágō, 'to lead, conduct, guide', from PIE *h₂eǵ-).

history.meaning: general, commander of an army, Athenian military magistrate
Greek military commander or civic magistrate
military general; figuratively a master planner or shrewd tactician

morphemes.meaning: leader, one who conducts (from Greek ágō)

stratège.notes: Epicene noun ('un fin stratège', 'une grande stratège'); frequently paired with the preposed adjective 'fin' ('un fin stratège') to praise a shrewd negotiator or agent.

cognates.meaning: distress, anguish (native doublet from Old French destrece)

stress.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-20th century (popularized through endocrinologist Hans Selye's medical research on general adaptation syndrome) from English stress ('mechanical pressure, physiological or psychological strain'), which comes from Middle English stresse ('hardship, coercion, distress'), an aphetic shortening of distresse, borrowed from Old French destrece ('narrowness, oppression, anguish', modern French détresse), from Vulgar Latin *districtia, derived from Classical Latin distringere ('to draw tight, detain, hinder'). Like sport and stage, it is a historical Franco-English boomerang word.

history.meaning: hardship, pressure, strain, physical or mental tension
physiological or psychological tension in response to pressure

stress.notes: Masculine noun ('le stress', 'un gros coup de stress'); completely naturalized in everyday French despite official recommendations in some technical contexts to use 'tension' or 'contrainte'.

cognates.meaning: to subject to stress or strain
to stress out, subject to nervous strain

stresser.etymology: Formed in the second half of the 20th century from the noun stress ('nervous tension, psychological strain', borrowed from English stress and ultimately tracing back to Old French destrece) plus the productive first-conjugation verbal suffix -er.

history.meaning: physiological and psychological tension under pressure
to cause nervous tension (transitive) or to feel anxious (intransitive)

stresser.notes: Works both transitively ('tu me stresses !' = 'you're stressing me out!') and intransitively ('arrête de stresser !' = 'stop stressing out!'), whereas the past participle 'être stressé(e)' describes feeling stressed.

stressé.etymology: Stressé is the past participle of stresser used as an adjective. Stresser is a twentieth-century derivative of stress; it is not an adjective whose origin can be inferred from the last letters alone.

history.stage: Old French -> Middle English -> Modern English

rootFamily.gloss: distress (native French cousin of the same root!)

stressé.notes: A fascinating linguistic boomerang: English 'stress' began as a clipped form of 'distress'—originally borrowed from Old French destrece (modern détresse)—and returned to French in the 20th century!

strict.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Classical Latin strictus ('drawn tight, close, exact, severe'), past participle of stringere ('to draw tight, bind, compress'; doublet of inherited étroit).

history.meaning: to bind tight -> drawn tight, rigorous

strictement.etymology: Formed in French from the feminine singular form stricte of the adjective strict (a learned borrowing from Classical Latin strictus 'drawn tight, close, rigorous, brief', past participle of stringere 'to draw tight, bind, compress') plus the adverbial suffix -ment (from the Classical Latin ablative noun mente 'with a ... mind').

history.meaning: rigorous, exact, admitting no laxity or exception

strictement.notes: Frequently used as an emphatic intensifier before negative pronouns: 'ça n'a strictement rien à voir' ('that has absolutely nothing to do with it') or 'je n'en sais strictement rien' ('I have no idea whatsoever').

rootFamily.gloss: narrow, tight, close (inherited popular doublet of strict)

cognates.meaning: performer of a striptease, exotic dancer

strip-teaseuse.etymology: Hybrid Anglo-French formation created in the mid-20th century by attaching the native French feminine agent suffix -euse (corresponding to masculine strip-teaseur) to the borrowed American English compound strip-tease ('burlesque performance involving gradual undressing'), itself composed of English strip ('to undress, remove clothing', from Old English *strīepan) and tease ('to tantalize, provoke playfully', from Old English tǣsan 'to pluck or comb wool fibers').

history.meaning: erotic cabaret dance in which the performer gradually undresses
male or female exotic dancer performing a striptease

strip-teaseuse.notes: Also spelled without a hyphen ('stripteaseuse') since the 1990 orthography rectifications; the stem 'teas-' keeps its English pronunciation /tiz/, yielding /stʁiptizøz/.

rootFamily.gloss: marketing teaser trailer (same English tease root)

cognates.meaning: artist's workroom; film or recording facility; studio apartment
study, notary's office (earlier borrowing from Latin studium)
