studio.etymology: Borrowed first in the 19th century from Italian studio ('study room, Renaissance artist's or sculptor's workshop'), and reinforced in the early 20th century by American and British English studio ('film set, photography or sound recording facility', as well as 'one-room apartment'). Italian studio descends directly from Classical Latin studium ('zeal, eagerness, study, place of study'), related to studēre ('to be diligent, apply oneself'), making studio a modern doublet of French étude.

history.meaning: eagerness, zeal, pursuit of learning, study room
scholar's study, painter's or sculptor's workshop (bottega/studio)
artist's workshop; film/recording production stage; single-room flat

studio.notes: In everyday Parisian life, 'un studio' almost always means a one-room apartment (with a kitchenette and bathroom), whereas in cinema and music ('les studios de cinéma', 'enregistrer en studio') it means a production stage or recording studio.

rootFamily.gloss: study, research; legal office (doublet from Latin studium)

stupide.etymology: Learned borrowing in 16th-century Middle French from Classical Latin stupidus ('struck senseless, stunned, amazed, dull-witted, foolish'), an adjective derived from the verb stupēre ('to be stunned, benumbed, dazed, or struck dumb with amazement'), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp- ('to push, hit, stun'). In early modern French it still meant 'numb or paralyzed with shock' before shifting primarily to 'foolish, unintelligent'.

history.meaning: to be stunned, benumbed, or motionless with astonishment
dazed with shock (16th–17th c.); foolish, absurd, unintelligent

stupide.notes: Notice how the original Latin sense of 'struck dumb with shock' survives in its close relatives 'stupeur' (stupor/astonishment) and 'stupéfait' (dumbfounded/flabbergasted).

rootFamily.gloss: astounding, mind-blowing; narcotic drug (as a noun)

stupéfait.etymology: Adapted in the 18th century (replacing earlier stupéfact) from Classical Latin stupefactus ('stunned, benumbed, astonished'), past participle of stupefacere ('to strike dumb, stun'), from stupere ('to be stunned or numb') + facere ('to make').

history.meaning: to be numb + to make -> stunned, astonished

style.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin stilus ('pointed writing instrument for wax tablets; manner of writing, mode of expression'), spelled with y under the false humanist association with Greek stylos ('pillar, column').

history.meaning: writing stylus -> manner of writing, literary style
style, manner of expression or design

stylo.etymology: Stylo is a twentieth-century shortening of stylographe. The shortened form became the ordinary French word for a pen.

morphemes.meaning: shortened from stylographe (< Greek stŷlos 'writing reed/pillar')

stylo.notes: False friend alert: French un crayon means a 'pencil' (never 'crayon'!), whereas an ink or ballpoint 'pen' is un stylo.

stylo-plume.etymology: Twentieth-century compound of stylo (shortening of stylographe 'fountain pen', coined from Greek stylos 'pillar, writing rod' + -graphe) and plume ('feather, pen nib', from Classical Latin pluma 'downy feather').

cognates.meaning: solid printing plate; fixed mental cliché or oversimplified image

stéréotype.etymology: Coined in French in 1798 by the printer Firmin Didot (first as an adjective and noun for printing from a solid cast metal plate rather than movable type) from Ancient Greek στερεός (stereós, 'solid, firm, rigid, three-dimensional') + τύπος (túpos, 'impression, mold, cast, mark', from τύπτω 'to strike'). In the 20th century, reinforced by American journalist Walter Lippmann's 1922 figurative use of English stereotype in Public Opinion, it came to denote a rigid, uncritical social cliché or stock character.

history.meaning: solid, firm + impression, cast, or character mark
printed from a solid metal cast plate; a solid printing plate (Didot, 1798)
fixed, conventional mental image, stock character, or social cliché

morphemes.meaning: impression, mold, type, model (from Greek túpos)

stéréotype.notes: Just Like 'cliché' (which also began as a 19th-century French printing term for a cast stereotype plate!), 'stéréotype' moved from the printing press into psychology, sociology, and scriptwriting critique.

rootFamily.gloss: to stereotype, fix in a rigid formula

subit.etymology: Learned borrowing in 13th-century Old French from Classical Latin subitus ('sudden, unexpected, coming on stealthily'), originally the perfect passive participle of subīre ('to go under, approach secretly, steal upon, occur suddenly'), compounded from sub- ('under, up from below') + īre ('to go', from PIE *h₁ey-). A Vulgar Latin derivative *subitānus yielded the synonymous native French adjective soudain.

history.meaning: to go under, creep up on, approach stealthily, occur
having come on stealthily; sudden, unexpected, unpremeditated

morphemes.meaning: gone, come (participial stem of Latin īre)

subit.notes: Slightly more literary or formal than 'soudain', and preserved in fixed expressions like 'une mort subite' (sudden death, both medical and in sports overtime) or 'un départ subit'.

rootFamily.gloss: to undergo, suffer, endure (from the same Latin verb subīre)
sudden (popular inherited relative via Vulgar Latin *subitānus)

sublime.etymology: Learned borrowing in 15th-century Middle French (and canonized in literary aesthetics by Nicolas Boileau's 1674 translation of Pseudo-Longinus's treatise On the Sublime) from Classical Latin sublīmis ('uplifted, high, lofty, borne aloft, exalted'), compounded from sub- ('up to, from under') + līmen ('lintel, threshold', or līmus 'oblique, slanting upward'), literally 'rising right up to the lintel'.

history.meaning: borne aloft, elevated, high, lofty in style or rank
lofty, elevated (in rhetoric and alchemy); reaching supreme moral or artistic grandeur
supreme in beauty or grandeur; in showbiz colloquialism, 'gorgeous, fabulous'

sublime.notes: In Parisian fashion, theater, and film circles (like Andrea and Gabriel in *Dix pour cent*), 'sublime' is an everyday hyperbolic compliment ('Tu es sublime, ma chérie !') meaning 'gorgeous, stunning, fabulous'.

rootFamily.gloss: to sublimate, elevate, bring out the best beauty in
subliminal, below the threshold of consciousness (shared Latin līmen root)

substance.etymology: Borrowed in 12th-century Old French as sustance (later re-Latinized in spelling and pronunciation to substance) from Classical and Late Latin substantia ('being, essence, underlying reality, material contents, property'), formed from the present participle stem (substant-) of substāre ('to stand under, be present, hold out'), from sub- ('under') + stāre ('to stand'), originally calquing Ancient Greek ὑπόστασις (hupóstasis, 'underlying foundation, reality').

history.meaning: to stand under or firm, be present, support
essential nature, underlying reality, material contents
essential matter, physical material, intellectual or artistic depth and gist

morphemes.meaning: abstract feminine noun suffix of state or essence (-ance)

substance.notes: Note the useful idiom 'en substance' ('in essence, basically, to sum up the gist of what was said') as well as Rabelais's famous phrase 'la substantifique moelle' ('the most substantial marrow/core').

rootFamily.gloss: to subsist, continue to exist (sibling compound from Latin subsistere)

cognates.meaning: success, triumph; also past participle of succedere ('happened')
event, occurrence, incident (preserving the neutral Latin sense of 'what happens')

succès.etymology: Learned borrowing in the 16th century from Classical Latin successus ('an advance, a coming up, succession, happy outcome'), an action noun built on the past participle stem of succēdere ('to go under, come after, follow, turn out well'), from sub- (assimilated to suc- before c-, 'under, next after') + cēdere ('to go, move, yield'). In 16th- and 17th-century French, succès meant any outcome or result (one could speak of 'un bon ou mauvais succès'), before narrowing positively to 'triumph, favorable result, box-office hit'.

history.meaning: to go under, follow after, take the place of, turn out well
a coming after, advance, course of events, favorable result
outcome or result (good or bad in 17th c.); triumph, hit, popularity

morphemes.meaning: under, closely after (assimilated form of sub-)
to go, move, yield (from participial stem of Latin cēdere)

succès.notes: In media and showbiz French, distinguish 'un succès d'estime' (a work praised by critics that sells modestly at the box office) from 'un succès fou' or 'un succès au box-office' (a smash commercial hit).

rootFamily.gloss: to succeed, follow after (note: 'to succeed in doing' is réussir, not succéder!)
successor, heir to a role or post

cognates.meaning: to suck (from the same Vulgar Latin *sūctiāre)
suction (from Late Latin sūctiō, built on the same Latin root sūgere)

sucette.etymology: Formed in 19th-century French from the verb stem suc- of sucer ('to suck') plus the feminine diminutive and instrumental suffix -ette. The verb sucer descends from Vulgar Latin *sūctiāre, a frequentative built on the past participle stem (sūct-) of Classical Latin sūgere ('to suck, draw in liquid', from Proto-Indo-European *sewk- / *sewg-). Originally denoting a linen rag filled with sugar given to infants to suck on (and hence a baby's pacifier), in the 20th century it came to mean a hard candy mounted on a stick ('lollipop').

history.meaning: to suck, draw in moisture or milk
to suck repeatedly, draw liquid with the lips
baby's pacifier or sugar-rag; hard candy on a stick (lollipop)

morphemes.meaning: feminine diminutive and instrumental noun suffix

sucette.notes: Means both 'lollipop' and (in some regions alongside 'tétine' or 'tutute') 'baby's pacifier'; in urban street furniture, 'une sucette (Decaux)' is the slang term for a tall sidewalk advertising panel mounted on a single post because of its lollipop shape.

rootFamily.gloss: hickey, love bite; also a flat lozenge candy
suction, act of drawing in by sucking

sucre.etymology: Sucre entered Old French via Medieval Latin succarum and Italian zucchero from Arabic sukkar, which traced back through Persian šakar to Sanskrit śárkarā ('gravel, grit, crystal sugar').

sucré.etymology: Past participle of sucrer ('to sweeten with sugar'), derived from sucre ('sugar', borrowed via Medieval Latin succarum and Italian zucchero from Arabic sukkar, from Persian šakar and Sanskrit śarkarā 'gravel, candied sugar').

sud.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Old English sūþ ('south', via Anglo-Norman maritime usage), from Proto-Germanic *sunþaz ('south, toward the sun').

suffire.etymology: Inherited (with stem reshaping on faire) from Classical Latin sufficere ('to put under, supply, be enough, suffice'), compound of sub- ('under') + facere ('to make, do').

suffisant.etymology: Derived in Old French (soufisant, later refashioned to suffisant after Latin) from the present participle of suffire ('to suffice, be enough'), reinforced by Classical Latin sufficiēns (accusative sufficientem, 'adequate, qualified, sufficient'), the present participle of sufficere ('to put under, supply, meet the need, suffice'), compounded from sub- (assimilated to suf- before f-, 'under') + facere ('to make, do'). In Classical and Modern French, when applied to a person or their demeanor, it developed the psychological sense 'full of oneself, conceited, smug'.

history.meaning: to supply, furnish, be strong enough, suffice
adequate, enough; also capable or proud
enough, adequate (of things); conceited, self-important, smug (of people)

morphemes.meaning: to suffice, be enough (stem of suffire)

suffisant.notes: Crucial semantic trap: while 'une somme suffisante' means 'a sufficient amount', calling a person or tone 'suffisant' ('il est d'un suffisant !', 'un air suffisant') means 'smug, conceited, self-important'—and the noun 'la suffisance' almost exclusively means 'smugness/conceit'!

rootFamily.gloss: to suffice, be enough ('ça suffit !' = 'that's enough!')
conceit, smugness, self-importance (rarely 'sufficiency' outside fixed phrases)

cognates.meaning: to suggest, propose, hint at (from the Latin past participle suggestus)

suggérer.etymology: Learned borrowing in 15th-century Middle French from Classical Latin suggerere ('to carry or lay under, supply, furnish, prompt, advise, suggest'), compounded from sub- (assimilated to sug- before g-, 'under, up from below') + gerere ('to carry, bear, bring, conduct').

history.meaning: to bring up from below, supply, furnish, prompt an idea or advice
to put into someone's mind, insinuate, propose discreetly or evoke artistically

morphemes.meaning: under, up from below (assimilated form of sub-)
to carry, bring, bear (from Latin gerere)

suggérer.notes: Watch both spelling and pronunciation: double 'g' takes a hard /g/ followed by a soft /ʒ/ before 'é' (/sygʒeʁe/), and the acute accent 'é' shifts to grave 'è' in stem-stressed forms ('je suggère', 'il suggère'), except in the future/conditional ('je suggérerai').

rootFamily.gloss: suggestion, proposal, subtle hint or mental influence
to ingest; (reflexive s'ingérer) to meddle or interfere (shared Latin gerere root)

suite.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sequita ('act of following, retinue, continuation'), substantivized feminine past participle of *sequire (Classical Latin sequi 'to follow').

suivant.etymology: Present participle of suivre ('to follow', from Vulgar Latin *sequire, Classical Latin sequi), used as an adjective ('following, next') and preposition ('according to').

suivre.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sequere (regularized active infinitive of Classical Latin deponent sequi 'to follow, come after, pursue'), from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- ('to follow').

history.meaning: to follow, attend, keep up with

sujet.etymology: Borrowed and adapted in the 12th century from Classical Latin subjectus / subiectus ('lying under, subjected; subject matter, underlying theme'), past participle of subicere ('to throw or place under'), from sub- ('under') + iacere ('to throw').

history.meaning: to place under -> subordinate, underlying topic
subject, topic, grammatical or political subject

super.etymology: Informal super is a twentieth-century use derived from the super- word family. The Académie distinguishes this favourable adjective or exclamation from the noun for a type of fuel.

rootFamily.gloss: on (inherited popular outcome of the same Latin super!)

super.notes: Pronounced /sypɛʁ/ and completely invariable in French: des amis super, une super idée (never *supers or *supère!).

superbe.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Latin superbus ('haughty, proud, arrogant; magnificent, lofty'), formed from super ('above, over') with an archaic suffix *-bho- (from PIE *bʰuH- 'to be, become', thus literally 'being above others'). In Old and Middle French, the word primarily denoted moral pride or arrogance (including the capital sin of pride as a feminine noun, la superbe), before gradually ameliorating from the 16th–17th centuries onward via the sense of 'imposing, sumptuous' into the modern enthusiastic meaning 'gorgeous, magnificent'.

history.meaning: standing above others; haughty, proud, lofty

superbe.notes: Epicene adjective (identical in masculine and feminine singular: un acteur superbe, une robe superbe); in archaic or literary French, 'la superbe' also survives as a noun meaning 'haughtiness, hubris'.

supplier.etymology: Inherited and semi-learnedly adapted from Classical Latin supplicāre ('to kneel down before, beseech humbly, pray to'), denominative from the adjective supplex ('kneeling in entreaty, humble'), itself compounded from sub- ('under, down') and the root of plicāre ('to fold, bend' — i.e., bending the knees under oneself). Attested in Old French as souploier ('to bow down, submit') before being reshaped as supplier under Latin influence.

history.meaning: to bend the knees under oneself; to kneel in humble entreaty
to bow down, submit; to beseech humbly

supplier.notes: Takes the construction 'supplier quelqu'un de faire quelque chose' (e.g., 'Je t'en supplie !' — 'I'm begging you!'). Do not confuse with the English false friend 'to supply' (French fournir or approvisionner).

cognates.meaning: added to supply what is lacking, extra

supplémentaire.etymology: Derived in 18th-century French from the noun supplément ('addition, that which fills up a deficiency') plus the learned relational suffix -aire (from Latin -ārius). Supplément itself was borrowed from Classical Latin supplēmentum ('that with which anything is made full, reinforcement'), from supplēre ('to fill up, make complete'), composed of sub- ('from under, up') and plēre ('to fill', from PIE *pleh₁- 'to fill').

history.meaning: that which fills up a gap or completes a whole; military reinforcement
addition that remedies a lack or extends a work
extra, additional, beyond the usual allocation

supplémentaire.notes: Common in workplace and film-production expressions such as 'heures supplémentaires' (overtime, colloquially shortened to 'heures sup') and 'cachet supplémentaire' (extra appearance fee).

rootFamily.gloss: to fill in for, make up for, compensate

cognates.meaning: to bear, put up with, endure
to bear weight; to back or assist

supporter.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Classical Latin supportāre ('to carry or convey from beneath, bring up'), formed from sub- ('under, from below', assimilated to sup-) and portāre ('to carry, bear'). In French, the verb developed the figurative sense 'to bear a burden, endure pain or annoyance, put up with someone', and later (reinforced in the 20th century by English 'to support') acquired the sports and media sense of 'to back, cheer for'.

history.meaning: to carry or convey up from beneath
to bear the weight of; to endure hardship or affliction
to tolerate, put up with; to bear; to cheer for a team

supporter.notes: Crucial partial false friend with English: in everyday French, 'Je ne le supporte plus' means 'I can't stand him anymore!' (not 'I no longer support him financially', which is soutenir or subvenir aux besoins de).

cognates.meaning: to abolish, cancel, do away with
to put down by authority or force, hold back

supprimer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin supprimere ('to press down, hold back, check, sink, conceal'), a compound of sub- ('down, under', assimilated to sup-) and premere ('to press, squeeze'). From 'pressing down out of sight or silencing', the verb evolved in French to mean 'to abolish, cancel (a role, scene, or budget line)' and in modern computing 'to delete'.

history.meaning: to press down, check, hold back, sink
to conceal, silence; to abolish or annul officially
to cut, remove, cancel, or delete

supprimer.notes: In French film editing, scripts, and digital interfaces, supprimer means simply 'to cut, remove, or delete' (e.g., supprimer une scène, supprimer un mail), whereas English 'suppress' carries a much heavier political or psychological connotation.

sur.etymology: Sur continues Latin super, on or above. The French preposition is recorded from the ninth century. It is separate from the accented adjective sûr.

history.form: sor / sour (crossed with sus < sūrsum) -> sur

history.meaning: on, on top of; about; out of (un sur dix)

sur.notes: Unaccented sur ('on, about') contrasts in writing with accented sûr ('sure, safe' < sēcūrus) and sour-tasting adj. sur ('tart').

cognates.meaning: outermost boundary or face of an object

surface.etymology: Coined in 16th-century French from sur- ('on, above, over', from Latin super) and face ('visage, outer side', from Vulgar Latin *facia, Classical Latin faciēs), constructed as a vernacular structural calque of Classical Latin superficiēs ('upper side, top layer, outer appearance', from super- + faciēs). English later borrowed 'surface' directly from French in the 17th century.

history.meaning: upper side, top layer, outer aspect
outer face or geometric boundary of a body (calque of superficiēs)
exterior, surface area, outward appearance; social standing

surface.notes: Used both for physical/real-estate area ('surface habitable', 'grande surface' = supermarket/hypermarket) and in idioms like 'refaire surface' ('to resurface / bounce back after a career slump').

rootFamily.gloss: exact area or learned term for surface

cognates.meaning: to prevail over, overcome; to top
to top, cap; to overcome an obstacle

surmonter.etymology: Formed in Old French (12th century, surmonter / sormonter) from the prefix sur- ('over, above', from Latin super) and monter ('to go up, climb, ascend', from Vulgar Latin *montāre, denominative of mōns, montem 'mountain'). Originally spatial ('to rise above, top, overtop'), it rapidly developed the figurative sense 'to rise above a difficulty, overcome an obstacle or fear'.

history.meaning: to climb above, rise higher than, surpass
to overcome an obstacle, master a crisis or emotion; to sit atop

surmonter.notes: Frequently collocated with abstract nouns of crisis or emotion: 'surmonter une épreuve' (to overcome an ordeal), 'surmonter son trac' (to overcome stage fright).

rootFamily.gloss: to climb, go up; to edit (a film) or stage (a play)

cognates.meaning: family name, last name (historically an added epithet)

surnom.etymology: Formed in Old French (surnon / sornom, 12th century) from sur- ('over, in addition to', from Latin super) and nom ('name', from Latin nōmen). In medieval usage, a sornom was an added epithet or byname appended to a person's baptismal name (which in Anglo-Norman and English became the hereditary family 'surname'), whereas in Modern French it specialized into an informal or affectionate 'nickname, moniker'.

history.meaning: added epithet or byname distinguishing individuals with the same given name

surnom.notes: Classic false friend with English 'surname': French surnom means 'nickname' (whereas 'surname / last name' in French is nom de famille).

surprenant.etymology: Lexicalized as an adjective from the present participle of surprendre ('to catch off guard, astonish'), itself formed in Old French from sur- ('over, upon') and prendre ('to take, seize', from Vulgar Latin *prendere, Classical Latin prehendere). Attested as an adjective meaning 'unexpected, astonishing, striking' from the 17th century onward.

history.meaning: seizing unexpectedly, overtaking (present participle of surprendre)

surprenant.notes: Remember the vowel alternation and single 'n' in 'surprenant' / 'surprenante' (pronounced /syʁ.pʁə.nɑ̃/) versus the double 'n' in the subjunctive/plural stem 'surprennent'.

cognates.meaning: to catch off guard, surprise, amaze

surprendre.etymology: Formed in Old French (sorprendre / surprendre, 12th century) from sur- ('over, upon', from Latin super) and prendre ('to take, seize', from Classical Latin prehendere via syncopated Vulgar Latin *prendere). Originally military and concrete ('to pounce upon, seize unawares, overtake an enemy'), it broadened in Classical and Modern French to mean 'to catch red-handed' and 'to astonish the mind with the unexpected'.

history.meaning: to grasp, seize, lay hold of
to seize from above, attack unawares, overtake
to catch off guard, walk in on, astonish

surprendre.notes: Means both 'to astonish' ('Ça me surprend') and 'to walk in on / catch someone in the act' ('Je les ai surpris en pleine négociation secrète' — 'I walked in on them in the middle of a secret negotiation').

surpris.etymology: Past participle of surprendre ('to catch unawares, astonish'), formed from sur- ('upon, over') and pris, the past participle of prendre (from Vulgar Latin *prēsus < *prehensus, Classical Latin prehensus 'seized, grasped'). Used adjectivally since Old French first for someone 'caught unawares or trapped', and since the 16th–17th centuries for 'astonished, taken aback'.
surpris.notes: The final '-s' is silent in the masculine singular (surpris /syʁ.pʁi/) but voiced as /z/ in the feminine singular (surprise /syʁ.pʁiz/), which is homophonous with the noun 'une surprise'. followed by 'de' + infinitive or 'que' + subjunctive.

cognates.meaning: an unexpected event, gift, or feeling of astonishment

surprise.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle (surprise) of Old French surprendre / sorprendre ('to seize unawares, overtake'), from sur- ('over, upon') + prise ('seizure, taking', from Vulgar Latin *prēsa, feminine of *prēsus < Classical Latin prehensus). Originally denoting a sudden military capture, ambush, or fiscal exaction, it shifted in Middle and Classical French to 'an unexpected event or sudden astonishment', whence English borrowed 'surprise'.

history.meaning: sudden seizure, unexpected military attack or ambush
unexpected event, astonishment, pleasant or unpleasant shock; unexpected gift

morphemes.meaning: taking, seizure (feminine past participle of prendre)

surprise.notes: Used frequently in apposition directly after another noun without a preposition ('un invité surprise', 'une fête surprise') as well as in the idiom 'à ma grande surprise' ('to my great surprise').

rootFamily.gloss: taking, grip, electrical socket; film take ('prise de vue')
mistake, misunderstanding, case of mistaken identity

surréaliste.etymology: Coined in French in 1917 by the poet Guillaume Apollinaire (who subtitled his play Les Mamelles de Tirésias 'drame surréaliste') and canonized in 1924 by André Breton's Manifeste du surréalisme. Formed from the prefix sur- ('above, beyond', from Latin super) + réaliste ('realist', from réel < Late Latin reālis, from Classical Latin rēs 'thing, reality' + suffix -iste < Greek -istēs), denoting an artistic truth superior to conventional realism, then in everyday speech 'bizarre, absurd, dreamlike'.

history.meaning: thing, matter; relating to actual things or reality
transcending conventional realism through the unconscious and dream logic
belonging to the Surrealist movement; colloquially, utterly bizarre, absurd, or unbelievable

morphemes.meaning: adherent or characteristic of a movement (Greek -istēs)

surréaliste.notes: Whereas English distinguishes between 'surrealist' (the 20th-century art movement) and 'surreal' (weird, dreamlike in everyday life), French normally uses 'surréaliste' for both senses ('C'est complètement surréaliste, cette réunion !').

sursaut.etymology: Inherited from Old French sorsaut / sursaut (12th century, 'sudden leap or start'), formed from sur- ('up, over', from Latin super) and saut ('leap, jump', from Classical Latin saltus, from salīre 'to leap, jump'), or as a deverbal noun from sursauter ('to jump up with a start'). It captures both a physical involuntary flinch and a sudden burst of energy or moral awakening.

history.meaning: sudden leap, bounding attack, abrupt startle反應 (start)
involuntary start or jolt; sudden last-minute surge of pride or energy

sursaut.notes: Very common in the adverbial phrase 'en sursaut' ('se réveiller en sursaut' — 'to wake up with a start/jolt') and figuratively 'un sursaut d'orgueil' ('a sudden surge/rally of pride').

rootFamily.gloss: to jump, leap; to be cut or skipped

surtout.etymology: Univerbation in Middle French of the prepositional phrase sur tout ('above all, over everything'), from sur ('on, above', from Latin super) + tout ('all', from Latin totus / *tottus).

surveiller.etymology: Formed in the 16th–17th century from sur- ('over, above', from Latin super-) + veiller ('to stay awake, keep watch', from Classical Latin vigilare 'to be awake, watch').

cognates.meaning: continuing to live after an ordeal or the death of others

survie.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in the 17th century from survivre ('to outlive, survive', from Late Latin supervīvere, composed of super 'beyond, over' + vīvere 'to live') on the model of vie ('life', from Latin vīta). Originally a legal term denoting the fact of outliving another person (as in a marriage contract), it generalized in the 19th and 20th centuries to mean 'survival' in extreme conditions or competitive environments.

history.meaning: to live beyond, outlive another person
legal state of outliving a spouse or testator
survival in face of danger, crisis, or extinction

survie.notes: Used both literally ('instinct de survie' — 'survival instinct') and hyperbolically in office/agency banter ('être en mode survie' — 'to be in survival mode').

survivre.etymology: Inherited or adapted in the 12th century from Late Latin supervivere ('to live beyond, outlive, survive'), compound of super- ('beyond, over') + vivere ('to live').

suspendre.etymology: Borrowed or semi-learned adaptation in the 12th–13th century from Classical Latin suspendere ('to hang up, support from above, interrupt, keep in suspense'), from sub- ('under, up from beneath') + pendere ('to hang, weigh').

cognates.meaning: anxious uncertainty; state of being undecided

suspens.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin suspēnsus ('hung up, suspended; hovering, uncertain, undecided'), the past participle of suspendere ('to hang up', from sub- 'under, up from beneath' + pendere 'to hang, weigh'). Originally used as an adjective meaning 'undecided, in ecclesiastical suspension', it survived primarily in the fixed phrase en suspens ('in abeyance, unresolved') before also becoming a spelling variant of the English re-borrowing suspense ('dramatic tension in cinema/fiction').

history.meaning: hung up, suspended; mentally wavering or uncertain
temporarily suspended from office; left undecided or in abeyance
in abeyance (en suspens); dramatic uncertainty or cliffhanger tension

suspens.notes: Pronounced carefully contrastively: in the traditional idiom 'en suspens' ('left hanging / unresolved'), the final '-s' is silent (/ɑ̃ sys.pɑ̃/), whereas for cinematic 'le suspens / le suspense', speakers pronounce the final /s/ (/sys.pɛns/) after English.

rootFamily.gloss: to hang up, suspend, adjourn, put on hold
suspension, temporary halt; hanging light fixture
dramatic tension in a thriller or screenplay (anglicism from French)

symbole.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th–15th century from Late Latin symbolum / symbolus ('token, creed, sign'), from Ancient Greek symbolon ('tally-piece, token of identity, sign'), from sym- ('together') + ballein ('to throw').

history.meaning: to throw together, match -> matching token, sign

cognates.meaning: by means of symbols; as a token gesture

symboliquement.etymology: Formed in French from the adjective symbolique ('symbolic', borrowed from Late Latin symbolicus, from Ancient Greek symbolikós, derived from sýmbolon 'token, sign, tally-half', from syn- 'together' + bállein 'to throw') and the adverbial suffix -ment (from the ablative singular mente of Classical Latin mēns 'with a ... mind/manner'). Literally 'in the manner of a token thrown together for recognition'.

history.meaning: matching half of a broken token used to verify identity; figurative sign
serving as a symbol or emblem; figurative
in a symbolic manner; as a meaningful token gesture rather than for material value

symboliquement.notes: In French business and entertainment contexts, 'symboliquement' (like 'un euro symbolique') often refers to doing or paying something as a token gesture of goodwill or principle rather than for commercial profit.

sympa.etymology: Twentieth-century colloquial apocope (clipping) of sympathique ('likeable, congenial, nice'), itself derived from sympathie (from Late Latin sympathia, from Ancient Greek sympatheia 'fellow-feeling', from syn- 'with' + pathos 'feeling').

cognates.meaning: showing compassion; congenial (false friend in primary sense)

sympathique.etymology: Derived in the 16th–17th centuries from sympathie ('natural affinity, shared feeling'), borrowed via Late Latin sympathīa from Ancient Greek sympátheia ('fellow-feeling, community of affection or physical affinity'), composed of syn- ('together, with') and páthos ('feeling, emotion, experience, suffering') plus the suffix -ique (Greek -ikos). Originally a philosophical and medical term for occult or physiological affinity between bodies, it shifted in 19th-century everyday French to mean 'naturally likable, pleasant, friendly'.

history.meaning: affected by like feelings; having natural affinity or resonance
operating by natural or physiological affinity (e.g., encre sympathique, système nerveux sympathique)
likable, pleasant, friendly, appealing (colloquially clipped to sympa)

sympathique.notes: Famous false friend with English 'sympathetic': French sympathique (ubiquitously clipped to 'sympa' in spoken French) means 'nice, friendly, likable, cool', whereas English 'sympathetic' (compassionate toward someone's distress) is 'compatissant' or 'compréhensif'.

rootFamily.gloss: natural liking, warmth, friendliness; condolences (at a funeral)
to hit it off, get along well with someone ('sympathiser avec')

cognates.meaning: sitting, session, meeting (parallel formation from sedere)
session, sitting, screening (from cognate Latin sessiō)

séance.etymology: Derived in Old/Middle French from séant, the present participle of the archaic verb seoir ('to sit, be seated; to be fitting/becoming'), inherited from Classical Latin sedēre ('to sit', from PIE *sed- 'to sit'), plus the nominal suffix -ance (from Latin -antia). Originally meaning the right or action of sitting in an assembly, it came to designate any timed sitting for a portrait, therapy, legislative meeting, or cinema screening.

history.meaning: act or right of sitting in a formal assembly; posture of sitting
session, meeting, sitting (photo/therapy), or movie screening

morphemes.meaning: to sit (from Old French seoir < Latin sedēre)
action or state nominal suffix (from Latin -antia)

séance.notes: Essential false friend in scope: while English 'séance' only means a spiritualist attempt to contact ghosts, French 'une séance' is the everyday word for a movie screening ('la séance de 20 heures'), a photoshoot ('séance photo'), a therapy session ('séance chez le psy'), or a workout ('séance de sport'), as well as the idiom 'séance tenante' ('on the spot, right then and there').

rootFamily.gloss: to sit, be becoming/suiting ('cette robe vous sied'); located ('sis')
fitting, proper, becoming; seat or buttocks ('le séant')

sécher.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin siccare ('to make dry, dry up, drain'), derived from the adjective siccus ('dry').

sécurité.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–15th century from Classical Latin securitas (accusative securitatem 'freedom from care, safety, security'), derived from securus ('free from care, safe', from se- 'without' + cura 'care, worry'; doublet of sûreté).

cognates.meaning: act of seducing or charming; allure

séduction.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French from Classical Latin sēductiōnem (nominative sēductiō, 'a leading aside, drawing away; in Christian Latin, leading astray into error or sin'), action noun derived from sēdūcere ('to lead aside or away'), composed of the privative/separative prefix sē- ('aside, apart') and dūcere ('to lead'). From theological 'leading astray', it softened in Classical and Modern French to include irresistible charm, persuasion, and romantic attraction.

history.meaning: a leading aside or drawing apart; moral leading astray (Late Latin)
enticement into error or sin; deceitful persuasion
romantic attraction, irresistible charm, or strategic persuasion ('opération séduction')

séduction.notes: In French media, politics, and talent agencies, 'séduction' is frequently non-sexual, referring to winning over an audience, director, or client (e.g., 'lancer une opération séduction' — 'to launch a charm offensive').

rootFamily.gloss: to charm, win over, entice, seduce
charming, appealing, attractive (of an idea, script, or person)

cognates.meaning: to entice into sexual intimacy or wrongdoing; to captivate

séduire.etymology: Adapted in Old/Middle French from Classical Latin sēdūcere ('to lead aside, take apart, separate; in Christian Latin, to lead astray, corrupt'), formed from the separative prefix sē- ('apart, aside') and dūcere ('to lead, guide'), conjugated on the model of conduire and réduire. In Modern French, its semantic range broadened far beyond moral or romantic enticement to mean 'to win over, charm, appeal strongly to'.

history.meaning: to lead aside, draw apart; (Late Latin) to lead astray
to lead into error, deceive, entice morally or romantically
to charm, captivate, win over (a person, audience, or investor); to seduce

séduire.notes: Watch the register difference with English 'seduce': in French it is completely normal and polite in professional settings to say 'Ce scénario m'a tout de suite séduit' ('This screenplay immediately won me over / appealed to me').

rootFamily.gloss: to lead, drive, conduct (same Latin root dūcere)

séjour.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 11th–12th century from Old French sojorner ('to stay for a time, rest, tarry', modern séjourner), from Vulgar Latin *subdiurnare ('to last for a day, stay awhile'), from sub- ('under, during') + diurnus ('of the day', from dies 'day').

history.meaning: to spend the day, abide for a while

cognates.meaning: act of choosing; a chosen assortment

sélection.etymology: Borrowed into French (first attested sporadically in the 16th century, then popularized in the 19th century via English 'selection', especially through Darwinian 'natural selection') from Classical Latin sēlectiōnem (nominative sēlectiō, 'a choosing out, selection'), derived from sēligere ('to choose out, cull, pick apart'), composed of sē- ('apart, aside') and legere ('to gather, pick, read').

history.meaning: a picking out or choosing apart from a group
act of choosing the best specimens; evolutionary natural selection (19th c.)
selection, shortlist, curated lineup (e.g., Festival de Cannes) or national team

morphemes.meaning: to pick, gather, choose (Latin legere / lect-)

sélection.notes: A cornerstone term in French cinema culture: 'la sélection officielle' (the Official Selection at the Cannes Film Festival) and 'être en sélection' (to be shortlisted/selected for a festival competition).

rootFamily.gloss: to select, shortlist, pick for a festival or team
selector, national team coach, festival programmer

cognates.meaning: act or state of separating or being parted

séparation.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (14th century) from Classical Latin sēparātiōnem (nominative sēparātiō, 'a severing, sundering, division'), action noun from sēparāre ('to pull apart, divide, sever'), composed of the separative prefix sē- ('apart, aside') and parāre ('to prepare, arrange, furnish'). It denotes both physical partitioning and the legal or romantic parting of a couple or business partners.

history.meaning: a setting apart, sundering, or division
act of dividing or parting; marital separation of bed and board
separation, breakup, partition, or institutional division (e.g., séparation des pouvoirs)

séparation.notes: Used both for romantic breakups ('une séparation douloureuse') and in French legal/contractual terminology ('séparation de biens' — separate property regime in marriage; 'se séparer à l'amiable' — to part ways amicably).

rootFamily.gloss: to separate, divide; (reflexive) to split up, part ways

séparer.etymology: Borrowed in Old/Middle French (13th–14th century) from Classical Latin sēparāre ('to disjoin, sever, part, set aside'), formed from the archaic separative prefix sē- ('apart, on one's own') and parāre ('to prepare, arrange, set in order'). Note that the inherited popular Old French reflex of Latin sēparāre is sevrer (which specialized into 'to wean a child from the breast'), whereas séparer is the learned restoration of the Latin verb.

history.meaning: to arrange apart, disjoin, sever, divide
to part, sever, divide; (sevrer) to wean
to divide, set apart; (se séparer) to split up, break up; (se séparer de) to let go of / sell

séparer.notes: Pay attention to the reflexive constructions: 'se séparer' without a preposition means 'to break up / split up' (of a couple or duo), whereas 'se séparer de quelqu'un / quelque chose' is a polite agency/corporate euphemism for 'to let someone go (fire/drop a client)' or 'to part with an asset'.

rootFamily.gloss: to wean; to deprive (inherited popular doublet of séparer)

cognates.meaning: continuous or connected series; cinematic sequence

séquence.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (13th–14th century) from Late and Medieval ecclesiastical Latin sequentia ('that which follows; a liturgical chant sung after the Alleluia'), substantivized neuter plural of sequēns (present participle of Classical Latin sequī 'to follow', from PIE *sekʷ- 'to follow'). In the 20th century, alongside its musical, card-game, and genetic senses, it acquired the technical cinematic meaning of a dramatic unit composed of several shots ('une séquence de film').

history.meaning: following; that which follows in order; liturgical prose chant after the Alleluia
liturgical chant; ordered run of playing cards of the same suit
ordered succession; dramatic film sequence or distinct episode ('séquence émotion')

séquence.notes: In filmmaking, 'un plan-séquence' is a 'long take / single-shot sequence' filmed without cuts; in everyday media French, 'une séquence émotion' refers (often ironicaly) to a tear-jerking or highly emotional moment.

rootFamily.gloss: sequel, aftermath, lingering aftereffect (usually plural: 'garder des séquelles')

cognates.meaning: a number of things or broadcasts in ordered succession

série.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–17th century as a learned mathematical and scientific term from Classical Latin seriēs ('row, chain, continuous succession, garland'), derived from the verb serere ('to join together, bind, plait, interweave in a row', from PIE *ser- 'to line up, bind together'). In the 20th century, under the influence of American and British broadcasting ('TV series'), une série (or série télévisée) became the standard French term for an episodic television show.

history.meaning: a row, chain, garland, or continuous succession of things bound together
ordered mathematical sequence, classification group, or industrial batch
succession, batch ('produire en série'); episodic television series ('série télé')

morphemes.meaning: to bind in a row, string together (Latin serere)

série.notes: Note useful idioms: 'hors série' (special edition/issue of a magazine, or exceptional), 'produire en série' (to mass-produce), 'tueur en série' (serial killer), and 'série B / série Z' (B-movie / ultra-low-budget schlock film).

rootFamily.gloss: serial, arranged in a series; serial (killer/story)
to classify or arrange into ordered series or priority categories
to insert, put into a sequence (from Latin inserere, same root serere)

cognates.meaning: in a serious or earnest manner; really?

sérieusement.etymology: Formed in Middle French (15th century) from the feminine form sérieuse of the adjective sérieux ('earnest, grave, weighty', from Medieval Latin sēriōsus, derived from Classical Latin sērius 'grave, earnest, weighty') and the adverbial suffix -ment (from Classical Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind'). It functions both as a manner adverb ('earnestly, thoroughly') and as a sentence-level discourse marker ('honestly, seriously?!').

history.meaning: earnestly, thoroughly, badly; as an exclamation, 'seriously?!'

sérieusement.notes: Famous French wisdom aphorism: 'Il faut faire les choses sérieusement sans se prendre au sérieux' ('One must do things seriously/thoroughly without taking oneself too seriously'). In casual speech, 'Sérieusement ?!' is often shortened to 'Sérieux ?!'.

rootFamily.gloss: serious, reliable, earnest; seriousness (as a noun, 'le sérieux')

sérieux.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Medieval Latin sēriōsus ('grave, earnest, weighty'), an extended suffixed form in -ōsus of Classical Latin sērius ('grave, earnest, important', commonly used in the phrase sēriō 'in earnest', from PIE *swer- 'heavy, weighty', cognate with German schwer 'heavy'). In French, alongside 'solemn, grave', it developed the prized professional sense of 'reliable, conscientious, trustworthy'.

history.meaning: weighty, grave, earnest, opposed to jesting (iocus)
serious, earnest; reliable, conscientious, professional; (as noun, le sérieux) reliability or straight face

morphemes.meaning: adjectival suffix denoting fullness or quality (Latin -iōsus)

sérieux.notes: Important positive nuance in French: calling a worker, agent, or student 'quelqu'un de sérieux' or 'un client sérieux' does NOT mean they are grim or humorless—it means they are 'reliable, professional, trustworthy, and diligent'. Also used as a masculine noun ('garder son sérieux' — 'to keep a straight face').

rootFamily.gloss: reliability, professionalism, or straight face (masculine noun conversion)

sûr.etymology: Sûr descends from Latin securus, free from concern or safe. The Académie records it from the eleventh century. The written accent distinguishes it from the unrelated preposition sur.

history.meaning: safe, certain (circumflex marks contraction of Old French hiatus eü)

cognates.meaning: Old French borrowing and learned Latin doublet

sûr.notes: Even under the 1990 French spelling rectifications (which dropped many circumflexes on u), masculine singular sûr keeps its circumflex so it never collides with the preposition sur ('on')!

sûrement.etymology: Formed in the 12th century from the feminine adjective sûre (Old French seüre, inherited from Classical Latin securus 'free from care, safe, certain') + the adverbial suffix -ment.

cognates.meaning: functional semantic equivalent blending 'sister' and 'friend/pal' (structural parallel)

sœpote.etymology: Contemporary colloquial French portmanteau (mot-valise) coined in playful youth and pop-culture register (featured in Dix pour cent / Call My Agent!), blending the initial syllable of sœur ('sister', pronounced /sœʁ/, from Classical Latin soror, sorōrem) with pote ('buddy, pal, best friend', an early 20th-century argotic clipping of poteau 'wooden post, pillar, reliable support', from Old French postel < Vulgar Latin *postellus, diminutive of Classical Latin postis 'doorpost'). It denotes a female friend who is simultaneously a sister and a best buddy—or a biological sister with whom one shares a best-friend bond.

history.meaning: sister + doorpost / supporting pillar (ultimate Latin roots of the two blended words)
sister + close buddy/pal ('one you can lean on like a post')
sister-buddy, sis-pal (playful blend of sœur and pote)

morphemes.meaning: colloquial noun meaning 'buddy, pal' (clipped from poteau 'post')

sœpote.notes: A quintessential French mot-valise (portmanteau): the 'œ' keeps the rounded vowel /œ/ of 'sœur' (/sœ.pɔt/), playfully fusing family kinship ('sœur') with informal camaraderie ('pote').

rootFamily.gloss: post, pole, goal-post; (old slang) loyal pal/sidekick

cognates.meaning: religious sister, nun (inherited from Latin soror)

sœur.etymology: Inherited from Old French suer / seror, where suer evolved directly from the Classical Latin nominative singular soror ('sister') via regular diphthongization of stressed open o in an open syllable (*sɔror > suer > sœur), while the oblique case seror came from the Latin accusative sorōrem. Latin soror itself descends from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr ('sister', compound of reflexive *swe- 'one's own [kin group]' + *-sōr 'woman, female'), making French sœur a deep Indo-European cognate of English sister and German Schwester.

history.meaning: female member of one's own kin group; sister
sister, female sibling; nun; close female comrade ('âme sœur')

sœur.notes: One of the rare French nouns surviving from the Old French nominative case (Latin soror > suer > sœur) rather than the accusative (sorōrem > seror); always spelled with the ligature 'œ' (and appears in the idiom 'l'âme sœur' — 'soulmate' and 'et ta sœur ?' — sarcastic dismissal 'and what about your sister? / who cares?').

rootFamily.gloss: sisterhood, female solidarity (learned derivative from Latin sorōritās)

table.etymology: Table comes from Latin tabula ('board, plank, writing tablet, table'), passing through Old French table into both modern French and English.
table.notes: **À table!** = Dinner/breakfast is ready!; **tablette** ('shelf; digital tablet') is its diminutive.

tableau.etymology: Derived in the 12th–13th century (Old French tablel) as a diminutive in -el / -eau of table ('board, plank, writing or painting tablet', inherited from Classical Latin tabula 'board, plank, painted panel, list').

history.meaning: small board -> painted panel, picture, board, chart

tablette.etymology: Derived in the 12th–13th century as a diminutive in -ette of table ('board, plank, tablet', inherited from Classical Latin tabula 'board, flat slab, writing tablet').

history.meaning: small shelf, lozenge/bar (of chocolate), electronic tablet

tablier.etymology: Inherited from Old French tablier (originally 'tablecloth', 'board for table games', and by the 15th century 'protective cloth worn in front at a workbench or kitchen table'), derived from table (< Latin tabula 'board, table').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tablier (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tablier

tablier.notes: In civil engineering, **le tablier d'un pont** still preserves the older 'flat planked board' sense: it means the deck of a bridge.

tabou.etymology: Borrowed in the late 18th century via English taboo (introduced by Captain James Cook in 1777) from Tongan tapu ('sacred, consecrated, forbidden, untouchable'), from Proto-Polynesian *tapu ('sacred, marked as off-limits').

history.meaning: consecrated or forbidden by Polynesia custom

tabou.notes: As an adjective, the masculine plural is tabous and the feminine is taboue (plural taboues), though some speakers treat it as invariable in informal speech.

tabouret.etymology: Formed in Middle French as the diminutive of Old French tabour ('cylindrical drum', an older cousin of tambour), because early round low stools were shaped like small drums!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tabouret (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tabouret

tabouret.notes: At the court of Versailles, being granted **le tabouret**—the right to sit on a folding stool in the Queen's presence—was one of the highest honours in France.

tache.etymology: Inherited from Old French tache / teche ('mark, badge, natural trait, blemish, stain'), from Vulgar Latin *tacca ('mark, spot, clasp'), borrowed from a Gothic or West Germanic *taikn ('sign, token, mark', cf. English token, German Zeichen).

taille.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 12th century from tailler ('to cut, prune, shape, carve'), inherited from Late Latin taliare ('to split, cut, prune shoots'), derived from Classical Latin talea ('cutting, twig, slip for planting').

taire.etymology: Inherited from Old French taisir, from Vulgar Latin *tacēre (remodeling of Classical Latin tacēre, 'to be silent, say nothing, pass over in silence'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tak- ('to be silent').

history.meaning: to be silent, utter no word

taire.notes: Used transitively (taire un secret, 'to keep a secret quiet') or reflexively (se taire, 'to be quiet / shut up'); note the irregular past participle tu.

talent.etymology: Inherited from Old French talent ('desire, inclination, will'), from Latin talentum ('balance weight, sum of money'), borrowed from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton, 'balance, scale, weight'). The modern sense of 'natural ability or gift' developed under the influence of the New Testament Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14–30).

history.meaning: scale, balance, standard weight or sum of money
weight, monetary sum, figuratively a treasure
inclination, desire, later natural gift or aptitude

talent.notes: In talent agency jargon (as in Dix pour cent), les talents is used in the plural or as a count noun to mean the artists/clients themselves ('the talent'), mirroring Hollywood English usage.

talentueux.etymology: Formed in the 18th century within French by adding the adjectival suffix -eux (from Latin -ōsus, 'full of') to the noun talent (with an epenthetic -u- modeled on learned formations like somptueux or spiritueux).
talentueux.notes: Long condemned by 19th-century purists as a neologism (though defended by Chateaubriand), it is now completely standard; feminine form is talentueuse.

talon.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *talonem (augmentative in -o, -onis of Classical Latin talus 'ankle-bone, heel').

tampon.etymology: Nasalized variant of Middle French tapon ('cloth plug, bung, stopper'), borrowed from Frankish *tappo ('plug, tap, peg'); shifted from a pad of cloth dabbed in ink to an ink stamp or postmark.

history.meaning: plug, wadded pad -> inked stamping pad

cognates.meaning: cognate from Old English tæppa ('cask plug, faucet')

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tampon (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tampon

tampon.notes: On French mail and official notices, **le cachet / le tampon de la poste faisant foi** ('postmark serving as proof of date') is a classic administrative phrase.

tango.etymology: Borrowed around 1900 from Rioplatense Spanish tango ('gathering of Black dancers, drum, Argentine ballroom dance'), likely of Niger-Congo (Bantu) origin (compare Kikongo ntangu or Ibibio tamgu, 'to dance, drum') or expressive onomatopoeia for a drumbeat, blended in folk etymology with Spanish tañer / Latin tangere ('to touch, play an instrument').

history.meaning: percussion gathering and dance in Buenos Aires and Montevideo
syncopated partner dance and musical genre

tango.notes: Parisian craze for le tango around 1910–1913 also gave rise to the invariable colour adjective tango ('deep reddish-orange').

tant.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin tantum ('so much, to such a degree, only'), neuter adverbial accusative of tantus ('so great, so much').

history.meaning: so great -> so much, to such an extent
so much, so many, as much

tante.etymology: Alteration by nursery reduplication in the 13th century of Old French ante ('aunt'), inherited from Classical Latin amita ('father's sister, paternal aunt').

tape-à-l'œil.etymology: A 19th-century phrasal compound (attested 1833 as a noun and adjective) combining the imperative/3rd-person singular of taper ('to strike, hit, slap', of expressive/onomatopoeic origin *tapp-) with à l'œil ('at the eye', from Latin oculus), literally 'that which strikes the eye' with ostentatious showiness.

history.meaning: to strike the eye, catch attention ostentatiously

tape-à-l'œil.notes: Completely invariable as an adjective (des tenues tape-à-l'œil) and also used as a masculine noun (du tape-à-l'œil, 'flashiness, cheap glitz'). Do not confuse with à l'œil alone, which means 'for free'.

taper.etymology: Attested since the 12th century ('to strike with the flat of the hand, slap, tap, bung'), from a Gallo-Romance or Germanic expressive root *tapp- ('to strike, slap, plug with a bung', cf. Middle Dutch tappen).

history.meaning: expressive root: to slap, tap, stopper
to pat, hit, tap, type on a keyboard

tapis.etymology: Inherited from Old French tapiz, borrowed via Medieval Latin tapetium from Byzantine Greek tapētion (diminutive of Ancient Greek tapēs, stem tapēt- 'carpet, rug, tapestry').

tapoter.etymology: Formed in Middle French (16th century) by adding the diminutive and frequentative verbal suffix -oter (expressing small, light, repeated actions) to taper ('to tap, slap, strike'), itself of expressive/onomatopoeic origin (*tapp-) imitating a light flat blow. Just as clignoter means 'to blink repeatedly' and chuchoter 'to whisper softly', tapoter means 'to pat or tap gently several times'.

history.meaning: to pat, tap lightly and repeatedly

tapoter.notes: The suffix **-oter** in French (**tapoter, pianoter, grignoter, siroter**) always softens an action into small, gentle repetitions.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tapoter

tard.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin tarde ('slowly, late'), adverb formed on tardus ('slow, sluggish, tardy, late').

tarder.etymology: Inherited from Old French tarder / targier ('to delay, linger, be slow'), from Classical Latin tardāre ('to make slow, hinder; to loiter, tarry'), derived from the adjective tardus ('slow, sluggish, late').

history.meaning: to delay, linger, take a long time

tarder.notes: Note the two distinct constructions: ne pas tarder à faire quelque chose ('to do something soon / before long') vs. impersonally il me tarde de... ('I can't wait to... / I long to...').

rootFamily.gloss: to delay, put off, run late

tardif.etymology: Inherited from Old French tardif ('slow, sluggish, late'), from Vulgar Latin *tardīvus, formed from Classical Latin tardus ('slow, late') + the adjectival suffix -īvus.

history.meaning: slow, belated, occurring after the normal time

tardif.notes: Whereas tard is primarily an adverb ('late in the day'), tardif is an adjective (feminine tardive) meaning 'belated' or 'occurring later than expected' (une prise de conscience tardive).

rootFamily.gloss: to delay, be long in coming

tarif.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian tariffa ('price schedule, assessment'), via Medieval Latin tarifa from Arabic تَعْرِيفَة (taʿrīfa, 'notification, inventory, official list of fees'), verbal noun of عَرَّفَ (ʿarrafa, 'to make known, notify, define'), from the Semitic root ʿ-r-f ('to know').

history.meaning: notification, official schedule of fees or customs duties

tarif.notes: False friend alert: while English tariff usually means a customs tax on imports, French tarif is the everyday word for any price, rate, admission fee, or fare (plein tarif, demi-tarif, les tarifs d'un hôtel).

rootFamily.gloss: to set a price or rate for
relating to rates or customs tariffs

tartare.etymology: From Middle French Tartare ('Tatar, member of the Turkic and Mongolic nomadic peoples of Central Asia'), via Medieval Latin Tartarus from Persian تاتار (Tātār) / Turkic Tatar, altered in medieval Europe by folk-etymological association with Latin Tartarus (Ancient Greek Τάρταρος, the infernal abyss). The culinary sense ('finely chopped raw beef or fish') arose in early 20th-century French gastronomy via sauce à la tartare.

history.meaning: member of the Tatar nomadic confederation
seasoned raw minced meat or fish dish

tartare.notes: In French bistro culture, ordering un tartare (de bœuf, de saumon, de thon) always refers to raw chopped meat or fish seasoned with capers, onions, and sauce.

rootFamily.gloss: Tatar language or person (modern ethnographic spelling)
Tartary, historical region of Central/Northern Asia

tarte.etymology: From twelfth-century Old French tarte ('flat open pastry'), related to Medieval Latin tarta / torta ('round loaf or twisted pastry'). English tart was borrowed directly from Old French tarte.

cognates.meaning: open pastry pie (borrowed from Old French tarte)

rootFamily.gloss: buttered slice of bread with spread

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tarte (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tarte

tartine.etymology: Attested from the sixteenth century (Rabelais) as a playful diminutive (-ine) of tarte: a slice of bread spread open-faced with butter, jam, or honey like a little flat tart.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: tartine (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: tartine

tas.etymology: Inherited from Old French tas ('heap, pile, stack of sheaves, crowd'), borrowed from Frankish *tas ('heap, stack of grain or hay'), from Proto-Germanic *tassaz ('heap, stack').

history.meaning: heap, stack of hay or grain

tas.notes: The final -s is silent (pronounced /ta/), and in everyday spoken French un tas de / des tas de + noun is the standard informal quantifier for 'a lot of / loads of'.

tasse.etymology: Tasse entered Old French (via Provençal tassa or Italian tazza) from Arabic ṭāsa ('shallow metal drinking bowl'), itself borrowed from Persian tāšt ('cup, basin').
tasse.notes: **Une tasse de thé / de café** = a cup of tea / coffee.

taupe.etymology: Inherited from Old French taupe, from Classical Latin talpa ('mole'), with regular Gallo-Romance vocalization of preconsonantal /l/ to /u/ (which later monophthongized to /o/).

history.meaning: mole; figuratively a blind or burrowing person

taupe.notes: Just as in English, une taupe refers both to the burrowing animal (hence myope comme une taupe, 'blind as a bat') and to an inside informant or 'mole' leaking confidential agency information.

rootFamily.gloss: molehill; dark cramped room or prep-school class
mole-catcher; student preparing for elite engineering schools

taxe.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Middle French from taxer ('to assess, fix an official price, impose a levy'), from Medieval Latin taxāre ('to estimate, assess value, impose a charge'), from Classical Latin taxāre ('to touch sharply, censure, appraise, rate').

history.meaning: to touch repeatedly, appraise, estimate value
to assess officially, levy a duty
fixed price, official assessment, indirect tax or duty

taxe.notes: Distinguish une taxe (an indirect tax or fee on goods/services, like la TVA — taxe sur la valeur ajoutée) from un impôt (direct income or wealth tax).

cognates.meaning: to levy a tax on; to strain or accuse

taxer.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Classical and Medieval Latin taxāre ('to touch sharply, reproach, estimate, assess for taxation'), frequentative of tangere ('to touch'). In 20th-century colloquial French, the fiscal sense 'to levy a charge on someone' shifted humorously to 'to bum, cadge, or borrow money/cigarettes from someone'.

history.meaning: to touch sharply, censure, appraise value
to assess a sum, impose a tax; to accuse someone (taxer de)
to cadge, bum, or borrow small items or cash from someone

taxer.notes: Has three distinct registers: fiscal (taxer les produits, 'to tax goods'), formal literary (taxer quelqu'un d'égoïsme, 'to accuse someone of selfishness'), and everyday colloquial (Je peux te taxer une clope / dix euros ?, 'Can I bum a cigarette / ten euros off you?').

taxi.etymology: Early 20th-century clipping of taximètre ('fare-meter cab', altered from taxamètre, coined in Germany in 1890 as Taxameter from Medieval Latin taxa 'tax, fixed rate of fare' + Greek metron 'measure').

tchin.etymology: Shortened from tchin-tchin, borrowed in the late 19th century via Chinese Pidgin English chin-chin from Mandarin 請請 / 请请 (qǐng qǐng) or Cantonese cing2 cing2 ('please-please, I cordially invite you'), later reinterpreted in Europe as an onomatopoeia for the clinking sound of glasses during a toast.
tchin.notes: Used singly (Tchin !) or reduplicated (Tchin-tchin !) when clinking glasses informally, alongside À la tienne ! / À la vôtre ! or Santé !

te.etymology: Te continues Latin te, the accusative form of tu, the second-person singular pronoun. The Académie records the French word from the tenth century. Modern te is the unstressed object form alongside subject tu and stressed toi; it is shortened to t' before a vowel or silent h.

tel.etymology: Inherited from Old French tel, from Classical Latin tālis ('such, of such a kind or nature'), correlated with quālis ('of what kind'), from the Proto-Indo-European demonstrative stem *to-.

history.meaning: such, of such a kind or quality

tel.notes: Notice the placement of the indefinite article: un tel succès ('such a success', literally 'a such success'), and key idioms like tel quel ('as is, unchanged') and tel père, tel fils ('like father, like son'). Feminine form is telle.

rootFamily.gloss: so much, to such an extent
of what kind, which (correlative of tel, from Latin qualis)

tellement.etymology: Formed in the 12th–13th century from the feminine adjective telle ('such', inherited from Classical Latin talis 'of such a kind') + the adverbial suffix -ment.

history.meaning: in such a way -> so much, so

temporaire.etymology: Learned borrowing (first attested 1560) from Classical Latin temporārius ('lasting only for a time, provisional, seasonal'), derived from tempus, temporis ('time, season, period').

history.meaning: of a time, lasting only for a limited period

temporaire.notes: Do not confuse temporaire ('temporary, lasting a short time') with temporel ('temporal, relating to time or secular/worldly affairs').

temporel.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin temporalis ('lasting for a time, belonging to time, secular/worldly'), derived from tempus, stem tempor- ('time, season').

temps.etymology: Temps continues Latin tempus, which referred to a division of duration, a season or time. The Académie also connects its weather sense with Latin caeli tempus, the state of the sky. That history helps explain why one French word covers both time and weather.

history.meaning: time, a division of duration, season
state of the sky; behind the weather sense

tempérament.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin temperāmentum ('proper measure, due proportion, moderation, mixture of humors'), from temperāre ('to mix in due proportion, moderate, regulate'), itself derived from tempus ('proper time or measure'). In ancient and Renaissance medicine, it referred to the balance of the four bodily humors determining personality.

history.meaning: to mix in due proportion, moderate, regulate
balance of bodily humors, character disposition, fiery personality

morphemes.meaning: to mix proportionally, moderate (from Latin temperāre)
noun-forming suffix of result or state (from Latin -mentum)

tempérament.notes: Avoir du tempérament means to have a strong, fiery, or passionate personality (or high libido in older colloquial usage).

cognates.meaning: degree of heat or cold; fever

température.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin temperātūra ('due measure, proportion, composition, state of the air or climate'), from temperātus, past participle of temperāre ('to mix in due proportion, moderate').

history.meaning: due mixture, proportion, mildness or state of climate
climatic condition, later measured degree of heat or bodily fever

morphemes.meaning: to mix in proportion, regulate (from Latin temperāt-)

température.notes: In idiomatic speech, prendre la température means 'to test the waters / gauge the mood' of a room, client, or negotiation before making a move.

tempête.etymology: Inherited from Old French tempeste ('violent storm, commotion'), from Vulgar Latin *tempesta (reanalyzed as a first-declension feminine singular from Classical Latin tempestās, tempestātis, 'period of time, weather, bad weather, storm'), derived from tempus ('time, season'). The circumflex on ê marks the historical loss of preconsonantal s.

history.meaning: portion of time, weather, stormy weather
storm, gale, emotional or social turmoil

tempête.notes: Compare the circumflex in tempête with the preserved s in English tempest and French tempétueux; common idioms include une tempête dans un verre d'eau ('a tempest in a teacup').

rootFamily.gloss: to rage, storm, rant and rave

tendre.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin tendere ('to stretch, extend, direct, hold out, strive'), from Proto-Indo-European *ten- ('to stretch'). (Homonymous adjective tendre 'tender' comes from Latin tenerum.)

tendrement.etymology: Formed in Old French from the adjective tendre ('soft, delicate, affectionate', from Classical Latin tenerum, accusative of tener, 'soft, delicate, young', with epenthetic -d- between n and r) + the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin ablative mente, 'with a ... mind').

history.meaning: with a delicate or affectionate mind/spirit

morphemes.meaning: adverbial suffix of manner (from Latin mente)

tendrement.notes: Illustrates the regular Gallo-Romance insertion of a transitional consonant /d/ in the cluster -n'r- (Latin tenerum -> Old French tendre).

tendresse.etymology: Formed in Middle French (replacing Old French tendror / tendreté in the emotional sense) from the adjective tendre ('soft, delicate, affectionate', from Latin tenerum) + the abstract nominal suffix -esse (from Vulgar Latin -itia).
tendresse.notes: While tendresse refers to emotional affection (plural des tendresses = 'caresses, words of affection'), the culinary tenderness of meat is called la tendreté.

tendu.etymology: Adjectival use of the past participle of tendre ('to stretch, pull taut, hold out'), from Vulgar Latin *tendūtus (replacing Classical Latin tēnsus / tentus), from Classical Latin tendere ('to stretch, extend, strain, direct'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ten- ('to stretch').

history.meaning: taut, strained, emotionally or socially tense

morphemes.meaning: past participle / adjectival ending (from Vulgar Latin -ūtus)

tendu.notes: Notice the homophony of the verb tendre ('to stretch/hold out', from Latin tendere, giving tendu) and the adjective tendre ('tender/soft', from Latin tener). In colloquial speech, C'est tendu ! means 'It's dicey / super stressful / tight!'.

tenir.etymology: Tenir developed from Popular Latin tenire, a remodelling of Classical Latin tenere, to hold or keep. The Académie records the French verb from the tenth century.

history.meaning: to hold, grasp, keep (shifted into -īre class like venīre)

cognates.meaning: from Latin tenāx and French tenant, tenable

tenir.notes: Tiens! / Tenez! ('Hold this!') is used constantly when handing someone an object AND as an exclamation of mild surprise ('Well look at that! / Hey!').

cognates.meaning: state of being stretched tight; mental or interpersonal strain

tension.etymology: Learned borrowing (attested in the 14th century in medical contexts) from Classical Latin tēnsiō, tēnsiōnis ('a stretching, drawing tight, cramp'), action noun derived from tēnsus, past participle of tendere ('to stretch, strain'), from Proto-Indo-European *ten- ('to stretch').

history.meaning: act of stretching, muscular tightness or spasm
physical tautness, blood pressure, voltage, psychological or interpersonal strain

morphemes.meaning: action or state noun suffix (from Latin -iōnem)

tension.notes: Besides emotional or dramatic strain (sous haute tension), la tension in everyday medical contexts means 'blood pressure' (avoir de la tension = to have high blood pressure).

tentant.etymology: Adjectival use of the present participle of tenter ('to tempt, entice, attempt'), from Classical Latin temptāre / tentāre ('to handle, touch, test, try, entice'), frequentative of tendere ('to stretch, reach out') or tenēre ('to hold').

history.meaning: to feel, test, try out, assail with temptation

tentant.notes: In French, tenter covers both 'to tempt' (Ça me tente bien !, 'That really tempts me / sounds great to me!') and 'to attempt' (tenter sa chance, 'to try one's luck'). Feminine is tentante.

tenter.etymology: Borrowed or semi-learned adaptation in the 12th century from Classical Latin temptare / tentare ('to handle, test, try, attempt, assail'), frequentative of tendere ('to stretch') or tenere ('to hold').

tenue.etymology: Noun formed in Old French from the feminine past participle (tenue) of tenir ('to hold, keep, maintain'), from Vulgar Latin *tenūta (replacing Classical Latin tenta), from Classical Latin tenēre ('to hold, grasp, maintain'). From the sense 'manner of holding oneself (posture, deportment)', it evolved to mean 'manner of dressing, attire, outfit'.

history.meaning: act of holding, session, posture, bearing

morphemes.meaning: feminine past-participle nominal suffix (from Vulgar Latin -ūta)

tenue.notes: Covers both 'outfit/attire' (tenue de soirée = 'evening wear / formal attire'; en petite tenue = 'scantily clad') and 'comportment / holding' (tenue de route = 'road handling').

rootFamily.gloss: to hold, keep; se tenir = to behave/stand

terminer.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin terminare ('to mark off by boundaries, limit, bring to an end, finish'), derived from terminus ('boundary stone, limit, end').

history.meaning: boundary, end -> to bound, bring to an end

cognates.meaning: stretch of land, physical features of ground

terrain.etymology: Inherited from Old French terrien / terrain ('earthly, piece of land'), from Vulgar Latin *terrānum (alteration of Classical Latin terrēnum, 'piece of ground, arable land', neuter substantive of terrēnus, 'of earth, earthen'), derived from terra ('earth, land, ground').

history.meaning: earthen ground, stretch of land (from terra, 'earth')
plot of land, sports field, field of operations, common ground

terrain.notes: Extremely rich in figurative negotiation idioms: préparer le terrain ('to pave the way'), trouver un terrain d'entente ('to find common ground'), and sur le terrain ('on the ground / in the field').

rootFamily.gloss: terrace, raised earth platform, café patio
to land (of an aircraft, literally 'to touch ground')

cognates.meaning: raised level earth platform, patio, row of houses

terrasse.etymology: Borrowed or adapted in Middle French from Old Occitan terrassa ('mound of earth, raised platform, rubble'), from Vulgar Latin *terrācea (feminine substantive of *terrāceus, 'made of earth, earthen'), derived from Classical Latin terra ('earth, ground').

history.meaning: earthenwork, raised bank or platform of earth
outdoor platform, balcony, sidewalk seating area of a café or restaurant

morphemes.meaning: collective or material nominal suffix (from Latin -ācea)

terrasse.notes: In Parisian daily life (and throughout Dix pour cent), faire une terrasse or boire un verre en terrasse refers specifically to sitting at the outdoor sidewalk tables of a café or bistro.

rootFamily.gloss: earthwork, grading, excavating; laying someone out flat
to knock down, overwhelm, lay low (like a fever)

terre.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin terra ('dry land, earth, ground, soil, country'), from Proto-Indo-European *ters- ('dry', cf. Latin torrere 'to parch').

terrible.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin terribilis ('frightful, dreadful, inspiring terror'), derived from terrere ('to frighten, terrify').

terriblement.etymology: Formed in Middle French (14th century) from the adjective terrible (borrowed from Classical Latin terribilis, 'frightful, dreadful', from terrēre, 'to frighten, terrify') + the adverbial suffix -ment (from Latin ablative mente). Like its English cognate, it weakened in conversational usage from 'in a terrifying manner' to an emphatic intensifier meaning 'extremely, awfully'.

history.meaning: in a terrifying or dreadful manner

morphemes.meaning: adverbial suffix of manner (from Latin mente)

terriblement.notes: Just like English 'terribly', it often functions as a positive or neutral intensifier in chic conversational French (Elle est terriblement attachante, 'She is awfully endearing'); also note that C'est pas terrible ironically means 'It's not great / pretty mediocre'.

test.etymology: Borrowed in the late 17th–19th century (first in political/religious history, then in psychology and science) from English test ('trial, examination'), itself borrowed from Old French test ('earthenware pot or cupel used by alchemists to assay gold and silver', from Latin testum 'earthen vessel').

history.meaning: assay of metal -> critical trial, examination

testament.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th century from Classical Latin testāmentum ('last will, publication of a will'), in Ecclesiastical Latin also translating Ancient Greek διαθήκη (diathḗkē, 'covenant, testament'), derived from testārī ('to bear witness, make a last will'), itself from testis ('witness'), from Proto-Indo-European *tristis ('third person standing by as impartial witness', from *treyes, 'three').

history.meaning: witness -> to call to witness, make a formal will
last will and testament; biblical covenant (Late Latin)
legal will disposing of one's estate; spiritual or artistic legacy; biblical Testament

morphemes.meaning: bear witness, declare one's will (from Latin testārī / testis)
instrument, result, or legal act (from Latin -mentum)

testament.notes: In French, 'a will' is always un testament (never *une volonté, which means 'willpower' or 'wish', though les dernières volontés means 'final wishes'). In cinema, un film-testament is a director's final, career-summing work.

rootFamily.gloss: relating to a will (e.g., exécuteur testamentaire)
to attest, certify, bear witness to
to contest, challenge (originally by calling witnesses)

tester.etymology: Derived in the late 19th–20th century from test ('examination, trial', borrowed from English test) or adapted directly from English to test. (Homonymous legal verb tester 'to make a will' comes from Latin testari.)

history.meaning: to subject to a test, try out

cognates.meaning: written work; borrowed via Old French

texte.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (12th century, originally designating the authoritative Latin text of the Gospels) from Classical Latin textus ('woven fabric, structure, framework, consecutive discourse'), a masculine action noun derived from the past-participle stem of texere ('to weave, plait, construct'), from Proto-Indo-European *teks- ('to weave, fabricate'). The classical rhetorical metaphor treats a written composition as a tightly woven fabric of words.

history.meaning: to weave, plait, construct with skill
woven texture; connected structure of a speech or narrative
sacred scripture, authoritative body of a written work

texte.notes: In French theatre and cinema ('Dix pour cent'), 'son texte' specifically means an actor's lines or script ('apprendre son texte' = to learn one's lines).

thym.etymology: Refashioned with learned Greek-Latin spelling from Old French tin, borrowed via Classical Latin thymum from Ancient Greek thýmon ('thyme'), connected to thýein ('to burn fragrant offerings, send up sweet smoke').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Old French tym, likewise given learned th- spelling

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: thym (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: thym

thym.notes: Tied with **persil** and bay leaf (**laurier**) using kitchen **ficelle**, **le thym** forms the classic French **bouquet garni**.

thé.etymology: Borrowed in the seventeenth century via Dutch thee (and Malay teh) from Hokkien Chinese tê ('tea'), brought through maritime trade, whereas land-route varieties of Chinese cha gave Russian čaj and Portuguese chá.
thé.notes: Gives **la théière** ('teapot'). **Du thé au citron / à la menthe** = lemon / mint tea.

théière.etymology: Théière was coined in late seventeenth-century French from thé ('tea') + the vessel suffix -ière (modelled on cafetière 'coffee pot').

théorie.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (15th–16th century) from Late Latin theōria, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek θεωρία (theōria, 'viewing, contemplation, philosophical speculation, spectacle'), derived from θεωρός (theōros, 'spectator, envoy sent to consult an oracle'), a compound of θέα (thea, 'a view, sight') and a stem related to ὁράω (horaō, 'to see, look attentively').

history.meaning: spectator, official observer at games or oracles

morphemes.meaning: abstract noun suffix forming domains of thought or practice

théorie.notes: Remember that 'th-' is always pronounced /t/ in French; 'en théorie' ('in theory') is constantly used to contrast idealized plans with chaotic agency reality.
