Initially used in medicine and physics for a medium that carries a substance or force, before generalizing to transport vehicles.

history.meaning: medium of transmission; vehicle, motor car

véhicule.notes: More formal or administrative than voiture ('car'); frequently heard in police, insurance, and film-production logistics (un véhicule de fonction, 'a company car'). The verb véhiculer is very common figuratively: véhiculer une idée / des clichés ('to convey an idea / perpetuate clichés').

rootFamily.gloss: to transport; to convey (an idea or image)
vehicular, used as a lingua franca (langue véhiculaire)
vector, carrier (from the same Latin verb vehere)

vélo.etymology: Late 19th-century apocope (clipping) of vélocipède ('bicycle, velocipede'), a neoclassical compound coined in France in 1818 by inventor Nicéphore Niépce and Baron Karl von Drais from Classical Latin vēlōx, vēlōcis ('swift, rapid, fleet') and pēs, pedis ('foot'), literally 'swift-foot'. As clipping in French regularly truncates after the linking vowel -o-, vélocipède shortened to vélo.

history.meaning: early human-powered wheeled vehicle propelled by the feet

vélo.notes: In contemporary France, vélo is the universal everyday word for 'bicycle' (more common than bicyclette). Note the prepositional rule: faire du vélo ('to ride a bike/go cycling') and aller au travail à vélo ('to go to work by bike').

vérification.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Medieval Latin verificatio ('act of establishing the truth or accuracy of something'), noun of action from verificare ('to make true, confirm, check'), compound of Classical Latin verus ('true') and -ficare (from facere 'to make'). Originally a legal term for registering and authenticating charters, it became the everyday French noun for any check or inspection.
vérification.notes: Pairs with the verb **vérifier** ('to check') and the root of **vrai** ('true') and **vérité** ('truth').

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: vérification

cognates.meaning: from the same Medieval Latin verificatio

vérifier.etymology: Vérifier was borrowed from Medieval Latin verificare ('to make true, confirm to be true', from verus 'true' + facere 'to make').
vérifier.notes: Everyday French verb for 'to check' (*vérifier la cave*, *vérifier l'adresse*).

véritable.etymology: Attested since the 12th century (Old French veritable, 'truthful, sincere, authentic'), formed from vérité ('truth', from Classical Latin vēritātem, accusative of vēritās, from vērus 'true') plus the adjectival suffix -able. Originally describing a person who speaks the truth or a statement that conforms to fact, it came to emphasize that something is a genuine, quintessential exemplar of its kind.

morphemes.meaning: adjectival suffix indicating quality or capacity

véritable.notes: Position matters: placed before a noun, véritable acts as an intensifier meaning 'real, regular, utter, quintessential' (C'est un véritable chef-d'œuvre / un véritable désastre); placed after a noun, it means 'authentic, not counterfeit' (du cuir véritable, 'genuine leather').

véritablement.etymology: Attested from the 12th century (Old French veritablement), formed by adding the adverbial suffix -ment (from the Classical Latin ablative singular mente, 'with a ... mind/manner', from mēns, mentis) to the adjective véritable ('truthful, genuine, real', from vérité, 'truth', from Latin vēritātem).

history.meaning: truth + with a [certain] mind or manner (ablative of mēns)
in accordance with truth, sincerely, truly

morphemes.meaning: adverbial suffix of manner (from Latin mente)

véritablement.notes: Serves as a slightly more elevated, emphatic alternative to vraiment ('really, truly') in persuasive or rhetorical speech—a staple of agents pitching actors or defending contracts in *Dix pour cent*.

rootFamily.gloss: to verify, check (from Medieval Latin verificāre)

vérité.etymology: Inherited or semi-learned adaptation in the 10th–11th century (Old French veritet) from Classical Latin veritas (accusative veritatem 'truth, reality, truthfulness'), derived from verus ('true').

cognates.meaning: vestment, ceremonial garment (borrowed from Old French)

vêtement.etymology: Inherited from Old French vestement ('garment, clothing, priestly vestment'), from Classical Latin vestīmentum ('article of clothing, garment, covering'), derived from the verb vestīre ('to clothe, dress, adorn'), from vestis ('garment, robe, clothing', from Proto-Indo-European *wes- 'to clothe', cognate with English wear). The circumflex in vêtement marks the historical loss of preconsonantal s (vestement > vêtement).

history.meaning: garment, article of clothing, bedclothes (from vestīre 'to dress')
article of clothing, attire, liturgical vestment

vêtement.notes: In singular (un vêtement), it denotes a single 'garment' or 'article of clothing'; in plural (des vêtements), it is the standard register word for 'clothes' (alongside colloquial fringues or habits). Notice how the circumflex in vêtement corresponds to the 's' preserved in English vest and vestment.

rootFamily.gloss: jacket, blazer (borrowed via Italian from the same Latin root vestis)

vôtre.etymology: Inherited (via the stressed Old French form vostre) from Vulgar Latin *voster, reshaped from Classical Latin vester ('your, yours', formed on vos 'you' by analogy with noster 'our').

cognates.meaning: the World Wide Web; spiderweb, woven fabric
to weave (from the same Germanic root)

web.etymology: Borrowed in the early 1990s from English web, clipping of World Wide Web (invented at CERN in 1989–1990 by Tim Berners-Lee and Robert Cailliau). The English noun web derives from Old English webb ('woven fabric, tapestry, cobweb'), from Proto-Germanic *wabją ('web, woven fabric'), from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- ('to weave, braid').

history.meaning: global hypertext information system accessed via the Internet
the Web, the Internet (masculine noun and invariable modifier)

web.notes: Always masculine in French (le Web, naviguer sur le Web). Official French terminology bodies recommended la Toile ('the web/canvas', calquing English web), which is occasionally used in journalism, though le web dominates everyday and industry speech (e.g., une web-série, un site web).

week.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English week, primarily through the compound week-end ('weekend', borrowed into French around 1906) and fashion/media terms like fashion week. English week derives from Middle English weke, from Old English wice, wucu ('seven-day period'), from Proto-Germanic *wikōn ('a turning, succession, change, week'), from Proto-Indo-European *weyk- ('to bend, wind, turn, yield').

history.meaning: seven-day period; end of the working week
weekend (colloquial clipping or in week-end); week (in fashion week)

week.notes: In French, week occurs either as a colloquial spoken clipping or transcription fragment of week-end (le week-end, 'the weekend') or in media/glamour anglicisms such as la Fashion Week de Paris; the standard French word for a seven-day week is la semaine (from Late Latin septimāna).

week-end.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century (attested in French around 1906) from English week-end / weekend, compound of week (Old English wice) + end (Old English ende).

history.meaning: end of the week, Saturday–Sunday break

whisky.etymology: Borrowed in the late 18th century from English whisky, which is an anglicized shortening of Scottish Gaelic uisge-beatha and Irish uisce beatha ('whisky', literally 'water of life'). The Gaelic phrase is a medieval monastic calque of Medieval Latin aqua vītae ('water of life'), the alchemical term for distilled spirits that also inspired French eau-de-vie.

history.meaning: water of life (alchemical term for distilled alcohol)
water of life; distilled grain spirit

whisky.notes: Masculine in French (un whisky). Fascinatingly, whisky is an etymological calque-doublet of native French eau-de-vie ('water of life', fruit brandy): both translate Medieval Latin aqua vitae! In mid-20th-century French photography and cinema sets, Saying 'Whisky !' was also used like English 'Cheese!' to make subjects smile.

rootFamily.gloss: fruit brandy, literally 'water of life' (semantic calque twin)

wi-fi.etymology: Borrowed around 2000 from American English Wi-Fi, a trademark coined in 1999 by the branding firm Interbrand for the Wireless Ethernet Compatibility Alliance (now the Wi-Fi Alliance) as a catchy, consumer-friendly name for the IEEE 802.11 standard. It was modeled phonetically on hi-fi (clipping of high fidelity, from English high + Latin fidēlitās), combining wi- (from wireless) with -fi.

history.meaning: high-quality sound reproduction (model for the rhyming compound)
wireless local area network technology (trademark coined in 1999)

wi-fi.notes: Prescriptively masculine (le wi-fi, short for le réseau wi-fi) according to the Académie française, though feminine la wi-fi (by analogy with la connexion) is frequently heard in casual speech. Pronounced /wi.fi/ in French (rhyming with oui-fi), never /waj.faj/.

rootFamily.gloss: high fidelity audio (hi-fi, the structural model)

wow.etymology: Borrowed in the second half of the 20th century from American English wow (exclamation of surprise, admiration, or excitement), originally attested in early 16th-century Scots (wow, vow) as an expressive, onomatopoeic interjection of wonder or dismay, popularized globally through 20th-century American cinema, comics, and pop culture.

history.meaning: natural exclamation of wonder, surprise, or sorrow
history.stage: Older Scots and Early Modern English

history.meaning: exclamation of strong admiration, excitement, or astonishment; a striking success

wow.notes: In French writing, it appears either in its English spelling wow (especially in scripts, subtitles, and marketing, like l'effet wow, 'the wow factor') or adapted to French phonics as waouh / wahou.

y.etymology: The pronoun y continues Latin hic, here. The Académie records it from the ninth century. It is a different dictionary entry from the name of the letter y.

cognates.meaning: frozen inside hay ('there is' < ha + y)

y.notes: Stands for places (j'y vais 'I'm going there') and inanimate à-phrases (j'y pense 'I'm thinking about it'), and sits at the heart of il y a ('there is/are').

cognates.meaning: hunt; fast light sailing vessel, yacht

yacht.etymology: Borrowed in the late 16th and 17th centuries via English yacht and directly from Early Modern Dutch jacht (clipping of jachtschip, literally 'hunting ship, fast pirate-chasing vessel'), derived from Middle Dutch jacht ('hunt, chase, pursuit'), from the verb jagen ('to hunt, chase, drive swiftly'). After Charles II of England used a Dutch jacht on his restoration in 1660, the vessel became a symbol of royal and aristocratic leisure.

history.meaning: hunt, pursuit; fast light vessel used by the Dutch navy to chase pirates and smugglers
fast sailing vessel used to convey royal or aristocratic passengers; pleasure craft
luxury pleasure boat or racing vessel

yacht.notes: Usually pronounced /jɔt/ in standard French (with a hard /t/ at the end, unlike silent final consonants in native words), and begins with an 'aspirated' y (le yacht, never *l'yacht, and no liaison in les yachts). A staple setting of the Cannes Film Festival in French cinema.

yoga.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century (via English and French orientalist scholarship) from Sanskrit योग (yoga, 'yoking, joining, harnessing, union, concentration, spiritual and ascetic discipline'), derived from the verbal root युज् (yuj, 'to yoke, join, harness, concentrate one's mind'), from Proto-Indo-European *yeug- ('to join, yoke'). Remarkably, Sanskrit yoga is a deep Indo-European cognate of Latin iugum and French joug ('yoke') as well as joindre ('to join').

history.meaning: yoking, harnessing; union, mental concentration, spiritual and bodily discipline
Hindu philosophical system and meditative/postural practice

yoga.notes: Treated as starting with a consonant (no elision or liaison: le yoga, faire du yoga, never *l'yoga). Etymologically, yoga ('yoking/harnessing the mind') comes from the exact same Proto-Indo-European root (*yeug-) as French joug ('yoke') and conjugal ('joined together')!

rootFamily.gloss: yoke (deep Indo-European cognate via Latin iugum)

zen.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from Japanese 禅 (zen, 'meditation, Zen Buddhism'), which is the Sino-Japanese reading of Middle Chinese 禪 (dzyen, shortened from 禪那, 'meditative absorption'), itself a phonetic borrowing of Prakrit jhāṇa and Sanskrit ध्यान (dhyāna, 'meditation, contemplation, thought'), from the Sanskrit root ध्यै (dhyai, 'to think, contemplate, meditate'). In late 20th-century French, zen underwent colloquial conversion into an everyday adjective meaning 'calm, unbothered, stress-free'.

history.meaning: meditative absorption; Chan / Zen school of Mahayana Buddhism
Zen Buddhism; (colloquial adjective) calm, relaxed, unflappable

zen.notes: As an everyday French adjective, zen is invariable in gender and number (Reste zen !, 'Stay calm/chill!'; des personnes très zen). In 1996, pop singer Zazie cemented its colloquial status in France with her hit song 'Zen' ('Restons zen').

rootFamily.gloss: calmness, relaxed attitude (colloquial blend of zen + attitude)

zeste.etymology: First attested in 16th-century French for the thin internal membrane dividing the halves of a walnut shell, and soon applied to the fragrant colored outer peel of a lemon or orange. Its ultimate origin is debated, most plausibly traced by Romance philologists to Latin schistus and Ancient Greek skhistos ('split, cleft, divided'). In late 17th-century kitchens, English borrowed zest directly from French zeste, first for citrus peel used as flavoring and later for lively enthusiasm.

history.meaning: inner membrane of a walnut; thin citrus peel
citrus zest; a tiny dash (un zeste de)

zeste.notes: Figuratively, **un zeste de** means 'a tiny dash or hint of' (**un zeste d'humour**), and English borrowed **zest** directly from French kitchen usage.

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: zeste

zombie.etymology: Entering French via Haitian and Caribbean French Creole zombi (attested in French colonial texts since the late 17th century for a spirit, revenant, or person magically deprived of consciousness) and reinforced in the 20th century by American English cinema (zombie). The Creole word derives from West Central African (Bantu) languages, specifically Kikongo nzambi ('god, supreme spirit') and Kimbundu nzumbi ('ghost, spirit of a dead person, fetish').

history.meaning: ancestral spirit, ghost of the dead, deity
phantom, spirit; person believed to be revived from death in Vodou folklore
undead monster in horror fiction; (figuratively) sleep-deprived or dazed person

zombie.notes: Spelled both zombie (under English cinema influence) and zombi (traditional French spelling promoted by the 1990 orthography rectifications). Figuratively very common: avoir l'air d'un zombie ('to look like a zombie', i.e., exhausted or half-asleep).

rootFamily.gloss: to turn into a zombie, daze, stupefy

zone.etymology: Learned borrowing (attested from the late 13th to 15th centuries in cosmography and geography) from Classical Latin zōna ('belt, girdle; climatic belt of the earth'), borrowed from Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē, 'belt, girdle; latitudinal belt of the terrestrial globe'), formed with the instrumental suffix -νη from the verb ζώννυμι (zōnnymi, 'to gird, put on a belt'), from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₃s- ('to gird'). In the late 19th century, la Zone referred specifically to the non-buildable military perimeter around Paris's fortifications, where impoverished settlements grew.

history.meaning: belt, girdle; one of the five climatic belts of the celestial or terrestrial sphere
climatic belt of the earth; geographical or administrative area, sector

zone.notes: Beyond standard 'area/region' (zone piétonne, zone euro), la zone in colloquial French means 'a rough, run-down suburban area' or 'a chaotic mess' (C'est la zone !), and the verb zoner means 'to hang around aimlessly'—all stemming from the 19th-century slums outside Paris's fortification belt (la Zone non aedificandi)!

rootFamily.gloss: to wander or hang around aimlessly (colloquial)

zut.etymology: Expressive and onomatopoeic interjection first attested in early 19th-century Parisian popular speech (originally meaning 'no!, enough!, go away!' accompanied by a dismissive flick of the hand, and soon 'darn!, shoot!, curses!'). Like earlier French ut! and flute!, it uses a sharp initial sibilant/fricative and a clipped final dental stop /t/ to mimic a sudden snapping gesture or polite deflection of stronger profanities.

history.meaning: expressive interjection of dismissal ('no way!, get lost!') or mild annoyance ('darn!, shoot!')
darn!, shoot!, rats! (mild, polite exclamation of frustration or forgetfulness)

zut.notes: A classic mild, family-friendly exclamation of annoyance ('Darn! Shoot! Oh no!'), often reinforced as Zut alors ! or Flûte ! Because it is completely clean, using zut in adult high-stress environments (like a talent agency crisis) can sound endearingly polite, old-fashioned, or ironic.

rootFamily.gloss: associated with or prone to saying 'zut' (19th-century literary group les Zutiques)

zéro.etymology: Borrowed in 1485–1515 from Italian zero (contracted from zefiro), from Medieval Latin zephirum (introduced by Fibonacci in 1202), adapted from Arabic ṣifr ('empty, nothing, zero'), a calque of Sanskrit śūnya ('void, zero').

à.etymology: À principally continues Latin ad, towards or for. Later spoken Latin extended its grammatical uses into relationships now expressed with à in French. The Académie also identifies a separate source a(b) in some expressions, so not every use has one simple origin.

history.form: ad (with traces of ab in select idioms)

rootFamily.gloss: see you tomorrow / see you soon

à.notes: Carries a grave accent since the 16th century to distinguish the preposition à ('to, at') from the verb form a ('has', 3sg. of avoir).

cognates.meaning: apart, separately (borrowed from Middle French a part)

à part.etymology: Prepositional and adverbial phrase formed in Old French (a part, 'aside, separately, to one side') from the preposition à (from Classical Latin ad, 'to, toward, at') and the noun part ('side, portion, share', from Classical Latin partem, accusative of pars, 'part, side, direction'). Literally 'to [one] side', it evolved from spatial separation ('putting aside') to logical exception ('apart from, except for'). English apart is a direct borrowing of this French phrase.

history.meaning: to one side, aside, in a separate direction
apart, separate; (preposition) apart from, except for

à part.notes: Extremely high-frequency in conversation: À part ça ? ('Aside from that / Otherwise, how are things?'), plaisanterie à part ('joking aside'), and être à part ('to be in a league of one's own / an outsider'). In theater and cinema, un aparté ('an aside' spoken to the audience) comes from the same phrase.

rootFamily.gloss: dramatic aside, private conversation (from Latin a parte)
full, fully-fledged (in the idiom à part entière)

âge.etymology: Âge was formed with the suffix -age from older French aé or ée, continuing Latin aetas, age. The Académie records early forms e(d)age and aage.

morphemes.meaning: lifetime (< Old French aé < Latin aetās)

cognates.meaning: borrowed directly from Old French aage / eage!

rootFamily.gloss: elderly; ... years old (âgé de dix ans)

âge.notes: Masculine in French (Quel âge as-tu? / Quel est votre âge?), and age is expressed with avoir ('to have'): j'ai trente ans.

âgé.etymology: Derived in the 14th century from âge ('age, time of life', Old French aage / eage, from Vulgar Latin *aetaticum, derived from Classical Latin aetas 'time of life, age') + participial adjective suffix -é.

history.meaning: of a specified age; elderly, aged

ça.etymology: In its everyday pronoun use, ça is a shortened or altered form of cela. The Académie dates that use to the seventeenth century. The psychoanalytic noun has a separate later history.
ça.notes: Written with a cedilla (ç) to keep the /s/ sound before a, and distinct from accented adverb çà in çà et là ('here and there' < Latin ecce hāc).

ébrécher.etymology: Formed in the 12th–13th century (Old French esbrechier) from prefix é- (Old French es-, from Latin ex- 'out') + brèche ('breach, gap, notch', borrowed from Frankish *breka 'breaking, gap', from *brekan 'to break').

history.meaning: to chip, notch the edge of a blade or vessel

écart.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 16th century from écarter ('to set apart, separate, move aside'), from Old French escart / esquarter ('to quarter, scatter, set apart'), from Vulgar Latin *exquartare (from ex- + quartus 'fourth').

cognates.meaning: exchange, reciprocal trade (borrowed from Anglo-Norman eschange)

échange.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from the verb échanger ('to exchange, barter, swap'), attested in Old French as eschange ('barter, trade, replacement'). The verb eschangier derives from Vulgar Latin *excambiāre, composed of the prefix ex- ('out of, reciprocally') and Late Latin cambiāre ('to exchange, barter'), itself borrowed from Gaulish *kambion / *kambiō ('to exchange, turn back and forth', from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kamb- 'to bend, curve, turn').

history.meaning: to barter, trade, exchange one thing for another (from Gaulish *kambiō)

morphemes.meaning: out, reciprocally (from Latin ex- via Old French es-)

échange.notes: Masculine noun (un échange). One of the few everyday French and English words (change, exchange) with a genuine Celtic (Gaulish) root rather than Latin! Common in idioms like en échange de ('in exchange for') and un libre-échange ('free trade').

échanger.etymology: Inherited from Old French eschangier ('to exchange, barter'), from Vulgar Latin *excambiare, compound of ex- ('out') + Late Latin cambiare ('to barter, exchange', of Gaulish origin *kambion).

cognates.meaning: to escape, get free (borrowed from Old Northern French escaper)

échapper.etymology: Inherited from Old French eschaper (Central Old French) and escaper (Old Northern French, source of English escape), from Vulgar Latin *excappāre ('to slip out of one's cloak to flee a pursuer, get free'), formed from the privative prefix ex- ('out of') and Late Latin cappa ('hooded cloak, cape'). The vivid underlying image is a captured person slipping out of their cloak—leaving it in the pursuer's hands—in order to run away.

history.meaning: to slip out of one's cloak (cappa) to flee a captor; hence to break free
to get free from captivity or danger, slip away
to escape, get away, elude notice

morphemes.meaning: out of, away from (from Latin ex-)

échapper.notes: Watch the construction carefully: échapper à quelque chose means 'to escape/avoid something before it catches you' (échapper à un danger; Ça m'a échappé, 'That slipped my mind/escaped my notice'), whereas reflexive s'échapper de means 'to break out of captivity or a closed place' (s'échapper de prison). Also note the idiom l'échapper belle ('to have a close call / narrow escape').

rootFamily.gloss: hooded cloak, cape (the literal root garment)

cognates.meaning: check (in chess; restraint; bank check, all from Old French eschec)
check (in chess); failure, setback; plural scacchi 'chess'

échec.etymology: Inherited from Old French eschec ('check!' in chess; plural esches, 'the game of chess'), borrowed via Medieval Latin and Arabic شَاه (šāh) from Classical Persian شاه (šāh, 'king', from Old Persian xšāyaθiya). In chess, calling šāh! warned that the king was under direct attack; the Persian phrase šāh māt ('the king is helpless/ambushed/dead') became Old French eschec et mat (échec et mat, 'checkmate'). From 'being put in check/checkmated', the singular noun developed the general sense of 'setback, defeat, failure, flop' by the 17th century.

history.meaning: king, monarch; 'the king!' (warning call in the game of chess)
check (to the king in chess); plural: the game of chess; obstacle or setback
failure, flop, defeat (singular); chess (plural les échecs)

échec.notes: A remarkable semantic journey from Persian šāh ('king'): in the singular, un échec means 'a failure, setback, or box-office flop' (un échec cuisant, 'a bitter failure'); in the plural, les échecs means 'the game of chess' (jouer aux échecs). English check, checkmate, cheque, and chessboard all come from this French word!

rootFamily.gloss: to fail, run aground (influenced in sense by échec)

échelle.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin scala ('ladder, flight of steps', related to scandere 'to climb'). Spoken Latin added a prosthetic vowel before initial sc- (*escala), yielding Old French eschiele, then échelle.

cognates.meaning: graduated measure; to climb (via Latin scala)

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: échelle (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: échelle

écho.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–14th century from Classical Latin echo, from Ancient Greek ēchō ('reflected sound, personified nymph Echo'), related to ēchē ('sound, ringing noise').

échographie.etymology: Twentieth-century medical neoclassical compound formed from écho- ('echo, reflected sound wave', from Classical Latin ēchō and Ancient Greek ἠχώ, ēkhṓ, 'reflected sound, echo', related to ἦχος, êkhos, 'sound') and -graphie ('writing, recording, imaging', from Ancient Greek -γραφία, -graphía, from γράφω, gráphō, 'to scratch, draw, write'). It denotes medical diagnostic imaging produced by recording the echoes of high-frequency ultrasonic waves bounced off internal tissues or a fetus.

history.meaning: sound, echo + writing, drawing, recording (Greek roots)
medical ultrasound imaging technique and the resulting sonogram image

morphemes.meaning: echo, reflected sound wave (from Greek ēkhṓ)

échographie.notes: The standard everyday French word for an 'ultrasound scan' or 'sonogram' (especially during pregnancy: passer / faire une échographie), often clipped in casual speech to une écho. English prefers 'ultrasound' or 'sonogram', whereas French reserves ultrason for the physical sound wave itself.

rootFamily.gloss: echo, reflected sound; gossip column item in press
relating to ultrasound imaging (e.g., examen échographique)

éclabousser.etymology: Attested in the 16th century (esclabousser 'to spatter with mud or water'), an expressive blend of éclater ('to burst, fly into splinters') and regional/Old French esbousser ('to dirty with mud or dung', from bouse 'cow dung').

history.meaning: to burst/fly + spatter with mire -> to splash, spatter

éclair.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 12th century (Old French esclair) from éclairer ('to flash lightning, light up'), from Vulgar Latin *exclariare ('to make bright, flash'), from ex- + clarus ('bright, clear').

history.meaning: flash of lightning; cream-filled pastry (since c. 1860)

éclairage.etymology: Derived in French from éclairer ("to light up, illuminate") with the collective/action suffix -age. Éclairer continues Old French esclairier ("to shine, dawn, make bright"), from Vulgar Latin *exclariare, an intensive enlargement of Classical Latin exclarare ("to make bright or clear"), composed of ex- ("out, thoroughly") + clarus ("bright, clear, distinct").
éclairage.notes: On a film set (plateau de tournage), l'éclairage refers both to the physical lighting rig and the visual mood crafted by the chef opérateur (cinematographer); figuratively, donner un nouvel éclairage sur une affaire means "to shed new light on a matter".

cognates.meaning: to brighten, clear up, thin out

éclaircir.etymology: Inherited from Old French esclaircir ("to make bright, become clear, explain"), an inchoative reformation in -cir of earlier esclairier, from Vulgar Latin *exclariare / Late Latin *exclaricire, ultimately built on Classical Latin ex- ("out, thoroughly") + clarus ("clear, bright, evident"). The figurative sense of resolving a mystery or misunderstanding developed alongside the literal meteorological sense of skies clearing up.

history.meaning: to brighten, clear up, make intelligible

éclaircir.notes: Distinct from éclairer ("to illuminate with light" or "to inform someone"): one éclaircit un mystère, un point, or un malentendu (clears up a misunderstanding), whereas one éclaire une pièce (lights a room) or éclaire le public (enlightens the audience).

rootFamily.gloss: bright spell, clearing in the clouds

éclairer.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exclariare (alteration of Classical Latin exclarare 'to make bright, illuminate, clarify'), compound of ex- ('out, thoroughly') + clarus ('bright, clear').

éclater.etymology: Inherited from Old French esclater ("to burst, shatter noisily into splinters"), formed either with the Gallo-Romance intensive prefix ex- + Frankish *slaitan ("to split, rend, tear apart", from Proto-Germanic *slaitijaną, causative of *slītaną "to slit, tear") or as an expressive denominative from Old French esclat ("splinter, sharp noise").

history.meaning: to shatter into splinters, burst noisily, resound

éclater.notes: Extremely common in idioms: éclater de rire means "to burst out laughing", éclater en sanglots means "to burst into tears", and colloquial reflexive s'éclater means "to have a blast, have the time of one's life".

école.etymology: Inherited (with prosthetic vowel before initial sc-) from Classical Latin schola ('leisure given to learning, lecture, school'), borrowed from Ancient Greek scholē ('leisure, spare time, philosophical discussion, school').

cognates.meaning: colloquial clipping for ecological or environmentalist
advocate for or specialist in ecology

écolo.etymology: Late 20th-century colloquial clipping (apocope) of écologiste ("environmentalist, ecologist") and écologique ("ecological, eco-friendly"), truncated after the Greco-Roman connecting vowel -o-. Écologie was coined as German Ökologie by biologist Ernst Haeckel in 1866 from Ancient Greek oîkos (οἶκος, "house, dwelling, habitat") + -logía (-λογία, "discourse, study").
écolo.notes: Functions as both an adjective (un tournage écolo, des mesures écolos) and an epicene noun (un/une écolo); standard in everyday spoken French with a friendly, informal register.

cognates.meaning: relating to the economy or thriftiness

économique.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Late Latin oeconomicus ("relating to domestic management or orderly arrangement"), from Ancient Greek oikonomikós (οἰκονομικός, "skilled in managing a household or state, thrifty"), derived from oikonomía ("household management"), a compound of oîkos (οἶκος, "house, estate") + némein (νέμειν, "to manage, distribute, allot").

history.meaning: pertaining to domestic management or rhetorical order
relating to household or public administration and thrift

économique.notes: Unlike English, which distinguishes "economic" (relating to the economy) from "economical" (money-saving, thrifty), French économique covers both senses depending on context (la crise économique vs. un tarif très économique).

cognates.meaning: to listen to internal sounds of the body (learned borrowing)

écoute.etymology: Post-verbal noun derived from écouter ("to listen"), from Old French escouter, esculter ("to listen attentively"), inherited from Vulgar Latin *ascultare (formed by dissimilation of initial au- before the back vowel -u- in the following syllable), from Classical Latin auscultare ("to listen with attention, overhear, heed"), built on an ancient root related to auris ("ear").
écoute.notes: Central to two high-frequency expressions: être à l'écoute (de quelqu'un) means "to be attentive, empathetic, and responsive to someone's needs", while in broadcasting être à l'écoute means "to be tuned in" (and être sur écoute means "to be wiretapped").

rootFamily.gloss: to examine medically by listening (learned doublet)

écouter.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ascultare (dissimilated from Classical Latin auscultare 'to listen attentively, overhear, obey').

écran.etymology: Inherited from Old French escran ('fire-screen, wicker or wooden shield against heat or wind'), borrowed from Middle Dutch scherm or Frankish *skrank / *skirm ('protective barrier, screen, shield').

history.meaning: fireplace heat shield -> projection or display screen

écraser.etymology: Attested in Middle French as escraser ("to shatter, squash, crush flat"), formed from the intensive prefix es- (from Latin ex- "out, thoroughly") + Old French crasir, craser ("to break, smash"), which was borrowed from Old Norse krasa ("to shatter, mash, grind to pieces") or a related Frankish imitative root.
écraser.notes: Beyond physical crushing or running someone over (se faire écraser), it is widely used figuratively for dominating rivals (écraser la concurrence) and in colloquial speech (s'écraser = "to back down, keep quiet, bow to pressure").

écrire.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin scribere ('to scratch, engrave, draw lines, write'), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kreybʰ- ('to scratch, incise').

écriture.etymology: Inherited or semi-learned adaptation in the 11th–12th century (Old French escriture) from Classical Latin scriptura ('writing, composition, scripture'), derived from scriptus, past participle of scribere ('to write').

cognates.meaning: historical clerk, notary, or copyist (borrowed via Anglo-Norman)

écrivain.etymology: Inherited from Old French escrivain ("scribe, copyist, public clerk, author"), from Vulgar Latin *scribanem (accusative of imparisyllabic *scriba, *scribanis), a Late Latin inflectional remodeling of Classical Latin scriba ("public clerk, secretary, scribe"), derived from scribere ("to write, draw lines, incise"), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skreybh- ("to scratch, incise").
écrivain.notes: Historically used as a masculine noun even for women (une femme écrivain), the feminized form une écrivaine—long standard in Quebec and Switzerland—was officially endorsed by the Académie française in 2019 and is now widespread.

écrouler.etymology: Derived in Middle French (escrouler) from the intensive prefix es- (from Latin ex-) + Old French crouler ("to shake, totter, rumble, fall down"), inherited from Vulgar Latin *corrotulare ("to roll together, cause to tumble down"), composed of com- ("together") + rotulare ("to roll"), from Classical Latin rotula ("little wheel", diminutive of rota "wheel").

history.meaning: to shake, totter / to collapse completely

morphemes.meaning: totter, tumble, roll down (from Vulgar Latin *corrotulare)

écrouler.notes: Almost always used pronominally as s'écrouler ("to collapse, crumble, break down in tears or exhaustion"), whereas its unprefixed base crouler survives especially in crouler sous le travail / les dettes ("to be swamped with work / buried in debt").

rootFamily.gloss: to totter, be swamped under (crouler sous)
to roll (distant cognate via Latin rotulare)

cognates.meaning: heartfelt, warm (related via Latin cor, cordis)

écœurer.etymology: Formed in Old and Middle French (escuirer, escœurer) from the privative/intensive prefix é- (from Latin ex- "out of") + cœur ("heart, courage, and by extension the pit of the stomach", from Classical Latin cor, cordis "heart"). Because cœur in older and idiomatic French also referred to the stomach (avoir mal au cœur = "to feel nauseous"), the verb evolved from "to tear the heart out, dishearten" to "to turn one's stomach, nauseate, disgust".

history.meaning: heart, courage, pit of the stomach
to dishearten, break the heart; to nauseate

écœurer.notes: Spelled with the mandatory ligature œ (écœurer); it describes both physical nausea caused by overly rich or sweet food (ce dessert m'écœure) and moral revulsion or bitter disillusionment.

rootFamily.gloss: heart; stomach (in avoir mal au cœur)

écœuré.etymology: Participial adjective from the past participle of écœurer ("to sicken, nauseate, disgust, dishearten"), formed from the prefix é- (from Latin ex- "out of") + cœur ("heart; pit of the stomach", from Classical Latin cor, cordis) + past participle ending -é (from Latin -atum).
écœuré.notes: In European French, être écœuré means to feel sickened, revolted, or bitterly disillusioned (je suis écœuré par son attitude), whereas in informal Quebec French the related adjective écœurant often means "amazing, mind-blowing".

cognates.meaning: to sweeten or cleanse of harsh/acidic substances (learned term)

édulcoré.etymology: Participial adjective from édulcorer ("to sweeten a medicine, remove harshness; figuratively, to tone down or sanitize"), borrowed in the 17th century from New/Medical Latin edulcorare ("to sweeten, wash out salts or acids"), composed of ex- ("out, thoroughly") + Late Latin dulcorare ("to make sweet"), from dulcor ("sweetness"), derived from Classical Latin dulcis ("sweet, pleasant").

history.meaning: to sweeten apothecary preparations, remove harshness

morphemes.meaning: sweetness (from Late Latin dulcor, from dulcis)

édulcoré.notes: A favorite term in cinema and literary criticism (un scénario édulcoré, une version édulcorée) for a script or adaptation that has been sugar-coated, watered down, or sanitized to avoid offending mainstream audiences or producers.

rootFamily.gloss: to sweeten; to tone down, bowdlerize
sweet, soft, gentle (inherited doublet from dulcis)

cognates.meaning: of the same measure, value, or status (borrowed from Latin)

égal.etymology: Inherited from Old French egal, igal, ivel ("level, equal, fair"), partially re-Latinized in spelling and pronunciation after its source, Classical Latin aequalis ("level, even, uniform, equal, of the same age"), derived from aequus ("level, flat, even, fair, just").
égal.notes: Forms its masculine plural as égaux (des droits égaux) and feminine plural as égales; the ubiquitous conversational idiom Ça m'est égal literally means "It is equal to me" ("I don't mind / It's all the same to me").

égaler.etymology: Derived in Old French (igaler, egaler, "to make level, put on the same footing, match") from the adjective egal ("equal, level") + first-conjugation verbal suffix -er, corresponding semantically to Classical Latin aequare ("to make level, equalize, match"), from aequus ("even, level, fair").

history.meaning: to make equal, match in value or rank

égaler.notes: Be careful not to confuse égaler ("to match or rival in quality or achievement", e.g., égaler un record, un talent difficile à égaler) with égaliser ("to smooth out a surface" or, in sports, "to equalize the score").

rootFamily.gloss: to level; to equalize the score in sports

cognates.meaning: state of being equal (borrowed from Old French)

égalité.etymology: Inherited and adapted from Old French igalté, egalité ("evenness, fairness, parity"), remodeled after its source, Classical Latin aequalitatem (accusative of aequalitas, "evenness, uniformity, equality of age or status"), abstract noun derived from aequalis ("level, equal"), from aequus ("even, fair, just").

history.meaning: evenness of surface, uniformity, equality of status

morphemes.meaning: abstract noun suffix of state or quality (from Latin -itatem)

égalité.notes: Alongside its civic prominence in the Republic's motto (Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité), être à égalité means "to be tied / on equal footing" in negotiations, awards, or sports.

égoïste.etymology: Formed in 18th-century French from égoïsme ("egoism, selfishness") by substituting the agentive/adjectival suffix -iste (from Ancient Greek -istēs). Égoïsme was coined in philosophical Modern Latin (egoismus) and French from Classical Latin ego ("I", first-person singular pronoun, from Proto-Indo-European *egh2), initially denoting philosophical solipsism before shifting to moral self-centeredness.

history.meaning: philosophical doctrine referring all things to the self
one who refers everything to oneself; selfish person

égoïste.notes: The diaeresis (tréma) on the ï in égoïste is essential: it indicates that the o and i are pronounced in separate syllables (/e.ɡɔ.ist/) rather than as the French diphthong oi (/wa/).

élan.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in Middle French (eslans, élan) from s'élancer / élancer ("to hurl oneself forward, dart, surge"), from Old French eslancier ("to fling out, lunge"), composed of outward/intensive prefix es- (from Latin ex-) + lancier ("to hurl a lance, fling"), from Late Latin lanceare ("to wield or throw a lance"), from Classical Latin lancea ("light spear, javelin"). (The homonym élan meaning "moose, elk" is an unrelated borrowing from Middle High German elend / Baltic.)

history.meaning: to wield or hurl a lance
to lunge forward / sudden dash, impetus

morphemes.meaning: lunge, hurl (post-verbal stem of élancer, from lancea)

élan.notes: Captures both physical momentum (prendre son élan = "to take a running start") and sudden emotional or creative surge (un élan du cœur, un élan de générosité, couper l'élan de quelqu'un).

rootFamily.gloss: to lunge, dart forward; to throb with pain

cognates.meaning: to make larger, expand (borrowed via Old French enlargier)

élargir.etymology: Inherited from Old French eslargir ("to widen, expand, bestow generously, release from confinement"), a parasynthetic verb formed from prefix es- (from Latin ex- "out") + large ("wide, broad, generous", inherited from Classical Latin largus "abundant, copious, bountiful, broad") + inchoative second-conjugation suffix -ir.

history.meaning: to widen, extend, set free from prison

élargir.notes: Remember the classic false friend: French large means "wide/broad" (not "big" in general), so élargir specifically means "to widen, broaden, expand the scope of" (élargir son public, élargir ses horizons).

rootFamily.gloss: widening, expansion, EU enlargement; release of a prisoner

cognates.meaning: relating to electricity; tense or thrilling

électrique.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th–18th century from New Latin electricus ("resembling amber in its attractive properties, electric"), coined by English physicist William Gilbert in De Magnete (1600) from Classical Latin electrum ("amber; alloy of gold and silver"), from Ancient Greek ēlektron (ἤλεκτρον, "amber; beaming sun"), because rubbed amber attracts light particles through static electricity.

history.meaning: having amber's property of attracting light bodies when rubbed

électrique.notes: Often used figuratively in production offices and on film sets (L'ambiance est électrique sur le plateau, il y a de l'électricité dans l'air) to describe an atmosphere crackling with tension, rivalry, or excitement.

rootFamily.gloss: electroshock; salutary wake-up call or jolt

cognates.meaning: to remove, exclude, get rid of

éliminer.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin eliminare ("to turn out of doors, banish, expel beyond the threshold"), a transparent spatial compound of ex- ("out of") + limen, liminis ("threshold, doorway, lintel") + first-conjugation verbal suffix -are.

history.meaning: to thrust out beyond the threshold, banish from the house

éliminer.notes: Shares the Latin root limen ("threshold") with préliminaire ("before the threshold") and subliminal ("below the threshold of consciousness")—so éliminer literally means "to put someone out across the doorstep".

rootFamily.gloss: introductory, placed at the threshold of a text

cognates.meaning: speech or tribute of praise, especially for the deceased

élogieux.etymology: Derived in Modern French from éloge ("praise, tribute, commendation") + adjectival suffix -ieux (from Latin -iosus "full of"). Éloge was borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin elogium ("short inscription on a statue or tomb, maxim"), reshaped in meaning through confluence with Ancient Greek eulogía (εὐλογία, "good speech, praise, panegyric", from eû "well" + lógos "word, speech").

morphemes.meaning: praise, tribute (from éloge, Latin elogium / Greek eulogía)

élogieux.notes: Unlike English eulogy (mostly restricted to funeral tributes unless qualified as éloge funèbre), French éloge and élogieux apply to any high praise or glowing press review (des critiques très élogieuses = "rave reviews").

cognates.meaning: to move away, distance (built on lontano)
archaic legal term: to remove goods to a distance (borrowed from Old French)

éloigner.etymology: Inherited from Old French esloignier ("to move away, distance, keep afar"), from Vulgar Latin *exlongiare, a parasynthetic verb built on Classical Latin ex- ("out, away") + longe ("far off, at a distance"), adverb of longus ("long, distant").

history.meaning: to put at a distance, remove far away
to move away, depart, keep at a distance

morphemes.meaning: far, distant (from Latin longe; compare loin)

éloigner.notes: Used both transitively (éloigner un importun = "to keep an unwanted person away") and reflexively (s'éloigner du sujet = "to stray from the topic", s'éloigner de quelqu'un = "to grow distant from someone").

cognates.meaning: grace, refinement of style or taste

élégance.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin elegantia ("taste, propriety, refinement, grace"), abstract noun derived from elegans, elegantis ("choice, select, tasteful, fastidious"), originally an active participial derivative of eligere ("to pick out, select carefully, choose"), from ex- ("out") + legere ("to gather, choose, read").

history.meaning: fastidious taste, refinement, grace of style
grace of style, refinement of manners and dress

élégance.notes: Etymologically cousin to élire ("to elect/choose"): elegance originally meant discerning selectivity; in modern French, avoir l'élégance de faire quelque chose also means having the moral class or grace to behave nobly.

rootFamily.gloss: lack of grace, tactlessness, bad form
to elect, choose (inherited doublet from Latin eligere)

élégant.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin elegantem (accusative of elegans, "choice, tasteful, refined, fastidious"), formed on the stem of eligere ("to pick out, select"), from ex- ("out") + legere ("to gather, select, read"). In Early Latin, elegans was a reproach ("overly picky, foppish"), before shifting in Classical Latin to high praise ("of discerning taste, graceful").

history.meaning: refined in dress, speech, or bearing

élégant.notes: Describes both sartorial chic (une silhouette élégante) and ethical fairness or courtesy in interpersonal dealings (Ce n'est pas très élégant de sa part = "That's not very classy/gracious of him").

rootFamily.gloss: to elect, choose (from the same Latin verb eligere)

cognates.meaning: act of sending out or discharging (heat, light, gas)
emission, issue; radio or TV broadcast

émission.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Classical Latin emissionem (accusative of emissio, "a sending out, hurling, release"), action noun from emittere ("to send out, let go, hurl, publish"), composed of ex- ("out") + mittere ("to send, let go, release"). In the 20th century, the technical radio sense of "transmitting waves" specialized into "radio or television broadcast/show".

history.meaning: to send out, let go, hurl, publish
sending out (of fluids, currency, radio waves); broadcast program

morphemes.meaning: send, release (supine stem of Latin mittere)
action or result noun suffix (from Latin -ionem)

émission.notes: While émission retains its scientific and financial senses (émission de carbone, émission d'actions), in everyday French une émission (de télé / de radio) is the standard word for a TV or radio show, talk show, or program.

rootFamily.gloss: to emit, issue, broadcast, voice an opinion

émotif.etymology: Coined in 19th-century French from the learned stem of émotion / Classical Latin emotus (past participle of emovere "to move out, stir up, agitate") + adjectival suffix -if (from Latin -ivus), modeled on pairs such as commotion / commotif and locomotion / locomotif.

history.meaning: to move out, stir up, agitate
relating to emotion; prone to strong emotional reactions

morphemes.meaning: adjectival suffix indicating tendency or relation (from Latin -ivus)

émotif.notes: Distinguish three adjectives that English often translates as "emotional": émotif (describes a person's temperament: easily moved, sensitive, high-strung), émotionnel (describes an abstract category: un choc émotionnel), and émouvant (describes something moving/touching: un discours émouvant).

cognates.meaning: strong feeling or affective state (borrowed from French)

émotion.etymology: Formed in Middle French (esmotion, émotion, originally meaning "popular uprising, civil commotion, disturbance") after mouvoir / émouvoir ("to stir up, set in motion"), modeled on Classical Latin motio, motionis ("movement, agitation") from emovere (ex- "out, thoroughly" + movere "to move, stir, shake"). The psychological sense of "inward affective stirring or feeling" developed in 16th–17th-century French and was borrowed into English and other European languages.

history.meaning: to move out, stir up, shake, agitate
popular uprising, social tumult; inward agitation of the soul
affective state, strong feeling or reaction

morphemes.meaning: noun suffix of action or state (from Latin -ionem)

émotion.notes: Originally a political word for a riot or public uprising (une émotion populaire) before shifting inward to the stirring of the heart; English emotion is a direct borrowing from this French innovation.

rootFamily.gloss: emotional (relating to emotions as a domain)
emotional, sensitive, easily moved (of a person)

ému.etymology: Participial adjective from the past participle of émouvoir ("to move, touch, stir up"), inherited from Old French esmovoir (past participle esmeu, "stirred up, set in motion, agitated"), from Vulgar Latin *exmovere, a remodeling of Classical Latin emovere ("to move out, shake, stir up"), composed of ex- ("out, thoroughly") + movere ("to move").

history.meaning: to move out, shake, stir up
to set in motion, agitate, stir emotionally

morphemes.meaning: moved (past participle of mouvoir, from Vulgar Latin *movutus)

ému.notes: Orthographic trap: although the simple verb mouvoir takes a circumflex in its masculine singular past participle (mû) to distinguish it from mu, the prefixed participle ému (along with émue, émus, émues) never takes a circumflex accent.

cognates.meaning: capacity for vigorous activity or work

énergie.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French from Late Latin energia ("force of expression, vividness, active vigor"), from Ancient Greek enérgeia (ἐνέργεια, "activity, operation, efficacy, actuality"), coined by Aristotle from energós (ἐνεργός, "active, at work, effective"), a compound of en- ("in, within") + érgon (ἔργον, "work, deed, action", from Proto-Indo-European *wergom "work").

history.meaning: activity, operation, actuality (as opposed to potentiality)
force of rhetorical expression, active vigor
force in action, spiritual or physical potency

énergie.notes: The Greek root érgon ("work") is an Indo-European cognate of English work and appears across French compounds such as ergonomie ("work-law"), synergie ("working together"), and chirurgie ("hand-work", i.e. surgery).

rootFamily.gloss: ranting fanatic, wild person (originally 'possessed by an active spirit')

cognates.meaning: false friend: to weaken, sap of strength or vitality
to weaken; in modern usage also to irritate, get on one's nerves

énerver.etymology: Borrowed in Middle French (enerver, originally "to weaken, sap strength, deprive of sinews") from Classical Latin enervare ("to cut the sinews from, weaken, render powerless"), composed of privative ex- ("out, away") + nervus ("sinew, tendon, nerve, vigor") + -are. In the 19th century, as nerf came to be understood primarily as a sensory/emotional nerve rather than a muscular tendon, énerver shifted from "to sap strength" to "to overstimulate the nerves, irritate, annoy".

history.meaning: to remove the sinews, weaken, sap of vigor
to weaken, debilitate, deprive of force
to fray the nerves, irritate, annoy

énerver.notes: A classic false friend with English enervate: while English enervate preserves the Classical Latin meaning ("to drain of energy, weaken"), modern French énerver means "to annoy, irritate" and reflexive s'énerver means "to get worked up, lose one's temper".

énigme.etymology: Learned Renaissance borrowing from Classical Latin aenigma, itself from Ancient Greek aínigma ('riddle, dark saying'), derived from ainíssomai ('to speak in hints', from aînos 'meaningful tale').

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: énigme (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: énigme

énigme.notes: Watch the gender: although Latin *aenigma* was neuter, **une énigme** settled in modern French as a feminine noun.

cognates.meaning: extremely large; borrowed via Middle French

énorme.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin ēnormis ("out of rule, irregular, immoderate, immense"), formed from the prefix ē- (variant of ex-, "out of") and norma ("carpenter's square, rule, standard"). Originally meaning "deviating from the norm", it shifted to "immense in size" and in modern colloquial French "fantastic or unbelievable".

morphemes.meaning: rule, standard, carpenter's square (from Latin norma)

énorme.notes: In spoken French and agency banter, "C'est énorme !" is a constant enthusiastic exclamation meaning "That's incredible / wild / hilarious!", not just physically large.

énormément.etymology: Formed in the 15th century from the adjective énorme ('outside the norm, immense, huge', borrowed from Classical Latin enormis, from ex- 'out of' + norma 'carpenter's square, rule') + the adverbial suffix -ment.

épais.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin spissus ('thick, dense, crowded, compact, slow').

épanouir.etymology: Inherited from Old French espanir, later enlarged to espanoïr ("to open up, spread out, blossom") on the pattern of verbs in -ouir, from Vulgar Latin *expandīre, a reshaping of Classical Latin expandere ("to spread out, unfold"), composed of ex- ("out") and pandere ("to spread, stretch").

history.meaning: to open up, blossom, spread forth
to cause to bloom; reflexively, to flourish or thrive

épanouir.notes: Most often used reflexively (s'épanouir) to describe personal or artistic fulfillment ("to blossom, thrive, come into one's own").

épaule.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin spatula ('broad flat blade, shoulder-blade, shoulder of an animal'), diminutive of Classical Latin spatha ('broad flat wooden blade, paddle, broadsword', from Ancient Greek spathē).

history.meaning: broad blade -> small flat blade, shoulder-blade

cognates.meaning: utter ruin or loss (from the same Latin root perdere)

éperdument.etymology: Formed in Old and Middle French from éperdu ("bewildered, beside oneself with emotion") and the adverbial suffix -ment. Éperdu is the past participle of the obsolete Old French verb esperdre ("to lose completely, ruin, bewilder"), an intensive compound of es- (from Latin ex-, "utterly") and perdre (from Latin perdere, "to lose, destroy").
éperdument.notes: Almost exclusively used in high-intensity romantic collocations such as "amoureux éperdument" or "aimer éperdument" ("to love madly / head over heels").

épicerie.etymology: Derived in the 13th–14th century (Old French espicerie) from épice ('spice', inherited from Late Latin species 'wares, spices, drugs') or épicier ('spice merchant, grocer') + suffix -erie.

épicier.etymology: Derived in the 12th–13th century (Old French espicier 'apothecary, merchant of spices and drugs', or from Medieval Latin speciarius) from épice ('spice', inherited from Late Latin species 'goods, spices, kinds', Classical Latin 'appearance, sort').

history.meaning: kind, sort -> spices, drugs -> spice dealer

éponge.etymology: Inherited via Old French esponge from Latin spongia, borrowed from Ancient Greek spongía ('sea sponge'). Gallo-Romance added a vowel before initial sp- (*ispongia -> esponge -> éponge).

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: éponge (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: éponge

éponge.notes: Initial **é-** regularly corresponds to English *s-* before *p, t, c* (**éponge** / *sponge*, **étoile** / *stellar*, **école** / *school*).

époque.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century from Medieval/Modern Latin epocha, from Ancient Greek epochē ('cessation, fixed point in time from which years are reckoned, astronomical position'), derived from epechein ('to hold back, stop, pause').

history.meaning: to pause, check -> fixed reference point in time

cognates.meaning: to marry; to adopt or support a cause (from Old French)

épouser.etymology: Inherited from Old French esposer ("to marry, wed"), from Late and Ecclesiastical Latin spōnsāre ("to betroth, give in marriage"), derived from Classical Latin spōnsus ("bridegroom, betrothed"), originally the past participle of spondēre ("to pledge solemnly, promise in marriage").

history.meaning: to pledge solemnly, promise in marriage

morphemes.meaning: spouse, betrothed (from Latin spōnsus with prosthetic é-)

épouser.notes: Grammar alert: unlike "se marier avec", "épouser" takes a direct object with no preposition ("épouser quelqu'un"); figuratively, it also means "to embrace a cause" or "to hug the contours of a shape".

cognates.meaning: to puff, pant, get out of breath

époustouflé.etymology: Past participle adjective of époustoufler ("to take someone's breath away, astound"), attested in the mid-19th century as an expressive alteration (likely via Provençal espoufar, "to puff, pant", crossed with étouffer, "to suffocate") of earlier French épouffer ("to put out of breath"), built on the onomatopoeic root pouf representing a burst of breath.

history.meaning: to puff, pant, lose one's breath
to knock the wind out of, astound

morphemes.meaning: expressive stem evoking puffing or knocking the breath out

époustouflé.notes: Once playful 19th-century slang, "époustouflé" ("blown away") and "époustouflant" ("breathtaking") are now ubiquitous in film reviews and celebrity praise.

épreuve.etymology: Post-verbal noun derived in Old French (esprueve, esprove) from the verb esprover (Modern French éprouver, "to test, put to the proof, experience"), from Late Latin exprobāre (re-analyzed in Gallo-Romance as "to test thoroughly"), composed of ex- ("out, thoroughly") and probāre ("to test, examine, judge the worth of", from probus, "good, genuine").

history.meaning: to put to the test, experience

épreuve.notes: Covers a wide range of "tests": a personal hardship ("traverser une épreuve"), an exam paper or Olympic event, and a printer's or photographer's proof ("épreuve").

cognates.meaning: water well, shaft (from the shared Latin root puteus)
well, pit, shaft (from the shared Latin root puteus)

épuisant.etymology: Present participle adjective of épuiser ("to drain dry, exhaust"), formed from Old French espuisier ("to empty a well by drawing out all its water") and the participial suffix -ant. Ultimately built on es- (Latin ex-, "out of") and puits ("well", from Classical Latin puteus, "well, pit").

history.meaning: to empty a water well completely
to drain of resources or strength, exhaust

morphemes.meaning: well, water shaft (from puits, Latin puteus)

épuisant.notes: Preserves the vivid metaphor of drawing water from a well ("puits") until it runs bone-dry, making it the exact semantic match for English "draining".

cognates.meaning: well, cistern (from the same Latin noun puteus)
well, shaft (from the same Latin noun puteus)

épuiser.etymology: Inherited from Old French espuisier ("to empty a well, draw all the water out"), derived from the prefix es- (from Latin ex-, "out of") and puisier (Modern French puiser, "to draw water from a well"), itself from puis (Modern French puits, "well"), inherited from Classical Latin puteus ("well, pit, cistern").

history.meaning: to draw water from a well
to drain a well dry; to wear out completely

épuiser.notes: Notice the contrast with its base verb: "puiser" means to draw water or inspiration from a rich source, whereas adding "é-" ("épuiser") means to drain that source dry.

rootFamily.gloss: to draw water or inspiration from

cognates.meaning: well, shaft (from the shared Latin root puteus)
well, shaft (from the shared Latin root puteus)

épuisé.etymology: Past participle adjective of épuiser ("to drain dry, exhaust"), from Old French espuisié ("emptied of water"), formed from es- (Latin ex-, "out") and puisier ("to draw water from a well", from Latin puteus, "well, pit"). It evolved from "drained of water" to "physically or mentally worn out" and, in commerce, "out of stock or out of print".

history.meaning: depleted of strength or stock, exhausted

épuisé.notes: Besides describing an overworked agent ("Je suis épuisé", "I'm wiped out"), "épuisé" is the standard retail and publishing term for "sold out" or "out of print".

équipe.etymology: Post-verbal noun formed in the 15th century ('line of barges towed together, work gang') from équiper ('to fit out a ship, supply'), derived from Old French eschipre / esquif, from Old Norse skipa ('to man or fit out a ship', from skip 'ship').

history.meaning: ship -> to man/fit out a vessel
fitted boat crew, work gang -> team, crew

équitation.etymology: Équitation is a sixteenth-century borrowing from imperial Latin equitatio, horse riding. Its history is a specific Latin borrowing rather than a generic story inferred from the French ending.

cognates.meaning: learned borrowings from the same Latin family

équitation.notes: While everyday French replaced Classical equus with cheval (< caballus), formal sports vocabulary borrowed équitation ('faire de l'équitation') directly from Latin.

cognates.meaning: relating to sexual desire or passion

érotique.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Ancient Greek erōtikós (ἐρωτικός, "of or caused by passionate love"), derived from érōs (ἔρως, genitive érōtos, "sexual passion, desire, love", personified as the god Eros) and the relational adjectival suffix -ikós.

history.meaning: pertaining to passionate desire or Eros
relating to love poetry or amorous passion

érotique.notes: In French cinema and literary criticism, "érotique" carries an aesthetic, artistic register carefully distinguished from "pornographique".

étage.etymology: Étage comes from Old French estage ('dwelling, floor level', from Vulgar Latin *staticum, built on stare 'to stand' — a 'standing level'). English 'stage' was borrowed from Old French estage.
étage.notes: Remember French floor numbering: **le rez-de-chaussée** = ground floor, **le premier étage** = one flight up.

étagère.etymology: Eighteenth-century derivative of étage ('storey, tier, level', from Old French estage 'standing place, level', built on Latin stare 'to stand'): originally an open piece of furniture with stacked tiers of shelves, then any individual shelf.

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: étagère (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: étagère

étanche.etymology: Inherited via Old French estanche ('watertight, stopping the flow of liquid') from the verb estanchier (Modern French étancher, 'to staunch a flow, quench thirst'). The verb likely descends from Vulgar Latin *stanticare ('to bring to a standstill, stop a leak'), derived from Classical Latin stare, stantem ('to stand firm'). The initial é- with acute accent reflects the regular loss of Old French s before t.

history.meaning: to make stand still, stop a flow

étanche.notes: English borrowed Old French **estanchier / estanche** as the verb **to staunch** (a flow) and the adjective **staunch** ('watertight, steadfast')!

sources.title: Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: étanche

état.etymology: Borrowed and adapted in the 12th–13th century (Old French estat) from Classical Latin status ('standing, posture, condition, rank, public order'), action noun from stare ('to stand').

history.meaning: state, condition, social estate, body politic

éteindre.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *extingere (reshaped from Classical Latin exstinguere 'to quench, put out a fire, wipe out'), compound of ex- ('out') + stinguere ('to quench, prick out').

history.meaning: to quench, put out a flame
to extinguish, put out, switch off

cognates.meaning: infinite or unending time (from Old French)

éternité.etymology: Borrowed in Old French (eternité, 12th century) from Classical Latin aeternitās (accusative aeternitātem, "eternity, endless duration"), derived from aeternus ("eternal, everlasting"), itself a contraction of earlier Latin aeviternus, from aevum ("age, eon, lifetime", from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyu-, "vital force, long time").

history.meaning: lifetime, eon; lasting for an age

morphemes.meaning: abstract noun suffix of state or quality (from Latin -itātem)

éternité.notes: Used constantly as an everyday hyperbole with the indefinite article: "Ça fait une éternité qu'on ne s'est pas vus !" ("It's been ages / forever since we last met!").

rootFamily.gloss: to drag on forever; to immortalize

cognates.meaning: the act of sneezing (learned borrowing from Latin)

éternuer.etymology: Inherited from Old French esternuer ("to sneeze"), from Vulgar Latin *sternūāre, a Gallo-Romance reshaping of Classical Latin sternūtāre (frequentative of sternuere, "to sneeze"), ultimately from an imitative Proto-Indo-European root *pster- echoing the sound of a sneeze.

morphemes.meaning: to sneeze (from Latin sternuere with prosthetic é-)

éternuer.notes: The initial "é-" here is not the Latin prefix "ex-", but a phonetic support vowel added in Old French before Latin "st-" clusters (followed by dropping the "s", as in "étoile" from "stēlla").

étiquette.etymology: From Middle French estiquette ('small pointed peg or paper slip stuck onto a courtroom sack of legal files'), derived from Old French estiquier ('to stick, pierce'), borrowed from Frankish *stikkan ('to prick, stick fast').

history.meaning: identifying label pinned to a file bag; court protocol card

cognates.meaning: ticket and etiquette both come from French étiquette!

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: étiquette (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: étiquette

étiquette.notes: Written slips (**étiquettes**) listing ceremonial rules at royal courts gave Europe the word **etiquette**, while earlier Middle French **estiquet** gave English **ticket**.

étoile.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *stēla (with long ē, altered from Classical Latin stella 'star'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr ('star').

étoilé.etymology: Formed in Old French (esteilé, estoilé, "studded with stars") from étoile ("star") and the adjectival suffix -é ("adorned with, shaped like"). Étoile descends from Old French esteile, from Late Latin stēla (Classical Latin stēlla, "star"), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr ("star").

morphemes.meaning: star (from Latin stēlla with prosthetic é-)
adjectival suffix meaning covered with or shaped like

étoilé.notes: Beyond "une nuit étoilée" ("a starry night"), in modern France "un chef étoilé" or "un restaurant étoilé" specifically denotes a Michelin-starred chef or restaurant.

rootFamily.gloss: to stud with stars; to crack in a star pattern

étonnamment.etymology: Formed in the 18th–19th century from the adjective étonnant ('astonishing, surprising', present participle of étonner) + the adverbial suffix -ment (with assimilation of -nt + -ment to -mment).

étonnant.etymology: Present participle used as an adjective (since the 16th century) of étonner ('to stun as if by thunder, astonish, surprise'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *extonare (Classical Latin attonare 'to strike with thunder, stun', from tonare 'to thunder').

history.meaning: to stun -> to astonish -> astonishing, surprising

cognates.meaning: to stew, braise; to bore or tire out
to braise, stew in a closed pot

étouffer.etymology: Inherited from Old French estouffer / estofer ("to suffocate, choke"), from Vulgar Latin *extūfāre, formed from Latin ex- and Late Latin tūfa / tūfus, borrowed from Ancient Greek tŷphos (τῦφος, "smoke, vapor, steam, stupor"), evolving from "to choke with thick fumes or steam" to "to suffocate, stifle, or hush up".

history.meaning: to choke with steam or fumes

morphemes.meaning: stifling vapor or heat (from Greek tŷphos)

étouffer.notes: In media, politics, and talent agencies, "étouffer une affaire" or "étouffer un scandale" is the go-to idiom for "to hush up / cover up a scandal".

étrange.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin extraneus ('external, foreign, from outside, strange'), derived from extra ('outside, beyond').

étranger.etymology: Derived in the 12th century (Old French estrangier) from Old French estrange ('foreign, from outside', modern étrange, from Classical Latin extraneus) + suffix -ier, taking over the sense 'foreign, foreigner, stranger' as étrange specialized to 'odd'.

cognates.meaning: to stroke, hit, level off grain with a strickle

étriqué.etymology: Past participle adjective of étriquer, borrowed in the 17th–18th century from Northern and Picard dialectal French estriquer ("to make narrow, tighten, trim down"), from Middle Dutch striken ("to stroke, smooth down, pull taut, level off"), originally describing garments cut too scantily before broadening to cramped spaces and petty minds.

history.meaning: to smooth down, draw tight, level off
to trim down, cut too scantily or tightly

morphemes.meaning: to pull tight or trim scantily (from Germanic striken with prosthetic é-)

étriqué.notes: Used both physically for tight clothes or tiny Parisian flats ("un costume / salon étriqué") and figuratively for petty, conventional thinking ("un esprit étriqué").

rootFamily.gloss: to make too narrow or scanty
in a cramped or narrow manner
strickle used to level grain in a measure (dialectal)

étroit.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin strictus ('drawn tight, compressed, narrow, close'), past participle of stringere ('to draw tight, bind, squeeze'; doublet of learned strict).

history.meaning: to bind tight -> drawn together, narrow

étudiant.etymology: Substantivized present participle of étudier ("to study"), attested from 13th-century Old French estudiant ("university scholar"), reinforced by Medieval Latin studiāns (genitive studiantis), ultimately derived from Classical Latin studium ("zeal, eagerness, painstaking application, study").

history.meaning: zeal, study; one applying oneself to learning

morphemes.meaning: to study, apply oneself (from Latin studium)
present participle and agentive noun suffix

étudiant.notes: Usage distinction: in France, "étudiant(e)" is reserved for university and higher-education students, whereas primary, middle, and high school pupils are called "élèves".

cognates.meaning: to apply the mind to learning (borrowed from Old French)

étudier.etymology: Semi-learned formation in 12th-century Old French (estudier, "to apply oneself, study") from Medieval Latin studiāre ("to pursue learning"), derived from Classical Latin studium ("eagerness, zeal, devotion, intellectual pursuit"), which comes from the verb studēre ("to be eager, be diligent, strive after").

history.meaning: to be eager, strive; zeal, intellectual pursuit
to apply oneself to learning, study

morphemes.meaning: zeal, study (from Latin studium with prosthetic é-)

étudier.notes: In professional and agency settings, "étudier une proposition" or "étudier un scénario" means "to review, examine, or consider a proposal or script carefully".

rootFamily.gloss: studio (borrowed from Italian, from the same Latin root)

étui.etymology: Deverbal noun from Old French estuier ('to enclose safely, treasure, keep with care'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *studiare ('to tend zealously to', from Classical Latin studium 'care, zeal').

history.meaning: to sheathe safely -> protective fitted case

cognates.meaning: learned cousin from the same Latin studium

sources.title: CNRTL / TLFi Étymologie: étui (citing Bloch-Wartburg & FEW)
Littré — Dictionnaire de la langue française: étui

étui.notes: Unlike a boxy **boîte**, **un étui** follows the shape of the treasured object inside (**un étui à violon**, **un étui à lunettes**).

été.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin aestas, accusative aestatem ('summer, summer heat'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- ('to burn, glow'). (Homonymous past participle été 'been' comes from Vulgar Latin *essitus / Classical Latin status.)

cognates.meaning: to empty out, clear a place of people

évacuer.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century (originally in medical usage for purging bodily humors) from Classical Latin ēvacuāre ("to empty out, hollow out, clear"), formed from ē- (variant of ex-, "out") and vacuāre ("to make empty"), derived from vacuus ("empty, unoccupied, devoid").

history.meaning: empty; to empty out, clear away
to purge humors, empty out, clear a garrison
to evacuate a building; to release stress or dismiss an issue

évacuer.notes: Very common in everyday psychological expressions: "évacuer le stress" or "évacuer la pression" ("to let off steam, release tension") and "évacuer une question" ("to brush aside a question").

cognates.meaning: to disappear suddenly (borrowed from Old French esvaniss-)

évanouissement.etymology: Derived in Old and Middle French (esvanuissement) from the verb s'évanouir ("to vanish, fade away; to faint") and the action-noun suffix -ement. Évanouir descends from Vulgar Latin *exvānīre, remodeled after Classical Latin ēvānēscere ("to vanish into thin air, pass away, die out"), from ē- ("out") and vānus ("empty, void, unsubstantial").

history.meaning: to vanish into thin air, fade away
to disappear; to lose consciousness, swoon

morphemes.meaning: nominal suffix denoting an action or state

évanouissement.notes: Shares its exact root with English "vanish": in French, fainting ("s'évanouir") literally pictures consciousness vanishing into thin air (and "s'évanouir dans la nature" still means "to vanish without a trace").

rootFamily.gloss: to faint, pass out; to vanish into thin air

évidemment.etymology: Formed in Middle French from the adjective évident ("obvious, plain to see") and the adverbial suffix -ment. Following the regular phonetic law of French adverbs built on Latin -entem stems, the vowel and nasal consonant assimilate to -emment (pronounced /a.mɑ̃/). Évident comes from Classical Latin ēvidēns ("visible, manifest"), from ē- ("out") and vidēre ("to see").

history.meaning: obvious, clear to the eye or mind

morphemes.meaning: adverbial suffix for adjectives ending in -ent (from -ent + -ment)

évidemment.notes: Pronunciation and nuance alert: the "-emment" ending is pronounced "-amment" (/e.vi.da.mɑ̃/), and "Évidemment !" means "Obviously! / Of course!", whereas English "evidently" is more tentative ("apparently").

rootFamily.gloss: to see (inherited from the same Latin verb vidēre)

cognates.meaning: proof, factual grounds (false friend in modern usage)

évidence.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin ēvidentia ("clearness, distinctness, vivid rhetorical illustration"), derived from ēvidēns ("plain to see, manifest"), formed from the prefix ē- (variant of ex-, "out, thoroughly") and vidēns, present participle of vidēre ("to see").
évidence.notes: Major false friend: in French, "une évidence" means "an obvious truth / a no-brainer" ("se rendre à l'évidence" = "to face the obvious facts"), whereas legal or police "evidence" is "des preuves" or "des indices".

évident.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th–14th century from Classical Latin ēvidēns (accusative ēvidentem, "visible, apparent, manifest, plain to see"), formed from ē- (variant of ex-, "out, clearly") and vidēns, the present participle of vidēre ("to see", from Proto-Indo-European *weyd-, "to see, know").
évident.notes: Idiomatic gem: in the negative, "Ce n'est pas évident" almost always means "It's not easy / It's quite tricky", rather than literally "It's not obvious".

éviter.etymology: Borrowed in the 14th century from Classical Latin evitare ('to shun, avoid, escape from'), compound of ex- ('out of, away') + vitare ('to shun, avoid').

cognates.meaning: to develop gradually, unfold (from Latin ēvolvere)

évoluer.etymology: Back-formed in the 19th century (first for military and dance movements, then biological and general development) from the noun évolution, borrowed in the 16th century from Classical Latin ēvolūtiō ("the unrolling of a papyrus scroll"), from ēvolvere ("to unroll, unfold"), composed of ē- ("out") and volvere ("to roll, turn").

history.meaning: to unroll a scroll; the unrolling of a book roll
tactical troop maneuver; gradual unfolding or development
to move in formation; to develop, change, or evolve

morphemes.meaning: to roll, turn, unfold (from Latin volvere)

évoluer.notes: Beyond meaning "to change or develop over time", "évoluer dans un milieu" means "to move in or operate within a social/professional sphere" (e.g., "évoluer dans le milieu du cinéma").

rootFamily.gloss: volume (originally a rolled scroll, from Latin volvere)

cognates.meaning: to bring a feeling, memory, or image to mind

évoquer.etymology: Borrowed in the 12th–14th century from Classical Latin ēvocāre ("to call out, summon forth, conjure up deities or spirits of the dead"), formed from ē- (variant of ex-, "out, forth") and vocāre ("to call"), itself derived from vōx (genitive vōcis, "voice").

history.meaning: to call forth, summon spirits or witnesses
to summon a spirit or legal case; to call to mind, mention

morphemes.meaning: to call, voice (from Latin vocāre / vōx)

évoquer.notes: In French news and office meetings, "évoquer" is used far more broadly than English "evoke" and often simply means "to mention, bring up, or discuss a topic" ("évoquer un contrat").

événementiel.etymology: Derived in 20th-century French from événement ("event, occurrence") and the relational adjectival suffix -iel. Événement was adapted in the 15th century (with suffix substitution of -ement) from Classical Latin ēventus ("outcome, result, occurrence"), from ēvenīre ("to come out, happen, come to pass"), composed of ē- ("out") and venīre ("to come").

history.meaning: to come out, happen; outcome, occurrence
event-based; relating to event planning and PR

morphemes.meaning: nominal suffix of action or result

événementiel.notes: Coined by historian Fernand Braudel ("histoire événementielle", surface-level history of events) and now used constantly as a masculine noun ("l'événementiel") for the events, gala, and PR industry.

être.etymology: Être combines two historical sources. Its main line is Latin esse through reconstructed popular Latin *essere. Forms such as étant, été and étais also continue Old French estere, from Latin stare, meaning to stand or remain.

history.meaning: to stand or remain; from Latin stare

être.notes: Être is highly irregular. It forms compound tenses with reflexive verbs and with verbs such as aller, venir and partir. Many other verbs of movement use avoir, so learn the auxiliary with the verb.

île.etymology: Inherited from Old French isle ("island"), from Vulgar Latin *īsula / *īsla, a syncopated spoken form of Classical Latin īnsula ("island; detached multi-story apartment block"). The circumflex accent on the î in Modern French île marks the historical loss of the preconsonantal s of Old French isle.
île.notes: The circumflex on "île" is a historical footprint of the lost "s" of Old French "isle" — an "s" still preserved in English "isle" and in the learned French adjective "insulaire".

rootFamily.gloss: insular, islander (learned borrowing from Latin īnsulāris)

œil.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin oculus (accusative oculum 'eye; bud of a plant'), diminutive formation from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- ('to see; eye'). Its irregular plural yeux continues the Latin accusative plural oculos.

œuf.etymology: Œuf comes from Popular Latin *ovum (Classical Latin ovum, 'egg'). Notice how French pronounces the final f in the singular **un œuf** (/œf/) while dropping it in the plural **des œufs** (/ø/), reflecting Old French sound changes before plural -s.

cognates.meaning: musical drama; an artist's complete body of work (borrowed from Italian and French)

œuvre.etymology: Inherited from Old French uevre, ovre ("work, action, creation"), from Classical Latin opera (feminine singular noun meaning "work, effort, labor, service", originally the collective neuter plural of opus, genitive operis, "work, accomplishment, artistic creation", from Proto-Indo-European *h₃épos, "work, abundance").

history.meaning: work of art, literary or cinematic piece; body of work

œuvre.notes: Gender nuance: "œuvre" is feminine for an individual work of art ("une œuvre majeure", "un chef-d'œuvre" is masculine because of "chef"), but can be masculine singular ("tout l'œuvre d'un cinéaste") when referring to an artist's entire lifetime body of work.

rootFamily.gloss: to work toward a goal, strive
